en: The Song dynasty monk Daoyuan of our own land, fearing that the Buddha-dharma would not be transmitted, divided it into patriarchs and established its schools, arranging their teachings in sequence.
He intended thereby to dispel the darkness of scholars, like a succession of lamps illuminating so that it cannot be obscured.
Ah! Did Dao-yuan’s composition perhaps capture the intent of our Master Zi Si and Yang Xiong?
When these two men spoke of the transmission of the Way, they said it extended from Yao and Shun down to Confucius, Zi Si, and Mencius.
When they spoke of the application of the Way, they said, "The Way of the gentleman is obscure at first but becomes manifest day by day," and further, "The Way of the sage is like the midday sun."
The words of these two [masters] are the source of the Way; they are what is called the "Lamp.

Although I have not yet attained a profound understanding of non-Buddhist scriptures, whenever I find leisure from official duties, I have never failed to regard the *Complete Enlightenment* (*Yuánjué*) as a teaching for engaging with the world.

Recently, having taken up this collection to read it, I observed its accounts of the origins of entering the Way, its pointing toward the subtlety of accord with principle, and its propagation of the fundamental tenets.
It has guided and supported later scholars; thus, its difference from the teachings of our own Confucian tradition is but slight.

Alas, it was not based on a good original, and as errors and corruptions have multiplied and the text has suffered great decay, I have once again collated it and commissioned artisans to carve the printing blocks, so as to broaden its dissemination.
"May this serve as a contribution for future generations.
On the twenty-second day of the fourth month in the sixth year of the Chunxi era, Prince Wei, the Son of Heaven’s Heir, inscribed this colophon.
In ancient times, the great canons and grand records of the state were invariably stored in the Jade Treasury, so that descendants might preserve them from generation to generation.
Guard it so that none dare let it stray or fall, thereby providing instruction for future generations; our ancestors relied upon it, and it has brought them great glory.

As for the great canons and treatises of the Teaching, they are of a different nature. The World-Honored Tathāgata, possessing perfect and universal knowledge, expounded the twelve divisions of the Sūtras to benefit the three realms.
Among these, the two divisions concerning past lives (*jātaka* and *itivṛttaka*) truly stem from his knowledge of past existences.
With the wisdom of knowing the minds of others, he clearly perceived throughout immeasurable kalpas of the past, present, and future:

the appearance of all Buddhas, the governance and transformation by universal monarchs (cakravartin), the formation and destruction of worlds, and the birth and sustenance of sentient beings and material things—all of which he beheld with his own eyes, heard with his own ears, and experienced with his own body.
As for the extensive hymns and long verses, Ānanda first committed them to memory, and Kāśyapa subsequently compiled them.
It is collected hereafter. At that time, one cannot help but regret that its circulation had not yet reached this land.
Even Confucius sighed with admiration over the missing portions of the historical records; how much more so for those who have beheld the location of the ultimate truth of the Noble Dharma!

The Dharma Master Huijiao was born in Kuaiji. He entered the monastic order and was attached to Jiaxiang Temple. His character and demeanor were pure and refined, and he naturally earned the high esteem of his fellow countrymen.

His extensive learning was admired by his contemporaries. Lamenting that the traces of past sages are difficult to follow and grieving that the reputations of future worthies are easily lost, he thought:
"If not for those who come after us, who shall bear this responsibility? Thereupon, following the precedents of secular historiography, he composed these biographies.

Beginning with Emperor Ming of the Han and ending with Emperor Wu of the Liang, all those monks who possessed great karmic fortune and, riding upon the power of their past vows, manifested transformations according to the needs of the times, were revered as teachers by the Son of Heaven and received the rites of hospitality from the feudal lords; they would set out toward the West, carrying incense and flowers in their arms.

Having obtained palm-leaf manuscripts, he returned to the East. He lived in humble seclusion and practiced asceticism to preserve his integrity; he sat in meditation and maintained a dignified composure to inspire and uplift others.
There was no one who did not inquire into the details of his origins and whereabouts, nor examine the reality of his words and deeds—such was the diligence of his resolve.
Subsequently, the masters Sengtong, Fazhao, and Daoxuan followed from the Liang dynasty through to the Tang, while Tonghui and Zanzhen... [continued].
As for Master Ning, he followed the tradition from the Tang through the Song and established ten categories [of literary composition], compiling a work that circulated throughout the world.

However, as for the prose that emerged therefrom, it was for the most part a continuation of the Six Dynasties and Five Dynasties period; its stylistic structure was weak and lacked even a trace of the spirit of the pre-Qin or Western Han eras.
Grand Historian Huang Gong Tingjian read it and found it inferior, intending to edit and refine it, but unfortunately never had the leisure to do so—this is to be regretted.
Master Juefan Dehong claimed that he alone refined the *Biographies of the Liang*, thereby continuing the legacy of Sima Qian and Fan Ye;

yet he ultimately had nothing to contribute to the biographies of the Tang and Song dynasties. Alas, how narrow-minded! For it is not without reason that the Buddha-dharma cannot be practiced without the vocation of the monastic, nor can the monastic vocation be clarified without the Buddha-dharma.
It is necessary that the Buddha-dharma be practiced through it, and the monastic vocation be clarified by means of it. This is the sixfold study...
It consists of merely twelve sections. Furthermore, the term *pāramitā* means "crossing over. Crossing over is the culmination of learning;

learning is simply the gradual process of crossing over. If one examines the Buddha by way of his learning, one will know that the Buddha reached the ultimate in the twelve [sections] and completed the crossing in the six [perfections].
If one examines the Saṃgha by way of these sections, one will know that the Saṃgha follows the twelve [sections] and practices the learning.
Sixth: Therefore, those who have not yet been able to translate the scriptures and transmit the lineage are insufficient for a discussion on wisdom (*prajñā*).

Those who have not yet been able to sacrifice their bodies to benefit sentient beings are insufficient for a discussion on giving (*dāna*). Those who have not yet been able to propagate the Dharma and protect the teachings are insufficient for a discussion on precepts (*śīla*).
Those who have not yet been able to collect their thoughts and maintain their resolve are insufficient for a discussion on patience (*kṣānti*).
Those who are unable to achieve resonance through the understanding of principle are not fit to be spoken of as possessing diligence.

Those who are unable to effect spiritual transformation through realization are not fit to be spoken of as possessing meditative concentration. Sixth: Study is truly like a boat or raft for crossing a river.

Once the crossing is achieved, it is abandoned; while the crossing is not yet achieved, it is used. In the context of the Buddha, this is called "deliverance," which refers to having already crossed over. In the context of the Sangha...
He said: "To speak of 'learning' (xué) refers to what is called 'not yet having crossed over' (wèijì).

Only the Buddha, because he did not forget those who have not yet crossed over despite his own state of having already crossed over, repeatedly extolled and praised the merits of the six types of learning during the assemblies of the Avataṃsaka, the Deer Park, the Vaipulya, the Prajñāpāramitā, the Lotus, and the Nirvāṇa Sūtras.
Thus, he used oars and paddles upon his boat and raft to await those who would cross over. — Great Historian Huang.
His Excellency took great care regarding the three commentaries on the *Liang*, *Tang*, and *Song* [versions of the *Lotus Sūtra*].
I, for my part, examined the various cave-treasures to unravel and synthesize them; subsequently, I combed through them like weeds and hair, compiled the draft, and preserved it.
This was during the period of Jǐchǒu (1349) of the Zhìpíng era. In the year Wǔmǎo (1373), having returned from Tiāntái, I went to live with my parents at Zhìmén Zèngqù in Xiàngshān.
The Abbot. Master Girām (Rik’an) Guanghui requested that I provide a draft for the purpose of carving it into woodblocks for printing. I did not grant permission immediately.
It so happened that Girām retired from his post to seek quietude, and Master Fuyuan (Fukuhō) was restored to the abbacy; he was indeed my fellow disciple and brother.
Having been elected to preside over this seat by public consensus, he urged me with great persistence and without ceasing. Consequently, the six studies were established to rectify [the tradition].
The essentials of the Buddha-dharma are arranged into twelve sections to distinguish the manifold aspects of the monastic vocation.
The "Prefaces" provide the order for study, thereby establishing the fundamental nature of the Buddha-dharma. The "Eulogies" offer praise for what is appropriate within the monastic vocation.

One thousand two hundred and seventy-three persons have received these transmissions; the number of people who received them matches the number of transmissions. Calculated by volume, this constitutes the ancient transmission.
The scrolls of the Old Traditions number seventy-four, while the scrolls of the New Traditions number thirty.

Why is it that the scrolls of the Old Traditions are excessive, whereas those of the New Traditions are deficient? An interpreter says: "The excess of the Old Traditions lies in the scrolls, not in the content of the traditions themselves;
the deficiency of the New Traditions lies in the scrolls, not in the content of the traditions themselves. It is just as if...
One studies the *Yi* (Change) in order to measure [all things], yet measurement has never changed; one classifies study according to categories, yet study has never been divided.
This is truly the canonical record of the gateway of instruction—is it not so? Let those who peruse this examine it closely.

Since the study of wisdom was transmitted from the Sanskrit manuscripts to the West, and the Buddha-dharma was subsequently spread to the East, it was through language and writing that this [transmission] reached its fulfillment.
It was only later that [the transmission] first became widespread. As for the Buddha-dharma, it is the profound depth of principle and meaning.
Yet, regarding principle and meaning within the world, there is nothing that differs; what differs is solely the sounds and languages of the five regions.
Language and writing are the loci of sound, and therein the principles and meanings of the Buddha-dharma are entrusted. If one truly understands this...

Regarding sounds, they consist of speech and written characters; through these, the profundity of the Buddha-dharma is universally communicated, and the debates concerning the various schools of *dharmatā* (nature) and *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics) can thus be transmitted. Is the merit of translation not therefore called "great"?
As the Sūtra clarifies: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind."

The text records a prophecy for this very day; therefore, the two categories of "Translating Scriptures" and "Transmitting the Lineage" are appended under the heading of "Wisdom Studies" (Hui-xue) to manifest the continuous succession of our teaching.
Section One: Translation of Scriptures.
Kāśyapa Mātanga was a man from Western India. He was well-versed in both the Mahayana and Hinayana vehicles and had long traveled among various kingdoms propagating the Buddha-dharma.
Once, he arrived at a small kingdom when a great nation launched an invasion; Mātanga then preached the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* on their behalf.

He rejected it. Thereupon, his fame resounded throughout the Five Indias. In the seventh year of Yongping, the *xinmao* year, the Emperor dreamed of a golden man wearing the radiance of the sun flying into the palace courtyard.
At dawn, he questioned his ministers Wang Zun and Fu Yi, saying, "What omen is this?
Fu Yi stepped forward and replied, "On the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of Zhou, the regular stars did not appear. The Grand Astrologer Su..."
The record states: "A sage of the Western Regions known as the Buddha was born there. A thousand years later, his teachings reached our land.
That which Your Majesty dreamed of was likely his divine manifestation. Thereupon, Cai Yin, Qin Jing, and eighteen others were dispatched to travel westward in search of the one seen in the dream.
Upon reaching the kingdom of Greater Yuezhi, they encountered [Dharmakṣema] Fotuo and traveled together with him. In the tenth year, the year of Jiachen...

In the fifth month, he arrived at Luoyang and presented a statue of Śākyamuni along with various scriptures on palm leaves (*pattraka*). By imperial decree, they were housed at the Court of State Ceremonial (*Honglu Si*).
The offerings were displayed at the Qingliang Terrace of the Southern Palace and atop the Xianjie Mausoleum in Guanyang, where he performed ancestral rites and worship.

Later, outside the Yong Gate to the west of Luoyang, he established the Baima Monastery as a separate residence for them. As for "White Horse," it was because—[the horse] from the West... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a historical record concerning the arrival of Buddhist relics and scriptures in China during the Eastern Han dynasty. The final sentence is incomplete, but the context refers to the famous legend of the white horse that carried the scriptures.)
Tradition has it that in former times there was a wicked king who intended to destroy all the stupas and temples. Suddenly, the king’s white horse circumambulated a stupa and neighed mournfully.
The king was awakened by this and consequently ceased the destruction; people relied upon his virtue. Thus, many of the stupas and temples were named after the white horse.
As for the monastery, its name originated from the fact that Kāśyapa Mātanga first resided in the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglù sì). The Emperor once...

He visited that temple. Xu Teng asked, "What building is this to the east of the temple? The Emperor replied, "In the past, the ground here suddenly rose up like a mound. When it was leveled, it did so again.
At night, there were strange lights and anomalies, so the people called it the 'Sacred Tomb. I suspect it is the Earth Deity of Luoyang;

therefore, we have worshipped it to this day. Xu Teng said, "Alas, that is not so. Your Majesty, read the *Commentary on the Golden Treasury of the Central Indian Land* (*Zhong Yin tu jin zang quan*):"
One hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, King Aśoka constructed eighty-four thousand jeweled stupas and enshrined the Buddha’s relics within them.
The Venerable Yaśas covered the sun with his hand and emitted various kinds of light that pervaded the realm of empty space.
He commanded the spirits and deities to carry the stupas and inter them simultaneously. Those buried in the land of Eastern China numbered nineteen locations; this is [the account].

This was the first instance. The Emperor was greatly astonished and immediately set out in his carriage to visit the Holy Tomb. A circular halo appeared above the tomb, and within the light, the Three Bodies manifested.

The attendants cried out, "Ten-thousand-year-old! The Emperor, both joyful and sorrowful, said: "Were it not for the Great Being who came from the West, how could I have known that the Great Sage was bestowing his protection?
He issued an edict to receive the ritual regulations from Huibian and constructed a pagoda over the site. The pagoda had nine stories and was [several] *zhang* in height.

It was five hundred *chi* [in height]. The following year, the light appeared once more; a celestial fragrance wafted intensely, and atop the stupa, a golden hand about one *chi* long emerged as if from within lapis lazuli.
When the Emperor arrived to pay his respects, the light circled around him in accordance with his footsteps.

It faded away after being present from noon until the third watch (*shen*). At that time, nine Indian monks, including Saṃghamara, had just arrived. They prostrated themselves and sighed in admiration, saying: "We..."
Regarding what was seen in Zhugan (India), there were three locations; now I have again been able to see this—is it not a matter of great fortune?
He passed away at the monastery where he resided in Luoyang.
The Han-period Zhu Falan was a native of Central India. From his youth, he left home to follow a teacher and recited several [volumes] of sutras and śāstras daily.
Ten thousand verses. Scholars from the Five Indias raised their master up; they traveled to the country of Yuezhi, where they happened to encounter the Han envoys Cai Yin and Chen Jing.
They further obtained Kāśyapa Mātanga, and together they led the way eastward. Their resolve was already firm. However, the various scholars earnestly obstructed and entreated them not to go.
Thereupon, they took a circuitous route through difficult terrain and eventually met Mātanga in Luoyang during the reign of Emperor Ming.
The Commandant Lao was diligent and devoted. Recently, he studied the Chinese language and translated five works offered [to the court]:
the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Buddha-jātaka*, the *Dharmasāgara-nidhi*, the *Buddha-carita*, and the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*. Now, only the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* remains;
the others have all been lost amidst the chaos and turmoil. Previously, when Emperor Wu opened the Kunming Pond, black ashes were found there.
In the depths of the pond, there was no one who knew [the answer]. Someone asked Dongfang Shuo about it, and Shuo said, "You may ask the Daoist from the Western Regions.
When Lan was subsequently questioned, he replied, "This is the ash from the kalpa-fire that consumed the world during the period when the universe was destroyed in a past kalpa."
Later, Falan passed away in Luoyang. As for his lifespan, judging by his appearance, he seemed to be fifty or sixty years old.

An Shigao, whose courtesy name was Shiga, was the legitimate son of the King of Parthia (Anxi). From childhood, he was renowned for his filial piety; he was extensively learned and there was nothing he did not know.
Once, hearing the chatter of swallows, he said to others, "Someone will arrive bringing food. Shortly thereafter, it indeed came to pass.

His reputation reached the Western Regions. While living at home, he maintained a simple diet of a single meal a day. Upon the death of the king, after he had completed the period of mourning, he immediately yielded the throne to his uncle and became a śramaṇa.
He studied the sūtras and was especially proficient in the Abhidharma, while he also mastered the subtleties of the dhyāna-sūtras.

He traveled through and transformed various kingdoms. At the beginning of Emperor Huan’s reign, he arrived in China and immediately mastered the Chinese language. The scriptures he translated over the course of his career numbered thirty-nine in total;
their phrasing was fluent and their meanings were clear, such that scholars took them as their authority. His spiritual traces from past lives were particularly renowned.
Toward the end of Emperor Ling’s reign, when the region of Guanzhong fell into great chaos, he said, "I shall go to Jiangnan. When asked the reason for this, he replied, "I..."
In a previous life, he was a bhikṣu who had a classmate prone to anger. Whenever this student received almsfood that slightly displeased him, he would grind his teeth against the donor.
This continued for twenty years. At that time, I was about to travel to Guangzhou to settle an old debt, so I took my leave of him, saying:

"If you were learned in the scriptures and diligent in practice, yet prone to much anger, you would receive an evil retribution upon death. When I have attained the Way, I shall be the first to deliver you.
Later, when he reached Guangzhou, a rebellion broke out. On the road, he encountered a wicked youth who spat at him, drew his sword, and said, "I have you now!
He was subsequently killed. His fellow student Guoqing was currently at Mount Lu. [Huiyuan] thought, "Can I go there and fail my original resolve? Thus, he went to Gongting.
The temple of the lake deity was extremely efficacious; it could divide the winds to send vessels arriving and departing on their way.

Once, someone took some divine bamboo without permission and cut it down, whereupon the deity grew angry and capsized his boat. At the spot where the bamboo had been planted and cut, passersby would hold their breath and break into sweat in awe.

Huiqing was traveling on the same boat with thirty companions, who offered a sacrificial animal and prayed for blessings. The deity immediately descended and spoke, saying, "There is a śramaṇa on this boat; you should invite him [ashore]. When Huiqing arrived, the deity...
He spoke again, saying: "I truly could not escape what I said during our parting. Now my family resides by this lake, which governs all within a thousand li.

Because I was prone to much anger, I have incurred this evil retribution; yet because I loved to give alms, I possess these precious treasures. Therefore, moved by human sentiment, you have come from afar.
I feel both sorrow and joy at once. However, I shall die this very day or tomorrow; fearing that my corpse might defile the rivers and lakes, I should be moved to die on the western mountain."

[The deity] said from within the marsh, "I must certainly enter hell. I have a thousand bolts of silk and various precious objects; I would be grateful if you would build a stupa and temple for me, to provide merit for my afterlife.
Sengqing said, "I have come from afar and we have been parted for a long time; why do you not manifest your form so that we may exchange greetings?
The spirit said, "My form is hideous and strange; how could I bear it? Sengqing said, "Just manifest it; there will be no harm. Thereupon, he manifested his form.
Inside the front tent was a large python. Huiqing recited a mantra in Sanskrit over it; as the python shed tears like rain, it suddenly vanished.
Before Huiqing’s boat had even departed, a handsome young man dressed in fine robes and a ceremonial cap knelt before him in the manner of one offering thanks.
Huiqing again recited a mantra, and the youth departed. The boatmen asked who he was, and he replied, "I am the deity of this temple. From that time on, the temple became a ruin.
The python eventually died in the marshes of the Western Mountains; this is the present-day Serpent Village (Shecun) in Xunyang.
Huiqing traveled to Nanchang, where he erected a stupa and built a temple, which was originally called Dongsi Temple; today, it is popularly known as Dajian Temple.

Consequently, Huiqing went to Guangzhou to seek out the youth who had harmed him in the past. He stayed at the youth’s home and recounted their previous encounter; they faced one another in mutual lamentation, and [Huiqing] said: "I..."

There remained further karmic retribution for him in Kuaiji. He was now about to go there, and his younger brother wished to accompany him. While walking through the marketplace in Yue, they were attacked by some who were brawling;
by mistake, [the assailant] struck Qing, and he subsequently passed away. Qing was originally of royal lineage, having come from the Western Regions to China.
To cite the case of An-hou (Dharmarakṣa): even foreign lands knew to hold such Chinese feudal titles in such high esteem.

As for the sūtras translated by the śramaṇa Dao’an, their phrasing is fluent and their meaning complete; they are truly no different from having received them directly from the Compassionate Honored One himself.
Zhi Loujiachen of the Han was originally a person of the Yuezhi. He was pure and sagacious by nature and was renowned for his strict observance of the Vinaya.

With the resolve to propagate the Great Dharma, he arrived in Luoyang during the reign of Emperor Ling. Between the Guanghe and Zhongping eras, he translated the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Āṭānāṭīya*, the *Śūraṅgama*, and other sūtras;
he also translated more than ten works, including the *Ajātaśatru-kumāra* and the *Ratnakūṭa*. Later...
His ultimate end is unknown.
The monk Zhu Foshuo of the Han dynasty brought the *Qidaoxing jing* (Sūtra on the Practice of the Path) from India to Luoyang.

In the second year of the Guanghe era, he produced the *Banzhou sanmei jing* (Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra). Zhi Chen transmitted the Indic language, while Meng Fu and Zhang Lian of Henan received it in writing.
The Chinese upāsaka An Xuan was a native of the country of Parthia (Anxi). By nature he was grave and resolute, and his extensive learning encompassed all manner of books.
Toward the end of Emperor Ling’s reign, he arrived in Luoyang and was honored with the title of Cavalry Commandant (Qiduwei) for his meritorious service.

Taking it as his personal mission to uphold the Dharma, he collaborated with the śramaṇa Yan Fotiao to produce the *Dharmādarśa-sūtra* (Fajing jing). An Xuan orally transmitted the Indic language, while Yan Fotiao transcribed it in writing. As Yan Fotiao approached...

A native of Huai, he was exceptionally intelligent and fond of learning from his youth. He was also renowned as a "Commander" (Dujū), and his excellence in translation was no less than that of the Marquis An (An Shigao).

He also compiled the *Shihuì zhuàn* (Biographies of the Ten Wisdoms). At that time, there were the śramaṇas Zhiyao, Kangju, and Kang Mengxiang, all of whom gained renown for their study of wisdom (*prajñā*) in the capital Luoyang during the reigns of Emperors Ling and Xian.
Zhiyao translated the *Chengjù dìngyì jīng* (Sūtra on the Attainment of Concentration) and the *Xiǎoběnqǐ jīng* (Minor Account of the Origins).
In the *Dacheng deng jing* (Mahāyāna Samādhi Sūtra), the *Juyi wen didu shi jing* (Sūtra on the Questions of Gṛhapati concerning the Matters of Hell) was translated by Juyi;

the *Zhongben qi jing* (Madhyamāgama Sūtra on Past Deeds) and the *Xiuxing benqi jing* (Sūtra on the Practice of Past Deeds) were both translated by Meng Xiang. This present sūtra was obtained by the śramaṇa Tanguo in the kingdom of Kapilavastu and translated together with Zhu Dalie;
however, it is not yet well-edited.
Seng-kai of the Wei dynasty arrived in Luoyang at the end of the Jiaping era and translated four sutras, including the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
Tan-di of the Wei dynasty arrived in Luoyang during the Zhengyuan era and translated the *Dharmaguptaka-karman*.

Wei Boyan was a man of unknown origins. Possessing talent and wisdom, he arrived in Luoyang during the Ganlu period and translated six sections of the *Wuliang qingjing pingdengjue jing* (The Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment). His ultimate end remains unknown.
Wu Kang Senghui was originally a native of the kingdom of Kangju. His father, a merchant traveling between China and the seas, eventually settled in Jiaozhi, where Senghui was born.
Orphaned at a young age, he became a śramaṇa; he was refined and elegant, possessed great intellectual capacity, was deeply committed to his studies, and excelled at literary composition.
When the Sun family established their rule over Jiangzuo, Buddhism had not yet been propagated there. Senghui’s ambition was to revitalize the faith. Red—
In the tenth year of [Sun] Wu, he arrived at Jianye. He constructed a thatched hut, established an image, and practiced the Way.

When the people of the state first saw the śramaṇa, they were struck with wonder and amazement. An official reported this to the throne. Sun Quan said, "Is this the lingering influence of the Buddha, the deity whom Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty dreamed of?

He issued an edict for Kāśyapa to come and explain his circumstances. Kāśyapa replied, "The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has been in parinirvāṇa for a thousand years. However, his sacred relics and śarīra..."
Its divine transformations are boundless. In the past, King Aśoka honored it by constructing eighty-four thousand stūpas;
this is one of its remaining traces. Sun Quan asked, "Can the śarīra be obtained? He replied, "It can be obtained. Sun Quan said, "If it can indeed be obtained, you shall build a stūpa for it;
otherwise, the crime of deceitful flattery shall not go unpunished. He requested a period of seven days. Thereupon, [the monk] observed the precepts.

His subordinates said, "The rise or fall of the Dharma depends on this single action; you ought to apply yourself with great care. When the appointed time arrived and there was no response, they extended the period by seven days.

Still there was no response. Quan said, "He has indeed deceived me face-to-face. Prepare to boil him! Hui was terrified and begged for another extension of the period, entreating him with his own life at stake.
After another seven days and nights, a resonant *keng* sound was heard coming from within the jar. Looking inside, [he saw] five...

The light of the relic flashed in various colors. He cried out loudly, "I have obtained a śarīra! At dawn, he presented it [to the throne]. Sun Quan, together with the high officials, gathered to observe it.

They were greatly amazed and said, "This is an auspicious omen rarely seen in the world. At that time, Hui said, "The majestic spiritual power of a śarīra is such that nothing in all the worlds can destroy it.
Sun Quan ordered strong men to crush it; though both the anvil and the hammer were dented, its radiance remained as before.
Consequently, the Buddha’s stupa was renamed Jianchu Temple to commemorate its origins. Thereupon, the teaching flourished greatly.
When Quan died and Sun Hao succeeded to the throne, he acted unrighteously and sought to destroy all shrines to the spirits, extending his purges to the monasteries as well.

His ministers remonstrated, saying, "The former emperor established this out of reverence for auspicious omens; how can it be destroyed? He dispatched Zhang Yu to interrogate Zhihui, but Zhihui refuted his arguments.

Lǐ Yù was humbled and departed. Huì accompanied him to the gate. Pointing to a licentious shrine beside the temple, Yù said, "The profound transformation reaches far, yet that which is near is not reformed.
Why is this? Huì replied at once, "When a swift thunderclap splits a mountain, the deaf do not hear it; this is not the fault of the thunder.

According to the principles of the world, when there is penetration, the myriad things respond in suspension; when there is obstruction, even between liver and gall, the distance is more than [mere miles]."
Chu Yue. Sun Yuzhi was renowned for his exceptional talent. Emperor Huo welcomed him and asked, "May I hear what the Buddha teaches regarding the retribution of good and evil?
He replied, "When a sagacious ruler governs the world with filial piety and compassion, red birds soar and the Old Man appears.
When he nurtures all things with benevolence and virtue, sweet springs gush forth and auspicious grain grows. Since goodness..."
There are auspicious omens; likewise, there are evil ones. Therefore, if one commits evil in secret, ghosts will find and punish them; if one commits evil in public, people will find and punish them.

The *I Ching* proclaims: "Accumulate goodness, and blessings will follow. The *Shijing* says: "Seek fortune without crookedness. Although these are the orthodox maxims of the Confucian classics, they are precisely the clear instructions of Buddhism.
Sun Hao said: "If that is so, then since the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius are already clear, what need is there for Buddhism?"

The Emperor asked, "Which is superior? He replied, "The teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius did not wish to speak deeply; therefore, they presented only a rough outline. The Buddhist teachings do not stop at shallow words;
therefore, they detail their essential points. Both are for the sake of goodness. The sages were only afraid that people would not practice goodness enough.

Why does Your Majesty regard this as a source of suspicion? Sun Hao had no reply and the matter was dropped. While the imperial guards were tending the gardens, they discovered a golden image. Sun Hao...

He ordered her to be placed in a filthy location and covered in impurities, treating this as a source of amusement. Suddenly, she contracted a swelling disease, her groans resounding through day and night.
A divination stated: "This is due to offending a great deity. Prayers were offered at various shrines to the gods without effect. Among the palace women was one who served the Buddha, who said:
"Why not pray to the Buddha instead? Huì understood this and welcomed the image into the hall, enshrining it in a niche to offer worship.
He also invited Huì to preach the Dharma. Huì pointed out the essential principles and explained them with illustrative analogies.

When Huì asked to read the *Śramaṇa-śīla-sūtra*, Huì took the *Pratimokṣa* of one hundred and twenty-five vows, divided them into two hundred and fifty items, and showed them to Huì, leading him to practice accordingly.

Whether standing, sitting, or reclining, he increased his wholesome intentions. Once Hao had received the five precepts and his illness was cured, he adorned a statue of the Buddha and served it with his own body;
thus, his cruelty and tyranny were somewhat diminished. Subsequently, he translated the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Small Prajñāpāramitā), the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-saṃgraha*, and the *Saṃyukta-avadāna*;
he also annotated the *Ānāpānasmṛti*, the *Dharmādarśa*, and the *Bodhimaṇḍa* sūtras. This occurred in the fourth month of the fourth year of the Tianji era of the Wu kingdom.
[The monk] passed away. In the ninth month, Hui met his end. During the Xianhe era of the Jin dynasty, when Su Jun rebelled, the stupa he had built was destroyed by fire.
He Chong, the Minister of Works, restored and completed it. Zhao You, General of the West, remarked to others, "To say the stupa emits light is mere exaggeration.

Shortly thereafter, light of five colors emerged from the top of the stupa; You was struck with solemn reverence and his respect increased. Furthermore, to the east of the temple, he constructed another small stupa. It is said that...
Before the assembly arrived in Wu, there was the upāsaka Zhi Qian, courtesy name Gongming, also known as Yue. He was originally a person of the Yuezhi.
There were also Zhi Chen and Zhi Liang; Liang’s courtesy name was Jiming. He studied under Chen, and Qian further studied under Liang.

He had read extensively across many books and was proficient in the languages of the six states. He was tall and thin with a dark complexion; his eyes were white with yellow pupils. At that time, he served as...
A saying regarding him went: "Zhi Lang’s eyes are yellow; though his physical frame is small, he is a treasury of wisdom. At the end of Emperor Xian’s reign, he sought refuge in Wu.
Sun Quan summoned him for an audience and was pleased with him, appointing him as a *boshi* (Court Doctor) and ordering him to assist the Crown Prince. This is recorded in the *Wu zhi lüe*.
Wu Weizhinan was a man from India whose family had for generations worshipped by fire and followed heterodox teachings. There was a śrāvaka monk who was skilled in incantations;
traveling from afar, he arrived at dusk and sought lodging at Weizhinan’s house. Weizhinan, harboring animosity toward the sons of Śākyamuni, lodged him outside the gate.
The monk then playfully used his incantations to extinguish the fire that Weizhinan worshipped. Only then did Weizhinan welcome the monk inside.
The fire blazed up again within the chamber. Finding this a great and wondrous marvel, Nalan took refuge in the Buddha-vehicle, abandoned his fire-worship, and served a śramaṇa as his preceptor.
He left the household life and mastered the profound meanings of the Tripiṭaka, becoming further proficient in the four Āgamas.

Traveling to various countries to propagate the teachings, in the third year of the Huangwu era, he arrived at Wuchang together with Zhu Lüyan, bringing with him the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Dharmapada-sūtra*, which they subsequently translated.
Dharmayaśas and Dharmapriya were both not yet proficient in the Chinese language; consequently, the phrasing of the sutra was often plain and direct.

Later, the Jin monk Fali retranslated it in five fascicles, with Faju acting as the scribe; the wording then began to convey the intended meaning clearly. Fali also separately translated more than one hundred minor sutras.
During the chaos of the Yongjia era, many [texts] were lost.
Zhu Tanmoluocha (translated as Dharmarakṣa) of the Jin dynasty was of Yuezhi descent; his family name was Zhi, and his family later resided in Dunhuang.
At the age of eight, he left home to serve the śramaṇa Zhu Gaozuo as his teacher. He could recite ten thousand words daily and was pure in character.

Diligent in ascetic practice and study, during the reign of Emperor Wu, although the temples and statues in the capital were magnificent and grand, the profound Vaipulya sutras had not yet arrived there.
Filled with lamentation, Saṃghavarman followed his master on a journey through the various kingdoms of the Western Regions.

He thoroughly investigated thirty-six different languages and scripts without omission. Thereupon he returned eastward; from Dunhuang to Chang’an, he assisted in the translation and transcription of texts under the imperial court.

During the Jin dynasty, Wen translated one hundred and sixty-five works, including the *Bhadrapāla-kalpa*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and the *Dharmapradīpa-saṃgraha*. Thus, the Dharma spread throughout China;

this was due to the protective power [of the deity]. Whenever Hu resided in the mountains and rinsed his mouth in a mountain stream, if woodcutters defiled the side of the stream, the stream would dry up.
Fahu sighed and said, "If a person lacks virtue, it causes clear springs to cease flowing. If there is truly nothing with which to provide for them, one should simply move away.

Immediately, the spring flowed as before. Later, he established a monastery outside the Qing Gate in Chang’an; its reputation spread far and wide, and the community regularly numbered over a thousand people.
When Emperor Hui fled westward and the region was thrown into turmoil, Fahu and his disciples traveled east, reaching Mianchi.
He passed away at the age of eighty-eight; he was popularly known as the Dunhuang Bodhisattva.
Zhu Shixing of Jinyin was a native of Yingchuan. Possessing great integrity, he left home to devote himself in silence to the study of the scriptures.

While reading the *Daoxing jing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāpāramitā Sūtra) translated by Zhu Foshuo, he lamented that the text was so concise and archaic that it did not fully convey the Buddha’s intent. In the fifth year of the Ganlu era, he traveled westward to Yong.
He crossed the shifting sands and arrived at Khotan, where he obtained an original copy of the lateral-script [Brahmi] texts.

He dispatched his disciple Farnatan—this being the Chinese translation of Dharmarāja—to send them to Luoyang, but they were only dispatched after some time. A scholar of the Hīnayāna then addressed the King, saying:

"It is not fitting that the writings of the Brahmins enter the land of Han; I fear they will confuse the orthodox scriptures and leave the people in spiritual deafness and blindness. The King accepted this argument and detained the texts.
Kumārajīva begged for fire to test the authenticity of the scripture. He then cast the scripture into the flames; the fire was extinguished, yet the scripture remained unharmed.

The people of the country marveled at this as a divine miracle. Subsequently, he traveled to the Southern Water Temple in Cangyuan, Chenliu, where the Indian upāsaka Zhu Shujian and the Daoist master Wuluocha joined him in translating the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* (The Light-Emitting Perfection of Wisdom) from leather scrolls.
Thus, his remains are currently at Dà'ān Monastery in Yúzhāng. He passed away in Yutian at the age of eighty.

When his body was cremated, it did not disperse. He had made a vow, saying: "If I have truly attained the Way, my body should be destroyed. At that very sound, it dispersed. His bones were collected and a stūpa was erected over them.
Bai Shili Miduoluo (帛尸梨蜜多羅), translated here as Jiyou (吉友), was a prince from a kingdom in the Western Regions.
Like Taibo of Wu, he abdicated the throne to his younger brother and entered the monastic life. He traveled east through various kingdoms and arrived in Guanzhong during the Yongjia era.

Encountering the chaos of the times, he crossed the Yangtze River and settled at Jianchu Monastery in Jianye. The world called him "Gaozuo" (The High Seat). When Prime Minister Wang Maohong saw him, he said:

"We are men of such caliber. The Grand Marshal Yu Yuangui, the Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Zhou Borin, the Director of the Court of State Ceremonial Xie Youyu, and the Minister of Justice Huan Maolun—these were all renowned scholars of the time who came to my door to form friendships, and our reputations were well-known among the official class.

When his friend once sat with Wang Dao, loosening his belt and reclining at ease, the Minister of the Secretariat Bian Wangzhi happened to arrive; the friend immediately assumed a solemn and dignified countenance.

When someone asked him the reason for this, he replied, "The Prince and Duke possess the *fengjian* (discernment of character) to anticipate people; Commandant Bian possesses the *fan-du* (comprehensive standard) to evaluate things.
It is precisely with these qualities that I respond to them. Huan Tingwei wished to compose a critical appraisal (*mu*) for his friend, but after a long time he had not succeeded.
Someone remarked, "Shili Mi may be called 'excellent and brilliant' (*zhuolang*). Huan immediately declared, "This is the ultimate pinnacle of all critical evaluations. The Great General...
Wang Chuzhong was in the southern regions when he heard that Yu was held in high esteem by the eminent officials; in his heart, he did not yet believe this.

However, upon meeting him, he could not help but feel a sense of joy and paid him respectful homage. When Zhou Yi served as Director of the Imperial Secretariat and presided over the selection of officials, he stopped to speak with Yu as he was entering the office and sighed in admiration, saying:
"In selecting worthy men for the court, to find one such as you truly makes one feel no shame. After Zhou Yi passed away, Yu consoled his orphaned children.
As they sat facing one another, he performed *brahman* chants; their pure resonance soared above the clouds. He then departed after reciting over a thousand words of incantation.
Dao said, "Among those in foreign lands who are not deluded by wealth and status, you are the only one.
Youxiao replied, "If I were like you gentlemen, how could I be here today? At that time, this was circulated as a famous saying. Youxiao was lofty and simple.
He did not learn the Jin language, but was known by his title as a mantra-holder. Originally, there were no mantras in Jiangxia;
Huizhi translated the *Mayūra-vijaya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* and various other divine mantras and bestowed them upon his disciple Mili. He passed away during the Xiankang era at an age of over eighty.
Huizhi had been fond of practicing *dhūta* austerities on Shizigang, so he was buried in that place. Emperor Cheng erected a stupa for him, and there was sand beside his tomb.
The name of the gatekeeper was lost to history. He came from the region west of the Passes to establish a monastery called Gaozuo (High Seat).
The Jin monk Saṃghabhūti—translated as "Manifestation of the Multitude"—was a native of Kaśmīra. He was profound, noble, and possessed great intellectual capacity;

he extensively studied the Tripiṭaka and was particularly skilled in the sūtras on meditation and numerical categories (*saṃkhyā*). He recited the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā* and penetrated its meaning with precision. Even when...
He traveled through various kingdoms, taking the propagation of the Dharma as his primary mission. In the seventeenth year of Fu Jian’s Jianyuan era, he arrived in Guanzhong.

At that time, Mahāyāna scriptures had not yet spread widely, while the study of dhyāna and mathematics was flourishing. Upon his arrival, both monastics and laypeople turned to him in devotion, regarding him as a master of the Dharma.
Zhao Zheng, the Secretary郎 (Lang), requested that he translate the Sanskrit original of the *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra*, and he [collaborated] with Dao’an.
Deng Xuan translated it and recited it orally. The foreign śramaṇa Dharmalan-di recorded the text in writing, while Fotuoluoche (Buddharakṣa) proclaimed and translated it.
The Qin śramaṇa Minzhi polished the phrasing. The translation was assembled in the fourth month of the nineteenth year of Jianyuan;
it was completed only in the autumn. Furthermore, he carried a manuscript of the *Vasumitra-śāstra* from India with him, and the following year, together with Dharmaruci...
Nandi Saṃghavarman personally held the Sanskrit manuscript. The śramaṇa Buddhasmṛti orally translated it; Huisong received it by pen; Da’an and Faho compared and corrected it.
He manifested majestic deportment, and those in Guanzhong followed his Dharma. His final destination was later unknown.

Dharmaratna (translated into Chinese as Fǎxǐ), a native of Tukhāra, entered the monastic life at the age of seven. Possessing a nature of keen intelligence, he was able to recite the *Ekottarika Āgama* from memory.

He became renowned throughout various kingdoms for his resolve to propagate the teachings of the Dharma. Braving the shifting sands of the Taklamakan Desert, he traveled eastward and arrived in Cháng'ān at the beginning of the Jiànyuán era of Fú Jiān.
Fú Jiān received him with exceptional courtesy and honor; such a figure had not yet appeared within the Central Kingdom.
Regarding the four Āgamas: Zhao Zheng, the Governor of Wuwei, requested that their original texts be produced.
At that time, as the rebel forces of慕容冲 (Murong Chong) rose up and the Guanzhong region was in turmoil, Zheng forgot his own life for the sake of the Dharma and petitioned tirelessly.

Consequently, together with Dao’an, he gathered those of scholarly learning to translate the *Madhyama-āgama* and the *Ekottarika-āgama*, as well as the previously translated *Abhidharmahṛdaya*, the *Samādhi*, the *Dhuta*, and other works. The Buddha—

He recalled the translation project; Huisong served as the scribe, and it was completed in two years. However, when Yao Chang’s troops occupied the Guannei region and the roads became impassable, he took his leave and returned to the Western Regions.
Buddharakṣa of the Jin dynasty was of unknown nationality. He was pure and possessed noble conduct. He had extensively studied historical records and was well-versed in the Chinese language.
Having traveled for a long time throughout China, he translated Sanskrit texts and was highly esteemed by the world.
The Jin dynasty monk Saṃghadeva—translated into Chinese as Zhòngtiān (Assembly of Devas)—was of the Gautama clan and a native of Jibin.

Having studied the Way since his youth, he made the diligent pursuit of teachers his primary concern. He thoroughly investigated and savored the Tripiṭaka, excelling particularly in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.

He once recited the *Tridharmaka-śāstra*, regarding it as the path for entering the Way. As a person, he possessed dignified deportment; his every movement was worthy of observation, and his discernment was profound.
Miaoyun was a man of humble and gentle virtue who excelled at guiding others. At the beginning of the Jianyuan era of Fu Jian, he arrived in Chang’an.

Previously, the *Bāshùmì* (Vasumitra), the two *Āhán* (Āgamas), the *Pítán Guǎngshuō* (Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra), the *Sān fǎdù* (Tripiṭaka-dharmapada), and other works totaling over one million words had been translated by Saṃghabhūti and Dharmanandin.
However, due to the turmoil of the Tuoba慕容 invasions and the disturbances of war, the full meaning of these texts had not yet been realized. Furthermore, Dao’an...
He passed away before he was able to revise and correct [the translations]. Later, when the Eastern Mountains were peaceful and settled, Saṃghadeva studied with the śramaṇa Fǎhé of Jìzhōu.

He gradually became familiar with the Chinese language and consequently realized that the previously translated scriptures contained errors and corruptions. Saṃghadeva then produced new versions of the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* and other various sutras as evidence for his corrections.
It happened that King Yáo Xīng ruled the Qín state, during which time the Way of the Dharma flourished exceptionally; Fǎhé entered [the capital].
Guān. Thereupon, Deva crossed the river to Mount Kuāng, where he was received with the courtesy due to a guest by Huìyuǎn.
During the Dàyuán era, at Huìyuǎn’s request, he translated the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* and the *Tri-dharmaka-śāstra* at the Bānruó Terrace.

In the first year of Lóng’ān, he traveled to the capital, where prominent scholars of the time vied with one another to seek an audience with him. He was also received with the courtesy due to a guest by Wáng Xūn of Lángyá.

He invited [Vasubandhu] to his residence to lecture on the Abhidharma. Eminent monks gathered in great numbers; Vasubandhu followed the principles of the doctrine, and his eloquent speech was as brilliant as refined prose.

At that time, King Mi was present in the assembly; he was moved to realization and his reverence increased. Yao Xun asked about the "Dharma-net" (the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*) and what the monk Ami had attained.
He replied, "In the main outline it is entirely correct; only in the minor details has he not yet reached full precision. The following year, Yao Xun convened another assembly.
More than forty śramaṇas from the monastic schools of the capital requested that the *Madhyama Āgama* be translated once more.

The Kasmīra śramaṇa Saṃgharakṣa held the Sanskrit manuscript, while Deva translated it into the language of Jin. When the transcription was completed, it was exquisitely refined and captured the intended meaning;
the world held it in profound secrecy and esteem. During his time in the regions of He and Luo, he translated a total of over one million words of various sūtras. Later...
His final whereabouts are unknown.

Zhu Fonian of the Jin dynasty was a native of Liangzhou. He entered the monastic order in his youth and possessed keen intelligence. He was compassionate and harmonious by nature, and his learning spanned both Buddhist and secular (inner and outer) traditions.
Being proficient in the languages of both the Chinese and the foreign (Hua and Rong), he became renowned throughout Guanzhong. During the Jianyuan era of the Qin dynasty, Saṃghabhūti...
Dharmaratna translated various sutras, at which time many were renowned scholars; however, Saṃghadeva alone excelled them.

When he came to translate the *Ekottarika Āgama*, Saṃghadeva analyzed and refined it extensively, exhausting its full meaning and flavor. It took two years to complete. Since the times of An Shigao and Zhi Qian, no one had equaled Saṃghadeva;
thus, he stood as the preeminent among translators during the reigns of the Fu and Yao dynasties. Furthermore, he produced the *Bodhi...* [text continues].
He was working on the *Sāraṅgavatī-śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Daśabhūmi-khaṇḍa-saṃyojana-cchedana-śrī-garbha-antarābhava-sūtra*, and other works;
however, as his drafts were not yet finalized, he passed away while ill in Chang’an. Monastics and laypeople alike lamented his loss.
Kumārajīva of the Jin dynasty—translated as "Child-Lifespan" (Tóngshòu)—was a native of India. His family had served as prime ministers for generations;
his grandfather, Dàduō, possessed a great reputation, and his father, Yán, was about to succeed him in the position of prime minister when he avoided this destiny by leaving the household life.

He traveled east across the Pamir Mountains, where the King of Kucha, having heard of his fame, went out from the suburbs to welcome him and honored him as the National Preceptor. The king had a younger sister, twenty years of age, who was exceptionally talented and quick-witted.

She was a woman of exceptional character; when envoys from various kingdoms sought to solicit her hand in marriage, she refused them all. However, when she saw that Śrīyān was pressing her to take him as her husband, she consented.
She bore two sons: the first was Kumārajīva, and the second was Puṣyadeva. From the time she became pregnant with Jīva, her mother’s wisdom and understanding were twice as great as usual.
She heard that the Great Temple of Kukkutārāma had many eminent monks, some of whom had attained the Way. She called her female companions and went there to listen to the Dharma;
suddenly, she attained mastery of the language of India, and her inquiries were sharp and incisive. One named Dharmaghoṣa saw this and said, "This woman must surely be carrying the child of wisdom."
He recounted for him the events concerning Śāriputra while he was in the womb. When Kumārajīva was seven years old, his mother, while walking in the wilderness, saw bones at a burial mound.

She requested from Yaśas that she be allowed to leave the household life, but Yaśas would not permit it. Consequently, she fasted for six days until her vital breath was like a single thread; only then did he grant her permission. He then shaved Kumārajīva’s head along with her own.
Through her exclusive devotion to meditative contemplation, the mother attained the first fruit of the path (*srotāpatti*). Kumārajīva recited a thousand verses of scripture every day.
The verses consist of thirty-two characters, totaling thirty-two thousand words; their meaning was also self-evident.
When the people of Kucha began to pay him ritual homage, his mother would invariably take Kumārajīva and flee to wander through various kingdoms.

At the age of nine, Kumārajīva crossed the Indus River and reached Kaśmīra, where he served the eminent monk Bandhudatta as his teacher and received the *Dīrgha-āgama* and *Madhyama-āgama* from the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*, totaling four hundred [sections].

[The king] spoke ten thousand words. Kumārajīva marveled at his eloquence. From that time on, Kumārajīva’s reputation reached the King. The King assembled followers of heterodox paths and established a debate for them to attack and refute one another.

The followers of the heterodox paths, being arrogant because Kumārajīva was young in years, made no preparations. Kumārajīva took advantage of this opening to defeat and exhaust them. The heterodox practitioners were ashamed and submitted.
The King provided the highest offerings and dispatched senior monks to attend to him, fearing only that he might leave. At the age of twelve, his mother took him back.
In Kucha, he declined all invitations from various kingdoms offering him honorary titles.

He was then escorted to the Yuezhi country, where the Venerable of the Northern Mountains saw him and said to his mother: "This śrāmaṇera will reach thirty-five years of age with his Vinaya remaining untainted;
he will deliver others like Upagupta, otherwise he will simply be a brilliant Dharma Master of the Single Orthodox School. He then arrived at Śāle.
Holding the Buddha’s bowl upon his head, he thought to himself, "How large yet light this bowl is! Immediately, it became so heavy that he could not bear its weight; he let out a cry and dropped it.
His mother asked him the reason for this, and he replied, "It was because my mind engaged in conceptual discrimination that the bowl appeared heavy or light.

He then remained at Śākala for one year, where he extensively studied the various treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), as well as the principles of *yoga*, astrology, and mathematics, mastering their essential points with great skill. The śramaṇas were delighted.

Upon seeing this, [Kumārajīva] was urged to request the King to open the Dharma for him. He said, "There shall be two benefits: the bhikṣus in the kingdom will feel ashamed that they have not reached his level and will increase their diligence;
furthermore, the King of Kucha will surely regard Kumārajīva as venerable, which will mean he honors me, and he will come to restore our former friendly relations."

The King agreed with this. Thereupon, he assembled both monastics and laypeople according to his advice. Kumārajīva was sincere and spontaneous, disregarding the constraints of formal rules; some, therefore, harbored doubts about him.
At that time, there were the Śākya prince Sūryabhadra and the military officer’s son Suyatrisoma, brothers who had both renounced their royal positions to become śramaṇas.
Suyatrisoma was particularly gifted in talent and eloquence; once, he explained the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* for Kumārajīva.
In the *Anavatapta Sūtra*, it is stated that the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are all empty and signless (*animitta*). Finding this strange, [Dao’an] asked:

"Does this sūtra go so far as to destroy and dismantle all dharmas? Thereupon, they together investigated the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna for some time, until Kumārajīva attained realization and sighed, saying: [This is indeed the ultimate truth.]
In the past, regarding the Hīnayāna, I was like one who mistakes brass for gold; consequently, I studied the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Śata-śāstra*, the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, and other such works.
In the kingdom of Wensu, on the northern border of Kucha, there was a follower of heterodox paths who set forth his tenets and beat a drum, seeking debate.
Kumārajīva happened to be there with his mother at the time, and he completely defeated him. From then on, his fame spread throughout the region west of the Pamirs, and he resided in Kucha.
He extensively expounded various sūtras. Disciples from many countries arrived like clouds gathering.

Nīlāñjanāvatī, the king’s daughter, had widely studied the various sūtras and had already realized the second fruit [of the path]. Hearing the Dharma, she rejoiced and requested him once more to further expound it.

Kumārajīva further analyzed the meaning of the dharmas, such as how all phenomena are fundamentally empty and that the aggregates (skandhas) and realms (dhātus) are merely provisional names and not real. Those who heard him were enlightened and awakened. [His age was... year.
20. This was at the royal palace. He received the precepts from Vimalākṣa and studied the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

Shortly thereafter, his mother said to the King of Kucha, "Your kingdom will soon decline; what can be done? She then said to Kumārajīva, "The profound teachings of the Vaipulya-sūtras are inconceivable.
That they have been transmitted to the Eastern Lands is solely due to your efforts. Yet you derive no benefit from them—how tragic! Kumārajīva replied:

"I must ensure that the Great Transformation is transmitted; even if it brings suffering, I shall have no regrets. His mother agreed with this, and he subsequently traveled to India, where he attained the third fruit of the path.

Kumārajīva remained alone at the New Temple in the kingdom. Later, he found the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* (The Scripture of Radiant Light) beside the temple, but its characters were obscured and could not be read.
Kumārajīva knew in his heart that this was the work of Māra and remained unmoved. After some time, the text became legible.
A voice from the air was heard saying, "O wise man, what use have you for this book? Kumārajīva replied, "This petty demon dares to act thus.

He remained there for two years, during which time he further studied Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras. The King of Kucha provided him with a golden seat and brocade mats, commanding that he sit upon them to preach the Dharma.
Kumārajīva, considering that his teacher Baṇḍumata had not yet awakened to the Mahāyāna, requested to go and convert him. Before long, the teacher arrived.

Kumārajīva first preached the *Sūtra on the Questions of the Virtuous Woman* (*Śrīmatī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*) for him; this was because it extensively clarifies dependent origination, emptiness, and the provisional, subjects which he and his teacher had previously both disbelieved.
The teacher said to Kumārajīva: "What extraordinary features have you seen in the Mahāyāna that you should so hastily..."

Shangzhi [listened]. Kumārajīva said, "The Mahāyāna is profound and subtle; its dharmas are all empty. It cannot be compared to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which clings to signs and is narrow and biased.
The Master said, "Your claim that 'all things are empty' is truly terrifying. Do you not also know the peril of abandoning existence while craving emptiness?
Long ago, there was a madman who ordered a craftsman to spin thread. When the craftsman had finished, it was extremely fine and excellent."
The madman still thought this was not enough. The craftsman pointed to the empty space and said, "This is the thread.

The madman asked, "Why do I not see it? The craftsman replied, "The thread is fine; even I, a skilled artisan, cannot see it, let alone another person. The madman was delighted and rewarded him handsomely.
"Your doctrine of emptiness is exactly like this. Kumārajīva said, "The Hīnayāna clings to existence; this is a great perversion.
It is like a person with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky and, thinking they are real, sits there waiting for fruit, demanding that others come to taste it.

Would he not be laughed at by those with clear vision? Thereupon, Guṇabhadra was enlightened and paid homage to Kumārajīva as his teacher. [This occurred] among the various kingdoms of the Western Regions.

Everyone was humbled by Kumārajīva’s spiritual wonders. Whenever he preached the Dharma, the various kings would all kneel long on their knees beside him, commanding Kumārajīva to step upon them to ascend the seat.
When Fu Jian heard of this, he had long harbored the intention to welcome Kumārajīva. In the twelfth year of Jianyuan, the first month of the dingchou year, the Grand Astrologer reported:
"A star has appeared in the celestial division corresponding to foreign lands; there shall be a man of great wisdom who enters to assist the state."
The King said, "I have heard that there is one named Kumārajīva in the Western Regions; could this be him?

He then dispatched General Lü Guang of the Xiaoqi Commandery with seventy thousand troops to campaign westward against Kucha. The King told Guang, "If you capture Kumārajīva, send him back immediately by relay station.
Before Guang’s army had arrived, Kumārajīva said to the King of Kucha, "There will soon be a formidable enemy approaching from—"
Day by day he drew closer. It would have been appropriate to receive him with due respect and not oppose his advance. But the King did not accept this advice;

he mobilized troops to resist Kumārajīva, only to be utterly defeated by him. Consequently, Kumārajīva captured Shi. Seeing that he was young in years, the King treated him with contempt and forcibly gave him the daughter of the King of Kucha as a wife.
Kumārajīva said, "That will not do. Zhu Faguang replied, "How could a Daoist not be born of qi and blood? Why should he refuse?
He then gave Kumārajīva strong wine and confined him in a sealed room. On his way back, Faguang halted at Mount Shansi. Kumārajīva said, "It would be better to proceed from the top of Mount Tungsong.
Faguang did not accept this advice. That night, indeed, there was heavy rain and floods arose; the water reached several zhang in depth, and thousands of people died. Faguang...

They found this strange. Kumārajīva wished to remain in the Western Regions, but Guṇabhadra said, "Judging by the movement of fortune and calculating the cycles of destiny, it is not appropriate for you to stay here.

There is a blessed land where you may dwell. They returned to Liangzhou, only to hear that Fu Jian had already been killed by Yao Chang, who was then usurping the title of emperor in the region west of the Yellow River with Guzang as his capital.
One day, a great wind arose, and Kumārajīva said, "This is an inauspicious wind; there will surely be treacherous rebellion."
Nevertheless, it was settled of its own accord without exertion. Before long, there were rebels, who were soon all exterminated.
Juqu Mengxun had previously enthroned Duan Ye, the Governor of Jiankang, as his sovereign. Yao Guang dispatched his son, Yao Zuan, to lead the troops and subdue him.

Contemporary opinion held that since Ye’s forces were a mere motley crowd while Zuan possessed a formidable reputation, victory would be certain. Yao Guang consulted Kumārajīva on the matter, and he replied: "I see no sign of success in this expedition."

As for his interests: when Fu Jian was defeated at Helirei, he encountered Guo Nuo’s uprising. Jian’s army retreated with light cavalry and was again defeated by Nuo; Jian barely escaped with his life.
When Zhang Zi, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, fell ill, Zhu Faguan personally sought means to treat him. A foreign monk named Luocha claimed he could cure Zi’s illness;
Faguan was delighted and bestowed upon him immeasurable rewards. Fashì realized that Luocha was a deceitful fraud and informed [the authorities].

Sengzi said, "Even if you perform the ritual again, it will be of no avail; it will merely be a waste of effort. "Although the workings of the unseen realm are hidden, they can be tested through ritual arts," [the other] replied.
He then took five-colored silk threads and made them into a cord, which he tied together, burned to ash, and cast into water.

If the ashes emerged from the water and reformed into a cord, the illness would be incurable. The ashes floated back as a cord just as before. Not long after, Sengzi passed away, and Guang followed suit shortly thereafter.
He died. His son Shao succeeded him, but Fu Zan killed him and established himself as ruler. A pig gave birth to a three-headed offspring;
a black dragon ascended into a well and coiled itself before the palace hall, vanishing by dawn. Zan took this to be an auspicious omen and renamed the hall Longxiang (Dragon Soaring).

Shortly thereafter, it ascended again at the gate of the Dangyang Palace, so he changed the name of that gate to Longxing (Dragon Rising). Kumārajīva remarked, "Recently, the hidden dragon has been out on its travels."

The anomaly of the boar-demon manifested its strangeness; for the dragon is a creature of the Yin, appearing and disappearing according to the seasons, yet now it has repeatedly appeared as a calamity.
This must surely mean that those below have plotted; one ought to overcome oneself and cultivate virtue to respond to the heavenly warning.

Zuan did not accept this advice and was eventually killed by his younger cousin Chao. Kumārajīva had resided in Liangzhou for many years; since Lü Guang and his son did not propagate the Way, he consequently kept [his teachings] hidden.
He possessed a profound understanding, yet there was nothing he would proclaim or teach. Yao Xing dispatched Yao Shuode to the west to defeat Lü Long and welcome [Kumārajīva] back as State Preceptor.
Initially, he was invited to enter the Ximing Pavilion and the Xiaoyao Garden, where he translated numerous sutras. He could recite many from memory.
Furthermore, observing the errors in the old translations, he, together with over eight hundred śramaṇas including Sengrui and Sengzhao, transmitted and received his teachings.

Furthermore, he produced over three hundred scrolls of sutras and treatises. Sengrui was of exceptionally high talent and insight; he constantly accompanied Kumārajīva to transcribe the texts. Kumārajīva frequently remarked to Sengrui:

"The literary style of the Western Regions places particular emphasis on formal composition. Its tonal patterns and rhythms are considered excellent when they can be adapted for wind and string instruments.
Whenever one has an audience with a king or beholds a Buddha, there must be verses of praise for their virtues; the gāthās found within the sutras all follow this model."
However, when translating from Sanskrit into Qin (Chinese), one loses its lush elegance. Although the general meaning may be captured, the literary style is utterly distorted.
It is just like chewing rice and feeding it to others; not only is it tasteless, but it even causes the recipient to retch. Kumārajīva once presented a verse to Fǎhuá, saying:

"The mountain of the mind nurtures brilliant virtue, its fragrance wafting for ten thousand *yojanas*. Like a grieving phoenix atop a solitary paulownia tree, its pure notes pierce through [the air]."

The *Jiūtiān* (Nine Heavens) consists of ten verses in total; both its diction and metaphors are of this nature. He was refined in his appreciation for the Mahāyāna and was determined to propagate it. He often sighed, saying:
"If I were to take up my pen to compose a Mahāyāna Abhidharma, it would not be comparable to that of Kātyāyanīputra. Finding no one of deep understanding, he consequently desisted in sadness.

He composed two fascicles of the *Shixiang lun* (Treatise on the True Characteristic) and provided commentaries on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*; all were completed with free-flowing brushwork, without [the need for further revision].

Kumārajīva settled there and served him with a reverence as if he were a deity. Once, while Kumārajīva was preaching the sutras at Caotang Temple, over a thousand people—including the Emperor, court officials, and eminent *śramaṇas*—listened with solemn countenances.
Kumārajīva remarked, "The Dharma Master’s talent and brilliance are so transcendent that he is peerless within the realm;
how can we allow the seeds of the Dharma to diminish? He then sent ten courtesans to compel Kumārajīva to accept them. Kumārajīva...
It is also said that while in meditative concentration, he frequently saw a small boy climb onto his shoulders, wishing to obstruct him.

From then on, he no longer resided in monasteries but established a separate residence. When various monks wished to emulate him, Kumārajīva gathered needles in his alms bowl and said, "If you can eat these, then you may do so.
He then took up his spoon and ate the needles as if they were ordinary food. [Regarding] the Vinaya Master Vimalākṣa, Kumārajīva...
He was ordained as a *dharmācārya*. Upon his arrival, [Bimbasara] welcomed him with joy and performed all the rites of hospitality. Vimardasena, unaware that he had been summoned, asked:

"You have great affinities in the land of Han; how many people have received the Dharma from you? Kumārajīva replied: "The sūtras and vinayas were not yet complete. All the new sūtras were transmitted by me.
More than three thousand people followed me to receive the Dharma. However, because my karma was heavy and my obscurations deep, regarding—"
The Vinaya was incomplete; he was simply unable to propagate it deeply. When the bhikṣu Beidu was in Pengcheng, he heard that Kumārajīva was in Chang’an and sighed, saying:
"I have been separated from this youth for over three hundred years in play. Our meeting is now remote and its timing uncertain;
we shall likely encounter one another again in a future life. That night, before Kumārajīva passed away, he felt his four elements were failing and spoke these three verses:

He recited divine mantras and instructed his foreign disciples to chant them for their own protection. Before he had yet applied himself fully to his task, he became increasingly aware that his condition was perilous.
Thus, despite his failing strength, he addressed the assembly, saying: "We have met through the Dharma, yet we have not been able to exhaust our hearts' intentions.

As we face the next life, I consider myself ignorant and obscure; I have mistakenly served as a translator. Among the sūtras and śāstras I have produced, only the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* remains; I have not yet reached the point of eliminating its redundancies. If...
His realization accorded with the Buddha-mind. On the day he performed self-immolation by fire, his tongue was not scorched or destroyed.

He passed away at the Xiaoyao Garden on the twelfth day of the eighth month in the eleventh year of the Hongshi era of the pseudo-Qin dynasty, which corresponds to the fifth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty. When his body was cremated, his tongue indeed remained intact.
There is a biography of him in the Book of Jin.

Fu Ruoduoluo (translated as "Flower of Merit") was a native of Kaśmīra. He entered the monastic order at a young age and devoted himself to the intensive study of the Tripiṭaka, taking particular delight in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
Because he upheld the Vinaya with such rigor, he became a preeminent model for scholars. At the beginning of the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty, he arrived in Guanzhong.

Yao Xing received him with great ceremony; even Kumārajīva increased his respect upon meeting him. In the tenth month of the sixth year, he convened a group of scholars to discuss the meaning [of the Vinaya].
Several hundred monks at Zhongsi Temple invited Puṇyatāra to produce the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. Kumārajīva translated it into the language of Jin;
when he had completed only half, Kumārajīva passed away, causing the students to mourn him deeply.
Buddhabhadra of the Jin dynasty—translated as Jue Xian (Awakened Virtue)—was a native of Kapilavastu and a descendant of King Amṛtodana.
His grandfather was Dharmadeva, translated as Fatiān (Dharma-Heaven), who traveled to Northern India and settled there.
His father, Dharmasūrya, translated as Farì (Dharma-Sun), died early along with his mother. Buddhabhadra was raised by his maternal uncle.
At the age of three, his paternal great-uncle, Jūvali, took a liking to his wisdom and acuity and ordained him as a śrāmaṇera.
At seventeen, he received instruction from the meditation master Buddhavarman. Once he had received full ordination, he became even more diligent in the study of the Sūtras and Vinaya.
Saṃghadatta had long been his fellow student and recognized his divine brilliance; however, he did not yet know the depths of his realization. He traveled to Kaśmīra...

While he was staying in a secret chamber in the kingdom of Bamiyan, Guṇabhadra suddenly arrived. [Daohui] asked him where he had come from. He replied, "I went briefly to Tuṣita Heaven to pay my respects to Maitreya.
As soon as he finished speaking, he vanished. Daohui knew that he had already realized the state of sainthood (*ārya*).

When the Qin śramaṇa Zhìyán arrived at Jibin, he requested that Guṇabhadra propagate and transmit the methods of dhyāna to the eastern lands. Guṇabhadra consented; thereupon, he traveled through six kingdoms and reached...
After Jiaozhi had submitted, [Bhadra] boarded a merchant ship. Seeing an island from afar, he pointed it out to the crowd, saying he wished to visit it.
The sailors, as the wind was favorable, were unwilling to stop. Suddenly, the wind shifted, and the ship arrived beneath the island. The crowd all considered this a divine miracle;

thus, for the duration of the voyage, they allowed him authority over the ship’s movements. After a short while, when they wished to depart, Bhadra stopped them again. Those who insisted on setting sail were indeed shipwrecked and drowned. Suddenly—
In the middle of the night, he called out to the assembly, intending to depart in haste. However, as the group was still fast asleep, they did not respond.
Guṇabhadra then set his sails himself and departed alone. The pirates plundered the remaining ships. Upon arriving in Qingzhou, he heard that Kumārajīva was in Chang’an and went there to follow him.

Kumārajīva stepped backward from his door to welcome him with great joy, regretting that they had met so late. Their discussions were many and profound. Guṇabhadra said to Kumārajīva: "That which you have explained has not yet..."
"This exceeds people's expectations. Why have you attained such high renown? Kumārajīva replied, "My years have already passed;

scholars vainly embellish one another, and you, sir, have joined in this chorus to call me 'high'—is this not possible? Prince Hong of Qin invited him to the Eastern Palace and, in the presence of Kumārajīva, discussed the Dharma with him.
He asked, "How is it that dharmas are empty? Kumārajīva answered, "The various atoms compose form (*rūpa*). Form has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); therefore, form is eternally [empty]."
"Empty. He asked again, "Since you have already refuted form by means of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), how do you further refute the single atom?

He replied, "Some masters may analyze and break down the single atom, but that is not my intention. He asked again, "Is the atom permanent? He replied, "Because of the single atom, the multitude of atoms is empty;
because of the multitude of atoms, the single atom is empty. When translated by Ratnamegha, this statement was not understood.

[Dao]an thought that all these were merely based on Guṇabhadra’s own calculations, namely that atoms are eternal. On another day, he requested further instruction. Guṇabhadra said: "Dharmas do not arise of themselves;

they arise through the convergence of conditions. Because of one atom as a condition, there are many atoms. Since atoms have no self-nature, they are empty. How could one say that a single atom is destroyed?
At that time, Emperor Yao Xing of the Qin dynasty held Guṇabhadra in such high esteem that more than three thousand people followed him in entering and leaving the palace gates.
The monk Xian was serene, tranquil, and withdrawn, appearing utterly composed. He once remarked to his disciples, "Yesterday I saw five ships from India set sail together.
When the multitude heard this, they took it as a manifestation of supernatural power. However, I have a disciple who claims to have attained the fruit of the *Āgama*.

There are those who report this with flighty words; disaster may arise from the unforeseen. Upon hearing this, many fled. Xian did not take it to heart. [This account is recorded by] Sengxuan and Daoheng.
[Dao’an] said: "The Buddha himself did not permit [the disciples] to preach the Dharma they had attained. Why, then, do you seek to interrogate me on this?
