Furthermore, my disciples have been mutually deluded and confused, giving rise to disagreements; this violates the Vinaya and prevents us from abiding in the same principle.

Xianxiao laughed and, together with Huiguan and over forty others, crossed the river. Yao Xing was startled and rebuked Sengsong and the others, immediately dispatching messengers to pursue them, but they could not be stopped.

He eventually arrived at Mount Kuang. There, the śramaṇa Huiyuan received him with great diligence and respect, and dispatched his disciple Tanyong to send a letter to Guanzhong to resolve the matter of his expulsion.
He further requested that he translate various sūtras on dhyāna and abhidharma. Consequently, five ships arrived;

he traveled to Jiangling, where his spiritual influence flourished greatly and donors flocked to him. Guṇabhadra, however, would not accept these offerings, but instead carried a single alms-bowl as he went begging for food.

Thus it was. When Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty was serving as Grand Marshal (Taishouwei), he was campaigning against Liu Yi at Jiangling. Yuan Bao of Chenjun served as the Chief Secretary (Changshi) accompanying the administration.
Buddhabhadra once requested food from him, but after he had not yet been satisfied, he took his leave. Yuan Bao said, "It seems your intention was not yet sufficient.

Buddhabhadra replied, "It is merely that the donor’s mind for giving has its limits. Yuan Bao called to his attendants to provide more rice, but the meal was indeed exhausted. Yuan Bao was deeply ashamed.

He immediately questioned Huiguan and came to know the man’s character. He subsequently informed the Grand Marshal (Taishou), requesting an audience and inviting him to reside together in the capital.
At that time, the śramaṇa Zhifaling of Daochang Monastery had obtained the first portion of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in thirty-six thousand verses from Khotan, but it had not yet been translated.
Meng Yi, the Interior Minister, and Chu Shudu, the Right Army General, [requested] Buddhabhadra to lecture on its translation.

As for the śramaṇa Faxian, while traveling through the Western Regions, he obtained the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya and requested Guṇabhadra to translate it; the details of this account are found in Faxian’s biography.

Guṇabhadra translated the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* in six fascicles, as well as fifteen treatises including the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Pratipad-sādhana-śāstra*, totaling one hundred and seventeen fascicles.
He passed away in the sixth year of the Yuanjia era at the age of seventy-two.
*Newly Compiled Biographies of Monks Classified into Six Categories of Study*, Scroll One (Engraved by Hu Taizhi of Siming).
*Newly Compiled Biographies of Monks Classified into Six Categories of Study*, Scroll Two.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Tanye of Zhedong.
Huìxué’s Translation of the Sūtra Section:
Buddhabhadra (translated as Juéshòu, "Awakened Longevity"), a native of Jibin, received his early training from the Bhikṣu Shàn.
Regarding the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*: at that time, he disciplined his body through the *vinaya* and purified his mind through *dhyāna*.

In the seventh month of the first year of the Jingping era, he arrived in Yangzhou. That winter, he assembled the community at Longguang Temple and translated the thirty-four fascicles of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* as the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*.
He personally held the Sanskrit original, while the śramaṇas Daosheng and Huiyan acted as scribes for the oral transmission.

The Palace Attendant (Shizhong) Wang Lai of Langye served as his patron (dan-yue). In the fourth month of the following year, he again excerpted and transcribed the *Jixin jiemofa* (Ritual Procedures for the Mind of Precepts).
His ultimate end is unknown.
Tanyayasha of the Song dynasty—translated as Faming—was a native of Jibin. From his youth he was fond of learning; at the age of fourteen, he was recognized by Puṇyatāra.
As he grew older, his character became exceptionally distinguished, and he attained a comprehensive mastery of the Sūtras and Vinaya, possessing extraordinary interpretive skills.
He had practiced meditative contemplation and was at times compared to Buddhabhadra. He traveled alone through mountains and marshes, frequently encountering tigers.
Whenever he sat beneath a tree, he would sigh, saying, "I am already thirty years of age and have yet to attain the fruits [of the path]; how negligent I have been!

He reached the point of forgetting both sleep and food, repenting his past transgressions through such rigorous asceticism. Then, in a dream, the Heavenly King Vaicravana exhorted him to travel to various regions to observe the Way. Not...

He said, "One should cultivate oneself well. It is said that the Way can be attained, but it cannot be sought after. Yet, if one seeks it with excessive force beyond one's lot, one will gain nothing even at death.
He then traveled through various countries and, during the Long’an period, arrived at Baisa Temple in Guangzhou.
He was skilled at reciting the *Vibhāṣā-vinaya* and was thus known as "Mahāvibhāṣā. He was already eighty-five years old and had eighty-five disciples. There was...
The woman Zhang, whose courtesy name was Jinming, lived in purity and self-restraint.
She received the essentials of the Way from Guṇavarman, who then explained for her the *Nidāna* (Origins) of the Buddha’s birth and translated the *Carmavastu Sūtra* in one fascicle.

During the Yixi era, she arrived in Chang’an, where Yao Xing treated her as his guest of honor. She formed a close friendship with the Indian śramaṇa Dharmakṣema. In the ninth year of Hongshi of the Qin dynasty:
Together they translated the *Śāriputrābhidharma*, completing it in the sixteenth year; it consists of twenty-two fascicles.
Later, he resided at Xinsi Temple in Jiangling, where he extensively propagated the essentials of Chan meditation. His students numbered over three hundred.

At first, both monastics and laypeople suspected him of being arrogant, but upon seeing him, there was none who did not bow in reverence. He frequently experienced extraordinary auspicious signs during his meditative concentration, which people spread by word of mouth.
He was regarded as one who had attained the fruit of realization. During the Yuanjia era, he took his leave and returned to the Western Regions.

His disciple Fadu was proficient in the Sanskrit language and assisted Guṇabhadra in translating the scriptures. Fadu was the son of Po-le from India; Po-le had lost his way in Guangzhou and fathered Fadu in Nankang.
He was originally named Jinka, but upon reaching adulthood, he left the household life and received his current name. Those who did not know this history took Fadu to be a native of the South.
He was a man from Kang. Having returned from the West with his master, he subsequently held heterodox views; he studied the Hīnayāna and prohibited the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) teachings.
He claimed that there were no Buddhas of the ten directions. By nature, he prostrated only to Śākyamuni, and for eating, he used a copper bowl without providing any other vessels.

He required the nuns to follow one another in performing repentance, which consisted merely of lying prostrate on the ground facing each other. The nun Fa Hong, Pu Ming, and others all received these [teachings].
Regarding its method, it is said that the various nuns mostly study and practice it.
Tánwúchèn of the Song dynasty was a native of Central India. Orphaned at a young age, his mother supported him by working as a hired weaver of *tǎnmáo* (woolen carpets).
At the age of six, he was placed under the tutelage of Master Dharmayaśas. By ten, he had studied the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) of the Hīnayāna;

he could recite ten thousand words of scripture daily, and none dared to oppose him. At that time, there was a white-haired meditation master known as Sūnà, whose polemical attacks could not humble him.
Suspecting that he possessed extraordinary scriptures, [the King] sought instruction from him. The Dhyāna Master bestowed upon him the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* written on tree bark.

Upon reading it, Śīlāditya attained awakening; he then assembled the great multitude to repent for his transgressions. By the age of twenty, he had recited two million words, and had thoroughly studied and mastered the various Mahāyāna sūtras.
His elder brother, skilled in training elephants, enjoyed the favor of the King. On another occasion, the King’s white elephant...
The elephant died, and the king ordered its execution. He issued a decree stating, "Whoever dares to collect and bury it shall have their three generations of kin exterminated.
Zhen (Chen) collected and buried it. The guards seized him and reported this to the king. The king was enraged and ordered that Zhen be boiled alive. Zhen said, "The King kills according to the law;

your brother collects [the corpse] according to righteousness. This is the universal principle of the world. Because of this, the king treated him with increased respect. Zhen was especially efficacious in his incantations and was titled the Great Master of Incantations.

Once, while traveling with Wang through the mountains, they ran short of water; [Dao'an] recited a mantra over a rock, causing it to gush forth. When the various kingdoms heard of this, they sent envoys to establish diplomatic relations with him one after another.
After some time, he received the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (the "prior portion") and the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*. He then traveled to Kaśmīra, where everyone followed the Hīnayāna and opposed his views.
He traveled to Kucha and stayed at the guest house in Guzang. Fearing there might be thieves, he fell asleep with the scriptures resting upon his pillow.

He dreamed of a person who pulled at his robe and said, "These are the Tathāgata’s treasury of liberation; how would you dare to forget your reverence for them? He was startled awake and placed the scriptures in a high location.

The thief indeed possessed great strength, yet could not lift them. At dawn, the monk Xian carried the scriptures away. The thief, regarding him as a divine being, confessed his transgressions and apologized to him.
Juqu Mengxun occupied the territory of Liang; however, he treated Kumārajīva with exceptional courtesy. He thereupon requested that the scriptural texts be translated.

Because Kumārajīva had not yet mastered the Chinese language, he did not grant permission immediately. After three years had passed, he translated sixty works, including the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* (First Part), the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Kṣitigarbha-sūtra*, the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the *Sāgara-nāgarāja-paripṛcchā*, and the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*.

The remaining [text] consists of ten thousand words; its composition is refined and meticulous, and its literary elegance is exquisite and abundant. The śramaṇas Huìsōng, Dàolǎng, and others held it in profound esteem.
Yet, because they felt the number of chapters in the *Nirvāṇa* was insufficient, they requested that he return to the West to investigate and seek out the complete version.

It comprises forty-two fascicles, stating: "This sūtra originally consisted of thirty-five thousand gāthās, whereas here in this land there are only one million words. This is what I have translated."
This work consists of ten thousand verses. Dharmakṣema performed many miraculous deeds. When Tuoba Tao of the Wei dynasty heard of his reputation, he dispatched an envoy to invite him, warning him:

"We know you hold your own honor and status in high regard; if you do not send him, we shall simply resort to military force. Consequently, Sengxun submitted a memorial requesting that Dharmakṣema be retained.

The Wei court further dispatched Li Shun, Duke of Gaoping, to confer upon Sengxun the title of Attendant-in-Ordinary and Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Liangzhou and the Western Regions.
The Grand Tutor, General of the Flying Cavalry, Governor of Liangzhou, and King of Liang, was granted the nine emoluments.
An edict was issued stating: "Dharmakṣema’s virtue and wisdom are vast and profound; I wish to pay him my respects in person. You must dispatch him by relay post. Xun addressed Shun, saying:

"I have served the imperial court with total loyalty and bear no debt of failure. Why then does Your Majesty believe the words of heretics and press me so? My previous memorial requested that Dharmakṣema be allowed to remain. Now...
He came rushing to pursue him, saying, "This is my master. I wish to die with him. Death is inevitable; it matters not whether it comes sooner or later.

Shun said, "The King was truly sincere when he first sent his son to serve you. The court held your loyalty and righteousness in high esteem, which is why they bestowed such exceptional honors upon you.
Now, because of this one barbarian monk, you have ruined your great achievement and forfeited the court's favor."

I privately believe that Your Majesty should not accept this. Zhi Dun said, "What the Grand Master of Ceremonies says is certainly admirable; however, I fear that his true intentions do not match these words.
Zhi Dun ultimately did not dispatch him. In the third month of the third year of Yihé, Daohui firmly requested to travel westward to seek a portion of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Zhi Dun was incensed by his departure and, fearing he might fall into the hands of the Wei, dispatched an assassin to kill him on the road.
He lived to the age of forty-nine, at which those who heard the news wept for him. This was in the tenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
When the prophecy first emerged as he passed through the pass, he said to his guests: "The karmic retribution has arrived; even though all the sages were present, they could not have saved me.
While Faxian was in Guzang, there was a śramaṇa named Daojin from Zhangye who received the Bodhisattva precepts from him. Faxian said to him: "You must purify your mind."
He repented of his conduct and came after seven days. Upon arriving at the place where Baoyi was, Baoyi suddenly became angry. Daolin said, "This is due to karmic obstacles from the past.

Daolin again applied himself with diligence for three years, during which he dreamed that Śākyamuni Buddha conferred the precepts upon him. On the same night, more than ten other people had dreams identical to those seen by Daolin.
Thereupon, Daolin went to see Baoyi once more. From afar, Baoyi saw him and was greatly astonished, saying, "Excellent! You have already attained the realization of the precepts."
"I shall now bear witness for you. The śramaṇa Daolang was likely one who shared the same dream. I pray that you lower your seniority and treat him as your elder brother.
Following this, more than a thousand people received the precepts from him. There was once a separate record stating:
"The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* shall be transmitted to this land by the Bodhisattva Iśvara. Later, Dharmakṣema indeed produced this sūtra; thus, such was Dharmakṣema’s spiritual status.
This can be known.
Buddhabhadra of the Song dynasty—translated as "Awakened Armor"—was a man from the Western Regions. From his youth, he possessed noble conduct and studied the Tripiṭaka;
he was particularly proficient in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, which he constantly recited and upheld as the essence of his heart. In the first year of the Yuanjia era, he arrived in Xiliang.
The śramaṇa Daotai was resolute and determined in his purpose. Having traveled through various kingdoms in his youth, he obtained a Sanskrit manuscript (*pi-p'o fan-ben*) of the *Vibhāṣā*.
In the fourteenth year [of the Yuanjia era], he invited Saṃghavarman to translate it; Daotai acted as the scribe, while Hui-gao, Dao-lang, and others verified and corrected the text.
The work comprised one hundred fascicles in total, of which forty were lost during the chaos of the civil wars. Later, Daotai returned to the Western Regions.
Sengzhiyan was a native of Xiliangzhou during the Song dynasty; his family name has been lost to history. He was renowned for his diligent practice.
In his youth, he sought out teachers and traveled to the Matara Vihāra in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, where he received the dhyāna teachings from the Venerable Buddhayaśas.

After three years, he had attained superior power, and Buddhayaśas praised him as a vessel for the Buddha’s Dharma. The monastics and laypeople of the Western Regions remarked, "Is there such a practitioner in the land of Qin? Qin...
Because his reputation had grown even greater, there was a certain Buddhabhadra, a master of the dhyāna tradition whose fame was widespread.

Daoxian invited him to travel east to transmit the Dharma and benefit sentient beings; thus, they returned together. Upon reaching Guanzhong, Buddhabhadra was subjected to the jealousy and malice of the monks of Qin after some time.
Consequently, Daoxian retired to Mount Kuang in Shandong, devoting himself solely to meditation and recitation. This was in the thirteenth year of the Yixi era.

When Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty was returning from his western expedition, he reached the east of the mountains. Prince Shixing Huai was traveling in the imperial entourage when they passed by Yanlu.
There were two bhikṣus seated in meditation, profoundly still. Huai snapped his fingers, and both looked up at him before immediately withdrawing their gaze;

they did not speak with him. Huai marveled at them in his heart and increased his reverence for them. He then petitioned Emperor Wu to invite them back to the capital. At first, neither was willing to go, but Yan eventually consented.
Upon arriving at the capital, he resided at Shixing Temple. Daohui also built Dongjiao Temple for him to dwell in; this was the Jiyuan [Grove].
In the fifth year of the Yuanjia era, together with the śramaṇa Baoyun, Huaiyan translated the *Lalitavistara*, the *Vaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka*, the *Caturmahārājakāyika-sūtra*, and other scriptures.

Huaiyan did not accept separate invitations. When mealtime arrived, he would enter the village carrying his alms bowl for a single meal, then remain in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) for the entire day. Huaiyan himself...

Reflecting that he had committed some transgressions against the precepts and suspecting they might fall under the category of "dharmas to be abandoned," he sailed by sea to India to seek a resolution from a distinguished venerable master.
The venerable master entered into meditative absorption, ascended to the Inner Court, and questioned Maitreya. Maitreya replied:
Having received the precepts, Huayan was filled with great joy. He passed away without illness in Jibin at the age of seventy-eight.

According to the custom of Jibin, when a bhikṣu passes away, they invariably distinguish between the areas for ordinary beings and those for sages before performing cremation. Huayan possessed both diligent effort and authentic practice.
Yet people did not know this; when they attempted to cremate him in an ordinary location, he was so heavy that he could not be lifted, but at the sacred site, he became light.
For this reason, it was known that Yan had attained the Way.
Seng Baoyun of the Song dynasty was a man of unknown origins. In his youth, he traveled back and forth between Liangzhou; he possessed both learning and virtuous conduct.

He was serene and withdrawn, refusing to involve himself in worldly affairs, and sought the Dharma at the cost of his own life. In the first year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty, he departed for the Western Regions.

Together with Faxian and Zhiyan, he successively journeyed through various kingdoms. Upon reaching the wilderness of the Rākṣasas, he heard the sound of celestial drums. There were many relics left behind by Śākyamuni.
He was venerated by all who beheld him. He was proficient in the Sanskrit language and studied the Brāhmī script. Later, he returned to Chang’an and became a disciple of Dhyāna Master Buddhabhadra.

When Buddhabhadra went to Mount Kuang, Huiyun followed him; wherever they went, he blended his presence with the crowd. After a long time, he returned home and settled at Daochang Temple, where he translated various sutras such as the *Sukhāvatīvyūha*.
He later resided at Liuhe Temple, where he translated the *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha-sūtra*. During the Yuanjia era...
He passed away at the end of the twenty-sixth year, at the age of seventy-four.
Guṇavarman of the Song dynasty—this name translates as "Armor of Merit"—was of the Kṣatriya caste. His family had long ruled the kingdom of Kaśmīra.

His grandfather was Haribhadra, which translates as "Lion-Worthy," and his father was Saṃghananda, which translates as "Joy of the Multitude"; both were... [possessed of... (Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at the end.)
King Qi-de-ba-mo was fourteen years old when his natural endowments were already exceptionally brilliant. His mother once required a soup made of wild animal meat and ordered him to prepare it.
Ba-mo said, "Among all living beings, there is none that does not loathe death.
To satisfy one's own cravings with what another loathes—is this truly the heart of a benevolent person? His mother replied in anger, "You say there certainly exists hell!"
"Is there retribution? On another day, I shall take your place and repay it; that is why I have no regrets. Later, Guṇavarman happened to overturn a pot of soup and scald his hand.
He said to his mother, "This pain is unbearable; can you take my place for me? His mother laughed and said, "The pain is yours. How could I possibly take its place?
Guṇavarman knelt and said, "Killing is indeed the cause of extreme suffering in the three miserable realms; one must experience the consequences with one's own body."

"It is certainly true that reason must not be abandoned. Was not the Great Man’s statement yesterday perhaps excessive? My mother has ceased killing for the rest of her life. At eighteen, he left home to become a śramaṇa.
A physiognomist said, "In thirty years, you shall face south and be called 'The Solitary' [a king].

Now that you have entered the religious life, it is certain that you will attain the fruits of the Way. When the time arrived, the King passed away, and the people of the country wished to welcome him back to be installed as ruler.
Guṇavarman suddenly withdrew and departed for the Lion Kingdom (Siṃhala). He traveled to Java. King Bhaṭāraka of Java had previously dreamed that a holy man would arrive;
he saw Guṇavarman there and received the five precepts from him. Initially, the king did not believe in him, but because of his mother’s dream, he changed his mind.
He also received [the teachings] from him, and after some time, he came to believe in them with great sincerity.
When a neighboring country launched an invasion, the King was about to repel it and asked Guṇavarman for a method to achieve victory without fighting. He replied, "Is it not through compassion?

Nevertheless, when the state faces calamity and hardship, how can one fail to exert oneself? "Your Majesty, proceed! After the King returned in triumph, he was struck by an arrow in the midst of the fray. Guṇa...
He washed it with water consecrated by mantras and was healed. The king wished to renounce the world, but his ministers strongly opposed it.
The king said, "I have three wishes; if you gentlemen will grant them, then I shall also grant your request. Otherwise, I will not."
First, one should collectively offer [the merit] to the Great Upādhyāya; second, one should prohibit killing; third, there should be surplus stores to provide relief to the poor and destitute.
Thereupon, the ministers respectfully accepted these stipulations and collectively observed the five precepts. The King personally oversaw the construction of a vihāra to welcome Guṇavarman.
His fame resounded throughout all nations. In the ninth month of the first year of the Yuánjiā era, the śramaṇa Huì... from the capital city...

Guān Huì, Cōng, and others submitted a memorial requesting that he be welcomed there. An imperial edict was issued to the Governor of Jiāozhōu, ordering him to send the śramaṇas Fǎcháng, Dàochōng, Dàojùn, and others by sea to Gāngzhōu.
By imperial decree, they were permitted to travel to the palace by post station; their route passed through Shǐxīng.
He loved Mount Hushan, as its form resembled Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; consequently, he changed the name of the monastery on the mountain to Lingjiu (Spiritual Vulture Peak).
He resided there for one year. The Prefect Cai Muzhi held him in profound reverence and respect. When [Cai] was about to die, [Guṇavarman] preached the Dharma to comfort him.

Furthermore, the family members dreamed that he was in the monastery expounding the Dharma to the assembly of monks. The monastery possessed a Baoyue Hall (Jewel Moon Hall), and Guṇavarman [inscribed] upon its eastern wall...
He playfully fashioned an image of the youth Megha-Dīpaṃkara spreading his hair [as a mat]; it was exquisitely beautiful and would constantly emit light at night.

The mountain had long been infested with tigers, but ever since Guṇavarman arrived, they were completely eradicated. His meditative concentration lasted for many days. A monk from the monastery once sent a novice to observe him;
the novice saw a white lion that looked up, stepped upon a pillar, and played there. The sky was filled with blue lotuses. Startled, the novice fled and cried out loudly. The monks...
He arrived in haste, but found that everything had vanished. In the first month of the eighth year, he reached Jianye and was summoned for an audience.
The Emperor questioned him with great diligence and said, "I wish to observe the fast and abstain from killing, yet I am constrained by the myriad affairs of state and cannot fulfill this desire.

Now that you, Dharma Master, have come from afar to this humble land, what instructions do you have for me? He replied, "The Way resides in the person, not in external affairs; the Dharma arises from oneself, not from [external conditions]."
Furthermore, the cultivation practiced by a sovereign differs from that of a commoner. A commoner is of humble station and minor renown; his words lack authority.
If he cannot overcome himself and undergo rigorous discipline, how can he be of any use? A sovereign takes the four seas as his home and the myriad people as his children.
When he utters a single virtuous word, both officials and commoners rejoice; when he implements a single benevolent policy, both humans and spirits are harmonized. As for punishments—

Lives will not be cut short prematurely, and laborers will not be exhausted by toil; thus, winds and rains will be timely, cold and heat will follow their seasons, the hundred grains will flourish, and mulberry and hemp will grow luxuriantly.
To regard this as the great merit of observing the fast and abstaining from killing—how could it be so?

Why must one cease eating for half a day and save the life of a single bird before it can be considered a vast salvation? The Emperor struck his desk and sighed, saying, "The common people are deluded."

The profound principle is remote, while the monastic community lags behind in its adherence to proximate teachings. Those who are deluded by the remote principle claim that the Ultimate Way is empty and vast;

those who lag behind in the proximate teachings merely cling to names and forms. As the Dharma Master has explained, such exhortations open and encourage the human mind, making it possible to discuss the boundary between heaven and humanity.
He resided at the Jetavana Monastery, where he lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the "Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmika*) chapter. The grandeur of these Dharma assemblies was unprecedented.

He translated twenty-six fascicles, including the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* in thirty chapters and the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, which completed the ten-fascicle *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* previously translated by Saṅghavarman.
In the sixth year of the Yuanjia era, he spent the summer retreat at Dinglin Monastery. Upon the conclusion of the retreat...
He returned to the Jetavana Monastery. On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month, before his midday meal was finished, he returned to his quarters.

His disciples followed him there, only to find that he had already passed away in a state of profound stillness. He was sixty-five years old. One day, he had said to his disciples: "I have already realized the second fruit [of the path]."
Furthermore, he spoke thirty-six lines of verse and bestowed them upon Aśvaghosa, saying: "These may be shown to the monks of India as well as to the monks of this land.
An imperial decree was issued to construct a stupa and translate these bequeathed verses; however, most of the verses have not been recorded here.

Saṃghavarman of the Song dynasty—translated as "Multitude of Armor"—was a native of India. Having renounced his home life in youth, he was refined and possessed deep learning in the Vinaya, being particularly proficient in the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
In the tenth year of the Yuanjia era, he arrived at Jianye, where both the clergy and the laity vied to honor him; he was titled a Tripitaka Master.
While residing at Pinglu Temple, he, together with the śramaṇa Huiguan, further renovated the temple’s pagodas.
The bhikṣuṇī Tiexialuo from Siṃhala arrived and conferred the precepts upon the nuns Huiguo and Jingyin of Yingfu Temple. Huiyi of Qihuan Temple criticized this;
however, Guṇavarman established the fundamental tenets and manifested the Dharma with such clarity and logical consistency that Huiyi was ultimately defeated and submitted. The monastic community...
There were several hundred nuns who received [her teachings]. Prince Yi Kang of Pengcheng held her in special esteem and served her with great devotion.
She translated the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, the *Mātṛkā*, the *Karmavibhaṅga*, the *Saṃkṣipta-rājapraśnīya-gāthā*, and the *Āryasaṃghasnāna-vinaya*.
Baoyun presided over the assembly while Huiguan transcribed the text with his brush. Later, he returned to the Western Regions.

[There was also] Kang Liangyeshe (translated as "Renowned for His Time"), a man from the Western Regions who lived during the Song dynasty. He possessed a grand and firm temperament and had no personal indulgences.

He was skilled at reciting the Abhidharma and was thoroughly versed in the various sutras, yet he specialized in teaching the methods of dhyāna contemplation to others. In the first year of the Yuanjia era, he arrived [in China].
In Jianye, he was revered by the Great Ancestor, Emperor Wen. He resided at the Daolin Vihāra on Mount Zhong, where the śramaṇa Bao honored his dhyāna methods.
He translated the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-bhaiṣajyasamudgata-aparimitāyur-jñāna-sūtra*, with Senghan receiving the text in writing.

Regarding these two sutras as secret arts for transforming obstacles and as the esoteric causes for the Pure Land, he pondered them deeply and savoring their meaning, he gave rise to verses of praise and eulogy.
When Meng Yi of Pingchang was appointed as the governor of Kuaiji, he requested [Huiyuan] to accompany him but would not let him go. Later, he moved his residence to Jiangling.
In the nineteenth year, he entered Shu to propagate the Way. Shortly thereafter, he returned to Jiangling and passed away at the age of sixty-two.
Qiunabidi (translated as Anjin), a native of Central India, entered the monastic order at a young age and served the Mahayana master Saṃghasena.
He was required to recite two hundred thousand words daily and was proficient in both Buddhist and secular studies. At the beginning of the Jian’an era, he arrived in Jianye.
He resided at the Vaiśālī Monastery, where his dignified deportment served as a model for those in training.

He translated one fascicle of *The Essential Parables from the Sūtra-piṭaka Compiled by Saṃghasena*, two fascicles on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and two fascicles of the *Sudatta Gṛhapati Sūtra*.
He passed away in the second year of the Zhongxing era.
Sengqiepoluo (Sanghapāla)—whose name means "Nurturer of the Multitude" in Chinese, also translated as "Armor of the Multitude"—was a native of the kingdom of Funan.

He was exceptionally intelligent from childhood and entered the monastic order at an early age. He specialized in the Abhidharma and enjoyed great renown throughout the South Seas. After completing his studies in the *Abhidharmakośa*, he proceeded to study the Vinaya.

He came from the Western Regions to observe and transform [the people]. Arriving by sea during the Qi dynasty, he resided at Zhengguan Temple in the capital as a disciple of the Indian śramaṇa Guṇabhadra.
He was widely learned and versatile, proficient in the scripts and languages of several countries. Following the fall of the Qi, he sought out those with specialized skills;
in the fifth year of the Tianjian era, he visited Zhengguan Temple within the Hualin Garden at Shouguang Palace in the capital of Yangdu.
The five locations, including the Yunguan and Funan Monasteries, completed the translation work. In the seventeenth year, a total of eleven works in forty-eight fascicles were finalized;
these included the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra* (Da yu wang jing) and the *Vimuktimārga-śāstra* (Jie tuo dao lun).
On the day the first translations were made, Emperor Wu personally attended to receive the dictation. The śramaṇas Baochang, Huichao, Sengzhi, Fayun, Yuan Tanyun, and others were present.
He produced commentaries that did not fall away from the tradition of translation. The Emperor treated him with great courtesy and invited him to serve as his personal monk (*kula-bhikṣu*).
Using the Emperor’s own offerings, he established the monastery where he resided. The Grand Marshal, Prince Hong of Linchuan, received him with exceptional honor.
In the fifth year of the Putong era, he passed away at Zhengguan Monastery due to illness at the age of sixty-five. There was also a śramaṇa named Mandāra, who was likewise a native of Funan.
The Chinese terms for these are "vast" (弘) and "weak" (弱). He brought the Sanskrit originals from afar;

the Imperial Envoy and the Brahmin translated them, resulting in three texts—the *Ratnamegha*, the *Dharmadhātuprakṛti*, and the *Mañjuśrīprajñāpāramitā*—totaling eleven fascicles. Their phrasing was profound and substantial.
Much of this remains unintelligible. In the fifteenth year of the Tianjian era, the lay practitioner Mudaoxian submitted one fascicle of the *Uruvilvā Sūtra*.

As the text was incomplete and its provenance unknown, it was rejected. At that time, the daughter of Jiang Bi, a Doctor of the National Academy, named the nun Sengfa, had entered the monastic life at a young age;
she would often sit in meditation with her eyes closed, reciting the sūtras as if she were possessed by some external spirit.
From the age of eight until sixteen, he produced a total of thirty-five fascicles, including the *Sukhāvatīvyūha* and the *Suśobhana-vyūha*.
During the Tianjian era, the Emperor personally inspected these works in the Huaguang Hall and marveled at their extraordinary nature.

The history of Tanyao of the Northern Wei does not mention his surname or place of origin. During the Heping era, he resided at the North Terrace as the *Zhaoxuantong* (Director of the Buddhist Clergy).

He lived at Tongle Monastery in the stone caves of Heng’an; this monastery was built by Emperor Wencheng. Previously, Emperor Wu had been deluded by the Daoist Kou Qianzhi and abolished the teachings of Śākyamuni.
Later, he died of a pestilential disease. Upon reaching this time [of Tanyao’s tenure], an imperial edict restored the teachings, including the stupas and monasteries.

Statues were placed before them, and this monastery was particularly exquisite and beautiful; it was constructed by carving into the mountains and valleys of the Wu Zhou region, extending for more than thirty li.
Inscribed steles still exist there. Before his work was finished, Chen Wei-yao produced the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (or *Dharmatrāta-saṃghāta*) and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* at the monastery.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Tan-jing produced two fascicles of the *Tivya-pāli-sūtra*.
Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei, whose Chinese name was Huāxī, was thoroughly versed in the Tripitaka and had attained mastery in dhāraṇīs.
His resolve was set upon propagating the Dharma. At the beginning of the Yongping era, he arrived at the capital of Luoyang. Emperor Xuānwǔ appointed him to the Great Yǒngníng Monastery.

At that time, among seven hundred Indian monks, he was esteemed as the preeminent master. When he first translated the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the Emperor personally received the oral transmission by pen. This continued until the reign of Emperor Xiàojìng.

After the capital was moved to Zhangye, more than twenty years passed during the Tianping era. During this time, he translated the *Buddhanāmasūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatārasūtra*, the *Dharmasaṃgrahasūtra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocanasūtra*, and other sutras;
as well as the *Suvikrāntavikramiparipṛcchā*, the *Mahāratnakūṭa*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra*, and other śāstras.

The śramaṇas Senglang and Daozhan, along with the Palace Attendant Cui Guang, served as scribes. In total, there were thirty-nine works comprising one hundred and twenty-seven fascicles. At that time...
The lay devotee Li Kuò compiled a catalogue of the various scriptures; his familiarity with the translations of Paramārtha was particularly thorough.
He once remarked that the Sanskrit manuscripts of sutras and śāstras in his residence nearly filled ten thousand [volumes], while the draft copies of his translations occupied an entire room.

Nevertheless, he possessed divine intuition and keen intelligence, was profoundly proficient in local dialects, and was exceptionally skilled in incantations and rituals. Once, while he was rinsing his mouth, no one needed to draw water for him.
He then spoke in Sanskrit; by joining his index fingers together and reciting it only a few times, the well-railing surged up from the water, which he then drew from and used.
Leṇamati (whose name means "Precious Intention" in the language of China) was a person from India who arrived during the Yuan Wei dynasty.

In the fifth year of the Zhengshi era, he translated the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*, the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, and other major works totaling twenty-four fascicles at the capital of Luoyang. Furthermore, he was skilled at expounding the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. His spirit...
The principles were clearly distinguished as they differed. He received and recorded the words of the Wei envoy, exhausting every subtle point and profound detail.

One day, while he was presiding over the high seat, a man arrived suddenly carrying a ceremonial tablet and a letter of introduction, appearing like a high official. He said, "I have come by imperial decree from the Lord of Heaven to invite you.

Dharmakṣema declined, saying that since the current dharma assembly had not yet concluded, it would be difficult for him to comply with the command. He further suggested that the *Dujiang* and *Weina*, who are essential for the performance of the dharma rites, should first [be sent].
He requested that [the monk] Ding be appointed as the *vīnāyaka* (lecturer) and *karmadāna* (disciplinarian). Subsequently, both Le-na-du and Ding passed away at the same time.

Buddhasanta of North India, whose name means "Awakened Stability" (*Jueding*) in the language of China, arrived from the region of Northern Wei between the Zhengguang era and the second year of the Yuanxiang era.
During this period, he translated the *Vajra-agrāsvāda-sūtra* and other scriptures at Baima Monastery in the capital of Luoyang and Jinhua Monastery in the capital of Ye.
Section Ten. At the capital of Luoyang, the śramaṇa Fa-chang translated the *Vimalakīrti-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Questions of the Elder Vimalakīrti), one fascicle.
[The translator] Prajñāruci—whose name in the language of China is Zhi-xi—was of the Gautama clan and of Brahmin descent; he was a native of Vārāṇasī in South India.

During the Xiping era, he arrived at the capital of Luoyang. From the first year of the Yuanxiang period until the end of the Xinghe period, he translated the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Lotus Sūtra).

The *Nian sheng shanzhu huizheng weishi deng jinglun* (Treatises on the Noble and Well-Established Mind-Only and the Turning Back of Disputes, etc. consists of fourteen works in eighty-five fascicles.
These were transcribed by the śramaṇas Tanlin, Sengfang, and others at the capital of Ye.

At that time, Bodhiruci and Prajñāruci produced scriptures both earlier and later; however, those who copied them generally omitted the characters for their names and simply wrote "Liu-zhi. Therefore—
The rain-like flow of these texts was so muddled and intermingled that it was difficult to establish them with precision.

In the second year of Emperor Wen’s reign of the Northern Zhou dynasty, the Vinaya Master Raṇabhadrā from the country of Pāṭaliputra—whose name means "Wise and Virtuous" (Zhìxián) in the Chinese language—together with Yaśogupta and others, translated the *Pañcavidyā-śāstra*. The five vidyās are:
grammar, medicine, mechanics, seals, and divination. The śramaṇa Zhìxiān acted as the scribe for the oral transmission. This occurred during the Tiānhé era of Emperor Wu.
Dharmaruci of the country of Mālava— whose name in the language of China means "Dharma-Desire"— translated the *Brahmaṇa-jyotiṣa* (Astronomy of the Brahmins) in twenty fascicles for Yuwen Hu,
the Duke of Jinyang and Grand Chancellor. Furthermore, the Dhyāna Master Jayayasa of the country of Magadha—
whose name in the language of China means "Treasure-Invocation"— together with his disciple Jñānagupta and others, [worked] at the former site in Chang’an.
Tianwang Temple. The *Dingyi tianzi wen jing* (Sūtra of the Questions of the Devaputra Samādhimati) in six fascicles was translated [by Paramārtha].
The śramaṇa Yuanming, Daobian, Chengyang Duke Xiao Ji, and others acted as scribes.
Chen: Kunāradatta; in the language of China, "Intimate Reliance" (*qīnyī*). Also called Paramārtha; in the language of China, "True Reality" (*zhēndì*). From the West...

He was a native of Ujjayinī in India. During the Datong era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, when the Three Jewels were flourishing, the court official Zhang Si and others sent him back to his country with an envoy from Funan bearing tribute. They were also commissioned to request a person of renowned virtue who was a Tripitaka master.
That country then dispatched Tanyi at the imperial command, and he arrived together with Mahāyāna treatises, various *Avataṃsaka* sūtras, and other texts. This was in the tenth year of Datong.
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month of the second year, he reached the South Sea. In the eighth month of the second year of the Daqing era, he arrived at the capital.
The Emperor prostrated before him in Baoyun Hall and immediately wished to commission the translation of his works; however, as the Hu invaders were encroaching and prevailing, this was not realized.
Dì also traveled extensively throughout the eastern lands. The patron Fuchun sent Lu Yuanzhe to invite him, along with the śramaṇa Baoqiong and two others.
Together with more than ten others, he translated the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (Seventeen Stages Treatise). Daobang [completed] five fascicles.

In the third year of the Taibao era, when Hou Jing summoned him back to provide offerings, Emperor Yuan established his reign. He resided at Zhengguan Temple in Jinling together with more than twenty people, including Master Huiyuan.

He translated the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, after which he traveled about to propagate the teachings according to the regions, finding no rest. He desired to board a ship and travel to the kingdom of Laṅkā;
however, both monastics and laypeople bound themselves by oath to detain him, so he remained in Nan Yue. There he re-examined his previous translations.

In the fourth year of the Tianjia era of Emperor Wen, the śramaṇas Sengzong, Fazhun, and the Vinaya Master Sengren, among others from Jianyuan Temple in the capital city of Yangdu, paid him their respects...

I have long been thirsty for new teachings. Having received your kind inquiry from afar, I am deeply moved by your intention. I have therefore translated the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* and other treatises.
While on my way back to the Western Regions, I arrived at Liáng'ān; however, driven by the winds of karma, my ship was blown back to Guǎngzhōu. There, the Regional Inspector, Duke Mù Wěi—
He resided at Zhiyi Temple, where, together with the śramaṇa Huikai and others, he translated the *Vipula-artha-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, and other works.

After Duke Mu passed away, his heir He served as his patron (*dānapati*), and the translation work continued. However, his spiritual insight reached into the profound and was beyond the comprehension of the world.
Once, while he was staying on a remote island, He went to visit him; the waves surged and overflowed, and he could not immediately cross over.
He gazed intently at it. Consequently, he spread his sitting mat upon the water and sat cross-legged; he crossed the current to reach the shore, yet the mat was hardly moistened.

Or, when riding upon lotus leaves, they did not tilt even slightly. In the sixth month of the second year of the Guangtai era, he entered the northern mountains of the South Sea intending to sacrifice his life.
When Huikai heard of this, he suspended his lectures and rushed to him. The Regional Inspector bowed his forehead to the ground in reverence.
He requested to remain, and the multitude blocked his departure and entreated him to stay for three days before he finally consented. Consequently, he was invited to the Wangyuan Monastery.

There, plans were made to return to Jianye, but upon encountering those who harbored resentment, the Emperor was dissuaded, and the matter was abandoned. On the eleventh day of the first month of the first year of the Dajian era, he fell ill and passed away at the age of seventy-one.
Regarding the sūtras and śāstras he had translated, Sengzong, Fazhun, and others respectfully returned them to Kuang... [the text ends here].

As for Paramārtha: although he extensively produced [translations of] various sūtras, he specifically took the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* as his primary school, and thus translated and transmitted it in various places.

There are both direct commentaries (*śāstra*) and indirect exegeses (*ṭīkā*); the latter commentary is that explained by Sengzong. As for Huikai, he thoroughly encompassed the source of the teachings and elucidated the meaning of the titles;
whenever he expounded them face-to-face, his reasoning and sentiments left nothing unexpressed. One day, Paramārtha sighed deeply and said to Huikai: "You gentlemen..."
"In truth, you have received the transmission of the Dharma; yet, meeting with such an untimely era, what is to be done? As he wept, Kai shed many rows of tears and knelt to address him, saying:
"The Dharma has reached the Middle Kingdom, yet the defilements of sentient beings are heavy, leading to this turmoil. When, then, will it be settled?"
Tandi pointed toward the northwest and said, "In this direction there is a great kingdom where my teaching shall flourish and spread widely before long;
it is only a pity that you will not live to see it. Alas! Is it not for today that he has waited?
From the end of the Liang dynasty until the beginning of the Chen dynasty, over a period of twenty-three years, Tandi produced sixty-four works consisting of sutras, commentaries, and records.
In total, there were two hundred and seventy-eight fascicles. At that time, there was a prince from the kingdom of Ujjayinī in Central India named Vajrabodhi (translated into Chinese as Gāokōng).
During the Yuánxiàng era of the Wèi dynasty, he produced three versions of the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* in seven fascicles at the residence of Sītu Gōng Sūn Téng in Yèchéng.
The śramaṇa Sēngfǎng acted as the scribe. This occurred just as the Qi dynasty received the abdication of the throne.

Traveling south, he reached Jinling (Nanjing). During the Dading era, he translated one fascicle of the *Mahāyāna-śikhara-rāja-sūtra*. Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty issued an edict appointing Guṇavarman as the General Overseer of Foreign Envoys.

In the second year of the Daqing era, he encountered the Khotanese śramaṇa Guṇabhadra—whose name means "Virtuous Sage" in Chinese—who arrived bringing the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Guṇavarman requested it from him and obtained it; this happened to coincide with the reign of [Prince] Hou.

During the chaos of Emperor Jing’s reign, there was no leisure to translate and transmit it. It was only in the year of the Earth-Bird (Biyou) of the Tianjia era of the Chen dynasty that the translation began at Xingye Monastery in Jiangzhou, with the śramaṇa Zhixin serving as the scribe for the oral transmission.
The monk Subhūti (Chinese: Shànjí) from the kingdom of Funan translated the *Mahāyāna-ratnamegha-sūtra* in eight fascicles at Zhìjìng Temple in Yangzhou.
Compared with the seven-fascicle version produced during the Liang dynasty by Mandra, this differs only slightly.
This is also recorded in the *Sui Sanbao lu* (Catalogue of the Three Jewels of the Sui Dynasty).
Chen Fatai was a man of unknown origins who had early on gained renown alongside Hui Kai, Sengzong, Farin, and others.
During the Liang dynasty, the Indian śramaṇa Paramārtha was living in exile in Lingnan; Fatai, together with Sengzong and Hui Kai, attended upon him. Upon [Paramārtha’s] departure...

At the request of Ou-yang Wei, the Governor of Kuang-chou, [the texts] were translated at Chih-chi Temple. In the third year of the Tai-jian era of the Chen dynasty, he lectured on the newly translated scriptures in Chiang-ye, astonishing the assembly of his time.
When Hsüan-tsung of P’eng-ch’eng came to consult him, Seng-t’ai expounded the teachings according to the occasion and in accordance with the essential principles, leaving nothing unexplained;
this account appears in the biography of Hsüan-tsung. Hui-k’ai’s surname was Ts’ao, and he was profoundly learned in the principles of the doctrine.
Bo was exceptionally prolific and his command of language was particularly abundant. He assisted Paramārtha in the work of translation, often lamenting that they had met so late in life.

While residing at Xianming Temple in Guangzhou, he invited Paramārtha into his quarters to lecture on the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*. During the Guangda era, there were monks such as Zong, Fazhun, and Farin.
Tandi studied diligently and lectured on the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*. He requested Huikai to lecture on the *Abhidharmakośa* at Zhihui Temple;
however, when they reached the ninth fascicle of the commentary on the "Chapter on Karma," Tandi fell ill and could not recover. In the spring of the following year, Tandi passed away.

Among his disciples who had received the Bodhisattva precepts was Cao Pi, the younger son of Huikai. Having followed Huikai to the South since his youth, he was already proficient [in these teachings].

Regarding the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra), he also inherited the traditions of various schools. Later, while residing in Jiangdu, he would occasionally take the seat to expound the teachings while dressed in the ceremonial square cap and wide-sleeved robes of a lay scholar;
at these times, the śramaṇas Sengrong, Riyen, Fakuan, and others all sought instruction from him. At that time, the nun Zhifu was also highly esteemed by Huikai;
thus, when Huikai passed away, Sengdi beat her breast in mournful lamentation and led Zhifu and the other nuns—numbering ten—in [the funeral rites].
The two men took up residence at Quānfáng (Quasi-Hall) on Mount Fǎ. There they maintained the incense and lamps and vowed to propagate the teachings of the Mahāyāna.

Later, although they encountered the Tripiṭaka Master Varmali’s disciple Huìgě and studied the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra* under him, they managed to complete only the section on the "Exposition" (*nirdeśa-parivarta*) before Huìgě passed away due to illness.
He then specialized in the study of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*.

Narendrayaśas (whose name means "Noble Renown" in the language of China) was a native of Wu-shang in Northern India. Having left the household life at the age of twenty, he heard the complete teachings of the True Dharma.

Once he had received full ordination, he traveled extensively to visit the sacred sites of the sages, witnessing the wonders of the Celestial Ladder and the Stone Terrace, as well as the Dragon... [text fragment].
He personally paid homage at all the sacred sites of temples and stupas, leaving none unvisited.

Once, a certain extraordinary venerable one saw him and said to him, "If you can cultivate in stillness, you shall realize the fruits of the Way; wandering about in vain labor will ultimately achieve nothing.
Śīha did not follow this advice and traveled through various difficult lands until he reached the borders of Qi. This was in the seventh year of the Tiānbǎo era of Emperor Wénxuān.

At that time, Xuanzang was in the prime of his career; his bearing was majestic and elegant, and public opinion held him in awe. By imperial decree, he was stationed at Tiantong Temple and titled "Tripitaka Master of Translated Scriptures.

The honors accorded to him were most profound: more than a thousand bundles of Sanskrit manuscripts were brought from the inner palace, and a ritual hall was constructed for him to demonstrate the Emperor's supreme veneration.
The Emperor personally prostrated himself before him and addressed the assembled officials, saying: "This is the great foundation of the Triple Gem."

Therefore, he was particularly worthy of veneration. Initially, he translated over fifty fascicles of various scriptures under the supervision of more than twenty individuals, including the Śramaṇa Fashang, the Great Overseer (Dàtǒng) of the Office for the Propagation of Mystery (Zháoxuán), who was appointed by imperial decree; the Śramaṇa Fazhi; and the layman Wàn Tiānyì, who served as the interpreter.

Not long thereafter, he was summoned by imperial decree to succeed [Fashang] as the Overseer of the Office for the Propagation of Mystery. Shortly after, he became the Director (Dū). When the Qi dynasty’s calendar came to an end, his teachings also declined accordingly. He [then] sought refuge...
To the southeast of the land [of India], he found no rest for four consecutive years. When the Sui dynasty took control of the realm, the Great Dharma was restored.
In the seventh month of the second year of the Kaihuang era, he received an imperial edict and entered the capital together with his disciple Daomi and others. He resided at Daxingshan Temple;

in the twelfth month of winter, he began the work of translation. Subsequently, he produced the *Bodhisattvadarśanaratnacandragarbhasūryagarbha* (The Bodhisattva Sees the Jewel-Moon-Treasury and Sun-Treasury).

The *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Xingtou Jingśe*, the *Mahāyāna-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, and other treatises, totaling seventeen works, were transcribed by the śramaṇas Fǎzuǎn, Sēngchén, and Míngfēn, along with the palace attendant Lì Dàobǎo and others.

They were supervised by more than twenty individuals, including the Śramaṇa Tányán, Director of the Office of Buddhist Affairs (Zhāoxuán), and the Śramaṇa Língzàng, Director of the Office of Buddhist Affairs. [The patron] Shè was advanced in years.

He practiced with rigorous diligence, constantly training himself through the practice of the Śāriputra-dhāraṇī. He dreamed that his own body became a Buddha, and the visions therein were exceptionally sublime.
Later, he resided at Guangji Temple as the chief prelate for foreign monks; he cared for and sustained those who were sojourning there, winning their hearts.
After a long time, he passed away without illness at exactly one hundred years of age, on the twenty-ninth day of the eighth month in the ninth year of the Kaihuang era.
Jñānagupta of the Sui dynasty—whose name in the language of China means "Virtuous Will"—was a native of Gandhāra in Northern India.

He entered the monastic order at the Great Forest Monastery (Mahāvana-vihāra) in his own country while still a child. Having received full ordination three summers prior, he was then twenty-seven years of age.
He immediately set out with his tonsure-master, Śrīnāman, and his preceptor for ordination, Candra, to travel abroad and propagate the Dharma. On their journey, they passed through...

Having crossed the Great Snow Mountains from the kingdom of Kāpiśī and endured every kind of perilous hardship, he arrived at Shanzhou during the first year after the founding of the Later Wei dynasty.
At the beginning of the Wucheng era of Emperor Ming of the Northern Zhou, he took up residence at Cudong Temple in Chang’an.

Before long, his reputation reached the imperial ear, and an edict was issued for him to debate the Dharma with the two renowned masters, Zhisheng and Miaoxian, in the Rear Garden; furthermore, the Emperor had four celestial palaces constructed for him.
He transmitted the Sanskrit texts at Wangsi Temple; these included the *Ekādaśamukha Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttamarāja-paripṛcchā Sūtra*.

When Prince Xiao of Qiao, Yuwen Jian, was stationed in Shu, he invited him to go there, where he stayed at Longyuan Temple. During the suppression of the Buddhist teachings under the Jiande era, he was coerced into taking up an official post, but he declined on the grounds of death.
By imperial decree, he was released to return home, but he fell into the hands of the Turks in the north and subsequently suffered the loss of both his parents. Initially, he had been a śramaṇa...
Baosheng, Daosui, Sengtan, and others traveled west during the Wuping era of the Qi dynasty to seek out Buddhist scriptures and teachings, obtaining two hundred and sixty volumes of Sanskrit texts.

Upon returning to the east, they also stayed for a time among the Turks to avoid the calamities of the Northern Zhou. They were overjoyed to meet one another. Soon after, the Sui dynasty received the mandate of heaven;
Baosheng and the others first brought the scriptures they had acquired to the capital, where the Emperor issued an edict to seek out and honor those of long-standing virtue and learning.

Translation: In the fifth year of the Kaihuang era, Ratnagupta accompanied by envoys visited Emperor Wen at Luoyang. An imperial decree was immediately issued for him to take up his post at Daxingshan Temple.
At that time, Yaśas had already passed away, and the office of the chief master had remained vacant for a long duration.

Consequently, another decree was issued for the Brahmin monk Dharmagupta, along with the laymen Gao Tiannu and the brothers Gao Heren, to jointly transmit the Sanskrit language; ten [monks] were appointed for this purpose.
The Venerable Śramaṇas Sengxiu, Facan, Fajing, Huizang, Hongzun, Huiyuan, Fazuan, Senghui, Mingmu, and Tanqian supervised the translation work and determined its fundamental tenets.
Mingmu and Yancong re-examined the Sanskrit manuscripts and scrutinized the phrasing and meaning.
In the twentieth year of the Kaihuang era, Kumārajīva [Kujūta] announced his passing at the age of seventy-eight.
From beginning to end, thirty-seven scriptures totaling one hundred and seventy-six fascicles were produced;
these include the *Buddhacarita-saṃgraha*, the *Dharmolkā*, the *Tejas*, the *Paritrāṇa*, the *Bhadrapāla*, and others.
Dharmagupta of the Sui dynasty—whose name translates into Chinese as Fami—was a native of Lāḷa in South India. His secular surname was Bhārgava, which translates into Chinese as Hushi;
he belonged to the Kṣatriya caste. At the age of twenty-three, he left the household life in Central India, where he served the śramaṇa Jñānagupta and underwent tonsure.
Twenty-five years later, he studied under the śramaṇas Guṇavardhana and Samantaprabha.

He received full ordination and became proficient in the sūtras and śāstras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Furthermore, he followed Master Zhao to practice alms-gathering and the methods of dhyāna-contemplation for three years, gaining a preliminary insight into their essential principles.
Soon thereafter, Master Zhao departed at the invitation of the King of the kingdom of Ṭhaka, remaining there for one year.
When the Master announced his return, [Daoshi] stayed behind alone for another four years, residing at Tianyou Monastery—a monastery built by that king.

From that time on, during my travels and service, my observations and experiences have been manifold. Merchants and travelers spoke extensively of how the Three Jewels had flourished in the great kingdom of China;
yet, I still did not believe it until I crossed the Snowy Mountains, where the accounts became increasingly authentic. Thereupon, I first set my heart upon this goal.

Wandering through difficult terrain and traversing vast distances, many years passed. In the winter of the tenth year of the Kaihuang era, I arrived at the capital and soon settled in the Great [Monastery].

At Xingshan Monastery, Dharmagupta [Jiduo] mastered the source of the scriptural characters and exhausted the nuances of sound and meaning; he was appointed as the chief among the translators, which truly satisfied public sentiment.
When Emperor Yang established his capital at Luoyang, he further increased his veneration and issued an edict to open a Translation Hall within the Shanglin Park.
He summoned men of eminent talent, and until the end of the Daye era—a total of twenty-eight years—altogether seventy-two fascicles comprising seven works of sutra and śāstra were produced:
namely, the *Lokaprajñapti*, the *Pratītyasamutpāda*, the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-praṇidhāna*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*.
...and so forth. He passed away in the second year of the Wude era of the Tang dynasty.
The Tang master Prabhākaramitra—whose name means "One Who Acts as a Lamp-Knower" in Chinese;
also known as Prajñā, meaning "Light-Wisdom"—was a native of Central India. He was of royal lineage, belonging to the Kṣatriya caste. He entered the monastic order at the age of ten. Following...

The Master studied and practiced, reciting one hundred thousand verses (*lakṣa*) of Mahāyāna sūtras. After receiving full ordination, he studied the Vinaya-piṭaka and gained a general understanding of its disciplinary framework.
Taking pleasure in meditative contemplation, he further studied dhyāna under a master of eminent virtue for twelve years.

He then traveled south to the country of Gauḍa and the Nālandā Monastery. At that time, the Master Śīlabhadra was propagating the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Seventeen Stages Treatise), and he was able to receive instruction from him. However—
Using this treatise, he also elucidated the Hinayana teachings, while reciting one hundred thousand verses (*lakṣa*) from a Hinayana śāstra.

His disciple Prajñendrabhadra transmitted the lamp to his native land, entrusting him with its succession; he then traveled northward in stages until he reached the headquarters of the Western Khan, Yehe.

There he instructed them in the Dharma, and before even ten days had passed, the Khan became a believer. *Note: The term "可汙" (kě wū) appears to be a transcription error for "可汗" (Khan), which is consistent with the context.*

In the ninth year of the Dede era, the Prince of Gaoping sent an envoy to meet him and intended to transport him away with him; however, the Yehe ruler and his ministers did not immediately grant permission.

The Gaoping post station reported this to the throne, and an imperial edict was issued for the Yehe to provide passage and not detain him. In the twelfth month, he accompanied the Prince of Gaoping to the capital to have an audience with the Emperor.
By imperial decree, he was lodged at Xingshan Monastery and granted silk brocade and a monastic robe; his stipend as a monk was increased from the standard amount.
Provisions were supplied, and he was visited with inquiries regarding his health with the utmost diligence.

In the third year, the third month, an imperial edict was issued to the relevant authorities to seek out nineteen men of eminent virtue to engage in translation at the monastery where Śīlabhadra resided. The śramaṇas Huìchéng and others served as proofreaders of the meaning;

the śramaṇas Xuánmù and others served as translators of the terminology; and the śramaṇas Huìzé, Huìjìng, Huìmíng, Fǎchén, and others composed the literary drafts. [The title] Shangzhuguo... [follows].

Edict. Left Vice President of the Secretariat, Fang Xuanling; Attendant-in-Ordinary and Director of the Household of the Crown Prince, Du Zhenglun, shall participate in and assist with the evaluation and determination [of the candidates].
Palace Grandee and Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury, Xiao Jing, shall take overall charge of supervision. Extract the *Bǎoxīng* (Jewel Star) and *Shèngguāng* (Victorious Light).
The *Prajñāpradīpa* and the *Mahāvyūha-sūtra-śāstra*, comprising three sections in thirty-five fascicles, were completed by transcription over the course of six years and reported to the Emperor.
The Emperor bestowed upon Bo Po one hundred rolls of brocade; others were granted bundles of silk according to their respective ranks.

At that time, some slandered him, claiming that he had gathered famous scholars together merely to abandon formal lectures and exegesis, seeking renown through such expedients rather than with the sincere intent of propagating the Dharma.
The supervising official did not heed the eloquent pleas of the śramaṇa Lingjia. It happened that the Crown Prince fell ill;

[Lingjia] was invited into the inner palace and attended to him during his consultations, and the favor he received became increasingly profound and generous. Nevertheless, his temperament was stern and his resolve firm; he could never reconcile with the former slander.
Consequently, he distributed his clothing and resources to cultivate various pure deeds. On the sixth day of the fourth month in the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, he beheld the Buddha.

He passed away while seated at Shenguang Temple. He left behind a memorial table requesting that his body be offered as alms. By imperial decree, he was cremated, his relics were collected, and a stupa was erected for them.
Huize of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Li and was a native of Jiangling in Jingzhou. At the age of nine, he entered the monastic order under Master Yin of his own locality.

As a śrāmaṇera, he held a volume and recited its text; the scrolls filled forty sheets. Initially, he studied the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and later he separately studied the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*).
During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, his hometown, recognizing that his capacity and character were precociously mature, requested him to serve as their Dharma master.

When he lectured on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, his eloquent responses invariably humbled even the most venerable elders. At that time, he was only twelve years old. The Regional Inspector, Kong Longgong Yuan Shou, heard of this...
He went to have an audience with him and was highly praised and rewarded. His name being made known, an imperial edict summoned him to the capital.

Once he had been granted an audience, the Emperor bestowed upon him a *saṃghāṭī* robe along with a full set of additional garments. He continued to reside at Qingchan Temple, where the arrival of officials and carriages daily crowded his gate; finding this troublesome, he grew weary of it.
He received the transmission of the study of the mind from Master Yingchan. At the end of the Daye era, he sought refuge on Gaoguan Ridge in Zhongnan Mountains.

When the Tang dynasty flourished, he traveled to the capital, where he frequently established dharma assemblies. At the beginning of the Wude era, by imperial decree, he presided over a hundred-seated recitation of the *Benevolent King Sūtra* at Yanxing Temple.
High officials gathered in great numbers; Jizang presented his formal discourse, and [Dao]ze’s words were clear and profound, pressing him with sharp inquiries.
When the brush-tip rose, the fourfold assembly was struck with awe, and Huizang sighed in admiration and submission. He was especially skilled in clerical calligraphy.
When Emperor Taizong Wen was still in the Qin Prince’s residence, he wished to invite him to his private quarters to honor him with offerings; messengers went six times, yet he firmly declined.

During the Zhenguan era, an imperial decree selected monks for the translation bureau; everyone recommended and yielded to him. When the task was completed and reported to the throne, the Emperor issued a decree bestowing upon him one hundred rolls of silk and a full set of robes.
Jia Ze also authored a preface to the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra*, most of which is not recorded here. On the sixth day of the fourth month in the tenth year, he passed away at his residence;
he was fifty-seven years of age. He was buried in the eastern suburbs of the capital. Chu Liang, the Court Musician and Doctor of Literature, composed the inscription for his stele.
His collected works in eight volumes were circulated in the world.
Tangga Fandamo (唐伽梵達磨), whose name in the language of China means "Venerable Dharma," was a native of Western India. Historical records lack detailed accounts of his origins.

During the Yonghui era, he translated the *Qianshou Qianyan Guanshiyin Pusa Guangda Yuanman Wuai Dabeixin Duanluo Ni Jing* (The Sutra of the Greatly Vast, Perfect, and Unobstructed Great Compassionate Heart Dhāraṇī of the Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva) in one fascicle.
Furthermore, according to the preface to the *Qianbi Jing* (Thousand-Armed Sutra), it states that he [collaborated] with śramaṇas...
Translated by Zhìtōng.
Āditya (whose name in the language of Huá means "Limitless Height") was a member of a noble clan who left the household life; his history is not recorded.

In the third year of the Yǒnghuī era, on the first month of the *rénzǐ* year, he arrived in Cháng'ān. He brought with him Sanskrit manuscripts from Western India, and by imperial decree, they were deposited at Címén Sī.

He was installed together with sixteen others, including the śramaṇas Dasheng Cong and others, as well as the Duke of Ying Li Shiji and the Duke of E Wei Zhidu and others, totaling twelve individuals.
At Huiri Monastery, within the Pagoda Courtyard, they established a *dhāraṇī* Universal Assembly Altar. All necessary provisions were prepared by the relevant authorities.
Miraculous omens appeared repeatedly, causing both monastics and laypeople to rejoice and marvel. In the fourth year, the translations were completed.
The *Jingang Dadaochang Jing Zhong Cuoyao Tuoaluni Ji Jing* (The Compendium of Essential Dhāraṇīs from the Vajramahāmaṇḍala Sūtra), twelve fascicles.
Transcribed by the śramaṇa Xuankai.
Zhitong was born in the Zhao clan of Anyi, Jiazhou during the Tang dynasty. During the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he entered the monastic order at Zongchi Temple. He received the precepts...

He was fully equipped [with these skills]. Later, while traveling to the capital of Luojing, he studied the Sanskrit script and language at the Translation Institute and became quite proficient in them.
During the Zhenguan era, a śramaṇa from North India arrived, bringing the Sanskrit original of the *Qianbi Qianyan Jing* (The Sutra of the Thousand Arms and Thousand Eyes).

Emperor Taizong issued an edict seeking individuals of talent and learning who were capable of composing the literary text and receiving the oral dictation to serve as officials of the Translation Institute. Xuanzang responded to this call and joined the Indian monks.
These were translated in two fascicles. In the fourth year of the Yonghui era of Emperor Gaozong, he further produced four works totaling five fascicles:

the *Sahasravartanī Dhāraṇī* (one fascicle), the *Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mantra* (one fascicle), the *Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva随心咒* [Mantra According to One’s Heart] (one fascicle), and the *Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Pure Dhāraṇī* (one fascicle).
Some have remarked that these are excellent examples of Yoga and Secret [Mantra] teachings.
Regarding his teachings, he frequently achieved spiritual resonance and communication.
Yanajia Boduo (Yanajia Boduo; Chinese: Zhixian) was a native of Puling in Nanhai. He was well-versed in the study of the Tripiṭaka.
During the Linqi era, the śramaṇa Huìníng of Chengdu traveled to the Western Regions.

On his way through Boliṅ, he obtained from Xuán the *Āgama Sūtra* and translated within it the events concerning the World-Honored One’s cremation and the collection of the *śarīra*, titled the *Nirvāṇa-hinduparivarta* in two fascicles.
He boarded a ship and reached Jiāozhōu; Níng then continued westward. At the beginning of the Yífēng era, the Regional Commander Liáng Nándí...
An envoy was dispatched along with Xuanzang’s disciple Yungi to present [the texts] to the Emperor.
In the third year, the śramaṇa Linghui of the Great Ci’en Monastery petitioned the Eastern Palace for their implementation. It is said that Xuanzang finally passed away in that country.
Buddhatāra of the Tang dynasty—whose name translates as "Awakened Savior"—was a native of Jibin in Northern India.

He brought forth the *Mahāvaipulya-tathāgatagarbha-bodhimaṇḍa-nirdeśa-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Perfect Enlightenment of the Great Vaipulya) at the Baima Monastery in Luoyang. Its literary style is harmonious and fluent, while its principles are subtle and profound;
it is truly the life-force of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and the ground of the minds of all sentient beings. Nevertheless, regarding the years he spent traveling and his past conduct...
Neither the Tibetan nor the Chinese histories record this; what a pity!

During the Tang dynasty, there was the monk Divākara (translated into Chinese as Rìzhào), a native of Central India. He was diligent in upholding the Vinaya and was particularly skilled in incantations and esoteric arts.

During the reign of Emperor Gāozōng, he traveled to China. In the fifth month of the fourth year of the Yífēng era, he submitted a memorial requesting permission to translate and transmit [the scriptures] he possessed.

Carrying the sūtra-fascicles, at the end of Empress Wu’s reign, he produced eighteen works in total—including the *Mahāyāna-vijñapti-mātrata-siddhi-śāstra* (The Scripture on the Manifestation of Consciousness in Mahāyāna) and the *Mahāyāna-pañcaskandhaka-śāstra* (The Treatise on the Five Aggregates in Mahāyāna)—at the East and West Taiyuan Temples in the two capitals, as well as at the Guangfu Temple in the Western Capital.
The śramaṇa Candraprabha-deva acted as the oral translator; Hui-zhi verified the Sanskrit; and Dao-cheng, Bo-chen, Jia-shang, and Yuan-ce served as assistants.
Lingbian, Mingxun, Huaidu, Zhengyi, Sixuan, and Fuli compiled the text, recorded the dictation, and composed the writings. Empress Wu personally wrote the preface for it.
He later passed away in his translation chamber at the age of seventy-five. His stupa was erected on Mount Xiangshan in Longmen, Luoyang.
Tang Tiyun Bore (also known as Tiyuntuo Ruona; in Chinese, Tianzhi) was born in the kingdom of Khotan.
In the first year of Yongchang, he first traveled eastward and had an audience with Empress Wu in Luoyang. By imperial decree, he translated at Weiguo Dongsì.
In the second year of Tianshou, he produced six works in seven fascicles, including the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Dharmadhātuviniścaya-śāstra*.
The śramaṇa Chuchu received the oral dictation in a single draft. Fuli then compiled the text. Dedan, Huiyan, Faming, Hengjing, and others served as proofreaders of the meaning.
Huizhi of the Tang dynasty was the son of an Indian Brahmin; having traveled east, he attained wisdom. From his youth, he aspired to leave secular life and followed [his teacher] for a long time.
The Brahmin monk Nāgabodhi was his disciple; he was well-versed in the scripts and languages of India.
Whenever the Tripiṭaka masters Śīladhara, Jñānagupta, Ratnacinta, and others produced translations, they would all summon him to certify the texts and assist with the linguistic nuances.
In the second year of the Changshou era, at Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital, Fazhi produced one fascicle of the *Guanshiyin Song*.
Mito of Tang (whose name in the language of Han is Jiyou) was a native of Duhuluo. During the reign of Empress Wu, he collaborated with Śikṣānanda to produce the *Mahāyāna-laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
During the Tian-shou era, he collaborated with the śramaṇa Fazang and others to produce one fascicle of the *Vimalaprabhā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.
Regarding the origins of this scripture, it concerns the Kapphiṇa-caṇḍa-brāhmaṇa...

The Master was on the verge of death due to illness. The Buddha, wishing to extend his life span, spoke [this teaching] for him. After he had presented his offerings, the Emperor provided a generous farewell banquet as he returned westward.
Tang Paramārtha—whose name means "Ultimate Measure" in the language of China—was a native of Central India. This occurred in the first year of the Shenlong era, the year of Yisi (705 CE).
On the twenty-third day of the fifth month, at the Zhiji Monastery in Guangzhou, with the śramaṇa Meghaśikṣa from the kingdom of Ujjayinī serving as the oral translator,
and the Bodhisattva-Precept disciple, former Minister of Justice, concurrently Chief Secretary and Vice President of the Secretariat,
Fang Rong of Qinghe, acting as the scribe, [the text was received by] the śramaṇa Huai... of Nanlou Temple on Mount Luofu in Xunzhou.
Di verified the meaning of the text, which is the *Mahābuddhoṣṇīṣa-tathāgataguhyakāraṇabhāvanā-siddhārtha-sarvabodhisattva-daśasāhasrika-śūraṅgama-sūtra* in ten fascicles.
This is indeed one chapter from within the *Abhiṣeka* section. Once it had been translated, it was transmitted.

Before he had yet presented [the texts] to the Emperor, it happened that his own country dispatched an envoy with royal orders to arrest him, on the grounds that he had illicitly taken out copies of secret scriptures.
Consequently, he took the Sanskrit manuscripts and returned westward by sea; what remained in this land was only the translated version.
Tang Zhiyan was a hostage from the Kingdom of Khotan. He had adopted the surname Wei-chi and was named Yue-shou.

He was registered under the Ministry of Rites (Honglu Si) and granted the rank of General of the Left Guard (Zuo Lingjun Wei Da Jiangjun), the title of Shangzhuguo, and the fief of Duke of Jinman Commandery. By nature he was sharp and intelligent;

he constantly contemplated casting off his worldly burdens like discarding shoes. In the fifth month of the second year of the Shenglong era, he submitted a memorial requesting that his residence be converted into a monastery. An imperial edict was issued.
