He was granted permission. The temple was bestowed the name Feng’en. On the fifth day of the eleventh month of the first year of the Jinglong era—the birthday of Emperor Zhongzong—he underwent tonsure and ordination to offer prayers for the Emperor’s longevity.
By imperial decree, he was to translate various scriptures at the monastery until they were completed in their respective sections; Yan played a significant role in this endeavor.
Furthermore, he re-translated the *Anantamukha-parivarta-dhāraṇī-sūtra*. Later, he practiced the dhūta austerities at Shíbi Gorge. He died there.
The Elder [Śikṣānanda] was at Zhìxiàng Monastery on Mount Zhōngnán.
Śikṣānanda—also known as Śikṣānanda; in the language of China, "Learner’s Joy" (Xuexi)—was a native of Yú Dùn in the region north of the Pamir Mountains during the Tang dynasty.

He was proficient in both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings and had a broad mastery of heterodox studies. Empress Wu [Zetian] took the existing version of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as the basis for her assembly.
It was not yet complete. An envoy was dispatched to Khotan to seek out Sanskrit manuscripts and to invite translators; these, along with the Sanskrit volumes, arrived together.

In the first year of the Zhengsheng era (the year of Yiwu), an imperial edict was issued for the śramaṇa Bodhiruci from South India and the śramaṇa Yijing to translate [the text] together at Dàbiànkōng Monastery in the Eastern Capital. Subsequently, the śramaṇas Fuli, Fazang, and others followed the Buddha...
At Foshouji Monastery, in the second year of the Shengli era, he completed eighty fascicles [of the *Lengqie jing*]. Later, the Empress personally composed a preface to serve as its introduction.

During the Jiusi era, he produced the *Mahāyāna-laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and also produced the *Mañjuśrī-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* at Qingchan Monastery in the capital and at Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang). In total, he produced nineteen sūtras over these periods. [In] Chang’an, four...
In the second year of the Jinglong era, he submitted a memorial requesting leave to return home and visit his mother. By imperial decree, the Censor Huo Siguang escorted him to the capital.
The Emperor personally went out to meet him outside the Kaiyuan Gate, where he resided at Dajianfu Monastery.

He passed away due to illness on the twelfth day of the tenth month in the first year of the Jingyun era. He was fifty-nine years of age. An imperial edict was issued for his burial according to foreign rites.
He was cremated outside the Kaiyuan Gate at the ancient site of the Lamp-Pillar Terrace. His tongue did not burn with the rest of his remains.
By imperial decree, Gośu Daoyuan escorted it back to his native country. Furthermore, a stupa was erected at the site where he was cremated, known as the Huayan Tripiṭaka Stupa.

Yijing of the Tang dynasty, courtesy name Wencming, was the son of the Zhang family of Fanyang. Having renounced secular life at the age of seven, he possessed a resolute intent to travel to the West.

Upon reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination and redoubled his former efforts. In the second year of the Xianheng era, at the age of thirty-seven, he gathered several dozen companions with the intention of boarding a ship;
however, they all withdrew and dispersed, leaving none to accompany him. Consequently, Yijing traveled alone for two...

Fifteen years had passed, during which he traveled through more than thirty countries. In the second month of summer in the year of Yiwu (685), the first year of the Zhengsheng era of Empress Wu, he returned to the region of the Yellow and Luo Rivers.
He obtained approximately four hundred volumes of Sanskrit manuscripts containing sutras, vinaya, and śāstras, totaling five million verses;
one set of images from the Vajrāsana; and three hundred grains of śarīra relics. Empress Wu personally went outside the Upper East Gate to welcome him with the utmost hospitality. All...

The monastery was adorned with banners, canopies, flowers, and incense as they escorted him. By imperial decree, all that he had brought was deposited at Foshouji Monastery, where he subsequently began his translations.

Initially, he worked alongside Śikṣānanda to produce the Avataṃsaka-sūtra. After the gengzi year of the Jiushi era, he resided at Fuxian Monastery and later at Ximing Monastery in Chang’an, where he devoted himself exclusively to translating the Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra and the Prajñāpāramitā-naya-sūtra.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Maitreya-buddhābhisaṃbodhi*, the *Ekākṣara-uṣṇīṣa-rāja*, the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī*, the *Dīrghanakha-parivrājaka-sūtra*, and others;
the *Vinaya* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda, including the *Nidāna*, the *Mātṛkā*, and the *Ekottarakarma-saṃgraha*;

the *Upāyikā-śāstra*, the *Pratītyasamutpādahṛdaya-vyākhyā*, the *Ṣaṭtrimśat-pada-śāstra*, and other treatises; and the works of Nāgārjuna—these he held within the palm of his hand. He was exhorted by... [text ends]
The *Caityastotra* (Verses of Admonition) comprises twenty sections in total. Later, [the Emperor] personally composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings" (*Śāsanaprastāvanā*).

In the first year of the Shénlóng era of Zhōngzōng, while encamped at Luóyáng, he issued an edict for [the Master] to reside at the Inner Chapel and Dàfúxiān Monastery. Furthermore, he produced scriptures to offer prayers for the four classes of the imperial family.

The Emperor composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripiṭaka of the Great Tang’s Dragon-Rising Era" (*Dàtáng Lóngxīng Sānzàng Shèngjiào Xù*) and personally presided over the western gate to proclaim the newly translated texts to all.

In the second year [of the reign], an imperial edict established the Institute for Translating Scriptures (*fanjing guan*) at the Great Jianfu Monastery in the capital. Jing followed the Emperor’s carriage back and took up residence there.

In the third year, he was summoned by imperial decree to enter the palace for the summer retreat (*zha-xia*). When the Emperor was at Fangling, he had once prayed to the Medicine Master Buddha (*Bhaiṣajyaguru*).

Consequently, an edict was issued to translate the *Benyuan jing* (Sutra of the Original Vows) in two fascicles at the Dafoguang Hall; the Emperor personally acted as the scribe for the oral transmission. This occurred in the first year of the Tanglong era of Emperor Ruizong.

In the year [blank], he produced twenty works, including the *Bath Image Merit Sūtra*, the *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, the *Two-Assembly Precept Sūtra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Ratnasaṃbhava*, and the *Ālambana-parīkṣā-vyākhyā*.
The Tokharian śramaṇa Dharmamitra verified the Sanskrit meanings; the śramaṇa Balanujña from Central India verified the Sanskrit terminology;
and the śramaṇa Dharmānanda from Kaśmīra verified the Sanskrit text. The layman Dong... [continued].
The Indian leader Īśvara verified the Sanskrit original. The śramaṇa Huìjī and the layman Zhōng Yìnzhù Lǐ Shèjiā translated the Sanskrit language.
The śramaṇas Wénɡāng, Huìzhǎo, Lìzhēn, Shèngzhuāng, Àitóng, Sīhéng, Zhèngyì, Xuánsǎn, and Zhìjī acted as scribes.
The layman Gōután Jīnɡāng from Eastern India and [the master] from Kaśmīra [assisted].

Translated by the Prince of Guo, A-shun (Āśuna). Polished by more than twenty persons, including the Grand Master for Literary Studies of the Xiuwen Pavilion Li Qiao, the Minister of War Wei Sili, the Vice Director of the Secretariat Zhao Yanzhao, the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel Lu Zangyong, the Vice Minister of the Ministry of War Zhang Yue, and the Palace Secretary Li Yi.
Supervised by the Left Vice President of the Department of State Affairs Wei Juyuan.
Su Gui, Right Vice President of the Secretariat, served as the supervising official. Prince Yong, the heir to the King of Guo, served as the co-supervising official.

In the second year of the Jingyun era, the *Ji zan rulai gongde shenzhu deng jing* (Scriptures on the Accumulated Praises of the Tathāgata’s Merits and Divine Incantations) and others were again brought forth at Dajianfu Monastery.

Xue Chongsu, Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, served as the supervising official. From the Jiushi era of Empress Wu until the Jingyun era of Emperor Ruizong, these scriptures were compiled and issued in their entirety.
There are sixteen sections totaling two hundred and thirty fascicles. Furthermore, he compiled five works totaling nine fascicles:

the *Biographies of Eminent Monks Who Sought the Dharma in the Western Regions*, the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* (Record of Buddhist Practices Sent Home from the Southern Seas), the *Separate Exposition on the Essential Methods for Confession of Offenses*, the *Essential Methods for the Use of the Three Waters*, and the *Ritual Procedures for Protecting Life through Releasing Animals*.
He also produced the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-bhikṣuṇī-karmavācanā*, which belongs to one of the various Vinaya schools.
His works included the *Khandhaka-varga* and other such texts, totaling seventy-eight fascicles. He was particularly skilled in the Vinaya section and never grew weary in instructing his disciples.

His practice of using a water-strainer to remove impurities was extraordinary. His students were widespread throughout the capital and Luoyang. In the second year of the Xiāntián era, he passed away at the age of seventy-nine, with fifty-nine years of *dharma-lakṣa*.
His stupa was erected on a high ridge north of Longmén in the capital and Luoyang.
Amoghavajra (translated into Chinese as Bǎosīwéi) was a native of Kaśmīra in Northern India and belonged to the Kṣatriya caste.
He arrived at the capital of Luò in the second year of the Chángshòu era of Empress Wu. By imperial decree, he transmitted [the teachings] at Tiāngōng Monastery.
During the Bingwǔ year of the Shénlóng era under Emperor Zhōngzōng, he moved to Fóshòujì, Tiāngōng, and Fúxiān Monasteries, where he produced the *Amoghapāśa* [sūtra].

The *Dhāraṇī Sūtra* and six other works, totaling seven texts, were decreed by imperial edict in the sixth month of the first year of the Taixi era of Emperor Ruizong to be formally determined for inclusion in the canon and put into practice.
From that time on, he increasingly devoted himself to ritual recitation; every morning, he would grind fragrant water and bathe the Buddha images before eating, never tiring of this until his death.
Aside from his robes and alms bowl, he gave away whatever he obtained as soon as he acquired it. Once, at Longmen Mountain...

He constructed a monastery according to the architectural systems of the Western Regions and resided there with his disciples, naming it after that region. He passed away in the ninth year of the Kaiyuan era at over one hundred years of age.
The Tang dynasty’s Bodhiruci was of the pure-practitioner Brahmin caste from the Southern Indian kingdom; his clan name was Kāśyapa. At the age of ten...
2. Shi (事) was a renunciant of the Pāśupata heretics who studied the grammatical treatises of the Sāṃkhya and other schools.

When he was over sixty years old, he first relied upon the Tripiṭaka Master Yaśogupta to study the True Dharma. In the second year of the Yongchun era, Emperor Gaozong dispatched an envoy to welcome him.
Empress Wu paid him exceptional honor and respect, issuing an edict for him to reside at Fuxian Monastery in East Luoyang. He translated the *Buddhagocarapariśuddhi-sūtra*.
He translated the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and other sūtras, totaling eleven works.

In the second year of the Shenlong era of the Zhongzong reign, he translated the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra* at Chongfu Temple in Jingzhao. The śramaṇa Sifeng, the Indian chief official Īśvara, and others translated the Sanskrit text.
The Indian śramaṇa Prajñākūṭa and the śramaṇa Dharma verified the Sanskrit meaning, while the śramaṇa Li... [verified the Chinese].
The principal editor was Fang Zongyi; Huìjué served as the scribe. The śramaṇas Shèngzhuāng, Chénwài, Wúzháo, and Huáidi verified the meaning.

The śramaṇas Chénglǐ, Yúnguàn, Shényǎn, and Dàoběn transcribed the text. The scholar Lú Càn and Xú Jiān, along with the Palace Secretary Sū Jìn and the Attendant-in-Ordinary Cú Qú, polished the language.
The Minister of the Department of State Affairs and the Vice-Chancellor of the Secretariat, both of the Third Rank, Lù Xiàngxiān, supervised the project.
Written by Guo Yuanzhen. Supervised by Zhang Yue, Grand Secretary of the Chancellery, and Wei Zhigu, Chief Minister.

Compiled during the Jingyun era of Emperor Ruizong, it was moved to the Gānlù Pavilion at the White Lotus Pond in Beiyuan, totaling one hundred and twenty fascicles. These contain the teachings spoken by the Buddha across forty-nine assemblies.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, it was presented to the throne, with an Imperial Preface placed at its head. The tenth year of the Kaiyuan era.

In the second year [of his reign], he accompanied the imperial entourage to reside at Changshou Monastery in Luojing. On the fourth day of the eleventh month of the fifteenth year, he passed away at the age of one hundred and fifty-six.
Upon hearing of this, the Emperor was moved with grief and bestowed upon him the posthumous title of Tripitaka Master Kaiyuan Yiqie Bianzhi.

The funeral expenses were provided from the Inner Treasury, and the procession was adorned with ceremonial insignia, feathered banners, streamers, and canopies; the eunuch Du Huaixin was dispatched to supervise the rites.
On the first day of the twelfth month, [the remains] were interred at the northwest plain of Longmen in Luonan; a stupa was erected and a stele was inscribed, in accordance with ritual propriety.
Tang Huaidi was a native of Xunzhou; he entered the monastic order and was registered at Nanlou Monastery. This monastery was situated on a site where land and sea met halfway.
It is truly a residence where sages and immortals dwell. Several Indian monks have stayed there;
Di You was proficient in their script and language, serving as the verifier of the meaning when Bodhiruci translated the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*.

Later, at the Zhizhi Monastery in Guangzhou, he also assisted in translating the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*—the "Ten Thousand Practices of the Buddha-Topknot"—which had been brought by an Indian monk from a palm-leaf manuscript.
Tang Feixi was a man of unknown origins. Initially, he investigated the *Vinaya*, and later he studied the principles of the three contemplations and the single mind according to the Tiantai school.
When he traveled to the capital, he resided frequently at Caotang Temple on Mount Zigé in Zhongnan.

He served alongside Amoghavajra as a translator, repeatedly holding the positions of scribe and editor for the texts. On the fifteenth day of the fourth month in the first year of the Yongtai era of Emperor Daizong.
An imperial decree was issued for sixteen śramaṇas of the same rank as the scholar-monk Liangbei, including himself,

to participate in the translation of the *Benevolent Kings’ Sūtra on the Prajñāpāramitā for Protecting the State* and the *Ghanavyūha Sūtra* within the Inner Court Dharma Hall of Daming Palace. As these sūtras were previously composed in verse,
whereas the current versions are in prose, it was appropriate that Amoghavajra and Xī, along with the Hanlin Academician Liu Kangzhi, should further refine and finalize them.
Furthermore, Xi Chong verified the meaning; his literary skill did not fail this task.
Tang Wuti was a person from Chanju (in the language of the Hu, this means "Lotus-Vigor"). He was a native of Guiji and had long resided at the Lotus Temple in that country.
The temple was located outside the western gate of the capital, near Mount Qianjian. On the mountain there was a flowing stream. From—
It produced a musical sound that was lovely. During the Kaiyuan era, an envoy from Anxi had a craftsman transcribe its melody and presented it as a musical piece titled "Yeboseshi.
It was exceptionally marvelous when incorporated into the *gegu* drum performance. Chang Chongfu once served as an envoy and happened to meet the Bhikṣu Tripiṭaka Master named Jingjin.
Chongfu then made a request, and the master produced one fascicle of the *Daśabala-sūtra*. This was [a teaching] given by the Buddha while he was in Śrāvastī.
That which was spoken by the Kingdom of Wei was presented to the Emperor by a returning court envoy. It was included in the Imperial Canon during the Zhenyuan era.
The Tang monk Prajña—whose name means "Wisdom" in the vernacular language—was of the Gautama clan and a native of Kāpiśī in North India.
By nature he was exceptionally intelligent. At the age of seven, he followed the Venerable Vinayavarma and entered the monastic order.
He recited the four Āgamas, totaling one hundred thousand stanzas, and the Abhidharma, totaling forty thousand stanzas.

Once he had received full ordination, he recited the Sarvāstivāda-vinaya for nearly forty thousand stanzas, the Abhidharmakośa in twenty-eight thousand stanzas, as well as the Mahāvibhāṣā and other texts; he mastered both their words and their meanings over a further period of seven years.
Regarding the Hīnayāna teachings: later, at Nālandā Monastery in Central India, he served the great virtuous masters Śīlabhadra, Jinamitra, and Jñānamitra.

For eighteen years, he studied Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*, as well as treatises on Vijñaptimātra, Yogācāra, Madhyāntavibhāga, Hetuvidyā (Logic), Śabdavidyā (Grammar), Cikitsāvidyā (Medicine), and Arthaśāstra (Royal Law). He received the Yoga-tantra methods and entered the maṇḍala of the three secrets.
Having received the mudrās of the Five Families for protecting the person from Dharmayaśas in South India, he recited more than three thousand five hundred verses in total.
Having long heard that the Great Kingdom of China was protected by Mañjuśrī, he embarked on a ship and sailed eastward.

After twenty-two years, he arrived once again at Fanyu, barely managing to survive the journey. In the second year of the Zhenyuan era, he finally settled in the capital, [where he resided at] the Shenche...
Junzheng Jiang Lu Hao was the son of his maternal uncle. At that time, he had achieved military merit during the rebellion of Zhu Ci. When they met, they were filled with both grief and joy.

He invited [the Master] to his home, where he remained for eight years, providing him with offerings and support. In the sixth month on the eighth day, the Sanskrit manuscript was brought out from within the palace;
by imperial decree, the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kapiśa was commissioned to explain and interpret the Sanskrit text for the Hanlin Academy.
By imperial decree, Liyan of Guangze Temple provided the oral translation; Yuanzhao of Ximing Temple received it by pen;
and Daoyi of Zisheng Temple, Liangxiu of Ximing Temple, Yingzhen of Zhuangyan Temple, Chaowu of Liquan Temple, Dao’an, Biankong, and Chongzhengyi served as assistants.
A hall was established at Ximing Temple for this purpose. On this day, offerings were bestowed in abundance, and the *Mahāyāna-naya-sūtra* (Dacheng liqu) was brought forth.

The *Ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra* in ten fascicles, the *Avataṃsaka-śreṣṭhī-paripṛcchā-nārāyaṇabala-sūtra*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, one fascicle each—these were transcribed and presented in the tenth month.
An imperial decree was issued for the Shen-ce Army Guard to provide a vegetarian feast.

He was granted five hundred rolls of *qiñ* silk and one set of winter robes; the remaining gifts of silk were distributed according to their respective ranks. Huì’s letter of thanks exists, but it is not recorded here.

His cousin Luo Haoxin’s letter of thanks addressed him as "Meritorious Official for Stabilizing the State under the Heavens," "Grand Master with the Rank of State Councilor," and "Acting Director of the Imperial Secretariat";
much of his wording is not recorded. Huì passed away in Luoyang, and a stupa was erected for him.

To the west of the gate was the country of Tang Liangxiu, surnamed Guo, a native of Pujin. Having reached the age for wearing the jade hairpin, he received the tonsure at Baiti Monastery on Mount Zhongtiao.

He mastered the scriptures and received full ordination, thereafter exerting himself in the study and exposition of the Dharma. In the fourth year of the Zhenyuan era, he was summoned by imperial decree to visit Kaśmīra.

The Tripitaka Master Prajñā translated the *Mahāyāna-nyāya-ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra*. On the fourth day of the second month of the fifth year, he completed the transcription in ten fascicles and presented them to the Emperor.
Subsequently, an imperial decree was issued for him to compose a commentary (*śāstra*). There is a memorial of thanks [for this honor].

He recommended the śramaṇas Tanshan, who had assisted in compiling the commentary, to lecture upon it at his own monastery. [The records] do not include the gift of ninety rolls of silk bestowed upon Xiu, Tanshan, Daoheng, and others. Internal...
The Palace Attendant Mao Qiyang was dispatched to deliver an imperial edict to offer his condolences.
Tang Lianhua, a man from India, arrived in Xingyuan at the beginning of the reign of Emperor Dezong carrying his monk’s staff.

He petitioned the Emperor, saying, "I wish to obtain one bell to take back to my western country to perform great Buddhist services for Your Majesty. An imperial decree was issued for Ji Fu, the Regional Commander of Guangzhou, to cast the bell.
It was cast and sent once more to Suvarṇakṣetra Monastery in South India. Hua then installed the bell at the Vairocana Buddha stūpa in the kingdom of Bhadraśilā.
Not long after, he received a shipment of the latter portion of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in Sanskrit via ship, which he offered as a token of gratitude.
An imperial edict was issued for the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā to translate [the text] at Chongfu Temple; it was completed in forty fascicles.
One version states that the King of Ujjayinī in South India offered the manuscript as tribute; it is unknown which account is correct.
Amoghavajra (Munīśrī), whose name means "Silent One" in the language of China, was a native of North India.
Having left the household life at Nālandā Monastery in Central India, he traveled eastward with his staff in the ninth year of the Zhenyuan era of Emperor Dezong.

He resided at Xingfu Monastery in Chang’an until the nineteenth year, when he moved to Chongfu Liquan Monastery, and subsequently to Cien Monastery, where he requested the Emperor to authorize the translation of the works produced by [Xuanzang].

The Master’s Sanskrit manuscripts included the *Rāṣṭrapāla-parirakṣaṇa-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in ten fascicles and six illustrated diagrams (*mǔtú*). The Emperor was delighted and bestowed generous offerings upon him.
Śīladharma (whose name translates into Chinese as Jièfǎ) was a man from Khotan who resided in Beiting; he served as a Great Dharma Master during the Zhenguan era.
In the Yuanzhong era, the śramaṇa Wukong, together with the Regional Commander Yang Xigu, requested the Dharma [Master] at Longxing Temple in Beiting to serve as the chief translator.
He produced translations of the *Daśabhūmika-pariṇāmanā-cakra* and other sūtras; the Dharma [Master] personally read the Sanskrit texts while simultaneously acting as the interpreter.
The śramaṇa Dazhen acted as the scribe (*bǐshòu*), Fachao polished the prose, Shanxin verified the meaning, and Wukong verified the Sanskrit text.

Once the transcription was complete, as the śramaṇas were not conversant with the original translated manuscript, they entrusted it to the imperial envoy for consolation, Duan Mingxiu, along with Niu Xin, an official of the Department of State Affairs, and Cheng E, an official on a mission to Anxi, to enter the capital via the Uighur route and present it to the Emperor. [Sanskrit text]
[This work] was preserved in the collection of Longxing Temple.

Prajñā of Kapiśī was a person of the Tang dynasty who entered our realm and served as a śramaṇa specializing in the study of doctrine (*yixue*). Emperor Xianzong deeply revered Buddhist principles and contemplated the task of translation with earnest thought;
however, due to many domestic affairs of state, on the fifth year of the Yuanhe era, the Gengyin year, an edict was issued by the Minister of Works...

Langgui Deng, Mengjian, Liu Boru, Xiao Mian, and others went to Liquan Temple, where they translated eight fascicles of a sutra titled *The Sutra on the Original Birth and the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground*.
The Sanskrit manuscript had been presented from Siṃhala Island during the reign of Emperor Gaozong. Once the transcription was complete, the sutra was submitted for the Emperor’s perusal.
An imperial edict requested that he compose a preface; subsequently, the text was distributed for viewing, and his composition was placed at the beginning of the work. (Dazhong)
In the interim, the Dharma Master Xuanchang of Fabao Temple requested that [the texts] be included in the Tripiṭaka.

The monk Man Yue was a man from the Western Regions; during the Kaicheng era, he presented Sanskrit manuscripts to the court. However, as the "Dew" (Ganlu) disaster occurred at that time, there was no leisure for translation.
National Teacher Wudai Zhi Xuan was fond of the study of *śabda-vidyā* (grammar/linguistics) and took Man Yue as his teacher; consequently, he requested that various [texts] be brought forth.
He translated the *Jinzhù* (Prohibitions and Incantations), together with the *Bodhivajra-siddhi*;

he produced the four-fascicle *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha*, and also produced the one-fascicle *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha for the sake of the Devaputra Viśuddha, which is more detailed than previous translations.
There was a Tripitaka Master named Prajñācakra, whose name in the language of Han means "Wheel of Wisdom.
During the Great Interim Period, he practiced the Mahāmāṇḍala initiation rites and served as an ācārya. He was firmly rooted in the fundamental teachings of the Buddha-dharma;
his doctrine held that dhāraṇīs are the root of all dharmas, for Mahāvairocana is indeed that upon which all Buddhas rely, and from whom they arise.
Regarding the boundless Dharma-gates, the student cultivates morality, concentration, and wisdom, using dhāraṇī to assist in their completion. One must strive for swiftness;
there is nothing that cannot be accomplished. Furthermore, he set forth the instructions and pointed out the ultimate goal.
The eulogy says:
The Buddha utters a single sound, Which pervades the entire Dharma-realm; Beings hear it according to their kind, Without confusion or destruction.
Yet, as karmic obstacles differ, This [limited tradition] is inferior and narrow. The flourishing of translation Is what the Eastern Land relies upon.
The recording was not of antiquity; the compilation was not of the present. Ānanda and Kāśyapa remained ever one-minded regarding the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables.
With the tongue dictating and the brush receiving, the structure is pure and profound.
Whether in the ocean-treasury or the celestial palace, such works are rare indeed. Compared to worldly compositions, they are like the towering peaks of Mount Tai.
*Newly Compiled Biographies of Monks Classified into Six Categories of Study*, Scroll II (Published by Hu Junxuan of Siming).
*Newly Compiled Biographies of Monks Classified into Six Categories of Study*, Scroll III.
Composed by the Sramana Tan'e of Zhedong.

The Transmission of the Lineage of the Wisdom-Training: Tánkējiāluó (Dharmakāla), whose name means "Time of the Dharma" in Chinese, was a native of Central India. His family had been wealthy for generations, and he delighted in performing meritorious deeds.
He possessed great eloquence and discernment. Upon reading a book once, he could recite it from memory. He was skilled in the four *Vaitulya* treatises.

Regarding the winds, clouds, stars, and constellations, as well as diagrams, prophecies, and the transformations of fortune, he was refined, proficient, and thoroughly versed in them all. He believed that the principles of the world were entirely exhausted within himself. He was over twenty years of age.

While traveling among monasteries, he read the *Vinaya* of Dharmatrāta; being utterly bewildered and not knowing what kind of discourse it was, he sighed, saying, "This suddenly transcends the realm of ordinary sentiment;
there must surely be profound meaning herein. He knelt and questioned a bhikṣu, whereupon he finally realized the principles of cause and effect across the three periods of time.

Thereupon, he abandoned his home to study the Way, reciting the sūtras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna as well as the various sections of the *Vinaya*, and traveled to convert others throughout various kingdoms. It was thus that he became renowned.
He traveled to Luoyang during the reign of Emperor Pingzhong. At that time, the Dharma was in its infancy;
monks in China merely shaved their hair, while their practices of fasting and repentance resembled those of secular sacrificial rites. The teachings of the Vinaya had never been heard there.

Upon Kālaya’s arrival, he began to clarify its origins, translating the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* so that the monastic precepts could serve as the daily practice. He further invited Indian monks to establish the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical procedures).
The Dharma was thus widely propagated, and his ultimate end remained unknown.
Bodhidharma of the Liang dynasty was the youngest son of the King of Xiangzhi in South India; he was of the Kṣatriya caste.
His natural disposition was open and bright, and his spiritual wisdom was boundless. His aspirations were set upon the Mahāyāna; his original name was Bodhidhara.
Later, he encountered the twenty-seventh patriarch, the Venerable Prajñātāra, who was traveling through and transforming that kingdom.

Having received the King’s offerings, the Patriarch used his supernormal powers to discern Bodhidhara’s secret potential and sent him with his two elder brothers, Candradhara and Guṇadhara, to distinguish [the truth].
Śibi gave him a pearl. [The boy] polished his wisdom and talent until they were unimpeded; his two elder brothers could not overcome him.

The Venerable One then said to him, "Regarding all dharmas, you have already attained thorough mastery (*pramāṇa*). Now, 'Dharma' has the meaning of 'thorough penetration. You should be named Dharmatrāta."
Entrusted with the lineage of succession, Moqiong received the teachings and served at his side with diligence for nearly forty years.

When the Venerable One passed away, he personally undertook the task of propagation and instruction, subduing the six heterodox schools. Thus, observing the land of China, he perceived the presence of Mahāyāna potential.

Therefore, he boarded a merchant vessel and traveled eastward. After enduring three cycles of winter and summer, he reached the South Sea. This was the first year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty.

Once Guangzhou had received him with full ceremonial honors, he immediately dispatched an official report to Emperor Wu. When the Emperor’s imperial decree arrived, his expressions of comfort and gratitude were most profound.
The Emperor asked, "Since I ascended the throne, I have built monasteries, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks; what merit do these deeds possess? He replied, "Man..."
"The heavens are but minor fruits. The Emperor asked, "What are called the merits of the Mahāyāna? He replied, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect;
its essence is inherently empty and tranquil. Such merits are not sought within the world. The Emperor asked, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths?"
He replied, “Vast emptiness; there is no sage. The Emperor asked, “Who is it that stands before me? He replied, “I do not know. The Emperor ultimately failed to gain any insight or realization.
Thereupon, he traveled north to the Wei dynasty and took up residence at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song. He sat upright facing a wall, remaining silent all day long.
People vied with one another to call him the Brahmin Bhikṣu of Wall-Gazing. This was during the first year of the Wutai era of Emperor Xiaoming.

The Emperor, admiring his cultivation of the Way and virtue, issued three edicts inviting him to court, yet he did not rise to accept them. The Emperor subsequently bestowed upon him a *mona* (patchwork) *kāṣāya*, a golden bowl, and a silver water flask as offerings.

Shortly thereafter, there were the śramaṇas Huìkě, Dào, Fúdào, and the nun Yù Zǒngchí, who followed his instructions and exhortations for nine years. He then addressed them, saying: "The time has come; you should each speak of what you have attained."
Hu Fu said, "As I see it, one does not cling to words and letters, yet does not depart from them, taking them as the functioning of the Way.
Sengmo said, "You have obtained my skin. Niti Zongchi said, "What I now understand is like Ananda seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha:
having seen it once, there is no need to see it again. Sengmo said, "You have obtained my flesh. Daoyu said, "The four great elements are fundamentally empty."
"The five aggregates do not exist. Yet, in my place of vision, not a single dharma can be apprehended. Bodhidharma said, "You have obtained my bones.
After Huike had prostrated, he stood in his place. Bodhidharma said, "You have obtained my marrow. Thereupon, he looked back and said to Huike:
"In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Dharma-eye treasury to the Great Being Kāśyapa, passing it down through successive entrustments until now."
"To me, I now entrust this to you; you must protect and uphold it. He then conferred the *kāṣāya* robe upon him as a token of faith and spoke these verses:
"I have come to this land To transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings. One flower opens into five petals; The fruiting will naturally follow. He further said:
"I observe that throughout China, only the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* can serve to seal the mind. You all should apply yourselves with diligence."
He then proceeded to Qiansheng Temple at Yumen, where he sat upright and manifested his passing. This was on the fifth day of the tenth month in the nineteenth year of Taihe, the Bingchen year.
On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month of that same year, he was buried at Dinglin Temple on Mount Xionger, and a stupa was erected over him.
Three years later, Song Yun, returning from the Western Regions on an imperial mission, encountered [the Master] at Mocong.
Ling took up his single sandal and departed alone with graceful ease. When asked where he was going, he replied, "I am returning to the West.

Upon receiving the imperial decree to open the tomb for inspection, only the single sandal remained. During the reign of Emperor Daizong of the Tang dynasty, he was posthumously honored with the title Chan Master Yuanjue, and his stupa was named Kongguan (Empty Contemplation).

Sengfu of the Liang dynasty was surnamed Wang. A native of Qi in Taiyuan, his disposition was focused and tranquil. He was fond of learning and sought out teachers, never shrinking from perilous distances.

Thereupon, he attended upon Master Bodhidharma in the mountain valleys and shaved his head. Having deeply penetrated the school of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he further extensively explored the sutras and śāstras.
Realizing that the holy Dharma is non-dual, he took it as his own. During the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty, he traveled south.
While traveling in the imperial carriage, he admired the excellence of the springs and rocks at Zhongshan’s Dinglin Monastery and consequently stayed at its lower temple.
When princes and nobles came to visit him, he would not rise from his seat. Although the palace was but a few paces away, he never once went to pay his respects.

Emperor Gao (Emperor Wu of Liang) held him in high esteem and issued an edict for the relevant authorities to prepare quarters for him at Kaishan Temple to serve him there. Huifu sighed, saying, "To live within the walls of a secular residence and sit upright amidst them."
This is still sufficient for joy; how much more so than the preciousness of rafters and eaves measuring several feet, or food spread out before one’s face covering a square zhang!
Furthermore, to abide peacefully yet be able to move on is what the ancients commended; why must one remain stagnant here to indulge the pleasures of the ears and eyes?

When I met with Xiao Yuanzao, the Marquis of Xichang, as he departed to govern the regions of Yong and Shu, I took advantage of the opportunity to follow him westward. Thus, the intent of our silent understanding was extended to Qiong and [Huo]. For a long time...
He returned south and resided at Kaishan Temple as before. Previously, when Prince Nanping had been visiting him while ill, a rustic man named Ke Gui found a set of Buddhist scriptures at Mount Huyi.
The one who gave him the scriptures said, "I am the deity of this mountain.
Speak these words to the Prince: his illness is not worth worrying about. He need only follow the methods of the scriptures and perform the *zhāi* fast for twenty-one days. Immediately—

He recovered. Furthermore, he said, "If you do not understand this, you should ask the Vice Abbot. Later, he took it to ask the Vice Abbot, who was astonished, thinking, "This must be the *Huiyin Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom).
Where did you obtain it? He then instructed [the king] in the method for performing a ritual fast (*zhāifǎ*).
The King’s illness was indeed cured. In the fifth year of the Putong era, at the age of sixty-one, before his passing, someone urged him to cultivate merit; he immediately...

He rose from his seat and said in a stern voice: "To exhaust wealth and resources merely to prolong life for the sake of future existence—is this truly the conduct of one who has realized the emptiness of nature?

Let all the household goods and utensils be given as offerings to the Sangha. Do not prepare a coffin or a tomb; cast the body into the mountains and valleys to satisfy the birds and beasts—is this not excellent?
His disciples wept and would not obey. Princess Yongxing, to whom he had always turned for refuge, [also supported him].
I respectfully request that the Crown Prince compose a text for this purpose. Prince Xiangdong Yi erected a stele for him.

[Huiwen] of the Qi dynasty was surnamed Gao and was a descendant of Shenwu. By nature he was exceptionally intelligent and had from early on received the teachings of the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇayāna*).

He constantly cultivated the methods of contemplation based on the doctrine of the "one mind and three wisdoms" found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitopadeśa* (Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom). Indeed, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitopadeśa*...
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "One who wishes to fulfill the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) with the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.

One who wishes to fulfill all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) with the knowledge of the paths should study the *prajñāpāramitā*. One who wishes to fulfill the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) with all-knowledge should study the *prajñāpāramitā*.
One who wishes to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their residual impressions (*vāsanā*) with the knowledge of all modes should study the *prajñāpāramitā*."

If, as the treatise itself asks: "Within a single moment of mind, one attains all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and severs all afflictions along with their residual impressions (*vāsanā*);
how is it now said that one fulfills the knowledge of all aspects by means of all-knowledge?"

By means of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), one abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their residual impressions (*vāsanā*). The answer is: in reality, all are attained simultaneously.
However, within this context, such a sequential distinction is taught in order to inspire faith in the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Nevertheless, although they are attained within a single moment of mind (*ekacitta*), there is still a sequence of beginning, middle, and end. For example, within a single moment of mind, there is the arising of causes and conditions for abiding, and then the abiding itself.

The causes and conditions are the three characteristics of cessation. Furthermore, regarding the mind, mental factors, teachings, non-associated formations, bodily actions, verbal actions, and so forth, one fulfills all-knowledge through the knowledge of the path; and through all-knowledge, one fulfills the knowledge of all modes.
It is likewise with the severance of afflictions and their residual habits by means of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Since the fruit is attained within a single mind, how could the causes be acquired sequentially? Therefore, when this contemplation is perfected, one realizes the threefold wisdom within a single mind;

being both simultaneously extinguished and simultaneously illumined, one immediately enters and abides in the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Furthermore, while reading the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, in the "Chapter on the Four Truths," a verse states: "The cause..."
"Those phenomena produced through conditions, I declare to be empty; they are also called provisional designations, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way.

At these words, [the assembly] suddenly and completely understood: all phenomena are nothing other than produced by causes and conditions, yet these causes and conditions are not fixed as existing, and emptiness is not fixed as empty.
That emptiness and existence are non-dual is called the Middle Way. At that time, [the Master] gathered a great multitude of disciples at the river.
The dharma-gates he entered between the Huai River regions were beyond the comprehension of the world.
When he propagated the teachings in the south at Mount Nanyue, his students inferred where he had come from and concluded that he had received his transmission remotely from Nāgārjuna.
Huike of Qi was a native of Wulao. His surname was Ji. His father, Ji, once prayed to the Buddha because he had no son.

One night, he was moved by a supernatural light that illuminated his chamber; consequently, his mother became pregnant. Upon her delivery, they named the child Guang (Light) in accordance with the auspicious omen of the light illuminating the room.

From childhood, he was extraordinary among his peers; he read widely in the *Shi* and *Shu*, and was particularly proficient in the profound principles of the *Xuanxue* school. Later, he studied Buddhist scriptures.
Being one who had transcended worldly concerns and attained something for himself, he was naturally fond of wandering and took no interest in domestic affairs or property.
He went directly to Mount Xiangshan at Longmen in Luoyang, where he joined the monastic order under Chan Master Baojing and received full ordination at Yongmu Temple.

He frequented lecture halls, studying the doctrines of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna exhaustively. At the age of thirty-two, he returned to Mount Xiangshan, where he sat in meditation throughout the day.
After eight years had passed, while in a state of profound silence, he beheld a divine being who said to him, "You are destined to receive the fruit of enlightenment in the south;
is it fitting that you remain stagnant here? The following day, he felt a pain in his head as if it were being pierced with needles. His teacher wished to summon a skilled physician to treat him.
Suddenly, a voice from the air said: "This is merely the shedding of bones; it is not particularly painful. You should go and report this miraculous event to your master.
The master examined his crown and saw that five bones stood out prominently, like five peaks rising majestically. He then remarked, "This is an auspicious sign.
I have heard that the Great Being Dharmatrāta resides at Shaolin in the south. You should go there at once and serve him as your teacher."
"You must certainly attain realization; this is what the deity has praised. You may receive instruction and go to Mount Shaoshi.
There, attend upon [the Master] morning and evening. When Bodhidharma sat facing the wall in meditation and gave no instruction, Huike thought to himself:

"In the past, those who sought the Way would break their bones to extract marrow, pierce their veins to relieve hunger, spread their hair to cover the mud, and throw themselves off cliffs to feed tigers. Looking at myself, what kind of person am I that I dare to be so casual?"
"False. On the ninth night of the twelfth month of that year, it rained and snowed heavily. [Bodhidharma] stood firm and unmoving.
At dawn, the accumulated snow reached above his knees. Bodhidharma asked him with compassion, "You have stood long in the snow; what do you seek?
He replied with tears of grief, "I pray that the Master, out of compassion, shall open the gate of ambrosia and extensively deliver all sentient beings. Bodhidharma said, "The Buddhas..."

The unsurpassed, wondrous Way cannot be attained by those who, lacking the diligent effort of kalpas, are unable to perform what is difficult to do or endure what is difficult to endure, yet hope for some gain through meager virtue and limited wisdom with a frivolous or arrogant mind; this is impossible.

When he heard these instructions, he secretly took a knife and severed his left arm, placing it before his teacher. As he ground it, he said: "When the Buddhas first sought the Way, they forgot themselves for the sake of the Dharma."
“Son, you have now severed your arm before me in pursuit of the Buddha’s wisdom; this is well. He then changed his name to Huike.
Huike asked, “May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas? Bodhidharma replied, “The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is precisely this mind.”
"How could it be obtained from another? Huik'e said, "My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to grant me peace. Mazu said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will grant you peace.
Huik'e said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable. Mazu said, "I have finished granting you peace.
Later, Mazu entrusted him with his robe and alms bowl, saying, "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Eye of the True Dharma to the Great Being Kāśyapa, who..."
Having successively transmitted these instructions down to me, I now entrust them to you. This robe and bowl are intended to serve as tokens of faith.

After two hundred years following my parinirvāṇa, the robe and bowl shall no longer be passed on; yet those who have secretly conformed to and secretly realized the Dharma throughout the entire realm will be beyond counting.
Having obtained the disciple Sengcan, he in turn was entrusted with the Bodhidharma robe and bowl. And...
He spoke in verse, saying: "Originally there was ground due to conditions; based on the ground, flowers grew from seeds. Originally there were no seeds; the flowers likewise never grew.
He further said, "You must protect and uphold this well. I have karmic debts from former lives which I must now repay.
In the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, he went to Zhengjiu Temple in Guancheng, Yedu, where he expounded the Unsurpassed Way. Those who listened gathered like clouds.

Previously, the Dharma Master Bianhe was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. When all his students departed, Bianhe could not overcome his indignation and consequently slandered the district magistrate, who then imposed an unjust punishment upon him.
He could have remained serene and passed away in accordance with the Way, yet he did not; he died at the age of one hundred and seven.
A stupa was erected in Fuyang County, Zizhou. Emperor Dezong of the Tang dynasty later posthumously conferred upon him the title of Grand Patriarch Chan Master.
Hui-guang of the Qi dynasty was born into the Yang family of Changlu in Dingzhou. At the age of thirteen, he accompanied his father to Luoyang.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, he received the Three Refuges precepts from Master Buddhatara. Buddhatara urged his father to keep him, saying, "This boy’s gaze shoots outward;

he is surely capable of being taught. Consequently, he was set to study and recite. When Hui-guang took up the scrolls and grasped the texts, it was as if they had been bestowed upon him in a previous life.

At the end of summer, he underwent tonsure; soon thereafter, he began expounding the words and principles he had studied with such elegance and abundance that his contemporaries dubbed him the "Holy Śrāmaṇera.
Whatever offerings and sustenance he received, he gave them all away to others. Daoyi listened to him without ever questioning him.
After some time, he returned to his native village. Upon arriving at Jetavana Monastery, he instructed those who had previously studied the Vinaya, saying:
"The Vinaya is the foundation of wisdom and the means by which one enters the Sūtras and Śāstras. If one were to prioritize the Sūtras and Śāstras, one would inevitably come to despise the Vinaya;

this is the very source of obstacles to the Path. From then on, he encouraged the study of the Vinaya-piṭaka. Previously, there was the Vinaya Master Daofu, who first opened the path for the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and composed commentaries upon it.

I have never heard of anyone who, while still a *kaiṣa* (novice), could uphold the grand framework [of the teachings]. Once Guang had completed his four summer retreats as a fully ordained monk, he lectured on the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, and those who listened gathered like clouds.
Thereafter, he investigated the sūtras and śāstras under Master Bian and refined his phonology in Luoyang.
He produced writings to serve as a substitute for memory, and thus his scholarly achievements became vast. On another day, Da saw the texts he had composed, summoned him, and said:
He said to him, "I had expected you to bear fruit by now, yet you are currently occupied with the petty matters of worldly discourse; you are merely fit to be a 'High and Bright' Dharma Master.
At this, [Hui]guang wept in response. Subsequently, as Paramārtha served as the head of Shaolin Temple and oversaw the translation work under Bodhiruci, Hui-guang was able to attend his lectures.
After some time, he was summoned by imperial decree to serve as the State Preceptor (Guo-sengdu). It happened that there was a great drought that year.

He prayed for rain at Mount Song, and it fell in abundance. Summoned by imperial decree to enter the capital of Ye, he was promoted to State Preceptor (*Guo-tong*) for his merits in pacifying and consolidating the realm.

When Er Zhu Shilong raised an army for the northern campaign, the military provisions were insufficient; consequently, monks and nuns were taxed to supply them. The enforcement was severe and cruel, and those who offered remonstrance were executed.
Sengguang stepped forward and rebuked Shilong, saying, "If you proceed in this manner, I fear it will not bring fortune to the state. Thereupon, the policy was abandoned.
At that time, renowned scholars such as Gao Cao, Gao Longzhi, and Lingju Ziru all paid him their respects. Feng Gun was a scholar from Ji province who had mastered the classics and histories;

having been recommended by his prefecture, he came to the capital to observe the imperial court. Believing he did not yet understand the principles of the Buddhist school, he sought an audience with Daoguang and happened to find him lecturing.
He sat down to listen and was deeply satisfied and convinced by what he heard. Consequently, he requested to be enrolled among Daoguang’s disciples.
He was unwilling to leave. Later, beneath the Gate of Radiance (Guangmen), he performed great meritorious deeds and was known as Layman Feng.

One day, as Guang was about to take his seat at the office while riding in a carriage, just as he stepped out the gate, a beam of the wooden structure suddenly split. While he sat there attending to official business, a block of wood fell before him;
though they examined it, no one knew where it had come from. Because of this, he lay ill for forty days until he passed away in Ye.

At Dajue Temple, he lived to the age of seventy. Throughout his life, Huiguang composed commentaries on the profound principles of the *Avataṃsaka*, *Nirvāṇa*, *Vimalakīrti*, *Daśabhūmika*, and *Bhūmisamādhi* sūtras.
He also provided annotated exegeses for the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda*, *Udānavarga*, *Jentaka*, *Ratnaketu*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras.
Furthermore, he produced a revised commentary of one hundred and twenty sheets on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, and compiled and edited the *Karmavācanā* and the *Prātimokṣa*. He also authored...
The *Xuanzong lun*, the *Dasheng yi*, the *Lüyi zhang*, the *Renwang qijie*, and the *Sengzhi shibabiao*. Among his disciples were Daoyun and Daohui;
Yun compiled a nine-fascicle commentary on the Vinaya (*Lüshu*), while Hui abridged it into seven fascicles. Thus, the proverb says:
"Master Yun at the head, Master Hui at the tail, with Master Hongli in between as the reason. Both have perished, and their details cannot be verified. Guang...
At the end of his life, he saw a celestial palace descend and said, "I wish to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). To be born in heaven is not my aspiration.
Thereupon, the celestial palace vanished.
Chen Huisi was born into the Li family of Wujin. From his youth, he was esteemed by his fellow villagers for his benevolence and forbearance.

While living at home, he dreamed of a monk from India who exhorted him to shave his head and leave the household life; he subsequently followed this advice. However, the temple where he resided was defiled and disorderly, yet Huisi alone remained pure and prudent.
If there were those who had previously been instructed and who possessed a nature of conduct that was increasingly lofty and sincere, they would recite the Lotus Sutra a thousand times daily.
When a hermit dwelling in the wilds burned down his hut and subsequently suffered from leprosy, they would again repair the dwelling for him and perform repentance on his behalf.
He then rectified his ordination. He once dreamed of several hundred monks, one of whom said to him, "The precepts you previously received were not supreme.
Now that you have encountered this pure assembly, you ought to re-consecrate the altar and receive the precepts again. Just as he was about to chant the *karmavācanā*, he suddenly woke up in alarm.

From then on, he practiced constant sitting without lying down and could see all the deeds he had performed throughout three lifetimes. Furthermore, within a state of meditative concentration, he dreamed that Maitreya and Amitābha expounded the Dharma for him.
He beheld the Dharma-body, as well as his own person together with his retinue, in Maitreya’s assembly at the Dragon-Flower Tree. He thought to himself alone:

"How fortunate I am that, during the final dharma-age of Śākyamuni, I upheld the Lotus Sūtra and now encounter the Compassionate Honored One! Furthermore, my water-jar is always full and celestial youths attend me.
While he was occasionally reading the *Sūtra on the Wondrous and Victorious Samādhi* and repeatedly cultivating the study of meditative concentration, at that time, Master Huì...

While Wén was gathering disciples to transmit the Dharma, [Hui]jìng went to consult him, undaunted by toil and hardship. During the day he attended to his duties, and at night he concentrated his mind.
Seasons of winter and summer passed swiftly, yet he had attained nothing. In the following summer, he redoubled his vigor; after only twenty-one days, he began to have realizations.

He gave rise to a minor state of calm observation (*śamatha*), which immediately stirred the eight tactile sensations and brought forth the fundamental first dhyāna. Subsequently, hindrances arose: his four limbs became limp and weak, making it difficult to move.
He reflected that these ailments all arise from karma, and that karma arises from the mind; since karma cannot be apprehended, he turned back to perceive the source of the mind.
Having observed in this way, his inverted perceptions were extinguished, the nature of his mind became pure, and his suffering was eliminated. Thereupon, [he] again gave rise to...

He practiced the meditative concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), yet his mind and its objects remained vast and empty. When summer retreat ended, he had gained nothing; grieving that he had passed the time in vain, he leaned his body against a wall.

Before he had even reached the wall, he was suddenly enlightened to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* and the Mahāyāna Dharma-gates. In a single thought-moment, he attained clear penetration of the sixteen special victories (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*), the stages of liberation (*vimokṣa*), and the bases of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*).
He immediately achieved thorough mastery. Later, he received the seal of approval from masters such as Juezhui and others, and traveled in all four directions.

He admired [the teachings] and, employing the methods of meditative concentration and wisdom from both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles to encompass himself and others, he remained unharmed despite the emergence of various slanders and the employment of treacherous plots and lethal poisons. He turned to his disciples and said, "Even when the Buddha was in the world, he could not avoid such things;
how much more so for me? However, the Buddha-dharma in the Central Kingdom will soon face difficulties; I am considering a way to avoid them."
Suddenly, a voice from the air said, "You may go to Mount Wudang or the Southern Peak (Mount Heng). At the beginning of the Qi Wuping era, he departed from Songyang and traveled south to Guangzhou.
At that time, due to the chaos of the collapse of Emperor Xiaoyuan of the Liang dynasty, the roads were blocked and he could not proceed. He stayed temporarily at Dasu Mountain for several years;
yet, because he was a man who valued the Dharma above his own life, even though it was on a strategic military frontier, people flocked to him like a marketplace to offer their support.
The offerings were abundant and the provisions ample. In establishing sutras and opening lectures, he never shied away from the great volume of work.

When Zhiyi of Jiangling asked him during a lecture session, "How can one mind be endowed with the myriad practices? Sengsi replied, "This is merely the sequential meaning of the *Mohebanruo Boluomi Jing* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra)."
"I shall grant you the Dharma-flower practice and the states of the three-week period; thus, your previous doubts will be resolved.
He asked again, "The stage realized by the Master—is it the tenth bhūmi? He replied, "No. It is merely my stage of the ten faiths, the Iron Wheel rank.

At the beginning of the Guangda era of the Chen dynasty, he moved to Mount Nanyue, where he often said, "I have resided on this mountain for only ten years; once I am gone, I shall surely be far away."
While traveling, he came to the base of a cliff at Hengyang and said, "This is the site of an ancient temple where I once sat in meditation. A bandit severed my head;
since the end of that life, I have received this present body. His attendant followed his words and dug there, and indeed they recovered bricks, tiles, utensils, as well as skeletal remains.
Desiring to honor the bones with worship, he erected a stupa for them. After he had lived there for some time, some people...
Sengsi heard that the Northern monks had received a recruitment drive to destroy the scenic splendors of Nanyue. Those who slandered him at court dispatched an envoy to investigate.
Just as two tigers were roaring and leaping across the path, the envoy was startled and retreated. After several days, he advanced again; Sengsi remained entirely indifferent to this.
Subsequently, three of the conspirators met their ends: one died a violent death, and another was torn apart by a snapping dog. Consequently, the Emperor...
He no longer questioned this. Previously, before his death, while Si was in the mountains, a bee stung him on the forehead.
Suddenly, a large bee bit the spot that had been stung and killed it, then placed its head before Si. This, indeed, was a sign of his impending fate.

By imperial decree, he was stationed at Qixuan Temple in the capital. He subsequently visited Waguan Temple; though he walked through the rain, he remained dry, and though he trod upon the mud, his feet were not soiled.
Hui’ao, the Chief Overseer of Monks (Sengzheng), encountered him on the road and regarded him as a divine being.

The entire court turned their eyes toward him, and the Grand Commander (Dadu du) Wu Mingche showed him exceptional respect, even presenting him with a rhinoceros horn pillow. Xiahou Xiaowei, a subordinate general of Mingche, wished to see what [the pillow looked like].
He presented a pillow as a gift. Once, while visiting a temple to pay his respects, Sengsi suddenly said to Xiaowei, "Do you wish to see the pillow of the General of the Interior of Wu?
He then ordered it to be brought out and shown to him. One day, at Xiaowei’s home, a voice suddenly rang out from the air:

"Quickly sweep and clean; a sage is arriving! Shortly thereafter, Sengsi arrived. In the ninth year of the Dajian era, he instructed his disciples, saying, "If there are ten people who do not begrudge..."

"Regarding body and life, I shall personally provide for those who constantly practice the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi*, and the Vaipulya repentances, as well as those who practice constant sitting and other such disciplines.
If there are none [who do so], I shall depart far away; for the practice of asceticism is difficult. Thus he asked three times.

There was no one who offered a reply; consequently, the assembly withdrew to a secluded place, collected their thoughts, and remained in silence. His disciple Lingbian was still young, yet his wailing cries of grief resounded both inside and outside the hall.
Sishi suddenly opened his eyes and said, "You are an evil demon. Why do you disturb and harass me? Begone!
He then once again withdrew his mind and sat upright until the end. When the assembly awoke, they found the fragrance filling the room, and his crown was warm while his body [remained supple].
His complexion was soft and appeared as if he were still alive. This was on the twenty-second day of the sixth month in the ninth year of the Taijian era of Emperor Chen.

He was sixty-four years of age. His physical form was exceptionally prominent; his gait and gaze were like those of an ox or an elephant. He possessed a *uṣṇīṣa* upon his crown and practiced great compassion.

He upheld the Bodhisattva precepts. Regarding such items as clothing, silk, cotton, or leather, he generally avoided them because they involve the harming of living beings; thus, his followers usually used plain cloth instead.
When it was cold, he would use *ainuo* (mugwort incense). All of his writings were transmitted orally and were never edited or polished.

He produced two fascicles on the "Gate of the Forty-two Letters" and two fascicles on the "Gate of Non-contention Practice," as well as the *Shelun xuansui ziyi anle* (The Profound Commentary on Following One’s Own Will for Peace and Bliss).
*The Sequential Practice of the Essentials of Dhyāna: The Three Wisdom Contemplation Gates*, one fascicle each; currently extant.
Chen Xuanguang was a native of Xiong Prefecture in the kingdom of Silla. From his youth, he was diligent in the pure conduct of *brahmacarya*.

Upon reaching maturity, he crossed the vast ocean to study the methods of Chan in the Middle Kingdom. There, he met the Great Master Sīta of Mount Heng and realized the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra. Having...

Having received this prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), he took his leave to return to his native land to propagate the Dharma. Just as he was boarding a ship and turning the rudder to depart from the shore, a divine being suddenly descended from the void holding a vermilion staff.
He called out, "The Celestial Emperor is journeying to the Dragon Palace to summon the Zen Master Xuanguang of海东 (Haidong) to expound the Dharma-gate of personal realization.
Immediately, those in blue robes led the way before him, while those with scales and shells guarded his rear as he ascended.
The Abbot ascended the throne and engaged in discourse for seven days; yet he suddenly realized he was on a boat, for the vessel had drifted without making any progress for barely half a day.
Such was the brevity of time and space for those of different realms.

After some time, he planted his staff at Mount Ong in that country, where seekers who responded to his call arrived one after another. He refined their Way and tempered their virtue, and many attained the Good.
One person was accomplished in the Fire-Light Samādhi; two persons were accomplished in the Water-Light Samādhi. By these examples, the remaining disciples may be understood accordingly.

Later, there was Huìchéng of the Liáng dynasty, surnamed Duàn, a native of Lǐyáng. Having long been affiliated with Shízhù Temple, he shaved his head to become a monk and recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.

He studied more than twenty Mahāyāna sūtras, such as the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra* (Mo-sheng-tian-wang-jing). After receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), he went to Jianye, where he stayed with Master Ling for ten years to master the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.

His understanding of its principles and phrasing became somewhat proficient. As he was about to return to his hometown, he encountered Master Tanyi, who was serving under Master Huisi of Mount Nanyue and transforming the people at Mount Lu.
Upon seeing him, [Zhiyi] felt great joy and admiration, wishing to follow him in his travels. Huisi asked him about his studies, and [Zhiyi] explained them in detail.
He replied, "I have thought it over: your lifelong studies have not even managed to warm your hands when held near mine;
you have wasted your efforts in vain—what a pity! Cheng returned home. After a long while, he said, "I trust the Great Master understands my intention well; please allow me to test this."
Sengsi sent him a rhinoceros-horn fan, a whisk, handkerchiefs, thread, and sandals as gifts.

Daocheng immediately burned his commentaries, manuscripts, pens, and inkstones, and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). At that time, there were several dozen senior practitioners whom Daocheng feared he might not be able to surpass;
thus, he practiced day and night, often sitting with eyes wide open for fifteen years, yet he attained almost no realization. Sengsi then instructed him to enter Fangshan.

He practiced the methods of Avalokiteśvara, the Lotus Sūtra, and the Pratyutpanna Samādhi at a place of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*), repenting his offenses and eliminating hindrances for three years. Thereupon, demonic activities were dispersed and dissolved;

thereafter, he exerted himself toward profound stillness and concentrated his mind upon the void and the wondrous, attaining realization of the *sattvabhāṣita-samādhi* (the samādhi of the languages of sentient beings).

Conceptual thoughts do not arise; stillness and distraction are unified as one. Compared to those who close their eyes, although their contemplation of the Way may be clear, they lose the vision of the objective realm;
thus, the difference in their progress is manifold. Zhiyi said: "My wisdom is perfected; my quiescent illumination, understanding, and practice are perfectly equal.
After Zhiyi manifested his passing, [Zhanran] went to Jiangzhou and founded Chanhui Temple. Between the Ming Gate on the sandy islet, he looked westward to draw upon the virtue of [the Master].
He followed the wind of Luan’s "Fleeing to Fatigue" (Feidun), continuing the legacy of Dao’an’s pioneering foundations. Those who speak of secluded excellence turn to him;

Prince Xiangdong built Jianzhong Temple for him to reside in. When the main hall lacked rafters and beams, the river rose in flood one night, and Cheng had men retrieve materials from within the water as if it were something they already possessed.
It was said that when Duan Hong, the master of the vihāra, died, his family requested Cheng [to perform rites].

As he was watching, Hong suddenly revived and said: "At first, I was taken into the presence of the King. Suddenly, the Meditation Master stood in the court and said, 'I am currently cultivating merit for this man;
his crime must be pardoned. The King rose, prostrated at my feet, and obeyed my command. Consequently, I was released and returned."

The Prince of Chen summoned him repeatedly, but he did not comply. Jiang Zong was dispatched as supervisor to compel him by force. As soon as Cheng entered the boat, he leaped up and stood upon the water.
Jiang Zong and the others prostrated themselves and wept, saying, "We would rather sacrifice our lives; please have pity on us and take us along.

Only then did he go to the capital to receive the precepts from the Prince of Chen before returning. While Cheng was at Mount Nanyue, it happened one winter night that he was lodging with Vinaya Master Chang. Chang threw [himself]...
While Hui Cheng was on the ground, the next day they parted ways. Cheng said to Hui Chang, "Yesterday a certain donor was frozen;

he is truly pitiable. Hui Chang looked on with deep sorrow. As Cheng neared his end, he instructed his disciples: "Hurry to lay the foundation for the hall; I intend to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Not long after, Zhiyi arrived from Yuquan Temple. They conversed for a long time, and Cheng passed away at Chanzhong Temple at the age of seventy-three.
Zhou Huiming, surnamed Guo, was a native of Jinyang in Taiyuan. She was a descendant of Guo Qizhi, a scholar-recluse of the Jin dynasty. Her family had moved to Changsha Commandery in Xiangzhou.
By nature she was exceptionally refined and elegant; her body emitted a radiant light. From an early age, she relied upon Master Zhen as a novice.
Master Zhen was a man from the Wei region, yet he was able to enter her inner sanctum—there must have been a profound reason for this. At the age of fifteen, she...
He practiced the recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and after more than ten days, he could recite it from memory without any omission or error.

Once he had undergone the tonsure, he constantly cultivated realization through the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and performed the repentance rites of the Vaipulya and Samantabhadra. Later, he sought instruction in the practices of meditative concentration from the two Chan masters En and Guangxian.
Previously, there was a Daoist named Meng Shou who had long resided on Mount Xiancheng; one day, he beheld [the Master].
The local spirits and deities provided a most magnificent guard. Climbing the cliffs to look out, he further saw a multitude of fellow practitioners gathered together.

Shortly thereafter, the summons arrived; Shou hurried to pay his respects and subsequently donated everything to establish Shan Guang Temple. His provisions were abundant and elaborate, and students gathered there in great numbers.
Later, he opened a lecture on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra at the provincial seat before returning to his native village. As for Dharma-voice (Fayin) Chan Master:
The son of the Wang family was surnamed Qi and was a native of Tongjun. In his youth, he served only Master Neng of Guoyuan Temple;

after only a few weeks, he traveled extensively throughout Jiangnan and Hebei to dispel whatever remained obstructed in his mind. It was only upon meeting the two masters Si and Miao that he finally ceased [his travels].
He subsequently stayed at Xiancheng for five years. One day, as they walked hand-in-hand through a pine grove, he laughed and said: "This..."

Both locations were truly fit for their final resting places. Those who heard of this remained unenlightened by it. On the fifth day of the twelfth month of the third year of the Tiānhé era, he passed away at Shànguāng Temple due to illness;
on the seventeenth day, his voice likewise ceased at Guòyuàn Temple. Yet in both cases, his spirit remained clear and undimmed as he faced west to recite the Buddha’s name.
Wondrous fragrances and extraordinary music were perceived, and some heard the sound of one chanting "Excellent! (Sādhu). Thus ends the account of his passing.

At the age of thirty-eight, Sengming was exceptionally skilled in literary composition. He authored works such as the *Dapin yizhang* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Larger Prajñāpāramitā), the *Rongxin lun* (Treatise on the Merging of the Mind), the *Huan yuan jing* (Mirror of Returning to the Source), the *Xing lu nan* (The Difficulty of Traveling the Path), and the *Xiangxuan fu* (Detailed Rhapsody on the Profound). These writings were circulated in the world.

Among them, the lay disciple of the Bodhisattva precepts, Dai Kui of Jibei, sent a letter requesting instruction; Sengming composed an elegant response to it. Much of this writing has not been recorded here. [The monk] Hui... [text fragment ends].
Xiao’s surname was Fu. His mind was clear and his learning was profound; his talent was nearly equal to that of [his teacher] Ming.

He traveled to Qi and resided at Lingyan Temple for several decades, yet people initially did not consider him extraordinary. On one occasion, due to a family mourning in his hometown, he went to visit the Magistrate of Shanchai.

He was instructed to decline immediate audiences with formal excuses for being occupied by others. He composed the "Fu on the Śramaṇa" (Xiao zuo shizi fu) to express his intent and subsequently departed.
His fame became prominent because of this. He was commanded to leave instructions to construct a brick tomb, and he directed his disciples and the lay devotee Zheng Ziwen to erect a stele.
Zhiyi of the Sui dynasty, courtesy name De’an, was of the Chen clan of Yingchuan. His ancestors had migrated south during the Jin dynasty and settled in Huāróng County in Jingzhou.
His father, Qizǔ, was the Duke of Méngyáng and a Court Gentleman for Horse Management under the Liang dynasty. His mother, Lady Xú, dreamed that five-colored incense smoke entered her bosom;
as she attempted to brush it away, she heard a voice say: "Due to karmic conditions from past lives, you have entrusted yourself to the Way of the King. This is a matter of merit and virtue."
"He has come of his own accord; why should you drive him away? Furthermore, she dreamed that she swallowed white mice two or three times. The divination stated, "This is an omen of a white dragon.
On the evening of her delivery, the room was filled with light, which ceased after two nights. Her relatives were preparing a grand feast to celebrate.

Without cause, he suffered from the burning sensations of hot water and fire, whereupon [the practice] was discontinued. Shortly thereafter, two monks appeared at night knocking at the door, saying, "This child’s virtue is profound;

he will surely leave the household life in the future. When they opened the door to look, nothing was seen. Consequently, he was named Wang Dao (Way King) and also Guang Dao (Way Light), both names derived from the auspicious signs in the dream.
His eyes had double pupils; when lying down, he would invariably join his palms; and when sitting, he would always face west to perform his prostrations.

He revered the Sangha as an image [of the Buddha] and never spoke frivolously; this was his constant practice. At the age of seven, he happened to go to a monastery, and when the *Pumenpin* (Universal Gate Chapter) was given to him, he could memorize it after a single recitation.
As for the other passages, he suddenly mastered them on his own. His parents tried to forbid him from going, but they could not stop him.

When he reached the age for beginning formal studies (*zhixue*), Emperor Yuan of the Liang dynasty passed away and the state fell into ruin. He subsequently went north to rely upon his maternal uncle.
He was born in Xiazhou. He soon entered Guoyuan Temple in Xiangzhou, where he served the śramaṇa Faxu as his teacher and left the household life.

While in the midst of prostrating before the Buddha, he suddenly perceived himself standing upon the vast ocean, which obscured the sun and floated across the heavens, boundless and shoreless. Above, jagged cliffs rose high;
a monk beckoned to him with his hand, then extended his arm to receive him and place him on a rugged slope at the foot of the cliffs, saying to him: "You shall..."
"Reside here; you shall spend your final years here. He immediately informed his disciples of this vision, and they all said, "This is Mount Tiantai.

During the Jin and Song dynasties, the monks Sengguang, Daoyou, Falan, and Tanmi resided there. Thereupon, [Hui]xu first guided them with the ten precepts, the stages of the path, and the monastic discipline (*vinaya*).
He then sent them north to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) from Vinaya Master Huikuang. Later, he resided at Dà...

Xianshan recited such scriptures as the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, and the *Universal Worthy Visualization Sūtra*; in barely twenty days, he had mastered them all without impediment.
He also studied under Master Huisi of Mount Dasu in Guangzhou, who extensively expounded upon mental contemplation (*cittabhāvanā*) to the fourfold assembly.
Thus, Huisi’s Way was obtained from Master Jiu, and Master Jiu obtained it from Master Zui. Initially, Yi...
Jian saw him and sighed, saying, "In the past at Mount Ling, we heard the Lotus Sutra together. Pursued by our karmic conditions from that former life, you have come here once more.
To show you the site of Samantabhadra’s practice, he preached the Four Practices of Peaceful Bliss. Zhiyi subsequently relied upon these teachings to practice the Lotus Samādhi.

After three nights, he arose from meditative concentration and began reciting the sutra; when he reached the passage in the "Chapter on King of Medicine" known as the "Verse of True Diligence," [he attained realization].
He attained a sudden and great enlightenment. He clearly perceived that the assembly of Buddhas on Mount Lingyan was still present.

He immediately went to visit Huisi to report what he had realized. Huisi said, "It is not you who could have been moved by this; it is not I who could have recognized it. This is the preliminary skillful means of the Lotus Samādhi.

Later, while practicing meditative concentration at Mount Baisha in Xizhou, he repeatedly saw Huisi expounding the sutras and giving him instructions. Subsequently, he frequently took Huisi’s place in lecturing.
Sengsi always held the *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling jewel) and sat by his side to listen to him.

He said to his disciples, "This boy has an abundance of insight into the meaning of the teachings, yet he lacks sufficient power of concentration (*samādhi*). Therefore, regarding the three samādhis and the wisdom of the three contemplations, he harbors some regret.
Subsequently, he took his leave and went to the capital, where, together with over thirty people including Falxi of Jinling, he founded the Waguan Temple.
