He propagated the Way. At that time, the Vice President Xu Ling and the Minister Mao Xi were both men of broad learning and insight; they both transmitted the Dharma of Incense.
Thereupon, Zhibian of Changgan Temple invited him to reside at Songxi and Tiangong Temples; Senghuang requested him to dwell at Fuku and Baima;
Jingshao, Chengcheng, Zhiwen, Chanzhong, Huiling, as well as the venerable elders of the Liang court such as Dari, all [sought his guidance].

The Master [Huiyi] completely abandoned his former occupation and followed him. Huirong of Yuxue resided at Zhuangyan Temple; he was commonly known as "Yilong" (Dragon of Meaning) and frequently engaged in rigorous cross-examinations.
Moreover, he was arrogant and boastful, even using a fan to perform a dance to display his prowess. Suddenly, the fan fell, and Huiyi rebuked him, saying:

The power of meditative concentration cannot be disturbed by those who are distracted. During the summer retreat of the śramaṇas, [Dao]sheng patted Yili’s back from the side and said, "Yili has now become a crouching deer; since the fan has already fallen to the ground, what is there left to hide?
Thus, after eight years had passed, he finished lecturing on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and subsequently opened the dharma-gate of *dhyāna*, bringing great benefit to many. Not yet...

When several of the newly enthroned kings went to station themselves at Lake Dongting, they passed by Waguan Temple to engage in discussion with him. Their profound satisfaction reached the core of their hearts;
they offered brave alms and reverent prostrations to exhaust their sincerity. Huiyi then sighed and said: "Last night, I dreamed that I encountered bandits.
Are these not soft-thief bandits? What is called 'a hair-cord severing bone' or 'dragging a tail through mud'—the impossibility of escaping them is even more severe than this."

As for the "robbers," they were previously the extraordinary monk Dingguang of Qingzhou, who practiced both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) while residing on Mount Tiantai for over forty years.
At this time, because of what he had seen in the past, Zhiyi wished to follow his conditions and return to seclusion; he then sent word to his disciples, saying:
"I have heard that the lips and tongue are like a bow, the mental deliberations are like the string, and vocal sounds are like the arrow. Throughout the long night, [they are] empty..."
He set out [to speak], yet there was nothing perceived or known; this is what is called "shooting in the dark. Having thus expounded this teaching, he further said: "The Dharma-gate is like a mirror;

it assumes square or round forms according to whatever image is presented. This refers to meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). However, when I first sat in the Waguan Temple, there were only about forty people present.
Yet only half have attained awakening. Of the two hundred people seated here today, barely ten have attained awakening;
thus, one can perceive the changes in worldly affairs. From now on, each may follow their own ease, for I too wish to follow my own will.
Upon reaching Mount Tai, he met with Daoguang. Daoguang said, "I remember when we were young, shaking our hands together on the mountain."

"The time for our mutual invitation has arrived. This was the seventh month of autumn in the seventh year of the Taijian era of Emperor Chen. Shortly thereafter, the sound of bells was heard filling the mountain crags and valleys.
Guang said, "The sound of the bells gathers the assembly; this is a sign that we shall succeed in reaching our destination. Thereupon, they ascended the southern side of Mount Fulong.

At the source of the Luoxi Stream, he established a hermitage, saying, "This shall serve as a temporary dwelling until the time of Guoqing, when a person of noble status will surely arise to establish a temple for me.

At that time, no one could fathom his words. Subsequently, while practicing *dhūta* austerities on Mount Huading, he was suddenly beset by wind, thunder, and *chimei* (goblins), whose forms and countenances were terrifying.
Furthermore, his body suffered from pain, and his late father appeared before him in person, weeping as he leaned upon his knee to plead with him.

Zhiyi relied upon the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), whereby both the harsh and the gentle Māras were simultaneously quelled. Shortly thereafter, a Brahmin monk remarked, "To overcome and conquer the enemy, one may truly be called brave.
Emperor Xuan issued an edict stating: "The Meditation Master is a preeminent hero of the Buddha-dharma, revered by the masters of our time.

His instruction extends to both the clergy and the laity; he is a national hope. Therefore, let the tax quota of Shifeng County be apportioned to provide for the community's expenses, and let two households of the common people be exempted from taxation."
He served as a stipendiary official. Yuan Zixiong of Chenjun, the Magistrate of Le’an, would regularly invite him to lecture on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* every summer.
Once, he saw three jeweled staircases extending from the sky to the ground; dozens of *brahmacārin* monks descended the stairs and entered the hall to perform prostrations.
Holding an incense burner, he circumambulated Zhiyi three times; after a long while, it extinguished itself. The entire assembly marveled at this wonder.
Prince Boyi of Yongyang came to govern Wuxing and went to the mountain to receive the precepts. He established the Fangdeng Repentance ritual for seven days and nights.
While in the commandery, he managed affairs by day and practiced contemplation by night. One day, Zhiyi said to his disciple Zhiyue, "I wish to exhort the Prince to cultivate [the Way]."

"Merit wards off calamity. Yue, having become king, was already diligent in advancing on the Path; if he were to speak further, those who did not understand would consider it flattery. He therefore desisted.

Shortly thereafter, the king went out hunting and fell from his horse, nearly losing his life. Fayi led the assembly in performing the *Guanyin Chanting Ritual* (*Guanyin Chanfa*), whereupon the king arose and sat leaning against a couch.
He saw a monk holding an incense burner, approaching to offer greetings to the king. At that time, the king’s tears...
He broke into a sweat and did not know how to answer. The monk then circumambulated the king once, and the pain immediately ceased.

The king composed a vow-text to demonstrate his reverence and faith; as it contains many words, it is not recorded here in full. After some time, an imperial edict was issued summoning him to bestow the precepts.

Zhiyi initially declined, but seven successive envoys arrived, each bearing a handwritten letter from the Emperor. He then reluctantly departed for the capital. By imperial decree, he was to travel in a sheep-drawn carriage, led by a youth.
The Master was escorted by the Chief Secretary and the Attendant Scribe; the ceremonial protocol followed the precedent established for the National Teacher, the Venerable Cui.

He was welcomed into the Eastern Hall of the Taiji Palace, where he lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. The Emperor and the hundred officials attended the assembly to listen. Consequently, an edict was issued to establish a community of Chan practitioners at Lingyao Monastery.
Later, the Master again lectured on the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* before the Emperor in the palace hall. The Sangha Rectifier Hui-geng and the Sangha Superintendent... [text ends]

Huìkuàng, a great virtuous monk of the capital, raised several difficult challenges. Zhìyǐ responded with detailed eloquence and agility. Huìkēng, holding an incense burner, congratulated him, saying:
"In the state’s assemblies, there were over ten seats [of masters], and I was humbled to be one of those invited for the four lectures. I considered myself unrivaled by others;
yet now the great sun has risen, while the moon and stars still shine—am I not a pitiful hand? Later, he resided at Guāngyào Temple, where he practiced both meditation and wisdom."

Jianhong followed him with an especially large retinue, and the Emperor issued an edict praising him. At that time, the government was conducting a census of monks and nuns and proposed that those who failed the scriptural examinations be forced to leave the monastic order.
Zhiyi submitted a memorial to remonstrate, saying: "Devadatta recited sixty thousand elephant-skin volumes of scripture yet could not escape hell;

Pindola recited a single line of verse yet attained the fruit of Arhatship. What matters in earnest discussion is the nature of the Way itself; how could it depend on the quantity [of one's learning]?"
He recited [the scriptures]. The Emperor then issued an edict halting the previous plan, intending to move him elsewhere because he felt Lingyao was too cramped.
He dreamed of a person providing solemn and orderly protection, from Bi to Guanda, requesting that he reside at Sanqiao. Zhiyi remarked, "Guanda is the Dharma-name of Emperor Wu of Liang."

Sankei Itsukō resided there; he moved his dwelling to that location. When the Emperor visited the temple, he bestowed great offerings and issued an imperial decree for him to lecture on the *Ninnō-kyō*.

Among the assembly, the Emperor prostrated himself before him in accordance with the rites. From the Crown Prince downward, all followed his disciplinary model. Thus, an edict issued from within the palace regarding the reception of the Dharma stated:
"I reverently reflect that [the Master’s] guidance is boundless, saving sentient beings according to their capacities, protecting the land, and drawing them upward."
O Celestial Being, your radiant brilliance illuminates all; you have entrusted your traces to teachers and friends. The omen of the bhikṣu entering the dream has long been manifest;
the arrival of the Honored One (Huiguo) makes the virtue of the high seat resplendent. Therefore, I direct my mind toward the Ten Stages and thirstily look up to the Four Reliances.

Regarding the two vehicles of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and the two teachings of the inner and outer [Buddhism], the honoring of teachers and the revering of the Way have been esteemed since time immemorial. I humbly hope that you will look down upon us with compassion;
may we form karmic ties through successive lifetimes so as to fulfill our original vows, and may these increase day by day. I now respectfully invite you to serve as my Bodhisattva Precept Master.
Suddenly, as the incense was passed to me, tears fell—how extraordinary! When Jinling fell into ruin, I took up my staff and traveled toward Jingzhou and Xiangzhou along the road.
Next, he arrived at Yicheng. An old monk appeared in a dream and said, "The auspicious image of Tao Kan respectfully requests that you deign to protect and uphold it.

He subsequently stayed at Mount Kuanglu, where he beheld the Mañjuśrī image painted by Huiyuan; he took up residence there and could not bear to leave. Shortly thereafter, rebels rose up and the temple buildings were completely destroyed.
Only this mountain stood towering and solitary; thus, that dream was fulfilled. When the Sui dynasty unified the realm, Prince Jin assumed the heavy responsibilities over the Huai and Hai regions.

Admiring his virtuous influence, he desired to receive and wear the precepts and took him as his teacher. Although he requested three times in writing, Huiyi declined with humility and had no leisure to comply.
Later, he set forth four vows, the first of which was: "Do not expect me to transmit the methods of Chan."
Second, it means not to demand strict adherence to formal rules. Third, it means that if one follows the constraints of monastic discipline, one’s comings and goings are heavy with obligation;
if one prioritizes the transmission of the Dharma lamp, one’s comings and goings are light. The essential point is to master the Dharma; do not begrudge slight movements or changes.

Fourth, it means that if thoughts of seclusion arise, one may follow one's heart in seeking food and drink to bring one’s remaining years to an end. Thereupon, the King personally composed a text to request [his presence]. This was in the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era.
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month, a thousand-monk assembly was convened at Jincheng, the Governor-General of Yangzhou.

[The King] respectfully invited [Zhiyi] to bestow the Bodhisattva precepts. At his residence, the Dharma of Incense was transmitted. Zhiyi bestowed the name "Zhongchi" upon the King, and the King likewise titled Zhiyi "Zhizhe.
When the assembly concluded, the King bestowed generous gifts upon him; Zhiyi gave them all away in dedication to the two [monks], Bei and Jing.
Tian immediately wished to take his leave, but the King earnestly entreated him to stay. Huiyi said, "We have already made a formal agreement; how could I violate it?

He shook out his robes and rose, returning once more to Mount Kuang before eventually going back to his native land. There he practiced the Way and cultivated merit to repay the kindness of the earth.

Elders and children came to welcome and attend him; his sites for ordination and lecture halls numbered in the tens of thousands. He selected Mount Yquan in Dangyang County to establish a vihāra, which was subsequently granted an imperial plaque.
Regarding the first sound: formerly, this land was desolate and perilous, with snakes and beasts preying upon one another. Once the vihāra was established, these atrocities ceased.
During a spring drought, the people spread a rumor that the deity was angry. Huiyi therefore led the assembly to the source of the spring and recited the sutras;

he moved the spirits to send down clouds and rain, and the false rumors subsided accordingly. Wang Jiji, the Duke of Yiyang and Regional Commander of Jiangling, broke into a profuse sweat during his prostrations.
He said to the man: "Having led armies many times, I have never been as fearful as I am today upon the battlefield; this must surely be because the devas and nāgas are reproaching and protecting me.

At that time, the Prince of Jin sent another personal letter requesting his presence. Zhiyi replied with a letter declining the invitation. When the request was repeated in a second letter, he finally consented to go.
For this occasion, he composed a commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. He was accompanied by Yingfeng, Liu Guyan of Hedong, and [others] from Donghai.

Xu Yi accepted [the scripture] and treasured it as a precious possession, entrusting it to Wang Shishi. Later, he sent Gu Yan with a letter requesting that [Zhiyi] save Princess Xiao from her illness.
Zhiyi then led his companions to perform the seven-day *Jin guangming* repentance ritual.
On the night of the sixth day, a strange bird flew into the altar; it writhed as if dead, then suddenly flew away. Furthermore, the sound of a pig was heard outside.
The sound [of the bird] was heard. Zhiyi said, "The Consort shall surely recover. That the bird died and was reborn, and the pig was hidden and then revealed—these are all auspicious omens.
At dawn, the Consort’s illness indeed abated, and the King was greatly delighted. Zhiyi returned to Mount Tai and performed the previous repentance rites once more, making a vow, saying:
"If I am able to bring benefit to the Triple Gem, I shall devote the remainder of these years to it; if there is no benefit, I shall immediately undergo transformation [into extinction]."
Thus he attained rebirth. He said, "The reason I have long desired to return to the mountains is precisely because the signs of my end were revealed by the spirits.

After my death, you must pile stones and plant pine trees, and bury me in a pit on the southwestern peak to provide a place of rest. Erect a white stupa above it so that those who see it may give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.
Furthermore, transmit the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith) and its commentary through oral instruction to serve as a lesson for future generations. He then commanded Zhi...
Zhiyi went to the Maitreya statue at Shicheng Temple in Shan County. He swept and sprinkled the area, arranged a bed against the eastern wall, and lit many incense sticks and lamps.
Zhiyi then faced west and lay down to visualize Amitābha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta. He divided his ritual implements into two portions.

One [robe] was offered to Maitreya; one was set aside for the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual). He requested his three robes, alms bowl, staff, and personal effects, or else he had medicine brought forward.
Zhiyi waved it away, saying: "Medicine can dispel illness, but can it preserve the remainder of one's years? Illness does not unite with the body; what, then, is there for medicine to dispel?"
"When one's years do not accord with the mind, what purpose do medicines serve? Furthermore, he advanced toward his meal and drink, then waved them away, saying:
'Is it by following one's shadow that one observes the fast? To be without observation and without conditions—that is the true fast. He said to Zhi Xi:

'Have you not heard the teachings within the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Discourse on Observing the Mind)? Why are you so preoccupied, disturbing yourself with medical treatments and worldly affairs? My life..."
The vessel of the poison of toil; death brings joyful rest. This is indeed the nature of the world; there is no need for excessive lamentation.
Furthermore, he wrote seven sheets by hand, along with his commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, a rhinoceros-horn *cintāmaṇi*, and a lotus incense burner, as parting gifts for Prince Jin.
He entrusted him with the Great Dharma. In those writings, it says: "The *cintāmaṇi* and incense burner were originally obtained from the Great King; I now return them to you as a gift in parting."
I hope that the fragrance of virtue may be spread forever and that you may always preserve your well-being as you wish.

Furthermore, chant together the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the praises of the *Amitāyus-sūtra*, and discourse upon such dharmas as the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*), the four non-arisings, the ten dharma-realms (*daśadhātuparyāya*), the three contemplations, the four teachings, the four immeasurables (*catvāryapramāṇāni*), and the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).

Someone asked about the stages and positions of spiritual cultivation. Zhiyi replied: "You all are too lazy to plant roots of goodness; regarding the merits of others, you are like a blind man asking about milk."

"Śāriputra, one who stumbles asks for the way. I do not lead a multitude; I must purify the six sense faculties and sacrifice myself for others, having barely attained the rank of the five internal stages.
Now that my teachers and friends have come to welcome me, how could I afford to look elsewhere?
However, the *Prātimokṣa* is what you revere, and the four kinds of samādhi are your clear guide. Have the *vina* master prepare the bells and chimes."
He took the exhaustion of his vital breath as his appointed end. Those who were forbidden from wailing sat upright and passed away as if entering meditative absorption.
He was sixty-seven years old. This was on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era.

Toward the end of the Renshou era, he shook his mendicant’s staff and donned his robes, manifesting his presence seven times: six times descending upon mountain monasteries and once traveling to Fulong. Such were his spiritual wonders. Upon reaching...
When Emperor Yang was on the throne, he was particularly strict in his supervision of the shrines and stupas; he kept the keys himself to ensure the doors were opened and closed with care.

On the anniversary of [the Master’s] death, the court was suspended, and an envoy was dispatched to the mountains to perform sacrifices. When the Chief Secretary Yang Su requested to personally visit the site, he still saw that the Master’s body remained whole and had not decomposed.
Furthermore, while the Master was still alive, ears grew upon the trees without waiting for cultivation; they could be gathered at will.
There was nothing lacking in what he gathered. By this time, even with diligent cultivation, nothing more could be obtained. Originally, the people of Linhai had made their livelihood by fishing;

the coastal barriers and river dams stretched for over four hundred li. Zhiyi used the funds from his offerings to purchase the land from government officials to establish it as a *fangsheng chi* (a pond for releasing living beings).
He dispatched the śramaṇa Huibai to submit a memorial to the throne. Emperor Xuan issued an edict imposing strict prohibitions against fishing in the area. The state...

His disciple, Xu Xiaokē, Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, composed an inscription for the stele erected on the seashore; its words were so profoundly sorrowful that readers wept as they read it.
Later, a flock of yellow sparrows flew up to the temple, crying out for three days before dispersing. Zhìyǐ believed this was because the fish had been moved by his virtue.
During the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, the previous prohibition was reaffirmed. He also authored commentaries on the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Mohe Zhiguan*.

He composed works such as the *Menxiu chandifa* (Methods for Cultivating Dhyāna at the Gate), each numbering several dozen fascicles, as well as thirty-seven fascicles of commentaries on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.

All of these were orally transmitted by him; his attendant Guanding recorded them in writing, and they have circulated in the world. He founded thirty-five monasteries and ordained over four thousand monks.

He transcribed fifteen sets of the Buddhist canon (*piṭaka*), using gold for their covers and sandalwood for their carving. He produced approximately one hundred thousand painted images of honored deities and received the Bodhisattva precepts.
His disciples who practiced meditation were too numerous to be recorded. Those who transmitted his teachings directly numbered thirty-two.
Huìyào of the Sui dynasty, surnamed Qí, was a native of Xiāngyáng. From his youth, he was grave and reserved; though slow of speech, he was quick in action. People held him in high esteem.
After receiving full ordination, he traveled extensively to seek the Way from Mìnggōng of Zhèngchuān and Sīgōng of Wèiyuè, and he served Sīgōng until the end.

Master Si [Tanyou] practiced for many years. He told Huiaoyuan that regarding the contemplation of the principle of *dharmatā* (the true nature of reality), there was a profound and subtle significance.

When Master Si announced his passing, Huiaoyuan happened to be traveling to propagate the Dharma in Baqiu, where he met the Dharma Master Daoyi; they traveled together westward and took up residence at Daoyin Temple in Jiangling.
There, he did not step outside his quarters for fourteen years. When Zhiyi returned to his native village, [Huiaoyuan’s practice] became even more profound.
I humbly pay my respects. In the second year of the Renshou era, he moved to Neihua Temple and established a separate *dōjō* to the west of Kaisheng Temple to practice the joy of *dhyāna*.
He also recited the mantras of the Seven Buddhas and others, which were especially efficacious. Whenever anyone suffered from illness, there was no request that did not prove effective.
Toward the end of the Daye era, tiger attacks became rampant; when Huoyao encountered a tiger, he stroked its head and spoke to it, saying, "Heaven..."
The disturbances below were in chaos; he told him, "You may depart to a distant place, lest you suffer at the hands of the common people. The tiger’s violence was subsequently extinguished.
Yang Daosheng, the leader of the eight garrisons' rebels, also extended sincere hospitality to him. When Xiao Xian usurped the throne, he continued to offer him honor and support.

Whenever there were gifts bestowed, [Huiyuan] would immediately plant them in the two fields of compassion and reverence, never hoarding even the slightest amount. He established the Longgui Vihāra within the city precincts.
Xian once asked him about the rise and fall of dynasties. He replied, "I, a man of meager virtue, shall not be able to remain long as a virtuous friend to my patron.
At that time, Xian could not fathom these words. Before long, the Tang army arrived and Xian perished. Huiaoyao passed away during the Wude era at the age of sixty;
he was buried beside the stupa of National Teacher Kaisheng Zikuang.

The Sui dynasty monk Sengcan was a man of unknown origins. Initially, while still a layman (*avadātavasana*), he went to see Master Ke and asked him, "I, your disciple, am afflicted with a chronic wind-illness;
this must surely be due to the accumulation of karmic offenses from past lives. I beg the Master to help me repent for these sins. Ke said, "Bring forth your offenses, and I will repent them for you.
Sengcan replied, "I have searched for my offenses, but they are utterly unfindable. Ke said, "I have repented them for you."
[The master’s] reprimand ended. [Nanyue] said, "One ought to rely upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Guanzhao said, "Now that I have seen the Upādhyāya, I already know who the Sangha is.
But I do not yet understand what is the Buddha and what is the Dharma. [The master] replied, "This very mind is the Buddha;

this very mind is the Dharma. The Dharma and the Buddha are non-dual; the Jewel of the Sangha is likewise so. Guanzhao said, "Only today do I begin to know that the nature of sin is neither within nor without."
In the interim, as the essence of mind is thus, the Buddha-dharma is non-dual; it may be called "My Treasure. He was then named Sengcan, tonsured, and ordained with full precepts.
The robe and alms bowl were transmitted to him, and he was further instructed: "In the past, the Great Master Bodhidharma entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to me;
I now entrust it to you. You must protect and uphold it well. This occurred during the period when Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty suppressed the Buddhist teachings.
He traveled to and from Mount Sīkōng for over ten years, concealing his brilliance and hiding his traces so that no one knew him.

At the beginning of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, he went to reside on Mount Huánggōng, where he found the śramaṇa Dàoxìn to inherit his lineage and entrusted him with the robe and bowl he had transmitted.
He then spoke this verse: "The seeds of flowers, though they depend upon the earth, From the earth the flowers grow. If there were no one to plant them..."
He planted flowers until the ground was entirely covered in non-arising. Thereupon, he went to Mount Luofu, where he lived in leisure for two years.

In the second year of the Daye era, he returned once more to his former mountain to preach the Dharma to the assembly. He passed away while standing solemnly with palms joined. His śarīra were enshrined at Shushan Valley Temple.
During the reign of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang dynasty, he was posthumously honored with the title Jingzhi (Mirror-Wisdom).
Zhiqian of the Sui dynasty was of the Xiahou clan of Yuzhang. In his youth, he relied upon Master Lang; at Xinghuang Temple in Yangzhou, he lectured on the Five Treatises.
In the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era, he studied Chan methods under Master Zhiyi of Tiantai. His power of mindfulness was exceptionally strong, and Zhiyi praised and esteemed him.
Shortly thereafter, he lectured on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Lotus Sūtra*, and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, among others. He was also proficient in non-Buddhist studies.
He was prolific in his writings. In his later years, he returned to Mount Lu, where he renovated both Dali and Xilin Monasteries.

However, he ultimately remained committed to Dali for twenty years. Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, drawn by his reputation, sent an invitation with great reverence, but the Master declined the summons.

Shortly thereafter, lay devotees from Yuzhang arrived at his mountain retreat requesting him to preach; he declined on account of his old age and illness, saying, "I am a man of the hills and valleys; I shall die among the hills."
"Could he have died amidst the bustle of a city? Before long, the virtuous of his home district urged him to go;
having no other choice, he departed, only to pass away shortly thereafter. Yet, death within a city was ultimately unavoidable—such is fate.

This occurred in the sixth month of the sixth year of the Daye era. He was seventy-eight years of age. His entire body was enshrined within a stone chamber, and his countenance remained largely undecayed."
It has undergone transformations, yet remains as if alive to this day.
The Sui dynasty śramaṇa Poyao was a native of Goguryeo. During the time when the Chen family held the kingdom, he traveled to study in Jinling;
by the Sui dynasty, he had come to attend at the imperial capital. In the sixteenth year of the Kaihuang era, he entered Tiantai to rely upon the Wisdom Teacher (Zhiyi). However...
His faculties were sharp and keen, and he quickly attained realization. A wise man once said to him, "You have a karmic affinity for this place.
Mount Huading is where I formerly practiced *dhūta* austerities; unless one possesses the capacity of a Mahāyāna vessel, one must not go there.
You should instead focus on perfecting your sublime conduct. As for all necessities such as food and clothing, you need have no cause for anxiety. In the eighteenth year of the Kaihuang era,
Having first set out alone with his staff to practice what he had been taught, sixteen years of cold and heat passed until the ninth year of the Daye era.
During this time, both body and shadow vanished, and he remained untouched by the secular world.

In the second month of that year, suddenly perceiving that his life was nearing its end, he went to Guoqing Temple. A few days later, he indeed passed away peacefully in the temple without illness at the age of fifty.
Second, when the funerary niche was about to exit the gate, the corpse turned around; it opened its eyes while facing inward, as if to bid farewell.
Afterward, it returned to its original position facing outward and closed its eyes as before. Those who witnessed this were struck with wonder.
The Sui dynasty śramaṇa Fayan was the son of the Zhang family of Qinghe. When the Northern Zhou abolished the Buddhist teachings, he traveled south and arrived at Jinling.

In the seventh year of the Taizhuan era of the Chen dynasty, he followed Zhiyi up Mount Tai, where he devoted himself to his instruction and edification. He frequently stayed among burial mounds and beneath the trees.

He sat constantly and never lay down; whenever he entered meditative concentration, he would remain for seven days before rising. Even when mountain deities attempted to disturb him, he remained unmoved.

He practiced in this manner for thirty years. He once sought confirmation of his realization from Zhiyi, who told him that this was the second stage of the "contemplation of the eight liberations" (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
On the thirtieth day of the second month in the seventh year of the Daye era, he passed away at Guoqing Temple at the age of sixty.
Zhi Yue of the Sui dynasty was born into the Zheng clan; he was a native of Nanyang. In his youth, his aspirations were already set on leaving secular life.

When his father wished to give him a wife, he would not consent. Upon reaching maturity, he possessed great capability and talent. Prince Yueyang summoned him to serve under him in Jingzhou, but he firmly declined. The prince perceived the sincerity of his fundamental character.
He was ordained as a renunciant. At that time, Zhiyi was preaching the Dharma in Jinling, and [the Master] followed him from the north to receive his teachings.
He studied the Six Subtle Gates and the Five Gates daily. His practice was dedicated to the Vinaya, and he had mastered the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

He lived with a water jar that remained perpetually full. On Mount Lushan by the sea, there was a monastery built by foreign monks; its spiritual wonders were manifold. Zhiyi frequently instructed [the Master] to sit in meditation there.
In the interim, once the Wise One (Zhiyi) had retired to Mount Tiantai, he was asked to lead the assembly. For more than twenty years, he guided others with gentle and sincere benevolence;

truly, he was without shame in bearing his heavy responsibility. When Empress Mu of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty passed away, he established a vegetarian feast and offered prayers, obtaining silk in the hundreds.
During the reign of Emperor Yang, on the anniversary of the Wise One’s death, the government provided for a thousand monks.

During his fasts, Yue would invariably provide from his own stores to fulfill the offerings for the alms. Zheng Xiebo, the Prefectural Governor of Kuaizhou, and Yang Shengui, the Garrison Commander of Linhai, shared a relationship with Yue that was both teacher and friend.
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month in the twelfth year of the Daye era, he fell ill while resting and passed away after ten days, lying on his right side; he was seventy-four years of age.
Daoyue of the Sui dynasty was a native of Zhaoqiu in Jingzhou. At the age of twelve, he left home to become a monk at Yuquan Temple.

He lived in poverty with austere integrity and devoted himself especially to the recitation of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Previously, Zhiyi had once found a piece of extraordinary stone in the waters of a mountain stream;
when suspended and struck, its resonance was clear and penetrating. To this day, it is used in place of bells and chimes, and Daoyue [was the one who utilized it].

Whenever he entrusted his thoughts to them, whenever he sought to perceive the former masters and brought forth their voices, his mind would become clear and cool. Such was the sincerity of his cultivation and the efficacy of his auspicious resonance;

it was only fitting. During the rebellion of Zhu Can, Huiyue suffered from chronic abdominal distension. As there were no skilled physicians in the region, he spent his days reading the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra, seeking its protective empowerment.

Suddenly, his abdomen felt as if it were being torn open, and upon going to the latrine, he discharged a torrent of waste. His illness was immediately cured. During the chaos of Zhu Can’s rebellion...

The monks of the temple fled, and none remained; Huiyue alone stayed behind to guard it, refusing to leave. When the bandits came to demand provisions, Huiyue reduced his own rations and gave them what he had.
The bandits’ fires could not cook the food, so they warned one another not to take anything. Other bandits did not yet believe this.

As they were about to drive him out and inflict harm upon him, Yue sat resolutely and said, "I wish to perish together with this temple. They then felt pity for him and released him, asking him to lead the way.
After walking only a few paces, he sat down again and said, "How could I, a śramaṇa, act as a guide for others? This physical form is but a floating illusion; why fear death?
The bandits marveled at him and escorted him back to the temple. When King Hanyang heard of his reputation, he revered and admired him, and invited him [to court].

In the "Chapter on Receiving the Precepts," [the King] offered a single set of robes as a gift, but [the Master] declined it. He then presented him with three robes made of coarse cloth and asked why he did not wear silk. He replied:

"Silk garments cause great harm to sentient beings, which contradicts the reputation of one who practices patience (*kṣānti*). Cloth robes are easy to produce, manifesting the appearance of compassion (*maitrī*).
The King said: "Zhongyou felt no shame [in wearing coarse clothes], yet Confucius praised him. Since a śramaṇa practices loving-kindness and patience, this is indeed what is appropriate for him."
He lived as a mountain dweller for over fifty years; by the time of his death, he was seventy-two years old.
During the Yonghui era, someone saw a monk at Qingxi carrying a staff and walking barefoot, who called himself Master Prajñā.
Commentators believed this was because when Huaiyue was still alive, he often recited the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra, and thus [the monk] spoke in that way.

The Section on the Transmission of the Lineage of the Wisdom-Training School: Zhi Xi of the Tang dynasty was a native of the Chen clan from Yingchuan. Later, due to official travel, he moved his residence to Min and Yue. Xi had long been awakened to the truth.

The world is an illusion. Desiring to escape the entanglements of the mundane, he heard that the Wise One (Zhi-zhe) was guiding the transformation of the realm from Mount Tiantai using the finger-pointing of the Three Contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).

At the age of twenty, he first obtained an audience with him; they were established as teacher and disciple. He became fully endowed with the monastic precepts (*vinaya*) and diligently advanced in the cultivation of meditative discipline.

Subsequently, when the Wise One manifested his passing, he left a final instruction for Xi to reside at the Xiu Chan Monastery on Mount Fulong. After a long time, he crossed the waters and was about to...
They were constructing a sutra platform. The workmen suggested that since Mount Xiangluo (Incense Burner Peak) abounded in *qing* and cypress trees, it would be appropriate to fell them for use.

Daoxi immediately informed [the Master], but Daoxi refused, saying, "The spirit of the mountain is not easily provoked. The next day, he suddenly ordered them to go there anyway. An attendant said, "Is the Master mistaken?
Yesterday you did not permit it, yet today you have reversed your decision. What is to be done? Daoxi told him the reason: "Last night I dreamed of someone coming to deliver [the timber]."
Regarding the offering of *chēng* and cypress wood: previously, Zhìzhě had purchased several hundred li of land by the sea to establish a *fangshēng chí* (a pond for releasing living beings).

Throughout the Chen and Sui dynasties, the local officials strictly prohibited fishing and hunting in accordance with the Dharma. However, at this time, lawless and insolent people completely disregarded these prohibitions.
When Xi learned of this, he joined Master Dǐng in burning incense and praying to Zhìzhě; from then on, there were no more [transgressions] along the Liáng and Hù rivers.
Having attained this, the fishermen made a pact to promote virtue. One day, he told his disciple Tongxuan:
"In the evening, a monk will arrive. Shortly thereafter, a monk wearing robes and carrying a staff and bowl appeared at a distance of one thousand twenty paces.
He hurried toward the east and vanished. Immediately, the sound of a bell resounded from the eastern valley. Xī said, "This is summoning me. He then had his disciples prepare his bath and robes.

Sitting upon the terrace at night, he held a *ruyi* (ceremonial fly-whisk) and preached the Dharma. His words were profound and silent for a long while. The disciples called out to one another in grief.
He opened his eyes again and said, "The phenomena of birth and death in this world—how can they be so worthy of sorrow? Depart; do not disturb me."
"Trouble me," [he said]. He further remarked, "Since I entered the Way, forty-nine years have passed without my side having touched a bed.
Yet, regarding the offerings of the faithful and the incense, I have never dared to be remiss; you disciples, moreover, ought to exert yourselves with diligence so as to carry on this work.
When his disciples asked where he would be reborn, he replied, "In a dream long ago, I saw the northwest of the Tuṣita Heaven; the palace there was blue..."
"Shaku, our former master, the Wise One, was here. The celestial beings and humans on both sides were all seated upon jeweled thrones, yet one throne alone was empty.
I asked for the reason, and the former master replied, 'Six years after my consecration, he shall come and sit upon this. Thus we know the efficacy of rebirth.
The following morning, he ordered the assembly of the temple to assemble early. Those who had come to inquire after his illness took their leave after the midday meal.
Xī detained him, saying, "You have come from afar with great hardship; wait but a moment. How can you go? The man firmly declined.
Xī spoke again, saying, "If you will not stay, you may depart quickly. It is about to rain. At that time, the sun was bright and clear, without a single cloud.
A short while later, Xī passed away, and the rain fell suddenly and heavily. This was the eighteenth day of the twelfth month in the first year of the Zhenguan era.
He lived to the age of seventy-two and was buried two hundred paces in front of the Zhi-zhe (Jñānabhadra) Grotto.
Fa-xiang of the Tang dynasty was born into the Li family of Ge-gang in Hai-ling, Yang-zhou. He stood eight *chi* tall, with refined and well-proportioned features and a majestic bearing.
By nature he was solemn and grave, speaking little and seldom smiling. There was a black mole on the sole of his foot, which physiognomists considered [a sign of great merit].
He was destined to attain great renown throughout the world. At the age of sixteen, he left the household life and practiced the dhūta austerities, dwelling in purity.

He especially devoted himself to the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Master Gong of Qixia Monastery on Mount She opened a retreat chamber beside the monastery for him, where he was instructed to practice the repentance rites of Zhiyi for twenty-one days;
he frequently witnessed auspicious responses. Later, he entered the capital and returned to his hometown of Daining.
He practiced seated meditation at a temple at the request of the monk Zhixi. One day, while napping during the day, he started up in alarm and cried out, "A fire has broken out!
Zhixi crawled out in all directions and looked around, but there was nothing there. [Tanyou] remarked, "It was merely a vision caused by the five delusions.
The next day it happened again, occurring three times in total. He then went to Ninghai; not long after, the rebel Li Zitong attacked and occupied the sea region.

The area was ravaged and nearly completely consumed by fire. At that time, tigers were causing extraordinary havoc, so [the people] were performing *zhai* (fasting) and offering prayers for protection.
Suddenly, a tiger entered a room and snatched a person away. [Seng]xiang pursued it from behind, calling out, "Why do you act so rashly? You must release this person! The tiger then released him.

It was as if there were someone who understood his intent. Shortly thereafter, a pack of tigers gathered; Xiang struck their heads all over with a staff while preaching the Dharma to them. He then intended to go wandering...
At Tiantai, he said to his disciples: "I cannot reach Tiantai by its own power; I have merely a karmic affinity with a certain mountain in Jiangnan.
Upon crossing the river, he stayed at Jiangyin. Monastics and laypeople alike looked up to him in reverence, and he established Dingshan Temple there.
After some time, he further established Zhengjian Temple on Mount Gu at Yanting and resided there. In the fourth year of the Zhenguan era...
In the winter, he suddenly took leave of his disciples, saying, "I have recently had evil dreams; my illness will likely not end.
After lying ill for twenty days, he requested hot water to bathe and washed his head, then sat in the full lotus position facing west and passed away at the age of eighty-seven.

Having originally wished to offer his body to birds and beasts, yet fearing that they would mangle it in a messy heap and provoke the derision of those who saw it, he instead ordered that he be buried to the west of the mountain.
In the southern corner, when they reached this spot and dug into the earth, they found a stone; the cavity was barely large enough to accommodate a coffin, yet a stupa had been built upon it.
Xiang’s previous words had often been proven prescient. In the second year of the Zhenguan era, Xiang spoke to herself alone, saying:

"A woman from Youzhou, wearing a black silk cloth headscarf, entrusted me with a message for a merchant in Changzhou. It has been a long time since she came; why has she not returned? She then dispatched [a messenger].
The disciples opposed this. Hardly had they reached the gate when someone indeed arrived with a headcloth. Those who had previously obtained one took it up, toyed with it, and sighed with regret;
they quickly tore it apart and divided it among themselves, giving a piece to each person. Those who did not receive a piece were at that time filled with suspicion.

Three years later, by imperial decree, all monks and nuns who had been privately ordained during the Yining era were summoned from throughout the realm; they were all dismissed and returned to the common registers of the population. As for the headcloths—
The prophecy proved true. That year there was a great snowfall, several feet deep. He called to his disciples to fetch fresh vegetables.

The disciples replied that because of the snow and the cold, it was not the season for obtaining vegetables. He said, "There are some on the mountain. Thereupon, they went up the mountain as instructed.
After traveling several li, they reached the foot of a tree and indeed found vegetables; they were all green and tender, fit for soup or eating.
Tang Guanding, whose courtesy name was Fayun, was surnamed Wu. His ancestors were originally from Yixing in Changzhou;
his grandfather moved to Zhang’an in Linhai and settled there. When Guanding was three months old, his father passed away.

Before he could speak, his mother happened to recite the names of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and Guanding mimicked her. His pronunciation and phrasing were clear and eloquent, which left his family members astonished. Thereupon—
When Master Zheng of Shejing Temple heard of this, he sighed in admiration, saying, "This child is no ordinary person. Consequently, his mother named him Fan-ping (No Ordinary).
At the age of seven, he was made a disciple of Zheng. His studies progressed daily, and at twenty, he received full ordination, whereupon his reputation grew even further.
This continued until the passing of Zheng, which occurred during the early years of the Zhide era of the Chen dynasty. [Then came] Tiantai Master Zhiyi.
When the Duke went forth to take up his post at Kuangzhai, Zhiying followed him. He delved deeply into the gates of contemplation and frequently received the Master’s seal of approval.
When the reign of the Chen dynasty came to an end, he followed Zhizhe on a tour of Mount Lu. He stayed for a long time at Yuquan Temple in Jiangling.

In the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Emperor Yang, while still the Prince of Jin, was stationed in Weiyang; there he received from Zhizhe the *rājā-śīla* (the precepts for kings). Shortly thereafter, [the Emperor] returned.
Tai-ling. Zhiyi followed him there once more. In the seventeenth year, when Zhiyi fell ill, Huiding attended to him with the utmost propriety. Before long, Zhiyi passed away.
Following his final instructions, Huiding presented the Master’s handwritten letters and personal effects as a report to the Prince of Jin.

Subsequently, by imperial decree, Wang Hong, the司马 (Sima) of the Yangzhou General Commandery, was dispatched to escort Huiding back to the mountain, where he further provided a meal for a thousand monks at the monastery.
He expressed his sentiments of longing remembrance and planned to establish Guoqing Temple.

In the first year of the Renshou era, when the Prince of Jin succeeded to the throne as Crown Prince, Zhiyi entered the capital to offer congratulations and to express his gratitude for the establishment of Guoqing.

By imperial decree, Zhang Qianwei, a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, was sent to escort him back to the mountain, where he was granted three thousand bolts of silk and three hundred rolls of felt. Furthermore, a meal was provided for one thousand monks at the mountain, and the temple was additionally adorned.
At that monastery, in the second year [of his reign], the Emperor issued an edict stating: "The summer season is scorching; the physical body of the Way requires rest and comfort.

The joy of *dhyāna* nourishes the spirit, and thus it possesses many excellent qualities. Recently, I have ordered the two masters Zhuang and Lun of the Huiri Monastery to lecture on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, using entirely the commentaries of Zhiyi to analyze and explain the scriptural text.
Since the Meditation Master is a preeminent disciple of the Great Master and has been entrusted with the Dharma-gate, now..."
He sent Yan Qu, who was certain to receive a gracious imperial favor; the commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was also dispatched with him to the capital.
[The Emperor] awaited his arrival, yet this letter could not fully express his intentions. Tíng subsequently entered the capital and remained there for three summers.

In the seventh year of the Daye era, when the Emperor marshaled his troops at Zhuoye, he issued an edict for Tíng to appear at his temporary residence. On the seventh day of the eighth month in the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away due to illness.
At Guoqing Temple, his lifespan was seventy-two years. Previously, he had said to his disciples:

"I have often heard from the Maitreya Sūtra that when the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa, incense smoke will rise like clouds; you must burn much incense, for I am about to depart. Thereupon, he bestowed final instructions upon his sons.
Thereupon, he rose and joined his palms in reverence as if beholding something sacred, while orally reciting the name of Amitābha.
Nine days later, he was interred on the southern mountain of the temple. Zixing was compassionate by nature and skillful in benefiting sentient beings.
When a person in that village fell ill, their child would run to him for rescue; Zixing would then burn sandalwood incense and recite sutras, and the illness—
Those who smelled its fragrance were immediately healed. Furthermore, the southern ridge of Anzhou Le’an was exceptionally sublime;

whenever the Master passed over its summit, he would look around and admire it, sighing, "I regret that it is not level and smooth. Could it not be used to establish a monastery for the sake of teaching and preaching?
Less than ten days later, white sand and yellow soil welled up like a mirror's surface. He once preached the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Lei.
At Kye-sa Temple, while the bells and drums were sounding together, pirates arrived. Amidst the chaotic clash of shields and spears, [the Master] showed no sign of fear on his face;

sitting upon a lion throne and holding a fly-whisk, he remained composed. The pirates, however, suddenly fled in terror. This was because [the Master] was actually a human being over ten feet tall, who had approached brandishing halberds and spears to confront him.
At Bul-nyong Temple, the disciples constructed a stone stupa using two separate stones for the door; among them was the disciple Gwangyeong.
He obtained a stone slab one zhang thick; striking its surface with his staff, he drew a line across it and said, "Only when it is thus shall it be usable.

Thereupon, the stone split into two pieces at his touch. He used it for the stupa, and even a master craftsman could not have achieved such a result. He propagated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* at Chengxin Jingśe Monastery.
At that time, Dharma Master Jizang was so deeply impressed by his interpretations of the doctrine that he disbanded his assembly and traveled eastward to meet him.
I have humbly received his instructions. As for the talent and eloquence of the Wise One, he alone was capable of upholding it—namely, Dharma Master Ding.
Therefore, his records remain complete; I shall not enumerate them here at length. The inscription on the stele was composed by the śramaṇa Faxuan of Hongshan Temple in Changzhou.

Tang Zhishou was born into the Huangfu clan of Anding; he was a descendant of the Master Xuanyan of the Jin dynasty. Later, his family moved to the banks of the Zhang River, where they resided for generations.
Initially, he took refuge with Chan Master Zhimin, a senior disciple of Master Chou at Yunmen Temple in Xiangzhou, and entered the monastic order.
Zhimin considered the precepts to be the foundation of concentration and wisdom; since Zhishou was still a mere child, he had him first practice and master them. Once...

Her mother also received the tonsure at a public monastery and was named Fashi. She was highly esteemed by the community of nuns for her observance of the Eight Respectful Precepts and the five codes of conduct.

Although Shou had severed her worldly attachments, she still harbored lingering emotions; wishing that she might early on enter the stream of the Dharma and be richly imbued with the flavor of the Path, she petitioned Min, who conferred upon her the full ordination (upasaṃpadā).
Shou then traveled extensively in search of a master worthy of emulation, yet such a person was truly difficult to find. Thus, three times—

In the year [X], he finally fulfilled his original aspiration; at that time, he was twenty-two years of age. Although he had previously experienced mystical responses and realizations, they remained difficult to fully comprehend.
Furthermore, when he prayed before an ancient Buddha stupa, the Buddha appeared and touched his head with his hand; only after this did his faith become even more profound and free from doubt.
From then on, his teaching was perfected and his conduct became complete as he presided over the seat of Daohong, where he gathered seven hundred fellow practitioners whose sharp wits [rivaled]...
His brilliance was like a forest. As for refining his rhetoric and scrutinizing the meaning to uphold the principles of his school, he was foremost and had no rival.

Thus, before reaching the age of twenty, he frequently ascended the high seat. Dharma Master Lingyu, a preeminent leader of the Buddhist community, led his assembly of monastics to personally attend his lectures;
scholars considered this a great honor. When the Sui dynasty arose, Emperor Wen commissioned the construction of the Da Chan Monastery for Empress Wenmu.

He established the Chan-ding (Meditation) Monastery in the capital to offer merit for the deceased. By imperial decree, Master Min and others were summoned; Min was the first attendant to enter the pass and reside at Chan-ding.

Whenever he had leisure from his extensive propagation of the Dharma, he examined and standardized the terminology and intent of the various scriptures of the Tripiṭaka, composing the *Wubu qufen chao* (Commentary on the Classification of the Five Divisions) in thirty-one fascicles.
Furthermore, as the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* was exclusively venerated in the region of Qin, Vinaya Master Hongzun first opened [the tradition] there.

This work establishes the fundamental tenets and governs the essential principles, resulting in a vast and clear understanding. Disciples carrying their books arrived daily to fill the halls, and Hui-zun likewise assisted in the proceedings to perfect its excellence.
At the beginning of the Daye era, an imperial decree ordered him to reside at the Great Chan-ding Monastery.
Shortly thereafter, he withdrew his remaining assets to erect two pagodas on the ruins of Yunmen to commemorate the site where he had left the household life and received the precepts. [Zheng]...

Observing the beginning [of the record]: The Tripiṭaka Master from India was appointed to oversee translation affairs; by imperial decree, he was commissioned to authenticate the meaning of the Vinaya.

In the eighth year, he was summoned to serve as the *upādhyāya* (abbot) of Hongfu Monastery. This monastery was established because Empress Mu had passed away while Gaozong was still in the Eastern Palace.
This was done to console the noble and virtuous thoughts [of the deceased] and, in particular, to ensure that his leadership would solemnize the administrative regulations.
On the twenty-second day of the fourth month in the ninth year, he passed away due to the aggravation of a chronic illness. He was sixty-nine years of age.

Upon hearing the report of his death, the Emperor expressed deep sorrow and issued an edict that the necessary provisions for the funeral rites must be made fully complete by the relevant authorities; furthermore, ten *mu* of burial land was granted to him in the capital.

On the Longshou Plains at the western outskirts of the city, the Vice-Director Fang Xuanling and the Chief Secretary Du Zhenglun—both of whom were his ordained disciples—jointly commissioned a stele to propagate his illustrious legacy.
Xu Jingzong composed the inscription. He began the lectures from the very beginning and recited them nearly one hundred times;
such was his earnestness in propagating and expounding [the teachings].
Zhi Zao of the Tang dynasty was born into the Zhang clan of Qinghe. After the Jin dynasty moved south, his family settled in Linhai.

His grandfather, Yuanxiu, and his father, Wenhui, were both prominent officials of the Liang and Chen dynasties. At the age of seventeen, he lost both his parents and contracted a chronic illness; he would often lie through the night under the moonlight.
She focused her mind on the Bodhisattva Candraprabha, praying for his compassionate salvation.

After some time, she had a dream in which a person of extraordinary appearance appeared and said, "I have come from the east to cure your illness. He then sucked at her body. This occurred for three nights, after which she gradually recovered.
Furthermore, knowing that the Three Jewels could be relied upon, he immediately went to Anjing Temple to take ordination under Dharma Master Huiping.

He soon followed the Venerable Zhiyi, receiving his teachings with devoted obedience. Thereupon, he performed the Lotus Sūtra Repentance in the mountains. On the night of the second seven-day period, [he had a vision].

He dreamed of a nine-headed dragon leaping from the earth into the sky. At dawn, he questioned Zhizhe (Zhiyi), who said, "This signifies that by means of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one shatters ignorance and enters the emptiness of the Dharma-nature.
In the fourth year of the Zhide era of the Chen dynasty, Prince Yongyang Zhibo was stationed in Kuaiji and dispatched an envoy to invite Zhizhe;
Bao accompanied him on the journey, whereupon they once again practiced the threefold recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
At Baolin Monastery, there was someone who would rattle the door panels at night; when questioned, he would say, "I have come merely to view the lamps.
There was a Chan Master named Huicheng residing in the monastery, whose quarters were separated from [the visitor's] by only a single wall.
He heard every word of the conversation at that time and said to his disciples, "This must be a ghost. Zao is in great danger! The next day, [he opened the door].
The door-bolt was intact and Huozao was unharmed; [the Master] marveled at this as something beyond human reach.

On the following night, six lamps within the hall were extinguished, leaving only one to illuminate the path for walking meditation. After three weeks had passed, he saw a person dressed in blue robes who praised him, saying, "Excellent!
and then vanished. Furthermore, he once went to beg for alms in Xiaoxing Village in Shan County; the host, by mistake, gave him a poisonous mushroom.
He served Zao with a meal. After Zao departed, the host’s attendants all suffered from violent vomiting and diarrhea, nearly dying;
only after taking potent medicine did they recover. Consequently, they sent the medicine he had taken to Zao from afar. Zao took no notice of it, merely smiling and declining it with thanks.

In the first year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he went to the Jiangdu palace to have an audience with Emperor Yang, receiving generous consolation and gifts. He made this journey a total of eight times over the course of seven years.
The honors accorded to him did not diminish in the least. He passed away in the twelfth year of the Zhenguan era at the age of eighty-three.
Tang Fashun’s surname was Du; he was a native of Wannian in Yongzhou. At the age of eighteen, he renounced secular life and left home under the Chan Master Sengzhen of Yingsheng Temple.
Sengzhen was surnamed Wei and had long practiced the study of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Previously, to the east of the capital...
The site was high and clear; the local people called it "Horse Head. He established his quarters there and was about to mobilize laborers when those of virtuous character came of their own accord.
Suddenly, the work began to take shape. There appeared a dog with a yellow body and white feet, though its origin remained unknown.

Day after day, it carried earth and timber with exceptional diligence. When midday passed, it would not eat despite being hungry. Upon hearing of this, an imperial edict was issued for the relevant authorities to provide it with three measures of rice daily.
