as Master Changjie remarked, he possessed a handsome appearance and a magnificent, dignified bearing. He was widely learned and skilled in exposition. Taking pity on Xuanzang’s extreme poverty, Su took him in to educate him.
At the age of eleven, Xuanzang was taught the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; he could recite them from memory upon merely looking at the text.
He constantly played with his younger brothers. When his elder brother took charge of Jingtu Monastery in the Eastern Capital, he was fifteen years old;

he applied himself even more diligently to his studies, and his reputation grew by the day. At the end of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, his father left his post as the Magistrate of Jiangling and retired to live in seclusion among the fields.
Suddenly, troops rose up and a famine ensued; having nowhere to beg or borrow, he followed his elder brother into Shu to rely upon Master Daoji.

There he received the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, and other treatises. He possessed the natural ability to hear and retain them; when he cited them, there was no impediment.

Daoji frequently looked back at him and sighed in admiration of his extraordinary talent. He also studied the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* under Sengjing, penetrating its profound depths and inner secrets. His elder brother resided at Konghui Temple in Yinan.

At the monastery, Xuanzang remained with them for a time before seeking an opportunity to take his leave. He took the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* from Master Daoshen at Zhaocheng, and thoroughly studied the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* under Master Huixiu at Ye.
He further studied the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* with Master Daoyue and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* with Master Xuangui.
Among the renowned masters of the time, there was none who did not recognize his talent. Prince Xiao Yu, the Chancellor (Puyue), submitted a memorial requesting that he be granted a residence.
Zhuangyan Temple was not his original intention. In the third year of the Zhenguan era, at the age of twenty-nine, he presented a memorial at the imperial palace and set out for the West.
The details of his travels are fully recorded in the biography composed by Yancong.
Having reached Central India, he attended upon Master Śīlabhadra at Nālandā Monastery, where he lectured on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and remained for five years.
He then traveled extensively to view them all, exhausting their splendors, before deliberating on his return. In the first month of the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he arrived at the capital.
By imperial decree, the śarīra relics and images he had obtained were enshrined within the side-aisles of Hongfu Monastery, and he was commissioned to perform translations there.
At that time, Gaozong was in the position of Crown Prince. He constructed Ci'en Temple to solemnize the posthumous merit of his mother, Empress Wen-de.

In the tenth month of winter, an imperial decree ordered him to move there. Once Gaozong ascended the throne, he bestowed even greater favor upon him. Shortly thereafter, an edict established official staff for the Translation Institute.
Accompanying the Emperor on his tours, his residence was not fixed in one place. In total, he produced seventy-three sections of sutras and treatises, amounting to one thousand [volumes].
He authored three hundred and thirty fascicles. In the first year of the Linde era, he passed away at Yuhua Monastery in Luoyang at the age of sixty-five.
Daoxuan of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Qian; he was a native of Dantu, though some say Changcheng. He was the descendant of Qian Rangzhi, the Governor of Guangling.
Later, Shen Chen was appointed as Minister of the Ministry of Personnel (Libu Shangshu). His mother dreamed that the moon pierced her womb and she became pregnant.
She further dreamed of a Buddhist monk who said to her, "The one you carry in your womb is none other than Sengyou of the Liang dynasty; Sengyou is the very same as Senghu of the Southern Qi."

It was fitting that he leave the household life and honor the teachings of Śākyamuni. At nine years of age, he was able to compose literary works; at fifteen, he studied the various sūtras and vinayas;

and at sixteen, he entered the monastic order under the Vinaya Master Zhìyún, receiving his training at Riyán Monastery. In his early twenties, he was moved by the manifestation of śarīra relics within a precious casket.
During the Dàyè period of the Sui dynasty, he received full ordination from the Vinaya Master Zhìshǒu. During the Wǔdé era, he continued his studies...

He was studying the Vinaya when, upon hearing it but once, he immediately wished to practice dhyāna. Master Ying rebuked him, saying: "One travels to the distant by starting from the near; one understands the profound by beginning with the subtle.
There is a proper time for practicing renunciation, and one's vows must first be fulfilled. It is not yet appropriate for you to abandon the Vinaya so abruptly.
After a long time, he finally began to cultivate samādhi and prajñā in Xiānzhang Valley on Mount Zhōngnán. His dwelling lacked fine drinking water, and whenever he passed by...
Pointing to a spot on the ground, he said, "One may dig a well here. They excavated it, and when it was only a foot or so deep, there was sufficient water for use.

Later, they established a temple there and named it Baekchun (White Spring). Subsequently, they moved to Chongui Jeongsa and then again to Pungdeoksa. Once, while sitting in solitary meditation, a divine being informed him:
"This site of Cheonggwan Village was formerly the grounds of Jeongyeosa Temple. If you construct a dwelling here and reside in it, it will be possible [to fulfill your purpose]."
He attained the Way. He then rebuilt and expanded his dwelling, relocating there. During the Zhenguan era, he lived in seclusion on Mount Yunshi in Qindu.
While he was at Zhongnan Mountain, a flock of dragons transformed into the forms of men and women to pay their respects with formal ceremony. Occasionally, the śrāmaṇeras would look back at them.

When he gave rise to a false thought, the dragon grew angry and was about to seize him; he immediately repented and spat his venom into the well. When Xuan departed, he instructed him not to draw water from it.
It has remained sealed until the present day, so they say. At that time, the scholar Sun Simiao was on very intimate terms with Xuan while wandering beneath the trees.
It happened that there was a drought, and a monk from the Western Regions requested an audience at court to establish an altar for a rain prayer at Kunming Lake. Kun-...
The waters of the Mingchi Pool were receding by several feet each day. Just as the sun was beginning its course through the sky, a man suddenly appeared who looked somewhat flustered.
He came forward and bowed, saying, "I am a disciple, a dragon of the Kunming Pool. That there has been no rain is the decree of Heaven;
it was not something I dared to do. Now, a foreign monk intends to take the treasure I guard and deceive the Son of Heaven in order to pray for rain."
"This has caused my disciples' lives to hang by a thread. I pray only that the Upādhyāya will look upon us with compassion and grant his protection.
Xuán said, "Though the barbarian monk is greedy, he is killing those of our own kind; how could we simply sit idly by? Mr. Sūn is a man of benevolence. Go to him for help;
perhaps he will take pity on you and save you. The old man approached Sīmiào as Xuán had instructed. Sīmiào said, "I have heard..."
"In the Dragon Palace of Kunming Lake, there are thirty divine prescriptions that can be granted to you; I shall then save you.
The old man said, "This is a decree of the Emperor that does not permit casual transmission. The situation is urgent; why indeed should I be stingy? After a short while, the prescriptions arrived.
Simao said to the old man, "Return without fear. From that time on, the water in the pond swelled greatly and overflowed the banks for several days.

There were those who sent extraordinary flowers whose fragrance and color did not fade for a long time; there were those who sent jimen, pear, and crabapple fruits whose flavors were unlike anything in the world;
and there were those who sent a package of an object called "thorn-forest incense" (jilinxiang). As for these matters...
An altar was constructed, where long-eyebrowed monks engaged in discourse; a young man supported one whose feet had stumbled.
He transmitted the illustrated scriptures of Jetavana and brought forth the Buddha’s tooth-relics. Celestial youths attended him on his left and right, and devas came and went to converse with him.

How inconceivable is his manifest transformation and profound resonance! When Ximing Monastery was completed, he served as the *sthavira* (upādhyāya) and assisted the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang in the translation work.
He was commissioned by imperial decree to deliver śarīra relics and to construct a stūpa at Wuyouwang Monastery in Fufeng.
Furthermore, he compiled the *Famen wenji*, the *Guang hongming ji*, the *Xu gaoseng zhuan*, the *Sanbao lu*, the *Jie mo jieshu*, and the *Xingshi*.

His commentaries, such as the *Yi-chao* (Commentary on Meaning), totaled more than two hundred and twenty fascicles. On the third day of the tenth month in the second year of the Qianfeng era, he passed away while sitting peacefully.

He was seventy-two years of age and had fifty-two years of ordination seniority. He was interred in a stone chamber at Tangu Valley. Throughout his life, he wore only the three robes made of ramie; he ate only a single meal of beans daily;
he traveled with a staff and alms bowl, and sat upon a simple mat. A monk from India who had attained the three fruits of the path offered praise for him.
It is said: Since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the period when the Semblance Dharma (śāsanapratirūpaka) abides in the world, you alone have been the one who practices the Vinaya.
In the tenth year of the Xiántóng era, an imperial edict conferred upon you the posthumous title Chénghào (Illuminating Clarity), and your stupa was named Jìngguāng (Pure Light).
Tang Hongren’s surname was Zhou. He was a native of Huangmei in Qi. From birth, he was exceptionally refined and extraordinary;

those who discerned his character believed that his physical marks fell short of the Buddha’s in only seven respects, and that by law he was destined to shoulder the burden of the Dharma-vehicle and succeed to the legacy of the lineage.
Initially, there was an ascetic monk on Mount Dongshan who made his living by planting pine trees; people casually referred to him as "The Pine-Planting Wayfarer. When he grew old...
He was about to die. He then went to knock at the abbot’s quarters to take his final leave. Chan Master Xin greeted him with a smile and said, "Are you leaving?
I have reserved the seat of the Patriarch for you; you shall return. The practitioner gave his word. Shortly thereafter, a woman of the Zhou family, before she was even married, gave birth to a son.
The Zhou residence was near a muddy creek, so she immediately sent a maidservant to cast the newborn far away into the water.
In the midst [of the river], he cast her out again and again, yet she did not sink. She wailed piteously as she drifted upstream until she reached the shore.

Having no other choice, he gathered her up and returned home. His father and elder brothers were enraged and demanded to know where she had come from. The girl said, "Yesterday, my child happened to go out for a stroll."

Seeing a man in a patched robe with disheveled hair, he approached the child and asked to be allowed to stay the night. The child felt ashamed and did not dare respond. The man suddenly vanished, leaving no trace of his whereabouts.
After a long while, she felt her body grow heavy; she had no other intentions. Her father and elder brother, however, ultimately did not believe her and suppressed the matter.
They eventually beat the girl and drove her away. She then fled together with the newborn, yet even as she fled, the newborn...
Yi was easy to raise. When he was just seven years old, his mother took him along as she went begging for alms. On the road, they encountered Chan Master Xin, who asked Yi’s surname.
He replied, "I have a surname, but it is not an ordinary one. The Master asked, "What is your surname? He replied, "My surname is Kūṅ (Emptiness).

Because of this past affinity, the Chan Master followed Yi’s mother and requested that Yi become his disciple. Once Yi had undergone tonsure and received full ordination, he further received the robe of Master Càn.
The Transmission of the Helmet was then conferred upon Huineng, who further spoke a verse to certify the orthodox lineage. The verse says:
"When sentient beings come to sow seeds, the fruit arises from the ground; since insentient things have no seeds, where there is no ground, there is no arising.
On the twenty-third day of the tenth month in the second year of the Shangyuan era, he passed away at Shuangfeng Temple on East Mountain at the age of seventy-four. He was interred...
His entire body was enshrined within a stupa erected above it. During the reign of Emperor Daizong, he was posthumously honored with the title Daman, and his stupa was named Fayu.

Huiming of the Tang dynasty was of the Chen clan and a native of Poyang; he was a descendant of the imperial lineage of Emperor Xuan. In his youth, he relied upon Yongchang Temple to receive the tonsure and enter the monastic order.
He immediately went to the Dharma seat at Mount Dongshan in Qi, where he visited and questioned [the Master] day and night. After a long time, he had not yet attained realization.

During the Xianheng era, Master Neng was personally engaged in the work of pounding grain with a mortar and pestle as a layman, while Master Xiu occupied the first seat; the assembly all turned their attention to him.
The thought was that what had been transmitted regarding the robe and bowl could certainly not be otherwise. Subsequently, he secretly entrusted them to the layman (Upāsaka).
Thereupon, the assembly felt ashamed and set out in pursuit, catching up with him at Mount Dayu. Huiming arrived first and saw the layman.
The layman suddenly threw the robe and bowl onto a rock, saying, "These serve as tokens of faith; can they be contested? You may take them yourself. Huiming was originally known as...
The man of great physical strength tried to pull it up two or three times but could not move it. He then said to Nanquan, "I have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for this.
I only pray that you, Layman, will instruct me. The Layman replied, "When you are neither thinking of good nor thinking of evil—at that very moment—what is the original face of Elder Ming?
At these words, Ming attained great enlightenment; sweat poured from his entire body and tears flowed down his cheeks.
Weeping, he performed a ritual prostration and said, "Beyond these secret words and secret meanings you have imparted thus far, is there anything further?
The Master replied, "What I am now telling you is not secret. If you turn back and reflect, the secret will reside within you. As they were about to part, he asked again:
"What should I do? the Master asked. The scholar said, "If you meet Yuan, you may stop; if you encounter Meng, you should stay.

Ming withdrew and deceived his followers, saying, "It is far away; it would only lead to exhaustion and fatigue. What benefit would there be? Shortly thereafter, he changed his name from Hui to Dao to avoid the name Neng.
Later, he indeed resided at Mount Mengding in Yuan.
Huineng of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Lu; he was a native of Xinxing in Nanhai. His ancestors originated from Fanyang.

His father, Xingtao, first held office at the imperial court, but during the Wude era, he was demoted due to slander and appointed as the Commandant of the Prefecture. On the *wuxu* day of the twelfth year of the Zhenguan era (628 CE), Neng was born in his official residence.
Not long after, his father passed away and his mother became a widow; they were extremely poor, and Neng grew up among the common people.
He sold firewood daily to provide for his parents' fine food and drink. One day, while at an inn, he heard a traveler reciting a sutra;
upon reaching the passage, "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere," he was suddenly awakened to the truth. He firmly questioned the traveler, "What sutra is this?

The traveler replied, "It is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He asked again, "Where did you obtain it? The traveler said, "I obtained it from Master Ren (Huineng) at Mount Fengmao in Huangmei, Qizhou."
The Master [Huineng] considered that by merely reciting this sutra, one would immediately see one's nature and become a Buddha.

Huineng said, "My ambition is to see the Great Master, yet I am burdened by my mother; what can be done? At that time, a guest offered ten taels of white silver to settle his family's affairs so that he might go.
During the Xianheng era, while passing through Shaoyang, the lay devotee Liu Zhilue invited him with great kindness.

Li was the paternal aunt of Zhilue. At that time, she was reading the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and had questions regarding its difficult passages; Zhilue was able to provide detailed explanations for them. Li then asked him about certain characters, to which he replied, "I do not recognize them.
Li found this strange and questioned him as to why he said so. He answered, "The wondrous meaning of all Buddhas does not fall within the realm of words and letters.

Li sighed in admiration and respect, calling him a "practitioner" (xingzhe) and spreading his reputation throughout the local community. Consequently, the people built and opened up the Baolin Monastery for him.
The old temple invited him to reside there so that he might have convenient access to the [monastic] community. Huineng said, "I have come here specifically to seek a teacher;
how can I settle down immediately? The next day, he went to rely upon Chan Master Zhìyuǎn at the West Grotto in Lèchāng County.
Yuan treated him with even greater esteem, saying, "You must first obtain certification from Qi, and only then return to instruct me.

Upon arriving at Qi, Master Ren asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Lingnan. Ren asked, "What do you seek? He replied, "I seek to become a Buddha. Ren said, "People of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature.
He replied, "People may be from the north or the south, but how could Buddha-nature be like that? Thereupon, he entered into service until he reached Xuan.
Huineng worked at the waist-stone, treading the pestle and mortar to demonstrate his diligence and endurance.

Previously, the senior monk Shenxiu had followed Huineng’s command to inscribe a verse on the wall to express his own understanding. Huineng then requested a guest to secretly write another verse beside it during the night.
When Huineng saw it, he privately summoned Shenxiu and transmitted to him the robe and alms bowl he had received, saying, "Since my former master, these have been used as tokens of faith."
Now, there are none among the arrogant and ignorant who do not covet [this position]. Therefore, wherever he resides, his life is as precarious as a thread suspended from above.
You must depart at once; do not linger here. Thereupon, he fled to the region between Sihui and Huaiji.

After some time, Dharma Master Yinzong of the Fasheng Temple in Nanhai, having heard of his discernment regarding the wind and the banner, sought an audience with him to request the robe and alms bowl he had received.
He had his hair shaved for him. Following Master Zhiguang, he ascended the altar to receive full ordination;
that altar was built by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇavarman of the Song dynasty. An inscription states: "In the future, there will be an incarnate Bodhisattva who shall receive the precepts here.
Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of the Liang dynasty personally planted a Bodhi tree beside the altar. An inscription states: "One hundred and twenty years hence, there will be..."

"O Mahāsattva! Herein is taught the Dharma of the Unsurpassed Vehicle. During the Shangyuan era, when the Great Master Ren entered parinirvāṇa at Dongshan in Qizhou, Huineng foresaw this and said, "My teacher is truly returning to his origin. Shortly thereafter, the news of the passing arrived.
He moved his residence to Baolin Monastery, but the Regional Inspector Wei Qu welcomed him to Dafan Monastery; he declined these efforts and entered Caoxi. Thus, from that day forth—

Scholars of inferior disposition turned toward Caoqi, yet Empress Wu Zetian and Emperor Zhongzong, having been petitioned regarding Chan Master Shenxiu, repeatedly issued imperial edicts summoning him to the capital.
Subsequently, they dispatched the palace eunuch Xue Jian to urge him with great earnestness; he declined both times on the grounds of illness and did not rise to the call.
Later, he was granted a *mohana* (worn-out) *kaṣāya*, an alms bowl, a prayer shawl (*kṣomapaṭa*) woven with strung beads, and a cotton handkerchief of green fabric with red borders;
five hundred bolts of silk were offered as sustenance. He donated his residence at Xinxing to establish a monastery and requested an imperial plaque from the state.

In the third year of the Shénlóng era, an imperial edict was issued for the restoration of the temple in Shàozhōu, with instructions to ensure it was as magnificent as possible, and its name was changed to Fǎquán.
In the first year of the Yánhé era, he instructed his disciples in advance to construct a stupa at Fǎquán Temple.

On the third day of the eighth month in the second year of the Xiāntiān era, he returned and announced his passing; he was seventy-six years of age. In the eleventh month, he was reburied at Cáoqī. (From the *Xìnbǎozàngjī*).
The imperial house posthumously conferred upon him the title Dajian; his stupa was named Yuanhe Zhengzhen.
In the third year of the Taiping Xingguo era of the Song dynasty, an imperial edict changed the name of Caoxi Fajian Temple to Nanhua Temple.

Shenhui of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Gao and was a native of Xiangyang. By nature he was upright and intelligent. While still young and engaged in his studies, he entered the monastic life under Dharma Master Xianyuan at Guochang Temple in the prefecture.
His reception of the scriptures and full ordination was exceptionally distinguished compared to his peers.

At that time, Master Neng was widely propagating the Dharma of the Mind in the regions south of the mountains; upon hearing of this, Shenhui rejoiced in it and went there without further hesitation. When he finally met him...
The Master asked Huai: "Where have you come from? Huai replied: "I have come from nowhere. The Master said: "If that is so, then you should go back. Huai replied:

"There is also nowhere to which I can return. The Master said: "How vast and boundless your life is! Huai replied: "My body is currently on the road. The Master said: "Even so, you have not yet arrived."
It is said that he did not linger there; thus, he resided at Caoxi for several years. In the eighth year of the Kaiyuan era, an imperial edict assigned him to Longxing Temple in Nanyang.
Later, he again went to guide disciples in Luoyang, and the teachings of the Southern School first flourished throughout the world.
Previously, the regions between the two capitals were all lands transformed by Shenxiu, and Puji was his successor; thus, the world called this the Northern School.
By the time of Huaiyi, the traces of Puji’s school had vanished, and so the Northern and Southern schools each established their own factions.
Consequently, they attacked one another with charges and counter-charges, and praise and slander arose in turn. At the beginning of the Tianbao era, the Censor Lu Yi—
A memorial was submitted [reporting that he] had gathered a multitude to plot treason. An imperial decree ordered him to appear for interrogation, but in the end, he was found innocent.
He was transferred to Junzhou. Two years later, he was again transferred to the Prajñā Hall of Kaiyuan Monastery in Jingzhou.

In the fourteenth year, An Lushan, the Regional Inspector of Yan’gang, rebelled and raised troops toward the capital, capturing both the Eastern and Western Capitals. The Imperial Carriage fled to Shu. By imperial decree, Guo Ziyi was appointed as the Vice Commander-in-Chief of the Realm.
He led the campaign against An Lushan. At that time, the state treasury was depleted and military expenditures were cut off.

Right Vice President of the Department of State Affairs Pei Mian proposed that sacrificial altars (*kaitan*) for ordaining monks (*du seng*) should be established in every prefecture and commandery, and that their offerings and profits should be collected to provide for the needs of the state.
Consequently, he was appointed to oversee affairs in Luoyang, where he contributed an especially large amount of revenue. During the reign of Emperor Suzong...
He entered the inner court to present offerings. An imperial edict was issued for the Chief Architect (Jiangzuo Dajiang) to construct a Chan monastery at Heze.

On the thirteenth day of the fifth month of the first year of the Shangyuan era, he took leave of his disciples; shortly thereafter, he rose from his seat, faced the void, and prostrated himself, then returned to his quarters.
That evening he passed away at the age of ninety-three. A stupa was erected for his burial at Baoying Temple in Luoyang, and he was posthumously granted the title Zhenzong;
his stupa was named Prajñā.

Tang Benjing’s secular surname was Zhang, and he was a native of Dongping. In his youth, he thoroughly investigated the study of emptiness and stillness, and his integrity and character were exceptionally solitary and distinct. He constructed...
Upon meeting Chan Master Huineng of Caoxi, the doubts and obstructions that had long lingered within him were suddenly resolved.

At the beginning of the Kaiyuan era, he withdrew to live in seclusion on Mount Sikong at Nan Yue. His spiritual practice was unfathomable, yet his traces never mingled with the bustle of the capital or the marketplace.
During the Tianbao era, the palace eunuch Yang Guangting encountered him while gathering medicinal herbs and asked: "Your disciple’s nature and understanding are dull and obscured; I have not yet—"

[The interlocutor] examined the relationship between the Buddha and the Way, asking, "What is the meaning of this? Jing said, "If you seek the Buddha, the mind itself is the Buddha. If you seek the Way, the absence of mind is the Way.
[The interlocutor] asked, "In what sense is the mind itself the Buddha? Jing said, "The Buddha is realized through the mind, and the mind is manifested by the Buddha.
If one realizes the absence of mind, even the Buddha does not exist. [The interlocutor] asked, "In what sense is the absence of mind the [Way]? Jing said...
Daowei said, "The Way is fundamentally without mind; no-mind is the Way. If one realizes no-mind, then no-mind is itself the Way.

Guangting paid his respects and accepted this with faith. Upon returning to the palace, he reported the exchange that had taken place in the mountains in full detail. The Emperor then issued an edict to Guangting.
The Emperor issued an edict for Jing to come to the capital. He was first accommodated at the White Lotus Pavilion.

The eminent masters of the Three Schools from the two streets, as well as Dharma Master Yuan of Taiping Temple and others, were summoned to expound the Buddha-dharma, while the Emperor attended in person.

On that day, Jing ascended the high seat and responded to the inquiries with grace and composure: "That which lies in others is always insufficient; that which resides within oneself is always sufficient. He spoke with dignified poise.

He was serene and composed; his every action was spontaneous. The multitude sighed in admiration and submission. In the fifth month of the second year of the Shangyuan era, he passed away at the age of ninety-five.
He was posthumously titled Chan Master Daxiao.
Zhiwei of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Chen. A native of Jiangning, he was precocious from childhood and took no pleasure in play.
He constantly maintained himself through stillness and silence, which those who saw him regarded as extraordinary. Not long after, one day he suddenly disappeared.

When they searched everywhere for him, it was discovered that he had already gone to rely on Master Tong of Tianbao Temple to leave the household life. Master Tong cherished him deeply and had him recite Mahāyāna scriptures daily.
At the age of twelve, he received the tonsure through the grace of the state and was enrolled at Youyan Temple.

There, he consulted with Master Chi regarding the principles of Chan and eventually became Chi’s successor. Chi subsequently retired to Yanzuo Temple, entrusting him with the sole responsibility of guiding others.
Those who received his benefit were beyond counting; among them was one named Huizhong, whom he designated as a vessel of the Dharma.
Wei once showed him a verse, saying: "Do not fixate on thoughts; thoughts create the river of birth and death. One wanders through the sea of the six realms;
no-thought exits the long waves. Zhong replied with a verse: "Thoughts and perceptions have always been illusions; the nature itself has neither beginning nor end."
If one grasps the meaning within this, the great waves will naturally cease. Daowei knew that [his disciple] had attained awakening and thus entrusted him with the mountain gate.
Thereupon, he followed conditions to transform and guide others. He passed away on the eighteenth day of the second month in the tenth year of the Kaiyuan era.

His final instruction was to move his body to Zhonglin Forest to be given to birds and beasts. His disciples, Xuanting and others, did not dare to disobey. He was seventy-seven years of age. This was the beginning of Daowei’s [legacy].
While practicing the dhūta austerities, he encountered three tigers at night but felt no fear. At dawn, the tigers followed him outside the gate as if acting as his guardians;
he merely gestured for them to depart, and they left. Such was the locus of his majesty. Every day, two rabbits and one dog would play together in the courtyard.
Was this not yet another sign of his compassion in transforming sentient beings?
Tang Kuījī, courtesy name Hóngdào, was surnamed Wèi. He was a descendant of the Chí clan, originating from the Wèichí tribe of the Tuóbá Wei dynasty; he was a native of Jīngzhào.
His grandfather was Luójiā, who served as the Western Garrison Commander of Dàizhōu during the Sui dynasty. His father was Zōng, a General of the Left Golden Myōrō Guard.
He was the Governor of Songzhou and the Duke of Kaiyu County in Jiangyou. His paternal uncle was the Duke of Bo, [Li] Gong.
His mother, Lady Pei, conceived him after dreaming of swallowing the lunar disk. Upon his birth, he was unlike other children. In his own preface, he wrote:

"At the age of nine, I encountered the mourning for my mother; gradually, I distanced myself from worldly customs. By the time I was seventeen, I had entered the monastic community (*zilin*) and took Master Xuanzang as my teacher."

The Master studied the languages of the Five Indias. He first resided at Guangfu Monastery and subsequently moved to Da Cien Monastery. His intelligence and acumen were far beyond those of ordinary men;
he could memorize the *Khandhaka-vagga* of the Vinaya upon a single reading. At the age of twenty-five, by imperial decree, he was admitted to the Translation Institute.

At that time, Master Xuanzang was translating the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, and the Emperor summoned Kuiji and Huifang to the Shangguang Monastery to serve together as editors for the refinement of the text. Kuiji was filled with profound resolve.

"I request that you alone take responsibility for this. Xuanzang consented and declined all others. Thereupon, he translated and annotated the text simultaneously, lecturing upon it morning and evening with the intent that it be circulated immediately.

Tang Huì'ān, surnamed Wèi, was a native of Zhījiāng in Jīngzhōu. Born at the beginning of the Kāihuáng era of the Sui dynasty, he possessed a dignified and elegant appearance and an exceptionally gentle and amiable disposition.

Fayue practiced the dhūta austerities. During the Zhenguan era, he traveled to Qizhou to pay respects to Master Ren, from whom he received the essential instructions of the mind-seal.

At that time, an early frost damaged the crops, yet his dwelling alone remained secure, while the surrounding forty li all yielded a bountiful harvest. Emperor Gaozong marveled at this and issued an edict summoning him for an audience, but he did not go.

How much more so for this stream of consciousness, which flows on without interval between arising and ceasing? From the initial consciousness until the point where the signs of movement do not arise, how could one record it by year or month?

In the [year of the] Sheep, the cremation was completed. Eighty *śarīra* relics were obtained; five of these were reddish-purple and were presented to the Emperor, while the remainder were used to construct a stupa for interment.

Daojun of the Tang dynasty was a native of Jiangling who resided for a long time at the Bixi Jingśe (Emerald Stream Monastery) in Zhijiang, where he cultivated the Dharma-gate of Mount Dongshan with great diligence.

He applied himself with diligent perseverance for more than forty years without his footsteps ever crossing the threshold of his door. Though his dwelling was nearby, he remained distant to others, and none dared to seek an audience;

During the Tang dynasty, Puo-zao-duo lived in seclusion on Mount Song. Having personally received the Dharma from Chan Master Lao’an, those who flocked to him from all quarters increased daily.

The monk bowed. Xuedou said, "Broken! Broken! Broken!"
Fazang of the Tang dynasty, styled Xianshou, was originally a native of Kangju and thus bore the surname Kang. From his youth, he was known for his devotion to Buddhist studies.

Layer upon layer of mutual reflection and concealment, it is beyond the reach of thought or speculation.

He opened the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. The Emperor was greatly pleased and, in order to ordain disciples, bestowed upon him various personal effects, colored silks, and other items.

Tang Dao’an’s surname was Tang. His ancestors were from Yingchuan; during the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty, they migrated south to Guangzhou, where they subsequently became residents of Guangzhou for generations.
Dao’an was born with an extraordinary character. Initially, he resolved to distinguish himself through Confucian studies, but later he repented of this and sought ordination as a monk.
One night, he dreamed that Kāśyapa instructed him with admonitions, and what he saw therein accorded with his reading of the scriptures.
His words in dreams were consistent with reality; consequently, his wisdom and understanding progressed daily, and his fame grew.

At that time, the Dharma Master Chu was once again exalting the Way through his virtue and character, and was popularly known as the Great Monk (Dashang). Hui'an followed him and resided at Longxing Temple in Kuaiji.
During the reign of Emperor Zhongzong, an imperial edict summoned him along with several eminent monks to the inner palace. He was treated with exceptional favor and honor.

The Emperor subsequently received the Bodhisattva precepts from him and ordered his portrait to be painted at the Lingguang Palace. Furthermore, he composed a eulogy for him, which read: "The pearl of the precepts is bright and pure; the stream of wisdom is clear and still.

His body is constrained by the five articles [of the Vinaya], yet his mind merges with the eight dhyānas. In study, he exhausts the true scriptures; in contemplation, he penetrates the ultimate nature."

He upheld the Dharma and attended to its affairs, serving as the administrative head of the monastic government. He hoped that the Vinaya-piṭaka would perpetuate the fragrant legacy [of the Buddha], so that the Elephant Teaching (Buddhism) might thereby flourish and shine.

Throughout his successive appointments at temples such as Baima, Zhongxing, Zhuangyan, Jianfu, and Wangle, he held the office of monastic administrator; this was considered an honor by all under heaven.

The passage of years and seasons has now reached two full cycles. Pressed by the approaching end of his allotted time, he recalled the places where he had fished and roamed.
On the tenth day of the eighth month in the fifth year of the Kaiyuan era, he passed away at Longxing Temple at the age of sixty-four. His disciples buried him according to the rites.

Upon reaching the shore, Dao’an became the preceptor to the Son of Heaven. All affairs were conducted according to his ink-written edicts; the monks of the southeast dared not dare to deviate from them.
As for the transmission of the four divisions of the Vinaya, was it not indeed due to Dao’an’s efforts?
Tang Xuánjué, whose courtesy name was Míngdào, was surnamed Dài and was a native of Yǒngjiā.
His elder brother Xuān, who was well-known within the school of Confucian education, ordained both of his nephews along with himself; they resided at Longxīng Monastery.

Having long practiced meditative concentration (*samādhi*), Xuánjué established a meditation hall beside the monastery where he lived to further his cultivation. Subsequently, inspired by the exhortations of Chan Master Zuǒxī Lǎng, he [joined] the East...

Chan Master Yangce went together with others to pay his respects to the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi. Upon first arriving, he carried his water jar and staff and circumambulated the Patriarch three times.

The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa is one who possesses the three thousand dignified demeanors and eighty thousand subtle practices. Great Virtue, you have come here after having cultivated these yourself."

He gave rise to great conceit. Huiké said, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. The Patriarch said, "Why do you not realize non-birth? Why do you not understand that there is no swiftness?
Huiké said, "Realizing it is non-birth; understanding it is fundamentally without swiftness. The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is.
Huiké then performed the full ritual of prostration and salutation. After a short while, he took his leave. The Patriarch said, "Are you returning too soon? Huiké—
Huineng said, "Fundamentally, it is not moving; how could there be speed? Huizang said, "Who knows it is not moving? Huineng said, "The benevolent one yourself gives rise to discrimination.
Huizang said, "You have deeply grasped the meaning of non-arising. Huineng said, "If there is no arising, how can there be meaning?"

The Patriarch said, "If there is no intention, who is it that makes distinctions? Huizhao replied, "Even making distinctions is without intention. The Patriarch sighed in praise, saying, "Excellent, excellent! Stay for a short while; you have one illness remaining.
At that time, he was called "One-Night Enlightenment" (Yi-xiu-jue). From then on, students flocked to him like spokes converging at the hub, and his transformation spread throughout the world.
On the seventeenth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Xiāntiān era, he passed away sitting upright as if entering meditative absorption. He was forty-nine years old.
On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month of that year, he was buried on the southern slope of the Western Mountains.
His disciples Huicao, Huchi, Cixuan, Jiji, and others succeeded to his legacy. Li Yong, the Prefectural Governor of Kuozhou, composed the inscription, which was engraved upon stone.
To record his deeds, Wei Jing, the Prefect of Qingzhou, compiled his lifetime writings for circulation in the world.
Later, he was posthumously titled "Wuxiang" (Formless), and his stupa was named "Jingguang" (Pure Light).
Tang Yuangui was the son of the Li family from Yiguan. He possessed an exceptionally brilliant temperament and an elegant, refined appearance.

In the second year of the Yongchun era, he received full ordination and enrolled at Xianju Monastery, where he studied the Vinaya. Furthermore, he awakened to the principles of Chan under the guidance of Chan Master Huian.
Thereupon, he built a hermitage at Pangwu on Mount Song to live in seclusion. In the second year of the Jinglong era.
There were several hundred attendants arrayed in ceremonial guards, wearing tall caps and trousers with pleated skirts, who came to pay their respects.
Xuan Gui perceived that they were no ordinary people and said to them, "Welcome, virtuous ones. For what purpose have you come? They replied, "Does the Master not recognize us?
Gui said, "I regard Buddhas and sentient beings as equal; how could I give rise to discrimination toward you alone? They said, "We are the spirits of this mountain..."
"You are a deity. Your office is to determine the benefit or harm, life or death, of human beings. How can you, Master, regard me as your equal?
Guī replied, "I regard my body as equal to empty space; I regard myself as equal to you. If you can destroy empty space and yourself, then you can destroy me."
"I am originally without birth; how could you destroy me? The spirit hurriedly bowed his head twice and said, "Your Master’s wisdom and eloquence are vast and great;
they are beyond my reach. I pray that you will grant me the five precepts and deliver me from this world. Guī said, "Since you have requested the precepts..."
"If one has already received the precepts, there are no precepts outside of those; what further precepts could there be? [The Master] said, "This is the principle. In practice, however, it is not so.
One must receive the precepts from a teacher, and only then may one become a disciple of that gate.

Guī then prepared a seat, set out the ritual table, and held the incense burner, saying, "I confer upon you the five precepts. If you can uphold them, you should say 'I can. If you cannot, you should..."
He replied, "I cannot. He then continued, singing out: "Are you able to be free from lust? He said, "Since I am already married, how could I not be?
Gui said, "I do not mean this; I mean whether you can be without the net of desire. He said, "I can. Gui said, "Are you able to be free from theft? He said, "My resources are sufficient;
why would I need to take anything? Gui said, "I do not mean this; I mean whether you can understand that good and evil bring about fortune and calamity, yet [you remain unmoved]."

[The Emperor] asked, "Is it because of performing sacrifices? [Guī] replied, "Yes. [The Emperor] said, "Can you refrain from killing? [Guī] replied, "I truly hold the office of its administration. Guī said, "That is not what I meant.
I meant that you can avoid being excessive, erroneous, confused, or doubtful. [Guī] replied, "I can. [The Emperor] said, "Can you refrain from speaking falsely?
[Guī] replied, "I am fundamentally upright; how would I dare speak falsely? Guī said, "That is not what I meant. I meant that you can avoid failing [in your duty]."
...and thus accord with the Will of Heaven. [The Emperor] said, "Can you? He replied, "I can. [The Emperor] asked, "Can you refrain from drinking wine?

He replied, "The world considers it a matter of ritual propriety; how could I do otherwise? Guì said, "I do not mean this. I mean that you can refrain from allowing drunkenness and excess to ruin your virtue.
He replied, "I can. Guì said, "The above are the wondrous precepts established by the Tathāgata. One is able to guard them with a conscious mind, yet without..."

The mind is bound by attachment. When there is a mind that restrains and upholds, yet no mind that opens the way to transgression, then being born before heaven and earth does not constitute longevity;
dying after heaven and earth does not constitute old age; changing and transforming all day long does not constitute movement;

and being ultimately silent and still does not constitute stillness. Therefore, taking a wife is not lust; partaking in sacrifices is not grasping; wielding the handles of government is not killing. It is as it should be.
To speak thus regarding what precedes and follows is not false speech; to be intoxicated by benevolence and righteousness is not to be drunk with wine.

This is surely because they possess a [fixed] mind. If they were without such a mind, then indulging in desires would not constitute lewdness, and one might receive blessings for evil while suffering calamity for goodness.

One does not steal. One does not kill through error, confusion, or doubt. One does not speak falsely when one's prior and subsequent actions contradict the Way of Heaven. One does not drink wine to the point of intoxication.
For where there is no mind, there are no precepts; where there are no precepts, there is no Buddha; where there is no Buddha, there are no sentient beings.
If there is neither you nor me, and neither me nor you, who is it that can observe the precepts? And what is it that is to be restrained? He replied: "It is my spirit."
Tong Ya bowed to the Master and asked, "What do you think of this? Guī replied, "As I understand it, even the Buddha possesses no supernatural powers; how much less so you!

Shen was struck with awe and said, "I pray you will instruct me. Guī said, "The Buddha can empty all phenomena and realize the wisdom of the myriad dharmas, yet he cannot immediately extinguish fixed karma.
The Buddha can know the nature of all beings and exhaustively comprehend the events of billions of kalpas, yet..."
One cannot transform and guide those for whom there is no karmic affinity. Although a Buddha can deliver immeasurable sentient beings, he cannot exhaust the realm of all sentient beings.
Can you cause the Supreme Deity to turn back? Can you make the Seven Luminaries travel east while the heavens move west?
Then I know you cannot do it. Can you seize the Earth-Spirit? Can you melt the Five Sacred Peaks and congeal the Four Seas? Then I know once more that you cannot do it.
Furthermore, if one claims to possess supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) yet there is something one cannot do, then it would be appropriate to say that one has no supernatural powers at all.

[The Master] said, "I am indeed shallow and ignorant, and have not yet heard the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Now that I have received the precepts from you, I beg to demonstrate what I am capable of, in order to repay your compassionate virtue.
Guì firmly declined, saying it was not permitted. Thereupon [the Master] said, "The layout of Dongyan Temple faces east, yet it is desolate and lacks trees. To the north..."

"The grotto possesses it, yet it is not for the purpose of shielding against the wind. You must not disturb the objects; simply move the northern tree to the eastern ridge for me, and that will suffice.
[The monk] replied, "Yes. Suddenly, a night wind shook the air; he cautioned him, "Be careful not to be afraid. He then took his leave.

Zhi Gui watched him depart until he was out of sight, seeing only banners and canopies fluttering in the sky, spears and halberds standing in dense array, and the sound of tinkling jade pendants swaying amidst the azure mist.
It vanished amidst the gathering crimson clouds, fading away into the vast distance. That evening at the third watch, a gale, lightning, rain, and hail indeed broke forth suddenly;

the roof beams seemed on the verge of collapsing. Yet when he looked, the pines and cypresses of the eastern cliff stood in rows as if they had been planted there for ages, while the northern ridge was no longer as it had been before.
Guī strictly forbade his disciples from speaking of this outside; he said that if they did, those who heard would not believe him. Furthermore—
"I am a spirit. On the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, the year Bingchen, he passed away at the age of seventy-three.

Yinzong of the Tang dynasty was born into the Yin clan of Wu Commandery. When his mother, Liu, was first pregnant, all her neighbors dreamed that a dignified and elegant śramaṇa entered her house with slow, deliberate steps.
Liu herself also dreamed that someone requested her to become his son, though she declined the offer repeatedly.
It did not stop there. That evening, his father again dreamed that a youth knelt and presented him with sandalwood for the Liu family.

Consequently, whenever the Liu family encountered meat or pungent foods, they would immediately feel revulsion and discard them. Upon the birth of Zong, he was immediately made to serve the Buddha, without any sense of stinginess or reluctance.

As he grew older, he relied on masters of long-standing virtue to study the sutras and śāstras, becoming especially proficient in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. In the first year of the Xianheng era, he began to propagate and guide others.
The imperial capital was extremely prosperous. During the Shangyuan era, an imperial decree invited him to reside at Dà'ài-jìng Temple, but he declined and did not go.

He instead proceeded to Mount Dōngshān in Qí to receive the Chan teachings from Master Rèn. He also once engaged in a dialogue with Chan Master Huínéng at Pányú, through which he deeply clarified the essentials of the mind.
After a long time, he returned to his native village, where he met the Regional Inspector Wáng Zhòu, who requested that he establish a *jìtán* (precept platform).
He ordained over a thousand people. Consequently, an imperial edict was issued for all monasteries in Jiangdong to establish ordination platforms and conduct ordinations on his behalf.

Later, he was summoned to the palace to construct a great statue of Maitreya. He composed the *Xinyao ji* (Collection of the Essentials of the Mind) and compiled works from the three teachings that elucidated the principles of the Buddha-dharma.
He passed away on the twentieth day of the second month in the second year of the Xiantian era at the age of eighty-seven.
Tang Shenying was a native of Cangzhou. At the age of seven, he followed a teacher to study the sutras and śāstras.
He later visited Chan Master Shenhui at Heze, who said to him, "You have a karmic affinity with Mount Wutai; you should go there. In the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, he departed.
In the middle of the sixth lunar month, I arrived at my destination. One day, after finishing my meal, I happened to wander through Xilin (Western Grove).

Suddenly, I entered a courtyard with a signboard that read "Fahua" (Lotus Sūtra). Its outer triple gate consisted of thirteen bays, and its walls were painted with scenes of the ten monasteries of Mount Wutai.

Inside, the inner triple gate featured sculpted images of the *Huoguo Renwang* (State-Protecting Benevolent Kings). There stood a lofty and towering pavilion enshrining images of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
Above these, the other palaces, processions, and ritual implements were so vast that they were obscured by their brilliance. At the very center stood the Stūpa of Many Jewels (*Prabhūtaratna*).

Its magnificent adornments were exactly as described in the sūtra; at that moment, my spirit was dazed and my senses bewildered, such that it was surely beyond the capacity of the ears and eyes to comprehend.
Upon emerging, the assembly of monks appeared with strange and extraordinary countenances, bowing to one another and exchanging greetings, as we then proceeded toward the east.
After walking about thirty paces, he heard the sound of a door closing; looking back, however, he saw nothing. Daoying then wept and said, "This Great Sage has awakened me.
How could I dare to be negligent? He then made a vow to construct [the temple] according to the regulations of the Huayan Monastery.

To cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish, he first constructed a hermitage at the site of the Huatapa (Huata) Stupa. He summoned craftsmen and procured materials, and before long the work was completed.

He commissioned Wu Daozi to depict what he had seen upon the walls and partitions, and he further inscribed the name "Fahua" (Lotus). There, he gathered disciples and preached the Dharma; his dignified bearing surpassed that of all other regions.
After a long time, he announced his passing, having reached the age of seventy-five.
The monk Da was surnamed Wang and was a native of Kuaiji. He entered the monastic life at the Miaoxi Temple on Mount Gui during his childhood.
As this temple had been established during the Liang dynasty, those residing there were all elderly and venerable; Da alone was young.
Subsequently, he traveled to various regions, visiting Master Ren at Huangmei, Master Yinzong at Caoxi, and Master Dao’an at Guangzhou.
The Master’s realization thus deepened day by day, and his fame spread ever wider. Those who followed him, carrying their mendicant staffs, flocked to him like waters flowing toward the sea.
In the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, he passed away due to illness at the age of eighty-two.

Zhiwei of the Tang dynasty was the son of the Jang clan from Jin-yun. He left home to become a monk at a young age on Mount Qianxuan, the mountain where the Yellow Emperor, Huangdi, refined his elixir.
Not long after, he carried his book-bundle to rely upon Chan Master Guanding at Shicheng Temple in Wozhou, where he received the teachings of Tiantai *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
However, his literary talent was rich and elegant; he composed two steles for Taoyan Temple and Touduo Temple, which were esteemed by men of letters.
He transmitted and recited [the teachings]. Those who recognized his worth considered him to be the reincarnation of Xu Ling. Huíwēi’s surname was Liú; he was a native of Dōngyáng.
He mastered the learning of Master Wēi of Jìnyún and was thus called "Little Wēi" by his contemporaries. He lived in mountain retreats and rarely interacted with the world.
Furthermore, among the disciples of the teaching school, he seldom granted approval to others, yet he alone deemed Zuǒxī Xuánlǎng capable of carrying on the lineage.
Truly, there was one who possessed true knowledge.
Tang Ju-fang, surnamed Cao, was a native of Anlu. In his youth, he received instruction from Master Ling of Langshan and enrolled as a student at Mingfu Monastery in the provincial seat.
He began by reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. After receiving full ordination, he traveled widely to seek out masters of the Southern School. Furthermore—

He founded the Northern School at the monastery of Master Xiu. Xiu asked him, "What is it like where the white clouds disperse? He replied, "It is not obscured. Xiu asked, "And what is it like after reaching this state?
He replied, "I clearly see one flower opening into five petals. Having received the secret seal, he took his leave and went to live on Cold Ridge in Shangdang.
Disciples came daily to challenge and stimulate him in their studies. The Regional Commander of Yuncheng, Palace Attendant Wu Wen-huan, [honored him].

Admiring his character, [the Governor] dispatched an envoy to welcome him back to the provincial seat to provide for his needs. He was soon thereafter established at Jian’anguo Temple. [The Governor] once asked him, “What will it be like after today?
He replied, “The ground shall be strewn with golden sand, and people shall dwell in peace within the jeweled sanctuary. The Prince of Wu increased his reverence and faith.
On the third day of the ninth month in the fifteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, he passed away at the temple where he resided; he was eighty-one years old. A stupa was erected to bury his remains.
[The Biography of] Quanshen. Tang Yifu’s secular surname was Jiang. He was a native of Tongdi in Luzhou. Having left the household life, he followed Chan Master Shenxiu and attained the Dharma.
He first resided at Guanghua Temple in Lantian for twenty years, and subsequently moved to Ci’en Temple in the capital. His Way...
His reputation grew increasingly eminent. In the eleventh year of the Kaiyuan era, when the Emperor’s carriage traveled to the Eastern Capital, he was summoned to attend the imperial entourage.
Wherever they passed, officials, soldiers, and commoners prepared magnificent banners to welcome and guide him, filling the roads; this was especially pronounced in the two prefectures of Pu and Guo.

This was because Master Xiu had originated from Huangmei and had spread his transformative teachings throughout Guanzhong and Luoyang; thus, although he was already revered by the Emperor, the Empress, and the princes and dukes, he was now accorded such formal ritual honors.
Wherever he resided, he never once proclaimed the fundamental tenets to instruct his disciples; thus, his merit was likewise [unmanifest].
One day, as he ascended the hall to preach, the Grand Marshal Fang Guan, the Vice Minister of War Zhang Jun, the Vice Minister of Rites Wei Zhi, and other eminent officials were all present.
He then said, "Today, I bid farewell to you all. Having finished speaking, he withdrew.
Zhang then spoke privately to Fang: "I have been taking elixirs of golden cinnabar since my youth, and I have always strictly avoided presiding over funerals.

Now that the Great Master has passed away in this manner, I dare not remain. He then departed, with no one knowing his reason. Fu Xing later said to Fang: "I have been traveling with Zhang for many years.
Yet, when the retribution of past karma arrives, it cannot be avoided in such a way. Had he been able to exercise a little patience, he might have seen it through to the end."
"I have met you; I still hold out some hope for you. Furthermore, he took Fan’s hand and said, "Exert yourself; you shall surely become a renowned minister of the Restoration.
Later, when Zhang Guo fell into the hands of the rebels, Fan rendered meritorious service in supporting the throne.
The postscript by Tang Ba states: Vajrabodhi—whose name translates into Chinese as Jīnagāngzhì (Vajrajñāna)—was a native of the country of Malaya in South India.
“Malaya” translates into Chinese as Guānmíng (Radiance). Because that country is near Mount Potalaka, the abode of Avalokiteśvara, it is so named.
His father was a Brahmin well-versed in the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*). King Jianzhi served him as his teacher. When Vajrabodhi was only a few years old, he...

He was immediately able to recite ten thousand words daily without forgetting them. At the age of sixteen, he left the household life and followed his teacher to study at Nālandā Monastery in Central India.
He practiced the Sūtras and Abhidharma until there was nothing he had not mastered. Upon receiving full ordination, he audited the Vinaya sections extensively.
Subsequently, he traveled to Western India to investigate the various schools of the Hīnayāna, as well as the Yoga, the Three Mysteries, and the Tārās.

He spent more than ten years on the *dhāraṇī* gates, during which time he became extensively versed in the Tripiṭaka. Subsequently, he traveled east to Laṅkā Mountain and journeyed through more than twenty countries, including Fu-shi (Funan) and the Nudists (*nagna*).
In the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, he arrived in Guangzhou. By imperial decree, he was invited to reside at Cien Monastery in the capital, and later moved to Jianfu Monastery.
Wherever he went, he invariably established the Great Maṇḍala and conferred the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) rites, ordaining four...

The assembly [included] the three masters Da-zhi, Da-hui, and Bu-kong, all of whom performed the rites of disciples toward him. In the nineteenth year, he accompanied the imperial entourage on its journey to Luoyang.
As it had not rained for a long time, an edict was issued to establish an altar and offer prayers for rain.

Thereupon, following the Bodhisattva ritual, at the place where they were staying, they used the *Amoghapāśa* (Unfailing Lasso) to dig a pit in the ground four cubits deep and erected an altar upon it, painting seven koṭis of Bodhisattvas there.
They performed rituals and chanted before the image, hoping that its eyes would open. On that day, it rained for seven days; the heat intensified and the sky remained cloudless.
After noon, the eyes opened, and a northwest wind arose with torrential rain. Roof tiles were blown away and trees uprooted, causing alarm and consternation throughout the region.
Yet the altar hall leaked through, and no one knew the cause. Some circulated the rumor that a dragon had flown away. The commoners and officials—
Day after day, tens of thousands came to visit. At that time, because the Emperor had adopted the Li surname, he held the followers of Laozi in high esteem.

An official, seeking to curry favor, requested that all foreign guests be expelled en masse. The Emperor granted this request. When his attendant informed Master Zhi of this, Zhi said, "I am a monk from India."
He was not a foreign guest; the imperial decree surely favored him. He ultimately did not leave. Not long after, he took his leave at the palace steps to travel to Yanmen.
The Emperor was greatly surprised and, taking him by the hand, led him up to the hall where they conversed for a long time. The Emperor’s daughter had been ill for a long time without improvement;

she had been moved to the Xianyi Outer Residence and had remained with her eyes closed for ten days, saying nothing. The Emperor summoned Zhì to bestow instructions upon her, and consequently selected [a consort] from among the palace women.
Two seven-year-old girls had their faces veiled with crimson silk and were lying on the ground. The Emperor ordered Niu Xiantong to burn the imperial edict elsewhere.
Zhi remained silent, yet she continued to recite it from memory. Suddenly, the two girls were able to recite the words of the burned edict without omitting a single character.
Shortly thereafter, the imperial princess also rose; hearing this, the Emperor did not wait for his guards but galloped off.
Upon her arrival, the Imperial Princess said to the Emperor, "The decrees of destiny are difficult to alter.
King Yama, moved by Your Majesty’s virtue, saw two women arrive bearing an imperial edict; he then ordered that my former nurse, Lady Liu, escort me back to follow those two women.
Thus, I have been granted half a day’s life to offer consolation to Your Majesty. From this point on, the Emperor held her in the highest esteem and honor. [Wu] was ennobled.
The Consort commissioned a statue of Vajrayus Bodhisattva, while the Prince of Hedong painted an image of Vairocana for the interior of a stupa;
both were undertaken with the intent of being cautioned by wisdom. He remarked, "I hope these two nobles may enjoy extended lifespans," yet both indeed passed away before long.
In the eleventh year, Master Da-hui Xing-yi requested that the *Abhiṣeka* sections of various scriptures be translated for circulation, and an imperial edict was issued.
A residence was established at Ziseng Temple. There, he produced the *Yogacaryābhūmi-japa-vidhi* in two fascicles and the *Saptakoṭi-dhāraṇī* in two fascicles.
The translator was Īśvara, a Brahmin from Eastern India, a high-ranking official and director of the Secretariat for Translations;
the scribe who received the oral transmission was the śramaṇa Wengu of Mount Song. In the eighteenth year, at Dajianfu Temple, he produced the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā*.
The *Five-Syllable Heart Dharani* and the *Essential Methods for the Yoga of Avalokiteśvara*, each in one fascicle.
Translated by the śramaṇa Zhizang; transcribed by Yixing. Furthermore, he supplemented the missing passages of the old translation of the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī*.
In the twentieth year, at Guangfu Temple in Luoyang, he said to his disciples: "When the white moon is full, I shall pass away. On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, [he departed].
He paid homage to the image of Vairocana Buddha and circumambulated it seven times. Returning to the monastery, he burned incense and made vows;

then, placing the Sanskrit manuscripts upon his head, he bowed to the translations he had produced. After entrusting his affairs with composure, he passed away in silence at the age of seventy-one, fifty-one years since his ordination.
His stupa was erected to the right of the Yi River at Longmen.
Tang’s Pujì was surnamed Fēng and was a native of Pú in Hedōng. Having ascended the ordination platform in his youth, he followed the Sūtras and Vinaya.
He served the Great Master Shénxiù at Yùquán Monastery in Jīngzhōu for six years, fully mastering his Way. During the Jiǔshì era, an imperial edict summoned Shénxiù to the capital;
Pujì then recommended himself. Emperor Zhōngzōng, considering that Shénxiù was venerable both in age and virtue, could not be treated with such casualness by [the world].

The affairs became so burdensome and turbulent that an imperial edict appointed Wujì to succeed him as leader of the community. In the twenty-third year of the Kaiyuan era, he moved his residence to the capital.

Nobles, officials, and commoners flocked to visit him in great numbers; his gate was as crowded as a marketplace. Wujì was naturally dignified and grave, speaking little and offering no formal instructions.

Yet, if one were merely granted the sight of his countenance, they would feel such overwhelming comfort and joy that they could not contain themselves, as if he had awakened them to some profound truth.
Those near and far were especially distinguished by this. In the twenty-seventh year [of the Tianbao era], he passed away at Tangxing Temple at the age of eighty-nine.

At his funeral, Pei Kuan, the Governor of Henan, along with his wife and children, donned mourning garments of hempen cloth and joined the ranks of the disciples, wailing bitterly as they saw him off until the streets were empty. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Dahui.

Yixing of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Zhang. A native of Julu, he was a descendant of Zhang Gongjin, a meritorious minister who assisted in founding the dynasty. From his earliest childhood, he displayed extraordinary intelligence;
when he read a book, he did not need to look at it a second time. Shortly thereafter, he received the Dharma from Chan Master Pujì and took him as his teacher to enter the monastic life.
Once, when Pujì was convening a great assembly, he invited the scholar Lu Hong, who was then living in seclusion on a separate peak.
Although the imperial court repeatedly invited him, he did not rise to accept. Jì requested that he compose a text to guide the local community.

Thereupon, Hóngxiù brought forth the text and placed it upon a table, saying to Jì, "The subject matter is abstruse and the language archaic; you must find someone brilliant and eloquent to proclaim it.
Otherwise, you may call him here, and I shall first instruct him. Jì hurriedly sent a messenger to summon Xíngzhì. When Xíngzhì arrived, he extended [his hands].
Senghong looked at him and merely smiled; he asked no questions and simply set the text down on his desk before departing.
Senghong was privately astonished by his casual and unrestrained manner. When Zhong and Fan performed together, a thousand people gathered in the courtyard.

Senghong stepped forward with his sleeves rolled up, and as they sang, their voices flowed forth like a cascade without the slightest error or omission. Senghong stared in amazement and sighed, remarking that Xuanji’s learning should be allowed to roam freely.
There was no profound principle within the Tripiṭaka that he did not master; he was particularly adept at the texts on *yīnyáng* (yin-yang) and *chènwěi* (prophetic commentaries).

He would travel a thousand *lǐ* to seek out and inquire after them, never ceasing until his purpose was fulfilled. Having heard that there was one at Guōqīng Temple on Mount Tiāntái who excelled in the study of mathematics, he set out to visit him.
However, his dwelling was beside a small stream where the current was extremely swift; standing on the bank, he did not immediately cross over, but from afar heard the sound of that man calculating.
He said to his attendant, "Today there will be a disciple coming from afar, though we have not yet seen him."

"If you remove one tally to frustrate the water, it will then cease to flow. Xing followed these words and saw the result; he prostrated himself at [the Master's] feet and mastered the entire art. The Daoist Xing Hepu was a man of unfathomable character. He said to Yin Yin: [The remainder of the text follows: "I have heard that when the Duke of Zhou was about to die, he entrusted the governance of the state to the Duke of Shao, saying: 'When the Duke of Shao dies, entrust the state to the Earl of Lü. When the Earl of Lü died, he entrusted the state to the Duke of Huan, saying: 'When the Duke of Huan dies, entrust the state to the Duke of Wen. Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he sighed, saying: "The Way of leaving home—how could it stop at this? At that time...
There was a Chan Master named Tan, who pointed him toward the elder An of Songshan. An, in turn, pointed him toward the Sixth Patriarch, Master Neng.
When the Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? he replied, "From Songshan. The Patriarch asked, "What thing comes in such a manner? He replied:
To say it resembles a single thing is immediately incorrect. He asked: "Can it still be cultivated and realized? He replied: "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent;
however, it cannot be defiled. The Patriarch said: "This very state of being undefiled is that which all Buddhas protect and keep in mind."
"Since you are thus, I am also thus. Having received this prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), Ràng served his Master for fifteen years.

In the second year of the Xiāntián era, he first went to Mount Héng to reside at Pánruò Monastery. During the Kāiyuán period, there was a śramaṇa named Dàoyì in the Fǎyuàn Monastery who sat in meditation day and night without lying down.
Ràng, recognizing him as a vessel for the Dharma, went to inquire of him, saying: "Virtuous One..."
“[Nanquan] asked, ‘What do you intend to accomplish by sitting in meditation? Nanquan replied, ‘I intend to become a Buddha. Nanquan then took a brick and began to grind it on a stone before him.
He asked [Nanquan], ‘What are you trying to accomplish by grinding this? Nanquan replied, ‘I am trying to make a mirror. Nanquan said, ‘Can grinding a brick ever produce a mirror?
Nanquan replied, ‘Can sitting in meditation ever produce a Buddha? Nanquan asked, ‘How then can it be so? Nanquan replied, ‘It is like this...’”
An ox draws a cart. If the cart does not move, one strikes the cart; this is the same as striking the ox. [The other] was speechless. The master said:
"You study sitting meditation; you study sitting as a Buddha. If it is sitting meditation, meditation is neither sitting nor lying down. If it is sitting as a Buddha..."
The Buddha has no fixed characteristics. Regarding the dharma of non-abiding, one should neither grasp nor reject. If you were to sit as the Buddha, that would be to kill the Buddha;
if you cling to the form of sitting, you have not realized the principle. One person prostrated once and asked, "How should I apply the mind so as to accord with the signless samādhi?
Huìràng replied, "Your study of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground is like planting seeds below; my explanation of the essential points of the Dharma is like..."
"That dew and rain—because of the convergence of conditions, you shall perceive its path. The first questioner asked, "The Path has no form or characteristics; how can it be perceived?
Rang replied, "When the mind’s eye opens and becomes clear, one is able to see that which is not seeing. The first questioner asked, "Is there arising and ceasing?
Rang replied, "If one perceives the Path through the lens of arising and ceasing, or gathering and dispersing, that is not perceiving the Path. Listen to my verse: Mind-ground..."
When the seeds are sown and meet with moisture, they all sprout. In the flower of samādhi, which is signless, what is there to destroy and what is there to create?

Huairang was born in the second year of the Yifeng era; he passed away on the tenth day of the eighth month in the third year of the Tianbao era. He was sixty-eight years old and had been a monk for forty-eight years.
During the Baoli era, an imperial edict conferred upon him the posthumous title of Chan Master Dahui, and his stupa was named "Supreme Wheel" (Zuisheng Lun). This occurred during the Yuanhe era.
Changshi Guiden composed the text and inscribed it upon a stele.
Liangling was of the Liu clan, a native of Mian in Basi. Having reached the age of *zhixue* (the age of resolving one's will), he entered the monastic life.

Once he had ascended to the level of full ordination, he continued his studies of the *vinaya*. As time passed and he reached the age of forty, in his later years he devoted himself solely to the propagation of the *Nirvāṇa* [Sūtra].
He first awakened to the essential purport of the school under Chan Master Dazhao. Guided day by day and month by month, he expounded the Supreme Vehicle at An Guo Temple in Chang’an.
Carrying his staff, he arrived [there], and those who did not cease [following him] numbered in the thousands.

On the fourteenth day of the fourth month in the fifth year of the Tianbao era, he passed away at the Shiling Jie Jingyuan (Stone Ridge Sutra Court) within the temple. He was fifty-six years of age and had thirty-six years of ordination seniority. Thereupon...
The cremation took place on the seventeenth day of the third week. On the tenth day of the tenth month of that year, the remains of the stupa were exhausted at Longshou Gorge.
To the right was the place where Buddhapāli enshrined the śarīra; to the left was the tomb of Empress Nüwa.
The eunuch Shangzhuguo Zhao Sikan of Tianshui erected this stele; the monk Shanyun composed the inscription, while his disciples Langzhi and Daoxun [assisted].
As with the one [preceding], they continue to commemorate his virtue, maintaining the incense and lamps to this day.
Tang Xuansu, whose courtesy name was Daoqing, was the son of the Ma family of Yanling in Runzhou.

During the Ruyi era, he received ordination by imperial decree and was registered at Changshou Monastery in Jiangning. Once he had received full ordination, his conduct became even more vigorous and resolute. In his later years—
Master Rujishi Wei entered the seclusion of Qianshan’s Youchan Temple, where he subsequently received the seal of transmission (*abhiṣeka*).

From that time forth, he exerted himself with diligent resolve and cultivated a state of tranquil harmony. Outwardly, he was not altered by cold or heat, hunger or thirst; inwardly, he was not moved by enemies or kin, nor by honor or disgrace.
Those who understood him considered his conduct to be the "infant-like practice" (*bāla-caryā*), and thus the world came to call him Infant-Like Practice Bodhisattva.
Suo’an. During the Kaiyuan era, Wei Xian, the Governor of Jingkou, dispatched the śramaṇa Sengwang to invite Su to reside at Helin Temple.

Although Su was frequently seen wearing a patched robe while sitting upon his meditation platform, he remained largely unmoved despite being honored by those of high rank and distinction; consequently, those who came to gaze upon him and pay their respects filled the area.

On one occasion, he personally accepted an invitation from a butcher’s household, which caused the crowd to be struck with amazement. Su said, “The Buddha-nature is the same for all; how could there be birthlessness [only for some]?”

It was different. Those who could be saved, I would immediately save them. At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era, intending to respond to the summons from Wúyuè, the śramaṇa Xīxuán of Yángzhōu secretly took [the image] at midnight and headed north across the river.
The waves were vast and the moon was dark, making it difficult to cross. He held the boat and waited for a favorable wind;

suddenly, a white light appeared, guiding the oars as they reached the shore, whereupon the light vanished. The entire city came out to welcome and pay their respects at the ferry crossing. Carriages [filled the road].

His horses were so numerous they crowded one another, yet he did not avoid mud or puddles on the roads. He bestowed gold and silk coins in such abundance that their gifts piled up like mountains; yet he never once took personal interest in them, using them all for the expenses of the "field of compassion" (for the poor).
At that time, Li Cheng, serving as the Governor of Yangzhou while holding the rank of Minister of the Ministry of Rites, treated him with exceptional courtesy.

He paid his respects. Subsequently, a formal letter was sent from Jingkou inviting him back to the two prefectures; however, the clergy and laity there were embroiled in such heated debate that no resolution could be reached.

Such was the power of his virtue to move both animate and inanimate beings. On the eleventh day of the eleventh month in the eleventh year of the Tiānbǎo era, at midnight, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.
He was eighty-five years old. On the twenty-first day of that same month, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Huángquè.
In Shanxi, the local governors, district magistrates, and officials of the various commanderies all offered their condolences and observed the rites of mourning for three years.
Among them, the Dharma-heir disciples Fajian and Faqin have separate biographies. The disciples by Bodhisattva precept were Qi Chao, Minister of the Ministry of Personnel;
Liang Qing, Commander-in-Chief of Guangzhou; Xu Qiao, Governor of Runzhou; and Wei Zhao of Jingzhao.
During the Dàhé period, the Secretariat Drafter Han Shang, the Censor-in-Chief Li Dan,
and the Minister of Rites Cui Lingqin posthumously conferred the title of Chan Master Dàjīn upon him, and named his stupa Dàbǎo Héng.
Tang Xiangyu was surnamed Li and was a native of Jiyin. His father served as a subordinate official in the Yanzhou Prefecture and was preoccupied with fame and status.

Xiangyu grew weary of this and began to take pleasure in the teachings of Laozi and Zhuangzi regarding tranquility and detachment. Upon reading the Buddhist scriptures (*bai shu*), his spirit resonated with their meaning and his mind attained harmony;
his thoughts and intentions became fully integrated. He subsequently went to Cangzhou’s Anding Temple to follow Vinaya Master Zhiguang and undergo tonsure. Having received full ordination, he...

He observed the precepts and further investigated the Vinaya teachings. Shortly thereafter, he took his leave. At that time, Master Xiu was flourishing in his propagation of the Dharma, and Fayu managed to join the ranks of his disciples.
After a long period, he fully grasped the essential instructions of Master Xiu. He then entered Dafoshan in Fushui to cultivate himself in seclusion.

The regional governor, Han Rui, deeply admired his virtue and repeatedly sent gifts and invitations for him to come out of the mountains; however, Fayu consistently feigned illness and refused to comply. Day by day...

He propagated the teachings of both the Black and White [sects], and his reputation was widespread. Master Han followed in his tracks with a carriage drawn by black oxen, and offerings from the laity accumulated in great numbers.
