Furthermore, he constructed a Dharma Hall to advance the monastic community. Master Han asked, "Regarding matters after the Buddha-dharma has passed away, what is it like? He replied:

He was like the vast void, leaving all matters to those with the capacity [to handle them]. His followers, coming and going, were always over a thousand in number. Once, as he ascended the seat, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"How excellent is this assembly! Those who encounter it do so with difficulty. You must resolve your doubts; do not let this time pass in vain.
Thereupon, he requested water for ablution, sat in the full-lotus posture, and passed away. He was seventy-three years of age.
Tang Zhifeng, surnamed Wu, was a native of Huai’an. In his middle years, he practiced as a *dhūta* while still a layman (*baiyi*).
Later, he relied upon Master Heng of Qingjing Temple in the prefecture, where he shaved his head and received full ordination. He began by studying the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.

Some criticized him for being mired in conceptual designations (*nāmākāra*), which prompted him to suddenly resolve to travel to Mount Wudang. There, upon meeting Master Xiu, the doubts in his mind melted away like ice. He then sought to cultivate [his realization].
The "Holy Fetus" (the Master) then took his leave and went to Mount Anfeng at Puzhen. There he lived on forest fruits and drank from mountain streams, observing the *brahmacarya* for ten years.
At that time, the Prefectural Governor, Wei Jian, invited him to reside at Ankoku-ji Temple; disciples flocked there in competition, and the community flourished and grew prosperous.
The Governor asked, "How is it today? He replied, "The sun rises from the Mongsu [the eastern ocean]; when it shines upon a tree, it is always without shadow. [This was] sent by Feng.

He went to Mount Zhongtiao twenty years ago; those who attained his Way there are beyond counting. After he manifested his passing into extinction, his disciples erected a stupa thirty *li* to the north of the prefecture.
Tang Xuānlǎng, courtesy name Huìmíng, was surnamed Chuán. His ancestors were originally from Púyáng Commandery;

when his great-grandfather Zhěng, the Governor of Jiāngxià, sought refuge in the region south of the Yangtze River, they settled in Wūshāng, Wù Prefecture. Xuānlǎng was the sixth-generation descendant of the Great Master Xī of the Liáng dynasty.
His mother, Lady Gě, dreamed that she was riding in a sheep-drawn carriage through the void; upon waking, she conceived. When the child was born, she laughed.
He did not cry. At the age of nine, he entered the monastic order and followed his teacher to recite the Indian scriptures, memorizing seven sheets of paper each day.
On the nineteenth day of the fifth month in the first year of the Ruyi era, an imperial edict was issued granting him ordination, and he was assigned to reside at Qingtai Monastery.

Upon reaching the age of twenty, he followed Vinaya Master An at Guangzhou to receive full ordination. His mastery of the *vinaya* was profound, and later, there were no sūtras or śāstras that he did not study. And...
He was particularly proficient in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and had long heard of the subtlety of the Tiantai school’s fundamental tenets.

He subsequently traveled to Tiangong Temple in Dongyang to receive instruction on the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation) dharma-gate from Master Huikaiwei. He then withdrew into seclusion within the cliffs of Zuoxi, which became his moniker for the rest of his life.
Vowing to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven, he once painted images of Avalokiteśvara and Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja on the walls of the temple hall. On one occasion, while burning incense—

Whenever he concentrated his mind in meditation, he would invariably perceive a divine light of five colors, drawing crowds of onlookers who gathered around him. At that time, there was a blind dog that would always arrive at the site and howl longingly while rolling on the ground.
Senglang took pity on it and performed repentance rituals for its sake; within barely ten days, both of the dog's eyes were completely restored to sight.

He dwelt leisurely among hills and valleys, instructing and exhorting his disciples without flagging for even a single day. For over forty years, he wore coarse clothing and ate simple food, never neglecting his small [duties].

Furthermore, he instructed his disciples to receive his spiritual legacy by constructing dwellings and repairing the sacred images. He also rebuilt two brick stupas, so that the layout of his residence became even more complete.

On the nineteenth day of the ninth month in the thirteenth year of the Tianbao era, he passed away from a slight illness at the age of eighty-two, having spent sixty-one summer retreats as a monk. His funeral carriage was placed within the grotto of the stupa; it lay level.
He entrusted the two fascicles of the *Fahua jing kewen* (Outline of the Lotus Sūtra), which he had composed, to his disciples Daobin,
Huitu, Fayuan, Shenyong, Shouzhen, Daozun, Daoyuan, Qingbian, and others.
Tang Jiangmozang (Conqueror of Demons) was the son of Wang of Zhaojun. From his childhood, his inclinations were extraordinary; he especially delighted in stillness and silence.
His father served as an official in Beizhou, where the family’s circumstances were humble and lowly. Consequently, [Jiangmozang] soon withdrew to live in a secluded and remote place.

However, the region of Qiao was particularly infested with malevolent spirits; anyone who encountered him would suddenly fall ill, become insane, or die. Yet, if they were permitted to dwell with Zang, no such harm occurred. For these reasons, he was called "The Conqueror of Demons."
He kept his practice hidden, and the world remained unaware of the heights he had attained. Later, while serving at Guangfu Monastery, he received the tonsure under Chan Master Mingzan;
he applied himself with great diligence to the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra* and the study of the Vinaya. Subsequently, he went to consult with Master Xiu of the Northern School.
Master Xiu asked him, "Your name is Jiangmo (Subduer of Demons). Here, I have no mountain spirits or water monsters; why do you instead act as a demon?"
He said, "There is a Buddha and there is a Māra. [The monk] replied, "If you are indeed Māra, you must dwell in the inconceivable realm.
He said, "Even this Buddha is empty; what inconceivability could there be? At that time, the assembly was without exception filled with admiration and submission.

Master Xiu then made a prophetic prediction, saying, "You have a karmic affinity for the ruins of Shaohao. After a long time, he entered Mount Tai, where his transformation of others through fruition flourished greatly. Thus it is recorded.
Some considered him to be the equal of Master Langgong of Jinyu Valley. Suddenly, he told his disciples: "I am now old and infirm;
I have a place to which I shall return. The time has come. He was ninety-two years of age.

Táng Zhìxián was surnamed Jiāng and was a native of Jiànyáng. He entered the monastic order in his youth and subsequently received full ordination, whereupon he devoted himself to the study of the teachings.
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era, he attended upon Master Dàoyī at Fójì Yán on the mountain in that prefecture; he drew water and gathered firewood without ever complaining of fatigue.
He eventually withdrew to live in Chìsōng Dòng on Mount Jīnhuá. During a great drought, Zhìxián gazed into the sky and struck a rock.
He spoke with arrogance and contempt, saying, "You are but dragons of karma; you have no power.
If you were truly Bodhisattva Dragon Kings, you would obey the Buddha’s command to save sentient beings. As soon as he finished striking the stone, rain fell in torrents.

Later, while traveling through Chang’an, the famous Tanluo invited him to reside as abbot of a great monastery, but Xian did not submit to his request. He subsequently ascended Mount Wutai and stayed at Ganquan in Taiyuan.
At the monastery, those who came to seek instruction from him arrived like a flock of deer. Suddenly, he passed away without illness; he was posthumously titled Chan Master Dayuan.
Huizhong of the Tang dynasty was the son of the Ran family from Zhuji in Yue. The historical records do not provide detailed accounts of his origins, his renunciation, or his practice of the Way.
He first resided at Mount Wudang in Jun. During the Kaiyuan era, the Prefect of Dengzhou, formerly a Palace Attendant...
Prince Wang Ju and Zhao Yizhen, the Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, met him at the Partyzigou Valley on Mount Baiya.

During their brief conversation, he attained a profound realization. They subsequently returned to report this to the Emperor, who immediately dispatched the Palace Attendant Sun Chaojin to welcome him with an imperial decree, receiving him with the etiquette due to a teacher.
Initially, he resided in the West Chan Hall of Qianfu Temple; later, during the reign of Emperor Daizong...

During the sixteenth year of his reign at Guangzhai Temple, as he preached the Dharma according to the capacities of his listeners, there was a Tripitaka Master from India named "Big-Ears," who claimed to have attained the supernormal power of knowing others' minds. The Emperor ordered Zhong to meet with him.
When the Tripitaka Master prostrated and stood to Zhong’s right, Zhong asked: "You claim to have attained the power of knowing others' minds; tell me, where is the old monk's mind right now?"
Dazhu said, "I was watching the boat races at Xichuan. Zhong asked again, and Dazhu said, "I was watching the monkey tricks at Tianjin Bridge.
When asked a third time, Dazhu was at a loss for words. Zhong scolded him, saying, "You wild fox spirit! Where is your *paracittajñāna* (knowledge of others' minds)?
One day, Zhong called to his attendant; the attendant responded. Zhong called him thus three times, and each time the attendant responded. Zhong said, "I had thought..."
"I have failed you; rather, it is you who have failed me. Nanquan arrived for an audience. Zhong asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Jiangxi.
Zhong said, "Have you brought back the portrait of Master Mazu? He replied, "This very one here.
Zhong said, "What about the one behind him? Nanquan was speechless. Zhong addressed the assembly, saying, "Students of the Chan school should follow the One Vehicle Buddha..."

Regarding speech: that which is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) accords with the source of one’s own mind; that which is not of definitive meaning (*neyārtha*) is mutually unaccepted, like parasites on a lion’s body.
Now, as for one who serves as a teacher to others, if they involve themselves in fame and profit or open up heterodox paths, what benefit is there for oneself or others?
It is like a master craftsman whose axe and hatchet do not injure his hand; it is like the load carried by a fragrant elephant, which a donkey cannot bear. Emperor Suzong asked the Master:
"What dharma have you attained? Zhong said, "Donor, do you see that single cloud in the sky? The Emperor said, "I see it. Zhong said, "Drive a nail into it; hang it up!
He asked again, "What is the Tamer of the Ten Bodies? Zhong stood up and said, "Do you understand?"
[The donor] said, "I do not understand. Zhong said, "Pass the pure pitcher to this old monk. He asked again, "What is the samādhi of non-contention?
Zhong said, "Donor, you are walking upon the crown of Vairocana’s head. [The donor] asked, "What is the meaning of this? Zhong said, "Do not mistake it for your own pure dharmakāya.
Yu Junrong asked the Master, "How should one cultivate and advance throughout the twelve periods of the day?"
Zhongmo said to the youth Dingyun: "Vigilant, you must simply be vigilant; distinct, you must simply be distinct. In the future, do not allow yourself to be deceived by others.
When Zhong was debating with the official Lin on the principles of doctrine, he ascended the seat. The official said, "I request the Master to state his thesis.
Zhong said, "The thesis has already been stated. The official asked, "What is this thesis? Zhong said, "As expected, it is difficult to refute. Then [he departed].
He descended from his seat. Tan-yuan asked, "After a hundred years, if someone asks about the ultimate matter, what will you say?

Zhong said, "Fortunately, you are already pitiable enough; why must you insist on having a talisman for protecting the body? When Zhong was about to conclude his fundraising efforts, he took leave of Emperor Daizong.
Daizong said, "After the Master has passed away, what shall I have to record as a memorial? Zhong said, "I request that the patron commission [a portrait]."
He took a seamless stupa and said, "I have come to borrow this stupa design from you, Master. Zhong gazed at him for a long time and asked, "Do you understand?
He replied, "I do not understand. Zhong said, "After I am gone, there will be an attendant named Yingzhen who will indeed know this matter.

On the ninth day of the twelfth month in the tenth year of the Dali era, he passed away lying on his right side. His stupa was enshrined in Dangzigu Valley, and he was posthumously titled "Da" (Great).

Later, Emperor Daizong issued an edict for Yingzhen. The Emperor raised the story of the "Seamless Stūpa" and questioned him. Yingzhen remained silent for a long time and then asked, "Do you understand?
The Emperor replied, "I do not understand. Yingzhen then recited a verse: "To the south of Xiang and to the north of Tan, Within lies gold sufficient to fill an entire kingdom."
"Under the shadowless tree, they share a single boat; in the lapis lazuli palace, there is no one to recognize them.
"Xiangtan" refers to the region of Danyuan.
Tang Jin was the son of the Wu family of Jingzhao; he left home at an early age at Mingfu Monastery on Yonganshan.
Feng was upright and elegant in appearance. He had thoroughly studied all the major Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras; when he expounded and interpreted the texts, his listeners forgot their weariness.

Later, while in Luoyang, he encountered Master Huizhao of Heze and awakened to the Dharma of the Mind. He sighed, saying, "Only today do I realize that everything obtained from the outside is not [the truth].
He subsequently resided at Mount Xiying in Tangzhou, where the Regional Inspector Zheng Wenjian welcomed him there.

Within the city, he raised the cry of the Dharma, and those who followed his guidance were numerous. When he passed away at the age of eighty-one, in the third month of the fourteenth year of the Dali era, he was enshrined in a stupa on a mountain.

Tanyi of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Zhang; his ancestors were originally from Han. From Zhang Liang, the Marquis of Liu, who served as the chief counselor to Emperor Yuan of Han, down through the Jin and Wei dynasties, his lineage of scholar-officials continued unbroken.
His great-grandfather, Heng, served as the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices under the Sui dynasty, attending the imperial entourage at the capital of Yangdu.
His descendants subsequently made their home there. At the age of sixteen, he attended Dharma Master Mōuliàng’s lectures on the sūtras and śāstras at Yúnmén Temple;
his profound understanding surpassed that of the assembly. The Dharma Master encouraged his mother, Lady Méng, to allow him to leave the household life.
Mōuliàng was the Bodhisattva Precept Master for Emperor Zhōngzōng. During the Jǐnglóng era, by imperial decree, he received the tonsure and, upon reaching the required age, followed Dānyáng Xuán...
Master Chang received full ordination. He studied the *Nanshan Shichao* under Master Tan-sheng of Dangyang.
In the fifth year of the Kaiyuan era, he traveled to the capital, where he relied upon Master Da-liang of Guanyin Temple to study the Vinaya-piṭaka.

Under Dharma Master Tan-zi of Chongsheng Temple, he thoroughly investigated treatises such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Abhidharmakośa*. At Anguo Temple, he received the Bodhisattva precepts from a śramaṇa from India.

He was entrusted with the compilation of the *Jie* (Precepts). Furthermore, he questioned Chu Wuliang, the Attendant-in-Ordinary on the Left, regarding the history, and Sima Zhen, the Director of Studies at the National Academy, regarding the observation of historical records.

Thus, his knowledge became comprehensive both within and without the court, and he achieved mastery in both Confucianism and Buddhism; consequently, his reputation began to flourish. He was patronized by Zhang Yi, the Duke of Yan and Chancellor;
Song Jing of Guangping; Su Gui, the Minister of the Court of Civil Office; Lu Xiangxian of Yanzhou; and He [Yuan], the Director of the Imperial Library.

Zhizhang and Wan Qirong, the Magistrate of Jing County in Xuanzhou, were both his companions in travel and feasting. In the twenty-fifth year [of the Kaiyuan era], he took up his staff and returned eastward.
The following year, an imperial edict was issued to establish Kaiyuan Temples in every prefecture and commandery; Zhang Chu, the Regional Inspector, nominated him to serve as the Abbot of the temple.
In the fourteenth year of the Tianbao era, the tide along the Zhejiang River became exceptionally violent, surging southward toward Qiantang Dayun Temple.

There was a monastery where he, together with about a thousand of his disciples, expounded the Vinaya nearby. Whenever the tide surged, they would all chant the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* Sūtra and would invariably stop when it subsided.
On the final day of the fifth month, while sitting in meditation at night, he beheld a divine being whose robes and cap were most magnificent.

He bowed his head in gratitude and said, "I have received your bestowed gift of the Dharma; I vow to reform my ways. Shortly thereafter, fifty *li* of sand surged forth at the site where the water had been driven.
Calculating it, this occurred only ninety days after the time of the Vinaya Master Faxian. Monastics and laypeople alike regarded this as divine.
During the era of Zhìdé, the state faced many hardships and the Buddhist teachings were in decline. The Prefectural Governor, Duke Wáng, with singular virtue—

He was sufficient to stabilize the drifting [minds] and it was appropriate for him to propagate the Way. I request that he be appointed as the *Sengtong* (Patriarch of the Monks), so that our customs and mores may remain pure and beautiful as before.

On the seventeenth day of the eleventh month in the sixth year of the Dali era, he passed away at the Vinaya Hall of Qian Temple. He was eighty years of age and had been a monk for sixty-one years (*lao*).
On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month of the following year, he was interred on Qinwang Mountain, to be enshrined alongside his ancestors.
This is the burial mound of the Upādhyāya. Previously, upon first entering the Pass, he paid his respects to Dharma Master Mingda, who gazed at him and said, "You are a lion among men.
There was also the nun Cihua of Zunsan Temple, who possessed spiritual powers and whose words were always proven true. She sang a song, saying:
Master Tanyi was a master of the Vinaya, possessed of great intelligence and free from all doubt; he was held in such high esteem by his predecessors.
He expounded the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* thirty-five times and revised and supplemented the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* more than twenty times.

Counting by the tens of thousands were the śramaṇas of Jianghuai who received the precepts from him; consequently, they donned mourning garments and carried the funeral ropes, wailing until the mountains were filled with their cries.
After the burial, Zhanran and others of Tiantai Guoqing Temple erected a stele, with Xu Gong Hao composing the inscription to perpetuate his enduring excellence.
Daojian of the Tang dynasty was born into the Wang family of Danyang; he initially attained awakening under Chan Master Huizhong at Mount Niutou.
[The Emperor] granted him leave. In the first year of the Dali era, he lived in seclusion at Nanquan Mountain in Chizhou. Later, he traveled through Xianghan and stayed as a guest at Ci’en Monastery.
At the beginning of the Yuanhe era, the State Councilor, Lord Yan, while governing the region south of the Han River, invited him to come and inquire about the Way.
He established the Dazao Monastery outside Fenglin Pass to receive students from afar. His offerings and provisions were abundant and generous; his preaching of the Dharma was but...
He passed away after two years, at the age of seventy-three.
Huikong of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Cui and was a native of Jiangling. His father served as an official in Lingbao County of Shan Prefecture and unfortunately died while on duty.
While observing the period of mourning, Huikong entered the monastic order under the śramaṇa Hengchao of Huiluan Temple to repay his debt of gratitude to his deceased parents.
He possessed the virtue of ultimate excellence. Before long, he passed the scriptural examinations with credit and was found to be exceptionally quick and sharp in his studies.

Consequently, he entered the Dharma assembly of Chan Master Ji of Songshao, where he received the seal of transmission (*kaji*). The regional governor, Duke Yuan, was deeply aware of his devotion and summoned him; however, he repeatedly declined on the grounds of illness.
When Emperor Daizong heard of his reputation, he issued an edict for him to reside at Guangfu Temple in the capital. The court placed its full trust in him for a long time.
He passed away at the temple at the age of seventy-eight. On the fourth day of the ninth month in the eighth year of the Dali era, his remains were subsequently enshrined in a stupa.
He was the Tang-dynasty Amoghavajra—whose name in the language of China means "Not-Empty Vajra"; nowadays, only "Amogha" is used, as it is an abbreviation.
He was originally a Brahmin from Northern India. In his youth, he traveled east with his younger uncle. At the age of fifteen, he took the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi as his teacher.
Within less than ten days, he was able to master the *Siddham* script, the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra*, and other texts from the Sanskrit originals.
His teacher marveled greatly at this. Shortly thereafter, he received the Bodhisattva precepts and entered the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu, where he cast a flower [into the mandala].

After examining his subsequent conduct, it was known that he was a vessel of auspicious signs for the Dharma gate. Upon reaching the age of full ordination, he became proficient in the Sarvāstivāda school and the scripts and languages of foreign lands.
In six months, he completed the great treatise on *śabda-vidyā* (grammar), and in two nights, he finished the *Mañjuśrī-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna*.
This was someone else; it was not a single decade or a single year, yet he had not yet mastered what is difficult to learn—how could his quick intelligence be anything less than remarkable?

He prayed to study the Five Families and Three Mysteries of the New Yoga (*Anuttarayoga*), but the Master did not grant permission for a long time. An imperial decree summoned Kūkai back to India, and people thought it certain that he would not remain.
One night, the Master alone dreamed that the images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the various temples of the capital all...
He traveled eastward. At dawn, the Emperor issued an edict to halt his journey at Kong. The Master considered this even more a divine sign.
He then fully transmitted the five divisions of the *Abhiṣeka*, the *Mahā-ācārya* rites, the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra*, the *Susiddhikara-vidhi*, and other texts.

In the twentieth year of the Kaiyuan era, the Tripiṭaka Master passed away. After the stupa and portrait hall had been renovated, [the Master] traveled through the Five Indias. His disciple was Han Guang.

Accompanied by thirty attendants, including Hui-bian and others, he first arrived at Nanhai. Liu Julin, the Commissioner for the Collection of Tribute, earnestly requested that he confer the *abhiṣeka* at Faying Temple, where he expounded the Dharma extensively;
those who received ordination numbered in the tens of thousands. He was moved by a vision of Mañjuśrī’s physical form. This was in the twenty-ninth year [of the Kaiyuan era].
Passing through the country of Ho-liṅ, he encountered a great wind; he performed a ritual to stop it. Upon reaching Siṃhala Island (Sri Lanka), he met the Ācārya Samantabhadra.

From this time on, he studied with no fixed teacher. Regarding all the secret treasury scriptures—five hundred volumes in total—including the samaya seals of the various deities, their ritual procedures, physical forms and images, altar methods and insignia, as well as their textual meanings and ontological characteristics, there was nothing he did not thoroughly master.

One day, the king let loose a mad elephant; people fled in all directions, none daring to approach. [The Master] stood in the middle of the road, reciting mantras with his hands and dwelling in the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*).
Though the elephant repeatedly struck him with its trunk and kicked him, he remained unharmed. Subsequently, he traveled through the Five Indias, where he frequently manifested miraculous responses.
In the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era, he returned to the capital and presented the letter from King Śīlāditya of Siṃhala, along with golden jewels, necklaces, and *vaipulya* [sūtras].

He was provided with Buddhist scriptures, various pearls, white woolen cloths (*kambala*), and other offerings, which were sent to the Court of State Ceremonial (*Honglu Si*). Subsequently, another edict ordered him to enter the palace, where an altar was established for the Emperor’s consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Later, he moved his residence to Jingju Monastery. That summer, there was a drought, and an edict was issued for him to pray for rain. The imperial decree stated:

At that time, the rain could not be delayed, nor could it be brought on suddenly. Dao-kong requested the establishment of a Peacock King altar (*mayūrajāla-maṇḍala*) to pray for it; before three days had passed, the rain fell.

The Emperor was greatly pleased and personally carried a basket containing a set of purple *kāṣāya* robes, which he ordered Dao-kong to don immediately, along with a gift of three hundred bolts of silk.
On another occasion, the Emperor summoned Dao-kong to stop a great windstorm; he requested a silver flask to perform a ritual, and the wind subsequently ceased. It happened by chance...
A goose at the pond bumped over a pitcher, and the wind rose even more violently. An imperial edict was issued to perform the ritual as before, which produced the desired effect accordingly.

He was granted the title Zhizang (Treasury of Wisdom). In the eighth year, an edict permitted him to return to the West; he traveled by relay station to Nanhai Commandery, where an edict ordered him to remain and proceed to Helong.
The Military Governor, Geshu Han, requested that his disciples Hanguang and others be separately appointed as Merit Commissioners. Li Yuancong was invested with the rank of Kaifu (Governor-General).
In the thirteenth year, Amoghavajra also conferred the Vajradhātu Mahāmaṇḍala at Kaiyuan Temple in Wuwei to several thousand officials and commoners.
On that day, the site of the ritual practice shook with an earthquake. Amoghavajra said, "This is the ultimate result of the collective devotion of the people's hearts.
In the fifteenth year, he returned to the capital and resided at Daxingshan Temple. At the beginning of Emperor Suzong’s reign, Amoghavajra constantly [remained] in secret...

He reported on the events at Fengxiang and Lingwu. The Emperor also dispatched an envoy to seek the secret dharma. When the territories were recovered and the throne restored, everything unfolded exactly as he had anticipated.

During the Qianyuan era, an imperial decree summoned him to the inner palace to establish a ritual site for homa. There he received the empowerment of the Seven Treasures and the initiation into the rank of a Cakravartin King.
Toward the end of the Shangyuan era, the Emperor fell ill; [the Master] performed purification rites in the air and recited the Mahāpratisarā mantra up to seven times.
The following day he recovered. He submitted a memorial requesting to return to the mountains, and Li Fuguo proclaimed an imperial edict granting his request.

Thereupon, he cultivated merit at Zhiju Temple on Mount Zhongnan. One night, he was moved by Mahāsattva Mahāratna, who manifested proof through the emission of light; thus, he drew near to the stage of *siddhi*.

Amoghavajra said, "While sentient beings have not yet been delivered, how could I deliver myself alone? When Emperor Daizong ascended the throne, his kindness and courtesy toward him were most profound and generous.

Amoghavajra translated the *Yanming Jing*, the *Mimi Jing*, and the *Renwang Jing*; the Emperor composed prefaces for them and issued edicts for their promulgation. On that day, auspicious clouds appeared, and the whole world presented congratulations.

In the first year of the Yongtai era, by imperial decree, he was granted the rank of Tetejin (Special Advancement) and appointed as Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (*Honglu Qing*), with the honorary title of Dayingguangzhi Sanzang (Great and Vast Wisdom Tripitaka Master).

In the third year of the Dali era, [Emperor Daizong] established a *dharmapūjā* site at Xingshan Temple. By imperial decree, the close attendants, high ministers, and various palace guards were all admitted to receive the *abhiṣeka*.
In the fourth year, he requested that from this time forward, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva be honored as the *sthavira* (senior elder) within the monastic halls throughout the empire.
This was because, although Kauṇḍinya had been ordained first, he belonged specifically to the Hīnayāna. The decree stated: "So be it. In the fifth year...
In the summer, a comet appeared. An imperial edict was issued for Xuanzang to perform meritorious rites at Mount Wutai. Upon the completion of the rites, the star vanished.
In the autumn, he returned from Mount Wutai; the Emperor sent his own steed, a lion-colored horse, to welcome him back and provided ceremonial canopies and supplies along the route.

On the second day of the twelfth month of the sixth year, he presented the scriptures he had translated, totaling more than one hundred and twenty scrolls in seventy-seven sections, and offered his congratulations.
This was the Emperor’s birthday. There is a memorial regarding this that has not been recorded. As the capital had suffered from a lack of rain, an edict was issued to establish an altar for prayers.

The imperial decree stated: "If it rains within three days, it shall be due to the power of the Dharma; if it is after three days, it is not due to the power of the Dharma. After barely two days, there was indeed a great downpour.
The Emperor bestowed upon him one set of purple silk robes and one hundred rolls of variegated brocade, and one set of robes for each of his disciples.

He provided meals for a thousand monks and requested the construction of a Mañjuśrī Pavilion, which was completed through the joint efforts of the Noble Consort, the Prince of Huaiyang, and the Princess of Huayang.
The Imperial Treasury contributed approximately thirty million coins to assist in its completion. In the ninth year, he manifested illness and submitted a memorial to resign.

The Emperor issued an edict to inquire after his health and bestowed medicine upon him, further conferring upon him the rank of Kai-fu-yi-tong-san-si and the title of Duke of Su with an appanage of three thousand households; however, he firmly declined these honors.
The request was not granted. He passed away on the fifteenth day of the sixth month at the age of seventy; his years as a monk (śrāmaṇera-vassa) were fifty.

He was posthumously titled the Tripitaka Master Dabian Guangzhengzhi. His disciple Huirang succeeded him in the position of consecration (abhiṣeka). In the mastery of dhāraṇīs, he was preeminent and most illustrious.

He benefited sentient beings even more extensively. Emperor Xuanzong once issued an edict to pray for rain. Amoghavajra said, "This is a matter of celestial timing. It shall rain naturally on a certain day; it cannot be forced.

To force it would likely cause violent storms. He therefore informed his teacher, Vajrabodhi, about this. Indeed, wind and rain broke out with great force, and there were those in the market districts who drowned and perished.
The Emperor immediately issued another edict for Amoghavajra to stop it. Amoghavajra, in the courtyard of the monastery, kneaded six...

Seven old women appeared and splashed water while reviling him in Sanskrit. After a short while, the weather cleared. One day, he was attending Emperor Xuanzong in the private hall alongside the master of arts Luo Gongyuan.
At times, Gongyuan would use his *ruyi* (magic wand) to scratch the Emperor’s back with his hand turned backward.
The Emperor became angry and snatched the *ruyi* away, smashing it to pieces before him. Gongyuan tried to pick it up from the floor two or three times, but it could not be found. The Emperor then...
As he rose to pick it up, Hui-kong hurriedly raised his hand and produced a *cintāmaṇi*, showing it to Gongyuan. He then said with a smile, "This was merely a jest.
That which was on the ground was its reflection; could it have been picked up? At that time, a giant serpent appeared at Beimang and spoke in human speech, begging Hui-kong for salvation.
It further said, "I, your disciple, have often wished to turn back the Yellow River to submerge Luoyang, so as to satisfy my long-held intent. Hui-kong [responded...]
He administered the precepts of refuge and explained the law of cause and effect, saying: "It is because your anger was so heavy in the past that you received this karmic body;
now it has become even more severe. What can my power do for you? You must reflect upon my words and not abandon yourself to your own impulses.

Later, a woodcutter saw the snake dead at the bottom of a stream, its stench reaching several *li* away. During the Tiānbǎo era, the armies of the three kingdoms of West蕃 (Tufan), Dàshí (Dàshì), and Kāngjū (Kangju) [invaded].
The Western Liang was surrounded. An imperial decree ordered Xuankong to recite the secret mantras of the *Ratnatripariṇāmanā Sūtra* within the inner chapel.
After only fourteen recitations (two weeks), the Emperor saw what appeared to be more than five hundred people in the palace courtyard.

Startled, he questioned Xuankong, who replied, "These are the sons of Vaiśravaṇa, leading their armies at Your Majesty’s command to rescue Western Liang. You should quickly provide them with food and dismiss them. Shortly thereafter, Western Liang...
An urgent dispatch arrived, reporting that the three kingdoms were besieging the city with great intensity.

Suddenly, more than thirty li to the northeast of the city, clouds and mist shrouded the sky, and the sound of drums and horns shook the mountains and valleys. Within the camps of the three kingdoms, at midnight, golden rats appeared;

they gnawed through the strings of bows and crossbows until none could be restrained. Consequently, their weapons failed whenever used, leading to a total rout and collapse. At that time, some beheld a deity.
The people were all clad in armor and stood with swords and blades. A light shone from atop the watchtower of the northern city gate, where a Heavenly King sat glaring in anger.
The Emperor examined the divination book and found it increasingly full of empty words. Some said that Kong had no other skills;

when there was a need for prayer for rain, he would simply set up an embroidered seat and hold a wooden deity several inches tall in his hand. He would shake and spin it, then cast it so that it stood upright upon the seat, waiting for its tusks to emerge and its eyes to open.
At that moment, it rained.
Huizhong of Tang was the son of the Wang family from Shangyuan in Runzhou. He was born at the beginning of the Shenlong era;

by the age of twenty-three, he had already attained ordination as a youth after passing the scriptural examinations. He was subsequently assigned to reside at Zhuangyan Temple. His resolve and integrity were such that he was held in high esteem by his contemporaries.
He was held in high esteem. He subsequently traveled abroad and attained a profound realization upon meeting Chan Master Wei at Mount Niutou.

Master Wei consequently entrusted the entire mountain gate to him, charging him to succeed him as the abbot. Thereupon, he redoubled his efforts, practicing the dhūta austerities amidst the mountains and marshes.

Clad in a single robe and using a single cauldron, he sat in meditation upon his rope-cot from morning until night. In the twenty-seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, the county magistrate Changsun Sui went to the mountain to inspect it;

when he reached the midpoint of the ascent, a tiger roared and pounced upon the path, preventing him from proceeding. Upon hearing this, Zhong hurriedly went out to meet Sui and caused the tiger to depart.
At the beginning of the Tianbao era, the provincial governor and local elites requested that he return from the mountain to the temple grounds to preside over its restoration.
The temple was dilapidated and prone to collapse; it was thus renovated entirely. Furthermore, he intended to relocate the Dharma Hall to the eastern corner of the main hall.
There, he was moved by two divine beings who demarcated the foundation for him. At that spot, there happened to be an ancient tree with a magpie’s nest upon it. Zhong could not bear to cut it down.
Later, the magpies eventually built their nest elsewhere, as if they possessed some foreknowledge—how extraordinary! The tenth day of the sixth month, the fourth year of the Dali era.

On the fifth day, he assembled the community for the *poṣadha* ceremony. In the evening, he instructed his attendants to prepare a bath and shave his hair, just as he had done when he was free from illness.

That night, clouds and vapors were brilliantly arrayed, as if the sound of celestial music could be heard from the sky. The following morning, he sat in meditation and passed away at the age of eighty-seven.
While he resided on Mount Zhong, there was a tree with suspended bells and a vine upon which he hung his robes; this occurred one year before his final nirvana.
The wisteria trees all withered. In the ninth month of that year, while Zhong was preaching from the high seat, water suddenly gushed forth, flowing in four directions;
wind and rain shook the earth, and a white rainbow pierced the southeast. Wei Sun, the Prefectural Governor, provided ceremonial guards to escort him back to the mountain.
Five years later, his body was cremated, and the resulting *śarīra* relics were beyond counting. His other deeds and utterances are recorded in the *Chuan deng lu*.
Tang Jueduo was a native of India. Since arriving in China, he had received the Dharma of the mind from the Great Master Neng of Caoxi.
He once traveled to Mount Wutai, taking a route through Dingxiang, where he encountered a Chan practitioner sitting alone in a thatched hut.

When Tang questioned him, the practitioner replied, "I am practicing contemplation of stillness. Tang asked repeatedly, "Who is the one who contemplates? What is this 'stillness'? The practitioner was left utterly bewildered.
He rose and prostrated himself to request further instruction. Huineng asked, "Whom do you follow? He replied, "The Great Master Shenxiu.
Huineng said, "In the Western Regions, even the most inferior of the non-Buddhists would not fall into such a view. Why do you not go to Shaoyang?"
Yet it was merely laborious toil and of no benefit. That monk followed the instruction and presented his previous words to National Teacher Neng.

The Master said, "You should simply observe yourself and rest in stillness. Do not observe characteristics, and do not observe suchness; then, amidst the activities of daily life, you will naturally find peace and joy.
This point was not significantly different from that of Huineng. Afterward, nothing further is known of Huiman’s end.
Tang Daoyin was born into the Wang family of Pengyuan. He left the household life at Nanshan Ersheng Monastery in Ningzhou.

While traveling, he received the essential instructions from Chan Master Shenhui of Hozhai. Upon returning to his hometown, he preached the Dharma to guide practitioners, and his reputation grew ever more prominent.
Offerings from the faithful arrived from all directions, eventually establishing a monastic center that would endure as an imperishable tradition. (The 13th year of the Dali era)
On the final day of the third month in that year, he passed away while sitting in meditation at midnight. He was seventy-two years of age and thirty-five years since his ordination.
His disciple Bianzhen succeeded him in leading the community, and his transformative influence was hardly diminished compared to that of Huian. Not long after, Bianzhen also passed away.
Today, the stupas for both master and disciple remain there.
Tang Hengyue, surnamed Han, was a native of Shangdang. Her father, a salt merchant, encountered bandits and drowned in the West River. Her mother subsequently remarried;

although Hengyue was young, she harbored deep feelings of shame and resentment. She thus entered the Shengshan Temple to seek refuge under Huichu, seeking to repay her debt of gratitude for her upbringing.
Having received the full precepts, she traveled to Mount Song to inquire about the essentials of the Bodhicitta. Thereafter, she propagated the Dharma at Cuiwei on Mount Wanghu.
In an ancient monastery beneath the cliffs, students from all quarters gathered in such numbers that their sleeves touched one another.

In the first year of the Jianzhong era, he manifested a slight illness and passed away at the age of seventy-nine. A stupa was erected for his burial on the twelfth day of the third month of that same year.
Zhanran of the Tang dynasty was the son of the Qi clan from Jingxi in Piling. His family had been of scholarly and humble background for generations.
At the age of twenty, he served as a lay practitioner under Master Xuanglang of Zuoqi, receiving the scriptures from him. On another occasion, Xuanglang asked him, "What did you dream of?
He replied, "Last night I dreamed that, wearing a saṃghāṭī robe and holding two wheels, I was traveling across a great river. Xuanglang—
He said, "Alas! Will you not employ the two dharmas of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to ferry sentient beings across the abyss of birth and death?
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era, he first donned the black robes of a monk. He subsequently followed the Dharma Master Tányì of Yuèzhōu to exhaustively study the *Vinaya-piṭaka*.

Later, at Kāiyuán Monastery in Wú, he extensively expounded what he had learned. Not long after, Master Lǎng passed away, whereupon he sighed, saying, "How difficult it is for the Way to be practiced!"
I understand this. The supreme persons of antiquity remained still to contemplate the fundamental source and moved to respond to phenomena;
they abided in neither, and only then were they nearly able to tread upon the Great Whole. People of today are either swept away by emptiness or stuck fast to existence.
If one sets me aside, who else is sufficient to provide a standard for correction? Thereupon, I have recounted the transmitted chapters and sentences, totaling ten.

It consists of tens of thousands of words, intended to be bequeathed to posterity. Although imperial edicts repeatedly summoned him, he ultimately declined on the grounds of illness and did not rise to the call.

Even during times of great military conflict and severe famine, those who sought refuge in him increased ever more, yet his guidance of the Way became even more diligent. Clad in coarse cloth and seated upon grass mats, he led others by his own example;
until his final years, he never ceased his efforts. On the fifth day of the second month in the third year of the Zhongzhong era, he manifested illness at the Fulong Monastery.
He said to his disciples: "Now, that a single thought is without marks is called Emptiness (śūnyatā). That no dharma is not fully contained within it is called Provisionality (prajñapti).
That it is neither one nor different is called the Middle (madhyama). In the state of ordinary beings, these are the three causes; in the state of the sages, they are the three virtues (triguṇa).

When lighting a wick, the beginning and the end share the same nature; when crossing the sea, the shallow and the deep flow differently. To benefit oneself and to benefit others lies solely in this. You all—"
"Do not be negligent. Thereupon, he leaned back against his armrest and passed away in stillness. He was seventy-two years of age and thirty-four years since his ordination.
A stupa was erected, and his entire body was interred in the southwest corner of the burial site of the Great Master Zhizhe. His successor in the Dharma was the śramaṇa Yuànhào of Wumen.

Among his writings during his lifetime were the *Fahua shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Lotus Sutra) and the *Fahua shuji* (Commentary and Records on the Lotus Sutra), each consisting of ten fascicles.

*Zhiguan fuxing zhuanhong jue* (Explanatory Instructions for the Transmission and Propagation of the *Mohe zhiguan*), ten fascicles; *Fahua sanmei bubo yi* (Supplementary Ritual for the Lotus Samādhi), one fascicle; *Fangdeng chan buque yi* (Supplementary Ritual for the Vaipulya Repentance), two fascicles;
*Lüe weimo shu* (Abridged Commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*), ten fascicles; *Weimo shuji* (Recorded Notes on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* Commentary), three fascicles;

*Chongzhiding niepan shu* (Revised and Determined Commentary on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*), fifteen fascicles; *Jinbi lun* (The Golden Scalpel Treatise), one fascicle; and the *Zhiyan yili dayi* (General Meaning of the Categories of the *Mohe zhiguan*). *Zhi*... [text ends]
The *Observations on Words and Phrases*, the *Ten Profundities*, the *Gate of Non-duality*, and other such works circulate in the world.

Among the scholar-officials who have attained the Way, the Academician Liang Su is preeminent; thus, he wielded his grand pen to reveal the Master’s profound treasury, and his inscription upon metal and stone is truly beyond reproach.
The Duke Si of Tang, surnamed Li, was a native of Hengyang. In his youth, he left the household life at Longxing Temple in his home prefecture.

Having received the tonsure and precepts, he traveled to the regions of Yi and Luo, where he met Chan Master Pujì. He thoroughly expounded the essentials of the mind and took great delight in them; consequently, he received the master’s prediction of enlightenment.
He lived in seclusion at Jia-shi Mountain in Nan-yong, where his reputation grew day by day. When Lord Niu governed Han-nan, he invited him into the city to pay his respects;

the Master firmly declined on the grounds of illness, and Lord Niu did not press him. Offerings and provisions followed one another along the road, and students gathered in great numbers to receive his instructions.
They came with empty hands but returned with full hearts, a practice worthy of high esteem. At the beginning of the Xingyuan era, he manifested signs of illness.
He passed away at the age of eighty-four.
Daoyi of Tang was of the Ma clan from Shifang in Hanzhou. From birth, he was grave and dignified; his gaze was like that of a tiger and his gait like that of an ox.

His tongue extended past the bridge of his nose, and the patterns on his feet formed the shape of a great character. In his childhood, he served Master Tang of Zizhou and received the tonsure. He followed Master Yuan of Yuzhou...
The Master received full ordination. After some time, he heard that Chan Master Ren of Mount Heng had received the direct pointing of the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi.
Thereupon, he emerged from the deep recesses of Mount Min and Mount E, as well as Mount Yulei, and traveled to the secluded stillness of the fragrant cassias and upright bamboos.
Upon his first visit to Master Ren, they merged seamlessly as one. He subsequently settled at the two mountains of Nankang and Gonggong in Linchuan. Previously...
That land was the dwelling place of all manner of *chimei* (goblins and specters); no one dared to approach it, for as soon as they drew near, calamities and misfortunes would instantly befall them.
Once, a figure appeared who wore purple robes and a black cap; he presented his respects before [the master] and requested that this land be granted to him to serve as a site for the Way (*dōjō*).

From that time on, the wild and fierce became docile, and the obstinate and violent were transformed. Furthermore, the Governor, Lord Pei of Hedong, held particularly deep faith and reverence. During the Dali era...
In the interim, when Lord Pei was transferred to the governorships of Lujiang and Shouchun, [the Master] once again registered his name at Kaiyuan Jingshe.

At that time, the Regional Commander, Lord Lu, considering that Zhongling was a great stronghold and ought to have a man of virtue and morality to benefit the fourfold assembly, invited him with the utmost diligence.

Thus he resided there for ten years. At the beginning of the Jianzhong era, all monks and nuns throughout the empire were required to return to their original territories; [the Master] accordingly returned to the region of Lian.

The General, Lord Bao, again detained him and would not let him go. Scholars from all over the world arrived, and they all addressed him by the title "Ancestor" (Zu), while their hearts followed his teachings;
thus the transmission flourished ever more greatly. Alas, how magnificent! He addressed the assembly, saying: "All of you, believe that your own mind is the Buddha."
Now, one who seeks the Dharma should have nothing to seek. Outside of the mind there is no separate Buddha; outside of the Buddha there is no separate mind. Do not grasp at good, do not reject evil.
Do not rely upon either of the two extremes of purity or defilement. Realize that the nature of sin is empty, for it cannot be apprehended in every thought-moment, as it lacks intrinsic nature.
A monk asked: "Why does the Master say 'this very mind is the Buddha'? He replied: [Because it is so].
To stop a child’s crying, he was asked, “After it has been stopped, what is it like? He replied, “Neither mind nor Buddha.
When asked how to instruct those who are neither of these two types of people, he replied, “Tell them it is not a thing.

One day, while presiding over the assembly, after a long silence, Baizhang gathered up the sitting mat before him, and Baoyi immediately descended from his seat. In the year Wuxu, he bathed without illness and passed away at the age of [blank].
He was eighty years old and had fifty years of ordination seniority. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Shimun. King Hyeon posthumously conferred upon him the title Daji (Great Quiescence).
Bao Ji, Duke of Danyang, constructed the stupa and erected a stele, while Quan Deyu composed the inscription.
Tang Fulin’s surname was Yuan. He was a native of Jingzhou. His father served as a judicial official in Xiangyang and had long been a devotee of the Buddha;
there were no so-called "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra) whom he did not visit. Fulin was thus steeped in these influences from his earliest years, appearing as if by natural instinct.

In his youth, he performed the rites of tonsure before the śramaṇa Qianzhu of Xuanjing Monastery. Having already received full ordination, he then sought the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West at Heze.

Master Hui-chan’s realization was fully manifested within his meditation hall, leaving no further latent tendencies. In his later years, he resided at Mount Dashan in Huangzhou, where students gathered like clouds and eventually formed a monastic community.
Lay patrons from all quarters contributed funds and materials to construct buildings for the monastery. He passed away after a long period of residence there.
At the age of eighty-two, he entered his stupa in the fourth month of the second year of the Xingyuan era.
Tang Haoyu was the son of Zhao of Shangdang. In his youth, he shaved his head at Qingjing Temple.

Later, he went to Luoyang to consult with Chan Master Heze Shenhui, receiving the seal of transmission for the sudden vehicle. In his later years, he withdrew to the mountains of Mount Heng. [The text continues: Hengyang Tai...
Shou Wang, the Vice Director, treated him with increasing respect and esteem. He passed away during the Xingyuan era at the age of eighty.
Tang Zhiman was surnamed Kang and was a native of Luoyang. As a young child, he saw his family preparing for a Buddhist assembly and felt a deep affinity for it.

He immediately entered the monastic order at Longxing Temple in Yingchuan and received full ordination. Upon hearing that the Dharma assembly of Chan Master Shenhui in Luoyang was flourishing, he went there at once and attained the essential points of the mind.
Traveling south, he arrived at Mount Huang, where he encountered a man gathering *huanglian* (Coptis).
He questioned him extensively, saying, "What is the name of this place? To which commandery does it belong? The man replied, "This is Mount Huánglián; it belongs to Xuān."
The city was plagued by many tigers. He requested that the Master remain there with gravity to exorcise and suppress them. Faman then burned incense and prayed to the Buddha;
consequently, the tiger calamity subsided. He subsequently built a thatched hut to dwell by Lingyang Spring, where he eventually established a great monastic center.
He passed away suddenly. He was ninety-one years of age. In the first year of the Yongzhen era, he was interred in a stupa.
Guangfu’s secular surname was Zheng and he was a native of Nanyan. In his youth, he relied upon the great virtuous master Si Hao at the capital to enter the monastic order.

Having received full ordination, he traveled among various monastic assemblies. While traveling between the Yi and Luo rivers, he met Chan Master Shenhui and received the separate transmission of Caoxi.
Following this intent, he crossed the river and traveled to Yichun, where he established a dwelling on Mount Yangqi and hung up his monk’s staff there.

Drinking from mountain streams and eating wild fruits, he remained seated throughout the day and night without lying down. The location was secluded and exceptionally beautiful; at first, no seekers came to visit him.
However, there were occasionally men wearing star-shaped crowns and feathered robes who passed by, riding cranes and phoenixes, engaging him in conversation.

He departed after the sun had shifted its course. Later, his transformation [of the Dharma] spread widely, and the doors of his followers were filled with shoes. He finally proclaimed his passing on the fourth day of the third month in the first year of the Zhenyuan era, at the age of ninety-one.
Tang Huai was the son of the Shang family of Heyang. His family possessed considerable assets, and he harbored no resentment toward his parents or siblings.

Yet, Huai resolutely sought liberation from worldly life. He thus relied upon Dushan Guangfu Monastery in his local district, where he served Chan Master Daming as his preceptor and left the household life.
Once he had received full ordination, Daming sent him to the capital to meet Chan Master Xiu, so that he might realize the truth.
Having completed his own affairs, he traveled to Jeongansan Mountain in Anok before long. There he happened upon an elderly man who said to him, "I pray that you, Master, will remain here;
it would be for our great benefit. Thus, Ung established a hermitage and stayed there.

One day, while local villagers were chasing a tiger, they saw Ung and said with joy, "The tigers in this area are violent and bring no peace; could you, Master, subdue them through your spiritual power?"
"No," he replied. "Regarding the tiger's violence, how does it differ from human violence? If humans do not harm tigers, then tigers will not harm humans;

this is the constant order of nature. From this day forward, you gentlemen should turn your hearts toward the good and completely cast away your hunting gear to establish a place of practice (*dōjō*).
Then the tiger’s violence may be quelled. The people followed his teaching. That very evening, a tiger stood before the hermitage with its eyes closed.

Fojing bowed. Kongdu said, "Because of your habitual anger and ferocity, you have received this retribution. If you do not cease now, you shall enter hell. Having finished speaking, the tiger finally departed.
The next day, after returning from the meal at the site of the Dharma assembly, the tiger again led its seven cubs to sit before the hermitage.
Fojing threw him the remains of the meal—cakes and food—and preached the precepts and repentance for him. From then on, the tiger...

The disturbances subsided. At that time, the provincial governor Zhang Liao dispatched his official Murong Xing to the mountain to welcome Daoxing. Upon entering the city, Daoxing was provided with offerings by the provincial administration;
however, Daoxing declined on the grounds of illness and did not rise from his seat. He remained at the mountain, where he constructed a monastery for his residence.
He passed away in the third year of the Zhenyuan era at the age of eighty-three. On the sixteenth day of the third month of that year, he was cremated, and his *śarīra* were collected and enshrined.

Stūpa. During the Tang dynasty, Zhenliang, whose secular surname was Hou, was a native of Jingcheng. In his youth, he entered Kaiyuan Temple in the prefecture to become a disciple under Master Zhiti, where he donned the dyed robes of a monk.

He performed menial tasks such as cutting firewood and drawing water, practicing the dhūta austerities. After receiving full ordination, he entered the Chan school of Pujie at Mount Song and Mount Shao.
He attained realization daily. Residing on Mount Longmen, those seeking his guidance gathered like clouds, and his reputation grew increasingly eminent.
It happened that the Imperial Commissioner, Minister Wang Duō, was governing this region; having heard of him and admiring his worth, he summoned him to Guang’ai Temple to facilitate his support.
In teaching others, he never showed even a hint of weariness, yet the subtlety of his refinement was such that it produced fine vessels.

He passed away. On the third day of the eleventh month in the fourth year of the Zhengyuan era, he suddenly informed his disciples that, as the final light of the setting sun, it was truly difficult to detain him;
after entrusting them with repeated instructions, he came to his end at the age of eighty-eight.
Tang Zangyong’s native place and lineage were unknown to anyone for generations. In his youth, he served Master Kong of Mount Song.
Upon reaching the required age, he received the full precepts from Vinaya Master Ju of Fenchuan. He then went to Master Ye of Luoyang to investigate and examine the Vinaya-piṭaka.

Furthermore, he traveled extensively through Mount Lu, Mount Huo, Xiang, Han, and Shuangfeng in Qi to explore the essential points of Chan. Thereupon, he returned to the capital, where he propagated and expounded [the teachings].
The Way was such that scholars flocked to it in great numbers. During the Jianzhong era, he was summoned by imperial decree to serve as a Great Virtuous One presiding over ordination platforms.
After Emperor Daizong had constructed the Huatayuan Monastery in the eastern city based on his former residence, he further decreed that [the Master] should take charge of its administration.

In the fourth year of the Zhenyuan era, Wang Xuan, the Director of the Left Office of the Imperial Secretariat, composed a poem in praise of him; Cui Gong of the Southern Terrace responded with a verse, and subsequently several other officials did the same.

The Preface to the Collection was composed by Cheng Hao, Rectifier of the Ministry of War. It was calligraphed by Wu Tongwei, Rectifier of the Office of Correct Standards and Director of the Chizhao Bureau.
Shen Yong of the Tang dynasty, styled Daogong, was of the Cai clan and a fifteenth-generation descendant of Cai Mo, the Grand Marshal of the Eastern Jin.
He resided in Jiyang, Kuaiji. During his mother, Lady Xuan’s pregnancy, there were many auspicious omens. While still in his swaddling clothes, he heard...
Whenever he heard the chanting of the scriptures, his demeanor was invariably one of rapt concentration and attentive listening. From his youth, he possessed keen intelligence;

whenever he read the two canons of Confucius and Śākyamuni, he immediately grasped their essential principles. At the age of twelve, he took leave of his parents and requested instruction from Master Jun of Fahua Temple.
In the twenty-sixth year of the Kaiyuan era, he received ordination by imperial decree and was assigned to Xiangli’s Xiangyan Temple.
He followed Master Xuanyan of the Fahua school to study the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*.

Xuanyan had produced the *Fujiao yilü pian*, and while others merely tasted its excellence, Wuyong alone mastered its profound essence without leaving anything out. Xuanyan said to others, "This disciple is the compass for scholars. Furthermore, he followed...

Master Xuānlǎng of Zuǒxī devoted himself to the study of the Chan gate of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Having completed only five summer retreats, he was already able to expound upon and realize its teachings.
During the Tiānbǎo era, Gùomì, a local resident, led the community in inviting him to reside in the western ward of Fǎlè Temple, where the buildings were made magnificent and grand.
Shortly thereafter, he traveled to the capital and stayed at Ānguó Temple; high officials flocked there daily. It was during the time of Lùshān...

He turned back and returned eastward. Passing through Xiangyang, he stayed for several months while Yu Guangxian, the Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief, was departing to govern the region south of the Jing River.
The Secretariat Drafter Dou Shao and the Palace Secretary Yuan Xian, who both revered his lofty character, received from him the essentials of his mind.
Wei Zichun, the Director of the Bureau of Historiography, was a man of great contemporary renown; he engaged in debate with [Sengcan] and was thereby refuted.
Regarding his character, the Director of the Imperial Garden sighed and said, "The Acharya may truly be called a *maṇi* jewel beyond the world, a lion among the masters of treatises.

Upon returning to his hometown, he continued to reside at Fahua Temple. There, the Palace Attendant for the Imperial Guard Huangfu Zeng, the Judicial Reviewer Zhang He, the Deputy Commandant of the Golden Myriad Guards Yan Wei, the Military Clerk Lü Wei, the Magistrate of Zhuji Qiu Dan, and the Proofreader Chen [Zixu] [all visited him].
Yunchu composed poems for their mutual exchange, continuing the literary legacy of Wenxuan’s travels. Lu Shishi wrote a preface for them so they might be transmitted to posterity.
He then ascended the ordination platform to confer the precepts upon śramaṇas and established monasteries to provide rest for travelers;
thus, the merit he bestowed upon all things was vast. Previously, the Daoist Wu Jun of Mount Zhong had composed several treatises which were refuted by him.

Alternatively, some believed him. Chen Shaoyou, the Regional Inspector (Cāngshǐ), requested a definitive resolution. Thereupon, Amoghavajra briefly employed his strategic insights and presented all the captured prisoners.
He subsequently composed the *Pòdǎofánmílùn* (Treatise on Breaking Down and Turning Back Delusion) in three fascicles.

On the fourteenth day of the eleventh month in the fourth year of the Zhenyuan era, he passed away due to illness in the Dharma Hall of Dayi Temple. This temple was [founded by] the patron Qi-du... [text ends].

It was established by Chen Shaokin, a military officer. Later, through the mediation of the local dignitary Xu Hao with the Inspector General Huangfu Wen, this title was submitted for imperial approval, whereby Yong was permitted to be buried at that site.
Was this not indeed destiny? He was seventy-nine years old and had been a monk for fifty years.

There is a collected works in ten volumes. Huangfu Zeng wrote the preface, while the inscription was composed by Lu Huai, a Proofreader at the Imperial Library, and the stele text by Qiu Shangqing, an Assistant Director of the Ministry of Revenue; all were masters of the literary brush.

Tang Xiqian’s surname was Chen. He was a native of Gaoyao in Duanzhou. While she was still pregnant with him, his mother loathed meat and blood. Upon his birth, he was precocious and stood out from other children.

After reaching adulthood, he was highly regarded for his reliability and integrity. His countenance and temperament were mild and easygoing, yet by nature he was firm and bold, inspiring awe and submission in others.
The local customs of his region were characterized by frequent licentious sacrifices; according to the seasons, they would slaughter oxen and pour out wine, dancing and singing within the shrines.

To pray for blessings, Zhixian frequently demolished local shrines and released the sacrificial oxen; his father and elder brothers could not restrain him. Nevertheless, no calamities or misfortunes ever occurred.
Consequently, people both near and far gradually began to believe in him. He then proceeded to Caoxi to pay homage to Dajian Huineng.
Huineng recognized his potential and said, "If you wish to be my disciple, you must be able to resemble me. Zhixian laughed and said:
"Yes. From that time on, he traveled between Luofu and the Three Gorges. In the sixteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, he received full ordination at Luofu and returned home.
That night, he dreamed that he and Dajian were riding a giant tortoise, traveling through the waters of a pond. Upon waking, he was filled with joy.
He said: "The tortoise possesses spiritual wisdom, and the pond is the ocean of nature. Thus, my master and I have long been riding upon spiritual wisdom to roam within the ocean of nature.
That we met in a dream was likely intended for the sake of transforming beings. Before long, Master Si of Mount Qingliang in Luling succeeded to the seat of Caoxi;
[Fahai] moved once more to receive him there. At that time, the number of scholars at Master Si’s gate could not be calculated.
Master Si pointed to Xuanzhao and said to others, "Though there are many horns, one qilin is sufficient. At the beginning of the Tianbao era, he built Nan Temple on Mount Heng.
To the east of the temple was a rock shaped like a platform, rising far above all other things; Xuanzhao constructed a hermitage there and dwelt upon it.

Consequently, the world came to call him Shitou Huashang (The Stonehead Monk). Among the long-established virtuous masters within the mountain were the three teachers Gu, Zan, and Rang, who [inherited] the lineage of Caoxi.
He was merely a disciple. Yet it was said: "Stonehead truly roars the lion’s roar; when the lion’s cub hears it, how could he not be courageous?
From this, his disciples progressed daily. A questioner asked: "What is liberation? He replied: "Who has bound you? Another asked: "What is the Pure Land?"

The response was, "Who has defiled you? His quick-wittedness and propriety were always of this kind. In the second year of Guangde (764), his disciples requested that he move to reside at the end of the beam.
At that time, as for the Buddha-dharma throughout the empire, Mazu Daoyi was the master of Jiangxi, while Shitou Xiqian was the master of Hunan.
On the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month of the sixth year of Zhenyuan (790), he passed away peacefully. He was ninety-one years old and had been a monk for sixty-three years. His disciples...
Ren Hui, Lang Zhen, Lang Bo, Dao Wu, Dao Xian, and Zhi Zhou together built a stupa on the eastern ridge.

Thirty years after the completion of the stupa, during the Changqing era, Liu Ke—a Doctor of the National University who was long-versed in profound principles and fundamentally esteemed the ancestral tradition—chanced to meet Dao Xian, who was eloquently recounting the Way of his former master.
Ke, seeking to honor the achievements of his predecessors, composed this inscription.
The inscription on his stele conferred upon him the posthumous title "Wuji" (Boundless).

His stupa was named "Jianxiang" (Manifesting the Signs). Yuanzhen was the son of the Chen family of Zhongshan during the Tang dynasty. His father served as an official in the prefectural administration; he delighted in goodness and was fond of the Way, earning the respect and esteem of his fellow villagers.
Once, a śramaṇa came to their home while wandering for alms and, at the close of day, requested lodging. Consequently, [Yuanzhen’s father] lit a candle to listen [to the Dharma].

While listening to his preaching of the Dharma, he attained awakening at dawn. On another day, Huizhen went to Mount Bazi and took refuge with Master Zhiyou, where he shaved his head and received full ordination.
Having traveled to Heze to receive the essential instructions on the ultimate meaning, he subsequently retired to live in seclusion at Mount Wuya in Nanyang.

Previously, this mountain was infested with many snakes and dragons; those who were bitten by their venom would invariably die, and no one could provide a cure. Upon his arrival there, however, these calamities were entirely eliminated.
He was no longer seen. One day, a strange man appeared before him and prostrated, saying, "I have resided here for nearly two hundred years, yet only now have I finally attained liberation.
Were it not for the virtue of the Zen Master, how could this have been possible?
In the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, Zhen passed away at the age of eighty-six. His disciples erected a stupa to bury his entire remains.

Tánzhēn of the Táng dynasty was surnamed Chén. A native of Wéiqīng, his family was poor; his father sold dates to provide for them. Tánzhēn followed him to Péngmén, where his father passed away while traveling.
Having no one to rely upon, Tánzhēn subsequently went to Dàyún Monastery in Xù to receive the tonsure and study the sutras and śāstras.
He traveled to Mount Sōng to realize the teachings of the Mind through awakening. At that time, Lǐ Zhōngchén Fěng was about to take up his post in Qiāo.

In the commandery, Zhen happened upon him in Rencheng. They struck their palms together in conversation and laughter, as if parting the clouds and mist; they lamented that they had known each other so late. Lord Li earnestly entreated him to accompany him to his post.

At the pavilions of wind and moon, they were able to engage in profound discourse day and night. Later, when the Lord was summoned to serve as the Governor of the Capital, he would frequently speak of Zhen with composure before the Emperor.

When an imperial decree was issued to summon him, Zhen did not rise to the call. (Zhenyuan) *Note: The term "尹京" (yǐnjīng) refers to the position of Governor of the Capital (Jingzhou), a high-ranking administrative office during the Tang dynasty.*
In the fourth month of the seventh year, he manifested his passing. His disciples erected a stupa to enshrine him.
Tang Fachin’s secular surname was Zhu; he was a native of Kunsan in Wu Commandery. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.

His mother, Guan, dreamed that she broke off a lotus flower and tied it to her sash; upon waking, she became pregnant. When he was born, his nature was gentle and refined; when playing with other children, he would invariably [compose verses].
Regarding his Buddhist practice: from a young age, he excelled in both vertical and horizontal studies, yet he did not exert himself under a formal teacher.

At the age of twenty-eight, intending to proceed to the capital to take the examinations, he passed through Dantu on his way and paid a visit to Master Sengsu at Heilin Monastery. Sengsu said to him, "Would you be able to follow me and study?"
He then personally shaved [the youth’s] head. Looking back at his disciple Fajian, he said, "This boy will greatly revitalize our school in the future.
Once he had received full ordination, the youth set out for the south to inquire widely about the various approaches and to seek instructions from the masters. Zhusu said:
He traveled along the current, stopping whenever he encountered a path. Upon reaching Lin’an, there was a mountain; woodcutters told him that this was the trail to Tianmu.
Accordingly, following Su’s words, he sat in meditation upon a rock and did not go elsewhere. One day, an old man bowed before him and said, "I am a dragon.
I have resided in this mountain’s abyss for a long time. Since your arrival, O Master, gods and humans [have gathered here]."
[The deity] provided protection; his majestic power was so blazing that neither my palace nor my retinue could remain at ease.

If you, Master, truly intend to teach and transform others, I pray that you relinquish this place to serve as a site for the Way. (The details of these words are recorded in a separate document. Previously, Wu Zhen, the Magistrate of Linhai, had also offered a separate island to him.
From then on, those who came to study became numerous. In the second month of the third year of the Dali era, an imperial edict stated: "I, the Emperor..."

I have heard that there is a Chan practitioner in the region east of the Yangtze River who embodies the Way; his virtuous nature is as pure as ice and frost, and his ascetic practices dwell in the forests and wilds.

With an empty mind, I gaze toward him with longing, my thirst for his presence ever increasing. Where there is resonance, there is surely communication; this would be a great celebration for the nation. I pray that the Venerable Master will descend from afar to the Middle Kingdom.

I, the Emperor, turn toward you with all my heart; may you not fail your vow of power. Manifesting forms in response to sentient beings, I now dispatch the inner attendant Huang Feng to deliver this decree and personally invite you to come.

Quickly fulfill my wishes. The weather is warm in spring; I hope you, Master, are at ease. I send this message and shall say no more. By imperial command, the local prefecture is ordered to provide transport for you.
Upon arriving at any prefecture or county, you shall be accommodated in a pure courtyard (*śuddha-āyatana*). Officials and clerks are not permitted to visit you.

The Master’s mental strength was exhausted, yet he did not calculate whether his disciples were many or few; he permitted them to attend upon him. When the Emperor saw this, he treated him with great gravity, inquired after the essentials of the Dharma, and provided offerings with the utmost diligence.
Yang Wan, the Minister of Education, sighed in admiration and said, "This is truly a high-minded gentleman beyond the secular world."

A hand-written imperial edict conferred upon him the title Guoyi (National One). At that time, those who observed the etiquette of disciples—including the Chancellor Cui Huan, Duke Jin Pei Du, Di Wu Qi, and Chen Shaoyou—accompanied him back to the mountain.
In the fifth year of the Zhenyuan era, an imperial letter was issued to commend his meritorious service.

The imperial favors bestowed upon him were exceptionally abundant. In the sixth year, while the Provincial Governor was administering the Jingyuan Monastery in Longxing, he requested that [the Master] descend from the mountain so that he might attend to his health.
In the eighth year, he manifested a slight illness; after preaching the Dharma, he passed away. He was seventy-nine years of age, and fifty years since his ordination.
He was posthumously titled "Great Awakened" (Dàjué). His disciples, including Shíxiàng and Chángjué, enshrined his entire remains in a stupa within the Jingyuàn (Pure Garden) of Longxīng Monastery.
The Prefect Wang Yán composed the inscription for the stele. There was also Huìchóng, who was likewise a disciple ordained by his own hand;
his deeds are detailed in a separate biography.
The Tang dynasty monk of unknown surname was surnamed Gao. His ancestors were from Bohai; his grandfather had traveled to Luoyang for official service and settled there.
At the age of twenty-eight, he registered at Tongde Temple to enter the monastic order and began his study of the Vinaya-piṭaka.
Subsequently, as the Chan school flourished, he received a prophetic transmission from Master Heze Shenhui. Prior to this, Shenhui had often said to others: "My Dharma must..."

He waited for those who were nameless before entrusting [the task] to them. When the time came and his sincerity was indeed proven, he traveled extensively and examined everything thoroughly to reach the pinnacle of his mastery;

thus, his ambition regarding his name was fulfilled. At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, the court officials Xianyu Shuming and Liu Hu urged the Emperor to cull the monks and nuns throughout the land to benefit the common people. Upon hearing of this, Wuming hastily submitted a memorial to remonstrate.
The matter was subsequently shelved. Li Shiming traveled south to Mount Heng. In the sixth year, he took up his staff and proceeded to Mount Wutai.
On the twelfth day of the twelfth month of the ninth year, he was just about to attend the midday meal at Foguang Temple. Having finished eating first, he sat cross-legged in meditation, motionless.
When he was shaken, he had already vanished. He was seventy-two years old by the spring-and-autumn reckoning and forty-three by the lunar calendar.
In the eleventh year, his body was cremated, and about one *sheng* of *śarīra* relics were collected. Li Baozhen, the Regional Inspector of Ze and Lu, erected a stupa to enshrine them.
Huiyan of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Mao and was a native of Xiangyang. His father served as the Magistrate of Judicial Affairs in Dongping.

At that time, Master Bianzhang was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Kaiyuan Temple. Huiyan, from a young age, followed him and received the tonsure; he listened to the teachings daily and remained free of any doubts or obstructions.

He subsequently began to expound the teachings himself to guide those who came to study. Before long, he joined like-minded companions to travel north to Mount Hua and Mount E, where he toured the sites.
At Maonü and Shanzhang, he visited the various peaks of excellence. Traveling through Luoyang, he met the Chan Master Heze and realized that what he had previously attained was not yet ultimate.
He proceeded to Mount Nanyue and settled in Liyang, where eminent disciples from all quarters gathered like moths to a flame.
He passed away in the thirteenth year of the Zhenyuan era at the age of seventy-nine.
Tang Chengxin, surnamed Zhu, was a native of Donghai. Her father served as the Magistrate of Jiuyuan and was killed during the An Lushan rebellion in the Tianbao era.
The family was ruined and impoverished, leaving them with no means of subsistence. Chengxin was still a mere infant when her mother took her to Henan to remarry.
