His heart found no joy [in worldly affairs]. He subsequently received the tonsure under Dharma Master Zhiming of Yingfu Temple and ascended to receive full ordination.

Traveling to various regions, he ultimately obtained the essential instructions of Master Xiù from one of his disciples. Later, he withdrew to dwell on Mount Nanyue, where seekers of instruction flocked to him in great numbers.
The Prefect, Wu Xianzhong, invited him to the prefectural administration; he declined and did not go. Only after being urged a second time did he go.
Upon arrival, he was lodged at Longxing Temple. In the eleventh month of the eighteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, he passed away, having reached the age of seventy-six.
Hengjue of the Tang dynasty was the son of the Liao family from Julu. In his youth, he received the tonsure at Yongtai Temple in his native village.
After receiving full ordination, he traveled to Luoyang, where he met Chan Master Heze Shenhui and attained awakening to the profound principles of the Dharma.
Upon reaching Jiangling, he happened to rest with his staff and alms bowl in an ancient temple. A woodcutter said to him, "This is Guochang Temple; it has been abandoned for a long time. If...

Those who possess the Way dwell therein; thus, through almsgiving, [the monastery] could be established. Daojue repaired the leaking roofs and raised up what had fallen, daily collecting alms to provide for guests.
Before long, it was transformed into a center for the Dharma. The regional governor and military commissioner, Minister Cui, wished to invite him into the city, but Daojue declined and did not go.
He passed away in the fifteenth year of the Zhenyuan era at the age of ninety.
Tang Shizang was surnamed Lü and was a native of Handong. When he was still young, he requested permission from his parents to leave the household life.
He followed [Master] Kai to the Kaiyuan Temple, where he shaved his head and received full ordination. After some time, he paid homage to Chan Master Ji of Mount Song and awakened to the subtle mind.

He spent several summers in silent meditation within a stone chamber on the Great Image Peak in Zhongshan, while those who sought him out as companions for inquiry [were so numerous that they] looked upon his reputation from afar.

It flourished until it became a great community, transforming the local customs of Boling. The regional governor, Lord Li Zhuo, looked up to him with the utmost sincerity and wished to invite him to his residence to provide offerings.
Daozang declined, saying, "My nature is that of a mountain recluse; I am unacquainted with formal etiquette.

I fear it would be an indignity to Your Majesty's majesty. Zhuo did not dare to insist. He then dismissed all his attendants and ascended the mountain to pay his respects as a disciple. He then submitted a memorial [requesting his presence].
The inscription on the temple plaque reads "Dingzhen. After Huizang’s passing, he bid farewell to the assembly one day prior and passed away while seated.
He was eighty-two years of age. In the first month of the sixteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, he was interred in a stupa.
Dizang of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Jin; he was the son of a royal clan of Silla. He was compassionate and forgiving within, yet stern and rigorous without.
His stature was tall and imposing, and his strength could match ten men. He often sighed, saying: "The Way of the Six Classics and the arts of the Three Clarities..."
How could he be spoken of on the same level as the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)? Thereupon, he shaved his head and traveled across the sea to the west to visit the Middle Kingdom.

Upon reaching Chiyang, he took a liking to Mount Jiuzi and chose it as his dwelling place. At the beginning of the Zhide era, the patron Zhuge Jie happened to ascend the summit to survey the scenic splendors;
seeing Sengzang sitting alone in a mountain cave, he found him truly worthy of admiration and examined his possessions.
One cauldron alone had its legs broken. When asked what he ate for his meals, he replied, "I take a small amount of rice each day, mix it with white clay, and make a gruel of it.
Jie was greatly shocked and prostrated himself in haste, saying, "If we were unaware that the Master’s ascetic practices were such as these, our transgression would be profound.
Thereupon, he announced this far and near, and people vied with one another to offer alms. Within less than a year, the monastery (Fan) was completed.
The hall was completed. In the early years of the Jianzhong era, the Prefectural Governor Zhang Yan submitted a memorial to bestow the name "Transformation City" (Huacheng) upon it.
Consequently, seekers of the Way flocked there from all directions. Previously, Zang had been bitten by a snake; when the venom flared up, no one could cure him.

Suddenly, a beautiful woman arrived with an excellent medicine and, after paying him respectful homage, said: "I was a child without knowledge who offended you, O Chan Master. I pray that you will forgive me."

Do not hold him accountable. However, as this mountain has long lacked fine water, I fear it may not be so [as you say]. This is surely a place where a community of practitioners has resided for generations;

there must be a spring emerging from within the courtyard. I hope you will stay for a long time so that we may receive your blessings. Shortly thereafter, a fine spring was indeed found. In the summer of the nineteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, he passed away.
Three years later, a stupa was erected for his burial. Fei Guanqing, Right Reminder of the Court of Remonstrance, composed a text which was engraved [upon the stele].
Stele. During the Tang dynasty, Dao Sui specialized from his youth in the study of the Three Contemplations (*trividha-śamatha-vipaśyanā*) of the Tiantai Zhiyi.

During the Dali era, the Master Zhannen of Jingxi entrusted him with the *Zhiguan fuxing chuanhong ji* (Record of the Supplementary Practice and Propagation of Stopping and Contemplation) to disseminate and propagate it. Among his fellow disciples was one named Hao Ran.
He was held in such high esteem that no one dared to challenge him; thus, it is evident that he was revered and submitted to by his contemporaries.
In the twenty-first year of the Zhenyuan era, the Japanese monk Saichō (Jie-zheng) traveled across the vast blue seas to receive his teachings.

He then transcribed the entire corpus of texts of this school and brought them eastward. Nevertheless, fearing that those in his native land who were as fragile as reeds might harbor doubts, he [proceeded as follows]:

He submitted a petition to the Prefect of Taizhou, requesting that the facts of his travels be officially recorded to serve as evidence. The Prefect, Lu Chun, immediately granted the request, stating:
"Master Zuizheng: although his physical form belongs to a foreign land, his nature is truly of the same source. He is uniquely endowed with innate wisdom."
He attained profound understanding through intuitive insight into all categories of phenomena and transmitted the teachings of Tiantai far and wide.

Furthermore, he encountered Master Sui, a "dragon and elephant" among practitioners, who unified the myriad practices within the single mind and realized that diverse paths converge within the three contemplations. Having personally received these secret instructions, their principles transcend all names and words. Disciples from other regions...
They were unable to believe and accept it. How could they not comply with the seal of authorization you requested? Therefore, you should hold this as a reliable testament.
After Fotudeng returned, this teaching spread widely; he then changed the name of a mountain to Tiantai and changed the name of a temple to Guoqing.
Furthermore, Hui-sui was honored from afar as the First Patriarch. Later, Hui-sui passed away at his place of residence.

Record of the Lineage of the Study of Wisdom, Composed by the Śramaṇa Tanne from Eastern Zhejiang (Part Four)
Tang Chengguan was born into the Xiahou clan of Kuaiji. At the age of eleven, he relied upon Chan Master Pài of Baolin Monastery on Mount Yingtian to recite the Lotus Sūtra.
At fourteen, by virtue of imperial favor, he was enrolled in this monastery and received the tonsure.
He immediately traveled in all directions to seek out teachers and friends. During the Qianyuan era, he followed Vinaya Master Li of Qixia Monastery in Runzhou, as well as...
Tanyi of his hometown was a master of the Vinaya-piṭaka. He visited Dharma Master Xuānbì of Jīnlíng to receive instruction in the Three Treatises (Sān-lùn) of Guānhé.
During the Dàlì era, he propagated the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Wàguān Temple.

Having received the commentaries and meanings of the *Awakening of Faith* from the Huáihǎn region, he subsequently studied the great scripture of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* under the guidance of Fǎshēn of Tiānzhú. He then traveled to Shànxī to seek [instruction].

Huiliang of Chengdu re-examined the *Sanlun* for ten years; he then studied the Tiantai *Zhiguan* under Dharma Master Zhanran at Suzhou, as well as the commentaries on the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and other scriptures.

Furthermore, he sought clarification regarding the meditative principles of the Southern School from Master Zhong of Niutou Mountain, Master Qin of Jingshan, Master Wuming of Luoyang, and Master Huiyun of the Northern School.

He perused widely and inquired broadly; there was nothing he did not master, from the Siddham script of India, the four Vedas, the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), secret mantras, and ritual manuals, to the classics and histories of the Eastern Land, the philosophical treatises (*zǐchuán*), the "Three Elegances" (*sānyǎ*), glossaries, and worldly arts and crafts. He would often say:

"Even sages of the fifth stage, who have realized *tathatā* through bodily realization, still give rise to conventional thoughts within their subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); how much more so for those of us currently abiding in the stage of learning?"
"Can one truly avoid this? In the eleventh year of the Dali era, he made a pilgrimage to Mount Wutai and Mount Emei, where he beheld the sacred images in their entirety.
He soon returned to reside at the Great Huayan Temple on Mount Wutai, where he devoted himself to the practice of the Vaipulya repentance rites.

Later, at the request of the temple abbot Xianlin, he was asked to lecture on the sutras and śāstras; thereupon, he became deeply contemplative and pondered that the *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra] embodies Mañjuśrī..."

This is wisdom—the principle of Samantabhadra. It manifests the ultimate limit of the myriad practices of Vairocana. However, the old commentaries were verbose in expression yet concise in meaning, insufficient for full illumination.
Between sleep and waking, I saw a golden person standing in the midday sun, grasping a *guan* (gourd) and placing it in my mouth, chewing it until it was entirely consumed.
Startled and sweating, I awoke and said with joy: "This is a sign of having swallowed and received the light that shines everywhere."
"How could I fail to transcribe the *Avataṃsaka* in order to repay the virtue of the Three Sages?

Thus, beginning on the first day of the first month of the first year of the Xingyuan era and ending on the twelfth month of the third year of the Zhenyuan era, he completed twenty fascicles. He hosted a meal for a thousand monks to consecrate the work.
Thereafter, while seeking someone worthy to transmit it to, he dreamed at night that he himself had transformed into a great dragon, its scales and whiskers gleaming like the sun as it seized...
It seized the azure void; its head was raised at the Southern Terrace and its coiled tail rested at the Northern Terrace.

After a short while, it produced several thousand small dragons from its body, which writhed and leaped about, dispersing into the blue heavens. In the first month of the spring of the fourth year, the abbot Xianlin requested that the new sutra be opened [recited].
In the seventh year, Li Ziliang, the Regional Inspector of Hedong, again requested that it be opened at Chongfu Temple. Virtue...

During the Zong dynasty, an imperial messenger, Li Fuguang, was dispatched to proclaim an edict. That very day, he entered the capital to participate in the translation work of the Kasmirian Tripitaka Master Prajñā.

When the King of Uḍḍiyāna offered the latter portion of the scriptures, [the Master] declined on the grounds that it should be done the following year; the Emperor granted this request. In the following year, he arrived at Putin.
The Minister of the Household, Lord Liang, invited him to reside for the summer retreat at Xiyuan Temple on Mount Zhongtiao. At the temple...

There was a certain monk whose actions were unfathomable, yet his words were frequently proven true. Before the [Bodhisattva] had even arrived, he suddenly drove the assembly of monks to sweep and sprinkle the grounds, saying, "The Bodhisattva will arrive here before long.
Previously, the temple had been plagued by many malevolent spirits, but once he took up residence there, they all ceased.

In the fifth month, the imperial envoy Huo Xianming arrived to proclaim the edict summoning him. Upon his arrival, the Emperor bestowed upon him the highest marks of respect and immediately invited him [to the palace].
He entered the monastery and revised his translations, producing forty fascicles. By imperial decree, he was commissioned to compose a commentary at the Cūtang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan;
this work consisted of ten fascicles. Furthermore, the Emperor decreed that the two monastic districts should each recite the new commentary once.

At the time he was composing the commentary, five lotus flowers appeared in the pond before the hall, manifesting the auspicious omen of double stalks and three nodes. Shortly thereafter, the Emperor decreed the translation of the *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā*.
In the *Jiezhujing* (Sutra on the Lord of the Realm), Zhi was appointed to compile the text. During the time when Emperor Shunzong was in the position of Crown Prince, Fazhao resided at Mount Wutai.

At that time, he received instructions and composed one scroll of the *Liaoyi* (Treatise on the Definitive Meaning) and one scroll of the *Xinyao* (Essentials of the Mind), as well as [treatises on] "The Causes and Conditions for the Sin of Eating Meat" and others.

Upon entering the imperial court at this time, the Emperor’s admiration and devotion were even greater. Fazhao had previously made ten vows, the first of which was to reside permanently in his quarters, possessing only the three robes and a single alms bowl.
1. Do not keep surplus possessions. 2. Renounce fame and profit as if discarding them. 3. Do not look upon women with lustful eyes. 4. Let not your shadow fall upon the homes of the laity. 5.
Until you have cast off this retribution-body, recite the *Lotus Sūtra* constantly. 6. Constantly read Mahāyāna sūtras and bestow their benefits universally upon all sentient beings.
7. Constantly lecture on the great *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. 8. Throughout one’s life, do not lie down to sleep by day or night.
Ninth, he did not seek fame to delude the masses or usurp the merit of others. Tenth, he never receded from his heart of great compassion to universally save all beings.
Therefore, he was able to contemplate, uphold, and practice these [precepts] throughout his life. He passed away at the beginning of the Yuanhe era, at an age of over seventy.
Among his disciples who succeeded him in the Dharma were more than a hundred people, including the State Councilors Qi Kang, Wu Yuanheng, Zheng Yin, Li Jifu, and Quan...
De-yu (Li Fengji), Palace Secretary Qian Hui, Vice Minister of War Gui Deng, Taichang (Temple Director) Wei Qumu,
Regional Commander of Xiangyang Yan Shou, Inspector of Yuezhou Meng Jian, and Wei Dan of Hongzhou.
All were moved to submit to his precepts and instructions. Furthermore, he authored the *Sui shu yanyi* (Explication of Meaning Following the Commentary) in forty fascicles;

the *Huayan gangyao* (Essentials of the Avataṃsaka) in one fascicle; the *Fajie xuylan* (Mysterious Survey of the Dharma Realm) in one fascicle; and the *Sansheng yuanrong guan* (Contemplation on the Perfect Interfusion of the Three Sages) in one fascicle.

He also produced separate minor commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka*, *Lotus*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, and other texts, totaling thirty fascicles. He established twelve assemblies for the *Amogha* Great Fast (*wu zhe da zhai*). At Yunhua [Monastery]...
Beneath the Prajñā Pavilion of the monastery, there is a painted diagram of the Avataṃsaka World;
the various sculpted and painted sacred images, as well as the transcribed scriptures, are fully detailed in the record composed by his disciple Qingman.
Tang Guangbao was the son of the Zhou family in Beijing. Having lost both his parents while still young, he subsequently pursued the study of emptiness and quiescence.
He visited every Zen monastery to seek instruction through inquiry and consultation. Initially, he met Chan Master Shenhui at Heze, who asked him, "What is your name?"
Zhangze replied, "Guangbao. Zhaowei said, "Your name is Guangbao. A 'name' defines the substance; 'treasure' (bao) is what you already possess. 'Light' (guang) does not come from without.
Even if you were to use it according to your own will, there would be no lack whatsoever. Throughout the long night, you have been illuminated without interruption.
Do you believe this? Zhangze replied, "I do indeed believe it. However, I do not yet know whether the light and the treasure are the same or different. Zhaowei said:
Light is itself the jewel; the jewel is itself the light. How could there be such names as "same" or "different"? Zhanran replied:

"When the eyes and ears perceive sounds and forms, do they proceed independently (*kàngxíng*) or do they interact (*huíhù*)? Let us set aside for a moment the question of independence versus interaction.
What dharma do you point to as the substance of sound and form? He replied: "As my teacher has taught, there is no sound or form to be found. Zhanran said:

If you realize that the essence of sound and form is empty, and further believe that the various faculties such as the eyes and ears, as well as ordinary and sagely beings, are all equal and like illusions, then the principle of their divergent actions and mutual interpenetration will become clear.
Thus, while he was first living in humble thatched huts on Mount Meng by the Yi River, the regions of Zeng and Fei were transformed by his influence.
The Grand Administrator of Shen then opened a quiet chamber for him in Yanzhou; at that time, the Minister of State Wang...

The high officials led the people of Yanzhou to welcome him into the government offices every time he visited, providing him with offerings. He was appointed to the post of Director of the Jing Room (Jingshi), and his plaque was inscribed with the characters "Baozhen" (Treasured Truth).
Vases and staffs were crowded about him in homage. In the second year of the Yuanhe era, he passed away at the age of ninety-two.
Tang Daowu was the son of the Zhang family from Dongyang in Wuzhou. At the age of fourteen, he informed his parents of his desire to leave the household life.
Although his parents did not grant permission immediately, he fasted for several days, vowing not to eat until death. Distressed by this, his parents relented and allowed him to do as he wished.
He went to rely on a Great Virtue in Mingzhou to have his hair shaved. At the age of twenty-five, he received full ordination at Zhulin Monastery in Hangzhou.

At the temple, he thereafter diligently maintained the monastic discipline and carefully selected his practices. He then traveled to Mount Jing, where he paid respects to National Teacher Guoyi and attained a profound realization.
In the eleventh year of the Dali era, he withdrew to live in seclusion at Damei Mountain in Yu’ao.
After three or four years there, he visited Master Mazu at Zhongling and spent another summer retreat with him. Subsequently, he went to Shitou at Mount Nanyue.
He asked, "Setting aside concentration and wisdom, by what dharma does the Master instruct people? The Master replied, "In my place, there are no slaves or servants;
what would there be to set aside? He asked, "How then can one attain clarity? The Master replied, "Can you grasp empty space?
He said, "If that is so, then from this day forward, I shall not go [anywhere]. The Master replied, "I do not know at what time or when you have departed."
"From where do you come? he asked. The man replied, "I am not a person from that place. The Master answered, "I have long been as you are when you arrive.
The man asked, "Why does the Master falsely accuse me with such impurity? The Master replied, "Your very self is present right now.

The man said, "Even so, after all, by what means will you show this to future generations? The Master replied, "Tell me, who is the 'future generation'? Through this, the man attained awakening and fully realized his former ignorance.
In the state of Guo, Master Ma employed his means, penetrating ever deeper into the marshes.
Suddenly, he built a dwelling at Liyang and moved to Chengkou, occupying Mount Zichai in Dangyang—the place where five hundred arhats had resided—to respond to karmic conditions. At that time:

When Pei Gong, the Right Vice President of the Secretariat, was serving as the Governor of Jiangling, he received a formal petition from Chongye Monastery requesting that Huiwu take up residence there. The Duke complied with this request.

Upon Huiwu’s arrival, both the clergy and the laity flocked to him, and offerings were piled up in abundance. The Duke himself also personally led his retinue to visit and pay his respects on a daily basis.

However, Huiwu always maintained the dignity of a venerable elder; when exchanging greetings, he never rose for anyone regardless of their rank, whether noble or humble. The Duke [was thus deeply impressed].

He especially marveled at his knowledge of the greater principles. Thus, the Imperial Temple Abbot Reigen said to his disciples, "Our temple is currently facing the calamity of being reduced to ashes.
If we could obtain Master Wuzhu, we might perhaps restore it from its ruins. Consequently, they carried Wuzhu by night to the abbot’s quarters.
The next day, Chongye and others clamored and disputed [over the matter], but when they could not prevail, they desisted. Later, the Emperor...
The imperial palace was indeed newly renovated. A monk asked, "What is the discourse on the profound mystery? He replied, "Do not say that I understand the Buddha-dharma.
The monk pressed further, "How can I, a student, resolve my lingering doubts? He replied, "Why do you not ask the old monk? The monk said, "I have already asked.
He replied, "That is not where you should rest. This was the last day of the fourth month in the summer of the Dinghai year of the Yuanhe era.

He entered parinirvāṇa at the age of sixty and with thirty-five years of ordination seniority. On the fifth day of the eighth month of that year, a stūpa was erected and his sacred reliquary (lingkan) was interred in the eastern corner of the commandery. The bhikṣus Huizhen, Wenben, and Chongxin succeeded him.
Tang Baoxiu, surnamed Zhou, was a native of Zizhou in Shu. In his youth, he left home to become a monk at Chunde Temple in his hometown.
Having entered a Chan assembly, he encountered the Dharma-heir of Master Ren of Qizhou, from whom he resolved all his doubts. Later, while traveling, he came to love Mount Luofu;
there, he remained in silent meditation day after day within a stone chamber. Subsequently, a donor completed the construction and expansion of the site, which became a flourishing center.
He established a great monastery. One day, he suddenly became somber and unhappy, saying to his disciples, "The conditions of cause and effect press upon me; what can be done?

None of the assembly could fathom his meaning. When Emperor Shunzong heard of his reputation, he issued an imperial decree for him to enter the capital, where he engaged in dialogue with the Tripitaka Master and corrected the translations he had produced.
He remained at the capital for three years, eventually passing away in a temple there.
Tang Faru, surnamed Han, was a native of Cizhou. In his youth, he engaged in trade to pursue profits of ten percent.

Suddenly feeling remorse, he followed Master Hongsi of the Xiangguosi Temple in Bianjing to enter the monastic order. After receiving full ordination, he traveled to the Song and Shao mountains to seek the Way.
There, he met Chan Master Shenhui in Luoyang, where his doubts were instantly resolved; he received the master’s seal of approval. Later, he withdrew to Mountaitai at Maitou.
At the foot of the peak, the garrison commander Wang Wenxin of Chu Dun led the assembly in constructing a hall for the purpose of expounding the Dharma and guiding his disciples.
When Li Yaqing, the Regional Inspector, invited him to the city, he did not go. He entered nirvana in the sixth year of the Yuanhe era at the age of eighty-nine.
In the third month, his remains were enshrined in a stupa.

Tang Daotong was born into the He clan of Lujiang. From childhood, his countenance was grave and composed; whenever he beheld Buddhist images or the ceremonial attire of monks, he would invariably pay them reverence.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era, he passed the scriptural examination and received ordination at Nán'ān in Qiānquán, where his father was stationed during his official travels.
After receiving full ordination, he visited the Chan Master Dàjí Yìgōng at Fójì Yán in Jiànyáng and later at Nánkāng.
At Mount Gonggong, he attained profound realization through secret accord, such that there was much he could not fathom.
In the second year of the Zhenyuan era, he visited Master Shitou Xiqian to further advance his studies. In the fourth year, when Daji (Mazu Daoyi) was about to enter nirvana, he said to Huizhong:
"The Mountain of Jade and Stone will support your path; you shall find a place there to dwell. That autumn, he went with Master Zizai of Funiu to survey the site.

In the capital of Jinglo, during the Tang dynasty, he encountered a mountain that was lush and verdant, lovely to behold. He asked a local resident, "What is this? The man replied, "This is Mount Ziyu.
Upon ascending its peak, he saw purple stones as brilliant and translucent as jade. He sighed, saying, "Is this not what my late master recorded?
Thereupon, he hung his staff and opened his satchel among them. Disciples who had come to study with him gathered like a mist; a monk asked him:
"How can one escape the three realms? He replied, "How long have you been inside them? The monk pressed further, "Ultimately, how can one escape them?
He replied, "The green mountains do not obstruct the flight of white clouds. Lord Yu Ti asked, "The scriptures say:
'A black wind blows their ship, casting it adrift and falling into the land of the rākṣasa demons. What is this 'falling into'?"
Tong said, “You, Yu Di, are a hired laborer! Why do you ask such things? Di flushed with anger.
Tong pointed and said, “You have fallen into the realm of the rākṣasa demons. One day he asked again, “What is the Buddha? Tong called out, “Lord! Di responded, “Yes?
Tong said, “Be careful not to seek it elsewhere. Later, when the Prefect Li Gonggu was serving as the Abbot of Ga... [text ends].
Lan. His disciple Jincang went separately to seek instruction from Chan Master Hai of Bai Zhang. In the eighth year of the Yuanhe era, Lan happened to return for a visit;
[Jincang] joyfully said, "You have come! This mountain now has its master. He immediately took up his staff and departed.
The monastics and laypeople of Xiangzhou welcomed and escorted him. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month of that year, he passed away without illness at the age of seventy-three.
Fapu of the Tang dynasty was the son of the Pan family of Lujiang. Historical records do not preserve the details of his initial entry into the monastic order or his tonsure.

During the Yuanhe era, he traveled to Huangguo in Qi, where he took a liking to the region’s extraordinary peaks and crags and its level stone altars; thereupon, he hung up his monk’s staff to take up residence.

After some time, he constructed a thatched hut by a tree to shelter himself. Suddenly, a person appeared, climbing through the vines and brambles and parting the weeds until they reached him. Upon seeing him—
Everyone hesitated and could not bear to leave. They all asked in astonishment, "How did you know to come here?

He replied, "At the foot of the mountain, I looked up toward the peak and saw purple qi swirling there. Thinking that there must surely be an extraordinary person there, I came. This report spread far and wide.
Day by day they flocked to him for instruction. Within a few years, his disciples numbered nearly a thousand. Huipu repeatedly declined their offerings, saying, "I am an old monk living alone;
I have nothing of benefit to offer. You yourselves lack for nothing, so why do you press me so persistently? His disciple Guangyan eventually constructed a magnificent monastery.
Those who received his Dharma teachings were beyond counting. As he was about to pass away, he gathered the assembly and told them: "I..."
He was about to depart. "You all must dwell well; take care of yourselves," he said. His physical body did not decay; because it had been coated and painted, it has survived to this day.
The Tang dynasty monk Zhizang, surnamed Liao, was a native of Qianhua. From birth he possessed extraordinary features, and those who recognized him knew him to be a man of great capacity.

At the age of eight, he followed a teacher to receive the tonsure. When Daji (Mazu) moved to Mount Gonggong, he went there to rely upon him. Furthermore, for the sake of Daji, he presented a letter to National Teacher Zhong. The National Teacher asked, "What Dharma does your teacher preach? Zang walked from east to west and stood there; the National Teacher said, "Is that all? Zang walked from west to east and stood there; the National Teacher said, "Is that all? Zang walked back to his original place and stood there; the National Teacher said, "Is that all? Zang then bowed. The National Teacher said, "Your teacher’s Dharma is indeed like this. Zang then bowed. The National Teacher said, "Your teacher’s Dharma is indeed like this. Zang returned to Daji and related the encounter. Daji said, "The National Teacher is a man of great capacity; you must go and see him again. Zang went again and stood before the National Teacher. The National Teacher said, "What Dharma does your teacher preach? Zang walked from east to west and stood there; the National Teacher said, "Is that all? Zang walked from west to east and stood there; the National Teacher said, "Is that all? Zang walked back to his original place and stood there; the National Teacher said, "Is that all? Zang then bowed. The National Teacher said, "Your teacher’s Dharma is indeed like this. Zang returned to Daji and related the encounter. Daji said, "The National Teacher is a man of great capacity; you must go and see him again. Zang went again and stood before the National Teacher. The National Teacher said, "What Dharma does your teacher preach? Zang walked from east to west and stood there; the National Teacher said, "Is that all? Zang walked from west to east and stood there; the National Teacher said, "Is that all? Zang walked back to his original place and stood there; the National Teacher said, "Is that all? Zang then bowed. The National Teacher said, "Your teacher’s Dharma is indeed like this. Zang returned to Daji and related the encounter. Daji said, "The National Teacher is
"This belongs to Master Ma. How about yours, worthy one? Mazu said, "I have already presented it long ago. He also sent a letter to Mount Jing.

At that time, Daji (Nanyue Huairang) was invited by the Regional Commander Lu Sigong to reside at the provincial seat, where he bestowed a patched *kāṣāya* upon Mazu and instructed the assembly to seek his guidance.
A monk asked Daji: "How does one transcend the four propositions and cut off the hundred negations?"
"Please, Master, point this out directly. Jì said, "Go and ask Zhìzàng. The monk asked Zàng, and Zàng said, "Go and ask Hǎi, your elder brother.
The monk asked Hǎi, and Hǎi said, "When I reached this point, I did not understand. The monk reported this to Jì, who said, "Zàng’s head is white;
Hǎi’s head is black. Later, while Zàng was residing at Xītáng, a layman asked about heaven and hell.
“Do these exist? Do the Triple Gems—the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—exist? Zang answered them all by saying, “They exist. The scholar said, “Master, you have made a mistake.
Zang asked, “What kind of venerable masters have you encountered? The scholar replied, “I have encountered Jingshan. Zang asked, “What did Jingshan say to you?
The scholar said, “He said that everything is entirely non-existent. Zang said, “Then you have a wife.”
The Master said, "No. The scholar said, "I have one. Zang asked, "Does Master Jing-shan have a wife? The scholar said, "No. Zang said, "If Master Jing-shan says there is none, then it is so.
The scholar bowed in thanks. At that time, Prime Minister Qi Gong Ying, Vice-Chancellor Li Gong Jian, Minister Li Gong Xiang, and General of the Household Pei Gong Tong all paid him their respects.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the ninth year of the Yuanhe era.

He passed away at the age of eighty and had fifty-five years of *śrāmaṇera* and *bhikṣu* ordination (*varṣa*). A stupa was erected to inter his entire remains. At the beginning of the Changqing era, he was posthumously titled "Great Enlightenment" (*Dàjué*).

Huaihài of the Tang dynasty was a native of Fújiàn. He left the secular world at the age of seven and became thoroughly proficient in the three studies of the Vinaya, Sūtra, and Abhidharma. It happened that Mazu was propagating his teachings in the south.
Dongshan Kang then surrendered his heart in devotion and became his follower; together with Xitang Zhizang, he was designated as one who had "entered the room.

One night, while attending the Patriarch as they gazed at the moon, the Patriarch asked, "At this very moment, what is it? Zhizang said, "It is precisely right for making offerings. Dongshan Hai said, "It is precisely right for practicing the Way.
The Patriarch remarked, "The Sutras enter the Canon; Chan returns to the Sea. One day, the Patriarch ascended the hall and the assembly gathered like clouds; Hai...
He then rolled up his sitting mat for prostration, and the Patriarch immediately descended from the seat. Hai went away and returned shortly thereafter to visit the Patriarch.
At the corner of the meditation platform, the Patriarch took up a fly-whisk and showed it to him. Hai said, "Is this all there is, or is there something else?
The Patriarch placed the fly-whisk back in its original spot and said, "What will you use to guide others in the future? Hai then picked up the fly-whisk. The Patriarch said, "Just this."
"This matter has something else entirely. Baizhang Hai hung his whisk back in its original place and stood in attendance. The Patriarch (Dongshan Liangjie) let out a thunderous shout.
Later, when Hai went into the world at Mount Baiyang in Xinwu, Hongzhou, guests seeking the profound mysteries flocked to him like deer.
Among them, Guishan Lingyou and Huangbo Xiyun were particularly outstanding. Hai said to them, "The Buddha-dharma is no small matter. I was struck by Master Ma..."
The Master gave a single shout, which left Huangbo’s ears deaf for three days.
Unconsciously, Huangbo stuck out his tongue and said, "Although I do not know Mazu, today I have truly seen Mazu in person. Baizhang said, "In the future, you must not take Mazu as your successor.
Huangbo said, "I will not succeed Mazu. Baizhang asked, "Why will you not succeed Mazu? Huangbo replied, "It would mean losing myself."
As for his descendants, Haiyun said, "It is so, it is so. He often remarked, "I practice the Mahāyāna Dharma;
how could it be appropriate to take the various Āgama teachings as my model? Others said, "The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Ābharaṇa-sūtra* are the Vinaya of the Mahāyāna."
"Why not follow him as well? Hai replied, "Within both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, I have sought a broad yet concise middle way, striving only to return to what is good.
My regulations are such that within a single monastery, there shall be only a Dharma Hall, a Sangha Hall, and a Vihāra (abbot’s quarters).
The Dharma Hall is for preaching the Dharma. Within the Sangha Hall, long benches are arranged, along with clothing racks; all those who..."
As for those who reside [in the monastery], regardless of their rank, they shall all hang their requisites upon the racks and sit upon the long connected beds, day and night without ceasing.
When weary, they may lean their heads against the edge of the bed and lie down; this is called "lying with the sword at the hip," intended to ensure that one does not settle into deep sleep.
The Elder (Sthavira) resides specifically in the Abbot’s Quarters (Vihāra) to demonstrate the dignity of his virtue and wisdom. As for laborious duties...

He established the practice of communal labor (*fǔqǐngfǎ*) to equalize the burdens of toil; this benefited the Chan school throughout the land, and all have followed and maintained it without daring to let it fall into disuse until the present day.
On the seventeenth day of the first month in the ninth year of the Yuanhe era (the *jiǎwǔ* year), he passed away at the age of ninety-five.
In the first year of the Changqing era, he was posthumously titled Chan Master Dazhi, and his stupa was named Dabao Shenglun.
Huaiyun of the Tang dynasty was the son of the Xie family of Quanzhou. After shaving his head and receiving full ordination, his mind had not yet entered the Way.
At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, he visited Chan Master Daji at Longxing Temple and immediately received his seal of approval. Later, he lived in seclusion at Qumuli in Lu.
Mountains such as Lingyan and Baijia in Qi, and Zhongtiaoshan, taught their disciples, saying: "The ultimate truth transcends words, yet people of this age do not recognize it;
they instead laboriously practice other matters, claiming them to be functional powers. They fail to realize that one's own nature is a subtle and wondrous gate of great liberation.
Its mirror-like awareness is luminous and has never ceased or been abandoned; it is like the great sun-disk, which shines upon both the near and the far. Although...
And as for the various forms, they do not combine with those various forms. The numinous candle and wondrous clarity require no artificial refinement;

yet, because one does not understand this, one falsely gives rise to empty flowers. It is merely like pressing upon the eyes—only to weary oneself in vain. If one can reflect back toward the source, there is no second person.
A monk asked, "Regarding this body composed of the four elements and five aggregates, which one is the original Buddha-nature? Yun called out the monk's name.
The monk responded, "Yes. After a long silence, Yun said, "You have no Buddha-nature. In the third year of the Yuanhe era, on the Emperor's birthday, [Yun was summoned].

He continued to use the Great Calendar (Dali) edict. All the famous monks and great virtuous ones (*mahāsattva*) throughout the empire who were proficient in the three studies were gathered together in the capital.
Thereupon, Wenyi was installed in the Vairocana Hall of Changjing Temple; he entered the Linde Palace and took the seat of honor, where he was granted a vegetarian feast.
Later, a monk circumambulated his corded bed three times and stood there shaking his mendicant’s staff. Wenyi said:
"It is so, it is so. When that monk arrived at Nanquan, they met as before. Nanquan said, "It is not so, it is not so.
The monk said, "Zhangjing said it is so; why does the Master say it is not so? Nanquan said, "Zhangjing is indeed so, but you are not so.
You are driven by the winds of karma and will ultimately meet with ruin. In the winter of the year Yimwei (1055), he suddenly manifested illness.
He passed away on the eleventh day of the eleventh month at the age of sixty-two.

In the second month of the following year, his disciples Zhilang, Zicao, and others enshrined his entire body for burial at Beiyuan on the north side of the Bashi Bridge. He was posthumously titled Dajue (Great Enlightenment), while Baoxiang (Precious Appearance) was the name of his stupa.
Jia Dao, the Registrar of the Department of Revenue in Luoyang, composed the inscription for his stele.
Tang Lingtan’s surname was Wu. He was a descendant of Empress Wu Zetian from Wen-shui in Taiyuan.

His father, Xuan, served as the Magistrate of Luoyang, and his mother was Lady Xiahou. She dreamed that a divine monk entrusted her with a precious mirror, its inner and outer surfaces brilliantly clear, saying, "Guard it well."

From birth, he was distinguished, upright, and lovely. At the age of seven, he had mastered his studies through recitation. He was recommended as a "Child Official" (*tóngzi*) and entered government service.

By the age of thirteen, he was promoted to *Tōngshì shèrén* (Attendant to the Crown Prince). He pursued his learning with even greater diligence and never grew weary; he perused the classics and scriptures of the Three Teachings until there was nothing left unexamined.
Nevertheless, he grew somewhat weary of worldly affairs and took a deep liking to the school of Emptiness (*kōngzōng*). At that time, Shenhui of Heze was flourishing in Luoyang.
When Hui-zhi was transforming [the people], Shan-tan went to join him and was subsequently recommended for his abilities; he was then appointed as an attendant. His parents could not dissuade him.
At the beginning of the Tianbao era, Hui-zhi said to Shan-tan, "I have a single phrase that has been transmitted from the First Patriarch Bodhidharma to Caoxi, and Caoxi has transmitted it to me.
You should receive it with careful attention so that it does not become extinct. Now, I am about to face a peril."
"I shall certainly leave you and go elsewhere. Before long, an imperial decree was indeed issued for him to move to Yiyang. Huitan also perused the Tripitaka at Fucha Temple in Luzhou.
In the fifth year of the Dali era, he was received with the honors due to a dharma-kinsman. He went to the capital to see National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang.
National Teacher Zhong submitted a petition on his behalf, and he obtained an imperial edict granting him the title "Great Compassionate One" (Dabei). At that time, the Chancellor Tian...
When Lord Shen-gong was about to lead his troops to Bianzhou, Tan Jiu accompanied him to propagate the transformation [of the people]. He was treated with exceptional courtesy and hospitality.
They then proceeded down through Wiyang and Liuhe. Suddenly, they heard a voice from the air saying, "I shall open the ground of your heart.

Immediately, they beheld a Bodhisattva image resembling Mañjuśrī, who pressed his hand against [Tan Jiu's] neck and said, "This is its seal of verification. Upon looking, there was a finger-mark [impressed there].
The four scars were all red in color and did not fade for a long time. When moistened with gold mountain water, clouds would arise, capable of poisoning people to death;
this was likely caused by a dragon hibernating within the cave, but it ceased at this point. Tan once remarked that he had personally traveled through that area.
Later, while at E'an on Mount Ding in Jiangyin, he heard the sound of chanting at night; upon investigation, he found it was two white tortoises. There was also a white snake.
He was several zhang tall. He prayed for the reception of the precepts and for repentance. He resided in Wuxing, where he built a *aranya* (hermitage) on Mount Lin.
Sometimes he saw three men dressed in gold and purple robes; he marveled at their magnificent appearance. In the fifth year of the Yuanhe era, the Chancellor, Lord Li Yong, governed Guangling.
Suyán was stern and lacked kindness, whereas Tǎn was open-minded, magnanimous, and broad-minded. Suyán lodged him at Huálín Monastery.

The monastery contained the tomb of Zhang Liao, a general of the Wu state, which was particularly haunted by dancing spirits and malevolent ghosts. Tǎn resided there, remaining unperturbed and encountering no opposition.
Ten years later, two foreigners arrived, claiming to be envoys from the kingdom of Kucha, and delivered a royal decree inviting Tǎn; yet it remained entirely unknown where they had come from. (11)
On the thirteenth day of the fifth month of that year, the assembly prepared a vegetarian feast for the anniversary of Heze’s passing. Xuantan addressed the assembly separately, saying:

"I have already accepted an invitation to travel afar. On the eighth day of the ninth month, he contracted a slight illness and passed away. He was interred in a stupa on the southern ridge of Xunzhai Village in the district.
He was one hundred and eight years of age; his dharma-age was eighty-four.

Tang Yuanhao, courtesy name Guangcheng, was surnamed Zou and was a native of Wu. In his youth, he followed Master Huiri of Lingshan Monastery in Jinling to renounce the world and received full ordination in the Vinaya.
He was assigned to reside at Longxing Monastery in his home province. Subsequently, he became a Dharma-heir disciple of Master Zhannen of Jingxi.
He once wrote a preface for the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* commentary [he had authored], stating: "I have heard from my predecessors..."
The great treasure of awakening is called "constancy" (*nitya*). The grand ceremony of granting repose and spreading harmony is called "instruction" (*śāsana*).

When all within the realm know transformation and return to the ultimate state, it is called "practice" (*caryā*). When the mutual resonance of the human heart reaches its ultimate limit, it is called "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*).

Thus, governing the age through the Way (*mārga*) and harmonizing with the movement of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), at the moment of responding to phenomena, one shares the same radiance as manifestation and concealment; expanding this supreme transformation, and—
That which is clearly manifest to oneself and others is truly disseminated through its grand reputation;

that one reverently hears and contemplates, attaining harmony to the ultimate degree, and that the four virtues are fully manifested, truly reside within its wondrous essence. It transforms the various schools and, surveying all the supreme classics, it is able to cultivate them thoroughly.
That the myriad achievements may reach fulfillment truly relies upon the fundamental source.

To faithfully transmit this to others, to clarify the ultimate principle of the source, and to fully expound its purport—so that it may perhaps benefit future generations—truly resides in its wondrous application.

To comprehensively synthesize all teachings to establish perfected instructions, so that they spread throughout the ten directions and all follow and submit to them, truly resides in its wondrous teaching. This is Hao’s [intention].

Through his discourses, one can know the depth of his realization. On the eleventh day of the eleventh month in the twelfth year of the Yuanhe era, he entered nirvana with his right side down and his feet stacked.

On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month the following year, his body was cremated, and a stupa was erected on the southern plain of Mount Dongshan at Tiger Hill in Suzhou. While Hao was still in good health, he [stayed] with Yunhua at the capital...
The Master Hua-yan Cheng-kuan of the monastery was a close friend of [the author].
When he annotated the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it was at the earnest invitation of the Hanlin Academician Lord Liang Su and the Prefect of Suzhou, Lord Tian.
His disciples included the śramaṇas Zhi-heng, Zi-yu, Dao-ru, Zhong-yi, and Zhong-liang, as well as the bhikṣuṇīs Shi-wei, Dao-xun, Zhi-zhen, Wu-ji, and others, who erected his stupa.
The Provincial Inspector was Cui Gongming.
Tang Shencon’s secular surname was Cheng; he was a native of Lantian in Jingzhao. From birth, he was extraordinary and refined; at the age of seven, he transcended the mundane world.
He relied upon Master Xiwei of Mount Nanyue to receive full ordination, and subsequently attended upon Chan Master Daji of Zhongling. In the eighth year of the Dali era, the court...

The court administered examinations for scholars throughout the realm based on the three categories of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. Those who wished to leave the household life flocked to these examinations, and Zong was selected among them.

By imperial decree, he was assigned to Xingguo Monastery in Jiuyang. Later, following the monk Sengwang, he moved to Donglin Monastery, which was the site of the former practice center of Master Huiyuan of Yanmen.
There stood the "Dew" (Ganlu) Precept Platform; Zong subsequently took up the restoration of Buddhist affairs there. Although...

He propagated both the Sūtras and the Śāstras, yet he dedicated the final years of his life to the Vinaya. By nature, he was frail and emaciated; looking at him, one would have thought he could not even bear the weight of his robes.
When his disciples requested that he seek medical treatment, he did not respond; when they brought medicine forward, he waved them away.

On the twenty-sixth day of the ninth month in the twelfth year of the Yuanhe era, he fell ill and passed away. On the nineteenth day of the tenth month of that same year, his entire body was enshrined in accordance with the tradition of Master Yuan.
He was enshrined in a mound and interred there. His life span was seventy-four years; his *laba* (monastic age) was fifty-one.
At that time, Bai Juyi, the Governor’s Assistant (*xunsima*), was a close friend. Upon hearing of this, he was filled with grief and sorrow, and composed an inscription for the stupa (*taming*).

Furthermore, he recounted a verse to mourn him, saying: "Originally we formed a community for the incense and lamps of Bodhi; Together we loathed this body, as transient as lightning or a bubble. There is no need for lingering grief."
The Master departed. He first invited the one from the West to serve as host.
Tang Weikuan was born into the Zhu clan of Xin’an in Quzhou; his grandfather An and father Jiao both lived in obscurity through their virtuous conduct.
When Weikuan was thirteen years old, he saw [a living being] being slaughtered to provide a meal for guests; unable to bear it, he withdrew to seek ordination and shaved his hair under the monk Tan.
He received the *śīla* from the Sangha Chong; he studied the *vinaya* under the Sangha Ru. Initially, he practiced *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, and later he beheld Great Quiescence (*mahā-śānti*).
Upon realizing the Dharma of the Mind, he propagated his transformative teachings throughout Min and Yue. In the seventh year of the Zhenyuan era, he established the Tengjia Dojo at Kuaiji;
in the eighth year, he established the Huixiang Dojo at Poyang; and in the thirteenth year, he resided at Shaolin Temple. Twenty...
He stayed at Weiguo Temple for one year; the following year, he moved to Tiangong Temple. A monk asked, "What is the Way? Kuang replied, "A magnificent mountain.
The monk pressed further, "The student asks about the Way; why does the Master speak of a 'fine mountain'?
He replied, "You recognize only the fine mountain, yet you do not recognize the Way. The monk asked, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? He replied, "It has. The monk pressed further.
[The monk] asked, "Does the Master have it? He replied, "I do not. [The monk] pressed, "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature;
why is it that you alone do not? He replied, "I am not a sentient being. [The monk] pressed, "If you are not a sentient being, are you a Buddha?
He replied, "I am not a Buddha. [The monk] pressed, "Ultimately, what kind of thing are you? He replied, "I do not even know what it is."
"What is it? Jin asked. "Is it visible or conceivable? He replied, "It is beyond the reach of thought and cannot be grasped through deliberation; therefore, it is called 'inconceivable' (*acintya*).
In the fourth year of the Yuanhe era, an imperial decree invited him to An Guo Temple. In the fifth year, he entered the Linde Hall, where the Emperor personally questioned him regarding the Way.
That same year, by means of the Dharma, he restored the Lingquan Spring—which had long been dry—to its former state for the Tripitaka Master Bukong.
At the pond, the Court Gentleman Bai Juyi once visited Huikuan and asked him, "Chan is beyond words and speech; yet you, Master, claim to abide in the Way of Chan.
How then can you preach the Dharma? Huikuan replied, "Unsurpassed Bodhi is manifested in the body as the Vinaya, proclaimed from the mouth as the Teaching, and realized in the mind as Chan.
Its applications are threefold, but its ultimate purpose is one. Why, then, do you falsely entertain doubts within this?"

He gave rise to a conceptual distinction. Again he asked: "If there is no conceptualization, why cultivate the mind? He replied: "The mind is fundamentally neither defiled nor pure; ultimately, what need is there for cultivation?

If one were to remove defilement and grasp purity, this is called 'the speck of gold-dust that blinds. Again he asked: "If there is no cultivation or realization, how does this differ from an ordinary person?
He replied: "Ordinary persons possess ignorance, while those of the Two Vehicles harbor attachments. To be free from these two..."
Sickness—this is called true cultivation. A monk asked, "Where does the Way reside? He replied, "It is before your eyes. The monk pressed further, "Why do I not see it?
He replied, "Because you harbor a sense of self (*ātman*), therefore you do not see it. The monk pressed further, "If I do not have a self, then I do not see; but does the Master see it?
He replied, "If there were you and there were me, we would still fail to see each other through our mutual existence. The monk pressed further, "What if there is no [self]?"
"Is there no 'you' and no 'self'? Do you still see [anything]? He replied, "There is no 'you' and no 'self. Whom would you have teach to see?

On the final day of the second month in the twelfth year, he ascended the seat to bid farewell to the assembly; then, suddenly, he passed away in accordance with the natural course of things. His age was sixty-three, and his years as a monk were thirty-nine.

He was buried at the Western Plains of Baling, posthumously titled Dache (Great Penetration), and his stupa was named Yuanhe Zhengzhen (True and Correct of the Yuanhe Era). He had over a thousand disciples.
Those who grasped his essential point numbered thirty-nine. Among those who entered the inner chamber and received his entrustment was Yichong Yuanzhao.

Tang Lingmo, surnamed Xuan, was the son of a man from Piling. In his early years, he had originally intended to succeed in the imperial examinations by answering the state policy questions, hoping thereby to bring glory to his parents and his home village.
Hearing that Master Mazu was gathering disciples and preaching the Dharma at Yuzhang, he went there to observe him. Upon seeing him, the Way was realized before his very eyes.
He subsequently sought ordination. After receiving full precepts, he visited Master Shitou Xiqian and attained realization of the fundamental principle.
At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, he entered the mountains of Mount Tiantai and resided at the Baisha Monastery, the site of the former Dharma-center of the Sui dynasty’s Zhiyi.
After two years had passed, a tiger gave birth to cubs in the nearby forest; its disposition became quite tame and docile. When Master Zhiyi first arrived to establish the monastery, for every...
Twelfth location. He recorded this, saying: "This site is wondrously adorned; it is not a place for those with impure vessels to dwell. If one can reside here, they will be no different from me.
Therefore, he lingered there in silence, unable to bear leaving. Later, he moved again to the Eastern Dharma Hall (Dong Daochang), where the terrain became even more secluded and remote.
Suddenly, one night, thunder crashed and a great tree fell, crushing cliffs and valleys. People thought that the disaster would surely extend to the place where Mo resided.

One morning he went to inspect his hermitage; it was undamaged. Once, while traveling at Mount Dongbai, he was poisoned. A neighboring elder summoned a physician for him, but he declined and sent him away.

He remained alone, sitting in meditation with the door closed. Upon emerging, he washed in foul water and was cured. After his passing in Puyang, he then accepted the invitation of Li Wang, a military commander at Yangling, to go to Wuxi.
At the beginning of the Yuanhe era, during a severe drought, he happened to be walking along a stream when he saw something green.

A large snake lay coiled and moist on its side, staring fixedly at passersby without moving in the slightest. [The Master] silently rebuked it, saying, "The common people are on the verge of dying of thirst;
do you truly have no heart of compassion? That night, indeed, a great rain fell, saturating the entire district. This was during the time of Meng Jian of Pingchang.
While serving as an Intendant on a temporary assignment in Zhejiang, he issued an edict to abolish all monastic schools within his jurisdiction, causing the students to disperse.
Subsequently, Cao Zhou, the Magistrate of Jishi, submitted a formal petition recommending Zhimen’s virtuous conduct, noting that he was capable of protecting the local community.
Permission was granted for him to rebuild the monastery to restore its former dignity. A monk asked, "What thing is greater than heaven and earth? He replied, "No one knows it. The monk—
[The Master] said, "Can it still be carved and polished? He replied, "Try taking a hand to it and see. A monk asked, "In this gate, what is the matter from beginning to end?
He replied, "Tell me, how much time has passed since that which is right now was formed? The monk said, "I do not understand.
He replied, "In my place here, there is nothing for you to ask about. The monk said, "Is there nothing at all, Reverend?"
At the place where he received visitors, he replied, "I shall receive you as soon as you seek my reception. A monk said, "I pray that the Master will receive me right now.

He replied, "What is it that you lack? On the twenty-third day of the third month in the thirteenth year, after bathing, burning incense, and entrusting his final instructions, he sat upright and passed away.
He was seventy-two years old and had been a monk for forty-one years. The eminent monk Zhixian recorded this.
His life’s deeds and activities were circulated throughout the world.
Zhi Chang of Tang was a disciple of Dayi of Jiangxi. During the Yuanhe era, he took up residence at Guizong Monastery on Mount Lu, where crowds of seekers flocked to visit him.
When Bai Juyi, known as Lord Baitu, was demoted to Jiangzhou as a Grand Master of the Palace Library, he was able to come and go [with the Master].
He consulted [Huineng] regarding the essentials for resolving his doubts. Out of the utmost reverence and admiration, whenever he saw him, he would sit facing south and pay his respects.

Later, when Li Bo was transferred from Qianzhou as a Regional Inspector (Cishi), he became even more deeply impressed and submissive. One day he asked: "In the teachings, it is said that Mount Sumeru can contain a mustard seed;
this is certainly logical. But it is also said that a mustard seed can contain Mount Sumeru—is this also logical?"
Chang said, "People say that a Doctor has read ten thousand scrolls of books. Is this true or not? Bo said, "I am unworthy to have earned such a reputation.
Chang said, "From the crown of one's head to the soles of one's feet, the body does not exceed a few feet in length. Where, then, are those ten thousand scrolls of books stored? Bo lowered his head.
After a short while, Chang could not help but sigh in admiration and, ascending the hall, said: "The ancient worthies of old were not without knowledge."
I understand your noble aspiration, which differs from that of the common crowd. Yet at present, you are unable to achieve self-reliance and are wasting your time in vain.

Hitherto, you have merely relied upon intellectual understanding; thus, every word you utter is obstructed, and your light does not penetrate through, simply because there is still something before your eyes.
My sons, do not misapply your minds. No one can take your place, nor is there any place for you to apply your mind.
Take heed. A monk asked, "What is the profound principle? Chang said, "No one can comprehend it. The monk asked, "How about if one moves toward it?
Chang said, "To move toward it is already to deviate. The monk asked, "How about if one does not move toward it? Chang said, "In departing, there is no place for you to apply your mind.
The monk asked, "Is there no skillful means? Chang said, "The wondrous power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom can save the world from suffering."
The monk asked, "What is the wondrous power of wisdom of Avalokiteśvara? Chang struck the lid of the cauldron three times and asked, "Did you hear that?
The monk replied, "I heard it. Chang said, "Why did I not hear it? The monk was speechless. Chang drove him away with a blow.

Once, while traveling as a *xiuxing* (wandering practitioner) with Nanquan, they were about to part after preparing tea. Nanquan asked, "From the past until now, I have discussed this with you, my elder brother..."
The matter was already known to both. After he had departed, someone asked, "In the end, how would you respond?
Chang said, "This patch of ground is very good for establishing a hermitage. Quan said, "Setting aside the establishment of the hermitage for a moment, in the end, how would you respond?
Chang then turned over the tea kettle and rose. Quan said, "Brother, you have finished your tea; Pu-yuan has not yet."
Changcha said, "This is a mere matter of talk; not even a drop of water can be digested. A monk asked, "How should one apply the mind to this matter?
Changcha replied, "An ox-hide drum covers a pillar; the pillar chirps and squeaks, yet ordinary ears do not hear it."
The various worthies laughed aloud. When an official from the secular government came to visit, Chang picked up his hat-strap and asked, "Do you understand?
The official said, "I do not understand. Chang said, "Do not blame this old monk for not removing my hat; it is because of a headache.

Once, while Chang was entering the garden to gather vegetables, he drew a circle around a single stalk of greens and said to the assembly, "You must not touch this by any means. The assembly did not [move it].
He dared not move. After a short while, Chang came by and saw that the vegetables were still there;

he immediately struck with his staff and drove away the assembly of monks, saying, "This lot of fellows—there isn't a single one among you who possesses wisdom. Once, while he was weeding, a monk came to pay his respects.
Suddenly, a snake passed right in front of him, and Guizong cut it through with his hoe. The monk said, "I have long heard of Guizong; I never expected he would be such a man of coarse conduct."
Gatekeeper Chang said, "The Master has returned; go drink tea. Chang had double pupils, yet he feared this might bring him misfortune.
He said, "I shall apply incense and massage [my eyes] to seek their elimination," and his eyes consequently turned red. Thus, he was known in the world as "Red-Eyed Guizong."
Tang Shenxuan was born into the Liu family of Liuyang in Jianyang. From childhood, he was grave and serene; he would only speak after being questioned.

As he grew older, he traveled to Wunü, where he entered Kaiyuan Temple as a *śrāmaṇera* (novice) to take ordination. One day, the Governor of Wunü visited him and, upon seeing him, remarked: "This youth possesses a spirit that is exceptionally clear and brilliant.
In the future, he will surely surround himself with a thousand followers and bring benefit to the world. You should encourage him [to pursue his vocation]."

He shaved his head to enter the monastic order and devoted himself to diligent cultivation. Once he had received full ordination, he stayed within a stone cave at Baijia Yan to the north of Mount Jinhuashan.
He constantly recited the *Saptabuddha-koṭi-mantra* day and night without ceasing. Above him was no roofed dwelling, and below him was no bed or mat;
yet when rain, dew, frost, or snow fell, a purple cloud would cover him like a canopy. After a long time, he moved.
He resided on the eastern peak of Chisongdong, where auspicious omens were particularly manifest.

In the second year of the Zhenyuan era, he met Chan Master Zhixian, who expounded the Dharma of the Mind for him; he thereby attained realization and his practice of recitation became even more effective.

In the eighth year of the Yuanhe era, the Vice Minister Fan Yang dispatched an envoy to bestow upon him frankincense, felt rugs, woolen cloth, and various vessels, yet Xuan immediately distributed them all and accepted nothing.
The Secretariat Drafter Wang Zhong requested that he go to Dayun Temple to bestow the Bodhisattva precepts upon the fourfold assembly.

In the twelfth year, the Minister Meng Jian invited him to preach the Dharma in Kuaiji; he firmly declined and did not go. In the eighth month, he finally returned and passed away at Kaiyuan Temple at the age of seventy-six.

Tang Yinfeng’s surname was Deng. He was a native of Shaowu in Jianzhou. His disposition appeared eccentric; though he seemed simple-minded, he was firm and resolute, possessing a tenacity that could not be shaken.
Having received full ordination, he first visited Mazu but attained nothing; he went again to Shitou but likewise found no resonance.
That he ultimately became a successor to Mazu allows us to know what he had realized. While at Shitou, Yinfeng asked:
"How can one attain accord with the Way? Tou said, "I, too, do not accord with the Way. Feng asked, "Ultimately, how is it?
Tou said, "You do not accord with the Way in coming here. How long has it been since you arrived? Feng was speechless.
One day, while Tou was weeding, Feng stood by with his hands folded. Tou threw his hoe toward Feng and, standing before him, weeded a single blade of grass. Feng said, "Master..."
Nanyue said, "You have only cleared away this; you have not cleared away that. He held up his hoe.
Feng received it and made a gesture of hoeing. Nanyue said, "You have only cleared away that; you have not cleared away this.
Feng said, "What place is this, where one speaks of 'this' and 'that'? One day, while Feng was pushing a cart of earth, Nanyue stretched out his feet.
Dazu was sitting on the road. Xuefeng said, "I ask the Master to withdraw your feet. The Patriarch said, "Once extended, they are not withdrawn.
Xuefeng said, "Once advanced, they do not retreat," and he pushed his cart past him. The Patriarch returned to the Dharma Hall, holding an axe, and said, "Come out here;
you just now crushed the soles of this old monk's feet! Xuefeng immediately stepped out before the Patriarch and extended his neck. The Patriarch then set down the axe. Xuefeng went to Nanquan.
Jianquan was in the midst of visiting with the assembly of monks. Jianquan pointed to a water pitcher and said, "The copper pitcher is an object; you must not disturb the object.
Bring me the water from within the pitcher. Fenyang then took the water pitcher and poured the water out before Jianquan.
"How could it have ever moved? At this, Quan stopped. Upon arriving at Guishan, he unpacked his robes and bowl in the presence of the head monk.
When Guishan heard of his arrival, he first assumed a formal demeanor and descended from the hall to see his "uncle" (the master).

Seeing Guishan approaching, Quan feigned sleep. Once Guishan returned to his quarters, Quan departed. A short while later, Guishan asked an attendant, "Is my uncle still here? The attendant replied, "He has already left."
Shan asked, "When you left, what words were there? The man replied, "There were no words. Shan said, "Do not say there were no words; that sound was like thunder.
During the Yuanhe era, while traveling to Mount Wutai, his path led through Huaisi. At that time, Wu Yuanji was besieging the city of Cai, resisting the imperial army;
they had held out against one another for a long time without a decisive victory. Fēng said, "I know how to bring it to an end."

When the violent and fierce ones [attempted to stop him], he cast his *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) into the air and passed over them by flying. The soldiers of both armies gazed upward in admiration and submission;
a spirit of compassion and yielding arose spontaneously within them, and the principles of good and evil, or opposition and compliance, were instantly discerned.
The binding of Yuan Ji and the capture of the city of Cai truly did not depend upon the schemes of Li Sù. Having thoroughly examined these spiritual traces, he then turned back.

He was interred within a Vajra Cave to demonstrate his passing into extinction. Observing him treading upon heaven and wearing the earth, his robes and trousers were neither trailing nor wrinkled, yet his limbs were not exposed.
When the multitude attempted to lift him, he was so solid that nothing could move him.
Later, his younger sister, who had become a nun, arrived and rebuked him, saying: "Brother, you lived with arrogance toward the Dharma and Vinaya; even in death, you remain deluded and confused."
"Is this worldly? He slowly pushed him down and toppled him. "Alas, how strange! He then performed the cremation and enshrined the *śarīra* relics in a stūpa at that site.
Zhi Cáng of the Tang dynasty was originally from Western India; having entered China, he adopted the surname Pí. His ancestors had once held office in Lúlíng.

Consequently, he registered his residence there. From a young age, Zang distanced himself from worldly affairs and frequented the mountain forests. He devoted himself to the Three Studies (*tri-śikṣā*) and was particularly proficient in the Vinaya Piṭaka.

In the third year of the Dali era, he enrolled at Tiangong Temple in Yuzhang. When the assembly requested him to ascend the platform and uphold the Dharma, every time he took his seat to preach, he would clarify names and principles and analyze subtle words;
the hall was filled to capacity and the seats were full, yet those who listened never grew weary. At that time, he was known as...
Lühù (Law Tiger). During the Zhenyuan era, he attained realization upon reading the *Jingsu* (Admonition) of Chan Master Daji.
He subsequently built a hermitage on Hang’u Mountain in Kuaiji and composed the *Miaoyi* (Sublime Meaning) of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Students gathered around him.

On the second month of the fourteenth year of the Yuanhe era, he passed away without illness at the age of seventy-nine. His stupa containing his relics was erected on the northern peak of the monastery; the common people call it Hang.
"Wu" is a corruption of "Hangwu"; it is merely an error in pronunciation.

Tang Daoxing was the son of a member of the Mei family of Kuaiji. His father was a local official. Daoxing was knowledgeable in the classics from a young age and eventually presented his refined compositions as a tribute to the Imperial Academy.
A monk, while on his alms-round, passed by his home; Daoxing conversed with him and attained a profound understanding of the essential points of Chan. He then took leave of his father.
The Master’s mother studied the Dharma of Emptiness and received the precepts from Zhiyou of Baoshou Monastery on Mount Siming as her teacher.
Having traveled to Mount Nanyue, she heard of the Way of Dayi of Jiangxi and went there to rely upon him. Later, she dwelt in a stone grotto on Mount Luofu.
Wood-spirits and water-monsters frequently manifested their forms, yet she regarded them with utter indifference as she walked about. There was an old man of dignified and solemn appearance.
His robes and cap were elegant and refined. He prostrated himself with his forehead touching the ground and said to Xing, "I have resided in this place for barely two hundred years.
That I am now able to escape suffering and attain joy is entirely due to the power of your transformative influence. He passed away from illness in the ninth year of the Baoli era.
He lived to the age of ninety-five. He was subsequently interred in a stupa built on a separate peak.
Tang’s Zhen Shu—whose family name, given name, and native place are unknown—left home to become a monk in his youth. His intelligence and acumen were peerless;

he sought the profound mechanism of reality from Chan Master Daji, who said to him: "The original source of all sentient beings is conventionally named 'Buddha. When the substance is exhausted and the form dissolves..."
It does not perish. Just as gold flows and its ingots disperse yet remain eternally present, the ocean of nature is windless, yet ripples surge forth spontaneously;
the mind is void and free of signs, yet the myriad phenomena are simultaneously manifested. Those who realize this principle do not speak, yet their voice pervades the sands of the Ganges;

they do not act, yet their merit supports the profound transformation. How can one turn one's back on awakening and instead unite with worldly toil, imprisoning oneself in delusion within the aggregates and realms?
Shu saw the Yangqishan of Yichun; the surrounding peaks converged from all four directions. He sighed and said, "The primal source of Earth acts as a guardian, constructing my Dharma-city.
As soon as a single word is uttered, the thousand crags respond with echoes. The heavens open to reveal the Moon Palace; the earth embraces the Cloud Gallery.

Within this realm of purity, a golden realm has manifested through transformation. Thereupon he sat in meditative repose for over forty years, until his transformative conditions were exhausted. The Yuanhe [era].
On the thirteenth day of the first month of the Gengzi year, he suddenly passed away while seated, as if entering a great meditative absorption.

His disciples, such as Rutan and Liangbao, were submerged in an ocean of grief; their sorrow moved like a mountain. They piled up various woods to construct an incense tower and cremated him with tea.
Seven hundred grains of śarīra were obtained; a stūpa was constructed on the eastern peak to enshrine them.
His senior disciple Yunming requested Zhi Xian to compose a text for the stele to record his eminent virtues.

Tang Zizai was born into the Li clan of Wuxing. From childhood, he possessed auspicious signs; whenever he sat, he would spontaneously assume the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), which those who saw him regarded as extraordinary.
He soon left the household life at Mount Jing in Qiantang and received full ordination (*upasampadā*) in Xinding.

He subsequently traveled extensively to visit various masters before entering the Dharma assembly of Daji at Nankang, where he received his formal transmission (*vyākaraṇa*). His movements were irregular, and he frequently lived in seclusion within the mountains.
At the Valley [Monastery], wherever he went, disciples gathered there. He once wrote a letter for Daji (Nanquan Puyuan) to be presented to National Teacher Huizhong.
The National Teacher asked, "With what words and teachings does Master Ma instruct his disciples? Nanquan replied, "The Great Master teaches people that 'mind itself is Buddha.
The National Teacher said, "What kind of talk is that? After a long silence, he asked again, "Is there anything further besides this? Nanquan replied:
[The Master] said, "Furthermore, it is said that the Way is neither mind nor Buddha. At other times, it is also said that it is not mind;
it is not mind, it is not an object. Guishan said, "It is still somewhat lacking. [Xuefeng] asked, "I do not know how it is here at your monastery, Master. Guishan said:
The three dots are like flowing water; the curve resembles a sickle for reaping grain. He addressed the assembly, saying: "‘Mind is Buddha’ is a phrase of seeking illness where there is no illness.
‘Neither mind nor Buddha’ is a phrase of seeking medicine where there is no illness. A monk asked, "What is the phrase of counteracting medicine and illness?
Yunju said, "It has been passed down from ancient times beneath Mount Funiu. Indeed, he was particularly fond of seeking out the traces left by former worthies.

He traveled extensively, visiting such sites as Kuaoyi Monastery, the site where the Tripitaka Master translated scriptures during the Later Wei dynasty at Longmen Mountain, the place where Chan Master Chou resolved a tiger fight at Wangwu Mountain, and the Tiger-Run Spring at Mount Song where Dharma Master Fan resided; yet he remained free from any attachment to them.
During the Yuanhe era, he lived at Mount Funiu near Luoyang and shared an unbreakable bond of friendship with Chan Master Tianran.

He composed the *Three Wounds* (Sānshāng) verses, which were exquisite both in diction and reasoning. Later, he dispatched his disciples to select the most magnificent mountain scenery south of the Yangtze River to paint his portrait.
He was about to return to Duchang Monastery in Jiangzhou when, upon reaching Ye, he was detained by both monastics and laypeople.
In the first year of the Changqing era, he entered nirvana at Kaiyuan Temple in Sui; it is said he was eighty-one years old. (1)
As for the bowl-monk (Bāohéshàng), historical records do not detail his name, surname, or native place. He once composed a "Song of the Bowl" to sing of the Way and exhort the world;
thus, people in common parlance came to call him by that name. At the beginning of the Qiandé era of the Later Shu, there was Lady Gao, the wife of General Chen.
She was a granddaughter of Tang Zhongling Bian. She had observed the precept against killing for more than twenty years.
Later, because her son was marrying a wife and invited his relatives, she was compelled to kill [a bird]. Less than ten days later, Lady Gao died suddenly. After two nights, she revived and said:
"At first, I was seized by messengers in black robes and taken to the City God Temple of Qifu. The temple god was wearing a tall ceremonial cap..."
Wearing voluminous sleeves, he sat upon the hall facing armored warriors. As the messenger led Gao forward, the warriors spoke in a tumultuous clamor, reproaching Gao for his breach of the precepts.
One of them gripped his own wrist and cursed him, saying: "I am a divine general who protects the precepts.
Because you were able to uphold them, I have not had leisure to sleep or eat for twenty years as I guarded you. How could I have expected that you would suddenly fail in your fundamental resolve?"
"Karmic retribution is spontaneous. Regarding what has happened today, I cannot serve as your refuge. City God, you must suddenly ask Gao: 'What other good deeds have you cultivated?
Perhaps by these you may redeem yourself? Gao had frequently recited the *Sutra on Rebirth Above* in the past."
