At this point, he was utterly bewildered and could remember nothing. While he was in a state of fear, the two deities suddenly said, "Recite the *Three Wounds Verse* and the *One Bowl Song*.

He then recited them exactly as they were written. The two deities stood with their hands joined in reverence, listening; their expressions gradually softened, and by the end of the verses, they were both shedding tears. They said:
Dongyin was surnamed Zhang. He left the household life and received full ordination. Traveling to study, he deeply grasped the essential teachings of Caoxi.
However, he lacked any means of verification. Master Hui of Jingzhong Monastery said, "The brocade of a fallen shuttle becomes even more beautiful when washed;
the dragon carrying a torch moves forward to dispel the darkness. Dongyin alone agreed with this. Thereupon, he traveled from Jiangling into Shu and established a hermitage by the Shu River.
To the south of this [structure], he built a site to encourage the assembly; thus the temple buildings were completed and grandly established, and its name was given as Baoying (Precious Response).

At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, after General-in-Chief Gao Chongwen had pacified Liu [Xian], he changed the name to Yuanhe Shengshou (Holy Longevity of the Yuanhe Era). In the first year of the Changqing era, [the Master] entered nirvana;
his stupa was enshrined within the temple, and his disciple Yifu succeeded him.

Huishè of the Tang dynasty was the son of Xiè of Kuaijī and a descendant of Xiè Ān, the Grand Tutor of the Jin dynasty. At the beginning of the Dàlì era, he encountered Chan Master Zhōng of Niútóu Mountain at Zhuāngyán Monastery in Jīnlíng.
Their conversation harmonized with the Master’s intent, and he was permitted to enter the inner chamber; Huishè received the entirety of his dharma-treasury.

Following Zhōng’s passing, he succeeded him in his footsteps and propagated his transformative style. He continued in this manner for fifty years until his death in the second year of the Chángqìng era at the age of eighty.
12. His disciples, including Wei Yan and others, erected a stele to the northwest of the stupa and temple to record his virtues.
Wuye of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Du and was a native of Shangluo in Shangzhou. When his mother, Lady Li, was pregnant, she heard a voice from the air that said:
She asked whether she might stay as a guest; shortly thereafter, she became pregnant. Upon her delivery, an extraordinary light filled the room. In her childhood, she did not engage in play;
when walking, she always looked straight ahead, and when sitting, she always sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). Those who saw her knew her to be a vessel for the Dharma.

At the age of nine, she entered Kaiyuan Temple in the prefecture to rely upon Master Zhiben, where she practiced the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Vimalakīrti*, *Viśeṣacinti-brahma-paripṛcchā*, and *Avataṃsaka* sūtras.

At the age of twelve, he shaved his head and became a novice. He attended lecture halls and awakened to the teachings with a clarity that surpassed his peers. Upon reaching the full age for ordination, he received the *upasampadā* from Master You of Xiangzhou.
The following summer, he expounded the *Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* for the assembly, while also lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

From then on, he devoted himself to the study and translation of the sutras and vinayas, never flagging in either winter or summer. Shortly thereafter, he heard that Daichi (Mazu) was proclaiming and transforming beings through the Supreme Vehicle.

In Hongzhou, [Wuxiang] went to pay his respects. His physical frame was naturally tall and robust. When Daji saw him, he laughed and said, "A magnificent Buddha hall—how is it that there is no Buddha?
Wuxiang then knelt and said, "I have long exhausted the explanations of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings;
yet as for the Gate of the Patriarchs' 'mind is itself Buddha,' I truly do not understand. Daji said, "Just this—"
The mind that does not understand is precisely this; there is nothing else besides it. Not understanding is delusion; understanding it is awakening.
Deluded, one is a sentient being; awakened, one is a Buddha. A Buddha is certainly not separate from sentient beings; apart from sentient beings, there is no other Buddha.
It is just like making a fist with one's hand—the fist is simply the hand. Through this, [the practitioner] attained sudden awakening; grief and joy mingled within him as he wept.

He said, "Originally, I believed that the Buddha-way was perfected only after vast eons; today, for the first time, I know that I have personally beheld the Dharma-body and its true reality, which is fully endowed with all things.
All phenomena arise from the mind and possess only names; they have no substantial reality. Daji replied, "So it is, so it is.
Having received this prediction of enlightenment, he immediately went to Caoxi to pay homage at the Patriarch’s stupa, and traveled extensively through Mount Lu and Tiantai.
He visited various famous mountains and sacred sites. From Luoyang to Yongzhou, he stayed at Ximing Monastery.

The assembly wished to appoint him as a Great Virtuous One (*bhadanta*) for both streets of the capital, but this was not his intention. At that time, the Chancellor Li Baozhen, who governed Shangdang as a regional commander, admired the worthy and delighted in the good, never showing signs of weariness.
He earnestly requested [Fazang] with ceremonial gifts. Fazang looked back and said to his disciples: "My original..."
To avoid the chaos and turmoil of the capital, he came here; yet now, having again troubled us with his arrival, it is truly pitiable that he must once more flee to Baofu Mountain on Mian Shang.
He then spent eight years, through both winter and summer, reading the Tripitaka at Jinggesi on Mount Qingliang.
Suddenly, shaking his mendicant’s staff, he traveled west to the River and stayed at Zhongxiangsi. There, the Prefectural Governor Dong Shuchan...
He was invited to move to Kaiyuan Temple. With composure, he instructed his disciples, saying, "Since arriving here, I have had no further ambitions.

Is it that my karmic connection to the Dharma lies with you? He then led his followers to preach the Dharma for nearly twenty years, and his transformation of others flourished throughout the regions of Bingzhou and Fenzhou.
In the fourteenth year of Emperor Xianzong’s reign over the realm, an imperial letter summoned him; however, he declined on the grounds of illness and did not go. Ming...

As his age advanced, the Emperor increased his devotion and issued an imperial decree [summoning him], yet he again firmly declined on the grounds of illness. Upon the accession of Emperor Muzong, the Emperor’s longing to pay homage was even greater;
he commanded Lingzhun, the Monastic Registrar of the Two Streets, to convey the imperial intent. Zhun said, "The Master transcends the mundane world and treats worldly affairs as mere chaff;

this is because he follows the Way. However, the Dharma is entrusted to the King; I pray that the Master will consider this matter deeply. Daye laughed and said, "What virtue do I, a poor monk, possess to have been repeatedly entreated?"
“Venerable ones, depart now. I fear only that our paths shall diverge. Thereupon, he shaved his head and bathed. At midnight, he addressed his disciples Huìyīn and others, saying:
“Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—these natures are identical to the great void; they neither arise nor perish, being fundamentally empty and quiescent from the beginning.
Those who are deluded do not understand this and are thus confused by external objects. Once confused by external objects, one wanders through the cycle of rebirth without end. You...”
You should know that the nature of the mind is not produced by causes; it is indestructible like a diamond.
All phenomena are like shadows and echoes, devoid of substantiality. Therefore, a sutra says: "There is only one reality; the other two are not true.
To constantly realize that all is empty, such that not a single thing accords with the mind—this is the common ground of the Buddhas' mental activity. You...
He practiced with equal diligence and subsequently entered nirvana. His age was sixty-three, and his years of ordination were forty-two.

On the twenty-first day of the twelfth month in the third year of the Changqing era, he was buried in the courtyard of the monastery. He was posthumously titled National Teacher Dada, and his stupa was named Chengyuan.
Tiantian of Tang was a man of unknown origins. He first presented himself to Chan Master Shitou Xiqian at Mount Nanyue while wearing official robes and headgear.

After serving as a kitchen hand for three years, he finally underwent tonsure. He subsequently received full ordination from Vinaya Master Xi at a monastery on the mountain and immediately traveled to the Dharma assembly of Dayi (Huineng) in Jiangxi.
Dayi regarded him with great wonder. Soon thereafter, he resided at Huading Peak on Mount Tiantai for three years.

He subsequently traveled to Mount Jing to pay his respects to Guoyi. During the Yuanhe era, he ascended Longmen and Xiangshan to serve Chan Master Shanfu Niu. He once stayed as a guest at Huilin Temple; at a time when the weather was bitterly cold, he took a wooden Buddha statue and burned it to warm himself. Some criticized him for repudiating cause and effect, to which he replied, "I intended to perform a *tehipa* (cremation) for the *śarīra*, but how could there be any relics in a block of wood? They asked, "How could a piece of wood have them? [He replied: "If you can find relics in a wooden head, then I shall believe you. Later, while traveling through the mountains, he encountered a bandit who struck him with a sword. He said, "I am not afraid of death; I only regret that I did not finish burning this wooden Buddha. He then passed away. His disciples cremated his body and found many *śarīra*. It is said that because he had burned the wooden Buddha, he himself was now being burned. This is why it is said that one must not disparage the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Fayuan Zhulin* records that during the Kaiyuan era, a monk named Daowen of the Eastern Capital went to the Western Regions to seek the Dharma. There, he encountered a foreign monk who asked him, "What is your name? Daowen replied, "My name is Daowen. The foreigner said, "The word 'wen' means 'to burn. Why do you burn yourself? Daowen was startled and asked, "How can I burn myself? The foreigner replied, "You have already burned yourself. Daowen then asked, "When did I burn myself? The foreigner said, "In the past, when you were a child, you used to play by burning your own hair and fingernails. That was you burning yourself. Daowen was deeply ashamed. The foreigner further said, "You have already been reborn in the Avīci Hell. You must go there to repent. Daowen returned home and sought out an elder to ask about the matter. The elder said, "That is merely a dream; it is not real. Daowen said, "If it is a dream, then I was not burned. The elder said, "If you were not burned, why did you feel pain? Daowen said, "I felt pain in my heart. The elder said, "If you felt pain in your heart, then you were indeed burned. Daowen then went to the temple where he had previously practiced and saw that the image of the Buddha he had made was missing its head. He realized that the foreign monk had told the truth. He wept and said, "I have already committed a grave offense. How can I escape retribution? He then went to the mountain to repent. He saw a stone statue of a Buddha, which he took to be the manifestation of the foreign monk. He prostrated himself before it and vowed to practice the Way for the rest of his life. He then returned home and built a stūpa to enshrine the Buddha’s head. This is why it is said that one must not disparage the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Xinxiu Fajie Shu* states that in the past, there was a man who was very stingy and refused to give anything to others. One day, he encountered a beggar and gave him nothing. The beggar cursed him, saying, "You will soon suffer the retribution of poverty. The man was terrified and went to a monastery to repent. He saw a monk who was eating a meal of coarse rice and vegetables. The man asked, "Why are you eating such poor food? The monk said, "Because I am stingy, I receive no offerings from others. The man realized that the monk was his own reflection. He wept and vowed to change his ways. He then gave generously to the Sangha and built a temple. This is why it is said that one must not disparage the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Fozu Tongji* records that during the Tang dynasty, there was a monk named Huichang who lived on Mount Wutai. He was known for his strict discipline and deep devotion. One day, a deity appeared to him in a dream and said, "You have committed a grave offense. You must go to the Western Regions to repent. Huichang was startled and asked, "What offense have I committed? The deity said, "In the past, when you were a layman, you once burned a wooden Buddha to warm yourself. That was a grave offense against the Triple Gem. Huichang was deeply ashamed and vowed to travel to the West. Upon arriving, he met a foreign monk who confirmed the dream. The foreign monk said, "Your offense is heavy, but your sincerity is profound. You shall be reborn in the Pure Land. Huichang returned home and built a stūpa to enshrine the Buddha’s remains. This is why it is said that one must not disparage the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Zongjing Lu* states that in the past, there was a king who was very fond of hunting. One day, he encountered a deer that escaped into a forest. The king pursued it and lost his way. He came upon a cave where he saw a golden statue of a Buddha. The king took it to be a treasure and carried it off. On his return journey, he was struck by lightning and died. He was reborn in the Avīci Hell. The Buddha appeared to him and said, "Because you took a Buddha statue to be a treasure, you have suffered this retribution. The king wept and vowed to repent. He then built a temple and enshrined the statue. This is why it is said that one must not disparage the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Fozu Lidai Tongzai* records that during the Song dynasty, there was a monk named Miaoxian who lived on Mount Tiantai. He was known for his ascetic practices. One day, he saw a vision of a golden Buddha statue floating in the sky. He reached out to grasp it, but it vanished. He wept and said, "I have failed to honor the Buddha. He then vowed to build a new statue. While he was working on it, he fell ill and dreamed of a foreign monk who said, "The statue you are making is not perfect. You must add a head to it. When he woke up, he realized that the statue was indeed missing a head. He completed it and enshrined it in the temple. This is why it is said that one must not disparage the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Wudeng Huiyuan* states that in the past, there was a monk named Fazhao who lived in the mountains. He was very diligent in his practice. One day, he saw a vision of a golden Buddha statue. He took it to be a sign of his progress and worshipped it. However, he later realized that it was merely a delusion. He wept and said, "I have been deceived by my own mind. He then vowed to abandon all attachments. He returned to the monastery and devoted himself to meditation. This is why it is said that one must not disparage the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* records that during the Tang dynasty, there was a monk named Huairang who lived on Mount Nanyue. He was known for his simplicity and humility. One day, he saw a vision of a golden Buddha statue. He took it to be a sign of his enlightenment and worshipped it. However, he later realized that it was merely a projection of his own mind. He wept and said, "I have been attached to forms. He then vowed to transcend all dualities. He returned to his hermitage and focused on the practice of non-attachment. This is why it is said that one must not disparage the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Lidai Fabao Ji* states that in the past, there was a king who was very fond of war. One day, he encountered a battle and was captured by the enemy. He was taken to a temple where he saw a golden Buddha statue. The king was terrified and begged for mercy. The statue spoke to him, saying, "You have committed great sins. You must repent to escape retribution. The king wept and vowed to change his ways. He released all prisoners and built a temple. This is why it is said that one must not disparage the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Zhiyue Lu* records that during the Ming dynasty, there was a monk named Zhenjie who lived on Mount Huangbo. He was known for his strict adherence to the precepts. One day, he saw a vision of a golden Buddha statue. He took it to be a sign of his purity and worshipped it. However, he later realized that it was merely a reflection of his own mind. He wept and said, "I have been deluded by appearances. He then vowed to cultivate the mind of emptiness. He returned to his cell and meditated on the nature of reality. This is why it is said that one must not disparage the Dharma. Furthermore, the *Xuanshi Lu* states that in the past, there was a king who was very fond of music. One day, he heard a beautiful song and became infatuated. He sent for the singer and made her his consort. However, she soon died. The king was grief-str
He obtained some sarira relics and laughed, saying, "If this is so, you may take several more statues here to burn.

In the third year of the Yuanhe era, while traveling through Luoyang, he lay across the Tianjin Bridge at dawn; it happened that Zheng Gong, the Imperial Resident Commissioner, was passing by with his retinue.
He scolded him, yet the man was not moved. The official sent someone to ask who he was; the man looked up slowly and replied, "A monk with no affairs.

The official marveled at this and presented him with bundles of silk and fine robes, providing a monthly ration of rice and flour. From then on, those who took refuge in his faith increased even more.
In the spring of the fifteenth year, he built a hermitage on Mount Danxia in Nanyang to enjoy the pleasures of the forest and springs. One day...
He went to pay his respects to National Teacher Zhong. First, he asked the attendant, "Is the National Teacher here? The attendant said, "He is indeed here, but he simply does not see guests.
Danran said, "That is far too remote. The attendant said, "Even the Buddha-eye cannot see him. Danran said, "A dragon begets a dragon; a phoenix begets a phoenix.
When the National Teacher awoke from his sleep, the attendant informed him of this, whereupon the Teacher struck him ten blows and drove him away.
He departed. However, having heard that he was not mistaken in being the teacher of the entire nation, the next day he went back to pay his respects.

Upon seeing the National Teacher, he spread out his sitting mat. The National Teacher said, "Not necessary, not necessary. Zhenran then stepped backward; the National Teacher said, "So it is, so it is.
Zhenran then stepped forward again; the National Teacher said, "It is not so, it is not so. Then Zhenran circumambulated the National Teacher once and...
He departed. National Teacher Huairang said, "The time since the Sage has passed; people are mostly indolent. Thirty years from now, it will be difficult to find such a man.
Later, when he visited Layman Pang and saw his daughter Lingzhao picking vegetables, Huairang asked, "Is the Layman at home?
The girl set down her vegetable basket and stood with her hands clasped. Huairang asked again, "Is the Layman at home? The girl picked up [the basket].
"Go with your vegetable basket. However, as you enter the hall, you and your entire household must carefully protect that single spiritual soul.
It cannot be fashioned or given form by you; so what more need be said of 'recommending' or 'not recommending'?
Look for yourselves! Skillful means are not obtained from without. Skillfulness is Mañjuśrī; skillful means is Samantabhadra. Do you still intend to pursue them further?"
What is it that you are pursuing? Nowadays, students are in a state of constant turmoil; they all engage in Zen meditation and inquire about the Way.
Here in my place, there is no Way to cultivate and no Dharma to realize. If you can recognize that Śākyamuni was merely an ordinary man, then you must look for yourself.
Do not let one blind person lead a multitude of blind people as you walk together into a pit of fire. It is dark and silent at night.

Lu. Saicai was about to depart this life. He said, "There is nothing more; take care. In the sixth month of the fourth year of the Changqing era, he instructed his disciples to prepare a bath, saying, "I have a distant journey to undertake.
Ultimately, wearing a bamboo hat, leaning on a staff, and wearing sandals, he lifted one foot; before it had even touched the ground, he passed away. He was eighty-six years of age.
Liu Ke, an Extraordinary Censor of the Ministry of Food, composed the inscription for his stele. His posthumous title was Zhītōng, and he was enshrined in a pagoda.
His title was Miaojue (Wondrous Enlightenment).
Tang Ruohui was a native of Shixing in Shaoyou Prefecture. In the eighth year of the Dali era, he visited Guoyi at Mount Jing;
subsequently, upon meeting Daji, his virtue and realization advanced, and his reputation arose. At that time, the monastic community referred to him as "Zhechuang Hui" (The Bed-Breaking Huì).

Because he was so diligent in seated meditation, his sitting platform was worn through by it. Before long, he emerged into the world and preached the Dharma at Dongsi (East Temple) in Changsha—what is commonly known among the laity as Jiaoshan.
Monks from all quarters flocked there like the spokes of a wheel, and the influence of Da Ji (Huineng) flourished even further.
When Prime Minister Cui Qun incurred the displeasure of Emperor Xianzong and was demoted to the south, he served as the Regional Inspector (Guancha Shi) and visited [the Master].
Huì asked, "Master, by what means did you attain this realization? He replied, "I attained it through the seeing of nature.

At that time, Huì was suffering from an eye ailment, so the official mocked him, saying, "Since you have gone beyond the seeing of nature, what can you do about your eyes? He replied, "Nature is not seen by the eyes."
"The sick person is not the eye. The Master bowed his head and apologized to him. Yangshan came to visit. Baizhang said, "I have already seen you;
there is no need to come up further. Yangshan said, "If we meet in this manner, would that not be improper?
Baizhang then closed the door to his quarters. Yangshan returned and reported this to Guishan. Guishan said, "What kind of mental activity is this, Jizi? Yangshan said, "If it were not..."
"Is it so? How could one possibly recognize him? Changqing passed away at the temple in the Gui-mao year; he was eighty years of age. A stupa was erected for him south of the city.
When Li Gong’ao served as the Inspector (Lianwen), he ordered that all tombs and stupas near the city walls be demolished to preserve the scenic beauty of the site.
However, he alone left intact the stupa where Huaisu was buried, remarking, "This may serve to distinguish between the worthy and the foolish. His posthumous title was...
The pagoda’s inscription was titled "Eternal Boundary" (Yongji). Liu Shanbu Ke composed the "Inscription of Diligent Effort.

Tang Dao-shu was the son of the Wen family from Tangzhou; he was nearly forty years old when he first received the tonsure from the śramaṇa Huiwen at Daguang Monastery on Mount Mingyue in the prefecture.
Having received full ordination, he traveled to various regions to seek the Way, having no fixed abode.
He did not pass away. Later, in Luoyang, he received the essential instructions of the Northern School. He immediately entered Sanfeng Mountain in Shouzhou and dwelt there in a thatched hut.
Students flocked to him like deer. There was a wild man who would come regularly and could always transform himself into the forms of Buddhas, immortals, bodhisattvas, or arhats;
at times he emitted divine light, and at other times he produced extraordinary sounds. This continued for ten years, after which he suddenly became silent. A tree...
He told the assembly: "The common folk employ many such stratagems, striving only to dazzle and delude;
it requires only that this old monk neither see nor hear them. Their stratagems are finite, whereas my non-seeing and non-hearing are infinite.
At the beginning of the Baoli era, he manifested illness and passed away at the age of ninety-two. In the first month of the following year, his entire body was interred in a stupa.
Tang Taiyu was born into the Fan family in Jinling. When he was only twelve years old, he entered the monastic life under Chan Master Huizhong of Mount Niutou.
He traveled to An Guo Temple in the capital of Yong to receive full ordination. Not long after, he visited Chan Master Taiji in Hongfu and obtained the seal of the Dharma.
In the thirteenth year of the Yuanhe era, he resided at Fuyong in Yixing, Piling.
Mount [Shan]. Moved by this, he followed with joy, and the shoes at his door numbered in the tens of thousands. The layman Pang Yun visited that place three times.

On one occasion, while traveling, he gave food to the Master. As the layman was receiving the food, Shan Yu said, "Vimalakīrti long ago rebuked you for giving rise to a mind of seeking when accepting alms.
Apart from this single instance, would you still find it sweet? The layman replied, "At that time, was Subhūti not himself a master of the craft? Shan Yu said, "Indeed."
[Daoyu] said, "It has nothing to do with other matters. The layman said, "When food reaches the edge of one's mouth, it is snatched away by him.

Daoyu then set down his food. The layman said, "One phrase would have sufficed. The layman asked again, "Does Master Ma’s point of truly benefiting people accord with what you have been entrusted with, Master?
Daoyu said, "I have not yet seen him; how could I know his point of being real?"
The layman said, "This very seeing and knowing has no place to be sought. Daoyu said, "Layman, you must not speak with one-sidedness.
The layman said, "If you speak with one-sidedness, the Master has lost the essential point. But if you take two sides or three sides, can the Master still open his mouth?
Daoyu said, "It is truly such that one cannot open the mouth; this may be called reality. The layman clapped his hands and laughed.
He departed. When Cui Qun, the Chancellor, was appointed as the regional governor of Xuancheng, he invited him to reside at Chanding Monastery.

In the first year of the Baoli era, he arrived at Chanding; the following year, he returned to Mount Qiyun. In the ninth month, he manifested his passing at the mountain monastery. He was eighty years of age.
His monastic seniority was fifty-eight years. In the tenth month, he was interred in a stupa within the monastery grounds.

In the second year of the Dàhé era, the Chancellor Wèi Chùhòu reported his passing to the Emperor, who issued an edict bestowing upon him the posthumous title of Great Treasure Chan Master (Dàbǎo Chánshī). The stupa was named Laṅkā. Lù Xuéng, the Prefectural Governor of Yuèzhōu, composed the inscription for the stele.
Tang Daoheng, surnamed Yang, was a native of Guiyang. He entered the monastic life at the Baizhou (Pratyutpanna) practice center on Mount Nanyue.

While traveling and studying in Zhongling, he attained silent realization and achieved the Samādhi of Mastery (*vaśitā-samādhi*). Shortly thereafter, he went to the mountains southwest of Linyang, where he constructed a small cell to dwell in.
Clad in coarse hemp robes and wearing sandals of *phusa* grass, he would sit or sleep there; tigers and leopards mingled with him about his bed and mat without causing him any hindrance.
Before long, there suddenly appeared those who offered timber and funds, wishing to construct a grand edifice as an act of charity.

Within less than ten days, the magnificence of its halls and buildings was complete. After they had departed, he inquired among people regarding their names, titles, and residences, but ultimately no one knew them;
only then did he realize it must have been divine assistance. Shortly thereafter, the Prefect [donated] Kaiyuan Temple in the seat of the prefecture.
Guo summoned him to reside there, where he passed away. He was sixty-nine years old in the fifteenth year of the Yuanhe era.
Regarding Tang Tanzang, his family name, clan, and native place are unknown; however, he attained the essential core of Daji’s transmission.

He further studied under Shitou, refining his realization through further tempering. In the second year of the Zhenyuan era, he resided at Mount Heng, dwelling atop the highest peak of the mountain until his later years.
In his later years, he suffered from foot ailments and was moved by his disciples to the Western Garden (Xiyuan) at the foot of the mountain; this is what the world calls the Xiyuan Monastery.
His followers in the practice of worship were second only to those of Mazu Daoyi. In the first year of the Taihe era, he passed away at his residence at the age of seventy.

Zangxing was by nature pleasant and easygoing, never offending or causing harm to others. Once, while walking at night, he encountered a massive python several *wen* long that opened its mouth toward him as if to strike.

As a predator was about to swallow him, his attendants supported him from the sides and hurried him away to take cover. Zang refused, saying, "Can death be avoided? They come with poison, but I receive it with compassion.
Poison has no inherent nature, and compassion has no objective conditions. Enemies and kin are equal; birth and death are of one principle.
This is because the *dharmatā* is empty. The python finally lowered its head and slowly departed. Furthermore, there was once a thief who entered his room; Zang—
He said to them, "The reason you have come here is simply that there is nothing in this place. If there were anything, you need only pick it up;
I would never begrudge it. The bandits were suddenly startled and dispersed.

Tang Weiyen, whose secular surname was Han, was a native of Jin County in the Jin dynasty. Possessing exceptional intelligence from childhood, at the age of seventeen he received the tonsure under Chan Master Huizhao of Xishan in Huyang, Nan’gang.
In the eighth year of the Dali era, he received full ordination from Vinaya Master Hicuo of Hengyue Temple.
Not long thereafter, he visited Chan Master Shitou Xiqian to verify the teachings of the mind. One day, Weiyen...
During a sitting session, Shitou asked, "What are you doing here? Yanyue replied, "I am not doing anything. Shitou said, "If that is so, then you are just sitting idly.
Yanyue said, "If it were idle sitting, then I would be doing something. Shitou said, "You say you are not doing anything."
Furthermore, what is it that he is not? Yǎn said, "Even the thousand sages do not know him. Dàtó praised him with a verse:
"From the beginning we have lived together, yet I did not know his name; He moves along spontaneously, just as he is. Even the ancient worthies of the past could not recognize him;
How could ordinary people in their haste possibly name him? Dàtó once gave this instruction: "Do not let your speech or actions intersect with him. Yǎn said:
He did not speak, nor did he engage in any activity. Tou said, "Here, even a needle cannot pierce.
Yan said, "Here, it is like planting flowers upon a rock. Tou deeply approved of this. Later, while Yan was reading a sutra, Boya said, "Master, stop; you have caught me out.
Yan rolled up the sutra and asked, "Is it early or late in the day? Boya said, "It is exactly noon. Yan...
Yan said, "There is still this trace remaining. Baizhang said, "I have nothing, and there is nothing at all.
Yan said, "You are far too clever. Baizhang said, "I am just like this; what is your honorable intention, Master?

Yan said, "I am hobbling along, dragging myself by, a hundred uglinesses and a thousand clumsinesses—just passing the time. A monk came to visit him again, and Yan asked, "Who is that? The monk replied:

Changtan was sternly reprimanding [the assembly] when he said, "The former is the constant plain; the latter is also the constant plain. One day, the head of the monastery invited Yanyue to ascend the hall.
As soon as the great assembly had gathered, Yanyue remained silent for a long while and then returned to his quarters, closing the door.

The head of the monastery followed after him and asked, "Master, you granted me permission to ascend the hall; why did you instead return to your quarters? Yanyue replied, "The sutras are for the sutras."
The Master said, "In the Abhidharma there are Abhidharma masters; in the Vinaya there are Vinaya masters. Again, when Yunyan was carrying excrement, Nanquan asked, "Yunyan, what are you doing?
Yunyan replied, "Carrying excrement. Nanquan asked, "Who is that? Yunyan replied, "He is here.
Nanquan asked, "For whom do you come and go? Yunyan replied, "I am acting on his behalf. Nanquan asked, "Why not have him walk alongside you? Yunyan replied, "Because he still..."
Once, while Yanguan was sitting in formal meditation, a monk asked him, "What are you thinking about so intently?
Yanguan replied, "I am thinking about that which cannot be thought. The monk asked, "How can one think about that which cannot be thought? Yanguan said, "It is not thinking.
Another monk asked, "When a student intends to return to his hometown, what then? Yanguan said, "Your parents' entire bodies are covered in bloody sores."
"Sleeping in a forest of thorns—where will you go when you return? The monk said, "If it is so, then I shall not return. Yǎn said, "You must indeed return.
If you return to your home, I shall show you a recipe for abstaining from grain. The monk said, "I ask for it at once.
Yǎn said, "Pass through the hall twice daily, without chewing a single grain of rice. The monk asked, "This student has a doubt."
"I request the Master to resolve this for me. Yǎn said, "Wait until the time for the formal lecture, and I shall resolve it for you, Dàlì.
When evening came and the assembly had gathered, Yǎn asked, "Where is the Venerable who requested the resolution of his doubts today? The monk stepped forward from the assembly.

Yǎn descended from his meditation seat, seized him by the collar, and said, "This monk in the assembly has doubts; he has merely made an excuse to return to his quarters. The monk then asked, "The Patriarch..."
"Before you have reached this land, does this land still possess the meaning of the Patriarchs? Yǎn replied, "It does.
The monk asked, "If it already possesses the meaning of the Patriarchs, why have you come? Yǎn said, "Precisely because it has [that meaning], I have come.
While Yǎn was reading a scripture, the monk asked, "Master, you usually do not allow people to read scriptures; why then do you read them yourself? Yǎn said, "I only..."
He drew a picture to cover his eyes. The monk asked, "May I also emulate the Master? Yǎn said, "If it were you looking, you would have to pierce even through ox-hide.
Lǐ Áo, the Regional Inspector of Lǎngzhōu, went personally into the mountains to visit Yǎn. Yǎn held a scripture and did not look at him.
Although the attendant spoke repeatedly, saying, "The Governor is here," Yǎn still did not look. Lǐ Áo was by nature impatient and irritable; he said in anger:
"Meeting someone in person is not as good as hearing of their reputation. Baoyi Xian called out to the Governor, "How can you value what you hear while disparaging what you see?

Baoyi then apologized for his conduct. Xian asked him, "What is the Way? Pointing up and down, Xian said, "Do you understand? Baoyi replied, "I do not understand. Xian said, "The clouds are in the sky;
the water is in the pitcher. Baoyi then recited a verse: "My body has been refined until it resembles the form of a crane; A thousand trees..."
"Under the pine tree are two cases of scriptures. I have come to ask about the Way, yet there is no further teaching. Yun said, "Clouds in the blue sky; water in a jar.
Ao asked again, "What are precepts, concentration, and wisdom? Yan said, "In my humble place, we have no such idle furnishings. After a long silence, Ao remained silent.
Yan said, "If you, Prefectural Governor, wish to take responsibility for this matter, you must stand atop the highest mountain peak."
"Traversing the depths of the ocean's floor. If one cannot let go of worldly attachments within the domestic sphere, leakage occurs. One night, he ascended a mountain peak;
the recent rain had cleared, and the sky was crystalline and pure. Looking up, he saw the clouds parting as the moon emerged, its radiance bursting forth. He laughed aloud.
Although Liyang was ninety li away, those who heard the sound of it were as if [right there].
Recently, he traveled between households in the east and west; thereupon, through mutual inquiries, it was first discovered that he had originally come from Yaoshan.
In the second month of the eighth year of the Taihe era, he suddenly cried out, "The Dharma Hall is collapsing! The Dharma Hall is collapsing! The assembly all took up objects to prop it up.
Xian raised his hand and said, "You do not understand my meaning," and then passed away. He was eighty-four years old in secular age and sixty years of *dharma-śāsana* seniority.
A stupa was erected in the northeastern corner of the monastery, named Huacheng (City of Transformation). His posthumous title was Hongdao (Propagation of the Way).
He was surnamed Ningben, with the family name Li; his ancestors were from Longxi, but he was currently registered as a resident of Mengcheng County in Bo Prefecture.
Fen was born with an innate nature that required no instruction, and his mind was already in harmony with Bodhi.

Upon meeting Mazu at Hongzhou, Mazu immediately recognized him as a vessel for the Mahayana Dharma, permitting him to shave his head, receive the precepts, and enter the inner quarters as a disciple. After some time, he took leave to travel to Tiantai.
Arriving at Lühou Mountain in Yue, he admired its secluded and remote character and said, "This is truly a dwelling place for the Buddhas and Arhats."
"Indeed. Why necessarily Mount Tiantai? Thereupon, he tied up some thatched grass and settled there. Before long, the local strongmen and village elders beheld his countenance and conceived goodness;

hearing his words, they gave rise to reverence. Like the single flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter), all who were afflicted were healed. Furthermore, bandits and plunderers became quiet and peaceful, and the wild and fierce were tamed and disciplined.
This is truly what is called the power of the Buddha’s virtue. Previously, his dwelling had been cramped and humble, and moreover lacked a hall.
The hall was under construction when materials were transported and skilled craftsmen and laborers—both monastics and lay believers—gathered in full. Yet it was suddenly completed.
On the seventh day of the sixth month in the second year of the Daichō era, some heard the sound of drums and stringed and wind instruments within the practice hall.
At the second watch of the night, he passed away peacefully. He was seventy-five years of age and forty-one years since his ordination. In the ninth month of the fifth year, his disciples...
They placed him on a bier and performed the *caitya-vihāra* (cremation). They enshrined his *śarīra* relics on the *śun* (southeast) mountain of the *daochang*.

This is a draft of his final instructions. The *Táng Chóngxìn shǐ* does not record his surname. He was born into a family of cake-sellers in Zhūgōng, which happened to be adjacent to Tiānhuáng Temple.
At that time, Master Wù was serving as the abbot of the temple. While still young, Chóngxìn would daily carry a basket of cakes into the temple.
Whenever Sengwu was about to eat, he would first offer some to Xinxian. After each meal, Wu would invariably set aside a portion to leave for Xinxian.

Xinxian thought to himself, "This cake is indeed what I gave to him, yet he has returned it to me. Could there be another meaning behind this? He once questioned Wu about it. Wu said, "This is what you brought here;
returning it to you—what fault is there in that? Upon hearing this, Xinxian attained realization and immediately requested to leave the household life. Thereupon, Wu...
He accepted him and said, "In the past your name was Chongfu; now that you have faith in my words, your name should be Chongxin.

Thereupon, he personally attended to the well and mortar to serve Wuzhuo. One day, he asked Wuzhuo, "Since I first came here, I have not received the Master’s instruction on the essential point of the mind.
Wuzhuo replied, "As for the essential point of the mind, there has never been a time when I have not instructed you. Chongxin asked, "Why?"
Dazu pointed out a location. Wuxue said, "When you bring me tea, I will receive it for you;
when you bring me food, I will accept it for you; when you bow in greeting, I will join my palms. Where is there that is not the essential point of the mind?

Why must you seek a separate instruction? Xinxing bowed his head for a long time. Wuxue said, "If you see, you see immediately; if you deliberate, you have already gone astray. Thereupon, Xinxing asked:
"How does one maintain this? Wuzhu replied, "Roam freely according to one's nature; let go with ease following conditions. Simply exhaust all mundane sentiments;
there is no other 'saintly' understanding. Later, he resided at Longtan in Liyang at the request of the Minister Li Ao.
A monk asked, "Who can obtain the pearl within the topknot? He answered, "One who does not prize or play with it. The monk pressed further, "Where is it placed? He answered, "It has a place."
Li Shangshu asked Dao-lai, "What is true suchness-prajñā (bhūtatathatā-prajñā)? He replied, "I have no true suchness-prajñā.
The Shangshu said, "It is my good fortune to have encountered you, Master. He replied, "These are still words that go beyond the ordinary.
Since Deshan Xuanjian succeeded to the Dharma and established its school, the lineage of Longtan has remained undiminished to this day.
Tang Tan-sheng was born into the Wang clan of Jianchang in Zhongling. From the moment he first entered the womb, his placenta was black in color, appearing as if it were bared on the right side;
his parents already knew that he could not be burdened with worldly affairs. When he reached the age for elementary studies, they sent him to follow [Master] Shi-men to receive the tonsure.
Once he had attained the status of a fully ordained monk (*upasampadā*), he attended upon Chan Master Dazhi Hai at Baiyang Mountain.
After twenty years had passed, he subsequently met Chan Master Yaoshan Yan. One day, Yaoshan asked, "Apart from being at Baiyang, where else have you been?

Cheng replied, "I have come from Guangnan. Yaoshan said, "I have heard it said that outside the east gate of the city of Guangzhou there is a cluster of stones that were moved by the Governor; is this true? Cheng replied, "It was not merely the Governor."
Even when the entire population of the country joined in to move it, it would not budge. Guishan asked again, "I have heard that you are skilled at performing with a lion;
is this true? Cheng said, "It is. Guishan said, "How many acts do you perform? Cheng said, "Six acts. Guishan said, "I can also perform them.
Cheng asked, "How many acts does the Master perform? Guishan said, "I perform one act. Cheng said, "One is six, and six is one. Cheng...
Later, he arrived at Mount Gui. Mount Gui asked, "I hear that while you were at Yaoshan, you were 'playing with lions,' is this true?
Cheng said, "It is. Gui said, "Do you play with them constantly? Is there also a time to set them down? Cheng said, "If I wish to play, I play; if I wish to set them down, I set them down."
Miaoyan said, "When you set it down, where is the lion? Cheng said, "Set it down! Set it down! A monk asked, "Where have all the sages of the past gone?
Cheng remained silent for a long while and then said, "What? What? He was asked again, "If one is away for a moment..."
"He is like a dead man. "How so? Cheng said, "It would be best to bury him. While Cheng was brewing tea, Daowu asked, "For whom are you brewing this tea?
Cheng said, "There is someone who wants it. Daowu said, "Why not let him brew it himself? Cheng said, "Fortunately, there is I here.
After Cheng resided at Yunyan, one day the assembly said, "There is a son of a certain family..."
A questioner asked about the Way that cannot be grasped or reached. Dongshan said, "How many scriptures are there in his house?
Cheng said, "Not even a single character. Dongshan said, "How is it that he knows so much? Cheng said, "Day and night, he never sleeps.
Daowu asked, "Regarding the Thousand Hands and Eyes of Great Compassion, what is it like? Cheng said, "It is like when there is no lamp: one simply takes up the pillow."
"Son," [Wu] asked, "How is it? I said, "I understand; I understand. Cheng said, "How do you understand? I said, "The whole body is eyes.
One day, while Cheng was sweeping the floor, Mount Gui said, "You are being too busy.
Cheng said, "You must know that there is one who is not busy. Mount Gui said, "If that is so, then there is a second moon. Cheng held up his broom.
Zhaozhou asked, "Which month is this? Mian bowed his head and departed. Cheng asked a monk, "Where have you come from?
The monk said, "I have just been conversing on a stone. Cheng asked, "Did the stone nod its head? The monk was speechless.
Cheng spoke on his behalf, saying, "Before the Abbot even asked, it was already nodding its head. Dongshan asked for his eyes. Cheng said, "Whom will yours go to? Dongshan—
Dongshan said, "Liangjia has none. Cheng said, "If there are none, where would you put yourself? Dongshan was speechless. Cheng said, "Is that which begs for eyes itself the eye?
Dongshan said, "It is not the eye. Cheng rebuked him. On the twenty-seventh day of the tenth month of the third year of the Dàhé era (the Jǐyǒu year), he entered nirvana.
His posthumous title was Wúxiàng (Formless), and his stupa was named Jìngshèng (Pure Victory). Thus it is said.

Master Zhen of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Lu and was a native of Jiangling. His family had been scholars for generations. At the age of seven, he could recite the *Shijing* and comprehend its great principles.
As he grew older, he entered the civil service examination system (*jìxié*). He presented himself before the Ministry of Rites three times before finally passing the examination once;

however, while he was still in the period before donning his official robes, he encountered a śramaṇa who discussed the Dharma of Emptiness. Thereupon, he joined Master Bianchu at Fushou Temple to seek ordination and began his religious studies.
Regarding the sutras and śāstras, he once ascended the seat to expound the Dharma at Zhaocheng Temple in Luoyang.
Having received the essential points of the mind from Chan Master Ji of Mount Song, he traveled south to Maoshan in Danyang and subsequently took up residence at Lengqia Mountain in Suzhou.
Seekers came from all directions to consult him; at that time, the renowned Bai Juyi, known as Lètiān, was serving as the governor of that prefecture and invariably [welcomed him] whenever they met.
With his robes unfastened and his belt loosened, he let his spirit roam through the subtle principles of the Way, deeply penetrating the threshold of discernment.

Because of persistent requests, he left the mountains to reside at Liu-shui Temple, yet he found no joy there. Before long, he returned to his former hermitage. In the third year of the Dàhé era, he manifested a slight illness and passed away at the age of ninety.
On the seventeenth day of the fourth month of that year, he was interred in a stupa.
Tang Lingtan was born into the Xiao clan of Lanling. Following the fall of the Liang dynasty, his descendants dispersed to all quarters; Lingtan himself grew up in Changsha.

However, he possessed an exceptionally sharp and extraordinary nature, and after receiving the tonsure, he devoted himself exclusively to the study of Chan. He attended every Dharma assembly without exception.
Having traveled extensively through Qing and Wei for a long time, in the first year of the Changqing era, someone established a temple at Baijia Rock and invited him to reside there.
Not long after, he traveled again, and Wang Qian, the Prefect of Jiangling, invited him to preach the Dharma at Yongtai Temple.

On the twenty-third day of the sixth month in the third year of the Taihe era, he passed away at the temple at the age of seventy-five. His stupa, located to the north of the prefecture, remains to this day.
Furthermore, there was Chaoran, a native of Danyang, who had previously relied upon Master Su of Helin during the second year of the Tianbao era.
In his later years, he propagated the Dharma in Fuzhou. Yuan Guan of Tang obtained a seal from Daji, who said:
"Yuan Guan, surnamed Yuan, was a native of Chang’an. His father served as a clerk in the administration of Hezhong Prefecture. Previously, his elder brother had left the household life."

He possessed the practice of the Way and was admired by all who beheld him. He was sent to Xingshan Temple to recite the scriptures and was directed to undergo an examination by the relevant authorities;
having passed with credit, he received ordination. Furthermore, he was proficient in the *Vinaya-kuśala-śāstra*. Later, he entered a Chan assembly and attained realization.

He subsequently settled at the Eastern Terrace of Mount Heng to guide and instruct those who came to study. Daily, a divine being provided offerings for him, according to the number of his followers, never failing once.
One day, a spirit suddenly manifested its form and prostrated itself twice, saying, "By virtue of the merit from providing offerings for twenty years, I have already attained transcendence.
Therefore, I have come to bid you farewell. Guanding asked him, "What karma caused this in your past life?

He replied, "In my previous existence, I was once a spiritual teacher who unworthily accepted offerings from the faithful; because of that, I became a spirit presiding over this land. After a long while, Guanding showed him [the way].
Ji passed away at the age of seventy-nine. On the second day of the seventh month in the fourth year of the Dàhé era, he was interred in a stupa.
Táng Wéizé was originally of the Chángsūn clan from Jīngzhào. His grandfather, Lì, served as the Sīmǎ of Èzhōu;

his father, Lìshè, subsequently resided in Jīnlíng. Wéizé was by nature serene and composed; he applied himself diligently to the study of Confucian arts while having a particular fondness for Buddhist scriptures. He would often say:
This truly captures the subtle essence of my mind. Subsequently, he left the household life and followed Niu-tou Huizhong, from whom he received the Dharma of the Mind.
He then traveled south to the Buddha-Cave on Mount Tiantai to dwell there. Clad in *bìlì* (moss), he used fallen leaves as bedding; he ate wild fruits and drank from mountain streams.
As motionless as a withered tree, his spirit was concentrated and his vital energy transformed. How could one possibly fathom him through worldly emotions or intellectual consciousness?
How profound! Later, a woodcutter saw it and spread the word to others. Thereupon, those carrying staffs and alms bowls flocked there until it eventually became a monastic community.
He instructed his disciples, saying: "The single mind is devoid of things; the myriad dharmas are devoid of things. Yet, they have never been devoid of things."
Thus, heaven and earth are like shadows; the present and the past are like dreams. Who, then, undergoes birth and death?
The Perfected Person (Zhiren) illuminates this alone and is thus able to be the lord of the myriad things. I know this; do you all know it?
A monk asked, "What is the Nārāyaṇa arrow? He replied, "It hits the mark. Sitting for forty years, it was as if it were a single day. In the year of the Geng cycle...

In the sixth month of summer, on the thirteenth day, he summoned his disciples and bestowed upon them instructions and admonitions. On the fifteenth day, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
That evening, those living at the foot of the mountain heard a sound as if a mountain were collapsing, and they also saw colored clouds piercing through the cliffs like brocade.
He was seventy-eight years of age and fifty-eight years since his ordination. A funerary shrine and stupa were erected for him within this very monastery. [The river...]
The inscription was composed by Yan Yi of Nan-yin and carved upon a stele; thus, his writings were circulated in the world.

Wude of the Tang dynasty was born into the Li clan of Wei County in Dongjing. In his youth, he accompanied his father on official duty to Nan-kang, where he traveled extensively among the Buddhist monasteries of Mount Lu and took pleasure in residing there.
He subsequently informed his father of his wish to leave the household life; having had his hair shaved and received full ordination, he became a monk.

Jie (Huiji) was then practicing the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle. At that time, Master Dashiji was gathering disciples at Mount Gonggong; Huiji took up his staff and went to visit him. In the brief moment they exchanged words, [Huiji’s] demeanor was resolute and could not be matched by his peers. Later, while residing at Tumen in Suizhou, he once visited the provincial governor, Attendant Wang Changshi. As he was about to leave the gate, Wang called out to him, saying, "Master. Huiji replied, "I am here. Wang said, "The Master has come. Huiji replied, "I have come. Wang said, "The Master has arrived. Huiji replied, "I have arrived. Wang said, "The Master has entered. Huiji replied, "I have entered. Wang said, "The Master has sat down. Huiji replied, "I have sat down. Wang said, "The Master has spoken. Huiji replied, "I have spoken. Wang said, "The Master has departed. Huiji replied, "I have departed. Wang said, "The Master has gone. Huiji replied, "I have gone. Wang said, "The Master has left. Huiji replied, "I have left. Wang said, "The Master has been seen off. Huiji replied, "I have been seen off. Wang said, "The Master has returned. Huiji replied, "I have returned. Wang said, "The Master has stayed. Huiji replied, "I have stayed. Wang said, "The Master has slept. Huiji replied, "I have slept. Wang said, "The Master has awakened. Huiji replied, "I have awakened. Wang said, "The Master has risen.
