Huiji replied, "I have attained Nirvana. Wang said, "The Master has entered Parinirvana. Huiji replied, "I have entered Parinirvana. Wang said, "The Master has transcended all phenomena. Huiji replied, "I have transcended all phenomena. Wang said, "The Master has realized the Way. Huiji replied, "I have realized the Way. Wang said, "The Master has fulfilled his vow. Huiji replied, "I have fulfilled my vow. Wang said, "The Master has completed his task. Huiji replied, "I have completed my task. Wang said, "The Master has ended his life. Huiji replied, "I have ended my life. Wang said, "The Master has reached the end. Huiji replied, "I have reached the end. Wang said, "The Master has attained liberation. Huiji replied, "I have attained liberation. Wang said, "The Master has attained the ultimate. Huiji replied, "I have attained the ultimate. Wang said, "The Master has reached the limit of reality. Huiji replied, "I have reached the limit of reality. Wang said, "The Master has exhausted all dharmas. Huiji replied, "I have exhausted all dharmas. Wang said, "The Master has transcended birth and death. Huiji replied, "I have transcended birth and death. Wang said, "The Master has entered the realm of non-arising. Huiji replied, "I have entered the realm of non-arising. Wang said, "The Master has realized the nature of emptiness. Huiji replied, "I have realized the nature of emptiness. Wang said, "The Master has attained the fruit of Buddhahood. Huiji replied, "I have attained the fruit of Buddhahood. Wang said, "The Master has become a true sage. Huiji replied, "I have become a true sage. Wang said, "The Master has become a great being. Huiji replied, "I have become a great being. Wang said, "The Master has become a field of merit. Huiji replied, "I have become a field of merit. Wang said, "The Master has become a refuge for all beings. Huiji replied, "I have become a refuge for all beings. Wang said, "The Master has become a lamp in the darkness. Huiji replied, "I have become a lamp in the darkness. Wang said, "The Master has become a boat on the ocean of suffering. Huiji replied, "I have become a boat on the ocean of suffering. Wang said, "The Master has become a bridge across the river of delusion. Huiji replied, "I have become a bridge across the river of delusion. Wang said, "The Master has become a physician for the sick. Huiji replied, "I have become a physician for the sick. Wang said, "The Master has become a guide for the lost. Huiji replied, "I have become a guide for the lost. Wang said, "The Master has become a teacher of men and gods. Huiji replied, "I have become a teacher of men and gods. Wang said, "The Master has become a protector of the Dharma. Huiji replied, "I have become a protector of the Dharma. Wang said, "The Master has become a sustainer of the lineage. Huiji replied, "I have become a sustainer of the lineage. Wang said, "The Master has become a vessel of the truth. Huiji replied, "I have become a vessel of the truth. Wang said, "The Master has become a treasury of wisdom. Huiji replied, "I have become a treasury of wisdom. Wang said, "The Master has become a mountain of virtue. Huiji replied, "I have become a mountain of virtue. Wang said, "The Master has become an ocean of compassion. Huiji replied, "I have become an ocean of compassion. Wang said, "The Master has become a sun of light. Huiji replied, "I have become a sun of light. Wang said, "The Master has become a moon of clarity. Huiji replied, "I have become a moon of clarity. Wang said, "The Master has become a wind of liberation. Huiji replied, "I have become a wind of liberation. Wang said, "The Master has become a rain of Dharma. Huiji replied, "I have become a rain of Dharma. Wang said, "The Master has become a fire of wisdom. Huiji replied, "I have become a fire of wisdom. Wang said, "The Master has become a jewel of the mind. Huiji replied, "I have become a jewel of the mind. Wang said, "The Master has become a diamond of reality. Huiji replied, "I have become a diamond of reality. Wang said, "The Master has become a lotus flower of purity. Huiji replied, "I have become a lotus flower of purity. Wang said, "The Master has become a lion of the Dharma. Huiji replied, "I have become a lion of the Dharma. Wang said, "The Master has become a dragon of the sky. Huiji replied, "I have become a dragon of the sky. Wang said, "The Master has become a phoenix of the world. Huiji replied, "I have become a phoenix of the world. Wang said, "The Master has become a crane of longevity. Huiji replied, "I have become a crane of longevity. Wang said, "The Master has become a crane of the Way. Huiji replied, "I have become a crane of the Way. Wang said, "The Master has become a crane of the ultimate. Huiji replied, "I have become a crane of the ultimate. Wang said, "The Master has become a crane of the absolute. Huiji replied, "I have become a crane of the absolute. Wang said, "The Master has become a crane of the unconditioned. Huiji replied, "I have become a crane of the unconditioned. Wang said, "The Master has become a crane of the ineffable. Huiji replied, "I have become a crane of the ineffable. Wang said, "The Master has become a crane of the ungraspable. Huiji replied, "I have become a crane of the ungraspable. Wang said, "The Master has become a crane of the unmanifest. Huiji replied, "I have become a crane of the unmanifest. Wang said, "The Master has become a crane of the unborn. Huiji replied, "I have become a crane of the unborn. Wang said, "The Master has become a
Looking back, the King struck the pillar three times, drew a circle with his hand, and then pushed it away three times before departing.
In the seventh year of the Yuanhe era, he thatched a hut on Mount Huanggu at Wuchang and sustained himself by begging for alms daily.

Consequently, those throughout Ba, Shu, Jing, and Xiang who were devoted to profound principles came from afar to seek him out. In the first year of the Dazhao era, he was invited by the Chancellor, Lord Niu Sengrou.
Zhenshang Jiang heard of Baizhang’s reputation and sent his carriage to visit him.
Fearing that Baizhang’s monastery was not registered in the official records, he specifically submitted a petition on his behalf, and Baizhang was granted the title "Daji" (Great Quiescence).

One evening during the formal assembly (*wanchan*), everyone addressed Baizhang as "Not-knowing" (*bushen*). Thereupon, Baizhang said to the assembly, "Where did that sound just now go? A monk raised one finger.
Dongshan said, "Take care. The next day, when the monk came for his formal visit, Dongshan turned his back and faced the wall, lying down with a groan.
He said to the monk, "I have not been very well for two or three days. Great Virtue, what medicine do you have on your person?
Give me a little. The monk pointed to a pure water pitcher and said, "This pure water pitcher—what is it?"
[The Master] asked, "Where did you get this? The monk replied, "This belongs to the old monk. [The Master] asked, "Where is yours, Venerable Sir?
The monk said, "It belongs to both the Master and myself. In the tenth month of the fourth year, he passed away at the age of eighty-two.
His disciples, including Shitong, enshrined his entire body in a stupa.
Tang Mingjue’s ancestors were of the You clan from Henei. His grandfather held office in Lingnan and subsequently moved his family there, making them natives of Jianyang.
Mingjue had long been trained in Confucian studies, yet he was particularly devoted to and admired the study of the Profound (Xuanxue).

Having previously heard that Daji was preaching the Way of Chan at Foji Ridge, he went there to rely upon him and left the household life. Thereafter, he traveled through various regions, extensively tasting the Dharma.
He stayed at Mount Lingji for several summers, personally undertaking the labor of gathering firewood and drawing water without any sense of weariness.
He subsequently confined himself to Dàyún Monastery in the city of Háng. Shortly thereafter, he lived in a hermitage atop Mount Qīngshān on Lake Tàihú.

It happened that Lú Gōng of Fányáng, having been appointed as the regional governor of Qiántáng from his post as a Minister of the Interior, invited him to reside at Dàyún Monastery and took charge of the affairs of the abbotship. In the fifteenth year of the Yuánhé era, he retired [to avoid the world].
Disliking the clamor of the world, he retreated to Mount Tianmu. Lay devotees flocked to him, and he eventually established a Buddhist monastery there.

In the spring of the fourth year of the Changqing era, a drought occurred; by the second month of the fifth year, it had still not rained. Wild fires broke out on all sides and reached the temple grounds.

The streams and gullies were completely dried up, leaving no means to extinguish the blaze. His disciples were terrified and requested that they move elsewhere. Huizhao said, "Do not be hasty. I am at this mountain..."

There were auspicious signs. Shortly thereafter, thunder and rain broke out suddenly, causing those who heard it to marvel in wonder. On the nineteenth day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Dàhé era, he entered *nirvāṇa*.
Táng Yuánxiū was the son of the Pán family of Fúmián; he shaved his head at an early age and received the full precepts at Huìshàn Monastery on Mount Sōngyáng.

At the temple, he studied the sutras and śāstras with great diligence. Soon thereafter, he paid his respects to Chan Master Dazhihai at Baiyang Mountain, whereupon he realized the essential point of the mind.
Not long after, Fubei traveled to the regions of Wu and Yue; entering Qinwang Mountain, he saw a pine tree with such twisted branches that it could serve as a seat.
He sat cross-legged upon it, with no shelter from wind, rain, frost, or dew. Although magpies nested beside him, they lived in peace.
In this manner, forty years of cold and heat passed. The world called him Master Niaoke (Nest-of-Birds).

Whenever a provincial governor arrived and heard of his reputation, calculating that he could not be brought down by invitation, would invariably go in person to see him beneath the tree. At the beginning of the Yuanhe era, Lord Pei...
Changdi treated him with even greater reverence and affection. He first established a hermitage on that site and requested [the Master] to preach the Dharma for the assembly;

he also constructed the Zhaoxian Monastery to provide a place for rest and seclusion. On the twenty-second day of the ninth month in the seventh year of the Taihe era, the year of Gui-chou, he passed away in profound stillness.
He was ninety-nine years of age and had been a monk for eighty years. He was buried beneath Shizeng Mountain by the śramaṇa of Nanyue.
Wei Zhen inscribed his stupa.

Tang Puyuan’s secular surname was Wang; he was a native of Xinzheng in Zhengzhou. He entered the monastic order in the second year of the Zhide era, receiving the tonsure under Chan Master Dahui of Daweishan in Mian County.
In the twelfth year of the Dali era, Puyuan was still in the prime of his youth. Subsequently, he followed...
Vinaya Master Gaofa of Huishan Si on Mount Songshan had received full ordination; there was no section of the Vinaya-piṭaka or its exegetical literature that he did not thoroughly investigate.
Ultimately, however, he established his definitive school under the gate of Great Stillness (Mazu). One day, while serving rice gruel to the monks, Master Ma asked him, "What is in this bucket?
Yuan replied, "This old fellow, shut your mouth! Do you speak such words? The rest was the same as before.
Those who followed him did not dare to question or challenge him. In the eleventh year of the Zhenyuan era, he hung up his staff at Nanquan Mountain in Chiyang.

Wearing garments of *xiang* and *pi* grass and eating from the cleared fields and pastures, he filled in valleys and cut down trees to clear a place for his dwelling. There, companions clad in coarse woolen robes gathered around him.
They advanced together and retreated in turn, crowding and filling the courtyard. He addressed the assembly, saying: "To utter the word 'Suchness' (tathatā) is already to have changed it.
The teachers and monks of the present day must walk among those of different species. Guizong said: "Though one performs the deeds of an animal, one does not receive the retribution of an animal.
Yuan said: "Meng Babang has gone off in that manner again. At other times he said: "Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra..."
Last night at the third watch, [Zhaozhou] gave rise to views of the Buddha and views of the Dharma; each was given twenty blows of the staff and expelled from the monastery.
Zhaozhou said, "Whom does the Master’s staff intend for me to eat? Yuan asked, "Tell me truly, where did Old Teacher Wang go wrong? Zhaozhou bowed and departed.
One day, while Yuan was visiting a manor, the master of the estate prepared a formal reception for him. Yuan asked the master of the estate:
The monk said, "How do you know that this old monk has come to mediate in such a manner? The Master said, "Last night the Earth Deity informed me, saying:
'Master Wang’s cultivation lacks power; he has been seen through by ghosts and spirits.
The monk then asked, "Since the Master is a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), why was he seen through by ghosts and spirits? He replied, "Before the Earth Deity, add yet another portion."
While eating his rice, he once said: "The Great Master Ma of Jiangxi says, 'This very mind is Buddha.
Teacher Wang says, 'It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing. In saying this, is there any fault? Zhaozhou came forward and bowed.
At that time, there was a monk who followed up on the question. The Abbot of the Prefecture (Zhaozhou) prostrated and asked, "What was his intention?
Zhaozhou said, "You should ask the Master instead. The monk then asked the Master, "Just now, when the Venerable Shen (Shenxiu) prostrated, what was his intention?
The Master replied, "He understood my meaning. One day, as he entered the hall carrying his alms bowl, Huangbo—who was then serving as the First Seat—was not present.
Wenyuan rose and asked, "Venerable sir, in what year did you practice the Way? Huangbo said, "In the time of the Buddha Wángwáng.
Wenyuan said, "You are still among the descendants of Old Master Wang. He then left.
One day he asked Huangbo, "If golden walls and moats surround it and silver forms its enclosures, whose dwelling place is this? Huangbo said, "It is the dwelling place of the Sages."
[The monk] said, "There is another person; in which land does he dwell? Huangbo stood with his palms joined and said, "I cannot say. [The monk] asked, "Why do you not ask the Old Teacher Wang?
Huangbo then took up the previous conversation and asked [the monk]. [The monk] replied, "It is truly a pity.

He asked again, "Regarding the study of the equality of concentration and wisdom (*samādhi* and *prajñā*), how should one practice? Huangbo said, "Throughout the twelve periods of the day, it is well not to rely upon a single thing. [The monk] said, "Do not..."
"Is this the elder's own view? Baizhang replied, "I dare not. [Baizhang] said, "Setting aside the price of the gruel for a moment, who will repay the cost of the straw sandals?
One day, he encountered the two head monks of the two halls disputing over a cat.
He immediately picked up the cat and asked the assembly, "If you can speak, I shall save the cat; if you cannot speak, I shall kill it. The assembly was speechless, so he killed it.
When Zhaozhou returned from outside, Yuan asked him to relate the previous conversation. Zhaozhou then took off his sandals, placed them on his head, and walked out.
Yuan said, "If you had been here just now, you would have saved the cat. Grand Master Lu Xian asked, "I have come from the Six Heavens;
does one still possess a body there? Zhaozhou replied, "Keep this clearly in mind," and related it as such.
Later, Lu once again said to Huiyuan, "I, your disciple, also have a slight understanding of the Buddha-dharma; I wish to ask: how do you, Great Officer, act during the twelve periods of the day?
Lu replied, "Not a single thread of silk hangs upon me. Huiyuan said, "You are still but a man standing below the steps.

One day, Lu said to Huiyuan, "Dharma Master Zhao is truly extraordinary; he understands that the myriad dharmas share a single root and that right and wrong are of one essence. Huiyuan [replied], "..."

Pointing to a peony flower in front of the courtyard, he said, "At that time, I saw this single stalk of a flower; it was like a dream. He addressed the assembly, saying, "Old Teacher Wang is selling himself;

who wants to buy him? A monk stepped forward and said, "I will buy him. Baizhang said, "Not at a high price, nor at a low price—how will you buy him? The monk had no reply. Later, Wulong spoke on his behalf, saying:
"The price is not high, the price is not low; The buyer and seller both know the value. If you wish to purchase the Teacher’s body, You must first purchase your own self."
"It belongs to so-and-so. One day, he made an appointment with Guizong and Magu to go together to pay their respects to National Teacher Nanyang.
As they were traveling, he drew a circle on the road and said, "If you can speak, then we shall go. Guizong sat within the circle;
Magu performed a woman’s bow and said, "If it is thus, there is no need to go. Guizong said, "It is."

Regarding his mental state and conduct, he wished only to be called back by others. In the first year of the Dàhé era, the Imperial Commissioner Lord Lù and the Military Protector Lord Liú paid their respects from the north, welcoming him down from the mountain.
On the twenty-first day of the tenth month in the eighth year, the Jiǎyīn year, he manifested illness.
Suddenly, a white rainbow pierced the rear peak, and a massive boulder collapsed upon itself with a sound heard for several tens of *li*. Tigers circled the forest trees, howling even by day.

Those who understood these signs were filled with anxiety. At dawn on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month, he suddenly instructed his disciples, saying, "The illusions of stars, shadows, lamps, and phantoms have long existed; do not say that I come or go. He then passed away abruptly at the age of eighty.
He had spent seven summers [in the monastic order] and was fifty-eight years of ordination seniority (*neng*). His disciples, including Qiyuan and Wenchang, numbered nine hundred in total;

all wore plain robes and black headbands and observed the rites of mourning for a heart-bereaved person. Those who hurried to attend his funeral procession followed one after another along the roads, the sound of their wailing shaking the forests and valleys.
In the following year, the Year of Yimao (715 CE), they were finally able to enshrine his entire remains in a spirit-stupa. [This was reported by] Yuanwailang of the Department of Food.
Liu Ke, Compiler of the History Bureau, composed the text for the inscription carved upon the stele to commemorate his virtuous excellence.
Tang Zhizang’s surname was Huang; he was a man from Shanggao in Yuzhang. His father served as a district clerk and was particularly devoted to the study of world-transcending teachings.

He once brought his collection [of scriptures] into Baoguo Temple to listen to the lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* given by the court chaplain Hào Yuè; he was immediately able to gain a subtle understanding of the meaning of the sutra.
He then took leave of his parents and went to Kaiyuan Temple to receive the tonsure under Master Zōng. At that time, he was only thirteen years old.
After some time, he visited Chan Master Dàjí and realized the essential points of the school. In the first year of the Jiànzhōng era, he arrived in Cháng'ān at the residence of Yuán Xiǎolú.
The Duke had long revered and served him; he was subsequently presented to the Imperial Court for offerings. By imperial decree, he was stationed at Huayan Temple.
Thereupon, disciples from all quarters flocked to him like rushing winds or gathering clouds. The benefits he brought to the world were such that they could not be fully exhausted by words.
In the ninth year of the Dàhé era, he passed away at the temple and was interred in a stupa.
Tang Yuanzhi, surnamed Zhang, was a native of Haihun in Yuzhang. In his youth, he served under Master Niepan and received the tonsure;
later, he received full ordination and immediately sought instruction at the gate of Chan. Subsequently, he received the seal of transmission from the chamber of Yaoshan. One day, Yaoshan asked him:
“Where have you been? Yunyan asked. Zhi said, “I have been wandering the mountains. Baizhang said, “Without leaving this room, quickly bring it here.
Zhi said, “The crows on the mountain are white as snow; the fish swimming in the stream are never at rest.
While Zhi was standing in attendance with Yungan, Baizhang said, “At the place where Zhi does not reach, you must strictly avoid speaking. If you speak, horns will grow. Zhi... [remained silent].
"How was the Dhūta born? Zhi then went out. Yunyan asked Yaoshan, "Why did Brother Zhi not respond to the Master?
Yaoshan said, "Today my back hurts. "He understands," [Yunyan] said, "you should go and ask him yourself."
Yanguan asked Zhi about this. Zhi said, "Go and ask the Abbot. When Yanguan passed away, he sent someone to deliver a letter to him.
Upon reading it, Zhi said, "Yunyan did not know [the Way]. I regret that I did not tell him back then.
Nevertheless, even so, he did not fail to be a son of Yaoshan. While lying down, Baishu asked, "What are you doing? He replied, "I am putting on my robe."
[The Master] covered [him]. Baizhang said, "Is this lying down? Is this sitting? He replied, "It is neither of the two. Baizhang said, "What about the covering?
He replied, "Do not speak in confusion. While Zhijian was sitting under a Baizhang tree, he asked, "What are you doing? Baizhang replied, "I bow. He replied, [silently].

"How long has it been since we last met? Baizhang said, "Just now," and then he shook out his sleeves and left. Later, on account of this, Muzhou asked Yunyan, "What do you take as your seat for Bodhi?
Yunyan replied, "I take non-action (wuwei) as my seat. Yunyan then asked Muzhou, to which Muzhou replied: [The text ends here.]

He took the emptiness of all phenomena as his seat. Guishan asked Zhi again, "Are you sitting? Zhi replied, "I am sitting. "If he is sitting, let him sit; if he is lying down, let him lie down," [Guishan said].
"But there is one who neither sits nor lies down—speak quickly, speak quickly! Guishan asked, "Where have you come from, Zhi?
He replied, "I have come from tending to the sick. Guishan said, "How many people are sick? He replied, "There are those who are sick, and there are those who..."
Zhaozhou said, "The one who is not ill. Baizhang said, "The one who is not ill—is that you, the Venerable Zhidu?
Zhaozhou replied, "Whether ill or not ill, it is entirely not a matter concerning another. One day he went to Wufeng, and Wufeng asked, "Do you still recognize the old master Yaoshan?"
He replied, “I do not know. Fēng asked, “Why do you not know? He replied, “I do not know; I do not know. A monk asked, “What is the house style of the Master?
Zhì descended from his meditation seat, performed a woman’s bow, and said, “Thank you for coming from afar; there is simply nothing to attend to you with.
A monk asked, “What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? He replied, “I have never encountered him in this land of the East.”
Shishuang asked: "After a hundred years, if someone asks about the ultimate matter, how would you answer them?
Zhi called out, "Novice! The novice responded, "Yes? Zhi said, "Add some water to the pure pitcher. After a long silence, he then questioned Shishuang.
When asked what he had come for, Huirang raised his whisk and immediately departed. In the ninth month of the Jiǎmǎo year (913), the ninth year of Tàihé, he manifested illness.
When the assembly of monks went to inquire after his suffering, Huizhi said, "There is the giving, but no receiving; do you understand this? The assembly was filled with sorrow.
On the eleventh day, he said to them, "I am now departing for the West; by principle, there shall be no returning to the East. Having spoken, he passed away in peace.
He lived to the age of sixty-seven. After his cremation, several pieces of sacred bone were obtained; they were golden in color and produced a jade-like sound when struck.
These were interred on the southern slope of Shishuang Mountain. He was posthumously titled the Great Master Xiuyi, and his stupa was named Baoxiang.

Dharma-rong of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Yan. He was a native of Langzhong. During his childhood, when his father sent him to hold a brush and practice calligraphy, he would instead paint images of the Buddha that were remarkably lifelike.
At the age of thirteen, whenever he saw a śramaṇa, he would immediately take up a scripture and inquire about its meaning.

Eventually, he entered the service of Dharma Master Huixiu of Changle Monastery as a disciple. After receiving full ordination, he recited the *Nanshan Lüchao* (the Vinaya Commentary of the Southern Mountain School) and traveled...
He then visited Chan Master Pujì at Mount Song, where he was secretly entrusted with the seal of mind.

He subsequently settled at Funing Temple in Guoyang, and scholars from all quarters flocked to him as if returning to a bustling market. In the ninth year of the Dàhé era, he manifested parinirvāṇa at the age of eighty-nine.
Fachang of the Tang dynasty was born into the Zheng family of Xiangyang. In his youth, he entered the monastic life at Yuquan Temple in Jingzhou.

Upon reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination at Longxing Temple. His appearance was refined and dignified, and his natural disposition was firm and quick-witted. Wearing his patched robes and carrying his alms bowl, he lived with a serene detachment from worldly affairs.
By nature, he cherished the joy of Chan meditation. At that time, Daji was flourishing in his propagation of the Dharma in Zhongling; Fachang therefore went to attend at his seat.
A question was asked: "What is the Buddha? Jì replied: "This very mind is the Buddha. Thereupon, he attained realization.

During the Zhènyuán period, he traveled from Tiantái to Sìmíng, where he found the former hermitage of Mèi Zǐzhēn, who had served as a Han dynasty magistrate of Nánchāng; he took up residence there. The location was deep and secluded.
Having no means to obtain food or clothing, he ate pine blossoms to satisfy his hunger and fashioned lotus leaves to cover his body.
He moved his hermitage into a deep cleft to avoid the traces of human contact. Initially, Master An of Yanguan had also propagated the Way of Daji on the sea;
there was a monk from his assembly who entered the mountains seeking a master to follow as his staff-bearer.
Upon seeing him, he reported this to Daji. Daji ordered a monk to ask, "What did you receive from Master Ma that caused you to dwell on this mountain?
He replied constantly, "Master Ma told me, 'The mind itself is Buddha,' so I have dwelt here.
The monk said, "Lately, Master Ma’s teaching of the Dharma has changed; he now says..."
"How do you distinguish them? The monk said, "And yet you say it is 'neither mind nor Buddha. Master Chang says that this old fellow is merely confusing people;
there will never be an end to it. Let him say 'neither mind nor Buddha' all he wants; I simply maintain 'this very mind is Buddha. The monk returned to Mazu and related this.
Mazu called out to the assembly, "The plum has ripened. Thereupon, Layman Pang went to visit him.
Dàmé asked, "I have long heard of Dàmé; I wonder if the plum has ripened? He replied, "It has ripened, but there is simply no place for you to bite into it.
The scholar made a gesture of chewing with his mouth and said, "Crushed to bits! He then reached out his hand and said, "Give me back the pit!
From then on, students gradually flocked to him, and his reputation for the Way grew ever more prominent. Addressing the assembly, he said: "You..."
May all such people each turn their minds back to realize the fundamental source. Do not pursue its branches; simply attain the root, and the branches will arrive of themselves.
If you wish to recognize the root, understand only your own mind. This mind is originally the very foundation of all mundane and supramundane phenomena.
Therefore, when the mind arises, all phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all phenomena cease. It is fundamentally and naturally as-it-is (*tathatā*); the myriad phenomena...
It was likewise so. A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? He replied, "The flowers of the *pú* tree, the willow catkins, the needle of the bamboo, and the hemp thread.
Once, while Jiashan and Dingshan were walking and conversing together, Dingshan said, "If there is no Buddha within birth and death, then there is no birth and death.
Jiashan said, "If there is a Buddha within birth and death, then one does not become deluded by birth and death. The two men then went up the mountain.
He paid his respects and then raised a question regarding Chang: "I do not yet understand which of these two perspectives is more intimate and which is more remote.
Chang said, "Go for now; come back tomorrow. The next day, Jia Shan asked again. Chang said, "That which is intimate is not questioned; that which is questioned is not intimate.
One day, he suddenly said to his disciples, "Coming cannot be stopped; going cannot be pursued. While they were at ease, they heard the cry of a flying squirrel.
Sheng then said, "This is that very thing and not another. You all must protect and uphold it well. Having spoken these words, he passed away.
His age was eighty-eight, and his years as a monk were sixty-nine. After cremation, countless śarīra relics were obtained, which were interred and enshrined within a stupa.
The inscription on the stele was composed by the Jinshi (Metropolitan Graduate) Jiang Ji.
*Newly Compiled Biographies of Monks Classified into Six Categories of Study*, Scroll Six (Engraved by Hu Shouju of Siming).
*Newly Compiled Biographies of Monks Classified into Six Categories of Study*, Scroll Seven.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Tanyu of Eastern Zhejiang.
Section on the Transmission of the Lineage of the Study of Wisdom (5):
Tang Chongyan was born into the Duan clan of Dongping. He left the household life as a disciple of Dharma Master Huichao of Longxing Temple.
While traveling, he visited Chan Master Pujì at Songyang and received the seal of his mind-ground. Later, he resided at Mount Duliang, where he gathered disciples and propagated the teachings.
The mountain stood at the confluence of the Huai and Si rivers; merchants and travelers thronged there, and guests in woolen robes lived in close proximity.
At that time, Prime Minister Li Shen was governing Guangling. Possessing great talent and learning, he looked down upon his peers; whenever he saw a monk, he would spit at him and dismiss him.
However, when someone reported the name "Yuan" (Huineng) to him, he dispatched an official of the yamen, Zhang Youcheng, to summon him into the government office.

After sitting for a short while, [the Master’s] speech became silent, yet his spirit reached toward the divine creation; he stripped away all boundaries and transcended all limitations. This was certainly not the mundane world of Li Shen.
He was one whom students aspired to emulate; thus, they sighed with great admiration and requested that he reside at Huizhao Temple so that they might receive his instruction.
Disciples from the four seas who came to seek him out numbered nearly a thousand. He passed away in the second year of the Kaicheng era at the age of eighty-four.
On the twenty-third day of the tenth month of that same year, he was interred in a stupa.
Tang Haozhi, surnamed Ding, was a native of Zhujia in Kuaiji. From his youth, he was pure and refined;
as for rich, fatty, or pungent foods, he never once allowed them to pass his lips. He went to Mount Hangwu to receive the tonsure under Master Zang.

At the beginning of the Yuanhe era, he received full ordination at Tianzhu Temple and extensively investigated the origins and lineages of the sutras, vinayas, śāstras, commentaries, and sub-commentaries. Suddenly, he took up his staff and traveled west to visit the Patriarch.
Fanglai’s lineage traces back to Mazu Daoyi of Hongzhou, from whom he received a formal prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
He resided at Daqing Temple in his native village, where seekers of the Way gathered like clouds. For twenty years, he brought great benefit to sentient beings.

Even when high-ranking officials on provincial tours or military governors passed through, there was none whom he did not receive with hospitality and instruct. Thus, the beauty of his reputation spread far and wide.
He traveled throughout the world. During the Dazhong era, while traveling to Mount Wutai, he passed through the capital and departed one night.
At that time, the two eunuchs Xi Zhirong, former Commander-in-Chief of the Guard, and Song Changchun learned of this and were determined to recruit him.

Based on the instructions he had previously received from Master Wen, at the beginning of the Kāicheng era, he returned to the imperial capital. The two noblemen lodged him in the abbot’s quarters of An Guo Temple. Long...
Elephants all hastened to follow him in submission. Not long after, he was summoned to serve as a Great Virtuous One (Bhadanta) in the imperial court, a position contrary to his own aspirations.

On the twenty-fifth day of the tenth month in the fourth year, having finished entrusting his final instructions to his disciples, he sat cross-legged and passed away. He was sixty-five years old and had spent thirty-two summer retreats.
His funeral and enshrinement were held to the east of the San River; all expenses were provided by the Qi and Song families. His disciple Jianzhu succeeded him.

A stupa was erected at Huayan on the southern side of Mount Chong, and he was buried there. In the fourth year of the Huichang era, Wei Xuan, a Gentleman of the Court for Attendance, composed the inscription.
Tang Zongmi’s secular surname was He; he was a native of Xichong in Guozhou. His family had long been devoted to the Confucian arts. At an early age, he desired to...
Having studied in the world to acquire fame and rank, in the second year of the Yuanhe era, he accompanied the census officials to the capital. On the way, he visited Chan Master Yuan of Suizhou;

upon seeing him, before even a word had been exchanged, Zhiyan felt a profound sense of admiration and joy. He immediately followed him to receive the tonsure. Shortly thereafter, he received full ordination from Vinaya Master Zheng.
Soon after, he visited Zhang at Jingnan, who said, "This is a person who transmits the teachings; in the future, he shall propagate and guide them."
In the capital city, he again visited Zhao of Luoyang. Zhao said, "This is a person who is a Bodhisattva; who could recognize him? Later, he visited Guan of Huayan on the Capital Plain.

Guan said, "As for those who follow me through the Vairocana Flower Treasury (Vairocanābhisambodhi) realm, you alone are they. Initially, while living in his native village, he once attended a vegetarian feast at a layperson's home.

There, he happened to receive a copy of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and obtained a copy of the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*). Upon reading it, he wondrously grasped its profound meaning and intent.
Thereupon, he vowed to transmit this sutra. Furthermore, because a sick monk from Hanchang had taught him the *Avataṃsaka*, he was immediately able to lecture upon it.

Consequently, he composed commentaries and sub-commentaries (*śāstra-ṭīkā*) on the *Avataṃsaka*, *Awakening of Faith*, *Nirvāṇa*, *Vajracchedikā*, *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, *Ullambana-sūtra*, *Dharmadhātudarśana*, *Sukhāvatīvyūha*, *Pratimokṣa-sūtra* (Four-Part Vinaya), and others;
as well as works on doctrinal categories and precedents, ritual repentance and spiritual realization, and illustrated biographies.
His writings on the esoteric methods of various schools, referred to as the *Zen-zō* (Zen Treasury), along with his letters and verses in response to inquiries, total more than two hundred fascicles.
His six scrolls of diagrams all take the single mind as their foundation to unify all phenomena;

they reveal the true essence to harmonize principle and phenomenon, transcending all dualistic existence and operating in solitary autonomy by merging the distinction between self and object. He was repeatedly summoned to the inner palace, where he was questioned regarding these secret essentials.

In the second year of the Taika era, on the occasion of the Emperor’s birthday, he was granted an imperial edict conferring upon him the purple robe and the title of Daidoku (Virtuous One). Shortly thereafter, he requested to return to the mountains.
On the sixth day of the first month of the first year of the Kōkai era, he passed away while seated at Kōfuku-in; his countenance appeared increasingly radiant and serene.

On the thirteenth day of the second month of that same year, the clergy and laity escorted his entire body to Kakegami Peak for cremation, where they obtained śarīra relics which were enshrined within a stone stupa.
His secular age was sixty-two; his dharma-ordination year was thirty-four. Previously, Mi had been on good terms with the minister Li Xun.
During the "Ganlu" disaster, when the eunuchs led the imperial guards and slaughtered everyone they encountered, Wang Ya, Jia Su, and Shu Yuanyu fled into Zhongnan Mountain to seek refuge with Mi.
Li Xun was also there, seeking to shave his hair to hide his identity, but this was refused; consequently, he fled.
Longxiang Qiu Shiliang ordered that Mi be arrested. When he was brought before the court at the Left Army, Qiu enumerated his crime of failing to report [the rebellion] and urged that he be executed.
Mi spoke slowly, saying: "I, a poor monk, have known the training for a long time and am also aware that he has always harbored intentions of rebellion.
Nevertheless, to sacrifice my own life to save all beings—this is the final instruction left by my original teacher; therefore, I have adhered to it with utmost sincerity."
I respectfully submit that my death today would have been a matter of willing acceptance. The eunuch Yu Hengzhi took pity on his sincerity and memorialized the throne for his release;

those who heard of it shed tears. The Chancellor Pei Xiu once composed a treatise to refute certain critics who claimed his learning and conduct were not entirely pure, yet most of these criticisms are not recorded here.
When Emperor Xuanzong ascended the throne, he posthumously conferred upon him the title of Chan Master Dinghui and named his stupa Qinglian (Blue Lotus).
Tang Chonggui was the son of the Jiang family of Shaanxi. His ancestors had attained high status and honor through the arts of Confucianism.

Since the Tianbao era, however, successive upheavals and displacements had occurred; his father died while engaged in trade between Gong and Luo. Chonggui, filled with lamentation, set out to seek ordination as a monk.
At the age of eighteen, he received the tonsure after passing the scriptural examinations. Not long thereafter, he traveled to Mount Nanyue, where he resided for several years. Furthermore...
Relying on Xiqia Temple on Mount Mao in Nanxu, his reputation grew even further. At that time, Li Gongyu, the Duke of De from Zannang, was serving as the regional inspector of this province.
He invited [Huigui] to meet him at Cihuo Temple; their conversation was mutually harmonious. Huigui said, "I suffer from a deep-seated melancholy;
how can one remain for long in a city wall or a village? The following year, he traveled to the Songxiao Mountains and hung his staff at Yue Temple.
In the *wushen* year of the Taika era, there was a drought in the capital. Only on Mount [Kōya], rain fell without failing its proper season. Some claimed this was moved by the virtue of [Dō]kai.
At the beginning of the Kaisei era, Lord Zannang entered the cabinet as Chancellor and requested that [Dō]kai propagate the Dharma at Ryūgyō-ji Temple in the capital.

The teachings he proclaimed were fundamentally those of [Eisai] Shū, yet his benefits to others were manifold. Subsequently, he entered into extinction; his lifespan was eighty-six years. [This concludes the] meeting.
On the tenth day of the eighth month of the first year of the Changyuan era, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa; the inscription was composed by the Senior Secretary Bai Gōng (Bai Juyi).

Tang Quan-zhi, surnamed Rui, was a native of Kuangzhou. In his youth, he relied upon the śramaṇa Dazhi at Rongguang Chan Monastery in that prefecture to recite and study the scriptures, eventually obtaining the tonsure.
After receiving full ordination, he traveled to the Chan assemblies in Luoyang, where he attained profound penetration of the mind-dharma.
Thereafter, he thatched a hut on Mount Duliang by the Huai River to gather disciples and propagate the teachings.

Subsequently, the Prefect Wei Wenqing invited him to the Changshou Temple in the seat of government so that the public might conveniently pay their respects. Wenqing asked about the future of the Buddha-dharma.
"How will its rise and fall unfold? Zhi replied, "That which is the true reality has never perished from ancient times until the present.
As for conditioned phenomena, they undergo the flux of the four marks and must inevitably meet with decay and obstruction; Your Highness need only wait upon the tips of your toes to see this.

This was a premonition of Emperor Wuzong’s suppression of the Buddhist teachings. Shortly thereafter, he passed away at the age of ninety-three. His disciples erected a stupa and a stele for him. At that time—
In the fourth year of the Chang era, on the seventh day of the ninth month of the Jiazi year, he was finally able to be buried.
Tang Qi’an was a member of the imperial clan. His ancestors had been displaced, and thus he was born in Hai-men Commandery.

From his initial conception until his birth, there were auspicious signs at every stage. In his childhood, an extraordinary monk knocked at his door seeking an audience; the monk rubbed the child’s head and said: [The rest of the text follows...]
The phoenix’s lair vibrates with majestic deportment; the dragon palace conceals precious treasures. Is not the vocation of perpetuating and exalting the Dharma found herein?
As he grew older, he repeatedly petitioned his parents, wishing to leave the household life. His parents could not restrain him and finally permitted him to follow Master Yuncong of Yunzhou.
He had his hair shaved in auspicious ceremony; upon reaching the age for full ordination, he went to the Vinaya Master Zhìyán of Nányuè to advance his studies in the *Vinaya*.

Later, following Dàjì Chánshī at Gōnggōng Mountain in Nánkāng, he profoundly mastered the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground (*cittabhūmi*). Toward the end of the Yuánhé era, he traveled to Fǎlè Temple in Xiāoshān, Yuè.
Although the temple followed ancient architectural standards, its pillars and walls were no longer intact; he repaired what was ruined and supported what was leaning.

I sat in quiet meditation for a while. At that time, Fa-xin of Hai-chang in Hangzhou—a preeminent figure among the monastic community—had begun to restore a piece of abandoned land on the shore of the Fang-sheng Pond (Pond for Releasing Living Beings) in Yan-guan to serve as a place for rest.

Hearing that Huian was in Yue, he hurriedly went to welcome him and offered him the site, yielding it to him. A monk asked, "What is the original body of Vairocana? Huian replied, "Bring me some clean water."
"Bring the water jar. The monk immediately took the pure water jar. Baizhang said, "Put it back in its original place.

The monk placed the jar back in its former spot and asked the question once more. Baizhang said, "The ancient buddhas have long since passed away. A presiding master came to visit him, and Baizhang asked:
"What work do you have to do? An said. "I am lecturing on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra," the lecturer replied. An asked, "How many kinds of *dharmadhātu* are there in the Avataṃsaka?
The lecturer replied, "In detail, they are infinitely layered; briefly, there are four kinds. An held up his whisk and asked, "Which kind is this?
Before the lecturer could answer, An snapped his fingers and said, "To know through thinking and to understand through deliberation—this is the way of ghosts."
Daily life: A solitary lamp beneath the sun; indeed, its light has failed. One day, Anan called to his attendant, saying, "Bring me the rhinoceros fan.
The attendant replied, "The fan is broken. Anan said, "The fan is broken, but give me back the rhinoceros!"
The attendant had no reply. [Dongshan] addressed the assembly, saying: "Space is the drum; Mount Sumeru is the mallet.
Who is it that beats them? The assembly had no reply. Emperor Xuanzong was then appearing in the guise of a bhikṣu; Anmo of the Zhatang Hall recognized him.
He appointed him as Secretary of the Monastery. Once, he was asked to compose a preface for a petition, and the rewards obtained were exceptionally abundant.
Dao’an marveled at the intensity of his karmic fortune and said, "The time has come; do not remain hidden like a dragon coiled in the mud. He then entrusted him with the Dharma.

In the second year of the Huichang era, on the twenty-first day of the twelfth month of the Renxu year, he passed away. Upon the Emperor’s accession to the throne, he heard of this and was moved with sorrow;
he immediately issued an edict through the eunuch Lu Jianqiu to construct a stupa and bestow the posthumous title Wukong (Awakened to Emptiness).
Tang Hengzheng, surnamed Zhou, was a native of Pingyuan. From his youth, he entered the local school; however, he paid little heed to the Confucian classics.

When he encountered Buddhist scriptures, he would study them with such relish that he could not put them down. Later, he went to Yanhe Temple in the prefecture to receive the tonsure under Dharma Master Quancheng.
Once he had received full ordination, he sought the Way at Mount Song and Mount Shao, retiring to the Three Peaks to nurture the "sacred embryo. There was no...
After some time, he entered Mount Taiyi, where he received disciples and propagated his teachings. During the Dazhong era, the Emperor developed a craving for clams and oysters;

the Grand Cook presented them regularly, and the coastal prefectures all took advantage of this to cause harm to the people. One day, there was a shell that, though a strong man tried to pry it open with all his might, remained stubbornly closed.
The Emperor found this extraordinary and burned incense to offer prayers. Suddenly, it opened of its own accord, revealing the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Inside [the stupa] was a statue of Śākyamuni, only about an inch in height; its features and attire were even more lovely than those of statues or paintings found in the world.
The Emperor ordered it to be placed in a casket of gold-dusted sandalwood and covered with a jade-cotton brocade cloth, granting it for veneration at Xingshan Temple.
Thereupon, he assembled his ministers and inquired as to what auspicious omen this portended. The Chancellor, Li Gongdeyu, stepped forward and said: "This..."
"This is not within the capacity of a minister to know; I know only that it is moved by the radiance of Your Majesty’s sagely virtue.
As for the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma, there is Zen Master Hengzheng of Mount Zhongnan. Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued to inquire of Zheng, who replied:
"I, a poor monk, have heard that nothing in this world responds without cause; this is precisely why I have sought to awaken Your Majesty’s faith.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: 'Those who are to be saved by means of this body, for them he manifests this very body and preaches the Dharma. " The Emperor said:
"The Bodhisattva’s body has indeed been seen by you. However, as for what is called the preaching of the Dharma, you have not yet heard it.
Jing said, "Now, does Your Majesty regard this as permanent or impermanent? Do you believe it or not? The Emperor replied, "This is an extraordinary matter; I believe it deeply.
Jing said, "If that is so, then Your Majesty has already heard the preaching of the Dharma. The Emperor was greatly pleased.
He remained in the Inner Court at the Palace Chapel. Although he repeatedly declined to return to the mountains, an imperial decree ordered him to reside at Shengshou Monastery.
When Emperor Wuzong first ascended the throne, he said to his attendants, "My enemy has arrived; can I not avoid him?

He then fled immediately into the Zhongnan Mountains, where he eventually passed away in a mountain hermitage at the age of eighty-seven. Following his cremation, forty-nine *śarīra* relics were recovered. (The third year of Huichang...)
On the fourth day of the ninth month of that year, he was interred in a stupa. Later, the imperial edict abolishing the teachings proved true to the words spoken regarding his avoidance of enemies.
Tang Puan, surnamed Cai, was a native of Handong. From a young age, he possessed exceptional intelligence and a refined, pure character;

he never allowed pungent or savory foods to enter his mouth. Having gone forth to study under a teacher, he mastered the meanings of the scriptures; when he took up the brush to compose prose, his works were worthy of admiration.

Once, he entered a monastic dwelling and perused the Buddhist scriptures; as he savored and studied them, he could not stop. He sighed, saying, "The Dharma that transcends the world is not something one can attain in haste.

He immediately took leave of his parents and went to Mount Baiyang to consult Master Huaihai of Baizhang regarding the essentials of the mind. After a long time, he shaved his head and received the precepts.
Soon thereafter, he received the transmission of the Dharma. Later, he appeared in the world at the Shou Mountain Monastery in Anxiu and addressed the assembly.
It is said: "The divine light is never obscured; its glorious legacy endures for ten thousand ages. Upon entering this gate, do not harbor intellectual understanding.
During the Dazhong era, Zhen set out eastward for Tiantai, where he traveled extensively to survey the scenic sites. Finding a level field, he chose it as a site for his hermitage.
A monk arrived to pay his respects; Baizhang struck him with his staff. As the monk stepped forward, Baizhang seized the staff and said, "Old monk!"
Just as the monk was about to act impulsively, Nanquan struck him with a staff once. Nanquan said, "An adept! An adept! The monk bowed;
Nanquan grabbed him and said, "It was you, Ācārya, who acted impulsively. The monk laughed heartily. Nanquan said, "This monk has met his downfall today.
He also once spoke a verse which says: "The Great Way is vast and empty; it is the ever-abiding, true mind. Do not contemplate good or evil."

His spirit was clear and transcended the mundane world; he lived out his days eating and drinking as circumstances required—what more need be said? In the third year of the Huichang era, he gathered his disciples to impart his final instructions and then passed away.
He was seventy-four years of age. His disciples included Quanliang, Wei, Yue, and others.
Tang Shenjian was born into the Han family in Xunyang. His father served as an official in Qian’an and was exceptionally sincere and devout in his service to the Buddha.

He would often display Buddhist images and chant hymns, providing meals for the monastic community within his official residence. Shenjian, while still a young child, wore an expression of overflowing joy and earnestly requested to leave the household life.
His relatives could not dissuade him, and he eventually followed the Vinaya Master Zhen-su of Donglin Temple to receive the tonsure. He mastered the *Nirvāṇa* [Sūtra].

At that time, Daji proclaimed the Heart-Essence (Cittamātra) school of Yuzhang. [Dongshan Liangjie] immediately went there to investigate and study. Later, he chose to reside in the mountains northwest of Huai’an.
Previously, those mountains had been infested with many fierce beasts; from then on, their violent depredations ceased. People from far and near relied upon him.
There was one who saw a magnificent man wearing a flat *zhai* cap, who paid homage toward the Dharma seat and then suddenly vanished. Seven days later—
Someone saw the ceremonial cap and robes arrive before the abbot’s quarters; ascending into the air, they praised him, saying, "This Great Master is a true treasure of the Dharma.

He has opened the eyes of the human and celestial realms; therefore, I have come to inform you. In the fourth year of the Huichang era, he entered nirvana. In the eighth month, he was enshrined in a stupa.

Táng Zhìyuǎn was the son of the Wù family of the Southern Song dynasty. He lost his father in childhood; his mother was intelligent and could recite the *Lotus Sūtra*, and he gradually mastered its meaning.
At the age of twenty-eight, he was sent by her to receive the tonsure under Chándé of Hézé, where he managed monastic affairs for six years.
Subsequently, he took leave to travel and pay his respects to various masters for another eight years, after which he came to understand the Way of Tiantái’s *Zhíguān*.
In this state of total dedication, he exhausted his will and toiled his body, practicing the four *samādhis*. He took but one meal at midday and did not accept separate invitations.

During years of famine, he would sometimes swallow air and rinse with mountain streams; yet his countenance showed no sign of hunger, and though his body was covered in sores and scabs, he would not scratch them with his hands.

In this manner, he persisted for nearly forty years. In the second month of the fourth year of the Huichang era, he suddenly ceased taking grain and remained in quiet contemplation for seventeen days.

He admonished his disciples daily, saying: "Throughout my life I have pursued spiritual cultivation, and now that I have attained this dream-like awakening and peace, is this not surely the retribution for what I have been moved by?
Furthermore, I transmit the commentaries and treatises of the Tiantai school to my disciple Yuankan and others."
Furthermore, it was said that he was about to tread upon the steps of the sages, yet before reaching such a rare attainment, he suddenly passed away.
He was seventy-seven years of age and had been a monk for forty-eight years. Yuankan was the son of the Ma family from Fufeng; he had long served Huiyuan as his teacher.

When Emperor Wuzong suppressed the Dharma, Yuankan concealed all the Tiantai commentaries and texts he had received within the walls of his house. Not long after, Emperor Xuanzong restored the religion, and Yuankan reconstructed them.
In his former residence, he established a separate shrine for Yuan Da and took the texts of that school, placing them all within it.
He performed the ritual circumambulations at the six periods of the day until the end of his life; thus, he truly did not fail the charge entrusted to him. Is such a person not to be called worthy?

Tang Lingyou’s surname was Zhao. He was a native of Changxi in Fuzhou. While he was still a young child playing in the courtyard, suddenly clouds gathered and swirled, and celestial music, clear and resonant, resounded.
Apparitions of divine sages and transcendents appeared and vanished amidst the sky.

After a short while, an old man whose appearance resembled that of a Kapiśa approached his father and said to him, “The origin of your son is lofty and sublime; he shall surely be of great importance.”
This is how these multitudes of spirits manifest their distinctiveness during the Buddha’s era of radiance. Furthermore, he departed after snapping his fingers four times.
Dao You served as an attendant to Vinaya Master Faheng; he shaved his head at the age of twenty and received full ordination three years later.
He studied the *Vinaya* under the śramaṇa Yibin of Qiantang and traveled to Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai, where he encountered Hanshan and Shide. For...
A verse says: "Across a thousand mountains and ten thousand waters, One stops whenever a deep pool is encountered. Having obtained a priceless treasure, One relieves the destitute son.
Thereupon, he went to visit the Chan Master Dazhi of Baizhang in Jiangxi. One day, while standing in attendance, Baizhang said, "Is there any fire in the hearth?
Huaiyu probed it and said, "No. Baizhang rose personally and probed deeply, finding a small ember; he held it up to show him.
[Zhaozhou] said, "What about this? Dayou attained enlightenment; he prostrated in thanks and presented his understanding. The Master said, "This is merely a temporary crossroads. As the Sūtra says:

"If you wish to see the Buddha-nature, you must contemplate the conditions of time and season. Once the time and season have arrived, one finally knows that one's own substance is not obtained from another.
Therefore, the Patriarch said: "Awakening is the same as non-awakening; there is no mind to attain and no dharma to grasp."
"It is simply a matter of eliminating the deluded minds of ordinary and saintly beings; as for these mental phenomena, they have been inherently complete from the very beginning.
Since you are now thus, you must skillfully protect and maintain them. At that time, the Dharma Master Sima arrived from Hunan, and Baizhang said to him:
"May this old monk go to Mount Gui? He replied, "Mount Gui is extraordinary and sublime; one may gather a community of fifteen hundred there.
You, Master, are a man of bone, while that place is a mountain of flesh; it is not a dwelling fit for you.
Baizhang asked, "Is there no one among my assembly who could dwell there? He replied, "I shall wait to observe them all. Baizhang then ordered his attendant to invite the head monk.
The Abbot called for the head cook (diànzuò). When the *dhūta* ascetic saw the Head Seat (shǒuzuò), he did not permit [the greeting].

Seeing the head cook, he said, "This is truly the master of Mount Guishan. The Head Seat showed a look of resentment. The Abbot immediately pointed to a water pitcher and asked, "It cannot be called a 'clean pitcher.
What do you two call it? The Head Seat replied, "It cannot be called a wooden stand. The head cook kicked it over.
Baizhang overturned the pure water jar. Zhang laughed and said, "The Head Seat has lost the mountain. The Head Seat was Hualin; the Kitchen Steward was Daoyou.

Baizhang subsequently dispatched Daoyou to reside at Mt. Mushi. Once the monastery had been established, the regional commander Li Jingrang submitted a memorial requesting that the temple’s name be changed to Tongqing.
The Prime Minister, Lord Pei Xu, also frequently consulted him on profound mysteries. Consequently, throughout the world...
Students flocked to him from all directions. He addressed the assembly, saying: "The mind of a man of the Way is straightforward and sincere, without artifice;
it has no 'back' and no 'face,' and is free from deceitful thoughts or actions. At all times, seeing and hearing are ordinary, with no further complications.

It is simply a matter of not allowing the emotions to attach to external objects, and one will attain it. The sages of the past have merely spoken of the faults and afflictions on the side of turbidity. If there were not so many..."
If one who possesses evil thoughts, emotional views, conceptualizations, and habitual tendencies is simply called a "person of the Way who has nothing," what is so wrong with that?

At that time, a monk asked: "For one who has attained sudden enlightenment, is there still further cultivation? He replied: "If one truly awakens to the source, then 'cultivation' and 'non-cultivation' are both dualistic expressions.
Although those of initial resolve now gain a point of entry through conditions, they still possess [dualistic notions of] existence and non-existence."

Since beginningless time, one has been habituated by latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) which cannot be suddenly purified; therefore, one must be taught to purify and eliminate the flowing consciousness of present karma—this is precisely what cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is.

It is not said that there is some separate dharma; rather, one is taught to practice so as to enter the principle through hearing. When the principle heard is profound and subtle, the mind naturally becomes perfectly luminous and no longer dwells in the realm of delusion.
Even if there are hundreds or thousands of wondrous meanings, one will be able to suppress or exalt them all appropriately. This is what it means to have attained [it].

Seated and donning the robe, it is the time to establish one's own livelihood. To state the essential point: within the ground of the principle of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single speck of dust is accepted;
within the gateway of the myriad practices, not a single dharma is abandoned. If one enters with a single blade, the sentiments of both ordinary beings and sages are exhausted.
The body is the manifestation of true permanence; phenomena and principle are non-dual. This is precisely the Buddha of Suchness. Xuansha asked Yangshan, "From where have you returned?
Yangshan said, "From the fields. Xuansha said, "Is the grain ready for harvest yet? Yangshan said, "It is ready for harvest. Xuansha said, "Do you see it as green? Do you see it as yellow?
Or do you see it as neither green nor yellow? Yangshan said, "What is behind the Master? Xuansha—
"Cloud-seed, do you see it? Nanquan picked up a stalk of grain and held it up. "Monk, why have you ever asked about this?
Danyuan said, "This is like the king of geese choosing its milk. While Danyuan was sleeping, Yangshan went to pay his respects.
Danyuan had turned his face toward the wall. Yangshan said, "Why has the Master become like this? Danyuan turned around and said, "I just had a dream; try to tell me [what it was]."
Yuanqian looked on. Yangshan took a basin of water and washed Danyou’s face. After a short while, Xiangyan came to pay his respects.
Danyou said, "I just had a dream; Jizi (Yuanqian) has already interpreted it for me. You, too, try to interpret it. Xiangyan brought a bowl of tea and offered it.
Danyou said, "The insights of these two disciples surpass even those of Śāriputra. On the ninth day of the first month in the Guiyou year of the Dazhong era.

Having finished washing his hands and rinsing his mouth, he sat in the lotus posture and passed away. He was eighty-three years of age and fifty-nine years since his ordination. He was buried in the Zizi Garden on the mountain.
The stele was composed by Lu Jianqiu, Right Attendant of the Household and Regional Inspector of the Four Garrisons, Biting, Xingjun, Jingyuan, and other prefectures;
the title was inscribed by the Jinshi (Metropolitan Graduate) Li Shangyin.

Tang Xuance was the son of the Lu family of Kuaiji. In his youth, he accompanied his father on a trading journey to Tiantai, where he witnessed the local people holding a "Glorious Assembly" (Guangming Hui) with great splendor; this had been originally established by the Sui dynasty’s Chan Master Zhiyi.

Regarding this practice, every year in the ninth month, they would gather a multitude from far and near, both monastics and laypeople, numbering perhaps many tens of millions. Xuance alone marveled at it in his heart.

He subsequently left the household life under Master Zhiguang of Chanlin Monastery. While traveling, he met Daji (Mazu) in Jiangxi, whereupon the long-standing burden that had obstructed his mind was suddenly cast off.
Later, because Mount Jiujing in Huangzhou was uniquely beautiful and charming, he settled there in a thatched hut to attract students.
Some, noting the seclusion and remoteness of the location, said to Ce: "Do you not detest [this place]?"

"Can one truly endure such solitude? Ce said, "I consider it precisely my joy; I do not perceive any solitude in it. In the eighth year of the Dazhong era, he demonstrated his passing into extinction.
His posthumous title was Yuanjí (Perfect Quiescence), and his stupa was named Zhìjué (Wisdom Enlightenment).
Tang Xiyun was a native of Min. In his early years, he left home to become a monk at Huangbo Mountain in Gaoyang.

After receiving full ordination, he traveled extensively to seek instruction from various masters. Once, while traveling with another monk along the road to Tiantai, they conversed at length; both were exceptionally brilliant and worthy of admiration.
His eyes sparkled, casting glances forward as he gazed ahead. They encountered a large stream that had been blocked by silt; following recent rain, the torrent had swollen. Not...
"You may cross by leaping over. Thereupon, Huizhun removed his hat, leaned on his staff, and stood still. The monk approached him and said, "It is better to cross; why do you stand there so long?
Huizhun feignedly replied, "I wish to cross for myself; do not urge me. A moment later, the monk finally crossed, walking as if treading upon level ground.
Once he had reached the other shore, he beckoned with his hand, saying, "Come across! Come across! Huizhun called out from afar, "Go away!"

He said, "You self-enlightened fellow! Had you known this beforehand, I would have surely cut off your shinbones. The monk, bowing in apology from across the water, said, "Truly a vessel for the Mahāyāna Dharma!
I am not his equal; I am not his equal! He then departed and was never seen again.
Furthermore, while once traveling through the capital, he went for alms at a donor's house at noon. After waiting for a long time behind a screen, he had obtained nothing. He then heard a voice...
The old woman said to those within, "This man is utterly insatiable. He harbors the thought that he has not yet given anything away, and thus claims to be unsatisfied;
there must surely be a reason for this. After a while, the old woman sent her young servant to summon him in and provide him with food, then asked:
"Have you ever met Master Baizhang Shanshi? He is the foremost spiritual friend of our time.

Furthermore, though I am a woman with the five obstacles, I have attained realization under National Teacher Huizhong. Given your majestic and dignified appearance, how could you possibly abandon yourself to such a state?
From this point on, go see Baizhang. He then asked Baizhang: "Regarding the ancestral vehicle of the Buddhas and patriarchs, what is it like?"
Baizhang remained silent for a long time. Yun said, "In that case, the lineage will be cut off by future generations. Baizhang said, "I thought you were a man of substance.
He then abruptly rose and entered the abbot’s quarters. Yun attained realization; following him in, he said, "Xiyun has come specifically to see you.
Baizhang said, "If that is so, you must not let me down hereafter. One day, Baizhang asked Yun, "What did Vasubandhu..."
"Where have you been coming from? Yun said, "I have been gathering mushrooms on the mountain. Zhaozhou asked, "Did you see a tiger? Yun then made the sound of a tiger.
Zhaozhou took up his axe and made a gesture as if to chop. Yun struck Zhaozhou with a slap.
Zhaozhou laughed heartily and immediately ascended the hall, saying, "There was a great tiger at the foot of Mount Daxiong; today, this old fellow has personally met its fangs."
"You all, look well! Yun was at Nanquan. During a communal work assignment to select vegetables, Nanquan asked, 'Where have you come from?
Yun replied, 'I have come from selecting vegetables. Nanquan asked, 'With what did you select them? Yun held up his knife. Nanquan said:"
Everyone was selecting vegetables. One day, Nanquan said to Xuanzhao, "I have recently composed a 'Song of Herding an Ox.
I ask you, Elder, to provide a response. Xuanzhao replied, "I already have my own teacher. When Xuanzhao took his leave, Nanquan saw him off at the gate;
picking up Xuanzhao’s bamboo hat, he said, "Elder, your physical stature is of vast capacity, yet this hat is far too small. Xuanzhao said, "Even so..."
"This entire great trichiliocosm is contained within it. Quan said, "What about Master Wang? Yun then put on his bamboo hat and departed.
Later, he resided at Da'an Temple in Hongzhou, where the assembly of monks gathered like a rushing torrent. At that time, the State Councilor Pei Xu was serving as the local governor;

he welcomed Yun to the prefectural seat to inquire about the Way and composed a single volume titled *The Essentials of the Mind-to-Mind Transmission* (*Chuanxin fayao*) to present to him. When Yun received it, he placed it [aside].
He did not open or examine [the text] while at the seat. After a long while, Yun said, "Do you understand? The Duke said, "I do not understand.
Yun said, "If you were to understand it in this way, you would still be somewhat close. From this, Duke Pei deeply honored and revered him;

wherever he served in office, he invariably observed the etiquette of a disciple, inviting him to expound the teachings. He once presented him with a poem that said: "You have transmitted the seal within the minds of the realized ones..."
With a round protuberance on his forehead and a body seven feet tall, he hung his mendicant’s staff for ten years while dwelling by the waters of Shu.
Today, floating his bowl, he crosses the banks of the Zhang River. A thousand dragon-elephants follow his lofty steps; ten thousand miles away, incense and flowers form a cause for supreme merit.

If you wish to serve this master as a disciple, you do not know to whom the Dharma will be entrusted. During the Dazhong era, he passed away at the monastery where he resided. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled "Duan."
The pagoda was named Guangye; the details are recorded in full in the *Chuan deng lu*.

During the Tang dynasty, Huanzhong’s surname was Lu, and he was a native of Pufan in Hedong. In his youth, he served as a scholar. At the age of twenty-five, he ranked first among those who passed the provincial examination (*jì*).
However, this did not satisfy his ambitions, and he intended to retake the examination at the Ministry of Rites (*lǐ bù*), but it coincided with the period of mourning for his mother. Consequently—
He maintained a funerary hut at his father’s grave. Upon the completion of his mourning period, he left home to become a monk at Tongzi Temple in the Northern Capital.
Within less than two years, he had thoroughly mastered the various sutras and subsequently traveled to Mount Song to receive full ordination. He further immersed himself in the Vinaya-piṭaka.

Later, he went to Baiyang Mountain to visit Master Dazhi Hai, through whom he investigated and realized the teaching of seeing one's own nature. Shortly thereafter, he built a hermitage on Mount Nanyue at Changle.
At the summit of the temple, Cui Gong, the Palace Counselor, held [the master] in particularly high esteem and had a separate abbot’s quarters built for him.
One day, Nanquan arrived and asked, "What is the master of this hermitage? He replied, "The blue sky! The blue sky!

Nanquan said, "Setting aside the blue sky for a moment, what is the master of this hermitage? He replied, "If you understand, then you understand; do not be distressed. Nanquan then shook out his sleeves and departed.
He departed and traveled to Qiántáng, where he stayed at Dàcí Mountain. The mountain lay above the Zhèjiāng River; the soil was saline and sandy, and no water could be found.
As he was about to leave for another place, a tiger suddenly knelt on the ground and a spring of water gushed forth, sweet and clear enough to drink.

Those who recognized this deemed it divine, and the assembly gathered in great numbers. Entering the hall, he said: "This mountain monk does not know how to answer questions; I can only diagnose the illness."

Zhuzhi placed his broom down, laughed loudly, and clapped his hands; he then returned directly to his quarters.
A monk was taking his leave to go to Jiangxi, and Zhuzhi asked, "Can you take me with you? The monk replied, "What would there be to take? Zhuzhi said, "I am asking you to take this old monk along.
The monk said, "Even those who surpass the Master could not take him either. Zhuzhi then desisted. Later, that monk...
He recounted this to Dongshan. Dongshan said, "How could you, Reverend, speak in such a manner? The monk asked, "What would you say, Master?

On one occasion, he addressed the assembly, saying: "To speak for ten feet is not as good as to practice for one foot;

It is said that when one practices grasping, one cannot reach the bottom; when one grasps at speech, one cannot reach the bottom of practice. Once he had mastered the principles and exhausted the teachings, the people submitted to him.

He moved from the Dai family estate to a secluded villa. At the beginning of the Dazhong era, an imperial edict removed previous prohibitions and restored his ceremonial status. Prefect Liu paid him increased reverence and respect.

The prosperity of the monastic community was no less than it had been in former times. On the fifteenth day of the second month in the third year of the Xiantong era, having finished his final instructions, he passed away while sitting peacefully.
He was eighty-three years of age and fifty-four years since his ordination. That winter, a stupa was erected and he was interred therein.
Dongshan Xuanjian was the son of the Zhou family in Jiannan. From childhood he was unlike his peers; as he grew older, he left the household life and received full ordination.

He studied the sutras and the Vinaya, earning a reputation for his excellence among his fellow villagers. At that time, the teachings of Bodhidharma were flourishing in the region of Xianghan, and the fame of Chan Master Longtan Xin was particularly widespread.
Consequently, Xuanjian traveled there specifically to visit him. Upon seeing him, he immediately said, "I have long admired Longtan; however, when it comes to..."
He arrived; yet the pond was not to be seen, nor did the dragon appear. Jian said, "You have come in person to Longtan.

One evening, while attending the Abbot for a long time, Jian was about to leave when the Abbot asked for a candle. Xian handed him a paper candle. Just as Jian was about to take it, [the Abbot struck him].
Xin immediately blew it out. Guanding prostrated. Xin asked, "What did you see that you prostrate?
Guanding replied, "From this day forward, I shall no longer doubt the tongues of the old monks throughout the land. The next day, he took his leave.
Xin said to his disciples, "Among you there is a fellow whose teeth are like a forest of swords and whose mouth is like a blood-basin; a single blow of my staff cannot turn him back."
[Daowu] said, "Head! In the future, you shall stand upon the summit of a solitary peak and establish my Way. Jian went to Mt. Mui and passed from the west side of the Dharma Hall to the east.

Looking back toward the abbot’s quarters, he said, "Non-existent, non-existent," and then departed. Upon reaching the front of the Sangha Hall, he said, "One must not act with such haste or negligence.
He then prepared his formal demeanor and went up for an audience. Stepping across the threshold, he lifted his sitting cloth and called out, "Venerable Master!"
When Guishan was about to take up his whisk, Jian gave a shout and flung open the sleeves of his robe and departed.

During the reign of Emperor Wuzong, when the Buddhist teachings were suppressed, he took refuge in a stone grotto on Mount Dufu.

If you have no concerns regarding yourself, do not seek them falsely; even if you were to obtain something through such false seeking, it would not be truly attained.

Yizhuo was a Han Chinese. On the third day of the twelfth month in the sixth year, the year of Yiyou (1605), he suddenly told his disciples:

He was eighty-four years of age and sixty-five years of *śīla* (precept-ordination).
Zang Huan of the Tang dynasty was born into the Zhu family of Huating in Suzhou. During her pregnancy and at the time of his birth, people perceived a wondrous fragrance.
When he was a child, he once fell into a well, but it was as if something had lifted him out. At the age of seven, he took refuge under the Chan Master Daokuang and received the tonsure.
Upon reaching the age of twenty, he went to Mount Song to receive full ordination. His mother would often weep with longing whenever she thought of him. Consequently—
When his mother lost her sight, upon returning home to visit her, he was immediately able to see as before. When his mother passed away, he grieved to such an extent that he wasted away;

he built a hut by her grave and brought about auspicious omens, thereby gaining renown for his filial piety within his local community. At Mount Wuxie, he met the Great Master Lingmo and attained awakening.

Throughout the fluctuations of the Buddhist teachings during the Huichang and Dazhong eras, he maintained the Way with unwavering composure. Later, when Luoyang was rebuilt, he established Changshou Temple.
By imperial decree, he was established there. With his own hands, he compiled the Sanskrit manuscripts (*bānjié*) to complete the Great Canon (*dàzàng*).
He once said to others, "In my previous life, I was truly Tanchui of Mount Tiantong in Mingzhou. My karmic conditions from former lives are now approaching; shall I not return?

Ren Jingqiu made a vow and donated his entire household to serve the Triple Gem. Admiring Huàn’s conduct and righteousness, he requested that Huàn become the first patriarch to open the mountain monastery.
The assembly crowded around him, detaining him and refusing to let him leave. Huàn left behind his *zōng* whisk and said to him, "As long as this remains here, I am with you;
what cause for doubt is there? Once he had preached the Dharma, eminent disciples gathered like clouds. Furthermore, he had a stupa constructed in the northwest corner.
He planted five cypress trees upon it to symbolize the five hundred mounds, saying, "This is the site of the Water Land;

I shall use this to suppress it. Shortly thereafter, the rebel Qiu Fu attacked Yinqian. One day, two thousand of his followers, all bearing weapons, charged in. Huàn sat calmly in the hall with his eyes closed.
When the rebels threatened him with blades, his expression remained unshaken. The rebels were struck with terror and cowered, bowing their heads to beg for forgiveness.

He departed. When the rebellion was quelled, the prefecture reported the matter to the throne. By imperial decree, the temple was granted the name Qixin (Resting the Mind) to commemorate Huian’s virtue;
it was also a place where Tiantong had occasionally resided. In the autumn of the seventh year of the Xiantong era, he manifested a slight illness.
He instructed his disciples in advance, saying, "Seven days from now, I shall pass away. You may temporarily inter me in the Tiantong Gorge, and after three years, perform the cremation."
He passed away on the third day of the eighth month at the age of seventy-seven and with fifty-seven years since his ordination.
