Tang Jian’s family name was Qian. He was a native of Changcheng in Huzhou. His grandfather, Wei, was a Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites; his father, Sheng, did not serve in office.

After his father had been bedridden for a long time with illness, Jian cut flesh from his own thigh to make a broth which he presented to him. Consequently, the father’s illness was cured. His filial reputation became widely renowned.
At that time, Gao Xian, an inner attendant and a Great Virtue who presided over ordination platforms at the capital, resided at Kaiyuan Temple in the prefecture.
Xian was skilled in cursive calligraphy and his reputation was widespread. Zong invited him to serve as his teacher, whereupon he shaved his head and received the precepts.

He then visited the Great Master Wukong of Yanguan and obtained his seal of approval. In the third year of the Xiantong era (the Xin-si year), he traveled through famous mountains and eventually settled at Tian...

Looking toward Mount Jing on the eastern peak, both clergy and laity turned their hearts toward him as he propagated and expounded the Dharma through transformation. He had a disciple named Hongxin, who took pride in his own lecturing and debating skills.
Zong said to him, "The True Dharma of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is direct and beyond verbal expression; you are merely counting the sands of the ocean."
"What benefit is there in this principle? Simply do not harbor cognitive views; extinguish external conditions and detach from all mental activity, and that is your true nature.

Upon hearing this, Huian was bewildered; he paid his respects and took leave to travel to various regions. Upon reaching Mount Wei, he realized the essential meaning, thereby knowing that Zongxun’s instructions were not false.
In the seventh year, the year of Bingxu, on the fifth day of the intercalary third month, he demonstrated his passing. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Dayi.

This eulogy and record was composed by the Master Yúnyá, Shěn Jìngxiū of Wǔxīng.

Tang Rizi, surnamed Liu, was a native of Qí. His family had been noble and wealthy for generations. He studied the classics, histories, and the works of Zhuāngzi and Lǎozǐ, yet he found them particularly trivial.
Consequently, he went to Dànxīngshàn Temple in Cháng'ān to seek ordination under Dánguāng Fǎshī.

Having received full ordination, he visited Mount Sōng and received the seal of transmission from him, becoming a successor in the lineage of Huángméi. Later, while traveling to Nányuè, he took a liking to Ángtóu Peak.
His appearance was elegant and towering, transcending worldly entanglements; he harbored the resolve to spend his final years there.

He lived in a hermitage for twenty years until, during the Huichang suppression of Buddhism, he subsisted on wild fruits and drank from mountain streams, barely sustaining his breath deep within remote crags and secluded valleys.

At the beginning of the Dazhong era, an imperial edict lifted the former prohibitions. Thereupon, he once again led his followers who were devoted to him to restore the old site so that they might receive future students.
In this manner, another fifteen years passed. In the first year of the Xiantong era, he manifested parinirvāṇa at the age of one hundred and eight.
Three years later, on the third day of the second month, his remains were enshrined in a stūpa, and a stele was erected to endure for eternity. The world called him Anguo.

Tang Liangjie was the son of the Yu family of Zhuji in Kuaiji. From his early childhood, he followed a teacher at Wuxie Mountain;
it was not until his twenty-first year that he finally received the tonsure. He went to Mount Song to receive full ordination.

Not long after, he met Chan Master Nanquan Yuan, who happened to be preparing a vegetarian feast on the anniversary of Mazu’s death. As Nanquan was conducting the ritual, he asked the assembly, "I wonder, who is this Great Ma?"
"Will the Master return? The assembly had no reply. Xuanjia stepped forward and said, "He will come if he has a companion.
Baizhang pointed at Xuanjia and said to the assembly, "This latecomer is quite capable of being refined. Xuanjia said, "Preceptor, do not press the noble into the lowly.

Upon arriving at Mount Gui, he asked, "I have long heard the story of National Teacher Huizhong regarding 'insentient beings preaching the Dharma,' yet I have not yet fathomed its subtlety. I beg the Preceptor to explain it."
Today I was discussing this with Liang-jia. Miu said, "The mouth born of my parents shall never speak for you.
Liang-jia asked, "Is there anyone else who shares the same realization as the Master? Miu replied, "There is a practitioner at Yunyan;
if you see him, he will surely speak for you. Upon arriving at Yunyan, Liang-jia immediately asked, "Who is it that can receive the Dharma from the insentient preaching the Dharma?"
Wumen said, "The insentient preach the Dharma; the insentient hear it. Jia asked, "Does the Master hear it?
Wumen said, "If I were to hear it, you would not hear me preaching the Dharma. Jia said, "If that is so, then I, Liang-jia, truly do not hear the Master preaching the Dharma.

he then passed away suddenly. At that time, the assembly of disciples wailed with grief and could not stop. Jia suddenly—
He opened his eyes and addressed the assembly, saying, "For one who has left the household life, the mind does not rely upon external things;

this is true cultivation. When the toil of life ceases and death comes to rest, what sorrow could there be? He then summoned the administrative monk and said, "Prepare the vegetarian feast. Once the feast is finished, I shall depart.
Thereupon, the assembly was filled with longing and affection, and they delayed the preparation of the feast for seven days before finally making it ready. Daoprajñā likewise—
He conformed to the assembly, yet he regarded their fast as a "fast of ignorance," for it lacked any portion of *prajñā*.

When the monks chanted the *suīyì* (the invitation for criticism), he said, "At the moment of departure, one must generally not be noisy or agitated; this is why the fast serves as a demonstration of the precepts.
The following day, after bathing, he sat in the lotus posture and passed away at the age of sixty-three, with forty years of *śīla* seniority.

Tang Zangyi, surnamed Cheng, was a native of Xin’an in Quzhou. From an early age, he resolved to seek ordination as a monk. During the Yuanhe era, [the Emperor]...
He went to Yuelu Temple on Mount Lu in Changsha and received the tonsure under Vinaya Master Lingzhi.

In the third year of the Changqing era, he received the full precepts from Vinaya Master Zhitong at Kaiyuan Temple in Wuling. He said to his fellow students, "The gates of the teachings are vast and extensive, difficult to fathom;
yet, though there exists a 'comprehensive gate' (the *Zongmen*), it remains unexplored. Can this truly be called wisdom? Thereupon, he traveled to Xiangtan and ascended [the mountain].

At Longya Mountain, he encountered a disciple of Masu who was then preaching the Dharma in the mountains. One day, the master said to Yi: "The aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*) are not real;
that which is born is not the self. What is the name of your fundamental source? From whom did you obtain it? At these words, Yi attained realization.
Not long after, he avoided the Huichang persecution by retiring to Keshan in his native village. In the sixth year of the Dazhong era...
In his later years, County Governor Mr. Cui Shou built a meditation hall at Longxing Temple in the county for him to reside in.

After several years had passed, he moved to Jiahe, where the community invited him to stay at Zhide Monastery. When Mr. Cui Jun governed Gusu, he had long heard of Xiyi’s reputation and invited him to reside at Nanchan Monastery.
In the eighth year of the Xiantong era, Zhou Bao, the Integrity Commissioner of Zhexi, commanded him to reside [there].
At Zhaoyin Temple, he spent the autumn; then he returned to Yong’an Temple in Jiahe. This temple had been built by the lay devotee Lü Jing, who donated his private villa for the purpose.
During the Qiánfú era, bandits were rampant; [Dàoxì] said, "The bandits will ultimately not reach this place. Afterwards, it was indeed so.

He was the son of Chen of Min during the Dà'ān era of the Táng dynasty. Having entered the path in his youth, his natural disposition was extraordinary.

The Regional Inspector, Yuan Xi, reported this auspicious omen, and by imperial decree the name was changed to its present one. Shortly thereafter, he traveled to Hongjing, where he was able to hear the essentials of the Vinaya studies."
He traveled to Mount Shigong in Linchuan, where he met Chan Master Huizang and received his prediction of attaining the "half-person" stage.

He then proceeded north to Mount Wutai, where he would frequently bathe naked in the Dragon Pond; onlookers were struck with awe and alarm, yet Huian remained composed. Later, he paid homage to Chan Master Dayuan of Mount Miao.

He was ninety-one years of age and had been a monk for sixty-seven years. His posthumous title was Yuanzhi (Perfect Wisdom), and his stupa was named Zhengzhen (Realization of Truth).
Huiji of the Tang dynasty was the son of the Ye family of Zhinchang in Shaozhou. At the age of fifteen, he earnestly sought to renounce the household life, but his parents would not permit it.
At seventeen, his persistence became even more intense, yet they still did not grant his request. That night, two white rays of light suddenly pierced through his house;
when he examined their origin, they were seen to emanate from Caoxi. Huiji then cut off his left ring finger.
Xiaozhi bowed and said, "I venture to repay your virtue for your diligent toil. Thereupon, he sent the Chan Master Yitong to receive the tonsure at Nanhua.
At the age of eighteen, Xiaozhi was ordained as a *śrāmaṇera* to advance on the Path. He first visited Danyuan;
having already experienced his ascent to the hall, he later met Guishan, through whom he was finally able to reach the profound depths. He asked Guishan, "What is the true Buddha’s dwelling?"

Dahui said: "By means of the subtlety of 'thinking without thinking,' reflect upon the inexhaustibility of the spiritual flame. When thought is exhausted, one returns to the source; this nature is eternally abiding.

The monk asked, "I have attained awakening. What is the meaning of 'entering the gate'? Jue said, "This matter is extremely difficult.
If one is under the guidance of a Patriarch, those of the highest capacity may awaken to a thousand things upon hearing it once and attain great dhāraṇī.

"What is the meaning of this? the lecturer asked. Xuanzhen said, "This meaning does not exist within the sūtra. Xuanzhen continued, "When the five hundred laborers lifted the rock, you immediately said it did not exist.
During the evening assembly, Xuanzhen said, "Tonight, let us go beyond words in answering questions. Is there anyone who understands how to ask?"
"Come forth! At that time, a monk came out and bowed. Xian said, "Recently, I have been throwing bricks to draw out jade; instead, I have drawn out a mere brick.
A monk traveling to Mount Wutai asked a woman, "In which direction does the path to Mount Wutai go?
The woman said, "Go straight ahead. The monk then departed. The woman said, "He has gone off in that way again. The monk reported this to [Master Xian].
Xuanzhen said, "Wait; I shall go and put that old woman to the test. The next day, Xuanzhen went there and asked about the path to Tiantai just as the previous monk had.
The old woman answered him exactly as she had before. Upon returning, Xuanzhen said to the monk, "I have finished putting that old woman to the test for you.
The monk asked, "Do you welcome those who come to you in such a manner? Xuanzhen replied, "I do. The monk asked, "..."
"A person who does not come in such a manner—does the Master still receive them? Xuanzhen replied, "I do.
The monk said, "If you receive those who come in such a manner, how do you receive those who do not? Xuanzhen said, "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak;
my Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive. A newly arrived monk said to Xuanzhen, "I have come from Chang'an, carrying a single staff slung across my shoulder."
[Zhang] never once struck a single person. Xuanjian said, "In that case, it is simply that your reverence’s staff is too short.
The monk had no reply. Another monk painted a portrait of Xuanjian and presented it to him. Xuanjian said, "Tell me, does it resemble me or not? If it resembles me, I shall beat you to death;
if it does not resemble me, I shall burn the portrait. Xuanjian ascended the hall and said: "As soon as there is right and wrong..."
In a state of utter confusion, he lost his mind. Was there even a portion of a reply for him? Later, a monk recounted this to Luopu, who clicked his teeth together.
The monk then recounted it to Yunju, who said, "Why bother? When the monk returned and recounted it to Xuanzhen, Zhen said, "In the South, many have lost their bodies and forfeited their lives.
The monk said, "Please, Master, give an example. As soon as Zhen uttered the previous words, the monk pointed to someone beside him.
The monk said, "This monk has finished eating his rice and is talking like this. Xuanzhen then left him alone.
One day, Wang Gong, the regional commander of Zhending, brought his sons into the monastery. As Xuanzhen sat there, he asked, "Does Your Majesty understand? The King replied, "I do not understand.
Xuanzhen said, "Since childhood I have observed the fasts until my body is old; seeing others, I lack the strength to descend from my meditation seat. Ming.
The King of Nihon sent an attendant to deliver a message. Dajian Zhenji descended from his meditation seat to receive him.
An attendant asked, "Yesterday when the Great King arrived, you did not descend from your meditation seat; today when the military commander arrives, why do you descend?"

Xuanzhen said, "This is not something you can understand. When a person of superior capacity comes, I receive them upon the meditation seat; when one of middling capacity comes, I receive them by descending from the meditation seat;
when one of inferior capacity comes, I receive them outside the mountain gate. As Xuanzhen was approaching his death, he entrusted his whisk to Wang Gong, saying:
If asked from where he came, he would simply say, "That which this old monk has used throughout his life remains inexhaustible.

On the second day of the eleventh month in the fourth year of the Qianning era, he passed away in the right-side reclining posture at the age of one hundred and twenty. He was posthumously titled Great Master Zhenji.

Hui-mu of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Zhu. His family had resided in Jiyang for generations and was a prominent clan. When Hui-mu was young, he studied the *Shi* and *Li* classics and attained a refined excellence.
While traveling to the capital as a candidate in the civil service examinations, he passed by Jue-zhi Temple and paid his respects to Chan Master Da-guan Qi-zhen.

Zhenwei was bathed by the wind of the [Master’s] teaching. Through this bath, he attained awakening and requested ordination; having received full precepts, he went to Hongjing to pay homage to Guanyin, whereupon he suddenly beheld his original mind.
In the seventh year of the Xiantong era, he returned to his native village to guide and transform others.

The local magistrate, Lord Wei, served as his patron, and through the offerings of the faithful, the Qizhen Monastery was established to accommodate scholars from all quarters. Not long after, the Provincial Inspector Pei Yan...

In Lu, he oversaw the construction and maintenance of a vihāra at Shuijianfang. Once it was completed, he summoned Moku to reside there. Shortly thereafter, Qi Zhao, an official of Mingzhou, invited him to dwell on Mount Yusi.
Wherever he went, he established a renowned legacy. Not long after, he passed away at the age of eighty-eight and with forty-five years of ordination.
This was the third day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Qianning era.
Tang Yuan’an, surnamed Tan, was a native of Linyou in Fengxiang. At the age of seven, he entered the care of his elder brother, Venerable You, at Huaien Temple in Qiyang.
Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he immediately began to seek instruction. He first visited Linji, after which he took his leave of him.
Jixian said, "A single arrow from the gate of Linji—dare anyone withstand its point? An was granted permission [to study], yet he considered himself sufficient.
He subsequently went to Jia Shan and pitched a hermitage there. Later, upon receiving a letter from Jia Shan, he read it and was struck with awe.
He then abandoned his hermitage and went to Jia Shan to pay his respects. Jia Shan said, 'A rooster nesting in a phoenix's nest—it is not of the same kind. Get out! An replied:"
Having come from afar to seek the Way, he requested that the Master receive him. Jia Shan said, "Before my eyes there is no you;
here there is no old monk. He immediately let out a shout. Jia Shan said, "Stop, stop! Disciple, do not be so hasty and reckless.
The clouds and moon are the same, yet the streams and mountains are each different. You may indeed cut off the tongues of all people in the world, but how can you [do so] to me?"
A tongueless man understands speech. Anmo was at a loss. Jia Shan struck him. Because of this, Anmo devoted himself to his service for several years.
One day he asked Jia Shan, "How does one realize the place where neither Buddha nor demons reach? He replied, "The candle illuminates the image for a thousand li."
The old monk in the dark room was deluded. Again he asked, "When the morning sun has already risen and the night moon is no longer seen, what then?

He replied, "The dragon’s palace holds the sea pearl; the swimming fish do not look back. When Jiashan was about to pass away, he said to the assembly, "The branch of Shitou is about to be extinguished.
An said, "Not so. Jiashan asked, "Why? An said, "There is naturally a green mountain that remains."
Jiashan said, "If it is thus, then my Way has not fallen into ruin. After Jiashan passed away, An settled at Luopo Mountain in Liyang. Later, he moved to Suxi in Langzhou.
Disciples from all quarters flocked to him like spokes converging on a hub. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The final phrase is where one first arrives at the secure barrier;
it locks off the vital thoroughfare, allowing passage neither to the mundane nor to the sagely. You must know that this is the..."

Those who drift in the currents do not take the insights of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and plaster them upon their foreheads; they are like the auspicious tortoise bearing the celestial charts, thereby bringing about the very cause of its own destruction.
A monk asked, "What is it like when one sees instantly? He replied, "The morning star divides the dawn's light; how can it compare to the brilliance of the sun?
A monk asked, "When coming thus, there is nothing established; when going thus, there is nothing extinguished. What then?"

"What? He replied, "The wood-seller is noble; the man in brocade is base. He asked, "The teachings state that feeding a hundred thousand Buddhas is not as good as feeding one who has neither cultivated nor realized.
What fault do the hundred thousand Buddhas have? What virtue does the one who has neither cultivated nor realized possess?
He answered, "A single sheet of white cloud spans the mouth of the valley; how many returning birds will find their way home at night?"
Minao asked, "What is this fundamental matter? The Master replied, "A single grain lies in a field overgrown with weeds; though the seedlings are not weeded, they flourish naturally.
The monk asked, "If one never weeds at all, will it not eventually be buried by the grass? The Master replied, "Its flesh and bone differ from those of common weeds;
thus, even wild oats and barnyard grass can never outshine it. Ascending the hall, he said, "Sun Bin has closed his shop and departed. At that moment, a diviner stepped forward.
A monk came forward and said, "I request a divination from the Master. He replied, "Your father has died. The monk was left speechless.

In the eighth month of autumn in the year of Wuyou (848 CE), the first year of the Guanghua era, he instructed his attendants: "According to the dharma of renunciation, one must not retain superfluous possessions.
At this time of sowing seeds, it is imperative to practice extreme frugality. All matters of construction and renovation must be completely suspended. Time flows swiftly; the Great Way—"
Profound and mysterious! If one merely follows along with the flow, by what means could one realize and awaken? The multitude take this as ordinary and fail to offer even the slightest admonition.
In the winter, he manifested a slight illness, yet he did not grow weary of leading the assembly in teaching. On the first day of the twelfth month, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"I will not remain for long. Now I have a matter to ask you: if you can penetrate it, then this is it; if you cannot, then it is like placing a head upon a head."
"If this one is not it," [Zhao] An said, "then you would be like cutting off your head to seek life.
At that time, the first seat replied, "The green mountains do not lift their feet; beneath the sun, one does not pick up a lamp. An said, "What kind of time is this for making such remarks?
Then there was the senior monk Yancong, who offered a different reply: "Apart from these two paths, I ask the Master not to question me. An [approved].
Hui'an said, "That is not it; speak further. Yancong replied, "The Way is inexhaustible. Hui'an said, "I do not concern myself with whether you have exhausted it or not.
Yancong replied, "Since I have no attendant, I am here to respond to the Master. Hui'an then descended from the hall. That night, he ordered an attendant to summon Yancong to the abbot’s quarters.
Upon entering, Hui'an said, "Disciple, your response to the old monk today was most reasonable. According to you—"
This accords with the intent of my late teacher. My late teacher said: "There is no dharma before the eyes; the intent is right before the eyes. It is not a dharma of the present moment;
it is not something reached by the ears or eyes. Now tell me, which phrase is the main sentence? If you can discern it, I will entrust you with the patriarch’s bowl.
Yancong replied, "I do not understand. An said, "You have grasped the meaning, just speak. Yancong replied, "Truly, I do not know."
He did not know. An shouted him out, saying, "Suffering! Suffering! On the afternoon of the second day, another monk raised the previous words and questioned An.
An spoke on his behalf, saying, "The Compassionate Boat does not row upon the clear waves; at Jianxia Pass, it is but a vain effort to release the wooden goose.
He then passed away. He was sixty-five years old and had been a monk for forty-six years. His stupa was erected in the northwest corner of the monastery.
Tang Wenxi was the son of Zhu Shi of Yuer in Jiahe. While his mother was pregnant, she dreamed that she obtained a peach with three stalks and swallowed it;
she subsequently gave birth to him. As an infant, he shunned the flavors of meat and pungent herbs.

At the age of seven, he entered the monastic life under the monk Qingguo of Changle Temple in the district—Qingguo being his maternal uncle—and was made to study the sutras and liturgical rites, whereupon he eventually underwent the tonsure. Shortly thereafter, he studied the *Lotus Sūtra*. And...
I read the *Wenju* (Textual Explanations) of Tiantai at Kaiyuan Temple in Yuezhou, expounding upon its contents as the occasion arose.
In the third year of the Kaicheng era, I received full ordination (*upasampadā*). Not long after, the Huichang persecution occurred; consequently, my practice became even more rigorous.
At the beginning of the Dazhong era, I was ordained once again at Qifeng Temple in Yanguan. Master Xingkong of Daci Mountain directed me to travel to various quarters to seek instruction.
In the year of Renwu during the Xiantong era, I met Master Ji of Yangshan at Guanyin Temple in Yuzhang. There, I suddenly attained realization of the Dharma of the mind.
Yangshan subsequently appointed me to oversee the temple’s permanent assets. One day, a visiting bhikṣu came after midday seeking food;

finding that all the food had been exhausted, I thought with joy, "He has other affairs to attend to and likely did not eat anyway," so I gave my own meal to the guest. Shortly thereafter, Yangshan asked, "Did you seek food recently?"
"Qiu, you have already realized the fruit of the path; will you provide [the offerings] for him? He replied, "I shall set aside my own portion and provide them.
Yangshan said, "Since you have obtained such benefit, how can you say it is nothing? For seven years he returned to live at Mount Qianqing in Yuhang.
Ten years later, patrons including Liu Yan and Ma Zheng invited him to reside at the Gucheng Monastery in Longquan. He lived there for eleven years. In the Jiafu year...
In the year of Hai, when the Nao rebels plundered the region of Yuhang, he moved again from Ye to Buting to seek refuge.
The Regional Inspector Du Ruxiu invited him to Renwang Monastery. In the third year of the Guangqi era, Qian Liu first took charge of Hangzhou and provided the offices of Longquan for his reception;
this is the present-day Ciguang Monastery. A monk asked, "What is the mark of nirvana? Xī—
It is said that this was verified at the point where the incense smoke vanished. [A monk] asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?

Xì called out to the monastery superintendent, saying, "This monk suffers from madness. [Another monk] asked, "What is one's own true self? Xì remained silent. The monk was at a loss for words and repeated his previous question.

Xiji remarked, "The blue sky is shrouded in night’s gloom; it does not fly toward the moon. At the beginning of the Dàshùn era, Dǒng Chāng, the Regional Commander of Wěishèng Army, along with Wǔsù, jointly submitted a memorial recommending him.
He was granted purple robes. In the fourth year of Qiánníng, he was bestowed the title Wúzhù (Non-attachment).
On the twenty-seventh day of the tenth month in the third year of Guanghua, he passed away while seated in his official residence. He was eighty years of age; sixty summers.
On the twenty-second day of the eleventh month, he was interred in a western valley of Mount Lingyin. His nature was pure and prudent;
his utmost sincerity could move all things. In the summer of the first year of Guangming, locusts and grasshoppers covered the land, and the wilds were thereby [devastated].
Zha Xǐ used his staff to mark out furrows in his *kāṣāya* robes; as he rebuked the locusts with a stern voice, not a single one descended.
That year, within the entire district, only the ten *qīng* of land that Xǐ had plowed yielded a bountiful harvest.
At the time of his death, a white light radiated from his quarters, and the bamboo and trees all turned white.
Tang Huanyu was a man of unknown origins. Having received the Dharma from Jia Shan in Liyang, he later propagated his teachings at Shao Shan in Luoyang.
One day, while descending the mountain, he encountered Nun Zun. Zun asked, "Where is Shao Shan?
Huanyu pointed to a grove of bamboo and said, "This very place is it. Zun said, "May I ask you a question? Huanyu—
Yun said, "Look at you—it was not made by a smith of golden teeth; how could you have known how to draw the bow to shoot Wei-chi?
Zun said, "The phoenix flies straight into the path of the misty clouds; who fears the wild sparrows in the woods? Pu said, "Even granting that you stand directly outside the realm of Vipaśyin."
"It is still half a month's journey from Shao Mountain. Huangbo Zhen asked, "Tell me, where does the fault lie? Guishan Pu said, "Such bold words are known by people of the age.
Huangbo Zhen said, "If that is so, then true jade differs from the mud; it brushes away the dust of ten thousand activities.
Guishan Pu said, "Under the workshop of Lu Ban, even skillful ingenuity is but labor in vain. Huangbo Zhen said, "The student only acts thus; what is your meaning, Master?"
"How is it? Nanquan asked. Puyuan said, "A jade maiden throws her shuttle at night, sending embroidered silk to a neighbor's house in the west.
Zhizun asked, "Is this not the very style of your monastery, Master? Puyuan said, "Stretching one's body across the universe—who is there to show their head? He passed away after some time;
his posthumous title was Wuweishan (The Fearless).
Tang Hongxin was of the Wu clan and a native of Wuxing. At the mere age of nineteen, he took ordination under National Teacher Wushang at Kaiyuan Temple.
By the age of twenty-two, he went to Huishan Temple on Mount Song to receive full ordination; in just seven days, he was able to master and recite the Mahābhikṣu precepts in their entirety.
He subsequently investigated the Vinaya and studied the sūtras and śāstras. Thereafter, he returned to visit his preceptor Wushang.
Wu Shang said, "During the twelve periods of the day and night, with what do you repay the four debts of gratitude and the beings of the three realms?
Xian was struck with dismay; for three days he could not eat. Wu Shang, perceiving his state of agitation and yearning, enlightened him. He immediately attained realization.
Thereupon, he traveled extensively to visit Yunyan and Moshan, and his spiritual capacity was already fully formed. During the upheaval of the Huichang era, everyone...
They wept with grief and lamented deeply; only Huiyin remained silent. He then said, "When a great man encounters such a calamity, is it not simply fate?
Since there are things that cannot be avoided by fate, why further display this manner of a weak woman?

Subsequently, the lay devotee Luo Yan of Changsha wished to enshrine him in his home to provide offerings. For a period of two years, he maintained the etiquette of a host toward him as if they were equals.

In the Dayong era, when the flourishing of the Dharma was restored, he returned to reside at Xifeng Monastery in his native village. In the sixth year of the Xiantong era, he ascended Mount Jing to pay his respects to his father.
The following year, the Great Master Wushang entered nirvana; the assembly requested that Huian succeed him as the head of the monastery.
When scholars came to him, they were more than ten times as many as during the time of Wushang.

During the rebellion of Huang Chao, one of his subordinate generals led over a thousand soldiers into the mountains to see Huixin. Huixin sat in meditation and did not rise. The general, enraged, brandished a sword at him;
the sword struck Huixin but did not pierce him, yet it struck the bed twice. Huixin’s expression remained unchanged. The general marveled at this and prostrated himself before him.

Having given what was to be given, he departed. A monk asked, "What is it like when the breath is stilled like ashes? He replied, "It is still merely the business of another house. The monk asked, "What is it like after that business is done?
He replied, "The farmer tills the field but does not sow. The monk asked, "Ultimately, what is it like? He replied, "The grain is ripe, yet one does not go to the market.
Emperor Xizong issued an imperial decree granting the monastery the name *Ganfu Zhenguó* (Dry Token National Pacification). In the second year of the Jingfu era, [the region of] Wu...
The King of Yue, Qian Shangfu, memorialized the throne to grant him the title of Grand Master Fajie.

On the eighteenth day of the ninth month in the fourth year of the Guanghua era, he took leave of the assembly and passed away. All expenses for his funeral were provided by the Wu-Yue government, which brought great honor to the Chan community.
Initially, Wang’s family lived at Shijianshan on Mount Tianmu; they were extremely poor. Yì happened to see him among the military garrison and immediately set him aside [to provide for].
The Master grasped his hand and whispered, "You should cherish yourself; in the future, when you reach the pinnacle of nobility, you must not harbor any aversion toward the Buddha-dharma.

Consequently, the King served him with reverence for the rest of his life. Among his foremost disciples were Master Ji of Xie Monastery on Mount Lu, Yi-zhi of Lin-chuan, and Ling-da of Gong-chen Yuan.
Ling-da was particularly eminent and outstanding; his teachings spread throughout the two Zhe regions. Upon his death, he was posthumously honored with the title "Guiji" (Returning to Quiescence).

Hui-gong of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Luo and was a native of Min. His mother dreamed that a stupa rising to the heavens sprang up from the ground where she resided, and she subsequently conceived him.
By the time he was a child, his intelligence and awakening were extraordinary. At the age of seventeen, he took the jinshi examination and arrived at the capital with the other candidates.

While traveling through Mount Zhongnan, he beheld the portrait of the Patriarch at Fengri Temple; he attained a state of serene realization and subsequently requested to be enrolled as a monk in that temple.
He served as a monastic laborer at Anguo Temple. When the temple was newly established and a ritual platform was inaugurated, he was twenty-two years old;
he then shaved his head for the first time and received full ordination. He went to visit Chan Master Xuanjian at Deshan. Deshan asked, "Do you understand? Cong replied, "What is there to understand?

Deshan said, "Please come forward for an audience. Cong said, "I have already recognized you. Deshan laughed heartily and permitted him to enter the inner quarters. After Deshan had passed away, it happened that...
The guest, having heard of the excellence of Mount Aiyu in Xinzhou, settled there. The Regional Inspector (Cishi) established Xichan Temple for him, where several hundred scholars gathered.
Not long after, because the city was noisy and defiled, he moved again to Maguan Mountain in Changxi, Fuzhou, and then to Fuyang Mountain in Quanzhou.
At every location, offerings from the laity poured in, and his disciples flocked to him in great numbers. This was his intention.
Yù (Deshou) established himself there. In the third year of the Jǐngfú era, he led his disciples to visit Mount Tiantai.
Dú Xióng, the Governor of the province and native of Jīngzhào, opened up Mount Zǐníng and constructed Ruìlóng Monastery to accommodate him.

On the twelfth month of the third year of Tiānfù, the *guīhài* year, he suddenly ordered the bells to be struck, looked around at those nearby and said, "I am departing," and then closed his eyes. He was eighty-four years of age. [Monk]...

In the sixty-second year of the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty, Dao Ying was born into the Wang family of Yutian in Jimen. At the age of twenty-five, he took the tonsure and received full ordination at Yanshou Monastery in Fanyang.
He began his studies of the Vinaya Piṭaka and sighed, saying: "A great man should seek liberation; how could he [otherwise]..."
"Am I bound by worldly concerns? Thinking thus, he went to Mount Cuī to inquire about the Way. He remained there in seclusion for three years, passing through both winter and summer.
Suddenly, he saw a person dressed in official robes, appearing like a messenger, who said to Huiying, "Why do you not travel south to visit spiritual friends?
Having spoken, the figure vanished instantly. Furthermore, a monk arrived from Yuzhang and spoke of Dong [shan].
This was the height of the Dharma assemblies of that time. Baizhang Ying eventually went to Dongshan. One day, Dongshan asked Ying, "What is your name, Acharya?
Ying replied, "Daoying. Dongshan said, "Say more than that. Ying replied, "If one goes beyond this, it is no longer called Daoying."
Later, Houshan asked Baizhang Huaiying, "I have heard that Dashi Huishang was born in Japan and became its king—is this true?
Ying said, "If it were Dashishe, he would not even become a Buddha; what need is there to mention becoming a king? One day, Houshan asked Ying, "Where have you come from?
Ying said, "I have come from treading the mountains. Houshan said, "Which mountain is fit for dwelling? Ying said, "Which one..."
Geshan said, "This mountain cannot be inhabited. Danyuan said, "If that is so, you have found a way of entry onto this mountain.
Geshan said, "There is no way. Danyuan said, "If there were no way, how could I have met with you, Old Monk? Geshan said, "If there were a way, I would not have met with you, Master.
Geshan said, "This fellow will, in the future, be beyond the grasp of thousands or ten thousands of people."
Thereupon, Dongshan deeply approved of him. He emerged from seclusion to reside at Sanfeng, later moving to Yunju to propagate the teachings; his style was much like that of Dongshan.

At that time, Zhong Chuan, the Prince of Nanping, controlled Jiangxi and held him in high esteem. He submitted a memorial to the throne requesting that he be granted purple robes and a monastic title.
Whenever he invited him to his residence, he would first order the Ganzi Hall to be swept clean to serve as his quarters. One thousand...
He was surrounded by a great multitude. Offerings and gifts were abundant and profuse; even Cheng Rui of Jingnan, admiring his virtue, sent contributions that frequently reached tens of thousands.
In the autumn of the first year of Tianfu (the Xin-you year), he manifested illness. On the third day of the first month of the following year, he passed away.
Tang Youyuan, surnamed Feng, was a native of Zizhong in Dongchuan. At the age when he first began his elementary studies, he entered Fugan Temple in Chengdu to serve the monk Dinglan.
Dinglan was the preceptor who had received the full precepts from Emperor Xuanzong. He frequently accompanied [the Emperor] in and out of the inner palace.
The Emperor once playfully wrote on the back of his robe, saying: "This youth has a karmic affinity with me."

Because of this, he was given the name Youlun (Yuan-lun) and received the tonsure. In the ninth year of the Dazhong era, Lord Minzhong Bai governed the region of Yibu and ordered the Jingzhong Temple to open a precept platform (*śīla-maṇḍala*).
Consequently, [the Master] was able to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). He subsequently returned to the capital to study and receive instruction in the Sūtras and Vinaya.
Later, he visited Xiaoma Shenzhao and grasped the essential points of the mind. He visited all the great monastic centers of the time...

Traveling extensively, he happened to stay at Huashan in Chuzhou. Later, during his southern tour, the Provincial Inspector, Lord Li Hui, built a separate meditation hall for him in Mount Wuyi to invite him to reside there.
In the third year of the Qiánfú era, he arrived at Jìnyún and established a monastery at Dàshài Mountain in Lóngquán.
When this matter was reported to the throne, an imperial edict was issued from the Ministry of Rites to grant it the name "Lóng'ān" and to ordain seven monks to dwell there. Ten...
In the eighth year, he moved to Lianyun. The Prefect, Lu Yue, further constructed a separate cloister at Kaiyuan Temple in the prefecture and provided him with the four requisites for his support.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the Dingmao year of Tianyou, he fell ill; on the first day of the sixth month, he passed away.
His secular age was seventy-three, and his years since ordination were fifty-two. At that time, Minister of Works Yang Xi was governing the region south of Xizhou;
he entrusted the master with the responsibility for his funeral arrangements. The cremation took place in the southern garden of the monastery, where over one hundred śarīras were obtained.
Forty of these grains, along with the cremated remains, were placed in a precious vase and interred in a stupa. This was in the third year of the Kaiyun era of the Jin dynasty.
In the year of Yisi (625 CE), the Vinaya Master Wentai composed this inscription and engraved it upon a stele to commemorate his noble conduct and illustrious virtue.

During the Tang dynasty, the Master Hengtong was born into the Li clan of Ping’en in Xingzhou. At the age of thirteen, having completed the mourning period for his parents, he went to Mount Que to rely upon a teacher.
There he studied and perused the Buddhist scriptures. At the age of twenty, he received the grace of tonsure at the [monastery] in the prefecture.
At Kaiyuan Temple, he soon received full ordination. He subsequently enrolled at Jianfu Temple to study and practice the sutras and vinaya.

Thereupon he asked: "When Kāśyapa Mātanga entered the Han, he translated and authored these texts; when the descendant of the Sage came to Liang, what further matters did he clarify? From this, he traveled southward to seek further inquiry.
He visited Master Zhaoxian Cen. Cen asked, "Where are you from? He replied, "Xingzhou. Cen said, "I say you did not come from there.
He replied, "Does the Master still reside here? After Cen entered *nirvāṇa*, Dàtōng served as his disciple and observed the rites of mourning with a focused mind.
While traveling in Xuancheng, the Minister Cui Yu treated him with exceptional courtesy and established the Ruisheng Chan Monastery for him.
Xie Xianshan invited him to reside there. During the Zhonghe and Wende eras, when the region was in turmoil due to banditry, in the second year of the Tongsun period, he led his disciples to Siming.
There, the Prefectural Governor, Huang Junseng, selected a site at Xuedou and established a residence for him to accommodate the assembly.

His flourishing and magnificent transformation was profound. On the seventh day of the seventh month in the second year of the Tiānyòu era, he manifested illness. Nine days later, having bathed, he passed away while seated.

He was seventy-two years of age and had fifty-two years of *śrāmaṇera* and *bhikṣu* ordination (*varṣa*). On the seventh day of the eighth month of that same year, his remains were enshrined in a stūpa.
The stupa is located two hundred paces southwest of the monastery.
He was a member of the Zhang clan from Chunan in Min during the Tang dynasty. In his youth, he served Master Tandai at Kaiyuan Temple in the prefecture.
Upon reaching the age of twenty, he shaved his head and became a monk. Shortly thereafter, he received full ordination on Mount Wutai and proceeded to Xiaoshan to study the Vinaya-piṭaka.

He subsequently traveled to the capital to study the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* and other texts. Thereupon, he sighed, saying, "The indications of the sudden and gradual teachings are as vastly different as this.
He then retired to Mount Furuang, yet found no realization. Later, he visited Master Yun at Huangbo, where he received a prophetic certification (*vyākaraṇa*). At that time—

During the Chang’an reign period, an imperial edict abolished the Buddhist teachings; he immediately withdrew to live in the forests and valleys. At the beginning of the Dazhong reign period, an edict restored the teachings.
When Pei Gongxiu, serving as Chancellor, was appointed as Governor of Wanling, he invited Huangbo to the provincial seat so that he might consult with him.
Nan attended upon Huangbo’s side with the utmost diligence. Before long, he took his leave to enter Zhejiang, where he hung up his staff at Ba’en Temple in Gusu, occupying a single room.
He practiced seated meditation for more than twenty years, never once stepping beyond the threshold of his dwelling.

In the fourth year of the Qiánfú era, the Prefect Zhou Shènsì followed his example and invited him to preach at Fǎlín Temple. Shortly thereafter, he moved to Zhīxíng Mountain, as he took pleasure in its tranquility and seclusion.
In the fifth year, Xu Zhèngyuán, the Magistrate of Chānghuà in Hángzhōu, and Ráo Jīng, the Commander of Zǐxī Garrison, [invited him].

Because the Ciyun Monastery on Mount Qianqing was exceptionally secluded and remote, he was invited to reside there as the abbot. Aside from instructing his disciples, he remained in constant silence.

Nevertheless, his influence spread throughout the regions of Wu and Yue. In the third year of the Guangqi era, the regional commander, Lord Qian Liu, provided offerings at the mountain and reported the Master’s virtue to the Emperor.
By imperial decree, he was granted one set of purple robes and five sets of deer-skin robes.
In the second month of the sixth year of the Wende era, two rainbows suddenly pierced through his hall and chamber; two deer entered the monastery; and the beam of the Dharma Hall broke.
In the fifth month, he fell ill and summoned the assembly to bid them farewell. On his bed, he gradually lowered his feet and extended his arms as if in the act of rising to walk.
He then passed away suddenly. His secular age was seventy, and his monastic seniority fifty-six years. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at the western corner of the monastery grounds.
Tang Yicun’s surname was Zeng, and he was a native of Nanan in Quanzhou. His family had served the Buddha for generations.

At the age of nine, he sought to leave secular life, but his parents did not grant permission as he was still young. When he was twelve years old, his father traveled to Yurun Temple in Putian, and Yicun attended him there.
The temple had a Vinaya Master named Qingxuan, whose conduct was exceptionally austere. Upon seeing him, Yicun immediately prostrated himself and said, "I..."
The Master then remained there, refusing to return home. In the seventeenth year [of the Dali era], he shaved his hair and went to pay respects to the Great Master Hengzhao of Mount Furong.
Coinciding with the calamity of the Huichang era, he subsequently went into hiding at that location.

After a long time, as the Great Dharma was restored during the Dazhong era, he traveled north through Wu, Chu, Liang, Song, Yan, and Qin. He received full ordination at Baocha Temple in Youzhou and visited numerous famous sites.
He traveled extensively, visiting various Chan assemblies, until he finally gained great benefit at Deshan in Wuling.
In the sixth year of the Xiantong era, he first established his residence at Xuefeng. Monks from all over the world flocked to him like shadows following forms.

During the Qianfu era, the Regional Inspector Wei Gong of Jingzhao, and during the Zhonghe era, the Minister of Works Chen Gong of Yingchuan, both looked up to him and entered his monastery to inquire about the essentials of the Way. Some [of these officials]...
I heard from Emperor Xizong that he dispatched the man from Min, Chen Yanchao, to bestow upon him purple *kāṣāya* robes and the honorary title of Master Zhenjue.
In the year *xinhai*, he traveled with staff and sandals to Danchun and Siming.

The following year, Wang Shenzhi first entered Min as Grand Guardian-in-Chief and took possession of the land; yet Cuncen was not there, as if they were avoiding one another. Two years later, he returned.

Since the time of the Wu dynasty, the Wang family has treated him with great honor and distinction. They have provided monastics with vegetarian feasts, constructed halls, established images, and cast bells.

Furthermore, they frequently welcome him and house him in their grand residences in the eastern and western wards of the prefecture; sometimes the family’s oil-canopyed carriages attend his seat to listen to the Dharma.

Consequently, both the scholar-officials and the commoners—whether farmers or hunters—all transform their dispositions and alter their conduct, becoming virtuous through the influence of his moral character. A monk asked: "What is the meaning of the Patriarchs?"
Regarding whether the intent of the teaching is the same or different, Xuefeng Cunen said: "Ācārya, for what purpose do you travel? He asked a monk, "Where have you recently departed from?
The monk replied, "I have come from the region of Zhejiang. Cunen said, "Did you come by boat or by land?
The monk said, "I did not take either path. Cunen said, "How then did you get here? The monk said, "What obstacle could there be? Cunen then struck him. He then ascended the hall.
He raised his whisk and said, "This one is for those of middle and lower capacity. A monk asked, "How about when a person of the highest capacity comes? Cunen raised the whisk.
The monk said, "You also say this one is for those of middle and lower capacity. Cunen struck him across the mouth with the whisk.

Cunen then cited the story of the Sixth Patriarch regarding the wind and the banner, saying, "How great [in stature yet small in action] was that patriarch! He left the head of the dragon but the tail of the snake. He deserves twenty blows of the staff!"
At that time, the Elder Taihara Fu was standing in attendance. Upon hearing this, he gnashed his teeth. Yunmen said, "I just now spoke in such a manner;
I too should be given twenty blows of the staff. In the third month of spring in the year of Wuchen (868), he manifested illness.

The King sent a physician to present medicine, but Yunmen refused it. On the second night of the second month of summer, he passed away at the age of eighty-seven and with five years of seniority in the monastic order.

Wuzuo, style name Buyong, surnamed Sima, was a native of Gusu. His father was the County Magistrate of Wanqiu; his mother was née Dai.
While she was pregnant, she dreamed of a strange śramaṇa who called himself surnamed Xu and resided at Liushui Temple; he earnestly requested lodging from her.

Her father also dreamed that characters were being written upon a platter, which he took great pleasure in and intended to present to the Son of Heaven. At dawn, each marveled at their respective dreams.
The mother then pointed to her own belly and said to her father, "If a son is indeed born, he shall surely belong to Liushui."
It was a temple; indeed, his family resided not far from it. When he was born, he was precocious and lovely. By nature, he was pure and aloof, detesting pungent or oily foods.
At the age of four, he was taught to recite and study, and he possessed a powerful memory. His father, Zizhi, rejoiced that his son resembled himself.

Furthermore, his parents intended to arrange a marriage for him so that he might settle down, but his mother would not permit it; consequently, he left the household life according to his original vow.

When he reached the required age, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*), and after becoming proficient in the sutras and śāstras through lecturing, he suddenly abandoned them and departed. Later, he entered Min and relied upon Master Xuefeng Cun, from whom he attained the essentials of Chan.
Not long after, lay devotees from Luling invited him to reside at Yunting Monastery on Mount Sangu; he also firmly declined an invitation to Nanping Monastery in Yuzhang.
At that time, the Zhong clan held power in Hongjing, where he stayed as a guest for ten years without ever being able to meet with them.

He eventually traveled to Kuaiji and settled at Kaopan in the mountains of Siming. When the Qian family of Wuyue heard of his reputation, they dispatched an envoy to summon him. [He declined briefly...]
Upon his arrival for an audience, he took his leave abruptly, offering a poem of thanks that read: "The nature of clouds and cranes is solitary; how could they endure the gates of fame and profit?

Though I entered the kingdom out of gratitude, I decline illness to return to the mountains. Sun He of Fangyi and Feng Lao of Fenghua were both naturally disdainful of monastic companions, yet they spent the entire day in conversation with him whenever he visited.
Yang Yan, an imperial scholar, also welcomed him as soon as their canopies met. During the Kaiping era, he passed away.
He passed away at the age of fifty-six. Throughout his life, he never entered a nunnery, did not visit official courts, did not compose visiting cards, and did not pursue worldly profit.
He produced models for cursive and clerical scripts, liturgical texts for the various scriptures, and commentaries on Dao’an’s *Six Periods of Buddha-Worship*.
His collected poems and songs were also circulated among the world. He styled himself the "Recluse of Ease" (Xiāoyáo zǐ).
Liang Shibei was born into the Xie clan of Min. In his youth, he followed his father while fishing in the South Terrace River;

whenever he caught a fish, he would immediately release it. Although his father grew angry, he paid no heed to him. At the beginning of the Xiantong era, he left the household life on Mount Furong and went to Kaiyuan Temple in Yuzhang to receive full ordination.
Upon returning, he took up service in the Vinaya Hall, enduring hardships without complaint. He wore robes made of coarse cloth and sandals of *máng* grass.
He ate but one meal at midday and remained constantly seated without lying down; thus, he was known throughout the monastic forests as "Tou-tuo Bei" (Prepared Dhūta).
Master Xuefeng Cunen, who was his senior fellow student, once said to him, "Tou-tuo Bei, why do you not go forth to travel and study with various teachers? Bei replied:
“Bodhidharma did not come to the Eastern Land, and the Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven. Xunshen agreed with this view.
When Xuansha appeared in the world, there were always about seven hundred followers among the monastics who attended him. One day, as he ascended the hall, he sat in silence for a long time.
The assembly, thinking that he would not preach the Dharma, all dispersed at once. Xuansha rebuked them, saying, “Look at this lot of fellows!”

There is not a single person among them who possesses true wisdom. Seeing only that I have opened up two flaps of skin, they all flock together to seek out words and phrases, claiming, "This is my teacher’s genuine concern for others.
Yet they do not understand at all. If things are like this, it is truly a great difficulty, indeed a great difficulty.
Baizhang once gave a formal discourse, saying: "The venerable elders of all quarters all say they 'welcome beings and benefit living creatures. But let me ask you:"
"Three kinds of sick people come; how will you receive them? If you strike the mallet or raise the whisk, the blind cannot see.

If you proclaim the teachings of the ancients and the present, the deaf cannot hear. If you wait for them to respond, the mute have no words. If you cannot receive them, the Buddha-dharma has no efficacy.
A monk stepped forward and said, "Regarding these three kinds of sick people, does the Master permit others to deliberate upon this?"
Baizhang said, "How do you resolve this? The monk then bowed respectfully and departed. Baizhang said, "Not so, not so.
Luohan said, "Guishen currently has eyes to see, ears to hear, and a mouth to speak; how would you receive him, Master?
Zhongta said, "As for those three types of sick people, where are they right now? Baizhang saw the monk [and realized his error].
He came to pay his respects and said, "It is because of me that you are able to pay homage. He then inquired in detail about Changsheng’s contemplation of the Buddha.
Changsheng replied, "The Buddha does not depart from the past, does not come from the future, and does not abide in the present.
How do you contemplate him? Changsheng said, "Let Jiaoran pass; I have a point to discuss. Beyu said, "I let you pass. What is your discussion? Changsheng remained silent for a long while.
Baizhang said, "I know full well that you are making your living inside a ghost cave. A monk asked, "What is it that makes it so difficult to see?
Baizhang said, "It is precisely because it is too near. The monk asked again, "Why is it that I cannot say anything?
Baizhang said, "My mouth is stuffed shut; how could you possibly speak? At that time, Wang Shenzhi was serving as the Grand Councilor (Shizhong).
There was a man from Min who petitioned for the bestowal of a purple *kāṣāya* robe; the master’s title was Zongyi.

On the twenty-seventh day of the eleventh month of the second year of Kaiping (the Wuchen year), he passed away at the age of seventy-four and with forty-four years of *dīkṣā*. King Zhongyi erected a stupa for him.
Liang Benren received the Dharma of the mind from Dongshan. He resided at Baishui Monastery in Junzhou, where his assembly numbered over three hundred.
His profound words were widely disseminated. Once, during the memorial feast for Dongshan, a monk asked, "When we make offerings to the former master, does the former master still come?
Ren replied, "Serve another portion of food. While the assembly of lay practitioners of the Western Mountain were prostrating, Ren asked them:
"Come here," Ren said. Xing said, "I have come to seek your instruction. Ren said, "With so many people here, whom am I to give it to?
When Jingqing arrived on his travels, Ren called out to him, "Monk, the weather is cold. Jingqing replied, "I dare not [complain].
Ren asked, "Do you have a bedding mat that can cover you? Jingqing said, "Even if I did, I would have no leisure to spread it out. Ren said, "..."
Even if you say, "The droplets of water freeze," it still has nothing to do with him. Qing said, "What business is there in 'the droplets of water freezing'?
Ren said, "On the summit of a high mountain, there is nothing for Daozhe to chew upon. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of non-transmigration?
Ren said, "Falling flowers follow the flowing stream; the bright moon ascends the solitary peak. When Ren was about to pass away, he burned [his body].
Sitting cross-legged in incense smoke, he said, "When the incense smoke has vanished, I shall depart. And so it was.
Liang Guangren was a man of unknown origins; the monastic community called him "Short Uncle" because of his short and unimposing physique.
Nevertheless, his spirit was refined and vigorous. In his preaching, he did not employ a staff or whisk, but would instead frequently stroke and caress [his audience].
Mushé (Wood Snake). When asked about him, people would say, "He is the daughter of the Cao family. His intellectual capacity and discernment were vast and profound;
scholars from all quarters held him in awe and respect. He was truly a preeminent and heroic figure among the disciples of Dongshan.
A monk asked, "What is the house style of the Master? Ren replied, "The five-cun head-wrap. The monk asked again, "What is the five-cun head-wrap? Ren replied, "Within the circle."
"It cannot be grasped. One day, Yunmen raised the case of Xiangyan’s "heavy meaning" (*zhìzhòng*)—which could not be fully expressed—and asked Jingqing, "How do you understand this?
Jingqing said, "It is entirely returned to the heavy meaning. Yunmen said, "Why can it not be fully [expressed]? Jingqing said, "Within this, there is no path of meaning.
Yunmen said, "Only then does it satisfy the sick monk's intent. On the winter solstice, he ascended the hall. A monk...
Question: "What is the meaning of winter's arrival? Ren replied: "The capital produces great yellow.

When Ren passed away, he spoke a verse: "My path lies beyond the azure void; White clouds rest in their leisurely stillness. In this world there is a rootless tree; Yellow leaves are sent back by the wind.

He also composed verses on the four elements and other topics. A brief version of Master Li’s *Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra* circulated in the world. After his remains had been placed in the sarcophagus, there was...

Zhi Xian of Qingzhou during the Liang dynasty stood seven chi tall. He had read secular books and possessed great talent and capability; his kinsmen and associates held him in high esteem.
Shortly thereafter, he left the household life and traveled to Tan and Xiang, where he served Chan Master Dayuan at Mount Wei. One day, the Master said:
[Zhaozhou] said: "I do not ask you about what you have been able to explain from the scriptures and commentaries throughout your life.
Rather, before you had even emerged from the womb and before you could distinguish east from west, bring me a single phrase; I wish to know you. Xian was at a loss for a long time.
After some moments, he advanced several words to set forth his understanding, but Zhaozhou would not accept it. Xian said, "Then I pray the Master [will speak]."
Xian said, "I shall speak with so-and-so. Shan replied, "I am capable of speaking; this is my own view. What benefit would it be for your eyes?
Xian then returned to the hall and searched through all the sayings he had collected from various quarters, yet not a single word could serve as a response.

He sighed, saying, "A painted cake cannot satisfy hunger. Thereupon, he burned them all and departed from the mountain in tears and lamentation, saying, "In this life I shall not study the Buddha-dharma;
I have already become a long-wandering monk who sells rice. This may perhaps spare me from forced labor.
Arriving at Nanyang, he beheld the traces left by National Teacher Huizhong and settled there to rest. One day, while weeding...
While clearing away grass and wood from his thatched cottage, he happened to throw down some tiles and pebbles, which struck a bamboo and produced a sound. At this, he attained great enlightenment.
He immediately returned home, bathed, and burned incense. Bowing toward the mountain from afar, he said, "The Master’s compassion surpasses that of my own parents.
Had he explained this to me at that time, would there have been such a thing as today? He then composed a verse, saying: "A single blow caused me to forget all that I knew."
There is no longer any need for further cultivation or maintenance. Every movement of the countenance reveals the ancient path; one does not fall into the trap of silent, obscure mechanisms.
Everywhere there are no traces; this is the majestic deportment beyond sound and form. Those who have attained the Way in all quarters all say this is the "highest-grade capacity.

He ascended the hall and said: "The Way arises from self-awakening; it does not reside in words and speech. Moreover, in its profound intimacy and majestic presence, it has never had any separation. There is no need to exert the mind or will."

Borrowing his majestic radiance for a time, the full efficacy of daily practice was realized. Those who had strayed on the path turned back of their own accord; those who came to inquire and study flowed together like water descending a slope, eventually forming a flourishing community.
He was posthumously titled "Inheriting the Lamp," and his stupa was named "Extended Blessings."
During the Datong era of the Liang dynasty, he was the son of the Liu family in Huaining. At an early age, he served under Chan Master Mantang of Baotang in Luoyang and left the household life.

He first practiced *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing), and when his mastery of this discipline was nearly complete, he felt that the ocean of nature in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* could not possibly be confined to such a limited scope.
He then took up his staff and hurried toward the assembly at Cuiwei, where he joined Yuan Tong of Funiu to seek further instruction on the Great Illumination of the Patriarchal Intent.
Upon returning to his hometown, he settled in a thatched hut on Mount Toudi to receive students. One day, the Venerable Zhaozhou Yan arrived in Tongcheng County while on alms-round;
Xitong also came out of the mountain, and they met on the road, though they did not yet know one another. Zhaozhou observed him closely.
Knowing they were the same person, he asked, "Are you not the Master of Mount Toudi? Tongsong replied, "Please give me some money for tea and salt.
Zhenzhou had already entered the mountain and was sitting in his hut when Tongsong arrived later, carrying a bottle of oil. Zhenzhou said, "I have long heard of Mount Toudi;
having come here, I see only an oil-seller. Tongsong replied, "You see only the oil-seller; as for the..."

He tested Touzi. Zhaozhou asked, "What is Touzi? Touzi lifted up an oil jar and said, "Oil! Oil! Zhaozhou asked again, "How is it when one attains life within death? Touzi said, "It is not permitted to travel by boat;

at dawn you must arrive. Zhaozhou said: [Note: This dialogue is a classic example from the *Wumenguan* (Gateless Barrier) case 30, where Zhaozhou’s final remark is often rendered as "If you do not understand this, you will be lost for a thousand years."]

"I have long been waiting for the white; you, moreover, wait for the black. From that time on, his reputation spread throughout the world, and those seeking his counsel flocked to him like spokes converging at the hub.
During the Zhonghe era, when the rebels of Chao were in turmoil across the realm, there was a ringleader who, brandishing a blade, questioned Tong, saying:
"What is the purpose of staying here? he asked. "The color remains the same and does not change. In response to this Buddhist teaching, they all disciplined their minds.
The ringleader suddenly prostrated himself, stripped off the clothes he was wearing, and offered them [to the master]. Moved to tears, he departed.

On the sixth day of the fourth month of the Jiashu year, the fourth year of the Qiandehua era of the Liang dynasty, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture at the age of ninety-six, with forty-six years of ordination. This was his total tenure on this mountain.
It has been more than thirty years since he passed away.
According to the Liang edition, Benji’s secular surname was Huang. He was a native of Putian in Quanzhou. At the age of nineteen, he entered the monastic order at Yunmian Mountain in Fuzhou.
At twenty-two, he received full ordination. His conduct was mature and dignified; those who knew him recognized him as [a man of great potential].
At the beginning of the Chengtong era, the study of Chan was flourishing. At that time, Chan Master Wuben Jia resided at Dongshan.
Xueji went back and forth to him to seek instruction. Dongshan asked, "What is your name, Ācārya? Xueji replied, "Benji. Dongshan said, "Speak further beyond this.
Xueji said, "I do not speak. Dongshan asked, "Why do you not speak? Xueji said, "Beyond this, there is no name 'Ben'."
Ji was a man of profound depth, and Dongshen held him in high esteem. When Ji took his leave of Dongshan, Dongshan asked, "Where are you going?
Ji replied, "I am going to the place that does not change. Dongshan said, "If it does not change, how can there be going? Ji replied, "Even going does not change.
Later, having accepted an invitation, he appeared in the world at Caoshan in Fu province and subsequently moved to Mount Heyu. At both locations, his Dharma assemblies were flourishing. A monk asked:
"Do the eyebrows and the eyes still recognize one another? Jì said, "They do not recognize one another. The monk asked, "Why do they not recognize one another?
Jì said, "Precisely because they are in the same place. The monk said, "If that is so, then they are not distinct. Jì said, "The eyebrow is simply not the eye.
The monk asked, "What is the eye? Jì said, "The very point. The monk asked, "What is the eyebrow? Jì said, "The very point."
Ji said, "Cao Shan, however, still harbors doubt. The monk asked, "Why does the Master harbor doubt?
Ji said, "If you did not harbor doubt, you would have reached the definitive point. He was asked: "The teachings state that 'the great ocean does not harbor corpses. What is the ocean?"
Ji said, "It encompasses all existence. The monk asked, "Why does it not harbor a corpse? Ji said, "That which has ceased breathing does not cling to it.
The monk asked, "Since it encompasses all existence, why does it not cling to that which has ceased breathing?
Ji said, "All existence is not its achievement; the cessation of breath possesses its virtue. The monk asked, "Is there still something further beyond this? Ji said, "I say there is."

The Way is attained through non-attainment; yet what can be done about the Dragon King brandishing his sword? While Xuán was occupied with responding to inquiries, he further expounded the theory of the "Five Ranks of Sovereign and Subject" to elucidate its subtleties.
He also composed poems in response to those of Hánshān Zǐ, which circulated throughout the world; their diction is elegant and refined, worthy of admiration.
Shortly thereafter, he manifested illness and passed away at the age of sixty-two and thirty-seven years since his ordination. His disciples erected a stupa to enshrine his remains.
Nanyue Xuantai later composed the inscription for his stupa.
Liang Cunsou was a disciple of Shishuang; he resided at Pusbak, where Wang Youqian, the military governor of the region, treated him with exceptional courtesy.

He frequently invited him into the provincial seat to discuss the Way, always arranging his own mat to face the master as a sign of respect. Furthermore, his offerings and provisions were abundant. And...
He was requested to serve as a Bodhisattva Preceptor. He resided on Mount Qishan, where his followers gathered in great numbers; he was truly no less than the "community of withered trees.

He passed away at the age of ninety-three. His remains were kept in the stupa for one month, during which time his beard and hair grew back; he therefore shaved them off once more before being interred in the pagoda.
Liang Shiyuan was the son of the Xu family of Minyue. Having received the mind-seal of Chan Master Yantou Quanhuo, he initially remained silent and withdrawn, but later became known for his wisdom.
Encouraged to benefit sentient beings, he acceded to the requests of the assembly and resided at Ruiyan Monastery in Tai.

In governing others and cultivating himself, he was rigorous and orderly, adhering strictly to the rules of discipline; thus, among those who discuss monastic centers in the region south of the Yangtze River, he is held in the highest esteem. Furthermore—
Yan’s discernment was sharp and swift; even Jingqing Daofu was once defeated by him whenever he posed a question. One day, three Indian monks arrived. Yan asked, "When did you leave India?
They replied, "This morning. Yan asked, "Are you not weary? They replied, "We forget weariness for the sake of the Dharma.
Yan summoned the *karmadāna* and had them enter the hall to be settled as visiting elders (*upādhyāya*). The next day, when Yan sought them out, they were nowhere to be seen. (Recorded in the *Wu*)
The Qian clan of Yue repeatedly invited him, but he accepted only once before resigning with great reluctance.

Some said that his granary was naturally full, so that it did not depend on cultivation or harvest, yet the community was constantly provided for. Suddenly, he encountered a village woman who said to him, "Return quickly;

you must save the lives of many hundreds and thousands of creatures. The woman immediately arrived home, where her daughter-in-law was just then carrying a bamboo basket, picking field snails. The woman—
He suddenly released them into the water, saying, "Clouds. Furthermore, several households of donors invited him to a vegetarian feast on the same day, yet Yan responded to all of them at once;

thus, his power of transformation can be known. When he passed away, just as the cremation was about to begin, a giant serpent climbed to the tip of a tree and threw itself into the mass of flames, transforming together with him.
Alas, how extraordinary! When the firewood was exhausted, the *śarīra* (relics) flew forth and scattered upon the grasses and trees, their brilliance and purity surpassing anything in the world.
Liang Judu, surnamed Guo, was a native of Nancheng in Linchuan. At the age of fourteen, he entered the monastic life at Mantian Temple in Luling.
He subsequently traveled to Mount Song to receive full ordination. Because he did not find resonance with the assembly at Cuiwei, nor with Deshan, he eventually settled at Dongshan.
One day he asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Dongshan replied, "Wait..."
"The cave-water flows upstream. He spoke thus to you; from this point, he first awakened.
Among the common crowd for eight years, King Ma of Chu heard of his reputation and revered him, inviting him to reside at Miaojian Monastery on Longya Mountain.

Those who followed him with their alms-staves numbered nearly five thousand. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Those who study the Way must pass through the Buddhas and patriarchs before they can attain it. What he...
According to the way of the ancient worthies, it is only when one regards the ancestral teachings of the Buddha as the enemy that gives birth to them, that one has the standing to converse with them.
If you do not penetrate beyond the Buddhas and patriarchs, you will be deceived by them. At that time, a monk asked, "Do the Buddhas and patriarchs have a mind to deceive people?
