During the Kaiping era of the Liang dynasty, he traveled north to Heshuo and south to the Jianghuai region, yet until then, he had attained nothing.

Upon arriving in Hannan, he met Yanjun of Guanyin Monastery, who asked Huai, "Have you heard of Chan Master Datong of Mount Touzi? He replied, "I have. The master asked, "Have you ever gone to see him? He replied, "No."
"I have never seen such a person before," he said. "You should go at once; do not delay. Thereupon, the assembly agreed that this was so. Having met him, their conversation indeed accorded perfectly.
In the second year of the Qianhua era, [Dongshan] went specifically to visit Master Jun and thanked him, saying, "Had it not been for you, I would have nearly spent this life in vain."
At that time, Master Jun was residing in Bianjing; he consequently remained at the assembly to assist with the Dharma seat.
In the autumn of the fourth year, Zhixiu, the abbot of the Arhat Temple in Baoji Ward, wished to nominate the assembly to succeed him.

The assembly would not permit it, further noting that the temple was cramped and dilapidated, insufficient to accommodate the multitude. Suddenly, the patrons Shangshu Zuocheng Wu Ai and Bingbu Shilang Zhang Gun together...
The Master requested a plaque from the court, and by imperial decree, the name "Tiānshòu" (Heavenly Longevity) was bestowed. From that time on, the community flourished and grew.
In the seventh year of the Tiānfú era, he was granted purple robes; at the beginning of the Kāiyùn era, he was conferred the title "Fǎxiàng" (Dharma-Aspect).

Thus, over a period of thirty-five years, he provided meals for more than two million monks. In all matters of acquisition and expenditure, there was not the slightest discrepancy, and his integrity and conduct remained pure and unblemished.
This can be seen in general. On the twenty-sixth day of the seventh month in the third year [of the reign], he entrusted his instructions to his disciples and passed away with serene composure.
He was sixty-seven years of age and forty-eight years since his ordination. His remains were cremated, and the *śarīra* relics were collected.
A stupa was erected in the Cangyang Township of the Eastern Suburbs, and Bian Guidang, the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice, composed the inscription for its stele.
Sengquan was a native of Kunshan in Wu. His father took him along to Jiyang for trade.

Although he was still young, Sengquan took delight in the practice of meditative stillness and earnestly entreated his father to allow him to leave the household life. His father grew angry and did not respond.

Later, observing that his father’s expression had softened slightly, he petitioned once more. He continued in this manner three or four times without ceasing. His father finally gave a perfunctory assent, whereupon Sengquan took his leave and fled.
He went to the abode of Master Qingping of Jiangxia. Qingping asked him, "What do you seek by coming here? He replied, "I am determined to seek the Dharma.
Qingping took pity on his youth and keen intelligence, and accepted him as a disciple. He served Qingping with exceptional diligence. Before long, he had his hair shaved and received full ordination.
On one occasion, he said to others, "I have heard that in learning there is no constant teacher. I am not a bitter gourd; how could I be tied down to one place?"
It was thus that he eventually arrived at the Southern Pagoda of Mount Yichun to serve under Master Yong. He attended him for several years and traveled frequently to Luling.
When Yang Gong, the Magistrate of Anfu County, established Yingguo Chan Monastery, he invited [the Master] there.
Upon Yang’s departure after his term ended, the Master moved to Qinghua Monastery on Mount Hegu. A monk from the same hometown said to him, "Your parents..."
"Is it not your intention to go to that state? The next day, he left Quehu Lake and traveled east to pay his respects to Wenmu Wang of the Wu-Yue Qian clan at Qiantang.
The king provided him with robes, bedding, and alms bowls in abundance. Having established a monastery on Yunfeng Mountain, he renamed it Qinghua and invited [Zhaozhou] to reside there.
Seekers flocked to him in great numbers. A monk asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?"
Fufu said: "A wooden crane flies atop the capital of a flower-tablet pillar; meeting a man who has attained the Way on the road, he does not respond with speech or silence.
I wonder, what does he use to respond? Fufu said: "The pupils in one's eyes are like a whistle blown. Question: "When a deceased monk passes away and undergoes transformation, where does he go?
Answer: "The long river flows without interruption; gathered foam drifts at the mercy of the wind. Question: "Does he still receive offerings?"

Question: Is there no ritual sacrifice? Answer: Ritual sacrifice is not non-existent. Question: How is the ritual sacrifice performed? Answer: When the fisherman’s song is raised with the oar, its sound is heard within the valley.
Chonghyeon (Chung-hyeon) presented a purple *kāṣāya* robe as a gift, which he bestowed upon Nae-ryang (Naeryang), who subsequently changed his name to Master Chunil (Chun-il).
In the seventh month of autumn in the fourth year of Kaewon (the Dingwei year), he manifested a slight illness and said to his disciples: "Life..."

When arising, it is according to the Dharma; when passing away, it is according to the Dharma. This arising and passing away is beyond the reach of verbal discourse. He passed away while seated in meditation.
At that time, there was a great wind and torrential rain that blew down houses and uprooted trees. He was sixty-six years of age and forty-five years since his ordination.
He was interred in a northern ravine of the mountain where he resided. The śramaṇa Huizheng composed the inscription.
Jingzhao of Jin was a native of Goryeo. Having entered China, he received the Dharma from Xuefeng.

Undaunted by cold or heat, he devoted himself to all communal duties, earning the awe and respect of the monastic community. He was known as Zhao Buna. Initially, he resided at Qiyun Mountain in Wuyi;
subsequently, he moved to Jingqing Hermitage in Yue, and later to Baoci Temple in Hangzhou. While Jingzhao was at Qiyun, he ascended the hall and addressed the assembly:
After a long silence, he suddenly raised his hand and looked at the assembly, saying, "Beg for a little bit! Beg for a little bit!
A monk asked, "At the assembly on Vulture Peak, the Dharma was transmitted from one to another; I wonder, with what will Qiyun entrust you? He replied, "I cannot let you waste Qiyun.
When he was at Jingqing, a monk asked, "The path beyond the ordinary, which not even a thousand sages can transmit—" [The text here is incomplete.]
[The Master] examined who had transmitted [the Dharma]. He said, "Even the thousand sages doubt me. [The student] asked, "Is this not the transmission itself?
He replied, "When Emperor Wu of Jin executed Ji Kang, it was during the time of Baozi. A monk asked, "Regarding 'saving sentient beings beneath the Bodhi tree,' what is the Bodhi tree?
He replied, "It is very much like a *kuli* tree. The monk asked, "Why is it like a *kuli* tree? He replied, "Originally, it is not..."

A fine horse requires no laborious striking with the shadow of a whip. Later, the Prince Zhongxian of Wu-Yue welcomed the sacred remains and ritual implements of the Great Being Fu Xi of Jinhua and enshrined them for worship at the Yuan-shuai Fu (Metropolitan Commandery).
He further constructed Longhua Temple and erected a stupa to house them, entrusting their care to the abbot.
Eventually, the stupa was moved to Mount Daci.
Ji Zhi-lang was the son of the Huang family of Chengwu in Danzhou. His mother, Liu, once dreamed that several śramaṇas were sitting in a circle preaching the Dharma;
upon waking, the sound still resonated clearly in her ears. She subsequently conceived, and Lang was born with a simple, pure, and tranquil nature.
He had no taste for luxury or ostentation. In his early years, he relied upon Hutong Monastery in Caizhou; having completed the required period of practice, he underwent tonsure and dyeing.

He immediately studied the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya) and the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra*, gaining a rough grasp of their essential threads. He sighed and said, "To call this 'leaving the secular world' yet to find oneself still hindered—how could this be my true aspiration?
Thereupon, carrying his alms bowl, he traveled southward. Arriving at Hengyang, he read the Tripitaka at Banyue Temple on Mount Heng. Upon reaching...
Dongshan ascended Xuefeng; having merged the Buddha-vehicle and the Patriarchal Seal with this very mind, he subsequently returned to instruct his native village for over forty years.

He passed away on the twenty-third day of the eleventh month of the Dingwei year, toward the end of the Kaiyun era. He was seventy-seven years of age and fifty-three years of *dharma-lakṣa* (monastic seniority).
His body was cremated, and after the *śarīra* were collected, a stupa was erected. [This record was written by] the Vice Governor of Daming Prefecture.
Li Hxuanwen composed the inscription for his stele.
Han Haengsu was a native of the Chen family of Quanzhou. In his youth, he relied upon Beoyeongam Hermitage to study and practice the sutras and vinaya.

At the age of thirteen, he shaved his hair; at eighteen, he went to the Precept Platform of Changnyeokbu to receive full ordination. At eighteen, he immediately traveled to Seongbong to follow [Master Cheonhui].
Chan Master Cunen was struck by the intensity of his mind-to-mind transmission. Although he had followed the assembly in requesting instruction, he had not yet found a clear direction.

Just as he was preparing to take his leave of Cunen to travel through the two Zhejiang provinces, Cunen pointed to his ear and said, "The contours of your ear are fortunately long, yet the pendants hanging from it are still short. I shall extend them for you."

On another day, he hoped that those who beheld his physical marks might be inspired to resolve their minds toward enlightenment; thus, he raised his hand and pulled [the tree] three times, and it immediately passed over his shoulder.
In the second year of the Tiānchéng era of the Later Táng dynasty, he arrived in Qiántáng, where the entire city came to gaze upon him in reverence and offerings poured in from all sides.

Consequently, he selected a site at the foot of Gāofēng Mountain to the west of the city gates and built a dwelling there. Before long, it became a large monastery complex. However, Huìxiū did not engage in public preaching or lead congregational chanting.
He sat upright all day long like a wooden puppet. When asked about matters concerning the Chan school, he would simply smile.

Whenever he went out, men and women would clamor after him, playfully pulling his ears down beneath his chin and tying them together; at that time, he was popularly known as "The Monk with Long Ears."
In the third month of the following year, he passed away while sitting in meditation at midnight.

His patrons and disciples had lacquered his seat and bedding as a means of securing their long-term security. After some time, he appeared again in a dream to the local governor, Chen Rong, saying, "My seat remains unfinished;
go and look at it. When they examined it, the seat was indeed not lacquered. They immediately ordered craftsmen to complete the work.
Zhou Wenyi, whose secular surname was Lu, was a native of Yuhang. At the age of seven, he took refuge with Chan Master Quanwei of Zhitong Monastery in Xinding and received the tonsure.
Barely having reached his early twenties, he followed Vinaya Master Huijiao to receive full ordination at Kaiyuan Temple in Yue.
Subsequently, Master Jiao further propagated the Way of the Vinaya extensively at Yuwang Temple on Mount Mao.
Yi continued to receive instructions from him. Before long, he traveled south and stayed at the Dharma assembly of Changqing. Shortly thereafter, he departed for Lake Xiang with a companion;
passing through Zhangpu, they encountered Master Luohan Chen at Dizang Temple. Master Chen asked, "Where are you going, Venerable?"

He replied, "I am traveling on foot. The Master asked, "What is the matter with traveling on foot? He replied, "I do not know. The Master said, "Not knowing is most intimate. Fayu attained realization;
he then sought instruction and resolution from Master Chen. Later, he arrived at Linchuan, where the Prefect invited him to take up the abbacy of Chongshou Monastery.
After the tea ceremony concluded, the fourfold assembly gathered around as he ascended the seat. Fayu addressed the assembly, saying, "Since all of you have come here..."
"In this matter, I, this mountain monk, cannot remain silent. I shall briefly cite a single, ready-made koan of an ancient master.
Take care. With these words, he descended from his seat. At that time, a monk came forward from below the seat to pay his respects. Yuanze said, "Ask well.
Just as the monk was about to pose his question, Yuanze said again, "Elder, before you have opened the hall, I do not converse with you. Thereupon, the monk stepped forward.
Zuò. Since Changqing’s time, Yì has frequently cited Master Lèng’s verse, asking: "What is the body that stands alone, revealed amidst the myriad phenomena?
As you were just now raising your whisk, Yì said: "Even understanding it this way, how can you attain it? You then stepped forward and said:
"What is the Master’s honorable view? Zhiyi said, "What do you call 'the myriad phenomena'? Zhenjin said, "The ancients did not negate the myriad phenomena.
Zhiyi said, "'Amidst the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. What is there to say about negating or not negating? At these words, Zhenjin finally attained awakening.

He recited a verse to express his sincere devotion. The Prince of Jiangnan, having received his instructions and admonitions, welcomed him to reside at Ba’en Chan Monastery and conferred upon him the title Jinghui (Pure Wisdom).
He ascended the hall and said: "The ancients said, 'I shall stand on the ground and wait for you to build it. Today, this mountain monk sits on the ground and waits for you to build it.
Is there any principle here? Or is there not? Which is intimate and which is distant? Try to judge for yourselves."

While at Qingliang, he ascended the hall and said: "For those who have left the household life, it is sufficient simply to accord with the times and seasons. When it is cold, it is cold; when it is hot, it is hot.
If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should contemplate the causes and conditions of the seasons.

Have you not seen how the Master Shitou, upon reading the *Zhaolun*, immediately understood the words of the *Cantongqi*: 'The mind of the Great Sage of India was secretly transmitted from east to west'? How could this be otherwise?
"Is it not that one realizes all things as oneself? If you, the Elder, were able to realize all things as yourself, then throughout the entire earth, not a single dharma would be visible.
Later he said, "Do not let your time be spent in vain. This was the ancient master’s earnest and repeated exhortation, fearing that you might lose your integrity as time passes.
Take care. The seventh month of autumn, the fifth year of Xian-de, the Wu-wu year.
On the seventeenth day, he manifested illness. On the fifth day of the intercalary month, having finished shaving his head and bathing, he assembled the community to bid them farewell;
sitting in the lotus posture, he passed away. He was seventy-four years of age and fifty-five years since his ordination. His posthumous title was Dharma-Eye (Dafayan).
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa named Wuxiang in Danyang Township, Jiangning County. The Later Ruler composed a text to commemorate his virtues, and Han Xi-zai inscribed the epitaph.
Zhou Huiming was the son of the Qiantang Jiang family. From his youth, he investigated the three studies (*tripiṭaka*).

Having traveled extensively to consult various masters, he eventually received the essential instructions of Master Qingliang Yigong from Linchuan. He subsequently retired to Baiisha on Mount Tiantai to further investigate his realization.

Whenever fellow practitioners of the profound path came to challenge him, they were all defeated and none dared approach; consequently, they branded his teachings as demonic and slandered him from all sides.

He arose [from his retreat] during the Qiandao era of the Han dynasty. At that time, Master Can of Cuiyan in Yinzhou led various Chan masters to the Sengzhu Sishen Monastery to examine and debate him.
His clear and responsive answers were all in accord with the fundamental tenets of the school.
Not long after, the Qian family of Wuyue built Dabao’en Temple and invited him to serve as its abbot, bestowing upon him the title Chan Master Yuantong Puzhao. Xiansha...

The Way [of Buddhism] relied upon him for its revitalization. He passed away during the Xian-de era. At that time, it was the height of the great summer heat, and the assembly wished to bury him immediately.
His disciple Yong’an said, "I know my Master’s intention; there will certainly be no burial, but rather cremation. From this, they obtained five-colored śarīras.
Zhouxing traveled on foot from Yamen, where he attained the Dharma at Lumen Mountain in Xiangyang.

He subsequently journeyed to Mount Konglu, where the Emperor of Southern Tang, having heard his reputation, invited him to take charge of Qixian Temple. Before even a month had passed, Zhouxing withdrew to reside in Fochuan Rock.
The rock was steep and precipitous, difficult to ascend; it contained a stone chamber, deep and secluded, suitable for meditative retreat, from which one could look down upon the Jinsiu Valley.
The valley was exceptionally secluded and magnificent. Because he had no disciples to attend to him, he relied on neighboring monks who came and went from time to time;
thus, his needs were never lacking. There was always a strange deer that stayed with him, which would lie beneath the stone eaves whenever night fell.

A bird with a scarlet pouch also nested among the stone walls. Emperor Yuanzong summoned him three times, yet he never rose to comply. One day, suffering from a slight illness, he spoke to the man [who attended him]:
He said, "Roll up the curtain; I am going, I am going. Just as the curtain was being rolled up, he descended from his bed and walked three or four steps.
He then stood upright and passed away. He was approximately seventy years of age. His remains were collected after cremation and enshrined in a stupa on the back of a cliff.
King Yeonjong commissioned an artisan to paint his portrait for veneration.
Song Yansheng was born into the Ye family of Jinyun. During the Zhengming era of the Liang dynasty, he shaved his head and received full ordination.

He immediately studied the *vinaya* under the Vinaya Master Jingxiao, from whom he attained its essential subtleties. Soon thereafter, he departed to travel through Min, where he followed Chan Master Changqing to inquire about the essentials of the mind.
He subsequently returned to Zhejiang at the invitation of patrons and resided at the Liutong Monastery in Danqiu for a long time.

When the Qian family of Wuyue heard of his reputation, they welcomed him to the Court of Meritorious Ministers. Later, he gathered disciples at Longhua Temple within the provincial administration seat.
He sought a life of detachment and had no personal嗜好 (shihao—pleasures or preferences); he took it as his sole responsibility to benefit all things and succor the masses.

Whatever offerings he received from lay devotees, he entrusted entirely to the temple’s permanent endowment. His gate remained unlocked and his rooms were free of chests or boxes. Whenever nuns came to pay their respects, he would immediately...
He dismissed them. When he encountered Dujie, monks from four directions gathered in great numbers, crowding around him; daily, thousands of monks were fed, yet he never suffered from want.
He passed away at his place of residence during the Jianlong era of the Song dynasty.
Song Daoyan was the son of the Wu family of Pujin. He possessed a handsome appearance and a tall, robust physique; on his chest were seven black moles, shaped like the Big Dipper.
In his youth, he relied upon Master Zhenji of Xiyuan Dadao Monastery on Mount Zhongtiao to receive the tonsure and ordination.
Once he had mastered the precepts and discipline, he entered Wutai Mountain in Yanmen to behold the Great Being Mañjuśrī. From then on, he traveled extensively through various Chan assemblies.
He also visited Chan Master Yi of Chongshou Monastery in Linchuan, where he suddenly attained realization of the mind-ground.

While reading the Tripitaka at an ancient temple in Quzhou, Mañjuśrī again manifested a wondrous form while he was sitting in meditation. Later, when he went to Ningbo to pay respects at the Yuyang Pagoda, he saw that the śarīra were red in color.
As he walked outside the hanging bell tower, a profound mixture of sorrow and joy welled up within him. Thereupon, Grand Master Guangwen compiled...
The Emperor invited him to the Mountain Hermitage (Shanzhai) to perform the Samantabhadra Repentance Rite for twenty-one days.
He was moved by the auspicious descent of Samantabhadra, whose elephant’s trunk rested upon the site of the ritual arena.

The King of Wuyue, the Qian family, welcomed him into his palace, conferred upon him the Bodhisattva Precepts, and constructed a great monastery named Huiri Yongming to house him; he further honored him with the title Chan Master Cihua Dinghui.

This was his title. He was granted a monthly stipend to demonstrate the honor accorded to him. On the eighteenth day of the ninth month of the second year of Jianlong (the *xin-you* year), he manifested illness and passed away.
As his body was being placed in the coffin, a white light radiated forth during the day. In the tenth month, he was cremated at Longjing, where countless *śarīra* relics were collected.
There was a butcher who, believing that his own transgressions could not be expiated, spread out his garment toward a pyre of fire.

He refused the request and died in the fire. Within a brief moment, seven grains were obtained. In the *Gengwu* year of the Kaibao era, National Teacher Shao of Tiantai constructed a stupa to bury him.
In the *Guiyou* year, a white light frequently rose from the top of the stupa. His karmic conditions, dialogues, and sayings are fully recorded in the *Chuan Deng Lu*.
Song Congyan, surnamed Mi, was a native of Jimen. At the age of fifteen, he took leave of his parents and entered the monastic life at Huijue Temple in Bingzhou.
Having received full ordination, he traveled extensively through the gardens of the teachings. He then sighed, saying, "The study of written texts merely exhausts the spirit;
how could it possibly serve to untangle entanglements or loosen bonds? Thereupon, he took up his staff and traveled south to seek instruction, where he met Master Dun.

In the mountains of Longya, he resolved his doubts. During the Qingtai era of the Tang dynasty, when the Central Plains were peaceful and tranquil, Yan returned to the north and took up residence at Mount Songxiao.
Before long, lay devotees flocked to him like echoes, and enlightened disciples followed him like shadows. Consequently, the halls, pavilions, altars, and courtyards were completed.

Throughout the three dynasties of Jin, Han, and Zhou, he received the utmost imperial favor and honors. On the third day of the eighth month in the second year of the Kaibao era, he manifested [his passing].
He fell ill and passed away.
Song Shaoyan was the son of the Liu family in Yongzhou; his mother was Lady Zhang. She conceived him after being moved by a miraculous dream.

When Shaoyan was seven years old, he left home to receive the tonsure under Master Ga’gan of Gao’an. At the age of eighteen, he received full ordination. Thereafter, he traveled throughout various regions. And...
The excellence of Tiantai and Siming was what he studied and contemplated most deeply.
Having resolved his lingering doubts with Chan Master Deshao at Mount Yi in Linchuan, he subsequently stayed at the Zhenshen Baota Temple on the West Lake in Qiantang.

There, he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* day and night without ceasing. Suddenly, lotus flowers blossomed within the temple courtyard; people regarded this as the fruit of his spiritual refinement.
It is said that he was moved by such sincerity. In the second year of the Jiànlóng era, he vowed to emulate the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja by burning his body as an offering;

however, the Qián family of Wuyue, out of profound devotion, earnestly entreated him to desist, and thus he stopped. Furthermore, he once went to the Cáo'ē River intending to drown himself to feed the fish, but was rescued by fishermen who pulled him out;
in the end, he suffered no harm. He subsequently moved to Mount Fǎhuá in Yuè, but was summoned again to reside in Hángchōu.
In the summer of the fourth year of the Kaibō era (1071), while staying at Jōgyō-in, he suddenly composed several gāthās and said to his disciples:
"Throughout my life, I have recited the sutras twenty thousand times. My sole wish was to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). Now, that time has come."
He passed away while seated in meditation. His age was seventy-three and his years of ordination fifty-five. All expenses for his funeral were provided by the royal court.
Through cremation, śarīra relics were obtained and enshrined within the portrait hall, where they remain imperishable.

Song Deshao was the son of the Chen family of Jin-yun. Having left home to become a monk and received full ordination in his youth, he traveled to seek out masters of wisdom during the Tong-guang era.
He first resolved his mind at Touzi, and subsequently visited Master Longya Dun, asking him: "The majestic and honored one..."
"Why can one not approach it? Ya said, "It is like fire meeting fire. Question: "What if you suddenly encounter water?
Answer: "You do not understand my words. Furthermore, when "Heaven does not cover and Earth does not support," what then?
Answer: "It is simply so. Shao did not understand and requested further instruction. Ya said to Shao, "You will understand it yourself in the future. [He] asked Shushan.
"A hundred circuits, a thousand layers—what kind of realm is this? Shushan said, "Twisting straw ropes on the left to bind the sons of ghosts.
Jian said, "It does not fall within the bounds of past or present; I request the Master to speak. Shushan said, "I will not speak. Jian said, "Why do you not speak? Shushan said, [silence].
Within this, there is no distinction between existence and non-existence. [Shou] Jìn said, "Master, you have now spoken well. Sūshū was greatly startled.

In this manner, he visited fifty-four spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). However, Shao eventually grew weary of seeking instruction. Later, upon arriving at Línchuān, he merely followed the assembly.
One day, a monk asked Jinghuì, "What is a single drop of water from the Cáo source? Huì replied, "It is the Cáo..."
Yuan drew a drop of water. The monk was bewildered, but Huishao suddenly attained awakening by his side. He then reported what he had seen to Huiri.
Huiri said, "In the future, you shall become a teacher to kings; the light of your ancestral path will be great, and I am not your equal."
While traveling to Mount Tiantai, Qian Chu, the Governor of the province, who was the Prince of the state, heard of Xuefeng Chao’s reputation and invited him to inquire about the Way.

Chao knew that he would surely become noble in the future, and thus entrusted him with the teachings of the Buddha-Dharma. In the first year of the Qianguyu era of the Han dynasty (the Wushen year), Qian Chu indeed succeeded to the throne as King Zhongyi;
he immediately dispatched an envoy to welcome Chao and prostrated himself before him in the manner of a disciple. He then selected...

This site of exceptional topographical beauty was established as a *dharmapada*. Among its teachings, the *Prajñāpāramitā* was one such focus. He held twelve assemblies for opening the hall and preaching the Dharma; most of his words have not been recorded. Those who grasped his essential meaning spread throughout the world. Furthermore, Master Zhiyi’s commentaries and sub-commentaries were particularly numerous, but following the chaos of the Five Dynasties at the end of the Tang, they were lost and scattered abroad to various kingdoms, including Silla. To: the Great Master of the Three Treasures of the Great Tang, the Venerable Zhiyi. I, [Name], respectfully address you. I humbly submit that I have long cherished the desire to propagate the Mahayana teachings. However, since the fall of the Tang dynasty, due to the turmoil of the Five Dynasties, these texts have been lost and dispersed to foreign lands, such as Silla and other nations. Now, having heard that the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang has returned from the Western Regions and is currently residing at Ci’en Monastery in the Eastern Capital, I have ventured to request that he be granted permission to translate the scriptures. I pray that you will grant me this favor. I shall take up my brush and inkstone to record your instructions. I hope you will not refuse my earnest plea. I remain, with utmost sincerity, your humble servant. Thereupon, Zhongyi sought [the scriptures] from Goguryeo with letters and gifts.
It was thanks to Zhaor’s efforts that the entirety of the teachings and contemplations of this family were returned intact. Thus, the world regarded Zhaor as an incarnation of Jizhe.
In the fourth year of Kaibao (Xinwei), the western peak of Huading suddenly collapsed, its sound shaking near and far. Zhaor said, "How could I remain much longer? The following year—
In the sixth month, a great star fell upon the mountain peak, and the forest trees turned white. At Shaofang, he manifested illness at Lotus Flower Peak;
his disciples came to inquire after him as usual. On the twenty-eighth day, he gathered his disciples to speak his final parting words and then passed away.
He was eighty-two years old and had been a monk for sixty-three years.
Song Xingman was a native of Nanpu, Wanzhou. In his youth, he left Sichuan and traveled through the Chan assemblies of Tan and Xiang.

He stayed at Shishuang for the longest period of time; once the various masters there had passed away, he proceeded to Yuzhang, where he finally received instruction within the chamber of Daji (Huairang).
Subsequently, he traveled to Tiantai to visit its famous sites, eventually serving as the head of the tea service at Zhiyi’s hermitage on Mount Huading.
The Master was always serene and joyful throughout his life. He lived together with him for nearly ten years, yet never once saw him show a trace of resentment.
At night he would sleep on a mat of earth, removing his clothes to feed the fleas and lice.

In the morning, as he sat inside and outside his room, small trees growing on the branches of massive pines would bend their low branches as if to pay him homage. Those who perceived this deemed it extraordinary. His appetite was somewhat small. Four...
For ten years, they were extremely intimate; [Yi] hardly ever saw him urinate or defecate. At the beginning of the Kaibao era, he suddenly said to his friend, "I am about to depart.
You should recite the names of Mañjuśrī for me to assist me. His friend followed his instructions, and he then passed away while sitting upright.
He was approximately eighty years old. A verse he sang on the Way is still recited and circulated in the world.
Yan-shou of the Song dynasty was born into the Wang family of Qiantang. During the reign of the Qian family, Yan-shou served as a clerk overseeing military supplies for the two circuits of Zhejiang.
He was upright and sincere by nature and never spoke falsely. Every day he sat and recited the *Lotus Sūtra* without ceasing.
At that time, Master Can was flourishing in his teachings at Cuiyan in Yinzhou; Shou abandoned his wife and children to seek ordination.

Having received the precepts, he practiced meditation for ninety days on Mount Tianzhu at Tiantai, where a bird resembling a lapwing nested within the folds of his robes. Shortly thereafter, he went to pay his respects to the National Teacher.

Master Shao resolved his views and moved his residence to Xuedou Mountain. At the request of the Prince of Zhongyi, the Qian family, he performed the Vaipulya Repentance Rite for the sake of sentient beings.

He recited the Lotus Sūtra approximately thirteen thousand times. He authored records such as the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) and the *Wanshan Tonggui* (The Ten Thousand Good Deeds Return to One Source).
His construction of stupas and images was beyond reckoning. The King of Goryeo heard of him from afar.
His reputation spread far and wide. He dispatched messengers to present him with a *kāṣāya* robe woven of gold thread, a rosary of purple crystal, a golden water pitcher, and other such items.
Yanshou was diligent in his instruction and guidance, yet he devoted his primary attention to receiving beings and benefiting sentient life.
From the time he moved from Lingyin to Yongming, his public teachings were numerous; here, one or two instances are recorded. A monk asked: "What is the sublime purport of Yongming? Yanshou—
[Shou] said, "Add more incense. [Yun] said, "Thank you for the teacher’s instruction. [Shou] said, "Be glad; do not engage in conceptualization. Thereupon he spoke this verse:
"If you wish to know Yongming, look at the lake before the gate: When the sun shines, radiance arises; When the wind blows, waves are stirred.

A monk asked, "If one attains Buddhahood or becomes an Ancestor, can one still not escape the six realms of samsara? "Indeed, one cannot escape," [Shou] replied. "Nor can one escape. "Have you not yet? [the monk asked].
"Examine closely what it is that cannot be produced. Shou said, "It cannot be produced from the place where you ask.
A monk asked, "What is the Great Perfect Mirror? Shou said, "A broken sandpot. In the eighth year of the Kaibao era, he passed away at his residence.
He was seventy-two years old and had thirty-seven years of ordination. He was buried on Mount Daci.

Song Yuande was of the Huang family of Qiantang. His father, Chaoxiu, was a Confucian scholar skilled in painting; he had copied the Buddhist sketches of Zhou Fang and received the methods of brushwork from Li Changshi Shao of Wuxing.
After Yuande left the household life and received full ordination, he followed Chan Master Daofu of Tianlong to receive the essentials of the mind.
He traveled extensively to visit Yunju and Lufu in Jiangxi, and was subsequently summoned by the Li clan of Jiangnan.
He entered the inner sanctum (neidaochang) and was separately provided with a *arhat* hall for his residence, but he declined these honors.

He was instead ordered to dwell in a new monastery on Mount Lu, where the relevant authorities were commanded to arrange a formal procession of dignitaries to escort him; yet Dezhi declined them all, departing alone with only his water jar and alms bowl.
When he ascended the seat to deliver his teachings, it was truly remarkable to behold. The Chancellor Song Qiqiu served as his disciple. He passed away during the Kaibao era.
Song Wuen, whose courtesy name was Xiujǐ, was a native of Chángshú in Gūsū. His surname was Lù and his mother was of the Zhāng clan.
She once dreamed that a Buddhist monk entered her residence before she conceived. While still a young child, whenever he saw a śramaṇa, he would invariably rise to welcome and prostrate before him.

At the age of thirteen, upon hearing the *Amitābha Sūtra* being recited, he experienced a profound awakening and consequently sought to leave the household life. Although his relatives and kin tried to detain him, he could not be persuaded and thus shaved his head and donned the monastic robes.

At Xingfu Temple on Mount Po, during the Changxing era of the Tang dynasty, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*). He subsequently investigated the Nanshan Vinaya school at Huiju Temple on Mount Kun.
At the beginning of the Tianfu era of the Jin dynasty, he studied under Master Hao Duan of Xieli, where his brilliance and talent surpassed his contemporaries.
During the Kaiyun era of the Han dynasty, he relied upon Master Zhiyin of Ciguang Monastery in Qiantang to receive the Tiantai [teachings].

Regarding his exposition on the "Three Contemplations" and the "Six Stages of Realization," he thoroughly investigated the meanings of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Sūtra of the Radiance of the Tathāgata’s Wisdom*, and the *Treatise on Meditation* (*Zhiguan*).
Having completed these works, he further recounted that he had earned the reputation of being like indigo dyeing blue cloth or ice forming from water.

On the first day of the eighth month in the third year of the Yongxi era, at midnight, he beheld a white light emerging from a well; its brightness flickered and did not remain constant. Looking toward it, he said to his disciples, "My karmic retribution has reached its end. From that time forth, he ceased [all activity].

He maintained a vow of silence and devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. In a dream, he received the consecration (abhiṣeka) of the Patriarch, who embraced him while holding a golden incense burner and burned incense;
he circumambulated the Patriarch’s chamber three times and said, "I have come to welcome you. Upon waking, he still smelled a fragrant aroma.

On the twenty-fifth day, he summoned his disciples and expounded for them the essential points of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Facing west, he sat upright and passed away at the age of seventy-three and [several] years of ordination.
55. Upon cremation, countless *śarīra* relics were obtained, perfectly round and lustrous.
Sengyiji, courtesy name Changzhao, was surnamed Hu and was a native of Yongjia in Wenzhou. While still in the womb, his mother suddenly grew weary of meat and blood;

at birth, he was enveloped in a purple caul. When he emerged from the birthing bed, he did not cry. Having reached the age of childhood, he ultimately renounced the secular world to become a monk under Kaiyuan.
The monk Sici of the temple was taught the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and was able to recite it from memory after one year; the senior monks praised him for this.
Having received full ordination, he went to Kuaiji to study the Nanshan Vinaya, and subsequently traveled to Tiantai to investigate the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Previously, the writings left behind by Zhiyi had been scattered and fragmented—destroyed in the distant past by the military chaos of An Lushan and Shi Siming, and more recently by the destruction during the Huichang persecution.

Jian: The traces of the teachings had nearly been extinguished. Jì once found a commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* within the ancient collection at Jinhua and subsequently conceived the intention to compile it in order to restore its former integrity.
At that time, Master Shao of Tongxuan served as a Chan master to Qian Chu, the Prince Zhongyi of the Two Zhe region.
One day, while casually perusing the *Zhengjue ji* (Anthology of True Enlightenment) by Yongjia, he came across the passage concerning the four types of co-residence.
[Zhi]zhu said, "This is the limit. Zhongyi asked, "What kind of language is this? Shaor replied, "It is the language of the Teaching school;
we practitioners of Chan do not know it. He then had Jie summoned to inquire about its meaning.
When Jie arrived, he understood the previous intent and requested that Zhongyi dispatch a messenger to the maritime kingdom to deliver the letter. Thus, the Tiantai school reached that land.

To this day, we rely upon it. In the fifth year of the Taiping Xingguo era, an imperial edict was issued for monks and nuns throughout the realm to undergo examinations on their mastery of the scriptures.
Jing led his disciples from Luoxi toward the provincial seat to take the examination; they first took up residence in the temple pavilion atop the provincial seat.

This pavilion was pressed against a great mountain, and at night Jing dreamed that the pillar of the stupa sank into the earth. He alone felt ill omens from this, and moreover, the rain was falling with great intensity.

The site was moved to the western sector, but the mountain collapsed and the pavilion was crushed. At the Ling-shi Rock by the Sea Gate, the former Master Zhi (Zhiyi) resided during winter at the Daochang Monastery.

This location belongs to Huangyan; the assembly requested that Jing travel by boat across the sea to preach the "Chapter on the Water-Bearer" from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and practice the rite of releasing living beings as his regular custom.
The monastery’s icons were renovated anew. Upon hearing of this, the Emperor issued an edict dispatching a high-ranking official to escort [the Master].
Fashao entered the mountains to rebuild Shouchang Temple and conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon local officials.
At the beginning of the Yongxi era, he again conferred the precepts at Guangming Temple in Yong’an County.

There, as the sacred image had fallen into decay, he happened to discover within its belly an inscription of a vow made by the śramaṇa Xi Jiao in the sixth year of the Xiantong era of the Tang dynasty. Those who observed it recognized the traces of his profound stillness.
There was a prior karmic affinity [between him and the patrons]. In the fourth year, he traveled at the invitation of the prefectures of Linhai, Jin’yun, Yongjia, and Dongyang.

In the ninth month, he arrived from Jin’yun. In the tenth month, he took up residence in the abbot’s quarters of Qian Temple. On the fourth day of the eleventh month, he delivered his final instructions and entrusted his affairs to his successors;
he then passed away suddenly. He was sixty-nine years of age and fifty years since his ordination (*śrāmaṇera*). Previously, Jì had resided in Siming...
At Yuwang Temple, he dreamed that he ascended to the upper story of Guoqing Temple, where there stood a precious, adorned bannered throne inscribed with the words "Mañjuśrī’s Terrace.

It was bordered in front by a barrier of horse-restraining poles that could not be entered. Suddenly, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva pushed back the poles with his hand and emerged from within to receive him.
He immediately felt his own body merge with that of the Bodhisattva; from then on, his superior spirit increased daily as he progressed further.
He was possessed of great eloquence. He lectured numerous times on such sutras as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the *Vimalakīrti*, and the *Brahmajāla*;
on treatises such as the *Mohe zhiguan*, the *Jinbi*, and others; on contemplations such as the *Fajie huanyuan guan*; and on works including the *Xuanyi*, the *Canyuan chuan*, and the *Yongjia ji*.
He also authored several volumes of works, including the *Zhiguan yili*, the *Fahua shimiao buer men kejie*, and others.
Song Yong’an, surnamed Weng, was a native of Yongjia in Wenzhou. In his youth, he heard that the Great Master Hui-zheng of the same prefecture had a close correspondence with Sun He of Le’an;
consequently, he went to him to seek ordination. However, Master Zheng was by nature lofty and haughty, such that those who served him often left because they could not harmonize with him.
Yet Yong’an was so flexible and thorough in his conduct that he never offended him. His peers marveled at this, deeming it difficult for anyone else to match.
During the Tiānchéng era of the Táng dynasty, he followed his master to Qiántáng. Shortly thereafter, he withdrew to a secluded place to practice the dhūta austerities.
Later, he traveled to Fúmián to seek instruction from Chan masters; however, in both instances, he was forced to desist because the roads were blocked by the chaos of bandits and rebels.

He then relied upon National Teacher Sháo at Tiantái, where he completely resolved all his lingering doubts. Upon returning home to visit his family, [his father] rebuked him, saying: "You have abandoned..."
"To turn one's back on filial piety and support—how can such a crime be forgiven? Now that you have fortunately returned, do you have any plan to remedy your previous transgressions?
An knelt and replied, "I have done nothing but remain idle to evade my responsibility. Zheng nodded his approval.
The King of Wuyue, the Qian family, summoned him to reside at Ba’en Temple and conferred upon him the title of Chan Master; furthermore, he combined the *Huayan* and *Li lun* into a single scripture.

He recruited others to carve printing blocks and obtained offerings through almsgiving; he cultivated both fields of merit and maintained virtually no personal savings. He was truly one who embodied the refined purity of a disciple.
He passed away in the seventh year of the Kaibao era at the age of sixty-four, with forty-four years of ordination seniority (*dharma-vassa*).
At his cremation, the tongue remained unburnt even after repeated incineration.
It was praised with these words:
"Precepts, concentration, and wisdom are the compass for the student; The precepts capture and concentration binds, While wisdom is ultimately used to destroy [defilements]."
Not three, yet one; not one, yet three. Roots vary in being sharp or dull; few are able to master both.
The *Sūtra*, *Abhidharma*, and *Vinaya*—these are what they investigate and explore.
They take the aggregates (*skandha*) as their profound understanding and give rise to wondrous discourse. Yet the seal of the mind of *Nirvāṇa* remains long sealed therein.
Entrusted to Mahākāśyapa: Truly worthy was he; down to the time of Dharmatrāta, the Dharma was spread far and wide.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Tanne from Zhedong.
To have nothing and yet insist on seeking it from others is greed; to have something and yet withhold it from others is stinginess. Only...
Greed, if it is stinginess, is a great affliction for sentient beings within the three realms.
Therefore, within the teachings of the former Buddhas, one is instructed to eliminate greed through internal giving—namely, the head, eyes, hands, feet, teeth, hair, skin, and nails.
To eliminate stinginess through external giving, one is instructed to give away kingdoms, cities, wives, children, clothing, food, utensils, and playthings. Indeed, that which is cherished is greed.
Stinginess is the root of [attachment], and the body is, in turn, the root of love. Since all share this same body, they all share this same love.
Now, one who can forget what they love is capable of casting aside the self; one who extends their love is capable of benefiting others.
How, then, could greed and stinginess exist? Furthermore, when Śākyamuni Bhagavān was a Bodhisattva—
At that time, throughout the trichiliocosm, there was not even a space as small as a mustard seed where he did not sacrifice his body and life in his quest for bodhi.
Alas! His love reached such a point that he relinquished his own person to benefit others and thereby achieve bodhi.
Thus, whether it be [the love] itself or its opposite, these two categories are appended under the training in giving (*dāna-śikṣā*) to serve as an exhortation to the world.
The section on "Leaving the Body":
Sengqun of the Jin dynasty was a man of unknown origins who possessed noble conduct. He resided at Mount Huo in the middle of Lake Luo Hai.
On this mountain was a large rock several *zhang* wide, with a hollow in its center some six or seven feet deep, from which a spring issued; the water was sweet in taste.
The water was clear and crisp; moreover, by drinking it, one could remain without hunger. It was named "Basin Spring" (*Yuanquan*). The community relied on it to avoid the need for the five grains.
Tao Kui, the Governor of Jin’an, requested some from the community and sent it out of the mountains; however, as soon as it left, its foul odor became unbearable.

Despite this, Kui insisted on obtaining it, so he personally crossed the sea and reached the foot of the mountain. The wind and rain were so dark and oppressive that he remained there for several days, yet he was unable to acquire it.
He went there and sighed, saying, "I was truly speaking of the mountain's spirit; it has merely turned back my worldly carriage. He then departed.

Outside the temple was a stream that separated the monastery from the Yúnquán (Alms-Bowl Spring); it could not be crossed except by a narrow footbridge. One day, a duck with broken wings suddenly appeared, its body spanning the bridge.
Zhìqún wished to move it aside with his staff, but fearing he might cause the duck’s death, he did not drink from the spring for several days. Thus it happened.
He passed away at the age of one hundred and forty. On his deathbed, he said, "In my youth, I once broke the wing of a duck; this is the retribution for that.
Tancheng of the Song dynasty—his clan name is lost from the records—was a native of Hebei. While traveling through Pengcheng, he stayed overnight at an inn.

The master and mistress of the house were both over eighty years old; they were impoverished and had no children. Tancheng remained there to care for them, treating them as his own parents until the end of their lives.
Having buried him, they departed. Upon reaching Mount Jia, the people of Mount Jia reported that a tiger was being violent and could not be stopped.
Chen said, "The tiger is merely hungry; I shall satisfy it with my own body. He then removed his clothes and sat in the grass at night, vowing:

"May this flesh and blood become the flavor of nectar, filling the Dharma-realm, so that all sentient beings may cease their greedy and harmful intentions and obtain the unsurpassed food of the Dharma until the end of time. When he went to look at it the next day, there remained only the skulls;
the local people collected them to build a stupa, and from then on, the tiger's violence ceased forever.
Seng Fa-jin (also known as Dao-jin or Fa-ying) was born into the Tang family in Zhangye, Liangzhou.
From his youth, he was renowned for his ascetic practices and was held in high esteem by Juqu Mengxun. After Mengxun passed away, his son Jinghuan was defeated by the Hu.
His younger brother, Anzhou, was in power. That year there was a great famine. Sengjin repeatedly requested relief aid, but Anzhou did not respond.

Jin then took a knife and wrapped himself in salt; he went to where the starving masses were gathered, conferred the Three Refuges upon them one by one, and immediately hung his robe and helmet upon a tree.

He lay down upon the ground and handed a knife to the hungry man, instructing him to cut the flesh from his own body so that they might share it together. The hungry man could not bring himself to do it;
thereupon, the Bodhisattva rose and cut the flesh himself, dipping it in salt and feeding it to the hungry man until both thighs were exhausted.
He then said to the hungry man, "I am weary; you take what remains yourself. Though it be but skin and bone, it will suffice for several days. Do not let the King know; if he should find out..."

He then seized them and departed. Those who were starving were all filled with grief and lamentation; they did not dare look directly at him. After a short while, his disciples and the king’s envoys arrived.
They carried [the remains] back to the palace. Anzhou was moved to realization and opened the granaries to save lives beyond counting.
The next day, he entered *nirvāṇa*. His funeral pyre burned with smoke and flames reaching to the heavens; the fire did not cease for seven days, and his tongue—
He was not harmed. A three-tiered stupa was erected to enshrine him. His disciple Sengzun possessed noble conduct.
Sengfu, whose style name was Shanshi, was a native of Gaoyang. Orphaned at a young age, he was devoted to his studies and was distinguished in his deportment.
Yang Yong, the General of the Guard under the Former Qin, and Xi Zuochi of Xiangyang were both his close friends. He listened to Dao’an lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (the *Fàngguāng*).
He was moved by this realization and subsequently shaved his head to become a śramaṇa. After Dao’an passed away, he returned to the Tingwei Temple in Wei Commandery to bid farewell to his guests.
While traveling through the mountains, he saw a young boy being dragged away by a band of bandits. When he questioned them, they said, "We wish to use his heart and liver as an offering to the deity.
The boy was crying, and as he wiped his face with dirt, he looked toward Fu. Fu immediately removed the garment he was wearing and gave it to the bandits, saying, "Please do not use him."
Human sacrifice was being performed, yet they used sheep and pigs for the offering; this garment was intended as the price for those sheep and pigs.

The bandit could not [bear it], so Fu followed the bandit and seized his knife, cutting open his belly. Blood flowed profusely as he collapsed by the roadside. The bandits were greatly alarmed and all fled in dispersal.
Although Fu was in distress, he was still able to speak. Those on the road asked about him and were moved with pity; they gathered together to embrace him and wept.
After escorting the young boy back to his home, they urgently used needles and thread to sew up his abdomen and applied medicinal ointments.
They carried him back to the monastery, and after a short time, he recovered.
Fayu of the Song dynasty was a native of Jizhou. At the age of fifteen, he became a novice under the śramaṇa Huishi.

Huishi applied himself to the Way with rigorous diligence, and Fayu, upon shaving his hair, was able to succeed to his conduct. He admired the bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja’s offering of his own body as described in the Lotus Sūtra.
Thereupon, he went from Puzhan to inform the Jin Prince Yao Xu. Xu said, "The paths to the Way are many;
why must you burn yourself? He replied, "I wish it to be so. He then donned scented oil and wrapped his body in cloth.
Reciting the sutras, he sat within a fire-rack until his voice failed as his eyebrows and forehead were scorched and charred, after which he passed away. He was forty-five years old at the time.
Huishao of the Song dynasty was a man of unknown origins. At the age of eight, he became a novice under the śramaṇa Sengyao. He received the tonsure at Zhaoti Temple in Linchuan.
He secretly accumulated firewood to a height of several zhang, hollowing it out in the shape of a shrine chamber. Then, using his desire [to die] as a pretext, he requested permission from Sengyao;
Sengyao earnestly tried to dissuade him, but he would not comply. Furthermore, when a gathering for the Eight Precepts (Bāguānzhāi) was being held, he went elsewhere...
On that day, people arrived in great numbers with carriages and horses, and gold and silk were piled up in abundance. In the middle of the night, Hui-shao suddenly vanished.
When they searched for him, he was already sitting inside a wooden shrine, but the fire had reached his head and forehead. Yet he was still heard chanting "One Mind.
Suddenly, a great star as large as a bushel fell into the midst of the smoke and flames; it fell again and rose again, its course unfathomable. The fire [subsided] three times...
The day passed. Three days later, a single wutong tree grew at that spot—exactly as Shao had previously remarked when he was still in good health, and he had cautioned that it must not be cut down.
At that time, he was twenty-eight years old. His teacher, Sengyao, lived to the age of one hundred and sixty and passed away at Zhaoti Temple.
Sengyu of the Song dynasty was born into the Zhou family. A native of Yuhang in Wuxing, he became a śramaṇa at the age of twelve.

He once lived as a hermit with Tanwen and Huiguang on the southern side of a mountain, where they were known as the "Retreat of the Summoning of the Hidden. Sengyu often said: "The cause of falling into the three miserable realms is the persistence of emotional attachments."
"When my emotions are exhausted, my physical form should likewise be relinquished; it would be fitting to follow afar the example of the Medicine King (Bhaiṣajyarāja) who burned his own body.

Thereupon, he recited the "Chapter on the Medicine King" and immediately entered the mass of flames. He was forty-four years old at the time. Later, twin paulownia trees grew in his chamber, and the world came to call him the Monk of the Twin Paulownias.

Sengqing of the Song dynasty was born into the Chen family. He was a native of Anhan in Baxi. His family had served the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice for generations, yet Sengqing alone perceived its fallacies.
At the age of thirteen, he became a śramaṇa and resided at Yixing Temple, where he purely cultivated the Brahma-conduct, vowing to seek a vision of the Buddha.

He first burned three fingers and thereafter abstained from grain. On the eighth day of the second month in the third year of the Daming era, at the western side of Wudanshan Temple, before the Vimalakīrti statue he had commissioned, he performed the offering of self-immolation by burning his body. A creature resembling a dragon ascended to heaven from the flames.
At that time, he was twenty-three years of age.
Huiyi of the Song dynasty was a native of Guangling; his clan name is not recorded in the histories. He became a śramaṇa in his youth and possessed exemplary conduct.

In the fourth year of the Daming era, he first began to abstain from grain, subsisting on hemp and wheat. In the sixth year, he ceased eating hemp and wheat and consumed ghee and oil. Shortly thereafter, he again abandoned the ghee and oil and took fragrant pills.
Although his limbs lacked strength at that time, his spirit remained exceptionally robust. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the seventh year...
On that day, cauldrons were set up at Mount Zhong, filled to the brim with oil. He traveled by ox-cart to Longmen to take leave of Emperor Xiaowu, and then entered the cauldron.
Sitting upon a small stool, he poured oil over himself while wrapping himself in cotton cloth (*karpāsa*), and he also poured oil over a long cap and placed it on his head.
The Emperor ordered the Grand Chancellor, Prince Yigong of Jiangxia, to go to the site of the cauldron and exhort him, saying: "There are many paths to the Way; why [do you do this]?"
He was determined to burn his body. He replied, "My original vow is such; there is no need to trouble Your Majesty’s holy mind with this.

I beg only that twenty monks be ordained to promote the Buddha-Dharma. An imperial edict granted his request. He then recited the "Chapter on the Medicine King" (*Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*); even as the flames reached his eyebrows, his voice remained clear and resonant.
On the following day, the Emperor established a vegetarian feast and founded a monastery named "Medicine King" (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*) in emulation of the events in that sūtra.
Tanhong of the Song dynasty was a native of Huanglong. His clan name is not recorded in historical records. In his youth, he became a śramaṇa and specialized in the Vinaya-piṭaka.

During the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty, he traveled to Panyu and stayed at Tai Temple; he later visited Xianshan Temple in Jiaozhi, where he recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, vowing to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
In the second year of the Xiaojian era, he gathered firewood and set himself ablaze. His disciples scrambled to embrace him.
When he was brought back, half of his body was already scorched and charred. After another month, he recovered slightly, but then lost him again.
Following his tracks, they found a blazing fire, and [Seng]ming had already passed away. The next day, someone saw Hong with a golden-yellow complexion.
Regarding the one who rode a single deer and galloped westward:
Qi Faguang was a native of Longxi in Qinzhou; the histories have lost his clan name. He became a śramaṇa at the age of twenty-nine.
He refused to wear fine silk or hemp and abstained from the five grains, subsisting instead on pine needles, pine resin, and fragrant oil.
He made a vow to cremate himself and gradually accumulated firewood at Jicheng Temple. On the twentieth day of the tenth month in the fifth year of the Daming era, he finally fulfilled his resolve.

When the flames reached his eyebrows and eyes, his voice reciting the scriptures remained perfectly clear. He was forty years old at the time. [This account was written by] the śramaṇa Facun of Shifeng.

He read the Lotus Sūtra and, admiring the account of the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja’s self-immolation as an offering, desired to transform those who were weak and lacking in resolve within his hometown.
He ultimately fulfilled this aspiration. The Governor, Xiao Mian, dispatched the śramaṇa Huishen to build a stūpa to commemorate him.
Qi Fening’s surname was Pang; he was a native of Huizhou. Initially, Emperor Wu once traveled to Mount Qi in a dream.
Upon waking, he inquired throughout his court about that location among his ministers, but none could identify it. He then issued an edict to search for it throughout the empire.
He obtained [the site] seven *li* north of the city of Huì. Consequently, he established a vihāra there, granted fields for its support, and ordained monks so that it might endure for all time.
Níng registered as a resident monk from Tóngzǐ. His observance of the precepts was rigorous and austere, and his cultivation of dhyāna and contemplation was brilliant.

Whenever he entered meditative absorption, he would remain for months at a time. Upon reaching the age of seventy, he happened to set up a high seat before a Buddha image and sat upon it to burn one [incense stick].
He pointed [at the fire] and remained almost motionless day and night. The flames and smoke from his arm grew ever more intense.

Whether disciples wished to extinguish the fire or shouted to forbid it, he would not listen. The fire eventually reached his body; for seven days and seven nights, there was only a single heap of ashes.
The multitude together buried his bones there and erected a stupa.

During the reign of Emperor Wudi of the Northern Zhou dynasty, Zhoupuyuan traveled to the Three Commanderies. He had long practiced the dhūta austerities and delighted in benefiting all beings through compassion.
Whenever young men wished to leave the household life, he would invariably ordain them without hesitation.

He would silently recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* until each fascicle was completed, though even his disciples were unaware of this. He frequently sat upon a rope chair amidst forests and burial grounds.

He practiced meditative concentration, reading and reciting scriptures repeatedly from morning until evening. When going for alms, he would travel alone into the villages; by nature, he was without fear.
There was often a ghost with four eyes and six tusks, whose body hair hung down and who held a curved staff before him, merely staring at him with wide, fixed eyes.
The ghost suddenly vanished. Someone begged Huanyuan for his head, intending to cut it off himself; the man then apologized and refused the request, causing him to desist.
Another begged for his hand, whereupon he tied his wrist to a tree with a rope and severed it from the elbow with a knife to give it away.

He subsequently fainted and fell to the ground, eventually dying at Fanchuan south of the outskirts. Monastics and laypeople alike admired his conduct and vied with one another to collect his remains.
He was buried. His corpse was subsequently divided into several sections and stūpas were erected for them at Mount Hu in Yongzhou, North China.
During the Sui dynasty, Puji first entered the monastic order on this mountain, where he followed the ritual protocols of Master Yuan and practiced the discipline of meditative concentration.

Nevertheless, he constantly recited the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as his regular devotional practice. When Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou abolished the Buddhist teachings, he again made a vow to cultivate [the Dharma].

He practiced the conduct of Samantabhadra so that the Great Dharma might flourish once again. If his vow were fulfilled, he intended to sacrifice his body as an offering and be reborn in the Land of Worthy Heads (Xianshou Guo).
Consequently, he dwelt among the Tai Bai Mountains, subsisting on mountain streams and wild grasses to pass the time.

When the Kaihuang era saw the widespread propagation of the Buddha-vehicle, his joy and celebration grew even more fervent; wishing to repay his vow, he threw himself from the western cliff of Tan Valley to end his life.
People from far and near flocked to him, such that the cliffs were increased in height and the valleys filled up.
He erected a white stupa upon a high peak. Tang Fa-kuang, surnamed Luo, was a native of Xianyang in Yong. In his youth, he specialized in Confucian studies;

later, he followed Master Rong at Hongshan Temple to hear the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. At the age of sixteen, his exegesis was thorough and fluent, and his responses were clear and resonant. The virtuous elders of the capital...

He was praised for his excellence; yet he was particularly adept at meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Without regard for time or place, he frequently perused the Tripitaka scriptures and strictly maintained the discipline of the Vinaya.
He devoted himself to the practice of the dhūta austerities until the end of his life. Furthermore, he constantly used detachment from worldly attachments to instruct his disciples, saying:
"I have been mired in the clinging of birth and death since beginningless time; therefore, I have undergone saṃsāra up to the present day."

Zhong was constantly dissatisfied and wished to test him. On the twenty-first day of the second month in the seventh year of the Zhenguan era, forty *li* from Mount Zhongnan, he went to within Carbon Valley, stripped off his clothes, hung them on a tree, and committed suicide by cutting his own throat.
At that time, no one knew of it. It was not until the eighth month that Jian finally sought out and found the place, where the corpse was found intact and clean.

In Dacheng Monastery of Fenzhou during the Tang dynasty, there was a monk whose name has been lost. Because he felt that this defiled world was difficult to transcend, he vowed to sacrifice his body, hoping to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
He first began to restrict his diet and took incense for several years. Thereupon, he selected an auspicious day and gathered the assembly.
A grand procession of banners and canopies escorted him to the cliff where Zixia had studied. Facing west, he stood for a long time contemplating the Buddha.
As the multitude cried out, "Excellent! he leaped from the high precipice and cast himself into the deep abyss. Those who watched saw him reach the ground.
He was still able to rise and sit; yet, when they went to look for him, he had already passed away.
Tang Huītong was a native of Wànnián in Yǒngzhōu, from the Õusù Stream. He left the household life and lived in seclusion in Bǎolín Valley on Mount Zhōngnán.

Every time he read the Lotus Sūtra, upon reaching the Chapter on the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, he would joyfully admire and emulate his example. He privately accumulated firewood to construct a cave, vowing that he must burn himself to ashes.
Toward the end of the Zhenguan era, in the stillness of a quiet night within the forest, he chanted the sūtra and set himself ablaze.

His clear voice and fierce flames traveled far with the wind. When the fire was finally extinguished, he was still seen sitting cross-legged as before. Shortly thereafter, [he vanished] toward the southwest.
A great white light appeared, flowing into the mass of flames, and only when his body had fallen prostrate did it subside at dawn.

Thereupon, they collected his remains, erected a stupa, and inscribed a commemorative stele. Furthermore, in Jingzhou, there were two sister bhikṣuṇīs who also resolved to practice the original vows of Bhaiṣajyarāja.
They gradually ceased eating grain, consuming instead various fragrant oils, honey, and other such substances, remaining spiritually lucid throughout.

She was highly intelligent and her physical strength did not decline. On the eighth day of the second month in the third year of the Zhenguan era, she set up two high seats on the main road of the prefecture.
Her sisters then wrapped their bodies in waxed cloth from their heels to the crown of their heads, leaving only their faces exposed.

The assembly collectively welcomed her to the high seat with flowers, incense, banners, and canopies. The sisters further applied torches to the crown of her head; she sat upright and recited the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Although smoke and flames reached her eyes, her voice remained loud and resonant. When it reached her mouth and nose, her breath finally ceased.
By dawn, the entire body had been consumed, yet two tongues alone remained. The assembly erected a stupa to enshrine them. The monks...

Shandao, following Daochuo’s teachings, propagated them throughout the capital. He personally transcribed the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* tens of thousands of times and distributed them among the men and women there;
those who received them and cultivated the practice of Pure Land Buddhism were beyond counting.

One day, while preaching at Guangming Temple, someone asked Shandao, "If one now recites the Buddha's name, will one definitely be reborn in the Pure Land? Shandao replied, "One will definitely be reborn."
He attained meditative concentration. After completing his prostrations, he chanted "Namo Amitābha Buddha," his voice continuing in an uninterrupted stream without a moment's pause.
He then left the temple and stood before a willow tree by the gate; with palms joined and gazing toward the west, he threw himself to the ground and died.
Tang Xuanlan, surnamed Li, was a native of Fangzi in Zhao. He had five brothers, of whom he was the youngest.
His paternal uncle, who served as the Magistrate of Wanquan in Pu, had no son and thus designated Xuanlan as his heir. However, Xuanlan’s heart longed for the monastic life, so he fled northward.
There he met Chan Master Chao in Fenzhou; his uncle sent men to search for and recover him, but Xuanlan ultimately refused to remain.

He then said, "My body belongs to my elder brother, but my heart belongs to the Buddhas. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, he entered the capital and received ordination, being registered at Hongfu Monastery.
He would often say to his fellow practitioners, "I vow to cast away this suffering wood [the body] to serve as a warning to the worldly masses."
On an auspicious day in the fourth month of the eighteenth year, he suddenly placed his robe and bundle in the hands of a temple official.

Wearing only a single garment, he went east to the Hongpo ward in Weiyin, where he chanted and performed prostrations by the water’s edge. Having finished, he immediately threw himself into the water.

The crowd rushed forward to rescue him and pull him out. Hui-lan said, "I am currently emulating the Great Being who was able to renounce what is difficult to renounce; please do not obstruct me. The assembly [desisted].
Wu listened to what he wished to do; he then joined his palms, made a vow, and chanted the name of the Buddha before plunging into the whirlpool.
Three days later, his corpse was recovered from the surface of the water. They erected a stupa at the original temple to bury him.

Previously, Lan had not returned for a long time, and those living with him found it quite strange; they searched everywhere but knew nothing of his whereabouts. Eventually, they untied the bundle he had left behind to verify [his fate].
Within his tracks, there was a letter left behind that said: "I respectfully address the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Your disciple Xuanlan has been a monk for twelve summers; though he has received the rank of a bhikṣu, his great task remains unfulfilled.
Now I wish to practice the dāna-pāramitā, as did the Sattva who threw himself [into the fire], Śibi who cut his own thigh, and the Fish King who became a mountain of flesh."
He followed the models of the former sages; his robes and belongings remain intact. I request that you act in accordance with the Buddha’s Vinaya.
Alas, at the moment of his passing, such was the thoroughness and detail of his arrangements—this is sufficient to reveal the depth of his intention.
A man from Tang who bound straw together suddenly saw him at Bodhi Monastery in the Pingkang Ward of the capital. His dwelling was untidy;
by night he would spread out a bundle of straw and sleep beneath the two eaves. He said, "This is the practice of a dhūta.

After several years had passed, the administrators of the monastery, regarding him as a man of long-standing virtue, constructed a room for him so that he might dwell in comfort, yet they did so with a sense of derision.
The mess was such that the grass said, "Do you weary me? This world is not worth cherishing; how can it endure for long?
That night, he then burned the bundle of grass upon which he had been lying. By dawn, his bones and remains were completely transformed, leaving nothing but ashes.
Now, with such a minute thing as a bundle of grass, he consumed a body seven feet tall, yet there was neither a stifling smoke nor the sound of a violent explosion. This is—
It is not that he had entered samādhi; it was impossible for anyone to destroy this body of flesh and blood by means of vajra-power.
The multitude collectively fashioned an image of him in the temple to enshrine it. When prayers were offered, it proved especially miraculous and efficacious.

Wu-ran of the Tang dynasty entered the monastic order and resided at Mount Zhongtiao. There he studied the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*, the *Śata-śāstra*, and other treatises.

He often remarked that according to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, together with ten thousand holy beings, has from time immemorial dwelt within the Golden World in the northeast, expounding the Dharma; at this thought, he would rejoice.
He then exposed his body to the elements. He wished to go there to pay his respects. In the seventh year of the Zhenyuan era, he hung up his monk’s staff at the Shanzhu Ge-yuan on Mount Wutai.
While gathering firewood, drawing water, and attending to the needs of the community, he traveled extensively through its secluded and magnificent sites.

The golden bridges, jeweled pagodas, bells, and gongs that appeared as auspicious omens were beyond counting. In this manner, twenty years passed. Later, to the east of the Central Terrace (Zhongtai), suddenly—
He saw a temple with a plaque inscribed "Fushō" (Birth of Blessings). Within were ten thousand *bhikṣus*. Enkan prostrated himself before them and offered his greetings according to the proper rites.
The Bodhisattva, appearing in the form of a monk, spoke to Enkan, saying: "You have a karmic affinity with this place; you must support the assembly. Do not have aspirations without practice.
Thereupon, Enkan resolved to provide meals for the monks and made a vow to himself: "If [the number of] monks reaches one hundred..."
When the number reached ten thousand, he would burn one finger as an offering of thanks. Once all his fingers were consumed, those who received his alms had already numbered in the millions;
offerings poured in like a vast ocean and accumulated like mountains, continuing without ceasing even as he approached his end.

During the Kaicheng era, he went alone to the summit of Mount Zhongtai to offer incense and bid farewell to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and ten thousand Bodhisattvas, accompanied by his younger brother.
Zhao Hua took two ends of waxed cloth, a bundle of coarse hemp, and one *dou* of fragrant oil, and went to that place.
On that day, he abstained from all food and drink. From dawn until dusk, his prostrations and recitations did not cease for even a moment. When it was nearly midnight, [the Master] said to Hua:
"I am now seventy-four years of age and have fifty-five years of summer retreat (*varṣa*). How much longer does this lingering breath remain?"
"If you still remain greedily attached and do not provide offerings, how could this truly be the conduct of my disciples? You are my younger brother;
I trust you will assist me in creating these conditions, for then there may be some hope for success. Although Huā wept and remonstrated four times, he would not consent.
[Huiyuan] then wrapped him in cloth, bound him with hemp, and doused him with oil. He raised a fire at his crown; while the smoke and flames were fiercely blazing, he stood firm and unswaying. When—
Only after his feet were firmly planted did he fall; thus, he may indeed be called extraordinary.
Tang Xingming was the son of the Lu family of Changzhou in Wu Commandery. Having left the household life, he visited various sacred sites such as Wutai, Emei, and Tiantai.
Upon reaching Mount Heng, he took a liking to it and eventually settled beneath Zhurong Peak, where he lived in simple cloth robes together with Xuantai.
Whenever he traveled back and forth, he would say to his friends: "I do not wish to emulate Sengya’s burning of the wooden tower, nor do I wish to emulate Qu Yuan’s burial in a fish’s belly;
nevertheless, in the end, I shall surely emulate Prince Sattva by feeding myself to a tiger.
One day, he surrendered his body before a predatory beast until his flesh and bones were entirely consumed. Da gathered what remained of his remains and performed a cremation for them.
He obtained śarīra relics that were perfectly round and lustrous. Consequently, he gathered flowers and drew water, composing a text to offer as a sacrifice.
The general purport of the text was that one can, through valorous effort, destroy greed and attachment, thereby perfecting the *dānapāramitā* of the Dharma.
Zhou Pujing, surnamed Ru, was a native of Hongdong in Jinzhou. In his youth, he left the household life under the Dharma Master Huiceng of his hometown.

He was diligent and devoted to reciting sutras and maintaining mantras. After shaving his head and receiving full ordination, he traveled to Fengxiang’s Famen Temple to pay homage to the True Body Relics.
He went to Suizhou to study and attended lectures at Longxing Temple; his lineages of transmission and instruction were all worthy of admiration.

Following circumstances, he traveled to guide and encourage others through the regions of Chen, Cai, Cao, Bo, Su, and Si. He eventually completed his missionary work in the capital of Bianjing and returned to his native village, where he resided at Ciyun Temple.
There, he met with the Prefectural Governor, Lord Yang, who invited him to escort the True Body Relic from the Pagoda in Fengxiang to bestow blessings upon the people.

Consequently, [the Master] submitted a petition seeking to contribute his own efforts. At that time, the Relic was enshrined in Guangsheng Temple. In the fourth month of the second year of the Xiande era...
