On the eighth day of the month, he sat in quietude before the stupa and performed the offering of self-immolation. He then made this vow: "I shall sacrifice a thousand bodies, hoping to attain perfect enlightenment;
today is but the first of those thousand. He immediately sat within a wooden shrine and cast a torch upon himself.
The sound of his mournful wailing resounded from all sides. Smoke and flames blazed fiercely, darkening the clouds and the sunlight. He was sixty-nine years of age.

Song Shouxian was from the Qiu clan of Yongchun, Quanzhou. From his youth, he was intelligent and quick-witted; he immediately followed a master to shave his head and don the robes at Jixiang Monastery.
Later, he traveled to study at Yunmen, where he attained the Dharma. Having established a community at Dasheng Temple in Hengyang, his integrity and conduct became increasingly solitary and austere.
He wore only a single cloth garment, which he never changed despite the repeated shifts of cold and heat, and used only a single cane staff.
He sat in meditation day and night like a stump. When questioned, he would respond without the slightest hesitation.
During the Qiandé era, he suddenly announced to the assembly, "I shall now fulfill my long-standing vow. The following day, he went directly into Nan-yao Mountain;
his disciples were initially unaware of this. One who sought him there found a pair of shinbones among the grass and stones. Thereafter—
It is believed that he surrendered his body to the jackals and tigers. After his cremation, his relics were collected and a stupa was erected.

He was seventy-four years old. Sengwen (Sung-wen) was a native of Pingyang in Yongjia; from childhood, he went to Jinhua to receive instruction and there he received the tonsure. Once he had completed the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*),...
He immediately took up his staff and traveled to Jin-yun to see Ming-zhao, where he attained the Dharma of the mind. Later, he went to the quarters of Master Shao at Tiantai, where he passed away.

He had served as an attendant for thirty years without the slightest slackening until he had exhausted the master’s profound treasury. Furthermore, he consulted the Tripitaka three times to verify his understanding.
In the third year of the Taiping Xingguo era, he suddenly piled up firewood and set himself ablaze, saying, "I offer this as a service..."

He nurtured the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time. Five-colored flames swirled about, and those who witnessed it were filled with a mixture of praise and lamentation.
Suddenly, he obtained śarīra relics from amidst the ashes in incalculable numbers. At that time, his age was eighty-four.
Sòng Huáidé was a man of Jiangnan. In his childhood, he traveled north and received the tonsure. Through listening to lectures, he attained a position of renown;
he was particularly well-versed in the *Lotus Sūtra* and recited it with singular devotion. Later, he paid homage at the image and stupa of Saṃgha at Sishang.

In the eighth year of the Tàipíng Xīngguó era, the Emperor issued an edict to the eunuch Lǐ Shénfú to present ceremonial banners and flowers as offerings, and to deliver the "Responsive Śarīra" to the temple.
He was buried in an annexed stupa. De then made a vow to offer his own body and life as an act of devotion.
He first gave away his robes, alms bowl, and all his personal belongings, using them entirely to feed the monastic community.

Thereafter, he dressed himself in paper garments soaked in oil, took leave of the assembly with a prostration, and holding two candles in his hands, ascended a pyre of piled wood and sat down. As the smoke and flames grew fierce, he continued to recite the sutras without ceasing. Eventually, his body...
The sound of his cries was crushed; his ashes were scattered. Alas! He may truly be called one of courageous and diligent exertion.
This was on the eighth day of the fourth month of that year. Shortly thereafter, Shenfu returned to the capital and reported the matter in full detail. The Emperor was moved to show his emotion.
The Praise says:
With craving as the cause, Craving for life is the fruit. How profound these maxims! Who can bear the burden of this body of birth and death?
A shackle binding one to the three realms— Alas, how the consciousness Mistakes it for "I" and clings to "self."
Desire is especially defiling, arising from the conditions of emotional attachment; life, too, is illusory, its length determined by heaven.
These two forms of craving are both brought about by one’s own body; therefore, one should be able to relinquish the body for the sake of the *dānapāramitā* of the Dharma.
The Tathāgatas protect and entrust [this teaching] to the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, whose sincerity is truly worthy of emulation.
*The Newly Compiled Classified Biographies of Monks of the Six Studies*, Scroll Nine;
*The Newly Compiled Classified Biographies of Monks of the Six Studies*, Scroll Ten.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Tanyu of Eastern Zhejiang.

Shi Xue, a master of the Liwu school from the Jin dynasty, resided at Changshan. He could recite over one hundred thousand words of scripture. At the shrine of Mount Tai, there was a large stone casket.

He was storing precious vessels when he happened to stay overnight by a shrine. A figure dressed in black robes and wearing a martial冠 (guān) appeared and ordered him to open the casket; suddenly, the figure vanished.
Xiang thought that the casket, containing a hundred oxen, would be impossible to move, yet upon attempting to lift it, he found it to be exceedingly light.

Thereupon, he took out the precious vessels and traded them for goods, which he distributed to the poor. Later, while crossing the river and staying at Yuecheng Temple, he suddenly became dissolute and indulgent in his conduct.

At dawn, Sima Tian, the General Who Guards the North, invited him and administered a poisoned drink to him. Yet he consumed three full goblets, his spirit and countenance becoming even more clear and refreshed.
Tian was greatly astonished by this.

Huilì of the Jin dynasty was a man of unknown origins. During the Yonghe era, he traveled to the capital. By the time of the Xingning era, he submitted a memorial requesting that the site where he had been living be converted into Waguan Monastery.
Once the monastery was completed, a stupa was erected. When the foundation for the stupa was first marked, a divine being appeared at night and moved it several dozen paces to the east;
Huilì then established the site there and would not allow it to be changed again. In the monastery, there were five [statues] crafted by Dai Andao.
There was also a sixteen-foot golden image repaired by Dai Yong. Initially, the face of the image appeared thin;
[Dai Yong] thought it was not the face that was thin, but rather the shoulders and arms that were too fleshy. He gradually removed the excess flesh, and thus the face became proportionate.
Shortly thereafter, this proved to be exactly so. Furthermore, King Siṃhala sent the śramaṇa Dharmayaśas to present a four-foot-two-inch jade image, which Emperor Xiaowu...

The Emperor issued an edict to enshrine it in the temple. There was also a golden image seven chi and two cun tall, which the Minister of Education Wang Mi had obtained outside the East Gate of the Palace.
Although his efforts were modestly devoted to the cultivation of merit, he simultaneously brought forth these manifold auspicious signs.
How magnificent! As for [Master] Li, his final whereabouts are unknown.
Huisou of the Song dynasty was a man from Anle; the histories have lost his clan name. In his youth he became a śramaṇa and traveled to the capital, where he stayed in Wang Tai’s Garden.
He dreamed that he was building a monastery within the garden. Upon waking, he marveled at this, and immediately fell asleep again to recount his previous dream.
At dawn, he spoke to the gardener Song-gi, instructing him to inform Baekdam.

Gi found this difficult, but when Baekdam himself came to request the construction of a monastery on his garden, he agreed to fulfill the dream. Furthermore, one night he dreamed that a blue dragon came from the south.

It transformed into a pillar for the temple. Consequently, he went to the riverside pavilion, where a massive log came floating down the current; just as he had seen it in his dream, he took it to be the pillar.
The temple was named Anle (Peaceful Bliss), as he did not forget his native land.

The Song monk Hong was a native of Yuzhou; his family name has been lost to history. He resided at Waguan Temple and, through his efforts in encouraging those with karmic affinity, he commissioned a sixteen-foot golden image.
At that time, Emperor Wu of the Song held the regency as Chancellor, and the prohibitions on copper were extremely strict. Consequently, Hong was imprisoned in the Chancellor’s office.
The official was due to die; he recited the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra day and night without ceasing. One night, he dreamed that the cast image appeared to him and said, "Do not fear;
there is no cause for sorrow. When the execution was to take place, the supervising officer suddenly had his carriage overturned by a charging bull, and he requested a new date for the execution.
Shortly thereafter, the Chancellor summoned Yuanzhi. Hong eventually passed away due to his ascetic practices.
Sengliang, a monk from the Song dynasty whose origins were unknown, wished to cast a sixteen-foot golden image.

He heard that the temple of Wu Zixu at Tongxi in Xiangchuan contained many bronze vessels, yet because the temple deity was so majestic and powerful, no one dared to approach it. Sengliang went there and [found] two large cauldrons.
Each vessel could hold a hundred *shu*. A snake over ten feet long guarded them. Zhi Liang recited incantations some dozens of times, and suddenly it vanished.

A deity appeared and said, "I wish for you to give these away to cultivate merit. Liang followed the instructions of the Regional Inspector Zhang Shao and borrowed labor and boat equipment to transport what he had obtained;
only a single spittoon remained. Someone remarked, "This was the deity's most cherished possession. Thus, the statue was completed.
It was placed in Pengcheng Temple. Emperor Wen commissioned a gilded circular halo for it. During the Taishi era, Emperor Ming moved it to Xianggong Temple, where it still exists today.
Fayi of the Song dynasty was a native of Jiangzuo. He constructed fifty-three *vihāras*.

During the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, Zhu Yingzi, the son of a Grand Master of Sacrifices, had previously been exiled to Mount Zhong. He partitioned his land to bestow upon Fayi, who established a temple named Yanxian.

The practitioner Beidu remarked, "This place shall undergo a transformation; nevertheless, it will ultimately be an excellent site. It faces directly toward the celestial palaces, making it easy to cultivate merit."
It was suddenly consumed by a wild fire. Zhang Yin of the *Qixie* [Record] wished to rebuild it based on the words of Beidu, but lamented that there was no water in the mountains.
He resolved to offer sincere repentance and prayers, vowing to beg for the waters of the Western Heavenly Pond.
After three days of increasingly diligent and reverent practice, he heard a sound falling to the ground; suspecting that a treasure must have appeared, he looked, but found nothing.
He dug at that very spot, and a spring gushed forth with a clear sound. It is now called the Water of Eight Virtues (*aṣṭāṅga-guṇa-vāri*). As for his intentions thereafter, his end is unknown.
The Song dynasty monk Huìbù was a man of unknown origin. During the Yixi era, he traveled with a man from Chang’an named Xíng Chángshēng and established [the practice].
The temple was located in Pōwǔ Village in the capital. When they first moved there to establish their quarters, they built thatched huts and assembled the monks at night.

Suddenly, two lamps advanced forward about ten paces as if being carried by someone. The assembly was greatly startled. Upon inquiring of the elder monks, they were told that the site had formerly been the foundation of a stupa for a foreign monk.
When they excavated it, it was indeed so; they therefore exerted themselves to raise it up, using the lamps [as a guide].
Therefore, it was named Chongming Temple.
The Song dynasty monk Jin was the son of Zhu Jian, a recluse from Pei-guo. In his youth, he read extensively and was particularly adept at the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*.
Upon arriving in Guangling, he went to the śramaṇa Tanyin to have his hair shaved and became his disciple. He traveled to Jianye, where the Prince of Xiangdong received the five precepts from him.
Regarding the Precepts: When Emperor Wu ascended the throne, he issued an edict appointing Huigjin as the Monastic Head (Sengzhu) of all under heaven.

He delighted in performing meritorious works; with the stipends and gifts he was granted, he established the two monasteries of Lingji and Lingzhao. Toward the end of his reign, the Emperor became increasingly irascible, and those who offended him were immediately executed.

Huigjin offered corrective counsel on their behalf, thereby sparing many from death. However, imperial favor and courtesy toward him declined from that point onward. He passed away during the Yuanhui era at the age of seventy.
Hui-kai of Liang was of the Yuan clan of Haiyan in Wu-jun. He left the household life as a disciple of Master Chong of Xuanwu Temple.

He subsequently studied the *Abhidharma* and the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* under him. During the Jianwu era, he traveled to the capital and resided at Daolin Temple, where he attended lectures on the sūtras and śāstras by the two masters Zang and Min.
Later, he moved to Pengcheng. By nature, he possessed a powerful memory; whatever passed through his ears he never forgot, and he was skilled in analyzing and distinguishing technical terminology.

Although his principles were formidable adversaries, none could pierce their core.磊落 (lěiluò), generous and fond of giving: when Xiè Miǎo of Chénjùn was appointed as Governor of Yùzhāng, he invited [Huìyuǎn] to preach and lecture.
The offerings and gifts bestowed upon him were exceedingly substantial; yet before he had even reached the capital, he had distributed them all, without the slightest hesitation.
Liu Ye of Pengcheng, the Governor of Jin’an, sent him ten thousand coins, which he immediately used to provide for the cold and hunger of others;

yet his own appearance remained soiled and neglected, as he lacked adequate clothing for both winter and summer, remaining unconcerned and at ease. He passed away in the sixth year of the Tianjian era at the age of thirty-nine. Tánjùn of the same monastery was similar in his conduct;
both were befriended by the Palace Attendant Wang Cí and the brothers Jiang Ge and his kin, who served as the Assistant Director of the Ministry of Works.
Fǎyǒu. Sēnghù of Liáng was a native of Shàn in Kuàijī. His clan name has been lost to history. In his youth, he became a śramaṇa and resided at Yìnyuè Temple on Mount Shíchéng.
To the north of the temple, there was a green cliff over a thousand feet high, from which a formation rose up like the radiant flames of a Buddha. Sēnghù went to it...
Below, he gazed upward every time, unable to look away for a long duration. Furthermore, he faintly heard the sounds of stringed and wind instruments, or witnessed strange manifestations of light.
He then made a vow to carve and chisel a statue of Maitreya one thousand *chi* in height, hoping thereby to establish a karmic connection for the Dragon Flower Assembly (*Nāgapuṣpa*).
Construction began during the Jianwu era of the Qi dynasty; however, before even the facial features were completed, Senghu died of illness, leaving behind—
The voice said, "I shall be reborn and fulfill my vow. Shortly thereafter, the śramaṇa Sengshu took up the task, but he was unable to complete it.
In the sixth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, Lu Xian, the Magistrate of Shifeng, was staying by Shanxi when he dreamed of three practitioners of the Way who said to him:
"Your sincerity and faith are firm and upright; you shall naturally find peace and security. However, His Highness the Prince of Jian’an is currently afflicted by illness and has not yet recovered."
"If you can complete the stone image being fashioned by the monk Senghu of Shan County, you shall surely be free from harm. The principles of the unseen world are not false;
you may open it. After about a year, Xian returned to the capital and happened to see a monk outside his gate who appeared to be someone he knew.
Xian made casual remarks regarding the matter of his prayers for Prince Jian’an at Shanxi, but [the Prince] was completely bewildered.
Xian smiled and departed. Suddenly, Xian remembered that this was the person he had seen in a dream at Shanxi. At that time, Prince Jian’an was staying in the capital;
upon hearing this account, he wished to act as the patron (*dānapati*). Thereupon, an imperial edict appointed Vinaya Master Sengyou to oversee the affair. Before Sengyou had arrived—
At the monastery, the monk Huicheng dreamed of a deity in black robes, accompanied by a very grand retinue, standing beneath a stone niche.
When Sengyou arrived, he deepened the niche and added a top-knot (uṣṇīṣa) above it. The seat was five *zhang* high, and the Buddha’s body was ten *zhang* tall;
in front, he constructed a three-tiered platform, along with gates, pavilions, and halls. This was in the fifteenth year of the Tianjian era. As Prince Jian’an’s chronic illness had already...
It is said that he was subsequently transferred to the fief of Nanping.
As for Fayue of the Liang dynasty, his origins are unknown. During the final years of the Qi dynasty, he served as the Sangha Master and resided at Zhengjue Temple in the capital.
Originally, at Songwang Temple in Pengcheng, there was a golden image eighteen chi in height whose spiritual anomalies were extremely well known.

Whenever there were calamities within the borders of the commandery, or instances of violence against monks and nuns, the image would break into a sweat. At that time, the north of Pengcheng belonged to the Wei; this occurred during the Taishi era of the Song dynasty.
When the Wei general attempted to transport the statue northward, it ultimately would not budge. At the beginning of the Qi dynasty, Pengcheng planned to submit to the south;
its defenses were sparse and insufficient, and even the monks were driven into labor. The Wei dispatched the Duke of Lanling, who attacked and captured the city.

The monk was taken prisoner, and the statue shed sweat that soaked the ground. Wang Liang, the Prince of Liang, was then stationed at Pengcheng; he hurried to the statue and had people wipe it, but they were unable to do so.
He stopped. The King made a vow, saying, "I, your disciple, shall personally protect the assembly of monks and ensure they suffer no calamity.

I pray only that you will take pity on me with great compassion. Having spoken, he wiped [the monk's face] with his own hand and then ceased. When the matter was reported to the Emperor, the monks' offenses were entirely pardoned. The monk’s heart was filled with joy and admiration;
he desired to pay his respects, but because the passes and bridges were blocked, he could not go. Yet his aspiration was so earnest that he vowed to sacrifice his very life.
In the fifth month of the eighth year of the Tianjian era, he and his fellow student Zhijing fashioned an image of Amitāyus at Xiaozhuangyan Temple using forty thousand *jin* of copper.
Once the mold had been cast, before he could submit a memorial for imperial approval, a decree arrived ordering an additional three thousand *jin* of copper to be provided.

Yet the officials were still not yet able to provide the necessary materials. Suddenly, a sheep-drawn cart arrived bearing an imperial edict; it carried copper in the required quantity and reached the side of the furnace.

As the molten metal was poured, it overflowed, and the casting was completed in a single pour. In an instant, the officials' copper finally arrived, but when they sought the aforementioned sheep-drawn cart, it could not be found.
Only then did they realize it was a manifestation of divine inspiration. Once the image emerged from the mold, it stood nineteen feet high.
It was one chi in height and had two large coins at the location of the waistband. By imperial decree, the image was entrusted to Dinglin Temple.
In the ninth month of that year, Sengyou moved it to Guangzhang Temple. It is said: [End of quote]
The monk Sengming of the Zhou dynasty was surnamed Jiang. A native of Neibu in Fuzhou, he was simple by nature and possessed integrity.

Although he had not studied the Buddhist scriptures (the *zhufen*) or the Confucian classics (the *Lugao*), people looked up to him with admiration. While traveling in Fangzhou, one day he happened to see a light emanating from between the mountains and valleys to the southwest.
Following it, he found a stone pedestal at the bottom of a stream; furthermore, looking off into the distance beside it, he saw...
As for the reclining stone that resembled a statue, half of it was buried in earth. Upon excavating it, it proved to be a solid image.

Although its *lakṣaṇas* and *anuvyañjanas* were perfectly complete, its color was pitch black. From the heels to the crown of the head, it stood over three *zhang* in height. Daoming immediately led his assembly to lift it, but none were able to move it.
At that time, Emperor Wu had already passed away and Emperor Tianyuan had succeeded to the throne. Daoming then took up an incense burner and prayed, saying: "If the Buddha-dharma..."

It was restored once more, providing the people with great reliance. They prayed that its majestic spirit might manifest so that their wishes might be fulfilled. Suddenly, the statue rose and walked, proceeding directly toward its stone pedestal, where it stood firm and upright.
Those who witnessed this were struck with awe and admiration. The officials reported these events to the Emperor, who was greatly delighted and issued an edict to restore [the temple].
He further changed the year’s name to "Great Elephant" (Daxiang) to commemorate this auspicious omen. By imperial decree, a temple was rebuilt on that site, and its plaque was inscribed.

Furthermore, there is the Great Image, which Ming obtained and enshrined; as well as the Prince’s Contemplation Image at Wu Temple in Xuzhou, the Stone Shadow Image at Chongyi Temple in the capital, and the sixteen-foot Amitābha Image at Jinxiang Temple in Xiangyang.
The image at Changsha Temple in Jingzhou; the Avalokiteśvara image from Dingzhou during the Northern Qi dynasty, along with the *Gaowang jing*;
the golden image cast by the "Heaven-Spreading" Śramaṇa in Xiangyang; the King Aśoka image at Changgan Temple in the capital of Yangdu;

the two life-sized golden and silver images used by the founder of the Liang dynasty; and the stone image of Saṃgharakṣita—all possess miraculous efficacy beyond measure. These are briefly described here.
To enlighten the common world, the Crown Prince reflected that an image is merely a representation of its form.
Formerly, during the Eastern Jin dynasty, the śramaṇa Faxian traveled through the Western Regions. While there, he fell slightly ill and longed for the fragrant rice of his native land.
He entered a monastery where the host was exceptionally hospitable and diligent; he ordered a novice to fetch some fragrant rice.

He advanced. He looked back at the śrāmaṇera; the blood on his heels was still wet. [The śrāmaṇera] said, "A short while ago, I went to the home of Wu Cangying in Pengcheng to beg for alms, but a dog bit me.
Daoyuan then realized that in the space of a mere instant he had traveled tens of thousands of li.

How could this be possible for an ordinary monk? Later, when he returned eastward, he visited Cangying in Pengcheng. Upon entering the gate, he saw blood smeared upon the door. When he questioned him, [Cangying] replied, "It was I..."
On a certain day of a certain month and year, a monk once came here to beg for alms, and a dog bit him. Calculating the date, there was no small error.
Xian said to the blue hawk, "This is the blood of an arhat and holy monk; guard it carefully and do not let it go.

Thereupon, the blue hawk established a temple at that very residence to repent for its transgression. It then sought a statue in the capital city of Yangdu; while crossing the River Jiang, their boat—
As the boat was tilting and on the verge of capsizing, two bones about one zhang long suddenly leapt from the current into the vessel, whereby it was safely delivered without further disturbance.
Upon reaching the shore, they were examined and found to be dragon teeth; they were subsequently submitted to the government authorities. Not long after, a hawk captured an image from a Brahmin monk.
Previously, while the hawk had happened to rest among the trees, the monk had arrived carrying the image and said, "I wish to offer this to you."
This was an offering by Wu Cangying of Xuzhou. Cangying said, "I am that very person. The monk joyfully entrusted it to him;
it is currently located at Daci Temple in Yechuan, Xiangzhou. As for the stone image, the stone is one chi in height and six cun in diameter;
it is purple and octagonal, transparent both inside and out, and features the Tathāgata, Bodhisattvas, stupas, monasteries, and devas.

The human and celestial oceans, the canopies and curtains, and the couches and seats—the manifestations of the three miserable realms are manifold. Sometimes they resemble one another from front to back;
sometimes each side is different. Their concealment and appearance are never constant; how could they be discussed in general terms?
During the Dading era of the Liang dynasty, a Śramaṇa from India brought it as a tribute. Encountering the chaos of Hou Jing’s rebellion, it was placed in the Xilin Monastery on Mount Lu.
It ascended to the zenith and departed. In the tenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Emperor Yang, while serving as the Prince of Jin, was stationed at Huaihai;
he dispatched the envoy Wang Yanshou to retrieve it. The Prince cherished it most dearly, and whenever he had other duties, he would carry it with him in a casket.
Upon ascending to the rank of Crown Prince, he enshrined it at Riyen Temple in Quchi, where it was not for outsiders to behold. In the seventh year of the Wude era...
In the [first] year of the Yongchu era, he returned to Chongyi Temple. In the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, an imperial decree summoned him into the palace.
As for the statue of Amitābha: it was commissioned by the Eastern Jin śramaṇa Dao’an on the eighth day of the eighth month of the third year of the Ningkang era.

In the late winter of the following year, once its adornments were complete, Xī Huī, the Regional Inspector, had newly assumed his post over this province; yet the statue walked alone toward Wànshān, where Huī led the multitude to welcome it.

It returned to its temple, but in the evening it emerged again and stayed outside the temple precincts. In the third year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, an imperial decree was issued to cast a gold-copper pedestal at Jianxing Garden to support it;

it was six feet high and one zhang wide. Liu Xiaoyi composed a eulogy for the inscription on the stele erected at Changsha Temple for the image, which had appeared at the north of the city during the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty; it stood seven feet high, and its radiant features were extraordinary.

In particular, there was once a man who encountered this image while walking at night. Thinking it was something inhuman, he struck it with a knife; yet when he looked closely, the image bore the marks of the blade.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty dispatched an envoy to welcome it for veneration. After three days, it was sent to Tongtai Temple.

Later, when the temple was destroyed by fire, the halls and pagodas were all consumed, but the image alone remained towering within its chamber. As for the image in Dingzhou, it was [originally] from the Yuan Wei dynasty, commissioned by Sun...

Jingde was a native of Fangzhou. He lived at home with great devotion, serving the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva image with reverence. During the Tianping era, he responded to a recruitment call for Dingzhou, where he was falsely accused by bandits.
He was arrested and imprisoned in the capital, where he was subjected to grueling torture; though innocent, he was forced to plead guilty and was about to be executed.
While sitting in his cell one night, Jingde wept and made a vow, saying: "To have been so unjustly treated must surely be the result of my having wronged others in past lives."
"Now that I have fortunately finished repaying my debt, I vow to take upon myself the misfortunes and injustices suffered by all sentient beings.
Thereafter, while he was dozing, a śramaṇa appeared in a dream and said, "The *Guanshiyin Jiu Sheng Jing* consists entirely of the names of various Buddhas.

If you can recite it a full thousand times, you may escape the calamity of death. He further instructed him to recite it several more times. Once Jingde awoke, he could not forget anything of what he had been taught. In the end—

He recited [the scripture] without ceasing from his mouth. By dawn, he had completed it one hundred times. Shortly thereafter, he was led to the marketplace for execution; as he walked, he continued to recite, reaching nearly a thousand times.
Yet, three times the executioner’s blade snapped, and even after three blades were replaced, there was not the slightest injury to his body.

When Minister Xiang Yuanchu heard of this, he marveled at it and immediately memorialized the throne to commute his sentence. An imperial edict was issued to transmit the scripture to the world. Once Jingde had returned to his post of defense, he...
Upon examining the image closely, the three scars from the sword wounds upon its neck were still clearly visible. Jingde was deeply moved and wept bitterly.

As for the golden image at Xiangyang: in the nineteenth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty, the year being Jiamu, the bhikṣu Dao’an fashioned a golden image eighteen feet tall at the western gate of Xiangyang.
This image has passed through three cycles of the sexagenary calendar, spanning one hundred and eighty years.
Thereafter, it was destroyed. This record was written on the image [of the Buddha] beneath its armpit, within the folds of the inverted robe.
In the third year of the Jiande era of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, the year of Jiawu, Changsun Zhe, a Grand Marshal, was stationed at Jingzhou, with Wang Cheng of Taiyuan serving as his deputy.

Zhe was by nature cruel and violent; as soon as he took office, he first ordered the destruction of the images. When the officials offered remonstrance, he became even more enraged, and the commoners and soldiers fled.
He hurriedly obeyed the command. He deceitfully tied a rope around the neck of the statue and led more than a hundred people to pull it.

The statue stood firm and did not move. Sengzhe thought they were lacking in strength and beat the supervisor a hundred times with his staff. They pulled again as before, yet it still would not budge.

Only when they increased the number of people to five hundred did it finally fall; the sound shook the earth and caused both people and things to tremble with terror. Sengzhe alone leaped for joy, unable to contain himself, and hurriedly...
He ordered the metal to be melted and the casting to begin. He hurriedly rode his horse to report this to the Duke of Taiyuan, but suddenly he fell from the horse, fracturing his limbs and bones;
he lost his voice and stared fixedly forward, passing away that very night. When one examines the dates and years recorded in his account, they match perfectly, like two halves of a tally.

Thus, the doctrine of "fixed karma" as determined by successive lifetimes is indeed correct. As for the image of King Aśoka at Changgan Temple, its halo, pedestal, and physical features were auspicious.

The auspicious responses and spiritual manifestations are fully detailed in the preceding biography. In years of severe drought, the Emperor would invariably mount his carriage to welcome the image into the palace.
He would personally don an oiled vestment and lead the procession with a ceremonial parasol, while the assembly of monks followed behind.

Although the heat was initially scorching, as soon as the image reached the midpoint of the journey, a steady drizzling rain would fall, saturating all living things. It was upon this reliance that the state ensured bountiful harvests. (Recorded by Chen Zhen)
During the day, the image suddenly turned to face west. The hall supervisor on duty repeatedly moved it toward the south, but when he rose at dawn to check it, it had again turned to face west.

When this matter was reported, an imperial decree ordered that the image be brought into the Taiji Hall, where vegetarian feasts were prepared and ritual circumambulations performed. Previously, the image had been wearing a crown of seven precious gems.
It was adorned with pearls and jade, weighing approximately one hundred *jin*. A brocade covering was further placed over it.

At dawn the following day, the crown hung from the hand of the image, yet the covering still remained over its head. The Emperor ordered that the crown be placed upon it and the covering restored as usual.
He then prostrated himself in prayer, saying: "If there is any misfortune for the state, let the crown fall off again. When he looked at it clearly the next morning, [he found the crown had fallen].
It was indeed so. In the ninth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, after the Chen had fallen, an imperial edict ordered that the image be brought to the inner palace for veneration.

Whenever the Emperor faced it, he did not dare to sit; this was because the image remained standing. After some time, an edict was issued stating: "I am advanced in years and cannot endure standing for long while attending the image.
Let the relevant authorities now fashion a seated Buddha, modeled after the image of King Aśoka, and send the original image to Xing[yang]."

The statue was enshrined at Shansi Temple; it was so magnificent that no location could contain it. When they moved it to face north in order to prepare for its relocation, the next day the statue had turned to face south.
Some suspected human interference, so they placed a banner facing north and locked the doors to observe it. Yet the statue’s face remained southward as before.
The assembly was struck with awe and all prostrated themselves in worship and apology to the Liang Emperor, who was the very embodiment of the Buddha.
Regarding the two statues of gold and silver: they were enshrined in the Chóngyún Hall, where he paid them homage morning and evening for fifty years.
During the usurpation by Hóu Jǐng, the Grand Marshal Wáng Sēngbiàn, having already executed Jǐng, plotted to welcome Prince Yuánmíng of Zhēnyáng from Qi to establish him on the throne.
While he remained hesitant and undecided, Sēngbiàn dispatched his son-in-law Dú Kān to serve as a guard for the palace gates; Kān was by nature greedy.
Hàn wished to destroy the two statues and cast them into gold and silver ingots. He first constructed a gallery surrounding the perimeter of the hall, naming it the "Three-Stop Gallery" (Sānhuī Gé).
The tops of the statues were positioned directly above this gallery. Hào dispatched several dozen men up the gallery to chisel at the tops of the statues.

Both statues turned their heads back to look at them. The multitude was struck with terror; they all became mute and fell into a stupor. Hào’s entire body subsequently swelled with a greenish hue, as if he had been beaten. He cried out in agony.

After several days of crying out, his wounds festered and he died. In the Chen dynasty, Emperor Wu (Wu Di) Fang had passed away in Jiangnan. Prince Linchuan (Lin Chuan Wang) Qian succeeded to the great lineage.
While he was preparing the funeral equipment and constructing a *wēnliǎng* carriage, the state treasury was found to be in short supply.

Consequently, an imperial edict ordered that the precious curtains and the jade pendants and pearls from the Buddha Hall be confiscated to provide for the expenses. The relevant officials gathered the necessary labor force to carry out the task.
The screens were withdrawn, yet clouds swirled and gathered so densely that they shrouded the interior and exterior of the hall in darkness. In other areas, however, the scenery was clear and bright.
Spectators gathered from all directions, vying with one another in their astonishment at this marvel. Then, as rain poured down and lightning flashed, smoke and flames suddenly surged forth.

The multitude saw the image in the hall lift off and soar, thinning the air against the Milky Way; it grew increasingly distant and faint until it vanished in an instant. A short while later, the clouds dispersed.
After the rain had passed, he went to inspect the site and found only the stone bases of the pillars remaining. Later, it was seen on the sea.
As for the Stone Image of Monk Hu, it was made during the Northern Qi period and stood eighteen feet tall. Initially, Hu made a vow to create it, but could not find a stone.

By chance, in a valley north of the temple, he saw a stone lying on the ground that was approximately the required size. He then looked for craftsmen to oversee its construction. [The text continues: Having undertaken the work...
After one year, it was barely finished; with its back to the ground, it was not easy to turn over, and despite the efforts of many people, it could not be moved.
On the following day, the stone suddenly turned of its own accord to allow for carving and polishing. When it was completed, it was moved and installed within the hall.

When the armies of the Northern Zhou destroyed the Qi dynasty, the image first began to sweat. When Jinzhou fell, all the temples were set on fire, yet this image alone remained perfectly intact. Although...
It possessed the strength of many oxen and could never be toppled. Soon thereafter, a monk named Zhou stacked tiles, wood, and earth to construct a protective trench around it;
however, in an instant, the monk’s whereabouts were lost. Someone broke off two fingers of the image with a wooden tool, whereupon the image appeared in a dream to people, saying:
"My fingers ache; please restore them. In the tenth year of the Kaihuang era, thieves returned to the image hall carrying banners and canopies; every night, [the image] would appear in dreams.
Zhang Ba rebuked him for this. The above accounts are all recorded in the *Dai jingyi ji* (Records of Wearing the Banner of Extraordinary Virtue).
Later, there was Fajing of the Liang dynasty; his ancestors were of the Sun clan from Taiyuan, later migrating to Jiangling.
While his mother was pregnant, she dreamed that her body entered a lotus pond and obtained a handsome boy. As she neared delivery, she again dreamed that she was riding a white lion, wandering about.
He sported amidst the void. At the age of seven, he left the household life at Changsha Temple. At thirteen, he ascended the seat to preach the Dharma;

his eloquence was unimpeded, such that even his fellow student Zhiyuan, though senior in years, could not surpass him. Consequently, offerings from the faithful arrived like clouds and piled up like mountains.
The small and large buildings of the Worthy King’s (Yǔwáng) Auspicious Image Hall, totaling fifteen hundred rooms, were all newly renovated, with the materials provided entirely from the capital.
An elder of the temple once dreamed that a person told him: "Jing was formerly a patron (*dānapati*) of this temple; he has now returned by the power of his vows.
Later, the Liang court appointed him as the *Sengzheng* (Chief Administrator of Monks) for that region. Before long, he fell gravely ill.
He then invited monks to perform the ritual circumambulation (*xingdao*) before the image for seven days. During this time, Sengjian and Fatai dreamed that the image came to Jing’s residence.
The chamberlain Jingren Yuanzhi saw the image emerge from the room of Lord Jing and return to the hall.
Shortly thereafter, his illness was cured, though he passed away not long after, at the age of seventy-six.
Sui Tongyou, surnamed Zhao, was a native of Pufan in Hedong. Having renounced the world at a young age, he entered the monastic order in his early twenties.

During the period between the Zhou and Qi dynasties, the Dharma-gate was beset by turmoil and adversity; consequently, he traveled south to Jinling, where he further advanced his studies. He applied himself with particular diligence to the study of the Vinaya.
With the rise of the Sui dynasty, he returned to Wei-yin to lecture and propagate the teachings. In his later years, he resided at Yanxing Temple, where he happened to encounter...
He undertook its initial construction without shrinking from the labor of earth and wood. Furthermore, he dug four large wells, each equipped with water-strainers to protect living beings.
In his daily life, whenever he opened a scripture, he would invariably wash his hands up to the wrists; even while staying within his private chambers, he never spat or sneezed.

He washed himself with water for convenience and did not use towels or head-covers; he allowed his hands to dry naturally. During the bitter cold, he layered his three robes—namely those of cotton and silk—so thickly that he no longer even noticed them.
He often sighed, saying: "To have failed to improve while alive is enough; that death does not repay my debts is sufficient. He admonished his disciples, saying:
"After I die, you must surely give [my remains] to birds and beasts. On the fifteenth day of the first month of the first year of the Daye era.
He passed away while sitting in meditation at the age of fifty-seven.
Huidá of the Sui dynasty was surnamed Wáng; he was a native of Xiāngyáng. Having entered the monastic path in his youth, he was particularly devoted to the restoration and repair of monasteries.
Later, he practiced *dhyāna* at Pùbù Temple on Mount Tiāntái. He also traveled north to Mount Wǔdāng, where he cultivated stillness as before. During the reign of the Chen dynasty...
An epidemic broke out extensively throughout Jiangnan. Sengda established a pharmacy in the city of Yangdu, providing extraordinary relief to many.

Among the Buddhist temples in Jinling, there were more than seven hundred; of these, those that Sengda restored—repairing what had collapsed and revitalizing what was dilapidated—numbered over three hundred.
During the Renshou era, he constructed a seven-story wooden pagoda at the Baita Temple in Yangzhou, and subsequently traveled upstream...
He traveled through Jiangxi to various prefectures such as Poyang and Yuzhang, transforming beings according to their conditions to bring them to spiritual fulfillment.
The śramaṇa Huiyuan invited him to stay at Mount Lu and constructed seven bays of the Xilin Multi-storied Hall, vowing to use yellow camphor wood for its materials.

The entire region searched for it, but it was completely impossible to find. Everyone wished to change their approach, but Da said, "It is simply because your sincere heart has not yet reached its full measure that you have had no success in your pursuit.
If your power of aspiration were firm, even the common *chūlì* trees would transform into *nán* timber.
Thereupon, the multitude went out in four directions to search, and they indeed found a valley of yellow *nán* trees within their borders at Mount Xiàcháo. Calculating their number, they could...

Having completed this pavilion, they found it was situated in such a perilous location that there was no way to exit. By chance, while traveling along the cliffside, Da happened to see a single spot through which people could pass.
He then hauled the materials down to the river, where they floated them downstream on rafts; not a single item was lost. When the pavilion was finished, its grandeur was unsurpassed in the world.
Later, it suddenly tilted three feet toward the south. This site lay at the Stone Gate Gorge, where it so happened that—
A great wind arose from the ravine and blew against the pavilion; the pavilion was thereby set upright. Later, when he went to Changsha, the trees grew even more luxuriantly.
Da reached the state of following his nature and acting with sincerity; his speech was devoid of flowery ornamentation, and his clothing was so tattered and worn that it was hardly fit to look at.

Yet, donors and believers looked up to him with admiration, and whatever he proposed was invariably successful—this was surely due to the principle of spiritual resonance. The seventh month of the sixth year of the Daye era.
In the month of Huì, her chronic illness intensified. A strange fragrance circulated within her chamber, and the consecrated images began to perspire. She passed away after reclining for seven days;
she was eighty-seven years of age.
Zhilin of the Sui dynasty was surnamed Lüqiu. He was a native of Fangyu in Gaoping. His grandfather, Yan, did not serve in office. His father, Tanzhen, was a Court Gentleman of the State of Liang.
When Zhilin was young, he requested instruction from the retired scholar Bian Quan; he thoroughly mastered the *Book of Rites*, the *Book of Changes*, the *Zhuangzi*, and the *Laozi*.
Upon reaching maturity, he entered the monastic order under the śramaṇa Fadun of Renxiao Temple, receiving the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. Not long after, [he...]

When Master Dun passed away, his precepts were not yet perfected, and no one followed his example. [The Master] then traveled to the capital and further relied upon Dharma Master Zhengkeng of Dongshan Temple to receive the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Cheng lun) and study the *Vinaya*.
In the tenth year of the Dajian era of the Chen dynasty, he returned to his native village.

Xiao Mohuo, the Regional Inspector of Nanxuzhou, treated him with profound courtesy and esteem, requesting that he turn the Wheel of Dharma. In the eleventh year, an imperial edict appointed him as... [Director of the Bureau of Sacrifices].

In the second year of Zhìdé, Sengzhèng was appointed by imperial decree as the *Sēngdū* (Chief Administrator) of Xuzhou. In the sixteenth year of the Kāiyuáng era, Lǐ Hǎiyóu, the Regional Inspector (*Císhǐ*) of Yùzhōu, appointed him as a judge.
The Renxiào Temple where he resided had been built from the private residence of Tán Sēngzhào, a former Consultant (*Zīyì*) to the General Who Conquered the West under the Liáng dynasty;
its construction was incomplete when the chaos of the civil wars ensued. Sēnglín then lavishly renovated it until it was magnificent and grand.

Hongchang truly exerted great effort in this regard. He fashioned six statues, one of which was made of lacquered cloth (niēzhù). Furthermore, he constructed a five-story brick stupa on the summit of Mount Yuyang.
He lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* numerous times.

He ordained more than a thousand disciples. In his later years, he resided at the Zhaoyin Monastery; its mountain dwellings were secluded and quiet, and the woods were lush and deep, making it a fitting place for spiritual cultivation.
He took dhyāna-concentration as his ferry for the Way, yet he was constrained by external conditions and never attained its fruit.

On the sixth day of the fifth month in the ninth year of the Daye era, he sat in the full lotus posture with palms joined and passed away in his temple quarters at the age of seventy. Previously, there was a lay devotee named Liu Zheng.

He was earnestly requested to expound the *Maitreya-sūtra on the Ascent to Tuṣita*, but Senglin declined, saying, "The impermanence of life has already arrived; how could I have the leisure for such a task? Furthermore, he left a final instruction:

"You must certainly perform the rites of the Śītavana cemetery. On the eleventh day of that month, his disciples Zhijian and others returned him to the King Aśoka Mountain at the Thousand Corpse Cemetery.
After a long passage of time, his physical remains showed no decay. Then, on the eighth day of the ninth month of that year...
On that day, a square mound was constructed and his entire body was interred. Cai Huan, a military officer from Jiangyang, composed the inscription for his stele.
Tang Zhuli’s surname was Chu; his ancestors were from Yangzhai in Henan. Later, there was one who sought refuge in Qiantang in Wu Commandery, and his descendants settled there.
At the age of eight, he entered the monastic order and became renowned among both the clergy and the laity. After a long time, during the Chen dynasty...
During the reign of Emperor Xuan, the Aśoka Monastery (Qínhuáng sì) was constructed to the left of the capital city; he was summoned by imperial decree to oversee the construction works.
In the second year of Zhìdé, he served as the abbot of the monastery. After the fall of the Chen dynasty, he moved to Chánglè Monastery in Jiāngdū.

In the thirteenth year of the Kāiyuáng era of the Sui dynasty, a five-story pagoda was built, its golden pinnacle shining brilliantly both near and far. In the seventeenth year, Emperor Yang, then the Prince of Jìn, went out to govern the Huái and Hǎi regions.

Entrusting the affairs to the head temple, he then returned to Longguang Temple in Danyang to welcome back the image of King Udayana obtained by Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, as well as the image of Dīpaṃkara obtained by Wang Mi. He constructed a high pavilion in the center, flanked on both sides by two towers.
An image was enshrined upon it, magnificent and exceptionally prominent, standing preeminent throughout the realm.

In the fourth year of the Daye era, he further constructed a four-sided complex of斋房 (zhāifáng), corridors, and galleries, along with storehouses, kitchens, and washrooms, so that his pure companions might dwell and rest there without weariness.

In the tenth year, he expended his own private resources to purchase sandalwood and commissioned carvings of a miraculous image together with two bodhisattvas, which were then installed and venerated within the pavilion.
In the fourteenth year, during the chaos and turmoil of the Sui dynasty, bandits and rebels were rampant. [The Master] vowed with all his might to sacrifice his life to protect the temple halls.
When Shendao (Emperor Gaozu) received the abdication and the world began anew, while other regions were in a state of total upheaval, these [halls] alone remained intact.

In the sixth year of Wude, the rebel leader Fu Gongwei rose in revolt; the temples and monasteries were all dismantled and transported to Jiangnan. [The Master] personally wrote a letter expressing his wish to burn himself rather than see them destroyed.
He intended to leave his body in the temple chamber, but the Abbot did not permit it. He said to his disciples with determination, "For immeasurable kalpas, I have accumulated greed and attachment;
I have been unable to sacrifice my life to repay the kindness of the Dharma. Now that this image is about to cross the river, I cannot bear to witness it.
You may pile wood and set fire to me to provide for its offering. My robes, provisions, and all personal effects shall likewise be bestowed upon the image. He was resolute.
After my parinirvāṇa, the image shall return south. He immediately bathed himself, sat in the lotus posture, and facing west, drew fire toward himself until his life came to an end;
yet his body remained with palms joined, steadfast and without decay. Although much fuel was added, it finally burned away from the west. He was eighty years of age.
It was the eighth day of the tenth month of that year. Subsequently, the image indeed returned south. His disciples Huian and Zhiyi erected a stele within the temple;
the text was composed by Yu Shinan, the Assistant Secretary of the Crown Prince.
Huizhou of the Tang dynasty was born into the Wang family in Puzha of Puzhou. Entering the monastic path in his youth, he delighted in honoring meritorious works.

After receiving full ordination, he immediately began studying the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. By the time he reached middle age, he was engaged both in meditation and recitation; however, he held the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in particularly high regard.
He resided at Qingchan Temple in the capital for over forty years, managing all its affairs, and never once complained of weariness.

Feeling weary, he caused gardens and orchards to surround his residence, where bamboo and trees grew in dense profusion; his fields and lands, both on water and on land, were filled with abundant stores in his treasuries.
Upon reaching the age of sixty, he retired to live in seclusion. Although the community, noting his long years of labor, permitted him this leisurely repose, there were matters that constrained him;
even then, he would certainly seek counsel before daring to take action. Such was the decisiveness of his discernment. As for the monastery...
There were many lay attendants (*upāsaka*). He selected twenty of them who were capable of rhythmic breathing and had them practice music.
Awaiting an auspicious festival day, he performed before the image to emulate the grandeur of the musical performances of the Western Regions (*Sīdēqí*) and to boast among the common folk.

Before long, his illness grew severe, and he said to his disciples: "I have committed minor transgressions, yet I am afflicted with a grave illness; this is because I engaged in construction and excavation."
He dug [the earth] because he had foreknowledge of the date of his death. Approaching the bath, he sat in the *paryaṅka* posture and said, "I have finished repaying my debts.
He then passed away. His lifespan was sixty-nine years; this was at the beginning of the Zhenguan era.
Tang Huizhu, surnamed Jia, was a native of Yonggui in Shizhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of six as a disciple of Dharma Master Bin.
He recited the *Śālistamba Sūtra* (Yijiao jing), and within a single night he was able to memorize it without forgetting.

However, observing that his master’s conduct frequently contravened the intent of the scriptures, he took his leave and went to rely upon Vinaya Master Jiang. There he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* (Fahua jing). In various quarters of the monastery, some were lecturing on secular laws.

As soon as the Master heard this, he asked ten questions regarding his prior training; at that time, there was no one who could answer them. From then on, both the ordained and the laity were awed and submissive.
The assembly urgently requested him to be their preceptor for the Vinaya, and they received the Bodhisattva precepts from him.

He established seven monasteries in Huang’an County, ten monasteries in Zizhong County, and three monasteries in Wulian County. Thus, the Buddha-dharma in Shu first flourished. Initially, the Master had received...
While studying at Kanro-ji Temple in the capital, he suddenly dreamed that heaven and earth were shrouded in darkness and sentient beings were blind;

only after three days and nights did it become bright and clear as before. Upon waking, he wondered about this omen. When Emperor Zhou suppressed the Dharma and he was subsequently restored to his teaching, barely a hundred days had passed—such was the manifestation of the sign.
Thereupon, he returned to live in seclusion on the Southern Mountain in his native village, where he paid homage to the Buddha and recited the scriptures.
The sutra recitations did not cease. Birds and beasts of various species gathered together, and he conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon those in both the hidden and manifest realms.

Moved by this, a deity presented him with gifts of *lingzhi* (tuberous fungus), *gansong* (sweet pine), and other fragrant substances. A troop of macaques gathered to help him repair the road. The Master said, "Your nature is restless and agitated; why are you doing this?
Suddenly, a monkey spoke in human speech, saying, "The ruler of this age is extraordinary; the Buddha-sun is now shining through. The Master found this most strange. Nevertheless...
He did not yet know what time it was in the world. It was only upon meeting eight men gathering bow materials that he later learned it was the Kaihuang era.
He soon left the mountains and reported his situation [to the authorities]. By imperial decree, he was granted tonsure.

During the Daye period, he followed an edict to propagate the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* at Xianglin Temple in his native village. At the beginning of the Wude era, Prince Lingyang governed Yi Province as a crown prince.

On his way to his official post, he passed through Shizhou and happened to rest within a temple. He inspected the lecture hall, the Buddha hall, and the monks' quarters, finding that his luggage had been placed everywhere throughout them.

Cattle and horses were let loose beneath the eaves, and their dung and urine overflowed. When the master and his attendants returned from the manor, he went straight into his room to retrieve his three robes and staff.
Uttering the words, "Life and death depend on this very day," he raised his staff and pointed it at the cattle and horses.
The oxen and horses immediately collapsed, and the luggage was all thrown into the ditch. The officials of the prefecture and county were greatly terrified;

they followed suit by reporting the situation to the Master and detained Wang, awaiting his orders. Upon hearing this, the Master was pleased and sent him a letter saying: "My disciple has been ill for some time."
He did not encounter any harm. The ghost was deeply grateful that Master Daolun had shattered its bag of stinginess and greed; this was a profound benefit to it.
Now, I respectfully present ten catties of agarwood and ten rolls of silk brocade as a gift. When you return to the capital later, you shall receive the precepts from me.
As for Master Ming of the temple, who was my close companion in former times, in the third year of the Zhenguan era, he suddenly saw himself missing half his body.
He said to his followers, "I and the Vinaya Master established this monastery. Now that what we see is such as this, if the Vinaya Master does not die, then I shall surely die.
Later, some outsiders saw several thousand monks with unusual appearances entering the monastery;
they thought a religious assembly was being held there, but when they inquired, it was not so. By noon, the Master had passed away at the age of eighty-nine.
Tang Daoji resided at Fugan Temple in Yizhou. Throughout his life, he specialized in the study of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Whenever he intended to preach or expound upon it, he would first bathe and change his robes before sitting down to open and display the text. By nature, he was exceptionally compassionate; he made it his urgent priority to succor all living beings.

When he encountered those suffering from carbuncles, leprosy, or other ailments that had caused their flesh to rot and溃 (fester), even when the stench and filth were so pervasive that people would cover their noses, Daoji would treat them with diligent care.
He gazed upon him day and night without weariness. Sometimes they ate from the same vessel; sometimes they lay upon the same mat, yet he showed no concern for his own comfort.
In the first year of the Zhenguan era, in the fifth month, he passed away at his residence. He was over seventy years of age. As it was the height of summer, his body was kept for one hundred days.
He sat cross-legged as he had done before, yet his body did not decay or smell foul. Consequently, the assembly applied lacquer and cloth to it.
The flourishing tradition of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in present-day Shu today can be traced back to this accumulation of merit. Furthermore, both Hóngyuǎn and Sēng'ēn recited the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*;

both were revered and honored by the common people and the elite alike. Later, Yuǎn resided at Huìchāng and Ēn resided at Hóngfú. [Both] practiced meditative concentration; furthermore, [Ēn] was at Hóngfú.

Zhiye was from a distinguished clan in the region south of the Yangtze River. He specialized in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and frequently transcribed it himself, while also commissioning others to do so;

in total, he produced more than two thousand copies. In his later years, while holding the administrative post at the monastery, he still wrote five sheets of paper every day. He lived to be over seventy years old.
He remained robust and healthy, showing no sign of decline.
Tang Demei, surnamed Wang, was a native of Linqing in Qinghe. At the age of sixteen, he took leave of his parents to enter the monastic life; at nineteen, he received full ordination.

Humble, prudent, reverent, and diligent, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the Dharma. Although he had thoroughly studied both the Sūtras and the Śāstras, he was particularly proficient in the Vinaya section.
Toward the end of the Kaihuang era, he took up residence in the capital, making it his daily practice to observe the precepts and perform rites of repentance.
Furthermore, while at Mount Taibai, he recited the *Sūtra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas* in twelve fascicles, prostrating himself before each name as he recited it.

A monk named Sengyong, a Dhyāna Master of Mount Jiulung on Mount Taibai, was long renowned for his spiritual conduct; [the Master] esteemed him highly and followed him to further his cultivation of the mind.
After completing his studies, he returned to the capital and resided at Huiyun Temple under the guidance of Chan Master Jinghei.
Jinghei was a spiritual disciple of Chan Master Daoshan, who maintained himself with frugality and was held in high esteem by the fourfold assembly. [Huiyuan] served Jinghei for over ten years.
All his arrangements were derived from what he had personally experienced and mastered. He remained in tranquil silence and aimed for nirvana, entrusting himself entirely to this single path.

He followed and maintained these practices without fail; thus, the two fields of compassion and reverence were never neglected for even a year. At all sites where merit was cultivated, he invariably provided offerings of wisdom.

At the end of summer, during the *bōn* (Ullambana) festival, he would also send goods to various monasteries, which the laity called "universal bowl money" (*pǔbōn qián*). This was during the final years of the Daye era.
In summer, he gathered a thousand monks and practiced the Way for seven days. Someone said to Daomei, "The weather is already sweltering;

you must not let the assembly suffer from hunger. Why do you not grind flour cakes to provide for them? Daomei replied, "Flour is easy to obtain, but what shall we do about it turning sour and spoiled?
The person said, "I can handle that; it will suffice simply to place many basins of cold water nearby. The next day, at the fifth watch, he rose.

Twenty hu of flour was prepared as provisions for two days. The kitchen staff were busy; from the striking with the mallet to the slicing with the knife, the cauldrons of boiling water were already bubbling.
As the meat was sliced, it was immediately cast into the broth. Once cooked, it was scooped out and thrown into the water.
Those cast into the broth were finite, but those thrown into the water were inexhaustible. At dawn, when the buns were served, everyone marveled at their firmness.

He was steadfast and resilient. The multitude believed this was due to the influence of his utmost sincerity. At the beginning of the Wude era, an imperial edict ordered him to reside at Huichang Temple.

Thereupon, he constructed a hall for repentance in the western courtyard; its statues and furnishings were solemn and magnificent, and its architecture was grand and beautiful. At that time, the bathing well suddenly ran dry.
Mei offered prayers, and the spring gushed forth as before. Throughout his life, he had not kept many śarīras, yet their miraculous efficacy was unfathomable;

whenever prayers were made, they were invariably provided from within a precious casket. He practiced the dhūta austerities with diligence, remaining barefoot throughout his life to avoid harming insects and ants.

Some practiced the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* without sitting; others studied the cessation of transgressions without speaking. Their various practices were so manifold and chaotic that it would be difficult to enumerate them all.
Nevertheless, they recited the name of Amitābha with their mouths and focused their minds on the return to the Pure Land. In the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era, [the Emperor]...
On the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month, he passed away with palms joined in homage while reciting the Buddha’s name. His age was sixty-three.

His body was laid out on Mount Nan-shan at Chiming Fu (Crows-Crying Hill), and his reliquary stupa was erected in Bianzi Gu (Bian and Zi Valley). His disciples erected a stele, the text of which was composed by Yu Zhining, Palace Attendant.

Furthermore, there was the śramaṇa Tanxian, a native of the capital, who also extensively propagated meritorious deeds; his achievements rivaled those of former sages, and he perfected himself in the precepts.
Fǎn was esteemed and revered by all; thus, the Pavilion of Radiant Jewels stands preeminent within the world, and the Hall of Compassionate Buddha is a marvel that strikes awe in its time.
His origins were humble, yet his traces have become manifest; these matters shall not be recounted in detail here.
Tánxiàn of the Táng dynasty was born into the Zhāng clan of Shǐpíng in Jīngzhào. In his youth, he served under the Vinaya Master Chāng. Chāng was of the Jiǎ clan of Yúxiāng;

his pure conduct was untainted and his meritorious deeds were renowned. He resided at Jìnglín Monastery. When Emperor Wǔ of the Zhōu dynasty suppressed the Dharma, although Chāng adapted to worldly conditions, his observance of the vinaya remained flawless.
With the rise of the Suí dynasty, the Buddha’s teachings were extensively propagated; Chāng was among the first to restore the status of one hundred and twenty monks.
Daohui was selected among them, and by imperial decree, each was permitted to ordain one śrāmaṇera as an attendant; Daoyuan was among those chosen. He resided at Daxingshan Temple.
Later, Daohui returned to his hometown, where he excavated the site for the image and constructed a monastery, restoring the Jinglin Hermitage.
Before his work was complete, he passed away. The donors and believers mourned him and subsequently offered Renshou Temple to Daoyuan, who succeeded to his legacy; thus, both monasteries...
Magnificent and worthy of full praise. Shortly thereafter, he was transferred to the post of Administrator of Baiti.

On the first day of the first month in the fifteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he manifested a slight illness. On the fifteenth day, he rose early intending to go to Jinglin, but the assembly urged him to stay.
At the hour of Mao (5–7 a.m.), clouds and mist darkened the sky, and he passed away at Baiti Temple. That evening, a radiant light appeared like a flower, extending from the southeast of Baiti.
On the mountain peak, his radiance illuminated everything near and far for three nights. His corpse and coffin were secretly taken away by Jinglin, yet those at Baiti did not know it.
Subsequently, the light also followed him out to the summit of the southern mountain of Jinglin;

only then did those at Baiti realize what had happened and lodge a complaint with the authorities. Ultimately, he was buried at Jinglin, where his disciples engraved an inscription to commemorate him.
Incident:
Fa-cheng of the Tang dynasty was the son of the Fan family from Wanzhou in Yongzhou. He entered the monastic order as a child and resided at Wangxiao Temple in Lantian.
There he served the monk Senghong, a śramaṇa of lofty conduct, as his teacher. After receiving the tonsure, he made it his daily discipline to recite the Lotus Sūtra. Furthermore...
He studied the practice of meditative concentration under Master Xiang at Chanlin Temple. In his later years, he oversaw the administrative affairs of Yunhua Temple.

At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, an imperial edict summoned him to serve as a preceptor for bestowing the precepts; he declined by submitting a memorial and subsequently traveled extensively through famous mountains in search of eminent companions.
There, he settled with Master Chao in Langu Valley—which is the present-day Wuzhen Temple—where they together practiced the Dharma.
Following his Flower Samādhi, he dreamed of Samantabhadra, who told him, "You should transcribe the Great Teaching. Upon waking, he took this to mean the Mahāyāna sūtras of the Great Teaching.
He immediately commissioned a skilled scribe to copy the *Prajñāpāramitā* and subsequently constructed a Hall of the *Avataṃsaka* atop the Horizontal Ridge to the south of the temple.
He invited the scholar-monk Zhang Jing to transcribe the sūtras for his offerings. As for the spiritual responses evoked by his devout reverence:

There was a strange bird that flew and danced, warbling and crying out between the incense burner and the altar. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, when he painted a thousand Buddha images, the bird gathered upon the shoulders and backs of the painters.
When he undertook the concurrent celebration of the scriptures and images, the bird followed him with rapidity, bathing in the fragrant water.

This, too, is extraordinary. I have indeed dreamt that beside the Qingni (Blue Mud) Hall there was a great sacred image. I went there occasionally to excavate it, and recovered a niche containing a statue;
however, it was largely eroded and its date could not be determined, appearing to be something buried during the period when the Zhou dynasty suppressed the teachings.
On the final day of the sixth month in the fourteenth year, I suddenly fell ill. After a short while, I sat up, sought a bath, and requested a sedan chair. At dawn the following day—

As the light of dawn was about to appear, he spoke these sincere words to himself: "If you wish to come, simply enter; why rely on the accompaniment of stringed music? He then looked back and said to his attendants:
"I have heard that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and that birth and death do not abide. That I have been reborn in the nine grades of the Pure Land is a verification of my compassion.
Now there is a youth to welcome me, who has been standing outside the gate for a long time. After I pass away, you should all strictly observe the Buddha's precepts. Do not...

It was as if something were lacking. Suddenly, light issued from his mouth, illuminating the room, and a wondrous fragrance filled the courtyard. He passed away while sitting upright at the age of seventy-eight.
Yet, he was truly sincere; every summer he would recite the scriptures five hundred times, and on other days he would certainly do so twice.
A rough calculation suggests that over ten years he must have recited them more than ten thousand times, let alone considering that his years of ordination exceeded this duration.
Tang Huizhen, surnamed Pang, stood eight *chi* tall. He possessed a powerful memory; upon hearing Master Gao’s exposition of the *Sanlun*, he was able to grasp its essential points.
He resided at Tongquan Temple in Zizhou, where the region of Shu was transformed by his teachings. Formerly, Master Gao had traveled south on a pilgrimage.
Upon his return, he obtained three hundred monastic robes (kāṣāya) offered along the way. After Seng’ao’s passing, he entrusted these to Sengzhen to be distributed every year in the first month.
He invariably gathered people to recite the Tripiṭaka and bestowed the robes upon them without ever ceasing for even a moment.
Daily, hundreds would assemble as he propagated the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises). One day, as if in a dream, someone said to him: "On the peak of the Western Mountains, it would be fitting..."
He commissioned the construction of a great statue. Upon waking, he inspected the site; there was a stone, fine and lustrous, with flowing springs on both sides and nothing else.
He immediately ordered artisans to carve it, forming a seated image one hundred and thirty feet high.

In the eighth year of the Zhenguan era, he gathered thirty thousand monastics and laypeople to perform the consecration ceremony. From the mouth of the statue, white light issued forth, illuminating everything near and far.
Those who saw him treated him with reverence and wonder. On the fifteenth day of the first month of the fifteenth year, he manifested his passing into extinction at the age of sixty-six.
Previously, in the seventh month of the fourteenth year, the fine horse he kept neighed loudly and refused to eat for three days. Shortly thereafter, a monk appeared whose origins were unknown;
calling himself Shi-li (Daśabala), he said to Zhen: "The horse is parting from its master; you, Master, should depart first. Furthermore—
He informed him of the exact date of his death and said, "Dharma Master, you should distribute all your wealth and property;
do not let it be a burden to your descendants after your passing. Having said this, he vanished. From then on, Huizhen increased his offerings to the two fields of compassion and reverence.

On the first day of the New Year that year, he invited monks to perform rites and held a great assembly of merit, scheduled to last for twenty-one days before reaching completion. On the eighth day of the assembly—

The fragrance of the various incenses wafted forth in dense clouds, filling the entire monastery. On the fifteenth day, lotus flowers sprang up across the grounds of the temple, and the vegetation likewise underwent a transformation.
Daozhen said, "My original intention was to fulfill the assembly for twenty-one days. Now that these auspicious signs have already appeared, how could I wait any longer?
He promptly proceeded to take his meal and distribute alms. Having finished eating, he held the incense burner and circumambulated the Lushena Buddha.
He circumambulated the image three times, then prostrated himself until he was exhausted and his breath ceased. At that time, the fragrance within the temple had still not dissipated.
Three lay brothers each contributed five hundred thousand coins to assist in constructing a stone stupa five *zhang* high, in which a couch was placed in a niche;
they supported the corpse upon it, and for over a hundred days, it did not decay or fall.
Zhitong of the Tang dynasty was born into the Chen family of Zizhou. At the age of eight, he renounced secular life and became a disciple of Dharma Master Daozheng.
Having undergone tonsure, he resided at Mount Niutou, where he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* more than one hundred times.
Those within the assembly all beheld a brilliant light that illuminated both the interior and exterior. Every time, a pair of geese would perch beneath his seat.
Although he listened to the Dharma, he maintained the Vinaya with strict rigor, such that the entire assembly stood in awe and submission of him. He particularly detested the teachings of Huang-Lao;

whenever the men and women of his village performed incantations or offered sacrifices, he would invariably summon those individuals to rebuke and humiliate them, sometimes even going so far as to flog them.
Throughout his life, he did not amass private wealth, yet the completion of his monastic buildings was entirely achieved through what he had acquired [from these very sources].

Regarding the property of the donor: on the thirteenth day of the tenth month in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era, he said to his disciples, "I have already spent one hundred thousand strings of cash for this temple; it is my regret that it is not yet complete. You must finish it.

At the time of his passing, while he was having a light meal, the rooms, halls, and grounds of the temple all shook and turned white. This lasted for the duration of a meal before subsiding. For a long time...
That was the end. His lifespan was ninety-seven years.
Huiyun of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Wang and was a native of Taiyuan. An ancestor of his had fled to Jiujiang to avoid trouble, and his descendants settled there.
At a young age, Yun relied upon the śramaṇa Zhikai of Dailin Monastery on Mount Lu to leave the household life. Zhikai—
There were also those renowned in their own time, yet Huiyun was particularly resolute and vigorous, standing alone apart from the common run.
Among the affairs of the Dharma-gate, there was never anything great or far-reaching that he did not keep in mind; yet the temple where he resided had never been repaired or maintained.
At that time, Master Da was just beginning to be sought after by donors for his spiritual practice. Huiyun was then twenty-five years old, and he made a vow:

He went to invite him. When he offered his wealth and property, Fotuo did not consent. Daoyun pleaded with him to the point of death, casting himself down and prostrating until his cheeks were swollen and split and his tears and mucus spread across the ground for five feet.
He even calculated that he might drown himself to manifest his resolve. Moved by this, Fotuo rose up.
Daoyun immediately ran ahead through the dangerous passes to inform the monastics and the laity, urging them to go out to welcome him. On the road, he encountered a group...
Tiger’s eyes could not rest for a moment. Once they reached the mountains, there were tasks to be performed, which Yun invariably carried out without the slightest negligence.

Once, while traveling by boat through a mountain valley during the freezing depths of winter, the riverbed was covered in crumbling sand and stones. Yun stripped off his clothes and waded waist-deep to pull the mooring rope;
though the ice bit into his bones and his blood congealed, he traveled over three hundred li without ever showing any sign of refusal.

[He was] intimidated. At the end of the Sui dynasty, when the world was in great chaos, Lin Shihong rose up in Yuzhang, styling himself King of Chu, and appointed the scholar Hu as his Minister of State.
Now that the rebels occupy Poyang and Jiujiang, [Hu] resolved to carve a replica of the Auspicious Image of Mañjuśrī from Mount Lu’s Donglin Temple.
Entrusting Yun with the timber, he charged him with its supervision. Shortly thereafter, the image emerged from the furnace.
However, the neck and sides of the statue were perforated and leaking. It was planned to recast it, but this was not accomplished as Hui was arrested on charges of slander.
There remained more than one hundred and twenty taels of gold-colored metal from the image, which Daoyun, fearing the calamity of war, stored in bamboo tubes.
He also sent a ring of bronze beads with an inscription as a token of trust, entrusting it to Hu. When Hu reached Gongting, his boat capsized and he lost both items.
Later, they floated back and were recovered thirty *li* away. Just as Hu was about to die, he further entrusted the gold to his uncle, Master Xiao Chan, instructing him to flee.
