Shortly thereafter, the Tang troops broke into Yuzhang; Xiao used the coins to wrap himself in silk.
He wrapped gold and carried it upon his back to avoid danger. He encountered bandits, yet the bandits did not know it was gold;

they abandoned it and departed. Thus, Yun was able to complete his work. On the day of the smelting and casting, Li Wujie first made a vow to burn one of her arms as an offering for the casting. When the task was finished, it turned out to be exactly as she had divined.

The Li family did not know of this. The image appeared to her in a dream and said, "You wish to burn your arm; how can you deceive me? Upon waking, the Li lady immediately fulfilled her vow as she had desired.
The monastery was well-provided with the *Sūtras* and *Śāstras*, yet the Vinaya section alone remained incomplete. At that time, the Venerable Shou was propagating the teachings in the capital.
Yun traveled there on blistering feet and, by imperial decree, resided at Hongfu Monastery. There he obtained all the missing texts and brought them back.
Facheng of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Wang; his original name was Shouchen. During the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, he rose to the rank of Censor-in-Chief.

Because he served as a cruel official who framed the Crown Prince to incite a great legal purge, he abruptly resigned from office to enter the monastic life, dedicating himself to rigorous ascetic discipline.
To transform and guide the customs of the people: In the second year of the Yi-feng era, a diviner reported that there was an extraordinary light at the Western Market in Jingzhao.

By imperial decree, the site was excavated, and a stone casket was discovered containing ten thousand grains of Buddha-relics (śarīra). These were translucent, brilliant, and so hard and compact that they could not be worn away by friction or tarnished.
The Emperor decreed that a Guangzhai Temple be built on that very spot and erected a Seven-Jewels Terrace. The relics were then distributed to various locations throughout the capital.

He made offerings to the Buddha-land. At that time, he established a cause by requesting the excavation of the remaining land and the diversion of the Yong’an Canal to form a large pond named Haichi (Sea Pond).
He erected Buddhist halls and sutra towers upon it to magnify its splendor.

Men and women who delighted in performing meritorious deeds all flocked there, releasing flying and aquatic creatures to pray for the prosperity of the state. While the excavation was underway, an inscription was discovered.

In the soil it was said: "For a hundred years it served as a marketplace; later it became a pond again. From the establishment of the capital at Dushi during the early Sui dynasty until this point, barely a century had passed.
Fangjie was a dharma-grandson of Chan Master Jietuo. Jietuo possessed supreme conduct, and Fangjie followed his precepts without fail.

Although he had passed away, he remained devoted to benefiting sentient beings and promoting merit. He was registered as a monk at Zhaoguo Temple in Taiyuan and was long regarded by men and women as a source of refuge.
Once, when a statue of Mañjuśrī from Mount Wutai arrived from afar only to sink into the waters of the Hutuo River, he rushed to report the news everywhere.
He then went to the riverbank, burned incense, and offered prayers; the water receded, and he recovered the image to restore its paint.

They carried him back through the marshes. The water rose and overflowed once more as before. When the cremation was completed, they enshrined his entire body in a stupa about one li to the northwest of the temple.
His western spirit remains miraculous to this day.

Huiyun of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Yao and was a native of Huxiang. At the beginning of the Linde era, when Yun was ten years old, she took leave of her parents and entered the monastic life at Mount Nanyue.

Upon reaching the age of twenty, she received full ordination. She traveled through secluded and magnificent sites, repairing and restoring every monastery she encountered that was in a state of decay;
in this manner, she attended to more than twenty such temples. During the early years of the Guanshi era, she halted her travels in Jun Prefecture and stayed overnight at Fantai.
He expected to see extraordinary vapors arising from the pond within the garden north of the Bian River.
Upon inquiring about the location, he learned it was the residence of Zheng Jing, the Vice Prefect of Xizhou. He proceeded there on foot, only to find that the pond was exceedingly vast;
its ripples were so immense and boundless that they reflected the heavens, appearing as a complex, interlacing array of palaces and towers. He could do nothing but sigh in wonder.
He said, "This is something I can apply my strength toward. In the second year of the Shenlong era, he moved his residence to Baocheng Temple in Puzhou.

He made a vow to solicit gold and commissioned the carving of a sixteen-foot Maitreya image, which he erected beside the temple pond. Furthermore, he intended to name the temple Fuhui (Blessing and Wisdom) as a place to enshrine it.
He felled timber and hired craftsmen, and was about to complete the work when, in the second year of the Jinglong era, he first [began...]

Jing purchased that residence. Among the earth, an ancient stone inscription was unearthed, which recorded: "In the sixth year of the Tianbao era of the Qi dynasty, the year of Yihai, Guosi Temple was founded.
Thereupon, an official on tour ordered the statue to be brought to that site and commanded that the temple's timber be dismantled.
The number of monasteries was fixed by imperial decree. At that time, Minister of Justice Wang Zhīqín served as an Imperial Commissioner for Investigation;
he was to carry out the instructions of the edict to completely dismantle all unauthorized monasteries throughout the empire and collect their bronze and iron statues to be sent to nearby temples.

By this time, the scale of the monastery at Yún had already been fully established, with only the decorative paintings remaining to be completed. Encountering this edict, the project was abruptly halted, and Yún subsequently burned [the materials].
He burned incense and wept, prostrating himself before the image day and night, saying: "If this matter must surely succeed, may a miraculous omen appear.
Shortly thereafter, golden light radiated from the head of the image, its brilliance illuminating heaven and earth. The entire city gathered to witness it, sighing in wonder.

Some who glared at it with anger or spoke slanderous words were struck blind or mute; however, when they repented before the image, they were restored, and all vowed to serve as slaves for the rest of their lives.

Regarding his physical remains: before they had even been placed upon the funeral carriage, an imperial edict was issued granting the temple the title "Xiangguo" (Minister of State). Previously, while the Emperor was still at his private residence, he had experienced a dream that corresponded with this event.

Furthermore, an edict was issued appointing Minggan, a Great Virtue of Foshouji Monastery, to oversee the meritorious works and ensure that the local government officials did not cause any disturbance.
Jia Zeng, Palace Secretary, and Cen Xi, Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, both donated their entire salaries and personal funds for this purpose.

[He] assisted [the Emperor]. During the Xuanzong era, when the inner abdication was received, the Retired Emperor personally took up the brush and calligraphy to write the plaque for the temple and bestow it upon him.

He issued an imperial decree for the Great Virtuous Zhendi and his disciple, the official Pingguan, to jointly carry banners and flowers to celebrate the occasion. After a long time, he passed away and was buried in the eastern suburbs.
To this day, the temple estate and the portrait hall remain there; he is titled the "Patriarch Founder of the Temple."
Tang Chongye initially had no knowledge of where he came from. Soon thereafter, he accompanied Yiyang Dao’an to rely upon Vinaya Master Wenwang to study the *Vinaya* (Piṇi).

He served with diligent devotion without negligence, and was esteemed as the preeminent leader among his peers at the monastic academy. From early on, he shared a reputation for excellence with Zichuan Ke;
however, he surpassed him in his exceptional integrity and resolute fortitude. His fame and virtue reached the imperial court during the reign of Emperor Ruizong, who [subsequently] exiled him.

He converted his former residence into a temple named Anguo and was summoned by imperial decree to reside there. He subsequently entered the Chengming Hall to practice meditation and was granted the Bodhisattva Precepts of the highest rank.
The Emperor bestowed upon him lavish gifts and provisions. At that time, the Bodhi Temple was undergoing construction on its halls and pavilions;

Jingye used all the wealth he had received to assist with the labor. Indeed, throughout his life, he never once allowed surplus wealth to accumulate. During the Kaiyuan era, he suffered from a slight illness and looked toward his younger brother.

The Master said, "My life's span has reached its end and my transformation is complete. You disciples must carefully observe the precepts and maintain self-restraint; do not allow yourselves to become negligent.
He then passed away in the residence where he lived, specifically in the separate quarters of Ximing Monastery. This is truly the account of his great-grandson, Chengzhao.
Tang Xuanlan’s surname was Chu. His ancestors were from Henan, but later they moved to Qiantang, where he established his family.

In his youth, he relied upon Master Huichang to enter the monastic life. Huichang was advanced in years and held in high esteem; he was truly a model for students. He resided at Huayan Temple in the vicinity of Linping.

Toward the end of the Sui dynasty, the world fell into chaos and turmoil, and consequently, the temple fell into ruin. At the beginning of the Tang dynasty, an imperial edict permitted its restoration.
He renovated it. Lan then made its architectural system magnificent and its foundations expansive. Backed by mountains and facing water, its strategic advantages were truly admirable.

Furthermore, he designated the lake in front of the temple as a "fish-releasing pool," and with the support of the Prefect Yuan Congli and the Magistrate Yang Minyan, he prohibited fishing and hunting there. He also cast three hundred and fifty images of gilded copper.

He sat [in meditation] and transcribed more than two thousand fascicles of sutras. He also painted images of the Four Heavenly Kings before the hall; thus, his power of manifestation was diligent indeed.

His father, Zong, was posthumously granted the title of Prefect of Hezhou and the honorific Right Attendant of the Imperial Household (You Sanqi Changshi), Duke of Shu. His elder brother, Wuliang, was renowned for his talent and learning.

His mother, the Great Lady, lived to the age of one hundred and ten, sustaining herself through her own efforts. Furthermore, Lan [the subject of the text] took his full ordination in India, the land where the precepts were originally received. And...
While serving as the Director of Monks (Senglù), he renovated the villa he had built for himself as well as three monasteries of Huayan, all of which he restored.

He spent his final years traveling leisurely between these sites, guiding and transforming others until his old age. In the twenty-second year of the Kaiyuan era, he manifested illness and passed away at the temple at the age of eighty-four.
His disciples, including Míngliǎo and Dàjué, interred him in the Xìlì Cave. Xu Ānzhēn, Vice Minister of Works, composed the inscription for his stele.
Táng Chǔjīn, whose surname was Chéng, was originally from Guǎngpíng; he now holds his household registration in Zhōuwěi, Jīngzhào. His mother...

Lady Gao dreamed of the Buddha one night and subsequently conceived. At the age of seven, she shaved her head and entered the monastic order; at eighteen, she had recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and mastered its great meaning.

At thirty, she vowed to construct a stūpa for the Buddha Prabhūtaratna. During the course of the construction work, Emperor Xuanzong saw the golden characters "Chu Jin" (Bearing the Golden) appear in the void.
The following morning, he dispatched an envoy to summon her and question her; she then completed the project and further increased the number of tiers. Furthermore, at Cuiwei...
He established one pagoda each at Wuzhen and Ersi Temples, saying, "In days to come, I shall surely dwell in seclusion here.

On the seventh day of the seventh month in the second year of the Qiannian era, he passed away lying on his right side. He was sixty-two years of age and thirty-seven years of *dharma-lakṣa* (monastic seniority).
On the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the thirteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, Dou Wen, Duke of Bin and Grand Marshal of the Left Street’s Merit Office, [erected a stele].

The Memorial Petition: Chujin of Qianfusi Temple was the Preceptor from Whom I Received the Precepts. At the beginning of the Tianbao era, he built the Many Treasures Pagoda for the sake of the state and established a Dharma Flower (Lotus Sūtra) Practice Hall.
More than sixty years have passed since then; the monks have performed their liturgical recitations during the six periods of the day, and the sound of the sūtra has never ceased.

Having served through four successive dynasties, his virtuous deeds have yet to be honored with a posthumous title. By imperial decree, he is hereby conferred the posthumous title of Chan Master Dayuan.
Tang Huaiyu, surnamed Xu, was a native of Taiyuan. He entered the monastic order at Chongfu Temple in his home prefecture.

From a young age, he was sharp and quick-witted, reciting a thousand words daily. His learning was excellent and his conduct rigorous; thus, his peers could not hope to equal him. Nevertheless, he remained diligent in his aspirations for spiritual cultivation.
In the regions of You and Bing, there was no one within the gates of the Dharma who did not exert themselves toward the maintenance of dwellings, ritual images, and sutra scrolls.
He served as the administrative head of three monasteries and collated more than twenty editions of the Tripitaka. He renovated and adorned the Pure Land Cloister (*Jingtu-yuan*).

During the reign of Emperor Daizong, he was summoned by imperial decree to serve as the presiding master of the Consecration Ritual (*Guanding-daochang*) site; the secret mantras and esoteric teachings all relied upon him. Later, he led [the community] at the monastery.
His lifespan was sixty-three years.

Tang Ming was a native of Tiantai. In his youth, he left the household life at Lingxu Daochang. He traveled through various regions until he reached the capital, where he took up residence at Chanding Temple.
There, he constantly reflected upon how the virtuous masters of antiquity had upheld the Buddha-Dharma, and his mind—

How immeasurable is this! For instance, the divine monk Zhiyuan, at Beishan in Fanyang, transcribed the scriptures and engraved them upon stone, pouring molten iron over them to pray that they might remain indestructible for the benefit of future generations;

this practice continues to this day. Following this precedent, Zhun resolved to have craftsmen carve the *Lotus Sūtra* into the cliffs of Langshan in the first month of the Wuyin year of the Zhenyuan era, so that it might endure for posterity. However, as for these stones...
Stubborn and evil, he was unfit for service. Zhun thereupon prayed to the mountain spirits to assist in virtuous deeds. Within his meditation, he saw several sheets of paper arranged upon a stone;

subsequently, the Regional Commander, Lord Cui of Boling, together with twenty-eight of his subordinates, each vowed to transcribe one chapter by hand, to be engraved on a stele and set up beneath the corridor. The first month of the eighth year of Yuanhe.
He shaved his head at Luocheng.
Tang Youxuan, surnamed Liu, was a native of Youzhou. At the age of twenty, he received the tonsure from Master Xian of Bingzhou. After some time, he attained the Dharma.
In the second year of the Yuanhe era, he struck his staff and traveled to the region south of the Yangtze River, where he visited Dayun Temple in Kuaiji and saw the drum lying silent.
The bells were silent and the alms-round did not turn. He sighed, saying, "Can this place alone not be used to propagate the teaching? Thereupon, he took a single bowl and went into the marketplace;
those who would give responded like an echo. Consequently, he had the abbot open the hall to receive the assembly according to the methods of all the patriarchs.
Not long after, he moved to the abandoned Miaoxi Temple on Mount Gui at the heart of Lake Dongting. In the ninth year, Meng Jian of Pingchang came to govern the prefecture;
he expanded the scale of the temple and renovated it entirely. In the twelfth year, he departed to travel to the Southern Peak (Nanyue), where he built a hermitage on the summit to dwell in.
Shang You, the Governor of Yuzhang, showed him even greater reverence and admiration. In the nineteenth year...
He was invited to reside at Dongming-sa. This temple was established during the reign of Emperor Jin’an; the gathering of eminent monastics there remains flourishing even to this day.

During the Baolì era, an imperial edict was issued to change its name to Shifu-sa, and a *jietan* (precept platform) was established within it. Furthermore, an imperial decree was issued for the ordination of monks.
It is said that all the statues and ritual implements in the temple were provided by Xuán. In the first year of the Dàhé era, Shen Zhongcheng Fu Gaxin developed faith in him. Moreover—
He constructed a five-story pagoda for the Buddha to the south of the temple. Shortly thereafter, he passed away; his entire body was lacquered and clothed, and it was enshrined within the pagoda.
Tang Jiran, whose secular surname was Bái, traveled to Mount Tiantai in the second year of the Taihe era. Upon reaching Wozhou Mountain in Shan County, he fell in love with [the place].
Its seclusion was so sublime that he chose it as the site for his hermitage. Once his spiritual transformation had taken root, eminent monastics gathered there in great numbers.
Yuan Xiangguo Zhen, the Integrity Commissioner of Eastern Zhejiang, once made a donation to him, and Governor Lu assisted in its restoration. Three years later the monastery was completed;

five years later, Buddhist rites were established. Yet whenever he ascended the seat to proclaim the essentials of the Dharma, he was especially revered and submitted to by those throughout the four seas.
He passed away later at that same monastery. The record was composed by the Court Gentleman Yue-tian Bai Juyi and calligraphed by the Palace Attendant Liu Yuxi.

Fa-xing of the Tang dynasty was a native of Luojing; he entered the monastic order at the age of seven, shaved his head, and received full ordination. Thereafter, he practiced the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

He was renowned for two scriptures and was particularly strict in observing the precepts without transgression. Traveling extensively to seek out sacred sites, he eventually settled among the forests and springs.

Thereupon, his name was again registered at Foguang Temple. Restraining his expenditures and utilizing offerings and profits, he constructed a Great Hall of Maitreya, seven bays wide and three stories high, measuring ninety-five feet in height.
Within it were seventy-two honored images, all of exquisite craftsmanship. Thus, at Mount Tai...

The assembly of monks collectively requested him to serve as the head administrator (*kangwei*) of the mountain gate, primarily because his character was harmonious and refined, and his learning and knowledge were comprehensive and extensive.
In the first month of the spring of the second year of the Dàhé era, he heard a voice from the air saying, "The assembly of Tuṣita Heaven has come specifically to welcome you.
Thereupon, he bathed, burned incense, sat upright, and passed away.
The monk Jie was a man of unknown origins who had long resided at Guangzhai Temple in the capital.
During the Jianzhong era, he intended to replicate the sacred sites of Mount Wutai by crafting an image of Mañjuśrī to inspire the devotion of the people, both men and women.

However, fearing that the act of excavation would inevitably harm living beings and their consciousness, he first established a ritual site (*dharmapūjā*) for three days to offer prayers before commencing the work.

He offered prayers: "May all wriggling creatures know how to avoid this place. When the baskets and shovels were finally deployed, there was not a single wriggling creature to be found amidst the mounds of excavated earth; such was the power of his sincere heart.

Previously, Jie had used double-layered silk to make water-strainers, straining water every day and pouring it into a well for insects. The well was always full and never ran dry, and because of this, the world [came to know him].
He named it the "Well for Protecting Life. He exhausted his ingenious ingenuity in its design;

furthermore, he cast a bronze toad to serve as a smoke-exhaust vent, so as to prevent moths and gnats from losing their lives in the lamp flames. Its construction was quite prevalent during that period.

Later, because he moved his residence to the Tai Temple that had been established, he was granted annual offerings of incense and the recitation of scriptures, which distinguished him from other monasteries.
During the Tang dynasty, there was one named Tanxiu, courtesy name Defu, surnamed Li. He had long relied upon Kaiyuan Temple in Yue to leave the household life and receive full ordination.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* in four fascicles is an excellent work that instructs scholars and possesses exceptional disciplinary rigor.

However, since the monastery was founded during the Southern Liang dynasty, more than four hundred years have passed, and its magnificent buildings have fallen into ruin. Recently, they have been renovated and expanded, surpassing their former beauty;
all of this is due to the efforts of Xiu. Furthermore, the outer gate towers of the Huguo Jinglou Monastery are likewise [restored].
Formerly, it was initiated by the Dharma Master Tanyi. During the Yonghui era, it was reformed through the manifested transformations of the Dharma Master Kang Senghui.
Now, it has all been restored so that its state is as if at its original inception; one may truly call this diligent.
During the Xiantong era, he passed away in that very temple, which is the present-day so-called Dashi (Great Goodness) Temple.
Tang Zhiguang, surnamed Cui, was first seen at Kaiyuan Temple in Yajou. Within the shrine of the deity Kārttikeya, he performed extraordinary arts and strange deeds that were unfathomable.
Whenever he encountered someone afflicted by illness, he would simply strike them once with a bamboo staff and give a single shout.
He burned paper currency and distributed food and drink; at times he even tore paper, dipped it in water, and applied it [to the sick], whereupon the paralyzed rose and the lame ran.

Illnesses were instantly cured. He was especially strict in disciplining himself. When women arrived at his door, he would invariably dismiss them. For his daily vegetarian meals, he permitted nothing other than rice, vegetables, and soybean sauce;
once the meal was finished, he would depart immediately without offering any thanks. If anyone offered him money as a religious gift, he would not accept it.
It shall not exceed twenty coins; if it exceeds that, it shall not be accepted. Furthermore, have them cast into a single basket.
When it is full, strike the bell at the Buddha Hall to assemble the community, who shall divide it equally. This applies even to households of men of rank; thus it was done during the Qianning era.
When the Wang clan first established their rule over Shu, Du Ya went to pay his respects to them, bringing with him Gong Nao of Luo.
The Wang clan addressed him as "Holy Master. Previously, during the Xiantong era, the Nanzhao Mian King Jieti Chuo had led an army to besiege Chengdu;

the situation was extremely perilous when the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa suddenly appeared in the form of a śramaṇa, about five zhang tall, standing upon the city wall and glaring at the enemy with wrath.

Blazing rays of light shot forth. Tichuo was terrified and immediately fled. The people of Shu subsequently built a pavilion at Baoli Temple, where they erected images of the Heavenly Kings and Śramaṇas to enshrine them.
Later, these were destroyed by Minister Niu; however, the military forces of Shu remained vast and continuous without end.

When it came to this time, the Wang family requested that Guang extensively restore and maintain them. Guang granted his consent, and donors crowded together like a suffocating mass. He collected the offerings until—

Two hundred thousand [people were involved]. Furthermore, he exhorted others to contribute timber; all of it arrived by water and was hauled by land. Laborers and craftsmen exerted their strength with axes and hatchets, while baskets and shovels worked in tandem.
In the first year of the Guanghua era, the pavilion was completed. Following the custom of the River God’s Pond, offerings were cast into the water.
The next day, fish measuring about two chi in length, numbering in the billions, floated to the surface dead. Could this not be what was meant [by the divine response]?
By the power of their merit, they transcend birth and are reborn in the good realms.

Huiwen of Tang was a native of Xin'an; he ascended the ranks of the precepts and resided at Lingshi Temple. Throughout his life, he constantly encouraged the secular world with the practice of giving, saying:
"In the cycle of transmigration through the five paths, if one wishes to advance in cultivation to seek liberation, one must not abandon the power of merit."
How secure his provisions were! Whenever there was construction or maintenance work, even for matters that were humble, lowly, or trivial, he would still attend to them personally.
Upon obtaining fish or meat, he would invariably carry it back with his own hands to provide for the craftsmen. One day, while traveling in the mountains, he encountered a tiger;
he immediately struck its head with his staff and said, "Do not devour people. I am now creating merit for you; you ought to assist me. The next day...
One day, a wild boar came, carrying a sun-disk in its mouth; such was the response evoked by his sincerity.

Previously, while casting a sixteen-foot image at the Lan River, he had calculated that the gold was sufficient for the purpose, yet he had not yet begun the molding and smelting, saying, "I shall wait for a great donor.
Not long after, he heard that a woman from Qingxi County had come to offer a precious mirror she possessed. He took it and...
He made a vow, saying: "If my resolve is truly sincere, then this mirror shall cast its reflection correctly upon the day it is cast.
Shortly thereafter, it was indeed so. He then visited Yuzhang and offered several *yi* of gold. On the way, he encountered bandits; he threw the gold into the water, saying:
"If you must dredge it out and then obtain it, then the merit-field (*puṇyakṣetra*) of you gentlemen will perhaps suffer no loss. Upon his return, he looked into his chest.
Since the golden fittings were found within it, was this not because his thoughts of compassion and forbearance were manifested, such that the spirits followed by bestowing their protection?
It is therefore fitting that the world honors his virtue.

Later, during the Zhenjun era of the Later Tang dynasty, Zheng Jùn, a son of the Zhang family from Xinzheng in Zhengzhou, at the age of fourteen, entered the monastic order under the Vinaya Master Guizheng of Xiangguo Monastery.
He studied and recited such sutras as the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa and the *Aparimitāyur-jñāna* (Renwang), soon becoming able to memorize them perfectly and never forgetting them.
Later, having donned the black robes and undergone tonsure, he studied the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*. At the age of eighteen, he ascended the lecture seat to propagate and expound it.

At his twentieth year, he received full ordination at Huishan Temple on Mount Song. Thereafter, he took up residence at Fengshan Temple—which is the present-day Kaibao Yuan—where he investigated the profound subtleties of the new commentaries on the Vinaya and taught them.
He was diligent and never for a moment slackened; at that time, he was only twenty years old.
In the second year of the Dàshùn era, the Xiāngguó Temple was destroyed by fire, leaving the ground completely bare.
The senior monks considered that without the power of great merit and virtue, it could not be restored. Some said, "If we invite Sengjùn, there is a good chance of success.
Thereupon, they went together to request him; Sengjùn did not decline or refuse, but returned to take upon himself the office of *upādhyāya*. Less than twelve years later, the donors...
Crowds gathered in great numbers. The temple’s halls, courtyards, and corridors were all newly renovated. The assembly elected him as the new Abbot, Wang.

His monks and nuns, numbering over one hundred and fifty, were of lofty and pure conduct; they truly possessed the power to move others. Thus, he was able to achieve such meritorious accomplishments while remaining seated.
On the twelfth day of the fourth month of the summer in the second year of the Tongguang era, he passed away from a slight illness. Spring.
He was seventy-eight years old at death and fifty-eight years of Dharma seniority. He was interred in the same burial mound as Chan Master Huiyun.

Later, Zhihui (of the Later Tang) was surnamed Gao and was a native of Xianyang. In his youth, he followed Chan Master Guifeng Wen to receive the tonsure. At the age of twenty, he received full ordination;
he studied the Vinaya and practiced meditation, extensively surveying the teachings of the Tripiṭaka. However, he was particularly skilled in calligraphy and poetry.
Yong also emulated the styles of Sengzhen and Daofen, and his paintings, executed according to the six methods, rendered objects and forms with lifelike movement.
As for his resolve to save sentient beings, it was clearly a matter of innate endowment rather than something practiced through forced effort.

In the fourth year of the Qiandehua era of the Liang dynasty, he came from Jiangbiao to the capital, where he toured various monasteries; he found that while all necessary provisions were complete, there was a particular deficiency regarding bathhouses.

The records were incomplete. Thereupon, he selected a site at the confluence of the Luo River and constructed several dozen rooms. He purchased land to provide firewood and excavated a pond to store water;
the water was drawn by a wheel and collected in troughs. The abundance of his medicinal decoctions was such that it could hardly be described.

Consequently, companions with flasks and alms-bowls, those wearing crowns and hairpins, and the class of gentry and scholars arrived in such numbers that there was no leisure even for a single day, and they would simply leave their shoes by the wooden [steps].
The writing was received with gratitude. Upon removing their robes, they used coarse hemp skirts (*sī*) to cover themselves;
these were opened once every five days. In total, seventy-two such openings occurred before the year was complete. Those who bathed there numbered nearly ten thousand.
Furthermore, a "Hall for Bathing the Holy Ones" was established along the western corridor to represent the sixteen *Arhats*, while within it was the Avalokiteśvara Hall. The attendant was Yang Ning.
Shi Duchi composed an inscription to commemorate the virtues of Zhijiang.
Zhijiang was a native of Youzhou, under the jurisdiction of the Three Rivers in Henan; he was the son of the Shi family.

His family was wealthy, yet while his elder and younger brothers were both men of the *youxia* (wandering knight) class who achieved nothing of note, Zhijiang alone devoted himself to goodness and cherished righteousness. He deeply admired the study of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*). In the fourth year of the Qianning era of the Tang dynasty...
In his fifteenth year, Jiang went to Ganhua Temple on Mount Pan to seek ordination as a śrāmaṇera.
In the third year of the Tianfu era, he received full ordination at Liyuan Temple on Mount Wutai. He mastered the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, and other scriptures.
At the beginning of the Longde era of the Liang dynasty, he lectured on the *Abhidharmakośa* at Kaiyuan Temple in Shangqiu and composed the *Ruìyìng Chāo*.

His disciples collectively transmitted and studied it. At the beginning of the Tongguang era of the Tang dynasty, he resided at Guangshou Monastery in Songzhou, where he constructed halls and buildings.
The structure was magnificent and worthy of admiration. Furthermore, he commissioned statues of the two venerable ones, Maitreya and Śākyamuni, as well as images of the sixteen Arhats;
these were exquisitely adorned with fine brushwork. In the early autumn of the fifth year of the Xiande era, he suddenly fell ill and passed away at the age of seventy-four.
Just as his breath was departing, some beheld celestial beings thronging about him in what appeared to be a ceremonial procession to welcome him. Observers attributed this to Jiang’s former vow.
This was the verification of his rebirth in Tuṣita Heaven. Li Huan, an official of the Ministry of Personnel, composed the inscription for his stupa.
Song Changjue’s secular surname was Li; he was a native of Chenliu. His family had long been scholars, yet they were impoverished and unable to support themselves.
At the age of seven, he studied at the local school, where his brilliance surpassed his peers. He traveled with fellow literati to Mount Lu, finding joy in its tranquility.

He subsequently entered the Guizong Temple to leave the household life as a *jìngrén* (lay attendant). In the second year of the Qiánhuà era of the Liáng dynasty, he first changed his secular attire and underwent tonsure.

He immediately received the full precepts at the Gānlù Altar of Dōnglín. Although he thoroughly investigated the Tripitaka in his studies, he ultimately devoted himself exclusively to the pointing-out instructions of Chan.
Having paid homage to the sacred traces of Mañjuśrī on Mount Wú tái, he thought to himself, "I am weary; shall I return?"
"Can this be used for the business of running about? In the third year of the Tiānchéng era of the Later Táng dynasty, he finally acquired land to the right of Lìjǐngmén in Bìnjīng.
He constructed several rooms to establish a bathhouse. Every month, on the third and eighth days, he would hold one bathing service;

monks from both near and far would come to bathe there. The annual expenditure was approximately ten million *mǐn*. Although this was entirely provided through the offerings of lay donors, it could not have been sustained without the guidance of the Awakened One.
Regarding the power of upholding [the precepts], who could possibly match him? He was particularly close friends with Tao Gu of Beihai and Zhang Zhongxun of Xiangdong;
the extant writings they exchanged can be verified. Tao Gu’s preface states that [the Master] took a single meal of hemp and wheat as his awakening, and a single set of robes for both heat and cold.

The kings and ministers before and after him petitioned for the title of "Imperial Preceptor" and purple robes; however, Daojue resolutely refused them. His conduct became all the more worthy of veneration.
He was praised, saying:
Alas, the world! Greed and stinginess cause all to perish. The Bodhisattva resolves his mind to universally rescue all living beings.
He draws near to those who beg; his words are warm and his countenance gentle. "You are destitute, you are in need," he says. "Take what you wish, seek what you desire!
Whether it be food and drink, clothing, playthings, precious jewels, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, or even his own head, eyes, marrow, and brain—he gives them all.
Internal giving and external giving—without things and without body; giver and receiver likewise have no person.
Only by being thus can one leave behind all marks of abiding, and together with emptiness, [attain] the Tathāgata, the treasury of great merit.

Precept Study (*Śīla-śikṣā*), composed by the Śramaṇa Tanyu of Eastern Zhejiang.
The Sūtra says: "The Prātimokṣa is your great teacher. To know this is to know how to propagate the Dharma. It further says:
"If the Vinaya is destroyed, the Buddha-dharma is destroyed. To know this is to know how to protect the Teaching.

Pervading the power of vows, it encompasses and restrains Māras and externalists, serving as a model for humans and devas.
Thus, that which was defiled is made to flourish, and that which was obstructed is made to flow through. It covers the three realms without limit and extends through billions of kalpas without end.
To act in such a manner and call oneself a disciple of the Buddha, continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom—how could this be limited merely to the *prātimokṣa*?

It is fitting for the Master. That the Vinaya remains unimpaired is indeed marvelous. As for the two sections—Promoting the Dharma and Protecting the Teachings—they are appended under the study of the precepts;

Zhi Dun of the Jin dynasty, styled Daolin, was born into the Guan clan. He was a native of Chenliu, though some say he was from Linlü. From his youth, he possessed a spirit of brilliance;
his divine insight was granted by Heaven. Upon first arriving in the capital, Wang Meng of Taiyuan saw him and remarked, "The power to penetrate the subtle."
He was truly no less than Wang Bi’s successor. Chen Qun and Yin Rong had once admired Wei Jie’s spirit and demeanor; among the younger generation, none could succeed him.
Upon meeting Zhi Dun, they sighed in admiration, feeling as though they were seeing such a person again. His family had served the Buddha for generations.

He lived in seclusion at Yuhang and became a śramaṇa at the age of twenty-five. His expositions of the scriptures were free and unencumbered by literalism, which led those who clung to the letter of the texts to disparage him.
When Xie An heard of this, he said, "It is like Jiu Fangyin’s appraisal of horses: he overlooks their dark or yellow coats and seeks only their noble spirit and elegance.

Wang Qia, Liu Tan, Xu Xun, Xi Chao, Sun Chuo, Huan Yanbiao, Wang Jingren, He Cidao, Wang Wendu, Xie Changxia, and Yuan Yanbo were all renowned scholars of the time who maintained a relationship of "external friendship" with Zhi Dun.
Once, while at Baima Temple, he discussed Zhuang Zhou with Liu Xizhi and others, saying: "To claim that 'following one's nature' constitutes *xīyáo* (carefree wandering) is not correct.
Furthermore, Jie and Zhi took cruelty and harm as their nature; could they also be said to have attained *xīyáo*? Thereupon, he annotated the "Xīyáo" chapter, which scholars came to revere.
He returned east to Zhishan Temple and later intended to enter the Shàn region, where Xie An was serving as governor.
In Wuxing, [Zhu Daoqian] sent a letter to Huida, saying: "My longing for you has accumulated day by day, becoming even more intense as the days pass.

Knowing that you intend to return to Shan to attend to yourself, I am filled with regret. Human life is merely a temporary lodging; since recent times, the refined pleasures and matters of worldly success have almost entirely vanished.
I am nothing but sorrowful all day long, looking forward only to your arrival to comfort me. This mountain county is quiet and secluded; it is quite suitable."
He was nursing his ailment at Shan, where the expenses were no less than before, yet medicine was easily obtained; thus he was fortunate enough to fulfill his long-cherished desire.

While Wang Xizhi was in Kuaiji, he had heard of Huida’s reputation but did not yet believe it, saying, "I must see him for myself before I am convinced. When Huida returned to Shan, his route passed through Mount Ji.
Wang Xizhi went to visit him and, struck by his refined demeanor, said, "Do you still remember the 'Verses on Wandering at Ease'? Huida then composed them for him.

His writings numbered in the thousands, brilliant and divinely composed, revealing the very heart of principle. Fuxi nodded in approval and invited him to reside at Lingjia Temple, desiring to see him every evening.
After some time, he entered the small ridge of Wozhou, where he built a vihāra and taught a multitude of over a thousand disciples.

Later, he moved to Qiguang Temple on Mount Shicheng, where he lived on wild fruits and drank from mountain streams, composing commentaries on the Ānāpāna-smṛti and the various sūtras on the four dhyānas.

He also authored the *Jise youxuan lun* (Treatise on Roaming the Profound within Immediate Form), the *Sheng bubian zhi lun* (Treatise that the Sage Does Not Discern or Know), the *Daowang zhiguai* (The Essential Return of the Practice of the Way), and the *Xue dao shi* (Model for Studying the Way).
Tracing his lineage back to Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna, he arrived at Shanyin and lectured on the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra*. Xu Xun served as the presiding lecturer (*dougjiang*).

Xuánbá was uniquely enlightened; for several hundred years, he alone has sustained and flourished the Great Dharma, ensuring that the True Principle does not perish.

Tán remained in the capital for three years, after which he submitted a memorial requesting to return to the mountain forests. The Emperor granted his request and provided him with the necessary provisions for his departure.
His provisions for every occasion were abundant. Once, when many famous figures of the time were seeing him off at Zhengluting, Cai Zishu arrived first and sat down near Hui Dun.

From this, [the Master] attained enlightenment; he ate only vegetarian food for the rest of his life. Once, while traveling through Yuyao Valley, he stayed for two nights and would not leave.

He was deeply grieved. He then moved [the remains] to the middle of the valley. On the fourth day of the intercalary fourth month in the first year of the Taihe era, he passed away at the age of fifty-three.

He sighed and said, "As the artisan Shi laid down his axe for the man of Ying, and Boya snapped his strings for Zhongzi, my own substance is lost.
Having completed the *Diao Zhang* (Chapter of Lament), he set aside his brush and passed away. His collected works comprise ten volumes. At that time, there was also Zhu Fayang in the eastern lands.
He also attained renown through his wisdom and understanding, and was highly esteemed by King Tai. After his death, he appeared in person before the king to exhort him regarding religious practice.
Zhu Daqian (style name Fashen) of the Jin dynasty was born into the Wang clan of Langya. At the age of eighteen, he became a disciple of Liu [Yuan] of Zhongzhou.
Yuanzhen. Yuanzhen possessed a fine reputation. He had secretly committed [the teachings] to his heart. Later, he shaved his head. He was skilled in deportment and conduct.

Emperor Xiaowu (Yuanhuang), Emperor Xiaoming (Mingdi) of the Zhongzong lineage, all held him in high esteem. Prime Minister Wang Maohong and Grand Marshal Yu Yuan gui both visited his door to form friendships with him. Once...

He wore wooden clogs as he entered the palace hall. People of the time marveled at his lofty character and moral integrity; at first, he was not even aware that there was such a thing as a court or marketplace.

He passed away in the second year of the Kāngníng era at the age of eighty-nine. By imperial decree, ten thousand coins were granted as funeral expenses, and he was buried by Zhú Fǎyǒu.
At the age of twenty-four, while reciting the *Abhidharma*, he mastered it after a single night; he subsequently lectured on the sutras at Nántái Temple.

people of the world could not distinguish between their respective writings. He was highly esteemed for transcribing various sutras. Zhu Fazhi possessed literary talent and composed the *Biographies of Eminent and Recluse Śramaṇas*. In total...

Zhu Sengfu of the Jin dynasty was a man of unknown origins. He was skilled in the *Prajñāpāramitā* of the Path of Radiance and resided at Waguan Temple to lecture and teach.

He was highly esteemed and praised by the eminent monks such as Dao’an and Sengtai. He passed away at the monastery where he resided at the age of over seventy.
Jin Daozheng’s surname was Zhao; he was a native of Qingshui in Luoyang, though some say he was from Jiyin. His original name was Zheng, and his courtesy name was Wenyue.
At the age of eighteen, he served as a Secretariat Drafter (*zhuozuolang*) under Fu Jian of the Former Qin, subsequently rising to the rank of Palace Attendant (*huangmenlang*) and Governor of Wuwei.

He was beardless and emaciated; though he had wives and concubines, he had no children, much like a eunuch. Furthermore, his learning encompassed both Buddhist and Confucian traditions, and he offered criticisms and admonitions without any fear or hesitation.
Toward the end of Fu Jian’s reign, as the ruler became negligent and addicted to the Xianbei people, [Tao Kan] sang this song:
"I have heard of old that the Mengjin River Bends in a single curve for a thousand li. This water was originally clear; Who has stirred it up?"
He caused [the water] to become turbid. Fu Jian said with indignation, "This is me! He then sang a song: "In the northern garden there is a jujube tree; its leaves spread wide, casting a deep shade.

Dao’an of the Jin dynasty was born into the Wei clan. He was a native of Fuliu in Changshan. His family had been of the scholar-official class for generations. Orphaned at an early age, he was raised by his maternal uncle, Kong Sheng.
Though his appearance was unremarkable, his character and disposition were exceptionally brilliant. At the age of seven, when he read books, he could take in five lines at once with a single glance;

his father marveled at this and knew he possessed no ordinary capacity. At twelve, he entered the monastic life. His teacher, judging him by his physical exterior, considered him dull-witted and set him to labor.

While out tending the fields, he stayed in a field hut for three years to seek out scriptures from his teacher. His teacher bestowed upon him one fascicle of the *Bianyi jing* (Sūtra on Resolving Doubts), consisting of five thousand words; in a single night, he returned it to his teacher. He then requested another scripture, and his teacher bestowed upon him one fascicle of the *Chengju guangming jing* (Sūtra of Perfect Radiance), consisting of ten thousand words; again, in a single night, he returned it to his teacher. The teacher asked, "Have you read it? [He replied,] "I have. The teacher said, "If you can retain it in your memory after reading it once, I shall give it to you. He then read it once and recited it back to his teacher without error. The teacher was amazed and gave it to him. He subsequently sought other scriptures, and his teacher bestowed upon him the *Damingdu jing* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra) in twenty-four fascicles. After reading it once, he could recite it fluently. His teachings are a source of liberation. His example is a source of inspiration. His legacy is a source of hope. His life is a source of wonder. His teachings are a source of understanding. His influence is a source of transformation. His legacy is a source of renewal. His life is a source of gratitude. His teachings are a source of peace. His example is a source of light. His legacy is a source of joy. His life is a source of meaning. His teachings are a source of truth. His influence is a source of unity. His legacy is a source of harmony. His life is a source of fulfillment.
He recited them all from memory without omission. His teacher considered this lack of sincerity and had him consult the scriptures to verify it; yet he did not miss a single character.
The teacher was greatly amazed by this and shaved his head for him, conferring the full precepts (*upasampadā*). He traveled to study in Ye (Yecheng), where he visited Fotudeng.
Deng spoke with him and was so struck that he exclaimed, "A man of talent of the age! The Buddha-Dharma in the eastern lands relies solely upon this person; others are not equal."
He was thus reached by [Dao'an's] influence and subsequently received Daocheng’s teachings. He lectured again upon them with such mastery that it was like pouring water from one vessel into another.

The assembly vied with one another to pose difficult challenges, saying, "We must surely defeat this 'Son of Kunlun' before we will cease. Yet Dao’an’s soaring eloquence pierced through their arguments like a sharp injection;

none among the crowd dared to look up at him. At that time, people had a proverb: "The lacquer-clad monk startles his neighbors. Later, he sought refuge in Huozhai, where there was Zhu Faji of Dayang.
He lectured on the *Śarīra-skandha-praveśa-sūtra* (Yin-chi-ru-jing), and Dao’an received his teachings from him. Shortly thereafter, he founded a monastery on Mount Taihang to reside in.
At the age of forty-five, he returned to Jizhou and stayed at Shoudu Monastery, where his disciples numbered several hundred. After Shi Hu passed away, Pengcheng Wang succeeded to the throne;
he then extensively renovated the quarters of the Hualin Garden and dispatched the imperial envoy Zhu Changpu to welcome Dao’an. Dao’an, regarding the state—
The crisis had not yet been relieved when Ran Min rebelled; moreover, there were natural disasters of drought and locusts, and bandits roamed everywhere.

The mountains of Wangwu and Nulin could no longer provide a place of refuge, so he intended to rely on Luguun. However, the troops of慕容俊 (Murong Jun) were pressing in from all sides, so he eventually fled south to Xiangyang.
Upon reaching Xinye, he dispatched Fa Tai to the Yangzhou region and Fa He to Shu, while he himself remained with Huiyuan.

More than four hundred followers traveled by night through rain and thunder, using flashes of lightning as their guide. When they saw a house, they noticed two horse feed-baskets hanging between two willow trees;
they could hold about one *hu*. Dao’an called out, “Lin Baisheng! and indeed someone came out to greet them. His disciples asked, “How did you know his name?
Dao’an simply pointed to the feed-baskets. Upon arriving in Xiangyang, he annotated the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Dàoxíng* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā), and the *Mìjì* (Guhyakādhipati).
The *Anapanasati-sutra* and other scriptures, as well as the *Zonglu-jing*, were translated and transmitted down to the present month; these were bestowed upon students.
Huan Lang, General Who Subdues the West, while stationed at Jiangling, forcibly took them along with him.

Upon his return, because the Bai Ma Pass was narrow and cramped, he established Tanxi Temple on the grounds of Zhang Yinzhi’s residence in Qinghe. He constructed a five-story pagoda and opened four hundred rooms. [At that time] the Liang...
Yang Hongzhong, the Regional Inspector of the province, offered ten thousand catties of copper to construct a dew-receiving basin (*lùpán*).
Dao’an said to Hongzhong, “The dew-receiving basin has already been entrusted to Master Taita for its construction; I request that you redirect this copper to cast a sixteen-foot-tall Great Image.

Would this be acceptable? Hongzhong respectfully agreed. When the image was completed, it emitted light and exhibited extraordinary features. Whenever Dao’an presided over a Dharma assembly, he would [invoke] Fu Jian.
The golden-foil relief image, the seated golden image, the embroidered golden-thread image, the woven image, and the pearl-beaded Maitreya image were presented as objects of verification;
those who beheld them revered and admired them. There was also a foreign bronze image of ancient and unusual craftsmanship that had long remained unadorned;
when he ordered his disciples to arrange its topknot, a śarīra was found within it, its radiance brilliant and magnificent.

It so obscured the hall and its steps that the multitude was struck with wonder and amazement. Xi Zuochi, a man of extraordinary talent from Xiangyang, first sent a letter to establish friendly relations, and only then went to visit Dao’an.
Upon meeting him, he introduced himself, saying, "Xi Zuochi of the Four Seas. Dao’an replied slowly, "Shi Dao’an who fills the heavens.
At the time, this was considered a famous exchange. Zuochi then sent a letter to Xie Anshi, praising Dao’an as truly peerless.
The Ever-Victorious One merely regrets not seeing you. For fifteen years while residing at Fandian, he constantly lectured on the *Prabhāsa-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

Emperor Xiaowu issued an edict stating: "The Dharma Master, by means of his virtue and the Way, illuminates both humans and devas, causing the Great Dharma to circulate and serving as a reliance for all living beings.
He ought to receive daily the stipend of a prince. When Fu Jian attacked Xiangyang, he captured [him].
Feeling at ease and joyful, Fu Jian said to his minister Quan Yi, "With an army of one hundred thousand, I have taken Xiangyang, yet I have gained but one person and a half.
When Yi asked who they were, he replied, "One is Master An; the other is Quan Yi, who is but half a man.
Fu Jian entered Guanzhong and resided at Wuchong Temple, where his followers numbered several thousand. Originally, when śramaṇas left the household life, they all followed their teacher’s surname.
Dao’an said, "The Master is no different from Śākyamuni Tathāgata. He therefore took "Śākya" as his clan name.

Later, he obtained the *Ekottarika Āgama*, which indeed stated that when the four rivers enter the sea, they no longer retain their individual names; likewise, those of the four castes who leave the household life all take the name of the Śākya clan.

This accorded with the scripture as perfectly as two halves of a tally. Dao’an was widely learned and skilled in literary composition. At Lántián, he discovered a bronze cauldron with a capacity of twenty-seven *dǒng*.
The *hu* [measuring vessel] had an inscription in seal script. He asked An about it, and An said, "It was cast by Duke Xiang of Lu. He also obtained a bronze *hu*;
its shape was perfectly circular, with a downward-facing *dou* serving as a horizontal beam. When the beam was raised, the *sheng* would rise; when lowered, they would join.

One end of the beam was the *yue*, which—like the *huangzhong* pitch-pipe—had a capacity of half a *he*. It also bore an inscription in seal script. He asked An about it, and An said, "This is from the time of Wang Mang."
He declared that he had emerged from the era of Emperor Shun during the year Wuchen (the fifth year of the sexagenary cycle).

Having rectified the calendar and attained the state of truth, he established a uniform standard of measurement to disseminate throughout the four quarters, desiring that vessels large and small be standardized so that the whole world might attain equilibrium. Thereupon, Yao Jian strictly commanded his attendants that anyone with doubts must take Dao’an as their teacher.
A contemporary proverb went: "If one studies without taking Dao’an as a teacher, one’s principles will not meet the challenge. Yao Jian succeeded the Shi clan.

Thereafter, the population and resources became abundant, and the four quarters were largely pacified. To the east, it reached the blue seas; to the west, it included Kucha; to the south, it encompassed Xiangyang;
and to the north, it extended as far as the desert. Only Jianye remained unsubdued. Fu Jian’s long-standing ambition was to seize and possess it, but his high ministers’ remonstrances went unheeded.
When Jian went out to the Eastern Garden, he ordered Yao An to ascend the imperial carriage and ride with him. The Chancellor Quan Yi remonstrated, saying:

"Your servant has heard that for the ceremonial carriage of the Son of Heaven, the Attendant-in-Chief (Shizhong) doubles his usual mount. Dao’an has destroyed his physical form [as a layman]; how could he be permitted to participate in this?
Fajian said angrily, "Master An’s Way and Virtue are worthy of the highest honor. I would rather exchange the glory of the imperial carriage for the world; it does not yet match his virtue.
He immediately issued an edict for Yao Yi to support Dao’an as he ascended the carriage. Thereupon, Yi knelt and assisted him by the arm as they climbed. Fajian looked back and said to Dao’an:
"I intend to travel south with you to Wu and Yue. I shall marshal the six armies on a tour of inspection, ascend Mount Kuaiji to gaze upon the vast ocean—is this not a source of great joy?
He replied, "Your Majesty responds to Heaven and governs the world; you possess the wealth of the eight provinces and preside from the center to control the four seas.
You ought to settle your spirit in non-action (*wuwei*) and rival the glory of Yao and Shun. Yet now you wish to lead an army of a million."
He sought lands of the lowest of the low grade. Furthermore, the terrain in the southeastern region is low-lying and its climate is miasmic;
in ancient times, Yu and Shun traveled there and did not return, and the First Emperor of Qin went there and did not come back. From my humble perspective, I see no reason for this to be feasible.

The Duke of Pingyang is a close relative of the imperial house, and Shi Yue is a high-ranking minister; both are profoundly concerned for the state, and their arguments are worthy of being heard. [Seng] Jian said: "This is not a minor matter..."
"It is not that the realm is not vast. It is simply that I wish to discern the will of Heaven and clarify where the Great Mandate resides.

To tour the provinces in accordance with the seasons is fully established in the canons of instruction. If it were as your esteemed argument suggests, would there then be no record of emperors inspecting the four quarters?

He replied, "If it is absolutely impossible [to proceed], you should instead station your capital at Luoyang. Rest your spear and harbor your sharpness while dispatching proclamations to Jiangnan. Should they fail to submit," [the Emperor continued,] "then we shall act accordingly."

"It would not be too late to attack him. Fu Jian did not listen. He dispatched two hundred and fifty thousand elite troops as the vanguard, followed by himself leading six million infantry and cavalry.
He was defeated by Xie Xuan, the Governor of Xuzhou, and fled on horseback alone.

Dao'an established the regulations for the Dharma-gate, organizing them into three categories: first, the incense offering, which fixed the order of the presiding elder and the recitation of scriptures.

The methods taught by the Master were as follows: first, the rules for daily practice during the six periods of the day; second, the method for chanting the time for walking meditation and taking meals;
and third, the procedures for the *poṣadha*, assigning duties, and repentance. These were observed and honored by all monasteries under heaven, with none daring to transgress them.

Every time he met his disciple Fayu, he would make a vow before an image of Maitreya, wishing to be reborn in the Inner Court (Tuṣita Heaven). During the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era of the Qin dynasty...
On the twenty-seventh day of the first month of one year, a strange monk suddenly arrived to stay overnight in the lecture hall.

When the *karmadāna* saw him entering and exiting through the window cracks during the night, he immediately informed Dao’an. Startled, Dao’an paid his respects and inquired about the purpose of his visit.

The monk replied, "I have come for your sake. Dao’an said, "I consider my own transgressions to be deep; how could I possibly be delivered? The monk said, "It is quite possible. However, you must further—"
When he bathed the holy monks, his sincere vows were surely fulfilled. He fully demonstrated the method of bathing. Anqian asked where he would be reborn;
he then pointed his finger toward the heavens, and immediately the clouds parted to reveal a pavilion appearing like a phantom in the northwest.

He said, "This is Tuṣita. That evening, some forty children came to join him for the bath. On the eighth day of the second month, he passed away and was buried at Wujie Temple within the city. This was that year.
This was the tenth year of the Taiyuan era of the Jin dynasty. Before he passed away, he visited Wang Jia, a recluse of Meigu Valley, to take his leave.
An said, "The affairs of the world are such that they will soon reach the common people; shall we depart together? Jia replied, "It is indeed as you say.
However, Master, you go on ahead; I have some small debts not yet settled and cannot go with you. Shortly thereafter, Yao Chang entered Chang’an and usurped the throne.
[He] bore the title [of General]. Furthermore, he held off Fu Deng. At that time, Jia was inside the city. Chang summoned Jia and questioned him, saying, "Will I capture Deng?
Jia replied, "I have roughly captured him. Chang said in anger, "If you have captured him, say so; why do you say 'roughly'? He then had him executed. Later, Deng was killed by Chang’s son, Xing.
Xing’s courtesy name was Zilüe. Jia’s courtesy name was Zinian; he was a native of Luoyang. His physical appearance...

He was humble and unpretentious, possessing a witty and humorous disposition that made him skilled in conversation. When questioned about matters of state, he would respond in a manner that seemed like mere jesting, such that the meaning was not immediately apparent.

However, after some time, his words proved frequently accurate. Fu Jian summoned him with the rank of Grand Herald, but he did not comply. Later, when the Emperor was about to launch a southern expedition, he sent an envoy to inquire whether the outcome would be auspicious or ominous.
Sengqie had no other words; he simply mounted the messenger’s horse, walked several hundred paces toward the east, and then removed both his boots and hat.
He discarded his robes and fled back home. On the very day he was to be executed, someone saw him atop a ridge and sent a letter to Daochang.
Previously, when Seng’an heard that Kumārajīva was in Guzang, he had urged Yao Jian to welcome him; Kumārajīva, for his part, also regarded Seng’an as a Bodhisattva from the East.
At birth, Seng’an had a piece of skin about an inch long on his left arm, like a cord, which could be stroked up and down. It was particularly...
He was simply unable to bring forth his hand; thus, he was known at that time as the Bodhisattva "Sealed Hand" (Yinshou).
Zhu Fatai of the Jin dynasty was a native of Dongguan. He stood eight chi tall and possessed a handsome appearance.

In his youth, he studied together with Dao’an before deciding to travel south. While traveling, he fell ill at Yangkou. At that time, Huan Wen was stationed in Jingzhou and invited him to visit, providing him with hospitality and medicinal care. Dao’an... [text ends]
He dispatched his disciple Huiyuan to inquire after [Seng]tan’s illness. When the illness had slightly abated, [Huiyuan] went to see Wen.
Wen wished to detain Tan for a long conversation, but Tan rose and departed because his illness flared up; he did not offer any formal farewell. The guests present marveled at his lofty character.

The śramaṇa Daoheng propagated the doctrine of "Mindlessness" (wuxin) extensively throughout the Jing and Chu regions. Tan declared, "This is a heterodox teaching; it must be refuted immediately," and he dispatched his disciple Tantan to do so.

First, when he assembled the monks to debate with Daoheng, the latter was consistently unable to yield immediately. However, Huiyuan took his seat; after only a few rounds, Daoheng felt he was losing the argument.
He struck the table with his fly-whisk, having failed to find an answer. Huiyuan said, "Why exert yourself in vain when you could have been swift without haste?
Those present all laughed, and Daoheng’s position was thus thwarted. Later, he went to Jianye and stayed at Waguan Temple during the reign of Emperor Taizong of the Jin dynasty.
Emperor Jianwen held him in deep reverence and paid him formal respects. He opened the Guangti Great Assembly, which the Emperor attended in person;

the high officials and nobles all assembled there, with a multitude reaching a thousand people. Waguan Temple was originally the site of the tomb of Shan Wan of Mount Henei, where Lord Shan had practiced pottery-making.
During the Xingning era, the śramaṇa Huili petitioned for the land to be established as a temple; it was now being renovated by Fatai. [This was recorded by] Wang Xun and Xie.
Anshi and others all visited one another. His disciples Tanyi and Taner were both renowned. He passed away in the second year of the Taiyuan era at the age of sixty-eight.
Fayu of the Jin dynasty was a man of unknown origins. From his youth, he was brilliant and versatile, possessing broad learning that eclipsed his contemporaries;

yet upon meeting Master Dao’an, he humbled himself and submitted, vowing to shave his head and become a disciple. When Ruan Bao, the Governor of Yiyang, heard of his reputation, he admired him from afar and provided him with continuous offerings of gifts.
To escape the disturbances, Fayu traveled eastward and settled at a monastery in Jiangling, where he lectured and taught a community of over four hundred followers. Once, a monk consumed...

Huiyu neglected his evening lectures; when he encountered this, [the Master] merely imposed a fine but did not dismiss him. When Master Dao’an heard of this, he placed a staff inside a bamboo tube, sealed and labeled it himself, and sent it to Huiyu.
Upon opening the seal and seeing the staff, Huiyu said, "This is because of a monk who drinks wine and is not diligent in leading the assembly."

Far from me, you have bestowed the gift of your concern; I immediately ordered the *vinaya-dhara* to administer three strokes of the staff as self-punishment, which I placed inside my staff-case while weeping and reproaching myself.
I then wrote a letter to Huiyuan, saying: "I am a man of shallow understanding and could not lead the assembly.
Although the Upādhyāya remains in a distant land, he still extends his compassionate concern toward me; my transgressions are beyond escape. He passed away at the age of sixty.

Sengshi of the Jin dynasty was born into the Fu clan; he was a native of Xunyang. He was the eldest son of Fu Xia, the Court Gentleman of Hedian during the Jin. In his youth, he served as a disciple of Dharma Master Hongjue.

He resided at the Great Monastery in Chang’an and traveled through the regions of Qingzhou, Sizhou, Fanzhou, and Mienzhou. He was well-versed in the Six Classics and had thoroughly mastered the Tripiṭaka.
His observance of the Vinaya was extremely rigorous, and he was held in high esteem by Yao Chang and Yao Xing. Since the arrival of Kumārajīva...

[The Emperor] closed [the discussion]. He was concerned that monks and nuns were committing many transgressions and causing calamity, so he deliberated on the establishment of a *Sengzhu* (Monastic Head) to oversee them.

He issued an edict stating: "Since the Great Dharma migrated to the East, it has flourished until now. As the number of monks and nuns increases, it is fitting to establish a governing structure to proclaim far-reaching regulations and rescue the declining order.
Master Senglang has long enjoyed a reputation for learning and later gained renown for his virtue; he may serve as the National Monastic Head. The monks...

Sengqian was appointed as the Director of the Assembly (Yuezhong). Faching and Huibin were appointed as the Monastic Registrars (Senglü). They were granted carriages, attendants, and laborers, and bestowed with the rank and stipends of Palace Attendants (Shizhong).

Each was assigned two messengers for imperial edicts and two for the sheep-cart. Sengqian and the others received various grants according to their status, which greatly satisfied contemporary expectations.

In the seventh year of Hongshi, an imperial decree added thirty personal attendants and thirty armed laymen to each of their retinues; the office of Monastic Director (Sengzheng) was established from this point onward.
At the outset, he maintained a very frugal lifestyle yet preached the Dharma without weariness. He passed away at Daishi, having reached the age of seventy.

Dharmaruci (translated into Chinese as Fǎlè) was a native of the Western Regions who came to China during the Jin dynasty. Having renounced his home life, he became renowned for his mastery of the Vinaya.
In the seventh year of the Hongshi era, he arrived in Guāngzhōng; at that time, Puṇyatāra had already passed away some time before. Huìyuǎn of Lúshān...

Having heard that you are well-versed in the Vinaya, I wish to complete my own studies of it. I have therefore sent this letter to convey our friendly greetings, saying: "The rise of the Buddha’s teachings first originated in Your Majesty’s kingdom.
Since their dissemination began, four hundred years have now passed. Yet, the fundamental basis of the bhikṣus remains unknown to us.
Recently, we were fortunate enough to have Puṇyatāra recite the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, but he passed away before half was finished. We harbor a lingering regret for this and have taken the liberty—"
"I have heard, O virtuous one, that you also carry this sutra; I pray you will surely grant me its exposition. Do not let my distress go unheeded.
Truly, you would cause those who have only just begun their journey not to lose the ford to the Unsurpassed Way. This kindness is beyond price—how could it ever be repaid?

When Zhi [Dao'an] received this letter, he then provided Kumārajīva with the remaining portions of the *Dharmapada* text that had not yet been completed. While Zhi resided at the Great Temple in Chang’an, the śramaṇa Huiguan desired...
Fayuan resided in Luoyang. Daopi said, "There are people in Luoyang who propagate the Dharma, which is sufficient to benefit the world.
I shall go to convert those places where the study of the Vinaya has not yet reached. Thereupon he departed, and his final destination remains unknown.
Dao Rong of Jin was a native of Linlü in Jijun. His family name has been lost to history. At the age of twelve, he left his home to follow a teacher.

Having no books of his own, he sent someone to borrow the *Analects* from a neighboring house; when it was late, he did not return it, saying, "I have already mastered it. When his teacher had him recite it, he missed not a single character.
The teacher marveled at this extraordinary feat and shaved his head for him. Upon receiving full ordination, he traveled extensively through the Guanzhong region.
He relied upon Kumārajīva. Kumārajīva said to Yao Xing, "Recently I have seen Master Rong; he is truly a rare and extraordinary human being.

[The Emperor] summoned him for an audience and spoke with him, after which he was deeply impressed. By imperial decree, he was invited to enter the Xiaoyao Garden to participate in the translation work.

At that time, Kumārajīva was translating the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* and the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, which had just reached two fascicles; Rong was already able to lecture upon them. Kumārajīva further commissioned him to give these lectures.
Regarding the *New Lotus Sūtra*, he himself listened to its analysis and judgment, remarking: "The flourishing of the Great Dharma truly depends upon this son.
There was a Brahmin in the kingdom who claimed to have read all the books of the Western Regions;

hearing that Kumārajīva was in Guanzhong, he said, "How can it be allowed that the teachings of the Śākya clan alone shall be transmitted to Zhendan? He then carried his books there, nearly causing Yao Xing to be deluded.
Regarding this matter, the Brahmin challenged the monks to a debate to determine their relative superiority. The monks of Guanzhong all looked at one another in dejection.
Kumārajīva said to Sengrui, "You should take on this challenge. Sengrui reflected that he had not yet read the non-Buddhist scriptures;

he therefore secretly had someone record the titles of all those books and recited them from memory after a single reading. They set a date for the debate, and Yao Xing gathered the dukes and ministers in a great assembly. The Brahmin—
The Brahmin took pride in his extensive learning. When Kumārajīva enumerated the scriptures he had read, including those from the land of Qin, they were three times as many as the Brahmin’s.
Kumārajīva mocked him, saying, "Have you not heard that there are scholars in the Great Qin? How dare you come from so far away with such arrogance?

Thereupon, the Brahmin was ashamed and submitted; he bowed twice at Kumārajīva’s feet and departed. Later, he returned to Pengcheng to lecture and teach, where his followers always numbered in the hundreds.
Baishu was by nature disinclined toward socializing and noise; he frequently ascended the tower to read his books, so few people ever recognized his face. He died at the age of seventy-four.

His writings include several fascicles of commentaries on the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Large Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, and the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*.
Vimalākṣa (translated into Chinese as Wugouyan, "Stainless Eye") was a native of Kaśmīra. He was a man of profound character and great willpower who disciplined himself through ascetic practices.
A master of the Vinaya, he became the preeminent authority for scholars in Kucha. When Kucha fell to the enemy, he fled to Uḍḍiyāna.
Hearing that Kumārajīva was in Chang’an, he wished to ensure that this supreme and exquisite flavor of the Dharma would once again reach the eastern lands. This was in the eighth year of Hongshi.

In the year he arrived in Guanzhong, Kumārajīva paid him respect as if to his own teacher. When Kumārajīva passed away, [Dao'an] immediately departed and traveled to Shouchun, where he translated the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) in fifty-eight fascicles.

The final recitation—concerning the methods for receiving the precepts and various matters for accomplishing wholesome dharmas—he renamed the "Good Recitation" (*Śubhabhāṇavāra*) to emphasize its essential meaning. Later, while residing at Shijian, he further expanded it to sixty fascicles.
It consisted of one fascicle. The final recitation was later changed to the *Vinaya* recitation; thus, both names still survive today.

Furthermore, while staying at Xinsi Temple in Jiangling during the summer retreat, he lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (the "Inaction" chapter) using the Han language, which became widely popular at the time.
Huiguan studied its essential points and compiled them into two fascicles. These were copied and circulated in the capital, causing the price of paper to rise. He eventually passed away at Shijian.
He lived to the age of seventy-seven. His eyes were blue, so he was known at the time as the Vinaya Master Blue-Eyed (Qingyan Lishi).

Sengrui of the Jin dynasty was a native of Changle in Wei Commandery; his family name has been lost to history. At the age of eighteen, he became a śramaṇa and served Dharma Master Sengxian as his teacher.
He was extensively learned in the sūtras and śāstras. When he listened to Senglang’s lectures on the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, he frequently posed challenging questions.
Lang said to Xian, "Yi possesses extraordinary courage and spirit; many of his difficult passages are ones that I myself cannot fully comprehend. He is truly an excellent disciple.

When Kumārajīva arrived in Guanzhong, he translated the *Dhyāna-yao* (Essentials of Meditation) in three fascicles. It begins with the works composed by Kumāralāta and concludes with those composed by the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa;
furthermore, it contains much of the terminology used by foreign worthies and sages, and is also titled *Bodhi*.
Sengrui refined the essentials of the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* and divided them into five sections. Yao Song, the nominal Minister of Education, held him in profound esteem and respect.
When Emperor Xiaowen asked Song, "To whom can Master Ruyi be compared? Song replied, "I have yet seen anyone who can compare with him.

Once, during a dharma assembly where the high officials were all present, the Emperor saw Sengrui and said to Song, "He is the foremost hope for the monastic community throughout the four seas. Zhu Fahu had previously translated the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The text says: "Heaven sees man, and man sees heaven. When Kumārajīva reached this passage, he remarked, "The meaning is the same as in the Western Regions, but its phrasing is excessively plain.
Sengrui said, "Could it not be that humans and devas meet, so that both are able to see one another? Kumārajīva agreed with him.
Sengrui lectured on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. Kumārajīva said, "Within this polemical treatise, there are seven passages that refute the *Abhidharmika* masters.
Can you identify them? Sengrui pointed out the locations in response, and they all met Kumārajīva’s approval. Kumārajīva remarked, "You truly possess refined discernment.

To have a connoisseur of sound in the transmission and translation—what cause for regret could I have? Sengrui sought rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; whether sitting or lying down, he did not dare turn his back toward the west. As he approached his end...

At the end, he said to his fellow student, "If my actions of body, speech, or mind have ever been in conflict with the precepts, I pray that you will bestow upon me great compassion so that we may remain dharma-companions for eternal kalpas.
Thereupon, having finished his bath, he prostrated himself, joined his palms, and passed away facing west at the age of sixty-seven.
He had a fellow student named Seng Kai, who possessed lofty conduct and was renowned as an equal to Huirui.

Sengzhao of the Jin dynasty was a native of Jingzhao; historical records do not specify his clan name. Being poor, he worked as a hired scribe and consequently read extensively across the Classics, Histories, and the various collections of philosophy.
He was particularly proficient in the *Zhuangzi* and the *Laozi*. At the age of twelve, he became a śramaṇa, and his reputation resounded throughout the Three Commanderies.

When Kumārajīva was in Guzang, Sengzhao went to follow him. Upon conversing with him, Kumārajīva was struck with amazement and exclaimed, "A dragon and elephant among the Dharma! Thereupon, he took him back with him.

In Guanzhong, he resided at the Xiaoyao Garden (Xiaoyuan) and meticulously edited and determined the sutras and śāstras. Scholars from all quarters flocked to him like the spokes of a wheel, launching difficult challenges and attacking one another;
yet Sengzhao resolved them as easily as a blade meeting a whetstone, leaving everyone satisfied and submissive.

At that time, there were Daosheng, Daorong, and Sengrui—all disciples of Kumārajīva—who were known as the "Four Sages of the Gate of Tongshou" (Kumārajīva). Sengzhao first composed the *Prajñā-wujilun* (Treatise on the Non-cognition of Prajñā), which Kumārajīva saw.
