He said, "I understand; I do not thank you for it. As for the text, I shall surely bow before it. Liu Yimin obtained this and presented it to Master Huiyuan.

Master Huiyuan struck his thigh and sighed, deeming it something that had never been seen before. Later, he further composed the *Treatise on Non-Emptiness*, the *Treatise on the Non-Transmigration of Things*, and a commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
When Kumārajīva passed away, he mourned him deeply and also composed the *Treatise on the Namelessness of Nirvāṇa*; all of these were exquisite.
He produced works of exquisite subtlety. Yao Xing held his calligraphy in high esteem and ordered its distribution. He passed away in the tenth year of the Yixi era at the age of thirty-two.
Huìyuǎn of the Jìn dynasty was born into the Jiā family; he was a native of Lóufán in Yànmén. At the age of twelve, he followed his maternal uncle, Língfú...
Your Reverence studied between the regions of Xu and Luo, where he exhaustively mastered a vast array of texts and grasped the essential tenets of Laozi and Zhuangzi.
His discernment was clear and outstanding; among his fellow students, his dragon-like insignia and phoenix-like bearing outshone even fish and birds.

Upon reaching adulthood, he intended to cross the Yangtze River to live in seclusion with Fan Xuanzi, but coinciding with the chaos of the Central Plains, the roads were blocked by war. He heard that Dao’an was preaching at Taixing Hengshan Temple.

Bānruò (Pragñā) subsequently went with his younger brother Huìchí to visit him. Upon meeting him, they paid their respects and wished to shave their hair, entering the ranks of his disciples to complete their studies.
Having received full ordination, he took it upon himself to propagate the Great Dharma. At the age of twenty-four, he immediately began giving lectures.
In the ninth year of the Jiànyuán era of the Qín dynasty, when Píng'ān Gōng of Xiāngyáng was captured by Zhú Xù, [Bānruò] consequently made a decision.
He traveled south to Jingzhou and stayed at Shangming Temple. Intending to visit Mount Luofu, he moored his boat at Xunyang; seeing Mount Kuang, he was captivated by it and settled at its base.
Pointing his staff at the ground, he said, "If there is a spring here, I shall stay. A spring suddenly gushed forth, and so he established his permanent residence there.
He frequently recited the sutras by the spring, whereupon a dragon appeared to listen. Consequently, it was named Longquan Temple (Dragon Spring Temple). This was the time of the śramaṇa Huiyong.
Dwelling in Xilin, he regretted that his residence was cramped and could not accommodate many people; thus, he requested the Governor Huan Yi to establish Donglin Temple for him.
According to ancient tradition, there was a shadow of the Buddha in a stone cave within an old city to the south of Nagarahāra in the kingdom of Mozhī.
The Flowing Sands are over fifteen thousand eight hundred li away. I wish to go there to pay my respects, yet I lament that my bones cannot fly.
There was a Daoist master from the Western Regions who painted [the scene] on a wall for me; Huiyuan composed five chapters of inscriptions, in which he was able to expound upon its wonders.
When Tao Kan was stationed at Guangzhou, a fisherman caught a statue of Mañjuśrī cast by King Aśoka while fishing in the sea.
He sent it to Hanchi Temple. The temple’s abbot, Sengzhen, was traveling directly toward Hankou when he dreamed that the temple was on fire, yet the statue remained unharmed.

He hurried back and found it to be exactly as he had seen in his dream. Because of its divine power, when Tao Kan moved his station elsewhere, he sent men to welcome the statue; ten men could not lift it. Thereupon—
He boarded the boat again, but it sank once more; in the end, he was unable to obtain it. When Huiyuan had completed the construction of the monastery, the statue arrived of its own accord.
This was surely due to the power of his sincere devotion. Thus, the people of the time composed a verse for him, saying: "Tao Kan was a hero among swordsmen; The statue is a paragon of the divine.
One soars through clouds, the other dwells in the mud— How vast the distance between them! It can be brought forth through sincerity, But is difficult to summon by force. —By Liu Yimin of Pengcheng.
Lei Cizong of Yuzhang, Zhou Xuzhi of Yanmen, Bi Yingzhi of Xincai, Zong Bing of Nanyang, Zhang Shimin, Ji Shuo, and eighteen others followed Huiyuan on his travels.
There, before an image of Amitābha Buddha, they commissioned Liu Yimin to compose a text for them to take an oath to vow to be reborn in the Western Land.
When Yin Zhongkan was traveling through Jingzhou, he visited [Huiyuan] at Mount Lu.
At Beijian, he heard Huiyuan lecture on the *Yi Jing* and sighed, saying, "His understanding exhausts the subtlest refinements; he cannot be fathomed by mere conjecture.
How could there be such a personage in this world? He lingered there all day before finally departing. When Lu Xun first occupied Jiangzhou, he once visited Huiyuan.
Huiyuan had been friends with Xun’s father, Ji, since his youth. Upon seeing Xun, he was delighted and spoke of their old friendship.

A counselor cautioned him, saying, "Xun is a rebel; you have been close with him. Disaster will surely come upon you. Huiyuan replied, "In our Buddhist Dharma, the mind is free from attachment or rejection.

How could I not know that I am being observed by those who possess discernment? This is not what I fear. When Emperor Wu launched his campaign against Xun and stationed his troops at Sangwei, someone [reported this].

Huiyuan sent a message to Emperor Wu, who said, "Master Huiyuan is a man beyond this world; how can he be measured by such standards? He dispatched an envoy to convey his respects and provide a meal for the monks.
Upon hearing that Kumārajīva had entered the Guanzhong region, he sent a letter to establish friendly relations and presented him with a robe of exquisite craftsmanship.

He invited Kumārajīva to ascend the high seat and personally donned it for him, along with a water-strainer, both of which were precious gifts. Kumārajīva’s reply, in brief, stated: [The text continues with the content of the letter.]
The Sūtra says: "In the final age, there will be a Bodhisattva named Dharmapāla in the East. Exert yourself, O benevolent one! Skillfully propagate this matter. There is a verse that says:
"Since you have already abandoned defiled pleasures, has your mind attained perfect mastery? If it does not wander or scatter, have you deeply entered the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)?
Within the ultimate mark of emptiness, your mind finds no delight; yet if you find joy in dhyāna and wisdom, this is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)."

There is no illumination; things such as the deceptive lack reality, nor do they provide a place for the mind to settle. "I pray that you, O Benevolent One, will graciously show me the essentials of the Dharma you have realized.
Yuan then replied to him with a verse, saying: "From where does the root of all things ultimately arise? Its arising and ceasing, its existence and non-existence—where is their limit?"

A single atom that stirs toward the realm of objects creates the momentum of this collapsing mountain; delusive appearances multiply one upon another, and upon touching the Principle, they naturally give rise to stagnation.

Although causes and conditions have no master, the opening of the path does not occur in a single lifetime. Since there is no enlightened master of the school at this time, who will grasp the profound seal?

The inquiries that come to us are still far from settled; let us agree to wait until the end of this year. Originally, in the Central Land (China), there was no teaching regarding *nirvāṇa* as being eternally abiding;
it was merely said that the lifespan is exceedingly long. Huiyuan said: "The Buddha is the ultimate. That which is ultimate is without change."
The principle of non-alteration—how could it ever be exhausted? He then composed the *Dharmatā-śāstra*, stating: "That which is ultimate takes non-alteration as its nature;
attaining this nature constitutes its essence, and the ultimate serves as its tenet. When Kumārajīva saw this treatise, he remarked: "People in a frontier land have not yet seen the sūtras."

This indeed accords perfectly with principle; how marvelous! King Yao Xing of the Qin dynasty sent a letter and presented a finely embroidered image of the Buddha from Kucha as a token of his sincere devotion.
Furthermore, Yao Song offered a pearl-encrusted image and a copy of the *Śāstra* (Treatise) stating: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is a new record composed by Nāgārjuna;
you, Dharma Master, should provide it with a preface to illuminate it for ten thousand generations. Thus, the Way was propagated in this land.
He was a scholar whose reputation was universally admired. Huiyuan declined his invitation with a letter, citing his own lack of talent;

though much of this correspondence is not recorded here, Huiyuan regretted that Daolun’s discourse was too voluminous, so he excerpted its essentials to form twenty fascicles. When Huan Xuan campaigned against Yin Zhongkan, his army passed north of the mountain.

He invited Huiyuan to come out to Tiger Brook, but Huiyuan feigned illness and did not emerge. Huan Xuan entered the mountain himself, and his attendants admonished him, saying, "Do not go further to pay your respects."
When Daoxuan saw Huiyuan, he unconsciously paid him respect. Daoxuan asked, "The precepts state that one must not damage one's body; why then do you shave your hair?

Huiyuan replied, "In establishing oneself and practicing the Way, there must naturally be one's own intention. How could one refuse to follow the example of King Taiji by shaving one's head and tattooing one's body simply because of Ji Li?
When Daoxuan left the mountain, he said to his attendants, "Truly, I have never seen such a person in my life. Later, Daoxuan [was accused of] usurping the authority of the sovereign.
Huiyuan’s majestic presence was such that Huijian desperately wished to bring him there, yet Huiyuan remained lying down in his retreat, refusing to move.

Shortly thereafter, Emperor Xuan intended to purge the monastic community, declaring that only Mount Kuang was the dwelling place of those possessing the Way and Virtue, and thus it should not be subject to the search and selection. Thereupon, Huiyuan sent a letter to Emperor Xuan;
its phrasing appeared to concede outwardly while actually subverting the proposal from within. At that time, Emperor Cheng was still a minor, and Yu Bing was the de facto ruler. Because...
"Śramaṇas ought to show respect to kings. However, Shangshu He Chong, Puyue Chu Yi, Zhuge Hui, and others submitted a memorial arguing that this was not the case.

The consensus among the assembly agreed with He Chong and his colleagues; consequently, the officials of the Menxia Gate looked on with hesitation, and conflicting dissenting opinions arose in abundance.

While Huiguan was at Gushu, he sent a letter to inquire whether Dao’an would agree or not, stating: "This is a momentous matter for the entire age; we must not allow the imperial court to fail in its duty."
[This is] the substance [of the matter]. I have received a letter from the Eight Ministers; they now treat me as if I were like you.

You should discuss in detail, point by point, the meaning of their lack of respect, so as to dispel their doubts, and then I shall act accordingly. Yuan responded with a letter, the gist of which was as follows: "The *kāṣāya* is not a garment for attending the imperial court;
the alms bowl is not a vessel for the corridors of the ancestral temple. When Hui Xuan usurped the throne, he issued an edict stating: "The Buddha-dharma is vast and grand..."

[The Emperor] could not fathom [Huiyuan’s intent]. Previously, he had honored him out of a sense of devotion to his sovereign, and thus gave rise to that respect. Now, however, since the matter rests with himself, he ought to exercise the utmost humility.
He commanded that the various monks no longer offer him salutations. Huiyuan then composed the "Treatise on Why Śramaṇas Do Not Pay Homage to Kings."

There are five pieces in total, which exhaustively capture the essence of things with subtle elegance. During the Xiban era, when Emperor An returned to the capital from Jiangling, He Wujī, the Protector of the State, urged Huiyuan to go out and welcome him.

Huiyuan feigned illness and did not go; the Emperor sent an envoy to inquire after his well-being, and Huiyuan composed a letter expressing his sincere devotion, for which the Emperor was highly pleased.
Xi Lingyun, relying on his superior talent and spirit, looked upon Huiyuan’s serene composure and...

He passed away. Yuan resided in seclusion for thirty years; his shadow never left the mountains, and his tracks never entered the secular world. Whenever he sent off guests on their travels, he used Tiger Creek as the boundary.
In the eighth month of the twelfth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, he first manifested illness. On the sixth day, his condition became critical.
Senior monks and elders requested that he drink fermented soybean wine, but he did not permit it. They further requested that he drink rice gruel, but he did not permit it. Furthermore...
He requested that honey-water be used as his drink. He then commanded the Vinaya Master to search through the volumes [of the scriptures], but he passed away before they could be found.
He was eighty-three years old. His final instruction was to leave his remains exposed beneath a pine tree; his disciples could not bear to collect them for burial.
Ruan Bao, the Governor of Xunyang, excavated a tomb and opened a passage on the mountain ridge to the west. There were ten volumes of his collected writings.
Daoheng of Jin was a native of Lantian; the histories have lost his family name. At the age of nine, the retired scholar Zhang Zhong saw him and said to others, "This boy has auspicious marks.
If he enters secular service, he will surely become a counselor to a king; if he leaves the household life, he will surely bring great glory to the Buddha-vehicle."

"I regret that my old age prevents me from seeing this. Sengheng was orphaned at a young age and served his stepmother with such filial piety that it became renowned. His family was poor, so he sold books and paintings to support himself.
At the age of twenty, after his stepmother passed away and he had completed his period of mourning, he became a śramaṇa. He heard that Kumārajīva had entered the Guanzhong region.
He went to rely upon him. Kumārajīva, admiring his lofty talent, ranked him as equal in fame to Daobiao.

Because Yao Xing considered both Sengheng and Daobiao to be men of divine brilliance who possessed the arts and learning for statecraft, he issued an edict ordering Yao Xian, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, to earnestly urge them to renounce the monastic life.
The two gentlemen thereupon submitted a memorial expressing their sentiments, the gist of which was as follows: "Emperor Guangwu of the Han fulfilled the integrity of Yan Ling;
Emperor Wen of Wei preserved the loftiness of Guan Ning. Your Majesty possesses Heaven-endowed sagacity, and your deliberations are consistently far superior to those of Yao and Shun."
Now, how can these two men, wearing crowns and head-covers, instead be placed beneath Emperor Guangwu and Emperor Wen of Wei?

Daoxing again wrote a letter to Kumārajīva and Sengquan, instructing them to persuade [Falin] and ensure he returned to his original lay attire. Kumārajīva and Sengquan both submitted memorials, setting forth the circumstances in detail, which stated in brief:
"Only the Sage is able to penetrate the wills of the world; [Falin] has already destroyed and discarded his lifelong vocation."
[His] hair and beard were grown, and he wore improper clothing. Now, to have him again don his hairpin and formal robes to stand in court would not be to fulfill his aspirations.
Furthermore, since the Great Qin has risen like a dragon and extraordinary talents have emerged in their ranks, those such as Hengbiao and others are not yet considered transcendent.

Thereupon, the assembly earnestly petitioned, and he was thus granted exemption from the requirement. Heng sighed and said, "A name is truly a burden to the Way. He then fled and subsequently disappeared.

In Mount Langya, in the thirteenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, at the age of seventy-three, he constantly composed the *Shixulun* (Discourse on the Explanation of the Teachings) and the *Baixingzhen* (Admonitions on the Hundred Practices);
he was also noted for his literary works.
Faxian of the Song dynasty was surnamed Gong and was a native of Wuyang in Pingyang. Three of his elder brothers all died of illness while still in their childhood.

When Faxian was three years old, he also fell ill; his father, fearing for his life, offered him to the monastic order so that he might be ordained, but in the end did not send him away. At the age of several years, he again fell ill and was on the verge of death.
He was then sent to a monastery. After one night, his illness abated; consequently, he remained there and did not return home. His mother built a hut outside the monastery gate for him.
When his father passed away, his uncle urged him to return to secular life. Xian said, "My mother has received sufficient care; what need is there for me?

He returned all the family's ancestral property to his uncle without making any inquiries. When his mother died, he buried her according to the rites. He once stayed with several dozen fellow student śramaṇas.
While a man was harvesting rice in a field, a bandit suddenly arrived. The crowd all fled in a state of panic, but Xian alone remained and said to the bandit:

"If you did not practice giving in previous lives, you have brought about this hunger in the present life. If you now further commit robbery, do you not consider the future life? The bandit felt ashamed and departed.
Having received the precepts, his will and conduct became clear and resolute; he constantly lamented that the sūtras and vinaya were incomplete and made a vow [to rectify them].
In the third year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty, he set out westward across the shifting sands together with the śramaṇas Huijing, Daozheng, and others.

There was a scorching wind and malevolent spirits; those who encountered them were certain to die. At the Onion Range (Pamir), there were perilous cliffs thousands of fathoms high, where snow accumulated through both winter and summer.

They had to pass through dangerous places by driving stakes into the ground, barely managing to cross. In total, they crossed more than seven hundred bodies of water, ten of which required crossing by means of ropes suspended from above.
The remaining regions were all places that neither Zhang Qian nor Gan Ying, who served as imperial envoys for the Han dynasty, had ever visited.
The Snow Mountains were so bitterly cold that Huìjǐng died of trembling. After passing through more than thirty such kingdoms, they finally reached India.
Thirty *li* from the city of Rājagṛha, there was a monastery. When they asked where Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa was located, the monks replied, "It is already nightfall."
Furthermore, there were many black lions that preyed upon humans, making it impossible to proceed. Xianlian thought to himself, "I have come here wishing to pay homage to these sacred traces.
If I were to die this very night, my aspirations would remain unfulfilled. He eventually reached Wusuowei (Abhayagiri), where he wandered alone through the mountains.
Prostrating before the sites and gazing upon them, he wept, saying, "I did not know of myself that my body had reached this place. He sat beneath a tree and recited the scriptures.
It was the third watch of the night. A lion crouched there, licking and gnawing at [the corpse]. Hsien stroked it with his hand and said, "You wish to intoxicate me with its flesh;

wait until I have finished reciting the sutras. Thereupon, the lion tucked its tail and departed. The next day, on his way home, he encountered an elderly practitioner (lao-su) standing with his staff planted in the ground.
Hsien bowed to him, but the man did not respond. After a short while, a young man approached. Hsien asked who the elder was, and the youth replied, "He is the dhūta Kāśyapa."

He was a great disciple. Xian pursued him as far as the mountain, but a rock blocked the cave opening so he could not proceed. He then went to the kingdom of Kāśi and observed the summer retreat there.

At a place known as Snake-Ear (Śravaṇa), he placed [the relics] in a copper bowl filled with curd; they traveled through the assembly from the senior monk to the junior ones until they had circled all, whereupon they vanished.
The monks of the monastery said, "This is the White-Eared Dragon. This temple was built by this dragon, who emerges once every year. When he arrived—

In the five regions of India—at the monastery of Southern India near the Aśoka Stūpa on the banks of the Pāṭaliputra River in the kingdom of Magadha—he obtained the Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya, as well as the Sarvāstivāda-vinaya, the *Saṃyukta-abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, and various sūtras such as the Vaipulya and the Nirvāṇa.
He remained there for three years to study the Brahmi script and the Sanskrit language. He then entrusted the scriptures and images to a merchant vessel and traveled to Siṃhala.
In that country, there was no one among his fellow practitioners remaining; he stayed there all alone.

A merchant offered him a fine silk fan for the Buddha, and upon seeing it, Faxian felt the desire to return home. Two years later, he obtained the Mahīśāsaka-vinaya and the Dīrgha-āgama and Madhyama-āgama.
All of these were things never before seen in the land of Han. He boarded a merchant vessel to return home, but suddenly a hurricane arose.
The crew all threw their belongings into the sea, while Xian called upon Avalokiteśvara, saying, "I have scriptures and images here, intended to open the eyes of those in the East.
Shortly thereafter, the storm ceased. They reached the kingdom of Yavadvīpa and stayed for five months to change ships. When they arrived at Guangzhou, a night hurricane broke out, and the ship—
A man said, "There is a śramaṇa on board with us. He intended to cast him into the sea, but someone rebuked and stopped him; thus he did not die.
When the water was exhausted and his provisions were also spent, they suddenly reached the shore and saw wild herbs. Entering a bay, he encountered hunters and asked them [the way].
They replied, "This is Mount Lao in Changguang Commandery, Qingzhou. The hunters brought him back home. Hearing of this, Prefect Li Gongyi went in person.
He welcomed him. Upon arriving at the prefecture, they rested briefly before proceeding to the capital, where he translated the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

There was a copyist who, one night, had a fire that completely destroyed all other items, yet the scripture remained unharmed. Later, he traveled to Jingzhou and passed away at Xinsi Temple at the age of eighty-six.
Tanwujie of the Song dynasty—translated as Fayong—was a native of Huanglong in Youzhou, born into the Li clan.
While still a śrāmaṇera, he practiced asceticism and, having read the account of Faxian’s journey to the West, desired to follow in his footsteps.

In the first year of the Yongchu era of the Song (420 CE), he departed from Haixi Commandery with twenty-five fellow śramaṇas, including Sengmeng and Tanlang, and entered the shifting sands of Gaochang. Thereupon...
Traveling from Kucha to Shule, he ascended Mount Xiling; looking toward the Snow Mountains, he saw them shrouded in mist for a thousand li, with a great river flowing with rapid currents below.
A bridge was constructed using ropes; it was so narrow that only one person could pass at a time. Those who first reached the opposite shore were required to raise a fire as a signal.
Those on this side could only advance upon seeing the smoke. If no smoke appeared for a long time, they knew that the person had fallen into the river.
After three days, they reached the Great Snow Mountain, which rose sheer for thousands of fathoms and was covered everywhere with notches for wooden pegs.

They proceeded by means of a relative system: each man held four wooden stakes and passed them alternately through holes in the cliff face, crossing like a monkey’s arm. Upon reaching level ground, twelve men were lost.

They entered the kingdom of Kaśmīra, where they paid homage to and beheld the Buddha’s almsbowl. They remained for over a year, studying the Sanskrit language and script, and obtained the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*.
Then, traveling westward along the Sindhu River, they entered the kingdom of Yuezhi (Gandhāra) and beheld [the Buddha’s shadow].
In the Inner Topknot Bone Contemplation, he visualized himself boarding a boat upon boiling water and arriving at the Stone Temple on the southern side of Mount Dantaka.

The monks of this temple studied the three vehicles in combination. There was a man from India named Buddhajīva (translated here as "Awakening Savior"), who was one who had attained the stage of fruition.

Without seeking an invitation, [the Master] took him as his preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and relied upon him to receive the full ordination (*mahā-śīla*). The Chinese śramaṇa Zhiding served as the *ācārya*. Because of this sitting...
In the summer, he set out during the summer retreat. The entire route lay within the borders of Central India; the land was vast and sparsely populated.

He carried rock honey as his provisions for the journey, and looking at his own shadow, he felt utterly alone, with only five other monks remaining as companions. Whenever he encountered danger or hardship, he would focus his mind on Avalokiteśvara to escape it.
As he was about to enter the kingdom of Śrāvastī, a herd of mad elephants approached. Just as he was returning his thoughts [to the Bodhisattva], a lion came forth from—
He emerged from the forest; the elephants, terrified, crouched down and departed while leaving behind their dung. Crossing the Ganges, a herd of wild oxen came bellowing toward him.
Again he called upon the name of the Holy One, whereupon a great vulture suddenly flew down. Thereupon the oxen also fled in all directions, and no one remained out of thirst to stay.

He thoroughly inspected the sites of the past traces, relying personally on the holy sages for a long time. Subsequently, he boarded a sea vessel to return home. Upon reaching Guangzhou, this was the end of his life.
There is a separate biography.

Huiyou of the Song dynasty was a native of Jiangyou; the histories have lost his clan name. In his youth he became a śramaṇa and specialized in the study of the Vinaya. By nature, he was upright and firm.

The Master was Vimalākṣa from the Western Regions, who had a profound mastery of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. He served as the preeminent authority for scholars in Shaanxi through his lectures and instruction.
He authored the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-artha* in eight fascicles.

Zhu Daosheng of the Song dynasty was a native of Julu in the Wei state. He lived as a guest in Pengcheng; his family had been of the scholar-official class for generations, and his father served as the Magistrate of Guangwei.
Daosheng was exceptionally gifted from childhood. When the śramaṇa Zhu Fatai saw him, he was greatly astonished and said, "Is this boy one who will be bound by fame, office, wealth, or honor?
Daosheng also felt joyful and wished to follow him back to the mountains to become a monk.
The disciple was fifteen years old when he was already able to lecture and teach. At that time, among the famous scholars, none dared to challenge his sharp intellectual edge.
Consequently, his reputation resounded throughout the garden of the Dharma. He lived on Mount Lu for seven years, after which he entered Chang’an with Huiyan and Huiri to study under Kumārajīva.
Among the hundreds of brilliant disciples in Kumārajīva’s school, none surpassed him. Upon returning to the capital, he took up residence at Qingyuan Temple.

At Yuansi Monastery, Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, the Taizu, showed him exceptional honor and respect. Just as he was preparing to hold a great assembly, the Emperor sat on the ground and personally joined the multitude for the meal.
When the food arrived, the assembly feared it was late in the day and did not dare to set down their chopsticks. The Emperor said, "It is not yet late; it is only midday.
Sengsheng replied, "When the sun shines upon the heavens, if the Emperor now says it is midday, how can it not be midday? Having said this, he lifted his bowl and began to eat.
[He] ate. The entire assembly followed his example, and the Emperor was greatly pleased. Wang Hong, Fan Tai, and Yan Yanzhi all visited his door to establish a friendship.

Daosheng often maintained that the translated scriptures from the land of True Dan (China) had not yet fully conveyed the Buddha’s intent, and that scholars, moreover, remained hindered by their limited experience and learning.

He held, however, that what is called "goodness not receiving retribution" and "attaining Buddhahood through sudden enlightenment" can only be grasped by those who transcend words to reach the essential meaning.

Having understood this, he then composed the *Treatise on the Two Truths*, the *Treatise on the Ever-Abiding Buddha-Nature*, the *Treatise on the Formless Dharmakāya*, the *Treatise on the Buddha Having No Pure Land*, and the *Treatise on the Existence of Conditions*.
These works comprehensively encompassed previous doctrines and revealed their profound depths with clarity as bright as the sun and stars;
yet some harbored resentment and jealousy toward him. Subsequently, the preliminary chapters of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* arrived first at the capital of Qin, where Kumārajīva read them thoroughly.
He said, "The icchantika shall naturally attain Buddhahood; it is only that this sutra has not yet reached its conclusion.

Thereupon, the assembly of lecturers attacked him from all sides, falsely accusing him of heretical teachings and stating that according to the Vinaya he should be expelled. Daosheng addressed the assembly with a vow, saying, "If what I have spoken..."
"This does not accord with the meaning of the scriptures. I vow that within this very life I shall witness the retribution for my evil deeds.

If it truly accords with the Buddha's mind, I vow that at the time of my passing, I shall occupy the lion throne; then, having received the dismissal, I shall fold my hands and return south, taking up residence in the Green Garden.

That summer, a thunderclap struck the Buddha Hall of the Green Garden, and a dragon ascended to heaven. Its light shot across the western wall, and the hall was renamed "Dragon Light" (Longguang). The assembly suspected its significance.
Shortly thereafter, he departed from Qingyuan for Mount Huqiu in Wu. Every day, he would set up a stone as an audience for his disciples while lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
When he reached the passage concerning the Buddha-nature of icchantikas, he would address the stone, saying, "Does the meaning of what I have explained accord with the Buddha’s mind?
Each time, the stone would move as if nodding its head in agreement. He subsequently returned to Mount Lu to seclude himself at Xiaojing Rock.

When the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* arrived in the Southern Capital, he indeed declared that even icchantikas possess buddha-nature. Daosheng saw this and was so overcome with joy that he could not contain himself.
On the gengzi day of the eleventh month in the eleventh year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he ascended the Dharma seat;

his voice was clear and resonant, and those who listened were delighted and awakened. Suddenly, his fly-whisk fell to the ground, and leaning on his armrest, he passed away. There was a monk named Shi Huisheng.
Ji Zhi Longguang was a man of noble conduct, whom his contemporaries distinguished by calling him "Elder" (Sheng) the Elder and "Elder" the Younger.
Hui Rui of Song was a native of Jizhou; the histories have lost his family name. He entered the monastic order in his youth and was renowned for his ascetic rigor.

While traveling to Shu, he was abducted by bandits and forced to herd sheep in the wilds. There was a merchant traveler who, seeing him and finding him extraordinary, questioned him regarding the Tripiṭaka.
He comprehended all meanings without exception. Thereupon, he provided gold to redeem his dharma robes and returned to wear them.

He traveled west to South India, where he became proficient in all matters of phonetic transcription and exegesis. Upon returning, he took up residence at Mount Lu, where he heard that Master Kumārajīva was in Guanzhong.

He tucked up his robes and went to receive instruction from him. Later, while residing at Wuyi Temple in Jianye, he lectured and taught; students gathered like clouds. Prince Yikang of Pengcheng requested that he serve as his teacher.
Sengrui declined three times with earnestness before finally granting permission. The Prince insisted that Sengrui come to his residence to confer the precepts upon him.
Sengrui said, "According to the rites, one hears of coming to study, but never of going to teach. The Prince was deeply ashamed and submitted to his refusal. He then visited [Sengrui at his temple].

While [Hui]yi was seated, [Shi Hu] presented him with a sable fur robe worth three hundred thousand [coins]. Sengrui had never worn it because he remained seated. Xie Lingyun frequently consulted Sengrui regarding the wonders of the scriptures and rare characters;

for this purpose, Sengrui composed the *Shisi yin xun* (Explanations of the Fourteen Phonemes), in which he provided a preface to systematically arrange the meanings and principles of the Sanskrit and Chinese terms.
He passed away during the Yuanjia era at the age of eighty-five.

Tánmómìduō (Dharmamitra) of the Song dynasty, translated as Fǎxiù, was a native of Jibin. At the age of seven, his spiritual intelligence was clear and upright; whenever he heard the chanting of the *brahman*, he would immediately laugh with joy.
Because of this, his parents permitted him to leave the household life. As his country abounded in men of virtue and erudition, he served them all extensively.

He was broadly versed in the various scriptures and possessed a profound understanding of the methods of *dhyāna*. He had joined eyebrows and possessed a dignified, refined bearing; thus, he was popularly known as "The Joined-Browed One."
The Dhyāna Master traveled through various kingdoms until he reached Kucha. One day prior [to his arrival], the King dreamed that a deity told him, "A Great Being shall arrive.

Consequently, the King went out to welcome him to the palace and conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon him. After several years had passed, he again dreamed that the deity told him, "The Great Being wishes to depart.

Although the King earnestly entreated him to remain, it was not possible. He proceeded to Dunhuang, where he built a vihāra and planted a thousand pomegranate trees; he stayed there for a short while.
He departed and traveled to Liangzhou, where he stayed at his former temple. He then journeyed through Shu and out to Jingzhou, where he established a meditation pavilion at Changsha Temple.
There he earnestly sought śarīra relics, making offerings for over ten days until he heard a tinkling sound as they fell onto the offering tray; looking, he saw that light filled the entire pavilion.
Returning east to the capital, he stayed at Zhongxing Temple, where monastics and laypeople erected a stūpa for him. Shortly thereafter, he moved to Qihuan Temple.

The Emperor, the Empress, the Crown Prince, and the various princes all observed the etiquette of disciples, receiving the precepts from him. High-ranking eunuchs came in constant succession to inquire after his well-being.
He translated sutras such as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna*, and the *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra*.

He instructed students in the methods of dhyāna, and scholars from near and far came to him without exception; he was titled the Great Dhyāna Master. Meng Ji, the Governor of Kuaiji, invited him to reside there.

He traveled among the various mountains of Moxian County and subsequently established a stupa and a monastery there. As the local customs of the East largely venerated shamans and sorcerers, from the time Guṇabhadra resided there, people turned en masse toward the orthodox Dharma.
In the tenth year of the Yuanjia era, he returned to Dinglin on Mount Zhong. By nature, he was fond of mountains and waters;

he constructed a dwelling overlooking a mountain stream to capture the finest scenic beauty. Among his disciples, Master Da was able to succeed to his legacy. When Guṇabhadra first departed from Kaśmīra...
The guest, the divine king Kāpiśī, escorted [her] as far as Kucha, where he intended to return.
He took leave of Tanmimide and vowed to travel together to the south, reaching Jiankang. Thereupon, she had his image painted upon the walls of the temple.
She passed away on the sixth day of the seventh month in the nineteenth year, at the age of eighty-seven. She was buried in front of Songxi Temple on Mount Zhong.

Sengzhi Meng was a native of Xinfeng in Jingzhao, Yongzhou during the Song dynasty. He was dignified and possessed virtuous conduct. Having left the household life, he recited the sutras from evening until dawn.
Deeply yearning for the sacred sites of the former Buddhas throughout the Five Indias, he felt a profound sense of lamentation and resolved to travel there with his own eyes.
Thus, in the sixth year of the Hongshi era of the Qin dynasty, the Jiachen year, he gathered a party of fifteen companions and crossed rivers and traversed valleys.
In total there were thirty-six locations. Upon reaching Liangzhou, he traveled west out of the Yang Pass, crossed the shifting sands, and passed through the various kingdoms of Kucha and Khotan.
Furthermore, two thousand li southwest of Khotan, he ascended Mount Sima, at which point nine of his companions turned back.
After another seventeen hundred li, he reached the kingdom of Boliu, where Zhu Daosong passed away. Fangtu She—

When Guṇamati lost sight of the corpse, he looked back at his four companions with sorrowful sighs and in wonder. Upon crossing the Snow Mountains and traversing the Indus River, he arrived at the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
There were five hundred *arhat* venerables in that land; they met Guṇamati with great joy and, in the interval, recounted to him the matters concerning the Four Heavenly Kings.
In the kingdom of Kiśa, he beheld the Buddha’s stone spittoon and also saw the Buddha’s helmet.
The helmet was purple-blue in luster; its weight changed according to his thoughts. He made offerings of fierce fragrances and flowers, knelt to don it while making vows, and then departed.
After another thirteen hundred *li*, he reached the kingdom of Kapilavastu. There he beheld the Buddha’s *uṣṇīṣa* bone, as well as the remains of his teeth, hair, and shadow, all preserved intact.
He visited the Forest of Firm Nirvāṇa and paid homage at the Bodhi tree where he subdued Māra. Then, at the site of subduing Māra...
He presented the image with a great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) and covered it with a precious canopy; furthermore, he prepared pure offerings to express his utmost respect.
The city of Pāṭaliputra was the former capital of King Aśoka. There lived a Brahmin named Rāvaṇa, whose entire clan propagated the Dharma and whom the king held in high esteem.
He asked Daorong: "Is there the study of the Mahāyāna in the land of Qin? Daorong replied: "All are students of the Mahāyāna. Rāvaṇa was astonished.
He marveled at this as something rare. Fǎměng obtained the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra, the *Saṃghāṭi-sūtra*, and various other scriptures from his home region and returned with them.
In the year Jiǎzǐ, he set out from India and reached Liángzhōu; he was accompanied only by Tánzuǎn. They translated twenty fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
In the fourteenth year of the Yuánjiā era, he entered Shǔ, and in the sixteenth year, he composed the *Record of the Western Journey*. He passed away in Chéngdū.

Huiyan of the Song dynasty was born into the Fan family; he was a native of Yuzhou. At the age of twelve, he studied as a Confucian scholar and attained a profound understanding of the *Shi* and *Li* classics.
At sixteen, he became a śramaṇa and gained renown for his exegesis of Buddhist doctrine. He traveled with Master Kumārajīva and was highly esteemed by his contemporaries.

Upon returning to Jianye, he resided at Dong'an Temple. Emperor Gaozu of the Song treated him with exceptional courtesy; when the Emperor was about to campaign against Chang’an, he took Huiyan along with him.

[He] practiced [the Way]. When Emperor Wen succeeded to the throne, he held him in even greater esteem and respect. Initially, the Emperor had not yet placed much faith in or veneration for the Dharma.

In the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era, Xiao Mozhi, the Prefect of the Capital, requested that regulations be established regarding the construction of temples and the casting of images among the common people.

The Emperor said to the Palace Attendant He Shangzhi and the Minister of Personnel Yang Xuanbao: "I have read the scriptures not many times since my youth; recently, moreover, I have become even less [interested]."

I have leisure. As for the matters of cause and effect, I am dimly aware of them and have not yet investigated them thoroughly; the reason I do not dare to propose a dissenting view is precisely because I hold you gentlemen, the eminent talents of the age, in deep respect and faith.
Fan Tai and Xie Lingyun once said: "The laws and regulations of the Six Classics are fundamentally intended to save the world.
If one seeks the subtle Way, one must take the Buddhist scriptures as a guide. Recently, I have seen Yan Yanzhi’s analysis of the *Daxing lun* (Treatise on the Attainment of Nature).
Zong Bing’s critique of the "Discourse on Black and White" is vast and profound; it elucidates the ultimate truth and is fully capable of inspiring and encouraging the human spirit.
If the people throughout the realm were all to earnestly embrace this transformation, then I would achieve Great Peace while sitting still—what further need would there be for action?
He submitted a memorial regarding the matter of the calligraphic copies, stating: "In your revisions and deletions, you must certainly have intended to curb frivolity and excess;

provided these do not harm the promotion of the Dharma, they should indeed be codified in the statutes. Shangzhi replied: "The customs of this land of horizontal-eyed folk are for the most part lacking in reverence and faith.

Because I am personally mediocre and unrefined, I possess only a simple diligence. I truly fear that my deficiencies might bring disgrace upon the Great Dharma. Yet, I have instead received your commendation."
Commentary: I am once again deeply ashamed. However, the eminent figures of previous dynasties did not fail to respond to the enlightened summons.

Those who came from the south of the Yangtze River include Wang Dao, Zhou Yi, Yu Liang, Wang Meng, Xie Shang, Xi Qi, Wang Tan, Wang Gong, Wang Mi, Guo Wen, Xie Fu, Dai Kui, Xu Xun, as well as my late High Ancestor and his brothers, the brothers Wang Yuanlin, and Fan Wang.

Sun Chuo, Zhang Xuan, and Yin Kai—some were the crowning ornaments of ministers and counselors, some were the paragon models for human relations, some placed their affections at the boundary between humanity and divinity, and others lofted their traces beyond the mists and clouds. All turned their hearts in reverent refuge [to the Dharma].
Among them, Lan Hu, Kai Qian, Yuan Yundao, and Liu Chong sui were like the secondary notes following the *huangzhong* in comparison; they were men of unfathomable depth. In recent times...

This brief discussion between the clergy and the laity is sufficient. Were one to enumerate them all, the extraordinary and eminent figures who appeared throughout the lands of the Yi and Xia, from the Han to the Wei dynasties, would be beyond counting.
Dharma Master Huiyuan said: "The transformation wrought by Śākyamuni is such that there is nothing it cannot encompass. Adapting to the Way is certainly the source of the teaching;

yet harmonizing with secular customs is likewise a matter of vital importance. I have personally savored these words and find they accord with the ultimate truth. If every household were to maintain [the precepts]...

If there were precepts, then the nation’s administration of punishments would cease; thus, when Fotudeng went to Zhao, the two Shi rulers were made to diminish their violence, and when Kumārajīva was in Qin, Fu Jian reduced his cruelty.
That the Way of the Spirits assists in governance is clearly observable and cannot be denied.

Yet, as for what you have requested, it is not that I consider it entirely wrong; however, those who harm both the clergy and the laity do so because their underlying intent lies in the absence of moral conduct.
Regarding the monastic community of monks and nuns, their sincerity and deceitfulness are difficult to distinguish, and thus it is not easy to decide what to adopt or reject.

As for works of earth and wood, although they may seem wasteful, the planting of merit and the repayment of kindness cannot easily be discontinued. I have recently deliberated on this matter, yet my decision regarding whether to proceed or retreat remained unsettled.

Today, having personally received Your Majesty’s virtuous decree, I am truly filled with joy and gratitude. Yang Xuanbao stepped forward and said: "This discussion concerns, in essence, the relationship between Heaven and man—"

"Your Majesty, how could I, a dull and ignorant subject, be fit to hear such matters? I only fear that the strategies for strengthening the military discussed by those of Qin and Chu, and the schemes for total annexation perfected by Sun Tzu and Wu Qi, would find no value in this [learning]. The Emperor said, "This is not the tool of the Warring States;

it is truly as you say. Shangzhi replied, "If the state honors the reclusive and the retired, the warriors will become indolent. If it prizes benevolence and virtue, the martial spirit of the troops will dissipate."

"If one were to set their will upon Sun Wu [Sun Bin and Wu Qi] and expect to achieve unification through military action, they likewise would find nothing to take from the Way of Yao and Shun—not to mention the teachings of Śākyamuni alone.
The Emperor was pleased and said, "The Śākya school having you is like the School of Confucius having Ji Lu (Zilu).
It is as the saying goes: 'Evil words do not enter the ear. From this time on, he revered and honored the Buddhist scriptures. Yan Yanzhi composed the *Liyu*...

Regarding the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Discourse on Consciousness): First, he used it to examine Emperor Wu. The Emperor commanded Yan to debate with him; they exchanged arguments throughout the entire day.
The Emperor smiled and said, "You gentlemen are truly not inferior to Zhi Dun and Xu Xun. He Chen-tian of Donghai asked Yan: "What calendar does the Buddha-land use?"

Yan said: "In India, on the day of the summer solstice, at solar noon there is no shadow; this is because it is the center of the heavens. In the Five Elements, earth is employed and yellow is the honored color;
the number five is used. Eight *cun* constitute one *chi*. Ten *liang* is equivalent to twelve *liang* in the Han system.

The month of Jichen (the ninth lunar month) is taken as the beginning of the year. They investigate the solstices and equinoxes, calculate eclipses, and observe the movement of light and shadow; such are their methods."
It was extremely detailed. He calculated the past ages and years, all according to established principles. Chengtian had no words with which to respond.
Later, people from the country of Pāri came, and their accounts indeed matched those spoken by Yan. The Emperor issued an edict for Ren Yu to receive [the text].

Yan, together with Huiquan and Xie Lingyun, meticulously finalized the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. A deity appeared in a dream and rebuked them, saying: "The *Nirvāṇa* is a most venerable scripture; why do you arbitrarily add revisions? Yan...
He was startled awake and wished to collect all his previous drafts. At that time, those who understood him said, "This is merely an attempt to admonish future generations.
If it were truly not to be, you would have seen the dream at the time of the final revision. Huiyan agreed with this.
Later, he again dreamed that a deity told him, "By the power of the Buddhist scriptures, you shall surely behold the Buddha. He passed away in the twentieth year of the Yuanjia era.
He lived to the age of eighty-one.
Sengye of the Song dynasty was surnamed Wang and was a native of Henei. He became a śramaṇa in his youth; he was intelligent and capable of extensively investigating the Tripiṭaka.
He received the Dharma from Kumārajīva and specialized in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*. Kumārajīva praised him, saying that he was the Upāli of future generations. He fled his homeland...
He crossed the Yangtze River. Zhang Shao of Wu established Xianju Monastery at Gusu to welcome him; the monastics and laypeople of the Three Wu regions vied with one another to honor and revere him.
A fragrant aroma was constantly present in his meditation chamber. He passed away in the eighteenth year of the Yuanjia era at the age of seventy-five.
The Song dynasty monk Dao was a native of Jingzhao; his clan name has been lost to history. He entered the monastic order at the age of ten.

His teacher gave him the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* (Guanshiyin jing), and Dao asked, "How many fascicles does this sūtra have? The teacher replied, "It consists of only one fascicle. Dao said, "Since the sūtra speaks of 'at that time' [the Bodhisattva] Akṣayamati, we know there must have been more before this.
The teacher was greatly amazed by his insight and gave him the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* (Lotus Sūtra). Thereupon, Dao attained profound understanding.

He was thoroughly proficient. His teachers, who had long been established in their studies, held him in great awe and respect. At the age of eighteen, Sengrui saw him and sighed in admiration, saying, "You shall become a Dharma Lord over ten thousand monks;
take good care of yourself. Yao Xing heard of his reputation and went to visit him to converse with him, even returning with him on the same carriage;
scholars considered this an honor. He frequently collaborated with Kumārajīva in the collation of his translations and authored the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and the *Three Treatises*.

He extensively elucidated the meaning of the *Śāstra* and the treatises on the two truths of Emptiness and Existence. When Emperor Gaozu of the Song dynasty pacified Guanzhong, he was delighted to obtain [Seng]dao.
Upon returning to Jianye, the Emperor pointed to Prince Guiyang, Yizhen, and said to Dao, "This boy is young and has been left here to govern;
we rely upon you to assist him. Later, when Yizhen was pressed by the barbarians, Dao was indeed able to organize a rescue. The barbarians then lifted the siege and withdrew. The Emperor...
When the Patriarch heard of this, he praised him. He established Dongshan Temple in Shouchun to serve as his residence.

When the Northern Wei suppressed the Buddhist teachings, those who fled there to seek refuge were all provided with food and clothing. For those from his old hometown who had died, he would organize assemblies and offer incense, weeping and lamenting in deep sorrow.
When Emperor Xiaowu ascended the throne, he issued an edict appointing him to Zhongxing Temple in Jianye. The Emperor [performed] the suburban sacrifices...

He welcomed [the teachings], and the Way of the Dharma flourished greatly. Whenever he lectured on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* at Waguan Temple, the Emperor would visit in person, and the high officials and nobles would all assemble.

After a long time, he took his leave and returned to Shouchun, where he passed away at the age of ninety-six. At that time, there were also the monks Sengyin and Sengwei, who likewise possessed extraordinary conduct.
Hui-xun of the Song dynasty was born into the Zhao clan; he was a native of Zhaojun. From his youth, he was diligent and austere.

He traveled to Guanzhong to study under Kumārajīva, where he thoroughly investigated the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, subsequently composing commentaries upon them. During the Yongchu era, he lectured on these texts in Guangling.

During the Yuanjia era, he arrived at the capital and resided at Daochang Temple, later moving to Changle Temple, where he widely propagated the study of the Vinaya. He passed away in the second year of the Daming era.
He lived to the age of eighty.
Guṇabhadra of the Song dynasty, translated here as "Virtuous Merit," was a native of Central India.

Originally, his family followed non-Buddhist teachings, but he fled from them to seek a teacher for his tonsure and ordination as a śramaṇa. His teacher ordered him to search through the sūtras, and he discovered the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin).
Huayan said with joy, "Do you have a karmic affinity for the Mahāyāna? He then conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon him, whereby his mastery of the Mahāyāna was further refined;
at that time, he was called Mahāyan. Subsequently, he sent a letter to inform his parents, urging them to return to the orthodox path.
Having traveled extensively through various kingdoms of Siṃhala, he boarded a ship and set sail toward the east. Upon reaching mid-journey, their drinking water was exhausted, and the wind ceased.

He was unable to proceed further. Xian performed a ritual incantation for him, and a torrential rain fell in abundance. Upon reaching Guangzhou, the Regional Inspector Che Lang reported the matter to the throne.

A messenger was dispatched to the capital; in the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era, [Faxian] first resided at Zhihuan Temple, after which he was summoned by imperial decree to enter the palace for offerings.

Langlang was Yan Yanzhi, a man of versatile talent and profound learning. When he arrived at the gate wearing his ceremonial belt, the high officials and nobles from near and far throughout the capital lined up in succession.
Both Prince Yikang of Pengcheng and Prince Yixuan of Nanqiao served him as their teacher.

He translated over one hundred fascicles of sutras, including the *Saṃyuktāgama*, the *Dharmabherī*, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda*, and the *Laṅkāvatāra*. Prince Yixuan invited him to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

However, Xian alone regretted that he was not yet proficient in the Chinese language. He prayed to Avalokiteśvara to seek a spiritual response; one night, he dreamed that a divine warrior replaced his head.
Upon rising the next morning, he suddenly understood the meaning of the language. He subsequently proceeded to give lectures.

When the King asked him about a series of strange dreams he had experienced, Xian replied, "There will be calamity in the capital. The King was hatching a rebellious plot, and Xian remonstrated with him until he wept. The King—

He was forced to go down with them. During the defeat at Liangshan, he fell into the river; single-mindedly reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara and clutching a bamboo staff, he saw a youth pulling at his robe.
Xian said, "You are but a small child, yet you can do this? When they reached the shore, he wished to take off his inner robe to repay the youth, but suddenly the youth vanished from sight.
Wang Xuemo, acting on imperial decree, escorted Xian to the palace to console him.
He settled him there and said, "I have long aspired to virtue, yet only today have we met. Having come from afar through such hardship, can you say you have no regrets?
He replied, "I have no regrets; I only think that our past affinity has now reached its full fruition. The Emperor again teased him, saying:
"Do you perhaps remember Prince Qiao? [The monk] replied, "The ancients did not forget a single meal. Your Majesty fed me for ten years; how could I dare suddenly forget it?
I wish to descend from these steps to pray for Your Majesty’s posthumous merit on your behalf. I only beg for your compassionate pity. The Emperor changed his expression accordingly.

When Zhongxing Temple was completed, an imperial decree appointed him as its abbot. Once, when the Emperor held a banquet at Dongfu, all the princes and dukes were assembled there, and the Emperor issued a decree...
Sengxian arrived. He was white-haired and appeared thin and emaciated. From above, the Emperor saw him and said to Xie Zhuang, "Mahāyāna possesses keen wit and eloquence;
you should engage him in debate. As Sengxian ascended the steps, the Emperor said, "Mahāyāna has not come in vain from afar; there is only one thing remaining."
He immediately replied, "This poor monk has been a guest at Your Majesty’s table for thirty years; the thickness of your kindness and favor has left nothing lacking.
What remains lacking is but one death. The Emperor was delighted and drew his seat closer; everyone present leaned forward in attention. In the sixth year of the Yongming era, there was a drought.
He traveled everywhere seeking a vision but found no sign. The Emperor issued an edict to Hsien, saying, "Only after a heavy rain shall we meet.

Hsien immediately ceased all food and drink and went up to the Fishing Terrace at Pei-hu, where he silently recited sutras and dharanis. The next day, there was a great downpour. The high officials entered to offer their congratulations.
His acts of charity increased ever further. In the first month of the fourth year of the Taishi era, he manifested illness and passed away at the age of seventy-five.
Sengqu of the Song dynasty was born into the Zhu family; he was a native of Wu. From his youth, he became a śramaṇa and served Sengye as his teacher.

He was particularly proficient in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) and skilled in literary composition. Having read widely across the classics and histories, he initially resided at Mount Huqiu. Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty heard of his reputation.

When the imperial decree arrived at the capital, he was appointed as the *Sengzheng* (Chief Administrator of Monks) and resided at Zhongxing Temple. At that time, there was a śramaṇa named Sengding who claimed to have attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*.

Sengqu assembled the congregation to investigate and adjudicate the matter, ordering him to manifest his supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). Sengding said, "I fear it would constitute a violation of the precepts; therefore, I shall not manifest them."
Qu said, "According to the Vinaya texts, there are four causes and conditions by which one may manifest supernatural powers: first, to sever the net of doubt;
second, to destroy false views; third, to eliminate arrogance; and fourth, to accomplish meritorious virtues. It is certainly impossible for you to do so.

He then expelled him and composed the *Jiezhuṅlùn* (Treatise on Expelling the Multitude) to instruct future generations. Emperor Xiaowu received the five precepts from him, and Prince Zishang of Yuzhang took him as his master for the Dharma.
His friend passed away at the age of fifty-eight. He annotated the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and compiled the *Essentials of Monks and Nuns*, both of which circulated in the world.
As for Shi Daoyan, he was a native of Xiaohuang in Xiongqiu. He was proficient in the Vinaya and had thoroughly researched the four sections of the Vinaya-piṭaka.

He synthesized the various schools and, further examining the differences between Sanskrit and Chinese phonology and their underlying meanings, he composed the *Treatise on the Determination and Correction of the Four Sections of the Vinaya*. He widely propagated the teachings of the Vinaya while traveling through Pengcheng.
The city was submerged. His lifespan was seventy-five years.
*Newly Compiled Classified Biographies of Monks of the Six Studies*, Scroll 11;
*Newly Compiled Classified Biographies of Monks of the Six Studies*, Scroll 12.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Tanne of Eastern Zhejiang.
*Jiexue Hongfa Ke* (Outline for the Propagation of the Dharma through the Study of Precepts), Part Two.
Qi Faying was born into the Su clan. A native of Dunhuang, at the age of thirteen he left his home to become a disciple under the śramaṇa Faxiang, receiving full ordination.
He resided at the Gongfu Monastery in Liangzhou, where he and Fali both became renowned for their mastery of the Vinaya.

Toward the end of the Yuanjia era, he traveled to the capital and resided at Xinting Temple. Emperor Xiaowu issued an edict appointing Huiming as the Sangha Rectifier (Sengzheng) of the metropolitan area.

He moved his residence to Duobao Temple to practice meditation and produce scriptures and images of exquisite magnificence. He also established a medicinal storehouse (yaocang) at Changgan to provide for the sick.
He compiled the *Jieben* (Manual of Precepts) for the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, along with the *Karmavācanā* texts and other writings. He passed away at the age of sixty-seven.
Qi Xuanchang was born to the Zhao family; he was a native of Jincheng in Hexi.
When he was young, the Qiang chieftain annihilated his entire family, but seeing Xuanchang, he forbade them from killing him, saying, "This boy’s gaze shoots outward; he is no ordinary vessel.

Consequently, Xuanchang became a disciple of Xuangao in Liangzhou. Later, when the Qiang destroyed the Buddha-dharma and harmed the various śramaṇas, Xuanchang struck [the assailant] with a willow branch.
Sand and dust obscured the sky, causing the pursuing cavalry to lose sight of him. In times of urgency, he would plug his nose with *xī* grass to breathe through it or cast himself into the water.
Traveling from Pingcheng through Daijun and Shanggu, he crossed the Taihang Mountains and the Mengjin River before reaching Yangzhou.

He was well-versed in the Vinaya and Sūtras and had extensively studied the works of the hundred schools of thought, including the histories and annals. Initially, the text and meaning of the *Avataṃsaka* were vast and profound; Daoyi was the first to...
The commentary explains this: as the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) was the school venerated by scholars, Emperor Wen invited him to serve as the preceptor for the Crown Prince, but he declined.
After a long time, he took leave to travel to Western Shu. Upon arriving at Dashi Temple, he personally painted sixteen figures of Vajrapāṇi.
He further established a temple on Mount Qi in Xiayang County, Minshan Prefecture, naming it Qixing. This day happened to coincide with...
At the time when Emperor Taizu received the nine emblems of investiture, certain celestial signs and human affairs coincided perfectly from ten thousand *li* away.

[Daosheng] composed the "Praise of Mount Qi" (*Qishan zan*) to narrate these events and sent it to Fu Yan of Chengdu. When Fu Yan heard of this, he inquired after him from various prefectures and commanderies at regular intervals.

[Daosheng] was able to stretch out his hand to produce incense and flow water from his palms. When Prince Ning of Yuzhang was stationed in Jingzhou, he welcomed [Daosheng] to the city. [The text ends here.]

Crown Prince Hui again dispatched an envoy to welcome him back to Linggen Monastery in Jianye. He passed away at the age of sixty-nine and was buried on Dulonggang in the winter of the second year of the Yongming era.
Qizhi Dao renounced his family name for the Liu clan. A native of Henei, he was prudent and upright. In his youth, he became a śramaṇa and extensively studied the various sūtras;
he was particularly adept in the Vinaya section. He Shangzhi admired his character and built Falun Temple to welcome him there to reside.

Since the Northern Wei barbarians had suppressed the teachings, the monastic precepts and laws had been neglected in the Central Plains. Dao, together with more than ten of his disciples, traveled to Hulao and gathered [the faithful].
The Daoists of the five provinces of Luo, Qin, Yong, and Yu gathered at Yinshui Temple to lecture on and transmit the complete Vinaya-piṭaka;

this was due to the power of the Way. After a long time, he arrived in the capital. When Wang Xuan was appointed as the regional governor of Xiangzhou, he took him along with him, whereupon he passed away.
He was seventy-three years old.
Sengyuan of the Qi dynasty was born into the Huang clan; he was a native of Chonghe in Bohai. At the age of sixteen, he wished to leave the household life, but his parents would not permit it.
Consequently, he engaged in ascetic practices and devoted himself to repentance and recitation. After another two years, he became a śramaṇa and studied under the Dharma Master Daohui.
He was well-versed in the sūtras and śāstras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. During the Daming era of the Song dynasty, he resided at Pengcheng Temple;
during the Shengming era, he resided at Longyuan Temple on Mount Niuluo. At the age of thirty-one, he began lecturing at Sunqin Temple in Qingzhou.

His delivery was clear and penetrating, and his demeanor was composed and profound, such that the entire assembly was captivated. Wang Sengda of Langye, who enjoyed great renown at the time, [held him in particular esteem].

Homage. He built a monastery to provide a place for them to reside. Yuan was benevolent by nature; as he walked through the green gardens, he would take off his own clothes to clothe those who were cold and give his alms-food to those who were hungry.
During a time of great pestilence, when the sick lay piled one upon another, he attended to each person and buried the deceased as if they were his own kin.
The people of the village were transformed by his filial piety and respect. Prince Luan built the Xin'an Monastery to offer memorial services for him.
Do not treat the nobles of Yin with excessive honor. Let an imperial edict be issued to select those of extraordinary virtue from throughout the realm; those who meet the criteria shall be summoned.

In the ninth month of the sixth year of the Daming era, the Right Counselor submitted this memorial: "Your servant has heard that the profound seclusion of the sovereign’s residence is not intended merely for loftiness, nor is the ritual of kneeling and prostrating before the food-tray simply a matter of yielding respect.

Rather, it is to manifest and extend the four cardinal virtues and to establish order within the eight realms. Therefore, although there are divergent branches of Confucianism and Legalism, as well as the schools of Name and Mo..."

Regarding the various regulations concerning the honoring of kin and the revering of superiors, there have been instances where these principles were neglected; only the Buddhist teachings are uniquely exceptional in this regard.
We, your ministers, have deliberated and concluded that when śramaṇas are received in audience, they must all manifest an appearance of utmost ritual respect. The Imperial Edict stated: "So be it."
Hearing of this from afar, Huiyuan sighed and said, "I am a shramana who has shaved my head; I originally left the household life to seek the Way. What concern have I with emperors?
He immediately declined on the grounds of illness and moved to reside at Dinglin Temple. When Emperor Ming ascended the throne, he invited Huiyuan to serve as his teacher, but Huiyuan did not accept.

Prince Jing-su of Jianping offered Qixuan Temple to him, yet again Huiyuan did not accept. When the Taizu of the Qi dynasty was about to pass the throne to his successor, he entered the mountains to visit him.

Huiyuan declined on the grounds of old age and illness, stating that his feet did not even reach the edge of his bed. Emperor Taizu visited him at the foot of the bed and consulted with him in full detail.

Upon ascending the throne, he again traveled by carriage to Huiyuan’s quarters; because the room and its chambers were so narrow as to not accommodate a palanquin or canopy, he halted his carriage, sent an envoy to inquire after his health, and departed.
For more than fifty years, Huiyuan had resided in the mountains. At first he still ate, but when food could no longer be sustained, he eventually subsisted only on water.
He resided at Jian for twenty years. In the first month of the second year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, he manifested illness.
The two princes, Wenhui and Wenxuan, attended him while he took medicine. He passed away at the age of seventy-one. The Emperor sent a letter to the śramaṇa Faxian, saying:
"I have heard that Master Yuan has passed away. As a disciple, I already knew this in the middle of the night. Master Yuan has departed to a most excellent place; there is no need for concern."
My compassion increases. There are more wonders than one or two. Only when I meet the Dharma Master can I recount the auspicious dream.

Now is precisely the time to perform meritorious deeds on his behalf; you may send a detailed list of what is required. Prince Wenxuan of Jingling has erected a stupa for him on the Southern Mountain.
Qizhilin was a native of Gaochang; his clan name has been lost to history. He took ordination under Master Liang and immediately traveled to Chang’an to extensively study the sūtras and the Vinaya.

He was particularly proficient in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*. When Master Liang was exiled to the regions beyond the southern peaks due to criminal charges, Zhilin went with twelve fellow students to the remote frontiers of the south.
There he lectured and taught daily; people from afar admired his noble character. Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty issued an edict summoning him to the capital.

He resided at Lingji Temple in the capital, where his students flourished even more. At that time, he established the doctrine of the Two Truths, for which there were three schools with differing views.
When Zhou Yong of Runan completed the *Sanzong lun* (Treatise on the Three Schools), he feared slander and did not circulate it; Senglin then wrote a letter to encourage him to do so.
The summary states: "I have humbly heard that the discourse on the Three Sects probes the profound and seeks out the hidden;

it exhausts the sentiments of sentient beings and clarifies and extends them to fulfill the intent of the Buddha. It ensures that the lamp of the Dharma has its seed and that its benefits are inexhaustible.
Even the giving of kingdoms, cities, wives, and children—how could these ever compare to this gift? The transmitter believed that because the donor feared criticism, he wished to...

He interrupted his work. How could he allow himself to remain entangled in the obstacles of doubt, thereby giving rise to views and conduct? When Sengyong received this letter, he was startled into awakening.
This treatise subsequently circulated throughout the world. Ling’s height was eight chi; his voice was clear and resonant. He returned to Gaochang to pass away, at the age of seventy-nine.
He authored the *Treatise on the Two Truths*, the *Commentary on the Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, as well as commentaries on the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, and other works.
Qi Fayuan was born into the Xin clan. He was a native of Longxi and a descendant of [Vimala]kīrti. His father had three sons:
the eldest, Yuanming, served the Wei dynasty and rose to the rank of Minister of the Interior (Shangshu); the middle son became a śramaṇa named Fa’ai; and Fayuan was the youngest.
He took the śramaṇa Huikai of Liangzhou as his teacher. Huikai was a man of unfathomable character, yet he held Fayuan in special affection, saying: "In the future, regarding the Buddha-dharma..."
He was capable and strong; he was sent to travel and study in the four directions. Relying on the wisdom of the *dharma-cakra*, he entered Mount Lu to practice meditation.

When Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty sought someone who could explain Master Sengzhao’s doctrine of "sudden enlightenment," Yu Dengzhi, the Regional Inspector of Jiangzhou, reported Huaiyuan’s name to the throne.
An imperial edict summoned him for an audience. Huaiyuan presented his arguments with clarity and precision. He Shangzhi sighed and said, "I had thought that Master Sengzhao had passed away."
Thereafter, subtle words were forever lost. Today, I have again heard discourse that transcends the mundane—truly, it can be said that Heaven has not yet abandoned these sacred texts.
The Princes of Nanping and Xiyang both served him as their teacher. He returned to Mount Lu and annotated the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.

When the Tianbao era was established, an imperial edict summoned Fayuan to reside there. When Wang Jingwen arrived, he encountered him in the midst of a lecture; Jingwen sighed in admiration, saying: "Everything he presents..."

What he had not heard before—all that he pointed out transcended the bounds of conventional thought; he was truly a dragon among the Dharma. When the Xianggong Monastery was completed, an imperial decree again invited Huai to reside there.

The Emperor visited in person to listen to the Dharma, and the high officials and dukes all assembled; at the time, this was considered a great honor. Later, during the reign of Emperor Wenhui of the Qi dynasty, he was again invited to reside at Linggen Monastery.
Wang Jian, the Grand Marshal, who possessed a preeminent reputation, specifically prepared a single couch for him and extended an invitation for him to sit upon it next to himself. Others...
No one associated with him. He passed away in the seventh year of the Yongming era at the age of eighty-one.
Qi Fawu was a native of Qizhou; the histories do not record his clan name. His family had been farmers for generations. He had six sons, all of whom left the household life.

When Fawu was fifty years old, he lost his wife and became a śramaṇa. He recited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras. Every time he did so, a tiger would crouch before him as if...
As for Tíngzhě: by nature he did not eat non-glutinous rice; each day he consumed nothing more than a single cup of wheat porridge.
Rǎn Huì, the Governor of Wuchang, cleared the southern slopes of Fán Mountain to provide a dwelling for the hermit Guō Chángxiáng, constructing halls and chambers for him to reside in.

He practiced the dhūta austerities with great rigor and was especially diligent in seated meditation; he would sometimes remain in samādhi for several days. He passed away in the seventh year of the Yongmíng era of the Qi dynasty.
He lived to the age of ninety-seven. There was also one named Huiming, born into the Kang clan; he was a native of Kangju and resided at Dong’an Temple.
Ascending Mount Chicheng, he admired the style of Daoyou and Tamlan and dwelt there in a thatched hut. He dreamed of a woman who called herself Old Lady Lü and said, "I shall protect you.
Wenxuan treated him with the utmost courtesy and brought him to the capital, but as soon as he arrived, the Master departed. He [subsequently] established...
Wu died at the age of seventy-one.
Qi Sengshen was born into the Wang family; he was a native of Qí in Taiyuan and a descendant of Shen, the Jin-era General of the Flying Cavalry.

Having settled in Qiao Commandery, he left home in his youth to take refuge at Shijian Monastery and receive ordination. He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, often saying that they were not [ordinary texts].

He felt that his meditation lacked wisdom. Thereupon, he devoted himself single-mindedly to *dhyāna*. Hearing that Dharmamitra was transforming the capital with his spiritual teachings, he went to pay him a visit;

however, [Dharmamitra] brushed aside his sleeves and crossed the river. He then stayed at Lingyao Temple, where he applied himself with diligence to receiving instruction until he had thoroughly mastered its profound depths.
When Wang Jingze entered the room to inquire after him, he saw him sitting in meditation. Wang snapped his fingers and departed, saying, "A holy man! He then paid him his respects.
He was granted a stipend of one thousand *shí* of rice. He was also revered by Wenhui and Wenxuan. He passed away in the eighth year of the Yongming era at the age of seventy-five.
At that time, there were the śramaṇas Sengqian, Chaozhi, Fadai, and Huisheng, all of whom were refined in dhyāna meditation and possessed extraordinary traces of spiritual attainment.
Qifa Lin was a descendant of the Yue clan and a native of Linqiong in Yuanzhou, Jin. In his youth, he relied upon Pei Monastery in Shu Commandery to receive the full precepts.

He followed Master Yin to study the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* with great diligence. When Master Yin returned to Shan, Lin followed him there as well. He mastered all the various sections of the Vinaya and applied himself wholeheartedly to the practice of the Pure Land contemplations.
At the time of his death, he beheld many extraordinary auspicious signs; with palms joined, he passed away.
Qifa Xian was born into the Xu family. A native of Yan Water in Xihai, he followed his maternal uncle to Liangzhou in his youth and subsequently left home to become a śramaṇa.
He devoted himself to the study of the sūtras and vinaya, gaining renown in his time. Residing at Dinglin Monastery on Mount Zhong, he heard that Master Meng had traveled westward;
wishing to emulate him, he departed from Ba and Shu for Henan, passing through the Rouran kingdom and arriving at...
From Khotan, he intended to cross the Pamir Mountains, but meeting with the suspension of the plank bridges, he was unable to proceed and thus returned.
There he obtained a single tooth of the Buddha, fifteen *śarīra* relics, the "Spell of Avalokiteśvara for the Extinction of Sins," and the "Chapter on Devadatta.

Upon reaching Kucha, he further acquired a gilded image struck with a golden hammer. He presented these—the image, the Buddha’s tooth, and the *śarīra*—to the capital, where he venerated them with great care.
For twenty-five years, no one was aware of its existence. Suddenly, Prince Wenxuan saw it in a dream; he went to the place where it resided to seek an audience and pay his respects.
It was then brought out and shown to him. There is a record stating that it originally came from the country of Udyāna, entered the Rouran from Udyāna, and reached the Han region from the Rouran.
Subsequently, Wang Su of Langya, Wang Rong, and Zhang Rong of Wuguo [all examined it].

Zhang Qu, the śramaṇa Huiling, and Zhizang all served as disciples of [Hui]xian. During the Yongming era, an imperial edict appointed him, along with the śramaṇa Xuanchang of Changgan Monastery, as the National Preceptor (Guosengzhu).
Whenever he appeared before the Emperor, he addressed him by name and did not take a formal seat.

One day, while at Qianhong Hall, the śramaṇa Sengzhong of Zhongxing Monastery addressed the Emperor as "this poor monk" (pindao). The Emperor was surprised by this and questioned the Court Historian (Shangshu).
