The Emperor asked Wang Jian: "When former generations of śramaṇas conversed with emperors, what title did they use? Were they permitted to enter the main hall and take their seats? Wang Jian replied:

"During the Han and Wei dynasties, the Buddha-dharma had not yet greatly flourished; thus, there are no records of such matters in the historical annals. During the Northern Wei, the Dharma began to flourish somewhat, and śramaṇas mostly referred to themselves as 'the poor man of the Way' (pindao).
Furthermore, they were permitted to sit together [with the emperor], and the practice of calling oneself 'the poor man of the Way' has continued to this day. The Emperor [approved].
It is said that even for the two Dukes, Chang and Xian, whose conduct was such as this, they were still addressed by their names; how much more so for others?
I believe it is appropriate to address them by name. Xian passed away at the end of the Jianwu era at the age of seventy-five.

Initially, when the pavilion was built at Dinglin Monastery to enshrine the Buddha’s tooth relic, on the night of the first month of the third year of the Putong era, several men appeared, knocking on the door while holding staffs, and claimed to be from the Netherworld.
Prince Shōsuke of Kawara arrived and urgently desired to ascend the pavilion to capture the rebel slave. The temple officials, struck with terror, issued the keys and allowed him to do as he pleased;
consequently, the Buddha’s tooth relic was lost.
Qi Zhicheng was a native of Wenxi in Hedong, a descendant of Pei Wei, the former Governor of Jizhou during the Wei dynasty.
Having fled to Jingkou to escape the turmoil, he was proficient in archery and horsemanship from his youth. He accompanied Wang Xuanmu on the northern expedition to Shentu;

subsequently, however, he felt remorse, saying, "To kill people in pursuit of honor and emolument is not my will. He abandoned his post and departed. Later, he heard someone reciting the *Ruixiang* (Auspicious Signs).
He experienced a profound awakening through his studies and went to the Chan Master Zong of Nanjian to receive the five precepts.

When Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty invited Chan Master Yin of Chengdu to the capital, he again relied upon him; subsequently, he followed him back to Shu to undergo the tonsure ceremony, at which time he was thirty-six years old.
He then devoted himself single-mindedly to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, traveling down to Jiangling to receive the instructions on meditation from the masters Yin and Ju.

During the rebellion of Yao Yijia, he moved to Xinghuang Monastery in the capital, where he listened to Master Ying’s lectures on the Vinaya. Faxian of Dinglin Monastery admired his discussions and took him back with him.
Later, the monk Sengzhi of Yuhang invited him to expound the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* at Bao’an Monastery in his native region. Furthermore, for...
As for Yunkisi, its abbot was [Dao]jing, who had been invited by Prince Wenxuan of Jingling to establish Puhong Temple; there he led several hundred students in the study of the Vinaya.
He subsequently preached the Dharma at Huishi in Zhufang. Whenever he encountered relatives or old acquaintances, he instructed them in filial piety and fraternal duty.
In the third year of the Yongyuan era of the Qi dynasty, at the age of seventy-two, he returned and passed away at Anle Temple in the capital.
The Monk Sengyou of the Liang Dynasty was born into the Yu clan. His ancestors were from Xiapi in Pengcheng, but they later moved their residence to Jianye.
When Sengyou was a child, he happened to enter Jianchu Monastery and stayed with the monk Fandao; when his parents called for him to return home, he refused to go. He was ten years old.
When four suitors sought to marry him, he fled from them. He entered the monastic order according to the Dharma at Dinglin Temple. Having received full ordination, he studied the Vinaya under Faying;
his realization surpassed that of his predecessors. Whenever he gave lectures, the audience always numbered in the thousands.
[He was honored by] Prince Wenxuan of Jingling of the Qi dynasty, Prince Hong of Linchuan and Prince Wei of Nanping of the Liang dynasty, General-in-Chief Yuan Ang, and Princess Yongkang.

Ding Guibin had over eleven thousand black and white disciples. All the offerings she received were used to repair and maintain stupas and monasteries, and to restore and complete scriptures and images;
thus, the Great Image at Guangzhai and the Great Mountain (Sheshan), as well as the stone Buddhas in Tan County, were all initiated by her.

The current Emperor treated her with profound courtesy; whenever he encountered significant doubts regarding monastic affairs, he would invariably consult her for a definitive decision. In her later years, she suffered from an ailment of the feet.
An imperial edict was issued permitting him to enter the inner palace in the imperial carriage to bestow the precepts upon the ladies of the six palaces.

He passed away on the twenty-sixth day of the fifth month in the seventeenth year of the Tianjian era at the age of seventy-four. His works—including the *Sanzang ji*, *Fayuan ji*, *Shijie ji*, *Shijia pu*, and *Hongming ji*—circulate in the world.

Fachao of the Liang dynasty was born into the Meng family. A native of Wuxi in Jinling, he was intelligent and precocious from childhood and pursued his studies with diligent devotion, never growing weary.
At the age of eleven, he left the household life and resided at Linggen Monastery, where he relied upon the monk Sengxiu for protection and instruction. He studied the sutras and śāstras;
though poor and unable to support himself through begging, he found no hardship in manual labor. Later in life, he followed the Vinaya Master Zhicheng of Anle Monastery.

He studied the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Shisong lü) under Huicheng, whom he praised as one whose teachings could be entrusted to his family. Huicheng spoke to him extensively regarding the principles that serve as the central pivot of the Dharma.
After Huicheng passed away, Sengchao became the peerless authority in the capital. At that time, Emperor Wu was fervently promoting the Buddha-vehicle;

he considered the study of the *vinaya* to be the foundation for concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), and held that self-cultivation and the eradication of transgressions were fundamentally dependent upon it. He therefore mandated that the monastic community...

Regarding the five categories and seven groups of offenses for *bhikṣuṇīs*, she guided their minds and encouraged their resolve. Fearing, however, that the texts of the various sections were so extensive and voluminous that they would be difficult to investigate when faced with actual matters, she compiled the *Lüyao* (Essentials of the Vinaya) in fourteen fascicles during her leisure time from study and recitation, and circulated it in the world.

She then appointed Chao as the *Sengzheng* (Monastic Rectifier) of the capital. In the sixth year of the Putong era, an imperial decree was issued for her to lecture at the Pingdeng Hall; she simply raised [the following points]:

This was merely a general outline intended to proclaim the grand purport. At that time, the Emperor personally attended to receive the teachings and further assembled the administrators, renowned virtuous monks, and the entire community of clergy and laity, ensuring there would be no criticism or debate that might lead to transgression. The project concluded within thirty days, and all quarters rejoiced.
In the winter of his seventy-first year, he passed away at the monastery where he resided in India. By imperial decree, the relevant authorities were ordered [to conduct the funeral rites].
The funeral cortege was escorted with full ceremonial decorum to Kaishan Temple on Mount Zhongshan.
Master Daochan was a native of Jiaozhi. Having early escaped the net of worldly existence, he was by nature upright and dignified. Initially, he resided at Xianzhou Mountain Temple in his hometown;
as the mountain had long been plagued by many fierce tigers, they ceased their depredations once Chan took up residence there. The local elders considered this a marvel.
At the beginning of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, Prince Jingling extensively propagated the Buddha-dharma. Huiyan heard of this and traveled from afar to participate in the eminent assembly.
He resided at the Lower Yunju Monastery on Mount Zhong, where he studied and excerpted various scriptural divisions; he was particularly proficient in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.

His disciples numbered over a hundred, and those who received his precepts and regulations in the capital and its suburbs exceeded one thousand. Furthermore, he delighted in quietude and solitude; whenever he encountered a secluded valley while traveling, he would immediately enter meditative absorption for a long duration.

Subsisting on vegetarian food and wearing tattered robes, he lived in a state of serene contentment. Whenever he obtained fragrant or delicious food, he would distribute it according to the needs of the poor and the sick.
In his later years, he withdrew from public life and severed all ties with the world. In the first year of the Datong era, he passed away at a mountain temple at the age of seventy.
Fayun of the Liang dynasty was surnamed Zhou and hailed from Yangxian. He was the seventh-generation descendant of Zhou Chu, the General Who Subdues the West during the Jin dynasty.

His mother was surnamed Wu; while she was pregnant with him, she saw clouds filling the room, and thus he was named Yun ("Clouds"). At the age of seven, he took the monk Sengcheng as his teacher, following the spiritual path of Bao Liang.
He entered the monastic order and resided at Zhuangyan Temple. At thirteen, he began his formal studies under Sengzong of Taichang Temple.
Sengda of Yan Temple and Baoliang always considered themselves inferior to him.

During the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, when Sengrou returned from the east and began lecturing at Daolin Temple, Fayun sat upon a small stool before him to consult and resolve doubts for several days; through this, he became renowned.
He was especially close with Sengmin of the same temple, where they collated the sūtras and śāstras, re-explaining the textual meanings whenever there were gaps or ambiguities.

Whenever he traveled along the road, he would reflect upon the meaning [of the Dharma] and frequently visit the temples he had built. Upon seeing the grand assembly at Changle Temple presided over by Fatio, he came forth and sighed, saying:
"In the capital of the Son of Heaven of Zhendan, the people are like this; it can truly be said that the Dharma seat is empty. He was thirty years old.
In the fourth year of the Jianwu era, in the early summer, he began the lectures on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* at Miaoyin Temple.

Xu Xiaosi of Dongguan, whenever he encountered Master Yun’s brilliant exposition, felt his own deficiencies. While observing the mourning rites for his mother, he emaciated himself beyond the prescribed ritual bounds. Sengmin remarked:

"The sages established the rituals so that the worthy might conform to them from below, while those who are not yet worthy might strive to reach them. This is especially true given the Buddha’s teachings."
While they are alive, one repays the kindness of their life by attending to their countenance and demeanor; when they have passed away, one awakens them to Bodhicitta to guide their consciousness.
If one merely follows private affection, it instead burdens one's closest kin and causes them to fall into the evil realms; only the wise can employ the power of skillful means.

If one governs and restrains them, one will be born in the happy realms. Fayun thereupon suppressed his feelings of grief and partook of food and drink. At the beginning of the Yongyuan era, he accepted an invitation to Piling;

both monastics and laypeople turned toward him, and they gathered from the capital in full numbers. In the second year of Emperor Wu of Liang’s Tianjian era, an imperial edict was issued for various eminent virtuous monks to each compose commentaries on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
Fayun synthesized the sutras and treatises, composing forty sections, which became the [Forty-Section] Commentary.
In two fascicles. In the seventh year, he composed a commentary on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The court nobles requested that Huìyún deliver a lecture, which he granted.

He also served as the Abbot of Guǎngzhái Monastery and established monastic regulations that were followed by later generations. The Crown Prince invited ten monks to enter Xuānpǔ Garden to lecture on the Way and discuss literature;
this continued for two consecutive summers. Huìyún was the foremost among them. Zhōngshū Jìshùn, Yáng Fàn Zhěn, authored the *Shén*... [text ends]
The Emperor issued an edict titled "On the Refutation of Annihilationism," to which Yun replied; this was promulgated to his subordinates, though the full text is not recorded here.
At the end of the Tianjian era, he further established a temple in Moling County, on the same level as the lower village, to repay the kindness of his patron.
It truly possessed a serene and elevated setting, situated on the western slope of Chan Mountain. He also translated three sections of scriptures presented by the kingdom of Funan. Furthermore, he...
He donated his personal belongings from outside his quarters to the Huālín Garden and Guānghuá Hall, where he convened a great assembly for a thousand monks.
At that time, Huiyún also fell ill. In the sixth year of the Pǔtōng era, an imperial edict appointed him as the Great Sangha-rectifier (Dà Sēngzhèng).

When the Emperor visited Tóngtài Temple to expound the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, he established a thousand-monk assembly and extensively gathered the administrators of various monasteries, as well as renowned monks of learning and conduct, to perform the *karmavācanā* rites.
An imperial edict permitted him to ascend the hall in the imperial carriage and listen to the lectures while leaning upon a couch.

Consequently, his illness became critical, and he passed away on the twenty-seventh day of the third month in the third year of the Datong era at the age of sixty-three. By imperial decree, he was buried beside Dinglin Temple.

Sengmin of the Liang dynasty was of the Sun clan; his ancestors had lived for generations in Fuchun, Wu, since the fall of the state of Wu during the Three Kingdoms period. He lost his father when young.
At the age of seven, he left home to become a monk and resided at Xishan Temple on Mount Huqiu. He served Master Senghui as his teacher and received from him the exegesis of the Five Classics.
Once, Zhang Bian, the Minister of Personnel of the Song dynasty and a native of Wu Commandery, asked him, "What is the śrāmaṇera’s surname? Where is his family from? Daomin replied:

This poor monk’s surname is Shi, and my family has resided on this mountain for generations. When Zhang Xu, who held the rank of Tèjìn, saw me, he sighed in admiration, saying, "Though these pine and cypress trees are small, they already possess a spirit that soars above the clouds.
At the age of thirteen, I accompanied Huì to the capital, where we stayed at Baima Temple.

Faguan would fold his outer robe at night to sleep and borrow other garments during the day to travel.

Emperor Wenhui of the Qi dynasty and Prince Jingling held him in profound esteem and respect. Wang Jian, the Minister of the Secretariat, once...

When the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* was being lectured, Fayin sat at the end of the assembly. His discussions were characterized by fresh and elegant phrasing, as well as profound and far-reaching insights, such that the listeners were completely captivated.

Oh, how magnificent! Since the Jin and Song dynasties, scholars have been intent on engaging in lofty discourse and grand rhetoric to outshine one another;

He merely provided outward polish, unable to provide internal benefit. Consequently, his reputation spread far and wide.

Wang Zhongbao of Langye and Zhang Siguang of Wu Commandery—both of whom were preeminent in learning at the time—formed a close bond with him and entered into friendship, exchanging white and black silk as tokens of their alliance. When the Qi dynasty fell into chaos, he fled to the East.

In the fifth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, an imperial edict summoned the *Sengzheng* (Director of Monks) Huichao to his quarters to request [his presence], along with Fachong and [Fadao].

He invited the five great Dharma masters of the capital to lecture at five monasteries, placing Bao Min at the head of the assembly; Daosheng was so pleased and satisfied with this that he [endorsed it].
Furthermore, by imperial decree, he lectured on the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra* in Hui-lun Hall, where the Emperor personally attended to listen. The monks Zhi and Huang were also present.

Liu Xie of Dongguan, the Secretariat Director for King Chuan, and twenty-nine others jointly excerpted all the sutras and treatises from Dailing Monastery, arranging them by category into eighty fascicles.

on this day, even it could not accommodate everyone. By imperial decree, the lectures were suspended for fifty days, and additional windows and doors were opened and fifty more seats provided;

Jingsi Temple. Previously, a five-bay hall had been constructed to expand upon its existing structures. On the appointed day, the assembly was fully complete; [Huishan] was particularly indifferent toward those of high status and influence.

Huiyue of the Liang dynasty, courtesy name Desu, was surnamed Lou. He was a native of Wushang in Dongyang. His family had been a prominent clan in the southeastern region for generations.

When she gave birth, her body was fragrant and pure, and her complexion was as white as snow; therefore, she was named Lingcan. At the age of seven, she entered school and immediately recited the *Xiaojing*, the *Lunyu*, and the historical records.

As she read the texts, she grasped their underlying meaning. To the south of her residence was an orchard where neighboring children would gather in groups to pick fruit and compete; yet the Master alone—

He then fled to another place, where slaughter was even more prevalent than before. Suddenly, he dreamed of a deity in red robes holding a spear and halberd, pointing them at him and saying:
"You did not heed the Bodhisattva’s teachings, but instead made killing your daily business. You may now go to your death."
Startled awake, he broke into a sweat. He immediately destroyed his hunting gear and repented his transgression.
On the appointed day, he went to his usual hunting grounds and saw several dozen deer; they leaped, stood, and followed him as if in a gesture of shame and apology.

Though his dwelling was remote and secluded, and he had no teachers or scriptures from which to learn, through the latent influence of his past habits, he came to a clear and thorough understanding of the principles of the teachings. He then thought of renouncing the secular life, yet he did not know where to go.
He went there and suddenly encountered a monk who pointed eastward and said, "In Shan, Buddhist activities are very flourishing. Having said this, the monk vanished; he was likely a divine being.

At the age of twelve, he went to Shan to pay respects at the stupas and temples and to study the scriptures. Thus, a chant circulated in the eastern region: "The youth Lou Jushi has attained the subtle principle.
In the fourth year of the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, he took leave of his parents and shaved his head at Dongshan Temple in Shangyu. At that time—
At the age of seventeen, he became a disciple of the śramaṇa Huìjìng of Nánlín Monastery, who was a preeminent leader among the monks of his generation.

Shortly thereafter, he followed Huìjìng to Fànjū Monastery in Shàn, where he served him with diligence and attended to his needs. More than twelve years passed until Huìjìng passed away; he then observed the full rites of mourning for his master.

Upon completing the period of mourning, he abstained from grain, consuming only pine and artemisia roots, and withdrew into seclusion. This occurred during the final years of the Qi dynasty, under the reign of Prince Jìnglíng.

The assembly was all displeased. The King said, "This man shall one day lead the Buddhist community. Gentlemen, please do not be overly critical. Zhou Yong of Runan, a Secretariat Drafter, issued an edict: [Text follows]
Shan treated him with even greater courtesy. He built a hermitage atop Mount Cong (Cóngshān) and invited [Hui]yong to reside there; it is now known as Caotang Temple.

Yuan once requested that he lecture on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*; Wang Jian did so as well.

He requested that the *Dafahua* (Lotus Sūtra) and the *Dapin* (Large Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra) be recited. While Yuan was bedridden with illness, he dreamed of a foreign monk who told him, "A Bodhisattva is about to arrive.
When Huixiang arrived as scheduled, his ailment was immediately cured. Yuan then requested and received the five precepts. Lou Youyu, the Director of the Palace Secretariat, was his clan ancestor.

Every time he saw him, he would invariably rise. Some asked, "This gentleman is a descendant of your grandson; why do you act thus? Yu replied, "When a Bodhisattva appears in the world, he becomes the teacher of all under heaven.

At the time of his departure, [the Master’s] longing was so profound that he remained for many years, during which time he provided extensive instruction.

Upon returning to the capital, he continued to reside at Caotang Temple. During the Longchang era, the Grand Tutor Shen Yue escorted him to his provincial post. While there, he found delight in meditation and recitation;
extraordinary fragrances filled his chambers, and fierce beasts grew tame before his steps. Whenever he went to Mount Jinhu to gather tangerines, or traveled elsewhere...
He stayed at the Crimson Stream Gorge (*Chisong-jian*), where divine lights appeared in succession. At Crimson Stream there was a lodge, the residence of Daoist practitioners.

One such practitioner, Ding Dejing, was afflicted by [the spirit] Chong; although he was accompanied by those skilled in the arts of healing, Chong became increasingly pervasive and his illness grew more severe until he suddenly died.

The Master had been ill for less than ten days when his condition suddenly subsided and he recovered. Later, while lying in bed, he saw two women dressed in green emerge from a mountain stream;

they prostrated themselves before him and repented, saying, "Our past karmic obstructions were deep and heavy, resulting in this retribution as water-crystal spirits. We pray that you will accept our refuge and precepts.

At the beginning of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, Shen Wei, who served as the Vice President of the Secretariat, submitted a memorial requesting that they accompany the Master [to the capital], which was granted. Previously, the Master had already predicted that this would happen.
It had been eleven years since the time of Shen Yin Danyang. At the moment of their parting, his words were sorrowful and plaintive. Shortly thereafter, Shen passed away.

It was not until eleven years later that an imperial decree summoned him for an audience. On the eighth day of the fourth month of the sixteenth year, the Jihai year, the Emperor received the Bodhisattva precepts from him at the Dengjue Hall.

From this experience, he attained the Way, and those disciples who were enrolled in the registers numbered forty-eight thousand. At that time, a female magpie ascended the steps, appearing as if it were listening to the teachings. When [the dream] ended—

he did not look at what kind of books they were from the very beginning. Yet the tree’s leaves remained green and its flowers red, spreading luxuriantly to this day.
Furthermore, birds resembling kingfishers—red in body with long tails—flock to the trees and woods. In the fourth year of the Datong era, he dreamed of his former residence.
With its white walls and vermilion gates, it was magnificent and imposing. He then made a vow to construct a temple, which by imperial decree was named Bensheng Temple.

On the sixth day of the ninth month of the first year of the Datong era, he manifested illness and lay down facing north on his right side; his spirit remained serene and joyful, entirely free from pain or distress.
He said to his disciples, "Last night in a dream, it was as if a great assembly with banners and flowers came to welcome me away."
"I am departing. On the sixteenth day, at the fifth watch of the night, an imperial attendant, Xu Yan, was dispatched by decree to inquire after him.

Diligently cultivate mindfulness and wisdom; be careful not to harbor delusive thoughts. Thereupon, he joined his palms as if entering meditative absorption. [His] lifespan was eight... [years].

Regarding the exposition of the Buddha-nature, I had long desired to provide a commentary on the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* because its words and meanings are so profound and subtle.

He recovered. Intending to pursue his former vocation, he reflected: "What is the span of a human life? The Dharma is inexhaustible.

They took pleasure together; yet, though she was in the prime of her years and possessed a radiant countenance, she longed to enter the Dharma-gate.

Fayuan then ascended the high seat and delivered a lecture on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. His discourse was profound and elegant, and his eloquence was unimpeded. He passed away in the second year of the Zhongding era of the Northern Zhou dynasty, at the age of seventy-seven. He was posthumously titled the Great Master Guangzhi. His remains were enshrined in the Xiangguo Monastery. His disciple Huixiu composed his biography. It is recorded that Fayuan was originally from the capital region. He also visited the eminent masters of the various schools, seeking out their teachings and refining his understanding. Upon returning north, he resided at the Xiangguo Monastery in the capital. He was renowned for his mastery of the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya*, the *Abhidharmakośa*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. His reputation for scholarship spread throughout the realm, and he was frequently summoned by the Emperor to participate in the Dharma assemblies. His lectures were always attended by several thousand people. He was particularly skilled at expounding the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*. Whenever he lectured, he would first provide a general overview, then analyze the text in detail, and finally summarize the essential points. His style was clear and concise, allowing listeners to grasp the meaning immediately. He also authored the *Vimalakīrti-śāstra*, the *Śrīmālā-śāstra*, and other works, totaling over ten volumes. He was also proficient in secular literature and could compose verses and prose with ease. His disciples numbered in the thousands, and he was widely revered by both the clergy and the laity. During the Sui dynasty, he was posthumously honored with the title of Great Master Guangzhi. The Emperor Taizong of Tang later bestowed upon him the posthumous title of Great Master Guangzhi, and the Emperor Xuanzong further conferred upon him the title of Great Master Guangzhi, the Venerable of the Dharma. His legacy remains celebrated to this day.

He lived in seclusion on Mount Taihang. Although the Emperor repeatedly summoned him to serve as a counselor, he did not go forth. During the Tianyuan era, when the Emperor fell ill, he issued a decree once again to erect a sacred image.

He ordained twenty bodhisattva-monks, among whom Yan was renowned for his fame. Nevertheless, [the Emperor] still did not permit it because he had not yet fully adopted the monastic appearance and robes.

His character was remarkably lofty and noble; as a successor to his master, he served as a standard for the Buddhist community.

In matters of food, drink, clothing, and carriage, he enjoyed a status second only to the imperial court—his wealth and honor were indeed supreme. Nevertheless, he remained humble in his conduct and compassionate in his guidance, benefiting both himself and others.

His magnanimity was so profound and harmonious that its limits could not be fathomed. In his daily life, he prayed for rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī), his contemplation unwavering until the end.
Prior to his passing, Sengren Jinbao and his son, who were neighbors of the monastery, still maintained their faith;

they saw banners and canopies in the air being led in two rows before the coffin from the south of the temple all the way to the Western Mountains. The Palace Secretary Xue Daoheng composed a text for the white mourning ritual, which is found in his separate collection.
Lingzang of the Sui dynasty was the son of the Wang family of Xinfeng in Yongzhou. In his youth, he took the Vinaya Master Ying as his preceptor and entered the monastic order.

He excelled in the profound and subtle, while simultaneously upholding the monastic regulations and administrative duties. He specialized in the *Prajñāpāramitā* (Zhidu) for his discourses and was proficient in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi).

Students bowed respectfully before him. At the beginning of the Zhou dynasty, the gates of the Dharma flourished greatly; the state annually ordained monks and nuns, specifically because Lingzang’s intellectual understanding was so brilliant.

Furthermore, he was permitted to select a site of natural beauty for himself to suit his own inclinations; this is the present-day Zunsanfang, or Daxingshan Temple.
From that time on, imperial envoys arrived in succession, treating him with abundant and elaborate courtesy, and he was frequently presented with gifts of rare delicacies and exotic dishes.
Furthermore, an imperial edict was issued for the Left and Right Vice Directors (Zuo-you Pu-xie) to enter the monastery twice a day to attend the assembly and provide stability.

An edict was also issued for the various gates of the palace to allow Hui-zang to pass through freely, without being required to follow the usual regulations of checking against official registers. In the fourth year of the Kaihuang era, the region of Guanzhong suffered from famine;
an edict was issued for the common people to go to Luoyang to seek food. Hui-zang consequently followed the imperial entourage to Luoyang, where men and women sought ordination.
Wherever he went, he gathered a following. The Emperor said, "My disciple is a layman, while the Vinaya Master is a man of the Way.

Over the course of time, the number of people ordained by them reached tens of thousands. When this news reached the Emperor, he was even more delighted and remarked, "The Vinaya Master’s ordaining of people is a virtuous deed."

He prohibited his disciples from committing evil. Although their specific duties differed, their underlying intent was no different. Regarding the translation of scriptures, he set a standard for all others by personal example.
Before he assumed the responsibilities of the monastery, his integrity and uprightness were already renowned. He passed away in the sixth year of the Kaihuang era at the age of sixty-eight.
He was buried at the Southern Suburb.
Sui Daozheng was a native of Bohai in Cangzhou. He had no fixed dwelling and no constant teacher;

he followed the *araṇya* (forest-dwelling) tradition, taking refuge in deep forests and seeking alms in villages. He sat and did not lie down. Whenever monastics or laypeople came to consult him, he would briefly [instruct them].

He merely demonstrated the fundamental principles thereof. Nevertheless, although he traveled extensively through the imperial lecture halls and debating assemblies, he was particularly renowned throughout Youzhou and Ji Province for his mastery of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
When Li Gongguan invited him to reside at a temple to rectify its affairs, Zheng ultimately showed no interest.

Consequently, he withdrew into the mountain valleys to compile and expound upon the canonical regulations, titling his work the "Six Practices" (*Liuxing*). This was essentially the method of cultivation for both ordinary beings and sages; it encompassed all [teachings].

One Transformation: It encompasses and integrates the myriad paths. The first is the course of action of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). The second is the course of meritorious action of ordinary beings.
The third is the course of action of those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). The fourth is the course of action of lesser bodhisattvas. The fifth is the course of action of great bodhisattvas.
The sixth is the course of action for realizing the fruit of Buddhahood. These comprise six sections; in brief, they constitute one fascicle, while in detail, they comprise twenty-one.
This scroll consists of two parts: the first half serves as the introductory section (*nidāna*), and the latter half constitutes the body of the practice.

The intention is that since those of the Śākya lineage in the Eastern Land (China) are often mired in names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) and rarely adhere to the true cause, he wished to cast aside the fishing net to examine the principle, establishing Chan meditation as the sole school to rescue the spirit and refresh the mind.
In the seventh year of the Kaihuang era, he submitted a formal petition; the Left Vice President of the Secretariat, Gao Ying, compiled the titles for him.
When Daozheng was debating at Chanlin Monastery, there was someone in the assembly who disparaged him, calling him a man from a remote corner of the sea who dared to surpass the imperial capital.
Upon hearing this, Daozheng sighed and said, "How could the Dharma be restricted by geographical location? It is simply used to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox;
whether a place is central or peripheral is not a matter of concern. Thereupon the assembly dispersed, and that [disparaging] discourse was ultimately suppressed. Daozheng.
Realizing that the decadence of the late age was inherently difficult to transform, he entrusted his writings to Master Fang and returned home;
the world knows nothing of his ultimate end.
Xinxing of the Sui dynasty was surnamed Wang and was a native of Wei Commandery. Originally, his mother had no children, so she prayed to the Buddha;

she then dreamed of a divine being bringing her a boy, and immediately became pregnant. When he was born, his appearance and character were exceptionally extraordinary. At the age of four, seeing an ox-cart stuck in the mud on the road, he exerted all his strength to pull it out;
his collar tore and blood flowed, yet the cart could not move forward. He then wept bitterly by its side, vowing to wait for it.
Once he was released, he departed. At the age of eight, he entered the school; his brilliant wisdom manifested uniquely.
A student asked him, "What is your family name? And what is your maternal family name? He replied, "My maternal family is surnamed Sun.

The student jokingly teased him, saying, "Your surname is not Fàn (飯), but Sūn (飱). Is there a reason for this? Xíng responded immediately: "Fàn removes hunger, but it does not remove thirst; Sūn [removes both]."
Thus, both hunger and thirst were simultaneously dispelled; for this reason, his surname was Sūn (Sun) rather than Fàn (Fàn). His various adroit and unconventional responses were all of this nature.

He always regarded reverence, diligence, and asceticism as the medicine for the diseases of arrogance, negligence, and indolence. Consequently, he would invariably circumambulate and prostrate before every stupa and image.
Furthermore, at Fazang Monastery in Xiangzhou, he renounced his precepts to take up manual labor and serve as a servant. This was his path...

When laypeople came to his door to question him, he would always respond directly according to the specific matter; there were none who did not completely abandon their former practices, receive his words upon their heads, and take him as their teacher.
At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, he was summoned by imperial decree to the capital. The Chancellor Gao Ying established a separate monastery at Zhenji Temple to provide him with lodging.
There he composed the *Dui-gen-qi-xing Sanjie Jilu* (Collected Records on the Three Stages Arising from the Roots of Response) and the *Dongshan*.

The various texts he composed total more than forty fascicles, which have been transmitted for eternity. He established five monasteries—Huadu, Guangming, Cimeng, Huiriji, and Hongshan—to support and promote the Great Teaching.
Not long after, his illness became critical; yet even then, he requested that a Buddhist image be brought into his room so that he might practice correct contemplation.
He passed away at Huadu Monastery on the fourth day of the first month of the fourteenth year. His age was...
At fifty-four years of age, seven days after his passing, he was cremated on Mount Zhongnan at Chiming Peak. When the ashes and bones were collected, a miraculous sign was found:
two ear canals were interconnected through a single opening. A stupa was erected at the foot of the mountain. The retired scholar Pei Xuanzheng of Hedong composed a text to inscribe upon its stele.
Xuanzheng had originally been a disciple of Master Xing, who had entered the monastic order at Huadu Monastery; at the time of Xuanzheng’s departure, the Master was in good health.

All that he wore at the time of his passing was evidence of his realization. While he was alive, he discarded his monastic robes and returned to lay dress; while alive, he himself composed the epitaph, and only after death was it carved and inscribed.
Today, three such steles still remain before the northern cliff of Zhixiang Temple.
Tanchong of the Sui dynasty was born into the Meng family in Xianyang. At the age of seven, he entered the religious life and followed various lecture halls for a long time.

Later, he relied upon Master Kai, a master of meditation (*dhyāna-ācārya*), and applied himself to the cultivation of mindfulness. By the time he received full ordination, his resolve had become even more pure and rigorous; he studied the *Saṃghāṭi-sūtra* (Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya).
He lectured and explained [the scriptures] more than ten times, attracting three hundred disciples who regarded him as their preeminent teacher in the capital and its surrounding regions.

Later, realizing that verbal exposition was of no benefit, he further cultivated his former practices; his body became like withered wood and his mind like extinguished ashes. Thereupon, the perception of form was eliminated.
Thereupon, radiance was emitted; his practice in the six modes of conduct became singularly refined, and he attained mastery through all five gates.

Master Kai praised him as the foremost leader, and his fellow students among the assembly turned to him with reverence. When Master Kai passed away, [Hui]zhao entrusted more than two hundred of his disciples to his instruction and guidance.

His reputation spread across the Long Mountains and the frontier passes; his transformation of others filled the passes and rivers. Those who sought to follow him in the lee of his influence were linked together for thousands of li.

Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou especially held him in high esteem and issued an edict stating: "Master Chong’s refined realization is peerless; the disciples he leads are virtuous in their conduct and righteousness."
It had never been heard that he had committed any transgression; he was fit to serve as a Tripitaka Master for the state and as the abbot of Zhuhusi.

Because his official duties were so burdensome and prolonged, he requested an exemption on the pretext of other circumstances, and the imperial decree granted his request. When the Buddhist teachings were suppressed, he conformed to secular customs rather than distinguishing himself from them.

By imperial decree, he was granted the rank of Jin-ziguanglu, yet he remained entirely unbending. At the beginning of the Daxiang era, Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty, recognizing that [Dao]chong had maintained his hidden virtue while governing the Zhou state and that the Great Dharma was about to be restored, issued an edict to ordain one hundred and twenty monks first; Daochong was included among their number.

He resided at Xingshan Monastery and was subsequently summoned by imperial decree to serve as its abbot, but he firmly declined. He then solicited donations to establish a monastery to fulfill his long-held vow. This was because of the Dharma...
Regarding its misfortune: formerly, [the Emperor] had granted permission, saying that once he ascended the throne, he would eventually establish nine temples to complete the number of ten.
At that time, our Tang Gaozu was serving as the Regional Inspector (Liushi) in Taiyuan; he also donated his residence to become Qingchan Temple in order to gather a community of monks.
When Emperor Yang resided at the Jin Prince’s residence, he granted seventy households of commoners, along with water-mills and grain-grinding stones, for the sake of the temple.

As for his foundation and legacy: at the beginning of the Kaihuang era, he was granted fourteen thousand bolts of silk, five thousand rolls of plain cloth, one thousand bales of cotton, two hundred pieces of brocade, twenty pieces of damask, one thousand *shí* of high-quality rice, five thousand strings of cash from the Empress, fifty rolls of felt, and fifty sets of razors.
Furthermore, when he constructed the stupa, he utilized the materials bestowed by the divine nun Zhixian.
Six grains of the Śarīra were used to assist in the propagation of the Buddha’s work. As the teachings were about to be fully inaugurated, this deeply accorded with the Emperor’s heart.

An edict was issued for the artisan Du Chong to construct the reliquary according to the Dharma, and more than three thousand strings of cash were granted for the cost of bricks and tiles; furthermore, all [precious materials] from the inner palace were collected.

The Prince of Jin resided in Yangyue; from his provincial seat, he constructed an eleven-tiered *lupan* (dew-dish) starting in the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era, which was completed and installed atop the pinnacle of the stupa by the fourteenth year. The Buddhist halls and monasteries were all established through the power of the King. By imperial decree, Master Chong was permitted to enter and exit the palace precincts without restriction, and it became the custom for him to have his name registered in the palace records.

Such was the weight of the honor and courtesy shown to him. On the thirtieth day of the tenth month in the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era, he passed away without illness.
He passed away in the room where he resided at the age of eighty. The Emperor was deeply grieved and issued an edict for the relevant authorities to provide for his funeral arrangements.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Mount Zhongnan.

Zhishun of the Sui dynasty was born into the Meng family of Dalu in Zhaozhou. In his youth, he served as a librarian; he was widely learned in the written word, skilled in calligraphy, and eloquent in exposition.
Those of scholarly character attached themselves to him. When he was over twenty years old, he grew weary of the world and left the household life to serve Yunmen Chou.
Master Gōng was by nature fond of secluded and obscure places; his will was fixed upon his vocation. He resided at Bailu for ten years, where he was constantly aided in secret by numinous deities.

Once, a pheasant, having been cornered by a hunter, flew into his hut and earnestly entreated him to release it; the hunter would not listen and departed with the bird in hand.
Shun immediately cut off his own ear and sent it after the hunter to move his heart, whereupon the hunter finally cast down his bow, released his hawk, and followed Shun to practice virtue.
He practiced [the Way], drawing near to what was proximate and yearning for what was remote. He utterly abolished the cruelty of killing living beings. His conduct was especially rigorous:

when in secluded places where no one was present, he would use fire to purify his hair; whenever his vigilance slightly slackened, he would draw a needle to prick his thigh. He ate coarse vegetables and plain grain, driving himself forward day and night with the whip.

He gathered in those who were cold and hungry, yet he himself remained constantly empty and destitute, remaining as composed as ever. Those close to him were transformed by him, relying upon him to refine themselves.

Master Xin was a man of ten *zhì*. On the twentieth day of the first month in the fourth year of the Renshou era, he passed away due to a respiratory ailment at the Chan Hall of Xuánqūlǐng in Yuánsì. He was seventy-two years old. He was buried beside the Chan Hall;
however, some later secretly moved his remains and interred them at Zhànghóngshān within the borders of Fángzǐ County. Three years later, they were exhumed and cremated. Thus it is said.
A white stupa was erected [in his honor], thereby establishing the fame of Mount Hong in the Fanzhi district of Zhaozhou; it is because of Shun that the mountain has become so renowned.

In the tenth year of the Kaihuang era, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "The Emperor respectfully inquires of Chan Master Zhishun of the Old Chanfang Temple in the Southern Valley of Mount Hong, within the Fanzhi district of Zhaozhou:
The winter is extremely cold; we hope the Master’s physical health remains clear and robust as he continues to instruct the common people. Early...
He has brought this to completion; we consider it most excellent. As I preside over the myriad people, I have extended my protection of the True Dharma, never flagging from morning until night.
I now dispatch Lu Yuanshou, a Grand Marshal of the Court, to proclaim my intent and deliver these offerings of incense, as detailed in the separate decree.

At that time, the Provincial Governor Yang Da, noting that Shun had no prior reputation and his whereabouts were uncertain, arbitrarily registered him at Guoyuan Temple to comply with the imperial decree.
Shun, however, declined and did not go. His disciple Zhizan was able to carry on his legacy.

Although he was repeatedly summoned and invited to serve, he ultimately retired to the forests and springs. In his leisure from quietude, he devoted himself particularly to the study of the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Fǎchún of the Sui dynasty was born into the Zhù clan; he was a native of Shǐpíng in Fúfēng.

Having entered the monastic path during the Zhou dynasty, he resided at the two temples of Zhǐhù and Tiāngōng in the capital, where he experienced the full severity of the suppression of the teachings. When the founder of the Sui dynasty was still in hiding, Fǎchún plotted to initiate the Dharma.
Yun was formerly a member of a community of one hundred and twenty bodhisattva-monks; Chun was one among them. Residing at Daxingshan Temple, he vigorously disciplined his three karmas.
When the Emperor heard of this, he invited him to serve as a preceptor for the precepts. However, Chun firmly declined on the grounds that his virtue was too meager.

Consequently, the Emperor visited the place where he resided to pay his respects and bestowed upon him generous gifts. Chun sighed and said, "Life and the body are impermanent; how can they be cherished or preserved?"

"The offerings of almsgiving are difficult to digest; I shall now practice the Fangdeng (Vaipulya) Repentance Method. For another forty-five years, with the exception of eating and relieving himself, he did not leave the pure precinct.
Consequently, he was moved by a spiritual response such that the lamps, though lacking oil, maintained a continuous flame for seven days and nights.
Sometimes he heard the sound of someone preaching or giving instruction within the marketplace; yet when he went to look, it was silent.
A moment later, he would change into monastic robes and walk through the streets and markets, performing manual labor as a hired servant. He did not shrink from even the most trivial or menial tasks.

When he received alms, he would say with a sorrowful expression, "The thief of craving has arrived; the King of Hell is approaching in secret. Before long, I shall be beaten and bound. Furthermore, by means of the sutras...

He requested images from people; his robes were merely those made of discarded rags (*pāṃśukūla*). He propagated the teachings using the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the *Sarvadharma-apravṛtti-nirdeśa*, and other works totaling twenty-five fascicles.

In the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era, he entered the inner palace and conferred the precepts upon the Empress. Whatever offerings and benefits he received were exhausted as soon as they were acquired. In the fifth month of the third year of the Renshou era...
On the twelfth day, he passed away peacefully at Jingzhu Temple at the age of eighty-five.

Prior to this, while he was sitting in meditation in a closed room, his disciple Huijin saw a youth in white robes holding a radiant light in his hands, standing respectfully to the master’s right. Huijin asked him:
"Who is this? He replied, "He is a deity from the sixth desire heaven who has repeatedly summoned me.

However, because I am hindered by attachment to pleasure, I have never granted him permission. "If there is no place for the Buddha’s Dharma, I vow to be born there to transform those who are deluded.
After a long time, a pair of pigeons gathered on the clothesline; they gazed intently at Sengchun without showing any sign of fear. Sengchun slowly said to his disciples:
He said: "Do not give yourself over to license; do not deceive yourself. He further asked: "Why is it that I now suddenly perceive my body mounted upon its own elephant?
Is this the result of deluded karma? He left instructions that his body be given as alms to birds and beasts. His disciple Hui’ang and others led various donors [to fulfill this wish].
A niche was excavated on the plains of Bailu (White Deer), with an entrance tunnel carved outside to house it.

Subsequently, when the flesh and sinews had completely vanished, the skeletal remains stood upright as if by themselves. Thereupon, the body was further adorned with clay sculptures to ensure its preservation for eternity.
The Śramaṇa Yanzong composed a preface and verses of praise to extol his virtue; the inscription on the stele, however, is the work of Fang. Fang was nurtured in purity from childhood.
His demeanor was leisurely, elegant, and refined. He had a collection of ten scrolls that circulated in the world.
Zhen Guan of the Sui dynasty, whose courtesy name was Shengda, was a native of Qiantang in Wu Commandery. His surname was Fan;

his grandfather was Yanzheng, a Grand Secretary of the Yellow Gate (Huangmen Silang), and his father was Dui, a Tongzhi Sanqi Changshi. His mother was of the Huan clan. Lamenting their lack of offspring, she made a vow.
She recited the *Bhaiṣajyaguru*, *Avalokiteśvara*, and *Vajracchedikā* Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras to seek a wise son.

Furthermore, she carved and wrote out an image of King Kapilavastu from Dinglin Shangsi Temple and served it with devotion, personally offering prayers. Following the ritual procedures of the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra*, she performed the seven-day practice;
on the third evening, a radiant light shone upon her body. From that time on, she became pregnant. When the child was born, there were patterns on the palms of his hands.
He attained the status of an immortal; his mouth flowed with vital essence, and his skin and body were moist and lustrous. Though aged, he never suffered from thirst.

His tongue was marked with patterns like fine silk, and his voice resonated like a bell. He was quick-witted and eloquent in discourse. At the age of five, he immediately adopted a vegetarian diet and sat upon a chest containing his robes.

He played with a fan and a broom, imitating the virtuous monks as they delivered lectures. At the age of eight, he was able to harmonize the verses of the *Elaeocarpus* (Lingqin) written by the Minister Yu.

By sixteen, he had thoroughly mastered the canonical texts of both Confucius and Laozi, while also engaging peripherally in the arts of the lute and chess. Once, he encountered a man of refined discernment who greeted him with a bow and said, "Young man, you shall one day become a teacher of devas and humans;
you should cherish yourself. Thereafter, he devoted himself exclusively to reciting the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and the *Prajñāpāramitā*. He lived on alms...
His parents wished for him to leave the secular world, yet they found it difficult to permit. Kāpilavastu sent a dream as an omen, whereupon they granted their consent.

Having received the imperial decree and been bestowed with robes and an alms bowl, he had the Dharma Master Sheng of Xiangyang shave his head, and the Vinaya Master Zhen of Yunyang served as his preceptor to confer the precepts.
Shortly thereafter, he studied the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* under the Dharma Master Guo of Hualin, and wishing to memorize the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he recited one fascicle daily.
He was moved by a dream which said: "You possess the faculties of the Mahāyāna; do not let yourself stagnate. Immediately seek instruction in the Mahāyāna at the feet of Master Lang of Xinghuang.
The Dharma Master Daren of Kaishan casts his shadow upon Mount Zhong; go there often to challenge and stimulate him. Upon hearing this, Daren sighed and remarked: [The rest of the passage follows].
The Way of Nāgārjuna spread to the East. The two masters Bian and Yong repeatedly received him as their honored guest upon the high seat.

The monastic community spoke of it, saying: "From Qiantang comes Zhen Guan; he shall occupy half the world. Hong Yan, a paragon of Confucianism and a hero among Buddhists, praised him to his face, saying:
"High cheekbones indicate great wisdom; white ears signify renown. I possess four excellences; you are endowed with eight abilities. From this point on—
Princes, dukes, and the nobility all desired to form alliances with him. When the Prince of Shixing was about to depart for his fief, he invited him to accompany him.

At that time, the assembly at Xinghuang Monastery had been deliberating on the teachings; the multitude recognized him as their leader. As soon as he ascended the seat, he expounded the doctrine of the Two Truths.

Amidst a hundred difficult challenges posed from every direction, a single word from him resolved them all like water melting away. The scholar Fu Zai sighed and said: "He is the foremost among the three thousand, the very beginning of the seventy disciples—that Superior Man!"
He was difficult to respond to in debate. Having arrived at Kuaiji, he resided at Xiangyan Temple and expounded the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Xinghuang sent letters three times summoning him, saying: "The regions of Yan, Zhao, Qi, and Qin are all looking up toward you with bated breath; the very hope of the Dharma-gate rests solely upon you. You ought to return quickly.
At that time, due to the failure of the campaign against Zhou, there were discussions regarding the conscription of all śramaṇas who did not possess official names.

He abandoned the monastic life. Daoguan Fen sent a letter to Xu Ling, the Palace Secretary, and the imperial decree was consequently revoked. When the Prince of Jiangxia went to govern Yue, he again earnestly invited him.
Master Lang choked with emotion and said, "If you can allow me to remain for three years, I shall entrust the lecture hall to you."
Nevertheless, in the end, he could not remain there. As for the Dukes of Yongyang and Poyang, who had attained the rank of Teci (Tèjìn), they all held him in the highest esteem.

The Wheel of the Dharma frequently turned in the eastern circuit; the Venerable Zhizhe of Tiantai was peerless in both reputation and conduct. Their years of ordination were equal, and in spirit they were like brothers.
Together they returned to the old chamber atop Qinling Mountain that reaches the clouds, where they discussed wisdom and illumination in the morning and settled into dhyāna in the evening.
Ji and Zhi both approached him with subtle inquiry, to which he responded by further expounding upon the teachings. When Yongyang returned to the capital, he frequently praised his virtue;

shortly thereafter, a special imperial edict was issued. However, as the mandate of the Chen dynasty came to an end, Emperor Wen of Sui sent imperial envoys three times, and Prince Qin twice invited him to his headquarters, yet he declined them all on the grounds of illness.
Prince Qi personally prostrated himself in worship at Jiangpu, transmitting the lineage of the incense and flame, and escorted him back to reside in his former village.
This was Zhongshan Monastery. In the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era, during a drought, the Prefect Liu Jing’an visited the monastery to pray for rain.

He requested that [Master] Guan preach the *Sāgara-nāgarāja-sūtra*; when he finished the introduction to the scripture, a torrential downpour ensued. Thus, the people of the southeast revered him as if he were a deity.
To the south of the county is Mount Lingyin, where in the past the Chan Master Dao’an practiced *dhūta* austerities in a stone chamber. His patron was Chen Zhongbao.
Leading his followers, he cleared the site and constructed a vihāra, naming it Nantianzhu (Southern India). Later, when Emperor Wenxuan built a stūpa, he also located it here;

thus, its secluded excellence may be known. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the seventh year of the Daye era, Sima Li Zishen was lecturing on the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra when he reached the "Chapter on Manifesting Illness.
He dreamed of three men whose appearance and attire were most magnificent, who held banners and paid homage.

It is said that the Śuddhāvāsa deities sent messengers to welcome him. On the sixth day of the sixth month, he lay ill. In a dream, he was in the same carriage as Zhezhì, escorting the Buddha back to the mountain.
Upon waking, he sighed and said: "I was destined to end my life at sixty-two; by lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra*, I have gained an extension of ten years."

Now at seventy-four, what more could he possibly seek? He immediately gathered his disciples to bestow his final instructions. That month, he traveled to Mount Tiantai, where he sent a letter accompanied by incense, ginger, and rock honey.
Upon reading the letter, [the recipient] remarked: "This is the very last message; is this not surely the result of karmic conditions from past lives?

He then sent back a single *ruyi* (wish-fulfilling) staff as a reply. On the first day of the seventh month, at midnight, he washed and rinsed his mouth, adjusted his robes, and sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
He sat down and suddenly spoke to himself, saying, "Someone has invited me to lecture on the Bodhisattva Precepts. Thereupon, he passed away with a serene expression.
At noon the following day, his chest and crown remained warm; three fingers of his right hand were bent inward, and sweat flowed from his entire body. This ceased after two nights.

On the fourth day, he was placed in the shrine. It was the time when the fire flows southward, yet the scorching heat remained intense; nevertheless, his limbs and body were supple and his countenance showed no change.
On the twenty-fifth day, monastics and laypeople from all quarters gathered in full splendor, all approaching the sacred hands to offer incense as a token of their parting.

Incense and flowers were offered in groups of thousands every day. On the appointed day, the shrine was opened; his physical features remained radiant and pure, and his eyebrows had grown even longer.
On the twenty-sixth day, the shrine was moved and interred at Lingyin Mountain. Observing the traces left by his opening [the shrine], he followed in the footsteps of the sages of old.

His merit in providing protection and rectification was equal to that of the sages of antiquity. In the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era, when the Imperial Army pacified Jiangnan, there were those who remained rebellious, which ultimately became a source of calamity.
When General Yuan Fuyou, also known as Yang Su, turned his banners back to drive them away, they were consequently completely shattered.
More than three hundred thousand were captured, enslaved, or executed. Because Guan’s reputation was flourishing, some prisoners falsely accused him of having authored the proclamations.
At that time, he was arrested together with the talented scholars of Jinling, Bao Heng and Xie Yu. Without waiting for interrogation or investigation, they were immediately brought to execution.
The magistrate approached him and rebuked him, saying, "A practitioner of the Way ought to practice meditation and recite the sutras;

why have you instead composed a manifesto to incite rebellion and bring upon yourself the penalty of the law? How can you deny your death? Sengguan replied, "What the Master of the Way studies is indeed as you say, sir. However—"

No proclamation had been issued, yet the innocent were being led to their deaths. Only Gong Mingjian remained unperturbed; he showed them the proclamation with an air of feigned anger and asked, "Who wrote this?
Having read it through, he said slowly, "If it were truly like this, how could it move people? I certainly did not write it. Had I actually written it, it would surely have surpassed this.
He then pointed out three or five specific phrases and asked, "Can these be put back onto the paper? They all looked on [in astonishment].
"What they do is merely the act of the ignorant and reckless; you must not believe them hastily. Sū (Sō) largely agreed with this.
He observed more than thirty people, including Bǎo (Bāo) and Xiè (Xiè), before him and said to him, "These are all of the same class as Guó (Guó), Bīn (Bīn), and Wáng (Wáng).
I hope you will give them careful consideration so that none suffer unjust grievance. Sū laughed and said, "The practitioner does not worry about himself, yet he worries further for others."
Huo Guan said, "Life and death are constants; why should they be a cause for grief? It is only when one is unjustly cast into calamity that one may rightly grieve.
Lu Su said, "Having been imprisoned for so long, I must surely grieve. You should compose a 'Rhapsody on Grief' (Chou fu). He looked to his attendants for paper and brush.

Guan took up the brush and wrote rapidly, as if in a flowing stream. Before long, the paper was exhausted. Su ordered more to be brought forward; as he read it aloud, he was struck with wonder and rose abruptly to his feet.
He summoned him to sit opposite him so that he might exhaust his arguments; as the text is voluminous, it is not recorded here in full.

Observing his lifelong carefulness in conduct, whenever he washed his hands, water would fall upon the ground without wetting it. While residing at Zhonsan Temple, the deity of Gaoting—whose surname was Chen and given name was Chong—communicated through a medium, requesting that he lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The deity provided him with money and goods, and further donated five bays of the temple hall to establish a new lecture hall. His disciple was Xuanjing.
He was indeed able to bear this burden.
Sui Lingyuan was a native of Hengzhou; his family name and given name are lost to history. His ancestors were scholars of the Confucian tradition.

Whenever he took up the classics and histories and encountered accounts of usurpation, pretension, warfare, or murder, he would close the volume and sigh, saying: "Alas, how men allow their hearts to be muddied by profit and desire!"
He was destined to receive the bodies of hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-dwellers among the various realms of suffering.
Yet, because his roots of goodness were not yet exhausted and his accumulation of evil had not yet reached its full measure, he was merely delayed for a brief moment.

How truly frantic, hasty, and forced was his pursuit [of worldly life]! Thereupon, he tore apart his scholar’s robes, donned the *kāṣāya*, and threw himself upon the community at Yanxing Temple to follow Master Huiyuan.

Yet he never once examined the essential meanings of the sūtras and śāstras. During the Renshou era, an imperial edict was issued to establish a stūpa at Longzang Temple in the prefecture to enshrine the śarīra;
once it was completed, he suddenly abandoned it and departed. He practiced dhyāna wherever he stayed.
Later, amidst a cluster of graves, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. It was only after a long time that people realized this. Alas! Truly a man of integrity.

Xuánjìng of the Sui dynasty was a native of Zhòuzhōu. He had long practiced the Vinaya, and his mastery of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* was so profound that it was as if he had heard the Buddha’s teachings directly from him.
Being able to maintain the precepts for his own benefit and likewise instructing others for their benefit, he was truly an *upādhyāya* of the degenerate age.
By imperial decree, a śarīra stūpa was established at Wújiè Temple in the prefecture; this was in the second year of the Rénshǒu era. Such were his Buddhist activities.
The power of mirrors is particularly great in this regard.

Jue Lang of the Sui dynasty was a native of Hedong. His physical appearance was magnificent and extraordinary, drawing the gaze of all who saw him. He had originally been affiliated with Xingshan Temple, where he studied the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya) and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
In the fourth year of the Renshou era, an imperial edict ordered the dispatch of śarīra relics to Chengzhou in Jizhou.

The auspicious signs manifested at Jue Temple are recorded in detail in a separate register. At the end of the Daye era, an imperial edict appointed him as the presiding master of the Great Chan-ding Monastery.

[His influence was such that] the arrogant and overbearing were brought to submission. At that time, there was the śramaṇa Haizang, who extensively expounded the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and was a preeminent leader of the Vinaya school.
At the beginning of the Tang dynasty, ten "Great Virtues" (*dashide*) were established, and Haizang was one of them. Furthermore, there was Faqiang, who [practiced] from seclusion...

Faxi retired to Dahu, where he lived secluded among crags and gullies, nurturing his aspirations and finding self-contentment. After his death, his remains were left exposed by the side of a mountain.
At night, a brilliant torchlight could be seen from afar; yet when one approached it, it vanished. This continued for two months before finally ceasing.

Fuliangyu (Sui Lingyu) was surnamed Zhao; he was a native of Quyang in Julu, Dingzhou. From childhood, he knew how to revere monks and prostrate before images, and he felt dread at the sound of slaughter.

At the age of six, he began to consume only vegetarian food, though his parents forcibly tried to break him of this practice, which he would not allow. At seven, he sought to leave the household life.

His two parents, considering his refined natural endowments, felt he ought to inherit their family profession; however, they firmly refused to grant him permission. Fayu sighed, saying, "My life’s purpose is ruined.

Thereupon, he redoubled his studies to further master his family's learning. At the age of fifteen, he intended to flee into seclusion, but it coincided with the mourning period for his father's death.
He observed the rites of wailing and living in a corner with the utmost devotion, never failing in his duty. Once the mourning garments were discarded, he traveled to Yingjue in Zhaojun.
At the temple, he received the tonsure from the two Zen masters Ming and Bao; his mother had never heard of this before.

At the age of twenty-two, he received full ordination and immediately began reciting the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. In eight days, he had both written out and mastered them. The Regional Inspector, Hou Jing, held him in especially high esteem.
Later, he traveled south to Zhanggan, where he specialized in the study of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* under Master Yin for five summer retreats, reaching a state of profound mastery.

In its innermost depths: Initially, Daoping had been instructed in the principles of the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) by Huiguang. Since Sengyu had long relied upon this Dharma seat, his analytical insights were extraordinary and his innovations were novel;

there was no one who did not defer to him. At that time, Emperor Xuan of the Qi dynasty was favorably promoting Fashang, issuing an edict appointing him as Grand Coordinator (*Datong*) to lead the eminent scholars.
Those who sought to curry favor with the prevailing trend stood shoulder to shoulder, yet only Sengyu maintained his integrity and steadfastness.

There was nothing he did not transform. His superiors consequently increased their respect for him. Regarding the *Avataṃsaka*, *Nirvāṇa*, *Daśabhūmika*, and Vinaya sections, he followed the traditional interpretations;

however, concerning the commentaries on the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Bhadrakalpika*, and *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā* (Yìjiào jīng), he alone produced profound insights, sweeping away all previous doctrines.

As for the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*, the three masters An, You, and Rong transmitted it orally and through the mind; as for the *Tattvasiddhi*, the two masters Song and Lin likewise transmitted it orally and through the mind.

In his reception [of teachings], he was never once mistaken; his vast and comprehensive erudition can thus be known. Those residing in the capital of Ye numbered twelve, and both inside and outside they were known as "Bodhisattva Yu.

During the illness of Emperor Xuan, an imperial decree was issued to expound the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. The various administrators of the Zhaoxuan Office recommended Yu as the presiding master of the Dharma (*dharmasvāmin*).
There was a rooster that would always follow the assembly; when the session concluded, it flew off toward the southwest, crowing loudly.

On the tree, he was struck down one night. The Emperor subsequently recovered from his illness. Three hundred monastic robes were issued from the palace to be bestowed upon Huìyù, who was then ordered to distribute them.
An imperial decree further commanded him to reside at an official monastery, but he firmly declined. At the time of his realization of destiny, he devoted himself to meditative stillness (*dhyāna*).

Before the summer heat had even reached its peak, he set out to respond to the invitation of the patron Lu of Fanyang. Those carrying their book-cases numbered in the tens of thousands. Not long after, he returned.
In Ye, his affairs were conducted as before. One day, Lou Rui, the Prince of Andong, performed prostrations before the assembly of monks;

when it was Huayu’s turn, he perceived something extraordinary about him and suddenly trembled with fear, breaking into a sweat. He immediately received ordination from him and further assisted in the restoration of Baoshan Temple.

When the Qi dynasty fell and the Northern Zhou abolished the two teachings (Buddhism and Daoism), Huayu donned the mourning garments of a son for his father and led twenty of his disciples [into exile].
He fled into the mountain valleys. By night he would expound the *Zhuzi Yanshi* (The Sayings of Master Zhu), and by day he would study the *Lunyu* (Analects).

He redoubled his efforts in his compositions, organizing them into categories and clusters with the hope of transmitting them to future generations. During a period of successive years of famine, he produced a volume of divination texts and sent someone to the marketplace to purchase rice;
as people crowded around to consult them, he obtained a considerable amount of grain. Daoyu then promptly burned the book. When the Sui dynasty arose, Daoyu’s teachings likewise...

During the Changsheng era, Fayu was first summoned by imperial decree. In the third year of the Kaihuang period, Fan Shulüe, the Regional Inspector of Xiangzhou, established the Assembly for the Dharma Master Qian, and Fayu presided over the primary seat.
By imperial edict, he was restored to his monastic office, and Shulüe subsequently recommended him as the General Overseer (Dutong).
Yùgù led the way and departed, traveling through Yān and Zhào. For ten years, the two river regions were thoroughly transformed by his influence.
He stayed at Língtōng Sī in Luò, where he obtained a document in the courtyard at night that spoke of the end of his karmic connection being in Xiányáng.

The following year, an imperial edict was issued from the capital to Dàcí Sī in Xiányáng to summon Yù to the capital. Yù remarked, "The calamity in Xiányáng has been verified," and he ultimately traveled there on foot.

Upon arriving at the capital, an imperial edict was issued for him to reside at Daxingshan Temple. Furthermore, the Emperor commanded the relevant authorities to deliberate on the establishment of a National Preceptor (Guotong).

Although Fayu declined the honor three times in his memorials, the Emperor then issued an edict for the Left Vice President Gao Ying, the Right Vice President Su Wei, the Palace Attendant Yu Qingze, the Regional Commander He Ruo Bi, and others to visit the temple to proclaim the imperial decree.
They were to receive the precepts on his behalf and perform repentance rituals for the Emperor, while he bestowed upon them three hundred rolls of silk, brocade, and fine cloth.

He assisted in the construction of Baoshan Temple. The Emperor personally inscribed the temple plaque with the characters "Lingquan" (Numinous Spring) and returned on foot, remarking to his attendants, "Is the toil of coming and going not a hardship?
Shortly thereafter, he moved to Yannong Temple, where the Emperor sent an imperial decree inquiring after his well-being.

During the Renshou era, the Emperor distributed the sacred *śarīra* of the Divine Nun that he had collected to various prefectures to erect stupas; wherever they were located, miraculous responses occurred.

They were exceedingly numerous, and everyone considered them auspicious omens. Yet Sengyu alone remarked that since everything he saw consisted of white flowers, white trees, and white clouds, how could these possibly be signs of good fortune?
"I merely fear," he said, "that there will be calamity and loss for the state. At first, people did not believe him.
Shortly thereafter, Empress Wen died and Emperor Wen passed away. Xue Zhou, the Duke of Yang and Governor of Xiangzhou, saw the foundation stones of his hall transform into jade;
he prepared a vegetarian feast to celebrate this auspicious sign. Sengyu said, "This is a 'flowing and scattering' omen; you should be cautious.

Zhou did not believe him, but later he was indeed exiled to the frontier on charges of involvement in Yang Liang’s rebellion. Toward the end of the Renshou era, nine-tiered pagodas were constructed at Hanzhuang Mountain.
When the construction had reached the fourth tier, the supervisor pressed him urgently, saying, "There may be some obstacle to this undertaking.
Day and night they exerted their full strength, and as they were about to reach the eighth tier, the rebellion at Jinyang broke out. His foresight was thus remarkable.

At that time, false rumors suddenly arose that Sengyu had passed away, yet the source from which they originated could not be found. Sengyu said, "I am about to die," and immediately he exhorted and urged his disciples until the seventh day.

Early in the morning, he composed two poems titled "Lamenting a Premature End" and "Sorrowing over a Long Enshrinement. That night, he spoke to his attendant, saying, "I am currently suffering from a severe backache.
At the third watch, he perceived a fragrance filling the room, and even as he lay there, his lips continued to recite the names of the Buddhas.
When the light of dawn appeared, he suddenly manifested parinirvāṇa at Yankong Temple on the twenty-second day of the first month of the first year of the Daye era. He was eighty years of age.
8. He erected a stupa for [his father] and buried him at the side of Lingquan Temple on Baoshan. Sengyu was upright by nature, dignified and imposing, and possessed a clear, refined presence.

Although his clothing and insignia were coarse and worn, he maintained no distinction in his etiquette whether toward the high and noble or the lowly and common. When people came and went, they never expected him to offer formal greetings or reception.
His body was adorned with a radiant white light that illuminated the gloom and darkness. By nature, he was endowed with filial piety and love;

when his mother fell ill and he was about to return home to care for her, he heard of her passing on the way back and turned around, saying, "I can now ensure the posthumous merit of my venerable mother. His aspirations were vast and great, and he did not confine himself to partial teachings;

thus, he exclusively lectured on both [the *Vimalakīrti* and *Śūraṅgama*] sutras, which became his constant practice. When he accepted invitations elsewhere, it was not out of mere deference or expectation.
He arrived, yet he would not deign to accept [the invitation]. Nevertheless, he never acted with negligence or simplification to solicit alms.

Once, when invited to lecture at a temple, he saw a garlic patch during a break that was situated close to his seat; upon inquiry, he learned the reason for it. Sengyu loathed this and immediately took his leave. The abbot apologized for the oversight.
He vowed to cultivate forty mu of garlic until he had planted grain instead. Having no prior savings, he was fond of giving.
At Baoshan, he constructed stone grottoes named the Vajravīrya-dhṛt-nārāyaṇa Cave. He carved the signs of the extinction of the Dharma upon the rock face.
Whenever he sat, he invariably faced west. His clothing and conduct were strictly in accordance with the Vinaya, serving as a model for those who came after.

Huiyu studied [the scriptures]. Some criticized him for seeking fame, to which Huiyu laughed and said, "If one truly seeks fame to perform good deeds, is that not still better than seeking profit to perform evil deeds?
There was a śramaṇa of unknown name from Yan who sought the benefit of a single word from him to distinguish himself.
Huiyu gave him the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks), saying, "Regarding the scriptures, proclamations, dhyāna, and vinaya, I fear they might confuse the sacred mind; I have not yet..."

If one practices in this manner, it constitutes attainment; such a person will depart with joy and reverence. Huìyù performed the *śīla-uddeśa* and the *karmavācanā*, but he did not transmit the practice of conveying one's consent (*chányù*).
Once, he entered Jingying Monastery just as the *poṣadha* ceremony was being held. Sitting in the hall, Huìyù saw Master Huiyuán transmitting his consent and raised his voice, saying:
"Huiyuán believes that because there are causes and conditions for dharma-affairs, one may thus convey consent. However—"
