"The assembly of monks is listening to the precepts; could this possibly be the work of Māra? He informed Huiyuan about this, and Huiyuan went to the hall. Huiguo said, "A virtuous person should lead others by example.
To preach the regulations regarding desire—who could be more suited for this than a Master of the Dharma? Huiyuan prostrated himself and accepted his words.

Among his writings were the *Commentary on the Ten Stages* in four volumes, and two volumes each of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā*. [The text continues with] the *Avataṃsaka*...

He composed the *Yan shu* (Commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*) and the *Zhigui* (Pointing to the Goal) in nine volumes combined; the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* commentary in six volumes; the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* commentary in eight volumes;
the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* commentary in five volumes; and the *Mahāyāna-yijiang* (Treatise on the Meaning of Mahāyāna) in four volumes.

Furthermore, he produced commentaries and records for various sutras, including the *Śrīmālā*, *Aṅgulimālya*, *Āyuṣmat*, *Avalokiteśvara*, *Ratnarāja*, *Vinayamātṛkā*, *Sukhāvatīvyūha*, the two *Maitreya* birth stories (*Upapatti*), and the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā*. He also wrote a commentary on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.

He compiled the *Abhidharma-jñāna-śāstra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Wisdom of Abhidharma) in five fascicles; the *Record of Sacred Sites* in two fascicles; the *Record of the Dharma’s Journey East*; the *Essentials of the Various Scriptures*; the *Model for Translating Scriptures*;

the *Method for Receiving the Bodhisattva Precepts*, including the beginning and end of the precept text (*śīla-sūtra*); commentaries on the introductory prefaces of the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras and śāstras;

and the *Treatise on the Similarities and Differences between Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna*. In addition to these, he composed the *Biographies of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana* and various rules for governing the monastic community.

*Anmin lun* (Treatise on Pacifying the People), ten fascicles; *Taoshen lun* (Treatise on Nurturing the Spirit), ten fascicles; *Luancheng sha lun* (Treatise on the Killing of Eggs), seven fascicles; *Ziben* (The Root of Characters), seven fascicles; *Zhuangji laogang shijing* (The Classic of the Master’s Framework for the Records of Zhuangzi);

*Zhaowei xianglu* (The Record of Portents and Patterns); *Yijue fujin fawen* (Texts on Medical Decisions, Talismans, and Prohibitions); *Duanshuichong xu* (Preface to the Extermination of Aquatic Insects); *Qishi sanbao ji* (Record of the Three Jewels in the Qi Dynasty); *Miefa ji* (Record of the Extinction of the Dharma);
*Guangshi dizu shide ji* (Record of the Ten Virtues of Master Guang’s Disciples); *Sengzhi sige* (Monastic Regulations and Temple Edicts); *Shiyuan shi* (Ten Grievances, Ten [Virtues]).

His works include the *Zhisong* (Verses on Aspiration), the *Qiwangxiaorizhong song* (Verses on the Decline of the Qi Dynasty and the Passing of Days), the *Chushi shenqing song* (Verses Extending Feelings upon Encountering Affairs), the *Sipo baoying ji* (Record of Retribution for the Destruction of the Temple),

the *Xiaojing yiji* (Record of the Meaning of the Classic of Filial Piety), the *Sanxing siqu song* (Verses on the Three Practices and Four Departures), and the *Shiping zají* (Collected Essays on Poetry Criticism), totaling fifty fascicles that circulated in the world.
Zhi Tuo of the Sui dynasty was originally of the Cai clan from Kaicheng in Jiyang. Later, due to his father’s official travels, he became a resident of Jiangdu.
His grandfather was Ping Qi, the Grand Governor of Xinchang; his father was Yuanzhen, the Assistant Director of the Northern Yanzhou Commandery of the Liang dynasty. When Tuo was first born...
Light arose in a dark chamber; a spring gushed forth from a dry well. Those who understood the signs regarded these as auspicious omens of his renunciation.

At the age of seven, he served Master Ying of Ye as his teacher and received the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Daśabhūmika*. After some time, he relied upon Master Qiang of Jiangdu to exhaustively study the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma*.

When he subsequently recited them, it was like pouring from one vessel into another or threading pearls together; the assembly marveled at him in submission. At that time, at Xingyan Temple in Danyang, [Master] Chao...

The Dharma Master was well-versed in the *Śāstra* (likely the *Abhidharmakośa*). He would frequently visit the wheel-beneath [the Buddha’s image] and, whenever engaged in informal conversation on the profound essentials of the Way, would discourse with tireless vigor.
The Master Jue held him in high esteem and deep appreciation. Before long, he passed away. His disciples all turned their attention toward Huide, intending for him to succeed to the Dharma seat.

Thus, the school of Xingyan remains flourishing even to this day. During the Zhide era of the Chen dynasty, he was repeatedly summoned by imperial decree to enter the palace to propagate the teachings, starting from Poyang.
Wang Boshan and his brothers, the Minister Wang Ke, the Secretariat Director Wang Gu, and others all extended their homage as disciples.
At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, the supreme teaching flourished once again. Once, while a vegetarian feast was being held at Qiyang Palace, the virtuous monks had all assembled;

the Emperor issued an edict for Sengtuō to ascend the Dharma seat first, and commanded the Attendant-in-Ordinary Cui Junde to proclaim the imperial decree, saying: "In the past, the Dharma Master was peerless in this world..."

At that time, [Hui]tuo was not yet sufficient to match his learning. Now that the four seas have been unified under one house and he has been appointed as the presiding master (*lun-zhu*), his extraordinary talent is finally made manifest.
When Emperor Yang was in the imperial residence, he went out to govern Weiyang and newly established Huiri Monastery, where he invited Hui[tuo] to reside there.

Hui[tuo] redoubled his efforts in study, becoming proficient in all fields of knowledge. Later, he followed [the Emperor] to the capital and stayed at Riyuan Monastery, where he was frequently summoned for instruction.
He elucidated [the teachings], and his reputation resounded even more prominently within the capital. Previously, there had never been a commentary on the *Tattvasiddhi* (Chengshi lun).

[Sengmin] thought that he must produce one, yet feared it might provoke dissenting opinions. It happened that the Emperor was installed as the Crown Prince; he issued an edict ordering its revision and refinement, which resulted in forty fascicles that were subsequently presented to the throne.
After the Empress Dowager passed away, memorial services were held in succession. An edict was then issued for the Riyang Monastery to select [monks].
More than fifty eminent and venerable masters entered the inner palace of Chengming to practice the Way. Soon after, an order was issued for them to lecture on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*.

The Emperor then commanded the śramaṇa Jizang to compose the commentary. Huida initially yielded to him, not yet wishing to conclude the matter immediately; however, as Jizang gradually became somewhat self-important, he began to offer subtle criticisms.
When the text reached the section on the Three Gates of Liberation, Huida asked: "With what arrow does one shoot through the Three Gates of Liberation? Jizang—

He said, "If one has not yet learned how to bend the bow, how can one discuss the release of the arrow? If you insist on citing these authorities, our investigation will become a chaotic mess. Although Sengzang wished to provide a defense and resolution, he was unable to do so.
When the Crown Prince personally visited him, he issued an order that there would be no debate; rather, he commanded that the text be analyzed solely according to its original meaning.
Furthermore, he ordered him to discourse on profound principles with Dharma Master Daozhuang; the dialogue between guest and host flowed without exhaustion. He then sent his attendant, Zhang...
Heng respectfully praised him, saying: "The Dharma Master’s erudition is such that it is rarely equaled in ancient or modern times.

If what you have expounded is indeed truthful and not false, then having perused the commentaries and treatises you have composed, I truly have no regrets. You should further compose a commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

Furthermore, regarding the terminology and teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, I shall provide scribes for you to transcribe. He subsequently produced four fascicles on the terminology and teachings of the Two Vehicles, as well as a commentary on the *Vimalakīrti*.
[He composed] ten scrolls. He then supervised the construction of a shrine and had his portrait painted there for veneration upon the Jewel Terrace (*ratnastūpa*).

Toward the end of the Renshou era, when the Emperor ascended the dragon throne, he bestowed four hundred bolts of silk as a reward for [the Master’s] past services. At the beginning of the Daye era, he accompanied the imperial entourage on its tour of Luoyang.

In the late winter of the second year, he first fell ill; yet even while holding his mat, he continued to instruct his disciples as usual. On the ninth day of the first month of the third year, a marvel occurred.
There was an auspicious omen of fragrant red light. At night, he rinsed his mouth and left behind a detailed testament. He passed away while sitting upright at the age of sixty-seven.
When the Emperor heard the news, he was struck with grief and issued an edict granting three hundred bolts of silk as funeral expenses;

the relevant authorities were to provide for the funeral rites, and Zhang Heng, the Palace Attendant (Huangmen Shilang), was appointed to supervise them. His voice was clear and resonant; even amidst a great clamor, it could never be drowned out. Whenever he received [the call to pray],...
The Imperial Edict issued the titles for his lectures. On the night prior, he invariably dreamed that the auspicious image of King Udayana stood alongside [the Buddha].

If the meaning was not yet fully resolved, he would immediately see a Brahman monk provide an explanation. He had previously dreamed of a youth holding a lotus flower who said, "The Heavenly Emperor has sent me to invite you.
On the evening of his death, he again dreamed as before. In total, he lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Vimaladatta*, and the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* thirty times each.

He recited other *Vaipulya* sutras fifty times each, as well as the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra*. His disciples, Huìquán and Dàoguàn, were both renowned for their excellence in both voice and virtue;
Guàn became famous throughout the world. On the twenty-fifth day of the second month of that year, he was interred in a square tomb on Mount Bǎimáng in Jīngŭ Village, Luóyáng.
Yú Shìnán, Secretary of the Imperial Library of Kuàijī, composed a text to be engraved upon a stele beside it.
Some say that he later again entrusted his consciousness to the sick monk Huiji, where he engaged in debate with Jizang;
there, he surrendered his heart and offered full courtesy to dispel their long-standing resentment, as if they were together as in former times.
The Sui monk Shan (whose secular surname was Xi) was a native of Zhengping in Jiang. Having left home as a youth, he devoted himself to the practice of dhyāna-concentration.
At that time, there was a master named Fang at the Linlu Spring in Jiji, who possessed an especially high reputation and was the equal of Shan.
Consequently, crowds of those who had submitted to the Way traveled incessantly between Mounts Bailu, Taihang, Baoduxi, and Linlu. Later, his disciple Sengxi...
He requested that Shan go to the bend of the Fen River to propagate the teachings. Shan had not yet consented. Xi said, "I have invited you back and forth some thirty times;
my heels may wear away, but my vow of heart is difficult to abandon. How could I bear to let this pass? Shan then complied.

He resided on Mount Mátóu, where scholars from both the Wei and Jin regions flocked to him like a herd. Thereupon, he divided them into four sections, assigning them to dwell in the two groves to the east and west.

In the era of Renshou, during the reign of Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty—a time when even the lands where cups and plates were discarded with great abandon saw his Way flourish most highly—it was precisely as the sutras describe regarding the ten *kṛtsnāyatana* (totalities).
As he approached the end of his life, he told his disciples: "When I was young, I lived in the mountains and attained nothing;
I sustained myself by eating small pebbles. Now I suffer from a cold accumulation within my intestines, which is merely the consequence of those chronic ailments. After I die, you may..."

He opened his belly to examine it and exhorted him to diligently advance in his practice. He was also ordered to be buried in an earthen jar, thereby sparing him from the destruction of life caused by cremation.
He passed away amidst the Great Yellow Rock on the eleventh day of the third month in the first year of the Daye era.
Xi Shi had originally been a man of Jiang; later he resided at Baoyan Temple in Jin, where he served as the temple steward (*zhisui*) and supervised the laborers in their cultivation.
Tian witnessed the cruelty with which insects on land and in water were being slaughtered. He returned to his former occupation until his death;

when his son Shan was away, after a long time he went to inquire after him, but no one knew where he was. Consequently, he went to the mountain to hold a memorial assembly and wailed in deep grief. Suddenly, the earth split open.
The sound [of his passing] shook the mountains and forests. At the time of the burial, the earthenware urn surged upward, and his skeletal remains were as brilliant as snow;

his tongue was a vivid, fresh crimson, reflecting light. He was subsequently divided into two parts and enshrined in stupas. He passed away on the ninth day of the first month in the fifteenth year of the Zhenguan era, at the age of sixty-four.
The monk Sengji of Xiaoyushan in Jin also possessed virtuous conduct; he gathered disciples without establishing formal rules of discipline, allowing them to follow their own inclinations.
As for his personal attainments, even the ground rats became so tame and submissive that they could be held in one's hands; this was not the case with others.

The Sui monk Zhao was a native of Jingzhao; his clan and lineage are unknown. In his youth, he studied under Jìng'ài and left the household life. Wherever he went, he brought about spiritual transformation.

She repeatedly obtained auspicious omens, yet fearing they might dazzle the masses, she kept them hidden and did not reveal them. When the Zhou dynasty abolished the Buddhist teachings, she once again lived in seclusion on Mount Qin, delighting herself in the tranquility of meditation.
Every time she looked at her reflection, she would smile and say, "In this world, can there truly be any joy greater than this?

Compared to that bustling marketplace, where one must bow and scrape amidst the dust and vulgarity of the secular world—how base and trivial it is! This continued until the Sui dynasty rose to prominence.
The Buddha’s transformative influence was further unfolding, and he subsequently established Shen-tian Monastery at Tian-gu in the Southern Mountains of Hu County.

There he gathered disciples and mastered his studies, his reputation resounding throughout the Wei River region. Just as Emperor Wen was on the throne, he issued an edict to the Chancellor Yang Su to enter the mountains and proclaim the imperial decree to invite him;

yet [the Master] did not comply with the summons. The Emperor’s reverence and admiration increased all the more, and he dispatched Yang Su again to present incense and ceremonial offerings, while simultaneously reiterating his invitation through an imperial edict.

The Emperor said: "The Chan Master’s virtue is esteemed by public opinion, and his Way reflects the profound origins. Dwelling in seclusion within mountain ravines, he nurtures his natural purity and honors his sacred vocation;

I greatly admire him. I have now sent attendants to express my reverent devotion, and I also wish to bestow gifts and request that he receive the returning precepts (śaraṇagamana), but he declined them all.
In the seventh year of the Daye era, he passed away at the monastery where he resided."

The Sui monk Can, surnamed Sun, was a native of Chenliu in Beiliang. In his youth, he traveled to study in Hebei, Henan, and throughout the eastern and western regions of Guanlong, traversing the territories of the Qi, Chen, and Zhou dynasties.
He was skilled in debate and adept at strategic maneuvers, styling himself the "Master of the Three Kingdoms.
In the tenth year of the Kaihuang era, by imperial decree, he resided at Xingshan Monastery in the capital. In the seventeenth year, by imperial decree, he was appointed to [the position of]...
He was the foremost Mahāyāna master among the twenty-five assemblies; thus, he composed ten treatises on the Mahāyāna, namely:
first, penetration; second, leveling; third, contrariety; fourth, conformity; fifth, reception; sixth, subduing; seventh, delusion; eighth, dream; ninth, characteristics; and tenth, the Middle Way.
He continued to reside at Tonghua Temple to oversee and guide the assembly of students. He also authored two fascicles of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

In the second year of the Renshou era, an imperial decree was issued to establish stupas in all prefectures. Relics previously kept within the palace were brought out, and monks from throughout the realm who were selected for their spiritual attainment and conduct were sent to enshrine them.
It was further stipulated that the foundations for the stupas would be laid on the same day. The Emperor performed extensive meritorious rites within the Inner Sanctuary.
He awaited reports of auspicious responses from the four quarters. Sengcan, leading the Vinaya Master Hongzun and others, took his leave of the Emperor.

The Emperor said, "May the Dharma Masters proceed with their mission of conversion so that you may return in glory to your native lands. Sengcan obtained the enshrinement of the śarīra at Guangfu Temple in Bianzhou;
the details of its radiant manifestations and fragrant omens are recorded in a separate account. Toward the end of the Renshou era, he again performed the enshrinement.
He resided at Xiude Temple in Huazhou, where its radiance and fragrance became increasingly wondrous and intense. The Emperor repeatedly expressed his admiration and praise.

There was a Daoist priest named Chu Rou, who was skilled in the teachings of Zhuangzi and Laozi; one day, by imperial decree, the high officials were all assembled to lecture on the *Laozi*, and it was stipulated that only śramaṇas were not permitted to take seats among them.
Upon hearing this, Sengcan led more than ten of his disciples, carrying portable stools and pushing aside the guards.

He went directly to that place and sat down. While the King of Fangxu was still smoothing his robes and had not yet issued his command for the writing to begin, Sengcan immediately spoke out with spirited and piercing words.
Although his phrasing seemed like humorous banter, its meaning was in fact profound and authoritative. Consequently, the assembly dispersed.

When someone reported this to the Emperor, the Emperor said, "If I am able to be contemporaneous with such a person, would it not be a blessing? Prince Jian of Qi was also filled with admiration and thirsted for his discourse. At that time, there was a śramaṇa...

Jizang had acquired the reputation for profound eloquence, and the King frequently sought to humiliate him. In the fifth year of the Daye era, a grand Dharma assembly was convened at Jizang’s residence;
more than thirty people were present, and they requested that Jizang ascend the seat. Fajian instructed Zhangbiao to pose questions, and the listeners thought Jizang would have no way to respond.
Yet, as Jizang cited the difficulties and provided seamless explanations, the audience further concluded that Fajian would certainly have nothing left to add. It was as if...

They engaged in this exchange more than forty times; Sengzang continued to analyze and expound upon the texts without hesitation. The King stopped him and ordered the next seat-holder to continue answering.

Sengcan then took up the questioning again for another twenty or thirty rounds before withdrawing. The King rose, took Sengcan’s hand, and thanked him, saying, "Your fame is not earned in vain. Your fame is not earned in vain.
He presented him with a fly-whisk and various personal effects to honor and manifest his excellence. In the ninth year, he passed away.

At Xingshan Monastery, he passed away at the age of eighty-five. His disciples were Sengluan and Sengfeng; Sengluan returned to secular life and entered government service, while Sengfeng has a separate biography.

During the Sui dynasty, Hongzun was the son of the Shi family from Xiangzhou; he left home to become a monk at the age of eight, and from the moment he began his studies under a master, he immediately gained renown. Once—
Having received full ordination, he devoted himself exclusively to the Vinaya section. He often remarked, "In upholding the bequeathed Dharma, we still rely upon this.

After three summer retreats of inquiry and consultation, he had only come to understand its general principles. Initially, he relied upon Master Ziyun at Shaolin Temple on Mount Songgao; in addition to studying the Vinaya, [he pursued other studies].
He concurrently studied the *Avataṃsaka-mahā-śāstra*. At that time, Master Huī of Ye was propagating the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*;

[Daoxuan] therefore carried his book-case and went to him. His disciples numbered five hundred, and none could surpass him. Yet even Huī was obscured by craftiness and flattery, and was unable to recognize [Daoxuan’s excellence].
One day, Daohui assembled his followers. Daozhun gathered all the commentaries he had composed, carried them into the hall, and placed them upon the lectern, saying:
"These have been relegated to the lower ranks of discourse for too long. In all my years of conducting lectures and formal debates, I have never once put them to the test.

Thus, the way of teacher and disciple has been stifled and not transmitted. I dare to return these commentaries to you. He then went to Huiyuan’s quarters, where Huiyuan immediately ordered him to ascend the seat.
Seated, he expounded the subtle and profound, far surpassing the common stream. Consequently, he completed his studies of the *Mahā-śāstra* to illuminate his wisdom and understanding.

Shortly thereafter, he entered the Chan forest (meditation grove), where his attainments became unfathomable. Over ten years passed; even upon returning home, he continued to propagate the teachings through the Vinaya.
From the four directions, people flocked to him like the wind, their numbers reaching a thousand. Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty issued an edict appointing him as a *śramaṇa* for judicial affairs;

whenever members of the fivefold assembly violated the disciplinary code, he was ordered to adjudicate according to the Vinaya. For long-standing disputes and litigation in Qingzhou and Qizhou, the Emperor commanded Sengzun to mediate and resolve them, while also punishing those who were unruly.
His judgments were consistently fair and resonated with public sentiment, such that his fellow practitioners rejoiced in and submitted to his authority during the chaos at the end of the Qi dynasty.
Accompanied by the renowned monk Huiyuan and others, he lived in seclusion at Bailu Rock. When the Zhou dynasty was unified, he moved to Mount Song.
In the seventh year of the Kaihuang era, an imperial decree summoned the five great virtuous monks to the palace;

the Emperor treated them with the utmost courtesy and diligence, ordering that they and ten disciples reside at Xingshan Temple, where the relevant authorities provided them with the four requisites for their sustenance. In the eleventh year, an imperial decree invited him along with [monks from] India.

The śramaṇa translated the scriptures for sixteen years. In the sixteenth year, by imperial decree, he was appointed as the Head of the Vinaya Assembly and began lecturing on the Vinaya at Chongjing Temple.

Previously, those within the Guannei region had long followed the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and rarely listened to or received instruction in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Sengzun then established expedient means for them, ultimately ensuring its widespread circulation.
In the second year of the Renshou era, an imperial edict ordered the dispatch of śarīra relics to Fojusi Temple in Wei. [There were] two types, red and crimson...
Its light shines brilliantly both near and far. In the fourth year, an imperial edict stated: "I, the Emperor, reverently receive the initial mandate and nurture the people.

I uphold the holy teachings and cause the Dharma of the Image (Xiangfa) to flourish once more. Now, the Great Compassion of the Tathāgata protects all classes of beings; moved by this grace, śarīras have appeared to guide and enlighten all living creatures.
I have already distributed them throughout the regions, both near and far, and erected sacred stupas for each. Yet, among the various provinces, there are still some where they have not yet reached."
Throughout [the realm], let them further invite virtuous monks (bhadanta) to escort the śarīra to each of the provinces, where they shall erect stūpas as previously instructed.

The monks so invited must necessarily possess moral virtue and be capable of following and correctly understanding the characteristics of the Dharma; only thus can they propagate the Buddhist teachings and inspire awakening in those who are deluded.

It is appropriate that the Three Heads (sangha officials) of all monasteries assemble to deliberate together and select [the candidates] with care. Their names shall be recorded and submitted for imperial report, so that [this merit] may be shared with all beings.
The common people shared in this meritorious karma. Sengzun followed his instructions in conducting the search and selection [of relics], which accorded well with contemporary discourse.

Furthermore, an imperial edict was issued for more than thirty prefectures to erect stupas to enshrine the śarīra; they were all placed within the stupas simultaneously. Sengzun then escorted them to Longsheng Temple.

The auspicious signs are detailed in a separate record. Shortly thereafter, he was appointed by imperial decree to oversee the affairs of the temple; his achievements were truly eminent. On the tenth day of the fifth month in the fourth year of the Daye era...
On the ninth day, he passed away at Xingshan Monastery at the age of seventy-nine. His writings include the *Datong chao* (Great Compendium) in five fascicles, which remains in circulation.
During the early Sui dynasty, Daohong, Fatai, Fayuan, and others were all renowned figures who served as the pillars of the True and Semblance Dharma.
Their ultimate fates, however, are unknown.
In his youth, Fa-jin of the Sui dynasty served as a disciple of Chan Master Hui at Yungnü Temple on Mount Yingxiang in Mianzhu County, Yizhou, where he left the household life.
Later, he received the ten precepts from Dharma Master Ding. He was reverent, diligent, humble, and respectful, constantly relying on Master Hui to study the "Water Contemplation" (shuǐguān).
In the bamboo grove of the temple lived four tigers; whenever Fa-jin entered into meditative concentration, the tigers would circle him on his left and right with docility, as if...
The area was so secluded that human tracks were completely absent. A woodcutter from a neighboring village peeked in furtively but saw nothing;

he only observed a pool of water solidified upon the corded meditation seat. He subsequently threw stones into it again. Shortly thereafter, the Master emerged from his concentration and felt pain in his heart.
He inquired extensively and learned the cause. The next day, he ordered that man to ensure all the stones thrown [into the water] were completely removed by the appointed time;
the pain then subsided. During the Kaihuang era, Prince Xiu was appointed as the King of Shu with his capital at Chengdu. His consort suffered from a severe affliction of the heart and abdomen.
At that time, the various practitioners of the Dao, such as Bai Ya and Ming He, were all unable to cure her. Consequently, he dispatched the Chief Secretary Zhang...
The King [Ying] immediately sent messengers to that monastery to request his arrival. Daolin refused, saying, "I have dwelt on this mountain for nearly eighty years;

my nature has remained unmoved, like wood or stone. Even if you force me, there will only be death. After he had returned with this report, the King dispatched his officials and attendants in carriages to welcome him, never flagging in their efforts.
Daolin’s resolve grew even more steadfast and vigorous, which provoked the King’s anger. He personally—
He went to that place intending to inflict punishment upon him. Upon seeing him approaching, the King looked back and was overcome with such trembling and sweat that he could not restrain himself;
he spoke urgently, saying, "Master Chan, you are compassionate; I pray you save me from this suffering.

Zhi Jin replied slowly, "If one were to slaughter a sheep and take its heart to serve in the kitchen, the pain of that sheep would be even greater than yours, yet Your Majesty did not show it the slightest mercy. Now, because your consort suffers but slight pain..."

"Affection is like this: thus, Your Majesty’s regard for worldly sentiments is heavy, while your regard for the Way is light. How can you still summon me? The King was immediately filled with shame and remorse, and he repented;
he then departed from the mountain. Furthermore, he refused to ride in a carriage, requesting instead to follow behind the King on foot with staff and sandals.
After a short while, he arrived two days ahead of the others. He went to the hall and saw the Consort, who was also perspiring profusely, as her illness followed him."
Feeling a sense of liberation, he presented five hundred bolts of silk, a *kāṣāya* robe, a *saṃghāṭī*, and various articles.

He invited [the Master] to wash his hands, and after holding the offered items and completing the prayers for blessings, he sent them all to Fǎzǔ Temple to assist in the construction project, whereupon he took his leave.
At that time, when the King was alone with his consort, he saw her feet raised about four or five inches off the ground.
On the eighth day of the first month in the thirteenth year of the Daye era, she passed away in the mountains.
Zhenhui of the Sui dynasty was surnamed Chen and was a native of Shan in Hebei. In his youth, he was compelled by his parents to marry, which was contrary to his own will.
Upon reaching the age of twenty, he suffered the loss of both his parents; consequently, he cast off worldly ties and entered the path under Master Qing at Datong Temple in his hometown.
This was in the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era. Having received full ordination, he relied upon Vinaya Master Jinghong.
He studied the Vinaya for years, enduring both winter and summer, before traveling to Master Xun at Linluoquan in Weizhou to investigate the teachings of Chan.
After more than a year, Huikai admired his character and demeanor; Master Xun bestowed upon him the record of the transmission of the lamp and appointed him to reside at Taoyan in Shanxi.
Before he had even arrived there, in the eighteenth year [of the Kaiyuan era], Huiyou sat out the summer retreat at Bailushan at the foot of Baijia Rock. Some have said:
Shoushan and Magu were especially eminent and peerless. In autumn, he proceeded to Pusan, where he built a dwelling to settle the fourfold assembly.

Carrying provisions and wearing straw sandals, they gathered there until it flourished as a great monastic community. Over the course of eighteen years, those who attained benefit from his teaching were beyond all reckoning.
However, Du Jie and Ang Er were the most eminent among his disciples. In the fourth year of the Renshou era, an imperial edict ordered him to reside at Xiyanshi Temple.

In the first year of the Daye era, he consumed yellow mustard to abstain from grain for one hundred days, yet his countenance became even more radiant and robust. Some of his followers attempted to emulate him in secret, but they were unable to do so.
He moved his residence to Beipan Valley; tigers avoided him there, and although it was remote and secluded, there was no way to measure the sun’s shadow [to determine the time].
His utensils remained as they were, and his daily activities—rising, sitting, eating, and drinking—did not deviate from their regular rhythm, as if he were sustained by some divine being.

On the seventh day of the tenth month in the eleventh year of the Daye era, he passed away due to illness at Magu at the age of forty-seven. His body was cremated according to the Dharma, and his *śarīra* relics were enshrined in a stupa.
*The Newly Compiled Biographies of Monks Classified into Six Categories of Study*, Scroll Thirteen;
*The Newly Compiled Biographies of Monks Classified into Six Categories of Study*, Scroll Fourteen.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Tanyu of Eastern Zhejiang.
Section on the Propagation of the Dharma through the Study of Precepts (4):
The Tang monk Huáng was the son of the Fēng family in Nánchāng, Fúchéng, Miánzhōu. He was tall and robust in stature, with a countenance and bearing that were bold and resolute.

He was broad in learning and quick-witted. From his youth, he enjoyed a reputation throughout his village. He once dreamed that he held the sun and moon in his hands while sitting amidst the great void;
seeing his own radiance shining brilliantly, he took this as the basis for his name. He earnestly requested his parents to allow him to leave the household life.
Fearing he might run away, his parents bound both his feet to a pillar in the house at night. Suddenly, they untied themselves; thereupon he sighed and said, "Wherever one's will lies..."
Heaven, earth, spirits, and ghosts followed him; how much more so would other beings? His parents were moved to realization and sent him to rely upon Dharma Master Huantan to receive instruction.

He was diligent day and night and eventually mastered the studies of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. During the transition from the end of the Liang dynasty to the beginning of the Zhou, the Dharma again became confused and corrupted.
Huáng maintained his integrity alone; he did not associate with those of a different kind. After ascending the dharma-seat, he specialized in the study of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
During the Baoding era of the Zhou dynasty, he further studied the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. He also received the mind-dharma from Chan Master Tánxiàng, Kāi Chan Master, and others.

Subsequently, his virtue was praised far and wide, and his reputation reached the Imperial Court. Emperor Wǔ issued an edict for him to preside over the Dharma Assembly at Míngdé Hall. He was then... [bestowed].
He served as the Tripiṭaka Master of his home province. When the Sui dynasty was established, he was appointed as the Sangha Rectifier (Sengzheng) to govern the local monastic community.

The people of Yizhou admired his reputation, and successive provincial governors all received the fragrance of his precepts from him. In the fifteenth year of the Kaihuang era, a separate group of dhūta practitioners was established at his residence, Zhenxiang Temple, to guide those who were indolent and negligent.
Following the Renshou era, he led the assembly of the temple in reciting the Tripitaka scriptures throughout the Zhou period.
He began once more to provide offerings and alms. He departed from his patron’s home and passed away at his residence during the early years of the Wude era.
He was eighty-five years of age. At the moment of his passing, the lotus pond dried up and the compassionate bamboo withered; yet roses bloomed profusely even in winter.
Those who understood these signs considered them two omens of flourishing and decay, surely portending the marks of birth and extinction.
Jizang of the Tang dynasty was a native of the kingdom of Anxi. His ancestors had settled in the South Sea to escape an enemy;
his father later moved to Jinling, where Jizang was born. At that time, the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha from Western India first arrived.

Jizang’s father took him to see the Master, who remarked, "This child is a gathering place for auspiciousness," and thus named him accordingly. The father also left the household life, taking the name Daoliang. Liang... [the text ends here].
From birth, his conduct was austere and peerless. He begged for food and listened to the Dharma without the slightest negligence.

Whenever he returned with his alms bowl, he would invariably enter the stupa barefoot to make offerings throughout to the Buddha images, and only then would he distribute the food as alms. Even when it came to tears, saliva, or excrement, he would always receive them in his hands, consecrating them with the prayer that they be food for all sentient beings.
His practice of such profound and meticulous discipline remained flawless from beginning to end; yet, he always carried [a small vessel] with him.
At the age of seven, he heard Dharma Master Daolang lecturing at Xinghuang Temple and subsequently followed Lang to leave the household life.

He frequented the master’s side daily, and by the age of nineteen, he was reciting the scriptures for the assembly; his refined discernment was sharp and incisive, earning him renown throughout the capital.

After receiving full ordination, his reputation grew even more prominent, and he was especially honored and venerated by Prince Guiyang of the Chen dynasty. When the Sui unified the realm, he traveled east and settled there.

At Jiaxiang Temple, he expounded the teachings as usual. Toward the end of the Kaihuang era, when Emperor Yang was still in his princely residence, he established four centers for the Way to attract and welcome men of virtue and talent.
[Zhiyan] was summoned to reside at Huiri Temple; subsequently, Riyang Temple was established in the capital, and the imperial decree further requested that he reside there.

Master Tanxian invited him to open the *Lotus Sūtra* (Fahua), and the assembly of the seven classes of disciples gathered in great numbers, with offerings of wealth and goods accumulating in abundance.

Having already established various fields of merit, he further served as the director for the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries (*daśākṣaya-kośa*). Entrusting the offerings to those practicing *dāna*, he ultimately completed the Great Image at Quqi.

It was so magnificent, towering, and prominent that all who beheld it could not help but feel a sense of reverent exertion. Prince Jian of the Qi dynasty invited Sengzang to his private residence for a Dharma assembly;
more than sixty people gathered at once, and they appointed Sengzang as the presiding master (*vādī*) of the discussion. Śramaṇa Seng...
Càn styled himself the "Master of the Three Kingdoms Treatise. He was the first to pose questions, engaging in more than forty rounds of exchange.

Sengzàng’s bearing was composed and leisurely, his rhetoric elegant and brilliant; his arguments surged and pierced with such force that they poured forth in abundance. All those present were moved to awe and withdrew.
King [Xin] wished to extend the discussion for two more days, yet none among the assembly dared to oppose him. At the beginning of the Daye era, he transcribed the *Lotus Sūtra*.
He recited two thousand sections of the sutras. During the final years of the Sui dynasty, he fashioned twenty-five statues and relinquished his residence to provide for their worship.

He separately established a statue of Samantabhadra and sat in meditation before it, contemplating the principle of the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). When the Banner of Righteousness first reached the capital, Emperor Wu received his audience at the Qianhua Gate.
In the preface to his collection, [Daoxuan] stated: "Alas, the four classes of people were submerged in the mire; I seized this opportunity to rescue those drowning."

Both monastics and laypeople looked up to his grace as if to the vast heavens; they could not contain their joy and gratitude. Emperor Wu was greatly pleased and visited him with frequent inquiries of courtesy.
At the beginning of the Wude era, an imperial decree selected ten "Great Virtues" (da-de) to oversee the affairs of the Dharma, and he was appointed as one of them.

Shortly thereafter, he concurrently presided over both Jishi and Dingshui Monasteries. Prince Yuanji, the Prince of Qi, wished to receive the precepts from him and invited him to reside at Yanxing Monastery; this was during that year.

His vital energy gradually declined, and he repeatedly suffered from the pains of illness. The Emperor issued an edict bestowing upon him excellent medicines, and imperial messengers visited him in succession.

He passed away in the fifth month of the sixth year of Wude at the age of seventy-five. When the Sovereign examined his final testament, he was moved by grief and sorrow; from the Crown Prince downward, all sent letters of condolence and inquiry. He was granted money and silk for burial.
His son, who was then in the Qin Residence (as a prince), composed a memorial of condolence, which is not recorded here. By imperial decree, he was buried to the south.

Shanzang lectured on the *Three Treatises* more than one hundred times, the *Lotus Sūtra* more than three hundred times, and the *Large Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* each several dozen times.

He composed commentaries for all of them, which circulated widely throughout the world. At the time of his death, he composed the "Treatise on the Absence of Fear at Death," though much of its text is not recorded here. His disciple Huiyuan succeeded him.
Tang Zhizang’s secular surname was Wei; he was a native of Zheng County in Huayin. At the age of thirteen, he entered the monastic order under Dharma Master Ai.
He resided at Zhuhusi Temple in Chang’an during the Western Wei dynasty. When the Zhou dynasty suppressed the Dharma, he alone went into hiding within the homes of various lay devotees.
Having shaved his hair and donned dyed robes, he never altered his practice. When the Sui dynasty moved the capital to Longshou, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Daxingshan Temple.
In the third year of the Kaihuang era, he chose a ridge to the east of Fenggu Valley on Mount Zhongnan to spend his final years; this was also the site of his former seclusion.
The Emperor dispatched Prince Jin Guang, Grand General of the Left Guard, to the mountain to proclaim the imperial edict and summon him for an audience.

Sengzang firmly declined. The Emperor’s respect and admiration for him increased further; he then dispatched the Palace Secretary (Neishi Sheren) Yu Shibiji to inquire after him, providing him with oil, incense, an incense burner, the three robes, and various household articles, while renaming his monastery Fengde.

Every year during the three months of the long retreat, Sengzang invariably expounded the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to propagate the teachings. At the beginning of the Wude era, when the monastic offices were established, Sengzang was appointed as...

This was his primary preference; however, in the end, it was not what worldly propriety favored. Because the official provisions at Xingshan Monastery were frequent and abundant, he wished to beg for food according to the Vinaya rules.
Later, while practicing *dhūta* austerities at the burial site of Bailin (Pine Forest) in the western suburbs, Emperor Wen went out on a tour.

Upon passing by, he marveled at him and ordered his attendants to all remove their robes to offer as alms. In total, more than one hundred bundles of clothing were collected, which he stored away entirely.
He filled his quarters with these. However, the only garment he wore was a heavy cotton robe (*nāgabhuja*) weighing about four *jin*.

He wore it until the end of his sixty-fifth summer, never for even a moment parting from it. He practiced constant sitting meditation and ate only once a day. His physical form was exceptionally distinguished;
he stood eight feet and two inches tall, yet his gait was light and composed. Whenever it was time to eat, he would first take up his water jar (*kamaṇḍalu*) a thousand times.
He walked upon wooden clogs through the dense thickets and marshy morasses. From the eastern mound, he traveled four *li* along a precipice before reaching his destination;

ascending again after midday, it was as if he had attained the supernatural power of the divine feet (*ṛddhipāda*). Therefore, his likeness has been depicted in portraits that have been preserved to this day.
The śramaṇa Xiaotan of Cimen Monastery in the capital erected a stele to the right of the monastery gate,
with the śramaṇa Falin of Yingchuan composing its inscription.
Tang Fasu resided at Huichang Monastery in the capital. His master, Zhìyǐ, was dedicated exclusively to meritorious works.

In the past, when he and Fasu were both staying in the region south of the Yangtze River, they invariably established great assemblies wherever they went, providing vegetarian meals for ten thousand people. At night, [Zhìyǐ] would inform Fasu to assemble the necessary materials;
yet when he rose to look at them the next morning, everything was exactly as desired. Such were the qualities of his talent and wisdom. (Sui...)
Ji was the governor of Dongdu. There, the starving lay piled one upon another; Ji could not bear the sight. In the monastery were two golden statues, each one *zhang* in height.
Consequently, Ji had one melted down to purchase rice and make gruel to sustain them. Before long, the rice was exhausted, and Ji intended to take the other statue to melt it as well.
The temple monk Bian summoned the other monks and together they resisted, refusing to allow it. Ji wept and said, "O Great..."
Virtue! In the past, the Tathāgata gave his head, eyes, marrow, and brain as alms to sentient beings;

at times he became a mountain of flesh, and at other times a great fish, to relieve their hunger and starvation. How much more so this manifested form? As for today’s matter, it shall serve as the price for my original body.
"I do not begrudge these two images either, yet they have become so emaciated and frail that they are no longer fit for their purpose.

Furthermore, since these images are made of precious materials, they will eventually perish and be lost. Why not instead benefit sentient beings and thereby fulfill the Tathāgata’s compassionate vows?
Although the monks firmly refused, later the city was destroyed and the images were lost, exactly as Su had predicted.
Huilin of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Xiao. Her grandfather was Emperor Ming of the Liang dynasty; her father served in the Sui dynasty as the Duke of Liang.
Her paternal aunt entered the inner palace of the Sui, becoming a consort to Emperor Yang. Her younger uncle is the present-day Marquis Song. Before Huilin left the household life, she...
She was nonetheless married to the daughter of the Qin Xiaowang (King Xiaowu of Qin) by virtue of her noble lineage; however, this was not her true aspiration.

After some time, when the Qin princess passed away, she shaved her head and donned the robes of a nun to study the supramundane Dharma. At the beginning of the Wude era, she returned to the capital and resided at Zhuangyan Monastery.

There, she extensively studied the various schools of Buddhist doctrine, applying her mind with particular diligence to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra*. Furthermore, she was proficient in literary composition and calligraphy; thus, throughout the capital—

Sutra titles and temple plaques frequently emerged from his hand. Whenever he composed verses with his elder brother, the Palace Attendant Donggong Zhongshe Jūn, their famous chapters and exquisite lines were relished by all, and those who understood them marveled at their brilliance.
Furthermore, Zhizheng was the elder brother of Duke Song and the son of the Grand Master of the Court of Finance;
though he was [Zhizheng’s] younger cousin in age, they lived together for a long time, encouraging one another in their religious practice and sharing a close bond.

His character was upright and refined; his peers praised him. Before long, both his elder brother Jūn and younger brother Shō died, yet Sōrei alone, by virtue of his family lineage, devoted himself exclusively to the Lotus Sutra, never daring to let it decline.
Toku-shin once compiled the finest portions of more than ten commentaries and sub-commentaries into a separate collection for circulation, and he frequently summoned renowned monks from the capital.
He pointed out errors and oversights, further propagating the teachings himself for the benefit of all classes of beings. His heart was set upon the principles of the Buddha;

he prioritized recitation and copying, producing nearly a thousand volumes. Despite the distractions of attending court audiences, he would still command his attendants to hold the scriptures before him.
Whenever there was even a slight interval from official duties, he would immediately open them to read. Alas! How truly did he carry on his predecessor’s will!
To describe the greatness of these events: how could the virtue of Emperor Wu, as it pertains to the world, be subject to further debate?
Tang Pujie was a śramaṇa who lived in the mountains during the early Zhen Guan era; he was valiant, bold, and resolute, such that even sleep could not deceive him.
He practiced frugality and modesty. As for those who profit from theft, he kept his distance. In all his discourse, he prioritized contentment.
Thus, while preaching the Dharma while seated, offerings accumulated like mountains, yet he never looked back upon them with attachment. He entrusted the supervision of the assembly to others.

He was particularly proficient in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, explaining them according to their literal phrasing. His voice was grand and resonant, reaching a radius of one *li*; the entire multitude heard him clearly.
Pei Jie resided at Guangming Temple, but soon fled due to the commotion and noise, and his whereabouts became unknown.
Zhi-man of the Tang dynasty was the son of the Jia family of Taiyuan; he entered the monastic order at the age of seven and immediately devoted himself to the study of the Vinaya.

Upon reaching manhood, he received full ordination and propagated the teachings of the Vinaya-piṭaka. He further studied the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and was able to master its essential principles. He resided at Shimo Mountain in Shangdang and gathered [disciples].
He traveled on foot. At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, the Dharma-vehicle flourished once more; as he propagated and expanded it, Man’s contribution was the greatest.

Thus, through ritual repentance, he gathered in those with lax emotions, and through seated meditation, he refined the burdens of the ordinary. Consequently, both monastics and laypeople looked up to him as their Bodhisattva Precept Master.
Yet, as there were no clear signs of realization, he did not lightly bestow the Dharma. Not long after, he moved his residence to Liuquan on Mount Dongshan in Licheng.
In the vihāra, those who sought to still the mind flocked to him as if returning to a marketplace. Shortly thereafter, he relied upon Chan Master Zan at Yanmen;

after a long time, he moved to the capital, where he further propagated the study of tranquility. During the chaos at the end of the Sui dynasty, he again joined with more than fifty like-minded companions.
He fled westward to T’uan-an Mountain in Lan-chou. While the world was in turmoil, this region remained deep and remote, such that he was never aware of it;

was this perhaps due to the power of his Way’s resonance? When the Banner of Righteousness was first raised, the High Ancestor issued an edict for him to receive offerings at the residence of Duke Hsü, and when the Emperor went in person to pay his respects, he felt a profound sense of awe. Turning to P’ai Chih, he said: "As for me and the Meditation Master..."
His hair stood on end in alarm, and he asked why. Jì replied, "This is because you are being protected by the deities of the precepts.

On another day, [the General] saw him again and said, "I, your disciple, have raised an army of righteousness and shall settle the empire with my halberd; this is all for the sake of rescuing and uplifting sentient beings.

I pray only that the Master’s compassion may extend its protection, ensuring that my movements come and go without hindrance. In the first year of the Wǔdé era, an imperial edict was issued to designate the residence of the Duke of Xǔ as [a monastery].
He was assigned to reside at Yixing Temple. Three years later, he was summoned to the capital by imperial decree.

At that time, Liu Hu, the Duke of Hongnong and Regional Commander (Dudu), submitted a memorial requesting that he not be sent, as the Xiongnu were currently raiding the borders and public sentiment was filled with fear and alarm.
In the fourth month of the summer in the second year of the Zhenguan era, he manifested a slight illness; however, he sat in meditation as usual. The śramaṇa Daochuo asked him: "The myriad..."
The Dharma is fundamentally empty. Yet, some enter through the contemplation of signs (*lakṣaṇa*), while others awaken through karmic conditions (*pratyaya*).

Why is this? He replied: "Conditions have nothing upon which to depend; signs have nothing by which to be characterized. Awakening and entering in this manner, there is likewise no dharma. Thereupon, he passed away suddenly.
This was on the ninth day of the sixth month of that year. He was seventy-eight years of age. A stupa was erected and a stele inscribed; he was buried at Longshan Tongzi.
Gu. Tang Daoxuan was born into the Zhou family; he was a native of Runan. Having left home to become a monk in his youth, his aspirations were lofty and pure.

Carrying his book-bundle, he resided at Gaozuo Temple in Jinling. He was proficient in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, yet he did not favor lecturing or recording commentaries on it. During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty...
In the twelfth year, he accompanied the Great General Zhou Luohou on a distant journey to Mount Lu.
He took up residence at Donglin Monastery, having been encouraged and invited there by the śramaṇa Faying; thus he settled into reclusion and no longer involved himself in worldly affairs.

He propagated the Way and saved sentient beings, and in the restoration and maintenance of shrines and stupas, he never grew weary. Even during the disturbances of bandits in his later years, he continued to guide and encourage his disciples as usual. [Zheng]...

In the ninth month of the second year, he fell ill. After more than ten days had passed, a great star suddenly fell into the pond at the West Pavilion, illuminating the mountains and valleys with a brilliance as if a thousand torches were being held aloft.
On the twenty-third day, at noon while eating his meal, he said to his disciples, "Has the Sangha finished their meal?
They replied, "Not yet. He said, "Call the Elder here," and immediately entrusted his final affairs to him before passing away. At that time, all...

The palace gates opened wide, and a wondrous fragrance filled the monastery for seven days. He was eighty-two years of age in both spring and autumn. The Tang monk Yong, surnamed Guo, was a native of Jiehou in Taiyuan.
His grandfather, Xian, was the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Jingzhou; his father, Shao, was the Prefectural Governor (Taishou) of Boling.
Yong possessed a profound and tranquil spirit; while still young, he entered the Imperial Academy. At the age of thirteen, he left his parents to enter [the monastic life].

Daofu practiced at Yunmen Monastery west of Ye, where he relied upon Master Chou and was immediately granted the methods of Chan. Within just a few days, his realization became exceptionally profound.
Chou patted him on the back and said to his disciples, "The five cessations and four foundations of mindfulness are all contained within this youth. Shortly thereafter, he moved to Mount Linli.
When the Zhou dynasty abolished Buddhism, he went into hiding in the White Deer Mountains. At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, he was brought out and established [in the monastic order].
The gates were opened once more. Master Xingxin of the Northern Wei had long heard of his reputation and wished to circulate his teachings;
he sent messengers to invite him down from the mountains. In the ninth year, Xingxin was summoned by imperial decree to the capital, and Daoyong accompanied him there.
Upon Xingxin’s passing, Daoyong led the assembly to inherit his legacy, never failing to uphold his standards. On the tenth day of the eleventh month in the fifth year of the Zhenguan era—
On the sixth day, he passed away at Huadu Temple at the age of eighty-nine. The Emperor bestowed silk for funeral offerings to cultivate merit on his behalf, expressing his profound reverence.
On the twenty-second day of that month, in accordance with his final instructions, his remains were cremated on Mount Zhongnan.
The disciples collected the śarīra relics and erected a stūpa to the left of the Xingxing Stūpa.
Its inscription was composed by Li Baiyao, Court Attendant for the Left, and calligraphed by Ou-yang Ts'un, Prefectural Magistrate.
Tang Daozhe was born into the Tang family of Linyi in Qijun. Initially, he followed Dharma Master Mingji of Yingchuan to exhaustively study the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
Later, he received the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* from Vinaya Master Xi of Wei Commandery and subsequently studied meditative concentration under Chan Master Xun of Henei.
Soon thereafter, as the practice of stillness and cultivation flourished particularly in the capital, he took up his staff and traveled there. Having been ordained at Renjue Temple...
Dànm qiān took up the essential principles of the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) and subsequently took his leave, retiring to Luògǔ in Zhōngnánshān.
Finding it difficult to sustain himself on grain, he required that the food offered to him be pure. At that time, a lay devotee named Zhāng Huī came down the mountain to seek instruction;

however, heavy snow obscured the path, and it was only after seven days that he arrived. Dànm qiān snapped his fingers to emerge from meditative concentration and accepted the food from him. This demonstrates how Zhé steadfastly maintained right mindfulness.
He maintained that there were no fixed rules regarding food, saying, "I would rather die than [compromise]. Subsequently, he moved his residence to the Flower Hall (Huaguan) of Dazhuangyan Monastery.

He went on alms rounds at midday and declined the offerings of the monastic community; thus, the assembly held him in even greater esteem. The people of Zhouti County constructed a Buddhist temple for him, and disciples gathered to advance their studies.
Monastics and laypeople flocked to him from all sides. Suddenly, he took leave of his disciples and returned east to Zhuangyan to pay his respects to the venerable elders. Then, abruptly—
However, he passed away on the first day of the first month in the ninth year of the Zhenguan era. He was seventy-two years of age.
His remains were initially buried in the western suburbs of the capital. After some time, the people of Zhouti exhumed them to transport them back for cremation.
Using the remaining ashes, a brick stupa was erected at the side of the Zhengdengshu tree in Long'an Township, west of the city.
Tang Shanhui, surnamed Xun, was a native of Wen in Henei. He studied astronomy and geography until there was nothing he did not master.
However, realizing that worldly phenomena are empty and fragile rather than solid or enduring, he subsequently shaved his head and donned the robes at Pengcheng Temple in Xuzhou.

There he first received full ordination, recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and studied the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra*. At that time, the world was ravaged by famine and turmoil; although Shanhui suffered from the cold...
Even in times of hunger, Fayi served the Dharma with self-exertion; his cleansing of defilements and protection of purity were more rigorous than on ordinary days.
Toward the end of the Daye era, he took up his staff and traveled westward. Along the way, he repeatedly encountered bandits; yet he carried a broken jar and shielded himself with a soiled cloth.

In the tenth month of winter, he arrived at the capital, where he happened upon Dharma Master Jizang, who was then expounding the *Lotus Sūtra*. He wished to follow him and receive instruction, but the assembly rejected him on account of his humble appearance.

Hui alone swept away the snow, spread it upon the ground, and sat there. Whatever words or meanings he acquired, Sengtai did not allow them to be lost; whenever someone questioned him, Tai would immediately cite their essentials.
The śramaṇa Faxi of Chanding Monastery invited Hui to his quarters, treating him with diligent kindness and generosity.
Because Hui’s wisdom and insight were clear and penetrating, he further took Faxi as his teacher. At the beginning of the Wude era, he followed [Faxi] to reside at Jinliang Monastery in Lantian.

He established many meditation halls to attract eminent companions. On the first day of the first month in the ninth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away at the Liangquan Vihāra on Mount Li at the age of forty-nine.
His disciples escorted his funeral carriage and interred him together with the śramaṇa Huida at the latter’s burial site in Taiyuan.
Huida recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* without ceasing his voice whether walking or sitting; the number of times he completed the recitation was vast.
Furthermore, among his five thousand followers, there was one whose nature was particularly compassionate toward living beings.

Whenever he lowered his eyes to look straight ahead and saw the form of an insect on the ground, he would invariably contract his body to avoid it, not daring to step over it. When someone questioned him about this, he replied: "The time of death is not fixed;
how can one know that this creature might not attain perfect enlightenment before oneself? In the fourth month of the eighth year of the Zhenguan era, he sat in the full lotus posture.
He passed away.

Tang Daoyue’s surname was Meng; he was a native of Luoyang in Henan. His father, Meng Gao, served as the Magistrate of Linzi under the Sui dynasty and possessed a reputation for administrative competence.
The recluse Xi Men Yi held himself in high esteem through the Way and had never previously gone to call upon him. Suddenly, he requested an audience to offer his praises.

Yan Gao then brought forth his sons, including Shao, Xuji, and others, and had them categorized by rank. Dao Yi remarked, "The Lord of the Prefecture has six sons, all of whom are men of great capacity.
However, three of the younger ones will certainly not be bound by the constraints of the secular world.

This was a reference to the Dharma Master Kuang of Jingtu Monastery, as well as Yue and others. They studied the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* under the two masters Zhinian and Zhitong.

Furthermore, he thoroughly investigated the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* under Master Daoni. Fearing the labor involved, he subsequently entered Mount Taibai to join Master Huian, where he refined his understanding of the master’s instructions.
Later, while residing at Mingjue Temple in the capital, he remained shut in his room for five years, finding no leisure even for eating or resting;

from that time on, he encountered no further minor obstructions. As for external doctrines and hidden texts, none could be understood without commentaries. All that was recorded by the Tripiṭaka masters—
He remained in the southern regions, where he continued to provide bribes to merchants to ensure the acquisition of the texts.

Indeed, at Guangzhou’s Xianming Monastery, he obtained the manuscript of the *Kuśala-śāstra* as orally transmitted by the Tripiṭaka Master, along with the records of the eighteen schools of Abhidharma.
Xianming was the very monastery where Master Kai had resided. This fully satisfied his aspirations; he subsequently followed Master An to Taibai to complete his studies.

Seng’an permitted him to stay and provided for his needs together with the community. Thus they lived through successive years without any lack of provisions. Although times were harsh and harvests poor, his virtuous lineage continued to advance.

Shortly thereafter, Seng’an retired from the mountain; he remained there for another two years. In the eighth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he was summoned to reside at the Da Chanding Daochang, where the assembly numbered over three hundred.
[The Master] considered that since the learning of Mount Yue had no teacher to transmit it, it would not be appropriate to propagate it yet.
There were śramaṇas of equal virtue, such as Fachang, Zhishou, Sengbian, and Huiqing, who together held him in high esteem and invited him [to lecture].
He then took the commentaries on the Tripiṭaka and adjudicated between the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*. At first, some were still not convinced;

however, once he set forth the fundamental principles and the comprehensive framework, revealing the vastness and unfathomable depth of the profound mysteries, the sharp edges of their disputes suddenly ceased. At the beginning of the Wude era, he was bedridden with illness at Huaguo Temple in Langu Valley.
On a cliff there was a spring of milk-water. Zhiyue received it in his hands; he could obtain two sheng before it ceased, at which point he said, "I have nothing to move it.
He then silently recited mantras, whereupon the water would suddenly boil and bubble; over the course of a day, he could obtain one sheng, which he used for food and drink.

His illness improved significantly. In the second year, because the original commentary by the Tripitaka Master contained many redundant words and phrases, he edited and abridged it into a single volume, totaling twenty [fascicles].
It consists of two fascicles, reduced by two-thirds from the original commentary to facilitate reading. He also composed commentaries on eighteen treatises, which have circulated in the world.
At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, the Tripitaka Master Prabhākaramitra arrived at the capital, and by imperial decree, translations were undertaken.

Sengyue was also appointed to an official post therein. During this time, he heard that Sengyue was skilled in the *Kosa* (Abhidharmakośa), yet he harbored doubts and said: "This man is from my own Western country..."
To say that "Ultimate Principle" (Jize) refers to his goodness now is a misconception. When questioned on matters of great significance, Huiyue answered as fluently as a flowing stream;
people often remarked, "A man of wisdom! A man of wisdom! His Majesty once invited Dharma Master Zong to the palace to assemble the multitude and establish the doctrines of the Three Schools.
When Huiyue questioned him regarding the universal or restricted application of the Eightfold Path for the worthy and the sage, Zong had no response. The Daoist Liu Jinxi [was present].

He first opened the way for Laozi. When [Liu] Yue questioned him regarding the evidence for the sequence of "the Dao giving birth to One and Two," the Daoist could only stare blankly. Yue said jokingly, "Master, you look down upon your predecessors; do you think one can attain realization merely by looking at them? The assembly laughed loudly. In the eighth month of the sixth year, his elder brother Kuang passed away. Yue’s grief was so overwhelming that he could not control himself. Someone advised him to restrain his sorrow, to which Yue replied: "I have heard that when a great man dies, the world loses its teacher. My brother was a man of the Way; how could I bear to suppress my grief? Furthermore, I am not yet free from the bonds of worldly affairs. How could I possibly find peace? He then composed a poem titled "In Response to the Exhortation to Suppress Grief. It read: "The Great Way is vast and boundless; How could it be contained within a single person? The myriad things arise and pass away; Who can remain forever? If one does not know the source of the Way, How can one avoid the cycle of birth and death? I have long since abandoned the pursuit of fame and profit; Yet I still harbor lingering attachments. My heart is like a wild horse, difficult to rein in; How can I suddenly bring it to rest? I fear that if I do not cultivate myself now, I shall fall back into the dust of the world. Therefore, I must strive with all my might; I cannot afford to be negligent. He then retired to Mount Wudang to practice the Way. Later, he traveled to Mount Luofu, where he encountered the immortal Wang Yuanzhi. Yuanzhi said to him, "Your physical form is already complete; you need only refine your spirit. You should return to the human world to propagate the teachings of the Way. Yue then returned to the capital.

During the Kaihuang era, he was summoned to the court and presented with the title of "Master of the Purple Chamber" (Zishui Daoshi). He declined the honor and instead requested to reside at Mount Songgao. Emperor Wen granted his request. He lived there for over thirty years, eventually passing away on the eighth day of the tenth month of the second year of the Daye era. At the time of his death, he was seventy-nine years old. His remains were enshrined in a stupa at Mount Songgao. Later, during the Zhenguan era, he was posthumously honored with the title "Great Master of the True Source" (Zhenshen Dashi). His disciples built a temple at Mount Songgao to house his image, which was named "Songgao Temple. This was the origin of the lineage of the Songgao school. Among those who received his transmission were the masters Zhongli Quan, Lü Dongbin, and Zhang Sanfeng. Their teachings flourished greatly throughout the world. (Note: The character [打-丁+(改-己)] appears to be a variant or error; based on context, it likely refers to a response or action taken by Yue.)
Tè said: "We dwell together in this burning house and are submerged together in the current of craving. As birth and death have not yet been severed, how could we not feel sorrow?

In the autumn of the eighth year, the Crown Prince gathered various eminent virtuous monks at the Hongwen Hall to debate the principles of doctrine. Sengyue’s eloquent discourse was particularly outstanding among his peers.
The Crown Prince turned and asked, "Who is this Dharma Master? Du Zhenglun, the Left Palace Attendant, replied, "The Great..."

This was Dharma Master Daoyue of Zongchi Monastery. Zongchi was formerly the Chan-ting Monastery of the Sui dynasty. The Crown Prince asked, "What office do you hold in this monastery? He replied, "I hold none.
The Crown Prince then said, "The Emperor has built this monastery for me specifically to summon men of renowned virtue and to propagate the Great Teachings.
Yet, if a person of such high standing as yours has no office, how can that be? He then invited him to accept one.

When he was appointed to serve as the Deputy Abbot (Furen) of the temple, he declined repeatedly with an open mind, but his request was not granted. He subsequently moved to reside at Puguang Temple. In the ninth year, his younger brother Minglue came to visit him;
he insisted that Minglue remain, but Minglue, who was skilled in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, stayed instead at Tiangong Temple in Eastern Luoyang. In the second month of the tenth year, he fell ill.

The Prince’s physicians sent offerings of medicine one after another, yet he passed away at the temple where he resided. He was sixty-nine years old. His funeral expenses were provided by [the state].

The Prince’s household ordered that he be buried at the southwestern corner of the Du City wall, south of the suburbs. Having briefly completed the funeral rites and returned home, his grief remained tightly bound within him.
He passed away in the twelfth year, at the age of sixty-seven.

Tang Xuǎnwǎn was born into the Yang clan of Huáyīn in Hóngnóng. Ancestors of this lineage had previously migrated to Xīnfēng in Yōng, where their descendants multiplied and subsequently established separate genealogical records.
When Xuǎnwǎn reached the age for study, he shaved his head and became a disciple of Dharma Master Tányán; Master Yán was a renowned master of his era.
Once Xuǎnwǎn had received full ordination, he followed Vinaya Master Hóngzūn to study the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya).

For three years, he expounded [the teachings], and his peers held him in the highest esteem. Furthermore, he studied under Dharma Master Tanqian the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, as well as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, and others; he investigated them all exhaustively, leaving no aspect unexamined.

Nevertheless, because Master Huiyan was still alive, he vowed to create a sixteen-foot golden image of Śākyamuni Buddha. He continued his predecessor’s resolve and carried out the task, never daring to let it falter. Thereupon—
In the second year of the Renshou era, he collected various offerings and cast [the statue] at his residence, Jingnian Temple.
At that time, the sky was clear and serene, and the bright sun shed its radiance. Heavenly flowers, like mica, drifted down from all directions and finally fell before the image.
Onlookers considered this a marvel. When the mold was removed, the light and features were exceptionally extraordinary; throughout the Guanzhong region, there was none to compare with it.

Furthermore, he compiled the four collections of scriptures, making them exceedingly magnificent. During the process of transcription, he meticulously verified the texts to ensure there were no omissions or errors.
Every year on the eighth day of the second month, he performed the ritual bathing of the sacred image, held lectures, and established vegetarian feasts.

The assembly, moved by both compassion and reverence, recognizes that while receiving the precepts has purity as its foundation, we now dwell in this age of the Semblance Dharma and fear the occurrence of transgressions.
Therefore, at the beginning of spring, they prostrate before the twenty-five Buddhas and recite the Thousand-Turn Divine Mantra, hoping that those who have violated the prohibitions may be restored.
Purifying his source and cleansing himself, he ascended the dharma-seat to receive the teachings with clarity and without doubt.

At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, an imperial decree was issued for the Crown Prince and various princes to receive the Bodhisattva precepts from him. Subsequently, when the Eastern Palace established Puguang Temple, he was summoned to reside there;

furthermore, by imperial decree, he was to bestow the precepts upon the Empress, the consorts, and the ladies of the six palaces. As offerings and gifts arrived in abundance, he distributed them accordingly. When the temple was being constructed...

He established meritorious deeds without amassing wealth. Before long, the Empress commissioned the transcription of one *piṭaka* of scriptures at De-yeh Monastery within the imperial gardens, and the construction of a scripture repository along with the transcription of scriptures at Yanxing Monastery;
in both instances, she issued an edict for Wǎn to oversee and protect the works.

Consequently, the scrolls and fascicles that had been damaged or lost since the Zhou dynasty were all subjected to collation and correction. Thus, the restoration of the Dharma-treasure in its entirety was due to the efforts of Wǎn. (9)

In the first month of that year, he submitted a memorial to the Eastern Palace (the Crown Prince) setting forth four articles for the practice of compassion and the prohibition of killing, as well as for the observance of fasting in accordance with the seasonal energies;

he provided a table of contents for these and composed several hundred words of detailed exposition, which were exceedingly earnest and profound. The Eastern Palace responded favorably, though much of his reply has not been recorded here.

In this year, an imperial decree was issued prohibiting the killing of living beings from the third month until the end of the fifth month; however, because Huian had petitioned again, the Emperor granted a special exemption for the remainder of that year.
In the winter of the tenth year, he fell ill and submitted a memorial to the Eastern Palace (the Crown Prince) entrusting him with the Great Dharma.

Shortly thereafter, he presented his final testament, consisting of one fascicle each of the *Treatise on the King’s Rewards and Punishments and the Three Jewels*, the *Treatise on Nurturing the Common People*, and the *Treatise on the Three Virtues*. [Twelfth Month]
Seven days later, he passed away in his quarters at Yanxing Temple at the age of seventy-five. When the news reached the Eastern Palace, the Crown Prince was stricken with grief.
A posthumous title was conferred according to ritual protocol, and an imperial edict expressed deep sorrow and granted additional gifts.

Xiao Yu (Tiejin), Xiao Jing (Taifu), Li Boyao (Zongzheng), Du Zhenglun (Jianshi), and others, having all personally served as his disciples and observed the mourning rites for a master, offered incense and flowers.
With banners and canopies, tens of thousands of people escorted [the remains]. His disciples numbered over five hundred.
Following his instructions, they performed the cremation at Zhongnan Mountain Temple. A stupa was erected to enshrine the charred bones, and a sacred image was venerated.

Xiao Jun of Lanling, serving as the Master of the Horse for the Crown Prince, composed the inscription, while Li Boyao, Minister of the Court of the Imperial Clan, wrote the epitaph. During Fayuan’s lifetime, three thousand people received full ordination from him.

Other individuals who received the precepts of refuge numbered more than twenty million. Du Ruhui, the Right Vice-Director of the Chancellery, made a vow at the time of his death to serve as [the Master’s] teacher throughout successive kalpas.
The mother and siblings of General Xue Wancheng also held him in profound reverence as their model.
He maintained a vegetarian diet for the rest of his life. Dharma Master Daoyue of Puguang Temple possessed a profound understanding of the subtle and the hidden;
