he was disciplined in the precepts he received. At the beginning of the Wude era, when the empire was in chaos and itinerant monks had no means to beg for alms, Sengwan sold all his property and took out loans to provide for their sustenance.
He especially delighted in promoting those of talent and virtue. Although Vinaya Master Zhishou resided among the forests and springs, his fame spread throughout the capital.
Hu Gu. Ultimately, it was due to him that the study of *vinaya* flourished during the Tang dynasty;
indeed, it has its origins there. Tang Zichao’s surname was Tian. His ancestors were from Fengyi in Tongzhou, later migrating to Yuci in Bingzhou.

Zichao desired to escape the secular world from a young age, but because his parents had no other children, they constantly suppressed and discouraged him. When he reached the age of twenty, they forcibly arranged a marriage for him.
In his chamber, he sat upon the bed through the night and preached the Dharma for his wife; the wife was likewise moved to tears. After a long while, he took his leave.
At the age of twenty-seven, he went to the Kaihua Monastery in Li to receive the tonsure under Chan Master Huizan.

Having received full ordination, he immediately traveled to Dingzhou to investigate the Vinaya and receive instruction. After five years, his studies had reached completion, and he entered the region west of Taiyuan.
At Beishan, he established a Chan monastery and practiced meditative concentration from dawn until dusk. Monks who heard of his reputation came from afar.

At the beginning of the Daye era, the authorities prohibited monks from leaving their monasteries to beg for alms; Sengchao entered the capital intending to report this matter to the Emperor, but the Secretariat suppressed the matter as being non-essential and did not allow it to pass.
In his final years, bandits and thieves were rampant, and the Bingzhou region was particularly severe.
Hui-chao’s followers arrived like clouds, and grain piled up like mountains. One night, torches were carried and the gates were forced open as sharp blades converged upon them;
yet Chao sat as firm as a tree stump, remaining utterly unmoved. The bandits all bowed down in submission. Chao then used appropriate means to guide and encourage them toward goodness.
When the High Ancestor rose in righteous rebellion, Chao also moved to reside at Ningding Temple. In the second year of the Yining era, he entered the capital.
He was congratulated on his accession to the throne and was summoned for an audience at the Taicheng Hall.
The Left Vice-Director, Duke of Wei, Pei Ji, invited him to reside in a private courtyard of his own residence.

Not long after, the śramaṇas Lingrun, Zhixin, and Zhiguang, considering that a place frequented by the nobility was not a field for the tranquility of meditation, invited him to Huaganshi Temple on Mount Lantian in the fifth year of Wude.
In his later years, he again moved to Baofu Rock on Mount Jie in Jin. Subsequently, he returned to Guangyan Monastery in Jixiu County, Fenzhou.
This was likely because mountain forests were conducive to spiritual cultivation, while cities and markets were easier for engaging with others.
On the eleventh day of the third month in the fifteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away at Guangyan Monastery at the age of seventy-one. He was buried in Fenzhou.
On the southern mountain of the city lived Tang Jinglin, whose surname was Zhang. His ancestors were from Nanyang, but later they migrated to Huayuan in Jingzhao.
When Jinglin was still a child, a foreign monk passed by his home and sighed, saying, "This boy shall cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish; he must not be kept here."

He was among the dust of the secular world. At the age of seven, he followed worldly custom by leaving home to become a monk; this was not his original intention, so he eventually departed to follow other teachers.

After the calamity of the Zhou dynasty had lasted for a long time, he remained submerged and unable to rise. At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, he relied upon Dharma Master Tanmeng to study the teachings of meditative concentration and wisdom.
At that time, the fortunes of the Dharma were once again flourishing. Still in his early twenties as a śrāmaṇera, Senglin traveled south to Fanyang.
Having received full ordination, Deng soon traveled to Qingzhou and Qizhou, where he perused and investigated the Vinaya-piṭaka. He further studied the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* under Dharma Master Jue.
Subsequently, he returned to the capital of Ye, where he followed Dharma Master Ju to receive instruction on the meanings of the *Avataṃsaka*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, and *Saṃcaya-gāthā* sūtras.

Thereafter, as he led assemblies and propagated the teachings, his reputation grew even more prominent. Coincidentally, while visiting Puzhou and Jinzhou, he encountered the two Dharma Masters Daoxun and Daoshun.
He remained to lecture on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. After a long time, he sighed and said, "Medicine is intended to cure disease, yet taking medicine increases the illness;

how can this be right? Scholarship, knowledge, talent, and eloquence only serve to give rise to arrogance. One should seek instead that which cures them. Thereupon, he began to practice the methods of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *smṛtyupasthāna* (the foundations of mindfulness).

Shortly thereafter, he gradually advanced toward the Mahāyāna realization of non-attainment (*anupalambha*), and practiced the contemplations of the departure from discursive thought (*amanasikāra*) and consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
He entered Mount Bailu several times to abstain from grain. At dusk, he would ascend dangerous peaks and tall trees to sit upon them, often remaining there for ten days or more.
Later, while traveling to Mount Tai, he saw a light at night that illuminated the surrounding peaks and ridges; he immediately went to search for its source.

He visited Master Shu, with whom he discussed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. Suddenly, the master vanished. Not long after, he entered Guanzhong, where he met Dhyāna Master Tanqian, who explained the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* for him.
In the fourth year of the Renshou era, by imperial decree, he was sent to deliver śarīra relics to Shende Temple on Mount Shimen in Huayan.
There, he devoted himself to his studies. In the third year of the Daye era, the śramaṇa Huan Yuan invited him to lecture on the *Saṃparigraha-śāstra*.
The brilliant wheels and wondrous images of the various monasteries under the imperial capital had long since reached the Eastern Metropolis.

Prince Qi Jian, whose devotion was profound and his principles well-established, constantly sought his counsel for decision-making. Su Kui of the Court of State Ceremonial received the essential instructions of the Master;

likewise, the Śramaṇas Daoxiong and Doti of Gaoyang, Daoxian and Mingze of Zhaojun, and Chengcheng all benefited from his excellent guidance, attaining a profound understanding of the subtle and reaching the heights of sublime wisdom.

Question: "Those who cherish the Way are many; what specific practice do they devote themselves to? Answer: "The mountains and valleys are high and deep; where does one’s mind find its stability? Zhe said:

"The mountains are high and the valleys are deep; this has been so from the beginning. Answer: "If it is as the Tathāgata says, should one not take earth from elsewhere to fill the valleys and level them with the mountains?
Zhe sighed in admiration and submission. In the thirteenth year, he prepared a memorial to inform the Emperor, intending to undertake a western tour.
Regarding his spiritual traces: as bandits and marauders ran rampant, the roads were blocked and travel hindered; he managed to reach Xiang and Deng with great difficulty.

In the second year of the Yining era, an imperial edict summoned him to reside at Dazongchi Monastery in the capital. In the third year of the Wude era, Li An-yuan, Duke of Zhengping, petitioned for the construction of Hongfa Monastery to welcome him there to dwell.
He expounded primarily upon the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, or occasionally the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*. At night, he would remain in tranquil seclusion.

The Vinaya Master Xuǎnwǎn personally received the imperial model [of patronage] from Prince of Rénchéng and his mother, the Dowager Grand Mistress of Chǔguó and Princess of Ānpíng, both of whom invited him to their residences to confer the precepts.
Xiāo Jǐng, Director of the National Academy; Zhāng Liàng, Minister of Works; Dù Zhènglún, Minister of the Household;
and Lǐ Dàoyù, Minister of Agriculture, all became his disciples. Furthermore, he was requested by Zhìshǒu to [confer] the Vinaya.
The Master expounded the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* ten times in total. Leading the assembly of students, he caused them to receive and submit to his teaching;
even the śrāmaṇeras and attendants in the capital became clear regarding the characteristics of the Vinaya—was this not his achievement?

On the twenty-sixth day of the tenth month in the fourteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away in his quarters at Hongfa due to illness. On that day, there was previously a friend in the Dharma...

He came frequently to visit him. Daolin said to him, "I do not cling to this life, nor do I crave its karmic retribution; when conditions assemble, they exist, and when conditions disperse, they cease.
He further said, "By means of my own illness, I take pity on the illnesses of others," and he shed tears, contemplating the various realms of suffering.
He again admonished his disciples, saying, "The path of birth and death is long; each of you should strive to extricate yourselves from it. At that time, he was seventy years of age.
This was the sixth time. When he was cremated at Zhongnan’s Xiangsi Temple, his tongue alone did not decay;
even after being burned a second time, it remained increasingly bright and clean. His donors constructed a five-丈 wooden pagoda to commemorate his virtue.

While in Luoyi, Senglin once served as a tutor for Li Haode, a *tongshi sheren*, in his preparation for the imperial examinations; when Haode violated the national laws, Lin consequently went into hiding.

He sought deliverance to avoid the sin. Later, when the matter was discovered, Daolin was arrested and imprisoned. The Emperor personally granted him clemency. There were three people who had conspired to harm an enemy;
one of them later felt remorse and went to the forest to receive the precepts. Shortly thereafter, the one who had received the precepts died and then revived, saying: "I saw King Yama.
The King ordered me to confront the other two regarding the matter of conspiring to harm our enemy. I..."
Cheng claimed that he had received the precepts from Lin and no longer knew where Lin was, citing him as his witness.

When the King ordered the witnesses to be pursued, it was reported that Lin had already been reborn in the Suvarṇabhadra World (Golden Grain World) in another direction. Because of this, I was spared from punishment and released to return home.
Tanyun of the Tang dynasty was a native of Gaoyang. Historical records do not provide details regarding his clan or lineage. Having initially left the household life, he recited the Lotus Sūtra;
however, with two fascicles still remaining, he found the secular world too full of clamor and bustle, and thus withdrew to Mount Puwu on Mount Heng to complete his studies there.
A practitioner of meditation instructed him, saying, "The Way lies in observing the mind and remaining free from discursive thought; it cannot be attained through the mere recitation of sutras.
Having received these words, Huìyùn traveled extensively to Mount Wutai. Carrying only his shadow as a companion, he resided at Papaya Monastery on the Northern Terrace for over twenty years.
However, because the terrain was high and the climate cold, Huìyùn would sit until late at night; yet his thoughts remained somewhat dull and distracted, and what he had previously recited...

He could recollect the sutras instantaneously without forgetting them. During the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty, Master Zàn was engaged in the practice of meditative concentration in the Yanmen Valley;
he carried his rope bed on his back and remained in quiet contemplation wherever he stayed. Huiyùn heard of his reputation and went to rely upon him.

Subsequently, when Zàn received the imperial summons to attend the imperial meditation assembly, Huiyùn returned to Mount Bigan and later traveled through the southern regions, including the commanderies of Lishi, Longquan, and Wencheng. At...
This is the study of tranquility, which has profoundly reached both the Central Plains and the foreign lands.

Furthermore, in regions where the rules of the Vinaya had not yet arrived, there were those who had been tonsured for as long as thirty years yet remained śrāmaṇeras; upon reaching this time, they all finally obtained full ordination. Thus, the merit of Huiyun was indeed great.
In the sixteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away at Mount Pingyao in Xihe while sitting upright without illness.
He was over eighty years of age. From the age of nineteen, he entered the mountains; sixty years had elapsed since then. He maintained his mind with unwavering diligence.

During the prime of his vigor, lice and nits grew upon his body; he would listen to their biting and sucking, unable to bear the thought of discarding them, even though the number of these earth-lice was great upon his felt mats.

The blood coagulated. He also said, "This is the repayment of my past karmic debts; if even one is not eliminated, it will persist. Later, in his sixtieth year, he was entirely free of fleas and lice.
He remarked, "This is merely due to the decline of my vital energy (*ojas*). Yet I still thought that my karma had not yet been exhausted—how could this have come to pass?
He once said to his disciples, "I see that Master Chao always stayed in rooms infested with wall-fleas, yet he never..."

He was troubled by this. Furthermore, he ate at the home of a family afflicted by *gū* (a type of contagious pestilence), where the spoon scooped up the insects and placed them at the bottom of his vessel so that they would not cause harm.
The master of the *gū* was terrified and thought, "By what virtue of mine has this been brought about? He also wished to transcribe the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Suddenly, an excellent calligrapher appeared and requested to write it for him. Within less than ten days, the work was completed. Just as he was about to offer a monetary gift in gratitude, the man vanished. Because of this—

He treasured this scripture and concealed it within a mountain cave. Having passed through numerous rebellions and disorders, all other possessions were plundered and nearly exhausted; yet this sutra alone was abandoned amidst the wild thickets.

Although its outer case and wrapping had rotted away, the scrolls themselves remained as if newly made. Yùn lived in a state of constant austerity, exerting himself with increasing vigor even in his old age.
Whenever he grew slightly weary while sitting in meditation, he would immediately rise to prostrate before the Buddha; such was the nature of his self-discipline.
Huijin of the Tang dynasty, surnamed Bao, was a native of Shangdang in Lu. From childhood, he followed the precepts and restraints, though he had not yet received the tonsure.

At the age of thirteen, his fellow villagers, noting his refined austerity and his severing of affection and renunciation of desire—his refusal to take a wife or raise children arising from his sincere resolve—recognized his dedication.
They then went together to inform his parents, who permitted him to leave the household life. He first resided at Fanjing Temple in the commandery.
After receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), he immediately traveled to the capital of Ye to study and gather teachings.

However, because the Vinaya relies on circumstantial conditions and is not in accord with [mere] texts, he subsequently closed himself in retreat to recite what he had previously lectured upon eighty times. Just as he was hearing that Master Hong was establishing a teaching seat in Xiang, one...
He sat in meditation for eight years, practicing with reverence and without indolence. Consequently, he followed his teacher north and south to further his studies.
Calculating roughly from beginning to end, he investigated and extensively expounded the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* approximately three hundred times.

Those who have such single-minded dedication and accumulated merit are truly rare. Toward the end of the Sui dynasty, a monk of the same monastery, jealous of his abilities, spread slander about him outside the temple.
Jin said, "In this world, people often harbor resentment toward those who leave behind a name and a record; yet, as for the practice of non-contention, only Śūnyatā-janman (Subhūti) was truly so.
Though I am not quick-witted, I beg to follow after him. He then hastily uncovered his bundle and departed. The assembly collectively tried to detain him, but Jin said:
"I am constrained by these circumstances; it is not that I am truly attached to departing or remaining. Farewell, my friends!
How could I remain here in dejection for long? Thereupon, he traveled extensively through the northern part of Dongchuan, surveying the scenic wonders of Wutai, Taishan, Changshan, and Yanmen.
At that time, Master Huizhan was traveling toward the distant desert lands, so [the Master] went there once more to take him as his teacher.
Thus it was. When Sengzàn entered Guān, he went to visit the ancient traces of Náo and Xǔ upon the summit of Mount Jī. There he discovered the foundations of an old temple;

he rebuilt it and made it his dwelling. For more than thirty years, monastics and laypeople alike followed his example and gathered there, transforming that secluded and desolate place [into a center of practice].
He established a hall for formal inquiries. On the fifteenth day of the first month in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away at the mountain temple at the age of eighty-six.
Among those from his same hometown was Mingzan, who also followed the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. His physical presence was naturally magnificent;

in his later years, he suffered from a wind-related ailment that caused him to lose his usual decorum. Although his clothing became tattered and worn, his appetite remained undiminished. He frequently presided over the assembly.
He resided at Fazhu Monastery, where his influence spread throughout the provinces of Han, Lu, Qin, and Ze.
It is said that Tang Qingmai was a native of Zitrong in Shu. In his youth, he traveled to the capital.

During the Zhenguan era, after Tripitaka Master Xuanzang returned from the Western Regions, an imperial decree was issued to construct Guangfu Monastery for the posthumous ordination of Empress Taemu; it was also established for the purpose of translation. Regarding him...
Regarding all necessary administrative labor, consult entirely with Xuanling to ensure they are provided with generous support.

Furthermore, summon eleven persons of great virtue from various regions—those well-versed in the Mahayana and Hinayana sutras and shastras and highly esteemed by their contemporities—to serve as members of the Commission for Examining Doctrines.

Mài was indeed selected among them; they resided together at Cien Monastery. He authored the *Yijing tuji* (Record of the Translation of Scriptures) in four fascicles, which has circulated in the world.
Táng Tánguāng was the son of the Zhāng family of Bìn; from childhood until adulthood, he maintained pure aspirations and a refined character, [mastering] the various profound and subtle gateways.
There was no one who did not ascend [the path] and practice it. By the time he reached his而立 (zìlì) years, he had mastered the Vinaya-piṭaka in its full brilliance;

he established the fundamental tenets and formulated their meanings, becoming an object of veneration for all, who all regarded him as having been inspired by the instructions of the two masters, Huilü and Huishao. Master Huilü once pointed to him and said to others:
"That my Way has been transmitted to the region west of the Yellow River is entirely due to this man alone. Shortly thereafter, he again listened to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
He studied the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) under Master Yufu and cultivated the methods of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* under Master Xiang at Mount Song.

His concentration and wisdom mutually supported one another, and his observance of the precepts became increasingly prominent. When he reached the Eastern Capital, his long-standing virtuous reputation was brought to light;

he was appointed to serve as the presiding abbot and issued an imperial decree for him to reside at Tiangong Temple, whereupon he was further appointed as the *sthavira* (senior elder) of the monastery to provide guidance and care for the pure assembly. Thus, he extended his universal love to all.
His sincerity was truly rare throughout antiquity; there were none among those of the Western Vinaya school who did not consult him.

Consequently, his disciples and followers joined shoulder to shoulder and followed one after another, achieving great accomplishments. The Vinaya Master of Ximing Monastery, Jundu, stood out as a preeminent figure of his time and was also one whom Guang promoted.
In the second year of the Linde era, he lectured in the Eastern Capital, where master and disciples mutually guided and inspired one another.
I deeply admire him.
Fu Li of the Tang dynasty was born into the Huangfu clan of Jingzhao. He was serene and had few desires, devoting his mind to inner learning.
He left the household life to reside at Xingshan Monastery. He was quite renowned for his skill in poetic composition and was frequently visited by famous scholars. The Tripiṭaka Master Divākara...
Bodhiruci, Śikṣānanda, and others translated the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and other works; all of them received imperial edicts to compose the definitive texts.
In the second year of the Yonglong era, Quan Wuer, a Court Literatus to the Crown Prince, set forth ten points of doubt regarding the Buddhist scriptures.
He questioned him, subsequently interrogating and analyzing his points to clear away his obstructions.

He then composed the *Ten Gates for Discerning Delusions* (*Shimen bianhuo lun*) in three fascicles, establishing a dialogue between host and guest, and presented it to him. In a subsequent letter, Wuxing wrote:

"To extend the legs of the morning duck and to bore through the apertures of the primordial chaos—centuries of doubt have been instantly exhausted in a single moment. We shall forever follow the path of awakening and eternally realize the source of delusion."
He burned the firewood of afflictions and partook of the meal of nirvana. I entreat you to take these words to heart and spend the remainder of your years in this practice.
Thus did he bring joy and submission to those outside the Buddhist teachings; moreover, he profoundly mastered the profound mechanisms of reality and uniquely harmonized with the Dharma of the Mind.

His "Verses on Reality and Delusion" were especially widely circulated throughout the world, and Master Zongmi of Caotang alone recognized his excellence. A collection of his writings remains in circulation today.

Táng Huáisù’s surname was Fàn. His ancestors were originally from Nányáng. His great-great-grandfather, Yuè, served as the Assistant Magistrate of Qūwò County in Jiāngzhōu during the time of Emperor Gāozōng.
His grandfather, Huī, was the Magistrate of Guǎngwǔ County in Yánzhōu. His father, Qiáng, was the Director of the Right Guard of the Right Military Command;

all of them resided in Jīngmào, where they subsequently registered their household. His mother, Lady Lǐ, conceived after dreaming of thunder and lightning shaking with awe. Upon his birth, he was divine...
A light filled the room. Divination indicated that he would become a teacher to a sovereign. From childhood, he was intelligent and wise, possessing a mature and dignified bearing.

When he was barely ten years old, he suddenly requested permission from his parents to leave the household life. In the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, when the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang was returning from the Western Regions, [the youth] was able to serve him.
He first explored the sutras and śāstras; having received full ordination, he devoted himself exclusively to the study of the Vinaya under Fali of Ye Prefecture.

Vinaya Master [Daoxuan] was a preeminent master of his time. Having relied upon [the *Sifen lü*] for three years, he thoroughly pointed out its flaws and shortcomings, whereupon he sighed and said, "How could I simply abandon it?
In the first year of the Xianheng era, he resolved to compose a separate commentary on the *Sifen lü*.
In the third year of the Shangyuan era, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Xitaiyuan Temple, where he was permitted to lecture alongside Vinaya Master Daocheng.

By the first year of the Yongchun era, his commentary on the *Jiwen* (Recorded Texts) was completed; it comprised ten volumes in total, including two volumes of the *Sifen Sengni Jie-mo Wen* (Four-Part Monastic and Lay Ritual Texts for Karmavācanā) and one volume each of the *Sifen Sengni Jieben* (Four-Part Monastic and Lay Precept Manuals). Shortly thereafter, he fell ill and said to his disciple Xiuzhang, "My retribution..."
As he was about to pass away, there was the sound of music in the air; he then departed suddenly. His age was seventy-four, and his years of ordination were fifty-three.
He followed the Sarvāstivāda school as his primary tradition, adopting its principles regarding the magnitude of the path of practice, while rejecting sixteen errors found in ancient commentaries.

This work is not without its points of contradiction with the *Nanshan* [commentary]. During the Kaiyuan era, Vinaya Master Bin of Mount Song composed the *Zhuangshi zongji* (Record of Adorning the School) to explain it, serving as a counter-pole to the old commentaries.
Tang Ai was of the same clan as Zhao, a native of Tianshui. Her family had been of the gentry for generations.
Having renounced worldly life in her youth, after receiving full ordination, she instructed those who came to study her using the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*.

Those who followed her were as submissive as grass before the wind and as receptive as a valley before a torrential rain. Formerly, during the Liu Song period, there was the Tripiṭaka Master Jue from Kaśmīra.
Śrīmitra translated this Vinaya, and a single fascicle of the *Karmavācanā* was also circulated alongside it. After some time, these were lost and scattered, becoming impossible to recover.

Consequently, those in later generations had no basis upon which to rely. Therefore, [the present text] was excerpted from within the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* to form a single fascicle for practical application;
it appears to be a complete and perfect work. During the Shénlóng era, the Tripiṭaka Master Yìjìng took charge of the translation bureau.
By imperial decree, he was appointed along with Wen-gang to serve as a "Verifier of Meaning" (*zhengyi*) for the various scriptures being produced, to which he contributed significantly.

He authored ten fascicles of a commentary on the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. At the time of his death, he left an instruction to the Vinaya Master Xuan-jin of Ximing Monastery to polish and refine the work;
however, due to the An Shi Rebellion, it was subsequently lost. How tragic!
Tang Daoliang was born into the Zhu family of Yue. He entered the monastic order at the age of eight and became thoroughly versed in the scriptural teachings.

Having received full ordination, he studied the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) under masters in the region of Hexi and subsequently expounded upon the great *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra. He later retired to a secluded and remote place to practice meditative concentration, until his reputation resounded throughout the seas and the lands.
In the first year of the Shenlong era, an imperial edict was issued for him to enter the Inner Daochang of Changle with ten masters to observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
At that time, the Emperor personally received the Bodhisattva precepts from him. While the Crown Prince was still the Prince of Xiang, he sent him a brocade quilt and felt mats.

In the second year, an edict was issued for him to discourse on the Way at the Western Garden. There, the Metropolitan Commander Li Xiaoyi, the Minister of Works Zhang Xi, and Zhou Ye of the National University [attended].
Cui Rong, Secretary-General; He Zhizhang, Director of the Imperial Library; and Kang Xun, Regional Inspector of Muzhou, all formed a teacher-disciple relationship with him.

They maintained the sacred incense and inquired after the essentials of Chan. He passed away at the age of eighty-two. His disciples, including Huiyuan, erected a stupa for him, and Wan Qirong composed the inscription.

Master Tang Xiugong was a native of Qian’an. Having encountered the mourning for his parents at the age of seven, he immediately took refuge with Vinaya Master Xing of the Shu region and entered the monastic order.
There he devoted himself to recitation and study, and subsequently received full ordination under him;

thus, his mastery of the *vinaya* flourished, and he became the foremost successor in the transmission of the precepts from Master Xing. After four years, he traveled to Chang’an and attended the lectures of Vinaya Master Xuanchong.
He refined and mastered the various sections of the canon with such diligence that he forgot all weariness. For sixteen years, he entered and emerged from his study cell;
how then could the depth of what he created and the richness of what he attained ever be exhausted by words? Thereafter, he returned to his native village like a brocade.
He repaid the kindness of his birthplace by traveling throughout Li’an, where he extensively disseminated his lectures and instructions.

Among his disciples, there was the Vinaya Master Zhen gu, whose understanding surpassed all others; those who achieved mastery under him were beyond counting. He passed away at Shili Temple in Anzhou at the age of seventy.

Táng Dégǎn, surnamed Hóu, was a native of Tàiyuán. He possessed a magnificent and handsome appearance and was exceptionally well-versed in his studies. Regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, he was as proficient as one could wish.
During the reign of Emperor Gāozōng, he was summoned by imperial decree to serve as a Great Virtuous One (*bhadanta*) for the translation of scriptures.

Furthermore, together with Shèngzhuāng, Dàyí, and others, he participated in the translation bureau of Yìjìng, where his expositions were highly commended by the Emperor. He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Chāngpíng County and received successive [honors].
His estate eventually comprised three thousand households. The Emperor bestowed upon him this encomium: "An excellence of the He-汾 region; an elite of the mountains and peaks.

Early on you cast off worldly burdens; long ago you untied the silken cords of dust. The monastic community looks up to your virtue; the blue-roofed temples spread your fame. You truly rival Nāgārjuna and equal Mātr̥ceṭa;
the gates of the teaching rejoice in your brilliance. Later, he served as the *karmadāna* (administrative head) of Foshouji Monastery in Henan. Shortly thereafter, he was promoted.
He was appointed to the monastic administration; both within and without the monastery, all were struck with solemn reverence. He passed away at over sixty years of age.
He authored the *Yimen* (Gate of Righteousness), which remains in circulation in the world. Dao Yin of the Tang dynasty was born into the Changsun family of Gaoqing in Chang’an.

His father was Rong, a Palace Attendant Censor, and his mother was Lady Ma. She conceived after dreaming that five-colored clouds covered her head. Upon giving birth, a fragrant aroma filled the room. As a child, he was exceptionally handsome and gifted.
He passed the examination for the Zhongjinshi degree, bringing glory to his kin and compatriots. Once, a Buddhist monk from India was passing by his gate while begging for alms;

having finished his meal, he wished to depart, but [Henyou] looked at him and said, "It is already dusk. Consequently, the monk stayed overnight. They conversed until the second watch of the night, during which the Indian monk frequently extolled the merits of leaving the household life (*pravrajyā*).
At dawn, the monk took his leave and departed; before they had gone far, he vanished from sight. From that time on, Henyou no longer pursued an official career.

He then went to the capital city and took the Vinaya Master Shenyan of Zhaofo Temple as his preceptor, whereupon he received the tonsure. After receiving full ordination, he diligently studied the sūtras and śāstras.
Previously, the Dharma Master Fuli of Xingshan Temple, who was skilled in composition, had him write a hymn in praise of the Western [Pure Land] to test his literary talent.
His phrasing was elegant and his meaning was profound; those who read it felt as though they were personally born in the Pure Land. And...

Beholding the venerable countenance with his own eyes, he bowed to the Master’s left and right and marveled at him for a long time. He then proclaimed to the assembly that Huiyin’s discourses were truly unsurpassed.
Upon receiving an imperial edict, he was ordered to accompany the Emperor—along with Fayou, Liangxiu, and Faxiu—to visit Luoyang.
Shortly thereafter, he composed a commentary on the *Sutra on Purifying Karmic Obstacles*. Once the commentary was completed, the Censor Li Jing requested it be presented at Tiangong Temple.
The discourse was opened. At that time, Master Xiying submitted a memorial requesting that a forum for debate be established at Fuxian Temple.

He proposed to assemble the most eminent scholars from throughout the land—those whose learning encompassed both the inner (Buddhist) and outer (non-Buddhist) traditions—to establish the systems of Yogācāra, Vijñaptimātra, Hetuvidyā, Śataśāstra, and so forth, and to discuss the fundamental tenets of these great doctrines in order to demonstrate the flourishing of the Buddha-dharma. Thereupon, the assembly collectively recommended Xiying to be the first to ascend the seat. And...
In the debates on the six categories of logic, [the opponents] were ultimately all defeated and humbled. Xingyi sighed and said to them, "The Dharma has its foundation;

even my death would be sufficient. Subsequently, as he was returning by carriage, the Emperor issued an edict for him to attend the imperial entourage as before. Just then, having contracted a slight illness, he submitted a memorial to decline the honor.

The Emperor dispatched an imperial messenger to bestow upon him a prescription and medicine. The edict stated: "If the Dharma Master takes this prescription along with the medicine, his ailment will surely be cured.
Once recovered, come early to the Western Capital so that we may meet. Such was the regard and favor shown to him. When Xingyuan passed away, he was buried at the Bronze Man Plain in Lantian.
Those who escorted him included officials from the Eastern Palace downward, as well as those of the ninth rank and above among the capital officials, together with the scholar-gentry.

There were approximately ten thousand men and women among the commoners. An imperial decree was issued to establish a *zhāi* (fasting ritual), and Yìn performed the *bái biǎo* (ritual of confession and dedication) services.
The Chancellor, Zhang Yan-gong Shuè, stepped forward alone and took Yìn’s hand, saying, "A later-generation talent of the Śākya gate, rare indeed within these borders.

I pray that you will record for me the lamentation I previously composed, so that it may be preserved within my precious casket. In the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, an imperial decree was issued [to perform the rites] at Huanao.
In the Hall, as they were deliberating on the relative superiority of the two teachings, the Daoist Yin Qian faltered in his responses and his arguments deviated from the core principles.

The Emperor bestowed five hundred bolts of silk upon Huìyī to honor his ability. When the Emperor reached the passage in his commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*—from "If there are those who, due to the karmic offenses of previous lives, should fall into evil realms" up to "their karmic offenses are extinguished, and they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi"—he remained in doubt at the end.

[The Emperor] found this erroneous, yet he did not immediately take up his brush. He subsequently issued an edict to inquire of Yinyuan. Yinyuan replied that it was due to the power of the Buddha and the power of the sutra;
even those of the Ten Sages and Three Worthies could not fathom it. "Your Majesty previously, within the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, received various perfumings [of the teachings].

If you further immerse yourself in focused contemplation, the manifest activities [of wisdom] will spontaneously appear. The Emperor attained a sudden and profound realization. Yinyuan then composed a commentary for him to lecture upon the *Qing* [Sutra].

At the three monasteries of Longxi, Ximing, and Chongfu, the floors of the lecture halls were all constructed using fragrant mud. Those scholars who came daily to listen, holding new commentaries, numbered in the thousands.
He authored one scroll of the *Duiyu lunheng* (A Balanced Discourse for the Imperial Presence) and five scrolls of the *Dasheng famen* (The Dharma Gates of the Mahāyāna).
He authored one fascicle each of *Mingjiao bing xin fayi* (The Name-Teachings and Faith in Ritual) and *Weishi shu* (Commentary on the Treatise on Consciousness-Only).

He also wrote six fascicles of *Fahua jing shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) and six fascicles of *Yuzhu jingang jing shu* (Imperial Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra). On the sixteenth day of the seventh month in the twenty-eighth year, he passed away and submitted a final memorial.
The Emperor dispatched the Inner Attendant Jia Wenxiang to deliver an imperial decree of condolence and bestow fifty rolls of silk.
This was to assist in his enshrinement. His age was seventy-three; his years as a monk were fifty-three.
On the thirteenth day of the eighth month of that year, he was buried beside the Xiaoyao Garden on Mount Zhongnan.

Tang Guangyi was a member of the imperial clan, the son of Prince Langye. During the reign of Empress Wu, he rose in arms with the Prince of Yue and was executed along with his entire clan for his offense.

At the time, Guangyi was still in his swaddling clothes; his wet nurse secretly carried him away and fled among the common people. When he reached the age of eight, an imperial edict was issued to search for him with great urgency.
The wet nurse, fearing [the consequences], abandoned him for good. Jingyi traveled alone and ultimately perished from cold and hunger.
He took refuge under an elderly monk and shaved his head at Qinglong Monastery. As he grew older, he became thoroughly versed in the *sūtras* and *vinaya*, and practiced meditation in seclusion.

He considered the joy of renunciation to be truly incomparable to worldly honor, profit, fame, or success. It happened that Emperor Zhongzong issued an edict to seek out the descendants of the Prince of Langye.
Yi Yin subsequently confessed the truth to the temple master. The temple master was greatly alarmed and immediately reported it to the Prefectural Governor of Fufeng.
The Governor, pleased with his appearance, pressured him to take his daughter as a wife, but Yi Yin refused. He promptly informed the authorities, who summoned him for an audience.

An imperial edict was issued ordering him to return to secular life and inherit his father’s fief, but he earnestly declined, expressing his wish to maintain his resolve and retire to the mountains and valleys. The Emperor granted his request and further permitted him to repair and maintain the *ārāma* (monastery).
He led his disciples to reside there. By nature, he had always cherished the sublime beauty of the mountains and waters of Zhongnan.

Since the restoration of various temples during the Faxing era, hermitages and monasteries have been established there in great numbers. Those who attended upon and looked after him were often several thousand people;
even high-ranking officials and ministers could not rival this, which was simply due to the power of the situation. In the twenty-third year of the Kaiyuan era.

On the twenty-third day of the sixth month, having finished gathering his disciples and bestowing his final instructions, he lay with his head to the north, his arm as a pillow, and passed away reclining on his right side.
His disciples, following his last testament, buried him at the southern end of Shaoling Yuan. They subsequently established Tianbao Temple on that site.
His disciples have maintained this tradition through the generations.
Xuanyan, whose secular surname was Xu, was a native of Zhuji in Yue. At the age of twelve, he entered the monastic order under the tutelage of the monk Huī of Fuchun.
In the first year of the Zhengsheng era, by imperial decree, he received full ordination and was registered at Xuānlìu Monastery. Upon reaching his early twenties, he followed Guang...
Master Zhou'an received the full precepts. At that time, the two Vinaya masters Chongfu and Rongji were both training disciples in the capital;

Yan went to rely upon them, entered their inner chambers, and received their certification of realization. Consequently, his reputation grew significant. When Emperor Ruizong received the precepts at An Guo Monastery, he was summoned by imperial decree to serve as a Great Virtue (Dade).
Later, he returned to the region south of the Yangtze River, where he specialized in instructing others through the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya). Shortly thereafter—
He resided at Mount Fahu and extensively expounded the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. Those who traveled with straw sandals and bamboo staffs came to hear his lectures and request the precepts;
they gathered like clouds and settled like still winds. In this manner, for nearly thirty years, he did not rise from his seat.

In the twenty-fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, an imperial edict was issued to promulgate the Emperor’s own commentary on the sutra throughout the realm. Yuan Yan-chong, the Regional Inspector of Henan, personally visited him.

While at Mount Zhong, he was invited to preside over the administration of the commandery, where a banquet was prepared and this sutra’s great meaning was chanted and expounded to accord with the Emperor’s wishes.
Previously, Master An of Guangzhou had once dreamed that a divine monk said to him, "Xuan Yan is truly a vessel for the Dharma of this age;
to instruct him in the Hīnayāna would be to let him go to waste. He had always exhorted him to propagate the Prajñāpāramitā, and now, at last, his aspirations were fulfilled.
Was this not, indeed, destiny? Before long, he donated his robes and alms bowl internally and exhorted lay donors externally to adorn the hundred-foot Maitreya statue at Shicheng.
Qi Han, the Regional Inspector of Runzhou, possessed an exceptionally vast mind and regarded all things with impartiality;
he provided a fleet of boats to welcome the image solemnly to Danyang. Furthermore, the prefectures of Yuhang and Wuxing [provided for] those newly ordained...
Wherever his influence reached, from Guangling to Xian’an, across a territory of a thousand *li*, nearly ten thousand people partook of his regulations and were bathed in his virtue;

the flourishing of such auspicious conditions was truly like this. On the seventh day of the eleventh month in the first year of the Tiānbǎo era, he manifested illness and passed away while seated at the Jìtán (Precept Altar) Hall of the monastery.
He was sixty-eight years of age. The site for his interment was selected on the second [day] of that same month.
Tenth: He was interred beneath Mount Qinwang, where a stupa was erected and pines were planted to mark the site. Wan Qirong composed a text to commemorate his virtues, which is not recorded here.
Yanyan recited the *Sūtra of the Names of the Buddhas* one hundred times and established ten banquets for the Unrestricted Assembly (*mucalinda-pūjā*).

He authored the *Fupian ji* (Record of the Auxiliary Chapters) in ten fascicles, the *Jie-mo shuchang* (Expositions on the Karma-vastu) in three sections, and the *Jingang yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Diamond Sūtra) in seven fascicles.
He lectured on the commentary to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* one hundred times.

Huideng of Tang was a native of Xing County in Donglai. Having received the tonsure during the reign of Emperor Zhongzong and subsequently attained full ordination, he came to admire the character of the Tripitaka Master Yijing and thus set out for the Western Regions.

He first traveled by sea for three years, visiting various kingdoms throughout the South Seas before reaching Central India, where he paid homage at sacred sites, sought out Sanskrit manuscripts, and consulted with learned masters.
"Good friend, for thirteen years there has been no one who did not take the Pure Land as their true refuge and Amitābha as their excellent guide.

Having received these dharma instructions, I have desired to benefit others; thus, carrying my mendicant's staff, I returned to my home country. After traveling for another four years, I reached the kingdom of Gandhāra in North India.
At a great mountain to the northeast, I fasted for seven days and nights, prostrating myself until the end of my life."
He vowed to pray for a manifestation of Avalokiteśvara. Suddenly, from the midst of the air, there appeared a figure of purple-gold color, over ten feet tall, seated upon a precious lotus flower.
With his right hand, the deity stroked [the practitioner’s] head and addressed him, saying: "You should exhort all sentient beings to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and recite the sutras."
"Having been reborn in the Western Pure Land, the World of Ultimate Bliss, the Land of Amitābha Buddha, once you have reached that realm, you shall see the Buddha and me;

the benefits you will obtain there will surpass those of all other practices. Having said this, he suddenly vanished. [Huiyuan] was so exhausted from fasting for days that he was severely weakened, yet upon hearing the Dharma, he felt restored with vigor.
He immediately crossed the Xiliang Ridge and traversed the shifting sands for eighteen years until he reached the capital, where he began his propagation of the teachings.
In the seventh year of the Yuan era, he presented a true image of the Buddha and Sanskrit scriptures [to the Emperor]. By imperial decree, he was granted the title "Tripitaka Master Cimin.

He also authored the *Wǎngshēng Jìngtǔ Jí* (Collection on Rebirth in the Pure Land), which circulated widely; furthermore, he established that *qú* (Asafoetida) is one of the five pungent vegetables (*wǔxīn*).

However, many scholars of the Vinaya in the Eastern Land could not identify it, some mistaking it for *yūntái* (mustard greens), *húsuī* (coriander), or *āwèi* (Asafoetida). Thus, regarding the Pure Land...
I have recorded this in detail to enlighten those who come after. Regarding the five pungent vegetables (*pañca-garaka*), there are only four in this land.
*Hiṅgu* is a corruption of the Sanskrit; in Chinese it is called "form-endowed" (*xingju*). Its root resembles a small turnip but is white in color, and its odor is like garlic.

I personally saw it in the kingdom of Yutian (Khotan); it does not exist in other countries. At that time it was mid-winter, and while the branches and leaves had already withered away, only the root remained.

He kept its roots to await consumption, speaking daily of the appearance of the roots, which were extraordinary; yet while he was detailed in his descriptions, he could not provide such detail regarding the branches and leaves.
He passed away in the seventh year of the Tiānbǎo era at the age of sixty-nine. His stupa was erected on Báilùyuán.

Fashen of the Tang dynasty was born into the Guo clan of Jiangdu. Having attained a degree of intellectual maturity, he resolved to leave the household life; though his parents loved him, they could not dissuade him.
Having received full ordination from Vinaya Master Cheng of Yaotai Monastery, he subsequently studied the Vinaya-piṭaka at Dongta Monastery in Taiyuan.

His discourse reached the subtle and profound, and his principles accorded with the mysterious essentials; those who understood him held him in the highest esteem and submission. The assembly requested him...

Appointed to a leadership position, he then returned quietly to the east. He devoted himself to reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the heart-mantra of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha* (the *Ruyilun Xinzhou*).

He transformed his native village; the details of all his undertakings cannot be fully recounted, but in brief, they were solely for the purpose of exalting the gates of the Exoteric Teachings (*Kyo*) and spreading the seats of the Dharma (*Hō*).
Furthermore, Yangzhou was a strategic hub in the southeast, where officials of the imperial court and the local gentry...

Whenever anyone came to visit him, they invariably had to submit a written request at his gate; yet, they considered it a source of great comfort to obtain an audience with him, and regarded failing to do so as a profound disgrace.
Consequently, the Palace Attendant Lu Zangyong sighed upon retiring and said:

"Within this universe, there truly are men of lofty character, such as Lu Xiangxian, Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent; Bi Gou, Minister of War; and the Director of the Imperial Household Office..."
Lu Yüqing; Yan Tingzhi, Minister of the Ministry of Personnel; Cui Xiyi, Governor of Henan; Fang Guan, Grand Marshal;
Cui Huan, Chief Secretary and Participant in State Affairs; Li Cheng, Vice Minister of Rites; Qi Mutian, Director of the Bureau of Historiography;
and the renowned scholar Wang Changling—all of whom provided support and wished to assist in the maintenance [of this site]. The tenth month of the seventh year of the Tiānbǎo era.

On the fourteenth day, he arose at dawn and, having washed and rinsed his mouth, sat cross-legged upon a low stool facing west in silence. At dusk, he passed away in the detached quarters of Longxing Temple.

He was eighty-three years of age, sixty-two years since his ordination. His disciples, both monastic and lay, extended from the Si and Yi rivers in the north to beyond the Ling and Jiao mountains in the south;
those who came to wail for him numbered in the thousands, and those who escorted his funeral procession reached ten thousand. This is how it was obtained:
The preeminent masters of the Dharma were Tanyi of Kuaiji and Huaiyi of Fujian, among others. They erected a stupa on the plains of Shugang to the west of the city.
Li Hua of Zhaojun, serving as Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel, composed the inscription which was engraved upon a stele.
Zhang Congshen, Rectifier of the Court of Judicial Review, performed the calligraphy, while Li Yangbing of Zhaojun inscribed the seal characters for the title.
Tang Daocuo’s secular surname was Wei, and he was a native of Fenshui in Bingzhou. While still young, living as a layman, he already displayed a spirit of reverence and humility.

At the age of fourteen, he left the household life. He lectured on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* twenty-four times. Later, he received the dhyāna teachings from Master Zàn, practicing them with exceptional diligence.
After some time, he inherited the legacy of Master Tanyou regarding the Pure Land, and subsequently established the Dharma [at] Xuanzhong Temple in Shibigou Valley.

In the region where the Master had previously resided, he practiced the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi* and the nine grades and ten contemplations of the Vaipulya sutras, and lectured on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* nearly two hundred times.
While Tanluan was practicing the path, a monk in meditative concentration saw the rosary he held; when he measured its size, it was as vast as a mountain of the seven treasures.
He beheld the wondrous realm of the West, so profuse and intricate that it was difficult to describe. Consequently, both monastics and laypeople vied with one another [to follow his example].
Biography. Huawang was born in the Shu region. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Zhenguan era, as his natural lifespan came to an end, he took leave of the assembly.
Upon hearing this, those who knew him rushed to him, filling the mountains and valleys.

All saw Dharma Master Luan arriving by floating through the air on a boat made of the seven treasures, who told Huawang: "Your Pure Land Hall is complete; it is only that your residual karmic retribution has not yet been exhausted."

Furthermore, he saw transformation-buddhas standing in the midst of the void, with celestial flowers raining down; both men and women were able to catch them on the hems of their robes, which were thin, smooth, and lovely.

At times, they would plant lotus flowers in dry ground, and they did not wither for seven days. When Daocuo reached the age of seventy, his appearance and physical strength remained exceptionally vigorous;
his teeth grew back like those of a child, and his speech was grand and eloquent. He redoubled his efforts in exhorting others to mindfulness. Daocuo further...
He personally drilled one hundred and eight wood *huánzǐ* beads to give to others and authored the two-fascicle *Jìngtǔ lùn* (Treatise on the Pure Land).

His citations and authorities were all drawn from Vasubandhu, Nāgārjuna, Huiyuan, and others; thus, among his followers, there were those who used hemp seeds as a measure, accumulating them until they filled several *hù*.
Daocuo never turned away from the west during his four daily postures, and he constantly recited the name of the Honored One.
The title [of this work] is dated to the seventh year of the [Tianbao] era. Meanwhile, the śramaṇa Daofu fled from the Hongfu Monastery in the capital to seek refuge there.
This year, Jue is eighty-four years old, yet he remains robust and free from ailment; is this not perhaps the result of the power of his diligent cultivation?
Jianzhen of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Chunyu and was a native of Jiangyang County in Guangling.

In his early childhood, while attending to his father at Dayun Temple, he was moved to realization upon seeing a Buddhist statue and requested to leave the household life. His father, marveling at his resolve, granted him permission.

He subsequently followed the Chan Master Zhiman to receive instruction. In the first year of the Chang’an era, an imperial edict was issued for the ordination of monks throughout the realm; consequently, he was enrolled in the temple.
He became a *śāntivihārin*. The "Great Cloud" [Temple] is the present-day Longxing Temple. At the beginning of the Shénlóng era, he first received the Bodhisattva precepts from Vinaya Master Dà'àn.
At the beginning of the Jǐnglóng era, he again went to Cháng'ān’s Shíjì Temple to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) from Vinaya Master Héngjǐng of Jingzhou.
He toured the two capitals, refined his understanding of the Tripiṭaka, and after several years had passed, he prepared to return home.
Huaihai benefited sentient beings through the precepts and regulations, becoming a preeminent leader of the school in that region.
During the Kaiyuan era, the Japanese śramaṇas Ryōe and Fushō paid homage at his true remains and requested, saying: "Our country lies within the great ocean;

In the world, there is certainly no obstruction caused by distinctions of self and other; yet, whenever a teacher or model arrives, people often find it difficult to accept him.

Zhenyin was moved by his intention and asked: "I have heard that in the past, Master Huisi of Mount Nanyue..."

He has become king and established a great teaching. Furthermore, we hear that the Prime Minister Chōbuku has commissioned a thousand *kāṣāyas* to be placed on a ship to be offered to the renowned and virtuous masters of the Middle Kingdom.
Moreover, he has embroidered a verse upon the hems of the robes, saying: "Though mountains and rivers lie in different regions, wind and moon share the same sky;
entrusted to you, O sons of the Buddha, may we together form future karmic bonds. Judging by this, it is truly a land of goodness; why should I remain here?

Abandoning [his original plan], he did not proceed with this journey. Instead, in the sixth month of the second year of the Tiānbǎo era, he recruited fourteen bhikṣus, including Sītuo, who purchased a boat and loaded it with the sūtras and vinaya.
They traveled by way of the Yangzi River to the port of Yuèzhōu, where they prepared to set sail for Fēngshān.
Encountering fierce winds and towering waves, the boat was on the verge of sinking. Suddenly, they saw a divine general standing in the sky, clad in armor.
The wind and waves soon subsided. After witnessing the wonders of the Snake Sea, the Fish Sea, and the Bird Sea that he traversed, he finally reached the shore and arrived in Japan.

The King personally came out to welcome him and led him into the city, where he was settled in a great temple. He immediately established a ritual altar in the Vairocana Hall of that temple and conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon the King;
