The local people regarded him as a śramaṇa of virtuous conduct and took him as their teacher. He ordained four hundred śrāmaṇeras, including Cheng and Xiu, and instructed them in the *śukla-karman* (white ritual) procedure.
Daily, those from the kingdom came to build monasteries and donate fields; he was thus titled "Great Upādhyāya.

Later, without illness, he took his leave of the assembly and passed away at Tiānpíng Bǎosì Monastery on the fifth day of the fifth month in the seventh year, the *guīmǎo* year. This was the [first] year of the Daì era.
The era was the first year of Zongguang. His lifespan was seventy-seven years.

Tang Weiqu was surnamed Lian, a descendant of Chen, a high official of the Qi dynasty. A native of Lu in Shangdang, he entered the monastic order at the age of nine under his maternal uncle, who was renowned within the Buddhist community.
After some time, he took his leave to travel for study, focusing on the teachings and principles of Chan.
He investigated the Way of the Vinaya without exception. At the age of forty, he was still residing in the capital. At that time, the former Chancellor Fang Rong had already passed away;
his descendants were living in the imperial mansion he had been granted. One day, they invited him for a vegetarian feast, but the meal had not yet been served.
He brought out one case of scriptures and said, "This is the ten-fascicle *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* translated by this official while he was in the South Sea. Now there are only ten monks at this banquet;

let each monk take one fascicle to establish a karmic connection. As Huìkè’s seat was the fourth, he received a fascicle and saw Pūrṇa’s inquiry regarding the meaning of the arising [of consciousness].
Finding the phrasing elegant and the principles profound, he then vowed to compose a commentary to circulate it. Upon reaching...
He returned to his residence at Chongfu Temple and immediately painted an image of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva while reciting the bodhisattva’s name.
For ten years, his resolve did not waver. Suddenly, he dreamed that Mañjuśrī, riding upon a lion, entered his mouth.

From then on, when he took up the brush, it was as if divinely assisted. This was the year Bingzi of the Dali era. When the commentary was completed, he again dreamed that Mañjuśrī emerged from his mouth; it consisted of three fascicles. Today...
It became widely prevalent in the world. According to one account, Chan Master Shenxiu of Dumensi Temple in Jingzhou obtained the original text while entering the palace.
Not long after, the śramaṇa Huizhen of Guntao transmitted it to Daoke, who circulated it.
Subsequently, Dharma Master Hengyuan of Zizhong in Shu composed the *Yizhang*, which is titled the *Zizhong Shu*.
Táng Shǒuzhí, courtesy name Jiāndào, was surnamed Fàn and was a native of Qiántán. He was the eighth-generation descendant of Fàn Wáng, the Táng dynasty Governor of Xìn'ān.
Having undergone tonsure, he subsequently relied upon Master Yuán of Zhīxíng Monastery in Sū to receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*).

On the evening of his ascent to the ordination platform, he alone beheld a light more than one *zhàng* in length; after a long while, it vanished. This was the sign of his attainment of the precepts. Thereafter, he relied upon...
The Venerable Zhen of Jiangling spent three years traveling throughout the land to pay homage to all sacred sites, thereby broadening his knowledge and experience.
He subsequently followed the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra to receive the Bodhisattva precepts. From the Great Master Pujì, he received the Heart-Seal of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
He lectured on the *Awakening of Faith* twenty times and the *Nanshan Vinaya Commentary* forty times. His original vow was to recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and so...
During the middle watch of the night, he dreamed that a divine being bestowed upon him a pearl. Upon waking, he felt a sense of wonder as if the pearl were still held in his grasp.
He subsequently entered Mount Wutai, where he read and recited [the scripture] some two hundred times to fulfill his vow. Furthermore, he perused the Tripitaka three times.
In the twenty-sixth year of the Kaiyuan era, by imperial decree, he was nominated for his eminent conduct and consequently registered at Dalin Monastery on Mount Lu. Great...
In the second year of the [Yongping] era, he moved his residence to Lingyin Peak in India (Tianzhu).

On the third month of the fifth year, he took up lodging at the Jingtu Monastery in Longxing and said to his disciples: "As for those of ultimate virtue, they come riding upon Suchness and depart riding upon Suchness.
Yet, how could those who wish to bind the bright sun with long ropes be worthy of even discussing this with me? On the second day of that same month...
On the nineteenth day, he passed away. His age was seventy-one; his years since ordination were forty-five. A stupa was erected for his interment.
His disciple Jiaoran (Jiao Ran) composed an inscription for him.
Tang Yuanzhao, surnamed Zhang, was a native of Lantian in Jingzhao. At the age of ten, he relied upon Vinaya Master Jingyun of Ximing Monastery and received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

He subsequently investigated the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Hetuvidyā*, *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, and the new translations of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

He frequently presided over Dharma assemblies and repeatedly served as the master of ordination platforms. During the Kaiyuan era, an imperial edict summoned him to participate in translation work. The tenth year of the Dali era...
In the third year, an imperial edict was issued for fourteen eminent monks (dàdé) presiding over ordination platforms from the two monastic districts to proceed to An Guo Temple.

There, they were to adjudicate the merits and defects of the new and old versions of the *Sūtra*. As their talent and learning were exceptionally abundant, the details of the compositions they compiled and produced are mostly not recorded here.

He rendered significant service to the gates of the teachings. During the reigns of the Daizong and Suzong emperors, he was particularly prominent in affairs. His official rank reached that of Yingfeng (Attendant).

He was granted the purple robe and appointed as a "Liantan" (Altar-Officiant) for the two streets, a "Ten-Wish" (Shiwang) Great Virtue, an Inner Chamber Attendant (Neichongfu), and an Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Shaqing).
He held a fief of one hundred households. He passed away at the Biyuan Monastery at the age of eighty-two and with fifty-eight years of ordination seniority.
Tang Biancai, surnamed Li, was a native of Xiangyang. At the age of seven, he entered the monastic order under Chan Master Ji of Mount Xian. As he grew older, he excelled in memory;

whenever he received a scripture, he invariably limited himself to one passage at a time. He would not ask about a matter twice, nor would he contemplate a meaning more than once. His teacher held him in high esteem.
At sixteen, he underwent the tonsure ceremony and was registered at Dayun Temple in his hometown. He then traveled extensively.
Traveling through the famous mountains of various commanderies, he was suddenly ordained at Yuquan Temple in Jingzhou.

Having long heard of the reputations of Vinaya Master Huaiwei of Anguo Temple and Vinaya Master Yiban of Ba’en Temple in the capital, he immediately went there to request instruction from them. Both masters esteemed him as their preeminent disciple.
In the fourteenth year of the Tianbao era, the Emperor observed that those in the northern regions were accustomed to horsemanship and archery, and were fond of slaughter.

Regarding those with a fierce and unruly temperament who indulge in military prowess and toy with weapons, it is appropriate that they be guided toward goodness and brought to submission through gentleness.

When the Emperor first ascended the throne, he issued an edict for [the Master] to preside over ordination ceremonies at the altar to provide instruction and admonition. At the beginning of the Zhide era, the Chancellor Du Hongjian petitioned that he reside at Longxing Temple.

An imperial edict was issued appointing him as the Great Virtuous One (Dade) and Professor within the jurisdiction of Shuofang, in the hope that the people of the Xianyun region might gain some understanding of the Vinaya teachings.
He was further commanded to establish a Lotus Sūtra practice hall for the state. Upon his return to the two capitals, he was repeatedly honored with imperial letters of praise.
In his later years, he applied himself particularly to the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna. In the second year of the Yongtai era, when Puqu Huai...
When An Pan incited the Tibetans to invade the borders, [the Master] enlightened him with discourse on cause and effect, fortune and calamity, whereby the horrors of slaughter were quelled.
In the third year of the Dali era, he was summoned by imperial decree to serve as the Great Virtue (Dade) of Zhangxin.
At that time, the Governor of the Prefecture, Lord Chang of Guo, and Ren Gong of Huru frequently visited him to discuss the Way. On the eighth day of the twelfth month of the thirteenth year, An...
He sat upon a rope bed and entered nirvana at the age of fifty-six. Not long after, his tomb was selected in the northwest corner of the monastery.
Previously, a local man named Shi Xian had been performing labor on the city walls; one night he heard the sound of pipes and strings and a wondrous fragrance wafted through the air.

From this, it was known that the place where Fayue’s rebirth would occur must be the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī). His posthumous title was bestowed as "Nengjue" (Capable Awakening), and he was provided with a purple shroud for his funeral attire.
His robes and the honor of his achievements were renowned beyond the Great Wall.

Huiming of the Tang was a descendant of Chen Shi, the Grand Marshal of Taichou during the Han dynasty. During the Southern Crossing at the end of the Jin Yongjia era, his great-grandfather, Zhongwen, assisted in founding the Chen dynasty and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Danyang.
His grandfather served as the magistrate of Shuangxi and Gushu counties, and his father served as the magistrate of Lanling.
He subsequently settled there. Ming was born in Lanling. At the age of seven, he left his parents to enter the monastic life; he received full ordination and studied the Vinaya. He sighed, saying:
"Since the divine Yu took possession of the world through his meritorious deeds, punishments and executions have proliferated.
Even Bo Cheng Zigao abandoned his status as a feudal lord to take up farming—how much more so for those like us who study emptiness and stillness? These clamorous disputes... [one]...
How could he have reached such an extreme? He then went to Fangyan to investigate the Dharma with all his heart.

At the beginning of the Tianbao era, he intended to travel to Mount Wutai, but because the Huai and Beihuang regions were beset by military conflict, he was unable to do so. Consequently, he built three *ārāmas* at Shimen in Wanling.

Previously, that area had suffered from the depredations of tigers and wolves, and the local people were particularly fond of hunting; since Ming, however, he had transformed and gathered them in through the power of compassion.
Everyone reformed their hearts and ceased harming one another. In the fifth year, he arrived at Yubei. At that time, there was Master Yu, a monk of divine and wondrous character.
Seeing him, [Master Yu] said, "The Bodhisattva who transmits the teachings of the Southern Patriarch—why have you come so late?

On another day, he ascended to the summit of Yubei with [Master Yu] and saw a peak to the southeast, strikingly prominent and lovely. He then pointed to it and said to Master Yu, "This is where our past karmic affinity lies."
He was here. Might he not perhaps attain [his goal]? In the eighth year, an imperial edict was issued for the ordination of persons throughout the realm.

The local governor, Wei Nanjin, having commended Ming’s eminent conduct, submitted a formal petition on behalf of both the ordained and the laity to enroll him at the Ninghua Monastery of the prefecture.

Ming declined and instead requested to be enrolled at Fuchuan, which is the peak visible from Yubi. According to the local gazetteer, this site was formerly the residence of Wu Yun of the Liang dynasty. In the past...
To the south of the Green Mountains, two ancient Buddha statues were excavated, whereupon the waters surged upward in response; for this reason, the site acquired its name.
Beside it stood an ancient shrine to the King of Wu, where shamans would sway the local community with threats of calamity and promises of fortune, inducing them to offer blood sacrifices.
When Ming arrived and moored his boat beneath the shrine, wind and rain suddenly broke out, causing trees and roof tiles to fly and break. After a short while, the weather cleared.

A majestic man came forward to pay his respects, requested ordination, and asked that the site of the practice hall be moved. When the practice hall was subsequently relocated, [the man appeared once more].
By chance, a bronze basin was unearthed from the earth; inscribed on its base were the characters "Huiming.

On the twelfth day of the first month of the first year of the Jianzhong era, he manifested illness and passed away. He was eighty-four years of age and fifty-one years since his ordination. A stupa was erected on the western mountain of the monastery.
And there the spirit-car was interred. His Dharma-disciples who attained realization were Huixie and Huimin, as well as Ruzhi.
His Bodhisattva-precept disciples were the Regional Inspector Lu Youping, Yan Zhenqing, Dudu Wensu, Du Wei, and Pei Qing.
Tang Daozun, courtesy name Zongda, was surnamed Zhang and was a native of Wuxing. In his youth, he entered the monastic order under Master Xing of Ba’en Temple.
At the age of twelve, he received full ordination from Vinaya Master Yiwu of Tianzhu and began to study the principles of the *vinaya* regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited.
Later, he transmitted the school of Mingjing of Tiantai. Thereupon, he extensively transcribed the *Lotus Sūtra* and established a scripture hall.
He established a *bodhimaṇḍa* at Zhixingshan to attract and gather students.

In the first year of the Dali era, the regional governor Wei Yuanfu, the Minister of War Liu Yan, the Censor-in-Chief Wang Yuan, the Prefectural Governor Lu Xiang, the Palace Attendant Censor Lu Xun, and the Court Counselor Zhang Xiang, having attained true satisfaction, wished to dedicate this supreme site to him. They...
He submitted a memorial to report this. An imperial decree was issued to specially designate it as the Fahua Daochang (Lotus Samādhi Monastery).

Consequently, throughout Jiangdong, a total of seventeen monasteries were established for the practice of samādhi, all of which originated with Zunsui. During the Tianbao era, he was practicing the samādhi at Lingyan Daochang when a brilliant light illuminated the heavens;

his body stood within the light such that no distinction could be made between himself and others. On another day, he asked Master Yan of Jingxi about this, and the Master said: [The rest of the text follows...]
The radiance of wisdom flows forth from the mind; this is brought about by the refinement of one's diligent resolve.

Furthermore, while once in the monastery’s place of practice, he perceived his body sitting in empty space, vast and unimpeded. Those who understood him recognized this as the sign of the exhaustion of defilements.
In the first year of the Xingyuan era, on the twenty-ninth day of the seventh month, he passed away at his residence temple. He was seventy-one years of age and had been a monk for forty-six years.
His disciples erected a stupa to commemorate his virtue.
Tang Modu (摩駄都), whose name in the language of Han means Dharmadhātu, was also known as Wukong (悟空). He was born into the Che (車) clan of Yunyang in Jingzhao;

he was a descendant of the Tuoba Wei. In the ninth year of the Tiānbǎo era, the kingdom of Kaśmīra requested to submit as a vassal state and dispatched its great chieftain, Śarvada-kan, along with the Tripiṭaka master Śrīyāmā, to pay court.
They also requested that an imperial envoy be sent on an inspection tour. The following year, an edict was issued.
The imperial envoy Zhang Taoguang, accompanied by forty attendants and officials on a mission to the foreign state, journeyed westward.
At that time, Kongming Fengchao was appointed as a separate general of the Four Gates Commandery of Jingzhou in the Left Guard; he followed the envoys out to Anxi.
After twelve years, they reached the kingdom of Gandhāra, the eastern capital of Jibin. Its king received the Tang envoys with formal courtesy.
When the messenger returned, he reported that Fang was critically ill and remained in the kingdom of Gandhāra.
Thereupon, [Fang] made a vow to serve Śrīlātama as his teacher and leave the household life; this was in the second year of the Zhide era of Emperor Suzong.
At the age of twenty-nine, he received full ordination in the kingdom of Kaśmīra with Mañjuśrīvajra as his preceptor (upādhyāya) and Upacandra as his instructor (ācārya).
He took Dì as his *karmācārya* and Dàlǐwèidì as his *śikṣācārya*. At Móngtí Monastery, he recited the Śrāvaka precepts and studied the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*.
Indeed, the learning of Northern India was entirely that of the Sarvāstivāda school. He visited the Eight Great Stūpas and consulted with the master Śāriputra.
Upon returning to visit his sovereign and parents, Śāriputra bestowed upon him the teachings on emptiness, the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*).
The Sanskrit manuscripts of the *Daśabalasūtra* and two other sūtras were distinguished by the Buddha’s tooth relic.
Upon reaching the country of Bamiyan (Bost), on the southern shore of a small sea, the earth suddenly shook; hail and rain fell together, and thunder struck incessantly.

At that time, a great multitude of merchants fled for refuge beneath a large tree. The merchant leader said, "The dragon spirits are so enraged; perhaps among you there is a śarīra or some extraordinary treasure."

He brought it out from the sea, lest it should harm life and limb. Because he secretly entreated the dragon deities to forgive his transgression for the sake of benefiting the Eastern Lands, the fish ultimately did not emerge.
From the hour of the Rabbit (5–7 a.m. until the hour of the Monkey (5–7 p.m.), the sky finally cleared. He then requested that the *Titi-ti-chan* fish be released.
He translated the *Daśabala-sūtra* at Qiuji Lianhua Temple and invited Śīladharma to translate the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
The *Xianglun jing* was at Beiting. In the fifth year of the Zhenyuan era (Jisi), it arrived at the capital. [The Emperor] presented the Buddha-tooth relic and the text of the sutra;
by imperial decree, the Commissioner for Merit and Virtue, Dou Wenchang, was ordered to entrust them to the Left Shenche Army for transcription and submission.

[The Master] was appointed as General of the Empty and Mighty Martial (Kongzhuangwu Jiangjun) and served as Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Shi Taichangqing). He resided at Zhangjing Temple before returning to Yunyang to tend to the tomb trees of his parents.
[The temple] was completed.

Daocheng of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Liang and was a native of Jingzhao. His father, She, was a Secretariat Drafter (Zhongshu Sheren). From childhood, Daocheng was sent to enter the monastic order;
he felt no lingering attachment [to worldly ties]. Once, a Chan practitioner happened to pass by him and said, "He may be named Daocheng," and then entrusted him with a monk’s staff and alms bowl.

A vessel of ritual propriety, he was known as the Vinaya Śrāmaṇera. After receiving full ordination, he traveled through various monasteries to study the *Nanshan Chao* (the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*).
He maintained the precepts with diligence and advanced in his studies; yet, by nature, he was straightforward and simple, and his residence was not constant.

He served at monasteries such as Feng'en, Zhuangyan, Caotang, and others, finding peace wherever he went. He made the protection of living beings his primary duty. In the second year of the Jianzhong era, he spent the summer retreat at Yunyang.
At Mount Shan, a tiger suddenly let out a roar as it entered the gate. Daoting appeared to be speaking to it; the tiger wagged its tail, pricked up its ears, and departed.
Later, when Daoting moved his residence to Changxin Temple, someone asked him the reason for this. Daoting replied, "Can one who has left the household life remain stagnant in a single place?"
According to the laws of the Western Regions, rooms were divided into three periods [of occupancy] to prevent attachment; alas, later generations changed this practice.

On the eighth day of the second month in the second year of the Zhenyuan era, the Emperor received the Bodhisattva precepts from Shandeng at the temple; the capital and its surrounding districts looked on with reverence, and the Emperor bestowed lavish gifts and rewards.

Shandeng dedicated them all entirely to the two fields of merit [the Sangha and the poor]. In the fifth year, the Emperor visited the place where Shandeng resided to inquire about his methods for cultivating the mind.

Regarding the Dharma-gate: she was subsequently summoned to serve as a consort among the principal ladies and palace attendants and received the Bodhisattva precepts. In the fourth month of the sixteenth year, she was granted the title Dayuan.
She passed away on the eighteenth day of the ninth month of the nineteenth year.
Tang Daguang was surnamed Tang and was a native of Anji in Huzhou. His mother was Mei; she conceived Daguang after being moved by a miraculous dream.
Upon his tonsure and ordination, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, and within three months, he was able to memorize it entirely.

While traveling to the capital, Emperor Suzong received him in private audience and gazed at him intently, saying, "Last night, I dreamed of a monk chanting the Mahāyāna scriptures while light radiated from his mouth."
Is he not indeed the man for this? Consequently, he was granted his current name. On the occasion of the Emperor’s birthday, he was summoned to Dingguo Temple and lodged at Qianfu Temple.

At the Scripture-Reading Hall, the eunuch Zhao Wen and others were dispatched to deliver an imperial decree, granting him permission to reside and preside over famous mountains throughout the empire as he pleased. Later, he moved to the Lantian Hermitage. As for the hermitage...
This monk had previously dreamed that a celestial youth descended and said to him, "The sound of the *Mahāprabhāsa Sūtra* has reached the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*);
its merit is immeasurable. One day, a sudden arm descended from the heavens and stroked his chest. He also dreamed that the monk drew out his breast and let the light suckle his milk.
From then on, his spirit and body were relaxed and comfortable, and his countenance became harmonious and flourishing. After some time, while walking in the mountains, he happened upon—
He fell into the Dragon Spring at the bottom of a deep ravine, yet his mind was not confused or disturbed;
he simply made a vow to recite the "Chapter on the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna" one hundred thousand times. Suddenly, he felt his body leap out as if being supported by something.

At the beginning of the Longshuo era, an imperial edict summoned him to reside at Zisheng Monastery, which was the former residence of the Duke of Zhao, Changsun Wuji. In the second year, an edict commanded him to compose a literary work.

Empress De performed memorial services for his merit. In the seventh year, Zisheng Temple suffered a fire; its buildings and furnishings were all consumed by the flames, yet the various Buddhist scriptures remained entirely undamaged.

When the matter was reported to the throne, he was granted exceptional favors. The common people also contributed vast sums of wealth and silk, exceeding ten thousand units in value, so that the temple was rebuilt.

Not long after, he submitted a petition requesting leave to return home for a visit, but the imperial decree did not immediately grant his request. Guang subsequently fell ill and could not be cured, wishing—

He threw himself into the water to die. [The official] forcibly raised him up and mounted him on a donkey to depart, but the donkey prostrated itself and would not move. A flock of crows cawed above its head; people gradually took notice of this.
After [the official] explained the situation to him with persuasion, he was finally released. He then carried the sutra scrolls upon his head as he traveled the roads.

Shortly thereafter, an imperial edict granted his request. Having returned home, he constructed a stupa at Wucheng. Every day he recited the "Prabhūtaratna" chapter to fulfill his former vow. In the first year of the Yongtai era, in Zhejiang...

The Western Circuit Inspector Wei Yuanfu submitted a memorial requesting that Guang be appointed as the head of the recitation assemblies for the six prefectures and that a separate *daochang* (meditation hall) be established for him.
During the Dali era, Yan Zhenqing, the Duke of Lu, was serving as the governor of the prefecture. The magistrate of Wucheng was Li Shen, the father of Gongchui.
When Shen fell ill before he had even completed his first year, he was cured by the name Guang performing Buddhist rites. Shen was young.

His posthumous name was Guang. It was for this reason that, during the Zhenyuan era, while Shen was serving at court, he occasionally went out to pay his respects at the Chan Hall where [the Master] recited the scriptures.
On the evening of the full moon in the twelfth month of the first year of the Yongzhen era, he passed away. He was seventy years of age.
At that time, Shen, then a Chancellor of State, composed a text to be engraved upon a stele. Alas, how glorious!
Huilin of the Tang dynasty was originally a native of the Kingdom of Shule. He took the surname Pei by adoption. Initially, he served the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra as a *śaikṣa*.

He thoroughly mastered Indian phonology (*śabda-vidyā*) as well as Chinese philology and lexicography; there was nothing he did not study with precision. He once remarked that translating from Sanskrit into Chinese...
The Chinese characters are concise while the Sanskrit is minute. Being concise, the meaning may be omitted; being minute, the expression may become prolix.

Yet, to ensure that the meaning does not become omitted and the expression does not become prolix, it is impossible for anyone who is not profoundly learned, comprehensive, and widely versed to achieve this easily.
Therefore, I have cited the *Zilin*, *Zitong*, *Shenglei*, *Sancang*, *Qieyun*, *Yupian*, various sutras, and miscellaneous histories to synthesize them, and have thus composed [this work].
The *Dazang yinyi* (Phonology and Meaning of the Great Canon), compiled from the fourth year of the Zhenyuan era until the fifth year of the Yuanhe era, consisted of one hundred fascicles.

Its original copy was deposited in the Ximing Monastery collection of the Great Canon so that it might be transcribed throughout the capital. He passed away in the seventeenth year, the Gengzi year, at the age of eighty-seven.

Tang Duǎnfú’s clan was Zhao; he resided in Tiānshuī, where his family had been a prominent lineage of Qín for generations. His mother, Zhāng, dreamed of a foreign monk who said to her, "You shall give birth to a noble son.
He then took a casket of *śarīra* relics from within his robe, made her swallow one, and departed. When she gave birth, she saw the monk from her dream.
One day, he entered the room during the daytime, rubbed [Falin’s] head, and said, "The teachings must surely rely on you to flourish greatly. Having finished speaking, he vanished from sight.
Falin had a high forehead, deep-set eyes, a large jaw, and a square mouth; he stood six chi and five cun tall, and his voice resonated like a bell.
At the age of ten, he became a śrāmaṇera and served Master Daowu of Chongfu Temple. At seventeen, he received full ordination.
The bhikṣu served at An-guo Temple, where he studied the Vinaya under Master Sheng of Chongfu Temple;
he transmitted the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* under Master Su of An-guo Temple; and he thoroughly investigated the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* under Master Yin of Folin Temple.

Shortly thereafter, he dreamed that a foreign monk presented him with a vessel of lapis lazuli filled with śarīra relics, commanding him to swallow them, saying: "The Great Teachings of the Tripitaka."
"Your belly shall contain them all. From that time forth, Miaozhi’s vast eloquence encompassed all like rivers pouring into the sea.
He visited Mañjuśrī at Mount Qingliang and expounded the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in Taiyuan; the excellence of his reputation reached the ears of the Emperor during the reign of Dezong.

He entered and exited the imperial palace precincts, engaging in debates on Confucianism and Daoism. By imperial decree, he was granted a purple cassock; on seasonal occasions, he was bestowed gifts of a quality beyond that of his peers.
When Emperor Shunzong was in the Spring Palace (Chunfang), they shared quarters and rose together, regarding one another as brothers; the favor and etiquette shown to him were exceptionally generous.

When Emperor Xianzong ascended the throne, he visited the monastery several times and frequently received his counsel, treating him no differently than a close friend or companion—such was Fu’s dignified demeanor.
Chao Mai was eloquent and refined in his speech; even in moments of haste, his responses never failed to lead toward the Buddha Vehicle and expound upon profound principles.
Consequently, the Son of Heaven held him in ever greater esteem. He then welcomed the true relics to pray for spiritual blessings.
He opened the secret palace to pray for blessings and oversaw the affairs of the monks of the Left Street for ten years.

He propagated the *Nirvāṇa* and *Vijñaptimātratā* teachings, and performed the *yoga-siddhi* recitations; he dedicated the offerings received from above to the adornment of stupas and temples, striving to reach the utmost excellence in carving and painting.
In his small chamber, he used but a single bed; his daily practice consisted solely of reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and silently contemplating purity and emptiness.

He received everyone—from princes and dukes down to commoners—with equal sincerity. Consequently, there was no one among the nobility or the gentry who did not look up to him with reverence. Commentators maintained that he practiced the conduct of Never-Despising (Sadāparibhūta).
He passed away on the first day of the sixth month in the first year of the Kaicheng era. On the sixth day of the seventh month of that same year, his cremation took place.

To the south of Changle, on a high plateau, he obtained lustrous and perfectly round śarīra relics; his posthumous title was Dada (Greatly Attained), and his stupa was named Xuansi (Mysterious and Secret).

He lived to the age of sixty-seven and had been a monk for forty-three years. Among his disciples were more than a thousand monks and nuns. During the Huichang era, the Minister of State, Lord Fei Xiu, composed a eulogy for his virtues and erected a stele upon the plateau.
Tang Zhixuan, whose courtesy name was Houjue, was surnamed Chen and was a native of Hongya in Meizhou. His great-grandfather was Tu Nan, who served as the Magistrate of Shehong in Zizhou;

his grandfather was Xian and his father was Miao, neither of whom had achieved success in the imperial examinations. His mother, Wei, dreamed that the moon entered her womb before she gave birth to him.

When he was still in his swaddling clothes, he would invariably laugh upon seeing images of the Buddha or the ceremonial deportment of monks. At the age of five, his grandfather pointed to a flower and commanded him to compose a poem on it;
within a few steps, he had finished, producing the lines: "Only one flower remains; tomorrow it will surely follow the wind. His grandfather recited them for a long time and sighed, saying:
"I hoped you would attain a high rank in the examinations to wipe away our family's shame. Now that this is so, your ambition is evident. Thus [he passed away] at the end.

Was he destined to enter the Gate of Emptiness? His residence was adjacent to Ningyi Temple. At the age of seven, while listening to Dharma Master Fatai lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he suddenly felt as though he had attained some awakening.
Furthermore, in a dream that night, the Buddha in the temple’s main hall placed his hand upon his head and stroked it.
Because he earnestly sought ordination, it could not be prevented. At the age of eleven, he went to Sian Temple in Tangxing to have his hair shaved.
His master bestowed upon him the Great Sutras along with Master Daoyuan’s commentaries and Master Huiben’s *Yuanzhi*; he studied them all until he mastered them without error.
At the age of thirteen, he ascended the seat to expound the Dharma at the Puxian Pavilion of Daci Temple. At that time, the Provincial Governor...

When Du Guang, Duke Yuan-ying, was about to depart to govern Shu, he heard of his reputation and summoned him. Those who listened numbered in the tens of thousands, and they were all struck with awe and submission.
From then on, no one dared to utter his name, but instead called him "Cen the Bodhisattva.

Some have transmitted that his previous incarnation was Zhi Xuan of Sanxue Mountain in Hanzhou; it is said that while he was lecturing on the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, the earth miraculously transformed into lapis lazuli.
Liyun received full ordination from Vinaya Master Bianzhen at Jingzhong Temple and studied the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* under Vinaya Master Gu of Shichang Mountain.

Thereupon, he traveled through the Three Gorges and passed through Jingzhou and Xiangyang before taking up residence at Zisheng Temple in the capital, where he was able to rely upon Dharma Master Xian of Anguo Temple to investigate the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. He also extensively studied the secular classics of the hundred schools.
He spoke thus; however, because his local accent was not standard, he was concerned about it. He then said, "I shall recite the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī at Mount Xiang'er.

In the middle of the night, he dreamed that a monk changed his tongue. At dawn, he was able to speak the language of Qin. Emperor Wen of the Tang dynasty treated him with even greater courtesy and respect. The Confucian scholar Yang Maoxian...

He paid close attention to the "Bamboo Tombs" (the Chinese classics) and admired the character of Xie Kangle. He annotated the meanings of the scriptures and would occasionally approach him to inquire about them.

When [Xie] passed away, Daoyuan alone saw him wearing purple robes and a green crown, bowing in thanks before him and then departing through the air. When the news of his death arrived, [Daoyuan] was struck by this vision.
He then learned that his son had been given a purple *kāṣāya* robe and a green lotus-flower crown for burial, and was told:

"Had I not been burdened by the constraints of official cap and robes, I would have long served Master Xuán as his attendant, carrying his water jar and holding his shoes. Now that he has suddenly passed away, what shall I do?

Emperor Wǔzōng initially still upheld the Inner Teachings (Buddhism), but later became deluded by heterodox doctrines; thus, none of the ministers dared to remonstrate with him. Once, on the occasion of the Deyáng Festival, he assembled the monastic community.

At the Huanglin De Hall, an imperial edict was issued for Xuan to debate the Daoist assembly alone. The Emperor personally brought forth the *Laozi*, specifically the passage on "governing a great state as one cooks small fish," and ordered them to engage in a dialogue.

Xuan’s responses totaled several thousand words, all of which maintained that the pursuit of immortality is inherently a matter for those dwelling in mountains and forests, and is not something suitable for an emperor to practice.
The Sovereign was greatly incensed. [The account continues with] Chou Shiliang of the Left Army and Yang... of the Inner Chancellery.

Qin Yi, appreciating his talent and virtue, privately exhorted him to present five stanzas of a poem on offering blessings to the Emperor Yao and explained its meaning to him. On that very day, Xuán returned to his hometown.
Subsequently, he traveled between the Xiang and Hu lakes with his cap and comb (as a recluse). Just then, Imperial Secretary Yang Han-gong was inquiring into affairs at Gui-ling;
he welcomed Xuán and accommodated him at Kaiyuan Temple. It happened that when Emperor Xuanzong ascended the throne, the Prime Minister Yang Gong commanded the left palace guard. Because...

His achievements were formally recorded in the imperial registers, and he was requested to resume his teaching duties. At the outset, he was summoned to seek out the traces of the profound [Buddhist] teachings; by imperial decree, he resided at Baoying Temple.

On the anniversary of the Emperor’s longevity, he delivered lectures and eulogies, for which he was granted a purple *kāṣāya* robe and appointed as the Head Seat (*śrāmaṇera*) of the Three Teachings. Shortly thereafter, he was summoned to move to the Yuxu Pavilion at Fagan Temple.
Regarding those [images] commissioned by the Emperor while at the imperial residence: in the third year of the Dazhong era, an edict was issued to restore all abandoned temples throughout the realm;
subsequently, portraits were painted in the inner palace to serve as models. In the eighth year, he submitted a memorial requesting to return to the mountains.

In the spring of the second year of the Guangming era, when Xizong fled to Sichuan to escape distant difficulties, he dispatched Guo Zuntao with an imperial decree to summon him to the imperial encampment.

He was permitted to follow him in a sedan chair. When the Emperor descended to receive him, he treated him with great courtesy and affection. Their conversation was most pleasing, and the Emperor wished to bestow upon him an honorific title.

He consulted the various scholars, but before they had even had time to report back, the Emperor suddenly took up his imperial brush and conferred the name "Wudada" (Awakened and Attained) upon him, saying:
"The purport of the *Lotus Sūtra* is to 'reveal, awaken, cause to attain, and cause to enter. It is fitting that his title be 'National Teacher Wudada' to express my intention."
Xuanchen declined the offer repeatedly, but it was not granted. He subsequently excused himself on the grounds of illness and returned to his old residence at Jiulong.
On the twenty-seventh day of the first month, he saw that the room where he lived was entirely transformed into a subtle and sublime realm.

On the seventh day of the second month, there was suddenly a voice in the air saying, "You will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land. When he asked who had made this voice, the reply came: "It is the Buddha. Or perhaps [the Bodhisattva]...

As he descended from his seat, a bright pearl fell from his hand onto his knee. Was this not the exhaustion of his retribution in this Sahā world, yet the sudden arrival of the karmic response of his past merits and faults?
In the seventh month, he summoned his disciple Cideng to compose a final testament and entrust him with his last affairs, instructing him to offer his body as alms to fish and birds.
Having delivered these earnest exhortations, he passed away in the right lateral position facing west. He was seventy-three years of age and fifty-four years since his ordination.
Xuánshēng was throughout his life scrupulous in maintaining his precepts and devoted to spiritual cultivation. Nevertheless, his efficacy in benefiting sentient beings was particularly prominent.
In Zhēnfú County of Lóugù, there was a man named Yōngshì whose residence stood above a large pond. In the pond lived a fish with feet and teeth, which was most extraordinary.
Whenever anyone wished to net or hook it, clouds and mist would arise to shroud and conceal it. Yōngshì raised this fish for four generations.
When Xuan arrived at that place, he recognized it and conferred the *śaraṇagamana* (refuge) precepts upon him. Upon emerging from the water, the dragon leaped about and departed.

That night, he dreamed that Lady Yong said, "I have already been reborn in heaven. Subsequently, the deity of Mount Yulei by the River Dao and the deity of Longmen on the northern outskirts of Yichang both received the precepts.
The verification of these events is recorded in the biography of my disciple Sengche; they shall not be recorded here again. [The] Stūpa.
He currently resides at Yousheng Temple on Mount Longshan in Jincheng. Throughout the regions of Qin and Shu, people depict his image in their household shrines;
some even include Li Shangyin holding a white whisk and standing in attendance, indicating that Shangyin once served as his attendant. Shangyin’s style name was Yishan;
he was a master of prose and verse. When [Hui]xuan resided at Xingshan Temple in the capital, Shangyin lived in Yongchong Ward.

He once suffered from an eye ailment and prayed for divine intervention to Xuán. The next day, Xuán sent him three stanzas of the *Divine Eye Gāthā* (*Tiān yǎn jì*), and his illness was subsequently cured.
Zhìxuān of Liáng was a native of Quanzhou. During the late Tang dynasty, the Buddha-dharma was particularly flourishing.

Xuān was in the prime of his youth and lamented that the circulation of the scriptures and teachings in this region was not yet complete. Furthermore, he considered India to be the land of auspicious responses for our World-Honored One. For...
His disciples had never before visited [the site]; was this not a cause for shame? Thereupon, he joined a fellowship and traveled westward;
they all attained their aspirations and returned. In the fifth month of the first year of the Kaiping era, he arrived at the capital and presented the bone of a Pratyekabuddha.

Xuanzang possessed Sanskrit manuscripts of the Sūtras and Vinaya written on palm leaves. Upon meeting the Taizu, who had recently received the abdication from the Tang, he was greatly pleased by his [Xuanzang’s] exposition.

The Emperor treated him with diligent courtesy and generosity. Xuanzang then requested permission to translate the Sanskrit manuscripts he had brought forth; however, because the empire was beset by many troubles, he was unable to do so at that time.
Jin Guangsì, surnamed Lǐ, was a native of Wénshuǐ in Tàiyuán. In his youth, he entered the monastic order under Hǎowēi at Zhēnróng Yùàn on Mount Tái.

Having received full ordination, he traveled abroad to receive the teachings of the Mind (Cittamātra). His dialectical skill was so versatile and formidable that none among his peers could withstand him.

Shortly thereafter, he traveled south to visit the Wáng family in Fúmián; King Zhōngyì held him in high esteem. He then proceeded to the Two Zhè regions to visit the Qián family, where Wǔsù [honored him].
The King treated him with even greater reverence. Both kings dispatched envoys to present offerings of incense and tea; furthermore, the two provinces of Zhe sent ten thousand sets of alms bowls.

By collecting the stipends of the governors and magistrates of various prefectures, they loaded them onto a great ship which reached Cangzhou. The envoy was then sent back to offer these as a consecration for Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the Great Master Jianglong was presiding over the various monasteries of Mount Tai, and he was held in awe by the multitude.

I prostrate myself and submit this for his consideration. The distribution was made so that the shares were equal among the many and the few. Thereupon, his disciples submitted a petition requesting that he succeed his master in presiding over the affairs of the monastery.

By imperial decree, he was appointed to the office of *Dugang* (Chief Administrator), with authority to oversee all the temples on Mount Tai. He was granted the honorary title "Chao-hua" (Transcendent Transformation).

In the fifteenth year, he restored ruined sites and provided food for the hungry; his deeds cannot be fully recorded. In the first year of the Tianfu era, he fell ill and passed away on the fifth day of the ninth month.
He subsequently entered parinirvāṇa; his disciples enshrined his śarīra in a stūpa, which remains to this day.

Jingchao of the Jin dynasty, having already upheld the model of the Vinaya, sought further instruction from him with particular diligence. Upon reaching Mount Lu, he resolved to spend the remainder of his life there.

He daily recited the *Lotus Sūtra* as a form of self-discipline, and before long, he had completed the ritual prostrations for both the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Lotus Sūtra*, each according to their respective lengths.
This happened twice. On both occasions, he again burned his fingers as an act of celebration. Thereupon, śarīra relics emerged from his body;
some were found on the ground where he sat, lay, or walked. They were perfectly round, lustrous, and lovely. During the Tianfu era, he passed away at his residence. His stupa still exists today.
Jingtong was the son of the Zhang family of Fufeng; his lineage had been illustrious and noble for generations.

Having left secular life while still a child, he traveled east to Luoyang during the turmoil at the end of the Tang dynasty. There, he received the *yogācāra* teachings from Vajrabodhi Tripiṭaka Master.
In the fourth year of the Tianfu era, when the imperial court dispatched an envoy to Wuyue, Jingtong obtained passage on the envoy’s ship to visit the scenic sites of Tiantai and Luofu. And...

He divined where he should turn his course. Accordingly, the Tripitaka Master also entrusted the circulation of the Sanskrit manuscripts to him. At that time, King Wenmu Yuanguan was residing at the headquarters of the military command;

he ordered the assembly of ceremonial regalia and musical troupes to welcome the master as he stepped ashore, and lodged him in the Zhenshen Pagoda Temple, providing abundant offerings and provisions.
Not long after, he traveled to Mount Chicheng and Mount Huading, where he took up residence at the Dharma-seat of the Venerable Zhizhe.

He further cultivated the practices for the Pure Land. On the mountain there was an ancient "Stone of the Waving Hand," traditionally said to be the place where Dīpaṃkara Buddha beckoned with his hand to receive Zhizhe.

It rose steeply and precipitously, nearly reaching halfway to the heavens. Zongzai twice climbed to its summit and threw himself down, praying to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nourishment (Sukhāvatī).
In one instance, he was rescued and revived; subsequently, he withdrew to hide at Mount Fahuashan in Yue. As he was about to pass away, he suddenly spoke white...

His vital energy overflowed; his sitting area was as if smeared with powdered rouge. He then passed away while seated. Upon cremation, five-colored clouds were seen swirling and coalescing above the mass of flames, and everyone smelled an extraordinary fragrance.

Jindaozhou, surnamed Guan, was a native of Huiluo in Shuofang. Having entered the monastic life at age seven at the Peacock Courtyard of Longxing Temple, he became an object of veneration for the lay faithful.
He was soon able to establish Yongxing Temple, thereby attracting a great multitude. At that time, Lord Han Su was serving as the military governor of Lingwu;
Daozhou subsequently took his leave and fled westward to Baicao Valley on Mount Helan. Through the power of his sincere devotion—

Upon his arrival, he was moved by the fact that the Sweet Spring (Ganquan), which had previously run dry, began to gush forth once more, and a miraculous serpent swam within its waters. Thereafter, he preached the Dharma to guide the common people;
he abstained from food and prayed for rain, and even drew blood to paint an image of the Great Compassionate One with a Thousand Hands and Eyes. This occurred in the second year of the Zhonghe era.

The region of Guanzhong remained in a state of unrest and turmoil. Thereupon, beneath the stupa at Nianding Monastery south of the city, he severed his left arm and burned it before the image, praying for its divine protection to bring peace and stability to the world. He received a response in the form of a sudden thunderstorm and torrential rain.
As for Zhifu, he used his left [hand] to pray for relief from drought; after long periods of famine, he prayed for the clearing of grievances, and all were fulfilled as he wished.

On the sixth day of the second month in the sixth year of Tianfu, having gathered his disciples and finished bestowing his final instructions, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away as if entering meditative absorption.

The assembly subsequently lacquered his body and prepared it for enshrinement. During the Jianlong era of the Song dynasty, the extraordinary scholar Guo Zhongshu composed a literary work in praise of his virtues.

Jin Zunhui’s secular surname was Li; he was a native of Qiao Commandery. For generations his ancestors had not served in office. His mother, Lady Zhang, became pregnant after dreaming that a divine being bestowed upon her a precious pearl.
While she was still nursing him, he was already adept at discerning the joys and sorrows of others. As he grew older, he frequented Buddhist temples and monasteries.

He lingered and looked back repeatedly, unable to bear the thought of leaving. At the age of eleven, he took refuge under the Vinaya master Chongyin of Kaiyuan Temple in Haocheng, shaving his head and beginning to recite the Lotus Sūtra, which he was able to memorize perfectly. Upon reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination.

Shortly thereafter, he traveled to Bian and Luo to seek the Way, receiving the meaning of the Lotus Sūtra from Dharma Master Zhipian. In the second year of the Kaiping era of the Liang dynasty, he first began to expound it.
His primary activity was at the Yakushi-in of Sōgoku-ji. In the second year of the Changxing era of the Later Tang dynasty, he instructed his disciples using commentaries and sub-commentaries;

those among his disciples who ascended to his hall numbered more than twenty. In the second year of the Tianfu era of the Jin dynasty, he taught and practiced the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and propagated it on Mount Wutai, continuing the legacy of Great Master Zhiyong. Monastics and laypeople gathered like clouds.
He had the scriptures engraved upon stone and installed them on three sides of the hall to ensure their permanence for all time.

Furthermore, in the fourth year, he assembled two hundred and forty monastics and laypeople, instructing each person to recite one fascicle; in total, they completed three sets of scriptures, which took one full year to accomplish.
In this manner, for twenty years, he did not neglect even a single interval. He further provided food as alms to exhort the spirits and deities to resolve upon the Bodhicitta.

His reputation reached the imperial court, and by decree he was granted the title Great Master Zhenxing (True Practice). On the sixteenth day of the first month in the second year of the Kaoyun era, he manifested illness.
He passed away lying on his right side while reciting the name of the Buddha. His age was seventy-one, and his years since ordination were fifty-one.
His disciples, honoring his final instructions, buried him on the eastern plain of Sizhuang in the region north of the Yellow River during the Sui dynasty.

Zhou Dao-pi was born into the noble lineage of the Chang'an aristocracy as a scion of the imperial clan. His father was Zongyan, the eldest of the five branches of the royal family of Emperor Zhaozong.
His mother was Lady Xu; because she had no offspring, she once personally recited the "Universal Gate Chapter" of the Lotus Sūtra before conceiving him.
When he was born, he was elegant and lovely. Hardly a year old, his father perished in the military forces at Mount Huo while on state business.

Daoping then ceased nursing and assumed a sorrowful countenance. At seven years of age, he abstained from meat and pungent flavors; whenever he visited Buddhist temples, he would never think of returning home.
As he frequently associated with the Dharma Master Jineng of Baoshou Temple, he informed his mother of his intention to follow him and leave the household life. Before long, he did so.

When Emperor Zhaozong fled to Shimen, Daopi was only nine years old; yet by the time the imperial procession returned, he was already able to accompany his teacher to welcome the Emperor according to ritual protocol.

At that time, Chen Bángōng, the Prince of Jìn'ān and Governor of Xiāngzhōu, invited the entire assembly to travel southward to propagate the teachings.
Mao Xi, Minister of the Ministry of Personnel, and Sun Zang, General of the Guard, both bowed their heads in reverent prostration.

Fu Zai, General of the Left Guard, was well-versed in both internal (Buddhist) and external (Confucian) studies; he was careful in his endorsements in daily life, and whenever he encountered [the Master] Jue, both his mind and his physical form became solemn.

Their discussions were so compelling that they persuaded [the Emperor]. Following the imperial decree issued over the region east of the Yangtze River, only two temples were permitted to remain in each prefecture, while all others were abolished and discarded.

Daohui heard of this and was filled with fear; he then traveled a hundred *she* to knock at the palace gates, and his petition was granted by the Imperial Hearing. This occurred while Emperor Yang was still in the Prince’s residence (*fan-di*).
He was dispatched to govern the region of Huaidian, where he was again granted a letter inviting him to reside at Huirisi Temple.

When the Crown Prince ascended to the position of heir apparent, an imperial decree appointed him as the overseer of the Bao Tai Sutra Repository in Jiangdu. In the second year of the Daye era, he accompanied the Emperor’s entourage into the capital, falling ill along the way.
On the twenty-second day of the third month, he passed away while staying at Suyu County in Sizhou. He was fifty-three years of age.
On the thirteenth day of the fifth month of that year, his remains were returned for interment in Zhuuyu Village, Jiangyang County.
The inscription on his stele was composed by Yu Shinan, a Secretariat Drafter of Imperial Edicts, with a preface written by the Jinzi Guanglu Dafu and Neishi Shilang [Li Ji].
Yu Shiji composed the inscription, and his disciple Zhiguo erected it.
Sui Jingduan (also known as Huiduan) followed Master Sengbao at the age of fourteen to receive the teachings of the mind.

Later, he further relied upon Master Tanxiang for investigation and verification; thus, the benefits he attained became increasingly subtle and wondrous. This continued until the Zhou dynasty abolished the Buddhist teachings.

Calamity arose; consequently, he collected all the scriptures and images and buried them in a remote location. When they were unearthed during the Sui dynasty, the various temples all relied upon their use.
Xuandu was humble, frugal, and retiring, never vying for fame or reputation. His conduct was such that he was revered and admired by his contemporaries.

Prince Han Wang Liang served him as his teacher. Both the Emperor and the ladies of the inner court received his instructions on the precepts. Once, when he was invited to stay overnight within the imperial palace, Duan alone withdrew, refusing to comply with the decree.
The ivory mat and sandalwood shrine bestowed upon him, along with various precious curiosities, remain suspended from the rafters of the building to this day.
During the Renshou era, an imperial edict ordered the interment of the śarīra at Yuzhou; a white light then curled and wound itself into five [spirals].

Vibrant colors overflowed [from the stone]. An inscription was carved upon the stone casing; when it reached the Emperor’s name, the characters transformed into gold. These matters are detailed in a separate biography.

When Emperor Yang succeeded to the throne, he established the Great Chan Ding Monastery in the capital and issued an edict to select those of renowned virtue from throughout the realm to reside there, in order to solemnly honor the late Emperor and secure his posthumous merit.
Yuanxian was appointed as the head administrator (*shoulinggangren*), and the assembly was all in solemn reverence. This was in the second year of the Daye era.
On the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month of winter, he passed away at Chanlin Temple at the age of sixty-four.
He was a son of the Gu clan of Shanyin, Kuaiji, during the Sui dynasty, named Dazhi. In his youth, he relied upon the Tiantai Zen Master Zhiyi for ordination.
His physical bearing and spirit were refined and detached, transcending the mundane world. Because the Master’s aspirations were so great, he was thus named after them.

He devoted himself exclusively to meditation and recitation, visiting and studying under all the eminent masters of his time. In the tenth year of the Kaihuang era, he traveled to Mount Lu and resided at Fengding Temple, where he daily recited the Lotus Sūtra without ceasing.
Later, on the southern side of Gānlù Peak on Mount Liánhuá, he established the Jingguān (Silent Contemplation) Dharma-hall;

there he practiced the dhūta ascetic disciplines, abstaining from grain for long periods without showing any sign of hunger. He would frequently sacrifice his own life out of compassion to save jackals and tigers.
Yet the jackals and tigers would always avoid him and not harm him. This continued for seven years, during which his resolve grew ever more steadfast.
Later, he resided at Fulin Temple on the mountain. During the upheaval of the Daye era, the teachings declined; he then donned mourning garments and wailed bitterly within the Buddha hall.
For three days and nights, he was comforted and consoled, saying: "Because of my karmic retribution, what I have encountered is thus; I must go to knock at the celestial gate to clarify this matter.

He then hurried to the capital to submit a memorial requesting that the Three Jewels be honored, and further expressing his wish to burn off one of his arms as an act of thanksgiving. The Emperor granted his request;
subsequently, the seven assemblies were gathered to perform a great *zhai* (fasting) ceremony to assist in the completion of his vow. This was his resolve.
He did not eat for three days. Then he ascended a high seat, where he burned his flesh with red-hot irons until it split open, and further cauterized his bones until they were entirely charred black.
Thereupon he wrapped them in cloth and doused them with wax, causing smoke and flames to erupt; the light reflected off the cliffs and valleys, and those who witnessed it were all ill at ease.
Yet Zhifang continued to chant the verses of the sutras, extolling the Buddha’s virtues and preaching the Dharma to the assembly, speaking and laughing as usual. At that time—
His arm was consumed until the fire was extinguished. He then descended from his seat, sat cross-legged, and entered meditative absorption. Seven days later, he passed away at the age of forty-three.
By nature, he was skilled in literary composition; he once authored a text of vows exceeding seventy sheets that has circulated in the world, inspiring those who read it.
Yanzong of the Sui dynasty was a native of Bo-ren in Zhao-jun. He was the son of the Li family, whose lineage had been of gentry status for generations. By nature, he possessed a powerful memory.
At the age of ten, he took refuge under Dharma Master Bian of Xin-du and entered the monastic order, receiving the name Daojiang;

there he studied the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*. At twelve, he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* at Mount Ju-mu. Shortly thereafter, he traveled to the capital of Ye, attending various lecture halls, before returning to his home temple to propagate the teachings.

Regarding the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, Wang Shao of Taiyuan, a district magistrate, held him in particularly high esteem and reverence. At the beginning of the Wuping era of the Qi dynasty, he entered Jinyang.
Coinciding with Emperor Wenxuan’s western excursion, Shao heard of his reputation and was summoned by imperial decree to lecture on the *Ratnaketuparivarta-sūtra* (Renwang jing) in Xuande Hall.

The Emperor, the Empress Dowager, the ladies of the six palaces, and the civil and military officials all assembled there. The Chief Minister Gao Yuanhai escorted Jiang to take his seat at the lectern. The State...

Dōshū Sōjū attended him; his two hundred disciples were all outstanding youths. His spirit was majestic and his speech firm and clear; his analytical discernment was bottomless and without stagnation.

The Emperor was struck with wonder, regarding him as a rare talent. At that time he was only fourteen years old. At sixteen, he encountered the mourning for his father and proceeded to receive full ordination.

The precepts consist of ten thousand words; by the afternoon of the following day, he had memorized them all through silent recitation. When Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty suppressed Buddhism, [he remained steadfast].
Shanglao (Jiang) then changed his former name, let his hair grow long, and altered his dress, adopting the *Daode jing* and *Zhuangzi* as his primary texts.
He attended the court debates and contributed his efforts to the imperial compositions on the Way, particularly the *Wushang biyao*. Emperor Xuan held him in especially high esteem.

He was repeatedly offered official rank but did not accept it. He was on close terms with court officials such as Wang Shao, Xin De-yuan, Lu Kai-ming, and Tang Yi, who were known as his "mystical friends beyond literature.
In the second year of the Daxiang era, he began to discourse on Prajñāpāramitā for various scholars.

In the ninth year of the Dading era, together with the śramaṇa Tan-yan and others, he obtained an imperial edict to undergo tonsure according to the old rites. Thereupon, Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty assumed the throne.

The Grand Chancellor was [Li] Zong, who was twenty-five years old. On the thirteenth day of the second month, the Emperor received the abdication from the Zhou dynasty and established the Kaishuang era.
He issued an edict that the lectures at the imperial academy be held in succession throughout the four seasons without negligence. Those who bathed in the Way numbered in the tens of thousands.

He compiled a collection of texts on the Inner Canon and reformed the methods for the *shamen* (monks) to lead the liturgical chants. In the third year, the Emperor visited the Daoist altar and witnessed the transformation of Laozi.

Hu Zhou found this strange and reported it. An imperial edict was issued for the śramaṇas and Daoists to debate one another, and Sū Wei, Yang Su, He Tuo, Zhang Bin, and others were ordered to examine and determine the matter in detail;

Daocong was also among them at that time. The Daoists were proven to be spurious, and Daocong composed the *Bianjiao lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Teachings) in twenty-five sections, citing authorities with great precision.
By imperial decree, he assisted in translating newly arrived Sanskrit manuscripts. When the Emperor’s carriage toured the East, he was ordered to accompany him as an attendant.
At that time, Emperor Yang was in the Jin Prince’s residence. Having been dispatched to take command in Hebei, he returned to the Bingzhou region to pay his respects.
There he lectured on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, *Śrīmālā*, and *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras. Prince Qin Wang Jun was stationed at Taiyuan and resided in the same mansion.

One night, he dreamed of a person with a golden body three zhang tall, who handed him a glass wine cup and said, "You may drink from this. He declined, saying, "I dare not, as it is prohibited by the Vinaya."

Upon arriving there, he saw that the image the King worshipped was identical to it. In the twelfth year [of the reign], an imperial edict ordered him to reside at Daxingshan Temple to oversee translation work.
Whenever a great vegetarian feast (mahā-pariṣad) was held, Sengcong would serve as the presiding master, exhausting his sincerity in every detail. The Emperor looked upon this and was deeply moved.

He then resided at Riyang Temple in Jinwang City, where he daily read the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, and other texts. Ren...
At the beginning of his life, he was sent to enshrine the śarīra at Kaiyi Temple in Bingzhou; at the end of his life, they were again enshrined at Longgai Temple in Fuzhou.

The auspicious responses were beyond the capacity of records to exhaust. He composed the *Śarīra-rui-tu-jing* (Sūtra on the Diagrams of the Auspicious Signs of the Śarīra) and the *Guojia-xiang-ru-i-lu* (Record of National Auspicious Omens). This was in the second year of the Daye era.
When the new capital was established in the East, the śramaṇas went to the palace gate to offer congratulations. By imperial decree, they were specially retained to reminisce about the past.

An edict was issued to station them at the Scripture Translation Hall in the Shanglin Park of Luoyang. When Lin’i was pacified, five hundred and sixty-four bundles comprising over one thousand three hundred and fifty sections of scriptures were obtained;
these were written on palm leaves in the script of Kūṇala. The Emperor ordered them to be sent to the hall, where Sengzong examined, collated, and cataloged them.
It consists of five fascicles and is further divided into seven categories: namely, Sūtras, Vinaya, Praśastis (Praises), Śāstras, Scripts, and Miscellaneous Works.
If translated using the language of the Sui dynasty, it would amount to more than two thousand two hundred fascicles. He compiled the *Record of India* together with Pei Ju.
The scriptures he translated before and after this total twenty-three works in approximately one hundred fascicles.

Having long suffered from chronic cold-natured ailments, he passed away at his lodgings on the twenty-fourth day of the seventh month in the sixth year due to dysentery. He was fifty-four years old; his remains were returned to Bo-ren for burial.
Zhangyuan, surnamed Zhao, was a native of Wugong in Jingzhao. His family had held high office for generations. He entered the monastic order at the age of thirteen.

When the calamity of the Northern Zhou arose, he lamented that the sun of the Buddha’s teachings had been eclipsed; he then made a solemn vow to gouge out his own eyes, pledging never to let the feet of the precepts be damaged.

During the Sui dynasty, when the True Dharma flourished, he underwent the tonsure and ordination once more, yet his wisdom and karmic legacy remained as they were before. From the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Yogācārabhūmi*...

He mastered the *Dhāraṇī*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, expounding them all upon hearing them but once; there was no one among the assembly who did not marvel and submit to his brilliance.
Yet, as for his personal conduct and his influence on others, how could they be fully detailed? He once stayed with Dharma Master Lingyu at Dongxia;

although the master’s disciples treated him with blunt disregard due to his straightforward nature, Master Lingyu alone marveled at his magnanimity and drew him in for conversation. Indeed, he proved exceptionally gifted, and the Master highly praised him.
Jushi said, "Truly, you are one of my disciples. He then shared his private quarters with him. They entered the Guanzhong region and lived in seclusion at Zhishang Temple on Mount Zhongnan.
When Sengyu was summoned to court by imperial decree, whenever he had leisure, he would visit Daoyuan, engaging in pleasant conversation and laughter.

Furthermore, he used the offerings bestowed upon him by the Emperor to relocate the temple's road; those who understood geomancy (fengshui) praised this decision. In the fourth month of the seventh year of the Daye era.

On the eighth day, he passed away at his residence in the monastery at the age of sixty-eight. Ten days prior to his death, the earthenware alms bowl he had carried throughout his life suddenly broke into five pieces for no apparent reason.
Huayan said to those around him, "The bowl is my life. Now that it has become thus, the five aggregates have dispersed.
Furthermore, as he was about to draw his last breath, when the bell was struck, it emitted a rasping sound and failed to produce its full resonance. His disciples...
Fali established a stupa and composed an inscription for it.
Jingxuan of the Sui dynasty was surnamed Zhao and was a native of Tianshui. At the age of seven, he became a student at the local academy.

At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, he received the teachings of Laozi, but soon thereafter he renounced them all and devoted himself exclusively to the scriptural division [of the Tripitaka]. He frequently ascended the high seat to guide the disciples of the profound mystery.

After he had received his full ordination, the reputation of the Śrāvakas spread even further. However, because the customs in the regions of Qin and Liang were corrupt and superficial, he sought to rectify them in order to perpetuate the life of wisdom;
the Emperor granted his request. He then issued the methods for advanced cultivation and decreed that they be implemented throughout the region west of the Yellow River.
Prince Yuande showed him exceptional respect and honor, issuing an edict to summon him and subsequently entrusting him with the Great Xingshan Monastery to propagate the teachings extensively.
During a lecture assembly, Dharma Master Can was seated in the audience and remarked, "From the time of Dao Lang until now, the West Land [China] has had its succession of eminent teachers;
it is you who shall now take up the reins. Subsequently, Emperor Wen passed away, and Yuanxing entered into meditative concentration. He then responded to the imperial summons and resided there.

On the twenty-ninth day of the first month in the seventh year of the Daye era, he passed away without illness at the age of forty-three. His countenance was profound and his nature was compassionate.
Shu [instructed]: "My final wish is that my remains must be discarded in the forests and wilds. Thereupon, his fellow villager Huiyan followed this instruction.
He subsequently collected the *śarīra* relics and constructed a stūpa on the western peak of Longchi Temple in Zhongnan Mountain, hoping to commemorate his virtue.
The śramaṇa Mingze of Jizhou composed an inscription for it to honor his merit. At first, Mingze had not yet attained a reputation; however, when he composed the [inscription for] Jueguan Temple...

Stele. [The character for] Ren (仁) minus two plus Ye (業) [refers to Jinye]. Yang Su saw him and marveled at his talent. He was subsequently recommended by imperial decree to reside at Sanchan Monastery in the Renshou Palace and to assist with the translation of scriptures in the Eastern Capital.
He further entered the Translation Institute to oversee the compilation of texts. Xue Daoheng remarked: "Master Ze’s writings repeatedly manifest fresh brilliance."
Yingying was uniquely enlightened. He passed away at the end of the Sui dynasty. A collection of his writings circulates in the world.
*Newly Compiled Biographies of Monks Classified into Six Categories of Study*, Scroll Fifteen;
*Newly Compiled Biographies of Monks Classified into Six Categories of Study*, Scroll Sixteen.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Tanne from Eastern Zhejiang.
*Jiexue hushetiao* (2) [Precepts, Study, and Protection of the Teachings].
Tang Zhishen, whose courtesy name was Huicheng, was surnamed Xu and a native of Xuzhou. He was the younger brother of Dharma Master Xuan.

Having grown up in Western Shu, he traveled extensively through the monasteries specializing in the Vinaya. Following the calamity of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, he entered the Guanzhong region from the east and lived in seclusion among the mountains of Zhongnan and Taibai, where he dwelt alone with only his own shadow for company.
During the Guangqi era of the Sui dynasty, when the True Dharma was being restored, he was summoned as a man of eminent virtue and took the lead in [the revival].
In Chang’an, he extensively propagated the Vinaya, and the assembly of listeners gathered in great crowds.
Later, as those seeking ordination became increasingly noisy and disruptive, he took his leave to enter Longju Mountain Monastery to dwell in quietude.

When Prince Xiu of Shu was appointed as the Governor-General of Yizhou, desiring to bring stability to the region of Kunwei and to clear and purify the territory of Jingluo, he first sent a letter to Tancong to convey his intentions to the people.

Furthermore, [the Emperor] sent this to invite Sēn. Thereupon, Sēn replied to him, the gist of which was as follows: "I have had the honor of receiving your letter and have read it over and over again, repeating each word three times.
Your prose is as clear as limpid water, and your analysis of principles is as precise as distinguishing a fine hair in autumn. This poor monk has resided in a secluded valley for over forty years;

I did not expect that in my old age I would have the good fortune to encounter such a time of auspicious clarity. I humbly reflect that the Prince of the State, His Highness, possesses virtues as lofty as those of the Three [Sovereigns]..."
The ancient Way shall be revitalized by a sovereign of a hundred generations. Rolling up his sleeves, he shall return to his native village; clad in brocade, he shall turn back to his home town.
The common people will have the prospect of a second birth, and all things will find relief from their burdens. The elders and youth of Jianan all await this coming salvation.

Need one rely on a gentle breeze for the grass to bow down? Naturally it will do so. You should urge the various leaders to cross the borders to welcome him. When Xiu received the report, he set fire [to the memorial].
Xiang paid his respects and announced to the army: "That people and things have come to this place is due to the power of the Vinaya Master.

From that time on, Daoxin returned to Shu and resided at Faju Temple. Both monastics and laypeople held him in extraordinary esteem. Once, he was presiding over a great *zhai* (vegetarian feast), and Dharma Master Xuan was seated among them.

Daoxin took up his chopsticks and asked him, "Is this place maintained in ritual purity (*hu jing*)? Xuan replied, "I have only just returned from the capital; it is too hurried and chaotic, so we have not maintained purity."
Xun threw down his chopsticks and rose, saying, "I would rather eat the food of a butcher than consume this molten copper!
At that time, the assembly of several thousand people dispersed together; such was the awe and dread they felt toward him. There was a monk named Dao Hui who was by nature violent and fierce;
whenever he saw Xun from afar, he would immediately flee and hide. Someone remarked, "You have never shown fear toward others before, so why do you alone stand in awe of Vinaya Master Xun?"
Yao said, "He is the King of the Buddha-dharma; how could he not be feared? [The Emperor] replied, "With your own physical strength, you can certainly match him one hundred or even ten times over.
Why, then, do you fear him? Yao said, "Now, as soon as I look upon him, all my vital channels sink and my four limbs fail to move.
How could I dare say I can match him? On the first day of the tenth month in the first year of Wude, he passed away without illness at the age of... (years).
80. Tang Pu Kuang’s secular surname was Fan; he was a native of Fufeng. At the age of seven, he followed Chan Master Shangyuan to leave the household life as a śrāmaṇera.
He dwelt in the mountains subsisting on cypress needles for fifteen years, where he devoted himself to recitation day and night with great diligence. After receiving full ordination, he practiced...
Regarding the Dhūta practices: he begged for food among the people, dwelling in forests and cemeteries for over twenty years.

Later, while traveling through villages to attend lecture assemblies, he would ascend the high seat to preach as soon as he heard their discussions; his expositions were always novel and brilliant, such that all who listened were won over and submitted to his authority.
During the time when Emperor Zhou Wu was still in concealment, [Sengyai] frequently engaged in debate at the Heshang River. He once resided in Fanchuan, where someone requested his...
As for Sengkuang: once, when he was about to sever his own throat with a blade, another man stopped him. The man then demanded his ears; Kuang cut them off without showing any sign of distress.

During the Jiande era of the Northern Zhou dynasty, the two teachings were about to be abolished, and the fivefold assembly in Guanzhong was unsettled. Kuang went in person to the imperial court to offer remonstrance, but it was not heard.
He withdrew and subsequently blended into secular life. The Emperor established the Tongdao Guan (Observatory of the Universal Way) to preserve the ancestral teachings. Furthermore—

Three hundred scholars were maintained within the palace, selected from among those of extraordinary talent in the Buddhist Way. Because Kuang was profoundly versed in doctrine and principle, he was appointed as the Director of Studies (*xuezheng*).

After Xiang’s dismissal, Kuang was further promoted to the post of *Chongshi* (Administrator) of Qishan. He habitually wore felt robes and silk caps, with his hair hanging down outside the cap and tied beneath his chin.
When adjudicating public affairs, he was as fluent as a flowing stream; even when matters became somewhat complex and urgent, he remained so.

He departed, saying, "I am originally a man of the Way. Who could endure this? During the Sui dynasty, the founder modeled himself after the Zhou dynasty by first establishing one hundred and twenty Bodhisattva monks.
Their appearance did not involve shaving or clipping the hair; instead, their headgear and robes followed secular etiquette.

He sought out those who had been renowned in previous days to serve as these monks, and Daokuang was indeed one of them. Shortly thereafter, they all returned to their former ways, and he resided at Xingshan Temple.
The Daoists collectively moved the bell of the Tongdao Monastery to the Xuandu Monastery, saying, "We have already received the imperial decree.
Sengkuang led his followers and contended with them, saying, "Our school is the orthodox one; we ought to receive the bell. The Daoists looked at one another and dispersed.
