During the reign of Emperor Yang, he was summoned to reside at the Chanding Monastery. At the end of the Daye era, an imperial edict appointed him to oversee the monastic administration. In the third month of the third year of the Wude era...
He passed away at Jimon-ji Temple at the age of seventy-three. By his final testament, he requested that his body be offered as an alms-gift and that no burial mound or grave be constructed.
His disciples gathered his remaining remains and enshrined them in a stupa on Longchi Peak in Zhongnan Mountain.

Tánxuǎn of the Táng dynasty was surnamed Cūi and was a native of Gāoyáng. By nature he was grand and extraordinary, not conforming to the customs of his time. Regarding the study of the scriptures, he pursued only their great principles;

he did not take the trivial details of phrasing as his primary object of study. Nevertheless, he was particularly profound in his mastery of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. In his later years, he resided at Xìngguó Temple in the Bìng region.
Whenever the assembly gathered, they invariably deferred to him to occupy the seat of honor. In his exchanges and responses to inquiries, his eloquence was vast and expansive.

He released [the prisoners]. Whenever they encountered the vanguard of his troops, he would immediately repel and crush them. People of the time referred to Yang Biao as "the Selector of Men" (Bao-xuan), because he identified Yang Liang’s rebellion before it had begun.

The rebels treated Xingguo Temple as their headquarters (Jia-fang) and Wude Temple as their supply depot (Shi-fang). When Yang Su entered the city with the imperial army, the rebels were all captured.
He then interrogated the various monks regarding their role as a nest for the rebels. The monks replied: "It was by the power of Your Majesty..."
[The King] was stern and urgent; [the monk] did not dare to obstruct or restrain him. This was because the garrison commander had instigated a mutiny. Thereupon, Suan-ru said:
"When the mutiny first broke out, there were several monks who remonstrated with the king and were killed. To say that the king's power is so stern and urgent—is this not a slander?
"Their sentiments are all identical to those of the rebels," [the King replied]. "You may proceed according to military law. At that time, he selected—

He stepped forward from the assembly and replied, "The fact that lawless people have recently disturbed the celestial order is entirely due to the gradual decline of the transformation of compassion to this point.
This is truly the fault of us monks. We would be honored by your instruction; how could we dare evade our responsibility? Suo was pleased.

Consequently, he dismissed the entire assembly of monks and remained alone with Xuan to engage in debate; they did not begin to part until late at night, and the other monks were likewise excluded from questioning him.
Toward the end of the Daye era, war and famine arrived in succession, such that alms could no longer suffice for their needs.
Although the state granaries were abundant, guest monks were especially barred by the gatekeepers. Xuan reflected on this, considering it a sign of the extinction of the Dharma. Every...
Taking up his staff, he drove away the gatekeepers and ushered guests into the hall until the seats were filled each day. His disciples, being young and lowly, remained silent and dared not speak;
after a long time, they reached an agreement that only Xu Nan was permitted to receive guests, while others were not allowed to follow this precedent.
Later, he placed [the offerings] in a large room and, daily, used what he received from the permanent endowment to provide gruel for beggars, combining those items with what he had obtained himself.

He personally supervised the distribution, seating the multitude of hungry ones in rows and apportioning the food with perfect fairness. He never slackened until harvest time, and the people relied upon him for their survival.

At the beginning of the dynasty, there was a śramaṇa named Zhiman who enjoyed great renown; he resided at Xinsi Temple in Yixing, where three hundred students came and went to study under his strict and orderly regulations.
One day, after the selection [of students] was complete, he went to the temple courtyard and questioned them, saying: "Have you all eaten your fill?"
"Wearing warm clothes—what further cultivation can there be in that? Yet its reputation spreads so widely; could this not be mere pretension?
Furthermore, what we practitioners perform must be based upon the scriptures and proclamations. As for what we rely on now, which scripture is it?

He replied, "It is the *Vaipulya* (fangděng) Sūtra repentance ritual. He said, "Then try reading it for me. Upon barely opening the first volume, he said, "This sūtra consists of four fascicles; it may be made to last four [days]."
The person was reading [the four fascicles] all at once. The śramaṇa Daocuo said from the side, "If one reads them all at once, the listeners may become confused and dazed.
[The reader] replied, "How can my hearing be the same as yours? Thereupon, he read the four fascicles all at once.
Before he had finished reading, [Daocuo] suddenly stopped him, saying, "The power of the dhāraṇī is such as this. He further remarked, "Vulgar customs are deceitful and corrupting."

Regarding the Buddha-dharma: if you can understand what it relies upon, you will come close to success. In the eighth year of the Wude era, he closed his door to nurse his illness and engaged in even greater self-reflection.
As visitors filled the corridors and courtyard, Daochuo lay on a mat like a corpse, drawing up his robes and extending his feet, saying, "Where shall I certainly be reborn now?
Daochuo replied, "The Master, the Western Land of Bliss, is named the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). That Buddha..."

His vows were profound. To those who wished to be reborn [in his presence], there was none whom he did not accept. He addressed them with a sigh, saying, "I am not your peer for one who seeks pleasure for the sake of the body.
Chao asked, "If this is truly so, then is there no rebirth? He replied, "Where there is no rebirth, there is nothing that is not reborn.
Thereupon, he stilled his breath. He lived to the age of ninety-five.

Fatong of the Tang dynasty was a native of Shilou in Longquan; the territory belonged to Xizhou. The region was characterized by perilous mountain passes and remote isolation, as seen in maps and records;
it was mostly inhabited by reclusive monks and solitary scholars. The local customs were particularly coarse and wicked.

If a wandering monk happened to encounter someone there who possessed some spiritual realization, that person would ask where he had come from, only to be met with the humiliation of having their face smeared with ashes. Although Fatong lived at such a time...
Before he left the household life, he was constantly weary of suffering. Toward the end of the Kaihuang era, his entire family followed him into the Buddhist path.

He said to others, "I have now finally been able to cast off my shackles and leave behind my chains. He settled in the prefecture, entrusting his two sons, two daughters, and his wife to the monasteries of the monks and nuns.
He himself served Master Ming of Tonghua Monastery with the etiquette due to a disciple. From that time on, the influence of his spiritual style reached everywhere.
Throughout the regions of Fen and Jin, there was no one who did not admire him. In villages and hamlets, monthly vegetarian assemblies (*zhāihuì*) were established;
furthermore, people would exchange cakes and food as offerings to break the fast. Even at great manor houses and noble residences, he would proceed directly to the inner chambers without obstruction;

the hosts would welcome him with smiles as if he were an old acquaintance. This custom persists to this day. Once, while traveling through the fields of Jia, he encountered the county magistrate and asked him what [scriptures] he had mastered.

The monk replied, "I am a mountain dweller. The magistrate ordered him to be bound and brought before him for interrogation. Tong immediately ceased eating grain and began circumambulating the prison while practicing the Way. That evening, foxes howled, causing the magistrate and his staff to hear them;

both the elders and the young found it impossible to sleep peacefully. The magistrate wished to release him, but Tong refused, saying: [...]* *Note: The original text fragment ends abruptly with "Tong refused, saying," indicating the remainder of the narrative is not provided.*

We considered this a source of joy. Even if we were left to our own devices, what else could we do? Furthermore, he continued his journey as usual without eating. The fox’s howling grew even more intense at night.
On the following day, the elders came together to reason with him and persuade him, whereupon he led his dog away. That evening, they sought lodging in a village house;
the dog bit his shin, and blood soaked his heels. The dog subsequently died of a seizure. Those who transmitted this account regarded it as extraordinary.
Fazang of the Tang dynasty was the son of the Xun family of Yingyin in Yingchuan. He lost his father at the age of three and his mother at the age of ten;
left alone and orphaned, he had no one upon whom to rely. In the second year of the Tianhe era of the Northern Zhou, Fazang was twenty-two years old.

It happened that on the eighth day of the second month, the Emperor was bestowing the tonsure upon monks to pray for blessings, and Fazang consequently entered the monastic order. In the fourth year, a crown prince was born.
An imperial edict was issued to select men of renowned virtue at Liquan Palace; Xuanzang was included among their number.

At that time, Emperor Wu was in the Chufang (Palace for Princes), and as [Xuanzang] hurried to the foot of the hall, he questioned the assembly of monks in the Xianbei language. The monks did not respond immediately, but Xuanzang alone stepped forward and answered the questions in Xianbei.
The court officials were all delighted, and the Emperor remarked, "This man is small in stature, yet his courage is great; he dares to [speak thus]."
The Prince replied to him as such, and furthermore bestowed money upon him as a reward and encouragement. From this, he received exceptional favor and patronage.

In the second year of the Jiande era, he moved his residence to Mount Zigai in Zhongnan. On the eighth day of the first month of the third year, he happened to find seven apricot fruits at the summit;
they were sweet and delicious when eaten. However, because the location was remote and the weather bitterly cold, it remained unknown from where they had come.
Before long, the calamity of the suppression of the teachings arose. Only Zang remained in seclusion in the mountains, as if alone and uninvolved. Thus it was for eight years.

Every time he thought of descending the mountain to sacrifice his life for the Dharma, in the ninth month of the first year of the Daxiang era, he knocked on the palace gates intending to have an audience with the Emperor.
The officials rebuked and stopped him. Zhao Wang Meng, the Senior Grand Master of the Prince of Wu’s household, and Yi Lou Qian, the Junior Grand Master, interrogated him regarding his purpose.
[He recorded] his own name, as well as those of his companions and the donors. The concluding words of the inscription state:

"This poor monk takes the mountain forests as his home, birds and beasts as his companions, and grasses and trees as his provisions. Furthermore, throughout the breadth of heaven, there is no land that is not the King’s domain;
and Mount Zigai lies within Your Majesty’s imperial borders. If this is so, then my companions and the donors are all Your Majesty. What more [need be said]?"
He asked about this, and Meng and the others reported it to him. The Emperor issued an edict saying: "I wish to govern and transform the people through the appearance and demeanor of a Bodhisattva.
Since this monk recently came from Mount Zigai, let him now keep his beard and hair long, wear robes and a cap, and serve as the abbot of Zhuhusi."
An imperial edict was issued to Yuwen Yi, Duke of Peiguo and Director of the Inner Secretariat, to inspect and implement [the reforms].
Tang Yi and Yuan Xinggong, both Assistant Directors of the Inner Secretariat, considered this to deviate from the established precedents and did not comply with the edict.

In the tenth month, they again presented themselves at the eastern city wall, citing the story of the two sons of King Wondrous Adornment who exhorted their father. They further remarked: "Your Majesty, when you were formerly our subject and son, we were unable to provide corrective counsel."

Consequently, he brought about the destruction of the late Emperor’s sacred scriptures and the melting down of divine images; his cruelty was even greater than Qin Shi Huang’s burning of books and burying of scholars.
The Emperor grew enraged and issued an edict for him to be executed immediately. Lord Pei (Liu Bang) interceded on his behalf, and the Emperor’s anger subsided slightly.

He then asked Lord Pei, "Was the practitioner afraid? Lord Pei replied, "The practitioner was foolish and ignorant, unaware of taboos. Having personally incurred the penalty of the law, how could he have been without fear?"
Terrified, [Hui]shang looked sorrowful and changed countenance, saying: "This is surely the 'goose-protecting bhikṣu' mentioned in the Buddhist scriptures.

I have heard of his deeds in the past; now I see the man himself. How could he be put to death? He should be pardoned. Grant him the robes and cap of a bodhisattva, and let him reside at Zhuchi Temple as previously decreed.
Sengzang immediately declined, wishing instead for personal freedom. The Emperor then issued an edict to the Censor Bao Hong, granting Sengzang permission.
He traveled through the five counties of Chang’an, Lántián, Zhòuwū, Hù, and Dú for ten thousand years, awaiting the opportunity to seek [the scriptures].
On the twenty-fifth day of the fifth month in the second year of the Dàxiàng era, Emperor Wén (Wǔ) acted as Grand Chancellor to promote the teachings of the Dharma.
In the sixth month, [the master] descended from the mountain and again underwent tonsure; the Emperor bestowed upon him a set of dharma robes and fifteen pieces of multicolored silk from Qingzhou.

One *shí* of jujubes. He returned to the mountains. In the seventh month, he again received an imperial decree to descend the mountain to deliberate on matters concerning the propagation of the Dharma.

On the fifteenth day, an edict was issued for Lord Jingling to accompany the Archivist Zang to ordain one hundred and twenty monks; all were granted monastic robes and sent back home, while Zang alone remained behind at the Chancellor’s residence.
On the twelfth day of the second month of the first year of the Dading era, the Sui dynasty succeeded to the mandate from Zhou, and the reign title was changed to Kaisheng.
On the fifteenth day of the first month of the [X]th year, an imperial edict was issued to summon the monks who had previously departed to perform religious rites at Daxingshan Temple.

In the second year, an edict was issued to Zhao Wei, the Secretariat Drafter, ordering the relevant authorities to provide a monthly stipend of *zangfu* (medicinal fungi), jujubes, apricots, oil, and firewood and charcoal as a permanent provision.
In the fourteenth year, the General of the Wuhou Command personally requested the cessation of these provided supplies.
Suheye donated his residence to construct a monastery to house the Tripitaka. Su Wei, the Right Vice President of the Secretariat, erected the main hall and the sacred images for the monastery.
A great vegetarian feast was prepared for ten thousand monks to consecrate the collection. Thereupon, the Attendant-in-Ordinary Pei Ju proclaimed the imperial decree, saying:

"Master Zang is the foremost among those who have shaved their heads; furthermore, he has personally hosted this great vegetarian feast. Who could equal the grandeur of his propagation of the Dharma? Now..."

The temple where he resided was named Faji. After a long time, his compassion extended even to animals; geese would circle the Buddha’s seat according to the proper times, and deer would not eat after midday.
When Emperor Yang was residing at the Jin residence, his younger son died prematurely, and the emperor had him interred in the Zang Temple.

As he was about to depart to govern the Huai and Hai regions, he wrote this inscription by hand and engraved it, saying: "The paths of the world are like illusions; birth and death are like floating bubbles.
Why is the child who died young so short-lived, and why is Pengzu so long-lived? Alas, my son! You have departed and shall not remain. May you forever become a seed of the Dharma."

He remained for a long time among his fellow Brahmans. He then took a *ling-shou* (myrobalan) staff and presented it to Xuanzang, saying, "Whenever you take up this staff, I hope you will remember me.
Xuanzang replied, "The King has entrusted his beloved son to the Dharma-gate with such affection; how could I ever forget that sentiment?
Just as the King cannot forget the staff in my hands, how would I dare to forget him? In the sixteenth year, the Emperor visited Qi.

The Emperor fell ill. Various princes and nobles fashioned images of Avalokiteśvara to pray for the Emperor’s well-being and longevity. By imperial decree, they were invited to be enshrined at Fazhi Temple for offerings.
In the first year of the Renshou era, the Emperor commissioned six life-sized statues of Śākyamuni; by imperial decree, they were welcomed and installed as previously done.
In the second year of the Daye era, Crown Prince Yuande passed away. Whenever there were offerings for the deceased’s merit, Zang was invariably entrusted with the management of the rites.
Toward the end of the Daye era, an imperial decree changed the name of Jiugong to a temple, and Zang was appointed as the *upādhyāya* of the newly established Taipinggong Temple.

At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, Prince Huai’an first began to show great reverence and devotion toward him; shortly thereafter, the Prince passed away, and Zang also departed this life. He was buried three years later.
At Nanyunji Temple on Mount Ganfu, the śramaṇa Xiaocai composed the inscription, which was engraved upon a slab of fine stone.
Tang Mingzhan, surnamed Du, was a native of Shiyi County in Hengzhou. From his youth he possessed noble conduct; by the time he had passed the age of learning, his character was already established.
He had already thoroughly mastered the classics and histories. When his commandery nominated him to take the imperial examinations, he did not comply with the order.

He soon followed the tonsure ceremony at Yingjue Temple on Mount Feilong. Shortly thereafter, he went to Da集 Temple in Ye to hear the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* under the guidance of Dharma Master Daochang.

When the persecution of the Dharma occurred, he fled to the mountain valleys of Dongjun. Upon the Sui dynasty’s accession to the throne, an imperial edict summoned him to reside at Fazang Monastery in Xiangzhou.

In the third year of the Kaihuang era, an imperial decree was issued for him to engage in translation, and he subsequently moved his residence to Daxingshan Temple. Shortly thereafter, the assembly recommended him for the administrative duties of the temple.
In the second year of the Daye era, there was a monk who, due to his foolishness and recklessness, violated the laws of the court; the authorities reported this to the Emperor.

At that time, the Emperor was extensively deploying his military forces and was about to perform the suburban sacrifice. He spoke with indignation, saying: "Regulations have long been promulgated; it is a matter of principle that one must pay due respect. Now..."

The monks all stepped forward and stood still; they no longer observed the customary etiquette. Why was this? Thereupon, among the followers of Huang-Lao, both men and women, there were none who did not prostrate themselves and pay homage, yet the monks remained as before.
Zhan then stepped out from the assembly and addressed the Emperor, saying: "If Your Majesty truly desires to honor the teachings..."
"Furthermore, it is certainly the rule that one in dharma-robes does not show reverence to the laity. The Emperor issued an edict, saying:

"If you claim that one in dharma-robes does not pay respect to the laity, why did Song Wu perform such acts? He replied: "That was an unprincipled ruler; how could he possibly be compared to Your Majesty’s sagely brilliance?

The Emperor asked this question five times in succession, and further ordered an attendant to speak to him repeatedly, yet he still would not bow. The Emperor turned to his attendants and had his defiant arguments recorded.

The man named Zhan visited the palace the following day to offer his thanks. The Emperor remained composed and immediately issued an edict for the two Chan temples to each provide a meal for the monastic community of the capital and bestow rolls of silk as offerings.

Later, the Emperor said to his ministers, "In all the realm today, there is perhaps but one monk who acts for the sake of the Great Dharma without fear of birth and death," referring specifically to Zhan.
By imperial decree, Zhan was appointed to reside at the Chan Temple and subsequently promoted to the position of *zhongyin* (Chief Administrator).

The administrative head (zhishi shangzuo) oversaw all monastic affairs. Upon entering the imperial court, he maintained his former status. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, he was summoned to the inner palace for an audience and granted a meal.
After the meal, he composedly and exhaustively expounded upon the principles of compassion. The Emperor was greatly pleased and issued an edict to prohibit slaughter;

every year on the sixth day of the third month, the court observed a vegetarian fast. Furthermore, at all sites where military expeditions had previously taken place, [monasteries] were necessarily established.
Regarding the Buddhist temples: they were established for the purpose of relying upon them for salvation and deliverance.

These include Choyun in Tongju, Jachoyun in Jinju, Pujŭi in Yŭju, Hungjŭi in Bunju, Choyok in Chiju, Tŭngja in Jeongju, and Chogyak in Nakju. The founding of these seven temples was indeed initiated by Chŏn.
Chŏn provided the resources for his gong, robes, and alms bowl, fed a thousand monks every year, and concurrently transcribed Mahāyāna sūtras.

Regarding his discourse on the practice of giving, he did so to repay the kindness of his mother. Shortly thereafter, he moved to Zhiju Monastery on Mount Taiyi; at that time, his years were already advanced.
As his physical decline and exhaustion increased, he required medical treatment and thus returned to Xingshan Monastery to take his medicines.

He subsequently established a grand communal support system and extended invitations to the great virtuous ones (*bhadanta*) of the capital to bid them farewell. Prime Minister Fang Xuanling and Duke Ruohui Du offered their contributions as alms.
Offerings were piled high. The next day, he returned the *zhijù* (wisdom torch) and sat contemplating the Pure Land. He said to his attendant, "Amitābha Buddha has come.
After a short while, he added, "The two great Bodhisattvas have also arrived. Regarding the contemplative gates (*guānmén*) described in the sutras, I have achieved them all;
only the remaining four gates were not yet accomplished. Now that I have seen them all clearly, how joyful this is!"
Alas! He then suddenly passed away on the twenty-seventh day of the tenth month of the second year. His age was seventy. By imperial decree, he was cremated;
when the fire was extinguished, his skeletal remains were found intact, with even the hair on his head preserved. Only upon his crown did there shine a brilliant purple light.
He was promptly interred beneath a cliff.

Huisheng of the Tang was the son of Liu [surname] of Pengcheng. His ancestors were descendants of the Han dynasty. His grandfather, Xin, was a General of the Right-Forward Division and Governor of Langya under the Liang dynasty.
His father, Ya, was a Minister of War under the Chen dynasty. His paternal great-uncle, Zhiqiang, entered the monastic order in his youth and bore a great reputation;

he served as the Great Sangzheng of Guangling under the Chen and was well-versed in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Huisheng was twelve years old [when he entered the order].

He immediately took Qiang as his teacher and devoted himself to the lecture halls. At the age of sixteen, he requested instruction from Master Zhijiao on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* at Zhuangyan Monastery in the capital of Yangdu.
At that time, the Chen dynasty succeeded the Liang in its governance, and Emperor Wu especially revered the Buddhist teachings;

he frequently recited the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (Renwang jing) and hosted grand vegetarian feasts. Taking advantage of these opportunities, [Seng]qiang was granted an audience to debate before the Emperor, and his eloquence was peerless.
He stood out from his peers and was held in high regard by the Emperor. On the eighth day of the fourth month, the Emperor again convened a religious assembly at the temple.

During this gathering, Shenxiang (Sheng) presented the argument that the Buddha-fruit transcends the two truths (*satya*). A Dharma Master, who had previously resided at Kaitai Temple and later entered Qihuan Temple, asked:
"Does the Buddha-fruit transcend the two truths, or do the two truths transcend the Buddha-fruit? Shenxiang replied: "It is the Dharma Master who transcends [the discussion]."
Kaitai acted as the Dharma Master for the opening ceremony. He said, "As a mandarin duck does not roost in a latrine;
as Śakra-devānām-indra does not dwell with ghosts; as the *kauśika* bird does not nest in a withered tree; and as the great ocean does not harbor a corpse.
At that time, Jiao was in the assembly and sighed, saying, "A formidable opponent! His edge is difficult to withstand. He stepped forward and removed the garment he was wearing.
Tianzhu received Nāgārjuna with great honor; consequently, his reputation grew even further. The Prince of Guiyang, Minister Mao, Jiang Renye, and others all extended their respect and admiration.
At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, the Prince of Jin, who was the Grand Marshal (Taifu), established the Huiri Monastery in Jiangdu.
Daoxuan, having received imperial edicts, moved there to reside and was treated with the courtesy accorded to a family priest, being invited to enter the capital where he encountered [the Emperor].
During a lecture, Jingying Huiyuan engaged in a discussion with him that flowed like a torrent. Huiyuan marveled, saying, "What kind of monk from Wu is this?
Could there truly be anyone in the world who surpasses him? This was because they had never met before and he was seeing him for the first time.

Upon returning to Huiri Monastery, [Daoxuan] further unleashed his talent and eloquence, such that the monastery’s veteran masters were all humbled by him. When the King heard of this, he was delighted and bestowed rewards upon him.
One hundred rolls of fine silk. Emperor Gaozu of the Sui dynasty, intending to tour Mount Dai, halted his carriage at the Yi and Luo rivers.

He issued an edict dispatching great virtuous monks from Jiangnan and Guandong to ascend the hall and expound upon the Dharma. Among those who responded to the summons, none could oppose him. The Emperor marveled at his extraordinary talent.

In the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui, he took the accumulated wealth he had amassed and used gold and jade to adorn a single incense altar, which he offered to Yongfu Temple in Weiyang.

In the sixth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, an imperial edict was issued to all commanderies to select three eminent monks (*mahāsattva*) each to expound the *Renwang jing* at the Si-fang guan in the Eastern Capital.

The Emperor then summoned Daoming to serve as the chief lecturer; for three consecutive days and nights, he did not lie down to rest. When the imperial carriage traveled to Zhangye, he accompanied it.
An edict was subsequently issued for him to expound the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* for the High Chang King, the Qu clan; Qu spread his hair upon the ground to serve as a mat for Daoming.

He ascended the throne. In the eighth year [of his reign], the Emperor visited the Eastern Capital (Luoyang). Two seven-story wooden pagodas were constructed in the capital to offer posthumous sacrifices for the Emperor’s deceased father and mother.

Consequently, an imperial edict was issued to enshrine and inter the Śāri-ratna (relics) therein. Shortly thereafter, high officials, scholars, and commoners erected more than thirty *vijaya-dhvaja* (victory banners/stupas) in rows.
From Xingshan Monastery, they escorted the Buddha’s sacred remains to Chanding Monastery, where the Master preached the *Ratnaketuparivarta-sūtra* (Renwang jing).

In the twelfth year [of the Zhenguan era], an imperial decree was issued to have a sandalwood image from the kingdom of Kucha copied at the Eastern Capital (Luoyang) and bestowed upon the various prefectures and commanderies.

In the fourth year of Wude, when the state had first stabilized the empire, an imperial decree stated that in regions recently disturbed by turmoil, it is difficult to distinguish between the right and wrong of the monastics.
It was therefore decreed that one monastery may be established in each prefecture and county, with thirty monks remaining there, as a demonstration of lenient grace. Its...
The rest were dismissed by Hui Tai. The Emperor considered Luoyang to be the capital of the world, certainly incomparable to any other place.
Nevertheless, despite the incident involving the "false Zheng," he still permitted over two hundred monks to reside at Tonghua Temple;

moreover, since Sengsheng had previously been defiled yet was someone the Emperor had long admired, no inquiry was made against him, and an imperial edict was issued for him to reside at Shengguang Temple.
The temple was indeed a meritorious achievement of the State of Qin. In the eighth year, the Emperor visited the National Academy and performed the ritual of *shidian* (sacrifice to the sages).

Previously, three seats had been arranged in the hall to represent the three traditions; thus, eminent Confucians and preeminent Buddhists, including the most outstanding figures of the Li clan, gathered like clouds and mist to enjoy the spectacle.
The Emperor decreed: "The teachings of Laozi and Confucius are the primary traditions of this land; the teaching of Śākyamuni arose later. It is fitting that..."

The guest rites were honored. The command was that the Confucians take precedence, followed by the Buddhists, and then the Daoists. At that time, Fasheng was highly esteemed and supported by the assembly;
having ascended the seat, he turned pale with alarm upon hearing the decree. Now, the Emperor was residing at the Qin residence, a position superior to all his ministers.
He looked directly at Fasheng and said, "Simply expound the imperial virtue; have no other concerns. Fasheng then proclaimed: "The Supreme Heaven..."

The lower realms are sustained by honor and nobility, and the conditions for karma arise from them; these must ultimately rely upon the Buddha and the sages. Now, I shall set forth the general principles and prescribe the appropriate rites:
everyone shall join their palms and kneel with devotion, so that there may be a standard for both teacher and disciple. Thereupon, beginning with the Crown Prince and those below him...
All descended from their seats and knelt to listen. As he mounted the platform, he first praised the imperial virtue; next, he expounded the principles of the Śākya school;
finally, he raised two difficult questions to simultaneously challenge both teachings. The Emperor responded with great admiration. After a short while, he issued an inquiry, saying:

"Yesterday, the Daoist Pan Dan submitted a memorial stating that Prince Siddhārtha could not have attained Buddhahood, but only became a Buddha after seeking the Way for six years. This, then, is the Way..."
One can give birth to a Buddha. A Buddha is accomplished through the Way; the Way is the father and teacher of the Buddha, while the Buddha is the child and disciple of the Way.
Therefore, a Buddhist scripture says: "Seek the unsurpassed, right, and true Way. It also says: "Realize and understand the Great Way, and give rise to the unsurpassed intention.
In the language of the foreign lands, it is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; in the Jin translation, it is rendered as "the unsurpassed Great Way. Judging by this, [it is clear that] the Way...
It can likewise be known that the Great Buddha is [chronologically] prior to the Small [Daoist] one. Regarding the principles of their mutual correspondence and regulation, it is briefly stated:

Lao Dan was born at the end of the Zhou dynasty, while the Buddha appeared at the beginning of the Zhou. Calculating the reigns between them, there were approximately twenty kings; discussing the years, there were over three hundred years.
How could the Buddha have existed during the time of King Zhao, and subsequently sought out the Way during the time of King Jing? As for the Daoist practitioner Li Zhongqing mentioned previously...

The discourse on the Way states: There is the Supreme Great Way, which was born before heaven and earth. It mists and billows within the vast void and blazes brilliantly above the Jade Purity (Yuqing).

This is the teacher of the Buddha; it does not refer to Lao Dan of Zhou. The Three Sovereigns had no Lao Dan, and the Five Emperors had no Lao Dan, yet that which is called the Way has never been absent.
Since Guanzi [Guan Yin] requested that he be commissioned to write the book, Empress Dou...
The Emperor issued an edict to promote learning; only then did the Way of Lǎn begin to circulate in the world. Yet, the Way does not point exclusively to Lǎn.
The *Yījīng* says: "One yīn and one yáng—this is called the Way. That yīn and yáng cannot be fathomed is called the Divine.

Now, if even yīn and yáng cannot be measured as to their origin, how much less could they give birth to a Buddha? Chē Yìn said: "To cultivate it within oneself is virtue; to extend it to things is benevolence."

Regarding the Way (*dào*), Yin Zhongwen said: "Virtue (*dé*) means attainment; the Way (*dào*) means following. The *Lunheng* states: "To establish one's person is called virtue; to achieve renown is called the Way.

As for virtue and the Way, it does not necessarily require that person to wear robes of cloud-mist, a golden crown, and jade pendants, to have the title 'Heavenly Honored One' (*Tiānzūn*), or to dwell atop Mount Dàluó within the Jade Capital (*Yùjīng*). Rather, [it is simply this]: [The text continues: "...to be able to cause others to attain the Way through one's own virtue, and to be able to cause others to attain virtue through one's own Way. This is what is meant by 'virtue and the Way.

It is not necessary for one to possess supernatural powers, to ascend to the heavens, or to descend to the earth, or to transform oneself into a dragon or a tiger, or to ride upon clouds and mist. It is sufficient if one can cause others to attain the Way through one's virtue and cause others to attain virtue through one's Way. This is what is meant by 'virtue and the Way.'"

He was one who was named for the Great Way. In the third year of the Zhenguan era, while at Shengguang Temple, he erected a precious stūpa for śarīra relics, adorned with magnificent images and endowed with various divine transformations.
He also established a Vaipulya (fangdeng) dharma-assembly hall and practiced the rite of repentance during the six periods of day and night to repay the kindness shown by His Majesty.
On the twentieth day of the tenth month in the fourth year, he passed away at his residence.
The Master was seventy-six years of age. His disciples, including Dazhang and others, followed his final instructions and performed the cremation at the mouth of the valley in the Southern Mountains.
They collected the remaining ashes and enshrined them in a stupa at Shengguang Monastery. The śramaṇa Falin composed the inscription for the stele.

As for Master Cheng, he served through three reigns and witnessed the succession of six emperors. He frequently encountered imperial favor and personally received the Emperor’s edicts; outwardly, he was honored by kings, dukes, and high officials.
As for the scholar [Zhang]: within the palace, the consorts, queens, ladies, and concubines all received the fragrance of his precepts and together offered him the rites due to a teacher.
He lectured on the *Nirvāṇa*, *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Golden Drum*, *Vimalakīrti*, *Daśabhūmika*, and *Tattvasiddhi* Sūtras and Śāstras, each several dozen times. Zhang was the adopted son of his clan;
he was skilled in chanting and hymns, and served as the Director of Lectures (*Dujiang*).
Tang Baoqiong was born into the Ma family in Mianzhu, Yizhou. She entered the monastic life at a young age and was pure, upright, frugal, and simple in her lifestyle.

She would invariably read the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* once every two days. Later, when she moved to Fushou Temple, she led the various districts in establishing a "Society of Righteousness," with thirty people in each group.
Every month they would prepare vegetarian feasts and recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, each person taking one scroll. This continued for nearly...
There were over a thousand communities. Originally, that region did not revere the Buddha-dharma, but followed only the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice (*Wǔdǒumǐdào*).

All those registered under it were called "Way-people" (*dàomin*). One day, they held a grand Daoist assembly and invited Sengqiong with great persistence; he arrived, and whenever he went, he would take his seat.

At first, no one prostrated. Everyone agreed that the Heavenly Honored One (the Buddha) ought to be bowed to. Sengqiong said to them, "The heterodox and the orthodox differ; what each serves is distinct.
In my dharma, even Heaven is not worshipped with prostration, much less the Lord Lao. If I were to prostrate where I ought not to prostrate, I would surely bring shame upon you all.
Although the assembly did not cease their pleading, he finally performed a single prostration. Immediately, both the image and its pedestal shook. A second time...
When he prostrated before the image, it collapsed and was destroyed. The assembly was struck with fear and requested that he receive the precepts for laypeople.
The County Magistrate Gao Da, recognizing his supportive contributions, further invited him to propagate the Dharma. He passed away in the eighth year of the Zhenguan era.

The Tang monk Fèng was surnamed Xiāo and was a descendant of the princes of the Liáng dynasty. His father, Cháng, served as the General for the Recruitment of Distant Regions and Governor of Xīnchāng during the Chen dynasty.

Because Fèng had enjoyed an excellent reputation from his youth and his physical bearing was such that he could not be contained by the mundane world, at the beginning of the Kāihuáng era of the Sui dynasty, the Dharma Master Sēngcàn...

His reputation was as weighty as the vast ocean; thus, he surrendered his heart to seek the Way, serving [Fazang] with the etiquette due to a teacher. Fazang observed his refined spirit and transmitted to him the True Vehicle (*samyak-yāna*).
He elucidated the distinctions of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and detailed the positions of the eight powers (*aṣṭa-vaśitā*). The Emperor [Wen] grasped these essentials without omission.

During the reign of Emperor Yang, when the cultural refinements reached their peak, the imperial camp halted at the southern suburbs during the Daye era. An edict was issued stating: "The military and state affairs..."
The customs of both the Chinese and the barbarians have not changed; they revere their sovereign and honor their superiors, preserving the distinction between names and substance for generations.

Since the regulations have long been promulgated, how can one dare to oppose these rites? Thereupon, the followers of Laozi all prostrated themselves, yet only the monks and nuns of the Buddha school looked at one another without bowing.

At that time, the śramaṇa Mingzhan had previously declined the imperial summons. Although the Emperor repeatedly issued edicts urging him to attend court, Sengfeng—who was then presiding over Chongjing Temple—held a significantly lower rank.
Having no choice but to proceed, Mingzhan presented his reasoning for why he could not show reverence; his arguments were so thoroughly substantiated that the matter was ultimately dropped.

After the Empress Dowager of the Sui dynasty passed away, the Chanding Monastery was constructed, and Mingzhan was invited to enter the ordination hall to provide exegesis. [He remained there] until the end of the Zhen... period.

During his stay at Zhongshan, Du Zhenglun, Chief Secretary of the Secretariat, submitted a memorial [recommending him]. He was subsequently transferred to the position of Senior Seat (Upādhyāya) at Dingshui Monastery.
Shortly thereafter, he was invited to Longgong Monastery in the western mountains of Qizhou; that monastery lay with its back against a series of tiered cliffs.
Facing south toward the clear Wei River, the stone mirror reflects the sun; pines and creepers overspread the sky. To fully satisfy his secluded sentiments, he went there without hesitation.
Even while ill, he was still able to rise and open the *Lotus Sūtra* to demonstrate the benefit of his final words of parting.
He passed away at the temple on the twenty-third day of the twelfth month of that year. He was seventy-seven years of age. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa.
On the northern plain of Chen Cang County, the disciple Fawei erected this inscription. The calligraphy is by Ren Ye, and the text is by Zhang Ting, Duke of Yan.
Huijing of the Tang dynasty was born into the Fang clan of Zhending in Changshan. His paternal uncle, Huiyuan, was a State Doctor of the National Academy during the Sui dynasty.

At the age of fourteen, Huijing entered the monastic order; he could memorize over eight thousand words daily. He studied treatises such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, and the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, as well as other scriptural divisions.
Toward the end of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, he arrived at the imperial capital, where his excellent reputation spread far and wide, attracting a multitude of disciples.

During the early years of the Daye era, while serving in Qin, he once traveled to Huaili. There, he encountered Yang Hong, the Magistrate of Shiping, who had assembled a gathering of monastics and laypeople at Zhicang Temple to debate the Dharma.
He intended for the Daoist priests to ascend the seat first; although the Buddhist monks were numerous at that time, none dared to speak out against this.
Jing stepped forward from the assembly and said to him: "Your Excellency has convened the fourfold assembly to weigh the merits of the two teachings. I venture to say—"
[The official] did not understand. He requested to inquire about his doubts, saying: "What is the reason? For there are constant rites for guest and host, just as a cap and shoes cannot be inverted.
How could one place a Daoist ahead of a Buddhist in a Buddhist temple? Your Excellency’s teachings have their proper order; please do not let the fundamental human relations fall into neglect.
The Prefect said: "How profound! I was nearly mistaken. Thereupon he placed the monk first, while the Daoist Yu Yongtong, whom the Prefect held in high esteem, followed.
The Emperor commanded that the six meanings [of the title] be explained as follows: "There is something formless yet complete, born before heaven and earth;
I do not know its name, but I style it 'the Way' (Dào). He then ordered Jing to provide an exegesis. Jing said, "A Dharma Master must employ words and principles with precise correspondence;

one must not commit the faults of 'flat heads' or 'tail-end rhymes. At that time, the Emperor was wearing a flat-topped cap (*pingmào*). Jing then remarked jokingly, "I, a poor monk, do not even wear a cap."
The magistrate said, "A hat—would you rather violate the rule against a flat top? If one does not violate the flat top, then one violates the upward-pointing tail.

Sengjing said, "When this poor monk casts off his shoes and ascends the seat, it is naturally upright and without a tail. Your Excellency, when you loosen your kerchief and wear your cap, it may be called level and without a head.
The magistrate was left with an embarrassed expression. Sengjing then asked Daotong, "There is a thing formed by blending; is it blended because its substance is one, or..."
If they are mixed because their substance is different, then at the very moment of being mixed, each has already established itself as a distinct entity; thus, oneness would not arise from the Way.
If they are mixed because their substance is one, then before they were mixed, each had already established itself as a single entity; thus, duality would not arise from a single source.
The Master said, "Your Way surpasses that of all others; I request you to resolve my doubts. Thereupon, Tong was utterly at a loss for a reply.
Jing said, "Since you, Master, have been able to open the gates and invite the enemy, how can you now cease the drums and lower the banners, thus suffering defeat so easily?

He then turned to the Magistrate and said, "Since Your Excellency has provided such assistance to the Way, how could you fail to save it? The Magistrate also felt abashed. After this, although [he] did so many times...

In providing reinforcements, he always struck down [opponents] in accordance with the occasion. At the beginning of the Wude era, Emperor Shendao visited the Fayuan Temple for a dharma assembly where officials from the three ministries were all gathered.
At that time, Dharma Master Qingce established the doctrine of "shattering emptiness" (*khaṇḍana-śūnyatā*).

Wang Jingye, the secretary of the Chancellor’s office, submitted an imperial decree requesting a formal debate. He asked: "I do not yet understand this 'shattering of emptiness. What is it that further shatters emptiness? He answered with "emptiness."

To refute emptiness is not to do so by means of existence; rather, it is said that grasping at emptiness is the disease, which is then cured by emptiness itself. Likewise, grasping at existence is the disease, which is then removed by existence itself.

In the second year of the Zhenguan era, newly arrived Sanskrit manuscripts were presented. An imperial edict was issued for the relevant authorities to select men of renowned virtue to perform the translation.

Jing served as the scribe (*bishou*), producing works such as the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra* (Da zhuangyan lun). He also composed thirty fascicles of commentaries. [The master] Prajñāvarman (Bopo Sanzang) [was also involved].

He said, "Is this not a Bodhisattva from the East? In the thirteenth year, while Gaozong was residing in the Eastern Palace, he assembled the palace officials and scholars of the Three Teachings in the Hongwen Hall and ordered them to debate with the Daoist Cai Huang.

Huang adjusted his appearance and asked, "The scriptures state that the 'Preface Chapter' is the first; I do not understand to which section the Preface belongs. Jing said, "When the Tathāgata entered meditative concentration..."

As for the portents: light was emitted, wonders appeared, the earth shook, and flowers rained down. By means of the distant to open the near, this serves as the grand foundation for breaking through duality and the gradual process for clarifying oneness;
therefore, it is called the "Preface. "First" (*di*) refers to a position; "one" (*yi*) refers to the beginning. Since the preface occupies the foremost position, it is called "the first.
Huáng says: "The character 'first' (*di*) is the same as 'younger brother' (*di*). If one is a younger brother, one cannot be called 'one' (*yi*). To speak thus—
On one hand, it cannot be called "di" (younger brother); on the other, the two characters are contradictory. How can this be reconciled? Jing said:
"Did I not say before that 'di' means 'to dwell' and 'yi' means 'beginning'? Since you, Master, failed to understand the former principle and instead mistakenly raised this latter objection."
"This is merely difficult for oneself; how can it be considered difficult for others? Huáng said, "If you do not understand what I have said, please explain it again.
Jìng then addressed the Prince of the East, saying: "In the past there were two men: one named Śreṇika, who forgot to sweep even when holding a broom;

the other was Śāriputra, who understood a thousand things upon hearing them once. Thus, while Śreṇika did not awaken even after hearing twice, Śāriputra grasped the meaning immediately upon the first utterance. This...
"It is not that you do not understand the Way; it is simply that you have received the Dharma, yet you are not of superior caliber.
Huáng said, "The Master’s words do not even leave his lips; what is there for you to comprehend? Jìng said, "When a Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma, his voice shakes the ten directions.

Yet the Daoist masters sitting here are as if lost or intoxicated. How can one say their physical forms are merely deaf or blind? Their wisdom is likewise suppressed. Huáng said, "This is like a jackal preaching the Dharma."

"How could this have been heard? Jing replied, "The celestial palaces are strictly guarded; by their very nature, they are beyond the tracks of beasts. The Daoist’s soul was bewildered, leading him to mistake a man for an animal.

Kong Yingda, the Director of the National Academy, stepped forward from the side and said, "There is no such person as 'Jing' in the Buddhist tradition; how could the Dharma Master have fabricated this?
Jing addressed the Prince of the Eastern Palace, saying, "Even during the lifetime of the Tathāgata, there were already such matters. It was the Buddha who refuted the non-Buddhists."
The non-Buddhist could not provide an explanation and, on the contrary, said to the Buddha: "You always claim for yourself that you are impartial.

Now that you have refuted me with these challenges, you are clearly not impartial. How can you be called impartial? The Buddha explained to him: "I used my own lack of partiality to refute your lack of partiality."

"If you attain equanimity, that is my own equanimity as well. It is the same now: by using the dispute of purity to break through their dispute, they will attain non-dispute, and purity itself will also be without dispute.
At that time, the Crown Prince said to Sengying: "Since you have spoken so incisively, you are truly a partisan of the Way.
Sengjing then replied: "I have heard that a gentleman does not take sides; how could this apply even to the Grand Master?"
"What is this faction? The Crown Prince smiled with composure and said, "I did not expect the Dharma-joy to reach such a state.

Shortly thereafter, the Crown Prince issued an order requesting that [Hui]zheng preside over Puguang Monastery and concurrently serve as the *upādhyāya* (abbot) of that monastery. [Hui]zheng declined the offer in a formal letter, which was not permitted.

Jingcai was both erudite and possessed of vast learning; having extensively propagated the sūtras and śāstras, he also compiled various treatises, including the thirty-fascicle *Xuanwen of the Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*. All [these works] were...
He compiled commentaries on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* in over thirty fascicles, for which Chu Liang, the Court Doctor of the Grand Music Bureau (*Taichang Boshi*), composed a preface.

He also produced a ten-fascicle commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Furthermore, he extracted the essential commentaries for the *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda*, the *Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Warm Bath Ritual*, the *Ullambana Sūtra*, and the *Birth Stories of the Upper and Lower Heavens*.
He also compiled the *Yinghua Shiji* (Collection of the Essence of Poetry) in ten fascicles, for which Liu Xiaosun, the Counselor to the Prince of Wu, wrote a preface.

His other writings are not recorded in full. In the nineteenth year, he was again summoned to engage in translation; however, after the imperial decree was issued, he declined on the grounds of illness.
At that time, he was sixty-eight years old. Nothing further is known of his final end.
Huijin of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Wu and was a native of Jiangdu in Yangzhou. At the age of seven, she entered the monastic order under Dharma Master Rong.
Whenever she accompanied Rong on his travels, she never dared to leave him. She would often wait upon him until late at night, whereupon she would lie down on the ground beneath Rong’s bed.

She studied and mastered the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra), becoming able to lecture upon it; her contemporaries praised her greatly. During the Renshou era, Rong received an imperial summons to enter the capital.
He dwelt in meditative concentration and traveled together with Xie Jin. Upon receiving full ordination, he applied himself with single-minded diligence to the Vinaya-piṭaka.

Under the guidance of his two teachers, Shan and Zun, he studied and expounded their teachings more than twenty times each. Consequently, regarding the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* and the Vinaya-piṭaka, he penetrated the most subtle and profound depths.
People considered him one who relied upon the Mahāyāna to propagate the monastic code—a feat difficult for others to emulate. Toward the end of the Daye era, the four suburbs...
The enemy lines were numerous. A band of bamboo-reed thieves marched forward with drums beating, and none dared to oppose them.

The veteran monks of Chanding Monastery, realizing that Yuanzhi possessed the strategic wisdom, courage, and strength required for the task, established watchtowers and defensive works at Kunchi Estate.

One day, when the thieves arrived in great force, their banners stretching for ten li, Yuanzhi consequently removed all his weapons of war and instead prepared a feast. He personally went to the camp.
In the midst of this, he invited the bandits to his residence and allowed them to eat and drink their fill before they would leave.
The thieves said to one another, "How could we betray such a capable practitioner? They took only ten oxen and departed. Having traveled halfway, they returned the oxen to Sengjin.
At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, he served as the *upādhyāya* (abbot) of Yunhua Temple. Not long thereafter, he was summoned to serve as the administrative head (*gaowei*) of Puguang Temple.
He passed away in the winter of the eighth year at an age of over fifty. As for those such as Man-de, Shan-zhi, Zhen-yi, and Jing-dao, they were all Faxin’s fellow students;
they admired one another’s integrity and formed a close circle, yet most have now perished. How tragic!
Tang Zhishi’s secular surname was Shao; he was a native of Wannian in Yongzhou. From childhood, he was extraordinary and possessed of marvelous qualities.

When playing with other children, his speech invariably concerned the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). A white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*) between his eyebrows was several inches long, its radiance illuminating his chin and forehead.

At the age of eleven, he left the household life and resided at Dazongchi Monastery, where he studied the doctrines of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, and the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.

They all mastered its subtle and profound depths. In the fourth year of the Wude era, shortly after the initial pacification of Wang Shichong, the Emperor resided at the Qin Residence and issued a distant summons for the Great Dharma Master Hui-cheng Dao-zong Bianxiang, along with more than twenty virtuous monks from the capital.
At the age of thirteen, he was in the assembly at Hongyi Palace. Seated in the lowest position, he was summoned by the Emperor to engage in debate;

his speech was clear and outstanding, startling those who had heard him before, and none among the others dared to follow with a response. The Emperor and the various princes sighed in admiration, saying, "This young monk is brilliant and fierce;
in the future, he will surely be able to propagate and uphold the Triple Gem. The śramaṇa Jizang said to him, "You possess..."
Regarding these auspicious signs, he remarked, "I shall surely follow in the footsteps of the Śākyamuni; it is only a regret that I am old and dying, and thus shall not live to see him.
In the seventh year, the Turks invaded Bingzhou, and the capital was placed on high alert. A monk named Fayaya had long been favored by Gaozu for his sycophancy and flattery;
Gaozu had granted him wives and concubines and treated him as a slave. Upon this occasion, Fayaya requested that monks from the capital temples who were both brave and robust be selected.
He formed a separate army of one thousand men and appointed his own general to lead them against the enemy.

At the age of twenty-one, he perceived that Master Ya’s undertaking was truly motivated by heterodox designs. Fearing that the coming disaster would bring great harm to the Dharma, he sent a letter to Ya, saying:
"We were born together in this age of semblance (Sāṃprata-yuga), sharing this era of decline. We grieve for the chaotic turmoil of the six realms and lament the suffering of the four [assemblies]."
Since you have not yet attained awakening, whenever you frequent the Phoenix Gate, you constantly encounter the Dragon Countenance.

It would have been fitting to sprinkle the nectar of immortality upon the Emperor’s heart and spread the compassionate clouds over all sentient beings; why then did you give rise to the perverse views of Sunakṣatra and stir up the evil winds of Devadatta?
This would cause a good reputation to vanish in that very moment, while an ill repute would spread through future generations.

Is it not because you harbor patience toward the court and heeded the counsel of the commoners, yet now indulge this foolish sentiment and articulate such obstinate views? Furthermore, once a *tāla* tree is cut down, it will never grow again;
once a rock is split apart, there is no sense in which it can be rejoined. Hurry and take up your robes and bowl; leave the monastery at once, so as to bring purity—

Turbidity and purity flow in different currents; the fragrant orchid and the stinking mugwort differ in their scents. If this were so, then the court would cease its critical discourse, and the Brahmins would fall silent amidst the sound of slander.

The water of meditative concentration, once choked, would flow anew; the lamp of wisdom, once obscured, would shine forth again. Do not remain forever self-concealed; I trust you will take these words to heart.
When Sengya received the letter, he became even more enraged. He intensified his supervision of provisions, grain, and weaponry, and set a date for the expedition to depart.
Shishi then declared to the assembly: "Sengya intends to incite rebellion and destroy the Great Dharma Wheel; this is truly the work of Māra.

Thereupon, he wept aloud, and a thousand monks wept simultaneously, their voices shaking the plains and wilds. Those who heard it were moved with sorrow. Shishi then stepped forward and struck Sengya several times with his fists. Sengya—
He fled and hid. The matter was immediately reported to the throne, and an imperial decree ordered him to be handed over for legal interrogation. Yet he showed no sign of fear.

Later, upon the petition of Xiao Yu, the Vice President of the Department of State Affairs, his crime was pardoned; he was released and permitted to return to lay life. The thousand monks [involved] were also dismissed from their positions, and each returned to his own monastery.
In the first year of the Zhenguan era, an imperial edict was issued dispatching Du Zhenglun, the Censor-in-Chief for Judicial Scrutiny, to inspect the Buddhist clergy.
Fearing that those of inferior character might be mixed among the pure assembly, [the monk] sent a letter to Lord Du, saying: "The humble monk Zhishi respectfully states:

At the age when one carries oranges, I already bore the name of a 'Pure Faith' layman; at the age when one gathers peaches, I have presumptuously assumed the rank of a 'Siksamana. Although my wisdom is shallow and my capacity narrow..."

I am capable. Nevertheless, I venture to look toward those who have attained mastery before me. I have privately observed the monk Fayā of Huadu Monastery, who accumulated the causes of goodness in past lives and has received the fruits of fortune in this present life.
He is like Anshang traveling to the Qin state, or similar to Huiyuan entering the Jin dynasty.

In principle, he ought to maintain the conduct of protecting the geese and uphold the resolve of binding with grass; he should contemplate repaying the grace of the Emperor and the sovereign, and offer thanks for the support of heaven and earth.

Regarding these virtues, I observe that stūpas and pure monasteries have constantly become slaughterhouses, while viharas and meditation groves have been permanently turned into chambers for wives and children.
Thousands of monks have been stripped of their robes; the fourfold repentance gives rise to earth-shaking sorrow.

The sūtras of the Seven Buddhas are slandered, and the myriad nations harbor grievances against Heaven. Since the time Emperor Ming of the Han was moved by a dream and Kāśyapa Mātanga entered Luoyang, it has been thus.
Such a monk, I have never heard of before. When the Emperor received the mandate of abdication, he nurtured the myriad regions of the world;

he sighed that the Way of the King might be pure and that the Dharma-realm be free from defilement. You, sir, registered your name under his auspices and served him with loyalty, yet you were permitted to abandon your life for the sake of the Way.

You eliminated the calamity of the sugarcane and uprooted the hollow trees, causing the Zen groves to flourish in lush splendor and the flowers of wisdom to spread wide. Your abundant fruits and noble reputation resound throughout the realm.
How can Your Majesty endure such wicked flattery? You still carry your almsbowl at Jetavana, yet you have abandoned me, your loyal and pure servant. Your tracks have ceased at the stūpas and temples;
the Dragon Gate is deep and precipitous, leaving no way for an audience. The celestial steps are suspended on high; when shall we meet before them?
May you, whose impartiality is like water and a mirror and whose wisdom perceives the subtle and hidden, deign to rescue us from this startled cage and save these parched fish.
To present such matters while in a state of extreme distress would only increase my trepidation. [Hui]lun reported this, and the Emperor issued an edict stating:

"Zhi indeed previously incurred the punishment of the late Emperor for his violent and rebellious conduct. Since returning to the secular life, however, his observance of the precepts has not declined, and his adherence to the Way has become even more earnest."
The decree for his ordination as a monk was left as it had been before. Later, Ya was ultimately executed on charges of madness.

In the eleventh year, when the Emperor traveled to Luoyang, he issued an edict stating that Daoists and female Daoists—specifically regarding places where they perform ritual offerings, processions, or stand in assembly—should all rank above the monks and nuns.
When I, Shi, heard of this, I submitted a memorial with the Venerable Fachang to offer counsel. Its summary stated: "The State’s imperial lineage originates from..."
Since the time of the Grand Scribe (Zhang Daoling), those who have sought to honor their ancestral lineage have elevated his teachings out of a heart that venerates their forebears.
However, they do not realize that the Daoists of today are merely the descendants of the Three Zhangs and are truly not the progeny of Laozi.

If their rank were placed above that of the monks and nuns, I fear that the genuine and the spurious would become confused, thereby harming the state’s civilizing influence. I have therefore carefully recorded the Daoist scriptures as well as the various histories of the Han and Wei dynasties.
The Buddha’s teachings on the sequence of cause and effect were presented as before. We humbly hope that Your Majesty’s divine compassion will graciously deign to grant us an audience.
The Emperor then dispatched Cen Wenben, Secretary of the Palace Secretariat, to proclaim an edict stating: "This clear mandate has long been in effect; those who do not submit shall be flogged.
Thereupon, each was flogged and released to return home. Subsequently, he went into seclusion at Sanyuan in Wei Yang. Those who admired and followed him gathered daily like clouds. Not long after—

After several days, he was stricken by a severe illness that nearly proved fatal. He ordered four of his disciples to carry his bed back to his residence at Dazongchi Monastery, where he took his leave, saying:
"In truth, I am but a person of meager merit, yet I have presumptuously joined the ranks of the Sangha. My lifespan is determined by fate; what cause for regret could there be?"
I am merely filled with lamentation because the Dharma teachings have declined and the faculties of people have become shallow and inferior. Recently, in a dream, the Seer Asita appeared and told me:
"From this life onward, you shall always be able to leave the household life. I believe these were no empty words. Shortly thereafter, he passed away.
This was the first month of the second year [of the Yonghui era]. He was thirty-eight years old. He was buried in the monastic cemetery at the South Suburb.

The śramaṇa Puying was bright and clear in character and possessed strategic talent; he was well-versed in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. This was precisely when Fu Yi was肆意 (indulging in) slander and defamation.

The assembly of monks sat by and watched, none of them exerting any effort. Daoying then entered the Bureau of Astronomy and summoned Xi Yi to debate. Whatever questions were posed, Yi was unable to answer;

he could only say, "These are the demonic ravings of a shaven-headed monk; who would deign to engage with him? Daoying replied, "From antiquity, the sages and worthies have held this in high esteem, yet you alone treat it with contempt and arrogance.
If it is not a demonic portent, what is it? Having retired, he composed the *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Destroying Heresy) in two parts.
Carrying the scrolls upon his back and slung over his shoulders, he went to the imperial court to present them.

Meanwhile, he further prepared a draft copy and entrusted it to the Secretariat and the various offices of the Hanlin Academy, so that it might reach the Emperor’s hearing and thereby sell his doctrine. Whenever he encountered Wang Yi, he would pull him aside and intercept him, refuting him with correct principles.
Since Yi had no learning, he was at such times forced to remain silent. His teacher, Fa-xing, was particularly firm and decisive. Fang...

In his daily life, he constantly exhorted himself to practice without the slightest negligence. Whenever he saw ruined stupas or dilapidated shrines, he invariably undertook their restoration and maintenance.
At the beginning of the Wude era, when Buddhist temples throughout the land had not yet resumed their activities, he opened up lodgings to provide for those traveling to and fro;
both the elderly and the young praised his virtue. As these sites were all affiliated with Dazongchi Monastery, they are recorded here as supplementary accounts.

Tang Falin’s surname was Chen; he was a native of Xiangyang. His ancestors resided in Yingchuan and had followed the Confucian profession for generations. Falin was exceptionally brilliant and spirited.
He left home at a young age and traveled through the regions of Chu and Ying, eventually retiring to the mountains of Qingxi. There his learning progressed even further;

whether speaking extemporaneously or writing with a brush, his literary style was consistently radiant, startling both those who saw and heard it. Subsequently, regarding the two teachings of Confucius and Laozi...
Together with us Buddhists, they form a triad. While Confucius established the teachings of worldly human relations, Li [Laozi] excelled in pure emptiness;
yet how could his traces not remain within the world? There must surely be extraordinary chapters and secret dharmas that those outside cannot perceive.
I shall seek them out to see them in their entirety. Thereupon, he let down his hair and donned a crown, gradually entering among their kind.

At the beginning of the Yining era of the Sui dynasty, he was again enrolled in the registers of a palace temple. Having long been well-versed in the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*, whenever he expounded upon them, the Daoists were invariably pleased and submissive.

From then on, he entrusted all the prohibited texts that they had previously hidden away to him for correction. The fabrications of Zhang [Jingxuan] and the falsehoods of Ge [Hong] could no longer be concealed;
as for those [texts] held by our own side, he was able to critique them. At the beginning of the Wude era of the Tang, he shaved his head once more and resided at...
At Jifa Temple in the capital, there was previously the Daoist Fu Yi, who had illicitly returned to secular life and served as the Director of the Bureau of Astronomy.

Because of his deep-seated prejudices from former habits, he harbored a profound aversion to the Buddha-dharma. In the fourth year [of the reign], he compiled eleven points regarding matters of the Buddha-dharma that were detrimental to the state and submitted them as a memorial.

The Emperor granted him an audience and issued an edict to assemble the great virtuous monks (*bhadanta*) of the capital for questioning. Daolin answered the imperial decree, asserting that the Ultimate Way transcends words.

How could the nine schools of thought discern it? The Dharma-body is formless and cannot be expounded by the Ten Wings [of the Book of Changes]. Yet, the four realms of existence are vast and boundless, drifting and sinking in the ocean of desire;
the three worlds are teeming with life, tumbling down the mountains of heterodoxy. The various sectarians are deluded and burn themselves; ordinary people are submerged and do not emerge.
Thereupon, one of the royal lineage of the Central Kingdom renounced worldly affection to leave the home-life, while the nobility of the Western Xia grew weary [of the world].
Entering the Way from amidst glory and splendor, he vowed to transcend the two kinds of birth-and-death and resolved to seek the single, wondrous Nirvana.

He propagated goodness to repay the four debts of gratitude and established merit to provide sustenance for those in the three realms of existence; such was his benefit to others. He altered his physical appearance to fulfill his resolve.
Therefore, they discard their fine hair and beard to transform their appearance and conform to the Way. Thus, they set aside the constant roles of ruler and subject;

though their outward form lacks the means to nourish their parents, they inwardly cherish filial piety. Though their ritual conduct deviates from serving a lord, their hearts retain gratitude for his kindness.

Their grace extends to both enemies and kin, thereby achieving great harmony; their blessings reach both the hidden and the manifest—how could this be restricted to minor transgressions? Those of superior wisdom rely upon the words of the Buddha.
Therefore, it is beneficial. For those of the lowest and common sort, it is detrimental because they undermine the holy teachings. By punishing evil, the profligate reform themselves;
by promoting goodness, the enlightened are moved to transformation. This is the general outline of the matter. Yet, although Yi submitted his memorial, the relevant authorities did not implement it.
Furthermore, he produced many copies of the petition and circulated them far and wide, so that from the capital to the villages, everyone spoke of the "bald-headed men" (monks).
He was subjected to such derision that, at banquet gatherings, people spoke with great vehemence, singing songs of "barbarian ghosts. The sun of the Buddha was obscured and failed to shine;

the prestige of the monks was dampened and they were left without influence. At that time, there were among both the clergy and the laity those who were clear-sighted and discerning, all of whom composed essays and proclamations to condemn [the game of] *yi*.

However, the Emperor ultimately maintained that his initial position was authoritative and would not listen to them in the end. Consequently, Daolun composed the *Poxie lun* (Treatise on Destroying Heresies); the text is extensive.
[The Emperor] did not record it. When the treatise was presented, the Emperor was slightly awakened; he had the memorial submitted by Yi set aside.

Yu Shinan, the Assistant Tutor to the Crown Prince, loved it and wrote a preface for it. Yi became even more dissatisfied and, together with his followers, composed further treatises to denounce the Buddha and the sages.

As the fragrant and the putrid became mixed, some grew suspicious. Daolin then authored the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Correct) in eight fascicles, annotated by Chen Ziliang of Yingchuan.

An explanation follows. Its preface states: "In the past, when Confucius dreamed of the man [Zhou Gong], the principles of the Ten Wings were fully revealed; when Boyang [Laozi] passed through the Pass, the meaning of the Two Chapters was thereby established.

Whether it be hooking into the profound to bind the images or exploring the mysteries of the unseen and the unheard, these matters cannot be proclaimed by conventional names and words, nor can they be fathomed by the principles of yin and yang.
Yet they are still able to encompass heaven and earth and include all spirits and deities. The Way is without..."

Pervading the great trichiliocosm, his words have not yet transcended the mundane realm; how much less so regarding the Dharmakāya’s perfect quiescence, which wondrously transcends both existence and non-existence?

Its ultimate principle is profound and mysterious, its traces vanish within the true and the conventional. Its essence is severed from the three marks, its afflictions exhausted through seven births; where there is no mind, this is precisely the mind.

That which is not form is form; beyond the fish-trap and rabbit snare, how could it be described in words? As for the Marquis of Xi being imprisoned at You, he subsequently manifested the subtle and profound;

as for Sima Qian being confined in the silkworm chamber, he ultimately fulfilled his predecessor’s will. Thus the *Yi* says: "The ancient makers of the *Yi*, did they not have their sorrows and anxieties?
This statement is indeed well-founded. There were two Daoist practitioners, Li Zhongqing and Liu Jinxi.
These and other such works were all composed in mediocre prose that slandered and defamed the True Dharma. Among the laypeople, some consequently gave rise to false beliefs.

The Dharma Master, pitying them for their blindness and ignorance, then composed this treatise, saying: "It may be said that he beats the drum upon this ocean of Dharma and brandishes his sword of rhetoric.

The sharpness of the 'Azure Cock' gallops in competition; the excellence of the 'Yellow Horse' rushes forward in contention. There is nothing that does not have its leaves fall and its branches broken, its clouds dispersed and its mists rolled away."
This treatise exhaustively elucidates the sources of the teachings of Śākyamuni and Laozi, and reaches the ultimate refinement of their principles and logic.

Fearing that later students who delight in such matters might have points they do not yet understand, I, your disciple, recently prostrated myself and followed it to seek its meaning. What I beheld was so brilliant it overflowed my eyes, like the sun and moon entering one’s own breast;
its silent response to my inquiry was like a precious jewel illuminating all things. Having thus awakened to the illusions of the four crossroads, [I am now at peace].
He then ceased his travels through the hundred cities and began to provide commentaries on what had not been heard before.

At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, the Emperor established Longtian Monastery at the former residence of the Dahuagong Palace in the Southern Mountains. Daolin, appreciating its tranquility and seclusion, took up residence there.

When the community nominated him for the administrative duties of the monastery, in the thirteenth year, the Daoist Qin Shiying, who frequented the Eastern Palace, privately extracted passages from Daolin’s treatises.
The central authorities spoke thus. The Crown Prince said, "This constitutes a slander against the Imperial House. The Prince agreed with this and reported it to the Emperor.
The Emperor was enraged and issued an edict to purge the monks and nuns. He decreed that those remaining must practice according to the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (Yijing jing);
otherwise, they too were to be purged. Subsequently, Senglin was summoned for interrogation. Lin presented himself at the public court and was placed in shackles.
The Emperor asked: "In the ancestral alliances of the Zhou, those of different surnames were ranked last. To honor the ancestors and value kinship is truly derived from antiquity.

For what reason do you fail to show mutual understanding, instead acting like a rat at both ends? You have extensively cited analogies of physical resemblance and fully set forth the metaphor of the 'polluting stream.
Senglin replied: 'King Wu was a Great Sage and the Duke of Zhou was a Great Virtuous One; yet they [had to deal with] Guan and Cai, who were all their brothers.'"
One's parents—perhaps they were honored with the ritual music of a Son of Heaven, or perhaps seven chariots were sent to release them into neighboring states.

This is due to nothing other than the retribution for good and evil. As the *Book of Documents* says: "The August Heaven has no favorites; it assists only those who possess virtue. Today, the world is one family;
who among us is not a relative? Laozi said: "My teacher is the Ancient Sovereign of Western India," and he further said: "I..."
The Master [the Buddha] skillfully entered *nirvāṇa*; he was subtle and pervasive, as if existing yet not. Thus, the Buddha was indeed the teacher of Laozi.
The followers of Liu and Li lacked true knowledge; having taken Laozi as their teacher, they further fabricated accounts to slander the Teacher of Laozi.

Since no one in the world could discern this, I have composed this treatise in eight fascicles, briefly responding to more than sixty points raised by the Daoists, all based upon [scriptural authority].
