In the historical records, he did not dare to offer any further debate regarding the state. Thus, they engaged in debate for more than twenty rounds, yet his arguments never faltered.

The Emperor again asked: "In the 'Chapter on Faithful and Defamatory Retribution' of the *Bianzheng lun*, it is stated that those who recite the name of Avalokiteśvara will suffer no injury even when facing the blade.
You should test this yourself; you may recite it with utmost sincerity. Seven days hence, I shall—"
"I shall execute you. If you have truly experienced the efficacy of recollecting Avalokiteśvara, then even execution will cause you no harm;

if there is no such efficacy, then the crime of deceitful falsehood shall certainly not be pardoned. Seven days later, the Emperor sent an edict to inquire: "Have you had any visions? Lingyun took up his brush and replied:
"Since the turmoil at the end of the Sui dynasty, poison has flowed through the four seas. Your Majesty, by the power of compassion, has rescued and protected all living beings."
"If it were not for the supreme power of the Buddha manifesting his spiritual mechanism, this would simply be the descent of Avalokiteśvara into this world.

Therefore, for the past seven days, I have thought of nothing else but Your Majesty. When the Imperial Secretary for Scrutiny Wei Zong was dispatched by imperial decree to inquire, "Yesterday you invoked Avalokiteśvara;
why do you now invoke the Emperor? Lin replied, "Because the virtue of Your Majesty is as great as that of Avalokiteśvara."
"To think of Your Majesty is precisely to think of Avalokiteśvara. Furthermore, the treatises composed by Lin were intended solely to enlighten the human mind.
Your Majesty, having misunderstood, has imposed punishment upon him; yet even if severe penalties are meted out, they do not diminish Lin’s spirit by so much as a single hair.

The Emperor was somewhat awakened to this truth and issued an edict commuting his sentence to death, banishing him to Yizhou. On his way, while passing through Bailao Pass, he passed away due to illness.
At Bodhi Monastery, his life lasted sixty-nine years. The śramaṇa Huixu was a native of Wugong in Yongzhou and was skilled in the *Śatya-siddhi-śāstra*.

Later, while he was establishing the conditions for the community through hospitality, Daolin arrived at Bailao; Xu attended to him with great care, exhausting every expression of kindness and affection.
When he died, [the Master] still rested his head upon his knees; he wailed and leaped about as if for a close relative.

He arranged for the burial on the summit of Mount Dongshan, erected a white stupa, and inscribed a commemorative stele to record the event. The Daoist Qin Shiying was subsequently impeached by the Censor Wei Cong and died in the大理 (Dali) prison.
Ling’s collected works in thirty fascicles circulate in the world.

Hui-man of the Liang family was from Chang’an in Yongzhou during the Tang dynasty. His father, Li Can, served as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Hai, Die, and other prefectures; he was particularly devoted to the Buddha-vehicle.

When Hui-man reached the age of seven, his resolve was to renounce secular life, and Li Can constantly praised and encouraged him. It so happened that an imperial edict was issued, permitting the people to leave the household life.
When Sengcan was serving as the Governor of Haizhou, he subsequently caused Faman to undergo tonsure. At that time, Dharma Master Xian’s fame resounded throughout the capital;
possessing both talent and learning, he resided at Daxingshan Temple. When Sengcan resigned his official seal and returned home, he sent Faman to receive instruction from him as a disciple.
Xian then took him with him to reside at Sanshan Temple within the Renshou Palace. At the beginning of the Daye era, they moved to reside at Dacanding Temple. Once there—
Upon receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), he studied the Vinaya under the Vinaya Master Zhishou, becoming proficient in its protocols and ritual decorum.

When it came to establishing boundaries (*sīmābandha*) and ascending the ordination platform (*maṇḍala*), he always took the lead among his companions. He was especially renowned for his meticulous and thorough investigation of doubtful points in the texts.

In the third year of the Zhenguan era, while he was lecturing on the *Karmavācanā* at the home of Wei Bingcao in Fucheng, a fire suddenly broke out in the thatched cottage. As the flames intensified with the wind, he searched everywhere for water.

He sprinkled water upon it and it was extinguished. Those who understood the matter attributed this to the power of his preceptual virtue. In the seventh year, by imperial decree, he resided at Xinsi Temple alongside various great virtuous monks.
Before long, he was summoned by decree to serve as the *upādhyāya* (abbot) of Hongji Temple. The strictness of its regulations remains such that people continue to stand in awe and submission.
A nun at Jixian Temple cast an image of Laozi, the Perfected One, for her own private veneration. She summoned Huang...

The group of officials gathered in the Hall of Celebration (*Qinghui-tang*) and, together with the bhikṣus, offered a vegetarian feast. Faman rebuked and stopped them, then assembled the Saṃgha to carry out the formal act of censure (*pravāsanīya-karman*).

He further changed the iconography of the Buddha image to that of a *rākṣasa*. Subsequently, he entered Taiyuan Temple. At the convent of Zhengguo Temple, the nun Huishang had managed to gain privileged access to the imperial palace.
Previously, when Emperor Shendao had passed away, the court deliberated on establishing a memorial service for his spirit at the convent where Huishang resided.
The official [Wei Shangman] summoned those residing at the Bhikṣu Monastery, saying: "The bhikṣus shall not remain here; you must all assemble.
Over two hundred people, including the three leaders and the virtuous elders of the capital, gathered. He then performed the ritual of expulsion, declaring:

"Since the propagation of the Buddha-dharma, there has never been a community of nuns who have used the power of the state to seize a monastery inhabited by bhikṣus. You should all leave this assembly!"

They continued to live together. If any of the fourfold assembly dared to associate with Shang and others, engage in social visits, or discuss religious matters with them, they were likewise expelled.

Thereupon, Shang became greatly afraid and appealed to the Prince of the East to seek a resolution. An imperial decree was issued dispatching Du Zhengyan, the Official in Charge of the Eaves (Yan Shi).
The assembly of bhikṣus gathered to lift the suspension. Huiman said, "Your Highness upholds the True Dharma, and I, Huiman, apply the principles according to the Dharma.
Now, however, you have violated principle and succumbed to sentiment; the established order is in chaos. He then grasped his sitting mat and withdrew, while those monks who remained—

Faru hastily followed the proposal for reconciliation. Upon hearing this, Sengman sighed and said, "Those who side with the good are few; what can be done? Later, although Shang repeatedly apologized, he ultimately paid no heed.
When the Emperor traveled to Luoyang, because the imperial surname was the same as that of the Buddha, he ordered the Daoist attendants to precede the Buddhist monks—a practice contrary to precedent.
Sengman gathered two hundred monks, each of whom removed his *kāṣāya* robe and placed it upon his head, then submitted a memorial to remonstrate.
In the evening, he bathed the monks and prayed to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). On the twelfth day of the fourth month in the sixteenth year, he contracted a slight illness.

He distributed all his accumulated possessions to the Triple Gem and sat cross-legged upon a rope bed. While answering questions from the assembly of another temple, his spirit remained clear and undimmed.
Suddenly, his breath ceased at the mouth, and he passed away. He was fifty-four years old. His body was cremated at...
Beside Longchi Temple on Mount Zhongnan, his tongue alone was not consumed by the fire; even after adding more wood and burning it for an entire night, its color became increasingly bright red.

He was buried together with the other remains in the mountains. During his lifetime, he lectured on the Vinaya more than thirty times and authored twenty fascicles of commentaries on the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya).
The śramaṇa Huisheng of Jingzhu Temple in the capital composed an inscription and eulogy for him, which is recorded in a separate collection.
Tang Daoji was a native of the Xiangli clan from Anyi in Hedong. His family name was Zi Cai.
At the age of twenty, he met the Vinaya Master Hongzhan and received the tonsure. He then withdrew to the Double Peaks (Shuangyan) to pursue his aspirations.

Furthermore, he devoted himself to the study of the Dharma under Chan Master Falang, remaining in seclusion within the mountains for three years, through both winter and summer. Thereafter, he sighed and said:

Profound realization is indeed difficult to attain; thus, one must thoroughly investigate the holy teachings. In the thirteenth year of the Kaihuang era, he studied the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* under Dharma Master Puxing at Yuanxing Monastery.
In the eighteenth year, he went to Baochang Monastery in the capital to consult with Dharma Master Mingji on the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Furthermore, relying on Dharma Master Biancai Zhenning, he practiced the study of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra*. In the third year of the Renshou era, he continued his studies and investigations.
In the seventh month of the fourth year [of the Wude era], while at Wude Monastery in Bingzhou, the śramaṇa Faleng was visited by Di-chi. At that time, Yang Liang rebelled;

consequently, Di-chi and his companions, including the masters Su and Jie, returned south to their native villages, where they extensively propagated and expounded the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, and various other treatises.

Zhilin Zhiming devoted himself exclusively to the *Dichijing* (Sutra on the Stages of Yogic Practice), declaring it to be the ultimate in moral exhortation and the essential core of mental discipline (*cittadharma*).

Thus, his virtue benefited those of humble station, and his Way harmonized with both the red-robed and blue-robed [lay and monastic] communities. Yet, he alone showed no regard for the community of nuns. He frequently said to his disciples:

"Women are truly a defilement to the precepts and are censured by the sacred scriptures. When the Buddha permitted their ordination and entry into the homeless life, it caused a diminution of the True Dharma. Upon hearing this name...
Yet your mind remains defiled; how can you claim to be untainted when facing such circumstances? Furthermore, the teachings value purity and clarity, excluding what is improper to avoid confusion.
In secular society, avoiding suspicion is highly esteemed, a principle upheld by gentlemen. Although I am not yet equal to this standard, I ask that you follow its measure;
thus, the spirit of purifying oneself and rising above the mundane can be envisioned. Previously, during the early years of the Sui dynasty, the śramaṇa Baoceng was at Pujiao...
At the temple, the construction of a hundred-foot Maitreya Great Image was commenced. Just as the work had begun, Fotudeng suddenly announced his passing. The elders requested Daoci to succeed him;
in barely ten years, the labor of carving and adorning it was completed. Both monastics and laypeople gathered to offer congratulations.

Previously, when Daoci had accepted the invitation, he had dreamed that two lions beside a cliff, at the side of the great image, continuously spat forth bright pearls without ceasing. Upon waking, [he realized this was a sign].
He then reflected: "The lion symbolizes the fearless flow of the Dharma; the bright pearl symbolizes the inexhaustible giving of wealth. Will my undertaking succeed?
He immediately ordered the dream to be depicted and displayed it before the image. The temple was situated on the southern slope of Pufan, a place of exceptional scenic beauty.
The statue, moreover, was extraordinary, truly a magnificent sight throughout all time and the world. Yet, long-standing decay had set in.
Wearing coarse clothing and eating simple food, he exhausted his will and toiled his body to bring it to completion; one may truly call this diligent.
Thus, the Vice-Director Pei Xuanzhen and the Regional Inspector Du Churong both sent incense as offerings and paid their respects, presenting robes and seeking the Dharma.

Toward the end of the Sui dynasty, Yao Junsu, the Administrator of Hedong, proposed that śramaṇas should defend the city against external enemies, issuing an edict stating: "Whoever dares to remonstrate shall be executed."
Ji Fen said, "We have established our traces beyond the dust of the mundane world, yet the world wishes to humiliate us with the status of common soldiers—is this right?
Thereupon, he joined Dao Xun and Shen Su in advancing [to the Emperor] and saying, "Have you not heard of those who do not fear death?
If death is of benefit, one has no fear even in dying. We fear only that it may be of no benefit and we die in vain. Furthermore, in the past, the High Ancestor of Han..."
The Emperor honored the Four Recluses, and the empire was at peace; Lord Wen held Gan Mu in high esteem, and the state of Wei was well-governed.

Today, these practitioners of the Way devote themselves to virtue and righteousness while distancing themselves from profit and fame; in this regard, they are nearly equal to the Four Recluses and Gan Mu. Such is the manner in which they are revered and honored.
If you do not see that it is right for the Duke to remain free, but instead detain him to compel him into military service, then the Duke’s departure from Han Gao Wenhou will be even more extreme;

yet those with discernment can already foresee this regarding the Duke. May the Duke consider this carefully. Junsu had always possessed a robust spirit and vigor of mind, so he was released without further interrogation.
Later, Junsu was ultimately murdered by Xue Zong, a local man of the commandery. Ji remained steadfast in his integrity.
In the tenth month of the tenth year, Fayi finally passed away at his residence. When he was initially approaching the end, he experienced no suffering whatsoever.
He addressed his disciples, saying, "I am now seventy-five years old; my death is certain. A disciple said, "The Master is only sixty-nine years old.
If you truly were seventy-five, there would still be six years remaining; why do you bid us farewell so abruptly? Fayi replied, "Death..."
It is a matter of birth and number. But how can numbers be real dharmas? They are merely provisional constructs consisting of speech and names.
When I was formerly registered in the census, the Provincial Governor added six years to my age. Calculating from that time until now, my lifespan should have come to an end;
indeed, within three days, I passed away.

Tang Fachang’s secular surname was Zhang. He was a native of Baishui in Nanyang. His great-grandfather, Long, served in Hebei during the Wei dynasty, and his descendants subsequently registered their residence there.
In his youth, he studied Confucianism; by nature, he loathed worldly complexity and distraction.

At the age of nineteen, he went to Dharma Master Tanyan to receive the tonsure and immediately began studying the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, subsequently lecturing upon it. Those who heard him marveled at his extraordinary talent. Tanyan once entered *samādhi*...

The Master [Hui]ding said, "You shall uphold the Buddha-dharma. At the age of twenty-two, when the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (She lun) was first emerging, he observed that his own teacher’s school mostly adhered to old conventions and rarely attained extraordinary insights.

Thereupon, he traveled extensively through the regions of Qin, Qi, Zhao, and Wei, thoroughly investigating the essential tenets of the *Satyasiddhi*, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and the *Yogācārabhūmi*. After five years of diligent labor, he finally produced commentaries on these works.
The Emperor relied upon him to resolve the doubts of the multitude. During the Sui dynasty, Prince Xiao Jian of Qi, on account of his reputation, summoned him to ascend the high seat.

From then on, his disciples gathered from all quarters, and his lectures and recitations continued without interruption. During the Daye era, an imperial decree appointed him to reside at the Chanding Monastery, where his influence in refining the teachings was exceptionally great.

Under the present dynasty, both near and far, peace prevailed; his transformative influence spread abroad. When the sutras were being translated during the Zhenguan era, he was commissioned to provide verification of the meanings, and the Emperor further decreed that he...

Recognizing his competence for the task of translation, when Puguang Temple was completed, an imperial decree ordered him to reside there. Not long after, an imperial decree was issued for the Crown Prince to receive the Bodhisattva precepts from him.
In the ninth year, he was appointed by imperial decree as the Precept Master for the Inner Palace and concurrently served as the *upādhyāya* (abbot) of Kongguan Temple.

King Kim Chijang of Silla abdicated his throne to enter the monastic path; he traveled by sea to seek an audience with the Master, received the Bodhisattva precepts from him, and returned home. In the fourteenth [year]...

In that year, there were monks who had mistakenly fallen into the net of the law. The authorities reported this to the Emperor, who issued an edict to assemble the virtuous elders of the capital temples at Xuanwu Gate to reprimand them collectively.
Thereupon, Daochang ascended the dais and addressed the Emperor, saying: "The monks have been graced by Your Majesty’s benevolence and permitted to participate in the Dharma-gate.
That we have failed to strictly observe the monastic precepts, thereby bringing this matter to Your Majesty’s imperial hearing, is entirely due to Daochang and my colleagues for our lack of virtue."

Feeling profound shame at this instruction, he then cited the words of entrustment from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The Emperor approved of this and consequently issued an edict to pardon the prisoners in the Grand Court of Justice (*Dàlǐ*).
He was further granted a meal before departing. Later, because the Emperor was confused regarding the origins of the Li clan, he issued an edict to have the monk Li Wei explain the matter to him.
[Daoxuan] repeatedly submitted memorials to contest this, but his requests were not granted. Soon thereafter, he fell ill and passed away at the monastery where he resided. (19)
This was the twenty-sixth day of the sixth month of that year. At the age of seventy-nine, on the second day of the seventh month, he was buried at Gaoyang in the southern suburbs.
His disciples, including De-xun and others, erected a stele; Li Boyao, the Minister of the Court of the Imperial Clan, composed the inscription.

He always practiced compassion and forbearance and diligently cultivated his conduct. He frequently experienced auspicious omens: divine beings, wearing white crowns and robes, surrounded him with their retinues as they circled his hall.

The Maitreya depicted on the wall suddenly rose up and began to dance. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, his physical form exquisite and magnificent, wearing a jeweled necklace, entered through the door from outside and hovered in mid-air for a long while before vanishing.

Samantabhadra Bodhisattva came from the east at a height of five or six *zhang* above the ground, his radiance surpassing the colors of the dawn. How could this possibly be a fabrication? Alas, how extraordinary!
Huilì of the Tang dynasty was originally named Zili; his current name was changed by Emperor Gaozong. His surname was Zhao, and he was a native of Tianshui.
Ancestors of his lineage had moved to Xinping due to holding official posts, and consequently became people of Bin. For generations, they had borne a reputation for high status and prestige.

He was the youngest son of Yi, who served as the Qiju-sheren (Attendant Secretary) and Sili Congshi (Official of the Office of the Metropolitan Superintendent) during the Sui dynasty. From birth, he was precocious and stood out from the crowd.
At the age when one’s will is set upon learning, he left the household life and registered at Zhaoren Temple in his native village; this was the third year of the Zhenguan era.
After a long time, by imperial decree, he was appointed as a Great Virtuous Monk for the Translation of Scriptures at Da Ci’en Monastery.

He was subsequently appointed as the Head Steward (Du Weina) of Ximing Monastery, and later received the position of Abbot of Taiyuan Monastery; in each case, he presided over the affairs of those monasteries. During the reign of Emperor Gaozong, the Emperor especially admired his extensive investigations into both Confucianism and Buddhism.

His elegant compositions were widely renowned; his eloquence soared like clouds, and his creative genius gushed forth like a spring. Furthermore, he possessed upright integrity and a dignified countenance, and would not [tolerate...]

He feared neither imperial majesty nor peril; even when entering fire or treading upon boiling water, he never yielded or flinched. Having repeatedly received imperial summons, he engaged in debate with the Daoist priests (huángguān).

The Emperor frequently marveled at the excellence of his character and resolve. He once composed a biography of the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of Cien Monastery; however, the draft remained unfinished when he passed away.
The śramaṇa Yanzong of Guangfu Monastery subsequently completed it in ten fascicles and presented it to the throne. It was then honored by the Emperor.
Lu Cai composed the *Shi yinming tu zhu* (Commentary on the Diagrams Explaining Hetuvidyā) in three fascicles.

Because it refuted and censured the correct principles of various masters, Lu sent a letter to reprimand them for their recklessness and to mock them for their superficiality and lack of self-awareness regarding their own limitations. When Liu Xuan, the Court Doctor of the Grand Commandant, heard of this, he [responded].
It was said to the Virtuous One of the Translation Bureau: "Li Cheng is today’s Qilu for the Buddhist community in warding off insults. Those who understand the matter agreed with this.
Tang Yibao was born into the Xue family of Jinling in Changzhou. Initially, he followed Master Xiaoming at Yongding Temple in Suzhou.
The Master received the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* from Master Lang of Xinghuang Temple; he was his successor.
Dharma Master Kuang resided at Yong’an Temple on Mount Jin’yun, so [Daoyou] took his leave to follow him there.

During the height of the Chen dynasty, Dharma Master Kuang was already renowned as a veteran master, such that his commentaries on the three sutras and four treatises were universally esteemed throughout the region south of the Yangtze. Daoyou investigated these works with sincere devotion for more than thirty years. Later...

He was transferred to Fanchang Temple in Jinhua, where he propagated the Way without indolence. During this time, he met Dharma Master Xuanzang of Ci’en Temple, who requested his presence for a later invitation.
The relevant authorities reported his name to the throne, and by imperial decree, he was summoned to the capital.

Whenever Master Xuanzang engaged him in discussion, he marveled at his comprehensive erudition and criticized those of later generations, asserting that they were mired in the obsession with names and essences and remained ignorant of profound illumination. Thereupon, [the Emperor]...

Cien recited it ten times in a single sitting. Thereafter, the various masters of the monastic community believed that both existence and emptiness were simultaneously discarded, and that medicine and disease had equally vanished—this was indeed not a false assessment.
Furthermore, he held that while the *Śāstra* certainly explains the *Sūtra*, the *Sūtra* is difficult and the *Śāstra* is easy;

lamenting that worldly customs had turned contrary, he remained seated, chanting the sacred scriptures in the morning and elucidating the wise *Śāstra* in the evening. In the winter of the third year of the Xianqing era, as the rain-prayer rituals had failed to bring rain...
It was snowing. He established a ritual altar within the palace to offer prayers. An imperial decree summoned Bao to debate the principles of the Way with the Daoist priest Li Rong of Dongming Guan.

Rong first established the principle of the "Ultimate Limit" (*benji*). Bao asked: "Regarding the principle that marks the Ultimate Limit, does the Way take the limit as its basis, or does the limit take the Way as its basis?
Rong replied: "Either way is acceptable. Bao asked: "If this is so, then the Way takes the limit as its basis, and the limit is the basis of the Way; is this not also the case?"
"Can the limit be rooted in the Way? Is the Way the original source of the limit? He replied, "It is also applicable.

Again he asked, "If it is granted that the Way and the original limit can mutually attain penetration, may it also be granted that spontaneity (*ziran*) and the Way mutually attain the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)? He replied, "The nature of phenomena is spontaneous."

"Spontaneity (*svabhāva*) does not take the Way as its law. He asked again, "If the Way takes spontaneity as its law, yet spontaneity does not take the Way as its law, then might it not be that the Way is rooted in the ultimate limit (*koṭi*), while the ultimate limit is not rooted in the Way? [Wang] Rong was unable to respond.

Thereupon, [Wang] Bi joked, saying, "Since you have called me 'Master' (*śāstr*), you are indeed my disciple. Wang Bao said, "The jesting of a commoner like myself offends Your Majesty's hearing; however—"
Although there was no question that he did not answer, one must consider what his adherence to ritual propriety was like.

As a disciple of our Buddha, he has traditionally taken the Buddha as his teacher. If you address him as "Master," then he would have been born before heaven and earth; since his teacher is the Patriarch of the Way, what further explanation could there be? Li Rong was put to shame and withdrew from his seat. Emperor Xiaowen then commanded Bao to establish a doctrinal argument.

Bao immediately established the doctrine of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Li’s followers vainly attempted to raise objections, but [Bao] crushed them as easily as snapping withered wood. The Emperor...
The Master was delighted. Thereafter, various monasteries requested him to lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, and the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and *Śata-śāstra*;

he granted his consent to all. In the first year of the Longshuo era, he accompanied the imperial entourage to the Eastern Capital (Luoyang). He frequently entered the palace precincts to debate the meaning of the scriptures and constantly expounded upon the Pure Land.
After a long time, he fell ill and passed away at Jingtu Monastery at the age of fifty-one. By imperial decree, his coffin was sent back to the capital.

Hua Jiu-zhu (of the Tang dynasty, personal name Wei Xiu). His native place and clan are not clearly known. He was widely learned and skilled in literary composition, and was particularly courageous in matters of righteousness.

On the fifteenth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Longshuo era, an imperial edict was issued to the monastics and the Daoists: "From this time forward, you shall all perform obeisance toward sovereigns and parents."

As was the custom, at that time the two schools were at a loss as to how to respond. Daoshou then cited precedents from the Jin and Song dynasties, as well as events from his own court that had never before been practiced;
thereafter, he relied upon the sūtras and śāstras to explain the reasons why [the practice] was untenable.
His arguments were clear, penetrating, and pertinent to the facts, which he presented to the Emperor. Thereupon, an edict was issued for the hundred officials to...
The deliberations held at the Central Terrace resulted in five hundred and thirty-nine people deeming it inappropriate to prostrate, while three hundred and fifty-four deemed it appropriate.

In the sixth month, an imperial edict was issued stating that one should not prostrate before the sovereign in order to preserve one's integrity, yet one should prostrate toward one’s kin as previously directed.
This policy was soon thereafter abolished. Hui-xiu’s submission of his memorial was precisely on the twenty-first day of this same month. Subsequently, various...

The monk was at the Penglai Palace, intending to submit a memorial once more to request [permission]. However, hearing that the Central Secretariat (Zhongtai) was currently convening a discussion, he desisted.
He then sent letters of petition to the high-ranking officials and nobles with whom he had established relations, seeking only their protection and support.
At that time, Vinaya Master Xuan also submitted petitions to the Governor of Yongzhou, Prince Pei, as well as to Lady Taifu of Rongguo, all of which were written by Xiu.
To chant it is subtle and excellent; the regulations of the former Buddhas have fallen into ruin.
Tángmíngdǎo, surnamed Yáo, was originally from Wŭxīng. An ancestor of his once held office in Shè, and thus the family settled there. From childhood he was extraordinary.

During the chaos at the end of the Sui dynasty, he lost both his parents and entered the monastic order, devoting himself exclusively to the observance of the precepts. At the beginning of the Zhengguān era, an imperial edict was issued.

When a monk is able to transform the people through virtue, the high officials shall select him and report his merits to the throne. At that time, Sengdao was serving as a subordinate official in Chenzhou;

the authorities suddenly summoned him in response to the imperial decree, yet he was deeply displeased. He sighed and said, "To be constrained by the narrow confines of a mere name and detained in one place—how can this be the way to achieve universal salvation?
Shortly thereafter, he sought out the two masters Shuo and Li, from whom he received instruction in the profound mysteries.

His profound learning was so comprehensive that his fellow practitioners all held him in the highest esteem. He was exceptionally skilled in making definitive judgments; whenever various monasteries had lingering grievances or disputes, they would invariably go to Huaidao to seek a resolution.
Huaidao would then settle and explain the matters with a single word, causing everyone to depart satisfied and submissive.

In the second year of the Longshuo era, an imperial edict summoned him to reside at Tiangong Temple in the Eastern Capital. In the first year of the Linde era, an edict ordered the relevant authorities to prepare ceremonial regalia to welcome him.

The statue of Laozi cast by the government of Luozhou was installed in the Mangshan Palace. Thereupon, the local magistrate Han Xiaowei sought to use this occasion to conscript the monks and nuns for labor;
he issued orders to all subordinate officials across twenty-two counties to assemble the monasteries and temples and lead their congregations out.

He addressed them, saying: "The two gates of Buddhism and Daoism have been naturally separated since ancient times. As for the command you have now received, its intent is the same [as that of secular service]."
Distressed and humiliated, and having received no separate imperial decree, he did not dare to obey the command. Xiaowei said angrily, "Does a monk reject the mandate of the state?
He immediately cast him out as a slave and stripped him of his monastic robes. Zhi Dao replied, "The monastic robe is a garment for those ordained by decree;
without a decree, I would not dare to remove it arbitrarily. This is just as I would not dare to deliver a Buddhist image without a decree. To send me with a Buddhist image without a decree—"
Furthermore, who would dare to falsely cast off their *kāṣāya* and thereby defy the decrees of the state? Xu Xiaowei, enraged, brandished his staff and ordered Zhi Dao to leave.
Zhi Dao alone stood firm and upright; the monks and nuns flocked to follow him, crowding and surrounding him in the courtyard without dispersing. Xu Xiaowei said:

"Are the practitioners of the Way rebels? At that time, the officials of the Six Ministries were all present. Sengdao immediately summoned them and said to them, "The high officials have gathered the monks and nuns and proclaimed that they are rebels;
this means the high officials themselves are rebelling. The monks and nuns have never rebelled. Such is their false accusation.
He insisted that they must appeal this to the Censorate. Thereupon, the officials all rushed out at once. Daowei was greatly terrified; he descended from the steps and humbled himself.
He apologized and then desisted. At that time, the imperial court was about to select and ordain monks; they assembled all the virtuous ones to deliberate.

An edict was issued for the Grand Kitchen to provide vegetarian food, which was brought forward as the sun had already passed its zenith. The assembly vied with one another to take and eat it. Tanyue said, "The Great Virtues are all the entrusted legacy of the Buddha-Dharma and the models for the world.
To consume food outside of the proper time in the presence of laypeople is a public violation of the Vinaya regulations. He manifested [this truth]...

"The conditions for the extinction of the Dharma are at hand; how lamentable! The assembly was filled with shame and remorse. The guide asked for water to rinse his mouth in sorrowful grief and intended to pass away.
Both monastics and laypeople earnestly exhorted him to desist, and subsequently offered him cakes and food. He had not eaten for one month.
This year he is over sixty years old and remains in good health.
Tang Fachong, courtesy name Xiaodun, was surnamed Li. He was a native of Chengji in Longxi. His ancestors served in succession during the Wei and Qi dynasties.
Chong was born in the region of Yanzhou. From childhood, he was exceptionally brilliant and talented, maintaining a haughty disdain for the conventions of his time.
By the age of twenty, he had already become close friends with the Minister of Works, Fang Xuanling.

Fang Xuanling once said to him, "When a man is in his youth and vigor, if his rank does not reach the fifth grade, it would be best to abandon official emolument and position, choosing instead to dwell in leisure and ease. Chong was twenty-four years old when he assumed office.

Langlüe of Yingyang encountered the mourning for his mother. While reading the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, upon reaching the passage concerning the narrowness of one’s dwelling, he resolved to leave the household life.

He attended lectures on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* more than thirty times. Furthermore, he listened to Dharma Master Gaofa of Anzhou lecture on the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Three Treatises*, and the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
Thereupon, he entered Mount Wudu and, based on what he had previously gained from the words and phrases of the texts...

He spoke thus and personally practiced what he preached. At the age of thirty, he traveled to Jizhou. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, an imperial decree was issued stating that those who had received private ordination would be executed.
At that time, monks were seeking refuge in the mountains of Yiyang, where their provisions were exhausted and dire. Sengchong vowed not to spare his own life;

he immediately shaved his head and hair and ran through the prefectures and counties, appealing for help from the local magistrates, saying: "If you simply provide grain and provisions, you will ultimately obtain blessings and protection. The various magistrates...
Appreciating his resolute integrity, Zhou provided for him; he divided the monks into two groups and allotted about ten *hu* of rice to each.
One group of over forty people consumed it, yet the rice never diminished throughout the year. The other group of fifty or sixty people ate it, and in barely two days, the rice was exhausted.
Sengchong said, "There is nothing to be wondered at; it is simply because their learning is of different capacities."
Since their cultivation involves diligence or negligence, the results they receive should likewise differ accordingly. After a long time, those who had come to seek refuge increased day by day.
Furthermore, they encountered heavy rains and flooding, leaving them with no place to stay. There was a great cave in the mountains where tigers and wolves dwelt;
Hui-chong eventually went there and told them to leave, and indeed they departed before he had even turned his heel. At that time, although Hui-chong—

While managing various affairs, he continued to rely on his wise mentor to investigate the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as usual. When it came to difficult passages requiring explanation, he went again to Dharma Master Gao in Anzhou, who had already passed away.
At that time, the Daoist Cai Yuhuang prided himself on his mastery of both internal (Buddhist) and external (Confucian/Daoist) classics;
however, those among our own ranks who visited him provided him with extensive assistance and encouragement. One day, the assembly of monastics and laypeople gathered in great numbers.
He assembled [the monks] and had Yu Huáng take the seat to expound the Buddhist sutras. Hóng opposed this because [Yu Huáng) was a non-Buddhist and strove to prevent it.

Those with discernment remarked that Hóng was a Dharma-protecting Bodhisattva of the Final Age. Suddenly, as the profound meaning of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra had long been neglected, he searched for it everywhere, regardless of whether the terrain was level or treacherous.
Initially, Meditation Master Huìkě, through the transmission of Bodhidharma, [received] the One Vehicle from South India.
The primary purpose [of this work] is that this scripture was extensively practiced; thus, its descendants, such as Dharma Master Gao, exerted themselves with particular diligence.
Zhi-chong relied upon and received instruction from him, frequently receiving his approval. Since then, he has expounded it more than thirty times.

Those among later students who have been enlightened by this reliance are almost beyond reckoning. Now, I shall record the lineage of masters so that those in the future may have a basis for verification. — By Da-mo.
The Chan Master [Dao]xuan produced two masters: Huikai and Daoyu. Master Yu received the Way but did not concern himself with verbal exposition.
Master Ke produced Master Can, Master Hui, Master Sheng, Master Nao, Master Duan, Master Changzang, Master Zhenfa, and Master Yufa (all of whom were lecturers but left no written works).
He also produced Master Shenlao (author of a four-fascicle *Cāo*), Master Feng (author of a five-fascicle *Shū*), Master Ming (author of a five-fascicle *Shū*), and Master Hu.

Master Ming (Five fascicles of commentary). Master Yuan, who inherited [the lineage] from Master Ke, had Master Dacong (Five fascicles of commentary) and Master Daoyin (Four fascicles of sub-commentary).
Dharma Master Chong (five fascicles of commentary); Dharma Master An (five fascicles of commentary); Dharma Master Chong (eight fascicles of commentary); Master Daming (ten fascicles of commentary).

There were those who could not be taken as teachers. Among those who relied on the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) themselves were Master Qiān (*Shu*, four fascicles), Vinaya Master Shangdé (who produced ten fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra-śāstra*), Dharma Master Kuàng, and Master Hóngzhì (invited to reside at Xīmíng Monastery in the capital; after his death, the transmission was lost).

Following Master Míngchán were Dharma Master Jiā, Master Bǎoyú, Master Bǎoyíng, and Master Dàoyíng (all of whom transmitted the lamp and propagated the teachings). Master Chōng specialized in making the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* the foundation of his school. The aforementioned—
Later, he extensively propagated [the teachings], doing so nearly two hundred times. When he preached, he never relied on written texts;

rather, he adapted his methods to suit the circumstances, employing various means to guide and transform others, ensuring that every aspect was perfectly appropriate. When fellow teachers and students earnestly requested him to set forth the underlying principles (*artha*), he told them:
"The very act of seeing and speaking of these principles is already coarse; how much more so when they are recorded upon paper? This is what is meant by 'the coarsest among the coarse.'"
The matter was difficult to resolve definitively. He composed a commentary in five fascicles, titled *Siji* (Private Notes), to show that he did not dare to make it public throughout the world.
Nevertheless, while Huichong traveled through Dongchuan, he did not hold an official rank; although he repeatedly received invitations for ordination, he nobly declined and would not accept them.

As he approached his fiftieth year, an imperial edict was issued for the state of Yanzhou to ordain persons; he was thus compelled to enter the monastic order and was assigned to Fazhi Temple under the jurisdiction of the prefecture.
Although his name was now registered among the clergy, his heart remained solely set on enjoying the springs and rocks and befriending those who were reclusive and neglected.

When Lord Fang, who held a position among the highest ministers of state, wrote a letter to summon him, Hui-chong inscribed upon the back of the letter: "I have no need for anything within the three realms."

The position of the Three Prime Ministers (Sānhuái) is also the ultimate limit; yet the Master repeatedly declined their invitations and refused to go, taking only the propagation of the Dharma as his own responsibility.

As soon as his seat was spread out, the carriages and canopies arrived like a flood. Du Zhenglun of the Secretariat personally joined those in the lower ranks to discuss the profound meaning of the teachings together with him.
The Dharma Master Rùn of Hongfú Monastery, having never known him before, asked, "Where does this great virtuous elder come from? He replied, "An old man from Yanzhou."
He was a monk. When asked why he had traveled so far, he replied, "I have heard that those who understand the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) are few in this region;
therefore, I wish to cast the net of the One Vehicle's teaching to scoop up the fish and dragons of the stage of faith. Run said, "This is truly a Bodhisattva of great resolve.
It happened that while traveling, he reached Daxingshan Temple, where Zheng Qintai, the Magistrate of Wannian, was beating someone at the temple. Hui-chong stopped him, saying, "Sir..."
"Do not strike anyone here. Qin Tai said, "I shall take upon myself the sin of striking others. Chong replied, "If you do not take the sin upon yourself, who else should bear it?
However, the state established this monastery originally with the intent to bring peace and security to the realm; one must simply practice what is good.
You are now striking people in this monastery—how can this be called praying for the blessing of the nation? Qin Tai bowed in gratitude. Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka Master Xuan...
Xuanzang replied, "I do not permit others to lecture on the scriptures translated previously. Huichong said, "You were ordained according to the old scriptures.

If you do not permit the propagation of those old scriptures, you may as well return to lay life and be ordained again according to the newly translated scriptures; only then will I grant your request."
Upon hearing this, Xuanzang desisted. Alas, how can such a person be equaled? Yu Zhining, the Vice President of the Secretariat, remarked: "Chongshi is a dhūta monk of the Dharma-realm;
he cannot easily be constrained by conventional names and realities. His words were indeed correct. During the Xianqing era, Chongshi returned to Yanzhou.
He lived until the Linde era, at the age of seventy-nine. Afterward, his final whereabouts remained unknown.

Tang Faming was a native of Jiangling in Jingchu. His learning encompassed both Buddhist and secular classics, and his eloquence and wisdom were particularly formidable. He was unrestrained in his conduct yet maintained himself with the strictest monastic discipline.

At the beginning of the Shénlóng era, he traveled to the capital, where an imperial decree had been issued for monks and Daoists to determine the authenticity of the *Huáhú chéngfó jīng* (The Scripture on the Conversion of the Barbarians to Buddhahood).
At that time, the Emperor presided over the inner palace, with all the officials standing in attendance. [Faming] was then compared with the great virtuous ones, including the Yellow...
Guàn raised his voice in debate, and the clamor did not cease. Míng suddenly stepped forward from the crowd and said:
"Laozi was a man of Han, while the Hu are people of a foreign land. Since their lands differ, so too do their speech and sounds.

At the time when he converted the Hu and became a Buddha, did he speak in the Han dialect or the foreign dialect? If he had used the Han dialect, then the foreign land would have been unable to understand him."
As for the foreign sounds, this scripture has reached its ultimate point and ought to be translated.
However, it is not yet known under which dynasty, in what year and month, and by which Tripiṭaka master this scripture was translated. The Daoist remained silent and speechless, unable to respond.

On the fourteenth day of the ninth month, an edict was issued throughout the empire to destroy all copies of these texts so that none should remain; furthermore, local officials were commanded to carry out this order.
He strictly imposed prohibitions and punishments, and moreover had this decree carved in clear characters at the Baima Temple in Luoyang to show posterity. Thereupon, the imperial edict stated:

"I, the Emperor, have humbly occupied the precious throne and twice restored the ancestral altars. Having performed the grand rites of the *mingqin* sacrifice, I have bestowed the great grace of thunder and rain.

This extends even to those in black and yellow robes, as I simultaneously issue both warnings and encouragement. I have heard that throughout the empire, all Daoist temples and monasteries depict [images of] transformations..."

The images of the Buddha’s transformation [depicted in] the *Hu chengfo bianxiang* (Transformation Images of the Buddha’s Conversion of the Barbarians) and the figures of Xuan Yuan (the Primordial Origin) painted in monasteries—since the honored countenances of both teachings are incompatible with one another, both must be removed within ten days of the date of this decree.
Should anyone persist in retaining them, the local officials are required to charge them with the offense of violating the decree.

As for the *Huahu jing* (Scripture on the Conversion of the Barbarians), successive imperial edicts have strictly prohibited it; yet recently, we have heard that it is still quite prevalent outside the capital.
The circulation [of these texts] continued. From this time forward, the *Huahu jing* and all other records containing accounts of the "conversion of the barbarians" were to be completely eliminated.

Should anyone privately possess such works, they shall be punished according to the established regulations. Shortly thereafter, Huan Daoyan, the master of Dahan Monastery in the capital Luoyang, submitted a memorial to argue against this.
The Emperor issued a response, stating: "I, your servant, am unworthy yet have received the great mandate. Although I..."

It would rather result in much loss; yet, impartiality and leniency are truly paramount. Moreover, since the two lineages share a glorious radiance and the Mysterious Origin (Xuan-yuan) presides over the cosmic order, how could one forget the teachings of Laozi while showing partiality toward the Buddhist school?
My resolve is to return to simplicity and my heart dwells on the removal of falsehood; as for those whose principles are deviant and whose practices are erroneous—
Though one may be a close relative, they must be eliminated if they oppose righteousness; though one may harbor enmity, they must be recorded if their name accords with the truth.

Recently, during the intervals between my myriad state affairs, I have briefly examined the texts of the two teachings. As for the *Laozi* and the two chapters on the Way and its Power (*Daode jing*), their subtlety transcends the realm of the rarefied and the ineffable.
In India, the two truths of emptiness and existence encompass the discourse on the principle of *tathatā*. There is nothing among them that does not fully expound the profound mysteries.
This school proclaims and expounds upon the most profound mysteries; why then should it rely on the spurious "Converting the Barbarians" (Huahu) to further the prestige of the Lord Lao (Laojun)?

Its doctrines contain contradictions, and its texts lack canonical authority. Regarding the claim that he became a Buddha, the four accounts differ; regarding his disciples, the records are inconsistent and conflicting.
Since Yin Xi is already said to have become a Buddha, this is already a flight into the void; to further claim he was transformed into Ānanda makes it even more absurd.

[This] agrees [with the truth]. Figures such as Guiguzi and Beiguo had not yet set foot in the Central Kingdom (Madhyadeśa); those like Śāriputra and Mañjuśrī falsely manifested themselves in this eastern land.
There is a confusion between Hu and Han, and the eras are also discordant. To preach *nirvāṇa* while treading upon water lacks any scriptural authority;

to discourse on the *saddharma* while walking through fire is akin to the antics of a clown. Their deceit and fraud are self-evident; what need is there for further elaboration? These scriptures are not of Laozi.

"This was composed by you; to destroy it would surely be called a deficiency in filial piety. This text, however, is what I, a vulgar person, have discussed; to remove it would further manifest the virtue of my predecessor.
Although your words are earnest, the principle is in fact not settled. You should fully understand my intention. Thereupon, he immediately rejected the submitted memorial.
Tang Lishè was a man from the Western Regions, of Brahmin lineage. In his youth, he formed a traveling party and journeyed to China (Zhendan).

He met the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang just as the latter was returning to the East; they encountered one another at Jinsuo Ridge, where Lishè sought to serve him as a disciple. Consequently, he became a preeminent senior student of Xuanzang’s school.

Magnanimous, profound, and erudite, he was held in especially high esteem by Emperor Zhongzong. Among the officials and nobles of both the court and the commonalty, there were none who did not [hold him in reverence].

I wish to engage in debate. During the Kaiyuan era, while he was lecturing on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at An Guo Temple, the fourfold assembly flocked there in such numbers that there was not even room for a knee to rest.

Offerings from the laity arrived like clouds, yet those who were envious and greedy cast sidelong glances at him. At that time, Wei Da, a Grand Master of Judicial Review (Dali Pingshi), submitted a memorial stating:
"The two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism have long been parasites upon the administration. I request that they be compared in their respective learning; if [the Buddhist] is indeed superior..."

"If he were long-lived, the state would have preserved him; what is there that is impossible? An imperial decree was issued for each of the three teachings to select one hundred men to assemble in the inner palace for debate to determine victory and defeat.
Thereupon, Jing first ascended the high seat and voiced his challenges. The Daoist Ye Jingneng and the Śramaṇa Siming were both defeated.
Next, Shi ascended the seat; his words were precise and his arguments piercing, as they exchanged challenges and responses several times.
Though [the discourse] underwent hundreds of thousands of turns, its thread was clear and flowing. While that [other school] is always deficient, this one is always sufficient;
those looking on were struck with awe and broke into sweat. Shuo涉 then asked Dongjing 玎 with composure: "You ascended the seat first; are you not the host? If so, what is the surname of the host?
If according to Confucianism, it is Kong; if according to Daoism, it is Li; if according to Buddhism, it is Shi. As such...
"This would mean your surname is Kong. Ding replied, "My surname is Wei. Shiye then chanted at length from his seat: "The Buddha-dharma of mine is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Why then have you come today with the surname Wei? It has been only three or four years since you were without the surname Wei; I do not know what kind of 'Wei' this is again.
When the hundred officials of the imperial guard heard this, they were struck with awe. The Emperor, because of this, recalled the affairs concerning Empress Wei.
He suddenly changed countenance and said, "Ding belongs to the commoner class, yet he has dared to treat the ancestral teachings with contempt and insult the Buddhist community!
Ding shall fearfully descend from the hall and prostrate himself to await punishment. He knelt and said, "Your servant does not belong to the commoner class. The Emperor’s anger remained unabated;

he issued an edict to demote [Ding] to Xiangzhou, while bestowing upon Shi the title of Master Mingjiao (Great Teacher of Illuminating Teaching) and granting him money and silk to construct Mingjiao Temple.
This served to manifest his capability. Later, due to a minor offense, he was exiled to Handong and subsequently transferred to Longxing Temple in Nanyang.

National Teacher Huizhong came to visit him in the mountains and fields; upon meeting him, Zhe recognized his potential and said, "In the future, you shall serve as a model for the Son of Heaven through your virtue and the Way.

Strive diligently; you are not someone who can be compared to those of my generation. He then presented him with clothing and other items, treating him with the same discernment and supervision as one would for a refined official.
This work, titled *Zhuli fapian lun* (Treatise on Establishing the Dharma Banner), circulated in one fascicle.
During the Dali era, the Śramaṇa Yuánzhào of Xīmíng Monastery compiled a biography for him in ten fascicles; from this, the abundance of his elegant words and noble conduct can be known.
Tang Shenwu, style name Tongxing, was of the Li clan. His ancestors resided in Longxi; during the Jin dynasty, they moved southward and became residents of Changshui.

For generations, his family had been devoted to Confucian and Buddhist studies. From childhood, Shenwu possessed exceptional talent, yet he suffered from a loathsome disease that no medicine could cure.

During the Kaiyuan era, Vinaya Master Xiguang instructed him in the two methods of ritual repentance—those pertaining to phenomena and those pertaining to principle. Consequently, Shenwu burned off one of his fingers as an act of devotion, thereby achieving such profound sincerity and diligence that he was moved by an auspicious omen.
His radiance was like that of the moon. In front of a statue of a Bodhisattva, in the fourth year of the Tianbao era, he first donned the black robes and received full ordination.
In the eighth year, his extraordinary conduct was recognized, and he was granted the privilege of being enrolled on this mountain—this mountain being Mount Shiui.

The site lay to the east of Laolao. In his later years, he constructed a dwelling in a secluded spot and regularly established a Lotus Sūtra ritual arena, practicing the Buddha-contemplation samādhi for a period of ninety days.
He once said to his disciples: "How can the shadows obscure the sun? How can the wind move through space without stirring it?

If one thoroughly understands that all is illusory, what is not of the nature (dharmatā)? After a long time, fierce beasts became tame beside his meditation seat, and auspicious clouds hung over his Dharma hall.
One night, a divine being appeared and said to Wù, "I am Cao Shì'ān, the Marquis of Xīnchéng of the Sui dynasty.
I am charged with presiding over this place. Now that you, Master, have arrived, I wish to serve you forever as you practice the Way. Having spoken, he vanished.

Later, Lǐ Huá, Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel, and Cúì Yì, Palace Attendant Censor, visited Wù together. In their leisurely conversation, they inquired about the relative superiority of the Three Teachings.
Huile said, "The scriptures of the Lokāyata are all phenomena external to the mind; those who savor them labor in vain without attaining realization.

It is like flowers blooming in decaying soil, or the moon reflected in a dried-up pond. Compared to the teachings of Śākyamuni, how vast and remote they are! Thus they exchanged verses back and forth several times.
Huayi merely acquiesced with repeated nods, unaware that he was repeatedly bowing his head in agreement. In the spring of the tenth year, he gradually fell ill.
He passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. His age was sixty-three, and his years of ordination were twenty-six. After cremation, more than five hundred śarīra relics were collected;
they were as bright as pearls and as lustrous as jade, truly lovely. His disciples, Zhan-yi and Yuan-yi, erected a stupa to enshrine them.
Tang Xingru’s clan and native place are not clearly known. He was a diligent scholar of the Vinaya-piṭaka and was particularly capable of practicing its precepts without slackening.
During the reign of Emperor Daizong, he served as a translator and concurrently held the office of presiding over ordinations for the two monastic districts (Lianjie). At that time:

All monasteries were subject to the jurisdiction of secular authorities. Consequently, when members of the five assemblies passed away, their clothing, provisions, and utensils were entirely transferred to the government treasury;

this was effectively equivalent to the confiscation of property for treason, which was utterly contrary to the intent of the Vinaya. Thereupon, he submitted the aforementioned petition requesting reform.

On the twenty-seventh day of the eleventh month in the second year of the Dali era, an imperial edict was issued stating that henceforth, the belongings of deceased monks shall be distributed among the monastic community, and they shall be publicly allocated accordingly.
The edict issued to the Secretariat and circulated throughout the empire for observance abruptly eliminated long-standing abuses. He exerted great effort on behalf of the Buddhist teachings;

he ultimately served as the *upādhyāya* (abbot) of both Ximing and Anguo Monasteries. Throughout his life, he produced a vast amount of writings, which Yuanzhao compiled into three fascicles that have been disseminated in the world.
During the Changqing era of the Tang dynasty, Emperor Wuzong was intensely devoted to Buddhist affairs. Fazhen received an imperial summons to enter the inner palace and served there for four years.

He attended the ritual assemblies within the Forbidden City, where the Emperor presided over the Dharma seat and inquired about the merits of the Triple Gem. Fazhen responded with detailed and thorough explanations;

his eloquence and citations were brilliant, whether advancing or withdrawing in his discourse. The Emperor was greatly pleased. Consequently, Fazhen petitioned that an altar be established to confer the precepts.

It had long been neglected and not revived. Since the commencement of military operations along the two rivers, even those among the monastics who had not entirely abandoned the Dharma have grown old and infirm.

May Your Majesty take pity on them; accordingly, an edict was issued that each of the monasteries of the two streets (the Eastern and Western Capital) should appoint monks and nuns to receive ordination.
The ordination platform ceremony may begin on the tenth day of the third month and conclude on the tenth day of the fourth month.
The Merit Commissioners of the Two Streets shall select monks of virtuous conduct, known as Mahāsthaviras, to examine the scriptures of the boys and girls candidates.
Those boys who can recite one hundred and fifty sheets from memory, and girls who can recite one hundred sheets, shall be granted ordination. This was approved by imperial edict.

Tang Changda, courtesy name Wenju, was surnamed Gu. His family had resided for generations in a coastal corner [of China]. In his early years, he traveled from Dayufu Mountain in Heyang to study at various monasteries throughout the Jianghuai region.

Beyond receiving full ordination, he specialized in lecturing on the *Nanshan Lüchao* (Commentary on the Vinaya of the Southern School). He also studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Yuanpin* (Perfect Sound), the *Lotus Sūtra*, and the *Zhi Guan* (Cessation and Contemplation).
He further perused the texts of the *Yinfu Jing*, Laozi, and Zhuangzi, and modeled his calligraphy after the styles of the two Wangs (Wang Xizhi and Wang Xianzhi).

His calligraphy was excellent, and his later study of Chan meditation reached a high degree of mastery. During the reign of Emperor Wuzong, who was deluded by heterodox teachings and suppressed the Great Dharma, he sighed, saying, "I was born at an inopportune time;
such things as these have occurred. Thereupon, he dwelt among mountains and wild places to adapt to the changing times.
During the reign of Emperor Xuanzong, the Buddha-dharma flourished once more, and monasteries and hermitages were frequently restored and expanded, particularly in his native region.
Thus, he fully realized the transformations of the past. Prefect Wei Shu increased his reverence and admiration.

In the twelfth year of the Xiantong era, the fourfold assembly of the entire commandery requested him to bestow teachings and precepts; yet Da remained carefree and aloof in the outskirts and pastures, never entering the city administration.

Several years passed in this manner, and though high-ranking officials and men of distinction came to his door with personal requests, none were able to see him. He was skilled in composing poetry and delighted in singing and responding to verses.
He composed the *Qīngshān Lǐdào Gē* (Song of the Green Mountains and Following the Way) in the style of Yuán Hé.

On the sixteenth day of the ninth month of the fifteenth year, while suffering from illness, he ceased taking food for seven days and passed away. He was seventy-four years of age and fifty-one years since his ordination.

His disciples, including Huìqīng and others, enshrined his coffin in a tomb three hundred paces southeast of the temple. Three years later, they constructed a stupa at the burial site. [Signed by] Yǐng.
Written by Chényán of Chuān as the inscription.
The eulogy says:
The Dharma has no dual nature; it is honored wherever it resides. Were it not for those of its own kind, how could it even be discussed?
The Kong and Li clans have long been held in high esteem by the Eastern Land; yet when the teachings of Śākyamuni reached the West, they alone surged forward with great vigor.

Consequently, disputes arose, and the various lords led one another to debate at court. It was only through their ability to rely on the scriptures and cite the classics that they could suppress the heterodox and eliminate the delusory, ensuring there was no further contention.
Thus, the Way and its Virtue were established as the governance, and benevolence and righteousness were put into practice.
Through the transformation of compassion, he guided and benefited all living beings; transcending the three realms, who could have been his equal?
*The Newly Compiled Classified Biographies of Monks of the Six Studies, Volume Sixteen* *The Newly Compiled Classified Biographies of Monks of the Six Studies, Volume Seventeen*
Composed by the Śramaṇa Tanne from Eastern Zhejiang.
The method of learning the Buddha’s Dharma through patience is truly not easy to advance in and cultivate. Nevertheless, for those who wish to advance in and cultivate it:

One must certainly maintain mindfulness. Regarding objects that may be liked or disliked, joyful or fearful, loathsome or admired, pitiable or angry—if one remains unmoved by them, then external insults will be dispelled. One must uphold the will;
regarding desires that can lead to arrogance or indulgence, obscuration or delusion, insolence or intimacy—[one must remain unmoved].
If one can be both compassionate and firm, yet does not give rise to [resentment], then the practice of patience within has been attained.

One should restrain dishonor through mindfulness and maintain patience through resolve. When there is nothing emerging from within to disturb the body, and nothing entering from without to vex the mind, the cultivation of the Buddha-dharma becomes easy.
These two categories—restraining mindfulness and maintaining resolve—are indeed the core of study.
This is the ultimate aim of those who practice patience; it is most appropriate to append it here. Regarding the section on "Collecting the Mind":
Bo Yuan (style name Fazu) was a man of the Jin dynasty. His surname was Wan, and he was a native of Henei. His father, Wei Da, was renowned for his literary talent.

He did not accept any appointments offered by the prefectures or counties. Huiyuan’s talent and brilliance far surpassed those of his contemporaries. After he left the household life, he recited several tens of thousands of words daily.
He studied and savored both the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras as well as the secular classics and histories, penetrating them all and knowing their essential points.

He once translated three sūtras, including the *Vaiśālī-praśnottara* and the *Pañcavargika-bhikṣu-vinaya*. He constructed a vihāra in Chang’an where he lectured on and explained their meanings, and others received and accepted these doctrines from him.
[He] always had a retinue of a thousand men. When Wang Yong of Hexian governed Guanzhong, he held [Hui]yuan in high esteem and regarded him as a teacher and friend.
Whenever he stayed at the Western Palace to lecture on the Way, the most eminent and talented scholars would all assemble there, and many eloquent debaters would submit to his wisdom.

At that time, because the region was embroiled in warfare, Huiyuan wished to flee. It happened that Zhang Fu was serving as the Prefect of Qinzhou, stationed in Longshang; Huiyuan traveled with him. Zhang Fu—

Huiyuan enjoyed great renown in distant regions. [Fu] Yu wished to dress him in scholar’s robes and appoint him as his own assistant. Huiyuan did not respond. Consequently, Fu became resentful toward him.
There was a man named Guan Fan who had once been defeated in debate by Huiyuan; because of this, he slandered and defamed Huiyuan without restraint.
When Huiyuan arrived at Pingcheng, he said to his disciples, "In a few days, my summons shall arrive. He then distributed his surplus belongings as a parting gift. The following day—

One day he went to visit Fu. His words offended Fu’s intentions, and [Fu] had him arrested and handed over to the official recorder. The entire assembly asked in alarm, and Huiyuan said, "This is the result of a past debt;

it is not a matter of the present. He then called upon the Buddha to make a vow: "Once this retribution is exhausted, I shall become a virtuous spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to Fu, so as not to let him suffer the sin of killing.
Subsequently, Fu was whipped to death. Fu soon felt remorse. Huiyuan then traveled to transform the people of Guanzhong and Longyou. The Qiang...
The Jin court honored him as if he were a deity; those who heard of his passing wept. The Qiang, with five thousand elite cavalry, intended to escort Fu Yuan back to the west.

Upon hearing midway that he had met with a violent death, they were all filled with indignation and desired to take revenge. Fu Jian dispatched troops to defend the Long Mountains, but the Qiang attacked them.
It happened that Fu Jian’s subordinate commander, Fu Zheng, slew Fu Jian, whereupon the Qiang finally withdrew. They then divided Fu Yuan’s bones and stones [for burial].

A stupa was erected for each of them. His younger brother, Fazuo, enjoyed a reputation for excellence from his youth. Summoned as a State Doctor (Boshi), he did not accept the appointment. At the age of twenty-five, he entered the monastic order.

His transformative influence spread throughout Guanzhong and Longzhou. Zhang Guang, the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Liangzhou, held him in particularly high esteem and served him with great devotion.

He repeatedly urged Fazuo to return to lay life, reasoning that since Fazuo had previously avenged his elder brother’s murder at the hands of Fu, he would surely follow his own advice. However, [Fazuo] remained firm.
Zuo Zhong had no desire for life, saying, "There is only death. Gao Guang ultimately murdered him; at that time, he was fifty-seven years of age.
Gao Guang’s courtesy name was Jingwu, and he was a native of Jiangxia. Later, he was besieged by Yang Nandi, the King of Wudu, and died out of indignation.

Faliang of the Jin dynasty was a native of Zhongshan. Having left home at a young age, he was well-versed in the Vinaya. While reciting the sutras, he encountered accounts of the Twin Trees and the Deer Park;
weeping, he said, "I am already unable to see the Holy Teacher in person. Can I not at least pay homage to his remaining traces?

He joined with three companions, and they crossed the shifting sands to the west. After three days, all traces of their path were lost, and the vegetation had grown so thick as to obscure everything; they were utterly disoriented.
He went there. Inside was an old, ruined temple consisting of two rooms, each occupied by one of two bhikṣus. One was reciting sutras while the other lay ill.
Although they lived side by side, they did not attend to one another; the sick man’s excrement and urine were strewn everywhere, so foul and filthy that no one could approach him.
Lang said to his disciples, "In the monastic life, the Dharma is our kin. If we do not see it, that is one thing; but once we have seen it—"
"How could it be discarded? He stayed for six days to wash and launder them. The next day, a fragrance suddenly filled the room.

[The monk] said to Lang, "The Master of our neighboring room has already attained the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa). You should go and see him. Lang went there and prostrated himself twice, requesting instruction.
The man said, "Your sincerity is such that you are in harmony with the sages; all of you shall surely enter the Way. However, as for your meritorious achievements..."

"You are simply not yet mature. However, why must you travel so far? It will be of no benefit to your practice; it would be better for you to exert yourself in the Way and ensure that you do not let this time pass in vain.
Consequently, Hui-lang traveled again through various kingdoms to study the sutras and śāstras. Later, he returned to China (Zhendan), where he gathered disciples and transmitted the Dharma;
his ultimate end is unknown. His disciple Ling-shao was born into the Lü family of Yanmen. In his youth, he took pleasure in hunting, but he later attained spiritual awakening.

He left the household life and studied the methods of skillful meditation. Whenever he entered meditative absorption, he would sometimes not emerge for several days. He moved to Liusquan Mountain, where he excavated a cave to sit in.
He carved wood to create an image of Bodhidharma and served it morning and evening as if it were alive. Thus, the world admired his conduct.

Jin Daobao was a native of Langye and the younger brother of the Chancellor Wang Dao. Having renounced his home in youth, his relatives wept and tried to dissuade him, but Daobao smiled and did not answer.
As he was about to have his hair shaved, he recited a verse: "Who would have known that ten thousand li of water / Initially began from a mere gushing spring?
He eventually became renowned for his mastery of the Way and its study.
Falan of Jin was a native of Gaoyang. Dissatisfied with living as a layperson, he abandoned his home to enter the Way at the age of fifteen.

He maintained himself with rigorous discipline; his physical bearing was tall and noble. His virtue transformed the people of the Three Rivers. By nature, he loved mountains and rivers; he practiced seated meditation among the rocky crags.
Even when heavy snow fell, a pack of tigers would stay by his side and not leave. The mountain deities also occasionally sought instruction from him. He was especially fond of Shicheng.
He then settled there permanently; it is the present-day Yuanhua Temple. He intended to travel to the Five Indias but passed away at Xianglin Temple in Jiaozhou.
Zhu Fachong of the Jin dynasty was a man of unknown origins. He was quick-witted and intelligent, possessed a mastery of the Vinaya, and was particularly proficient in the Lotus Sūtra.

While traveling to Lushan in Xiangzhou, a mountain spirit transformed into a beautiful woman and came to request the bestowal of the precepts. She offered her own dwelling to be converted into a monastery for his use.
Later, he returned to Gexianshan in Shan, where he lived in a thatched hut and drank from the mountain streams; students gathered there in great numbers.

Kong Chunzhi of the state of Lu would often stay for two nights during his excursions and, finding his spirit profoundly expansive and serene, sighed with admiration: "The dust of worldly desire has been cleared away."

He was thirty years old at the time of his death. He regretted that they had met so late. He authored the *Fahua yizhu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) in four fascicles and passed away in the mountains.
Fǎhé of the Jin dynasty was a native of Hóngyáng; in his youth, he studied together with Master Ān and shared a deep friendship with him. As a person, he was respectful and yielding.
His discourses were pure and correct, capable of resolving doubts and dispelling delusions. During the calamity of the Shi clan, he fled to Western Shu.

Upon hearing that Xiangyang had fallen, he entered Guanzhong and resided at Yangping Temple. Later, during a religious assembly held at Jinyu, he climbed a mountain ridge with Dao’an and gazed out toward the horizon.
After a while, he said, "This mountain rises high, and many who come to wander and look about are here. From this point on, all things..."

When [the monk] Huihua asked, "In the end, where can one measure his destination? Dao’an replied, "The Dharma Master maintains his mind with purpose; why fear future lives? If the wisdom-mind does not sprout, that is truly to be pitied.
Thereupon, he and Master Dao’an together carefully determined the terminology and meanings of the new scriptures. Shortly thereafter, he traveled to the lecture hall at Puzha under Yao Xu.
He then said to his disciples, "The worldly nets of affliction are manifold"; and so he straightened his countenance and adjusted his robes.
He circumambulated the Buddha, prostrated, and rose; returning to his chamber, he covered his head with his *kāṣāya* robe and passed away.

His lifespan was eighty years. Tanyong of the Jin dynasty was born into the Yang family; a native of Guanzhong, he served the illegitimate Qin in his youth as General of the Guard. He stood eight chi tall.
Xiongwu was capable of accomplishing great deeds. In the eighth year of the Taiyuan era, he followed Fu Jian on his southern invasion, where he was defeated by the Jin forces.

Upon returning to Chang’an, he served as a disciple of Master Dao’an. After Dao’an passed away, he also served Huìyuǎn. He thoroughly mastered the sūtras and śāstras, gaining extensive understanding of them.

Furthermore, he frequently accompanied Huìyuǎn back to Guanzhong to deliver letters to Kumārajīva; he handled these diplomatic missions with such dignity that he never brought shame upon them. His contemporaries were envious of him, yet Huìyuǎn [valued him for his] subtle...
Zuī sent Yong away. Yong understood his intention and maintained an expression free of resentment; he instead built a thatched hut to the southwest of the mountain and resided there.

A mountain deity came to request the precepts, and Yong conferred them upon him according to the Dharma. The deity presented him with foreign-style chopsticks and a spoon, which were exquisitely crafted and extraordinary.
When Huiyuan passed away, Yong rushed to the funeral and wailed with grief in accordance with the rites. Later, he died at Zhulin Monastery in Jingzhou.

Facheng of the Song dynasty was a native of Liang. From his youth, he became a śramaṇa; he abstained from grains and subsisted on pine resin. He studied and practiced Chan and the Vinaya, traveling as far as Guanghan.
Once, while reciting the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, when he had reached only halfway through, he suddenly fell ill. He urgently ordered his attendant to read the entire scripture for him.
Then he transformed. Some saw a dark-blue horse carrying a coffin depart through the air.

Hui-guo of Song was a native of Yuzhou; at the beginning of the Song dynasty, he traveled to the capital and resided at Waguan Temple. He recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, and other scriptures.
Once, after finishing his visit to the latrine, a ghost appeared before him and said, "In a previous life, I was the *karmadāna* (steward) of this temple. Because of my transgressions..."
He died and was reborn in a latrine. Because the Dharma Master possessed the profound virtue of recitation and upholding the scriptures, he was able to bring liberation from the miserable realms;
thus, [the ghost] prayed for his deliverance. "I have three thousand coins buried beneath a persimmon tree," [the ghost said]. "You may take them to provide for the expenses of meritorious deeds.

Consequently, the Master informed the assembly of this matter, took the coins, and commissioned a copy of the *Lotus Sūtra*. He then held an assembly to perform repentance. Later, he dreamed that the ghost had been reborn in a superior realm.
He came to offer his thanks. However, upon observing his appearance, it was entirely unlike that of the previous day.
The Song monk Yin was born into the Li clan; he was a native of Longxi in Qinzhou. At the age of eight, he left home, and at twelve, he became a śramaṇa.

He mastered the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and recited the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Under Dharma Master Xuangao of Xiliang, he thoroughly investigated and clarified the wisdom of dhyāna.

He had a profound understanding of the essentials of the Vinaya. He subsequently traveled west to Ba and Shu, and upon his return, resided at Pipa Temple in Jiangling, where he further studied under Huiche;
