his reputation spread throughout the Jing and Chu regions. At that time, Liu Xiyou, Prince of Shanyang, served as the regional governor, and Zhang Dai served as the Chief Secretary (Changshi);
both received the precepts from him. Furthermore, Liu Xiuruo, Prince of Baling, and Jing Su, Prince of Jianping, halted their carriages there to inquire about the Way.

He was also ill. When asked whether it was early or late in the day, he replied, "It is already noon. He then sought water for washing and rinsing his mouth, and passed away in a state of profound stillness.
There was a śramaṇa named Daofang, born into the Zhang family, a native of Wucheng in Guanghan. He was learned in the Vinaya and lived to the age of one hundred and twenty.
Furthermore, there was a śramaṇa named Daorong, whose origins were unknown; he was learned in the Vinaya and resided at Wenxin Temple.
He lectured and taught. He passed away at the age of eighty-three.
Tánbǐn of the Sū clan was a native of Nányáng. At the age of ten or so, he took Dàoxuī as his teacher and became a śramaṇa.
He studied the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* under Sengye at Wujun; he studied the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* at Jinglin in Jianye;
he studied the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* under Fayao at Wuxing; and he studied the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* under Faye at Nanlin.

He thoroughly mastered a multitude of doctrines, and students followed him in great numbers. Upon returning, he resided in the region of Fandeng, where he lectured and taught. At the beginning of the Xiaojian era, he moved to Xin'an.

While he was lecturing on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, Yuan Can of Chenjun—whose reputation was preeminent at the time—personally visited him to pay his respects and urged him to enter the imperial court for an audience.

Sengbin declined, stating that as one who dwells beyond the mundane world (*fangwai*), how could such a thing be appropriate? He further expounded upon the principles of sudden and gradual enlightenment.

At that time, those who vied for intellectual supremacy raised numerous objections; however, because Sengbin’s responses were eloquent and his arguments reached the core of the truth, they ultimately could not prevail. Yuan Can [was thus impressed].
He further increased [his reputation]. He passed away at the age of sixty-seven.
Seng Huiliang of the Song dynasty was born into the Dong family; he was a native of Dong'e. He served as a disciple of Huijing and enjoyed a high reputation.

He was able to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. After crossing the Yangtze River, he resided at Heyuan Temple, where students gathered like clouds. Yan Yanzhi, Zhang... [text truncated]

Xu sighed and said, "Hui'an and Fayu brought forth the 'jade resonance' in the past; Daobin and Huilang followed with the 'golden sound. These subtle words and wondrous discourses, which were nearly extinguished, are now flourishing once more.
How could such things have been easily obtained? He passed away during the Yuanhui era at the age of sixty-three. He authored the *Tongxuan lun* (Discourse on Penetrating Mystery).

The Song dynasty monk Jing was born into the Jiao clan; he was a native of Longxi who lived as a guest in the region of Wu. He was renowned for his filial piety, disdained wealth, and delighted in charity.

When his mother passed away, the Prefect offered him funeral gifts, which he refused. He carried soil on his back to build a tomb and lived in a thatched hut beside it, planting pine and cypress trees.

After three years, he became a śramaṇa and resided at Huashan Temple in Wu County. He entered the Guanzhong region to seek out teachers and receive the Dharma. [He was later invited by] Xu Zhan of Donghai.
He requested [Huiyuan] to serve as his teacher for the entire lineage. Later, he returned to Gusu and visited Xie Lingyun of Shangyu, with whom he shared a profound and sincere bond.

They traveled together through the Yan and Sheng mountains. During the Yuanhui era, by imperial decree, he was summoned to the capital and resided at the Lower Dinglin Monastery, where he frequently established Dharma assemblies.
He annotated the *Fahua*, the *Weimo*, the *Yishu*, and the *Pitan Xuantun*. He passed away at the age of sixty-seven.
At the same time, there was also Shi Tanlong, who was likewise renowned in the world for his noble conduct.
Song Chaojin was born into the Zhuanxu clan. A native of Chang’an, he possessed high moral integrity and was learned in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras.
He entered the monastic order at a young age and became renowned throughout Guanzhong. When the Xiqiang leader Helian Bobo invaded Chang’an, he took refuge in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang).
After a long time, he traveled to Wu. Meng Yi, the Governor of Kuaiji, welcomed him to reside at Lingjia Temple in Shanyin.

At the beginning of the Taishi era, he was summoned by imperial decree to the capital, where he lectured on such scriptures as the *Mahādharmānda-sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Monastics and laypeople regularly numbered in the thousands.
Because he was so devoted to reading, he became doubly blind; nevertheless, he still had his disciples chant the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* once every day. During the Yuanhui era—
He passed away at the age of ninety-four. At that time, there were Tanji and Daoping, both of whom were renowned for their scholarly exegesis.
Fayao of the Song dynasty was born into the Yang family; a native of Hedong, he was fond of learning from his youth and was capable of seeking out teachers ten thousand *li* away.
During the Yuanjia era, he crossed the Yangtze River and resided at Xiaoshan Temple in Wukang, Wuxing. For nineteen years, his traces did not enter the world of men.
In the sixth year of the Taiming era, an imperial edict ordered the local commandery to escort him with ceremonial rites to the capital.

There, he stayed together with Daoyou at Xin'an Temple and lectured on the meaning of the two awakenings—sudden and gradual. The Emperor halted his carriage to attend the assembly, accompanied by the hundred officials of the court. In the ninth year, he composed the *Niepan*... [text fragment].

He authored commentaries on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, and others. He passed away during the Yuánhuí era at the age of seventy-six.
Sēngzōng of the Qi dynasty was born into the Yán clan; he was a native of Fēngyì in Yōngzhōu. At the age of nine, he took the master Yuàn as his teacher and received the full precepts.

He studied the Way under the two masters Bīn and Jì and became proficient in such scriptures as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. Whenever he ascended the lecture hall to preach, [he encountered] difficult [questions].

None were able to break it. His nature was transcendent and unrestrained; he disregarded the rules of measurement. Whenever he had something on his mind, he would go directly to it, passing through walls without obstruction. People criticized him for this.
Prince Wenhui of the Qi dynasty conceived an evil thought toward him, whereupon he suddenly dreamed of being tormented by someone. Thereupon, he changed his mind and apologized to him.
The Ruler of Wei sent a letter requesting that he open a lecture hall, but Emperor Shizu of the Qi dynasty did not grant permission. [The Master] took the offerings made throughout his life...
He founded Taichang Temple; he passed away when the temple was completed, at the age of fifty-nine.
Senglín of the Liáng dynasty was a native of Wú. During the Dàtóng era, he traveled to Shǔ and reached Tóngzhōu, where he resided in a divine shrine on Mount Dòuchuí.

To the northwest of the city, one hundred and forty *li* away, there was a mountain where the deity was exceptionally numinous and strange, a place to which the people offered sacrifices and paid their respects.

Senglin often practiced meditation there in silence. One day, a giant python coiled itself before his rope bed; it raised its head and looked up and down as if performing a ritual of bowing and yielding.

After Senglin had administered the Three Refuges to it, the serpent immediately departed. From then on, he gradually expanded the construction and settled there peacefully, and in the end, no further harm occurred. This was at Shushan.

There were many monkeys. However, to the north of this mountain and on the southern bank of the Fu River, there had previously been none at all. When [the Master] came to dwell in the forest, two monkeys suddenly appeared from nowhere;
they settled there and did not leave for a long time. As the years passed, their offspring multiplied until their number reached over a hundred.

Whenever he happened to leave the forest and go out of the mountains, the troop would escort him as far as the Dragon Gate, where they would stand waiting expectantly for his return. Such was the nature of these creatures.
His longing and devotion were such as this. Before long, he stayed at Chishui (Red Water). His old residence had fallen into ruin, and the buildings were completely collapsed.
Upon his return, he sat exposed in the thickets; a tiger crouched before him, gazing into the forest as if waiting for someone. When Lin preached the Dharma to it, the tiger departed.
Ultimately, Lin passed away at Tongguan.
Liang Shangyuan, surnamed Chen, was a native of Luocheng in Guanghan. Throughout his life, he benefited living beings through the arts of exorcism.
At that time, the concubines and maidens in the palace of Prince Wuling Ji were all possessed by ghosts; they sang or wailed, creating such a tumultuous disorder that peace could not be restored.
The ghosts suddenly manifested their forms, and when the Prince ordered a skilled archer to shoot them, the ghosts immediately caught the arrows.
The arrows he threw back at his assailants invariably struck and wounded them. This continued for a long time without ceasing, until he went to the palace of Yuanchi to offer prayers.
Upon his initial arrival, he beheld dragons, snakes, wolves, and tigers roaring, galloping, appearing and disappearing, or remaining hidden, with various strange apparitions crowding before him.
Yuan sat calmly and said to them: "You are but ghosts of a lowly household; how dare you recklessly enter the royal palace? You..."
"Does it mean that you are able to effect transformations? If you can indeed cause my body to transform, only then can it be called 'transformation.
However, though you may transform your own bodies into ten thousand varieties, you are merely minor spirits; you are not among the great spirits.
"Stay where you are for a moment and listen to these words of mine. Then all the spirits stood with palms joined. Yuan Yin cried out: "Namo Buddhāya! All the spirits...
At one time, they all suddenly vanished from their location. When Emperor Wu heard of this, he bestowed great praise and favor upon him.
Later, he passed away at Yecheng, where he resided, at the age of eighty-one.
Liang Daozhen’s place of origin is unknown. Initially, while at Mount Lu, he practiced the visualization of Amitābha.

Once, during a state of meditative concentration, he saw a person traveling by boat upon the great ocean, who said, "I am going to the Land of Amitābha Buddha. Daozhen then requested to be taken along.
The man said, "If one has not performed the practices for the Pure Land, how could this be possible?

At that time, he thought to himself, "Building and maintaining a bathhouse and reciting the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* shall constitute my practice for the Pure Land. Once he emerged from meditative absorption, he acted according to his intention.
As the years and months passed, there suddenly appeared a silver platform above the mountain pond in his room; no one else knew of it, but he alone did.
He recorded these matters on the bottom of his scripture case. On the evening of his death, hundreds of torches appeared as if arrayed across Mount Ban;

those who saw it considered it a marvel. Later, he happened to recover the old record written on the bottom of the scripture case, and only then did he again verify the evidence of his rebirth in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, there was the Chan Master Fagui, a native of Hanyin in Xiangyang. Having long practiced the discipline of Chan, he once, while in meditative concentration—
There was a divine being who invited him to travel to Mount Lu. Although he had never known Mount Lu in his lifetime, upon emerging from meditative concentration, he went there;
the trees, rocks, temples, and stupas were exactly as he had seen them within his concentration. He subsequently built a dwelling there and resided.
This is the present-day Fengding Temple (Fengding-ji). Gānlù Peak (Amṛta Peak) is also a secondary peak of this mountain.

Formerly, when Chan Master Huìjǐng was about to pass away, he held up two fingers; though they were extended, they would bend back again. Commentators considered this a verification of his attainment of the second fruit [of the śrāvaka path].
Furthermore, the flora and fauna of the mountain were all bathed in *amṛta* (sweet dew), and the peak was named accordingly. (The third virtue, one.)
This event remains a celebrated wonder of the mountain to this day; I have recorded it here in full.

Dao Bian of Wei was born to a woman of the Tian clan of Fanyang when she dreamed that a monk wearing a *kaṣāya* and holding a *khakkhara* entered her womb. From childhood, he displayed many miraculous signs.

As he grew older, however, he became deaf and mute due to illness. Consequently, he renounced worldly ties and took ordination. Regarding the profound meanings of the *sūtras* and the *vinaya*, he required no formal study.

He was particularly adept at analyzing the heterodox and the orthodox and elucidating obstructed or stagnant points. Once, when preaching the Great Teaching before Emperor Xiaowen, he pleased the Emperor’s mind.
Initially residing at Beitaishan, he later followed the court southward; his reputation spread throughout the regions of Hede and Luoyang.

At that time, there was a scripture titled the *Dafazunwang Jing* in eighty fascicles, which was claimed to have been spoken by the Buddha. Bianyi read it once and recognized its falsity, subsequently ordering it to be burned.
Furthermore, he intended to provide exhaustive commentaries on the entire Tripitaka in order to refute other erroneous views; however, upon encountering various unusual omens, he eventually desisted.

His commentaries on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda*, and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*, as well as his *Mahāyāna-yìzhāng*, *Hīnayāna-yìzhāng*, and *Shēn xuánzhào*, have been circulated in the world.
The two disciples were Tanyong and Wangming. Yong possessed great talent yet was disdainful of the world; he lived in seclusion to maintain his integrity.
Sengbian often rebuked him, yet Yong harbored no resentment from the start. Instead, morning and evening, he would offer prostrations to him from afar, saying: "..."

Huisong of Qi was a native of Gaochang. He left home to become a monk in his youth; he was intelligent and quick-witted. While studying the *Zaxin lun* (Treatise on Miscellaneous Minds), he became a figure toward whom his own country looked for guidance.
His elder brother, who served as a state doctor for his literary talents, repeatedly urged him to return to lay life, but Huisong would simply shake his head and walk away.

He then used the *Yilin* (Forest of Changes) to inquire about its esoteric and hidden meanings. Since Huisong had never read it before, he immediately divided it into sections and analyzed them without any obstruction or hesitation.
His elder brother was amazed by this; yet, he still did not believe that the Buddha-dharma was so profound and vast.
Thereupon, Huisong gave him a single verse from the *Abhidharma* (*Pitan*) and asked him to explain its meaning. He pondered it for two months, struggling in vain with confusion, yet his explanation—
This was even more erroneous. When Hui-sōng was in a state of frustration and yearning for understanding, [Hui-]yǒu briefly opened up the initial end of the path for him;

thereupon, he attained a clear and spiritual realization and finally turned his great respect toward [the Buddha]. From that time on, nothing could ever again deter Hui-sōng from his religious vocation. Toward the end of the Wei dynasty, Hui-sōng still upheld our teaching.

When the King sent Hui-sōng along with his younger brother to the court, the Prime Minister Gāo treated them with exceptional courtesy and generosity. Master Zhìyóu was renowned throughout the world as a *lùnshī* (master of treatises).

He followed the Master of the School, Sengsong, to study the *Abhidharma* and the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*. He grasped the essential meaning of the texts and commentaries; those who listened to him forgot their weariness.

His reputation for brilliance spread in his early years, and formidable opponents submitted by the time of his later years. With his learning eminent and his reputation far-reaching, his own country requested that he return.
Sengsong would not listen. When he was summoned a second time, he did as before. The king resented this and exterminated Sengsong’s three clans.

Sengsong said to his disciples, "Does the Sūtra not say that the three realms are impermanent and all conditioned existence is not pleasure? How much more so for the three miserable paths and the eight sufferings through which we have passed since time immemorial—what is there to be surprised at?
Shortly thereafter, the Gao Qi dynasty underwent a revolution. At the beginning of the Tianbao era, Emperor Xuan ascended the throne. The Emperor [issued] an edict...

He was held in high esteem primarily because of his official position, yet Huiyuan constantly surpassed him in learning and erudition. By imperial decree, he was transferred to Xuzhou to serve as the *Sengtong* (Patriarch) of the Longnian Monastery;
throughout Henan and Jiangbiao, people generally followed his teachings. The Dharma Master Zhinian of the Sui dynasty was indeed his spiritual successor.
He subsequently passed away.
Qi Daoji’s surname was He. His native village is unknown. He specialized in the *Abhidharmakośa* and had a particularly large following of disciples.
During the Tianbao era, he would regularly begin his lectures at the beginning of autumn in the capital of Ye. One day, Daoji led the assembly southward out of the city of Ye.
There were some former disciples who led a crowd in to meet him; even when they encountered him directly, they did not retreat or yield.

Sengji rebuked them, to which they replied, "The Dharma drums resound in competition; this is precisely where benefit is established. When fame and reputation are directed toward one, what distinction can there be between teacher and disciple?
Sengji remained silent and gave no answer, eventually departing for the outskirts of the city. There, he dismissed all his disciples, saying, "I have already lectured three times..."

It has been ten years. As for those whom I have brought to spiritual accomplishment, one knows not how many there may be. Furthermore, to establish practice based upon understanding is the legacy of the ancients.
Now, to possess understanding yet lack practice—how can this be endured? The past cannot be pursued, but the future may still be reached.
I shall now close my door to reflect upon my transgressions; therefore, I have swept out a room and am reading the sutras and śāstras extensively, drawing from the monastery...

He composed one set of seven fascicles of the *Jin zang lun* (Discourse on the Golden Treasury), explaining the origins of pagodas, banners, and lamps, as well as the fundamental principles of scriptures, images, and the precepts.
He recited it once every seven days to expound upon these matters for the laypeople and clergy, leading them to take refuge and believe.

Furthermore, he exhorted them to uphold the eight precepts and practice the *fashè* (Dharma-society) fasts, forbidding slaughter. Within a few years, throughout the region surrounding Ye, everyone followed his teachings. Therefore—

The world collectively praised him. Why then would he conceal his teacher? He served him with the utmost reverence. Ji considered the task of sweeping the pagoda for his mother to be his most urgent duty, saying:
"According to the sutras, sweeping a monastic ground as vast as Jambudvīpa is not as meritorious as sweeping the ground of the Buddha."
To say it was as small as a single palm is to speak of the excellence of his field of wisdom. His mother was equal to a Bodhisattva who has ascended the stages (*bhūmi*).

Therefore, in serving her—whether in matters of food, clothing, or daily activities—he always performed them with his own body and did not permit others to assist him. He said: "My mother is the root of my physical form.
The burdens of this physical form are my own burdens; how could I dare to burden another? In the dwelling where I reside, there shall be no more menial servants. If...
Whenever he traveled, he would pack his shoulder-pole with two loads: at one end were the stupa, the image, and the scriptures;
at the other end was only his old mother’s broom. Someone asked, "In the past, your disciples contended for the right way. Do you still harbor any regret?
He replied, "It was largely through their efforts that I have reached this day. Why should I have any cause for regret?"
Zhou Wei Yuansong was a native of Chengdu in Yizhou. In his youth, he entered the monastic order under an unnamed Dharma Master.

He was exceptionally intelligent and stood out from his peers. Once, while attending the Dharma Master during a night vigil, he suddenly sighed and said, "The world values the ears and despises the eyes;
how, then, can it distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy? The unnamed master replied, "If you wish to pursue fame and reputation, then feign madness."

It may be appropriate to cause confusion in order to startle the common world; Sōng agreed with this in his heart. Thereupon, he "played upon the field" as the occasion arose, composing verses upon whatever he encountered.
In this manner, for more than twenty years, everyone among the people of the four quarters—whether they knew him or not—regarded Yuan Sōng as a sincere man of the world.

Subsequently, he disappeared from public view and entered Guān, moving his residence to Yě'ān, where he composed the *Tiānnǚyuàn* (Lament of the Celestial Woman) and the *Xīnfēngnòng* (Play of the Mind-Wind).
He played the lute and once said to his elder brother, "The land of Shu is narrow and small; it is insufficient to unfold my inner ambitions.
I must certainly travel to the capital to contend with the heroes and sages. What do you think? His brother deemed this improper, and Yuansong took his leave.
Upon arriving in the capital, he reflected that there was ultimately no way to move the Emperor, so he drafted a memorial on the matter of abolishing Buddhism for submission. It happened that...
The scholar Zhang Bin acted as his confidant. Thereupon, the Emperor accepted his proposal and abolished the Buddhist teachings without hesitation.
In the eighth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Du Qi of Jingzhao died; after three days he revived and said that he had gone to the Netherworld and seen King Yama.
The King asked, "What office did your father once hold? He replied, "In the Zhou dynasty, my father served as a Commandant of the Upper Grade.
The King said, "If that is so, then I have wrongly pursued you. You may be released immediately to return home. The King then asked, "Do you know Emperor Wu of the Zhou?
He answered, "I formerly served as a Judicial Officer of the Left Imperial Guard and was constantly at the palace steps; I knew him very well. The King said, "You may..."
Upon first looking at Emperor Wu, an official led him to a certain place. The doors, windows, rafters, and tiles were all made of iron.
Through the iron window, he saw the Emperor’s body; his complexion was as dark as iron, he was extremely emaciated, and he was bound with an iron collar and shackles. He knelt and wept, saying:
"Master, for what reason are you so distressed? He replied, "My distress is even greater than it is now;
you simply have not seen it yet. Qiji asked, "What sin has brought you to such distress? He replied, "Do you not know?
It is because I used my influence to protect Yuan Song, thereby causing the Buddhist teachings to be abolished. Qiji said, "Master, why do you not bring Yuan Song here as a witness?"
He replied: "I have frequently cited and quoted him. However, the authorities maintain that even if one were to search throughout the three realms, no one could be found.
If he had indeed been seen, I would have attained liberation; what more would there be to discuss? Return and tell the people of the world that it was Yuan Song."
"Perform meritorious deeds; come early to save us. If you ultimately do not arrive, there will be no time for our liberation.
Inferring from this, Yuan Song’s approach toward the Buddha-dharma was indeed acting perversely and contrary to principle, intended perhaps to provoke and stir others.
Falin of the Liang dynasty was surnamed Yan. A native of Zhiyang, at the age of fifteen, he received the tonsure at Yquan Mountain Temple.

There he joined the assembly to study the flavors of the Dharma for many years. In the intervals between his meditation and leisure, he continued to recite the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra-ṭīkā*.
He wore no silk or cotton, and ate from fields that had not been plowed or tilled for three years. He lived on discarded rags and alms, and never slept while seated in meditation. His...
In his travels, he visited Mount Lu, Mount Tai, Mount Heng, Mount Luo, and Mount Heng; in seeking the profound and investigating the mysterious, there was nothing he did not observe.
While traveling slowly toward Mount Dai, he encountered a county magistrate who asked for his travel documents. Senglin pointed to the box he was carrying and said, "This is it.
When the magistrate opened it, it was the *Lotus Sūtra*. Thinking he had been deceived, the magistrate was extremely angry. Senglin spoke calmly, saying, "This..."
"It is indeed the trace of the Buddhas' appearance in the world. As for what I, a poor practitioner, cultivate and perform, may it not be fitting to call it 'practicing the Way'?
This further enraged Liu Yu, who had him arrested and imprisoned. Despite this, he remained steadfast in seated meditation and recited the sutras without ceasing for seven days.
This caused him to experience bad dreams, so [the Emperor] ordered his release. Not long after, he passed away at the age of sixty-two. Fǎrěn of the Liáng dynasty was a native of Jīnglíng.
He received the tonsure and full ordination at Tiānhuáng Monastery. Every day he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* twice.
After some time, finding the environment noisy and distracting, he moved to live beneath Fùzhōu Yán. There he practiced the dhūta austerities with diligence for over thirty years.

He practiced the contemplation of suffering with clarity and tranquility for seven consecutive days. His provisions were always abundant; should they ever fail, he would subsist on nothing but water and fruit.

His meditation cell was barely large enough to accommodate his knees; through the freezing winter and the scorching summer, he never once stepped outside his door. He wore neither linen nor cotton clothing.

Wearing a tattered robe, he endured both cold and heat. Before long, an elephant appeared of its own accord. Shortly thereafter, he manifested illness and passed away in a cave to the north of the cliff at the age of sixty-seven.
Chen Zhiyuan was of the Wang clan; his ancestral home was Taiyuan, but he resided in the Shan region as a youth.

He relied upon the Chan quarters of Changsha Monastery in Jingzhou, where he studied under the śramaṇa Fajing. Having shaved his head and received the precepts, he cultivated his conduct with vigor and earnestness.

Carrying his book-cases on a carriage, he traveled to Jianye to study the advanced teachings of wisdom under Sengchao at Longguang Monastery. Within three years, he had mastered the Tripiṭaka. During the Liang dynasty...

Marquis Jian'an, Xiao Zhengli, established Puming Monastery and invited [the Master] to reside there. At that time, Chan Master Huizhan was leading his disciples with the study of meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
the Master subsequently consulted him on its secret essentials. Thereafter, he traveled to famous mountains to cultivate his will and propagate the Way.
Later, he again encountered the śramaṇa Daohui at Longpan, where he resolved the subtle mysteries; thus, throughout the four modes of deportment (*catur-īryāpatha*), [he attained mastery].

Throughout his life, he never departed from meditative absorption (*samādhi*). He resided at Kaishan Temple, dedicating his will to the pursuit of springs and rocks; in silent seclusion, he found his own delight. To the end of his life, he remained free from worldly ambition.
He passed away on the first day of the twelfth month in the third year of the Taian era. At seventy-seven years of age, he was buried at Dulongsan Mountain.
The *śramaṇa* Huigao erected a stele for him, and Xiao Ji, the Minister of the Five Armies, composed the inscription.

Chen Huifeng was a man of unknown origins who resided at Xiqia Temple in Jiangdu. Having studied the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) under Master Xuan, he attained a profound realization of their essential meaning;
thus, he was highly esteemed by the assembly. Master Xuan often remarked with admiration: "As for Huifeng’s penetrating understanding and power of reflection, I cannot surpass him.
Since I am advanced in years, let him remain to rely upon me. Huifeng devoted his mind to the contemplation of Chan meditation and modeled his conduct after the monastic discipline (*vinaya*).

He concentrated his mindfulness amidst the pine forest, taking but a single meal a day. His robes were coarse and tattered, yet he possessed a refined elegance that caused those of his time to admire him with envy.

In his later years, he focused particularly on the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) to skillfully guide students; those who came to listen and receive his instruction were especially numerous. Some, however, criticized him.
"Since you have long practiced the Mahāyāna and yet lecture on the Vinaya, how could this be logical? Fēng said, "This is not something you can know.
In the Buddha-dharma, what distinction of 'Great' and 'Small' could there possibly be? He passed away during the Tiānjiā period at the age of sixty.
Before his death, he said to his disciple Zhìkūn, "The place to which I am departing—how could you possibly fathom it? It is so remote and vast. Upon [his passing]...
When he was encoffined, one finger remained bent; it could not be extended even after death. Those who understood this took it as proof that he had realized the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).
Huikong of the Sui dynasty was originally of the Zhou clan from Runan; later, fleeing the turmoil, he settled in the region south of the Yangtze River and became a native of Yangxian in Yixing.

His grandfather, Shao, was a General of the Palace Interior under the Qi dynasty; his father, Fu, was a Colonel of the Longshui Cavalry under the Liang dynasty. Huikong mastered the Six Classics from his youth.
At the age of eighteen, Da Yi sighed deeply and said: "I have held the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius close to my heart, prioritizing benevolence and righteousness;

I have turned my mind toward Huang-Lao, valuing emptiness and non-being. Yet, coming and going through birth and death, entering and exiting the toil of the mundane world, are but burdens within the realm—they are not the Way that transcends the world.
Shortly thereafter, he dreamed of a five-storied pagoda, magnificent and towering in its splendor. He paid homage to it...
He prostrated and offered prayers. Ascending to its summit, he suddenly sat upon the spire of the stupa and could not contain his joy.

Thereupon, following the Dharma Master Xu of Zhufang Zhulin Temple, he left the household life and received the ten precepts. Shortly thereafter, he arrived at the capital and resided at Gandhakuṭī Temple.
Upon receiving full ordination, he studied the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* under Master Jingzhong Feng and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* under Master Longguang Chuo.
After Master Chuo passed away, he further studied the *Aṣṭagrantha-abhidharma* under other masters, desiring to savor its profound essence and extract its finest flowers.
He also conducted an exhaustive investigation of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* under the Great Sangha Rectifier (Sengzheng) Master Shu of Longguang Temple. And Shu...

He passed away. Having been entrusted with the succession of the lineage, he accepted his final testament. When the destiny of the Liang dynasty came to an end and the monasteries in the capital were devastated, the founder of the Chen dynasty was testing his fortunes in Zhufang;
[the Master] then traveled south with his staff and returned. He was especially held in high esteem and veneration. Subsequently, Lord Hou succeeded in governing this province;
with a sincere heart, he took refuge in him, and no ritual could surpass his devotion. In the third year of Yongding, he departed for the capital once more and stayed there.

At the Baima Monastery, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* were lectured upon in alternation. Students flocked there in great numbers, traveling from as far as a thousand li without hesitation;
the magnificence of these dharma assemblies was unsurpassed. In the second year of the Tianjia era, two hundred and seventy śramaṇas, including Baochi and others, [gathered there].
He was invited to propagate the teachings at Xianggong Temple. In the fourth year of the Dajian era, Emperor Xuan issued an edict transferring him to Dong'an Temple.

When the Later Emperor was still in the Eastern Palace, he repeatedly summoned him for assemblies on the Dharma; having long admired his talent and eloquence, the Emperor’s esteem for him grew even more profound once he ascended the throne.

In the first year of the Zhide era, he was appointed by imperial decree as the Great Archbishop (Dāsengdu) of the capital. In the fourth year, he was elevated to the rank of Great Archpriest (Dāsengzheng). During this time, the empire was unified under one rule.
He returned once more to guide the people of Zhufang. On the tenth day of the seventh month in the ninth year of the Kaihuang era, he passed away at Zhongsi Temple at the age of seventy-five.
On the twenty-eighth day of that same month, he was interred on Mount Zhong.

During the height of the Chen dynasty, every summer during the ancestral temple sacrifices, the Emperor would invariably summon Sengxiong to the Leyou Garden to recite the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, thereby solemnizing the merit for the afterlife. And as for Feng...
The dragon banners were furled; the emerald streamers and the great canopy cast their shadows over the divine seat.

Sometimes, after his meal, he would take a brief nap and immediately dream that a person in vermilion robes said to him, "Dharma Master, it is time for you to rise. General-in-Chief Ren Zhong was by nature fond of hunting.
One day, the kitchen fires emitted a brilliant light. Zhong was filled with anxiety and fear. That night, he dreamed of a man who said, "Have no anxiety or fear;

you need only invite Dong’an to lecture. His disciple Zhiyu and others erected a stele at his tomb. The text was composed by Wang Zhou, a *pusa-jie* (bodhisattva-precept) disciple and Court Historian of Langye.
Faxing of the Sui dynasty was a native of Yanzhou. In his youth, he studied Chan Buddhism. He traveled alone along the coast;
although he relied on alms for sustenance, he would occasionally enter villages, yet he never once set foot in places of fame, status, or worldly profit.

When Emperor Wen went on a tour to the east, he searched out those dwelling in mountain caves and consequently issued an edict for Faxing to enter the capital, where he resided at Shengguang Temple. During the Renshou era, when pagodas were being erected, the Emperor again sent śarīra relics to him.
It was at Pule Temple in the prefecture. This great master of dhyāna-concentration was specially built for Xing by the Emperor during his final years;
subsequently, he indeed passed away in this temple.
Baoji of the Sui dynasty was surnamed Zhu. A native of Tiaocheng in Jizhou, he left the household life to seek the Way; his resolve was worthy of respect.

When the Qi dynasty fell and the Buddhist teachings were suppressed, he withdrew to Mount Tai to cultivate his fundamental nature. In the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era, Emperor Wen went on a tour of the east and received Baoji’s audience.

The Emperor was greatly pleased and issued an edict for him to reside at Shengguang Temple in the capital. He was profoundly learned in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra*, which were as interconnected as a chain of rings.
He lectured and expounded [the scriptures] without ever ceasing. By nature he was broad-minded and forgiving; even when people pressed him or offended him, he showed no resentment.
If anyone spoke ill of him, he would immediately take off his robe and give it to them, saying: "If you can see my faults and not conceal them for me, you are truly my teacher and friend.
At the beginning of the Renshou era, an imperial edict ordered the dispatch of a śarīra stupa to Sijue Temple on Mount Hua. Its auspicious responses were recorded separately.

There is a tradition concerning Daochan of the Sui dynasty, a native of Hengzhou; his family name and clan, however, have not been heard of. Regarding his wisdom-studies, he had long taken the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra* as his guiding compass.
He was capable of raising profound doubts and resolving hidden meanings during the course of his lectures and debates, for his aspirations were set upon the profound and subtle.
Jing was truly not one who delighted in traveling by imperial carriage; his later residence at Jingguang Monastery was merely because he had no choice.
During the Renshou era, when a stupa was being constructed, an imperial decree ordered him to deliver śarīra relics to Xuzhou. His final whereabouts thereafter remain unknown.

Zhi Jiao of the Sui dynasty was a native of Yongzhou. He first studied the teachings and contemplation, lecturing by day and practicing meditation by night, never for a moment showing even the slightest laxity.
Later, weary of verbal exposition, he devoted himself exclusively to quiet seclusion; his spiritual orientation was such that it could not be fathomed by worldly people.

During the Renshou era, he erected a stupa at Yongning Temple in Qinzhou. Wherever the śarīra relics arrived, officials and commoners, monastics and laity alike, celebrated together as auspicious omens appeared.
It would have been chaotic; yet those who saw it believed it.
Sengfan, a monk of the Sui dynasty, was a native of Ji. His learning encompassed both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, yet he was particularly devoted to the practice of tranquility.

His realization was profound and far-reaching, such that his contemporaries could not help but submit to him. He resided at Shengguang Temple, where scholars from the mountains and forests heard of his reputation.

They arrived in great numbers. While he remained in his daily life without offering formal instruction, his laughter, jesting, and even his scoldings caused people to attain awakening and insight at every turn.
How extraordinary! By imperial decree, his śarīra were enshrined in Jueguan Temple in the prefecture; the stupa remains there to this day.
Tánguān of the Sui dynasty was a native of Jǔshān. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and became thoroughly versed in the sutras and liturgical repentances.

Upon receiving full ordination, he studied the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*; his mastery of its principles left no room for stagnation or confusion. Later, he devoted himself to the practice of dhyāna and contemplation, attaining exceptional proficiency in the "Sixteen Special Victories" (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*).

Furthermore, by reciting various vidyās, he obtained divine efficacy, and his reputation reached the celestial gates. Consequently, he was summoned to reside at Dàxīngshàn Monastery in the capital, where he was provided with offerings.

His influence was grand and extensive. Whenever he entered the inner court, he was provided with counsel and consultation; yet all the rewards and gifts he received were returned to the permanent endowment of the monastery, and he accepted nothing for himself.
His three robes and single alms bowl were as simple and austere as ever. During the Renshou era, a stupa was established to enshrine the śarīra relics at Dinglin Temple in the prefecture.

Emperor Gaozong summoned him to oversee the planning and design; consequently, when the stupa was completed, the people suffered no hardship. Alas! As for Guanzhi within the gates of the Dharma, his contribution was truly unsurpassed.
Such a person may indeed be called one of great power. Jingning of the Sui dynasty was a native of Bian.
At that time, Master Xuanjue (Shenxiang) was just then renowned in the world for his study of emptiness and stillness.
Jingning consequently took him as his teacher; thus, what he attained through hearing and seeing—how could it ever be sought again through written characters or spoken language?

Is this not strange? Yet he sits in silence all day long like a fool. When someone asks him questions regarding the meaning of the scriptures or their doctrinal principles, he answers without deliberation, his insights emerging with marvelous subtlety beyond the reach of the mind.
During the Renshou era, a stupa was erected at Liugou Temple in the prefecture; this was a great honor for returning to one’s hometown, as it involved the enshrinement of śarīra relics.
Is this not far superior to the act of walking by day in one’s native land while dressed in brocade?

Xuánjǐng of the Sui dynasty was the son of the Shì family of Cāngzhōu. From childhood, he was intelligent and quick-witted; whenever he read a book, he could immediately cite its meanings without omission.
In barely five years, he had thoroughly mastered the Classics, Histories, Philosophical Works, and Collections. At the age of eighteen, he was recommended as a *xiùcái* (talented scholar).
To simplify matters for the Prince of He, at that time Master He was lecturing on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* in the capital of Ye.
Sengjing happened to stand by the side of the door listening; finding Jing’s comprehension to be exceptionally outstanding, he subsequently enrolled under Master He to study.

He was nearly eighty years old. Mingcan of the Sui dynasty was born into the Wei clan in Yishui, Ju. His family had been of scholarly and simple virtue for generations. From his youth, he studied the classics and histories;

before he had even reached the age of *zhixue*, he left the household life. By the time he received full ordination (*jijie*), he was already in his early twenties. Nevertheless, regarding the maintenance of the monastic community, he was considered a consummate master.

Shi was truly devoted to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, lecturing upon it without ceasing. Although he withdrew to the forests and marshes when the teachings were suppressed under Emperor Zhou, his enlightened companions followed him, and he never forgot what he had expounded.
At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, his fame spread far and wide, and by imperial decree he resided at Daxingshan Temple in the capital.
At the beginning of the Renshou era, he was summoned to deliver a śarīra relic, which was interred at Qixia in Jiangzhou—this being the present-day She.
He was a monk of a mountain temple. However, he had previously obtained over a hundred volumes of ancient Sanskrit scriptures in the region south of the Yangtze River.

He longed to translate them for inclusion in the Tripiṭaka, yet lacked the necessary funds; thus, he was driven by this concern, never ceasing his efforts even as he traveled through remote areas where bamboo screens were suspended.
His resolve to propagate the Dharma remained steadfast until his death at the beginning of the Tang dynasty.
The Sui monk Senggai was a native of Hengzhou. Initially, he studied the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* in the regions of Fen and Luo.

Later, calculating that his wisdom surpassed his precepts, he focused exclusively on the study of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). He then took up his staff and traveled to the capital, visiting meditation masters everywhere.

Da Xingshan Temple was located in the midst of a bustling marketplace, yet Senggai resided there; throughout the day, he remained in quiet seclusion, maintaining the perception that he was in deep mountains and dense forests. Thereupon—
The commentators extolled his lofty achievements. In the second year of the Renshou era, an imperial edict sent a śarīra stūpa to Cangzhou;
in the fourth year, another śarīra stūpa was sent to Yizhou. His final whereabouts remain unknown.
Daoshun of Sui was a native of Juzu. He studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and possessed a particularly profound resolve for compassion and salvation.

Once, while he was under self-reproach and imprisoned, his explanations converted the other inmates; those who were virtuous could not bear it when the officials seized them as criminals despite their innocence—a manifest injustice.
Consequently, they were forcibly compelled to leave. At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, he entered the capital and resided at Xuangfa Temple.
An imperial edict was issued to send the śarīra relics to Songzhou; at the time the stupa was erected, auspicious responses were exceedingly numerous.
Daofa Ying was the son of the Wang family of Kuaiji. From his youth, he was exceptionally brilliant and insightful; he left the household life and attended upon the śramaṇa Tanchong.

He devoted himself to the study and practice of Chan. As Master Chong’s transformative influence permeated the Zhou court, his followers gathered like a marketplace, and Daoying was foremost among them.

Subsequently, he withdrew to Mount Zhongnan, where he sustained himself on pine needles and water from the vines to avoid the calamity of the suppression of the teachings. He applied his mind to emptiness and stillness with ever-increasing rigor;
he frequently moved wild beasts to become tame and submissive, to whom he administered the precepts of refuge. Master Chong deeply approved of him and thus entrusted [him with the lineage].
His disciples numbered five hundred, all of whom were worthy of hearing the teachings and precepts.

In the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, an imperial edict was issued throughout the realm to select the most eminent among those versed in the three studies to serve as preachers for the five assemblies, with a particular emphasis on the study of Chan. Twenty-five individuals were thus selected.

He was commissioned to travel afar to propagate the teachings, yet he alone was recommended for the capital’s Bao Ta Si (Treasure Pagoda Monastery), where he led a community of three hundred and received the highest offerings.
From then on, his reputation as a śrāvaka spread even further. At the beginning of the Wude era, he passed away at Qing Chan Si (Pure Meditation Monastery) at the age of eighty.

The Dharma Master Tang Shao was surnamed Pu and was a native of Xuanwu in Zizhou. Before he left the household life, while traveling in the mountains, he once saw a tigress and her cub catching shrimp in a mountain stream.
The shrimp were so small they could no longer be caught, and even if some were obtained, they would not suffice to stave off hunger.
Tang Shao thought to himself that such was the suffering caused by the compulsion of karmic conditions. He then sighed, saying: "My own body..."
Whether earlier or later, we shall all die alike; it would be better to sacrifice myself to save them from starvation, thereby benefiting all living beings.

He then lay down naked before the tiger, and the tiger immediately retreated, causing him no injury. After he had shaved his head and received full ordination, he was even more diligent in his conduct.

At the beginning of the Daye era, the region of Ruizhou was plagued by many violent tigers; on the roads, travelers could not venture out unless they were gathered in groups of thirty, fifty, or more.
He did not dare to go. When Shao heard of this, he went to that place and sat for a long time under a thatched shelter, waiting to be devoured.
The tiger drew back to a distance, and the region subsequently became peaceful. He lived to the age of one hundred and nine before his death. As he was about to die, he said to his disciples:
"I wish to leave my body exposed as an offering to the various insects and birds. However, while alive they already detested me; how much more so when I am dead? You must certainly fence it in."

The body was left until it was completely decayed. His disciples could not bear to follow his words, yet they did follow his intent; they left the corpse for over a month, during which time no creatures whatsoever dared to invade or damage it.
In the end, they collected the remains to perform the burial.
Tang Baogong was surnamed Cui and was a native of Qingzhou. During the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty, his family moved south and settled in Jianye.
His father, Chudao, served as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of that province. When Baogong was eleven years old, Dharma Master Jing had him recite the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*;

he was able to recite it from memory after only one period of the first watch of the night. Consequently, Jing permitted him to leave the household life. Shortly after Jing passed away, Baogong dreamed of two snakes emerging from Jing’s feet.

Upon emerging from meditation, he entered [the hall] with respectful composure and became aware that his spiritual state was extraordinary compared to ordinary days. He then followed Master Tche of K'ai-shan to hear the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.

Master Tche provided him with a commentary on the treatise for him to study and recite; its characters were as small as a fly’s head, amounting to eight sheets of paper per section, yet he never forgot a single word.
Among his five hundred fellow students, there was none who did not submit to his excellence. Having received full ordination, he devoted himself to the practice of meditative concentration.
Regarding Master Huixiao, he further inquired about the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* with Master Gaochang Song, who had been stymied by his doubts.
Consequently, he studied the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*; in less than a year, their great meanings became thoroughly clear, and his former doubts were dissolved like melting ice.

He then established his practice based on the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* while specializing in lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. At the beginning of the Zhide era of the Chen dynasty, Huibu of Mount She returned from Beiyang and visited him.
He was invited to visit Xiqia Temple to propagate the Chan school. After Sengbu’s death, he redoubled his efforts in guiding and encouraging others.

At the end of the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty, following the demise of Empress Wenxian, an imperial edict summoned him to the capital to serve as the presiding master of the Chanding Monastery and assume the administrative duties of the Sangha.

Prince Qi Wang Jian requested that he confer the precepts upon him, bestowing five hundred robes; however, he distributed them all and retained nothing for himself. At the beginning of the Tang dynasty, he sought refuge in Wushan at Lantian.
Zhensi. In the second year of the Wude era, an imperial edict was issued to maintain the existing monastic appointments and to rename Chan ding Temple as Dazhuangyan Temple.
Furthermore, ten great virtuous monks (*da-de*) were appointed to oversee the community. At that time, they still hesitated and did not immediately comply.

Emperor Gaozu sent messengers to urge them to take office, and the various masters gradually advanced. On the nineteenth day of the twelfth month of the fourth year, he passed away at Dazhuangyan Temple.
He lived to the age of eighty and was buried in the southwest of the capital's suburbs; his epitaph was inscribed by Xiao Deyan, the Director of the Secretariat.

Initially, when Sengcong was traveling through the mountains, he passed directly through the place where a tiger was crouching without the slightest trace of fear. During the rebellion of Yang Xuan gan, some falsely accused Sengcong of being involved in the conspiracy.
Just as he was ascending the seat to deliver a formal lecture, armed soldiers suddenly burst in to arrest him, causing the assembly to be struck with terror.
As the assembly was about to disperse, Gong said slowly, "I have examined myself and find no fault; I shall wait until the lecture is concluded to come forward and debate. Such was his magnanimity.

Fa Xiang of Tang was a native of Tongzhou. He entered the monastic order as a child and received full ordination upon reaching adulthood. When the Zhou dynasty suppressed the Buddhist teachings, he immediately—

He supported himself with his stipend while never ceasing to recite the *Rites*. His colleagues and subordinates admired his sincerity, and their superior intended to submit his name to the Imperial Academy and the Ministries for a prominent appointment;
however, he firmly declined. When the Sui dynasty arose, he shaved his head again and took up residence at Daxingguo Temple. By nature, he was lofty and spirited.
He did not attend to anything obscure or hidden. The room where he lived had its front and rear doors entirely opened through;

he sat and slept on a single bed, positioned directly in the wind, remaining unchanged through both cold and heat for over thirty years. When monastics or laypeople came to inquire after him, they did not dare to do so unless he had finished reciting a scroll of scripture.
Even when questioned, he would not offer a reply. Once, he contracted a severe case of smallpox; some urged him to seek medical treatment with medicine.
He would not accept it. Furthermore, he suffered from dysentery. His advisors urged him to do as they suggested, but he said, "Dysentery is water; I can treat it. He then ate dry rice.
In the seventh year of the Wude era, after having been ill for a long time, he sat up. With a faint voice, he said, "Buddha image, Buddha image.
When his attendant turned to look, he saw the majestic form of the Buddha on the western wall, its radiance perfectly complete. He also heard the sound of incense and music for a short while.
He passed away. He was buried in the southeastern corner of the city.
The monk Sengding was a native of Danyang. Having first studied the *Abhidharmakośa* (Chengshi), his investigations were so arduous that he eventually contracted a wind-fever.

Thereupon, he sighed, saying, "Since my physical form has already been discarded by the world, why not turn my heart toward the stillness of Chan? He resided at Mount Zhong, where he consumed [only] water daily.
He ate one cup of white congee made from non-glutinous rice and remained seated constantly without lying down, awaiting his death. After several years had passed, his ailments were entirely cured.
His limbs, face, and head became suddenly radiant and pure; both his beard and hair grew back, though his eyebrows were particularly fine and extraordinary, measuring about an inch in length.
Tiger tracks appeared as paths within his room, yet he felt not the slightest fear or agitation. Whenever thoughts momentarily drifted, he would remain so throughout the entire night.
He wandered about, never avoiding thickets or brushwood; when wild beasts and birds of prey saw him, they regarded him as one of their own kind.

At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, an imperial edict summoned him to reside at the New Monastery in the capital, but he did not go. When another edict was issued later, bestowing upon him the higher precepts (*upāsaka-śīla*), he again declined and did not attend.
Once, he suffered severely from a cold, yet he completely abstained from food and drink, sitting upright as usual. After three days, his disciple Bao Gong feared for him...

He was on the verge of collapse. [The thief] urged him, "Please sustain yourself with some food and drink," and then hurriedly departed. Zhi Ding said slowly, "Is it not permissible to take the Dharma as medicine?
After seven days had passed, his ailment was suddenly cured. Toward the end of the Daye era, he moved his residence to Tahe Temple on Mount Zhongnan.
A thief entered his room at night; Zhi Ding sat in meditative concentration (dhyāna) without moving. The thief said, "Have you ever heard of a 'slave-thief' in this world? Zhi Ding replied:
"I am not even afraid of bandits; how much less so of these slaves? The thieves stripped him of his clothes, which he gave up without a trace of stinginess.
When they attempted to seize the woolen rug upon which he sat, he firmly refused, saying, "I have relied solely on this for the entire winter.
You may take it away, but if you wish to do so, you must kill me. The thieves looked at one another and desisted. In the sixth month of the seventh year of Wude, due to a slight illness...
He passed away while seated; his lifespan was over eighty years.

Tang Manyi’s family name and origins are not detailed in historical records. Toward the end of the Wude era, the Vinaya Master Fali at the capital of Ye was composing a commentary on the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya.
Manyi subsequently approached him to study under him. Having extensively heard and seen [the teachings], he composed...
His arrival was likewise profound. Thus, he led his disciples in preaching and guidance for over thirty years, and it was from his school that Daoliang of Guanyin and Tanyi of Yuezhou emerged.
Hui’ao of the Tang dynasty was a native of Lu’an. Having entered the Way at a young age, he immediately possessed a far-reaching capacity and aspired to honor the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

Though his aspirations were obstructed and could not yet be fully realized, at that time Dharma Master Bao-shan Ming succeeded the lineage of Xinghuang and was renowned in the world as a master craftsman. Hui’ao therefore followed him to receive instruction.

Just as he reached the prime of his years, he began to propagate and expound the teachings for the assembly. From then on, those who received his teachings and shared his lamp of wisdom were beyond counting.
Record. However, he considered that while the state of Chu was already flourishing, the region of Min had not yet been fully reached by the Dharma.

During the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he traveled up the Yangtze River and passed through Chengdu, where he extensively established Dharma assemblies. He subsequently moved to Zizhou, Mianzhou, and Suizhou, providing guidance according to the needs of each locality. His followers became numerous.
He improved from his previous state. When some people began to slander him, claiming he was deluding the masses with heterodox arts, word of this reached the authorities.

At the beginning of the Wude era, an imperial edict ordered a thorough investigation; although the charges were not substantiated, Sengao nonetheless returned to the south. Finding the clamor and distractions of his hometown burdensome, he soon withdrew to the western slopes of the mountains.
After five years of refining his practice through the "Middle View" (Madhyama-darśana), before long, both monastics and laypeople yearned for him and came to the mountain.
He was welcomed and brought [to the capital]. In the seventh year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away at Fangdeng Temple in his native village at the age of eighty-seven.
Daogao’s conduct was strictly pure; he took only one meal a day, eating whatever he obtained immediately without regard for whether it was morning or noon, nor did he wait to beg for alms.

His physical constitution was so emaciated that he could not even bear the weight of his robes. While he was in Shu, his disciple Daoqin feared that he would not survive, so he secretly informed outsiders to provide him with generous offerings.
When the offerings arrived, Seng’ao marveled at their extraordinary nature; upon questioning, he learned the reason and immediately expelled Daoqin, refusing to live with him.
He said, "The food of those who follow wrong livelihoods is evil and cannot be consumed. Therefore, whenever a donor sent [offerings] during his ordinary daily life...
The offerings were abundant and exquisite. All were commanded to enter the Saṃgha in accordance with the Vinaya.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Tanne from Eastern Zhejiang.
Section on Training in Patience and Gathering the Mind (2).
Tang Huixiao was born into the Liu clan of Pengcheng during the Sui dynasty; later, his family moved to Changge in Xuchang, where he now resides.

His grandfather followed the tradition of Confucian simplicity. When Xiao was eighteen, he fulfilled the local tax quota by serving as a student of the *Shi* and *Li* classics, but this was not his true aspiration.

He subsequently followed a master on Mount Songgao to enter the monastic life. His observance of the precepts was strict and pure, earning him the highest esteem among the elder scholars of his hometown.
It is permitted. At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, he traveled to study in Ye (Yecheng), where he thoroughly mastered the various Vinaya schools and specialized in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
He resided for a long time at Lingyan Temple on Mount Tai, later returning to Mount Zhong to attend to and support his teacher.

When Minglang of Longmen—renowned as a preeminent master of the Vinaya in Hedong—heard of Xiao’s reputation, he traveled from afar to follow him. Although Minglang was older than Xiao, he [Xiao] constantly...
He regarded Xiao as his elder brother; such was their mutual forgetting of worldly concerns within the Way. Subsequently, Xiao’s teacher reached the end of his natural lifespan.
Thereupon, Senglang requested that they both return together to Longmen Dinglin Temple. At that time, there was the Venerable Master Shanchan of Mount Maitreya.

He was then practicing *śamatha-vipaśyanā* in the forest and, because he was extensively expounding the *Vinaya*, found it particularly delightful. During the Renshou era, he once spent the summer retreat at Mount Huangjie.
Someone fleeing for their life sought refuge with him; when the matter was discovered, the pursuit and arrest of Xiao were urgent.

It happened that Hui-lang and Shan-bing had both passed away, leaving him solitary and without anyone to provide assistance. At that time, Daoji of Jinchuan and Daosuo and Daojie... [the text continues]. The Dharma...

He was a preeminent talent among the scholars of his gate. Thereupon, he traveled south and sought refuge there, remaining for many years. Toward the end of the Daye era, laws and regulations arose like bristling bristles.
Having been stripped of his official registration due to his offenses, Xiao subsequently traveled extensively through the Zhongtiao and Wangwu mountains.
Ding Rong, the governor of Hedong Commandery, invited him to reside in Renshou, so that amidst the chaos and upheaval of the Central Plains, he might open [the Way].

Regarding the section on the teachings for protecting living beings, his application of the mind was likewise benevolent. During the Yining era, when fierce bandits ravaged Hedong, Renshou continued to expound the Dharma as if nothing were amiss.
He passed away in the fourteenth year of the Zhenguan era at the age of seventy-three. Xiao Su was a man of profound integrity;
he always cherished the friendship between himself and Senglang. Although he would ascend heights to gaze into the distance in order to disperse his emotional entanglements, his feelings...

As I turned toward this [goal], my grief and distress increased all the more. In my entire life, I had opened the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* only about ten times; I still regretted having achieved no merit regarding the Mahāyāna.
For several years I read the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, yet whenever someone requested that I expound it for the assembly, I would say, "I have not yet understood the meaning of this scripture.
Alas! How truly sincere [this confession] is!
Tang Kongzang’s family name was Wang. His ancestors were originally from Jinyang, but by the time of Zang, they had moved to Guji in Xinfeng, Yongzhou.
While Zang was still in the womb, his mother did not refrain from consuming pungent foods, alcohol, or fresh meat. Upon his birth, [she...]
He was precocious and extraordinary from birth. At the age of nineteen, he requested his parents for permission to leave the household life, but they would not grant it.

Consequently, he prostrated himself before them for seven days. His parents, distressed by this, allowed him to go as he wished. He immediately entered Mount Lan-tien (Mount Liang) and received the tonsure in the mountains.
He obtained six pecks of flour and consumed it daily without ceasing; after three years had passed, there was still a surplus. From that time on, he practiced meditation.

He recited [the scriptures] without fail day and night. Later, he followed Master Panfa and resided at Longchi Temple, where he thoroughly investigated the essential tenets of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*).
He recited ten thousand words daily and was said to have mastered a total of one hundred million characters; in all, he acquired more than three hundred fascicles.

At the beginning of the Daye era, an imperial edict summoned him to reside at Chandeng Temple. During the present dynasty, when Huichang Temple was established in the Jincheng Ward, another edict again commanded him to dwell there.

However, Zangxing delighted in secluded places and was dedicated to quietude and silence. Every year during the second month of spring, he would leisurely wander among the mountains and waters, eventually selecting a site at Yüquan to build a residence as a plan for his final years.
He never grew weary of preaching and guiding others, and those who attained awakening became ever more numerous.

Later, during a severe drought, he offered prayers, and the dried-up spring gushed forth once again. During the summer months, he regularly practiced the Fangdeng Repentance Rite and daily paid homage to the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.

He remained seated and did not lie down for nearly twenty years. On the twelfth day of the fifth month in the sixteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away at Huichang Temple at the age of seventy-four.
His final testament was that his body be given as alms to birds and beasts; later, his remaining bones were collected and a stupa was erected beside Longchi Temple.
[This was recorded by] Yu Zhi, Grand Master of the Golden Purple Rank of the Court of Imperial Entertainments and Director of the Court of the Imperial Household.
I shall rather record this in writing and erect a stele.
Fahu of the Tang dynasty was originally of the Zhao clan of Zhaojun. His grandfather, Kang, served as the Governor of Jiyin, and his descendants made their home there.

At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, there was one Zhao Heng, who, as a "Xiucai" (talented scholar), passed the examinations alongside Cui Wang of Qinghe; they were then known as the "Four Sages. It was he—
His father was still living when, at the age of twelve, he encountered the successive misfortunes of his parents' deaths. He wailed so bitterly that he lost consciousness several times.

After completing his period of mourning, he intended to travel north of the River to study under renowned Confucian scholars; however, upon encountering favorable conditions for the Dharma, he immediately shaved his head and became a monk without showing any sign of reluctance.

Within seven days, he could recite the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* from memory. Subsequently, he studied the *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra* under Master Zhinian and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* under Master Fayan.
After the Master received full ordination, he followed [the teachings] to investigate the Vinaya-piṭaka. He further studied the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* under the Master Sengsong in Pengcheng.
Consequently, he became known as a master of the *Saṃparigraha*. In the third year of the Daye era, by imperial decree, he resided at Huayuan Temple;

shortly thereafter, he was again summoned to reside at Huiriji Temple. At that time, he was thirty-two years old. He constantly lectured on the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, and the *Saṃparigraha-śāstra*. His present majesty...

While at the Qin residence, he was specially invited to join a group of five men of renowned virtue, and Hu was included among their ranks. At that time, the new version of the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) had been produced;

some considered its rigorous pruning to be insufficient for reliance, yet Hu alone grasped its meaning in his heart. Later, when the Tang translation circulated, it proved to be an excellent match with what he had understood.
People considered him to possess foresight. In the twelfth year of the Zhenguan era, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Tiangong Monastery and was appointed to oversee its affairs.
On the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the seventeenth year, he passed away in his quarters at the monastery at the age of sixty-eight.

He compiled more than twenty treatises on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* which were circulated in the world. Huihu was simple and straightforward by nature, yet he took pleasure in the arts of immortality;
he frequently ingested medicines made of gold and stone. On one occasion, these caused him to suffer a severe reaction, leaving him delirious for several days.

His disciples were terrified and, at night, deceitfully spoke of other matters while offering him the dregs of their rice cakes. Later, when he heard what had happened, he assumed a stern expression and said, "I have been deceived; I must now exert self-mastery."
To reprimand him would be to involve the Master in unrighteousness; what logic is there in this? A śramaṇa from Mount Song, named Zhida, was over ninety years old;

he was simple, aloof, and serene, having not descended from the mountain for thirty years. Upon hearing the news of the death, he arrived carrying his staff and, after weeping to the full extent of his grief, said:
"Among those learned in the sūtras and śāstras, there has never been a lack in our generation. Yet as for pure integrity, there has been only this man."
Huibin of the Tang dynasty was surnamed He and was a native of Yanzhou. His family had practiced Confucianism for generations. Huibin was widely versed in the classics and histories.

At the age of nineteen, he served as a local assistant teacher; at twenty-three, he received the tonsure and entered the monastic order. He traveled extensively through various academies and centers for the study of the Vinaya, before suddenly entering Mount Tai to cultivate various forms of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
He remained there in this manner for eight years, and subsequently trained in ascetic practices at various temples on Mount Tai and Mount Lingyan.
At the age of thirty-four, he first registered his official affiliation and resided at Cundao Temple on Mount Zeng in Liangfu, Qinzhou.
During the Sui dynasty, for the sake of Empress Xian, a meditation hall was constructed to advance her posthumous merit. An imperial edict summoned him along with several eminent and senior monks;

although Sengbin had the youngest number of years since his ordination (*śrāmaṇera*), his reputation was most exalted, making him a preeminent figure in this degenerate age of the Dharma. Later, he served as the abbot of Hongfu Temple. [The text ends with] "Zhen..."
On the sixth day of the tenth month in the nineteenth year of the Guanghua era, he passed away due to illness at the age of seventy-two.

Huixiu of the Tang dynasty was born in Leshi, Yingzhou; his family had long pursued the occupations of sericulture and fishing. However, Huixiu possessed an early awareness of transcending his worldly lot.

At the age of sixteen, he encountered the śramaṇa Xun begging for alms in the village and was moved to resolve his mind toward the Way. He subsequently left his parents and fled to join Xu, seeking the discipline of the Vinaya.
When the Master left the household life, Dharma Master Lingyu—who possessed a great reputation—was then residing in Ye, providing guidance and exhortation.
[The Master] followed him on his travels and began to study the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. He reached more than fifty recitations, yet ultimately made no progress.

Residing in Bohai, he listened to Dharma Master Mingyan’s exposition of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. Not long after, Yan passed away; thereupon, [the Master] received the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Minor Matters) from the *Vinaya-mātṛkā*.
Shan recited the *Dharmasaṃgraha* several times for the sake of the Dharma Master Zhinian. Zhinian said, "I have spent many years studying the Hīnayāna;
having now met you, how could I let this time pass in vain? Thereupon, he set aside his previous distinctions between the various schools and composed works such as the *Zaxin xuanchang chao shu*.

Although he opened the way for the school of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) within the realm of the unseen, he still adhered to the principles of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), seeking enlightenment through manifold means. Thus they were reconciled.

Master Yu entered the Guanzhong region, where he engaged in scholarly exchange with Dhyāna Master Tanqian, Vinaya Master Niren, and others. He propagated and refuted the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra), grasping its essential meanings and principles;

after studying it three times through and through, he immediately composed commentaries and treatises. From that time on, the lineages of the various *piṭakas*, both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, became accessible for study.

However, he alone had not yet found the leisure to examine the Vinaya section thoroughly, so he further studied the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya) under Vinaya Master Hong, sitting in meditation for a single session.
During the session, he recited it more than thirty times, yet Gao could not fathom its depths or boundaries. Looking at his disciples, he said, "Regarding the sutras and treatises, it was like that;
regarding the Vinaya, it is like this. Is it not the case that while principles may be sought abstractly, the actual facts are difficult to reconcile?

When Master Li saw that even in his advanced years the Master remained so diligent and thorough, he once remarked, "Even a Great Virtuous Dharma Master such as you still exerts such tireless effort. The Master replied, "Rest."
I recall that when I first escaped the mundane entanglements, I was finally able to undergo spiritual refinement; how could I dare to be separated from it for even a moment?
The temple where I resided was defiled on four occasions. During the Wude era, Liu Heitan rebelled; I then led twenty disciples to guard Xiangzhou and the Tiance Commandery.
When Lord Cao Xu Shici led his troops to suppress and execute the rebels, I was further able to provide from my private stores to support them. Subsequently...

Upon the pacification of the raiders, Cao Gong reported the matter to the Emperor. An imperial edict was issued stating that, with the exception of Xiangzhou which was restored to its former status, only thirty monks and nuns were to remain in each of the other prefectures and commanderies.
In the ninth year of the Zhenguan era, an edict summoned him to the capital, but he firmly declined.
He was ninety-eight years old at the time. He resided at Cizhun Temple in his native village, where his disciples were Tanyuan and Lingfan.

He was able to propagate his teachings. Yuan was pure and lofty, aspiring to the joy of dhyāna; he lived in seclusion at Linyu Mountain, while Fan resided at Hongfu Monastery, where his reputation resounded throughout the capital.
He remained healthy and vigorous until the present day. When the Emperor campaigned against Liaodong, he personally visited his residence.
Huibì of the Tang dynasty was born into the Hong family of Jiaxing, Suzhou. At the age of seven, he entered the monastic life at Liushui Temple.

After receiving the full precepts, he traveled in all directions in search of the Way, undaunted by either level ground or rugged terrain. Regarding the *Tripiṭaka* and the *Four Treatises*, he consulted with the elders again and again until there remained no further points of stagnation.
He then returned to his native village to encourage those who came to study under him. He sat constantly and did not lie down for over forty years, relying on his aged frame.

He used a curved armrest and had several hundred disciples. In his instruction and guidance, he never showed the slightest sign of weariness. At the end of the Zhenguan era, he passed away at the age of seventy-something.
In Chang’an, within the Ma family of Yongzhou, there was Baoxiang. At nineteen, he left the household life and resided at Luohan Temple.

He specialized in the study of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and was particularly devoted to the practice of *dhūta* austerities to subdue deluded consciousness. At night, he recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* seven times.
He recited the name of the Buddha sixty thousand times. During the day he read the *Tripiṭaka*, and throughout the six periods of the day he performed prostrations and repentance.

In this manner, for over forty years, he never ceased or rested. Later, he further read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* one thousand eight hundred times, while also concurrently reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Yet his body was free from illness or affliction, and his food and clothing were provided according to conditions; thus he may be said to have been excellent in his cultivation.

When he was about to pass away, he entrusted himself to both the monastics and the laity, insisting that they must first practice mindfulness of the Buddha. He further said, "My corpse should be cremated and scattered.

As for matters such as building a stupa or carving an inscription, I wish for these not to be discussed. Having spoken thus, he passed away at the age of eighty-three and with sixty-two years of *śrāmaṇera* ordination.
Also in the same monastery was Fada, who was by nature diligent and frugal; whenever he attended a vegetarian feast, he would receive offerings.
He used his offerings to copy and repair the Huayan Sūtra and personally burned incense while reciting the Eight Divisions of the Prajñāpāramitā more than a hundred times.
