In his daily life, he did not maintain any disciples or followers. At the age of seventy, he retired to Yunyang Rock, where he passed away after four years.
Tang Daohui was a native of Wuyang in Jianwei, the son of the Shi family. He possessed a lofty and simple bearing that transcended the common crowd.

When he first left the household life, he resided at Yanyuan Temple, where he became a source of refuge for monastics and laypeople from all quarters. However, he felt that because Sichuan was remote and secluded, his learning and experience were not broad enough;
thus, he entered the capital to seek out teachers and friends, further investigating the sutras, śāstras, and historical records. In this manner, ten years passed. And...
He was about to return to his native village to lecture and guide the younger generation, but as the times were marked by turmoil and separation, he did not succeed in doing so.

At the beginning of the Yining era, the imperial court dispatched Zhan Jun, Li Yuan, and others to Shu to conduct pacification efforts. They happened upon a memorial addressed to the Chancellor, Lord Tang, which stated:

"I have a younger brother whose character and disposition are unworthy; our family lineage has declined and fallen. Regarding the conferment of his fief and the posthumous honors for him, there are questions concerning the imperial edicts."
They still remain. The descendants of former students and old officials stand in orderly ranks, all raising their arms and gnashing their teeth, eager to offer their services.
On this very day, although the Jianmen Pass has been opened, the Wuxia Gorge remains defiant. I shall soon personally lead my followers, shaking my monk’s staff as we set out on the road.

With but a single letter, I will proclaim our majesty and open my heart to receive their submission. Thus, the army will suffer no toil from arrows or stones, and the ruler will enjoy the ease of achieving success through waiting. This—
This would also have been a benefit for the time being. I hope you will consider this, Lord. Lord Tang could not accept this advice.
In various places, there were many instances of privately ordaining monks, nuns, and Daoists; Song Ji was particularly prominent among these Daoists.

He made offerings in Longshan County and established the Daiguan Monastery, ordaining thirty people within it. Subsequently, he submitted a petition to the Prefectural Governor, Duan Lun, requesting that [the monastery] be...
The temple belonged to Li Xiyu, the Grand Commissioner for Pacification. While leading his troops on a tour of inspection through the prefectures and counties, he happened to pass by it.

The Daoist priests were startled, believing him to be coming to expel them, and they all fled in disarray at once. The site was subsequently established as a Buddhist temple, which remains so to this day. This occurred at the beginning of the Zhenguan era.
He traveled to the capital and subsequently attended upon Master Lin, where he composed the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Distinguishing the Correct).

At that time, someone falsely accused Dharma Master Gaofa of Anzhou, claiming that while in Shu he had gathered a large assembly for lectures with the intent of plotting a return [to the north], and further alleged that Senghui was acting as his scout.

The authorities arrested him and cast him into prison. Despite this, Senghui’s spirit remained undaunted and unshakable; he constantly expounded the sūtras and śāstras for the other prisoners from spring until—
In winter, he never ceased [his practice]. Among those prisoners who had been confined for a long time, some were so ragged they could not endure the bitter cold.

Hui then sent a letter to his patrons (dānapati) requesting that they provide furs and shoes for the *wujinzang* (inexhaustible storehouse). When the matter was settled and he returned to his home village, the renowned monks of the Three Prefectures all saw him off outside the city gate.
Hui composed a poem, saying: "Both leaving and staying, we are but guests; Sharing sorrow impairs one's nature and spirit. Together..."
Having parted without a time for reunion, he was able to inquire after the living and the dead; those who heard him shed tears.
Shortly thereafter, Pei Xiren, a scholar from the Gate Academy (Menxue), came to seek an audience. During their conversation, [Hui] seemed slightly to disparage the people and things of that region.
Hui said, "Although Shu is remote and secluded, since the Western Capital of Han, there have been scholars who have achieved renown in heaven through their literary works and accomplishments."
As for those of lower standing, when compared to the Central Plains, they truly do not fall short. Your Excellency ought to maintain an open mind and honor the worthy and talented;
how could you deign to disparage yourself on account of the narrowness of your own experience? Xi-ren apologized with shame. He passed away at the end of the Zhenguan era at the age of seventy.
Tang Hongzhi was born into the Wan family of Huaili Township in Shisheng. In the eleventh year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he entered the Zhongnan Mountains to become a Daoist practitioner.
He abstained from grain and practiced the cultivation of qi, vowing to achieve transcendence. After a long time, his physical form became withered and emaciated.
My mind and spirit were weary and exhausted. I happened to go to Jingfasi Temple in the capital and followed Master Hui to inquire about the methods for advancing on the Path.
Hui said, "For living beings, food is the source of life; for the Path, the body is the foundation. When there is food, one can nourish the life;
when there is a body, one can plan for the Path. This is a universal principle throughout ancient and modern times. I have never heard of anyone discarding..."
Those who exhaust their bodies to pursue the Way—such as the arts of cultivation practiced by immortals and spirits—are like trying to tie up the wind or catch a shadow;
it is no wonder that few achieve success. Thus, he showed them the method for settling the mind and casting off burdens.

At the beginning of the Yining era, he cast off his yellow cap and devoted himself to his studies according to the teachings of Master Hui. This continued until the Wude era, when the empire was unified.
The two gates of the Buddha-way stood side by side; knowing this, he went to the provincial governor’s office and requested to be enrolled among the ranks of the Śramaṇas.

The high officials granted his request and permitted him to reside wherever he pleased. However, as his nature delighted in seclusion and solitude, he eventually chose the most remote location within Xiangsi Temple to establish his dwelling.

There he lectured on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, and other texts. He refined the common people and welcomed those who were spiritually hungry, providing them with the sustenance of the Dharma.

He provided for them with all necessary resources. Although the public regulations and monastic rules prohibited such acceptance, he nevertheless guided and protected them, never showing any hesitation or avoidance.
It is evident that this arose from his utmost sincerity. He passed away on the ninth day of the fifth month in the sixth year of the Yonghui era;
he was sixty-one years of age.
The Tang dynasty recluse Ming studied the sequential meditations (*anupūrva-vipaśyanā*) and the ten totalities (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*) in his youth, yet he resided exclusively on Mount Wutai.
Initially, he stayed at Papaya Valley Temple on the Central Terrace for thirty years; then, at Buddhaprabha Mountain Temple for seven years;
and finally, at Dafu Temple for nine years. Disciples seeking the Way followed him without ceasing, and monastics and laypeople alike came in such numbers that they filled the mountain forests.
In the second year of the Yonghui era, the Governor of Dazhou returned Huiyin to Zhaoguo Temple from where he had previously been assigned, ordering him to take charge of the temple’s affairs.
In the tenth month of the first year of the Longshuo era, he passed away at the temple; sitting upright with a serene and joyful countenance, he appeared as if in meditative absorption.

Tang Mingjie, surnamed Yao, resided at Puguang Temple in the capital. He was refined, alert, and quick-witted; his mind roamed through the arts, and he was renowned in the capital for his skill in the lute, poetry, calligraphy, and painting.
However, he was haughty and disdainful toward others, gradually becoming steeped in corrupt customs until he was rejected by the elders and the virtuous.
During the Longshuo era, an imperial edict was issued to examine and test all those possessing learning, scholarship, or artistic talent within the Three Teachings.

In the Eastern Capital, he ranked them according to their merit to prepare for their appointment. Upon his release from the monastery, he immediately ceased his monastic life, intending to seek high office through this opportunity.
He hastily cast off the *kāṣāya* he was wearing, saying, "I now shed this donkey skin to enter the teachings of the world.
He then prepared wine and gathered his friends and associates, composing a poem which said: "The One Vehicle is fundamentally non-existent; what of the Three Emptinesses?"

He returned to his place of origin and soon passed away from illness. Later, he appeared in a dream to a monk who had been kind to him, saying, "Because I died with a lack of faith, I have been reborn in the evil realms.
I pray that you will show compassion for my hunger and thirst out of our former friendship.
The monk prepared food and offered it as a sacrifice for him. Furthermore, the painter who had worked alongside him at that time also dreamed of the same thing.
He said to him, "The place where I was born is extremely wretched; I long to acquire merit, but have no means to accomplish it.

If, by your power, you could transcribe one or two scrolls of a sutra, the benefit gained would be great. Furthermore, please recite the poem he composed until it is thoroughly mastered and committed to memory.
The painter was exceptionally dull-witted; he recited the poem eighteen times before he finally mastered it.
He said: "Holding hands, we cannot part; I stroke my chest, grieving for myself. How painful that life’s shadow is so short; how tragic that the road to the spring is so long.
The wild forests tremble at the evening breeze; the desolate tombway falls under the cold frost. What can I offer as a parting gift? Only this:
that our nature is the very precept of the Inner Canon. Alas! To lose but a single thought is to incur the burden of ten thousand kalpas. How lamentable! — Sung of Míngzhōu.
Shangli was a man of refined etiquette whose family had been scholars for generations. His writings favored eccentric and frivolous expressions.
As his circumstances were long impoverished, he frequently begged loans from Jiede Temple; after some time, the monks grew increasingly weary and annoyed by him.

Shangli composed the "Fu on the Ga-dou" to mock them, which the common folk vied to recite as a source of amusement. During the Zhenguan era, Shangli fell gravely ill and was filled with regret and distress.
Rang’s two eyes were round and blood-red; he manifested the appearance of a hungry ghost (*preta*), and all who saw him were struck with fear.
After a short while, he passed away. Zhou Shenkai’s secular surname was Guo; he was a native of Taiyuan and a descendant of Linzong of the Han dynasty.

Later, because his father held office, he registered his lineage in Jingzhao. He had six brothers and sisters, and Shenkai was the youngest. From childhood, his aspirations were extraordinary, and he subsequently became a disciple.
He attended upon Dharma Master Mingxun for his tonsure; this Mingxun was none other than Da-cheng Xun. Upon reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination.
He studied all the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras without exception, and subsequently expounded treatises such as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Abhidharmakośa*.

Later, while lecturing on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, he encountered the interpretive positions of ancient masters and sighed that they were incomplete. Thereupon, at Mount Baimiao in Anlu, he composed [the following].

Master Shu, whose own mind was naturally skillful and wise, once fashioned a clay image of himself beneath the southern cliff of Shan Creek, reflecting it in the pool water so that it was a perfect likeness.
Later, by imperial decree, eminent practitioners of high conduct and great learning were summoned to the capital to participate in the translation of sutras and treatises;
Fayue was assigned to Chongye Monastery. During the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, he passed away at that monastery. His disciples erected a stupa for him there.
Nanxiao Garden. This was indeed the Dharma-gate of the spiritual son of Dashengji.
Master Quan of the Tang dynasty was a native of Wutai County. Having left the household life and received full ordination, he immediately studied the Vinaya.
His disposition was profound and tranquil; in his daily life, he was never disturbed by external things, devoting himself solely to instructing his disciples. Thus, from far and near...
There was nothing he did not know in advance. Whenever there was a matter related to the teachings, he would invariably inform others so that they might prepare themselves and remain on guard;

at that time, it was said that he had attained the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*). Aside from his three robes and one alms bowl, he maintained no other possessions. His quarters were empty and silent;
when guests arrived, he would simply engage them in pure conversation for a long while, and once they had departed, he would not even provide tea or hot water. Upon entering [the room],...

On the day of his passing, auspicious signs appeared spontaneously from the heavens and celestial music resounded with a piercing clarity; these sounds were heard throughout the entire monastery, and an extraordinary fragrance wafted everywhere.
Then, he spoke a final word to the assembly, sat cross-legged, and passed away into stillness.
Tang Fawan was born into the Feng family of Qiantang. His ancestors were originally from Changle in Min.
His grandfather, while serving as an official on a tour of duty in Jiangdong, settled there and made it his home. For generations, the family had admired the Way of Vimalakīrti;

they would regularly place members of the monastic community in separate quarters to provide them with equal alms, while praying for the continuation of their lineage. Soon thereafter, Yanwan was born—exceptionally gifted and precociously wise, with a naturally refined disposition.
He was extraordinary. Slightly older than his elder brother, he petitioned his father to request release from worldly burdens. His father marveled at this and granted his permission.

He shaved his head and received full ordination, whereupon he investigated the Mahāyāna teachings until there was no longer any stagnation in his understanding. He reflected alone that wisdom does not arise without meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
thus, for five years, how could he afford even the slightest negligence regarding *dhyāna*? Consequently, beside the Lingzhi Temple where he resided, he constructed a separate hermitage (*ārāma*).
He remained in profound silence regarding worldly affairs. Fellow practitioners of like mind came to his door to seek instruction, and he enlightened them greatly.
On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Tiānbǎo era, he instructed his attendants and passed away while sitting upright.

He was sixty-five years of age; his monastic seniority was slightly less than twenty years. On the nineteenth day of that same month, his stupa was enshrined on the mountain slope of the monastery. The stupa was white.
His disciple was Yu Fajie; his son was Huai Fu, and his nephew was Xi Xiu, among others who established [this].
Tang Xuanyi, surnamed Du, was a man of unknown origin. He first became a Daoist practitioner, titled Master Du, and presided over the Dadao Hengguan Temple in Jifu.
Shortly thereafter, he shaved his head and took ordination, residing at Foshouji Temple. Someone asked him: "Why did you suddenly [leave the Daoist path]?"
"Do you believe in the Buddha? Yi replied, "I certainly regard him as one described in the *Book of Changes* as 'returning before one has gone far, so that there will be no cause for regret.

Furthermore, birth and death pass as swiftly as a gale; one ought to plan for them early. If one only straightens the reins when reaching the crossroads, or halts the oars while in midstream, those who can avoid overturning their carriage or drowning in their boat are few indeed.
As for worshipping the True One and the Dipper, exorcising ghosts, and seeking immortality—this is not the proper application of the mind."

This was the ultimate [attainment]. During the reign of Empress Wu, who venerated the Great Dharma and propagated the Supreme Vehicle, she heard that Yi was capable of abandoning heterodoxy for orthodoxy and emerging from the shallow to enter the profound.

She issued an imperial decree appointing him as the Chief Steward (Du Weina) of the monastery. Since Yi had already thoroughly mastered both Chan and doctrinal teachings, he felt all the more ashamed of his initial errors.
He subsequently established a system of formal question-and-answer sessions and composed the *Jianzheng lun* (Treatise on Discerning Orthodoxy) in one fascicle. His final whereabouts remain unknown.
Tang Yuanchong’s surname was Wang. His ancestors were from Linyi in Langya. He was the descendant of Wang Hui, the son of the Jin Prime Minister, Duke Wenxian of Shixing;
because Hui resided in Gourong, his lineage subsequently registered its household registers there. From childhood, Yuanchong stood alone, his aspirations being serene and simple.

At the age of fifteen, he cast off worldly burdens and associated with those who followed Tao Hongjing and Xu Xun. Nevertheless, he felt that the ultimate principle had not yet been fully integrated within him.

He then further devoted himself to the study of the Indian scriptures (*Zhudi*), investigating their subtleties and exploring their profound mysteries; his mastery was so transcendent that it surpassed all conventional praise. Monastics and laypeople throughout the regions of Wu and Yue all partook of the fragrance of his virtue.

When Qi Ying, the Duke of Pingyang and Prefectural Governor of Runzhou serving as Imperial Commissioner for the Collection of Talent, heard of his religious conduct, he waited expectantly for a long time.

Coinciding with an imperial decree to recruit men of talent, he recommended [the Master] to serve as a tribute. Toward the end of the Kaiyuan era, [the Master] received the essential points of the mind from him.
At Waguan Temple, Master Xuán’s reputation for spiritual attainment grew ever more far-reaching.
The virtuous monks of Jinling revered him with even greater longing and requested that he be transferred to Xiqia Temple. At the beginning of the Zhìdé era, he traveled to the capital with his staff.
At that time, Right Vice-Minister Wang Wéi was building a private estate at Wǎngchuān, where he frequently visited with the Secretariat Drafter Xiāo Xīn; they would burn incense [to welcome him].
They sipped tea and exchanged verses on Prajñāpāramitā, remaining entirely unaware of the peace or turmoil of the realm, nor the safety or peril of the Sovereign.

When Huichong entered Zhongnan Mountain, he happened to pass by them; they debated with him for an entire day, whereupon Wang Xiao sighed in admiration, saying, "The Buddha-dharma truly has its rightful heirs.

Shortly thereafter, Huichong traveled through the Yellow and Luo Rivers and ascended Mount Song and Mount Shao; wherever he went, he was invited to serve as abbot, yet he repeatedly declined and departed.
He had no fixed attachment. He traveled east through Tiantai and Siming, where he gazed afar at the magnificent scenery and explored its secrets until almost nothing remained undiscovered.

After several years of this, he returned to grow old on Mount Zhong; was this not his benevolence toward his ancestral home? In the fifth year of the Dali era, the Prefectural Governor, Lord Fan of Nanyang, bowed his head in the direction of the Master’s dwelling and sought out the essentials of the school.
In accordance with the wishes of both the clergy and the laity, the Master was humbly requested to preside over the monastery.

For twenty years, he oversaw the restoration of the buildings until they were newly renovated and magnificent. Subsequently, he retired to Mount Gaoding, where disciples from all quarters flocked to him like the spokes of a wheel converging at the hub.
On the second day of the eighth month in the twelfth year, he manifested illness and passed away at the age of sixty-five.
Eight days later, he was buried on the southern slope of Mount She. His disciples collectively erected a grand monument at the gate of the monastery to record his life and transformative deeds.
The first was Tang Lingyi, born into the Wu family of Guangling. At the age of nine, he shaved his head and donned the monastic robes; upon reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination.

He subsequently studied the Vinaya and achieved great proficiency in it. His family had long been engaged in commerce and usury, and his brothers vied with one another in luxury and extravagance, yet Lingyi alone wore the saffron robes.
Holding his *khakkhara* staff with composure, he first studied the *Vinaya* of the Xiangbu school under Master Fayi of Weiyang.
He later relied upon the Chan practitioners Yinkong and Qianjing at Xuaniu Temple on the southern slopes of Mount Kuaiji to investigate the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
At times he traveled to Qingyun Temple and Yifeng Temple in Yuhang, yet his footsteps never entered the gates of lay households. Heaven...
Tai Dao’s Pan Zhiqing, Xiangyang’s Zhu Fang, Nanyang’s Zhang Ji, Anding’s Huangfu Zeng, Fanyang’s Zhang Nanshi,
Wujun’s Lu Xun, Donghai’s Xu Yi, and Jingling’s Lu Hongjian— all drew upon their allotted lot to desire friendship with him,
knocking at his breast in admiration and regarding him as a companion in their pursuit of the Way. Among those he was most intimate with were Huining, Mingyou, Lingyou, Tanyi, and Yizhen.
Xuancheng was truly one of my three beneficial friends from the same school and one of the four robes that remain in this world. He was skilled in literary composition and delighted in poetic verse;
having already authored the *Faxing lun*, whenever he encountered a fine season or an exquisite landscape, he would invariably take up his brush and spread his paper to express his inspiration.
Those who recorded these events titled it the *Jianqi ji* (Anthology of Interstitial Spirit).
On the sixteenth day of the tenth month of winter in the first year of the Baoying era, he passed away at Longxing Temple in Hangzhou at the age of thirty-five.

His disciples, following his final instructions, performed the *jhāpaka* (cremation) rites and erected a stūpa to mark the site. Li Shu, Military Aide to the Left Guard, and Li Tang, Magistrate of Jiaxing, [recorded this].
Du Guofan, Military Aide to the Judicial Office of the Left Golden Archer Guard, together with others, lamented the collapse of the foundational beam and feared the shifting of hills and valleys;
they thus carved this inscription upon the southern slope of the East Peak of Mount Wulin.
During the Tang dynasty, there was a famous monk who was skilled at reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. However, he lived in a state of carefree abandon and did not observe minor rules of conduct.
During the Shangyuan era, he encountered a Vinaya master from Guang’ai Temple in Luoyang at an inn in Yongyang. The monk followed his host’s lead and purchased wine and meat to refresh himself.
The Vinaya master scolded him in great anger, but the monk continued to eat and drink as usual, paying it no mind. At dusk, he asked for water.

Having rinsed his mouth and washed his hands, he sat cross-legged upon the bed to recite. As soon as he began the title of the scripture, two rays of golden light issued from the corners of the monk’s mouth.
The Vinaya Master was filled with shame and distress, and eventually went to lie down.

After a short while, he perceived that the sound of the recitation grew even more resonant and expansive, and the golden light pervaded the courtyard and the halls. Thereupon, the Vinaya Master rose to observe him; the monk was already reciting the fourth fascicle.
When the fifth bundle was reached, dawn was approaching and the light gradually faded; the monk also fell into a light sleep, as if in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Then, Master Vinaya, assuming a dignified demeanor, wept and prostrated himself in repentance; yet, in the end, he could not discern who this monk truly was.
Tang Hongzheng, surnamed Chang, was a man of unknown origins who lived between Min and Shu.

He silently upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, reciting it day and night without ceasing. At that time, the śramaṇa Shouxian was in the adjacent room; one night, while sitting, he could not fall asleep.
Hearing voices from the next room, as if two people were conversing, one said: "I have received this command to oversee the great and correct [order];
alas, how can I do so when there is a benevolent deity providing protection nearby? Although I wish to draw close, it is impossible.
Yet, regarding the sin of violating my mandate, what plan can I devise to avoid it? The other replied: "I know how to avoid it. On the ground by the East Gate, there is..."
"His name and appearance are similar to his. He is currently a commoner, yet he once served as a monk; we must surely take him to fulfill our obligation. Subsequently, they all became silent.
Xian immediately went out the door and searched everywhere, but saw no one. The next day, Xian told Zheng what had happened.
He went again to the eastern gate to inquire about the Chang family. It turned out that the one named Hongzheng had indeed died last night.
Xian had previously specialized in the *Amitābha Sūtra*, but upon this news, he also changed his practice to follow the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Tang Weishi, surnamed Yang, was a native of Fuyang. During the Tianbao era, he traveled to Mount Yuanpeng in Siming;

finding its seclusion and remoteness pleasing, he resolved to spend the remainder of his life there. The mountain crags and caves were deep and mysterious, and upon them were Buddha footprints that had first appeared during the Kaiyuan era.
Not long after he settled there, the sea pirate Yuan Chao rose up, releasing his hordes to plunder the region. At that time, Weishi was seated in meditation within a cave.
When bandits arrived, they detested him. Thereupon, two or three hundred people joined together to lift a massive rock and block the cave opening so that he could not escape.
Suddenly, Zhishi rose from his meditative state; letting out a thunderous roar, he used his palms to lift the rock as if intending to hurl it at the bandits.
The bandits were struck with great fear; they prostrated themselves in rows and begged for their lives. The villagers held him in high esteem and built a vihāra for him. The Dali...

In the eighth year [of the reign], the Prefect Pei Jing requested that he inscribe the title plaque for Xiangshan Temple; the Emperor subsequently granted an edict permitting the ordination of seven monks to be enrolled in the temple’s registers.
In the winter of the second year of the Zhenyuan era, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. He was sixty-two years of age and thirty-one years since his ordination.
Tang Zhihong was surnamed Qian. He was a native of Xiajue in Changcheng, Lake District. His original name was Yan; Zhihong was his courtesy name.
In his youth, he left home to become a monk at Shimen Temple in his hometown—which was the same as Jinglin Temple during the Liang dynasty. After receiving full ordination, he...
Relying on Master Daoheng of Moyuan, he investigated and scrutinized the Vinaya section and engaged in mutual refinement with Tanqing and Xinggong.

He believed that the commentaries on the *Nanshan chao* by previous masters were not entirely exhaustive; thus, he composed the twenty-fascicle *Souxuan lu*, which comprehensively encompassed the teachings of more than forty schools from Daci and Lingyan onwards.
Master Chengguan, the commentator on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, [was among those whose works were included].
During the Dali era, [the Emperor] composed a preface for him to serve as its introduction. He was one hundred and eight years of age and remained free from ailment;

by imperial decree he was titled the Great Master Changshou (Longevity). The world did not dare address him by his given name but used his courtesy name instead, which is sufficient to show the honor accorded to him.
Yanjun of the Tang dynasty was the son of Fan Shi of Weizhou. His father was the Governor of Xiazhou and the Court Secretary of Prince Zhao’s Household.

Yanjun was both talented and possessed of extensive learning. At the age of nineteen, he entered the examinations for the jinshi degree; however, upon encountering the hardships caused by his father’s death, he retired to a Buddhist temple in Nanyang to leave the household life.
Shortly thereafter, he followed Chan Master Yuzhen at the Yuquan Hermitage in Jingzhou to study the method of *vipaśyanā* (contemplation). He entered...

He stayed at Dayun Monastery in Chengqi. Because the assembly knew that he had long investigated the *Vinaya*, they earnestly requested him to preside over the ordination platform to serve as a model for later generations.
Reluctantly, he accepted the command. Later, he suddenly attained realization of the essentials of the mind under Chan Master Guanjing.

At the beginning of the Dali era, intending to go to Qingyuan to verify his insights with Chan Master Si, he met Yan Zhenqing, the Duke of Lu, before reaching Luling; with a single word [from the Duke], [his path was altered].
In the second year [of his tenure], during the spring, the Governor of Yichun requested that the Chief Monk (Sengzheng) submit a formal petition on his behalf.

In the fourth year, Li Hua, the Prefect of Hongzhou, welcomed him to reside at Daming Temple. In the third month of that year, he bathed, changed his robes, and passed away while facing the sky with palms joined.
He was fifty-nine years of age. After his remains were enshrined in a stupa, his disciple Yuan Yue erected a commemorative stele.
Tang Zhixuan was a native of Hexuochao. He was skilled in reciting the incantations of the Five Indias.
Driven by a compassionate vow to save sentient beings, he felt no concern even for his own life. Once, while traveling through a forest, he saw a fox at an ancient tomb;

it wore a human skull and was clad in weeds and brush, appearing like a beautiful woman in elegant finery. At dusk, she stood alone by the side of a post station road, where she encountered a young man.
The carriage followed him there. He then asked, "What is this woman doing here? The woman wept and said, "I am from Yishui.
My parents married me to the Zhang family of Jiang. Not long after, my husband died. My parents-in-law are old and cruel, so I have no one to rely upon.
Although my own parents are still alive, I think of the great distance and cannot return to visit them. That is why I linger here. And...
She thought to herself that she would end her life there. The young man was startled and hurried; he alighted from his carriage and knelt, saying, "I am a soldier from the waters of Yi River.

I am currently on my way out for garrison duty, having received my replacement and returning home. If you, Madam, truly have this intention, it would suffice for me to serve as your charioteer by virtue of our shared hometown.
Why must you go so far as to take your own life? The woman thanked him repeatedly with joy. Just as they were about to mount the carriage, Xuan—
He rebuked and stopped her. As he shook his monk’s staff and recited incantations, the woman suddenly resumed her fox form; she prostrated herself before him and could not leave.
When he looked at her slowly, she was already dead.
Regarding Huiling of the Tang dynasty, his surname, clan name, and native place are unknown. In the seventh year of the Taizhong era, the Emperor visited Zangyan Temple.

He paid homage to the Buddha’s tooth relic. While ascending the Great Stūpa to look out in the four directions, he saw a ruined site to the northwest and said, "This was formerly the Zongchi Monastery.
He remained filled with regret for a long time. By imperial decree, he questioned the senior monks about past events; the assembly recommended Ling to respond.

The Emperor praised his detailed account and immediately conferred upon him the purple robe, while also decreeing the restoration of the Zongchi Monastery. On the eleventh day of the third month, the Head Seat of the Three Teachings [passed away].
He oversaw the restoration of the temple, completing the work in the sixth month. By imperial decree, Hui-ling was appointed as the head administrator (*sanghan*).

Once he occupied this office, the monastic community was established in proper order, and the Emperor frequently bestowed honors and rewards upon him. The temple annually contributed pear blossoms and honey; the color was white and the flavor was excellent.
He was highly esteemed by the world. Ling died at the temple.
During the Tang dynasty, there was one named Danyi, whose courtesy name was Yuanzhen. His surname was Xu, and he was a native of Xiaoshan in Kuaiji. From birth, he was exceptionally bright;
when he was only seven years old, his father instructed him in the classics, and he could memorize several thousand words a day. At the age of twelve, he entered the service of Ling at Shanyin.

He stayed at Yinsi Monastery and practiced the inner Dharma; whenever he opened a scroll, he immediately mastered its meaning, such that those who saw him marveled and praised him. It happened that Emperor Zhongzong ascended the throne, and by imperial grace, the monks and Daoists of Tian-shan were granted ordination.

Hu Yuanli, the Regional Commander, examined their mastery of the scriptures and their doctrinal understanding, and [Wang] ranked first, thereby obtaining permission to shave his head and receive the monastic precepts.

He was assigned to Guanzhao Xuan Temple. From that time on, his application to study became exceptionally diligent. At the beginning of the Kaiyuan era, he received full ordination from Vinaya Master Yuan of Wu Commandery.
He then proceeded to Vinaya Master Shen of Kaiyuan Temple in his hometown to thoroughly investigate the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Once Master Shen had passed away, he traveled to the capital. Vinaya Master Xuanyan of the Fahua Temple took a liking to his outstanding brilliance and said to him: "In these present times..."

As for the transmission of the Dharma, who else but you could have done it? Not long after, the Vinaya Master Chao of Chengxin Temple in his native village requested that he take charge of the temple’s affairs.
During the Kaiyuan era, due to the loss of his parents, he recited the Tripitaka at Fulong Mountain on Mount Tiantai.

During the Tianbao era, he built a dwelling in the former site of Zhi Dun’s Wozhou and resided there; this place was commonly known as Beiwu (The Northern Ravine). There, he initially dreamed of two Brahmans...
The monk told him, "You have a twenty-day matter to attend to here. At the beginning of the Baoying era, he again dreamed that the previous monk said, "The original period was twenty days;
it has now passed. The demonic rebels are approaching; you should not remain any longer.

Subsequently, Yuan Chao occupied Shan and Danqiu, and the harm inflicted upon [the community] became increasingly severe. Consequently, Huiyi, together with Dahuai and Huilü, went to visit Chan Master Zuoxi Lang.
At the Master’s residence, he refined and cultivated *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Consequently, the scholar-officials of both the court and the countryside turned their hearts toward him.
These included the Chancellor Du Hongjian, the Minister of Revenue Xue Jiaxun, the Vice Censor-in-Chief Du Guojun, and Xu Jiao, the Prefect of Mingzhou, along with his son Hao.

He was universally esteemed for his profound kindness. In the fifth month of the year Jiwu (1779) of the Dali era, he passed away at Chenchin. He was eighty-nine years of age and had been a monk for sixty-two years.
His remains were interred at his former residence in Beiwu.
Tang Qingjiang was a native of Kuaiji. His clan and lineage are unknown. From his youth, he set his aspirations beyond the mundane world;

however, constrained by his parents' affection, it was only after a long time that he entered the monastic order. He served as a disciple under the Vinaya Master Tanli, reciting the scriptures with such fluency and mastery that those who discerned his talent regarded him as a "thousand-li colt" of the Buddhist gate.
Shortly thereafter, he followed the Vinaya Master Shouzhi at Tiantong Temple in Zhiyang.

He prepared the ritual implements for the altar and continued his studies under Master Yi, training in the *Nanshan Lüchao* (Commentary on the Vinaya of the Southern Mountain) and researching the *Xiangshu* (Commentary on the Vinaya).
He mastered them all thoroughly without any deficiency. He was skilled in literary composition; whenever he wrote poems or verses, he immediately gained renown in his time.

By nature, however, he was narrow-minded and impetuous, constantly provoking even his seniors and superiors. Master Yi always showed him great forbearance, yet in the end he departed, with no one able to restrain or dissuade him. Having thus traveled...

He traveled on until he encountered no one; thereupon, he regretted his departure and returned. He prostrated before Master Yi-gong and said, "My former thoughts were ignorant, but my subsequent mind has attained awakening.

I hope that through the Great Compassion of the Venerable Master, you will grant me the gift of joy. Moved by his sincerity, Master Yi-gong accepted him as his disciple once again, just as they had been before.
In the eighth year of the Dali era, Jiang Yu, while staying at Runfen in his native region, met the National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang. The Teacher once recounted a transmission he had received:
"Tang Xiongjun, surnamed Zhou, was a native of Chengdu. He was broad in learning and possessed great talent, yet he lacked restraint regarding the precepts. Whenever he gave lectures,"
Whenever he received offerings or benefits, he immediately diverted them for other uses. Furthermore, he once let his hair and beard grow long and concealed himself within the military ranks.
When he was accused of a crime, he fled again and shaved his head as before. During the Dali era, he died of illness. At that time, there were those who died suddenly and then revived.
It is said that Yun-jun was brought before King Yama. The King, filled with rage, ordered him to be cast into prison.
Yun-jun raised his voice and cried out, "If I, Ung-jun, were to enter hell, then the Buddhas of the three periods would all be speaking falsehoods.

Furthermore, according to the sutras, even those who have committed the five heinous crimes may attain rebirth in the lower grade through ten recitations at the moment of death; how much more so for one like me who has never committed the five?"
He replied, "I have been reciting the Buddha's name, though its number is unknown. Having finished speaking, a jeweled platform immediately arrived from the west, and Jun ascended it and departed.
Táng Qiánzhēn, whose courtesy name was Yìzhāng, was surnamed Wáng and was a native of Tàiyuán. Later he moved to Xiàzhōu, to Chóngdào Xiāng in Shuōfāng.
His father was Zhēn, who had two sons; Qiánzhēn was the second. Having reached the age of twenty, he entered the monastic order.
In the twenty-sixth year of the Kāiyuán era, he enrolled for tonsure at Língjué Temple in his hometown. The following year, he received full ordination and began his studies.
He studied the Vinaya-piṭaka, the sūtras, and the chapters and verses of the śāstras without exception.

During the reign of Emperor Daizong, when the newly translated *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha-sūtra* was issued by imperial decree, he was commissioned to compose a commentary. On the eleventh month of the eighth year of the Dali era, the three-fascicle commentary was completed.
He advanced [his studies] by composing the *Bodhicittārtha* (The Meaning of the Bodhicitta) and the *Bodhicittotpāda-śīla* (The Vow for the Arising of the Bodhicitta), each in one fascicle.
He also compiled the *Tri-saṃvara-śuddha-śīla* (The Threefold Pure Vows) and the *Daśakuśala-dharma-śīla* (The Vow of the Ten Wholesome Dharmas) together in one fascicle.

Furthermore, he received the esoteric teachings of the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra, entered the maṇḍala, and received the seals of Buddhahood; thus, he became proficient in both the Exoteric and Esoteric divisions. This was in the fifth month of the second year of the Zhenyuan era.
On the fourteenth day, he fell ill. He soon gathered his disciples, and his final instructions were most earnest.

On the twenty-first day, with his right side down and feet stacked, he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha and passed away at Xingshan Temple. He was seventy-one years of age; he had spent forty-nine summer retreats.
Tang Shen-hao, whose courtesy name was Heng-du, was surnamed Xu. His eighth-generation ancestor was Xu Chi, a scholar at the Western Residence of Prince Jingling of the Qi dynasty.

His son, Xu Ling, served as the Left Vice-Minister of the Department of State Affairs during the Liang dynasty; he was a man of letters whose reputation for literary talent rivaled that of Ruan Ji (Gengzi-shan).

After the fall of the Chen dynasty, Xu Ling assisted in the administration of Wu County and subsequently made his home there. Shen-hao was a native of Wu; by nature he was upright and resolute, possessing a lofty spirit that sought liberation from worldly constraints.
In his secular life, he followed Master Yi of Longquan Monastery in Qiantang and left the household life.

In the sixth year of the Tiānbǎo era, an imperial edict was issued to carefully select those of refined purity, permitting each prefecture to ordain three individuals. Sòng Hào obtained registration at Fòyuàn Monastery on Mount Bāoshān.
Initially, he received full ordination under Master Xīng; later, he studied the *Nánshān Lǜchão* (Commentary on the Nanshan Vinaya) under Master Tányì. Not long after, he again...

He retired to live in seclusion at Baoshan. At the beginning of the Qianyuan era, an imperial edict was issued to select seven virtuous monks (*dàdé*) from each of the twenty-seven monasteries throughout the empire to preside over the long-term lectures on the Vinaya.

The assembly requested that he reside at Kaiyuan Temple. In his later years, he devoted himself to the Perfect Teaching (*yuánzōng*), establishing a Western Pure Land Society (*xīfāng jìngshè*) where he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* more than nine thousand times.
In the tenth month of the sixth year of the Zhenyuan era, he fell ill. Upon reaching [the end of his life], he...
In his thirteenth month, his illness became critical. He looked toward his disciple Weiliang and said, "You must return my remains to Dongting to erect a stupa.
That night, though the sky was free of clouds, stars fell like rain. He subsequently passed away at Kaiyuan Temple at the age of seventy-five, with forty-three years since his ordination.
Regarding his burial, Xi Zhou composed an inscription for his stele.
Tang Lingche was endowed with a pure and refined nature. He was a diligent scholar skilled in literary composition and excelled particularly in poetry.

Residing at Yunmen Temple by the Yuexi River, his reputation spread far and wide from the very year he came of age. Those who followed him to study the Vinaya teachings flocked to him like crowds rushing through a marketplace.
Among those who attended were Yan Wei, Director of the Imperial Library, and Liu Changqing, Regional Inspector of Suizhou. The palace... [text truncated]

The Palace Attendant Censor Huangfu Zeng not only excelled at composing verses such as "yellow silk and colored threads," but also realized the underlying meaning of the "green bamboo and yellow flowers.
When he visited Zhushan in Wuxing, Jiaoran was already as renowned as day; upon meeting him, they immediately established a bond as fellow recluses.
He presented all of his correspondence to the Imperial Commissioner Bao Ji, who highly recommended him. When [Huangfu] finally met him...
Ji’s ritual decorum was beyond what ordinary people could attain. Later, Quan De’u sent a letter inquiring about Zhe’s daily conduct;

Zhe replied to him as he had done in his previous correspondence. Such was the esteem in which he was held by his peers. He authored the *Lüzong yinyuan* (The Source of the Vinaya School) in twenty-one fascicles.
Tang Shaokang’s surname was Zhou; he was a native of Jinyun. His mother dreamed that a cauldron traveled to Lake Feng, where she encountered a jade maiden who presented her with a blue lotus, saying:
"This flower is auspicious; entrust it to your keeping. In another life, you shall give birth to a noble son; you must cherish and protect him."
At birth, a blue-green light filled the room, and its fragrance was like that of the lotus. As she grew slightly older, her eyes were azure and her lips vermilion;

her white teeth were so beautiful they seemed as if painted. Yet, even at seven years of age, she still did not speak. On the Buddha’s birthday, her nurse carried her to play at Mount Ling-shan Temple.
Pointing to the Buddha [in a painting], he asked him, "Do you recognize this? He immediately replied, "Śākyamuni Buddha. Those who heard this were amazed.

His parents, knowing he was no vessel for the secular world, eventually relinquished him so that he might leave the household life. At the age of fifteen, having already recited the scriptures, he was able to master all five divisions (*piṭaka*).
Once he had undergone the tonsure, he completed his ordination at Jiaxiang Temple in Yue, where he studied the Vinaya and further listened to lectures on the *Huayan* (Avataṃsaka).
While at Longxing Temple during the Shangyuan era, [Hui]yan traveled to Luoyang at the beginning of the Zhenyuan era and stayed at Baima Temple.
Suddenly, he saw an object emitting light that illuminated the hall. As he hurried to look at it, it was the *Pure Land Practice Text* (Jingtu wen) by Master Shandao.
Overjoyed beyond measure, he immediately made a vow, saying: "If there truly exists [a Pure Land] in the West..."

"As for the conditions," he said, "this text shall again emit light. As soon as he finished speaking, the light grew even more intense, and within it appeared countless manifested Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Before long, he went to the Hall of the Shadow of Shandao in Chang’an to offer his prayers. Suddenly, the statue of the Venerable One transformed into the body of a Buddha and spoke to Kang, saying:
"To bring benefit and joy to all sentient beings, we shall be reborn together in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing; it is only I and you who shall do so."
There was such a man. Shortly thereafter, he encountered a monk from Guoyuan Temple in Jiangling, who said to him, "Your karmic conditions lie in Xin-ding;
you should go there quickly. Having spoken, the monk vanished. Thereupon, Kang went to Xin-ding and daily practiced alms-gathering among the villages.
Whenever he obtained money, he would give it all to small children, making them chant the name of the Buddha—one coin for one recitation. He continued in this manner for over a month.
A group of children pursued Kang, chanting "Buddha" while seeking money; their voices resounded throughout the market stalls.
For a year, whenever they saw Kang, they would invariably chant "Buddha," not only the children, but even men, women, the elderly, and the young did likewise.

He then established a Pure Land practice hall on Mount Wulong, constructing a three-tiered altar and composing twenty-four hymns of praise. Day and night he performed the ritual practices to extol the Pure Land.
On a day of fasting, Hui Kang ascended the high seat and gathered more than three thousand disciples whom he was transforming beneath it.
He instructed them, saying, "You all should observe me with sincere devotion as I chant the Buddha’s name.
Kang then raised his voice and cried out, "Namo Amitābha Buddha! Suddenly, a Buddha emerged from Kang’s mouth; as he chanted ten times in succession, ten Buddhas appeared.
His mouth was shaped as if strung with pearls. Kangfu addressed the assembly, saying, "Do you all see the Buddha now?
If you see the Buddha, you shall surely attain rebirth. On the tenth month of the twenty-first year of the Zhenyuan era, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture, emitting light.
A violent wind arose from all directions, and hundreds of birds wailed in grief; the color of Mount Wulong turned white because of it. He was enshrined in a stupa within the prefecture.
Dongzhitaiziyan: Tang Shangheng, surnamed Rao, was a native of Nancheng in Linchuan. At the age when one resolves to study the Way, he followed his maternal uncle into the monastic life.
He recited Buddhist scriptures daily, totaling a thousand words. Upon reaching maturity, he received the precepts from Master Dayuan of Mount Nanyue.

Although he was diligent in his studies and listening to the teachings, he was reluctant to travel long distances. During the Dali era, he requested to be affiliated with Jingyun Temple so that he might more conveniently attend to his parents' care.

As many years passed, his cultivation remained without deficiency; he was particularly proficient in lecturing upon and thoroughly mastering the *Nanshan Shisao* (The Southern Mountain Commentary on the Vinaya). At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, he moved...
He resided at Longxing Monastery in Juyi, where he formed friendships with Fazhen of Mount Lu, Lingyou of Tiantai, Faye of Jingmen, Shencou of Xingguo, and Huizhi of Jianchang.
He was also close friends with the State Councilor Jiang Gongfu and the Duke Yan Zhenqing.
Yang, Feng, Wei, and Dan—these four gentlemen traveled together, and thus the teaching of "dividing into four parts to transfer merit and extinguish transgressions" arose.
Those benefited by this were many. For some twenty years, they sat upon the Amṛta-maṇḍala; among the men and women of Jambudvīpa and China, those who attained deliverance were numerous.
There were more than fifteen thousand followers. In the tenth year of the Yuanhe era, he manifested a slight illness.
On the day of Jihai in the tenth month, he passed away at Donglin Monastery on Mount Lu. His entire body was interred in a stone tomb on the southern ridge.

He lived in this world for seventy-seven years and spent fifty-five summer retreats in formal seclusion. His disciples planted pine and cypress trees, and Bai Juyi of Taiyuan composed an inscription for his stone stupa.
Tang Qingche initially had no knowledge of where he came from. He traveled extensively through the monasteries specializing in the Vinaya, closely guarding the gates of his senses.

However, he held no fixed teacher; wherever there was excellence, he would devote himself to it with reverence. He first associated with Vinaya Master Daoheng of the Northern Courtyard at Kaiyuan Temple in Wu.
Daoheng’s realization was profound and far-reaching, and there were none among those of great reputation and eminent virtue who did not praise him. During the Yuanhe era...

In the eighth year, he compiled the essential and authoritative explanations from various schools to comment upon the *Nanshan Chao*, composing the *Jiyi Ji* (Record of Collected Meanings) in twenty fascicles.
By the tenth year, the work was completed; today, it is widely transmitted and recited in Yuzhang, Wuchang, and Jinling.

Tang Weizhe traveled to the capital during his youth. Beyond his studies in the three traditional branches of learning, he devoted himself particularly to the sculpting of images to inspire reverence and admiration.
He said, "To rely upon images as an aid for accomplishing the path of contemplation is the essential technique for spiritual cultivation.

It so happened that during the Yuanhe era, Empress Dowager Guo of Emperor Xianzong commissioned the construction of Fengci Monastery to cultivate merit on behalf of her mother, the Grand Princess of Qi.

The Princess was then selected for entry [into the palace] to serve through her artistic talents. Before long, she again traveled eastward to Zhejiang, where she paid homage at the Aśoka Stūpa in Moxian County, Siming.
This stūpa was one that Liu Sahuo had previously worshipped during the Eastern Jin dynasty;
its meritorious significance cannot be fully recounted here. Thereupon, she used powdered seven precious gems mixed with glue and lacquer to fashion a mold for it. When...

He cast off his mold and cut [the statue] with perfect fidelity. The multitude marveled that he possessed such a karmic affinity; thus, they carried him back home to provide for the offerings at Chongbong Temple.
Throughout the capital, none failed to have faith and take refuge in him. Later, he passed away at Chongbong.

Huilin of the Tang dynasty, courtesy name Baoyu, was the son of the Kē clan of Xīn'ān. At the age of seven, he entered the monastic order at Xīfēng of Línghǐn Temple to serve under Master Jīn, where he received instruction in the Buddhist scriptures.
At the beginning of the Dàlì era, he received full ordination; he brought the three studies into harmony, leaving nothing deficient.

By nature, he delighted in springs and rocks, and so he lived in seclusion at Tiānyǎn—this being Mount Tiānmù. It rises three thousand *zhàng* high and spans three hundred *lǐ* in circumference. Together with...
Mount Lufu is like Mount Tianzhu; it possesses two lakes known as the Eastern and Western Eyes. The terrain is deep and secluded, abounding in strange and supernatural phenomena.

Yet Ling alone remained undisturbed by them. In the *dinghai* year of the Yuanhe era, Du Zhi—the Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies and Governor of Chennan—invited him to leave the mountains and go to Yongfu Temple to ascend the altar and ordain people.
In the spring of the *jichou* year, Pei [Xuan], the Minister of War and Regional Inspector...
Changdi requested to ascend the altar of Tianzhu Monastery to ordain others and lecture to his disciples for nearly twenty years.

Throughout this time, his lofty and pure conduct remained unchanged from beginning to end. On the twenty-fifth day of the fourth month in the sixth year of the Dàhé era, he passed away at the age of eighty-three and with sixty-four years of monastic seniority (*lǎ*).
On the twelfth day of the fifth month of that same year, he was buried at Yongan Monastery.

On the southern slope of the Western Mountains lived Tang Guangxiu, who was born in Dongyang and descended from the Liu clan. Having shaved his head, he enrolled at Chanlin Temple and entered the gate of Master Sui to investigate the essential teachings of the scriptures.
Students gathered there like clouds, and he would daily recite the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.

The *Guangming Fanwang Sifen Jieben* (The Four-Part Brahma Net Precept Manual of Radiant Light), the practice of the Six Periods of the Day, and furthermore, the performance of the Repentance Rite for seven weeks every year;
the fourth is the Samādhi of Following One’s Own Intent (*Sui-zhuyi Sanmei*). In the third year of the Kaicheng era, the Japanese monk Enzai came in person to request the Dharma.
Wei Heng, the Prefectural Governor of Taizhou, welcomed him to lecture on *Zhi Guan* (Stilling and Contemplation) in the provincial office. The third year of the Huichang era...
He passed away on the sixteenth day of the third month of that year. His age was seventy-two; his years since ordination were fifty-two.

He was buried at the Jindao (Golden Earth) Site of Enlightenment. His dharma successor was Wuwai. In the seventh year of the Xiantong era, his disciple Liangwen exhumed the remains and performed cremation.
Over a thousand śarīra relics were obtained and enshrined in a stūpa.

Tang Zongliang, surnamed Feng, was a native of Fenghua in Mingzhou. During the Kaicheng era, he shaved his head and entered the monastic order, becoming affiliated with Guoning Temple in the prefecture.

Having received full ordination, he studied the *vinaya* (monastic discipline) until there were no lapses in his conduct. During the persecutions of the Huichang era, he fled to live among the mountain crags and valleys of his hometown.
When the state was restored during the Dazhong era, twenty-eight men of renowned virtue were summoned and selected for office, and Liang was one of them.
Li Pin, the Governor of Jianzhou, composed an inscription for the temple which states: "The Vinaya monk Zongliang and the Chan monk Quanyou were such men.
In their later years, they increasingly withdrew from worldly affairs, rarely leaving their chambers for months at a time. Regarding their occasional visits, Fang Yu sent them a poem that says:
"A single pool of autumn water, its bottom always visible; a thousand-foot mountain pine, its branches never branching out. [The] Empty Gate...
"How much have you learned of the Buddha? he asked. "I have only shaved away the dust of my mind; I have no other teacher. He passed away at the age of eighty.
Throughout his life, Liang associated with more than several dozen individuals, such as Guànshuāng and Zéwú, all of whom maintained pure integrity and formed friendships beyond the monastic groves.

He composed an inscription for Yuèlín Monastery and a collection of approximately three hundred poems, along with eulogies and hymns, which have been circulated in the world. Nevertheless, he was keenly devoted to merit and reverence.
Second, as for his fields of merit: he was already held in high esteem and admired by Luo Yin of Jiangdong and Sun He of Anle.
When Sun He composed the *Sīmíng Cáimíng Zhì* (Record of Talented and Famous Men of Siming), he specifically included his name among the ranks of eminent scholars and outstanding men of letters.
Such was the degree of reverence bestowed upon him by the leading literary figures of his time.
Tang Wen-zhi, surnamed Zhu, was a native of Xujiang in Quzhou. His paternal uncle was the Venerable Wei-kuan, who was highly esteemed at the time.

Wen-zhi entered the monastic order as a youth; when Wei-kuan received an imperial summons to enter Chang’an and reside at Daxingshan Temple, he was further invited to bestow the Bodhisattva precepts at the Inner Court (Neidaochang), and Wen-zhi accompanied him on both occasions. At the age of fifteen, he had already mastered [the scriptures].

He studied the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and other scriptures—twenty-three in total. At twenty-three, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*). After seven days, he was able to master the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
Two years later, during the summer retreat, he lectured on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. At the age of twenty-seven, he lectured on the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. In this manner, forty years passed.
There were many who thoroughly mastered the great sutras and treatises. Later, he inquired about the dharma of the mind from the two Chan masters Beici and Yujie;

he then returned to lead his disciples at Fale Monastery in Zhuji. A tiger crouched beneath his seat as if listening to his teachings, and when he stroked its head, he commanded it not to devour living beings;
the tiger tucked its tail and departed. During the Huichang era, an imperial edict was issued to purge the Buddhist clergy.
Zhi Dun retired to Mount Dafurong in Leqing County during the Yongjia era. At the beginning of the Taizhong period, the Prefect, Lord Wei, repeatedly issued summonses, but Zhi firmly declined them.
Thereupon, they forcibly carried him into the city administration seat. He resided at Kaiyuan Temple for many years;
all the offerings he received from the faithful were used to construct the Buddha hall, the lecture hall, and the surrounding corridors and buildings, as well as to establish the sacred images.

The elaborate adornments and the complete restoration of the temple buildings were all expenses incurred for this purpose. Shortly thereafter, the Vice Commissioner of Kuaiji, the Second Minister Shen Gong, welcomed him back to the Lühou Mountain Monastery.
This monastery was originally the site where Master Ningfen had once propagated the Dharma. Upon his arrival, [Zhao] Qi occupied nothing more than a single mat within a thatched hut.
On the fourteenth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Xiantong era, he took his leave.
On the fifteenth day of the month, he passed away while sitting upright. He was eighty-four years of age and sixty-two years since his ordination. His entire body was interred at Linggu Monastery.
Once the stupa had been constructed, Duan Chengshi, the Regional Inspector of Yue Province, composed a narrative of his life and deeds.

Tang Zengren was the son of the Shi family of Chéngliú in Pèiguó. In his youth, he studied at the local school; as he grew older, he accompanied others to the capital to present his policy proposals for the imperial examination.

Failing to achieve his ambition, he departed and soon traveled west to the Helán Mountains. Taking a liking to Báicǎo Valley, he finally cast off his official cap and shaved his head, constructing a thatched hut to dwell in.
The people of his hometown admired him so much that they did not wait for him to go on alms rounds; instead, offerings of butter and milk products arrived daily.

[Gift]. In the fifth year of the Huichang era, an imperial edict was issued to abolish the Buddhist teachings; however, because [his location] was remote from the borders, it was not included in the prohibitions.
Li Yanzo, the Regional Commander (Jiedushi), showed him exceptional respect and constructed a separate Baicao Cloister within Longxing Temple to welcome him.

In the seventh year of the Dazhong era, he drew blood from his finger to transcribe the various sutras, totaling two hundred and eighty-three fascicles. Yanzo feared that his work might remain incomplete.
He fell ill. [The Master] exhorted him, saying: "Master, as a student of the Mahāyāna, you ought to remain long in this world to shoulder the True Dharma and benefit all sentient beings.
Yet here you are, inflicting wounds upon your flesh and draining your very marrow for the sake of the brush and inkstone, thereby hastening the end of your life.
Is this not what Confucius meant when he said that one 'dares not damage the body, hair, or skin'? Thereupon, he composed the *Sanjiao huibian* (Compendium on the Destruction of the Three Teachings).
In his *Treatise on the Compassionate One* (*Beichan lun*), he expressed his intent: "In the ninth year, I read the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* and investigated the dharmas symbolized by the forty-two arms.

Upon reaching the 'Fearless Hand,' I harbored doubts. Thereupon, I established a ritual altar and offered prayers for ten days. I was moved by the appearance of two hands forming the *mudrā* of the correct seal in the void, clearly visible to the eye.
Consequently, I commissioned an artisan to paint it so that it might be transmitted, and I composed the six-fascicle *Treatise on the Mahākaruṇā*. Or...
They slandered him, claiming it was not so. He endured this and again earnestly entreated them, having the artisans wash their brushes and prepare a copper bowl to await [the flower].

Suddenly, a single flower emerged from the bowl; its branches and leaves were exceptionally fresh and brilliant. This was a manifestation of spiritual resonance on the tenth day of the seventh month in the twelfth year.
He passed away at Baik-sa Temple (Baekcho-won), reaching the age of fifty-nine. On the seventeenth day of the tenth month of that same year, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa.

To the south of Suiguan, there was Tang Yuantiao, whose character was outspoken and straightforward. In his daily life, he delighted in evaluating the characters of others; consequently, he frequently came into conflict with the world.

He had mastered the Vinaya and was skilled in the learning of the Zhousi (Confucian) tradition. There was no branch of arts, techniques, or crafts that he did not comprehend. In his early years, he relied upon Ximing Monastery in the capital.
During the Guangming era, when the region was overrun by the Chao rebels, the Dharma Master Sifabao traveled south and stayed at Dashiensi in Yue.

There he expounded his *Nanshan chao* (Commentary on the Nanshan School); its principles were comprehensive and its discourse grand and eloquent. Whenever he brandished his fly-whisk, his disciples forgot their weariness.
The masters throughout the Jiangbiao region all submitted with joy and respect; he was popularly known as the "Liaoshi of Jian-shui. He authored five volumes of writings, titled... [title missing].
*Jiānshuǐ jí* (Collection on Examining Water).
Yuàncéng, whose secular surname was Sòng, was a native of Hexi. His lineage traced back to Confucian scholars, yet he was particularly devoted to the study of the *Zhū* (Buddhist) teachings.

One night, his mother, Yīn, dreamed that the trees in her courtyard were laden with thousands of blossoms, yet they bore only a single fruit, which was extraordinary and lovely; she subsequently conceived. Upon [the birth],...
As she was about to give birth, [the master] named her Cheng (Sincerity) based on his sincere vow, and it remained unchanged even when she entered the monastic life.

As she grew older, she served Xingyan as her teacher and received his instructions. In the third year of the Dahuang Taihe era, she first shaved her head; in the fifth year, she received full ordination.

Not long after, the Huichang persecution of Buddhism occurred, and Cheng immediately went into hiding. She did not change her appearance or attire. At the beginning of the Dazhong era, the Dharma gate flourished once more, and Cheng obtained...

He returned to reside at Foguang Temple. When the Emperor heard of this, he issued an edict bestowing upon him purple robes. When the Li clan occupied the Bingmen region, they would frequently come to visit with several hundred horsemen;

having seen and recognized him, they showed him great reverence and affection. They submitted a memorial to the Son of Heaven requesting a title for him, and by imperial decree, he was titled Yuanshang (Circle-Mark).
He concurrently served as the General Inspector of the Mountain Gate. In the third year of the Guangqi era, he prepared sacrificial food and offered robes, inviting monks for a ritual offering.
Just as the bell was struck and he was about to enter the refectory, he passed away. A stupa was erected and a stele inscribed at a distance of one *li* to the northwest of the temple.
Tang Quanqi was a native of Yuhang. At that time, the Great Master Faji was propagating the Dharma at Mount Jing.

Quanqi immediately requested to be tonsured under him. Later, he built a grass hut on Mount Heng to advance in the Way. He lived on wild fruits and drank from mountain streams, relying on no one for his needs.

He endured both cold and heat, sheltering himself with oak leaves; this remained unchanged even through the winter and summer solstices. A guest once presented Quanqi with a poem that said: [Poem omitted as per instructions]
Since the one who dwelt in the nest has passed, who else remains? He has transmitted the true seal of the Tathāgata’s Dharma. Yesterday, the Fire God was seen above and below;
his grass-clothed body is none other than the body of the Snowy Mountains.
Liang Yanqing, surnamed Gong, was a native of Chushan in Wu Commandery. He was dedicated to seeking out teachers and, in his later years, encountered Jizong Jizhu, from whom he requested instruction.
His peers flocked to him like echoes, and the influence of the Vinaya spread widely; that region subsequently became a reservoir for the *vinaya*.
Once, a tiger lay in wait on the night at the temple’s pavilion, roaring loudly. Yanqing perceived that it was merely a decoy, set there by hunters with arrows hidden within.
He thought of ascending the pavilion to rescue him, but his disciples remonstrated against it, saying, "The tiger is a predatory beast; its every movement causes injury.
Moreover, that creature has been driven mad by medicinal drugs. Although you, Great Man, have compassion for all beings, how can you face its ferocity?
At the third watch, while everyone else was exhausted and lying down, Daoceng alone took up a torch, extracted the arrow from which the tiger had been struck, and [removed the poison].
The tiger lowered its ears and bowed its head as if in a gesture of prostration and thanks. The next day, the hunter Zhu De, believing the tiger was dead, went to the temple to search for it;
Huiqing showed him the arrow, and De subsequently repented his transgression. King Qian of Wusuku treated him with exceptional respect and honor;

whenever he performed Buddhist rites, he invariably summoned Huiqing to recite prayers, offer incantations, and distribute food to the hungry ghosts. One day, the robe covering his shoulders fell off.
The ground suddenly returned to its former state as if nothing had happened. There were frequent sightings of spirits and deities standing in attendance by his side.
In the sixth month of the sixth year of the Zhengming era, he passed away at Xingfu Temple on Mount Poshan at the age of ninety-nine.

Furthermore, there was the śramaṇa Shou, who devoted himself exclusively to the *Nanshan chao*. Toward the end of the Tang dynasty, when the Yang family illegitimately seized the lands of Jiangnan, [Shou] frequently...
He was summoned to his residence to receive offerings, yet he did not maintain a permanent household. He lived in a state of serene spontaneity; truly, no worldly affairs could disturb his thoughts.

Just as he was presiding over a ritual altar and holding the *karmavācanā*, he suddenly passed away on the slopes of Mount Bofu. When the Yang family heard the news of his death, they were struck with wonder and lamentation.
A man of the Way from Liangguo lived in seclusion at Shuangxi Monastery on Mount Lu. In his leisure time between meditation and recitation, he devoted himself solely to tending a garden.
As for the vegetables, he allowed others to take as they pleased and did not forbid them. When asked the reason for this, he said: "I cultivate with a mind of non-attachment."
He grasps with no-mind; both he and I are without mind. How could the things that exist within it ever come to an end?
Thus, heaven and earth are my garden, and wind, frost, rain, and dew are my irrigation. What toil could I possibly have?

When the Zen Master Sōmoku heard this, he approved of it and presented him with a poem, which said: "Entering the gate, the emptiness and stillness are profound; truly, you are a child who has left the home-life."
When he went out as a ghost, no one saw him; those without spiritual insight called him a fool. After a long time, he passed away and was buried in the mountains.

Qi Ji of the Liang dynasty was born into the Hu family of Huya. He left home to become a monk at Daming Mountain Temple while still young, and having received full ordination, [he continued his practice].
He subsequently trained in the Vinaya precepts until he reached their profound depths. By nature, he delighted in poetic composition and attained great renown at an early age.
Yet, he always harbored a regret that he had not yet grasped the subtle essence of the Dharma. Thereupon, he traveled abroad, visiting the seats of Master Yaoshan, Lumen, and Huguo in succession.
Sudianbin served at Shichuang. When the Liang dynasty overthrew the Tang, the empire was in a state of turmoil.

Gao Jichang expelled Lei Man from Zhugong and styled himself the "Leftover Protector" (Liuhou) of Jingmen; he subsequently received an appointment as a Regional Commander (Jiedushi) from the imperial court.
By the time Zhuangzong entered the capital from Hedong to replace the Liang, the Gao family had already come to control one region, while men of integrity and principle [fled] in all four directions.

Upon reaching the beginning of the Longde era, [the Emperor] appointed him as the Sangzheng (Chief Administrator of the Monks) and granted him a monthly stipend. He was housed in the Jingyuan (Pure Court) of Longxing Temple, which was not to his liking.
He composed fifteen chapters of the "Mowen Pian" (Unclassified Chapters on Zhu-gong) to express his sentiments. He had a goiter on his neck.

His robes hung down like gourds; he was popularly known as the "Poetry Sack. Clad in tattered rags, he traveled among the mountains and waters, living in contented joy, never aware of whether the world was in order or in chaos.
He never once casually presented a single word to seek an audience with the feudal lords. What a sublime aspiration this was!
His poems were exchanged in song with the Hermit of Mount Hua, and at the end, he was styled Chongyue Sha.
There is the *Bailian ji* (Collection of White Lotuses) by Men, which circulates in the world.
Later, Congli was born in Xiangyang; he was exceptionally filial and fraternal, and his reputation was highly praised throughout his village. When he lost his parents...

He then left the household life and received full ordination; at that time, he was already advanced in years. When he studied the Vinaya-piṭaka under his teacher, he suffered particularly from the demon of sleep.
Because his natural disposition was dull and clouded, he would frequently use an iron awl to pierce his own forehead and palms. This continued for more than half a year.
What he transmitted were merely the words of instruction and dialogue; yet he maintained them with such diligent vigor that he never deviated from them, even in moments of haste or distress.
During the Qiánhuà era of the Liáng dynasty, he traveled to Tiantái and stayed at the Píngtián Monastery, where he was soon appointed as the *upādhyāya* (abbot) of the temple.
He was grave, dignified, and silent, never allowing his joy or anger to manifest on his countenance. He once said to the assembly: "The *Prātimokṣa* is my..."
"Great Master, like an elephant without a hook or a monkey that has found a tree, how easy is it to restrain this mind? One must maintain the *poṣadha* even in ordinary times;

thus, his sincere resolve allowed him to commune with ghosts and spirits. During a summer drought, the administrative monk requested that he offer prayers for rain because the vegetables in the garden were withering.
The Master said, 'It will suffice simply to burn incense in the Hall of the True Lord. After two or three days, [the rain] did not cease."
Furthermore, he required timber to construct a wooden walkway over the water to ferry people across; the labor was not easily obtained, so he reported this to his superior.

The ritual master said, "I shall speak of this to the True Lord. Suddenly, a great wind blew down the trees. When the Wukus Wang, the Qian family, heard of this, they summoned him into their residence and established a *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light) Dharma assembly.
Alms were distributed as needed, yet he wore only a single robe through both cold and heat. At night, he sat constantly and did not lie down, eating but once a day.

Externally, he left no surplus or possessions. In the third year of the Tongguang era, in the eleventh month of winter, he passed away at the age of seventy-nine and with fifty-two years of ordination.
His body was cremated, and his relics were collected to erect a stupa.

Later Tang Wuji was surnamed Shi and was a native of Shuofang. In the ninth year of the Dazhong era, at the age of thirteen, he renounced secular life and received the tonsure under Master Fakong of Baicao Monastery.
In the third year of the Xiantong era, he received full ordination at Ximing Monastery in the capital.
Having become skilled in lecturing and exegesis, he was also proficient in the lute and calligraphy. Previously, Lord Tang Hengfu had once...

While he was pacifying Shuofang, [the Emperor] treated him as a member of his own household. He requested that [the Master] be registered with the Merit Commissioner of the Two Streets and was enrolled at Ximing Monastery.

Later, when an imperial edict invited the True Body from Famen Monastery in Fengxiang, the Deputy Commander of the Right Army, Zhang Siguang, petitioned for him to serve as a guide for the procession.
At that time, the Sovereign personally presided over the Dharma assembly and was greatly pleased, bestowing lavish rewards upon him. During the Guangqi era...

He returned to his native village and, based on the *Buddhapiṭaka-uṣṇīṣa-jvālā-śrī-samaya-maṇḍala-dharmaparyāya* he had transmitted from the capital, established a ritual altar for the Governor of the Prefecture, Lord Han, to perform the rite. He evoked numerous auspicious responses.

During the Jingfu era of the Later Jin dynasty, Lord Han submitted a petition requesting him to serve as the abbot of Guangfu Temple. Those seeking to receive the Bodhisattva precepts at the frontier walls gathered there daily in great numbers.
In the second year of the Zhengming era of the Liang dynasty, Han Zou, the Chief Secretary of the Secretariat, submitted a memorial bestowing upon him the title Hongyuan.
On the first day of the fourth month in the third year of the Tongguang era, he passed away in his chamber; his countenance remained as if alive, causing onlookers to marvel at the wonder.
The Chief Secretary ordered that lacquer be applied to preserve the remains, and Xue Zhao, an official of the military administration, recorded these events in an inscription.
Hou Tang Chenghui was surnamed Li and was a native of Lingqiu in Weizhou. His parents once traveled to Mount Wutai and, together before an image of Mañjuśrī, offered prayers for his birth.
Later, when Shi Faron of the Zhenrong Hall beheld his outstanding appearance, he exhorted him to leave the household life;
thus, he shaved his head and received full ordination. Chenghui studied the sutras and śāstras with diligence, and by nature he delighted in...
Línquán. The śramaṇas Zhànchóng and others of Wángzǐ Temple had long admired his reputation and wished to receive his pure regulations.

Consequently, they collectively requested him to serve as the temple’s abbot. In his leisure time from attending to administrative affairs, he recited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* more than a hundred times.
