At that time, Kèyòng was serving as the Military Commissioner (Jiédùshǐ) holding the gates of Bìng, while Liáng Tàizǔ was just then receiving the abdication of the Táng dynasty; as such, weapons and war drums followed one another across the Central Plains.
"Tu-tan. Previously, Li Kuyong had been acquainted with Huì. During a campaign, he was struck by a stray arrow;

the wound did not heal for some time, and he wished to see Huì to disclose his inner thoughts and entrust him with prayers for his recovery. When Huì arrived, Kuyong personally prostrated himself before him and addressed him as "National Teacher.

After Zhuangzong ascended the throne, he issued an imperial decree bestowing upon him purple robes and a posthumous title, which Huì firmly declined. In the tenth month of the third year of the Tongguang era...

In the second month, he entrusted his disciple Tinggui, saying, "My karmic conditions for transformation have come to an end; I request leave from this point on. Each of you should advance in the Way; there is no principle of one person substituting for another.
Having spoken these words, he entered his chamber and passed away lying on his right side. He was fifty years of age and thirty years since his ordination.

Upon hearing the news, the Emperor expressed deep sorrow and dispatched an attendant of the Inner Service to oversee the funeral arrangements. Three days of sacrificial offerings were granted, and his remains were cremated and collected.
He benefited the five regions and erected a stupa. He was posthumously titled Fayu (Dharma Rain), and the stupa was named Ciyun (Cloud of Compassion).
Later, Tang Kezhou, surnamed Fu, was a native of Jinling. In his youth, he left home to become a monk at Jianyuan Temple.

By nature and disposition, he was diligent and quick-witted; he subsequently traveled to Yuzhang to receive the *Fahua* and *Cien* commentaries from Dharma Master Yuntao, where his progress was daily increasing.
Master Yuejiang’s exposition reached the profoundest depths. He then arrived at Taiyue to benefit the multitudes.
In the second year of the Qiandehua era of the Liang dynasty, he traveled to Longxing Temple in Hangzhou to expound the teachings; monks and laypeople gathered there in great numbers.

At that time, the Prince of Wusu, the Qian family, who held sway over the two Zhe circuits, ordered him to reside in the Tianbao Hall at Xiguan. There, he continued his lectures day and night without ceasing, even through the nights.

He became a spirit. Could this have been stopped? From then on, people occasionally saw objects guarding his side. Furthermore, there was a shaman who summoned spirits; for a long time they did not descend.
After a while, the spirit spoke through the shaman, saying: "I followed the great deities to the Western Gate Tianbao Hall to listen to the Dharma, which is why I was late.
When the King heard this, he increased his veneration and bestowed upon him a golden *ruyi* bowl and purple robes.
He was posthumously titled Great Master Jingzhitongming. In the first year of the Tiānchéng era, he passed away at Guānyīn Temple.
He once authored one fascicle of a sub-commentary (*chāo*) explaining the preface to Vinaya Master Xuán’s *Fǎhuá jīng xù*, but it no longer exists today.
Later Tang Bianguang, courtesy name Dengfeng, was surnamed Wu and was a native of Yongjia. He was a descendant of Wu Jing, the Left Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Tang dynasty.
In his youth, he left home and entered Taoshan Temple, where he shaved his head and received full ordination. He was skilled in poetry and proficient in cursive and clerical scripts.

Hearing that Lu Xisheng had been exiled to Yuzhang, he went to visit him and mastered his method of calligraphy, specifically the "Five-Finger Pen-Wielder" (Wǔzhǐ bōdēng) technique. From then on, Bianguang’s own calligraphy...

His skill advanced further; as he turned his wrist and wielded his brush, he became even more exquisitely marvelous. He subsequently traveled west to the capital, where Emperor Zhaozong was on the throne.

By imperial decree, he was summoned to the presence of the throne to paint, and was bestowed a purple square-cut robe. Later, he visited the military governor of Hua, Wang Jian, who petitioned for his appointment and granted him the title Guangli.

Returning from China to his native village, he paid a visit to the Wu-Yue King, the Qian family of Wuhusu. The King treated him with the etiquette due to a guest. During the Changxing era, he returned to Yongdong and passed away.
The Prefect, Yang Quan, who had long held Huijue in high esteem, oversaw his funeral arrangements. Three years later, it was again proposed that he be cremated;
however, upon opening the coffin, his countenance showed no sign of decay. His beard, hair, nails, and cuticles had all grown long. The assembly then collected the remaining ashes.
There are other pagodas as well. His disciples, including Zhi and Zong, both received his oral instructions on calligraphy.

There is one collection of songs and poems presented by contemporary scholars and officials, such as Wu Rong (the Internal Secretary of Wu) and Luo Jiangdong Yin; and there is another collection of his writings from throughout his life.
Xin of the Sun clan from Linzi in Jin province left the household life, shaved his head, and received full ordination. He immediately devoted himself to the study of emptiness and stillness.

Hearing that Chan Master Yunju Deng was spreading his transformative influence in Zhongling, Xin traveled there to visit him. Having grasped the Master’s essential instructions, he attended by his side and could not bear to leave.
After a long time, when Yunju passed away, Xin went into seclusion on Mount Guangde. At that time, King Wenmu Qian...
The Marquis was then leading an army from Wu and Yue to attack Wanling. By chance, he entered a mountain temple, where the monks had all fled and were nowhere to be found;
only Xin sat upright in meditation, showing no sign of fear. When questioned as to the reason for this, he replied, "At present, both the east and the west are occupied by rebels.
Even if one wished to flee, where could one possibly go? The Marquis, impressed by his integrity, took him along when the army returned in triumph.
He returned, and King Wusuku treated him with special affection, assigning him residence in Ruiying Yuan and bestowing upon him the title Guangxian.

Initially, while Xing was gathering medicinal herbs in the mountains of Xuancheng, he first entered a cave that was exceptionally dark and obscure; after traveling only a few li, the sunlight suddenly shone brilliantly.

Beside it was a cavern, empty, bright, and spacious. A clear stream and ancient pines reflected and obscured one another from above and below. In a secluded corner stood a thatched hut, cut off from human tracks.
There, an old monk sat in meditation with his robes drawn close; suddenly opening his eyes, he asked Xin, "Where have you come from? Xin recounted the circumstances to him.

He said, "Alas, I am thirsty. He took out some fire embers from within the ashes to brew tea, which he drank. At dusk, Xīn said to him, "Please stay here; I have somewhere else to go," and eventually climbed up to the treetops.
There, he sat in the lotus position inside a bird's nest. At midnight, he heard the sound of someone reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*, followed by the sound of someone scolding a tiger;
the voice was clear and resonant, surpassing the whistling of the forest. The next day, Xīn requested to remain there. The monk said, "Since..."

"I have come here," he said. "I have seen the grass wither a hundred times; you cannot remain here. He asked if I was hungry. Just then, there were several hundred stalks of rice on the bank of a stream.
We led each other to gather more than ten stalks, rubbed them to extract the grain, pounded it into rice, and mixed it with wild vegetables to make a porridge for me to eat.
He hurriedly escorted me out to the mouth of the cave and thanked me, saying, "How could this be mere coincidence? That we should meet like this. A short while later, tea and—
The gruel was not produced by fire or smoke. "I know that from now on you will no longer suffer from hunger or thirst. Later, he went there again, but in the end could not find the way.
In his later years, he served as the presiding master for the reconstruction of the Treasure Pagoda. He passed away during the Tianfu era at the age of eighty.
Hong Zhen of the Han dynasty was born into the Hong family of Suizao in Huazhou. Having entered the monastic order, he recited the Lotus Sūtra and mastered its great meaning;

moreover, he made it his daily practice, accumulating a total of ten thousand fascicles. Subsequently, he presented a memorial to the imperial court, expressing his wish to burn his own body as an offering to a Buddhist stūpa.
Some slandered him, claiming that this would delude the masses and was an ill omen for the state. Consequently, an imperial edict sternly rebuked him and placed him under prohibition.
He stopped her. Zhenshen sighed and said, "This is surely because his roots of goodness are shallow while demonic obstacles are strong. What can be done?

He then withdrew to reside at Guang’ai Temple, where he gave away all his robes and alms bowls as offerings to the fourfold assembly. Shortly thereafter, he passed away without illness; his corpse remained seated in the lotus position.

After several more days, his countenance showed no sign of decay or change. When he was cremated, his tongue remained exceptionally fresh and pure. His fame spread throughout the regions between the Yi and Luo rivers.
He was only fifty-two years of age.
Han Ruoxu lived in seclusion on Mount Lu, reciting the sutras without leaving his room for several years.
Li Shi of Jiangnan admired him and repeatedly issued summons to invite him, yet he never rose to accept them. He would say each time, "This old monk has no virtue;
how could I dare trouble Your Majesty’s commands in such a manner? If you continue to insist without ceasing, I shall simply flee to the deep mountains and remote valleys."

He bid eternal farewell to the world, and from that time on, the court did not dare to compel him. Occasionally, they presented him with incense, tea, and clothing, yet there were many instances where he declined them;
thus, his purity and prudence are evident. During the Qianguo era, he passed away while sitting in meditation during the height of summer.
Although his body remained for a long time, it showed almost no signs of decay, nor was there any foul odor. How extraordinary!
Song Shilu’s secular surname was Jia; he was a native of Fanyang and a descendant of Wei Guogong Tan, the Tang Prime Minister.
At the age of fifteen, he received the tonsure at Minzhong Temple under the tutelage of Master Zhen She. Subsequently, he completed his full ordination.

He then traveled south to inquire into the essentials of the mind. Since the capital had been moved to Bianzhou at the end of the Tang dynasty, people throughout the realm had generally looked to him for guidance;
thus, wherever he stopped, scholars and officials alike revered him as their master. Consequently, he established a monastery in Mount Yimen to propagate his teachings.
By imperial decree, the temple was named Kaibao after the current era, and he was honored with official robes and titles, receiving abundant favor and prestige.

Yet the Vinaya-regulations viewed him with utter disdain. On the twenty-third day of the first month in the second year of the Qiandé era, he summoned his disciples to deliver his final instructions and passed away.
He was eighty-one years of age and sixty-two years of *dharma-śrāmaṇera* seniority.
In the third month of the fifth year of the Tàipíng Xīngguó era, his bier was moved for burial at the site of Xūnyú in the northern district. Jǐa Shǒulián, a Jinshi, composed the inscription for it.
The Pagoda.

Song Shouzhen’s secular surname was Ji. He was a native of Wannian in Yongxing. His ancestors had migrated west to Shu during the chaos of Huang Chao’s rebellion and settled there to register their households.
By the time of Shouzhen, he was a product of Shu. When he first reached the age for capping, he happened to visit Shengshou Temple and saw...

The Vinaya Master Xiujin admired his conduct and subsequently relied upon him to undergo the tonsure. He studied the *Awakening of Faith* under Master Lang and received the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* from Master Guang.
He transmitted the *Yogācāra* teachings from the Upādhyāya Yanmi. In all these matters, he reached the ultimate essentials of the mind-dharma.
For forty years, he expounded them without weariness. Consequently, he was granted the honorary title "Zhaoxin" (Illuminating Faith). Part One.
Ri said to his disciples on one occasion: "The proverb that 'one cannot guarantee the next breath upon exhaling' is indeed a worldly saying, yet it is profoundly true to principle.
How can you and I not apply ourselves to this? Thereupon, he constructed two stupas to the right of the Guangdu Monastery.

Since they were completed at the beginning of the Kaibao era, he inscribed them with the name "Kaibao. On the fifth day of the eighth month in the fourth year [of Kaibao], he assembled the congregation and proclaimed:

The Buddha’s name was Yishi (With-Gone). His age at death was seventy-eight, and his dharma-age was fifty-three. After cremation, he obtained crystalline and lustrous śarīra, which were enshrined in an opened treasure stūpa.
Song Yanjun, surnamed Lian, was a native of Jingzhou. He entered the monastic order in his youth and, upon reaching adulthood, perfected his precepts and virtue.

He subsequently traveled extensively across Mount Heng and Mount Lu to investigate the essential points of Chan. Once, while traveling with a companion to Fenglin, they lost their way and entered a deep valley.
He saw gold and silver objects scattered all over the ground. His friend’s expression suddenly changed; looking back at him, he said, "Fortunately, there is no one else here. We could pick them up.
Furthermore, if Heaven provides something and you do not take it, you will instead suffer for it. Why do you treat this with such indifference? Zunjing did not answer immediately.

Daozong of the Liang dynasty was a native of Jiangling in Jingzhou. His clan and lineage are unknown. He took the tonsure at an early age and resided at Waguan Monastery. By nature he was pure and refined;
his conduct, whether in motion or stillness, was always measured by constant standards. He applied himself diligently to study and was content with poverty and hardship.

At the end of the Qi dynasty, during a great famine, his alms-gathering did not suffice for his needs, so he traveled south to the regions beyond the Ling Mountains, where his Way flourished greatly. Furthermore, he vowed to convert others through the example of death, and subsequently passed away.
He lived for over fifty years. He resided at Juyan Xiansi Monastery, where his diligent cultivation of the Dharma was steadfast despite his poverty. His mastery of the teachings was truly peerless.
At the beginning of the Tianjian era, he traveled west to the "land of the sea" (the Western Regions) and returned east to the whole of Chu, where he performed great service in propagating the faith.

Huijian of the Liang dynasty was possessed of the Way and its practice, as well as strict observance of the precepts. By nature, he was bold and courageous. He served as a gatekeeper for the Duke Jianwu;
when the Master and the Duke went out to fill the vacancy in Jingzhou, they invited him to accompany them. To the east of the provincial seat, there was a separate chamber consisting of three rooms.
It was particularly convenient; however, it had been uninhabited for a long time, as strange anomalies were frequently observed there, making it prone to misfortune.
Upon arriving, he found a single room within the complex, which he used to enshrine a Buddha image, with two adjacent rooms to house his scriptures and receive guests.
While Simjian was still lying down and had not yet risen, he suddenly saw a blind man dressed in black robes approaching from—
The figure emerged from the wall and stood leaning against the door. Sim Xian’s mind and eyes were perfectly clear, yet he was unable to speak.
Nevertheless, his mental recollection of Avalokiteśvara did not cease for even a moment. The person said, "I knew your diligence, so I came to test you.
Since you can maintain such self-possession and composure, how would I dare to press you further? Suddenly, he entered the wall and did not emerge again. Sim Xian [recorded this].
He rose slowly to wash and rinse his face. After completing his ritual recitations, he returned to bed because of exhaustion.

He dreamed that the person he had seen before said to him, "I have resided here since the end of the Han dynasty for several hundred years. By nature, I am upright and rigid, and I often find it difficult to tolerate others.

Since you have cultivated yourself through pure conduct, I have yielded this place to you; do not be afraid. From then on, there was no further disturbance. Although many years passed, they felt like a single day.
After his departure, there was never again anyone who could succeed him in his lineage.
Wei Daodeng was born into the Rui clan of Dongguan; he was intelligent, alert, and possessed faith and vigor.

Having heard that the monk Sengyao in Xuzhou was elucidating the sutras and treatises, he took up his books and followed him, thoroughly investigating the *Nirvāṇa*, *Lotus*, and *Śrīmālā* sūtras. Later, he followed Sengyuan to study the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
His reputation shook the capital of Wei, and he was repeatedly summoned for official appointments. His fellow student Fadu said, "Why not go?

To transform others according to their circumstances and serve as a bridge and raft for sentient beings. That Huiyuan brushed off his robes at Mount Lu and Tan-di vanished from Kunshan were merely matters of a single era;
how can they be compared to the present? When [Dao'an] arrived in Luoyang, imperial favor extended to his entire clan. Because of his origins...
His surname was Bu-hua (Fuhua), and by imperial decree it was changed to Nai. He was followed by a multitude of monastics, and his lectures were held in great abundance.
In his later years, he resided at Mount Heng, where he eventually passed away at Baode Temple at the age of eighty-five, during the Jingming era.
Fazhen of the Wei dynasty’s lineage is unknown. He was a native of Dongguan in Bohai. At the age of nine, he left the household life and resided at Guangde Monastery in Luoyang.
At eleven, he took Daoji as his teacher and began reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Whenever there were points he could not understand, he would immediately pose questions;
thus, he came to master its meaning. Daoji especially praised him for this. As he grew older, he became proficient in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, becoming the equal of Sengjian.
As for their names: at that time, people regarded Jian as peerless in his construction of phrases and sentences, and Zhen as solitary in his subtle penetration of the mysteries;
moreover, they were mutual friends. Every time they lectured, there were thousands of listeners. With the offerings they received, they fashioned images for worship.

Wang Yi, Prince of Qinghe, and Wang Yue, Prince of Runan, both prostrated themselves before them and received their instructions. As the virtue of the Wei dynasty declined, they planned to travel southward during the Putong era of the Liang dynasty.
In the second year [of the Tianjian era], Sengzhen was overtaken by an advancing cavalry and died at the age of sixty-one. Sengjian was a native of Qinghe;
there were also Huicong and Daoji, both of whom were disciples of Master [Seng]gong and whose learning was likewise admirable. Sengjian traveled south to Jiangyin and resided at Heyuan Temple.
Emperor Wu issued an edict to assemble the monks at Leishou Hall to establish doctrinal positions, and it was Sengjian who carried out this undertaking.
Dunjin was intelligent and tranquil, and his final whereabouts remain unknown.
The monk Sengyi of the Wei dynasty frequently gathered disciples at the Shanshi Temple in the valley of Mount Tai.
This temple housed seven statues—of Goryeo, Xiangguo, Nüguo, Wuguo, Kunyang, and Daijing—all of which were made of gilded bronze.

The model [of the Buddha] was exquisitely beautiful in its physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). It was displayed within the hall without locks or keys, so as to allow for unrestrained veneration;
yet, not even birds or beasts dared to enter. Thus, the *Lingyan zan* (Inscription on the Spirit-Response) says: "They come through spiritual resonance, truly beyond designation.

This means that while their supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) were manifest in the unseen realm, no one knew from where they came. Consequently, I have restrained myself to offer worship until my final years.

One evening before his death, he saw a śrāmaṇera who had already passed away. The śrāmaṇera prostrated and said, "Since I first disobeyed you and entered your service, I have been constantly driven and employed by the Heavenly Emperor, which has caused me to neglect my cultivation of the Way.
I have heard in secret that the Heavenly Emperor will soon invite the Master to lecture on the sutras;

I pray that through a single word from you, I may be granted release from this physical suffering. Thereupon, [the Master] immediately bathed, changed his robes, burned incense, and sat upright in expectation. Before long, [the śrāmaṇera appeared].
When Guo, adorned with official robes and ceremonial insignia like a person of high rank and distinction in the world, entered the monastery, his spirit ultimately departed.

Furthermore, the *dujiang* (lecturer) and the *weina* (chant master)—the officials in charge of monastic affairs—each resided in different counties; yet it was verified that their deaths all occurred on the same day.
Tanzun of Qi was the son of the Cheng family of Hebei. From his youth, he felt weary of the dust of desire; yet his physical appearance remained exceptionally handsome and flourishing.

He once sought ordination under Master Faguang, but Master Guang, fearing that Tanzun might be swayed between worldly defilement and pure monasticism, sent him back to lay life. Once his resources for study were clear and his learning was established, he became a worthy vessel for the times.
The Wei dynasty appointed him as a Yuanwailang (Junior Court Official), but this was not his heart’s intent. He requested permission to return to Master Guang once more, and Master Guang...

The Duke still refused, citing his previous apprehensions. Sengzun knelt and petitioned him, saying, "I now dedicate my life to taking refuge [in the Triple Gem] and shall forever honor the Ultimate Way.

If you do not grant me your favor, I will surely follow false views and bring ruin to the Three Jewels. When Hui Guang examined his insight and found it profound, he immediately conferred upon him the full precepts (*upasampadā*) and directed him toward diligent study.
After more than twelve years, [he mastered] the sudden meaning of the One Vehicle and the source of the mind within the Dharma-realm. Both...

He analyzed and expounded upon the principles of doctrine with such brilliance that he far surpassed his contemporaries. Initially, he propagated his teachings in Luoyang; subsequently, they spread throughout Qi, Chu, Jin, and Wei, reaching as far as Yan and Zhao.

He relied exclusively on oral instruction to guide and govern his followers, following a tradition of succession without producing written works. Prince Wang Gong of Huaiyin, the Chancellor, held him in high esteem and treated him with profound respect.

When he was over seventy years old, the Prince appointed him as the head of the national capital, and he soon thereafter ascended to the position of Commander-in-Chief. Shortly after, he fell slightly ill.

Sitting in meditation, he recited the *Vimalakīrti* and *Śrīmālādevī* sūtras; having finished the final fascicle, he passed away at the age of eighty-five. Sengzun was by nature pure and lofty; his deportment was always dignified and lawful.
When opening doors or drawing back curtains, his body never intruded upon the secular world. His mouth never uttered vulgar speech, and his eyes never looked upon anything improper.

Nevertheless, his reverence for former masters and his nurturing of junior disciples were rarely equaled in his time. When Master Guang passed away, [Daoyuan] followed the prescribed rites while residing in Qizhou;
upon hearing the news of the funeral announcement, he wailed with such grief that he fainted and fell from his bed, and warm blood gushed from his mouth—such was his filial piety.
Qi Tan-yan was of the Xiahou clan from Nan-yuan Province. He was born with his teeth and gums already fully formed, which people regarded as extraordinary.

At the age of seven, he entered a local school; at fifteen, his province selected him to serve in the provincial capital. During his leisure time from official duties, he would attend lectures at Buddhist monasteries.

At eighteen, he was recommended as a *xiucai* (talented scholar) and traveled to the capital city of Ye. Upon passing by Master Guang’s dharma seat, he immediately received the precepts of taking refuge and devoted himself to the study of the mind.

At the age of twenty-three, he followed Master Guang to tonsure his hair and receive full ordination. He applied himself to his studies with ever-increasing diligence, to the point of forgetting both eating and resting.
Whenever he encountered a point of doubt, he would consult the eminent and venerable masters; yet they all declined, saying they were unable to answer him.

He once turned to his disciples and said, "Since I followed my teacher, there have been points I did not understand. Every time I contemplated them, I attained realization. It is like looking down with a lowered gaze."
In the darkness, he could see nothing. When he gradually extended his neck and stepped out of the door, everything near and far became visible.

From this point on, the profound transformation spread throughout Qi, Zheng, Yan, and Zhao, with people flocking to him like spokes converging at a hub. Although he encountered obstacles and discouragement, his composure in the face of hardship remained unshakable.
Thus, the Prince of Zhaojun, Rong Rui; the Prince of Shangluo, Yuan Hai; and Du Bi, the Regional Inspector of Jiaozhou—all being high-ranking relatives and eminent ministers—deeply [honored him].
Respectfully submitted. Zu Xiaozheng, the Palace Secretary, memorialized that [the site] should be made the capital of the state.

On the eighteenth day of the third month of the first year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, with palms joined, he invoked the name of Maitreya, his countenance serene and joyful; at the meridian, he passed away in Mingzhou.

Regarding the Lu family: previously, there was a dream in which Huayan was dressed in vermilion robes with his topknot hanging down to his shoulders, attended by two children behind him, as he traveled through the air toward the northwest.
The world took this to mean that he had been reborn in heaven.
Sengyuan of the Qi dynasty was by nature lax and unrestrained; he did not cultivate refined conduct.

While residing at Xue Temple in Liangzhou, in the third year of the Wuping era, he dreamed of a great man who bit his teeth in anger and rebuked him, saying: "You are a renunciant, yet your countenance is such as this, and you still allow yourself to commit evil.
Why do you not take a mirror and look upon it? Upon waking, he was struck with terror and broke into a sweat. He then reflected the sunlight into a basin of water to examine himself.
He saw that the colors around his eyes were dark and murky. At first, he thought it was due to grime and oil, so he immediately felt them with his hand to wipe them away.

Suddenly, his eyebrows fell off entirely as he touched them. Greatly alarmed, he thereafter followed the rules and laws in every matter, never daring to transgress them. After more than a month, he again dreamed of the same person, who said joyfully:
"To recognize one's faults and reform—this is what is called wisdom. Exert yourself; do not repeat the errors of the past. The next day...
His face and eyes were moist and lustrous, and his eyebrows grew slightly longer; through such disciplined cultivation, he became a refuge for those in his village.
Tanyi of the Qi dynasty was the son of Shi, the Regional Inspector of Henei. From his youth, he felt weary of the mundane world and strictly observed the monastic precepts.

He recited the scriptures to the extent of three hundred thousand words, constantly memorizing and retaining them day and night as his regular practice. Upon reaching the required age, he received full ordination from Vinaya Master Daofu. Furthermore...

Relying upon him, he listened to and received instruction with such diligent application that he surpassed his contemporaries. Later, through the transformative influence of Master Guang, he underwent a change and refinement;
thus, he ultimately completed his mastery under Master Guang. Hou Jing, the Regional Inspector of Dingzhou, admired him and invited him to serve, providing him with all necessary provisions.
Gao Longzhi, the Minister of the Interior, likewise treated him with exceptional courtesy and honor. Consequently, the banks of the Zhang River were permeated by his profound teachings. When Jing...
The Xingtai [Governor’s Office] built Dayan Temple east of Ye. Daoyin widely disseminated the monastic rules and precepts; the five groups of disciples looked up to him as their teacher.

He resolved and adjudicated questions as they arose, his explanations of the texts and meanings being elegant and correct. At that time, there was a śramaṇa named Daole, whose practice and understanding were both exemplary, and whom all people admired.
Thus, a proverb in Ye went: "Regarding the Vinaya school, for clarity and brevity, there is only Yin and Le. Such was the weight of their reputations. However, Daoyin...
By nature, Daoxing did not keep disciples; he traveled alone with his staff, while his robes and bowl followed him constantly like the wings of a bird.
To the east of India, those who were truly skilled in the Vinaya were few, and Huiyin was the only one. At the age of sixty-three, he passed away at Dajue Temple in Ye.
He authored a four-fascicle commentary (*chao*) that remains in circulation today. His more than ten disciples all became accomplished masters, which is truly praiseworthy.

Furthermore, there was one named Hongli who authored a two-fascicle sub-commentary (*chao*). Later, Zhishou expanded and clarified its terminology and meaning, reorganized its structural headings, and edited it into four fascicles, which were recited everywhere.
Qifa’s family name was Liu, and he was a native of Chaoge. At five years of age, he entered a local school and mastered what he studied and recited.
At six, he once accompanied his younger paternal uncle to a Buddhist temple, where he would immediately prostrate and offer praise. At nine, he happened to read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
He immediately grew weary of the world and sought to leave the household life. At the age of twelve, he went to the Chan Master Daoyao to receive the tonsure.

As he traveled through various regions, those who knew him in the Eastern Capital called him the "Holy Śrāmaṇera. Later, he lived in seclusion on Mount Linlü, where he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*.

Within barely ten days, he had mastered both sections [of the Vinaya] and thoroughly comprehended their meanings. Shortly thereafter, he entered Luoyang, where his reputation became exceedingly great. At the age of fifteen, he lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
those who challenged him with doubts and difficulties were all left sighing in admiration and submission. He was skilled at interrogation and delighted in rigorous examination.
Yet, because his appearance was dark and emaciated, people of the time had a proverb regarding him: "If the Black Śrāmaṇera comes, the high seat meets with disaster."
During a year of famine, he subsisted on vegetables and mended his robes from grass to avoid hunger and cold, while devoting himself single-mindedly to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

His spiritual cultivation progressed daily, and he subsequently followed Master Guang to receive the full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*). He soon went to attend to his father’s illness; upon his arrival, the father had already passed away.

Consequently, he took his mother’s elder sister as a nun by hand and brought her to the capital of Ye. He spent the summer at Shaolin and returned home for a visit in the autumn; however, due to the recurring state of famine, their reunion was not yet complete.

The region was tranquil and peaceful. The assembly requested that he propagate the teachings extensively. Thereupon, he turned the wheels of the *Daśabhūmika*, *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, *Laṅkāvatāra*, *Nirvāṇa*, and other sūtras without ceasing, while also composing commentaries and sub-commentaries upon them.
Furthermore, his mental acuity was unshakable and his organizational principles were systematic. Consequently, people of the time spoke of him in verse, saying:
"Looking toward the capital, the foremost place for the Way is the Dharma Hall; [Dharmottara] is nearly forty years of age, traveling and transforming beings in Huai and Wei."

Recently, the Great General Gao Cheng submitted a memorial appointing him as the Director of the Office of the Orthodox and Mysterious (Zhāoxuántóng) to oversee monastic affairs. When the Qi dynasty underwent its revolution, he continued to hold this office.
During the reign of Emperor Wenxuan, an imperial edict conferred upon him the Bodhisattva Precepts; the Emperor personally spread his hair upon the ground so that [Huiyuan] might step upon it.
In the second year of the Tiānbão era, an edict was issued to convert the grounds of the Eagle Master’s Bureau into Bàodé Temple, and a precious stupa was erected there.
On behalf of the Grand Empress Dowager, he prayed for her posthumous merit. Before long, he was elevated to the rank of *Dàtǒng* (Great Patriarch).

Initially, the court deliberated on establishing ten *tǒngs*, but they were concerned that the titles were not sufficiently distinguished. Upon submitting a memorial, the Emperor personally annotated the document, stating:

"The *Shàngfǎshī* (Supreme Dharma Master) shall be the *Dàtǒng*; the others shall be *Shàngtǒng*s. At that time, Wang Gaode, the Chancellor of the State of Goguryeo, sent a letter inquiring about the teachings of the Gate.
He wrote a detailed response to [the inquiry] regarding the origins [of the matter], which is not recorded here. By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Dingguo Temple in Xiangzhou.
Furthermore, using offerings and profits, he constructed a meditation temple on the western mountains of Ye. The mountain was originally named He-shui;

at its summit, he built a Maitreya Hall and provided for one hundred and fifty monks. When the Qi dynasty fell and the Zhou regime suppressed the Buddhist teachings, the Master donned lay clothing and lived in seclusion, offering prayers.

He was reborn in Maitreya’s Inner Court and would no longer return to Xiuding Monastery. At the beginning of the Great Tang, when Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty was acting as regent for the Zhou, the Great Dharma gradually flourished.
Upon hearing of this, the Emperor’s joy was manifest on his countenance; though his body was frail and weak, he immediately draped a *kāṣāya* over his head.
He had his disciples carry him to Xiuding Monastery. There, he joined his palms, performed three prostrations, and circumambulated the building to the right before departing.

He immediately returned to his hermitage at Heishui Mountain, where he recited the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra, the Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra, and other texts until he passed away on the eighteenth day of the seventh month in the second year [of the Kaihuang era].
He was eighty-six years old. His writings include the *Zengyi shufafa* (Forty fascicles), the *Foxing lun* (Two fascicles), and the *Dasheng yizhang*.
Six fascicles. One fascicle of the *Zhongjing lu* (Catalogue of All Scriptures) circulates in the world.

His disciple Lingyu has a biography. Chen Hongyan was born into the Xie family of Shanyin, Kuaiji. His grandfather, Mao-gong, lived in seclusion and did not serve in office. His father, Zang, was an official associate of the Prince of Hengyang of the Liang dynasty.
At a tender age, Yan left the household life; his spirit and appearance were exceptionally refined, and he studied both Buddhist and secular classics. He possessed...

He was praised throughout his home village. Upon reaching adulthood, he traveled to the capital, where he audited the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya* and *Tattvasiddhi* extensively. He ultimately received instruction from Dharma Master Chao of Longguang Temple.

After three or four years of study, he was able to penetrate its profound and subtle depths; the assembly turned to him for guidance, and he propagated the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* with great success, as well as various other treatises.
His exegesis was unprecedented; at that time, even those of advanced age remained stuck in their stagnation, and the ancient commentaries had not been elucidated—until he [brought them] to rest.

He alone raised the pure and stirred up the turbid, refusing to yield or compromise. Consequently, those who came to study under him distanced themselves from him because of his forthright and critical manner;

he thus cultivated his aspirations in a secluded chamber, holding his principles in high esteem. When Emperor Tai Zong of the Liang dynasty was still the Crown Prince, he admired his outstanding brilliance.
He wished to have him return to secular life so that he might serve as a scholar-official, but Sengyan remained steadfastly humble and retired, maintaining his self-possession.

It happened that Emperor Wu summoned all the great virtuous monks to the Chongyun Hall to lecture; although Sengyan was the youngest in seniority and sat at the furthest end of the assembly, his arguments were profound and inspired, earning the Emperor’s special appreciation.
Shortly thereafter, due to the calamities caused by the non-Chinese tribes and successive years of famine, he moved to Jinyun, where he found joy.
Regarding those springs and rocks: before long, he was forced to flee from mountain bandits and found no peace anywhere.

When Xiao Shaor, the Prince of Changsha of the Liang dynasty, filled the city of Ying and invited him to Zhugong, Zhugong fell into ruin. With the upper reaches blocked by chaos, he returned eastward.

He then traveled extensively through Ruoye and Yunmen; he once ascended the Shengping Pavilion in Wu and composed a poem to record his inspiration, the words of which are recorded [in the *Gaoseng Zhuan*].
Separate Collection. At the beginning of the Tianjia era of the Chen dynasty, he gathered disciples and established a lecture hall at Wuxian Temple.

Whenever there was an interval between lectures, he would invariably visit Kaishan and Dinglin on Mount Zhong to rest his mind through seated meditation. The poems he composed therein were not recorded. By imperial decree, he was appointed as an attendant for the envoy from Northern Qi, Cui Ziwu;
he was highly praised for his conduct, yet he firmly declined all gifts and rewards. On the twentieth day of the ninth month of the fifth year...
One day, he passed away at Xuānwǔ Temple due to illness at the age of sixty-one.

On the twenty-ninth day of that month, his entire body was enshrined as a *śītavana* (charnel ground) offering on the eastern ridge of Kāishàn Monastery, in accordance with his final testament. His collected works, comprising twenty fascicles, were circulated in the world.
Chen Huiming was a man of unknown origins. Because his physical appearance resembled that of a foreigner (*hu*), he was popularly known as "Hu Ming.

He drew extensively from the sutras and śāstras and read widely across books and histories. His extraordinary eloquence and grand discourses were so swift and his analogies so ingenious that none among his peers could withstand him.
During the Tianjia period, whenever the court organized merit-making vegetarian feasts, the common people followed suit in a wave of imitation; yet Huiming alone maintained his own course.
He possessed a clever and eloquent tongue. When many came to invite him for audiences, the assembly would defer to him and not contest his position.

Thereupon, he clearly drew upon examples from antiquity and the present, encompassing both Confucius and Laozi, striving only to ensure that his listeners were pleased and satisfied. In the fifth year of the Dajian era, he was about to undertake a northern expedition.

He dispatched the Grand Commander Cheng Wenji and others to lead troops to the banks of the Huai River; their morale surpassed that of the Qi fortifications, yet victory and defeat remained undecided.
The Emperor was deeply concerned and, at the Dajidian Palace, ordered a tortoise to be used for divination. Suddenly, the markings on its belly split wide open.

The ruler and his ministers looked at one another with expressions of fear, generally regarding it as an omen of misfortune. He immediately provided a vegetarian feast for a hundred monks, and once the rite was performed—

When the incense had been offered, he was about to state the purpose of the vegetarian feast when Ming suddenly responded by composing a narrative. He further recounted its origins, saying: "The tortoise shell cracked when divining the expedition;
this may be called the opening of a road of a thousand li. For the patterns on the belly of a tortoise are what the common folk call 'a thousand li.
At that time, it was regarded as merely a temporary embellishment. Yet when the army reached the Great and Small Xia Mountains, every battle was victorious, and they captured Qin."
Xing harmonized the four prefectures and brought them back [to the central authority]. An imperial edict was issued to commend and exhort him; thus, Ming’s legacy flourished even further.
Regarding the fundamental principles of the school, he was especially renowned for his profound understanding. His final whereabouts remained unknown thereafter.

Chen Falang’s secular surname was Zhou; he was a native of Pei in Pei Commandery, Xuzhou. His grandfather, Zhong Fengshu, served as the Palace Attendant for the Yellow Gate (Gishilō Ōmon Shōrō) and Regional Inspector of Qingzhou.
His father, Zhong Shenguī, served as an Extraordinary Cavalier Attendant (Enge Sanjisōji) and Governor of Pei Commandery.

His mother, Lady Liu, dreamed that a divine being riding in a celestial palace entered her womb, and her body became as vast as empty space. Upon waking, her four limbs felt light and at ease, and she subsequently conceived.
She strictly avoided the five pungent vegetables and various strong flavors. When Senglang was born, he was endowed with pure filial piety and possessed high moral integrity.
As he grew older, an imperial decree assigned him to General Xu Ziyuan—who held the rank of Acting Commander-in-Chief—to lead the northern campaign. He alone...

He reflected: "Warfare is an instrument of cruelty, and the body is a source of suffering. To kill others for the sake of exalting oneself—even if one were victorious in battle and received the reward of a noble fief—such a thing should not be done;

how much less so for that which is yet uncertain. On the second day of the second month in the second year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty, he consequently shaved his head and became a monk in Qingzhou.
He traveled to study in the capital, Yangdu, where he followed Master Bao of Daming Temple.
Master Zhi received the methods of Chan meditation; he listened to Vinaya Master Tuan lecture on the Vinaya;
he investigated the *Tattvasiddhi* under Master Xian of Nanjian; and he studied the *Abhidharma* under Master Jing of Zhujian.

His reputation stirred the capital, yet he considered that the sublime teachings of Vulture Peak and the legacy of Nāgārjuna still remained to be inherited and must certainly be explored. Thereupon, he [studied] with Sengquan of Zhiguan Temple on Mount She.

The Master was then propagating the teachings of the late virtuous master Lang in the world. He further studied and received the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Dvādaśanikāya-śāstra*, and scriptures such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
In the eleventh month of the second year of the Yongding era, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Xinghuang Monastery.
Disciples gathered like clouds, prostrating themselves with sweat pouring from their brows. He expounded the sutras and śāstras more than twenty times each. During the Dajian [era]...
In the thirteenth year, on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month, he moved to the quarters of Shen Temple.
At the age of seventy-five, on the twenty-eighth day of that same month, he was interred on the western ridge of Sheshan in Luoluo Village, Jiangsheng County.
Initially, Master Lang had silently transmitted the profound principles of the Madhyamaka to Sengquan; Sengquan, in turn, transmitted them to Lang and Bianbu.
Yong and others considered these teachings to be refined and subtle, fit only for the wise to practice. Thus, the Sūtra states: "Do not preach this sūtra to those who harbor views of a self;
do not speak of it extensively to those who merely delight in the Dharma. This was truly because there must be a correspondence between the medicine and the ailment.
Later, as they gradually spread their influence, none surpassed Hui-lang. Formerly, the divine monk Baozhi once recorded: "A person in black robes shall open the temple..."
The scholar [Shi] widely propagated the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, there was the layman Du Facan of Nanmo, who was over eighty years old; he devoted his life to the Dharma with single-minded resolve.

He once dreamed that within the temple, banners, flowers, and musical instruments filled the halls and pavilions, while monks and laypeople crowded the seats. At this time, the signs were especially manifest:
when the temple attendants struck the bell for the conclusion of the meal, they missed the proper hour. Lang knocked on the door at dawn to urge them, but the whale-bell...

The bells of the musical stands resounded spontaneously; was this not the Way of resonance and response? In the Spring Hall, Prince Shubao of the Eastern Palace convened an assembly on the meaning of [Buddhist] terminology;

he personally recounted the provisional names established by Senglang, and finally composed an inscription to manifest his intent. Jiang Zong of Jiyang, the Court Counselor to the Crown Prince, wrote the epitaph for his tomb.
Fayuan of the Sui dynasty was born into the Ren clan in Hexi. He was by nature alert and discerning, possessing a high-minded character that set him apart from his peers.
While still a layman, he traveled east to the capital of Ye. There, Fashang—the Great Patriarch of the *Zhaoxuan* [Buddhist Registry]—was struck by his conversation and marveled at him;

he subsequently took him under his care and ordained him as a monk. Thereupon, Fayuan traveled extensively among lecture halls, seeking the Dharma without weariness, and followed in the footsteps of Upāli.

He specialized exclusively in the Vinaya-piṭaka. Regarding all that was transmitted to the Eastern Land (China), he composed commentaries on their principles (*yìshù*), masterfully reconciling differences and establishing or refuting more than one hundred various interpretations of the schools.
At the time, he was renowned as the "Tiger of the Vinaya. As for matters concerning legal adjudication and administrative procedures, he mostly followed the literal phrasing of the texts;

his deliberations and final rulings were universally accepted as authoritative. By imperial decree, he was appointed to serve as the *shàngzǎo* (Superior Administrator) of both the Dazhuangyan and Shiku Monasteries.
During the Sui dynasty, after they had received the abdication of the throne, he was again summoned by imperial decree to serve as the head of Daxingguo Monastery in Bingzhou.

He repeatedly held the position of administrative director, managing the assembly with great skill; commentators praised him for this. On the twenty-second day of the sixth month in the seventh year of the Kaihuang era, he passed away at the monastery where he resided.
He was sixty-four years old. A stupa was erected and he was buried in a corner of the city. Of his writings, only those on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* remain.

It was not a transcription; only two fascicles remain, while the rest have been lost. His disciples, Daohang, Kan, and others, were sufficient to uphold the lineage and exalt the ancestral tradition, their reputations being preeminent in their time.
Fǎ'ān of the Sui dynasty was born into the Tián family in Zhījiāng. He entered the monastic order in his youth. At the age of eighteen, he traveled to Jīnlíng.
Initially, he studied the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, and later he relied upon Master Lǎng of Xīnghuáng to investigate the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.

Among his fellow students, he was renowned for being "triple-superlative," meaning that his dignified bearing was tall and elegant, his understanding of the doctrines was profound and excellent, and his asceticism and purity of character were unsurpassed. He frequently [discussed] the different interpretations regarding the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

He ordered the assembly to attack him with arguments, yet despite their eloquence, none could defeat him. When Master Lang questioned him, his responses were like echoes following sounds. Subsequently, Lang asked, "Is your meaning exhausted?
He replied, "Meanings are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; how could they ever be exhausted? At that time, many students referred to themselves by the name "An" (Peaceful).
Consequently, he alone was distinguished by being called "Sha-an" (Sands-An). Regarding the *Three Treatises* and the *Four Scriptures*, he expounded upon them all through his chanting and preaching.
On his behalf, he composed the *Guangchu*, *Lujiao*, and other chapters, which circulated throughout the regions of the Yangtze and Han rivers.

Shortly thereafter, he followed Master Cheng in the practice of meditation, abstaining from monastic food and refusing to drink fermented grain liquors. He refined his mind and nature in such a manner.
At the age of sixty-seven, he passed away at Dengjie Temple. To the west of the temple lay Shazhou, where the scholar Liu Qiu had annotated the *Lotus Sūtra*.
This was the site of the monastery. Today, the remains of the sutra platform still exist.
The Sui monk Yuan (淵) was of the Li clan and a native of Qi in Guanghan, Shu. His family possessed abundant wealth;

at the time of his birth, it rained coins from heaven and grain gushed forth from the earth—surely this was due to the fruition of his merit. At the age of eighteen, he entered the Conquest Monastery (Kāngxīng) in his hometown.
He shaved his head and became a monk. Shortly thereafter, he entered the capital and relied upon the śramaṇa Sengbao of Zhuhu Temple to practice meditative concentration.

Having been on friendly terms with Dharma Master Yi of the same temple since his youth, he now once again studied together with him. Yi was particularly well-versed in non-Buddhist classics and skilled in cursive and clerical scripts.

When the Zhou dynasty suppressed the teachings, [Sengbian] immediately returned to demolish the temple where he had previously resided. With the rise of the Sui dynasty, he reconstructed it anew; leading the craftsmen, he oversaw the felling of timber.
Once, after a long period of rain, the weather cleared as soon as he prayed for it. When constructing the *cakra* (spire) for a stupa, he was determined to have it made of gold;
he then dug into the earth and recovered gold to provide for its use. Later, he built a bridge over the Jinjiang River.

It was rumored that Zhuge Wuhou had once sunk an iron *dun* (gong) into the water, measuring eight or nine feet in length and three feet in diameter, though such a thing has never been seen by the world. Once the bridge was completed...
The *dui* gong floated up on its own; having done so, it was subsequently lost again. People regarded this as a divine sign.
Sengyi passed away on the twelfth day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Renshou era at the age of sixty-nine. Yuan said, "How could I possibly remain here alone?"

He continued his studies for another day before passing away at the age of eighty-four. His final instruction was that he be buried together with [his teacher], so his disciples did not dare to disobey it.
The Sui monk Shi was a native of Qingzhou; carrying his book-bag, he traveled to seek the Way, his traces extending throughout Qi and Lu. He possessed a formidable spirit and a resolute will.
In his discourses, no one was able to withstand the sharpness of his brilliance. During the Kaihuang era, he entered the capital and resided at Xingshan Monastery.

At the beginning of the Renshou era, he received an imperial decree to deliver a śarīra relic to Hongzang Monastery in Laizhou; in the fourth year, he again delivered it to Maosheng Monastery in Mizhou, in both cases establishing stupas for its enshrinement.
As for the man known as Fushang of the Sui dynasty, no one knew who he was. He was frequently seen in Yizhou;

at night he would stay at Jingde Temple, and during the day he would hang his rain hat by the side of the road and sit beneath it to read the sutras. To those who passed by, he never called out to them to solicit alms.
Even when people threw coins into his hat, he did not offer prayers of thanks. However, though his location was secluded and remote, there were many who visited him daily.

"How much have you gained? A person of faith passed by and said to him, "Why have you abandoned the bustling marketplace of Gogŭng-dong to the west of the city and come here? Pu replied, "One or two coins are enough."
"What need is there for such elaboration? Liangzhou Prefect Zhao Zhongshu was by nature a cruel official. Upon hearing of this, he went to test him.
Riding past him, he feigned dropping one thousand coins on the ground and continued on his way without looking back. Fuyi continued reading his scriptures as if nothing had happened.
After they had gone some distance, Zhongshu sent someone back to retrieve the dropped coins, but Fuyi paid them no mind at all. Zhongshu was suddenly struck with awe.
He turned back and questioned Fu, saying, "Did you see me drop coins on the ground? Fu replied, "I saw them. Feng said, "Where are those coins now?
Fu replied, "I saw someone take them away. Feng said, "You sat here all day and could not obtain a single coin.
When there were strings of coins that you could have taken, you did not take them, but instead allowed others to take them. How, then, can your mind be described? Fu replied, "My..."
"There is no such thing. Furthermore, how could I dare to falsely claim it? Zhongshu said, "Give me the *kāṣāya* on your body; may I have it?
Fu folded it and gave it to him, saying, "If you can take it with you, there will surely be others who will offer it to you. This may be called 'gain and loss being of one accord.
Zhongshu dismounted from his horse and bowed in thanks, saying, "My family has served the Zhou dynasty for generations, reaching back to this third generation..."

"Generations have passed, yet the monks I have encountered number no fewer than tens of millions. However, those who are not greedy are rare; people come to visit me merely because they have heard my name, for no other reason.
I request that you go to Lingzhou to provide offerings. Fu said, "That is most excellent. I only wish that you, sir, would govern with compassion and forbearance to bring peace to the common people;
in doing so, you would bestow much more upon this poor monk than could ever be achieved by the four requisites. What further need is there to wait for those four things? Zhong—
He sighed deeply and departed; Fu also soon went into hiding. Later, a man from Yizhou named Su Xiang encountered him in Yangzhou;
his countenance always appeared as if he were fifty years of age.
Mingfen of the Sui dynasty was a native of Xiang. During the Qi period, the Tripitaka Master Yaśas from India was renowned throughout the world for his expertise in translation;

Mingfen admired him deeply and requested instruction, subsequently serving him as his teacher. At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, when the four seas were unified under one rule, an imperial edict summoned him to work alongside Indian monks on the simultaneous translation of the Dharma-texts, with Mingfen specifically charged with the duty of verifying errors. During the Renshou era, pagodas were erected.
An imperial edict was issued to dispatch śarīra relics to Shikuzan in Cizhou; [the Master] did not dare to treat this with negligence.
Fayaun of the Sui dynasty was the son of Chen of Su; he was widely learned and possessed integrity of character.

Having thoroughly mastered the various texts of Confucius and Laozi, he even mastered the works of Zi Xia and below, as well as the epitaphs and biographies composed by Wang Sengru and others—there were none that he could not recall and retain. He was particularly skilled in the *xi* (seating/ritual) arts.

He would lead the chanting of scriptures for the upper classes, serving as a ritual guide for vegetarian feasts; he prepared more than a hundred scrolls of ancient liturgical texts and mastered over seven hundred melodic variations (*kṣetra*) of scriptural recitation with exceptional fluency.
Consequently, invitations arrived one after another, and he rushed to respond to them so busily that he had no leisure even by the day.
At the age of thirty, on the first day of the New Year, he resolutely severed these ties and ceased such activities altogether. He then began to study the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and was able to—

He recited the scriptures again and again until he was free from error or omission. He soon settled at Xixia, where he received the dharma of dhyāna. He later traveled to Lingyan on Mount Tai to practice the *pratyutpanna-samādhi*.

In his leisure time, he drew water, split firewood, and swept the corridors and eaves. Later, he returned to his native village, where he encountered the famous statue of Fushi being reduced to ashes, with nothing remaining.
Sengyun wished to recreate it, but as the proportions were not clearly defined, he ultimately installed a new image.
Thus, he established the foundations and performed the rites for eighty-four thousand stupas to seek a spiritual response. Suddenly, he encountered an old woman who gave him a scroll.

Upon casually examining it, he found it contained the causal conditions and architectural models for the images. He then constructed them strictly according to these instructions, and they yielded great signs of efficacy.

Furthermore, while once residing on Yanghu Island in the sea, he remained calm and composed amidst hurricanes and malevolent spirits; even at midday, his mind was as tranquil as if he were sitting under a mulberry tree.
Mai died in the fourth year of the Renshou era (604 CE). He was thirty-five years of age.
Sui Fashun was a monk at Yanxing Temple in the capital; later, he resided at Donglin Temple on Mount Lu in Jiangzhou.
During the Renshou era, an imperial edict was issued to construct a stūpa on that very site to enshrine the śarīra.

Sui Mingyu was a native of Yingzhou; he was a master of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*. In the eighth year of the Kaihuang era, he further studied under Master Xian, seeking instruction and inquiry.
His level of realization was difficult to fathom. By nature, he was magnanimous and forgiving; even when others provoked him with anger or abuse, he never showed a look of resentment.
He resided at the Anāsrava Monastery (*Anāsrava-vihāra*), where students carrying their book-cases followed one another in shoulder-to-shoulder crowds and footstep-after-footstep succession.

By imperial decree during the Renshou era, he was sent with śarīra relics to Chongfan Monastery in Jizhou; offerings poured in like mountains and clouds, providing everything necessary for the construction of the stupa without any deficiency.
Zhi Guo of the Sui dynasty was a native of Shan in Kuaiji. He was a man of refined talent and noble character. He recited the Lotus Sūtra and understood its great meaning;

he was particularly fond of literary composition and was highly esteemed by his contemporaries. His calligraphy rivaled that of the Right General (Wang Xizhi). When Emperor Yang was still a prince at Jin, someone presented Zhi Guo’s writing to him.
The Emperor summoned him to perform a brushwork demonstration, but Zhi Guo declined, remarking with a sigh: "I am a man who has left the household life; how could I serve as a subject to a king?"

He was a gatekeeper who declined the appointment on the pretext of impaired vision. The King grew angry and imprisoned him at Jiangdu, ordering him to guard the treasure tower and the sutra repository.
Upon the Emperor’s accession to the Eastern Palace and his subsequent tour of Jiangdu, [Zhi] submitted the "Eulogy on the Prince’s Eastern Tour. Its preface states in brief:
"Zhi Guo shook out his robes to leave the mundane world and traveled to Liang in pursuit of righteousness. Moved by the patronage he received in the past, he rejoices this morning..."
In celebration of this auspicious occasion, he issued an order to release him, granted him ten thousand coins and two golden bells, and summoned him to the capital.
He resided at Huiji Temple until his death in the Eastern Capital.
Sui Jing was born into the Zhang family of Gu’an in Zhuojun. At the age of fifteen, he left the household life to become a monk.

There was a śramaṇa named Jingrong, who had thoroughly investigated the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* and was well-versed in both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras. Jing initially relied upon him, frequently inquiring about profound doctrines; however, Jingrong was unable to provide answers.
Consequently, he urged Jing to go to the capital or Ye to pursue his studies, saying, "You will surely become a vessel of great achievement. Once...
Upon reaching adulthood, he followed the Vinaya Master Rongzhi of Taixue Temple to exhaustively study the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*.
He subsequently visited the two Vinaya Masters Hui and Yun to seek their instruction; his only regret was that he had not yet had the leisure to examine the Hīnayāna teachings in detail.

Furthermore, he approached the two masters of the śāstras, Daoyou and Fadan, to investigate the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Samyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*. Regarding works such as the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, the *Jñānaprasthāna*, and the *Śāriputrābhidharma*, he attained a comprehensive understanding of them all.
He was widely renowned and his fame was great. King Langya of the Qi dynasty held him in high esteem and respect.
Every spring, he would gather disciples and arrange seats, honoring [the Master] as the Dharma Lord to encourage later students.

Amidst the upheavals caused by the Zhou dynasty, he subsequently crossed the Yangtze River together with over three hundred monks, including fellow practitioners Xuanlu, Faguī, and Fakǎn. At that time, Emperor Xuan dispatched the Palace Attendant Yuan Xian to Jingkou to pay his respects.
[The Emperor] received him. He subsequently dispatched the Prince Consort Cai Ning to proclaim an imperial decree, saying: "The person of ultimate attainment dedicates their body to the Way.
You Dharma Masters have clarified the principles of order and chaos; your devotion and reliance [upon the teachings] are well-ordered and deeply praiseworthy.

You should be accommodated in the great monasteries within the capital city, and the relevant authorities shall provide for your needs with full attention to ensure they are met completely. Thereupon, Sengzheng Shi Songgui presided over the assembly, while the listeners numbered more than five hundred.
Once, he met the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of India. Although the Master had already translated the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Triṃśikā*, he had not yet lectured upon them.
Fǎmén and Fǎtài were the only ones who received their transmission. Huìsōng consulted and resolved his doubts for several years, eventually reaching the profound depths of the teachings.

From the various divergent interpretations regarding Buddha-nature, the Middle and the Extremes, signlessness (*animitta*), and consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), there were over forty treatises; in reality, however, they were all categorized under two main works.
In the tenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, he returned north. By imperial decree, his former temple, the Wangsi of Jingzhao, was renamed Chongsheng, and he resided there.

He specialized in teaching the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) and composed a six-fascicle commentary on the *She lun*, as well as a five-fascicle commentary on the *Zaxin lun* (Abhidharmahṛdaya-vibhāṣā).

His profound treatises on the nine consciousnesses, the three baskets, the three clusters of precepts, and the two types of birth-and-death circulated throughout the world. When Emperor Yang was still in the prince’s residence, he traveled to Tianmen, Yangzhou, and Yuezhou.

He established four sites for the Way. He was once summoned by Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei, but Huisong did not rise to the call. Later, when the Emperor ascended the throne, he summoned him again, yet Huisong firmly declined.
When his disciples asked him the reason, he said: "A śramaṇa is named 'Liberation. Why should I burden myself with such things as this?

In the past, I traveled between the two capitals and was repeatedly subjected to laborious service. Even within an inner palace chapel, it is not like being beyond the mundane world. Therefore, my recitation and cultivation have continued for nearly thirty years."

Zai practiced asceticism with such intensity that it was as if he had been doing so for but a single day. The marks left by his hands pressing against his knees while kneeling and his head bowing in prostration remained vividly indelible even after a long time.
By nature, he loved elegant literature and delighted in springs and rocks. He passed away in the tenth year of the Daye era at the age of seventy-eight.
Hui-zan of the Sui dynasty was the son of the Wang family from Cangzhou. He entered the monastic order in his prime, his aspirations being lofty and far-reaching.

After receiving full ordination, he studied the Vinaya at the Xingyu Monastery in Dingzhou. Whenever the lectures reached the topic of wealth and profit, the Dharma Master would wish to pose difficult questions to refute them;
however, Hui-zan viewed this with disdain. At one time, there were three hundred coins in his bundle, which he immediately cast away. From that point on...
Throughout his life, he never spoke of wealth or profit. To escape the cruelties of the Zhou dynasty, he took refuge in the region south of the Yangtze River.

During the Kaihuang era, he returned north and resided at Longshan in Xifeng, Zhaozhou. There, he gathered disciples and guided their minds toward detachment from worldly attachments; he himself practiced the dhūta ascetic observances.
He practiced the dharmas of an araṇya-dweller. Scholars who came to him from afar numbered more than two thousand, and his reputation resounded throughout the region north of the Yellow River.

When Prince Jin of Qin governed the Bing province, he constructed Kaichua Temple and summoned Daozan to preside over its affairs; there, he governed the community by exclusively upholding the settled practice of meditation and was particularly strict regarding the poṣadha ceremony.
His disciple, Chan Master Mingyin, followed these precepts with unwavering diligence. In his later years, he returned to Ye to receive disciples.

Shugu was able to establish himself as a preeminent figure. When the Chan-ting Temple was established in the capital to commemorate the late Empress Xian, he was summoned by imperial decree to join several men of renowned virtue.
He was subsequently invited to reside at Longchi Temple on Mount Zhongnan, where seekers of instruction gathered there in great numbers.
He passed away in his mountain retreat shortly thereafter at the age of ninety-two, in the ninth month of the third year of the Daye era. His disciple was Zhi-chao.
See the *Biézhuan*.

Huichang of the Sui dynasty was a native of Jingzhao; he resided at Riyang Monastery. Regarding his *fanbai* (Buddhist chanting), he was able to suppress the resonance of the *va* sound so that the voice issued from his throat without the movement of his lips or tongue.
When standing side-by-side with others, those who did not previously know him could not [distinguish] him at all.

This refers to the matter of emulation. From Emperor Wen down to Emperor Yang, although the grandeur of their Buddhist rites was consistently maintained, their traditions regarding the study of *bhāṣa* (chanting) differed according to their respective family styles;
thus, they did not grant one another mutual recognition. As for Chang, however, he would simply acknowledge their excellence while inwardly feeling a sense of trepidation.
When others wished to emulate him, none were generally able to reach his level. Later, he entered the Eastern Capital during the rebellion of Xuan Gan.

Qiang Chang was serving as the Governor of Qi when Hui Xuan gained the upper hand and fled in defeat. Chang went into hiding in the region of Guanzhong and Shaanxi. Some claimed that he had previously disparaged the state;
consequently, an imperial edict was issued for his arrest, and he was bound and sent to the Eastern Capital. Upon reaching Shazhai, a guest stopped him, saying, "Do not go, lest you be put to death.
Chang declined, saying, "How can one escape an old debt? He ultimately met his death at the age of over forty. There was also another man named Dao...
As for the eminent and spirited Ying: his voice was resonant and his countenance noble and majestic; his diction and breath were powerful and far-reaching.

Even amidst a multitude of tens of thousands, he could still project his voice with great clarity. The foundation of Xingshàn Hall was ten *mǔ* wide, and its windows, lattices, doors, and panels were so tall, large, and solid that they could not easily be shaken.
When Ying led the assembly in circumambulation, the lingering echoes reached everywhere, causing them all to tremble. As for Shuǎng:
The calligraphy was elegant and flowing, with continuous curves and turns; its rhythm, both expansive and concise, was pleasing to the mind. [He] resided at Xingshan Temple.
During the Zhenguan era, there was Chan Master Tanbao of Zhaoji Temple in Yuzhou. He abstained from grain to discipline his body, and his observance of the precepts was flawless.

When he was about sixty years old, the Emperor requested him to lecture on the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* to instruct the officials and the common people. His intonation was resonant and clear, remarkably distinct from that of ordinary people.
Every quiet night, he would offer praise and prostrations upon the foundations of a temple pagoda; his voice and words could be heard clearly for thirty *li* around.
Hui Bian of the Sui dynasty was a native of Qi who resided at Lingyan Temple on Mount Tai. During the Daye era, he was over seventy years of age. Together with...
Shinben of Tōri came to travel through the Kanto region. He researched astronomy and geography and predicted auspicious and calamitous events with divine accuracy.

He once remarked, "The Zenju-ji temple is already situated at the very peak of the mountain's terrain; why then build a pavilion in front of it? It will surely lead to disputes. Later, this proved to be no falsehood.
A layman requested that he inspect his ancestral graves; Shinben traversed the plains and hills and pointed to one [grave].
It was said: "This [site] can provide sufficient food and abundant wealth. At a depth of three feet, one shall obtain one *sheng* of millet;

at a depth of ten feet, one shall obtain two pieces of five-colored patterned stone. Everything occurred exactly as he had spoken, and so they proceeded with the burial. Consequently, his family has remained prosperous to this day.
Furthermore, it is said that not a single night has passed without visitors staying there to observe the site. Formerly, Dharma Master Yu used to say:
I, [the author], have studied Dao’an’s teachings of the Jin dynasty; he too was masterful in this art. His commentary on the *Sūnǚ jīng* (Classic of the Lady Sūn) is the most essential of all.

My only regret was that its original text had been lost. At that time, a monk happened to obtain it and presented it to me. I read through it daily, never setting it aside, and sighed, saying: [...the rest of the passage...]

The world regards you with eyes as vast as the heavens; I have long held this in mind, and from now on, it shall be confirmed. Although these are but four sheets of paper, they encompass everything without omission.
At that time, the moon was about to invade the asterism of Jing (Well). You suddenly remarked, "Jing belongs to the domain of Chu, and the moon is the sign of water; will Chu suffer from flooding?
Before long, the Han River rose in a great flood, and in the city of Xiangcheng, barely one board’s width remained above the water. O Confucian!
There was Yuan Shansong, who, having heard that Bian was profoundly learned, visited him to discuss Yanziyun’s *Taixuan* and Wang Faji’s commentary on the *Yi*.

Bian said, "The doctrines of Yang Xiong and Wang Bi seem not to be particularly profound or abstruse. Shansong’s face suddenly flushed with indignation, and he accused Bian of being envious of the worthy.
Bian replied, "Sir, why do you go so far in your credulity regarding antiquity? It is simply that you have not yet perceived their errors. Thereupon, he proceeded to cite the *Taixuan*.
He thus disparaged and criticized [the practice]. By nature, he was fond of the furnace-fire; whenever he obtained money, he would purchase cinnabar, lead, and mercury.

Someone once told him that he should be cautious regarding his expenditures and ought to guard against theft. Bian replied, "I have no fear. He reasoned that the methods for detecting thieves necessarily rely on the *duñjiǎ* (遁甲) system and the six *dīng* (六丁) days, which require adding the lunar phase to the date.
"Now," he said, "since it is like this, I have no fear. During the Yínníng era, he traveled south to the regions beyond the Ling Mountains. He did not...
He knew the time of his passing.
Honglin of the Sui dynasty was a native of Taiyuan; his clan and lineage are not detailed. Having entered the religious life in his youth, he resided at Daxingguo Monastery in Bingzhou.
He lived alone in a single room for fifty years. Apart from eating, drinking, and attending to the calls of nature, he engaged in no other activities.
His feet never once crossed the threshold [of his cell], yet his appearance was refined and elegant, and his conduct was serene and retiring; those who saw him felt a sense of solemn awe.
Consequently, although there were many monks at the temple, all looked up to him as a model. He passed away during the Wude period at the age of eighty.
Tang Zhizhou, courtesy name Yuanlang, was surnamed Zhao. His ancestors were from Xiapi in Xuzhou. During the Jin dynasty, they migrated to Qufu in Lou County.
By nature, his character was transcendent and lofty. At the age of seven, he entered the monastic life under Dharma Master Tao of Liushui Temple.
He served him with diligence, never wasting even a moment of time. Before long, carrying his book-box, he proceeded to the Da-zhuangyan Temple to study under the Dharma Master Jiao.
The Master, reasoning with his former karma, remained for one *jī* (twelve years), yet it did not satisfy his aspirations.

Upon the fall of Jinling and the unification of the realm under the sea, he returned eastward from there to propagate the Great Dharma. After a long time, he moved his residence to Huìjù Monastery on Mount Mǎ'ānshān.
He thus concealed his traces. Shortly thereafter, he emerged from the mountains once more to benefit the masses.
Soon after, the rebellion broke out in Jiangdu and the empire collapsed like crumbling earth; he then drifted along without attachment, moving in harmony with the Dao.
On the fifth day of the seventh month in the fifth year of Wude, he passed away at the residence of Xue Shitong, the Regional Inspector of Wuzhou, due to illness. He was sixty years of age.
7. On the twentieth day of the eleventh month of this year, as the roads were level and tranquil, my disciples Fadu and others were finally able to escort the coffin back to the mountains.
On the fifteenth day of the second month of the fourth year of the Zhenguan era, my disciples Huiman and others...
A circular burial mound was established on the western ridge for his interment. Zhou Jing alone refined his mind and nature, distancing himself from the realm of sensory consciousness.

He encouraged and uplifted those who came after him, while holding the predecessors in high esteem. Furthermore, he was proficient in maps, histories, and verse, as well as in seal, clerical, cursive, and regular scripts; he shared a deep affection with his elder brother, Bao.
He was renowned both in the north and the south; as for the greatness of his achievements, none could rival those of Zhou.
At that time, there was the śramaṇa Daogong of Huixiang Temple who composed a eulogy for him, though most of it is not recorded here.
Tang Zhi, surnamed Zheng, was named Ting. He was of a prominent lineage from Rongyang, a family renowned for generations for its literary talent.

When he first entered official service, he held the post of Commandant of Cavalry in the Feathered Forest Guard (Yulin Qiduwei), but he soon resigned. He went to listen to Dharma Master Jizang lecture on the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) and other sutras such as the *Lotus Sutra*, and he took refuge with sincere devotion in emptiness and stillness.
At the beginning of the Daye era, the Chancellor Yang Su saw him and recognized his potential, recommending him for an appointment at court.
He served as a Secretary of the Chancellery during the reign of Emperor Huangtai of the Yue Kingdom.
After Wang Shichong assassinated the King and usurped the throne—founding the state of Zheng with the era name Kaiming—he appointed him to assist in governance while retaining his former office.

At that time, the Tang dynasty had already received the abdication of power; when Taizong, leading the Tiance Army, pressed against the Western Garden, Wang Shichong was in extreme distress and consequently ordered [him] to...
