His wife and he shaved each other's heads to become a monk and a nun, saying, "Our vows are fulfilled.

He immediately donned the *kāṣāya* robe, took up his mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), and went to see Shi Chong, saying, "Zheng Ting has now left the household life. Shi Chong was greatly incensed and dispatched his attendants to execute him.
He addressed Xī (Huiji), saying: "My vow is now fulfilled. Thereupon, he prostrated himself before the Buddhas of the ten directions, reciting the name of Prajñā aloud.

He took up his brush and wrote this verse as his parting from the world: "Illusory birth returns to illusory extinction; Nothing is a greater illusion than the body. The mind at rest has its own place."
Seeking someone to perform the execution, he found no one. He then took leave of his relatives and friends; closing his eyes for a brief moment, he said, "You may strike the blade.

Until the end, his countenance remained unchanged. Previously, there had been a monk skilled in physiognomy who told him: "Your skull, forehead, and jaw indicate that by the laws of fate you are destined for wealth and nobility.
However, you have a 'wolf's glance'; how then can you die beneath the window? He replied, "It shall surely be as you have pointed out."
This truly accords with my heart. Whenever I see those who die while lying ill, their spirits are dazed and confused as they suddenly depart for the afterlife;
it is surely not as good as having cultivated vast vows so that one's contemplation remains firm and clear when the blade falls and the breath ceases.
His wife was a bhikṣuṇī who later resided at a temple in Luozhou.
Tang Xuanjian was the son of the Jiao family of Gaoping in Zhezhou; at the age of nineteen, he renounced secular life and resided at Qinghua Temple.

He studied the sūtras and śāstras under Master Huiyuan, mastering them all through extensive study. However, he was particularly profound and well-versed in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Toward the end of the Sui dynasty...
During this period of turmoil, the stūpas and temples in every location were reduced to ashes and charred remains; the monastics were emaciated by hunger, perishing in the ditches and ravines.

Huijian subsisted on hempen clothing and coarse vegetables, yet he maintained his discipline with even greater rigor. When the harvest became bountiful again, he returned to his native village and gathered funds to rebuild, restoring them to their former state.

Consequently, both the clergy and the laity turned toward the faith, and local customs underwent a transformation; they became strict regarding food and drink, and upon seeing those who were fond of wine, [they would reproach them].
He would immediately remonstrate with them face-to-face, speaking bluntly of their transgressions. If they did not reform even slightly, he would seek out their tools and break them.

When the powerful families were holding banquets, upon hearing that Sengjian had arrived, they would generally hasten to avoid him. Whenever there was labor service, some would send wine and meat to provide him with refreshments, to which he would reply:
"I would rather not rise. He thought, "I must certainly not burden others with the karma of hell," and he dismissed them all.
There was a man named Zhangsun Yi who once presented two carriages of goods; Sengjian declined them as he had previously explained. Yi became angry and sought to slander him under some other pretext.
At night, he dreamed that a divine being threatened him with a sword, whereupon he immediately cast himself down in repentance. At that time, the pestilence was raging fiercely, and many were dying.
They lay prostrate upon one another. Had they simply received the precepts and abstained from wine and meat, they would have been spared; though already ill, they soon recovered.
Formerly, when Li Qianruo was deeply immersed in drunkenness, he later did not allow even a drop to enter his mouth.

He said to others: "In the past, I lay ill beneath a window, knowing no way to be saved. Fortunately, Master Jian happened to pass by. Since my illness was cured by him, I have feared him ever since as if he were a venomous insect. Furthermore—
Li, the Clerk of Huozhai County, died and was buried. Seven days later, his wife heard a voice say:
"According to my allotted lifespan, I still have six years remaining. Yet the Lord of Fate has erred by placing me among the registers of the dead.

Although King Yama has permitted me to wander temporarily among the living, there is no matter of good or ill fortune that I do not know. Considering your poverty and distress, I now wish to engage in divination for you."

"Your Excellency, it is beneficial. After a long while, he spoke again: "I wish to go to Master Jian’s place to listen to the Dharma. His wife then went and set up a curtain at the corner of the house to screen it off.
When she questioned him, he responded with excellent replies. Jian expounded upon the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* without ceasing for four seasons.
Though old, he remained vigorous and robust; this year he is eighty-three years of age.

Tang Zhibao was a native of Hedong. He entered the monastic path in his youth and did not conform to worldly customs. After receiving full ordination, he was particularly rigorous in maintaining his discipline and exerting himself in self-cultivation.
Having read extensively through the classical texts, he responded to both Buddhist and Confucian inquiries with brilliant literary elegance, which earned him the high esteem of his contemporaries.

The far-reaching influence of the Vinaya tradition truly relied upon this man. Initially, he resided at Shengguang Temple; later, he stayed at the Chan-ding Daochang, where offerings and alms were abundant.

He accumulated [merit] and never once used it for his own enjoyment. When the four hundred members of the monastic community ate together in a single hall, if there were melons, vegetables, or other items, each person would invariably take the most fragrant and delicious portions;
however, he would preserve the seeds as soon as he obtained them, fearing that they might damage the characteristics of the species. Such was the detail with which he understood the Dharma.

Upon reaching old age at Śrīprabha Monastery, his religious practice became even more rigorous; though he served as the monastery’s steward (*vārṣika*) and performed irrigation duties, [he remained steadfast].

Regarding the vegetables from his garden, he would also personally carry the filtering equipment to tend to them. Even the smallest bits of straw and chaff, he would invariably gather and collect, sending them down to the servants.
Toward the end of the Wude era, when his illness became grave, his spirit grew even more clear and lucid. He said to his friend Huiman:
"I am now dying; yet my consciousness still cannot transcend [this state]. What can be done? Man asked him about this.
He replied, "My future existence seems to be that of a guardian deity of this monastery. However, it dwells only within the Buddha hall of the Western Courtyard.

I have repeatedly attempted to depart from it through wholesome dharmas, but in the end, I could not succeed. Having said this, he passed away. From then on, no one dared to go to that place unbidden.
As for the pointing toward the earth, it was likely because his spiritual influence resided there.

Huīyùn of the Tang dynasty, surnamed Li, was of the Longxi clan. Because his eleventh-generation ancestor, Zhòng, had been enfeoffed as Marquis of Dōngtíng during the Jin dynasty, they migrated south and became people of Jiāngxia.
When Huīyùn was ten years old, he took up discipleship under Fǎmíng of Gúāngyán Sè, who was a member of his maternal clan.
When the Master entered the monastic order, Emperor Wen of the Chen dynasty held the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra) in high esteem;

every year he would select men of renowned virtue to preside over grand Dharma assemblies. At the age of twenty, the Master was granted entry into this circle, from which one can discern the extent of his reputation and influence.
When Heaven grew weary of the Chen dynasty’s virtue and the destiny of the Sui flourished, he accepted the invitation of Liu Quan, the Prefect of Suzhou, and settled at Tongxuan Temple.
Based on the miraculous image, he propagated [the teachings]. During the final years of the Sui dynasty, he sought refuge at Xianling and Ruixiang Monasteries in Piling.

There were two śramaṇas, Zhishi and Zhimeng, who successively expounded and disseminated [the doctrine]. Just as Du Wei was usurping the title of Emperor, the High Ancestor (Emperor Wen of Sui) had already stabilized the empire and subsequently summoned them to court.
At first, Wei still harbored hesitation regarding his advancement or retreat; however, [Zhishi] explained his past lives for him.
He bowed at Huī’s feet and departed with tears. The śramaṇas Dàoxiǎn and Fǎjì of Yúháng had long been devoted to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*;
upon this occasion, they further advanced in their cultivation. When they intended to offer gifts, Huī merely waved his hand to dismiss them, taking nothing.
Thereupon, he went to the Lóngquán and Xíngyáng monasteries and commissioned one gilded-bronze Maitreya statue for each, each with a seated height of... [one chi].

He was five zhang and five chi tall. He used this [height] to form the conditions for rebirth. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, he further assisted the Great Virtuous Dharma Master Huiyi in constructing the Ruixiang Hall.
Not long after, Chen Shichuo, the Magistrate of Wu County, invited him to expound upon the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
When the scrolls were nearly finished, he suddenly handed his fly-whisk to his disciple Zhizang, saying: "Study diligently to await questions; do not let the wind of wisdom decline."
He passed away peacefully with eyes closed. This was in the eleventh month of the fourth year [of the reign].
He was sixty-seven years of age. He was interred on the southern ridge of Mount Baitu. More than a thousand disciples erected a stele to commemorate his virtues;
the scholar Zhulín of Jiang Wang composed the inscription. Later, a five-story brick pagoda was constructed. The monk Fǎxuān of Chángzhōu composed the epitaph, which is not recorded here.

Huijun of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Zhang by secular custom. He was a native of Qinghe. His ancestors had moved south of the Yangtze River during the Jin dynasty and settled in Jianye, where they had followed the Confucian profession for generations.
In his youth, he advanced in the arts at the local schools. His father, Zhengjian, was renowned for his literary talent during the Chen dynasty;

he had his own collected works. Huijun’s resolve was set on transcending and casting off worldly burdens. Because his parents could not overcome his determination, they reluctantly permitted him to become a Daoist. Not long after...

He immediately underwent the tonsure. During the Daye era of the Chen dynasty, he was able to travel north to collate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Having been selected for this task, he received the imperial favor of ordination and resided at Tongtai Temple.
When his parents heard of this, they rejoiced; the neighbors and kinsmen all offered their congratulations, as they had previously been unaware of his situation.
After the fall of the Chen, he stayed at Hualin Temple in Jiangdu, where he followed Master Jie to thoroughly study the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. The Sui dynasty... [open]... began.

Toward the end of the Sui dynasty, when Emperor Yang resided as the Prince of Jin, he constructed Riyen Temple in the capital and extensively invited the most eminent and virtuous masters from across the realm to propagate the teachings.
Zhongying was among them; there, he was able to freely examine various schools of thought and widely collect new insights.

He subsequently returned to the lineage of Nāgārjuna, researching treatises such as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Śata-śāstra*, the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, and the *Vijñaptimātratā-siddhi*. At that time, the śramaṇas Zhishou and Daoyue frequently visited him.

The Vinaya Master Xuǎnwǎn held him in particularly high esteem. In the summer of the eleventh year of the Zhengguān era, when he suffered frequent bouts of wind-related illness, he said to his disciples, "My physical condition will not last much longer.
You should exert yourselves with even greater diligence and ensure that you do not leave me with cause for regret.

He further said, "Should my consciousness become clouded and I request food at an improper time, you must not comply with such wishes recklessly, lest you incur the karmic fault of acting contrary to my final instructions."

At dusk, he asked for gruel. Someone informed him that the time for the midday meal had already passed; he then departed in silence. This was on the twenty-sixth day of the seventh month of that year.
He was seventy-four years of age. His burial site was first excavated at the western edge of Gāoyáng Plains.
He was buried there. Later, he was moved to the eastern cliff of Pungdok-sa Temple on the Southern Mountains, where an inscription was engraved upon a stone niche.
Since the author’s name is not recorded in the text, it can be known that this was composed by Cheongjo. Furthermore, in his own account, he wrote:

"I have served [my master] since my student years for more than twenty years, devoting myself exclusively to the observance of the precepts (*śīla*) and their transgressions (*āpatti*). When I traveled throughout the four quarters..."
His extensive learning was indeed inherited from his Upādhyāya.
Bao Yan of the Tang dynasty resided at Fahai Monastery in the capital; his demeanor was relaxed and expansive, and his heart was set upon both the monastic and the lay worlds.

People of the time collectively referred to him as the "Dharma Master. This was because his exposition of the sūtras and śāstras differed from that of other virtuous masters; thus, his phrasing and terminology were unique.
All other matters are omitted; we simply take the matters of the auspicious paths of merit and the evil realms of the netherworld as the basis for generating joy and revulsion.
Furthermore, we cite the writings of Master Guan that guide King Wenru in his method of repentance, corroborated by dozens of authorities such as Emperor Wu of Liang and Shen Yue.

He was able to move his listeners so that they would take off their sashes and girdles, pull out their hairpins, and cast away their bracelets, providing the means for the grandeur of the stūpas and temples and the abundance of offerings.
Someone once questioned him, saying: "One who preaches the Dharma should preach in accordance with the Dharma.

If the aggregates (skandhas) and elements (dhātus) are empty, then you have not yet explained that; instead, you speak only of past lives and events—how can this be? Huiyan replied: "The aggregates enter into birth and death."
The Lord of Saṃsāra, seeing that the sentient beings of this turbid age are dull-witted, designates this as "sleep. Therefore, I have expanded upon it through Jātaka tales and past events.
If, by means of these, they awaken, then even the Jātakas and past events are empty. His adaptation to the capacities of beings is like this.
He passed away at his residence during the Zhenguan era; he was over seventy years of age.
Huichi of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Zhou and was a native of Runan. He was born in the early Kaihuang period of the Sui dynasty while his father was stationed in Yuzhang.

He was quick-witted and possessed keen intelligence. In his youth, he traveled extensively to fulfill his aspirations. Upon arriving in Danyang, he took up the life of a śrāmaṇera and served Master Fǎmǎn of Kāiśān.

He could recite five pages of the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* daily. Barely having reached the age of twenty, he stood eight feet tall; his appearance was majestic and his deportment was orderly and elegant.
He never looked around, and thus he was known at the time as an "Elephant King. Having completed his studies, he subsequently listened to the teachings of Zhu Fashang at Dong'an.
Dharma Master Gao-li Shi was a master of the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*), and he was also proficient in the *Zhuangzi*, *Laozi*, *Yijing*, and the histories.

At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, Yang Su, the Duke of Yue, while governing the military forces along the Huai and Hai rivers, heard of his reputation and went to pay him a visit. In his later years, as the world fell into turmoil, he took refuge in the Yu-xue (Amphitheater of Yu) and resided at Hongdao Temple.
There, he extensively propagated the *Sanlun*, *Mohebanruo* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā), *Niepan* (Nirvāṇa), and *Huayan* (Avataṃsaka) sutras, and he also greatly promoted [the teachings].
He was well-versed in the teachings of Zhuangzi and Laozi. In this manner, he spent thirty years constantly sitting without reclining, practicing with diligent perseverance and without indolence.
On the twenty-third day of the eighth month in the sixteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he addressed his disciples, saying, "Prepare food quickly;

I wish to go to other regions to teach and transform beings. When the time came and the meal was finished, he returned to his room, sat cross-legged upon his rope bed, and passed away. Those who first saw him...

He entered meditative absorption and did not dare to move for three days. Du Fuhu, the Assistant Magistrate of Kuaiji, was a man of vegetarian and ascetic practice who attended upon [the Master] with devotion, making no distinction between those within and without the inner circle.
At this time, he suddenly smelled a strange fragrance; when he went to look, [the Master] had passed away. He was buried at Dayu Mountain at the age of sixty-eight.

Tang Daozong was born into the Wei family of Fengyi. In his youth, he followed the Buddhist path and devoted himself exclusively to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. When the Northern Zhou dynasty suppressed the two religions, he returned to lay life.
Once the Sui dynasty held the empire, he immediately shaved his head and donned the robes of a monk, residing at Daxingguo Monastery in Tongzhou—the very place where his ancestors had lived.

He extensively propagated the teachings alongside other masters, attracting disciples in great numbers like the legs of a tripod. Offerings from donors arrived in such abundance that they were sufficient for all needs.
Yu. At the end of the Sui Daye era, there was successive famine; the emaciated commoners and starving scholars all carried their infants on their backs to seek food.
His reputation, along with that of Daoxun of Pudu, was celebrated throughout the Guanzhong and Hedong regions.

When the assembly recommended him for the position of Abbot of Zhiyuan Temple, Huiyong, observing that the clergy lacked discipline due to the chaos of war, personally traveled to the capital to welcome the śramaṇa Zhishou, who then lectured during the summer retreat.
He spoke thus, leading more than three hundred followers who crossed their sūtras across their chests to listen without a trace of weariness.

When the commentary reached the section on establishing boundaries (*sīmābandha*), it was noted that if a monastery lacks pure ground (*śuci-bhūmi*), one cannot maintain the Dharma while observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*). Consequently, he suspended his lectures and translated the *Sai* (the *Vinaya-mātṛkā*).

Furthermore, during every *poṣadha*, he never failed to speak of the *chanda* (consent). Whenever he addressed Xi, he would invariably weep until his tears soaked his kerchief, sighing with deep emotion.
Thus it was. In the twelfth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away due to illness at the age of eighty-five; he was interred to the east of the city.
Tang Zhiheng’s secular surname was Bai; he was a native of Anxi in Dingzhou. At the age of eleven, he shaved his head and left home, severing ties with his parents and relatives.
He wept before him, yet his countenance remained composed without the slightest change. His teacher, recognizing his past predispositions (*pūrvābhyāsa*), diligently instructed him;

consequently, his studies progressed daily, and he observed the precepts with such rigorous discipline that his peers marveled at his excellence. Though still in his early twenties, his reputation for wisdom spread far and wide.
In the tenth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, the imperial court widely sought out men of brilliance and virtue, and he thus accompanied Tanqian [to the capital].
The Chan Master entered the capital, where an imperial edict granted him consolation and rewards. He resided at Shengguang Temple.

In the first year of the Renshou era, Yu Qingze, the Left Vice Director of the Chancellery, built Renjue Temple and petitioned for him to dwell there. Shortly thereafter, he followed Master Yuan of Zhongnan Zhiyang Temple.

For twenty-eight years, he propagated the Dharma outwardly while clarifying the practice of meditative concentration inwardly; he disciplined himself through the six periods of the day, never involving himself in worldly affairs. Zheng...
On the twenty-eighth day of the second month in the thirteenth year of the Guanghua era, he passed away at the monastery where he resided. He was eighty-one years of age.
His disciple Zhixian and others enshrined his remains in a stone chamber, carving it into a cliff to the northwest of the monastery;

an inscription exists that can still be seen. Zhixian had received instruction from him since his youth and never deviated from his teachings; all of [the Master’s] writings were transcribed by Zhixian’s hand.
Whenever he sat upright in meditation, [Daoxuan] would attend to him by his side, following his every word and every movement; though many years passed, he never once allowed him to sit down.

On occasions when he grew weary late at night and stumbled or fell, Daoxuan would immediately reprimand him, saying: "In the past, a man stood on one foot for seven days—how great was his sincerity and reverence!
Today you have become so negligent and disrespectful that this has happened. It is not the elephant that should be pitied. He lectured on the *Huayan*...

He produced commentaries on the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, among others, too numerous to enumerate, all of which he recorded as notes (*caojì*). He alone, however, composed a commentary (*shū*) on the *Avataṃsaka*.
Zhībá of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Zhāng; a native of Xiānyáng, he entered the monastic order at the age of six and became a disciple of Master Rùn. Rùn commanded him to receive [the teachings].

He taught Master Zhe. Zhe was at Xiangyang; Gu was a figure of monastic renown and has his own biography. Initially, when reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*, he would cover five sheets of paper per day and had a rough grasp of its general meaning.
Subsequently, he relied upon Master Jizang in the capital, where he listened to the lectures only twice.

When Jizang commanded him to recount what he had heard, he extracted a point and questioned him, saying: "The One Vehicle is like a cloud; it is subsequently divided into three. Could it not also be the One Vehicle?"
He asked, "Is it raining? Is it divided into three? No one in the assembly dared to answer. Daozang said, "This question is truly excellent," and he ultimately entrusted him with the Great Dharma.
Thereupon, he returned to his hometown. At that time, a band of robbers was causing turmoil; he had to hide by day and flee by night, finding no leisure for peace.

When the rebellion was suppressed, he resided at Qishu Temple, where he lectured without ceasing, completing five cycles of the text each year. His disciple Fachang saw him staying at Fanyun Temple and took up the lineage of his teachings.
On the seventeenth day of the ninth month in the fourteenth year of the Zhenguan era, the lay devotee Zhang Ying invited him to his home for a gathering.

There, he established the principles and opened the topic of the discourse. Someone asked about the meaning of the "three-in-one" (san-yi) throughout the past and present; [the Master] extracted the essence of what had not yet been clarified.
Upon meeting him, he immediately told Dharma Master Ling: "I, Zhi Ba, am now bidding farewell to my fellow countrymen, the virtuous monks, and the donors.
He then passed away; his countenance remained as if alive, and he sat upright in the full lotus posture. Both the local elite and the common people sighed in lamentation.
The Provincial Governor, Lord Jiang, personally attended to offer incense and presented him with one hundred bolts of silk. A vegetarian feast was held at his burial site;
he was sixty-six years old. Daoxuan’s secular surname was Sang, and he was a native of Chengdu in Shu Commandery.

Having long since renounced the world, he possessed a profound mastery of the *Nirvāṇa* and *Satyasiddhi* schools, yet the *Lotus Sūtra* was that which he constantly lectured upon. His character was refined and noble, and he was well-versed in non-Buddhist classics.
He was skilled in the cursive and clerical scripts. His writings were elegant and abundant. Furthermore, he humbled himself and bowed down to men of humble station;

yet toward those of wealth, rank, or fame, he never yielded, instead treating them with contempt and insult. Xiao Pingzhong, the Assistant Secretary of the Eastern Office in Zizhou, was a descendant of the Liang dynasty.

While conversing by chance, [the Master] treated the various literary compositions with profound courtesy and deference. Hui Pingzhong said, "I have often heard that you, Master, are habitually disdainful;
yet now I receive such honor from you, I am deeply ashamed of my own unworthiness. The Master continued, "I was merely being disdainful toward that which ought to be disregarded.
But how could I possibly be disdainful of you, Illustrious Sir? Pingzhong replied, "Master has never been thus before; surely this present attitude is not your true intention?"
"Is it merely a matter of empty appearances? He replied, "The way I, a poor monk, await the truth or falsehood of your honor is just like the way you, my lord, await the truth or falsehood of Xu.
They looked at one another and laughed. He once composed the inscription for the Bao Yuan Temple stele, which read: "Laozi was called a Sage; Zhuangzi was styled a Philosopher.

To hold a firefly up to the sun, or to compare a mountain to a speck of dust—such is our endeavor. It happened that there was a Daoist, Feng Shanying, who, by imperial decree, went to offer sacrifices at the river."
When Daoxuan saw this, he considered it a repudiation and said to Xu: "To compose writings to praise their teachings is the constant way of principle;
why have you gone so far as to slander their teachings in this manner? He then ordered the passage to be deleted and revised. Otherwise, I shall report this to my superiors. Xu replied:
"As for the structural style of such compositions, how could I possibly know? If you wish to use intimidation to force me to make changes, I—"
The monastery’s estate was situated close to the capital; every year, those who collected its revenues came and went with the various nobles of the court.
Your conduct has been unlawful—could it not have been reported to the Emperor? I, Ying, alone harbor great resentment and sigh constantly.

I recall the passage in the *Zhuangzi* where the Peng bird and the quail serve as metaphors for the ultimate extremes of greatness and smallness, and say: how could that quail know that Mount Sumeru cannot contain it?
Jinshi entered a world as minute as a pore of a neighbor-atom. Furthermore, he was swift; having gathered the assembly, he renounced everything, saying, "Birth and death are but constants.
I pray that each of you will quickly find your own salvation. That evening he passed away; this was indeed during the Zhenguan era.
Tang Xing was the son of the Ji family of Fengyi. He entered the monastic order at the age of twelve. There was one named Xuánhuì with whom he served Master Zhǒng;
they also studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* together under Master Yuǎn of Jingyǐng Monastery. Later, while residing at Cíbēi Monastery, they remained together there as well.
Whenever [Yuǎn] ascended the seat to preach, Xing would go first and Huì would follow him. Altogether, those whom they assisted in expounding the Dharma numbered one hundred and one.
Ten times. Thus is the way in which the path of sympathetic resonance (*zàncéng*) functions. If there should be any obstacles or difficulties, we shall certainly know of them in advance;

therefore, I request that the assembly recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and the demonic affairs will immediately cease. For this reason, at the conclusion of the assembly, each person must pay homage to the Buddha and recite the scriptures.
This is based on the account of a person who received the precepts from us, who, after dying and then reviving, said: "The officials of the underworld..."
Because he was a disciple of the Buddha, he was permitted to return home. The rooster he kept would always wait for the sound of the bells and drums and would crouch beneath his seat.

On the sixth day of the third month in the sixteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away from illness at the age of seventy-three. His final instruction was to donate his body to birds and beasts;
however, his disciples could not bear this, so they prepared a grand funeral ceremony, sought an auspicious burial site, and intended to lift the body the following day.

The funeral procession was proceeding toward the burial mound when it suddenly began to rain at night and continued for several days. Those escorting the remains were ultimately prevented from proceeding.
Following his final instructions, the *śarīra* were interred at Shenhe Yuan on the southern outskirts of the capital once the weather cleared.

Huisi of the Tang dynasty was born into the Guo family of Jiexiu in Fenzhou. His family had practiced Confucianism for generations; from his youth, he was well-versed in the classics and histories and held a particular affinity for the profound and abstruse.
He excelled in literary composition and was skilled in the seal and clerical scripts, earning a reputation throughout his local community.

At the age of twenty-five, he began teaching in the Bingzhou region, yet he still did not understand what was known as the Buddha-dharma. It happened that the śramaṇa Daoye was lecturing on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and Huisi occasionally went to attend.

He listened to them, and upon gaining some realization, he sought to leave the household life. He further understood that for essential practice, nothing compares to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), yet such masters are rarely encountered.

Consequently, he traveled throughout the land seeking the Indian scriptures for about thirty years, thoroughly investigating their profound meanings while wearing coarse clothing and eating simple food.
Those who beheld him were moved to resolve their minds [on the Way], and men of ambition flocked to him in great numbers.

Consequently, the assembly gathered at the foot of Mount Ji, where they devoted themselves to their daily recitations during the six periods of the day, never failing in the noble tradition. Once, while discussing his aspirations with his peers, Sengsi remarked, "For those who study the Buddha-dharma, birth and death follow conditions;
what need is there for such elaborate funeral rites? At that time, people took this to be merely a jest. However, by the time...
While suffering from illness, after only two months had passed, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying, "I am about to die.

He then proceeded to an empty cave, cleared away his remaining remains, and took leave of his disciples. Seated in meditation within it, the forested cemetery stood tall and solemn; the assembly could not bear to part with him.
He kept watch by his side through the night and observed him; then, with hands folded in formal repose, he passed away.
He was fifty-five years old, in the fifth month of the sixteenth year of the Zhenguan era.
Huixi of the Tang dynasty was born into the Zhao family of Pei County in Yizhou; he entered the monastic path as a youth. He devoted himself to reading and was proficient in literary composition.
He was equally renowned as Rongzhi of Zhenxiang Temple in Mianzhou; both were truly the most outstanding among śrāmaṇeras.

Later, while composing poetry together with a śrāmaṇera from Dàshí Temple in Chengdu, a disagreement arose over a particular line. Consequently, he withdrew into seclusion, severed all worldly affairs, and devoted his mind to the study of Chan.

Having received full ordination, he thoroughly mastered the Sūtras and Vinaya, was proficient in the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises), and was especially well-versed in the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) and the *Zaxin lun* (Abhidharmahṛdaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra).
He once challenged Master Jì on the meaning of "dust-consciousness" (*rajas-vijñāna*) in the Hīnayāna; Jì explained it through the Mahāyāna perspective, whereupon [Huijun] laughed and said:

There is nothing great that he does not encompass; however, he has lost his minor tenets. Later, while residing at Kōe-ji Temple south of the prefecture, he closed his quarters and sat without food for over twenty days.
The community feared he would perish from starvation, so they deceived him by saying, "The state is currently searching for those of moral virtue."

"If you simply do not eat, the world will consider you a sage. You may occasionally attend public assemblies to quell outside gossip, but do not indulge in self-adornment, lest it burden the permanent residence.
Xi hurriedly followed this advice. Consequently, his single room became a mere wall-standing space, with moss and ferns covering the floor and no trace of people coming or going.
On his bed remained only a worn-out mat covered in dust; there was only the mark of his cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*) remaining within it. Sometimes...

Those who admired him went to visit him, yet it took several days before they could even catch a glimpse of his face. On such occasions, he would deliver clear and elegant discourses that rose far above the mundane world.
He continued in this manner for nearly thirty years until his peers were awestruck by him; he passed away at the age of ninety.
Tang Sanguihui was a native of Loufan. In his youth, he specialized in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, and later entered the Huirì Monastery.

At the beginning of the Daye era, an imperial edict summoned him to Ba and Shu to recruit those of artistic talent. Upon reaching Qiong and Bi, the Sui dynasty came to an end. He subsequently retired to live in seclusion, propagating the Dharma until his final years.
During the present dynasty, when Dou Gui, the Duke of Zan, served as the regional governor, he held Sanguihui in particularly high esteem and paid him great honor. Wu... [text fragment]

In the ninth year of the Daye era, he traveled to the capital, where the Emperor’s inquiries and audiences were most gracious and abundant. Du Gongbu Shangshu Duan Lun memorialized that Hui was the one who had established Linghua Monastery.
During the Zhenguan era, by imperial decree, he entered the Translation Hall to compile texts, verify meanings, and composed the prefaces and introductions for the hall.
He passed away that same year at the age of seventy. While Hui was once staying in a separate courtyard in Jiang, he suddenly beheld a divine being.
His physical form was strange and uncanny. He paid his respects before him and said, "I beg you to exhort the administrator not to plow the grave.
Hui had not yet had time to speak when he saw him again later. The spirit urged him on the previous matter, saying, "If you do not speak at all by the end [of this], I will surely kill this monk.
Hui immediately questioned him; it turned out they were about to plow an old tomb. Thereupon, he hurriedly stopped them. It was nothing else.

Tang Shen-su was surnamed Wang; his ancestors were originally from Taiyuan. His distant ancestor, Yong, followed official service to Yuzhou and subsequently moved his residence to An-yi, in the wilds of Ming-tiao.
From childhood, he pursued the study of Confucianism and was particularly proficient in the *I Ching*. When he set pen to paper, his writings were brilliant.

He was especially close to Dharma Master Daojie, following him in every movement, whether traveling abroad or staying at home. This remained so until Daojie practiced meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

As for his activities, he first expounded the *ānāpāna-smṛti* (breath-meditation) methods of various schools. He subsequently occupied the seat [of his teacher] to propagate the teachings, lecturing on the *Abhidharma* more than forty times and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* nearly twenty times.
In the second year of the Zhenguan era, the assembly at Xiyuan requested that he assume the administrative duties of the monastery.

He declined on the grounds that religious duties and monastic administration could not be undertaken simultaneously; he firmly refused the request. However, based on the precedent set by Master Jie, he was permitted to accept.

For a long time, relations between the superior and subordinates remained harmonious without change. On the twenty-third day of the second month in the seventeenth year, he passed away at Xiyān at the age of seventy-two.
Having always envisioned the Pure Land throughout his life, he summoned all his disciples on that very day.

The assembly, having reached this moment of final service, resolved to assist him. They adjusted their appearance and sat in the lotus posture, causing him to recite the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* twice and to personally invoke "Namo Amitābha Buddha," while they themselves joined in the chanting.
At midnight, he passed away, sitting upright without shifting. They immediately moved him to a coffin;
although his flesh had completely withered away, his skeletal frame remained seated as it was before. This was the account of Dharma Master Zhikuan of Renshou Temple.
The Master dreamed that his former companion was sleeping in the same bed with him and then departed, saying:

"The Tathāgata, out of great compassion for all sentient beings, diligently sought the Great Dharma throughout vast eons to propagate it among humans and devas, desiring that it never be interrupted. We have received the Buddha’s final entrustment;

yet in this degenerate age, we have been unable to bring forth its brilliance. We harbor deep feelings of failure and have often wished to submit our lives and our utmost sincerity to the heavenly ear."
"Now my great destiny may not be stayed; I must bid you long farewell. Farewell and strive diligently! Alas, how strange it is!
Tang Zhikuan, surnamed Yao, was a native of Puzhou in Hedong. His father, Yao Shaoshi, served as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Qingzhou.

Zhikuan had studied various sutras and śāstras throughout his life, regarding the *Nirvāṇa* and *Daśabhūmika* sūtras as the essentials of his heart. He traveled east and west in search of the Dharma, never wasting even a moment of time.
Furthermore, he practiced faith without pretense or deceit. Once, while purchasing silk garments in the Chang'an market, the vendor said, "You may pay the price now;

I shall deliver them to you tomorrow at the agreed amount. When [Seng]kuan asked for the location so that they might be sent there, the man agreed. Upon returning, [Seng]kuan told the monks about it. The monks laughed, thinking he had been deceived.
[Seng]kuan said, "I reflect that throughout my life I have never deceived anyone; how could things themselves then be willing to deceive me?"

Indeed! That man truly acted according to his vow; he was especially diligent in tending to the sick. Whether from near or far, he brought those sent by carriage to his room for treatment, never neglecting even the slightest care.
If an abscess on the abdomen would not readily discharge its pus, he would simply suck it out with his mouth.

When Emperor Yang heard of his conduct and realization, he issued an edict for him to reside at Huiri Monastery. During the rebellion of Yang Xuanfan, he was implicated and imprisoned to await punishment. Thereupon, an envoy was dispatched...

The provisions were distributed entirely among all, with no partiality shown toward anyone. Later, when he was assigned to labor as a convict to carry earth and build the imperial road, his fellow laborers told him that since there was no official supervision, he might take some liberties.
Dao-kuan said, "If such is the nature of karmic retribution, how can one deceive oneself? Shortly thereafter, they were all sent westward to Shu.
Upon reaching Shan Prefecture, various donors pooled their resources to provide him with parting gifts; he immediately distributed these among them, leaving behind only a single [item].

He traveled on a donkey carrying his sutra scrolls. Upon reaching Tongguan Pass, the eminent master Baoxian’s feet were so severely blistered that he could not proceed; he lay twisting and turning by the side of the road.
Daokuan took pity on him and gave up his own donkey to carry the master, while he himself bore the sutra scrolls on his back until they reached Shu. There, he prayed for rain and exorcised tigers.
His transformative influence spread far and wide. Whenever he held a lecture or a public assembly, the offerings presented to him were exhausted as soon as they were distributed.

Yet, his own clothing and personal effects were always simple, humble, and frugal. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, when he returned to his native village, a severe drought occurred. Fayuan established an altar there and prayed for rain.
He declared that if it did not rain, he would not remain in his residence and would expose his body to the sun for three days. Consequently, the rain fell in great abundance. Fayuan...
In his dwelling, there was the sound of armor-clad men. When he peered out at night, he saw divine beings circumambulating beside him.
Commentators attributed this to the fact that he had regularly recited the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* and the *Prātimokṣa*. There was also a Dharma Master named Su, a lifelong friend;
they were able to communicate with one another, and even after [Su] had died, [Sengshao] continued to comfort him with letters. These matters are not recorded here. The seventeenth year.
On the sixteenth day of the fifth month in summer, he passed away at Renshou Temple at the age of seventy-eight. He was narrow-mouthed and did not seek profit; his hands never grasped treasures.
As for the hoarding of chests and boxes, he had long since abandoned such thoughts; as for riding in carriages or using labor-saving tools, he never engaged in them throughout his life.
On the verge of death, he left an instruction to his disciples: "Wrap my corpse in coarse mats and carry it on two rafters through the forests and wilds. There was no [funerary procession].
Such confusion leads to nothing but useless affairs. Alas, how profound! Tang Lingrun’s secular surname was Yu;
he was a native of Yuxiang in Hedong during the Liang dynasty. His family consisted of ten brothers, all born of the same parents. Among them, three wished to enter the Way.
Their father said, "Simply practice the recitation of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra; if you can first memorize it by heart, then I will grant your request."

Run held the scroll from dawn until noon and immediately memorized it without forgetting even a single word. He subsequently received the tonsure and resided at Xingshan Monastery under Dharma Master Lingcan.
At the age of thirteen, he was instructed in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; at fifteen, he ascended the lecture seat like a veteran elder.
During the Renshou era, an imperial edict ordered his master, Càn, to escort śarīras to Huai Prefecture to construct a stūpa;
however, Zhìrùn traveled with them as a disciple, providing for himself by begging for alms and declining all official expenses. Commentators praised his integrity and steadfastness.

Upon reaching Mount Tai, he followed the vice-abbot of Lingyan Temple to practice the *pratyutpanna-samādhi*. At that time, while five hundred fellow practitioners were present, Zhìrùn alone excelled in his practice.

He sat without substitution [in his practice] for some time, whereupon he received the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* from Dharma Master Daozang. He remained in service to Master Zang, taking him as his preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*).
At the age of twenty-three, he returned to the capital with his mendicant’s staff. There he encountered Dharma Master Zhinian, who was then propagating the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.
He again approached the teacher’s feet to study under him. There was also a Dharma Master Bianxiang, whose learning encompassed both the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna, at Jingying Monastery.
He composed the *Śāstra-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*) in five fascicles. Among his five hundred disciples, two hundred were capable of establishing formal arguments;

they would cross-examine one another, and while Rùn would initiate the discussion, Zhìfèn would vigorously present extraordinary propositions, such that the entire assembly marveled and submitted in admiration. Dàbiàn Fǎshī held him in particularly high esteem.
At the beginning of the Dayè era, he suddenly suffered from a wind-related ailment. Although he later required no medicine, his weariness with the illusory nature of phenomena only increased.

He divined a site north of Zhongnan Mountain, between Li and Hu, below Mount Yushan, where he intended to spend the remainder of his life with the śramaṇas Kōzō, Eijin, Chishin, Chikō, and others, wandering among groves of shrines and wild graves—a place where ghosts and spirits shriek and howl in packs.
In the tenth year of the Daye era, an imperial edict summoned him to the Honglu Guest House to instruct the monks of the Three Han kingdoms. Furthermore—
While residing at his monastery, he translated various sūtras. In the final years of his life, as the four seas were in turmoil, the authorities prohibited monks from traveling outside.
Thereupon, he retired to the western courtyard of Xingshan Monastery. For three years, he disciplined himself in meditation and study;

subsequently, he moved to Ganhua Monastery in Lantian, where, together with Chan Master Huiding and the śramaṇa Zhichao, he maintained a single daily meal and observed profound silence for fifteen years.
In his later years, as successive years of famine struck, he would share meals of beans and wheat with visiting guests; even Master Lingcan marveled at the grandeur of such a Dharma assembly.
When the Tang dynasty rose, an imperial edict appointed him as the abbot of Xingshan Monastery. This was in accordance with the legacy that Master Run had previously entrusted to him.

I did not dare decline. In the eighth year of the Zhenguan era, an imperial edict was issued to move him to Hongfu Monastery to engage in translation, while he continued to serve as the *zhengyi* (certifier of meaning).
This is the general outline of the matter. As for the hardships and sufferings encountered along the way, they were all fortunately met with divine providence, such that he never fell into distress.
Is this not the power of the latent impressions (*āśraya*) evoked by his virtuous conditions?
Once, while he was exiled to Huánzhōu for defending the Dharma, an imperial edict ordered him to be settled in Eastern Luò; yet the clergy and laity flocked to him as they had before.

He sent a report to the capital, and when his disciples discussed it at length, the Chancellor Fáng Xuánlíng saw it and sighed, saying: "The words and principles are earnest and sincere. One who possesses the name must surely possess the reality."
How true it is! He lectured on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* more than seventy times and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra* more than thirty times.

As for the *Vimalakīrti*, *Śrīmālādevī*, and *Aśvabhāva’s Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* and other treatises, they are beyond counting; all of them have their commentaries (*yi-shu*) circulating in the world.

These commentaries—such as those on the ālayavijñāna in the *Saṃgraha*, or the contemplations of the non-characteristic and non-arising of the ultimate and conventional truths—are particularly distinct from other expositions. His disciple Jingyuan succeeded him. [End of] Sha...
Men Zhiyan was his cousin. Having received instruction and exhortation from his youth, he was well-versed in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*.
He resided at Fachisi on Mount Lantian.
Tang Yuankang was of sharp intelligence; his physique was stout and short. Previously, he had lived in the forests and wilds, where he constantly maintained his recitation and contemplation.
Regarding his title, "Yinhao": Suddenly, there was a deer with eight-pronged antlers that would follow and playfully roam the courtyard steps as if it had been raised there for generations.

Whenever he mounted it, he could travel to great distances without weariness. Consequently, he placed the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) upon its back, hung the commentaries and sub-commentaries from its horns, and tied other small scrolls to its tail.
When at leisure, Kang wore coarse cloth and trailed a *nà* (Sanskrit: *lipa*; Chinese: "stomach-wrapping garment," also called "chest-wrap"; its construction is like a vest).
The Patriarch wore a large bamboo hat, which those who saw him considered strange. Upon entering the capital, he encountered a public lecture;

he immediately went to the assembly, approached the lecturer to present his own interpretation, and engaged in a dialogue of several hundred words before concluding. The lecturer then teased him, saying: "The sweet peach bears no fruit;
the bitter plum bends its branches low. The Patriarch replied: "The Wheel-Turning King has a thousand sons; the Street Official has no grandson. This was intended as a rebuke.
Kang had no disciples. Kang said, "That which is near cinnabar becomes red; that which is near lacquer becomes black.
Your redness cannot be used for vermilion or crimson, and your blackness cannot be used for lead or ink. No one could fathom where his understanding led.

When word of this reached the Emperor, he issued an edict for him to propagate and expound [the teachings] at Anguo Temple. Consequently, he composed the *Commentary on the Madhyamaka-śāstra* (Zhongguan lun shu) and the *Commentary on the Śata-śāstra* (Zhongbai lun).
The *Menlun xuanshu* (Mysterious Pivot of the Gate Treatise) in two volumes circulated in the world.
Wú'ài of the Táng dynasty was originally of the Chén clan from Zhōngzhōu. During the Yǒngjiā era of the Jìn dynasty, his ancestors migrated south and settled in Jiànyé.

His father, Kuàng, served as a scholar-official to Emperor Yuán of Liáng. In the first year of the Chéngshèng era, Wú'ài was born in Chéngdū; his divine appearance was exceptionally extraordinary. Upon seeing him—

He was known as a vessel for the present age. At nine years of age, he was able to respond to inquiries; at ten, he entered a private school, where he possessed a powerful memory and never forgot what he had learned.
He once traveled to Chang’an, where the Dharma Master Dao’an spoke with him and marveled at his talent, encouraging him to leave the household life.

He first studied the *Prince’s Sutra of Auspicious Omens*, and his longing and admiration for it were so overwhelming that he could not contain himself, even shedding tears. In the third year of the Tiānhé era, during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of the Northern Zhou...

Upon the Empress’s accession, he was graciously permitted to receive the tonsure. In the third year of the Jiande era, when an imperial decree abolished the Buddhist teachings, he sank into obscurity amidst the dust and grime;

nevertheless, his observance of the precepts became even more rigorous. At the beginning of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, he subsequently participated in the restoration of the Dharma. By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Yongning Temple.

He immediately proceeded to the Qi region, where he relied upon Master Chao to hear lectures on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Not long after, he entered Chang’an to study the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and the *Abhidharma*.
At that time, Dharma Master Tǐ of Xìngshàn was just beginning his exposition of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. He commanded Sè to lecture on its meaning without obstruction;
however, some of the textual passages were occasionally omitted. Thereupon, Sè spent day and night thoroughly reciting the sixty fascicles of the original text until he suffered a heart ailment.
He subsequently returned to Yǒngníng Temple for medical treatment. After ten years, the Regional Commander, Prince of Héjiān, appointed him to oversee the affairs of the temple. Great...
In the second year [of the Kaihuang era], an imperial edict ordered him to revise and finalize the Buddhist teachings at the Sifang Guan in Luoyang.

In the fifth year, when Emperor Yang was on his western campaign, he passed by the monastery, summoned him for an audience, and bestowed upon him exceptional honors and gifts. In the thirteenth year, when the Tang dynasty succeeded the Sui through abdication, he went to the capital and resided at Zhuangyan Monastery.

As the community recognized his broad knowledge and insight, they requested that he take charge of the monastery’s affairs; however, this was not to his liking, as it was similar to his previous experience at Yongning Monastery.
In the eighth year of the Wude era, he turned toward the practice of *nirnimitta-vipaśyanā* (contemplation of signlessness) at Yongning Temple to subdue his mental afflictions.
On the twenty-eighth day of the second month in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away without any pain; he was eighty-four years of age.
Tang Fayan, surnamed Yan, was a native of Jinling in Jiangbiao. Originally named Fazang, he resided at Yuanli Temple. There he studied Vasubandhu’s *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* under Master Zhuangyan Jue;

whenever he heard other scriptures, they seemed as familiar to him as subjects he had previously mastered. He would then test his understanding by privately searching for and emulating their words and meanings, finding that there were no points that did not harmonize with his comprehension.
He immediately consulted various senior masters, all of whom said, "This is due to the karmic conditions you have cultivated over many past lives."
Thus, I have not forgotten him. Later, he entered the capital and resided at Riyen Temple, where he passed away at the end of the Wude era.
Furthermore, those who dwelt in the profound were advanced in years, yet being content, they did not accumulate wealth or currency; whatever they received was immediately distributed and exhausted.
In the tenth year of the Zhenguan era, he died at the temple at the age of over ninety.

Tang Zhikai, surnamed Feng, was a native of Danyang. Orphaned at a young age, when he was six years old, he happened to follow the Dharma Master Jizang to hear the "Fire-House" chapter (*Agnighara-parivarta*) of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Upon returning home, he said to his mother, "The one described in the scripture as the 'fire-house' is my own body.
If I were the fire-house, I should burn others; since I cannot burn them, it can be known that there is no 'self'. That evening...

He remained awake until dawn and urgently took leave of his mother to go to [Jñānagupta] Zang to seek ordination. Because his complexion was very dark, he was commonly called "Wukai" (Black K'ai) at the time.
At the age of thirteen, Zang had him recite [the scriptures], and he did not rely on the sutras or śāstras but followed Zang’s own interpretations.
He resided at Jiaxiang and other monasteries in Kuaiji. When Zang entered the capital, he returned to Jinglin to gather disciples. In the seventh year of the Wude era, someone again invited him.

He propagated the teachings in Shan County, where his followers reached five hundred. In the first year of the Zhenguan era, he resided at Xiaolongquan Temple in Yu’ao County, where he expounded the *Three Treatises*, the *Large Perfection of Wisdom Sutra*, and other scriptures.
He vowed never to travel elsewhere, to remain free from sleep, and to reject offerings of beds, seats, water, or food, accepting only what was necessary.
Behind the Buddha hall, a pond suddenly overflowed, leading him to say, "I can spend my final years here."

Ordinary people treated dogs as wicked creatures; as soon as they were born, they would abandon them, leaving them to die of hunger and cold. When Seng-kai heard of this, he felt pity for them and collected and raised them all.
He harbored no resentment even when they stepped upon or soiled his bedding. In the nineteenth year [of the Tianjian era], the Duke of Qi, the Regional Inspector, welcomed him to Jiaxiang Temple.
There, over eight hundred people gathered to study the exegesis of the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises), with officials and commoners all present in their proper order to receive his instruction.
The temple gates were made magnificent and radiant. At that time, the Dragon Spring dried up. Huikai sighed and said, "I shall not return.
On the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month in the twentieth year, he finally ascended the seat; holding a *ruyi* (ceremonial fly-whisk) in his hand, he sat in silence and passed away.
His entire body was buried at Dayu Mountain, and a seven-story pagoda was erected to commemorate his virtue.
Hui-min of the Tang dynasty, whose courtesy name was Xuansu, was originally from Hedong. He entered the monastic order at the age of nine;

after one month of reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*, he was able to repeat it from memory. At fifteen, he followed Dharma Master Guang of Silla to Huixiang Temple to study the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Cheng-lun).
At seventeen, he lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* at Guangxing Temple in Haiyan, where fragrant incense filled the courtyard, and some even heard [divine voices].

In mid-air, he snapped his fingers, and the assembled guests all marveled at this extraordinary feat. Once he had received full ordination, he studied the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* under Master Zhi of Zhuyuan Temple;
his mastery of both its principles and phrasing was so profound that he also became well-versed in other Vinaya schools. Master Zhi entrusted all his disciples to him before passing away.
Shortly thereafter, he traveled to Kuaiji and Tiantai, where he paid homage to the Stone Buddha in Shan County. After several years, he returned to Wu.

He formed a bond with his companions to cultivate their practice at Tongxuan Temple. Wearing plain clothes and subsisting on simple vegetarian fare, seventeen years passed before his feet ever crossed the threshold of his door.
During the chaos at the end of the Sui dynasty, he never ceased his meditation and recitation. Su Zongguan Wen Si’an invited him to visit twice.

Thereafter, he visited [the region] once more. The Regional Governors Li Lian, Xue Tong, Wang Rong, and others held him in particularly high esteem and wished to detain him firmly for the welfare of the common people;
however, hearing that the Master would ultimately not comply, they consequently built a temple for him in Guanduan Mountain at Huating.
He intended to practice the Way there; however, as the ground was damp and infested with mosquitoes and gadflies, he feared it might lead to illness or calamity.

Early in the Tang dynasty, he moved to Mount Haiyu, where he planted hundreds of thousands of catalpa trees. Students from distant regions who came to study under him were often more than a hundred at a time.

In his later years, he resided in a thatched hut at Nanjian, where two rabbits and a tiger were always with him whether he went out or stayed home. Birds, beasts, and even deities received the precepts of refuge from him. Thus did he serve them.
His legacy is vast and worthy of record. Li Shijia, Duke of Yangwu and Commander-in-Chief, dispatched an envoy with gifts and a letter to summon him, but he did not comply with the command.
In the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, Prince Jiang, serving as a Regional Inspector, wished to receive the precepts from him, yet he again firmly declined and did not emerge from the mountains.

He revised and corrected those parts of the ancient Vinaya commentaries that were deficient or erroneous, and authored the *Private Record on the Ten Recitations Vinaya* (Shisong siji) in thirteen fascicles.

He authored the *Sengni xingshi* (Practices of Monks and Nuns) in two fascicles, the *Nizhong jiemmo* (Karmavācanā for the Community of Nuns) in two fascicles, and the *Daosu pusa jie yi shu* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Bodhisattva Precepts for the Clergy and Laity) in four fascicles.
He had more than twenty disciples who attained the Dharma. On the eleventh day of the eighth month in the twentieth year, he passed away at his place of seclusion at the age of seventy-seven.
The Newly Compiled Biographies of Monks Categorized by the Six Fields of Study, Scroll Nineteen;
The Newly Compiled Biographies of Monks Categorized by the Six Fields of Study, Scroll Twenty.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Tanyu of Eastern Zhejiang.
The Section on Enduring Suffering, Studying, and Maintaining Resolve.
During the Tang Dynasty, Faxian was born into the Ding family in Jiangling, Nanjun. At the age of twelve, he relied upon the Dharma Master Baoming of Silong Temple.
The Master [Hui] received the tonsure and served him diligently for a long time. One day, he suddenly asked, "The realm of desire is a land of turmoil;

it is not inherently a condition for the Way. Since one has been born within it, how can one escape? Daoming replied, "All sentient beings possess the 'taste of dhyāna' of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), which they do not forget throughout kalpas.
When the time comes, it will manifest. Now, Grand Master Hui is the preeminent master among scholars; you should go and serve him. Soon after, Daoming departed for Hui’s presence.
When Emperor Yang summoned him, he was about to return to Jinling, but on the way, he turned back to his hometown. He stayed at this temple to receive visitors;
with four hundred disciples, it flourished into a great monastic center. Later, he again followed Chengyan, Xi Hao, and others to refine his practice, increasing his progress day by day.
However, he ultimately found his final resting place at the monastery of Xi Hao. At that time, natural disasters and banditry repeatedly struck the region, and the temple—
The multitude fled and dispersed, but Xuán alone remained to guard the Great Hall for over thirty years. Within, he frequently went without even vegetables or water;

without, the clash of weapons raged incessantly. Yet he remained silent and composed as if nothing were amiss. The canopy of the hall was constructed by Dharma Master Mítiān, using plum wood for its beams.
It was popularly known as the Mei-liang Hall. Within it was placed a statue of Maitreya, both the halo and the pedestal of which were forty feet high.

It was surrounded by the eight classes of supernatural beings, whose appearance inspired the utmost awe and reverence. At this time, a precious crown and flowered curtains were displayed, along with ritual implements and a sutra platform.
Five lamps burned perpetually without ceasing; suddenly, one lamp blazed up alone, its flame rising more than ten feet high. Such was the response to his utmost sincerity.
During the Zhenguan era, Xian began to reside in a separate quarters. One night, there appeared one wearing five-colored robes and holding a golden pitcher, who presented it to him.
Furthermore, he once dreamed that a strange monk told him, "You should go to Qizhou to see Chan Master Xin. Upon going there, he indeed attained realization.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month of the third year of the Yonghui era, he dreamed that he was sitting in a jeweled hall, bestowing [the teachings] upon the fourfold assembly.
He observed the precepts with such diligence that he fell ill. On the tenth day of the first month of the fourth year, he rose from his bed and bathed and shaved his head as he usually did.
At noon on the eleventh day, he passed away. On the seventeenth day, his disciples buried him at the northern plain of Daming Monastery.
Before his death, a disciple saw the western wall of the room crack open, and white light pervaded it.
At the northwest of the temple was a place called Tou. At night, two paths of white clouds stretched across the sky, and the statues, furnishings, and utensils within the hall all began to shake.
Those who discussed the matter believed that Xian had resided at this temple for more than fifty years without ever stepping outside his door;
therefore, at the time of his death, auspicious signs were particularly numerous. Prince Ji, the Governor-General of Jingzhou, had long since received [his teachings].
He returned to the precepts. He commissioned Guo Yu, the Secretary of Records, to inscribe a memorial for him, thereby expressing his remembrance and longing to the slightest degree.
Hui-ming of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Wang; he was a native of Hangzhou. He left home to become a monk in his youth and traveled to seek the Way, going everywhere.
He constantly wore a robe of coarse cloth and followed Master Min of Yue for twenty-five years. His profound understanding was such that, among a multitude of thousands, he stood out as...
First, he was known as Qingbuming during his time. Later, he studied the methods of Chan under Chan Master Yan of Jiangshan for ten years.
Once, when accumulated snow blocked the road and he had not eaten for seven days, he thought to himself alone: "I have heard that one dies after seven days without food;
since I do not die now, could this be my karmic destiny? I shall test this by observing it. Thereupon, he suspended himself with a rope.
At the edge of the cliff, it was as if someone had suddenly severed the rope; he fell all the way to the bottom.
Suddenly, as if someone were lifting him up, he was restored to his former position, without the slightest injury.

Not long after, while practicing *dhūta* austerities on Mount Siwang in Jingzhou, his form and shadow were always together, wearing but a single robe through both cold and heat, having forgotten both self and others. And as for the two tigers—
As for those who were fighting, he was able to cause them to reconcile. He took the *Sūtra of Additional Benefits* (*Śrīmālā-sūtra*) exclusively as his standard for practice.
During the Longshuo era, while traveling through Zhongnan Mountain, he visited the capital for a short time before departing.

Tang Daoxing, surnamed Liu, was a native of Qinzhou. During the final years of the Sui dynasty, when the empire was in great turmoil, Daoxing was eight or nine years old and constantly desired to leave the household life.
His parents did not grant their permission, so he would frequently run away to the monastery; though they pulled him back, he had no intention of returning. His parents grew weary of this.
At the age of nineteen, he eventually went into seclusion at Daguang Temple. His parents searched for him everywhere but could not find him.

The community, pitying his resolve, exhorted him; he immediately shaved his head and became a monk. He once said to his disciples, "A human body is difficult to obtain; you should uphold the precepts and not be negligent.
When bandits abducted his mother and departed, Sengxing was still a novice (śrāmaṇera) managing the temple affairs. Upon hearing this, he hurriedly set out that very night.

He galloped sixty *li* to reach the bandits' location. Prostrating himself and weeping, he begged to be allowed to return with his mother. Before the bandits could strike him with their blades, they had not yet wounded him;
he thought to himself, "This monk faces death without fear for the sake of his mother—is this not the height of filial piety? To kill one who is supremely filial would bring misfortune."
He tore his own clothes to bandage his wounds and had [the monk] carry his mother. They fled through a secret path toward the city.
Later, while seeking refuge, they entered the road to Shu and encountered an elderly monk who traveled with them. The old monk said to Sengxing, "I have ten taels of gold.
If you reach a place of safety, I hope we may share it together; I pray you do not disdain the burden. Sengxing thought to himself that gold is a thing that brings misfortune. As...
"Furthermore, since even holding a jewel in one's hand is not permitted, how much less so carrying it on one's back?

Thereupon, he took leave of the old monk and traveled alone until he reached Hechi County, where Duke Zhanhuang happened to recognize him. The Duke provided him with servants and guards and escorted him as far as Liangzhou.
Some reports state that the old monk encountered bandits at Sanquan County, who killed him and took his gold. Once Xing had completed his ordination, he practiced the dhūta ascetic observances.
Dharma Master Zhishun studied the Vinaya and could listen to the five types of transgressions and then recite them back from memory. Zhishun was profoundly amazed by his wisdom and understanding.
Furthermore, having received the teachings from Dharma Master Shou in the capital, his mastery of the great principles became even more comprehensive.

Upon returning to Shu, he extensively synthesized the sutras and śāstras, and also received the essential points of the mind under Chan Master Jiang. Nevertheless, it was toward the Vinaya that he applied his greatest effort of study. He would often sigh and say: "The Buddha..."
The Dharma gradually declined, and irreverence increased day by day; how could I dare to treat it with such profanity?
Therefore, unless a request for the precepts was made twenty or thirty times, I never permitted their transmission; thus, one can know the weight he placed on the Dharma.

When he delivered impassioned discourses on the suffering of birth and death within the six realms of existence to exhort the assembly, some were moved to shed tears. He served as the *upadhivāra* (administrator) of Fushō-ji Temple.

At that time, the temple master possessed a *sīmā-sthāpana* (boundary-setting) charter which forbade him from harboring guests. Yet, whenever a guest arrived, Daoxing would always provide them with lodging and food, refusing no one.
The master became greatly incensed and said, "How dare you, young man, act this way? My words are not being heeded; do you think the office of the *sīmā-sthāpana* does not exist?
Daoxing replied calmly, "The public office does not admit even a needle, yet private matters allow for carriages and horses. This is the case for the Sangha and the Three Jewels."

One should accept [the offerings] according to the Dharma; otherwise, one violates the Buddha’s regulations. Regarding the Buddha’s regulations and the mandates of secular officials, which is more weighty?
The Prefect became even more enraged. After some time, he finally repented. During the Zhenguan era, Dai Ling of Chengdu arrived and stayed overnight in the Xingfang hall.

When the drums were struck for the third time, he suddenly started up in alarm and ran outside, saying, "I see a monk dressed in red who, holding a staff, strikes my back and asks, 'Why are you staying here?
He hurriedly called for a lamp to examine his back; there was a mark from the staff, three fingers wide. He immediately went to Xing to repent his transgressions and departed.
Once, while suffering from an illness, he heard music intensely; sitting alone in his room, he reflected, "Throughout my life, I have sought the Buddha."

As for the fruit [of his practice], the retributions of humans and devas were not what he sought. As soon as he brought it to mind, the pain ceased; he recovered swiftly. From that time on, he prostrated before a thousand Buddhas daily.
During the Yonghui era, Dharma Master Xuanzang sent him the śarīra relics he had obtained from the Western Heaven (India) so that he might make offerings to them.

He established his practice within his private chambers and separately erected a *bodhimaṇḍa*. He made this vow: "If my transmission of the Dharma and my worship of the Buddha accord with the holy mind, I pray that you grant a miraculous sign of light as witness.
Shortly thereafter, the entire room became golden in color. He passed away in the fourth year of the Xianqing era at the age of sixty-seven.
Tang Falang was a native of Gusu. She had long been devoted to the recitation of the Avalokiteśvara mantra.
Among the people of the capital, those who prayed for relief from illness and distress frequently received its efficacy. Princess Chengyang was the biological sister of Emperor Gaozong;
she was first married to Du He, the son of Du Ruhui, and after He’s death, she was remarried to Xue Guan. In the second year of the Longshuo era, her illness became critical.
There were several dozen other skilled physicians, yet none could cure him. Someone then recommended Daolang’s name to the attendants, who summoned him to establish a ritual altar.

He performed the recitations according to the dharma, and soon the illness was indeed healed. The reward bestowed upon him was generous, and he further petitioned the Emperor to restore the temple where he resided;
this temple was formerly the Linggan Temple of the Sui dynasty. In the third year of the Kaihuang era, when Emperor Wen was about to relocate the capital, he first issued an order...
All the imperial mausoleums and burial mounds were exhumed and relocated to the outskirts, and the site was walled off.

The construction of this monastery was intended for it to serve as the guardian of the incense and lamps for all these imperial mausoleums and burial sites. It had been abolished in the fourth year of the Wude era, but by this time it had been fully restored and adorned.
Furthermore, he was granted the title "Blue Dragon" (Qinglong) as a mark of praise and honor. Later, Hui-lang passed away at the monastery.
There was a Tang-dynasty monk named Yuan, whose courtesy name was Biankong; his secular surname was Yu, and he was a native of Changyi in Gaoping.

While his mother, Lady Zhao, was pregnant, she dreamed that she was attending upon sages and worthies by her side as they traveled joyfully through the air. When Yuan was six years old, he accompanied his mother to pay homage at the Śāriputra Stūpa, where he beheld a holy monk.
He was like one who, beside a stupa, joyfully leaped for joy and embraced it as if it were an old acquaintance. He then said to his mother, "I wish to leave the household life.
Because he was still young, his mother did not grant permission. At the age of thirteen, she sent him to become a disciple of Dharma Master Huìyán of Hǔqīu Monastery.
In the second year of the Lóngshuò era, he underwent the examination of his training in tonsure and received full ordination from Meditation Master Huìxǔ. His feet were complete.
Jie listened as the Dharma Master Cong of Changle Temple visited Master Rong of Jiangning to study the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) and the teachings on the mind.

On the twentieth day of the twelfth month in the second year of the Yongchang era, his illness became critical. He said to his disciples, "The place where a corpse resides is overcome with foulness and impurity;
I wish to depart for another realm. His disciples escorted him, and he stayed at Tongbi Pavilion.
At Jingzhi Abbey, he suddenly perceived a wondrous fragrance filling the air. Fayuan maintained right mindfulness without distraction;
mindful of his late master’s earnest instructions, he passed away with palms joined. He was fifty-one years of age.
Tang Daoying left home to become a monk in his early years and was particularly meticulous in observing the precepts. His monastery was located in Buzheng Ward in the capital.
During the Xianheng era, the abbot Huilian happened to be standing in the courtyard at dawn when he perceived two people entering Daoying’s quarters;
looking down, he saw that their feet never actually touched the ground. Finding this strange, Huilian went to Daoying to ask about what he had encountered. Daoying said: "These..."
He was, in fact, an envoy sent by King Zhuangxiang of Qin. Now, King Zhuangxiang brought about the destruction of the Eastern Zhou and severed the ancestral sacrifices of the Ji clan;

for this he has incurred sin beneath the earth, and it has been eighty years since he has been able to receive offerings. Lately, however, due to the pangs of hunger and emptiness, [he has become restless].
He then came to me and requested, saying, "Master, you are greatly compassionate; I pray you do not decline. Furthermore, I have three hundred followers;
can the expenses for the Master be measured? I shall attend tomorrow; I hope the Master will provide for us. Thereupon, Hyang-ji prepared all the necessary provisions, yet there was no wine.
Thus, he sent a messenger back to fetch more to assist him. When the appointed time arrived, they sat in rows as follows.
Li Zhuangxiang turned toward Yingli and pointed, saying, "This is Bai Qi; this is Wang Jian; this is Chen Zhen.
Some were executed for slaughter, others for treachery; all have become our adversaries. As he spoke these words, they all offered their thanks repeatedly.
As they walked along, looking at one another, they said, "When will we ever obtain a full meal again, such as today? Thereafter—
He said, "Wait twenty years. Then, Ying spoke slowly, saying, "The wine was not mine; it was actually taken from Jian in the past.
When the ruler and his ministers heard this, they were moved by even deeper gratitude. They asked Ying, "Does the Master know the tombs outside Tonghuamen Gate to the east of the city?"

"In the past, when I was buried, the various items used for my funeral amounted to nearly ten thousand. Since the onset of this chaos and disorder, although the tomb has been excavated many times, some things still remain.
If you have the good fortune to employ these with baskets and shovels, I shall perhaps be able to repay you slightly. Ying laughed and said:
"I am one who has left the household life; how could I possibly serve as a 'Gold-Seeking' officer for Dong Zhuo? He then took a long bow and departed.
Tang Huìjǐng was born into the Zhāng family of Qí; at only three years of age, she was able to recite the *Dayún jīng* from memory with exceptional fluency.

When the Empress Dowager heard of this, she issued an imperial decree for him to be summoned so that she might stroke his head; she bestowed upon him a purple *kāṣāya* robe and ordained him at Chongfu Monastery in Taiyuan.
As he grew older, he served as the monastery’s *upādhyāya*. His countenance was stern and upright, such that all who saw him were struck with awe and respect.

When walking through the marketplace, if he observed the two assemblies (monks and nuns) failing in their decorum, he would invariably reprimand them, never showing the slightest leniency. In his later years, he devoted himself especially to the practice of meditative stillness.
