I respectfully submit this. He subsequently passed away at the age of over eighty. His portrait and the robes he was granted both remain preserved in the Nine Sons Mother Hall of the temple.
During the Tang dynasty, Xuanzang was registered as a youth at Baima Temple in Jingzhou; he mastered the teachings of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and was particularly devoted to the Lotus Sūtra.
He established a private chamber, burned incense, and recited [the scripture] seven times daily. He once experienced the arrival of celestial beings to listen to his recitation.
In this manner, he did not cease for fifteen years. At that time, he and Dharma Master Daojun were both summoned to remain in the capital.

On the eighth day of the second month in the third year of the Jinglong era, the Emperor broke his fast at the Lingguang Palace while the various scholars were assembled in great numbers; Xuanzang and the others then presented [their memorial].

The Master requested leave to return to the mountains. The Emperor composed a poem to see him off and issued an edict for all the scholars to write verses in response. Consequently, those who composed such verses filled both the court and the common world;
Linxia considered this a great honor. Many of these poems have not been recorded here.
Dharma Master Zhen of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Wang and was a native of Jinhua. He resided at Xiuguang Temple in Yuyao;

he upheld the Vinaya and was proficient in the sutras, enjoying a flourishing reputation that was highly esteemed by the eminent scholars of his time. In the sixth year of the Tianbao era, the Governor, Lord Qin, and the Chief Secretary, Lord Di, recommended him to preside over this temple.
The two officials said to one another, "Master Zhen understands the profound and subtle Dharma and has attained awakening..."
Regarding the supreme meaning, he asked about one thing and attained three; hearing one, he knew ten. His eloquence was as vast as that of Lishi, and his wisdom as comprehensive as that of Senghui;
it would be appropriate to say he could drive side by side with them. In the eighth year, the County Magistrate Wang Rui composed a text to inscribe this memorial.
The Epitaph for Hong Yuanshen.
The Tang official Dajia was surnamed Wang; he was a native of Jinshui County in Jianzhou, Shu. From his youth, he renounced worldly life, and his conduct was solitary and austere.
Toward the end of the Tianbao era, when the Emperor visited Chengdu, Dajia went to the imperial residence as a youth to seek ordination.

The Emperor was struck by this and, having attained such a name [for his monastery], he subsequently built a hermitage on Mount Shicheng. Within a short time, it was expanded into a temple, initially named Yunding.
When the Emperor entered Shu, he once ascended the eastern terrace of Wuyan and beheld auspicious clouds and a fine atmosphere;
furthermore, he had a dream in which a divine being surnamed Li said, "I come from Shicheng and wish to serve as Your Majesty’s attendant. Upon reaching this point, the imperial carriage [arrived].

Once, while attending the Emperor during a private banquet, the Emperor asked with ease where the Master resided. The Master replied accordingly. The Emperor realized it and said, "I have indeed known of you.

He subsequently changed the name of the temple to Ciyun (Cloud of Compassion) and bestowed upon the Master the divine title Xuansun (Mystic Grandson), as he was a descendant of the Mystic Origin (Xuanyuan).
Ultimately, the Master passed away at this very temple.

Tang Fajiong resided at Kaiyuan Temple in Guangzhou. He practiced the dhūta austerities with exceptional diligence. There was an ancient bell that had sunk into the sea at Lianmen Port within Jiangnei.
Every month on the fifteenth day, when the great tide receded, the Pu-lao (the dragon-shaped clapper) would emerge from the mud;
its cavity could accommodate a single person. From this, one can know the immense size of the bell. During the Dali era, Fajiong constructed a pavilion for it.

At that monastery, [Daohui] desired to ascend this bell to perform Buddhist services. He first established a great vegetarian feast assembly and had the monks recite divine incantations, sending a novice monk to submerge himself in the water to convey his intent to the Dragon Palace. Shortly thereafter, the novice emerged holding three pearls and reported:
"The bell serves to stabilize the sea; it cannot be obtained. However, although Daohui wished to bring forth the bell, he has instead obtained these pearls. This was surely because the object...
There is that which cannot be taken for granted.
Tánchútuóhuā (Dharmatāta), whose name translates as "Without Cause," was a man from the Western Regions. During the Shàngyuán era, he came to travel in the capital.
At that time, his age was already six hundred years; some say it was eighty. His countenance possessed the appearance of a child, and his physical strength was light and robust.
His movements were exceptionally graceful and convenient. The Emperor questioned him about this and issued an edict for him to enter the palace, where he asked about the way of longevity.
Puṇyatāra said, "The way of longevity lies in nothing else but the reduction of desire. When desire is reduced, the mind becomes tranquil; when the mind is tranquil, the spirit becomes settled."
"When the spirit is at peace, one attains longevity. To abandon this is something beyond my humble understanding. Because of this, the Emperor held him in even greater esteem.

In the third year of the Yongtai era, he foreknew the date of his own death. He sent a disciple to present his robes and alms bowl to the throne as a parting gift, and subsequently passed away at Zhanguo Temple.
By imperial decree, his disciple was granted purple robes.

Tang Yixuan was a native of Jinling. By nature he was intelligent and sharp, possessing a serene air that transcended the mundane. After receiving the Dharma, he applied himself with diligence to the Vinaya;
his efforts at self-discipline were such that he never wasted even a moment of time. At the beginning of the Tianbao era, he relied upon the Vinaya Master Fashen of Yangzhou.
Master Fashen patted him on the back and sighed, saying: "Confucius said that 'the younger generation is to be feared. This son of mine is exactly what he meant."
Later, I listened to Vinaya Master Zhou lecture on the *Zhongnan Shichao*. His investigations were meticulous and refined, leading him to compose the *Zhezhong Ji* (Record of Resolving the Middle).

"Resolving the middle" means resolving what is erroneous to hit upon what is correct. By affirming my own correctness while resolving the errors of masters such as Min, Rong, Ji, E, and Sheng, he demonstrated that it was not yet too late to settle matters of right and wrong.
Nevertheless, regarding the School of the Lineage (the Chan/Zen tradition), one simply cannot help but act in this way.
In his later years, his influence through transformation was especially flourishing; in the end, no one knew where he passed away.

During the Tang dynasty, She Guang became a monk and was affiliated with Daxingshan Monastery in Jingzhao. During the Kaiyuan era, the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra’s fame was preeminent throughout the realm;
among the scholars and gentlemen of the time, there were none who did not look up to him with reverence. Guang consequently attached himself to him. When [Amoghavajra]...
He traveled westward into the void, and his light followed him as well. Having endured many hardships and perils, he reached the Kingdom of Siṃhala (Sri Lanka).

There, he encountered the Venerable Ācārya Śrīmitra, who was establishing the Mahāvairocana Maṇḍala of the *Mahāvairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra*. Kūkai, together with Huiguan, received the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the five divisions of the teachings.
In the sixth year of the Tiānbǎo era, he returned to the capital alongside Amoghavajra and was subsequently appointed to participate in the affairs of translation. Before long, Amogha...

Amoghavajra was silent. Emperor Daizong waited for the light [to appear] and received him with the ritual of Amoghavajra. By imperial decree, he was commissioned to perform meritorious rites at Mount Wutai.
There, he encountered Master Zhanran, a scholar of the Tiantai school, who was leading more than forty monks from Jianghuai on a pilgrimage to Mount Wutai.
Master Zhanran followed Amoghavajra and inquired about matters concerning the Western Regions, saying, "In our own school as well, there was once [a tradition] regarding the Western Regions..."

"Is there anyone who knows this? Does anyone possess the excellence of the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of this school? Guṅ replied, "There is indeed such a person. I have commissioned a translation of it to send to you.
Furthermore, the teachings of Nāgārjuna flourish in South India; as for the wise one [Zhiyi], he is not at all far removed from him."
Langran of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Wei and was a native of Nanxu. During the Kaiyuan era, he received the tonsure from Master Qi at Kuangguang Temple in Danyang.
At the beginning of the Tianbao era, he relied upon Master Guang of Huayan Temple in Hangzhou to receive full ordination.

Later, he moved to Lingyin Temple, where he served under Master Yuan and mastered the *Sifenlü shanbu suiji jiemo* (The Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya). He also studied under Master Tanli of Yuezhou.

He researched its meaning and provided detailed and clear expositions. Students from all quarters flocked to him. In the second year of the Zhide era, an imperial edict appointed him to reside at Cihesi.
During the Shangyuan era, the Prefectural Governor Wei Xuan welcomed him as the Great Virtuous Head of the Zhaoyin Monastery. Thereupon, during his leisure time, he...

He composed the *Jin-gu-jue* (Decisions on the Ancient and Modern) and the commentary on the *Shi-sifen-lü-chao* (Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya), totaling hundreds of thousands of words, which circulated widely throughout the world;

his own preface is particularly detailed, but it is not recorded here in full. In the twelfth year of the Dali era, during winter, he passed away while seated in the lotus posture at the age of fifty-four.

He was thirty-five sui. In the spring of the following year, a stupa was erected on the western plain of the mountain. Liu Shi, a Court Gentleman for Agricultural Supervision, composed an inscription for it.

Yuanquan of the Tang dynasty was simple and straightforward by nature; in his leisure time between Chan meditation and lecturing, he also managed agricultural enterprises, achieving considerable profit from his lands and gardens.
He resided at Huilin Temple in Luoyang, where he was renowned as a "Yi Dun of the Empty Gate" (a master of the Buddhist way). He was particularly close with Li Yuan.
Yuan’s father, Li Cheng, had served as the Imperial Commissioner for the Capital during the Tianbao era; he died maintaining his integrity during the rebellion of An Lushan.

Consequently, Yuan vowed never to marry or hold office, renounced all his property, and entered the permanent endowment of Huilin Temple. There, he took his meals daily alongside the monks to manifest his resolve.
We once intended to travel together to Sichuan to explore the splendors of Mount Min, Mount Emei, Wanglei, and Qingcheng;
however, we could not decide for a long time upon the route to take. Guān wished to go by way of the Xiagou Valley from Chang’an, while Yuán wished to go by way of the Three Gorges from Jingmen.
Soon thereafter, he ultimately followed Yuan’s counsel. As the boat moored at Nanpu, they saw a woman wearing a brocade apron, carrying a water jar on her back to draw water.
Observing her, [Yuan] wept and said, "I originally did not wish to go by this route; how could it be otherwise now? Yuan asked her, saying, "The woman is surnamed Wang.
She has been pregnant for three years, yet she has still not given birth. It is only because my time of death was still far off. He died there.
He replied, "I have no regrets. I bid you farewell. Twelve years from now, on the evening of the Mid-Autumn Festival, we shall meet outside the Tiantzhi Temple in Qiantang.
After Yuan finished attending to the funeral rites, he went to wait upon the Wang family to seek an audience with their son.
The boy smiled; from this, Yuan knew where his karmic affinity lay, for it was truly not easy to evade. After a long time, Yuan arrived as he had promised.
In Qiantang, he heard that a cowherd was singing a *zhuzhi* song beside the Ge Hong Well. He hurried there to pay his respects and said, "I wonder if you, sir, are in good health?
The cowherd replied, "Master Li is truly a man of faith; since you have traveled so far, it is fitting that we converse."

"Your current worldly entanglements will bring you no further benefit; be careful not to draw near them. Diligently apply yourself to cultivation so that we may eventually achieve our union—this would be most fortunate.
Having spoken thus, Xu struck his elbow against the horn and departed.

Regarding Tang Ruǐng’s surname and native place, there has not yet been time for a detailed investigation. Previously, Master Xingzhi of the capital had produced a commentary on the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya);
later, Master Fali of Weixun County composed a separate commentary that circulated independently, which seems to have contained some slight discrepancies.

During the transition between the Sui and Tang dynasties, Master Daoxuan, based on Master Xingzhi’s primary commentary, authored the three-fascicle *Shanbu chao* (Excerpts on Deletion and Supplementation).
Since the Zhenguan era, this [text] has been widely transmitted and chanted throughout Jianghuai, Min, and Shu.
Later, Huaisu—the disciple of Tripitaka Master Xuanzang—composed the *Kai-sifenlü-ji* (Record of the Opening of the Four-Part Vinaya) during the Xianheng period.

Scholars flocked to it, and his work was titled the "New Commentary" (*Xinshu*), as the work of Master Daoxuan was designated the "Old Commentary" (*Jiushu*). Thus, the two commentaries, new and old, circulated side by side.

Regarding the length of the [Buddha’s] physical marks: in the thirteenth year of the Dali era, an imperial edict was issued to assemble the virtuous monks (*bhadanta*) presiding over the ordination platforms of the two monastic streets to deliberate and decide the matter.
At that time, Jing was recommended as the presiding master (*zhuzong*). In the second year of the Jianzhong era, he submitted two memorials which were both implemented.
This was because Prime Minister Yuan Zai held Master Su in high esteem; consequently, Jing had no choice but to comply. Furthermore, Zai commissioned Jing to compose a new memorial.
Biography.
Wei Zhong was born into the Tong family in Chengdu during the Tang dynasty. In his youth, he entered the monastic order under Chan Master Daoguanshi Dao-yuan.
Subsequently, he traveled to Mount Song, where he met Chan Master Shenhui and received definitive instruction from him. Thereafter, he went on to visit various sacred sites.
To the left of the river, there was a secluded mountain, elegant and beautiful, worthy of love. He subsequently built a thatched hut and settled into meditative concentration therein.

For this place had long been infested with dragons and snakes, and shrouded in miasmic smoke and pestilential fogs; even during the day it was pitch black, and those who went there to gather firewood or graze cattle often met their death instantly.
Though the kingdom possessed state physicians, they could exert no skill against such conditions. Since Zhong’s arrival, [the area] for those near and far...
In tranquility, he heard a voice from the air saying, "By the power of the Dharma Master, you have now attained liberation.
He entered nirvana in the third year of the Jianzhong era at the age of seventy-eight.
Tang Bianxiu’s secular surname was Liu; he was a descendant of Jiao, the Prince of Chu of the Han dynasty. Orphaned at a young age, he was raised by his paternal uncles.

He left the household life and received the tonsure under Chan Master Mou of Lingyin. In the fourth year of the Tiānbǎo era, he received full ordination from Master Jiànzhēn of Dōnghǎi and transmitted the Vinaya under Master Tányī of Huìkēi.
During the Zhìdé era, by imperial decree, he was nominated for his eminent conduct and was granted a place on the official register in Wú.

At Kaiyuan Temple in the commandery, during the Qianyuan era, an imperial decree was issued for twenty-five temples throughout the realm to each designate seven eminent monks (*dàdé*) to take turns requesting the Vinaya-piṭaka.
The commandery selected Xiu to respond to this mandate; however, he remained particularly devoted to the Pure Land. He once said to others:
Some have heard it said that in the West (India), the precepts are considered the "Mahāyāna with characteristics" (*sanimitta-mahāyāna*).

This is not so. Why? For all speech is the very nature [of reality], and every thought is suchness (*tathatā*). A single form or a single fragrance is none other than the Middle Way; how much more so, then, is right mindfulness?
As for the Mahāyāna, what could possibly be "with characteristics" and what "without characteristics"? Written on the fifteenth day of the sixth month in the first year of the Jianzhong era. [Seal].
He passed away suddenly at the age of sixty-seven and with thirty-five years of ordination.

On the fifth day of the seventh month of that year, his coffin was moved and interred at the West Temple on Mount Huqiu, to the right of the pine gate. The monk Ruzhou of Zhe compiled the inscription for the epitaph.
Tang Wuce was a man of unknown origins; some say he came from the Western Regions during the Jianzhong era.

Upon arriving in Kuaiji, he took a liking to the sublime scenery of Mount Ruoye and subsequently resided at Yunmen Temple. He was skilled at making friends and would associate with anyone who came and went.
There was nothing that did not accord with his intent. Jiaoran of Wuxing inscribed on the walls of his room: "The mountains of Yue are exquisite, and Yunmen is peerless;

The Western monk has an ancient countenance, yet his heart is like the moon. In the clear morning he sweeps the stones and returns from his practice; Beneath the trees he sleeps in meditation, gazing at the pines and snow.
Readers remarked that Jiaoran had truly succeeded in capturing the master’s distinctive character and refined demeanor.
Táng Jiǎorán, whose courtesy name was Rúzhòu, was a native of Chángchéng in Wŭxīng. His surname was Xiè; he was a tenth-generation descendant of the Marquis Língyùn of Kānglè.
From childhood, he possessed extraordinary talent and was not bound by worldly conventions. He subsequently shaved his head and received the full precepts at the Línghyǐn Ordination Platform.

Later, he relied upon the Vinaya Master Shǒuzhēn to exhaustively study the *vinaya* (monastic discipline). As for the Confucian classics and the works of Lǎozi and Kāśyapa Mātanga, there were none that he did not master.

He reached the ultimate perfection in his craft and was especially skilled in composition; his prose and verse were elegant and beautiful, and his poetic laments particularly delved into the subtlest mysteries.
He was renowned alongside Lingche of Kuaiji and Daobiao of Qiantang. Thus, a contemporary proverb said: "Lingche of Yue penetrates like ice and snow;

Daobiao of Hangzhou rubs the clouds and reaches the heavens; and Daoshou of Xie is capable of refined elegance. In his middle years, he traveled extensively to visit various Chan seats, including those of Nanquan Puyuan and Huineng of Beishou.
These were the points upon which he inquired and reflected. At the beginning of the Zhenyuan era, while residing at the East Creek Hermitage, he sighed and said:

"Even if one possessed the broad knowledge of Zhongni or the vast learning of Xuchen, to spend one’s entire day before others boasting of the Way and flaunting its principles would only serve to disturb the true nature of one's being.
How could this compare to a solitary pine and a fragment of cloud, sitting opposite on a rush mat, attaining the meaning through silence? Thus it reached its ultimate point.
Truly, it was one in whom stillness and spirit were in harmony. Thereupon, he composed a text to bid farewell to his brush and inkstone and withdrew to live in seclusion on Zhufeng Peak.
In the fifth month of the fifth year, he met with Li Hong, the former Censor-in-Chief, who had incurred reprimands in Hebei and was once again appointed as the Governor of Wuxing.
Upon their first meeting, they spoke in harmony. [Jiao] requested instruction on the general outlines of the Chan school (zongmen).
On another day, as they were discussing poetry in general, Jiao ordered his disciples to produce a volume of his drafts to show him, explaining that he had recently discarded them.

Hong was struck with amazement and said, "In the past, I have read Shen Yue’s *Pingsao* (Appraisals), Huixiu’s *Hanlin*, and Yu Xin’s *Shizhen* (Poetic Admonitions). The arguments of these three masters do not come close to this."
"It would have been appropriate to further exert your own strength to inspire the world, yet you have instead abandoned your progress by ceasing midway;
can this truly be right? Every night, he offered food to the ghosts and spirits. He formerly resided at Xingguo Temple in the capital.

An army officer named Shen Jiao, a native of Deqing, was riding his horse toward Luotuo Bridge at dusk when the moonlight was like a roll of silk. He saw several men standing there, dressed in magnificent robes and caps. Jiao asked them—"
Therefore, it was said: "The monk Jiao of Xingguo Temple, east of the shrine of Xiang Wang, has prepared a vegetarian feast and summoned me.
Qian Pei, a soldier of the Changcheng regiment, while moored at Mount Lü, saw several hundred people carrying food and bearing silk passing by with laughter and conversation.

When he questioned them, they replied, "We are returning from attending the feast for Master Jiao. Later, Jiao passed away at Shufeng, the very place where the scholar-junior friends with whom he had spent his life had gathered.
Among the great officers (daifu) were Wei Yingwu, Lu Youping, Wu Jide, Li Ze, Huangfu Zeng, Liang Su, Xue Feng, Lü Wei, Yang Da, and Lu Yu.

As for their literary compositions, there are the *Hao'nuzi* in ten fascicles, the *Neidian leiju* in forty fascicles, the *Rushixiaoyou zhuan*, and externally, the *Yunhai* in twenty fascicles. These were indeed produced by the Chancellor (xiangguo).
The biography was compiled by Lord Gong Di and Lord Yan Zhenqing, while Jiao Shi supplemented its conduct.
Tang Xuanyan was surnamed Li and was a native of Jiangxia. His grandfather, Shan, was widely learned and possessed a powerful memory; his commentary on the *Wenxuan* circulated throughout the world.

His father was Yong, who served as the Governor of Beihai; there is a biography of him in the Histories. From his childhood, Yan had renounced worldly ways. At the beginning of the Zhidu era, he ranked high in the state examinations for the Buddhist scriptures.
He followed the śramaṇa Chongzhen to receive the tonsure and was enrolled at Kaiyuan Temple. In the third year of the Dali era, he received the full precepts from the ācārya Wuzhen.

He immediately conducted himself according to the monastic rules and regulations without even the slightest blemish, and subsequently devoted himself to the study of the Vinaya-piṭaka. Shortly thereafter—

Having received the instructions of the Vajra-like realization that emptiness shatters all marks, he was skilled in poetic composition. Liu Changqing of Pengcheng especially esteemed and recognized his talent.
Among the renowned scholars who frequented him at that time were Yuan Zi of Chen Commandery, Li Ze of Zhao Commandery, Lu Laiqing, Yu Wenxuan, Cai Zhiyang, Heng Li, and Yan;
they would often sit together with him, burning incense and brewing tea, engaging in conversation.
[The Master] smiled. Furthermore, [the authorities] provided funds to expand his residence; how could he fail to be moved and submit?

At the beginning of the Jianzhong era, He Gong, the regional commander of E-yue, summoned him from Jin’an, but he firmly declined. On the fourteenth day of the ninth month in the sixteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, he passed away.
He was fifty years of age and had thirty years of seniority as a monk. He was buried on the southern plain of Mount Huanghe.

Nanta (Nanda) of the Tang dynasty was a man from the Western Regions; "Nanda" translates as "Joy. In the early years of the Jianzhong era, he arrived in Min and Shu, bringing with him three nuns who were all young and beautiful.
They indulged in drinking and wandered about wildly, gathering crowds of the vulgar and reckless wherever they went.

At that time, Zhang Yanshak, the Duke of Wei, was the governor of Chengdu and sought to restrain his subordinates through propriety and righteousness. When the garrison commander heard of this, he felt deep resentment and dispatched soldiers to arrest them.
Bao Da arrived and said to him, "I, a poor monk, have studied Buddhism since childhood and attained the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*).
Entering water, I am not wetted; entering fire, I am not burned; I can transform earth and stone into gold and jade. My arts are inexhaustible.
He then pointed to three nuns and said, "These women are exceptionally skilled in music and dance. Prefect, you should test them. Thereupon, he held a banquet and had them perform.

He observed their performance; their singing and dancing were entirely in accord with the rhythm and the musical laws. When they had become intoxicated with wine, Dharmagupta further commanded them to perform a "trampling dance.
Their trailing of ribbons and whirling like falling snow, as well as their rapid rising and touching of the *maṇḍala*, were particularly extraordinary.

While the military commander was laughing and exchanging pleasantries with them, Dharmagupta suddenly exclaimed, "How dare these women act thus! In all dances, one must stop when the melody ends; yet now she still remains bent over..."

It tilted precariously and would not remain upright; was it perhaps possessed by a wind-spirit? He then took a knife and severed its head. The three nuns followed suit and collapsed to the ground, with blood flowing for more than a zhang.
The guests looked on in astonishment, only to find that they were actually three bamboo staffs. As for the blood, it was merely the wine they had previously drunk.
Puṇyatāra slowly lifted the heads of the three staffs and nailed them to a pillar, then leaned the bodies of the three staffs against the wall. The wine was served.
Then, as he took up the bamboo staff at the point where it was broken and raised its upper end, the head of the staff immediately turned red.
When he sang, the head of the bamboo staff also made a sound; when he danced, the body of the bamboo staff likewise moved in rhythmic gestures.
Once the banquet had ended, the body of the bamboo staff suddenly joined the head of the staff, forming three nuns as before. Upon examining the point where they were joined, it was almost...

There were no traces [of his passage]. Furthermore, he once stayed for several days at the home of a lay donor (*dānapati*). When he was about to take his leave and depart elsewhere, the donor tried to detain him;
he refused, and the donor immediately closed the door to cut off his intention to leave. However, Huìtú hid himself within a crack in the wall.
The host hurriedly grabbed at his robes and caught a corner of the *kāṣāya*. As he pulled harder on the *kāṣāya*, Huìtú drew deeper inside until he finally vanished, never to be seen again.

It was obtained. On the following day, there appeared on the wall a shadow of the Buddha (Bhagavān) as if it were a painting. On the next day, its color gradually faded to a dark hue, yet it still resembled the shadow of the Buddha.
After seven days, the shadow of the Buddha was no longer present; there remained only ink traces. On the eighth day, even the ink traces vanished.
It is said that someone encountered the Buddha in the territory of Pengzhou.
Tang Yun Sui was a man of unknown origins. He was distinguished in his learning and possessed abundant talent. In his social dealings, he was particularly characterized by kindness and benevolence.
He was frequently summoned by imperial decree to enter the Inner Daochang (Palace Monastery). During the reign of Emperor Shunzong, he presided over translation affairs.

At the beginning of Emperor Xianzong’s reign, he was appointed to manage the various monasteries and temples of the Right Street, overseeing matters pertaining to both the Daoist and Buddhist teachings. By special imperial edict, he was further charged with the supervision of the two temples, Ximing and Qianfu.
This is not a matter of mere morality; how could it be otherwise?
Tang Zhencheng, surnamed Shen, was a native of Deqing in Huzhou. His father, Xuanwang, was promoted to the rank of Sima of Yanzhou for his integrity and filial piety.

While Zhencheng was still in the womb, there were auspicious signs of divine light and extraordinary vapors. From birth, he was magnificent and noble; his capacity and bearing surpassed those of his peers.

The boy did not resemble [his father]. Sima instructed him, saying, "You must cultivate the literary arts so that you may obtain an official post. At this, the boy looked sorrowful with an expression of being compelled against his will.
It happened that Yan Zhenqing, the Duke of Lu, passed by his home and ordered him to recite what he had studied.

The boy then recited five hundred scrolls of Buddhist scriptures alone, without a single error. The Duke greatly praised and marveled at this, shaved his head, and enrolled him as a resident monk at Bashi Monastery.
Daosi received the precepts from Master Changjin at Tongxuan Temple. Thereafter, he devoted himself to the study of the *Vinaya*, for which he was especially beloved by Master Jin.
The master said to his disciples, "As for Cheng, among you, he is no mere brother.

Not long after, he traveled west to the capital, where he investigated the commentaries on the *Lotus Sūtra* and the teachings of Tiantai at Yunhua Temple; his reputation spread widely, and his writings—

The venerable elders of Xinsi Temple also invited him there. During his periods of lecturing and instruction, he simultaneously excelled in the mastery of the essentials of the Sūtras and Vinaya, such that he felt no shame before the assembly.
During the Zhenyuan era, the Duke Liang, as the Commissioner for Meritorious Works, frequently visited An Guo Temple on imperial errands;

since it was impossible to respond to his inquiries and counsel without a carriage, the Duke petitioned for him to be appointed as a Court-Provided Great Virtue (Gongfeng Dade), and he subsequently moved his residence there.

At that time, his former teacher, Wuzhi, who had likewise attained great success in his religious career and received imperial favor, submitted a memorial recommending Daoxuan to pray for the blessing of the state.

Daoxuan, however, requested leave to return home due to illness, and the Emperor granted his request. Previously, Wuzhi had dreamed that Daoxuan was walking southward while holding a white lotus flower in his hand;
this dream was now proven true. Nevertheless, in his native village, Daoxuan served as the presiding master (*śāstrin*) of the Vinaya school eight times and four times...

The members of the officiating assembly at the altar were all appointed in response to the requests of various public figures. He further made pilgrimages to Mount Wutai, where the manifestations of Mañjuśrī appeared and vanished beyond measure.
In the evening, he stayed at Huguo Temple, where he recited the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* one hundred times daily and never omitted his daily practice of repentance.

He composed commentaries and sub-commentaries on the *Lotus Sūtra*. In the tenth month of winter in the fifteenth year of the Yuanhe era, he manifested slight illness and passed away. His [life span was] long...
On the thirteenth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Qianqing era, he was cremated; his remains were enshrined in a stupa in accordance with his final testament.
Wang Zhen, the Commandant of Wannian, composed the inscription for the stele.
Tánqīng of the Táng dynasty: his clan and native place are not detailed in historical records. Initially, he relied upon Vinaya Master Dàohéng at the Northern Monastery in Wú.
He was close friends with Shěnggōng. Shortly thereafter, he remained at Nányuè, where he lectured and instructed a multitude of disciples.

During the Yuánhé era, the boundary (sīmā) was demarcated at Longxìng Temple in Làngzhōu; at that time, Yìsōng was expounding Huáisù’s new commentary, and [Tánqīng] consequently cited the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.
It says: "At a distance of seven tree-lengths from one another, those who perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) shall be said to have performed the *karmavācanā* well.

According to this principle, one should take sixty-three paces on each of the four sides. Such a natural boundary (*prakṛtisthā sīmā*) serves as the basis for establishing the formal ritual boundary (*kṛtā sīmā*).

The monks were required to assemble in full, and Huiqing was also present. He subsequently raised extensive challenges and objections without ceasing. As the matter passed through the provincial and metropolitan administrations, it reached the imperial hearing.

An edict was issued for the two monastic districts to convene representatives of the three schools to adjudicate between the new and old petitions. It was found that what Master Song had stated truly lacked logical consistency.

Linghu Chu, the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, issued a formal judgment stating: "According to the testimony of the Great Virtuous Ones who transmit the Vinaya in the two monastic districts..."
The interpretation cited by Tancheng is deemed correct. Later, he composed the *Xianzong ji* (Record of Manifesting the Doctrine), which circulated throughout the world.
Tang Qingyuan was born into the Feng family of Yanling in Nanxu. In his youth, he entered Mount She and took Master She as his teacher. He shaved his head and received full ordination;

thereafter, he thoroughly investigated the study of the ritual particulars (*śīla-vinaya*) of the *vinaya*, becoming a peerless master in the field. Shortly thereafter, he suddenly attained comprehensive realization.

Regarding the essentials of Chan: without relying on the instructions of a teacher, at the beginning of the Changqing era, Li Deyu, the Minister of Works, while stationed in Zhexi, invited [the Master] to reside in Jingkou.
He consulted him regarding the mind-dharma, and they were in profound accord with his long-held aspirations. When Lord Li left the prefecture, the Master returned to Xixia.
He passed away at the temple.
Dao-biao of the Tang dynasty was born into the Qin family of Fuchun. At the age of seven, the Venerable Hai of Baiyun Peak on Mount Lingyin saw him and stroked the crown of his head, saying:
"This boy’s eyes are like blue lotuses; if he can renounce the household life to follow me, he will surely [attain great things]."

He had a reputation for virtue. His father agreed with this assessment. In the second year of the Zhidu era, an imperial edict was issued to all laypeople throughout the realm stating that those who could recite seven hundred sheets of Buddhist scriptures were permitted to become *bhikṣu*s.
Baoliao was selected according to this standard and received ordination; he was subsequently registered as a resident of Tianzhu Monastery.
At the beginning of the Yongtai era, he received full ordination at Lingguang Temple under Vinaya Master Yi. At that time, people already recognized his excellence in upholding the precepts.
During the Zhenyuan era, he built a separate dwelling on the lower slopes of the Western Ridge, which he called "Cao Tang" (The Hermitage).

There, he enjoyed the pleasure of chanting and whistling—a realm where worldly fame and profit could never reach. The people of Hangzhou called him the "Western Ridge Monk. His literary compositions were of a lofty and peerless caliber.
The ancient author [Zhang Yue] once exchanged verses with Ru Zhou of Wuxing and Lingche of Kuaiji; these dialogues are recorded in the biography of Ru Zhou.
Li Gongyi of Guzang, the Right Attendant-in-Ordinary, remarked: "Beneath a great reputation, such literary works truly exist. Lu Yu of Jingling said:
"The sun, moon, clouds, and mists are the insignia of heaven; mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees are the insignia of earth; sages, worthies, and heroes..."
Jie was the standard for human character; recommending ability and attributing beauty to others was the standard for virtue; dwelling in leisure and seeking tranquility was the standard for the Way.
Alas! This is the ultimate in discernment. When one draws upon Heaven, Earth, and humanity to compare him with them, what can be said of his sincerity, reverence, and yearning?
Thus, the famous statesmen and high officials of the time, as well as the eminent talents among the recluses, all felt a deep bond of affinity and shared his purpose.
He engaged in generous discourse on friendship. On the seventh day of the sixth month in the third year of the Changqing era, he passed away at his residence.
On the second day of the tenth month of that same winter, he was buried in the mountains. He was eighty-four years of age and fifty-eight years since his ordination.
In the fifth year of the Kaicheng era, Zheng Suqing erected a stele to commemorate his virtues.

Fazang of the Tang dynasty was the son of Zhou of Nankang. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations; later, he further advanced in the study of the Yellow Emperor and Qi (i.e., medicine).
Whenever monks fell ill, he would be summoned to treat them, and he invariably administered effective remedies to restore those who were in critical condition.

He declined the ceremonial gifts and, for that reason, frequented the depths of the forest. He took particular delight in the benefits of meditative joy (*dhyāna-prīti*) and the bliss of the Dharma (*dharma-prīti*).
Consequently, he went to the Baoji Monastery on Mount Pingtian in the prefecture and received the tonsure under the śramaṇa Shi Yuan.
Subsequently, he visited Master Daji in Yuzhang and attained the heart-Dharma (*citta-dharma*). He then ascended Mount Lu and chose a dwelling place among the Five Elders (*Wulao*).
Feng ate acorns and chestnuts and drank from mountain streams and ravines for several years in this manner. Spiritual beings, immortals, and sages occasionally passed by him.

Suddenly, offerings of silk and cloth arrived in abundance like falling clouds, and the sound of footsteps at his door became constant. During the Baoli era, he manifested parinirvāṇa at the age of eighty-two.
Huishao of the Tang dynasty was a man of unknown origins. In the eleventh year of the Yuanhe era, he resided at Kaiyuan Temple in Wuling.

At that time, there was a man named Chen Guang who had just been appointed to an official post in this commandery by virtue of his status as a filial and incorruptible scholar. When Huishao saw him, he felt both sorrow and joy, saying:

"Master Chen, why have you come so late? Guang was startled; in his mind, he thought they had never met before and marveled at the lateness of this encounter, wondering if there might be some deeper significance.
He therefore requested an explanation. Zhao said, "How could this be done in haste? On another day, I shall seek out the words for you.
One night, Guang went to stay with Zhao, whereupon they sat side by side on their beds and poured forth all that was held within them. Zhao said, "I—"
I am the son of the Liu family, a great-grandson of Emperor Xiaowen of the Song dynasty. My great-great-grandfather was Prince Ye-xie of Poyang, and my grandfather was Shi-hong;
both are detailed in the historical records. My ancestors were known for their literary talent and were recognized by Prince Ziliang of Jingling during the Qi dynasty;

he served as the Magistrate of Kuaiji. I was born in the fifth month of the seventh year of the Putong era of the Liang dynasty. At the age of thirty, I began my official career under Emperor Xuan of the Chen dynasty.
The Emperor then dismissed him, and he went to associate with Shen Yanwen. Later, both Prince Shujian of Changsha and Prince Shuling of Shixing treated him as a guest;
they raised a great clamor and sought his favor through their influence and power. I, together with Yanwen, remained under the patronage of the Prince of Changsha.
When the Prince of Shixing was executed, we also perished along with him. Acorns and chestnuts were our only provisions, and our days and nights were short.
Wearing coarse cloth to ward off the cold and heat, they hid themselves in deep forests and remote valleys to find joy in their destiny.

Before long, an elderly śramaṇa passed by them and said, "The physical constitutions of both of you are extraordinary; however, Mr. Liu shall live even longer. Yanwen bowed twice and requested the medicine he had taken.
The monk smiled, took his leave, and further told us: "Worldly people pursue fame and profit; it is merely weary toil and suffering."
[He] said, "I wish to know further what you have accomplished. I believe that only the Way of the Śākya clan comes close to it. You should continue to exert yourself.
Thereupon, I received these instructions and did not dare to let them fall into neglect. Fifteen years later, the Chen dynasty fell.
When the former Emperor’s princes entered Chang’an, I led Yanwen to beg for alms and travel westward to pay my respects and offer condolences at Changsha. At Gua...
I stayed overnight at the frontier post of the Hu Qiang in Jinchang. Several years later, I passed away in Changsha; another few years later, Yanwen died.
I then took refuge in a Buddhist temple in Kuaiji and shaved my head. This was already twenty years after the death of Yanwen, and I am now surely a hundred years old.
Although my physical frame is withered and emaciated, my strength has not declined; I still [practice] daily—
I traveled for a hundred *li*. During the Tang dynasty’s accession to the throne, I happened to travel with a monk once more to the capital.

In the sixth year of the Wude era, when the empire was unified and all usurpers and rebels had been quelled, I was able to journey extensively through the scenic sites of the Yellow and Luo Rivers, the Yangtze and Huai Rivers, the three regions of Shu, and the five ridges of the South.
At every place I visited, I lingered for a long time to fully savor its charm. Up to this present day, it has been two hundred and ninety [years].
Many years have passed. Although my own life has been fraught with hardships and I have experienced many trials, I have never for a single day suffered the anxiety of carrying firewood.
Toward the end of the Yuanzhen era, I hung up my monk’s staff at this temple. One night, I dreamed that Changsha spoke to me, saying:
"Ten years hence, my sixth-generation descendant Guang shall meet with you; you must fortunately instruct him. Upon waking, I recorded these words.
In a dream, I was among books and scrolls; calculating it, last year’s tally had already reached that number. Yet when I inquired of those who passed by, you had still not arrived.
I have often felt despondent, thinking my dream must have been erroneous—how could I have known you would appear this very day?
"Moreover, your high cheekbones, receding hairline, and features closely resemble those of Changsha; this truly gives rise to my lament that I arrived so late.

Consequently, he produced his books and scrolls to show him the places where [Changsha] had recorded [his teachings]. Weeping with grief and shedding many tears, Guang bowed deeply and wished to become his disciple immediately, offering to serve him with staff and sandals.
Daoshao said, 'Plan it for now, but it is not yet possible. You should come again tomorrow. Guang Ming—"

Whenever Sengzhao went out, Sengzhao would have already fled. At the beginning of the Dàhé era, Hui Guang went to serve as a clerk in Bāzhou. On the road in the southern mountains, he encountered Sengzhao at an inn.
That night, Guang prostrated before a lamp and followed him to travel, having no other ambition. Sengzhao consented, but when they rose early the next morning, Sengzhao had already departed;
Guang could do nothing but sigh in regret.
Tang Wenju was the son of the Zhang family of Dongyang in Wuzhou. His physique was tall and robust, standing firm like a mountain; his countenance was as mild and refined as jade.

He moved and rested according to the proper seasons, and his faculties of sight and hearing were disciplined; moreover, he was particularly cautious in speech—this was truly the natural emergence of a model for discipline.
At the age of fifteen, he entered the service of a master to study the sutras and the Dharma; at nineteen, he shaved his head and received the full precepts. He settled into the monastic life.
In the third year of the Zhenyuan era, an imperial edict permitted the ordination of monks and Daoists throughout the realm; he thus received the precepts.

Nevertheless, he never dared to be negligent in his study of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya). When he ascended the lecture hall to provide instruction, his disciples gathered daily in great numbers.

He was also thoroughly versed in the commentaries on the *Lotus Sūtra*, and his influence extended to the kings of Tiantai. At that time, Master Fokuze was highly esteemed for the path of Chan, yet [Cishi] was still recommended for his learning.
He became renowned alongside [his contemporaries]. Soon after, by imperial decree, he was appointed as a Great Virtue (Mahādeśaka) at Guoqing Temple.

Originally, Master Zhizhe had established a *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* Sūtra practice hall (*dharmapada*), where every year in the ninth month, the fourfold assembly would gather to engage in intensive cultivation for a period of seven days.

At that time, donors arrived like clouds, and the offerings were abundant and elaborate. Since the passing of the Great Master, however, the practice hall had been altered and gradually fallen into silence.

[The lineage] became desolate; by this time, it was nearly extinguished. During the Dàhé period, the incumbent monk Qīngyùn consulted with Jǔ and established twelve *qǐng* of fields and gardens to provide for the expenses of food and drink for the Guānmíng Assembly.
Thereupon, the provisions first became sufficient to be transmitted for a long duration.
He passed away on the [blank] day of the fifth month in the second year of Huìchāng, at the age of eighty-three (*suó*) and fifty-five *xià*. His disciples erected [a monument].
On the western peak of the stupa-temple, Han again composed an inscription.
During the Tang dynasty, Huaixin resided at Xiling Temple in Guangling. He had long been friends with Liu Yinzhi, a literary scholar from Huainan.
The temple originally possessed a stupa, magnificent and towering, which stood preeminent throughout the region. During the Huichang era, Yinzhi traveled to the four directions...

One night, Ming dreamed that the stupa was flying over the sea. Xìn then erected the third tier; leaning against the railing, he spoke with Yǐnzhī, saying, "I am now sending this stupa across the East Sea;
it shall return within ten days, and we shall meet again. Not long after, Guanglíng was struck by a fire.
The stupa was reduced to ashes. When Huiyin returned from Siming to visit Faxin, Faxin asked, "Do you remember our meeting by the sea?
Huiyin was deeply astonished by this.
Tang Dinglan was the son of the Yang family from Chengdu. By nature he was initially fierce and cruel. After his parents passed away, he entered the ranks of hired laborers.

Later, he shaved his head and took the tonsure, enrolling himself at Fugan Temple. Nevertheless, he endured toil, hardship, and humiliation. Whenever he encountered the anniversary of his parents' deaths, he would wail and lament until he collapsed in exhaustion.
He entered Mount Qingcheng, where he exposed himself to feed mosquitoes and gadflies, plucking out his ears and gouging out his eyes.
He gouged out his eyes to feed to birds of prey and wild beasts, saying, "This is the internal giving (adhyātma-dāna). Is it not fitting to use this to repay my parents' toil?
Someone encouraged him, and he drew blood to copy the scriptures and raised funds to construct a monastery, which was named Shengshou (Holy Longevity).
By the time he grew old, he had already gouged out his eyes; when he walked, he could not avoid stumbling unless supported by others, and he did not know where he was going. Suddenly—
There was a guest who came seeking him as a skilled physician. [The Master] took a pearl from his own eye and placed it within the guest’s socket; consequently, the guest was able to see as before.
Not long after, the guest appeared in a dream and said, "I am the Heavenly King of the South. Because you have diligently practiced your cultivation, I have returned this eye-pearl to you.

Those who heard of this, both far and near, were all struck with wonder. In the third year of the Dazhong era, an imperial edict summoned him to provide offerings within the palace, and he was granted permission to do so.
A disciple who had served him with a karmic affinity submitted a memorial in the second month of the sixth year, requesting permission to burn his own arm to repay the grace of the state.

Once the arm was already burning, an imperial edict arrived forbidding it; the assembly thereupon extinguished the fire, whereupon he died from the burns. Because of his karmic affinity, another memorial was submitted requesting [his remains].

His name was changed and a stupa was erected for him; by imperial decree, he was posthumously titled "Juexing" (Awakened Nature), and his stupa was named "Wuzhen" (Realization of Truth). Today, in Shu, it is simply called the Dinglan Stupa Monastery.
Zhiyong of the Tang dynasty was a native of Zhongshan; in his youth, he served as a disciple under Xianlin of the Xianzhu Ge Monastery on Mount Wutai.

He was a member of the [Qing] family. Later, having passed the scriptural examinations, he received ordination. He traveled abroad, visiting lecture halls everywhere; among these, he was particularly well-versed in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

He retired to Gaofeng, where he swept away all worldly entangments. During the Yuanhe era, the community collectively requested that he be appointed as the *dujianchaoshenglao* (General Inspector and Head of Monks) for Mount Wutai.
Yǐng firmly declined, saying it was not possible. At that time, there was a famine, and at Huayan Temple—[it was]... (Note: The source text appears to be fragmentary at this point.)

This was the site where the Great Sage constantly manifested his responses; it was a place where pilgrims from the four directions flocked. Now that [the temple] had fallen into such distress and depletion, it was truly a matter of shame for the mountain.
Consequently, he again entrusted [the responsibility] to Yún, appointing him as the Chief Administrator of Offerings (*du-gongyang-zhu*) for Huayan Monastery.

At that time, the three great virtuous masters Fǎzhào, Wúzháo, and Chéngguān were present; since Chéngguān was then composing a commentary (*shū*) on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, he also charged [Yún with this duty].

Fayun served as the lecture master (*kangzhu*). Every day he gathered a thousand monks, and the offerings of alms were so frequent that the provisions for their sustenance were more than double those of other days.
Among them was a śramaṇa named Yiyuan, who slandered him, saying, "Fayun has known the monastic community for a long time;
how could he not have private interests? One night, a deity appeared to him in a dream and said, "The Abbot is one of the thousand Buddhas. You have uttered words of arrogance."
"You shall surely fall into the evil realms; you must repent without delay. At dawn the following day, Yuán went to the temple to perform repentance according to the ritual.

Not long after, an imperial decree was issued to purge the monastic community throughout the land. Yuan fled into the mountain valleys. At the beginning of the Dàzhōng era, an edict was issued to ordain fifty monks at the various temples of Mount Wǔtái, and they were granted robes and vestments.
Thereupon, Yuan was again appointed as the abbot of ten monasteries and concurrently served as the Director of Construction for the Mountain Gate.
The Master of Offerings held a great *pañcavārṣika* (unrestricted) assembly for seven years, lasting one month each time. Subsequently, he gathered his disciples and imparted his instructions:
"I wish to quiet my mind and withdraw from public view to enjoy personal tranquility. You should entrust the administration of the community's affairs to those of future wisdom.
He then sat cross-legged in a pure chamber and passed away at the age of seventy-seven, with fifty-eight years of monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-varṣa*).
Tang Xingyan was a native of Hongyang. His family had been of official lineage for generations. By chance, he listened to the *Lotus Sūtra* until reaching the "Chapter on King Miaozhuangyan.
He then informed his parents and requested to be tonsured. Having received the precepts, he traveled to various regions to seek the Way, finding that what he attained was most personally satisfying.
He had long heard that Mount Wutai was the place where Mañjuśrī manifested his traces; that among all who went there to seek him out, there were none who failed to behold auspicious responses. At...
He remained there to reside and register his name. During the Dàhé period, he extensively exhorted the common people to cultivate meritorious deeds;
among the princes, dukes, and high officials, there were none who did not turn toward him in devotion. He further established a great vegetarian feast, providing for a thousand people daily;
those who understood him marveled at and admired this. In the third year, he passed away lying on his right side. A stupa was erected one *li* to the west of the temple.
Tangdangyu, surnamed Yin, was a native of Fanyang. In his youth, he left the household life at Anji Temple in northern Ji.

In the fourth year of the Dazhong era, he took up his staff and ascended Mount Wutai. At the Bodhisattva image in Huayan Temple, he set fire to the middle finger of his right hand and remained there for two full years.
The auspicious signs he beheld were beyond counting. Later, he traveled to Bimoyan on the Western Terrace.

This was the site where the Great Sage subdued the dragon in the past. Upon seeing its golden radiance, which rose like the battlements of a city wall, it appeared no different from the present-day city walls.
He therefore questioned the monk residing there, who replied, "This is what is called the Golden Light World (*Suvarṇaprabhāsa-loka*).
In ancient times, a master of virtue resided here, and the imperial court conferred upon him the title 'Golden Light Illumination' (*Jinguangzhao*). Having heard this, [he]...
With a heart intermingled with both sorrow and joy, he once again thatched a hut to practice in stillness. He remained in *samāhita* (meditative equipoise) for a total of forty-nine days.
Lay devotees gathered in great numbers, and thus a forest hermitage (*āranya*) was established. In this manner, for seventeen years, he did not descend from the mountain;

his daily practice consisted solely of contemplating the teachings of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in its nine assemblies and other scriptures. Through this, he attained the realization of the holy and manifested supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). His speech and every movement were [in accordance with his realization].

He was unfathomable. Toward the end of Emperor Yizong’s reign, he suddenly lost his usual composure, laughing boisterously and shouting in anger; he became utterly unrestrained by any moral discipline.
Shortly thereafter, the Central Plains fell into turmoil and the imperial carriage was forced to flee. His prescience was thus manifested in this way.

At that time, Li Kuyong, who held the title of Prince of Jin over Hedong, remembered the virtue he had previously encountered him with and sent him respectful greetings from afar. In the first year of the Wende era, [the Emperor]...
In the fourth month of summer, he issued a command to Ma Sisu, the Prefectural Governor of Xianzhou, to convey his intent and extend an invitation.

Huigu replied, "How could I be burdened by the honors and insults of this floating world? He firmly declined and did not go. On the eighteenth day of the seventh month, he gathered his disciples, delivered his final instructions, and passed away.
He was seventy-two years of age and fifty-one years since his ordination. On the eighteenth day of the fourth month of the first year of the Longji era, his disciples... [at the gate].
Ren Taiwen and others followed the Indian custom of cremation. They obtained *śarīra* relics and erected a separate stupa to enshrine them.
Tang Gaoxian was a native of Wucheng by Lake Haokuan. Having left secular life in his childhood, he received full ordination and resided at Kaiyuan Temple.
He was extensively learned and proficient in all subjects; he was particularly skilled in calligraphy, and his cursive script was often compared to that of Zhang Xu. He traveled...

In the capital, he received instruction in the sutras and vinaya at Jianfu, Ximing, and other monasteries. Emperor Xuanzong summoned him into the palace; there, the Emperor personally supervised his painting and bestowed upon him purple robes.
He was further granted access to the ritual platforms for the *linsi* (confession) and *chanjie* (precepts), and was titled a "Virtuous One of Ten Aspirations" (*shiwang dade*).

When he grew old and requested to return home, he passed away at the monastery. His disciple Jiazong inherited his brushwork and was granted the title "Unsurpassed Great Master" (*wushang dashi*) by the Emperor. He lived in seclusion and peace.
While residing there, he frequently wrote in the cursive and clerical styles using white ramie silk; even today, some of these works remain with connoisseurs in the regions of Tiáo and Zhè.
Táng Quánqīng was a native of Huìjī who was skilled in incantations and capable of exorcising spirits and demons. A certain monk’s wife from the market district fell ill;
her speech became deranged, and she wept and laughed without restraint for several years. Eventually, Quánqīng was summoned to treat her. Quánqīng immediately bound straw figures as [effigies].
The human effigy was about one chi in height and dressed in five-colored cloth. A ritual altar was prepared and the straw figure placed within it, whereupon the master performed the rite.
Suddenly, the woman bowed deeply and said, "I beg for my life! I shall confess: some years ago, during the springtime, we happened to meet before the Temple of Yu.
If you, O Monk, will not kill me, I shall depart far away; I dare not remain any longer."
Thereupon, he struck the straw figure with a clear whip until it let out a lowing sound.

He placed it inside a jar, sealed the mouth of the jar with "Six-One Clay" (liu-yi ni), and closed it with vermilion-colored talismanic characters. He buried it beneath a mulberry tree, warning: "Do not move. Five years later...
Dong Chang rebelled with the city. Liu Hanhong attacked and captured it, unleashing his soldiers to plunder within the city. Some dug pits to hide their treasures;

beneath a mulberry tree, they unearthed a jar, but when they broke it open, only a single crow flew away. Perched on a tree branch, a person cried out: "Only now do we see the light of heaven and sun!
At that time, Qing had already been dead for some time.
Tangsheng Che was a man of unknown origins. For a long time he attended upon Wuda, who also delighted in educating and bringing him to full maturity.
Consequently, his capacity was ultimately employed throughout the world; the two acted as a complementary pair to propagate and clarify the Great Dharma.
For instance, Wuda authored the *Commentary on the Assembly of the Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* in two fascicles, while Che expanded upon the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* in four fascicles.
*The Commentary on the Mahā-amitāyus Sūtra*, two fascicles; *The Elucidation of the Dharma-Lamp*, two fascicles; *The Commentary on the Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda Sūtra*, four fascicles;

and *The Garden of the Dharma*, ten fascicles. He also produced commentaries and exegeses for both the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra*, which he likewise compiled into fascicles following the style of Zhiyi.
Furthermore, there are six fascicles of liturgical repentance texts (*chánwén*) and various miscellaneous writings, all of which were composed by Zhiyi.
He propagated [the teachings] so they might circulate in the world. Initially residing at the Fagan Inner Monastery, he was increasingly revered by the officials and courtiers.
Subsequently, he served as a lecturer for the imperial court in both the Left and Right Quarters. Every year on the Emperor’s birthday, he would ascend the seat at Linqide Hall to deliver lectures;

the Emperor further bestowed upon him a purple *kāṣāya*. Emperor Yizong held the Buddhist vehicle in especially high esteem; whenever the eighth day of the month arrived, he invariably provided meals for ten thousand monks within the inner palace.

Not only that, but he personally performed hymns of praise and ordered Che-lang to chant them aloud atop a high platform. The imperial favors bestowed upon him were manifold, even to the point of commissioning a sandalwood throne for him to occupy.

At that time, an edict was issued for the two monastic districts and four temples to perform the Vaipulya repentance rites, to establish altars for the reception of precepts, and to ordain monks, each for twenty-one days.
Furthermore, a separate edict summoned twenty virtuous monks (Mahāsattvas) to enter the Xianqin Hall.
He conferred the full precepts upon the nuns of Neifushou Temple, transcribed the Tripitaka, and carved one thousand sandalwood statues—all under the supervision of the Imperial Inspector.
Furthermore, on the fourteenth day of the eleventh month, he returned to celebrate the consecration; by imperial decree, the monastics and Daoists of the capital were summoned.
He attended the debate at Linqide Palace. Zhe then expounded upon the imperial will and expanded the ancestral Way as he had done on other occasions.
On another day, he was granted the title of Jingguang Dashi. In the eleventh year of the Xiantong era, an edict was issued to record the affairs of the monks of the two streets.

During the Guangming era, the rebels of Chao invaded the capital. Emperor Xizong fled to Shu. That evening, Zhe stayed overnight within the palace; at dawn, together with Du Guangting, he [attended] the granary...
Huang Hu followed him and again met Wuda; such was the continuity between teacher and disciple from beginning to end. His writings were particularly abundant.

Le Penggui, an Inner Secretary and Vice Minister, composed a eulogy for his portrait. With many disciples throughout the regions of Qin and Shu, he may truly be said to have enjoyed honor in life and mourning at death.
Tang Wenzan, surnamed Zhang, was a native of Jinyang. In her youth, she took refuge at Chongfu Monastery in Bingzhou and received the tonsure.

Her learning encompassed the various classics, and her instruction permeated the Three Vehicles. As for the records of the golden tablets and jade cords, and the texts concerning the dragon-strategy and celestial phenomena, there were none whose origins and branches she did not investigate and extract.
When it came to expounding matters before the vermilion palace floor or praising them within the Yellow Gate, she was always ready.

Blessings have spread throughout the vast territories, and grace has reached even the corners of the sea. By imperial decree, he was appointed as a translator and concurrently served as a Great Virtue (Mahāsattva) at the Foshouji, Anguo, He'en, Chongfu, and other monasteries.
Throughout his life, he collectively established one hundred assemblies of the Unrestricted Great Fast (Amogha-pūjā). At each fast assembly, he...
Then the dark clouds cleared and the sky brightened; the freezing snow gave way to spring. Such was the power of his utmost sincerity.
Tang Yunwen, whose courtesy name was Zhi-jing, was the son of the Zhu family of Jiahe in Xiuzhou. When he was nine years old, his father fell ill and was on the verge of death.
He called him and instructed him, saying: "After I have closed my eyes, you shall immediately leave the household life; do not remain hindered by worldly affairs.

The Master bestowed upon him the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. After two years of study, he had thoroughly mastered the phrasing, readings, and underlying principles of both.
Someone once asked him in jest what he was doing, and he replied spontaneously: "I am sitting upon a lotus pedestal and uttering the lion's roar—is this not my task?"

That which his peers were expected to undertake, he did at the age when one first aspires to learning: he underwent tonsure. Upon ascending Mount Song, he relied upon Master Yuan to receive full ordination;
at that time, he was already twenty-three years old. Thereupon, he applied himself to the Vinaya-piṭaka while simultaneously investigating the essential points of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
After four cycles of winter and summer had passed, he had reached the ultimate depths of both the Dharma-nature school and the Abhidharma studies. In the fifth year of the Dàhé era, he returned.
In his hometown, he suddenly heard that the Nirvāṇa Sūtra was being lectured at Tiantzhi Monastery in Qiandang, so he went there to listen.
At the beginning of the Kaicheng era, he traveled east to Mount Tai and happened to stay at Jiaxiang Monastery in Yue. The fourfold assembly requested him to expound upon the sūtras and the vinaya;

he exhorted them with constant diligence, and some were moved to tears. In the third year of the Huichang era, he moved to Jinglin Monastery, where he devoted himself exclusively to proclaiming the Nirvāṇa Sūtra.

He was summoned to participate in the imperial deliberations on the purification of the monastic community. Consequently, he wore the *shenyi* (scholar’s robe) by day and the *kāṣāya* (monk’s robe) by night, awaiting the change of times.

When the Dharma was restored during the Dazhong era, he was enrolled as a member of the Kaiyuan Temple. In the seventh year, he became a venerable elder of the temple and elucidated the essentials of the Vinaya.
In the third year of the Qiánfú era, he first began to peruse the scriptures of the Tripiṭaka.

On the twenty-ninth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Zhōnghé era, he passed away due to illness at the age of seventy-eight, having been a monk for fifty-five years. On the twelfth day of the seventh month of that same year, he was buried on Shíqí Mountain;

no mound was raised and no trees were planted, in accordance with his final instructions. His demeanor was always solemn and dignified whenever he ascended the seat to hold the *daolü* (ceremonial whisk).
When his disciples looked upon him with expressions of solemn dread, it was sufficient to discern the principles he upheld. He was particularly fond of literary composition;
during his lifetime, he emulated the style of Bai Juyi (the Grand Councilor) by composing an epitaph for his own square tomb, which he kept within his bookcase. His disciple Huaiyi—
Later, seeing this, he felt compassion for him. He then erected a small stupa, engraved with this inscription, and placed it beside [the remains].
Tang Hongxiu was a monk from Huangbo Mountain Temple in Min; he had long practiced dhyāna-concentration, and his mastery of the subtle art of mental cultivation was profound.
He was especially capable of leading the masses with authority. He often said to his disciples:

"The cycle of birth and death within the three realms exists because of the presence of karmic debts from beginningless time. If one can fully repay these, then one will ultimately attain liberation and transcend the three realms."

Those who heard this could not comprehend its meaning. During the Guangming era, when the rebels of Chao were rampant, he once went out the gate of the monastery, stripped off his clothes, and sat naked upon a large rock, saying: "Today my karmic retribution has arrived;
how can I fail to await it? Yet this is the pure ground of my monastic community; how would I dare to defile it with my corpse? A short while later—

When a great band of marauders arrived, they plunged their blades into his neck, yet there was no blood at all. The marauders were struck with awe; they bowed in a prostrate line, repented their transgressions, and departed.

His disciple Jingxian performed the cremation (jiewei), from which he obtained seven *śarīra* relics. He erected a stupa to enshrine them, and the monk Qinghuo composed a text in verse to eulogize his virtue.
Tang Xiyuan was born into the Zhang clan of Gusu. His family had been wealthy and powerful for generations, yet he alone renounced it to follow the Dharma of emptiness and stillness.
Once he had received full ordination, he devoted himself to the study of the sutras and śāstras. After some time, his contemporaries recommended him as a teacher and guide.
During the Guangqi era, Xu Yue rebelled and dispatched Sun Ru to raid the territories of Wu and Kuaiji. Xiyuan departed from Tongxuan Temple, boarded a ship, and crossed the sea, reaching Yongning.
To the east, he resided at Baolin Mountain Monastery in Kuaiji. By nature, he was tranquil and composed, frequently engaging in the leisure of meditative practice (*dhyāna*).

No one was able to fathom the depths of his realization. During the Jingfu era, he traveled to the monastery to expound the teachings, constantly exhorting students to diligently cultivate the karma for rebirth in the upper realms.

He would say, "It is not difficult to know; it is only the practice that is difficult. He authored several fascicles of the *Xuanchong chao* (Excerpts from the Profundities). Yuan Xiaofang [resided] at Lang...
It rises to the very peak of the heterodox. Thus, an ancient tradition says that the mountain flew here from Langye Terrace; it was for this reason that it received its name. It is indeed Baolin.
On the mountain there is a well whose water waxes and wanes in accordance with the tides of the Great River.

Some believe that when Yu the Great came to Zhejiang to regulate the waters, he bound the monstrous creature known as the *ju* here; the form of this *ju* is like that of a large eel, with two ears and a dark-green hue.

It was yellow in color with bamboo and wood at its upper edge; it invariably brought wind and rain. It would constantly come and go within the temple's ditches and channels, and people became so familiar with it that they felt no fear.
If one tried to grasp it, it would leap about as if in a fit of rage. It was especially frequently seen in the room where Yuán resided.

Because Yuán had conferred the precepts of refuge upon it, from the time of Yuán’s passing until his own end, it never once caused violent winds or rain. On the first day of the fourth month of the second year of Qianning...
One day, Yuánfāng delivered a lecture; he sat upright and passed away upon his Dharma seat. After his cremation, more than seven hundred śarīra relics were collected.
Once they had been interred and he had returned, the monastery’s permanent residents prepared offerings at the gate to await him.
They saw someone in a vermilion robe and holding an ivory tablet prostrating in worship, who vanished in an instant. In the end, it was never known whose spirit it was.
Tang Huize’s surname was Mi. He was a native of Kunshan in Wu. At the age of nine, he already felt a sense of weary detachment from worldly life.
In the seventh year of the Dazhong era, he hurried to Ximing Monastery in the capital to undergo tonsure. In the ninth year, by imperial decree, he received full ordination at Mushi Monastery.

In the fourteenth year, he listened to the lectures of Master Fabao and excelled his peers in his ability to recite and expound upon them. That same year, an imperial edict appointed him [to an official ecclesiastical position].

Serving as a member of the Great Virtuous Assembly (*mahāśramaṇa*), in the third year of the Xiantong era, he lectured on the *Kosa-śāstra* and the *Sangfu yi* (Rituals for Mourning Garments) at Chongsheng Temple.
He compiled one scroll of the *Sanjie tu* (Diagram of the Three Realms). In the seventh year, he succeeded Master Chang in presiding over the propagation of the teachings at the ancestral monastery.

In the fifteenth year, by imperial decree, he was appointed as a regular member of the ordination platform (*litan zhengyuan*). In the first year of the Guangming era, when the rebels of Chao invaded the capital, he fled the chaos to Biankui in Huazhou.
In the second year of the Zhonghe era, the Marquis Gao Bian of Huainan welcomed him to propagate [the teachings] at Fayun Temple.

Upon returning to his hometown, the fourfold assembly earnestly entreated him to remain and provide guidance; Prefect Yang was particularly diligent in his efforts, yet he declined both offers firmly.

He subsequently traveled eastward and took up residence at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai. In the first year of the Qianning era, he arrived at Yuyang Temple in Yinzhou and composed one "Epitaph for the Stupa."
*Jiyao ji* (Collection of Essentials), twelve fascicles. Invited by the Prince of Wu, Qian Hongchu, to preside over the ritual platform in Yuezhou.

On the eighth day of the eighth month in the second year of the Kaiyuan era, he fell slightly ill and sat down with his eyes closed. He was seventy-four years old; he had completed fifty-four summer retreats.
He was interred on a ridge of Mount Mù.
Táng Yuánhui was of the Lù clan of Jiāhuó; he was a descendant of Lù Jī, the Inner Historian of Pínyuán during the Jìn dynasty.

His father was Lù Dān, a Scholar of the Literary Forest (Wénlín láng) and Cavalry Commander (Yúnqí wèi), serving as the Judicial Official (Jiūcáo) of Wēnzhōu. In the first year of the Kāichéng era, at the Fākōng Monastery in the capital...

At the temple, he served Master Qingjin and shaved his head. At the beginning of the Huichang era, he traveled to Huanyang to receive the full precepts and immediately began studying the Vinaya-piṭaka.
He subsequently journeyed to Mount Wutai, where he beheld ineffable manifestations of light beyond measure.

In the second year, he returned to his hometown and resided at Jianxing Temple, where he observed the "three whites"—meaning consuming only white salt, white broth, and white rice—and recited the mantras of the five classes of Maṇḍalas while burning incense.
He burned his arm for five years. An imperial edict was issued to purge the monks and nuns throughout the land; he immediately hid himself in the house of a layperson.
At the beginning of the Dazhong era, an edict restored the teachings. In the seventh year, he rebuilt Fawang Monastery and resumed his religious duties there.
He enshrined the Buddha’s tooth relic from Mount Baoyuan and burned incense upon his arm as an offering. He visited the sublime beauty of the Stone Bridge at Tiantai during the Xian Tong era.
The Buddha’s middle finger bone relic was returned to Chongzhen Temple in Fengxiang. Huìcóng went there and burned his left thumb as an offering, reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* to express his gratitude.
The burned finger was restored within less than a month, appearing as if it had never been burned at all.
On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month of the third year of the Qianning era, he passed away from illness at Zunseng Monastery at the age of [report].

He was seventy-eight years of age and had fifty-eight years of monastic seniority. His disciples, Duan Su and others, performed the funeral rites according to protocol and buried him in the Wu region.
He was popularly known as the "Three Whites" (Sānbái) Master.
Wuming lived in obscurity among the kilns south of the city of Youzhou during the Tang dynasty.

During the Tianyou era, when Yan and Ji suffered from famine and the dead lay piled one upon another, Wuming was out on his alms-rounds when he heard the sound of wailing by the roadside. Upon looking, he saw a young girl who had been abandoned by the people;
he took her back with him and daily sought cow’s milk to nourish her. When she reached the age of losing her baby teeth, Wuming...

She begged for materials within the city and obtained silks and brocades with which to make clothes. By the time she reached the age of marriage, her appearance was exceptionally radiant and beautiful.

Some criticized her for violating the monastic rules, but Wangming showed no sign of shame. At that time, Liu Rencong had usurped the title of ruler in that region; while out hunting, he happened to see her.
He then requested [the image] from Wangming and ultimately took it back with him, enshrining it in his inner palace; thus, the integrity of Wangming’s guardianship was further demonstrated.
Ren Gong subsequently built a separate vihāra for it and paid homage twice every ten days. Was it not because of some profound reason that Ren Gong acted thus toward Wangming?
Later, when Wangming passed away, he suddenly informed the woman [of her husband's death]; the woman, upon hearing this, [was overcome].
He grieved so deeply that he fell into a swoon.
Bao’an of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Xia; he was a native of Changshu in Gusu. Having shaved his head, he resided at Lingguang Temple in Jiahe.

After receiving full ordination, he specialized in the gate of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). He traveled to Mount Wutai, where he beheld auspicious radiances and sacred traces that cannot be fully described here.
However, among those from the south, there were some who had never once visited that land in their entire lives and thus knew nothing of it;

how, then, could they have given rise to a heart of reverence and admiration? Consequently, he commissioned skilled artisans to create a likeness of him and brought it back to propagate his image widely.
Later, he passed away without illness at the age of one hundred and eighteen, with seventy-eight years of ordination.
Liang Guànxiū, courtesy name Déyǐn, was the son of the Jiāng family of Lánxī in Jīnhuá.

At the age of seven, his parents sent him to rely upon the Chan Master Yuánzhēn of Huó'ān Temple in the district to serve as a novice attendant. Each day he could recite more than a thousand words of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
His residence was adjacent to that of Chùmó, and since they were ordained at the same time, their bond of friendship was even closer than that of others. Every...
