They conversed across a fence, and those listening by the side were all struck with wonder and amazement. When he first received full ordination (*upasampadā*), his fame as a poet was already widely established.

He then traveled to Yuzhang to study the sutras and śāstras. The Regional Governor (Commandant) Wang Zao was deeply devoted to him. Later, Jiang Kuai commissioned him to oversee the purification and repentance rites at the ordination platform.
At the beginning of the Qianning era of the Tang dynasty, he went to visit the King of Wuyue, the Qian clan, and presented five poems, each consisting of eight lines. Because...
He composed a verse praising the merit of the subjugation of Wuyue. The King was pleased and bestowed upon him abundant gifts;
furthermore, he erected a stele inscribing the names of all the ministers who had assisted in the campaign, and appended Huixiu’s poem to the back of the stele to glorify the imperial court.

Consequently, Wuyue was granted an iron covenant and its ruler was titled a Meritorious Minister; Huixiu was instrumental in this achievement. Huixiu possessed knowledge of the six principles of calligraphy, and his painting was excellent.
In ink and wash, he produced the images of the Eighteen Arhats for the Qiang family of Zhongan Bridge at their request; connoisseurs declared them to be of the "Divine" (shen) grade.

He said, "When I set down my brush, I did not dare to do so unless I could truly visualize their forms. Upon passing through Shixi, he visited Master Lan of Tang'an Temple and stayed there for three years.
He then traveled south to Mount Heng and north to visit Cheng Rui, the military governor of Jingzhou, who received him with great courtesy.

During the reign of Emperor Ai, Fayuan was repeatedly summoned to the capital, where he lectured on the *Fàngguāng* (Prabhūtaratna) Sūtra; Xi Anshi and Wang Wéndù held him in especially high esteem. Someone once asked:

"I use the medicine of the six perfections to treat the diseases of the four māras. Is this not magnificent? He passed away at the age of sixty-four.
Jin Yu Dao-sui was a native of Dunhuang. He lost his father at an early age and was raised by his uncle; he served his mother with exceptional filial piety and reverence.

At the age of sixteen, he entered the monastic order under Falan, becoming a śramaṇa. He was proficient in both Buddhist and secular learning, as well as in medicine, pharmacology, calligraphy, and epigraphy.

When it came to investigating profound principles and engaging in spirited debate, none among his teachers or disciples could claim superiority over him. Having a passion for springs and rocks, he crossed the Yangtze River and was highly esteemed by Xie Qingxu.
Shi [Fashu] traveled west with his teacher until his death at the age of thirty-one.
The Jin monk Guang was a native of Jizhou and a disciple of Master Yuan of Changshan. In his youth, he met Dao’an at an inn;
at that time, neither had yet received full ordination. They fully disclosed their aspirations to one another, and upon parting, Dao’an said to him: “If you grow up...”

"Do not forget one another. Later, he practiced with rigorous austerity and attained profound mastery of the sūtras and śāstras. During the chaos caused by the Shi clan, he went into hiding at Feilong Mountain.

Dao'an followed him there to engage in philosophical discourse. Dao'an said, "Much of what has been established in the past deviates from the Buddha's intent. Guang replied, "I shall simply do my utmost."

"How could I dare to rank my predecessors as superior or inferior? Dao'an replied, "It is not so. In propagating and extolling the principles and teachings, one should ensure they are fully satisfying.
When the Dharma drums resound in competition, what priority or sequence can there be? Having traveled south, he returned to Xiangyang, where he encountered an illness and passed away.
Daohu was a native of Jizhou. Possessing a strong sense of integrity, his learning and understanding were thorough and penetrating; he likewise lived in seclusion on Mount Feilong.
Zhu Sengfu of Ye was a man of the Jin dynasty who gained renown for his lecturing in the capitals of Jing and Luo.

Encountering the famine and turmoil of the Western Jin, he went into hiding at Huozhai together with Dao’an and others, where they analyzed the subtle and profound points of doctrine. Later, he resided at Shangming Temple in Jingzhou, where he performed rites of repentance and made spiritual progress.
Xiu vowed to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven and served as the preceptor for Wang Chen of Langye. He lived to the age of sixty and passed away without illness.

Zhu Faya of the Jin dynasty was a native of Hejian; he was profound and possessed great personal dignity. In his youth, he was skilled in literary composition, and in his maturity, he became thoroughly versed in Buddhist scriptures.

Those of the scholar-official class delighted in following him. In instructing others, he would adapt to their existing inclinations, using analogies from secular texts to clarify the meaning of the Dharma.
Following the Buddhist scriptures, he employed what is known as "matching meanings" (*geyi*). His peers, such as Vibhūtiṣeṇa, also imitated this method in instructing their disciples.
The monastery where he resided was located in Gaoyi, and his community numbered in the thousands. His disciple, Tanyu, was able to carry on his scholarly tradition.
Tanhui of the Jin dynasty was a native of Henei. At the age of twelve, he served Master Dao’an as a novice. His spirit was greater than his physical stature.
Dao’an had him study the *Shi* and *Li* classics; four years later, he shaved his head. Tanhui devoted himself to the master’s instructions.
Upon reaching maturity, he gained a high reputation for lecturing. He remained with Dao’an in Xiangyang until Dao’an passed away, after which he traveled east to Jingzhou and settled at Shangming.

At the temple, someone asked the Dharma Master about his spiritual transformation, comparing it to that of the Bodhisattva Yinshou (Hand-Seal). Huī replied, "The depth of a monk’s inner cultivation is not easily measured;
however, regarding the external conditions he influences, there are many miraculous responses. My single drop can hardly be compared to the rivers and seas.

He passed away in the twentieth year of the Taiyuan era at the age of seventy-three. He authored the *Liben lun* (Treatise on Establishing the Foundation) in nine fascicles and the *Lishi zhi* (Index to the Six Consciousnesses).
There are twelve poems in total, all of which are extraordinary works that have been transmitted through the world.

Dao-li of the Jin dynasty was a man of unknown origins. In his youth, he served Master Dao-an and was skilled in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* of the Radiant Light. Whenever he lectured and taught it, [the assembly would be moved].
He adorned his teachings with the principles of Zhuangzi and Laozi; thus, students who were accustomed to these works found it easy to attain enlightenment.

Delighting in leisure and vastness, he lived in seclusion on the cliffs of Mount Zhoushan, refusing all offerings and service. He would often remain in deep meditation for ten days or more without rising. Suddenly, he left the mountain to assemble a crowd and lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
When asked the reason for this, he said, "I shall travel far away this autumn. When autumn arrived, he indeed passed away.
Zhu Daoci of the Jin dynasty was originally from the Lu clan; he was a native of Wu.

From the moment he shaved his head, he took great pains to remain in seclusion, such that no one could recognize him except for the brothers of the Prince of Langye, who alone knew of him and treated him with reverence.

During the Daming era, he arrived at the capital and stayed at Waguan Temple, where he studied under Master Taisi. Within a few years, he attained a profound mastery of the innermost sanctuaries of the teachings. Taisi had a disciple named Tan...
First: He also possessed an elegant demeanor. At that time, people would call out "Elder One" or "Junior One" to distinguish him. Emperor Jianwen held him in particularly high esteem.
After the Emperor passed away and Daotai entered nirvana, Huichi returned east to take refuge at Huqiu Mountain.

Disciples flocked to him like ants drawn to honey. On Mount Ruoye, there was one named Baidaoyou, who sent him a poem saying: "Successive peaks stretch for thousands of li; Long forests border the level marshes."

Clouds pass over the distant mountains, obscuring them; the wind arrives, brushing through the wild thickets. The thatched cottage is hidden from view, yet one knows there is someone within by the sound of the rooster’s crow.

I stroll leisurely along its path, seeing discarded firewood everywhere at every turn. Only then do I realize that even beneath a hundred generations, there still remain the people of the Sovereign on High.

Having received a letter, Yi subsequently traveled east to Yexi to establish a bond with him beneath the trees. Later, when Governor Wang Hui founded Jiashang Temple, he invited Yi to serve as the head of the monastic community.
After a long time, Yi returned to Wu and resided at Tiger Hill, where he passed away due to illness during the Long’an era.
Tanyi of the Jin dynasty was a man of unknown origins. He was reclusive and fond of learning; his appearance was grave and slow, yet his mental agility and transformations were swift and intense.

He lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and brilliantly extolled the *Prajñāpāramitā*. His reputation resounded throughout Guanzhong, and Yao Xing held him in high esteem. Kumārajīva remarked, "Tanyi is the paragon among monks.
He entered the Xiaoyao Garden to assist Kumārajīva in the transmission and translation of scriptures. When the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* was first produced, within it—
He compiled five rounds of questions and answers based on these dialogues and presented them to Kumārajīva. Kumārajīva praised him greatly, saying, "You have deeply grasped my meaning.
Consequently, he composed a commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and also annotated the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*. He passed away during the Yixi era at the age of seventy.
Daozu of the Jin dynasty was a native of Wuguo. His clan name is not recorded in the histories. In his youth, he served as a disciple to Zhi Faji of the Tai Temple.

Possessing keen talent, he studied under Sengqian and Daoliu, following the teachings of Huiyuan. Huiyuan sighed in admiration, saying, "These individuals are quick to awaken; I need no longer worry about future generations.
Shortly thereafter, Qian and Liuliu died prematurely, which caused Huiyuan particular grief and regret. Daoliu compiled a catalogue of various scriptures, but—
Thus Daozu brought it to completion. Later, he returned to the Capital and lectured at Waguan Temple. Huan Xuan went there frequently to observe and listen, remarking to others:
"Daozu surpasses Master Yuan; it is only that his breadth of learning and experience has not yet reached his level. While Huan Xuan was administering the government, [Daozu]—
Desiring to compel the śramaṇas to show respect to the king, Hui-zu (Hui-zu) declined the invitation and returned to Tai Temple in Wu.

When Xuán usurped the throne, he issued an imperial decree for the commandery to escort Hui-zu to the capital; however, Hui-zu declined on the grounds of illness. He passed away in the first year of the Yuánxī era at the age of seventy-three.
Huìyào, Tánshùn, and Tánshēn were all disciples of Master Yuǎn. Huìyào excelled in ingenious craftsmanship; he carved a lotus flower out of wood.
He constructed a twelve-petaled wheel that floated upon water; it served as a sundial on Mount Ding, its measurements never erring by even a fraction.
Furthermore, he once fashioned a wooden kite that could fly for several hundred paces.
Hui guan of the Song dynasty was born into the Cui family and was a native of Qinghe. At the age of ten, he was renowned for his keen intelligence. He left home to become a śramaṇa;
first, he went to Mount Lu to follow Master Huiyuan, and later he went to Chang’an to follow Master Kumārajīva. Thereupon, he mastered the profound and subtle meanings of the teachings.
Scholars gathered around him wherever he went. After Kumārajīva passed away, he traveled to Jingzhou. The regional commander Sima Xiuzhi built Gaoxing Temple to welcome him.
His teachings flourished throughout the Jing and Chu regions. When Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty pacified Jingzhou, he saw Guṇavarman as if seeing an old acquaintance.

At that time, Emperor Wen was accompanying the expedition as a General of the Household (Zhonglang), and he held him in particular esteem and affection. He was escorted back to Jianye and resided at Daochang Temple.
At the Temple, on the Shangji festival of the third year of the Yuanjia era, the Emperor went to the Qu-shui (Flowing Water) banquet. The high officials and ministers all assembled, as did Sengguan.

By imperial decree, they were all to compose poems. Sengguan completed his first and presented it; its phrasing possessed a marvelous and sublime resonance. The Emperor was greatly pleased and showed it to the hundred officials.
All marveled at his superior talent. He passed away at the age of seventy-one. At the same time, there was a monk named Sengfu, who also produced writings and possessed noble conduct.
Hui’an of the Song dynasty was a man of unknown origins; he lectured on the teachings and had recited over three hundred thousand words of scripture from childhood. He served as...
The śramaṇa resided at Lingyun Temple on Mount Lu. Students came to him from afar. He once cast down a staff that was radiant, fragrant, and pure;
upon it were inscribed transverse characters that no one could recognize. It was said that he had obtained it from a monk from the Western Regions.
When Kumārajīva saw it, he said in astonishment, "Does this staff accompany you on your travels? He translated the characters as follows: "Originally born in the Śāla forest of India."

In the south, the period of turmoil and ruin was about to subside. Later, after Kumārajīva obtained the Daoist teachings, Long’an entrusted his staff to the Western Region monk Pōshànà (Vasunanda) and returned home.
He passed away during the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty.
Senghuijing of the Song dynasty was born into the Wang clan. A native of Dong'e, he became a śramaṇa in his youth and traveled between the Yi and Luo rivers, where he acquired a high reputation.

He was dark-complexioned and thin, yet his insight and understanding far surpassed those of others. At that time, there was also the śramaṇa Daojing, whose ears were large and who was profoundly learned.
People of the time said: "In Luoyang, Da is long-eared; in Dong'e, Jing is as black as ink. When questioned, there is nothing he does not answer;
when he answers, there is nothing that does not satisfy. Jing would often grasp a handful of dust while exerting his eloquence, leaving even a thousand people speechless.

He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, wrote commentaries on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, and composed the *Nirvāṇa-lüejì*, the *Dapin-zhiguī*, and the *Daminglùn*. This was during the Yuanjia era."
He passed away at the age of sixty.
Sengbao of the Song dynasty was a native of Jingzhao; his clan name has been lost to history. He became a śramaṇa and received the Dharma-path from Kumārajīva.

He could recite ten thousand words daily. During the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty, he further increased his intellectual realization under the two masters Huangshan and Jingding, and [his influence] was universal.
Xian Qi’s cultivation of repentance frequently brought about auspicious responses. Upon arriving at the capital, he encountered a lecture being held at Qihuan Temple.

Bao, wearing tattered clothes and with a soiled face, tethered his donkey outside and stood in the doorway. Once the high seat had finished announcing the title of the discourse, Bao hurried out, intending to ask a question.

The person on the high seat asked, "What is your name, guest? He replied, "My name is Bao. The master asked again, "What does 'Bao' (to contain) contain? He replied, "Even a person seated upon a high seat may be contained within it.
Thereupon, they engaged in several rounds of debate, and no one dared to oppose his words. Then, he himself took on the roles of both host and guest, analyzing and dissecting the arguments;
the entire assembly stared in amazement. The master on the high seat felt ashamed and ceased. At that time, Wang Hong and Fan Tai heard of this...
He sighed in admiration and wished to form a friendship with him, inviting him to stay at the Jetavana Monastery.

When Xie Lingyun saw Bao, he marveled at him, considering him an extraordinary and superior companion. Someone asked, "How does Master Xie compare? Bao replied, "Lingyun’s insight is far superior to mine;
his talent is merely such that we might bow to one another. He passed away during the Yuanjia period. At that time, the śramaṇa Fahé of Waguan Monastery was also...
He was well-versed in the sūtras and śāstras and was honored by the High Ancestor (Emperor Wu).
As for Sòng Tánjiàn, his surname was Zhào and he was a native of Jìzhōu. He served Zhú Dàozǔ as his teacher and was renowned for his mastery of the Vinaya.
He traveled to Guanzhong and studied under Kumārajīva. Kumārajīva said, "You are truly one who has attained *śrutadhara* (the capacity to retain what is heard).

He resided at Xinsi in Jiangling, where he cultivated his resolve to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*). At the time of his death, he indeed witnessed extraordinary omens; as he closed his eyes, a wondrous fragrance filled the air.
He lived to the age of seventy.
Tánwúchéng of the Song dynasty was a native of Fúfǎng who moved to Hánglóng to escape the chaos. At the age of thirteen, he became a śrāmaṇera;
his character and disposition were exceptionally brilliant. Before receiving full ordination, he carried his book-box into Guānzhōng to follow Kumārajīva. Kumārajīva asked him, "Śrāmaṇera..."

"Have you come from so far away? He replied, "Wherever the Way resides, why inquire about near or far? Kumārajīva was pleased and thereupon transmitted to him the profound essentials of the various sutras.
One day Yao Xing said to him, "Ma Qilang was a man of vast learning and brilliant intelligence, yet he was naturally arrogant toward his contemporaries.
You, Dharma Master, truly ought not to be like that. He replied, "I govern my mind with the Way precisely because I wish to eliminate this very fault."

Xing sighed in admiration of his extraordinary nature. When the Yao dynasty declined, he resided at Zhong Temple in Huainan, where he constantly lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He composed treatises such as the *Shixiang lun* (Treatise on the True Mark) and the *Mingjian lun* (Treatise Clarifying the Gradual). He passed away during the Yuanjia era at the age of sixty-four.
The Song dynasty monk Sengnian was a man of unknown origins. He was widely learned and possessed a profound mastery of astronomy.

Having renounced his family life to become a śramaṇa, he delved deeply into the "Dharma-cave" (the scriptures) and lectured on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, becoming a model for students. In the seventh year of the Yuanjia era, Tao Zhongzu, the Governor of Xinxing, established Lingwei Monastery to provide him with a residence.
At that time, Ren Han of Pengcheng composed the *Treatise on the Non-existence of the Three Times*. [He] abandoned it...
He composed the *Treatise on the Immortality of the Spirit* (*Shen bumie lun*) to oppose [the prevailing views].

He also authored the *Treatise on the Perfect Mirror of Sagely Wisdom*, the *Treatise on the Unborn Dharmakāya*, and the *Commentary on the Meaning of the Lotus School*. Without falling ill, he passed away in Xun.

Sengbi of the Song dynasty was a native of Wu; his clan name has been lost to history. He excelled in dignified deportment and, together with the śramaṇa Tanka, relied upon Kumārajīva to receive instruction.

He possessed great scholarly learning, for which Kumārajīva praised him and appointed him to participate in the translation work. Later, he traveled through famous regions, where some requested that he serve as the abbot of a monastery.
He declined, stating that unless one is fully endowed with both meditative concentration and wisdom, they cannot establish a lasting legacy of virtuous conduct. Afterwards, he went south...

Residing in Ying, Chu, he brought about a great transformation throughout the region south of the Yangtze. Juqu Mengxun, the Prince of Hexi, heard of his reputation and dispatched an envoy with offerings.
At that time, he entered the capital to lecture; while at Pengcheng Temple, Emperor Wen held him in particularly high esteem.
He passed away in the ninth year of the Yuanjia era at the age of seventy-eight.
Sengche of the Song dynasty was a native of Taiyuan of the Wang clan. Initially, he lived as a guest in Xiangyang. At the age of sixteen, he visited Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu.

The Master regarded him with wonder and asked, "Do you have the aspiration to leave the household life? He replied, "To distance myself from the dust and depart from the secular world is my original intent;
as for becoming a vessel of the Dharma, I shall trouble the craftsman. Huiyuan smiled and said, "Your spiritual lineage is already capable of fearlessness."
"What he will achieve in the future shall be immeasurable. Thereupon, he shaved his head. Through his diligent study of the sutras and śāstras, his literary reputation became renowned in his time.

Once, while traveling in the southern mountains, he leaned against a withered pine tree and let out a long, resonant whistle. The mountain breeze reached him from afar, and the birds of the crags sang in harmony.

He felt a transcendent sense of self-sufficiency and thus questioned Huiyuan: "It is certainly true that the monastic discipline prohibits string and wind instruments and bans singing and dancing. Yet, as for this single chant—"

Hao Yi asked, "Could one achieve this with a single sigh? Huiyuan replied, "In terms of what constitutes distraction, all such acts are said to violate the Dharma. Thereupon, Hao Yi never again engaged in frivolous talk or laughter for the rest of his life.
Huiyuan was commissioned to lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Small Version); his eloquence overwhelmed his contemporaries, and no challenger could refute him.
He traveled south and stayed at Wuceng Temple in Jiangling, where he was held in high esteem by Prince Yikang of Pengcheng. The twenty-ninth year of the Yuanjia era...
He passed away at the age of seventy.
As for Senghuijing of the Song dynasty, he was born into the Shao clan and was a native of Yuhang in Wuxing. He possessed refined decorum, literary talent, and high-spirited integrity.
He was skilled in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and resided at Yecheng Temple. He passed away during the Taishi era at the age of fifty.
Sengfanmin was the son of Lady Li of the Song dynasty. A native of Hedong, he traveled to Guanzhong in his youth to become a śramaṇa.
He frequented the regions of Pengcheng and Sishui, where he became widely versed in both Buddhist and secular scriptures and gained a fine reputation. He settled in Danyang to lecture and teach;
Xie Zhuang, Zhang Yong, Liu Qiu, and Lü Daohui were all his close friends. Having grasped the essential tenets of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he passed away in Danyang at the age of seventy.

Agreed. Dao Meng of the Song dynasty was a native of Xiliang; his clan name has been lost to history. He studied the Tripiṭaka and the nine divisions of the scriptures, as well as the Abhidharma and the Sāṃkhya treatises, mastering them all with profound insight and penetration.
He was particularly skilled in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and enjoyed great renown in the lecture halls. In the twenty-sixth year of the Yuanjia era, he arrived at the capital.
The Master resided at Dong’an Temple. Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty paid him special honor and reverence, constructing a temple outside Jianyang Gate and appointing Daomeng as its head.
He named the temple Huangxing. Whenever the Master gave lectures, the Emperor would personally attend, and the high officials and nobles would all assemble there.
He bestowed his gifts most generously. He passed away in the third year of the Yuanhui era at the age of sixty-five.
Sengdaoyou of the Song dynasty was a native of Wu; the histories do not record his clan name. He was a disciple of Master Daosheng. He lived with Master Daosheng on Mount Lu for a long time.
After Master Daosheng passed away, he traveled to Linchuan and, upon seeing the newly translated *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*, sighed and remarked, "This is what my late master had spoken of."

The meaning [of this] accords with the *Āgama* scriptures; it is only a pity that our former masters did not see it. I have therefore annotated it to demonstrate that I do not forget their bequeathed instructions.
When Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty asked Huiguan about Master Sengzhong’s doctrine of "attaining Buddhahood through sudden enlightenment," he inquired who else could further expound it.

Huiguan replied with [Seng]you. The Emperor immediately issued an edict for him to travel from Linchuan to the capital. Once he had returned and set forth his expositions, those who vied in debate [were silenced].

As mutual challenges arose, Sengyou invariably seized the opportunity to blunt the opponent's momentum; there were none who were not defeated and humiliated. The Emperor struck his thigh in approval and sighed, saying:
"Master Daosheng’s solitary spirit shines with absolute clarity, while Master Sengyou drives straight ahead on his own path. They may truly be called masters who fully illuminate their craft."
He did not disgrace his illustrious reputation. He resided at Xinxian as the presiding master of the temple. When Emperor Wu ascended the throne, he treated him with exceptional reverence.
He passed away during the Yuanhui era at the age of seventy.

Huitong of the Song dynasty was born into the Liu family. A native of Peiguo, he became a śramaṇa in his youth. His spirit was profound and refined, and his scholarly exegesis was precise and brilliant.
He resided at Yecheng Temple, where those who came to listen and learn from him filled the capital and the markets.
Xu Zhanzhi of Donghai and Yuan Can of Chenjun held him in especially high esteem. Emperor Xiaowu issued an edict appointing him as a friend to the two princes, Hailing and Jianping. There was...

He composed commentaries on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, and the *Abhidharma*, as well as three treatises titled *Buo yixia xianzheng faxing* (Refuting Barbarians and Revealing the Chinese to Manifest the Dharma-nature) and the *Yi yaoxiang ji* (Record of the Hexagrams and Images of the *I Ching*).
He was highly revered by Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty. He passed away during the Shengping era at the age of sixty-two.
Sengrou of the Song dynasty was born into the Tao family. A native of Danyang, he was upright and resolute from childhood and possessed a resolve to transcend the mundane world.

At nineteen, he became a *śramaṇa* under the disciple of Hongcheng and underwent tonsure. He devoted himself to the study of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras. At the age of twenty, he ascended the lecture platform;
at that time, prominent officials and nobles vied with one another to serve him as their teacher. Later, he traveled to the Cave of Yu (Yuxue) and spent the summer retreat there together with Huiji.
He entered Shan County and stayed at Lingjiu Temple on White Mountain. During the Qi dynasty, Emperor Daizu established a temple for him; he was summoned to the capital and resided at Dinglin Temple.
The two princes, Wenhui and Wenxuan, sought his counsel on the Way day and night. He passed away in the spring of the first year of the Yanxing era at the age of sixty.
Rou suppressed his worldly desires and sought rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). Upon reaching this point, he indeed beheld extraordinary auspicious clouds.
Sengyuan of the Qi dynasty was born into the Zhao clan; he was a native of Yingchuan and a descendant of Yan, the Minister of Works under the Wei dynasty. In his youth, he served as a scholar.

Suddenly abandoning his former life, he became a śramaṇa and traveled to Pengcheng, where he studied the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma* under the Dharma Master Sengsong of the White Stupa (*Baita*).
By virtue of his wisdom and eloquence, he gained great renown. His physical presence was robust and imposing, with a waist ten spans in circumference;
his speech resonated like a bell. As he walked tall and dignified amidst ten thousand monks, he was like a phoenix or a peacock in the midst of a flock of chickens. The reclusive scholar Liu Yin...

He donated his residence to serve as a vihāra to welcome him. He passed away in the fifth year of the Tahe era of the Wei dynasty at the age of sixty-eight, which was the second year of the Jianyuan era.
His disciples were Tandu, Huiji, and Dengdao.
Qí Dàhuì (齊道慧), born into the Wáng family, was a native of Yúyáo. While residing as a guest in Jiānyè, at the age of eleven, he took refuge under the monk Sēngyuǎn and shaved his head.

Upon reading the *Biography of Master Yuǎn of Lúshān*, he came to admire his character. He traveled to Lúshān to visit the master’s remains and chose to reside at Xīlín for three years before returning to the capital.
At that time, Wáng Shì was gathering a large assembly of students to debate the meaning of the "three characteristics" (*trilakṣaṇa*). Daòhuì was then only... [years old].
Seventeen. He immediately posed questions several times; his intent reached the profound and subtle, and his expositions followed a logical sequence.

The assembly all admired his extraordinary brilliance. Furthermore, he attended Master Meng’s lectures on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. Because Zhang Rong raised a dense succession of difficult challenges, Master Meng grew particularly weary of them.

Consequently, he sent Huiyu to confront him. Upon seeing that Huiyu was young, Zhang Rong harbored a sense of pride and condescension toward him. Huiyu, however, maintained a resolute spirit and was determined to prevail.
Shangqiu, Chudeng, and Xie Chaozong all held him in high esteem. Because his mother was elderly, he moved to Zhuangyan Temple to live with her so as to provide for her needs.
His mother, out of affection for him, also shaved her head and converted their former residence into a temple. He passed away in the third year of the Jianyuan era at the age of thirty-one.
There was a monk named Xuanzu Sengda, both of whom were refined in the sūtras and śāstras and were highly praised by their contemporaries.

Qi Hongchong was a native of Liangzhou; his clan name has been lost to history. In his youth, he was well-versed in the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi* and excelled at pure discourse (*qingyan*). He left home to become a śramaṇa and gained a thorough understanding of the sūtras and śāstras.
Toward the end of the Daming era, he crossed the Yangtze River and resided at Duobao Monastery, where many senior scholars and venerable monks held him in high esteem.

He was held in awe. He lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, and the hall was filled with listeners. Prince Wenxian Yigong paid him special honor and respect.
When Emperor Ming ascended the throne, he issued an edict for him to reside at Xianggong Monastery. He passed away during the Qi dynasty’s Qiuming era at the age of seventy-two.
The *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhi-śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
Seng Huisheng of the Huangfu clan was a monk of the Qi dynasty. He was a native of Chaonao in Anding and later moved to Xiangyang; his family had been of the gentry for generations.

In his youth, he served Master Tanshun of Zhulin Monastery in Jingzhou. At the age of twenty-five, he lectured on the *Nirvāṇa*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Daśabhūmika*, *Vimalakīrti*, and *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya* sūtras and śāstras.
He was also proficient in the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*. Whenever he preached the Buddha’s teachings, he did not require a formal lecturer (*dougang*); his eloquence flowed forth like clouds.

High-ranking scholars such as Zong Bing, Liu Qiu, and Zhang Chang all served him. Emperor Gaozu of the Qi dynasty issued an edict stating: "The Monastic Head of Jingzhou possesses a refined and simple character;
he has harmonized with the Way to assist the world and has rendered service to the state. As his years have advanced, I grant special permission for him to travel to the capital in a sedan chair.
Crowds gathered to watch, regarding it as an honor. Together with Xuanchang, he was favored by the Emperor's acquaintance and patronage, and was renowned as a "Black-robed [Buddhist] Minister."
The two were both eminent. [The former] passed away in the fourth year of the Yongming era at the age of seventy-nine.

As for Qi Tandu, he was a native of Jiangling from the Cai clan. By nature, he was reverent and prudent. Having become a śramaṇa, he excelled in dignified deportment and was renowned for his mastery of the precepts and monastic regulations.
He traveled to the capital to study, thoroughly mastering the *Nirvāṇa*, *Lotus Sūtra*, *Vimalakīrti*, and *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* sūtras. Later, he went to Pengcheng.
In Chengdu, he received the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* from Sengyuan; consequently, he was highly esteemed for this school during his time.

Emperor Xiaowen of the Wei dynasty heard of his reputation and summoned him to Pingcheng to lecture and transmit the teachings, where more than a thousand disciples gathered. He compiled the *Chengshi shu* (Commentary on the *Satyasiddhi*). He passed away in the thirteenth year of the Dahuang period.
Huiji of the Yin clan of Qi was a native of Jizhou. In his youth, he served as a disciple to the śramaṇa Zhiquin and received the full precepts.
At that time, the śramaṇa Fajian of Xuzhou possessed great renown; his mastery of the sūtras and śāstras was refined and thorough. Zhiquin therefore entrusted Huiji to him.
When Master Fajian traveled south, Huiji followed him and resided at Zhulin Temple in Jingkou. At the age of fifteen, he returned with him to Pengcheng, where he [studied] the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*...
His reputation for debate spread throughout the lecture halls, and he entered the capital to reside at Xie Temple. The śramaṇas Zhizang, Sengmin, and Fayun were all eminent figures of the time;
nevertheless, they all followed his teachings as their standard of judgment. The two princes, Wenhui and Wenxuan, served him as their teachers.

In the eighth year of the Yongming era, while lecturing on the *Śataśāstra* (Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas), he smiled upon reaching the chapter on "Breaking Through Dust" and passed away. He was fifty years old.

Seven: Hui-long of Qi was a descendant of the Cheng clan and a native of Pingyang. In his youth, he was poor; having no teachers or friends for his studies, he attained profound realization through his own efforts.

At the age of twenty-three, he first became a śramaṇa. For barely more than ten years, he concentrated his mind upon the teachings of the Buddha-vehicle and mastered the doctrines of the hundred schools of thought. He studied...

He followed this school. During the Taishi era of the Song dynasty, he resided at Heyuan Temple in the capital. Emperor Ming invited him to stay at Xianggong Temple, where he lectured on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
He established the doctrine of "real dharmas severing the fetters" (*satya-dharma-prahāṇa*) to expand upon and clarify previous traditional interpretations.
More than eight hundred scholars attended his lectures. Zhou Yong of Runan described him, saying: "Master Lung’s demeanor is detached and refined; he is like a pine tree standing amidst the frost."
Song. He passed away in the eighth year of the Yongming era at the age of sixty-two.

Huiji of the Qi dynasty was born into the Lü family of Qiantang. From childhood, he was exceptionally brilliant and outstanding. Having first renounced his home, he became a novice under Huiyi of Zhiyuan Temple.
When he reached the age of fifteen, Huiyi petitioned Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty for his tonsure. Huiji established a rigorous and austere character.
He had a profound mastery of the Classics and Histories. When Saṃghavarman arrived from the Western Regions, Fayi sent Daohui to enter his quarters and serve him as a disciple.
He then traveled to Caizhou to receive full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*). Saṃghavarman said, "You are destined to be a king of the Way in Jiangdong; you must not remain long in the capital.

Thereupon, he traveled extensively through the lecture halls of the Yangtze and Huai regions, specializing in the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Cintāmaṇicakra-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda* sūtras, Daoyi cherished their profound and elegant meaning. He resided for a long time in the capital, living together with them.

Upon Daoyi’s death, he returned to Qiantang and stayed at Xianming Temple. Subsequently, he crossed the Zhe River to settle at Fahua Temple in Shanyin, Kuaiji, where more than a thousand students gathered around him.
Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty issued an imperial decree summoning him, but he declined on the grounds of illness. At the beginning of the Yuanhui era, another decree was issued.

Having no other choice, he set out. On his way across the Zhejiang River, his illness flared up again. He returned to Guishan and established Baolin Monastery, where he inaugurated the practice of the Samantabhadra Repentance Rite.

The eminent scholars Zhou Yong, Liu Huan, and Zhang Rong all came to him, adjusting their robes as a mark of respect, to inquire about the Way. Prince Wenxuan, filled with admiration and reverence, sent him a letter inquiring about the essential principles of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Daoci subsequently composed the *Commentary on the Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra* in three fascicles and wrote a sub-commentary on the *Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching*.

The *Jing* (Sūtra) says: The world revered his writings and esteemed him as a leader of the Sangha; his fame was great throughout the Three Wu regions. He passed away in the winter of the third year of Jianwu at the age of eighty-three.
Fǎ'ān of the Qi dynasty was born into the Bì family; he was a native of Dōngpíng and a descendant of Bì Guǐ, the Wei-era Minister of Retainers. At seven years of age...
He left his home and went to rely upon Huiguang at Baima Temple as a novice. Because his spirit was exceptionally outstanding, Huiguang shaved his head and had him recite books and scriptures.
By nature he possessed a powerful memory, and his reputation for being extraordinary and brilliant spread throughout the age.

When Zhang Yong invited Master Bin to lecture, he asked about the youth of the capital; Bin recommended Seng’an. He invited An to come and have him recite the *Buddha-nature* treatise and various other texts.
He was without any impediment. Yong asked him how old he was; he replied, "Eighteen.

Yong sighed and said, "In the past, Zhu Bo of Fufeng was able to recite books and chant poems at the age of twelve, yet that was not enough to be considered remarkable. When Wang Sengqian went to govern Xiangzhou, he took [the boy] along with him.
They subsequently traveled to Panyu, where [the boy] debated the meaning of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* with Master You. You felt ashamed and submitted, yielding his seat to him. He then resided there.
In the second year [of the Yongtai era], he spread the teachings by sea. Upon returning to the capital, he lectured on the *Nirvāṇa*, *Tattvasiddhi*, and *Vimalakīrti* sūtras;

many renowned scholars of the time followed him. He passed away in the first year of the Yongtai era at the age of forty-five. He authored commentaries on the *Vimalakīrti* and the *Daśabhūmika* as well as five fascicles of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
Sengyin of the Qi dynasty was born into the Zhu family. A native of Shouchun, he was grave and steady from his youth and could endure toil and hardship.
He left home to receive the full precepts and studied the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) under Tan-du of Pengcheng. He further studied the meaning of the *Lotus Sūtra* under Hui-long of Mount Lu.
Returning to the capital, he resided at Zhongxing Temple. During the Daming era, the retired scholar He Mo invited Sengyin to serve as a master of the Dharma and extensively expound its teachings.
The audience numbered more than seven hundred people. Although Zhiyin’s learning was broad and extensive, he was particularly fond of the Lotus Sūtra;
thus, while holding the fly-whisk, he recited it a total of two hundred and fifty-two times. He passed away in the first year of the Yongming era at the age of sixty-five.
Liang Zhixiu was born into the Chou clan. A native of Jingzhao, he lived as a guest in Jianye. In his youth, he left home and received ordination at Lingyao Temple on Mount Jiang.

He was proficient in various sutras, including the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra (both Great and Small versions), the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra, and the Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras. Renowned for his eloquence and wisdom, he became a preeminent teacher of his time.
He passed away in the third year of the Tianjian era at the age of sixty-three.
Liang Daochao’s surname was Lu; he was of a prominent clan from Wu Commandery and the sixth-generation descendant of Chancellor Jingfeng.

His grandfather, Zhao, served as the Director of the Gold Bureau in the Ministry of Personnel, and his father, Zun, was a Court Gentleman Attendant. From his youth, Daochao was diligent and earnest, and he formed a close friendship with Hui’an of the same commandery.
While traveling to the capital, he encountered Dharma Master Min, who was lecturing on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* at Lingji Temple; Daochao came to revere him with the utmost devotion.
He spent his nights reflecting on his days, frequently patting his thigh and sighing, "For your sake, I have lived in obscurity and become a laughingstock to others.
Furthermore, hearing that the monk Zheng of Longguang Temple was being invited by the assembly to expound the teachings, he sighed, "How can one with a seven-foot frame remain behind others?

Thereupon, he performed prostrations and recited scriptures, seeking divine protection so that he might become like [Seng]min. This matter is recorded in the Biography of Dharma Master Min. Shortly thereafter, it indeed came to pass as he had hoped.

He possessed a certain degree of attainment; he would speak to himself and laugh alone, maintaining an air of haughty superiority over the common world. Yet, when it came to analyzing and resolving doubts or subduing opponents, he never failed to leave anything out.
When encountering an opportunity or facing an adversary, he sought to strike back and resist, never failing to step forward in response.

In the same monastery was Daoben, who was slightly senior in years; though he followed the assembly in their studies, his character was exceptionally indolent and lax. One day, he said to Sengchao, "I and you..."

As for their relative merits, [the critics] could do nothing but stare up in astonishment and sigh with disdain. With the classics and histories piled around his knees, he lived in seclusion, shunning all guests;

dust filled the rooms, and crickets chirped against the walls. Zhang Shuai, a fellow townsman and Gentleman of the Central Secretariat, exclaimed, "How can one remain unperturbed in such surroundings?
He replied, "It is precisely because of this that I find my joy. Contemporaries held his unconventional liberation in high esteem.
Dada was thirty-six years old when he passed away at the beginning of the Tianjian era. Hui’an died at Xianggong Temple at the age of only thirty-two.
Alas! These two men were identical in their aspirations, their studies, and their conduct; even their lifespans were nearly the same. What a pity!
Huilin of the Liang dynasty was the son of the Ma family. A native of Fufeng Commandery, at the age of sixteen, he served as a disciple to Daoxin of Zhulin Temple in Jingzhou.
He entered Mount Xiang and the foot of Mount Yue to practice dhyāna and contemplation. Later, he traveled to Pengcheng, where he received instruction on the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* from Sengyuan.

He returned to Jingzhou to serve as the head of the monastic community (*saṃghapati*). His transformative influence spread throughout the regions of Jing and Chu. He passed away in the third year of the Tianjian era at the age of seventy-four.
His disciples intended to leave his remains exposed beneath a pine tree, but they could not bear to do so.

Sengsheng of the Liang dynasty was born into the He clan. A native of Jianye, he became a śramaṇa in his youth. He was exceptionally intelligent, surpassing his contemporaries, and was proficient in the exegesis of sūtras and śāstras.
Possessing noble conduct, he was also quite skilled in literary composition and was held in high esteem by the dukes and ministers. He passed away during the Tianjian era at the age of fifty.
Sengshao of the Liang dynasty was surnamed Wang. A native of Gaoyang in the state of Qi, he resided at Jianyuan Temple in the capital during the early Yuanhui era of the Song dynasty.
He maintained his practice in a secluded chamber, refraining from frivolous socializing. Only after the Qi dynasty had received the abdication of the throne did he begin to engage in public lectures;

his studies of the *Abhidharma* spread throughout the realm. Prince Wenhui and Prince Jingling of the Qi dynasty held him in high esteem and paid him respectful homage. [He was also honored by] Cui Hui of Qinghe.
I personally received his instructions. In the third year of the Tianjian era, he passed away at the monastery where he resided, at the age of fifty-eight.

During the Jianyuan period, there were the brothers Faliang and Falang. Faliang was of the Shen clan of Wukang in Wuxing; his conduct was lofty and pure, and his mastery of the Buddhist scriptures was refined and brilliant.
By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Yaowang Monastery. Falang compiled a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Both brothers died during the Tianjian era.
Sengmi of the Liang dynasty, whose clan and lineage are unknown, entered the monastic order at Anle Village in his youth. Early on, he bore a reputation for excellence;

however, because his learning and experience were not yet extensive, he wished to travel abroad to seek further instruction. When he requested permission from his teacher, the teacher did not grant it, so he eventually departed in secret.
He received instruction from the śramaṇa Daoming and, at the beginning of the Taishi era, crossed the Yangtze River to reside at Zhuangyan Temple. His...

His appearance was dignified and his demeanor profound, grave, and upright. He did not allow matters of profit or loss to entangle his mind; though he lived among others, none could fathom the depth of his capacity.
His contemporaries compared him to Fatai; although he lectured on various scriptures, he devoted his whole being to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.

Nevertheless, relying on his own scholarly prowess, he was arrogant in his talent and temper, showing little deference to others. He even fabricated faults against Prince Jingling, failing to defend himself in secret;
consequently, he was banished to Huainan, where he carried his book-cases (*gēng*) and traveled with some thirty followers.
He passed away in the fourth year of the Tianjian era at the age of seventy-three.
Liang Zhixin was the son of the Pan family of Jiankang in Danyang. From childhood, he was intelligent and quick-witted; even trivial matters that reached his ears were never forgotten.
At the age of seven or eight, he entered Qijing Temple, where he happened to attend a lecture on the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination.
He said, "The cycle of birth and death revolves without end," and was filled with lamentation. He immediately went to the monastery to seek ordination from the monk Master Shen.
Although he was widely learned, he took pleasure in practicing menial tasks. The Master said to him, "I observe that you are not one who acts in mere haste."

"Why is it that what he studies is not profound or remote? He replied, "I simply wish to broaden the scope of its categories. After receiving full ordination, he studied the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* under Daomeng of Dong’an Temple;

having completed only four recitations, he bound the volumes together and returned home. Yet when it came to his own lectures, his mastery of both text and meaning was so precise and exhaustive that the fourfold assembly honored and admired him.
More than eight hundred people attended his teachings. Toward the end of the Yongming era, the Crown Prince...
On several fortunate occasions, he visited Dongtian Temple, bringing several inner attendants with him; he frequently passed through the monastery, alternating between joy and weariness.

Consequently, he declined his post at Mount Zhongshan and resided at Songxi Temple, where he strictly avoided associating with those of wealth and status. He passed away in the fifth year of the Tianjian era at the age of sixty-one and was buried in the mountains.

According to the ordinances of the Liang dynasty, [the monk] surnamed Dong was a man of unknown origins who resided in Jiankang. He left home to become a monk in his youth and lived at Dinglin Shangsi Temple.

He was fond of studying the sutras and śāstras, attaining mastery in many areas. He was skilled in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Mahā- and Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras*, and was especially proficient in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.
When he lectured, he would first set forth the essential framework and then analyze the detailed branches; his words were concise yet their meaning far-reaching, and he enjoyed great renown.

In the capital city, he frequently engaged in seated meditation and quiet contemplation to observe the essence of the mind; however, he was repeatedly afflicted by illness, which caused his practice to decline.
He constantly reproached himself, saying, "In my previous lives, I clung to signs and made distinctions, giving rise to various contradictions and harms. Now I have received this retribution.

From that time forward, for thirty-three years, his feet did not descend from the mountain. He maintained pure harmony and conformed to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), while continuing to recite one volume of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He removed obstructions and cleared away stagnation. He passed away in the fifth year of the Tianjian era at the age of sixty-nine. Huitai and Huizuan resided in the same monastery;

both were renowned for their learning. Huitai was diligent and devoted to meditation and wisdom, while Huizuan’s character was pure and straightforward; both possessed the bearing of eminent statesmen.

Zhishun of the Liang dynasty was born into the Xu family in Linyi, Langye. At the age of fifteen, he entered the monastic order under Zhidu of Mount Zhongshan. From his youth, he was exceptionally gifted;
he was widely versed in the various scriptures and was particularly proficient in the *Nirvāṇa* and *Satyasiddhi* treatises. He had several hundred disciples.
Although he was once beset by worldly affairs that caused him distress and hardship, Zhishun never wavered from his principles. Prince Wenxuan of Jingling treated him with great esteem.
He resided at Yecheng Temple. Xu Xiaosi, the Minister of Works, held his conduct in high esteem and took him as his teacher.
When Donghun’s lack of virtue led to the execution of Xu Xiaosi, Xiaosi’s son, Xu Gun, was spared thanks to Sengshun’s protection and care.
Once, there was a thief in the night who was captured by the guards; Shun kept him in a secret room and, at dawn, bestowed gold and silk upon him to guide him toward goodness. Thus...
He was sent away to travel to the Cave of Yu (Yuxue) and reside at Yunmen, where his reputation resounded throughout Jiangzuo. His spirit was so solemn that those who saw him were struck with awe.
He passed away during the Tianjian era at the age of sixty. At the time of his death, he instructed his disciples to leave his body exposed as alms for birds;
his followers then buried him beside the temple.
Fahū of the Liang dynasty was surnamed Zhang and was a native of Dongping. At the age of thirteen, he was skilled in cursive and clerical scripts.
His teacher, Daoyong, who also enjoyed a reputation for integrity, once patted his head and said: "With such spirit and resolve as yours, you will surely be able to revitalize the bequeathed Dharma."
Having received full ordination, he subsequently encountered the death of his father. He lived in seclusion for four years and did not participate in formal dharma assemblies.

During the Xiaojian era of the Song dynasty, he went to the capital and resided at Jianyuan Temple, where he frequently lectured on the *Abhidharma*. His discourse eschewed superficiality and flourishes, instead seeking to penetrate the underlying principles and logic.

Those who followed him numbered more than one hundred. During the Qi dynasty, Prince Jingling established a "Seminary for Establishing Doctrines" (Juyi Zhai) at Falin Temple, appointing Hu as its presiding leader.

Those with whom he associated were all eminent figures of his time: Ruan Tao of Chenliu, Attendant-in-Ordinary to the Qi court; Ruan Hui, Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices; and Zhou Yong of Runan, Secretariat Drafter.
All of them treated him with sincere respect and courtesy. In the sixth year of the Tianjian era, he passed away at the monastery where he resided, reaching the age of sixty-nine.
At that time, Zhiyuan of Xin’an Monastery and Sengda of Tianbao Monastery were both diligent in their studies and steadfast in their resolve.
He did not focus on lecturing or preaching, but preferred to cultivate meritorious deeds.
Bao Liang of the Liang dynasty was born into the Xu clan; his ancestors were of the Dongguan lineage, who moved to Jian County in Donglai to escape the chaos of the Jin dynasty.
At the age of twelve, Sengliang followed the master Daoming of Qingzhou to become a śramaṇa. Daoming’s learning in the doctrinal studies was preeminent in his time.

Liang applied himself with such diligence that he achieved daily progress. When it came time for him to receive full ordination, he wished to remain [with his teacher] to repay his kindness in training and nurturing him.

Daoming said to him, "A śramaṇa differs from the laity; his principle is to propagate and transmit [the Dharma]. How can you linger within the net of attachment and cause my Way not to spread to the East?"
Sengliang was moved by this realization. He traveled to the capital and stayed at Zhongxing Temple. Yuan Can saw him and marveled at his extraordinary nature, sending a letter to Sengming.

Its gist was as follows: "I have frequently seen Master Liang and find him to be no ordinary man. Lately, I have heard what I have never heard before, and I am unaware that the year is drawing to a close.
Yet, when pearls are produced in Hepu, the people of Wei take them to illuminate their chariots; when jade is found in Handan, the King of Qin requests it."
To adorn the state with flowers is a treasure of the world that should be shared with all under heaven; it is no longer something that a superior man may monopolize for himself.
From this point on, his fame grew even more prominent. After his parents passed away, because the roads were blocked and he could not return home, he lived in seclusion and withdrew from the world.
Prince Wenxuan of Jingling personally visited him; having no choice, Sengliang responded to the Prince's request and established the fourfold causal conditions for the Bodhisattvas.
He subsequently moved to Lingwei Monastery, where his lectures and studies flourished in the capital. He had thirty disciples;

Liang’s brilliant spirit overwhelmed others, and his verbal acuity was sharp and soaring. Whenever there were those who were obscured regarding the principles, Liang would explain them until everyone was completely enlightened.

In the eighth year of the Tianjian era, the Emperor issued an edict for him to compose a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* totaling over one hundred thousand words, for which the Emperor himself wrote the preface. Ten months later...
He passed away at Lingwei Temple at the age of sixty-six and was buried to the south of Zhongshan.
Liang’s Fataong was born into the Chu clan; he was a native of Yangzhai in Henan and a descendant of Su, the Jin General Who Pacifies the East.

Even in his childhood, his capacity and character were exceptionally brilliant. At the age of twelve, he became a śramaṇa. He studied the Tripiṭaka extensively, with particular depth in the Vaipulya Mahāprajñāpāramitā and the Lotus Sūtra.
Disciples gathered from as far as a thousand *li*, and he traveled to the capital, where he initially resided at Zhuangyan Monastery and later at Dinglin Shangsi.
Students also flocked to him, drawn by his reputation, including Prince Wenxuan of Jingling during the Qi dynasty.
The Chancellor Wenxian Wang and others all admired his virtue. Xie Ju, Lu Guo, and Zhang Xiaoxiu personally visited him to receive the precepts.
He had over a thousand disciples, both monastic and lay. He resided on Mount Zhong for more than thirty years, diligently cultivating meditation and recitation.
He passed away during the Tianjian era at the age of seventy.
Huiji of the Liang dynasty was originally from the Qian clan of Wuxing. At the age of eighteen, he left home to enter Mount Kuaiji and became a disciple of Huiji.
By nature he was sincere and not ornate; he was a specialist in the *Abhidharma* (Pitan), and students took him as their model. He passed away during the Tianjian era at the age of sixty.
It is said that his sub-commentary on the *Abhidharma*, consisting of over one hundred thousand words, remains in circulation today.

Sengxun of the Liang dynasty was surnamed Ming. He was the nephew of Shanbin, the Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary. When he had just reached the age of childhood, he would often listen as Shanbin discussed matters with guests;
he could follow the exchange of arguments and grasp their nuances without any error. Shanbin patted his head and remarked that he would surely be the one to revitalize our lineage.
His father, Fengbo, was a devout believer in the Great Teaching (Buddhism). At the age of twelve, Sengxun was sent by him to Fengcheng.

He entered the monastic order at a temple as a disciple of the Vinaya Master Sengbian. Sengbian was by nature upright and honest; his observance of the precepts was as pure and rigorous as ice, and he maintained himself with diligent self-discipline.

He constantly lectured on the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Shisong). After Xun, [Dao]xuan resided at Yecheng Temple, where he followed the teachings of Fayun of Guangzhai Temple to inquire about and receive instruction in the sūtras and śāstras.

Whatever reached his ears or met his eyes, he never forgot even slightly. Whenever he recited what he had mastered, it flowed forth like water poured from one vessel into another, spreading throughout the monastery without obstruction.

He managed various affairs, for which his contemporaries praised him. He recorded everything he saw and heard, and among his fellow students and friends, there was none who did not copy these records.
He passed away in the sixteenth year of the Tianjian era at the age of thirty-five. At that time, there were Dao-sui and Dao-biao;
as they were both natives of Hailang and had likewise studied under Fayun, they were close associates.
Tán Pèi of the Wáng family was a native of Shàn in Kuàijī during the Liáng dynasty. In his youth, he left the household life and attended upon Huìjī.

He attained profound mastery of the deep Mahāyāna sūtras and was well-versed in the texts of Zhuāngzi, Lǎozǐ, Confucius, and Mozi. He traveled extensively to investigate doubtful points regarding the scriptures;

upon returning to his hometown, he resided at Fǎhuá Tái Temple, where his disciples were very numerous. Pèi’s spirit and demeanor were refined and bright, and his speech possessed a superior cadence, like the movement of the wind.
Sengchuan’s reputation flourished greatly during his lifetime. Xiao Yuanjian, the Prince of Hengyang, as well as He Yin of Lujiang, both took him as their teacher.
Zhang Rong and Zhou Yong also frequented his company. He passed away during the Tianjian era at the age of seventy.
At the same time, there was a śramaṇa named Mingqing, a native of Yuyao, whose observance of the precepts was pure and whose refined character was particularly profound.
Sengruo of the Liang dynasty was the nephew of Sengqu (whose biography appears in the preceding section). At the age of fifteen, Ruo entered the monastic order at Dongshan on Mount Huqiu.
By nature he loved learning, and after several years his mastery of the scriptures was thorough; both the clergy and the laity held him in high esteem.

He went to the capital and resided at Yecheng Temple for more than twenty years, where he was deeply welcomed and supported by Lu Hui, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices of Wu Commandery, and Lu Cheng, the Minister of the Department of State Affairs.

In the thirty-second year, he returned to Mount Huqiu to live in seclusion. Although his vegetarian fare was sometimes insufficient and his robes were occasionally inadequate, he remained free and easy, never engaging in calculation or anxiety.
When Wang Bin, the Protector of Wu, governed Langye, he always took pleasure in gathering for Dharma assemblies.
Upon returning to the capital, he said to those who knew him: "While in the commandery, I relied upon you, sir, so that I could almost forget my old age.

In recent years, I have observed your practice of releasing living beings; your benevolence extends even to the birds and beasts. Although my own lectures are infrequent, the bridge across the stream has not been severed.

Why must one vanish into mountain caves to be considered noble? It is simply that one must not miss the opportune moment regarding whether to emerge from or remain in seclusion. In the eighth year of the Tianjian era, an imperial decree appointed him as...
The Monastic Chief (Sengzheng) of the Commandery passed away in the first year of the Putong era at the age of seventy.

His elder brother, Ling, was also renowned for his profound learning but unfortunately died young. Fadu of Dinglin Temple, Huifan and Huirang of Zhuangyan Temple, were all highly esteemed by their contemporaries.
Huifan was originally of the Wu clan of Shan County; he was resolute and decisive. Huirang’s complexion was as pure as frost, earning him the nickname "White [Huirang]."
Lang (Liang Mingche), surnamed Xia, was a native of Qiantang in Wu Commandery. He lost his father at the age of six and immediately entered the monastic life at Wangguo Temple in Shangyu.

By nature he was fond of learning and possessed a particularly profound capacity for emotional resonance and vigorous self-exertion. Once, while with a guest, he happened to read the biography of Dao’an of the Jin dynasty.
He said, "I was orphaned at a young age and raised by my maternal uncle. Thereupon, he sighed and wept for a long while before finally stopping.
On another day, having investigated further, he beheld the beauty of Dao’an’s propagation of the Dharma; rubbing his thighs, he sighed and said, "Living in this world, how could one not act thus?

From then on, he devoted himself single-mindedly, never discarding even an inch of time. His dwelling was dilapidated and old, and as the wind blew, it was on the verge of collapsing. Everyone feared it.

He pressed down on it and departed, while Sengche continued his practice beneath it as if nothing had happened. Kong Guang of Kuaiji heard of this and considered that he was destined for a position of great renown.
In the tenth year of the Yongming era of the Qi dynasty, Prince Jingling invited the Vinaya Master Sengyou to lecture; Sengche followed him to receive instruction in the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
He followed [his teacher] to the capital of Yangdu and resided at Jianchu Monastery. At the beginning of the Jianwu era, he further studied the sutras and śāstras under Dharma Master Min.

When Xiao Yingzhou, the Grand Tutor and Governor of Jingzhou, took him along to his residence, they opened a lecture on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. After the Grand Tutor passed away, he presented him with a fly-whisk and a soft chair as a parting gift.
At the beginning of the Tianjian era, he returned to the capital and frequently provided exegesis for Master Min; Emperor Wu held him in high esteem.
While waiting for an opportunity to present his work, an imperial decree was issued to assemble the essential points of the *Vinaya* at the Baoyun Monastery in Huilin Garden.

When the compilation was nearly complete, he suddenly fell gravely ill at Shouguang Hall. The Emperor personally visited him to offer consolation and inquiry after his health, and he was moved to the monastery where he resided to seek medical treatment.
Imperial envoys came to inquire after his health without ceasing on the roads. Tche left behind a memorial petition; as its text is extensive, it is not recorded here in full.

When the Emperor examined the petition, he was moved to grief by it, and the attendants were likewise affected. By imperial decree, a vegetarian feast for three hundred monks was established at the monastery.

The Emperor personally composed a text for the vow of repentance. This was on the seventh day of the twelfth month of the third year of the Putong era. An imperial decree provided him with a secret coffin from the Eastern Garden, and he was interred at Dinglin Monastery.
Mù. Sengqiān of the Liáng dynasty was surnamed Lè. A native of Dūlíng in Xiānyáng, he left home to become a monk in his youth and traveled to the capital, where he resided at Línggēn Temple.
He studied under Bǎoliàng of Língwèi Temple and was appointed as a domestic priest by Emperor Wŭ. [He was also patronized by] Tīngpíng Hóu Xiāo Bǐng.
He was treated with exceptional kindness. In the summer of the sixteenth year of the Tianjian era, the Emperor once saw the śramaṇa Huixu at night.
On another day, during a dharma assembly, he asked Huixu, "What did you say when I saw you before me last night?
Huixu replied, "Why do you suddenly ask this? His tone was extremely stern. Qian raised his voice and said, "I and you both came from Xizhou; we are both śramaṇas. One..."
At that time, whenever he encountered those who sought him out, he would immediately surpass his peers; he thought only of serving the Buddha and looked upon his fellow villagers with utter disdain.
Xu was deeply ashamed [of his own conduct]. He passed away in the fourth year of the Putong era at the age of fifty-five.
Fakai of the Liang dynasty was of the Yu clan of Yuhang in Wu Commandery. In his youth, he left the household life under Tanzhen of Beicang Temple.

Tanzhen possessed both profound understanding and spiritual practice; his disciples, Sengliu and Tanyan, were from families overflowing with wealth and fine clothing, and their food and lodgings were exceptionally luxurious.

Yet, when they suddenly turned to study under Fakai, none could equal him. Later, Fakai traveled west and resided at Chengan Temple, where he relied upon the two masters Rou and Ci to exhaustively investigate [the teachings].

Although he was impoverished, he applied himself with even greater diligence to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. Once his work was complete and excellent, he grew increasingly leisurely. However, by nature he was quick-witted and sharp;
skilled in debate, he would secretly ascend and strike out suddenly, leaving those who encountered him utterly defeated.
Both Wang Jun of Langya, the Minister of Personnel, and Bing Di of Wuxing, the Governor of Yongjia, bowed in respect and praised him. Upon returning to his hometown, he stayed at Xisi. Previously...

Those who sought to challenge him would flee at the mere sight of his presence, even unto death. Consequently, lecture halls were established in succession, and both monastics and laypeople turned toward him in devotion.
When the Dharma Master Zhizang was lecturing on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* at the Yuxue (Cavern of Yu), Huikai went there to observe him.
For several days, he raised difficult points of contention. Zhizang said, "Master Huikai has already spoken much; you may leave now. I wish to enter into the text. Upon hearing this, Huikai departed.
He said to him: "When Śākyamuni preached the Dharma, Prabhūtaratna emerged from the earth; why then did the Dharma Master point his finger toward the south and dismiss you, sir?
Zang turned red with shame. He passed away in the fourth year of the Putong era at the age of sixty-five.
Hui-chao of the Liang dynasty was surnamed Wang and was a native of Taiyuan. During the chaos of the Yongjia era, he took up residence in Xiangyang.

He entered the monastic life at the age of seven as a disciple of Hui-jing of Tanxi Temple. Because the assembly was too noisy and distracting, he requested to move to a meditation hall to study the practice of concentration under the guidance of Master Seng-chong.
At the age of twelve, he further studied under a monk of the same temple and mastered the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan). [Qi]...

During the Yongming era, Prince Jingling invited Dharma Master Zhixiu to preach the teachings according to the needs of the region. Among those who aspired to follow him as his disciples was there no limit.
Sengchao consequently received instruction from him. When Zhixiu returned to the capital and resided at Linggen Monastery, Chao requested full ordination from Dharma Master Fachang.

It took less than two days for him to recite the precepts, and he had not even finished the second session of listening to the Vinaya before he mastered it; in both cases, his understanding of the texts was profound and his grasp of their meaning complete.
He grasped its subtle and profound mysteries. At the beginning of the Putong era, Emperor Wu issued an edict appointing his master to oversee monastic affairs in the province;

he was renowned for his frugality. Upon his master’s passing, he relied upon Zhizang to investigate the sūtras and śāstras. Zhizang said, "This youth is exceptionally brilliant and will surely become a vessel of great beauty.

Consequently, they lived together whether in seclusion or in public, discussing all the various schools of thought in detail. When it came time for him to take the pulpit and lecture on their behalf, he declined.
Kendang further investigated the Vinaya. Huiji praised him, saying, "I did not expect that one who had only recently begun his studies would already be as cold as ice.
By imperial decree, he was appointed as a Scholar of the Shouguang Hall. Saṃghabhadra translated the *Aśokarāja-sūtra* at Zhengguan Temple.

The Emperor issued an edict for him to transcribe the imperial brush. By nature, he was free from self-aggrandizement. He excelled at debate, striking upon the essential points and penetrating the core contradictions with a skill that seemed divine.
When Prince Xiao Ya-xiu, the Prince of Ancheng and Kang, and Prince Xiao Bing, the Marquis of Wuping, were appointed to frontier provinces, they both invited him to accompany them;
in both instances, he provided great benefit through his propagation of the teachings. He passed away at the age of fifty-two, which was indeed the seventh year of the Putong era.
Liang Hui-cheng, whose secular surname was Lan, was a native of Gaoyao in Panyu. At the age of fourteen, he followed the Venerable Daoda to leave the household life and resided at Suixi Temple.

During the chaos at the end of the Qi dynasty, people’s moral conduct was easily compromised; yet Cheng maintained his observance of the precepts and continued his ritual recitations without ceasing, even while confined within his room.
At the beginning of the Tianjian era, although the world was trending toward clarity, the southern roads remained obstructed. He traveled with great difficulty to find refuge.

He eventually arrived at the capital and stayed at Zhuangyan Temple, where he studied the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras under the monk Sengmin. For ten years, he diligently applied himself to unraveling the profound and seeking out the hidden.
When Xiao Xiang, Prince of Guiyang, heard of his reputation, he invited him to lecture; consequently, he was held in high esteem and venerated by those both near and far.

When the Prince of Guiyang was appointed Governor of Nanyue, he requested that [Huiyuan] accompany him there. However, as it had been many years since he had last seen his parents, he intended to return home for a short visit.
Furthermore, in accordance with the local community’s desire to welcome him, in the fourth year of the Putong era, he continued to reside at Suixi, where he expounded the subtle and profound Dharma.
Those who gathered around him were as dense as a forest; within barely five years, the benefits of the Dharma were boundless.
In the first year of the Datong era, he passed away at his residence temple at the age of fifty-two. At that time, there were fellow students such as Huirang, Huili, Fasheng, and Huwu, all of whom—
Jie Chengshi was a man of refined character; Lang was poor yet fond of learning, possessing broad erudition and adaptability, as well as skill in oral transmission.

Lue was intelligent and quick-witted, and his expositions followed established principles. Sheng sought out the extraordinary and pursued the rare, weighing matters according to their profound mysteries. Wu propagated the literary meanings with vigor, being concise and avoiding prolixity.
Although all of them had long served as master teachers, alas, they have not widely disseminated [their teachings]. All were over thirty years of age.
He passed away.

Wei Daochong was formerly the Confucian scholar Zhang Bin. During the transition between the Northern Qi and the Northern Wei, there was a Master Xuan’an at the National Academy who was widely learned and skilled in literary composition, serving as a model for his generation. His disciple Li Fan followed in An’s footsteps with equal distinction.

Xi was one among those who had gathered there as masters of various arts and skills, yet he was the sole guest. He once went to Yanjiao Temple in Zhaozhou—which is the present-day Yingjue Temple—and being thirsty, he asked the temple for water.
A novice monk asked Xi, "How many atoms does this water contain? You must state it; only then may you drink. Xi was utterly at a loss.

The novice then splashed water in his face, leaving Xi deeply ashamed. He said to himself: [...]* *Note: The original text ends abruptly with "謂其" (he said to...). The intended meaning is that Xi realized his own lack of wisdom compared to the monk's profound knowledge.*
The man said, "It is not merely that you have brought me to shame; it is sufficient to see that the Buddha-dharma is so difficult to understand.
I shall now cast myself in sincere devotion toward it. Thereupon, he took leave of all his attendants and entered the monastery as a renunciant.

According to the monastic regulations, one must undergo a three-year period of testing before being ordained through tonsure; however, because he was a man of renown and distinction, he was permitted to do so immediately.

Having received full ordination, he entered the Western Mountains to extensively seek out the *Pitaka* collections, reaching the depths of their profound mysteries; he sighed that he had been late in devoting his spirit to them.

During the reign of Emperor Xuanwu, who held the Great Teaching in high esteem, in the first year of the Yongping era, an imperial edict was issued for the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of India to translate the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* at Ziji Hall, and for Ratnamati at Taiji Hall. Furthermore, each [master] was provided with—
The imperial guards were forbidden from coming and going; it was only after four years that the work was completed. When the rival versions were collated, the meanings and phrases matched exactly.
Where they differed, it was by only a single character—either one took it as "non-dual" (不二) or the other as "inexhaustible" (不盡).

Later, Narendrayaśas definitively established it as "not different" (不異), which everyone praised as being in accord with the Sage’s intent. Emperor Wencheng heard of this and consequently went to visit Ratnamati.
Based on the essential meaning of his translations, Daopeng bestowed upon him the detailed instructions for the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* during the three months of winter;

he then produced a commentary for them all in their entirety. He subsequently lectured on them, and his audience gathered like clouds, such that those in Ye City were filled with admiration. At that time, Wei Shou, Xing Zicai, Yang Xiuzhi, and others were present in the assembly.
Daopeng silently observed them and remarked, "Since these worthy men are all the finest flowers of the nation and the eminent talents of the court..."
"Do you recall from whom you originally received your studies? They replied, "We all began by studying under Master Zhang.

However, this master has now grown weary of the mundane world, and we know not where he has gone. Zongchong rebuked them, saying, "The rites between teacher and disciple are fully preserved in the classics;

why do you act thus now? The three disciples immediately prostrated themselves to apologize for their transgression. This was reported to the Emperor, who issued an edict granting them three taels of gold daily.
He was thus distinguished for his excellence throughout his entire life. Hui-shun of Qi was surnamed Cui;
he was the younger brother of [Cui] Guang, a Palace Attendant (Shizhong). From childhood, he grew weary of the net of worldly dust, and as an adult, he became a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*).

He followed [the teachings] to listen to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* until no meaning remained unclarified. Once, while resting in a doze upon his seat, he heard a voice in a dream saying: "This interpretation is indeed..."

He realized that his understanding was still not ultimate; his mind harbored doubts that he could not resolve. At the age of twenty-five, he entered the monastic order under Master Guang at the capital and studied under him.
Through this, both the paths of doctrine and realization were clarified for him like ice melting away.

He lectured on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, composing commentaries and records for each. As he approached the age of fifty, he returned to his native region in the east.
