Li extensively bestowed the precepts and teachings. As soon as the grand assembly was convened, more than a thousand people attended. Throughout Qi, Zhao, Ying, and Ji, all placed their faith and devotion in him.
The Palace Secretary Zu Xiaozheng memorialized that he be established as the National Preceptor. At the age of seventy-two, he passed away at Zongchi Temple in Ye.
Qi Dao was surnamed Han. A native of Pí'ēn, at the age of twelve he entered the monastic life at Shǎo Temple in Guìxiāng.
He first studied the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra*, memorizing it upon hearing it once. Later, he studied the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and subsequently sought out the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.

He was particularly drawn toward the practice of dhyāna meditation. Having traveled extensively through Zhāng, Fǔ, Yī, and Luò to inquire into its essential principles, he eventually arrived at Shaolin Temple.
One who had sat in long meditation with a concentrated mind for eight summers came there seeking the Way, braving thorns and thistles to arrive.
When he reached Master Guang’s propagation of the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra*, he went to listen to it; it was truly satisfying to his Mahāyāna aspirations and deeply fulfilled his long-held hopes.

He remained for ten years, spreading the teachings throughout Zhao and Wei. Regarding the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, he neither raised a brush nor consulted written texts.
His speech was clear and refreshing, and he penetrated the profound meaning of the scriptures as if he had personally realized them. Thus, a saying circulated in the capital:

"Master Ping’s [Píngshī] Dharma-characteristics and Master [Fǎxiàng]’s literary phrasing," speaking of how both were peerless in their generation. Some even compared his eloquence to that of Śāriputra; truly so.
On the seventh day of the third month in the tenth year of the Tenpō era, he passed away at Bǎoshān Temple to the southwest of Yecheng at the age of seventy.

Twelve years passed. Initially, he vowed to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). At the time of his death, he alone saw a brilliant light filling the room, and those who came to him especially smelled an extraordinary fragrance.
The temple formerly possessed two large bells; at this time, one of them also broke with only a slight touch.

Furthermore, relying on the wealth and status of his family lineage, he sustained himself by begging for alms. Though originally descended from a noble clan of officials and scholars, he now washed [his feet] with his shoulders bared.
His legs and arms were bare and without clothing; moreover, he did not rely on the embellishments of written words or spoken language, yet his propagation of the Dharma was unsurpassed.
How could one possibly measure the depth of his realization?
Qī Língxūn was born into the Fù clan of Yúyáng. Having left the household life while still a child, he received no formal instruction from a teacher;

nevertheless, he was immediately able to produce annotated editions of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* for circulation. Later, he relied upon Master Guāng for over ten years, conducting his research with the utmost thoroughness.

Yet, regarding the subtle purports and esoteric intentions [of the scriptures], he was entirely free from obstruction. Although he was extensively versed in the myriad classics, he specialized in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, for which he also composed commentaries and records.
When he moved the capital to Zhangye and Ye, he traveled through Yan and Zhao, spreading his transformative influence among the fourfold assembly.

He was particularly fond of calligraphy, painting, and the elegance of verse and prose; he possessed a handsome appearance and a refined bearing, and his eloquence was both elegant and pure, such that those who listened to him... [could not be satiated].

Jian. Initially he served as the State Preceptor (Guotong), and later as the Chief Overseer of Monks (Sengtong) for Bingzhou. He passed away in Jinyang at the beginning of the Qi dynasty, at the age of sixty-nine.

Dao Shen of the Qi dynasty was surnamed Shi and was a native of Gaoyang. He entered the monastic order at the age of fourteen; having received full ordination, he went to Luoyang to rely upon Master Guang.

He continued his studies under the master who presided over the *Dilun* school, while specializing in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. By nature, he was humble and simple, taking it as his personal responsibility to uphold the Great Dharma.

Whenever he attended the recitation of the precepts (*śīla*), he would kneel and listen until the very end of the session. When preaching to accommodate the various capacities of his audience, his words were never prolix;

the wise did not find them too brief, nor did the ignorant complain that they were too much. He traveled with empty bags yet returned laden with cargo; thus, the fivefold assembly held him in deep affection and esteem. Emperor Wenxuan...

An imperial decree established him as the capital of the state; his efforts in pacifying and governing were without flaw. At that time, there were masters of meditation such as Sengda and scholars of debate such as Faling;

the talent of these men in debate was admired and respected by all the world. Yet, in terms of refined elegance, inner cultivation, and correcting worldly customs while inspiring others, [Huiguan] surpassed them by far.
Later, while returning from escorting the Emperor in a carriage, both axles broke simultaneously, and he passed away in Yecheng.
Dingguo Temple. He was sixty-five years old.

During the Zhou dynasty, Huishan entered the monastic order at Xiuxuan Temple in the capital of Yang when he was young. He investigated and mastered the principles of the *Abhidharma-vijñānakāya-śāstra*.
Those who heard him were filled with admiration and submission. However, as the legacy of the Liang dynasty declined, he fled to the territory of Qin.

Toward the end of the Chengsheng era, he resided at Chonghua Monastery in Chang’an, where he was recognized by the Grand Chancellor (Dazhongzai), who provided him with special offerings and support until his life’s end. This was during the Tianhe period.
He reached the age of sixty; it was during this time that he skillfully expounded upon the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, frequently citing teachings from the Hīnayāna to corroborate its points.
The meaning is as follows: it is like the various stars and the moon assisting the sun in its brilliance, or like a profusion of flowers scattered about.

Therefore, what he has composed is titled the *Sanhua Shu* (Commentary on the Scattered Flowers). Its preface states briefly: "The essence of composition values brevity of expression and richness of principle.

I am quite familiar with various works, yet the reason I now provide such a detailed exposition is precisely because of this path [of concision]. Few people are thoroughly practiced in this; hence, whenever I encounter [a passage]..."
The meaning is earnest. Encountering the text, it is as clear as pointing at one’s palm. Even those who have read it extensively should still examine this point.
Zhou Baotuan was of the Anhan Zhao clan; he moved his residence to Suxi in Longchang, Mianzhou.
When he was just one year old, his parents laid various objects before him and observed what he would take to discern his past habits. Baotuan pushed them all aside.
He discarded [all else] and took up only books and correspondence. The multitude marveled at this as extraordinary. At the age of seven, he reached Baxi.
The Regional Inspector Yang Tiao asked him, "Some say you have read much; tell me, why is Laozi so named? He replied, "Because when he was born, his head was already white.
At sixteen, he became a novice attendant (*dàotóng*) under the Prince of Pingxi of the Liang dynasty, serving as the supervisor of the camp.

Regarding his meritorious deeds: he happened to encounter a Buddhist scripture, and upon reading it, he rejoiced. From then on, he constantly sought out its profound meanings in order to dispel his ignorance and delusions.
At the age of twenty-four, he was able to leave the household life and receive full ordination. He first investigated the Vinaya-piṭaka and subsequently studied the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
Delighting in the transmission of the teachings, whenever anyone wished to obtain his private notes, he would give them to that person without any reluctance.

Alas. Before long, he again listened to Dharma Master Shao lecture. At the request of the Gate-Master of Prince Wuling, he was commanded to lecture on the *Qingguanyin jing* (Sutra of the Invocation of Avalokiteśvara) in the Mahā Assembly Hall.
As this sutra had previously lacked any commentaries or sub-commentaries (*vṛtti*), he initiated its exposition here, providing a detailed and comprehensive introduction.
The meaning of his words was profoundly fluent, and the four assemblies rejoiced. He therefore compiled these teachings into a literary treatise for circulation in the world.

He subsequently returned to Fuchuan, where he transformed both monastics and laypeople. He provided continuous exegesis on the inner (Buddhist) and outer (secular) classics, leading nine out of ten households to abandon heterodoxy and return to the orthodox path.
Furthermore, he transcribed medical prescriptions to alleviate the suffering of illness; though some offered him gold and silk in gratitude, he accepted nothing. It was because of this that—
Because those who had surrendered their hearts and renounced secular life were so numerous, others likewise observed the eight precepts to manifest their devotion and reverence.

He once composed a commentary on the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, but when he reached the "Chapter on the Storehouse of Space," the meaning was not yet fully penetrated; thereupon, he closed his eyes and entered into deep contemplation.
He was unaware that his body had risen into the air, hovering three or four feet above the seat where he sat. Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment.

Having completed the commentary, the monk Bao of Wudansi in Yizhou requested him to lecture upon it; at that time, the Bodhisattva Sengya commissioned the production of the manuscript, which has circulated to the present day.
He also authored commentaries on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Lotus Sūtra*, and other texts. He often remarked, "My life will not last long," and then suddenly fell ill with a wind-disorder.
He was so ill that he could not produce a sound. As his end approached, he urgently instructed his disciples and entrusted them with his belongings. Thereafter, he returned to his normal state.

When the attendant offered him some rice gruel, he closed his mouth and refused it. For the rest of the day, he remained motionless, showing no concern for anything, but only recited the name of the Buddha.
He would repeatedly join his palms and place them upon his forehead until he finally passed away at Guangxing Temple in Tongzhou, which is present-day Mianzhou.
This is Dazhenxiang Temple. On the twenty-third day of the tenth month in the first year of the Baoding era, at the age of fifty, the mountain behind the temple suddenly collapsed without cause.
People to the north of the mountain saw the temple image ascending into the air toward the north;

banners and flowers preceded it, while the assembly of monks followed behind. At that time, Daotuan was in the midst of preaching. Someone reported what they had seen to him, and Daotuan said, "Generally speaking, those who..."
I did so as well. After some time, he passed away.
Zhou Baohai was born into the Gong family in Langzhong, Baxi. He left home to become a monk in his youth and heard that the Buddha-dharma was flourishing in the capital.
He immediately descended from the gorges and followed Master Fayun to study the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*. He attended various lecture halls alongside him, quickly gaining a reputation for purity.

Consequently, he gathered his own disciples and eventually became the preeminent figure of his time. Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty personally presided over the opening of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* lectures and summoned Hai-sheng to the debate platform to establish the doctrine of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
The Emperor himself held a brass incense burner and said, "Since you, Dharma Master, have severed stinginess and greed, this burner..."
[The Emperor] held a brass vessel [and asked], "Is this reasonable? Hǎi replied at once, "Your Majesty is currently practicing compassion and forbearance;
yet as for wearing a cap with a hairpin and carrying a banner—does this not also have its own explanation? The Emperor was greatly pleased. Later, he returned to Shu and resided at Xīshè Temple.

When Prince Yì of Wǔlíng established his military headquarters there, he would frequently stay overnight at Hǎi’s quarters to discuss profound principles, forgetting weariness day and night. One day, the Prince rose early; while washing his hands, he saw [Hǎi].
The clear weather was delightful. Guhaima looked at the sea and said, "The sunlight upon the plastered walls resembles the sound of wind-bell chimes atop a pagoda within the city;
thus I know there is a temple inside. Shortly thereafter, a carriage canopy came to meet the King, and his horses neighed in a chorus.

Guhaima then said, "From afar I see the canopy move; I joyfully encounter Chen Si. Suddenly I hear the horses neigh; I celebrate meeting Longji. He went out with a joyful smile. The King said to his charioteer:
His conversation with Dharma Master Hai was truly such that it left one lingering, unable to depart. His eloquence was consistently like this.
When the Zhou dynasty came to possess both Liang and Yi, the Provincial Governor, Duke Yong, showed him even greater reverence. At the age of eighty, he instructed his disciple Faming, saying:
"When I die, my body should be exposed for birds and beasts to consume. If a stupa were built for me, it would ultimately only lead to its own ruin. His disciples did not...
"I dare not disobey. During the Jiande era, he indeed demolished the stūpas and images.

Later, there was a monk named Qian of the Liang dynasty, whose secular surname was Yan. He was a native of Wu in Wu Commandery. He served as a disciple under Dharma Master Daoze of Lingyao on Mount Zhong.

Later, he traveled among the lecture halls and once challenged the meaning of the *Dhyāna-pāda* (Chapter on Meditation) in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* before Huayan [Huiyan] of Zhaoti Monastery. Zhaoti consequently revised his commentary.
In the Xingshan Hall, Emperor Gaozu held a Dharma assembly. [Hui]gui’s sharp eloquence flowed like a stream, and the Emperor praised him.

Furthermore, by special imperial decree, he was promoted to preach the *Shengman-yishu* (Commentary on the Śrīmālā-sūtra), which the Emperor had composed himself, in the Shouguang Hall. The Crown Prince and Minister of the Secretariat, He Jingrong, [was present].

He also engaged in vigorous debate and was subsequently appointed as the Great Sangha Rectifier (Daisōjō) of Jingye. He was so humble and gentle that the seven assemblies were brought to harmony without the need for strict discipline.
On the seventeenth day of the fourth month in the twelfth year of the Tenpō era, he passed away at Dabō Seisha at the age of seventy-nine.
He was buried at Mount Zhonghua in Jiangling. Returning to his youth, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* six thousand times.

He personally beheld Samantabhadra within his dreams, who illuminated him with fragrant light and bestowed empowerment by touching the crown of his head; he kept this secret and did not speak of it, until now, when he finally told others.
Furthermore, Emperor Ming of the Liang dynasty sent a memorial requesting that [the image] be moved, stating: "In my equal contemplation, I face north."

I took refuge [in the Triple Gem]. Time passed for three cycles of twelve years (*tri-yuga*). For thirteen years, I upheld the sutras and inquired after the Way, until I finally came to realize suffering and emptiness. This merit was due to the guidance of Shandao;
he is truly one who contemplates the Dharma of the Emperor (the Buddha). This is his name.
*The Newly Compiled Biographies of Monks Classified into Six Categories of Study*, Scroll Twenty-one;
*The Newly Compiled Biographies of Monks Classified into Six Categories of Study*, Scroll Twenty-two.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Tán’è of Eastern Zhejiang.
Jingzhixue Yijieke (2): Chen Huiyong of the Huan clan.
His ancestors were from Longkang in Qiaoguo. Later, because his grandfather served as the Magistrate of Qian...
During the Tang dynasty, [Fayun] resided in Huán Village, East Township, Wú County, Wú Commandery. His father, Xiàn, died early.

His mother, Lady Zhāng, once dreamed that she ascended a Buddhist pagoda and obtained two golden images of Bodhisattvas; she subsequently conceived and gave birth to twins. Both were boys. From their youth, they both entered the monastic path.
When grown, Huì was the more intelligent, while Cóng was the more courageous. He first departed for the capital and took refuge with...

The Master received instruction at Lingyao Temple according to his circumstances, not specializing in any single field. Upon reaching the age for full ordination, he studied the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* under Vinaya Master Feng of Jingzhong Temple;
subsequently, he devoted himself to the teachings of Sengchuo of Longguang Temple and Fapeng of Jianyuan Temple, receiving their core doctrines from the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Soon thereafter, the Wheel of Dharma turned extensively and lecture halls flourished; at that time, he was only thirty years old.
He was merely a year old when the chaos at the end of the Liang dynasty left him with no place of rest.

Thereupon, he went to She and stayed at Zhiguan Temple, where he sought formal instruction from the Dharma Master Sengquan. Sengquan also treated him with exceptional kindness, regretting that they had met so late.
Previously, before Yong had departed, he had obtained a bamboo *ruyi* (ceremonial fly-whisk) in front of Ba’en Temple; the person who gave it to him said it had come from Mount She.

"Come," he said, "and you shall surely achieve your aspirations as you wish. Suddenly, he vanished. A short while later, a lacquered box containing a copy of the *Sanlun* (Treatise on the Three Treatises) was found.
Although he searched the windows and doors of his room, he could not discern where it had come from; it seemed as though some being had encouraged and inspired him.
In the fifth year of the Tianjia era, Emperor Shizu invited him to expound the teachings at the Taiji Hall, and his reputation became widely renowned.
He served as the abbot of Chanzhong Temple for eighteen years. He constructed a Great Dharma Hall, naming it "Prajñā," which was vast in scale and magnificent in its architecture.
On the twenty-eighth day of the fifth month in the first year of the Zhide era, he passed away from a slight illness;

his countenance remained unchanged, and after one night had passed, the crown of his head was warm. On the sixth day of the sixth month, he was interred on the western ridge of the mountain at the age of sixty.
Ninth: From beginning to end, he lectured on the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Vaipulya*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* twenty times each;

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, and the *Dvādaśanikāya-śāstra* thirty-five times each; and other works such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Saṃthukta-prajñāpāramitā*, the number of recitations for which is not recorded.
Jiang Zong of Jiyang, the Grand Secretary, composed the inscription for his funerary stele.
Chen Baohui’s surname was Xu. His ancestors were from Dongguan; later, fleeing from danger, they moved to Qu’acha County in Kunling. His grandfather was Qi, a General of the Right Army.
His father was Sengda, a Counselor to the Prince of Linchuan under the Liang dynasty. Baohui stood seven chi and five cun tall;
his back and shoulder blades bore dragon patterns, and he had thirty-nine teeth. In his youth, he served the śramaṇa Fatao and then left the secular life.

The authorities recognized his exceptional talent and did not allow him to serve alongside the common ranks. Having passed the age of *zhixue* (the age of fifteen), he was about to receive instruction from Master Yun of Guangzhai Temple, but this did not come to pass.
Instead, he studied the *Śāstra on the Number of Categories* (*Saṃkhyā-śāstra*) under Master Xian of Nanjian. Master Xian had previously obtained his private notes, which he read and praised.
Later, when Master Xian ascended the seat, he urged his disciples to copy the text and have them recite it back; at that time, [Hui]ji had only just begun to receive [the teachings].

Jù-ěr served as the Dharma Master for less than five years before succeeding Xian to propagate the teachings. It was during this time that Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty brought forth the sublime purport of the Three Teachings for circulation in the world;
Jù-ěr investigated their meanings with particular depth. The Emperor held him in exceptional esteem and summoned him to an audience at the Shòuguāng Palace.
Upon returning to his hometown, he resided at Jiān'ān Temple. At that time, Hóu Yè served as the local governor and treated him with profound respect and reverence. Suddenly—
The people of the commandery spread a rumor that a white dragon had appeared within the temple; for several days, they scrambled to see it, unable to stop themselves.
Jiaohai was a great dragon among men, and those who understood him recognized this as a prophecy concerning [Jing]qiong.

He had long been on friendly terms with Jianzi Zhou Hongzheng, who said to him, "You truly possess the talent to guide and enlighten the capital. Thereupon, he requested permission to return to the capital and began expounding upon the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.

Waving his fly-whisk, he answered the sharp and incisive challenges of the Chief Monk Hui-ling. His deportment was dignified and worthy of admiration. Shi Dao-mao and Shi Guan assumed the heavy responsibility of public reputation;

as for Shi Ren-xiao and Shi Gong-cong, they were both rich in literary talent, holding scrolls to resolve their doubts and receiving instruction with devoted hearts. Shi Shi-mu was the son of Shi Gong-cong;

by nature he loved learning and was particularly profound in the study of the *Mysterious Meanings* (xuan-yi). When he lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it was like water being poured from one vessel into another. He was about to—
While he was planning to enter the Way, he suddenly met with his death. His crown remained warm for two nights; his fingers were curled into three.
On the day after his burial, his father still saw Shi-mu amidst several divine figures descending from the heavens. They conversed face-to-face as if it were their former lives together.
He praised his renunciation of the world and extolled the benefits of the Dharma. After a short while, they departed together through the air, ascending toward the tomb. The room—
A fragrant aroma wafted from within, lingering for days without dispersing. In the summer of the third year of the Yongding era, Emperor Gaozu fell ill.

He issued an edict to propagate the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) within the Great Hall of the Chongyun Palace to offer prayers for his recovery. In a dream, a deity clad in crimson robes approached him with reverence and said, "The Prajñā is vast and difficult;
I pray you will preach it as soon as possible. Sengqiong declined on the grounds that the number of fascicles was still too great, requesting further instruction.
He was earnest and diligent. On the tenth day of the seventh month, he informed the assembly, saying, "Last night in a dream, a divine being urged me to conclude the Dharma assembly;
only one fascicle remains, and it shall be finished before noon. Upon leaving the hall and returning to the monastery, thunder suddenly broke out, and the High Ancestor subsequently passed away.

When Emperor Wen succeeded to the throne, he issued an edict appointing [the Master] as the Great *Sengzheng* (Chief Overseer of Monks) for the capital. The seven classes of disciples were struck with solemn reverence, and the various kingdoms of the Eastern Sea sought him out.
Xiangyao paid his respects. On the twenty-third day of the second month in the second year of the Zhide era, he manifested a slight illness.
On the twentieth day of the third month, he passed away. Previously, Baoqiong of Jianchu Monastery had studied together with him since their youth; their reputations and virtues were well-matched.

One evening, Baoqiong dreamed that he was informed [Fajing] had already entered extinction, and furthermore, he dreamed of ascending to heaven where there was a request for him to lecture on a commentary. These signs corresponded perfectly with reality, without the slightest discrepancy.
In his final instructions, he stipulated that no stele or epitaph should be used to mark the burial pit, and that only what was strictly necessary for funeral rites should be provided.

He further decreed that the imperial ceremonial procession (*lǔbù*) should be employed to honor the occasion. On the eighteenth day of the fourth month, he was interred at the tomb of a famous monk on Mount Zhong.

Previously, when Huìjué had entered the capital, he went to Nanjian Temple to pay his respects to Huìchāo, the Head of the Sangha (*sēngzhèng*), seeking to reside there. Huìchāo did not grant him permission at first; however, upon seeing him, he was struck with awe and said:
"This boy shall hereafter hold my position; he is one upon whom the Dharma-gate relies. Why should it be only Fang? He immediately ordered the monastery administration to take charge of him.

Emperor Xiaozhuang repeatedly issued edicts to propagate and expound [the teachings]. When the Crown Prince saw his attendants, they were all refined and majestic; indeed, they were said to be divine beings.
The Great General Zhang Zhao-da once welcomed and invited [the Master], and his observations were likewise [consistent with the truth].

His nephew, Pu-guang, following the instructions he had inherited, together with his fellow student Dao-zhuang and others who possessed clear understanding, erected a stele at the ancient site of Jin-ling.
The text was composed by Shi Fa-lun of the Hui-ri Monastery.
Chen Jingshao was born into the Yan family of Shangyu in Kuaiji. At the age of [blank] years, he entered the path under his younger uncle, Sengguang, as his teacher.

Sengguang’s observance of the Vinaya was such that he was a leader of his time. Jingshao possessed a character of lofty integrity; as soon as he traveled to the capital, he returned to his hometown to receive the precepts.
He maintained them with such rigorous care that it was as if he were holding an oil bowl. The śramaṇa Daolin requested that he remain [in the capital] to open [the Way].

He returned to his native region. In a dream, he saw that his tongue was long and broad, yet on the verge of being severed; consequently, he repented his previous failure and exhorted him to return once more to the capital to propagate the Dharma.
He first succeeded to the legacy of Master Zhuangyan Min, and subsequently received instruction from Sengchao of Longguang Monastery, who was himself a descendant of Master Quan of Kaishan.
In his later years, he further explored and studied the Tripiṭaka, extensively synthesizing the teachings of various schools.

At the age of twenty-three, he began lecturing on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin), and those who came to listen filled the roads. Later, he returned to Jinling to expound the teachings at Jianyuan and other monasteries;

his understanding was preeminent among the multitude of scholars. By nature, Huishao delighted in meditative stillness and often wished that once he reached the age of forty, he would cease his teaching duties.

Yet his fellow students looked upon him with such profound admiration that they could not bear to let him go. At that time, he was already thirty-nine years old. It happened that the [construction of]... was undertaken.
The former Abbot, at the time of his death, sent word that he was transmitting the Dharma to Shao; thereupon, Shao took his seat in the hall and taught without any hesitation or refusal.
Emperors Jianwen and Shaoling of the Liang dynasty, as well as Prince Yueyang, received his instructions and treated him with exceptional reverence.

As the world fell into decadence during the final age, he went to Yuzhang to bestow the Bodhisattva precepts upon Yu, the Regional Inspector of Yuzhou, the General of State Carriages Huang, and others. It happened that...

He encountered the foreign Tripitaka Master Paramārtha in discussion. Paramārtha sighed in admiration, saying: "I have traveled much throughout the world, yet a person such as this is truly not easily found.

[The Master] translated the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Dīrghāgama*, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* (or *Dīrghāgama*), and the *Caturdaśasvara-śāstra*.
In the fourth year of the Tianjia era, Huizao, along with Daolun and others from Tongtai Temple, numbering two hundred...
The people granted his request; they prepared a formal petition with joint signatures, requesting that he lecture continuously at the Baima Monastery in Kuaiji for ten years.
By then, Huijiao was already advanced in age, so he appointed Huizao to succeed him in leading the assembly, while he himself sat in meditation at Waguan Temple, fulfilling his original vow.
The śramaṇa Zhiyi requested that he recount his past deeds, but he firmly declined on account of illness. As for his other engagements, they are not recorded here. Until...
On the eleventh day of the tenth month in the first year of the Daye era, he passed away at Kaishan Temple while lying on his right side.
On the sixteenth day of that same month, he was interred at Dulonggang on Mount Zhong. He reached the age of seventy-six.

He lectured on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* more than fifty times, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* more than thirty times, and the new translation of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* more than thirty times, as well as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, the *Devendraparipṛcchā*, and the *Brahmaparipṛcchā*.
The scripture does not record the number of times [it was recited].
Chen Anlin (styled Qin), a seventh-generation descendant of Qin Jing, the Grand Secretary of the Jin dynasty, moved southward and settled in Jiangyin.
His father, Zheng, was skilled in the study of geomancy (dili) and had previously authored two works titled *Rushen* and *Dongli*. When Anlin reached the age of ten...
Third: His noble virtue was thus manifest. He attended to the ancestral rites and followed his father’s teachings within the courtyard, extensively studying and practicing them.

As for the pure tranquility of Laozi and Zhuangzi, as well as the strategic artifice of Sun Wu and Wu Qi, there was nothing he did not master; yet none of these were what he truly cherished. At the age of twenty-five, he took leave of his parents to enter the monastic life.

He then traveled north to the state of Wei, where he relied upon Master Rong of Guangrong Monastery in Sizhou to investigate and receive the sutras and śāstras, and to listen to the teachings at Mount Song.
At Shaolin Temple, he recited the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* over ten times and further elucidated the methods of meditation (*dhyāna*). He thoroughly explored the profound gates of the Dharma.

Having remained in the Wei dynasty for twelve years, he lectured on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* approximately twenty times, while continuously teaching Mahayana sutras and śāstras without interruption.

In the first year of the Taiching era of the Liang dynasty, he returned to the capital at Yangdu. By imperial decree, he resided at Tian’an Temple, where he expounded the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* with such grand and subtle elegance that it was easily understood.

Regarding his realization: once the fortunes of the Liang dynasty had ended and the turning of the Wheel of Dharma had ceased, he was summoned to the inner palace during the first year of the Yongding era of the Great Chen dynasty.

There, he personally transmitted the incense and lamps, attended upon the Master’s feet, and rendered the utmost devotion. He received the precepts and followed the Master’s instructions, after which an imperial decree was issued for him to move and reside at Qisheshan Temple.

The officials provided for his needs, and he perpetually propagated the teachings. Thereupon, he formed the resolve to retire from public life. Emperor Shizu issued an imperial decree to convene a Great Assembly at Zhaode Hall.
Emperor Xiaozhuang, in turn, personally received his instruction on the Way while facing north within Hualin Garden.
In the first month of the first year of Zhide, he fell ill and passed away. He was interred on the western mountains of Kaishan, having reached the age of seventy.
7. Chen Huirong was born into the Gu clan of Shanyin, Kuaiji. During the Datong era of the Liang dynasty, the *Abhidharmakośa* was flourishing greatly in the capital.

Huirong began her studies at that time, yet she was immediately able to master all its dialectical arguments. The entire assembly was struck with wonder and amazement; from this, her reputation spread far and wide.

He applied himself even more diligently to his studies and attended to no worldly affairs. Whenever he received letters from his parents, he would immediately burn and discard them without ever looking at them.
He said to his friends, "Is it that I have no feelings? It is simply that within those letters there are but two characters. To see them would only cause me to neglect my studies.
When pressed as to what those two characters were, he replied, "They are merely 'good fortune' and 'misfortune. In this manner, more than thirty years passed until he reached the age of fifty.
Tenth: This was a grand occasion for the propagation of the Dharma. When Prince Zhaoming of the Liang dynasty was present in the assembly, he sent someone to ask the lecturer, "Who is this?
Huirong immediately raised his voice and replied, "I am Huirong from the Cave of Yu. The Crown Prince, the heir apparent of the state, did not even recognize him;

how narrow is his vision! Those who heard this covered their ears. Huirong remained composed as if nothing had happened. Later, he returned to his hometown with his disciples, leaving them all behind. Only he...
His mother was unwell. He sighed and said, "At fifteen I left my old neighborhood; at fifty I am returning to it.

The youths do not recognize me, and among the elders there is not a single person [who does]. The people of the village vied with one another to admire him, yet they detested his arrogance and bombast.

They subsequently convened a great assembly and ordered him to establish a formal thesis (*vāda*). Daorong said, "How could my learning possibly be matched by you gentlemen? If I were to establish a thesis, I fear that you—"
The Master found it difficult to respond and requested that the assembly choose a topic for him to address.

The assembly then selected the "Eight-Inch Seedling" (Bācùn zhǒnghào), likely intending that he would be unable to retain its full contents in memory. Huìróng said, "Is this the proper method for establishing a thesis?

Although this text is voluminous, its meaning is easy to understand; one simply divides it into upper and lower sections, lists the categories, enumerates the names, and sets forth the essential nature. The assembly was [impressed].
The turbulence of those times was difficult to endure. Toward the end of the era of supreme virtue, he passed away in the capital of Yangdu.

Huibì of the Sui dynasty was born into the Jiǎng clan of Yíxīng, Chángzhōu; his grandfather was Xuánlüè, his father Yuánniàn, and his younger uncle Yuǎnjǔ, all of whom held distinguished positions and reputations.
From childhood, Huibì possessed a brilliant spirit, such that all who saw him marveled at his extraordinary nature. In the second year of the Yongdìng era, during the Chen dynasty—

The Dragon Flourished. Emperor Wu personally donned the *gǔnmian* robes and trimmed [Sengliang’s] *zhōuluó* hair. He issued an imperial decree for the Imperial Workshop (*shàngfāng*) to provide him with the three robes and ritual implements, and he subsequently served as a disciple under the Dharma Master Ling of Huidian Temple.
Ling was a preeminent figure among the monastic community of the Southeast. Initially, Sengliang followed him to receive instruction in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.

At the age of twenty, he relied upon Master Ming of Baoliang Temple to propagate the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, and later followed Master Huang of Tiangong Temple to study the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*. Thus, he...

He studied with meticulous diligence and thorough investigation until he could grasp the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma*, the *Aṣṭagrantha*, the Four Noble Truths, and the Five Aggregates as clearly as if pointing at his own palm.

In the first year of the Tianjia era, he abandoned minor affairs for the greater purpose and studied the *Catuḥśāstra* under Master Shaolong Zhe. Within several decades, he had mastered its profound depths;
yet while his wisdom remained deeply internalized and his speech was measured and restrained, his reputation grew ever more weighty. In the tenth year of the Taijian era—

By imperial decree, he resided at Baode Temple on the Great Wall, where he lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Lotus Sūtra*. His water jar and staff filled the hall, and scholars in official robes sat full upon the mats;

those who received his precepts and sought refuge in him gathered like a marketplace. When Master Zhe was approaching death, he dispatched a messenger to summon him, entrusting him with a curved armrest, a fly-whisk, scriptures, and other items, charging him with his final affairs.
Upon the submission of the region south of the Yangtze, he returned to his native village and renovated the Chen [Temple].
He settled at Anguo Temple, which he had established, and spent his final years there. Dharma Master Zhi guan composed an inscription for the temple; the text is recorded in a separate collection.
In the first month of the nineteenth year of the Kaihuang era, he fell ill, and on the fifteenth day of the third month, he passed away suddenly.
He was sixty-two years of age. He was interred at Huayang Mountain, where his disciple Hui fang erected a stele.

Huizhe of the Sui dynasty was the son of the Zhao family of Xiangyang. Initially, he relied upon Master Jué of Jianchu Monastery during the Chen period. At that time, Jué served as the Great Sangzheng (Chief Administrator of the Monks);
his complexion was dark purple, so the assembly nicknamed him "Black Jué. Later, Huizhe relied upon Master Baojué of Pengcheng; his complexion was pure and fair, so he was nicknamed "White Jué.

Under both, Huizhe made great progress in his studies. However, by nature he was self-aggrandizing, arrogant, and boastful. Shortly thereafter, he transferred his service to Master Daoláng of Xinghuang Monastery.

He pursued what he had not yet mastered. Once, while traveling on a road during a thunderstorm, he proceeded to the monastery with composed and steady steps, yet his boots were already filled with water.
In his daily life, his gaze never wandered, and his movements always followed established rules. He was skilled at guarding the gates of the senses and was moderate in his diet.
Even when attending to invitations and staying overnight in the homes of laypeople, one never saw him soiled or unclean, whether regarding his excretions or his bathing.
Thus, those who possess discernment submit to his steadfast maintenance of the Dharma. He succeeded in opening up the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises), causing their reputation and value to double.

Subsequently, he led his disciples back to his native village and resided at the Guangfu Chan Chamber of Longquan Temple on Mount Wangchu to the west of the city. There, he propagated and expounded both the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Sanlun* in alternation. Among his followers, there were over three hundred people;

about fifty became capable vessels for the transmission of the lamp. [As for] Huipin and F... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from a Buddhist historical record or biography, likely concerning the master Jizang or a similar figure of the Sanlun school.)
Cànzhì, Sōngfǎtóng, Huìxuán, Huìléng, and others passed away at Longquan in the fourth month of the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era.
They were fifty-nine years of age and were buried on Mount Xiwàng. The śramaṇa Huìxiǎng composed the inscription for their tomb stele;

Huìxiǎng’s power of reflection was robust and vigorous, and Dào Héng held him in especially high esteem. Furthermore, Hóngzhé was well-versed in both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings, and was popularly known as "The Former and the Latter."

Zhe says: According to the *Sui Zhifang Shi*, his surname is not recorded. His ancestors lived in Eastern Wu; because his grandfather had once served in Shu, he subsequently registered his residence in Zizhong.
In his childhood, he relied upon Dharma Master Lun at Longyuan Temple in the prefecture. For a long time, he was associated with Baohai.

He traveled back and forth until he and his companions went together to the capital of Yangdu to study under Dharma Master Yun. His intellectual discernment was sharp and agile, which earned him a reputation for excellence.

Whenever he spoke, scholars and laypeople alike vied with one another to transcribe his words on paper. When he first began expounding the *Lotus Sūtra*, upon reaching the "Jeweled Stupa" chapter, he said:
"The seven-tiered [pagoda] that fills the heavens vies in brilliance with the sun and moon; the nine-storied [tower] of Tongtai..."
The mists and clouds vie with one another in color; at the square wells, lotus leaves hang downward, and at the circular rafters, lotus flowers are spread askew.
When comparing their sublime and majestic adornments, how could they exist only in the Buddha-lands? Indeed, they abound even in the Yangdu capital. One day, Hai asked:
"The transformation of the pure and the impure resides in the land, and thus it is so. Does the transformation of the ordinary and the sage likewise follow in accordance with the person? He replied:
He said, "Transformation Buddhas are exceedingly numerous; because they are narrow, they must be expanded. This is simply the nature of ordinary beings and sages—why labor to alter it?
He further asked, "If this were so, would sixty minor kalpas be perceived as a mere mealtime for the sage, while remaining unnoticed by the ordinary being?
If both the ordinary being and the sage were to perceive it, then both the ordinary being and the sage would be sages. Then he laughed and said, "What did the High Seat ever say of this? Hai.
He teased him, saying, "What do you mean by calling a three-cornered wooden ladle 'square in wisdom'? He replied, "Between tiles, rubble, and a filthy pond, what could be called a precious ocean?

The assembly all laughed heartily and dispersed. When his illness became critical, Haisang constantly sent inquiries after his well-being. [Hui]zhi thanked him, saying, "I, Zhifang, have been unable to maintain my health.
I rely on your kindness to come and visit me frequently. I wish to be reborn in a good realm so that we may travel together."
He was joyful. Suddenly, a strange fragrance filled the inner quarters. He passed away at midnight at the age of over ninety.
Hui-long of the Sui dynasty was the son of the He family of Ju-rong in Dan-yang. His grandfather, Jian, was the Chief Secretary to the Prince of Wu-ling during the Liang dynasty;
his father, Yi, was a Court Gentleman of the Household during the Liang. When Long was eleven years old, he entered the service of the monk Hui-shu, the Superintendent of Monks at Xuan-wu Temple.
At home, he was respectful, humble, reverent, and cautious, fulfilling all the duties of a disciple toward his teacher.

At the age of thirteen, he listened to Master Que of Fayun Temple lecture on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, thoroughly investigating its profound and hidden meanings. After receiving full ordination, he further studied the *Vinaya*, scrutinizing its essential points. Before long—
When the mandate of the Liang dynasty came to an end, he retired from the world to Pengcheng Temple. There, he remained intent upon guiding others.

When the Chen dynasty took up the imperial mantle, the Vinaya Master Sengzheng, the Venerable Xiong, opened a dharma assembly at this temple; seekers of the profound truth flocked there like the spokes of a wheel. Daolung entered his chamber and subsequently was commissioned to expound the teachings.

By the time Sengzheng was about to pass away, he entrusted the lineage to him. When the Sui dynasty governed the realm, bringing the nine regions under its sway, an imperial edict was issued to the eminent monks of the empire.

Sengde gathered [his disciples] in the capital. Longzhi remained in seclusion, firmly declining the invitation on account of old age and illness. He passed away on the sixteenth day of the eleventh month in the first year of the Renshou era.
He had lectured on the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (Cheng lun) thirty times and on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) more than ten times each.

He did not recount this in detail. Previously, while he was still a novice (śrāmaṇera) at Longfang, someone suddenly presented him with a copy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and identified himself as surnamed Jiang, entrusting him specifically with the Buddha-dharma. Alas, how extraordinary!

Zhiyin of the Sui dynasty was surnamed Li. He was born in Beizhou. In his youth, he became a disciple of Master Huayan Zang. Upon reaching adulthood, his wisdom and understanding were vast and expansive;
there was nothing he did not master. In the seventh year of the Kaihuang era, an imperial edict summoned Zang to reside at Daxingshan Temple, and Zhiyin accompanied him.
In the sixteenth year, an edict proclaimed that Zhiyin was proficient in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-śāstra*.

[He] was appointed as the presiding master of the assembly for lectures and exegesis. Residing at Jingzang Monastery, during the Renshou era, he was summoned by imperial decree to deliver śarīra relics to Fayu Monastery in Yizhou;
subsequently, they were sent to Huazhou, where auspicious responses were repeatedly obtained.
It coincided with the arrival from Central India, the kingdom of Magadha, of Śrīmitra, who reported that the ground of his own country had once split open, yielding a stone relic.
The inscription states: "In the east lies Zhendan; its kingdom is named Da-sui (Great Sui), its city Da-xing (Great Flourishing), and its king Jian-yi (Firm Resolve).

He has established the Triple Gem and erected a stūpa for the śarīra. Thereupon, that king dispatched an envoy to offer congratulations. When the Emperor heard of this, he was exceedingly joyful and bestowed upon him most generous gifts.
Only after much persuasion did the envoy accept them, subsequently distributing them among various sacred sites to assist in the cultivation of wholesome conditions."
It is said that he was especially generous toward those in seclusion.
Fǎlǎng of the Sui dynasty was a native of Pú. His studies encompassed the Tripiṭaka, yet he devoted himself particularly to the Vinaya.

Whenever doubts regarding the scriptural texts or clusters of confusion arose, his inquiries caused them to melt away like ice and snow, leaving nothing hidden or concealed. In the second year of the Rénshòu era, an imperial edict summoned him to the capital.
It was deemed auspicious to erect a stupa at Daxingguo Temple in Shanxi; this temple was the birthplace of His Imperial Father, Emperor Wuyuan.
Consequently, the ceremonial rites were particularly grand and auspicious responses were especially abundant. Could this truly not be the result of the interaction between Heaven and man?
Fayuan (also known as Fazun) was a man of Qi Prefecture whose family name and origins are unknown. He first lived in seclusion at Mount Tai, practicing the dhūta austerities.

In the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era, when the Emperor traveled through the provinces in his carriage, he sought out men of renowned virtue. Someone reported Fayuan’s name to him; the Emperor issued an edict to summon him for an audience and invited him to travel together with him.

Upon arriving in the capital, the Emperor decreed that he reside at Shengguang Temple. There, he served as a model for others through his conduct, and his fellow practitioners of Chan held him in high esteem.
I look up. At the beginning of the Renshou era, an imperial edict ordered that śarīra relics be sent to Shentong Temple on Mount Tai in Qizhou.
This temple was originally built by the South Yan ruler Murong De for the Chan Master Senglang; the account is recorded in the historical annals. It was anciently known as Langgong Temple.

He was named [Seng]gan because of his spiritual inspiration. In the third year of the Kaihuang era, this title was changed. When the śarīra arrived at the temple, its auspicious signs were as recorded in a separate account.
Later, Gan used his settled vocation to guide others, and finally passed away in the temple.

Sui Baoru was a native of Youzhou. He entered the monastic order as a youth and traveled among various lecture halls. Later, he relied upon Master Huiyuan at Ye, where he thoroughly studied the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
During the Zhou dynasty’s suppression of the teachings, he returned south. By the time the Chen and Sui dynasties unified the realm under one rule, [he had already established his reputation].

He immediately returned north to Luochui, where he listened to Master Yuan’s exposition on the beginning and end of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for three years. He was then commissioned to recite it from memory, and Master Yuan gave his seal of approval.

Disciples who admired his righteousness gathered there from the four directions, and he continued to reside at Jingying Temple. At the beginning of the Renshou era, an imperial edict ordered him to reside at Daxingguo Temple in Dengzhou;
furthermore, as that site had been the place where the Emperor had once lived in concealment, plans were made to construct a stupa there. However, he was concerned about the lack of fine materials.
He was a man of stone-like integrity. When he was about to take a rough stone from within the temple and polish it, the finished vessel suddenly transformed into agate.

Furthermore, there appeared an inscription in the Eight-Part Script (Lishu) reading: "The Righteous State Has Attained It. He reported this in full to the authorities. In his later years, he closed his door to devote himself to his studies;
those who wished to visit him could not see him except during mealtimes. He eventually passed away at the temple.

Huizui of the Sui dynasty was a native of Yingzhou. Initially, he studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in Ye; later, he traveled south to the Jiangbiao region to avoid the calamities of the Northern Zhou dynasty.

He possessed strategic acumen and was skilled in adaptive means. Furthermore, while most northern monks residing in the Chen dynasty were often at odds with local customs, Huizui was entirely free from such contradictions.
Those who discussed him praised him in unison. When the Sui house rose like a dragon, he immediately went to observe the capital city and resided at Guang... (Guangzhai Monastery).
Regarding Ming Temple: During the Renshou era, an imperial edict was issued to dispatch śarīra relics to Daxingguo Temple in Jingzhou.

A stupa was erected there at the site of the Dragon’s Latency (Longqian Daochang) as a means of repaying past kindness. When the Emperor was in his humble years, he once encountered a śramaṇa with whom he formed a close bond. It is said that [the śramaṇa] remarked: [text continues].

Previously, the covered walkway in front of the site of practice had collapsed; it was repaired and restored. Upon reaching this point, the foundations were measured and planned so that their breadth and width were perfectly proportioned.
Subsequently, [the image] was sent to Fameng Temple in Jizhou. All the auspicious signs witnessed there are fully recorded in a separate account.
After a long time, he passed away at the monastery where he resided.

Huichang of the Sui dynasty was the son of the Xu family of Xuzhou. He specialized in the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* and, regarding the Mahāyāna as empty and exaggerated, initially did not believe in it.
Just as Master Huiyuan established his presence in Luoyang and his disciples gathered like clouds, Huichang became suspicious of him; thereupon, he went to visit him.
He listened to their discussions and found them lofty, profound, and magnificent, such that nothing could rival them.

Looking back at his own learning, it appeared to him like drifting dust against the sky or a mustard seed covering the earth. He lamented his belated realization of the truth. During the Renshou era, he established a stupa.
An imperial edict was issued to send śarīras to Jushe Mountain Temple in Muzhou. The mountain yielded yellow silver, and a cave remains there.
In the past, the First Emperor of Qin wished to lash stone beams across the sea, but they were able to resist him; thus, the mountain was named accordingly. The stupa stands on Wen Gongfou.
Some say that during the Northern Qi dynasty, there was a śramaṇa named Sengwen, seventy years of age, whose spiritual practice was unfathomable. He once traveled south...
He received offerings from Emperor Gao of the Liang dynasty for twelve years. Afterward, he returned to reside here; however, tigers and wolves howled and roared.
When those who were frightened by them spoke to him, Wen calmly said to them: "You are beasts, brought forth by the ten non-virtuous actions.

I am a human being, summoned by the ten virtuous actions. Sin and merit are as far apart as heaven and earth; why should they concern one another? Depart quickly, depart quickly! From that time on, the birds and beasts of this mountain [became peaceful].
He was permanently cut off from the world. Wen’s body was seven chi tall; his eyebrows covered his face. Chang returned to the capital to attend to his duties, while Zong managed his former affairs.
He did not leave his gate for matters of mourning or celebration. He predicted the date of his own death, bathed, sat upright, and passed away at an age of over seventy.
Mingdan of the Sui dynasty was the son of the Shi family from Ji County in Wei Prefecture. He entered the monastic order and became renowned for his mastery of the Vinaya.

He lectured extensively on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, becoming a preeminent authority revered by scholars. Later, he resided at Shengguang Temple in the capital.

Possessing a gentle, broad-minded, and magnanimous character, students flocked to him with their books in bamboo cases. By imperial decree, he was sent to Xiangzhou to enshrine the śarīra relics atop Feng Mountain.

At a forest monastery, he dug into the ground and discovered a golden image one zhang and six chi in height, its marks and signs perfectly complete. Other auspicious responses are not recorded in full.
Dao-Endu of the Sui dynasty was a native of Lu; after leaving the household life and receiving full ordination, he devoted himself exclusively to the study of the Vinaya-piṭaka.
The essential points are as follows: Later, he entered Renfasi Temple in the capital, where he expounded upon the regulations concerning grave and minor offenses without any error.
Furthermore, he had a profound understanding of Indian scriptures and Sanskrit; his interpretations did not conflict with those of China, making him a model for scholars to emulate.

During the Renshou era, an imperial edict was issued to establish a stupa at Fanjing Temple in the prefecture to enshrine the śarīra relics, and Yuan listened to the command with devotion. He subsequently passed away at that location.
He resided at the monastery.
During the Sui dynasty, Baohuan came from Zhengzhou and began his studies in the Vinaya. He was a disciple of Master Baozhen and enjoyed a reputation for being as pure as ice and water;

those who discerned his character watched him with bated breath. During the Kaihuang era, he lived together with Baozhen at Daxingshan Monastery, where his conduct was regulated by strict rules and his speech was measured.
He proceeded to strictly conform to the established regulations. During the Renshou era, an imperial edict was issued to enshrine śarīra relics and erect a stūpa to mark the site;

it has remained a place of veneration for humans and devas to this day. The Sui monk Xin was a native of Shangdang in Luozhou. By nature he was serene and silent, never speaking or laughing frivolously. When someone presented him with a scripture...
When questioned regarding the subtle purport and profound meaning of the treatises, he would explain them without any hesitation or obstruction.

This was because his learning had been acquired from Master Yuan (Yuǎn gōng) through the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. Later, he entered the capital and resided at Xingshàn Temple. His character and demeanor were lofty and refined;
he did not associate with those of his own rank. During the Renshòu era, he escorted śarīra relics and established a stūpa at Máo’s Hùfǎ Temple, where he presented them to the Emperor.
This was his destiny. The auspicious responses are recorded in detail in a separate collection.
Zhi Kui of the Sui dynasty was born in Jizhou. From childhood, he attended lecture halls and devoted himself exclusively to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

He was affiliated with Hongji Temple, where he shut his door and declined visitors, savoring the essential meanings of the teachings. Unaware that the years were passing and he was growing old, an imperial decree ordered that his śarīra be enshrined in a stupa.
At Kaijue Temple in the Wei dynasty, incense, flowers, and ceremonial processions were supervised to accompany the ritual offerings.
Sui Ba’an was a native of Yanzhou. Initially, he followed Dharma Master Huiyuan to study the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. His reputation for exegetical mastery was widespread throughout the north.
Upon the fall of the Northern Zhou and Qi dynasties, he fled south to the Chen state in order to investigate those points he had not yet fully mastered. He established [the temple].
At the beginning of the reign of Emperor Huang, the imperial domains were unified. Dao’an entered the Pass and resided at Jingying Temple.

In the second year of the Renshou era, an imperial edict was issued to erect a stupa in Yingzhou, which is the ancient city of Huanglong. Consequently, there was the Fanchuang Temple with a seventeen-story pagoda;
at that time, the śarīra relics were enshrined therein, and those who deliberated on the matter considered this a successful strategy.

Fobao Yan was a native of Youzhou. He left the household life and received full ordination, exerting great effort in the study of the Vinaya. Nevertheless, he had also extensively studied the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
By nature, he was exceptionally quiet and reserved; beyond his preaching and exposition, he would do nothing but sit in the lotus posture to rest in meditation.

He first resided at Renjue Temple in the capital. Those who followed him were all men of outstanding talent and noble character. During the Renshou era, by imperial decree, he was sent to deliver the śarīra relics.
The stupa was enshrined at Hongye Monastery in the prefecture. Once the task was completed, Yan also passed away. Dao Sheng of the Sui dynasty was a native of Puchuan.
In his youth, he served as a disciple under Master Yan, the Director of the Office for Buddhist Affairs (Zhaoxuantong).

His learning possessed a profound depth and continuity; he was handsome in appearance and skilled in ritual protocols. His daily practices were entirely based on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. Furthermore, what need is there to mention... [the rest of the text follows].
This has been explained. During the Renshou era, an imperial decree sent śarīra relics to Chu Prefecture. Wild deer arrived and were able to become tame;
they bowed and prostrated themselves, listening to and receiving the precepts of refuge. Thus, the benefits of the śarīra are vast, and through this, the virtue of the living is also made manifest.
Fenji of the Sui dynasty was a native of Xuzhou. For a long time, he had traveled about giving lectures on the study of wisdom (*prajñā*), yet remained without a fixed place of residence.

During the Qi dynasty, while staying in the capital, he specialized in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitopadeśa* (Da lun) and the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* (Apitan xin), and it was then that his reputation first began to spread.

Toward the end of the Wuping era, when the state fell, he traveled south to Jiangyin to attend to his former studies. After the Kaishuang dynasty unified the realm, he took up his staff and traveled west into the Guanzhong region, where he stayed with various eminent and venerable masters.

Everyone was present, and their spirits were once again uplifted. During the Renshou era, a stupa was erected; by imperial decree, śarīra relics were sent to Liugou Temple to bring glory to the local region.
His final whereabouts remained unknown thereafter.

Fǎkǎi of the Sui dynasty was born in Qīngqiū. In his youth, when he first resolved to study the Way, he left the household life under the Venerable Xuántǒng at Yédū and studied the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, making exceptional progress.
Later, he further consulted the two masters Yúnhuī and [the other], whereby his lingering doubts were dissolved. Following the fall of the Qi dynasty, he fled south to the region of Huái-diàn.
With the rise of the Sui, he widely opened the gates of the Dharma and established a monastery approximately three li north of Cáo City.
He accepted those who came to study him. Thereafter, he entered the pass and resided at Yanghua Temple, where his reputation grew even more prominent.
During the Renshou era, an official petitioned to establish a stupa at Caoshang; this was granted. The Emperor further ordered that śarīra be sent for interment there.
The abundance of auspicious responses compared to other locations was unsurpassed, as is fully recorded in the separate chronicle.
Sui Zhìnéng, surnamed Lǐ, was a native of Hénèi in Huái. He had long been accomplished in the study of the Vinaya. Those who followed him were all sufficient to serve as models for their generation.

At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, he resided at Zhuǎnlún Temple in Wèiyīn. During the Rénshòu era, by imperial decree, he escorted śarīra relics to Fúshèng Temple in Qīngzhōu, where a stūpa was erected.
In his later years, he honored the practice of meditative concentration, retiring to dwell among forests and springs; ultimately, he did not...
He knew his destined end.
Sui Dao-sōng was born into the Liu family of Hejian in Yingzhou. Orphaned and suffering in his early years, he left the household life and served various renowned sages in Luoyang.
Although his robes were tattered and worn, he paid them no heed. Later, he followed Huìyuǎn to refine his understanding of the sutras and śāstras. First...
His reputation reached the capital, where scholars were filled with admiration. During the Renshou era, a stupa was erected at Gusu;
while excavating the ground, ancient śarīra were discovered, which were subsequently interred together with his remains. Later, he resided at Zonghua Temple, where he passed away.
Hui-zang of the Sui dynasty was the son of the Hao family from Pingji in Zhao Commandery. He entered the monastic order at the age of eleven.

When he lectured on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, his exposition was perfectly in accordance with the Dharma. Once he had received full ordination, he devoted himself to the study of the Vinaya. After some time, he mastered such scriptures and treatises as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
At the age of forty, he wished to compose a commentary on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, yet he found it difficult to set pen to paper; thereupon, he withdrew into seclusion.

He dwelt on Mount Que, drinking from mountain streams and eating forest fruits. He severed all ties with worldly entanglements to contemplate the meaning of the teachings with refined concentration, aspiring upward toward the realization of the sages to resolve his doubts.

Suddenly, one night, he heard a voice in the air saying, "It is so; it is so. During the reign of Emperor Wucheng of the Qi dynasty, he was invited to expound the teachings in the Taiji Hall, where their influence reached its peak at that time.
When the Zhou dynasty abolished the Buddhist teachings, he likewise went into seclusion. At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, he resumed his practice.

He received the tonsure and traveled to propagate the Dharma in Dongchuan. In the seventh year of the Kaihuang era, an imperial decree summoned the six Great Virtuous Ones to the capital to have an audience with the Emperor.

At the Chengming Hall, he expounded upon the subtle and profound mysteries of the teachings, which fully accorded with the Sovereign’s mind; consequently, he was treated with exceptional courtesy and honor. By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Kongguan Monastery.
There, śramaṇas such as Zhishun, Senglang, and Fayan requested him to propagate the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, for which he established a distinct and eminent standard.

Xinli synthesized the terminology and meanings [of the scriptures], ensuring his discourse was free from superficiality or frivolity. Those who received his instruction all held him in profound reverence.
On the twenty-ninth day of the eleventh month in the first year of the Daye era, he passed away due to illness at the age of eighty-four.

His disciples, honoring his final instructions, laid his body at the foot of a forested slope to bury the remains and erected a stupa on Mount Zhongnan. The śramaṇa Mingze composed a text to be inscribed [upon it].

Stele. Daozhuang of the Sui dynasty was a native of Jianye in Yangzhou. He possessed a bold and spirited nature, and his deportment was upright and elegant. From his youth, he was held in high esteem by his peers.
Initially, he received instruction in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* from Dharma Master Qiong of Pengcheng Temple; scholars especially revered him for this. Furthermore—
When Fayong was ill, he deliberated on who should succeed him. The assembly all declined, not daring to accept the position, yet Sengzhuang alone felt no hesitation.

Fayong said, "Sengzhuang has a large head but small feet; in the end, he will achieve nothing. Moreover, I fear he will divert his efforts toward other schools. Later, Sengzhuang indeed followed this prediction.

He went to listen to the *Catuḥśataka-śāstra* under Dharma Master Lang of Xinghuang Temple and entered the Inner Court to propagate the teachings. At that time, Emperor Yang was in the Chunfang (Palace of the Heir Apparent).
His imperial favor increased day by day. Indeed, while he was still in the frontier regions, he had already sent letters and composed verses in response to the Emperor’s works.

Shortly thereafter, he entered Riyen Monastery, where he was frequently granted audiences and feasts; the Emperor even went to the palace precincts to receive his instruction. Later, he again lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* at Riyen, composing a commentary in three fascicles.
When the Emperor first ascended the throne, out of regard for their former connection, he bestowed upon him five hundred bolts of silk and thirty felt rugs.

He was appointed as a *ling* (attendant) and accompanied the imperial entourage to Luoyang. He passed away at the age of eighty-one, which was at the beginning of the Daye era. His collected works comprise several dozen scrolls. Sui Faching was a native of Wu Commandery;

he was quick-witted from youth and excelled in discourse. He had a broad mastery of the classics and histories, having initially followed [the teachings of] Xing... (Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at the end.)
Master Huang Lang commented upon and elucidated the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises), resolving obstructions and pruning away the superfluous; he truly rendered great service to the religious tradition.

Later, he gathered disciples and established a teaching seat at Kaishan Temple in Jiangdu. When Emperor Yang resided in the Jin Prince’s residence, he established four centers for the Way and summoned the eminent virtuous men of the realm;
at that time, Sengcheng was also among them. In the third year of the Renshou era, he moved his residence to Guanzhong.

The reputation of Riyen Temple grew ever more eminent. When the Emperor established his capital at Yi and Luo, he followed the imperial entourage as far as the right side of the Xiaoshan Pass, where [the Master] passed away due to illness at the age of over seventy.
Fali of the Sui dynasty was a native of Nanjun. Initially residing at Tianhuang Temple in Jingzhou, he soon departed of his own accord and went into seclusion on Mount Fuzhou by Qingxi.
He specialized in the *Tattvasiddhi* and was particularly skilled in literary composition. Emperor Ming of the Liang dynasty held him in high esteem; though summoned repeatedly, Fali did not go.
When Emperor Yang was still in the prince’s residence, he personally paid him homage and invited him to come to the capital, where Fali resided at Riyen Monastery.

He visited Emperor Wen at the Renshou Palace. An imperial decree was issued for him to be granted pure offerings (śuddhāhāra) in the Dabao Hall, where he recited verses on the throne praising the Emperor’s virtues;
the Emperor marveled with admiration. When Emperor Yang was in the position of Crown Prince, his favor and patronage were even more profound.

In the first year of the Daye era, as he was about to move the Eastern Gate, an imperial decree granted him one set of *kaṣāya* robes made from the bark of the Qianqiu tree, five hundred rolls of silk, and forty pieces of felt.
He received from the Empress a fox-axil fur cushion, Dharma robes, and other gifts. Following the imperial entourage to Luoyang, he passed away shortly thereafter at the age of seventy-eight.
Hui-lun intended to embellish and adorn the Great Vehicle (Zong-cheng) with his writings; he once continued the *Biographies of Famous Monks* (*Chuan-ming-seng*).
He left no formal works behind; however, a separate collection in eight fascicles exists and circulates in the world.
The Sui monk Tanchu was born into the Zhang family of Luozhou. Having renounced secular life at a young age, he lamented that the Buddhist teachings were not yet fully established.
Thereupon, he formed a fellowship and traveled westward in search of it. He barely reached the Xi-ling (Sili) Pass when his journey was blocked by the road and he returned.

Nevertheless, he became thoroughly proficient in both the phonology and the script of the Sanskrit language. Upon arriving at the capital, his fame spread far and wide. In the tenth year of the Kaihuang era, an imperial edict ordered him to translate [the scriptures];
he resided at Daxingshan Monastery. Not long after, an edict sent śarīra relics to Xiyuan Monastery in Puzhou. Xiyuan is...
This was the ancient Yunju Monastery. The mountain is named Zhongchao; it borders the banks of the Yellow River to the west and is renowned throughout the world for its magnificent scenery.

Later, he was again summoned by imperial decree to reside at Zhidu Monastery in Yinzhou, where he likewise experienced auspicious responses, as recorded in detail in a separate account. He passed away at the beginning of the Daye era.

At that time, there was one named Huizhong, a son of the Guo family from Yongzhou, who was skilled in the *Śatashāstra* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. He too received an imperial decree to go to Taizhou.
A stupa was erected at Daie Temple. However, the gates of the mountain shrine were usually kept locked and never opened; yet on this occasion, they opened spontaneously three times.

Zhi Ju of the Sui dynasty was born into the Wu clan of Wuxing. He was dignified and solemn, skilled in literary composition, and possessed a refined and elegant appearance. Initially, he listened to...

When Master Lang of Xinghuang lectured, he subsequently expounded the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the Four Treatises (*Catuḥśāstra*) himself. At that time, even the great masters of the East rushed westward to attend his teachings.
Later, he propagated the Three Treatises at Jianchu Temple, where there were always over a hundred people in the assembly. Duke Wushan Guo Yan once paid him a formal visit.
When Emperor Yang was in the provinces, stationed as governor in Yangzhou and Yuezhou, he summoned the Master to reside at Huiri Temple. There, he [began] to expound...

In the nineteenth year of the [Sui] Huang era, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Riyen-ji Temple in the capital. All provisions for his support were provided solely from the Prince’s estate.

At that time, Dharma Master Jizang, an eminent figure among his fellow disciples, invariably composed new prefaces and various verses whenever [Jingying] preached or propagated the teachings, thereby providing encouragement.
Consequently, those who gathered around him as followers became numerous. This occurred in the first month of the second year of the Daye era.
He passed away at the age of seventy-two and was buried south of the capital’s outskirts.
Bianyi was the son of Ma Shi of Qinghe in Jiu Prefecture; he renounced secular life at a young age and immediately began studying the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.

By the time he had reached the age of twenty, he was already capable of delivering lectures. There was one named Tansan who prided himself on his talent and understanding, yet he considered Bianyi’s views to be merely superficial.
He was easily discouraged. Thus, they exchanged arguments ten times; however, Daosan was unable to continue. Fayi said, "The logical momentum has not yet been exhausted;
why do you not proceed further? Daosan replied, "This was what I had originally intended. Even if I wished to proceed further, how could I possibly do so?

At that time, the tyranny of Zhou was flaring up, so he eventually traveled south to Jinling and soon arrived in the Central Lands. While Emperor Yang was still in the imperial residence, he issued a recruitment for men of renown.

De was appointed to reside at Riyans Temple. Later, he entered the capital, where eminent scholars of the time—such as Tancong, Daofu, Jie, Jing, and others—all attended his lectures, holding his texts beneath their seats and consulting him on profound and obscure points. In the second year of the Renshou era, Prince Han Liang came to court;
Master Zhinian paid him five visits of respect and subsequently established a Dharma assembly at Chanlin Temple, mobilizing the scholars of the Three Fu regions.

Everyone abandoned their original practices and turned toward this [new teaching] together. Daoyi also initially joined their ranks, but his mind was not at peace with it. He subsequently examined the points where they were obstructed;

after three days of deliberation, he found that their arguments were consistently blocked and he could offer no rebuttal. When Empress Wenhui passed away, Emperor Yang resided in the Chufang (Palace of Spring).
He summoned forty monks of great virtue, including Daori, to debate the profound principles of the Dharma, and Daoyi was deemed the most competent. The sandalwood... [text ends].
Mendao of Mount Yue studied the *Abhidharmakośa* under his own initiative, as he had received no formal instruction from a teacher; he relied on [Fajing] to resolve his doubts.
His reputation for extensive learning was celebrated by his contemporaries. Over thirty people, including Zhijiu, Jizang, and Huisheng, resided together at Riyuan Monastery;
whenever they discussed the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, the assembly would defer to him. In the second year of the Daye era, he passed away at the monastery due to illness at the age of sixty-four.
Sixteen. He was buried south of the capital’s outskirts. Zheng Ting, Attendant-in-Ordinary to the Crown Prince, composed the inscription for the erected stele.
Previously, in the second year of the Renshou era, an imperial edict had ordered that śarīra relics be sent to Bao Rong Temple in various prefectures and commanderies to establish stupas.

In the fourth year, they were again sent to Liang Jing Temple on Mount Du in Lu Zhou. Although the auspicious signs witnessed therein differed, they were both magnificent. [The details are] fully recorded.

This is recorded in the *Biezhuàn* (Separate Biography). Huǐhǎi of the Zhāng clan was a native of Yúxiāng in Hédōng. At the age of fourteen, he shaved his head and became a disciple of the Great Śramaṇa-samgha-pati Dámiány Fǎshī.
At eighteen, he already lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. After receiving full ordination, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of dhyāna.
Daoye hid himself on Mount Fudu in Hongnong. When Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty completely destroyed Buddhist temples, he entered the Chen state to avoid persecution;
thus, his precepts remained unimpaired and he never laid aside his dharma robes. Furthermore, he studied the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra), investigating its profound meaning to the utmost.
Upon the Great Sui dynasty’s accession to the throne, he first arrived at the capital. His Imperial Sister, Princess Cheng’an Chang, established Jingfa Temple for him to reside in.
His disciples gathered in great numbers, and his excellence has been passed down to this day. However, by nature he delighted in quietude and silence, and did not engage in formal preaching;
his directness of mind toward the *dōjō* (place of practice) was evident therein. At the beginning of the Renshou era, an imperial decree sent śarīra relics to Dinglin [Temple] in Heng [Prefecture].

He was enshrined at Yuesi Temple, where a stupa was erected for him shortly thereafter; he was subsequently sent to Shishan Temple in Xiongzhou, and the details of these auspicious responses are all recorded in his separate biography.
On the twenty-seventh day of the fifth month in the second year of the Daye era, he passed away at the temple at the age of fifty-seven.
His final instruction was that his burial be simple, and his disciples did not dare to disobey it.
