The nun was the daughter of Liu Shi of Puzhan; her name was Zhixian. She entered the monastic life at the age of seven. One day, while sitting in meditation, she entered a state of meditative absorption (dhyāna) from the very top of the building.
Her teacher searched everywhere for her without success and concluded that she must have drowned in a well. From then on, whatever she said or did was invariably accompanied by divine verification.

When the Zhou dynasty abolished the teachings, the nuns relied upon the imperial household; they never moved their temple, and it consequently grew ever larger. The auspicious responses of the śarīra relics are recorded in the *Biézhuàn* (Separate Biography).
Zhi Ju of the Sui dynasty was of the Zhu clan; his spirit was pure and far-reaching, manifesting even while he was still in his swaddling clothes. He left the household life at Suzhou’s...
At Dongshan Temple on Mount Huqiu, there was Dharma Master Yin, a preeminent master of both the Way and the arts. [Zhu] Fu gathered there to study, never being idle for even a moment of time.
From his hometown came Gu Xipeng, and from Kuaiji came Xie Juyue; these two further illuminated his understanding through their mastery of the forest of rhetoric and the cave of principle.
Thus, by the age of twenty, he was already engaged in lecturing, and he especially admired the profound and pure [teachings].
The Master [Huiyuan] attained perfection in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and took it to heart. After a long period of inquiry and discussion, all his doubts and obstructions were resolved.

Zhou Hongzheng of Runan, who was profoundly versed in both Buddhist and secular learning and possessed the discernment to evaluate the worth of men, saw him and sighed in admiration, saying: "He is truly a 'hu-lian' vessel of the Śākya gate.
The Chen princes Bo-shan, the Prince of Poyang; Bo, the Prince of Xin'an; and Shu-qie, the Prince of Xincai, all held him in high esteem and sought his company. Up to this point—

In the second year of the Daye era, an imperial decree was issued for the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* to be recited in the Taiji Hall. The Emperor personally presided over the Dharma assembly, with all his ministers and officials in attendance.

At that time, [the monks] poured forth [their eloquence] like clouds and wrote [their insights] like from a vase; there were none who did not admire them. In the third year, he returned to his native village to grieve for his mother’s passing, yet he did not cease his propagation of the teachings.

In the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era, an imperial letter was sent to commend him and inquire after his well-being. [The decree was signed by] the Chancellor of the Department of State Affairs, Chu...

Lord Su and Lord Wei of Pi, the Left Vice President of the Secretariat, personally visited the meditation hall to prostrate at his feet in worship and presented offerings to manifest their sincere devotion.
In the twelfth year, by imperial decree, monastic offices were established, and he was appointed to the position of Administrator of Equality (Pingdeng).

When Lord Zongcheng Liu served as the Regional Commander, he received the Bodhisattva precepts from him. Later, when Prince Jian of Qi governed the Huaihai region, he sent a letter inviting him there, but he did not rise to accept the summons.
He passed away on the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month in the fifth year of the Daye era. His age was seventy-two.
In the twelfth month of that same year, he was interred on the southern ridge of the mountain. His disciples, including Daogong and others, erected a stele to commemorate his conduct;
the inscription was composed by Yu Shinan of the Secretariat.
Jingyuan of the Sui dynasty’s lineage and surname are unknown. A native of Dazhou, he entered the monastic order in his prime and applied himself with vigor to the study of the sūtras and śāstras.

Having received the full ordination (*mahā-śīla*), he specialized in the Vinaya-piṭaka. Possessing vast learning and a powerful memory, he would examine and extract insights from the texts morning and night;

after only five recitations, he was already able to lecture upon them. From then on, he successively expounded the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (*Caturvarga-vinaya*). He also studied the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the *Daśabhūmika*, and various minor treatises. In his later years, he practiced the *Zhun*...
Master Gongshe lectured on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* while residing at Baocha Temple in the capital. When he ascended the seat to establish the doctrine, those who followed him were numerous.
He composed a ten-fascicle commentary on the *Śarīra-abhidharma*, which was extremely comprehensive and exhaustive. By imperial decree, he was sent to deliver a relic to Lushan Temple in Tanzhou.

As they were crossing the Xiang River and approaching the mountain, there appeared fifty thousand extraordinary birds of five colors, flocking together and floating over the water to welcome and lead them toward the boat.

Upon reaching the shore, the birds continued to fly through the air together until they arrived at the site of the stupa. [The monks] wished for this auspicious omen to be reported to the Emperor, who was greatly delighted.
At the beginning of the Daye era, Master Xiang entered into seclusion at Huiri Monastery and entrusted his disciples to Master Yuan; through this, his reputation grew even more far-reaching.
In the fifth month of the fifth year, he suddenly passed away.
Sui Zhi: Nian was a member of the Su lineage and a native of Xindu in Jizhou. His ancestors were descendants of Gai Fan of Yingchuan, who later migrated there due to official service.

Having entered the monastic order, Nian was determined to seek the Way. Upon receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), he proceeded to the capital of Ye to study the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* under Dharma Master Daochang.
After several years, he ultimately became one of those known as the "Four Disciples" (*sisheng*) under Daochang’s guidance.
Xiuji and his peers were renowned for their equal fame. Shortly thereafter, they went to the Dharma Master Daocong to study the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*.

After the master had translated treatises such as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, as well as sūtras such as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, he was about to propagate and expound them, yet had not yet found a suitable person for the task.

Consequently, he and his fellow masters Zongkai and Zhunyun received instruction from him, sitting at his feet. When the Tripitaka Master passed away and his companions followed him in death, [Fashang] again joined his fellow student Sengzong.
He dwelt in the seclusion of Kuangxiu to propagate the Dharma; the two princes who governed the province, those of Poyang and Changsha, revered him as their teacher.

He thus formed the resolve to spend his final years there. On the sixteenth day of the fifth month in the ninth year of the Daye era, he passed away at the age of eighty.

His crown remained warm and his fingers remained flexed; this was yet another sign of his rebirth in the higher realms and attainment of the Way. On the twentieth day of that same month, he was interred on the western mountain of the monastery.
Tongzhen of the Sui dynasty was originally of the Li clan from Longxi; later, while residing in Pufan in Hedong, he left the household life and studied under Dharma Master Tanyan.

On the fourth day of the second month in the ninth year, he passed away at the monastery at the age of seventy-five. His final wish was to offer his body to the mountain forests;
his disciples followed this, collecting his remaining remains and enshrining them in a stupa on Mount Zhongnan.

Zhi Run of the Sui dynasty’s lineage and surname are unknown. A native of Xiangyang, his disposition toward the Buddha-dharma was as if it were the result of past habituation. At the age of twenty, he went to Ye (Yecheng).
Coinciding with the time when Huizun presided over the exposition of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, he followed him to receive instruction. He further studied the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Subsequently, he relied on Daoguang to hear the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, while simultaneously studying the *Abhidharma-śāstra*; he thoroughly mastered both its points of penetration and its obstructions. At that time, he was renowned as "Broadly Vast."

Rarely was there anyone able to surpass him. After some time, he crossed the Yangtze River to serve as an attendant to Master Digan at Changgan Temple, where he thoroughly studied the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises). Later, he returned to Hanyin to guide and transform others.

At the beginning of the Daye era, while residing at Huiri Temple, he encountered an imperial decree to offer prayers for the expedition against Liaodong, so he traveled through the regions of Jiang, Yu, Min, and Shu.
He returned to the Western Capital and passed away at Chanding Monastery due to illness at the age of seventy-five; this was the tenth year of the Daye era.

Jingye of the Sui dynasty was a layman by history, a native of Suizhou in Handong. Having left the household life and received full ordination, he devoted himself to the meticulous study of the Vinaya-piṭaka.
He followed Dharma Master Huiyuan to receive instruction on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Subsequently, carrying his book-cases, he followed Huiyuan into Guanzhong at the Emperor's command.
There he absorbed the profound principles of the teaching. Later, he studied the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* under Chan Master Tanqian, his devotion and veneration being most sincere.
During the Kaihuang era, he lived in seclusion on Mount Fucheshan in Lantian; the community built a dwelling for him, which is the present-day Wuzhen Temple.
In the second year of the Renshou era, an imperial edict ordered the transport of the śarīra to Jingcheng Temple in Anzhou;

the auspicious signs accompanying the erection of the stupa are recorded in a separate biography. In the fourth year of the Daye era, an edict summoned him to the Honglu Temple to instruct visiting monks.
In the ninth year, an edict appointed him to reside at Chandeng Temple. He suddenly said to his disciples, "I now wish to turn my cart around; this shall be my final departure."
Not long after, he passed away on the eighteenth day of the second month in the twelfth year of the Daye era.

Zhi Guang of the Sui dynasty was a native of Jiangzhou; in his youth, he followed Master Ju to study the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra), and his reputation rose far above his peers.

In the tenth year of the Kaihuang era, an imperial decree summoned Master Jueju to the capital, where he resided at Daxingshan Monastery. During the Renshou era, when pagodas were being erected, an edict ordered him to deliver śarīra relics to Xunzhou.
Since Xunzhou was situated far away in the south of the Ling Mountains, he forgot his weariness for the sake of the Dharma; his devotion to the light [of the Buddha] was indeed exemplary.
Upon returning to the territory of Qin, he grew weary of clamor and yearned for tranquility; ultimately, he spent his final years in a mountain retreat on Mount Lu.

Sui’s Tan sui was a man of magnificent talent and capacity; consequently, regarding the principles of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Vijñaptimātratā*, and the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha*—both in their ontological and phenomenological aspects—he was thoroughly proficient in all of them.
Whenever students arrived at his door with their bundles of books, they all departed fully satisfied, having gained what they sought, and were moved to joyful submission.

Thus it was. During the Renshou era, an imperial edict ordered that śarīra relics be sent to Jinzhou, where they were enshrined in Fahou Temple within the prefecture—a site of superior geomantic excellence.

Tánliángshēng of the Lì clan from Lù, who was of the Tang dynasty, left home to become a monk after his years exceeded those of the *zhìxué* stage. He lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and those who understood the Dharma praised him as one who possessed a refined ear for the music of the teachings.
He entered the capital and resided at Zhēnjì Temple. During the Rénshǒu era, by imperial decree, he escorted śarīra relics to Bózhōu to be enshrined at Kāijí Temple.
The monastery was not far from the Temple of Laojun. Thereupon, a stupa was erected and he was interred there; he passed away at the age of over eighty.

As soon as he first shaved his head, he was proficient in the great Mahāyāna texts; he also transmitted the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* of Huiyuan.

After receiving full ordination, he entered the Guanzhong region and resided in silence at Jingfasi. During the Renshou era, a stupa was erected for him at Guazhou Chongjing Temple. Yi passed away... [text ends]

Lingcan of Tang was a disciple of Master Yuan of Huazhou. He traveled to study at the capital of Ye, where he investigated and mastered the correct principles.

Having thoroughly studied and lectured upon the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, he accompanied a group of ten companions to enter the Guanzhong region following Master Yuan, where they resided at Daxingshan Monastery.

Later, Huicān moved him again to Dà Chándìng Temple. At the beginning of the Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty, he passed away at his residence at the age of seventy.
Tang Haishun’s secular surname was Ren. She was a native of Puzhak in Hedong. Orphaned at a young age, she served her mother with filial piety.

When she reached the age for formal study, she first left the household life under the śramaṇa Daosun. Her recitation and practice were diligent, swift, and admirable. After receiving full ordination, her observance of the precepts was lofty and pure;

she was especially courageous in her dedication to the practice of meditative concentration. She then concluded that among the three wheels [of body, speech, and mind], faults of speech were particularly severe, and thus she maintained silence.

He did not speak; he merely swept his thatched door and sat upright in meditation. At that time, there was a śramaṇa from Qiyán Monastery named Shénsù, who by nature delighted in secluded seclusion and specialized in the study of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Sēn carried his book-cases to consult with him. However, his disciples were quite numerous, and those who sought instruction from him were especially many.

"First I attained three things; now I have attained two more. Su asked, "What do you mean? He replied, "First, I beheld your countenance of displeasure;

second, I heard the wondrous meaning [of the Dharma]. Su was ashamed. He once spoke to Su in a relaxed manner, saying, "In the vast eons of the past, I have deeply failed to encounter sages and saints.
Wandering through the five realms of existence, I could not free myself, and thus was born in this defiled land to face these ordinary conditions."
I have not yet been able to cross the river of desire or ascend the shore of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). Is this not because the horse of the mind has lost its bridle and plunged into a dark pit?

For this reason, my tears drenched my breast. Furthermore, I thought: whenever I recall the two wheels of the chariot meeting on the same track and coming to rest, how can one allow them to gallop long through the six realms?
I long for the way home, yet find no path. It is only by virtue of having been born as a human that I may open up a period of carefree ease and be free from sorrow.

I am poor and lowly. To leave the household life and propagate the Way as a monk is no easy matter for one of my status compared to a prince or nobleman; yet now I have attained both. How truly cause for celebration!

Furthermore, within this chamber of great darkness, I look up to you who transmits the lamp of the Dharma. Although I do not have the fortune to behold the Tathāgata in person, I am fortunate to have encountered a Dharma Master.
Without weighing my own meager capacity, I venture to fathom the profound source. I pray that you will immediately bestow upon me the bright pearl and cast it into the depths of the vast ocean.
[If you] act thus, then in one lifetime you shall have gained [the truth], and for a thousand ages you will have no regrets. Su said, "I respectfully hear the aspirations of the gentleman.

Later, Su repeatedly held various monastic offices, yet he ultimately withdrew from the dharma-seat. Not long after, he again sent a letter to the śramaṇa Daojie to exhaustively inquire about the principles of Chan.
Daojie’s replies were all omitted from the record; furthermore, [Su] composed the "Three Non-Doings" (San bu wei pian). The first says: "I desire..."

Cease arms and cultivate culture; though the body dies, the name remains. By grinding stones one opens the Way; by praying at the well, the spring flows. Your liver was within him, while my body remained on the periphery.
Jing Ke drew his sword and Mao Sui held forth the basin; had they not acted, it would have been so, but having acted, it could not be otherwise.
I fear that if two tigers fight, neither can remain whole; thus, the present friendship would be severed forever and resentment for the future would endure.

For this reason, I have retraced my steps onto the wild paths and stilled my shadow at the brushwood gate. The second verse says: I wish to prick my thigh like Mencius and suspend my head by a needle-point like Sui Yue;

to study by the window beam like He Yan and write by the snow like Wang Xizhi; for my colorful scrolls to reflect the glow of fireflies. In a single morning, I shall soar like a Peng bird across ten thousand li, flying like a phoenix, letting my talent run free.

Discerning the art of persuasion: when a sovereign ascends a high carriage to return to his capital, or wears brocade to return to his hometown, there is fear that the bird will be maimed for its feathers or the orchid broken for its fragrance.

They exchange greetings, displaying their forms and drawing out their influence; their status is elevated and their reputation transcends the ordinary. Their chests are filled with elegant robes, and their kitchens abound with sweet delicacies.

They recite and extol the works of the *Xuan Guan*, and sing praises in beautiful songs and ballads. Yet, fearing that they may dwell like dust upon fragile grass or lodge like dew upon precarious branches, they pass their days without excess and their mornings without transgression.

Tang Zhiju, surnamed Li, was a native of Shouchang in Xin’an. His father, Hui, was a *sanqi yuanwailang* (an outer court attendant of the Imperial Secretariat) during the Liang dynasty.

Zhiju first studied the *Śāstra on the Exposition of the Mahāyāna* under Master Tan; next, he studied the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* under Master Ya; and he further studied the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) under Master Yu. At that age—
27. He immediately proceeded to expound the Dharma with unimpeded eloquence. Renowned among all, he was entrusted by Emperor Wu with the five divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras.
His reputation flourished greatly, and both the learned and the common alike looked up to him in reverence. He once said to his senior disciple, Mingyan:
"I entrust to you the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the *Nirvāṇa*, the commentaries (*śāstra*), and the fourfold expository treatises (*piṇḍārtha*)."
You, [Master] Ruzhen, suddenly passed away while holding hands with me after we had conversed twice or thrice.

This was on the tenth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Wude era at Jian'an Temple in Changzhou. He was interred at his former burial site at Beitan Nan Temple. His secular surname was Qiu, and he belonged to a prominent clan of Jinling.

Tánqiān of the Tang dynasty was a native of Jiāngdū. His mastery of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* was profound, and he was also well-versed in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and other scriptures.

Whenever he sat at the dharma assembly, his inquiries and challenges arose like swarms of bees; scholars were intimidated by him. When Emperor Yáng was still the Prince of Jìn, he established a monastery in the capital.
Yanqian resided there. Xiao Zong, the Director of the Secretariat, along with his brothers, humbled themselves to receive instruction from him; such was the way he won others over through his virtue.
Toward the end of the Renshou era, an imperial edict sent the śarīra to Huangu Valley Mountain at Shangu Valley Temple in Xizhou, where auspicious responses were obtained.
These are not recorded here, as they have a separate record.
Tang Fakǎn was the son of the Zheng family of Róngyáng. In his youth, he entered the monastic order at Lìngyán Monastery on Mount Tàishān.

After receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), he followed Dharma Master Yuǎn to study the principles of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*. When the Qi calendar came to an end and the Northern Zhou abolished the Great Teaching, he traveled south to Jiàn'ye.
Once the Sui had pacified the Chen, he resided at Ānlè Monastery in Jiāngdū. Cáo Pī placed his faith in him.

Daoshi composed a commentary on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, which he intended to explain and recite with eloquence. Sengbi listened to it himself, and whenever there were points of profound meaning, Bi would invariably join his palms and exclaim, "Excellent!

When Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty was residing at the Jin residence and was stationed in Yangzhou and Yue, he summoned Daoshi to reside at Riyang Monastery; however, shortly thereafter, Daoshi retired and returned home.

He devoted his mind to contemplation and ceased worldly activities, yet the objects he crafted were vast in number. At the beginning of the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty, an imperial edict ordered Daoshi to go to Xuanzhou for his placement.
Śarīra. Not long after, he traveled again to Lizhou and obtained auspicious signs in each case, as detailed in a separate record.

At the beginning of the dynasty, an imperial edict selected ten "Great Virtuous Ones" (da-de) to serve as administrators over monks and nuns; Huikan was included among their number due to his dignified demeanor and tranquil solemnity.
Later, he moved his residence to Xingshan Temple. On the eleventh month of the sixth year of the Wude era, he passed away at the temple at the age of seventy-three.

His physician advised him to increase his intake of pork to suppress the ailment. Huikuan said, "All humans must die; how could one possibly obtain such [a remedy]? Thus, he remained steadfast in guarding the foundation of the precepts.

Thus it was. Shanzhou of the Tang dynasty, surnamed Huai, was born in Yingzhou. He renounced worldly life and devoted himself to the study of the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samāsa-śāstra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

When the Qi dynasty fell, he fled south to the borders of Chen. At that time, a severe famine prevailed; having no means to beg for alms, he would occasionally obtain a single cake to barely sustain his breath, until—
He was so emaciated and haggard that those who saw him treated him with indifference. He happened to go to a temple where a lecture was being held;

he entered and engaged in debate three times before the high seat, but was unable to respond. He died of suppressed indignation, and [Fazhou] Guizhou initially did not know the reason. When Guizhou visited him on another day, he saw that preparations for a funeral were underway.
Upon asking the cause, he was told, "The Dharma Master died yesterday after being challenged by a monk from the North. Only then did Guizhou realize what had happened.
Having fled, he later attended another lecture and acted in the same manner; in succession, he caused three men to die. Consequently, his reputation spread throughout the regions of Wu and Yue.

At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, he returned north and relied upon Master Fayuan, residing at Jingying Temple in the capital. As he restated and established his doctrinal positions, their sharpness was irresistible.

His fellow seekers of the profound numbered in the thousands, all of whom marveled at and submitted to him. When Fayuan composed a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Jizhou was immediately commanded to take up the brush.
Huiyuan criticized him, saying, "This may be done after my death; is it not excessive for you to do so now?
Huizhou replied, "If the Dharma Master were to pass away immediately, who would know of Zhou? What would be the point of practicing meditation then? Huiyuan followed his advice.

Upon Huiyuan’s passing, he was summoned by imperial decree to serve as the presiding master of the Nirvāṇa Assembly and resided at Jingying Monastery. At the end of the Kaihuang era, he followed Prince Xiu of Shu to open [the teachings].
He guided the construction of shrines at Min and Bo, and oversaw the creation of sacred images for all of them, which were sent to the capital for veneration.

During the reign of Emperor Wen, when pagodas were established to enshrine the śarīra relics, he was summoned by imperial decree to Hua-lin Monastery on Mount Niutou in Zizhou; the auspicious responses are detailed in a separate record.

He founded monasteries during the Taiye era and was repeatedly selected for high appointments, yet he soon retired to Chan-ting Monastery. Although his reputation for propagating the Dharma flourished, he suffered from chronic illness; nevertheless, the assembly at his dharma seat remained magnificent.

He did not diminish from his former state. Not long after, Liang Chazhou said, "How can I remain for long? When someone asked him the reason, he replied, "To grow old and die is simply the way of natural law.
In the thirteenth year [of the Sui dynasty], he wished to return to the monastery where he had originally resided, but the assembly would not permit it.
Consequently, he took earth and stuffed his mouth; the assembly, fearing for him, granted his request. In the eighth month of the third year of Wude, he passed away at Jingying Monastery. Spring.
In the autumn, at the age of seventy-one, while initially bedridden with illness, Zou addressed his disciples, saying:

"Throughout my life, I have maintained right faith and applied myself to the teaching of the Dharma without ever becoming lax. It is certain that I shall be reborn in the Pure Land. Prepare the chambers by sweeping and cleaning them, so that I may await it."
Suddenly rising from his seat, he joined his palms and said, "The World-Honored One has arrived. Looking toward his attendant, he said, "Prepare a seat for the World-Honored One.
He then assumed an air of repentance and shame. After a long while, he said, "The World-Honored One has departed," and bowed as if seeing off a guest.
Thereupon he lay down and did not speak again; he passed away. He was buried on the northern slope of Weiqu, south of the city. His disciple Huikai succeeded him. Now...
It is recorded that he resided at Dazongchi Monastery.

Huìjué of the Tang dynasty was the son of the Fàn family of Qí. He had long been well-versed in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and its Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), and his illustrious reputation was far-reaching;

his disciples followed his teachings as a prevailing custom. During the Great Sui dynasty, when the Buddha-dharma flourished, an imperial edict established Wǔdé Monastery to the south of the city of Bìngzhōu. It was vast in scale.
In the past, when Emperor Wen governed the Zhou dynasty, he personally trod upon the edge of blades; this was the place where he lost his way and sought refuge.

Because his awakening and wisdom were manifest, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside there. When he accepted an invitation from Gao Yang, the assembly numbered more than a thousand, yet the land was too narrow to accommodate them.

A patron constructed a great hall for him, which was completed in less than a day. He ascended the seat to establish the Dharma, and those who heard him were satisfied and awakened. He composed the *Huayan*... [text continues]

He composed commentaries on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, as well as the *Zuanyizhang* (Compendium of Meaning) in thirteen fascicles, all of which circulate in the world.
In the third year of the Wude era, when the Xianyun tribes invaded from the south, Fayue suffered a slight illness and said to his disciples, "I am departing.
His disciples asked, "The barbarian invaders have cut off all roads; where will you go? He replied, "The path of birth and death is long; we shall surely part ways again."
He then brought out all that he had stored and distributed it as alms to the assembly. With right mindfulness and a serene composure, he passed away;
he was ninety years of age.
Dao Yan of Dingzhou was the son of the Li family. Initially, he studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* under Master Huiyuan, and he lectured on them.

He bestowed the transmission of enlightenment upon many more than others. Upon entering the capital, he resided at Jingying Monastery. During the Renshou era, when pagodas were being established, an imperial decree ordered that śarīra relics be sent to Guizhou for interment;
however, because the region was remote and the local customs were vulgar, the Buddhist rites could not have been carried out without the steadfast resolve of Daoyuan.
Tang Baoxi was a native of Beizhou. He left the household life as a disciple of the Tripiṭaka Master Sengxiu of Yongzhou.

At the age of eighteen, he took the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Zhidu lun) as his primary study, and his reputation moved the eminent figures of his time. In the sixteenth year of the Kaihuang era, an imperial edict appointed him as the presiding master of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* assembly;

he subsequently taught and transformed others during all four seasons at Tonghua Temple. During the Renshou era, when the construction of pagodas was decreed, an edict ordered him to escort the relics.
He resided at Songyue Temple in Songzhou for some time. Later, he was sent to Shen'ai Temple in Xingzhou; his spiritual wonders are recorded in the *Biézhuan*.
When Emperor Wen passed away, he established the Chan-ding Daochang (Meditation and Concentration Monastery) and invited [the Master] to receive offerings there.
At the end of the Wude era, he passed away at his residence at the age of eighty. His disciples, Tan-gong and Ming-hong, were both skilled in their former practices; Tan-gong, during the Zhenguan...
At the beginning of his tenure, Guan-chu served as the *sthavira* (Dharma Elder) for Chong-ji Temple; later, he entered Hongfu Temple to assume the duties of Puguang Temple.
Daohong also entered Puguang Temple to oversee bathing affairs, providing monks with baths twice a month. Furthermore, Zhisheng resided in the inner courtyard.

Huiqian of the Tang dynasty was a native of Yingzhou. Having shaved his head at an early age, he took a deep interest in the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages). Carrying his staff, he traveled in search of a master of the craft.

Upon meeting Master Huiyuan, he became thoroughly versed in the teachings of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Dichizhi* (*Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*), and the doctrines of a hundred schools. Whenever he delivered lectures, he would provide detailed accounts of the various masters’ perspectives.
When the Qi dynasty fell and the Dharma declined, he fled south to Chen. With the rise of the Sui, he returned north and followed Master Huiyuan into the Guanzhong region.
He resided at Daxingshan Temple. In the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, by imperial decree, the five assemblies were established;

he was appointed as the presiding master of the Ten Grounds Assembly (*daśabhūmi*) and propagated the teachings extensively at Baoguang Temple. In the second year of the Renshou era, an imperial edict sent śarīra relics to Hongbo Temple in his native village, where a stupa was erected;
the auspicious responses are detailed in a separate record. In the fourth year, another stupa was established at Anhe Temple in Haizhou.
His śarīra were enshrined in the capital, where he frequently opened dharma assemblies of the Ten Stages; the magnificence of these dharma feasts was beyond compare.
In his later years, he resided at the Chan-ting Monastery. Toward the end of the Wude era, he passed away at his residence at the age of seventy-nine.
Tang Daoqing was originally of the Dai clan of Guangling; later, his family crossed the Yangtze River and settled in Wuxi.
At the age of eleven, he entered the Jian-shan Temple in Wu-jun to serve under Preceptor Zang and received the tonsure.

At seventeen, he went to the capital to study the profound texts and abstruse meanings of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* at Pengcheng Temple, mastering them without omission. Consequently, the masters of his time remarked that he had "suspended the sun and moon within his breast."

He poured the rivers and streams into his mouth; this truly corresponds to his eyes. After the fall of the Chen dynasty, his companions perished one by one, so he returned to Fengguang Temple in his native village, where he continued to transform and guide others as before.
Later, he moved to Hongye Temple on Mount Bitan, where he propagated the teachings without ceasing through both cold and heat.
In the eighth month of the ninth year of the Wude era, he passed away in his temple quarters on the twentieth day of that same month.
On the third day, he was interred on Mount Futang. The inscription for the stele composed by the monk Faxuan of the same monastery is not recorded here.
Jingzang of the Tang dynasty, whose secular surname was Zhang, was a native of Gaodu in Zezhou. At the age of nine, he entered the service of Chan Master Quan of Qinghua Temple.

He left the household life and devoted himself to the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). After receiving full ordination, he further exhausted the depths of the Dharma’s principles, becoming a refuge for his fellow disciples.

At the age of twenty-three, he went to the capital to study under the Great Virtuous Master Daoyuan of his native region. Upon Yuan’s passing, he attended various Dharma assemblies to listen to and receive instruction on the *sūtras* and *śāstras*.
He applied himself with particular dedication to the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. Returning home, he resided at Jingying Monastery to propagate the teachings.

He led a great multitude of followers. In the ninth year of the Daye era, an imperial edict summoned him to enter the Grand Court of State Ceremonial (Dahonglu) to instruct the monks of the three kingdoms of the Eastern Dependencies, all of whom followed his righteous teachings.
At the beginning of the Wude era, an edict appointed Yu Wenmingda as Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stables (Dapuju) to go with full powers to pacify Henan and the north.
Just before his departure, Wenmingda, having previously received the precepts for returning to the Buddha from Xuanzang, went to see Xuanzang to seek further instruction.
Sengzang said, "The world is impermanent; the Buddha has given us sincere warnings. It is easy to part, but difficult to meet again. I pray that you will take care of yourself.
Da bowed twice and said, "I, your disciple, shall certainly not return. I pray that you, Master, will secretly bestow your blessings upon me.
