In the twelfth month, he entered the capital and fell ill while dyeing his robes; he passed away at his lodgings at the age of fifty-six.
His disciple Daoshan now resides at Zhongnan Zixiang Temple.
Tang Puming was born into the Wei clan; he was a native of Anyi in Pu. At the age of thirteen, he first left the household life under his maternal uncle, Dharma Master Daoxun.
Daoxun further sent him as a disciple of the śramaṇa Tongzhen at Yanxing Temple. By nature intelligent and quick-witted, he took the Great Dharma as his own responsibility.
Carrying his book-box, he traveled extensively, never remaining in one place for long. Consequently, his mastery of the sūtras and śāstras became complete.
He embraced [the teachings], and his peers were all humbled and won over by him. At the age of eighteen, he expounded the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.

After receiving full ordination, he specialized in the study of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, and the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. At twenty-four, he expounded the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*; at thirty, he expounded the *Triṃśikā*.

His speech was refined and his meanings were lucid; students gathered there in great numbers. In the sixth year of the Daye era, an imperial edict appointed him to the Dà Chándìng Dàochǎng, where his name was ranked among the highest.

He was ordained at the age of one and had spent eighteen summer retreats [since his full ordination]. In the first year of the Wude era, by imperial decree, he resided at Renshou Temple in his native village, in accordance with the wishes of the people.

By day he lectured and by night he practiced meditation, strictly adhering to the scriptural teachings. Every morning he recited the *Prātimokṣa* once and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* twenty times.

He performed prostrations and repentance during the six periods of the day, dedicating all of it toward the Pure Land; he practiced this throughout his life without ceasing. There was nothing [he did not do].
His various sculptures and transcribed scriptures are not recorded here again. He passed away at the age of eighty-six.

His disciple Yiyān was particularly refined and pure, capable of continuing his master’s work. He excavated a site on the eastern plain of Púbǎn and reverently relocated the burial there, erecting a stele beside it.

Dharma Master Zhou of the Tang dynasty lost his place of origin and his family name in historical records. He studied the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, applying himself with exceptional dedication and vigor.

He traveled to the capital and resided at Jingjue Temple on Quqi Hill; the site was distinguished by its springs, rocks, bamboo, and trees, where he would often engage in joyful conversation with like-minded companions.
Through this, his virtue grew ever more profound and his reputation rose accordingly. During the Renshou era, he was honored...
By imperial decree, his śarīra were sent to the Xujì Temple stupa in Hànzhōu. He died of illness during the early years of the Zhōu dynasty’s Táng Zhēnguān era at the age of eighty.

Huidan of the Tang dynasty was a native of Yongzhou. From his youth, he followed Dharma Master Tanyan to hear lectures on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, through which he thoroughly mastered their essential meanings.
His expositions were such that there were those who found them worthy of admiration. Initially, he resided at Yanxing Temple.

During the Renshou era, by imperial decree, he escorted śarīra relics to Tianzhu Temple in Hangzhou; while digging a pit to enshrine them, an ancient casket was discovered, which he interred within the site.
He was not at all regretful in his final moments. After his birth, during the early years of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, he passed away at the monastery where he resided.
Tanbian (also known as Bianxiang) was the son of the Shi family from Yingzhou; he early on relied upon Master Huiyuan to study the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* at Shaolin Monastery.

He thoroughly investigated both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna Tripiṭakas, penetrating their profound mysteries, and was particularly meticulous and skilled in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. Later, he traveled south to the Xu region to further his research.

He studied the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and perused the *Abhidharma*, his fame spreading throughout the eastern lands. In the seventh year of the Kaihuang era, he followed Daoyuan into Guanzhong and resided at Jingying Temple.

There, both the propagation of the Dharma and the care of his parents reached their peak. During the Renshou era, when stupas were being erected, he was summoned by imperial decree to deliver śarīra relics to Dayu Temple in Yuezhou;

the miraculous responses are detailed in a separate record. Upon his return to the capital, his guidance and instruction flourished even more. At the beginning of the Daye era, he was summoned by imperial decree to enter [the palace].
He served in the Inner Sanctuary of the Eastern Capital. When the present Emperor resided at the Qin Residence, he was summoned by imperial decree to stay at Shengguang Temple.

Later, drawing upon the resources of his lifelong practice and having first opened the gate of wisdom, he paid homage to Jingying Huiyuan; subsequently, he proceeded to lecture and expound the teachings.
He also painted a portrait of Daoyuan to pay him respectful veneration. In the first year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away due to illness at the age of over seventy.
Tang Daojie was originally of the Yang clan of Hongnong, descendants of Yang Zhen, the Grand Marshal of the Han dynasty. His family had moved to Mingtiao in Anyi, Hedong.
In the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, when he had just reached the age of twenty, he traveled east to Wenxi to rely upon Dharma Master Zhenyuan and received the tonsure.
He soon received full ordination and was sent to study the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. Later, he went to Mount Xiantou to recite and practice the Dharma.
Huā reflected to himself: "Does not the Sūtra say, 'What one has heard may be little, but what one understands must be much'? To penetrate the essentials, one must wait for extensive travel.
In the fourteenth year [of his monastic life], he followed Master Hé Jìlùn of Qīngzhōu and studied the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* for two years.
Hé remarked, "I believe my treatise is about to flourish. If you, my son, can maintain it from beginning to end, I shall dare to instruct you further."

Alas! Before long, he recorded the Master’s passing. Thereupon, he traveled throughout the land of Qi, visiting the gates of Zhu Sengzhuang, Sengji, Seng'an, and Fayi, whereby his realization of the Way flourished and progressed.
He continued to rely upon the two masters Cang and Jiwei. Under Master Nian at Wei, he studied the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Later, relying on Daoshang at Qinghe and Honggai at Jijun, he refined his mastery of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* for four years. He once [studied] with Honggai...
The Master defines this, stating that a treatise says: "There is but a single sensation of suffering, yet it has three distinctions.

Does this passage not take the nature of pervasive suffering (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) as the sensation of suffering? As for the three distinctions, they are precisely the three sensations spoken of according to conventional designation with respect to that single sensation of suffering.
Is this not the position held by the Sautrāntika masters, which Guṇavarmadeva describes as his own tenet? Could it be otherwise?

He replied, "That is so. Jie said, "If it were truly the case that an arising sensation repays its cause, then one could say that a painful sensation is a pleasant sensation, and likewise, a cause could be established as producing a result by saying that an evil karma is a virtuous karma.

If you say that a virtuous karma produces a pleasant result because a virtuous karma is not an evil karma, then one could also say that a pleasant sensation repays a virtuous cause because a pleasant sensation is not a painful sensation. If you say that a pleasant sensation repays a virtuous cause..."
Furthermore, the substance [of the experience] is itself the feeling of suffering; thus, even a wholesome karma may produce an evil fruit, and its substance is itself an evil karma.

If one says that there is only this single feeling of suffering, which is called "false pleasure" according to worldly sentiment, then it can likewise be said that there is only this single evil karma, which is called "false goodness" according to worldly sentiment.

In this context, the meaning of the phrasing—where the examples are inverted to reach a definitive conclusion—is ultimately a point of obstruction that leaves one utterly bewildered. (The year) was the ninth year of the Kaihuang era.
He traveled to Ye to study the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* under Master Lin. He also received the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* from Master Hong, as well as from Masters Zhi-nian and Fa-leng.
When he went to the Sui dynasty, Prince Han summoned him, and they studied the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* together; after three years, he had thoroughly mastered its essential points.

He once challenged Master Nian, saying: "If tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*) is not included within the sphere of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), then consciousness (*vijñāna*) should likewise not be included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)."

"Space is not an abode of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). If that which is not a constituent part of consciousness were an abode of consciousness, then contact (*sparśa*), which is not a constituent part of contact, would likewise be the locus of entry for contact.
Master Nian smiled and simply gazed straight ahead. In the second year of the Renshou era, he received the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra* and other treatises from Dharma Master Leng;
at that time, he was as proficient as Daorong, Zhijing, and Dalun in the *Daśabala-śāstra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Regarding *Nirvāṇa*, the Vinaya section of the *Shun-kān* [collection], and others, all were gathered together during the Jin dynasty to investigate their similarities and differences;

these works are worthy of admiration. Thus, the people of the time had a proverb that said: "Dàtóu Jié is difficult for others to defeat. When Emperor Wen passed away and chaos broke out in Jinyang, he fled back to his hometown.
There, he expounded the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, the *Dhāraṇī*, and other texts five or six times. He sighed, saying: "The delusions of verbal expression ultimately have no..."

This was of great benefit to his progress through birth and death. He subsequently relied upon the Chan Master Zhenhui at Magu to contemplate and discern the principle of reality, gaining deep insight into dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Master Hui, recognizing that this was the result of his past cultivation, praised him most highly. Later, he further clarified the teachings on the *Abhidharmakośa* and the methods of *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing).
He then commissioned Dharma Master Shensu to compile the various scriptural passages concerning the methods of *ānāpāna* for the sake of others.

Later, in the first year of the Wude era, someone requested that he expound upon the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. Huizhe laughed and said, "My resolve is firm: to lecture by day and practice dhyāna by night.
He then proceeded to expound it, doing so some thirty times or more. Furthermore, he dispatched twenty of his disciples to propagate the teachings abroad.
On the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month in the first year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away due to illness at the age of fifty-five.

Initially, Fan Chuo of Sangquan had long been on friendly terms with Jie. After Chuo passed away, his two daughters suddenly dreamed that he arrived traveling through the air, saying, "I have been reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss;
I have come now specifically to welcome Master Jie. While Jie was lying ill, he also once saw Chuo by his side.
Chuo had previously served as a śramaṇa, but when the Zhou dynasty suppressed the teachings, he returned to lay life. It was at this time [that he appeared].
Jiémíng. Regarding the account of Zhòngwén, whose music and fragrant incense filled the air:

his secular surname was Táng, his given name Huìng, and he was a native of Jùnyí in Bìnzhōu. At the age of six, his compassionate parents orally transmitted the *Guānyīn jīng* (Sutra of Avalokiteśvara) to him;

he memorized it as if it were the result of past habituation. At sixteen, he cast off his lay attire and entered Mount Tài, where he applied himself with such diligence that he forgot all weariness. He was twenty-five [when he passed away].

In that year, he began lecturing on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* at Huifusi Temple. Later, he composed a five-fascicle commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which he expounded more than fifty times in total.
Whenever he reached the "Herbs" chapter (*Oṣadhivarga*), rain would invariably fall from the heavens.

He also composed commentaries on the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, and the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*. Not long after, he passed away at the age of sixty-six. Shortly before his death, there were extraordinary...

A fragrant spiritual light continued for two nights, appearing within the room where he resided. He then addressed his disciples, saying, "I wish to rely on this auspicious omen to be reborn in the Land of Bliss.
Thereupon, he abstained from food for twenty days. On the day of his passing, even the well he regularly drew water from ran dry;
it returned to its former state only several days after his body had been encoffined.
Tang Shenhui’s secular surname was Tian. He was a native of Linjin in Fengyi. Having renounced the world at a young age, he traveled in all directions seeking the Way.
Although he had extensively mastered the Tripiṭaka, he became renowned for his mastery of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. He was particularly adept at literary composition;

having written prefaces, introductions, and commentaries on various sūtras, more than forty volumes of his collected works were circulated in the world. Every spring, he would wander freely through hills and valleys. In summer...

Consequently, the monasteries in the capital entered the retreat period (*kaji*), with prohibitions against leaving the gates or stepping outside. Despite his exceptional air of detachment and disdain for convention, he was a preeminent monk of this degenerate age.
Thus, the people of the time had a proverb concerning him: "The Great Master of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* has returned; Śākyamitra and Dharmatāla have simultaneously arrived."

At the time he established his doctrinal positions, he required three or five men of exceptional talent to debate with him individually; only then would he provide a comprehensive summary and lead them to a thorough understanding.

In the tenth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he was summoned to reside at Chanding Temple. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, an imperial decree invited him to the Court of State Ceremonial (*Honglu*) to instruct the monks from the Three Han kingdoms using the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
In the third year, he took up his monk’s staff and traveled to Shu, where his transformative influence caused all things to bow like grass before the wind. In the fourth year...
On the first day of the seventh month, his spirit was transferred to Faju Temple, where he was cremated south of Shengxian Bridge.
His disciple Xuancha collected the remaining ashes and, together with his fellow student Xuanjiu, constructed a stupa at Xianyou Temple on Mount Zhongnan.
Jiujiu composed a text to serve as an inscription; he was a man of considerable literary talent, yet he died before achieving his full potential.
Tang Zhiyan, courtesy name Mingcan, was born into the Zhu clan of Wu. His grandfather, Xian, served as a *yuanwai sanqi shilang* under the Liang dynasty;

his father, Min, served as a *fengchaoqing* under the Chen dynasty. His mother, Lady Zhang, dreamed of ascending the pagoda of Tongxuan Temple and sitting upon its spire to gaze far into the void, feeling no sense of fear at all.
She subsequently conceived Zhiyan. From birth, he was extraordinary among other children; at the age of eight...
Shitong Xuanqiu became a monk under Dharma Master [Fajing]. At the age of twelve, he could recite the *Lotus Sūtra* from memory.

At sixteen, he entered the capital to study at Ba’en Temple under Dharma Master Chihui, where he mastered the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*. His analytical brilliance was outstanding and his innate wisdom was fully awakened.
At nineteen, he returned to his hometown to visit his parents and subsequently began preaching extensively at his home temple, responding to inquiries with effortless fluency. Four...

Zuo was struck with awe and admiration. He subsequently received full ordination at Qinhuang Temple in the capital under Dharma Master Yan. Before long, he relied upon Dharma Master Zhuo of Dazhuangyan Temple to further investigate the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
Through this, he gained a profound and heartfelt understanding of the new edition’s meaning; his achievement was doubled.

In the third year of the Zhiz德 era of the Chen dynasty, when he was twenty-two years old, the imperial court established the Renwang Assembly, and by imperial decree, one hundred men of renowned virtue were summoned.
When [the Emperor] ascended the high seat, Yan sat in his ranks; as he posed difficult questions with his debating skill, the Emperor especially appreciated him.

Among the dukes, ministers, and officials, there was none who did not admire his refined elegance or submit to his quick-wittedness. After the fall of the Chen dynasty, he fled east to Mount Huqiu, remaining there for nearly thirty years.
During that time, [he encountered] Yang Su, Duke of Chu and former Minister of State of the Sui, and the Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs, Pei...
As Duke Su Wei, he sometimes set aside his weapons to receive guests with courtesy, and at other times entrusted his envoys to attend to their countenances.

When Emperor Yang was in the imperial residence and later went to govern the Yangzhou region, he extensively recruited men of talent and virtue; when the summons arrived, Su Wei could not decline it. Shortly thereafter, however, he returned to his former seclusion due to illness.
Emperor Wen frequently sent imperial letters to inquire after his well-being. In his final years, the clamor of war drums and blades rose up, and the entire realm fell into ruin. Tán... [text ends]
The disciples of Yue escorted him out to Beitán. He served at the imperial court for ten years, during which time the empire enjoyed tranquility and peace.
In the seventh year of the Wude era, Li Shijia, the Duke of Wuyang and Governor-General of Suzhou, made a joint request on behalf of both the public and private sectors.

On the eleventh day of the tenth month in the eighth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away at the Eastern Temple of Huqiu at the age of seventy-one. On the twenty-second day of that same month, [his remains were interred].
He was interred on the southern ridge of the monastery. The Śramaṇa Faxuan of Hongye Monastery in Changzhou, together with the monastery’s abbot Zhifeng and others, erected a stele.

It records that throughout his life, Yan cultivated the sixteen subtle contemplations and prayed for rebirth in the Pure Land; he practiced the repentance rites of the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
The extent of his spiritual responses was such that smoke rose from the incense burner before it had even been lit, and as soon as the vessel was emptied, [the water returned].
The waters overflowed. He commissioned an image of Amitābha and practiced the three types of pure karma.
He convened five hundred people to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and *Vimalakīrti* sūtras thirty times each, and the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra* one hundred and ten times.
Fali of the Tang dynasty was originally of the Li clan of Zhao. Later, due to official service and travel, he settled in Xiangzhou;
Fali was born there. From the time of his birth until his death in old age, his teeth remained firm throughout; they were perfectly intact, never wavering or falling out.

At the age of fifteen, he was ordained as a disciple by Dharma Master Lingyu. After receiving full ordination, he studied the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* under Vinaya Master Jinghong and listened to the great expositions of Master Yuan of Hengzhou.
Consequently, when expounding the teachings, his speech was concise and penetrating, and his rigorous refutations were even more steadfast;
he was especially praised and admired by those with discernment. Later, he traveled through Jiangnan, where he grew weary of...
During the suppression [of the rebellion], he returned to Ye to instruct his brothers. When the Sui calendar came to an end, his disciples dispersed.

Coinciding with the inauguration of the Tang dynasty, Pei Shiyuan, the Magistrate of Linzhang, welcomed him to preach the Dharma. After a long time, the influence of his transformative teachings spread widely.

Among those who ascended the hall and entered the inner chamber [of the Master’s teaching], the Dharma Master Huixiu was at that time just beginning to gain renown in his generation for his studies in doctrinal principles.
Daoli was on friendly terms with him; consequently, he composed this fundamental commentary (*shu*), which earned him praise for its comprehensiveness and breadth.
On the tenth month of the ninth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away at Rizhuang Monastery in Ye at the age of sixty-seven. Throughout his life, he had lectured on the Vinaya.

He lectured more than forty times and composed the *Commentary on the Four-Part Vinaya* in ten fascicles, the *Exegesis on the Karma-vinaya* in three fascicles, as well as the *Ritual for the Abandonment of Confession*, the *Discourse on the Gravity of Offenses*, and other works.
His disciple Dàshuò followed his example to the Wèi Prefecture; truly, they were like the blue dye from the indigo plant and ice from water.

Tang Daoji’s secular surname was Lü. A native of Dongping in Henan, he was only fourteen years old when he traveled to Pengcheng with his book-bag on his back to study among various masters, discussing their profound tenets.

When Yang Su—the current Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and former Grand Marshal of the Sui dynasty—saw him, he looked upon him with favor and said to the assembled officials, "Master Daoji is the very embodiment of the Buddha-dharma.
He immediately invited him to the Eastern Capital to expound the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (Heart Treatise). Great...

Regarding his works, he first composed the *Zhuxuan zhang* (Commentary on the Mysterious Chapters) along with its sub-commentary in eight fascicles, which circulated throughout the world. In the fifth year [of the Kaiyuan era], by imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Huiri Daochang (the Temple of Wisdom Sun).

Whenever there were assemblies for doctrinal discussion, the Imperial carriage would visit in person, attended by all the high officials and ministers. As the various virtuous monks deferred to him, they did not dare to ascend the seat before him.

Later, when the Central Plains were ravaged by rebels, he again took up his staff and traveled to Ba and Shu, where he diligently studied the Mahāyāna and subsequently summarized the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*.
He authored the *Zhu Zhangchao* (Commentary on the Chapters) in eight fascicles, which has been transmitted through successive generations throughout the realm.

At the beginning of the Zhenguan era of our dynasty, he was about to compose a sub-commentary (*shu*), but passed away at Fugan Temple in the capital in the second month of the tenth year. He was over sixty years of age. At that time, Huijing and Baoxian of Shu were both followers of the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra).

Tang Zhihui’s secular surname was Jiao; he was a native of Gaoping in Zezhou. At the age of thirteen, he entered the monastic order and relied upon Dharma Master Yuan at Qinghua Temple in the prefecture.
He followed the master to study the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* with particular depth. By nature diligent and reverent, he attended to the affairs of the Sangha during the day.
He read the commentaries and treatises by night. After receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), he became even more earnest and diligent in observing the precepts.

Every year, he regularly lectured on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*. Emperor Yang held him in high esteem and treated him with special courtesy.

In the seventh year of the Daye era, an imperial decree summoned him to the Inner Chapel in the Eastern Capital. After some time, the rebellion broke out; Huiming took up his staff and returned to his native village, exhausting his accumulated wealth in acts of charity.

He accumulated [merit] without stinginess, and those he brought to salvation were many. Zhang Liang, the Duke of Yún and Governor-General of Huái Prefecture, requested to receive the Bodhisattva precepts and also expounded the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
When the summer retreat concluded and the assembly dispersed, Daohui also reached the end of his life on the twentieth day of the third month in the twelfth year of the Zhenguan era.
He was seventy-nine years of age. Daohui was exceedingly filial and compassionate; whenever he ascended the seat, those under his jurisdiction...
Xie said, "The Great Master’s intention was such. Thereupon, he shed several rows of tears. He would often say to his disciples, "My parents gave birth to my physical body;
the Dharma Master gave birth to my Dharma-body. To repay this kindness, there is only the propagation of the teachings to benefit all beings.
Apart from this, there is nothing else that can be done."

Fagong of the Tang dynasty was born into the Gu clan of Wu. At his birth, an extraordinary light illuminated the room. In his childhood, he served the Dharma Master Ju of Wuchiu and entered the monastic life.
After receiving full ordination, he studied the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* under Master Chong of Yuhang and the *Abhidharma* under Master Xi.
When Master Chong was nearing death, he entrusted Fagong with his fly-whisk (*cūrṇī*) as a symbol of his dharma lineage. From that time on, his dharma assemblies flourished.

He did not fall short of his predecessors. He traveled again to Jiankang, where he consulted various masters of the tradition until all the doubts that had long obstructed him were completely dispelled.

Upon returning to his native village, his spiritual cultivation surpassed what it had been before. During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, the Regional Inspector Liu Quan personally visited his mountain retreat and invited him to reside at Huixiang Temple.
In the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era of our present dynasty, an imperial edict summoned him to Changzhou along with [Master] Fa...

Xuān went together with him to Luò, where they attended Emperor Yang’s private audience and the Imperial Lecture Hall (Jīngxián). On several occasions, he was granted silk bolts and invited to remain for his support.
When the Prince of Wèi was appointed to govern Yōngzhōu, he heard of Xuān and admired him from afar, sending letters and petitions requesting him to serve as his preceptor (*jìshī*).

Once Xuān had resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), the Prince bestowed abundant offerings. Consequently, monastics and laypeople alike from both the court and the countryside flocked there in great numbers, traveling shoulder to shoulder and carrying their books on bamboo frames.
On the sixteenth day of the tenth month in the fourteenth year, he passed away at Dazhuangyan Temple in the Western Capital. He was seventy-three years of age.

By imperial decree, funeral gifts were bestowed and the state provided a ceremonial carriage and the necessary expenses for the journey. His disciple Huiqian was commissioned to escort his remains back for burial.
On the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifteenth year, he was interred on the southern ridge of the mountain. The inscription was composed by the [Emperor].
The Preface was written by Cen Wenben, Duke of Jiangling and Director of the Secretariat; the Epitaph by Liu Ziyi, Court Dispersing Gentleman and Director of the Bureau of Historiography.

Shenzhao of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Chunyu and was a native of Zhongmou in Bianzhou. At the age of nine, during the chaos of the Sui dynasty’s collapse, his relatives and old friends had all perished or scattered.
The only person upon whom he could rely was his mother alone. Before long, his mother also passed away, leaving him with no one to turn to for support.
At the age of twelve, he entered the monastic order under the Vinaya Master Mingzhi of Weishi. At that time, the realm had only recently been pacified, and students were gathering like clouds;
however, as provisions were not yet sufficient, Sengzhao traveled from village to town begging for alms, providing for them for six years without weariness.

He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* at night, yet though he did so for a long time, no one knew of it. Having received full ordination, he listened to the Vinaya and subsequently went to Xiuhe in Ye.
At the Master of Dharma’s residence, he thoroughly studied the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra* until he had completed it one full time without omission.

Consequently, he was called "Yipianzhao" (One-Time Illuminator), and the name "Henan Yipianzhao" subsequently became established and persists to this day. Later, relying on Master Kong at Xuzhou, he researched the *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*;
having reached only the eighth fascicle, he ceased his studies due to his preceptor’s illness. On another day, he resumed and mastered the work, penetrating its entirety without obstruction.
It was different. Thereafter, he did not decline invitations to visit the *Avataṃsaka*, *Nirvāṇa*, *Tattvasiddhi*, and *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* [lectures].

He commissioned several hundred Buddha images and transcribed several thousand scrolls of sutras, exhausting all his accumulated wealth. Regarding the newly translated *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, upon examining its phrasing and principles, it appeared to be missing one line;
when he verified the palm-leaf manuscript, this was indeed the case. During the Zhenguan era, he passed away due to illness at...
An-ye Temple. [His] lifespan was fifty-nine years.
Tang Xuanhui, courtesy name Huaimo, was surnamed Xi. His ancestors were from Anding; his grandfather held office in Jingzhao and consequently settled at Bisan in Fanchuan.
At the age of twelve, his ascetic diligence was peerless, and his dignified bearing was exceptionally eminent. Prince Han...

Liang saw him and marveled at his extraordinary qualities. He granted him special permission to leave the household life. He resided at Haijue Temple, where he studied under Dharma Master Zong to investigate the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Based on this, he composed the four-fascicle *Nirvāṇa-yi-zhang* (Treatise on the Meaning of Nirvāṇa), the four-fascicle *Yiyuan-wenben-shiwenshi-chao* (Explanatory Commentary on the Source Texts of the Meaning), and the *Shiwen-shichao* (Commentary on the Explanations of the Text).
At the beginning of the Wude era, the śramaṇas Tanyan and Daokai, who were renowned figures of the realm, established Cizbei Temple and submitted a petition to have [the author] serve as its abbot.

The Master thereupon guided and received his successors, extensively expounding this section nearly forty times. By nature he was exceptionally humble and self-effacing, never remaining confined to a single school.
Whenever there was a seat for study, he would investigate it thoroughly; even with texts he had previously mastered, he could expound them as if they were entirely new.
Truly, in this degenerate age of the Dharma, he is without peer. Master Sengzong said: "What virtue do I possess that I am able to attain such entry into his inner circle?"
"Is this not the 'Son'? Master Xiang said, "The sutras speak of those with merit and wisdom appearing in the final five hundred years;
could this be that very person? If it were not so, how could he be sufficient to revitalize the Great Teaching in these present days?

Master Yue said, "This gentleman came to me to study the *Abhidharmakośa*, wishing to gather others through the means of 'common purpose. He is a wondrously adorned and virtuous spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); he is no ordinary man."
As for who this person was, Dharma Master Zhen said: "This gentleman came to me to study the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra*; he likely wished to assist and support my own efforts.
For one who follows the Great Way to descend and inquire about minor arts—is this not like turning an elephant or a dragon onto the path of a rabbit?

In the eighth year of the Zhenguan era, an imperial decree appointed him to reside at Hongfu Monastery, where his cultivation of the Path became even more advanced. He once dreamed of ascending onto the hand of Amitābha Buddha.
He then fashioned a single statue of Amitābha and constantly intended to fix his mindfulness upon it, desiring to retire to the mountain forests to spend the remainder of his life there.

The assembly entreated him to remain, and he began lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Zhenglun*. Thereupon, demonic disturbances arose; consequently, he returned to Cibei Temple where he lay ill.
Seeing the Buddha coming to welcome him, he passed away on the twenty-seventh day of the fifth month in the fourteenth year [of the Kaihuang era]. He was fifty years of age.
19. He was buried at Gaoyang Plains in the southwestern corner of the city. A brick stupa was erected and his remains were enshrined there for veneration.
The Tang monk Bian, whose secular surname was Zhang, had lived for generations in Nanyang by Zhugong. After the Liang dynasty lost its hold on power, he subsequently entered [the monastic order].
Guan was a native of Fengyi. At the age of seven, he could recite a thousand words daily from his studies.

By the age of ten, although he had not yet undergone tonsure, he frequently ascended the seat to rehearse and expound upon the Vimalakīrti and Renwang (Benevolent Kings) Sūtras, earning him renown at the time. This was during the early Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.

An imperial edict was issued for Su Wei to ordain three thousand monks. First, their mastery of their respective fields of study was tested; one who was the youngest in age but had studied his subject most thoroughly was approved by the presiding officials.

Consequently, he was exempted from the general examination and permitted to leave the household life. After receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), he followed Dharma Master Zhineng to investigate the sutras and śāstras.
He spent many years of winter and summer in this pursuit. During the Daye period, he resided at the Chanding Monastery. Emperor Wu...

The Origin of Virtue: Having passed through the Passes, he propagated the teachings among the regions of Pu, Yu, Shan, and Guo. Once, while expounding the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) in Ruicheng, the listeners crowded together like a wall.
A donor provided curtains and canopies above them to shelter them from the open air. Shortly thereafter, a Daoist priest came to pose questions.

Bian said, "The True Dharma is inherently luminous; it is only because of heterodox winds that it is obscured. As the Daoist wished to advance further, suddenly a wind arose, causing the curtains and canopies to entangle and knot together.
His cap and coarse robes were blown about, and dust filled his mouth and nose. The others all remained unaware, but the Daoist suddenly burst into loud laughter and departed.

During the Zhenguan era, the Institute for Translating Scriptures was established, and by imperial decree, Bian was transferred to Hongfu Monastery. There, the Master Daoyue, who served as the Proofreader of Meaning (*zhèngyì*), expounded upon the *Abhidharmakośa*.
When he discussed the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, [Daoxuan] would suspend his own lectures to listen to him. He subsequently compiled more than three hundred sheets of notes.

On the thirteenth day of the sixth month in the thirteenth year, he passed away at the monastery where he resided. At that time, a severe drought prevailed and the scorching sun blazed intensely; yet for twenty days after his coffin was placed there, his countenance remained bright and radiant.

By the time of the burial, rain fell throughout the land, bringing joy and celebration to all. He was seventy-five years old. Among his works is the *She lun zhong* (Commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*).
Treatises and commentaries on such subjects as the "Ultimate Consciousness-Only," the "Contemplation of Objects," the "Buddha-nature," and the "Equality" were all circulated in the world.
Dao Liang of Tang was the son of the Zhao family of Luancheng in Zhao. At the age of fifteen, he entered the Sha-tu Chan Monastery to take ordination under Master Bei.
From the age of sixteen until eighty, Bei expounded and propagated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, his fame spreading throughout the two river regions. Liang consulted [Bei]...
During the Jōkyū era, he was commissioned to go to Ryūzan to recite sutras. He was accompanied by thirty companions, all of whom were devoted to Zen practice.
As they had no attendants (*jōnin*) and Hōryō was young in years and low in rank, he personally managed all communal affairs; he would go barefoot to husk the grain, continuing this for seven years.

Hearing that Zen Master Zōn was flourishing his teachings in the province of Byōbu, and having already received full ordination, he immediately went to follow him in order to investigate the principles of meditation (*samādhi*).
He studied further under Vinaya Master Yan at Wuliangshou Monastery, where he trained in the Vinaya. From that time on, he specialized in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
Not long after, he accompanied Master Yan to Shizhou to hear the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, acting as a representative for the local scholars and officials of that region.
He began by opening the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith). He went to Lǚzhōu to listen to Vinaya Master Kān’s lectures before returning home.
Early in the Tang dynasty, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Yìxīng Temple in Mǎnsì, where he constantly expounded the teachings to inspire and encourage his juniors.

When he later returned to his hometown, his teacher, Master Bèi, was still in good health; delighted that his disciple had achieved such accomplishment, Bèi came to visit him and established a formal assembly for the Vinaya.
Those who crossed over to him to request instruction numbered more than eight hundred; those who shared his lamp [as disciples] were over forty people.
Up until the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he was seventy years of age.

Tang Daohong’s secular surname was Yin; his family had resided in Hedong for generations. His father, Yin Di, served as the Magistrate of Jiangling under the Sui dynasty. Daohong was the third of five sons.
In the sixth year of the Kaihuang era, at the age of thirteen, he left the household life to serve Master Tanyan of the capital, where he specialized in the study of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
He recited and expounded upon it with thorough mastery. Furthermore, he received the *Dilun* from Master Yuan and concurrently studied other scriptures.

His virtuous character was lofty and renowned. Following the demise of Emperor Wen, an imperial edict appointed him to reside at the Chan-ting Monastery. From that time forth, he was occupied with the propagation of the Dharma without a moment’s leisure.

At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, an edict appointed him as the *upādhyāya* (abbot) of Lüzang Monastery; not long thereafter, another edict appointed him as the chief administrator (*vihārasvāmin*) of Dazongchi Monastery.

In the fourteenth year [of the reign], he went to Baochang Temple at the request to preach the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. At that time, a white pheasant was so tame that it would not leave his side until the conclusion of the assembly.
Later, while translating scriptures at Hongfu Temple, by imperial decree he served as a proofreader for the meaning of the texts and lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* eighty-seven times.
In his final years, he passed away due to illness at the age of seventy-nine.
Tang Daoyin was surnamed Hou and was a native of Puyang. At the age of seven, he encountered the death of his mother;
upon completing the period of mourning, he sought a teacher at Lingyan Temple in his hometown. Within less than ten days, he had memorized and mastered two fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

After shaving his hair, he redoubled his efforts in cultivation and immediately began giving lectures. Upon receiving full ordination, he proceeded to study the Vinaya rules. At that time, Dharma Master Song of Pengcheng transmitted...
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra* was flourishing among his disciples. Once, while passing through a crowd, he was respectfully saluted;
he subsequently ordered them to lecture on the text again, after which he withdrew to Mount Tai for four autumns. When he was about to travel to Luoyang, no one accompanied him.

Just as he reflected that he could not travel alone due to the prohibitions of the times, he called upon Avalokiteśvara. A white-haired śramaṇa appeared from somewhere nearby, and they entered [the city] together.

The city suddenly vanished from sight, and people attributed this to the power of spiritual resonance. He took refuge at Duobao Monastery in the Three Shu region, where he expounded the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (She lun) and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*;
those who listened numbered in the thousands. Dharma Master Baoxian was a native of Donghai and was exceptionally gifted in the arts;

he looked down upon the multitude with arrogance, yet every time he encountered Yuan, he would immediately alter his demeanor. He served as an advisor to the Generalissimo, Duke of Deng, Dou... [text ends].
Dui Jin, Left Vice Director of the Regional Inspectorate; Dou Gui, Counselor to the State; Gao Shilian, Duke of Shenguo;
and Lu Chengqing, Duke of Fanyang—along with the officials of the provincial administrations—all expressed their profound reverence.

Consequently, taking advantage of the intervals between their practice of the Way and their official duties, they reconstructed the dilapidated and ruined mountain temple at Pengmen, transforming it into a magnificent pure monastery (*śuddhāvasa*) and carving all three [scriptures] in full.
The Tibetan scriptures were stored in the northern cliffs of the monastery. Dharma Master Xuanzang translated them at the Great Ci’en Monastery in the capital;
by imperial decree, they were commissioned for collation and verification, serving as the definitive commentary. Master Xuanzang praised them with profound admiration.

Kai, the Abbot of Huiri Monastery, invited him to preach the Dharma. The monastics of the imperial city heard what they had never before encountered, specializing particularly in the *Nirvāṇa* and *Avataṃsaka* sūtras.
He lectured on the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, and other sūtras;

as well as the *Daśabhūmika*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the *Abhidharma*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Buddhabhūmi*, and other śāstras; and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and other vinayas. He also produced commentaries on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and the *Vimalakīrti*.
In the third month of the third year of the Xianqing era, he passed away at Huiri Monastery. The following year, his remains were returned for burial at Pengmen. He was seventy years of age.
There were two [commentaries].
Tang Puguang’s history omits his surname; he was originally from a local family that had long served the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang.

His diligence and parsimony were beyond the reach of his peers, and his intellectual understanding was especially unfathomable. Later, he participated in the translation project, whereupon his outstanding insights became uniquely manifest.

Regarding the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*: Initially, Xuanzang observed that the previous translations of the *Kośa* were deficient in both text and meaning. Consequently, he produced a Sanskrit manuscript and retranslated it for Puguang.

Much of this material consisted of the private memorized recollections of Sarvāstivāda masters from Western India. Puguang then composed a commentary (*ṭīkā*) to explain and adjudicate its meaning, which was subsequently disseminated.
Furthermore, from the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era until his death in the first year of the Linde era, Xuanzang produced [the following works]:
Of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras, seventy-five works totaling one thousand three hundred and thirty-five fascicles were transcribed by Kuang as pen-receiver (bishou).
During seventeen or eighteen years, and later at the Yuhua Palace, his contribution in assisting with the production of the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras was exceptionally great.
Táng Dàoshì, courtesy name Xuányùn, was originally of the Hán clan from Yíkǎn. His ancestors served as officials in Jīngzhào, where his descendants settled.
At the age of twelve, he entered Qīnglóng Monastery to renounce secular life; because his given name violated the taboo names of the imperial ancestral temple, he was known by his courtesy name.

He studied and scrutinized the Vinaya sections of the canon and was especially devoted to the Mahāyāna (shàngchéng). During the Xiǎnqìng era, he entered the palace together with Master Xuánzàng to [collate] the newly translated sūtras and śāstras.

He was supported by the state, which further selected virtuous monks (*bhadanta*) from Ci’en Temple to perform ritual circumambulations in rotation, without fail at any time; Daoshi was included among their ranks.
When the Western Ming Temple (*Ximing Si*) was established for the Crown Prince, he was summoned to reside there due to his brilliance and erudition.

At that time, Vinaya Master Xuanchang was vigorously expounding the *Vinaya*, and Daoshi assisted him with such diligence as to never dare to be remiss. He further compiled and categorized a work titled *Fayuan zhulin* (The Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma) in one hundred chapters.
He organized [his works] into ten bundles so that those studying the inner teachings might consult them. His other writings were quite numerous; he subsequently passed away.
Detailed accounts of his lifespan and years of ordination are not fully recorded in the histories.
The Tang dynasty monk Fabao had long relied upon Master Xuanzang to study the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* prior to its translation.

Regarding his doubts concerning the afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), Fabao requested further instruction from Xuanzang. Consequently, Xuanzang separately composed sixteen characters as a refutation to be inserted into the treatise. Fabao said:

"Is this indeed the language of the Sanskrit original? Xuanzang replied, "I have composed it based on the meaning and intent. Puji said, "Should you not refrain from adorning the sublime measure of the Sage with ordinary sentiments?
As for the meaning of the six types of *vigraha* (analytical explanations) in the *Abhidharmakośa*, I consider Puji’s version to be definitive.
At that time, the two masters Puji and Sengbao regarded Master Xuanzang as Kumārajīva did with Sengrui and Daorong.

In the third year of the Chang’an era, Tripitaka Master Yijing translated [the texts] at Fuxian Monastery and Ximing Monastery. By imperial decree, Fazang, Shengzhuang, and others were invited to serve as proofreaders for the meaning;
his fame and reputation thus grew even more renowned.
Táng Dàguāng was surnamed Chǔ; his place of origin is unknown. Having passed the age of childhood, he entered the monastic order.
After receiving full ordination, he studied the Vinaya under Master Ān of Guāngzhōu. He had long been devoted to the recitation of the Lotus Sūtra, never flagging even until old age.
In the first year of the Shàngyuán era (760 CE), he manifested illness and passed away at Fànhuá Temple in Qiántáng at the age of seventy.
9. His dharma-ordination age was fifty-eight.
Zhou Huiyin’s history omits his clan and surname. He had long been renowned in the capital for his moral integrity, learning, and scholarship.
In the second year of the Linde era, an imperial edict summoned him, along with ten others including Xuanze of Ximing Monastery, to compile the *Chanlin yaocao* at the Northern Gate.

At the Western Dragon Gate, he compiled the *Xiūshūsuō* (The Studio for Cultivating Writings), which was essentially a collection of the various scriptures of the Great Canon (*Mahāpiṭaka*) formed through refined meaning.
It was presented to the Emperor, who issued an edict to enshrine it in the Secret Library (*Bìgé*). Yan had also previously participated in translation work, but that is not recorded here.
Zhou Yuance was intelligent and quick-witted from his youth. He lectured on the newly translated *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* and soon gained renown.

Later, he lectured on the new *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, gaining an especially profound mastery of its essential points. It appears that after these two treatises were completed, Master Ci’en (Xuanzang) privately entrusted them to his disciple, Master Ji, to propagate and expound, so as to monopolize their merit.
Yet Yuance clandestinely studied them and, by being the first to lecture upon them, frustrated Ji’s plans.

Yet he was able to find such joy in the Dharma. At the beginning of the Tianhou period, he was summoned by imperial decree to enter the Translation Institute as a member of the Commission for Verifying Meanings (*zhèngyìyuán*).
There, he produced translations of the *Mahāyāna-vijñaptimātratā-siddhi-śāstra* and other sutras.
Zhou Jia had early on followed the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang to study various treatises.
Later, at Yuhua Palace, while the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* was being translated, he served in the capacity of verifying the meaning and compiling the text.

When Xuanzang fell ill, he [Jia] recorded the number of fascicles for all the sūtras and treatises translated, and read aloud the merits he had performed before the Master. Xuanzang joined his palms in joy and gratitude. Tian...
At the beginning of the later period [of the Tang], an imperial edict summoned him to the translation hall of Tripiṭaka Master Yijing. At that time, he was acclaimed as a veteran master.

Zhou Yancong had long studied under the gate of Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang. Toward the end of the Zhenguan era, when the Translation Institute was established, the assembly of scholars was exceptionally flourishing;
among the disciples of Puguang and Huibao, many stood out like the points of a horn, yet Yancong excelled in composition. He associated with the śramaṇa Huili...

Liu Ya once composed the *Records of the Western Regions of the Tripitaka*, which provides detailed accounts of the mountains, rivers, topography, distances, terrains—whether level or rugged—and the customs, whether refined or crude, of all the countries he visited.
Li Cong annotated and explained this work for its circulation among the world.
Zhou Yizhong was born into the Yin clan of Xiangyuan in Lu. At the age of nine, he entered the monastic life under the guidance of Upādhyāya Zhao of Zizhou.
Zhao had him recite the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*; before long, he had mastered it such that there were no minor errors or omissions. At that time, he was thirteen years old.
At twenty, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*) and deeply studied the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, while also gaining a comprehensive understanding of the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*.
The treatise was then expounded for the assembly. Yuanzhao said to him, "How can the water of a puddle in a horse's hoofprint suffice to contain a fish that swallows a boat?
Master Ci'en Ji is currently renowned throughout the world; let us therefore go together to study under him. Thus, they took each other’s hands and went to study there.

After five years had passed, he studied such sutras as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, as well as treatises such as the *Śataśāstra*, the *Hetuvidyā*, the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Tattvasiddhi*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
He frequently ascended the high seat and regularly presided over long assemblies; it was then that he composed the *Cheng weishi zanyaoyao*.
He authored commentaries on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, as well as a sub-commentary on the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*.
During his daily life, Chō always faced the northwest; whether walking or sitting, he would settle his mind in meditation, praying for rebirth in the Inner Court of Tuṣita.

One morning, after rising and completing his ritual washing and rinsing, he gazed toward the sky and bowed as if offering a prayer. Shortly thereafter, he sat in the full lotus posture and instructed his sons with words of admonition.
Suddenly, a rare fragrance filled the courtyard, and its radiance illuminated the chamber. Zhong joined his palms and gazed upward, saying, "I am but a weak and defiled bhikṣu;
why trouble the Great Sage to come in person to guide me? Thereupon he passed away. He was seventy-two years old at the time.
Zhou Huizhao’s past karma led him to translate scriptures; he first relied upon the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang at the Great Ci’en Monastery,

and later followed the Master Dasheng Ji and Bodhiruci to translate the *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra* at Chongfu Monastery, where he was selected to serve as a member of the Translation Committee for Verifying the Meaning.

Zhou Zongzhe was a native of Pingyao in Xihe. From his early years, he possessed a naturally brilliant intellect. Having sought out a teacher, he happened upon the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang, who was then translating sūtras and śāstras;
Zongzhe followed him. As time passed through several cycles of the seven stars (years), he exhausted the study of all the scriptures.

His profound mastery and vast erudition were such that among the disciples of Xuanzang, he was known as "the one who has attained the true meaning" (Deyi). Later, he was also called "the Dharma-river Zongzhe."
Zhe said: "To express my thanks to all these people, do not treat this matter as something exceptional. You do not know that the 'Ocean of Dharma' (Fahai) is actually near Taiyuan.

As for what was pointed out, it refers to Fuyou. He once composed the *Yili* (Exemplary Precedents), in which he took the three matters of the Buddha’s rank from Master Zhao and—using the metaphors of the three dots and three eyes—arbitrarily divided them into superior and inferior, assigning them to the high and low. This is an excessive and clever fabrication. Alas!"

How truly wise he was! Tang Fuchou, surnamed Zhang, was a native of Taiyuan. He possessed an exceptionally striking appearance and an intelligence that surpassed all others. He had extensively mastered a multitude of scriptures and could distinguish between elegant and vernacular speech.
He applied himself with particular diligence to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, such that scholars from all quarters vied with one another [to study under him].

He visited his gate; however, he was reticent in articulating his insights and remained profoundly humble as if empty. At that time, Master Zhe was at the height of his reputation for eloquent exposition;
he alone recognized the Master’s worth and bestowed upon him the title "Ocean of Dharma. He passed away at the age of over seventy at Chongfu Temple, his place of residence.
Tang Daocheng was a man of unknown origins. During the Xianqing era, he established a lecture seat in the capital to propagate the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya).

Those who came to receive his instruction were as numerous as the crowds in a misty marketplace. Although Wenguang had emerged from the school of Sengzhao, he had nonetheless ascended to the hall and entered the inner chamber [of Daocheng’s teaching] on several occasions.
Furthermore, many of Huaisu’s writings were based upon those of Daocheng. During the Chuigong era, the sun shone three times...
He translated the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun) and other scriptures; Emperor Gaozong and Mingxun praised his realization of the meaning.
His final years are not well documented. Tang Hengjing was born into the Wen family of Dangyang. In the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era, he entered the monastic order through imperial favor.
Initially, he relied upon Vinaya Master Wen Gang to study the *Vinaya*. Later, at a location ten *li* south of Yquan on Fuzhou Mountain, he established a separate [monastery].
He established a vihāra, naming it Longxing (Prospering and Flourishing) to commemorate the former traces of Master Zhizhe. There he cultivated the dharma-gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

From the reign of Empress Wu Zetian until the accession of Emperor Zhongzong, he was summoned to the inner palace for offerings on three occasions; the Emperor honored him with the etiquette due to a teacher and received the precepts from him.

In the third year of the Jinglong era, an imperial edict permitted him to return to the mountains. Previously, he had been summoned by imperial decree to investigate those of high moral conduct throughout the empire.
More than twenty monks were constantly performing meritorious rites in the inner palace.
Upon the conclusion of these assemblies, an imperial edict was issued to the Secretariat (Zhongshu), the Chancellery (Menxia), and various scholars to escort the relics to the Lingguang Palace.

The Emperor personally composed a poem, while the Chief Secretary Li Qiao, the Secretary of the Chancellery Li Yi, and others all responded to the imperial composition with their own verses. At that time, Daojun of Jiangling and Xuanzang were also present.
He returned to his hometown. Receiving imperial gifts was far more honorable than the ancient proverb of "walking by day in brocade.
He authored the *Treatise on the Many Meanings of Accordance* in two fascicles, the *Compendium of the True Dharma* in seven fascicles, and the *Treatise on Buddha-nature* in two fascicles.

On the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month in the first year of the Xiantian era, he passed away at the age of seventy-nine. His disciples performed his funeral rites and interred him to the west of the monastery where he resided.
Original Text:
Tang Zhisheng was of unknown origins. He possessed profound insight beyond the Two Vehicles and was particularly skilled in the Vinaya. Furthermore, his talent for composition appeared to be innate;
he frequently [revised] the catalog of the Great Canon, even though there were already those such as Nie Daozhen, Dao’an, and Mingquan who had done so.
The catalogs compiled for the Jin, Wei, Han, and other dynasties merely serve as provisional records of the dates of translation and transmission, as well as the names of the individuals involved.

As for such matters as different translations from the same source, conflating one into two, presenting old works as new, the confusion between earlier and later periods, and the intermixture of authentic and spurious texts—their faults are beyond enumeration.
Thus, in the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, the Gengwu year, [he] compiled [this work].
The *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu* (Record of Buddhist Teachings Compiled during the Kaiyuan Era) in twenty fascicles reaches the pinnacle of critical discernment;

it was thus able to exclude the writings of Jiang Mi and the female practitioner, thereby blocking the source of demonic delusions. Even later works such as Yuanzhao’s *Zhenyuan Lu* remain far removed from its excellence.
Furthermore, there is one fascicle of the *Xu Daoshuan Neidian Lu* (Continued Record of Inner Scriptures by Daoshuan) and one fascicle of the *Jingmai Tujì* (Illustrated Record by Jingmai).

The secular surname of the Tang dynasty monk Yuanhui is lost to history. From an early age, he was renowned throughout the Guanzhong region; his studies encompassed both the *Xing* (Dharmalakṣaṇa) and *Xiang* (Yogācāra) schools, yet he devoted himself particularly to the *Abhidharmakośa*.
At that time, Jia Zeng, the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, was a great admirer of him and frequently invited Yuanhui to engage in discussion and exposition.

Whenever they reached those chapters deemed most complex and difficult—such as the sections on "non-perception," "delusive attachments," "acquisition," and "non-acquisition"—he would provide a thorough and lucid elucidation of their underlying principles.
In general, there was nothing that did not become clear [to them]. [Daoxuan] often lamented that the commentaries of the ancient masters were difficult to consult;

he therefore collaborated with the Vinaya Master Huaiyuan of Shengshan Temple to produce an abridged commentary, making it direct and expedient for the convenience of students. Later, one named Chongyi produced an excerpt (chao) to further explain it.
Regarding the ancient commentaries, those by Masters Daoguang and Fazhao exist, but currently only the commentary by [Daoshi] Huikai (Huishu) is widely circulated in the world.
Tang Xuan-yi, surnamed Dou, was the maternal grandfather of Emperor Xuanzong Shenwu. His bearing was extraordinary and transcended the mundane;
he was a man of renowned learning. Having entered the monastic order, he perused the *Nāga-kośa* (the Buddhist canon) and sighed deeply, saying:

"The time since the Sage has passed is so remote that the texts have become disordered and confused to such an extent! He then consulted the catalogs of both ancient and modern times regarding the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna [scriptures].

He collated one thousand eight hundred sections from the Sūtras, Vinayas, and Śāstras collected by sages and worthies of the East and West, verifying their volumes and meticulously examining their phonetics and characters.

He compiled these into thirty volumes in total, including commentaries and exegeses on the *Guangpin* (Broad Chapters) and the *Lizhang* (Chronological Chapters), which were circulated throughout the world.
Yet, he was not led astray by wealth or status, but was able to govern himself through emptiness and stillness. Had it not been for his great... [text ends]
How could one who has transcended the ordinary reach such a state? How magnificent and sublime! Tang Ling’er was a man of unknown origins.
During the Qiánfēng era, he obtained the opportunity to attend the Dharma seat of Master Xuán of Nánshān at Xīmíng Monastery.

He inquired earnestly and reflected deeply, never shrinking from the hardships of travel. Yet, as for his spiritual lineage, he was unable to definitively establish it. Toward the end of his life, he grew apprehensive...

Having lost the intended meaning of the original teachings, he then proceeded to collect and extract from what was being recited, providing explanations, deletions, and additions. He designated these separately as "Records" (Ji) within his compendium.
He also composed the *Qingzhong jue* (Decisions on Light and Heavy Offenses), which, due to the chaos and turmoil of the times, was subsequently lost and forgotten. How tragic!
Fahai, whose courtesy name was Wenyun, was a man of Wu-xing during the Tang dynasty. He was born into the Zhang family of Dan-yang.

In his youth, he entered the monastic order at He-lin Temple, where he sought out teachers and friends to study the sūtras and śāstras. Consequently, he thoroughly explored the profound origins of both the texts of Eastern Lu (Confucianism) and the teachings transmitted from the West (Buddhism).
He once said to others: "The study of Buddhism has nothing else; it consists solely of the mind-ground. All other matters are merely..."
He was a man of humble means. During the Tianbao era, he attended the lecture halls of Fashen Vinaya Monastery in Yangzhou;

at that time, figures such as Tanyi and Lingyi all esteemed him as their Yan Hui and Ran Geng. He was particularly close with Zhushan Huizhao, and many followers from both the monastic and lay communities joined them in their leisurely excursions beneath the trees.
Huiyuan of the Tang dynasty was a native of Jingzhao. In his youth, he served as a disciple of Xianshou Fazang and received the essential instructions of the Huayan school.

He then relied upon the *Pao-tsang lun* (Treatise on the Precious Treasury) to establish four types of teaching: first, the teaching of deluded attachment to the unreal, which refers to ordinary worldlings;

second, the teaching of one part of the real and half of the unreal, which refers to those of the two vehicles; and third, the teaching of one part of the real and the full [unreal], which refers to bodhisattvas at the initial stage.
The teaching that fully possesses the four truths refers to the Bodhisattvas of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).

Now, while the Tathāgatagarbha has never been absent from sentient beings, those who are able to recognize it are exceedingly few—much like a person born blind who has never recognized his own parents or wife and children.

The various masters have offered their judgments, some conforming to and others contradicting [the original intent]. Furthermore, I have compiled two fascicles of glosses and explanations, focusing exclusively on phonology.
The commentary on the text and meaning of this school states:
Shenhui of the Tang dynasty entered the stream of the Dharma in his youth; his conduct was solitary and lofty.

During the Baoying era, together with the Vinaya Master Dayi of Chengxin Temple, he studied the Three Contemplations under Chan Master Zuoxi Lang and attained a profound understanding of the Tiantai teachings. Furthermore, his literary compositions—

His calligraphy was grand, expansive, and vigorous yet elegant. He composed the *Praise of the True Image of Lang* and the *Preface to the Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sūtra*, both of which were highly esteemed by the world.
His later life remains undetailed.

Tang Zheng was the son of the Hou family of Taiyuan. In his youth, he entered the monastic order at Chongfu Temple in the prefecture. He recited over a thousand sheets of scripture, mastering them all through repeated review;

thus, he was known at the time as Zhengjingzang (the Treasury of the Correct Scriptures). However, he possessed a majestic bearing and a solemn spirit, with a dignified and elegant appearance that inspired those who beheld him.
Once, Wang Gong Jin, the Chancellor of the State, requested that Zheng extensively expound upon the *Kusha-śāstra*, for which he offered praise.
His mastery in analytical discernment and his appropriateness in responding to inquiries were such that they far exceeded the capabilities of others.

During the reign of Emperor Daizong, he was summoned by imperial decree to serve as the Great Virtuous One (Dade) of Zhangxin Temple, but he did not accept. He passed away at the temple at the age of fifty-eight.
Tang Liangben, surnamed Guo, was a native of Yuxiang in Hezhong. His appearance was dignified and upright, and his discernment was profound and far-reaching.
During the Yongtai era, he assisted the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra in transmitting and translating Sanskrit texts. Emperor Daizong invited him to serve as a Bodhisattva Precept Master.

At that time, the *Renwang Huguo Jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra for the Protection of the State) had newly appeared; by imperial decree, Liangben composed a commentary (*shu*) that fully captured the intent of the scripture. He subsequently submitted a memorial to present it to the throne.
Later, he submitted a petition requesting that his works be circulated; the texts of his memorials and imperial responses are not recorded here.

He subsequently taught and guided at both Zhangxin and Anguo Monasteries, where listeners always numbered several hundred and official provisions were never lacking. In the first month of the seventh year of the Dali era, he passed away.
Fabu not empty-handed submitted a petition to have [the Master’s works] included in the catalog; the imperial decree granted his request. Fabu had previously moved to Jizhou in the sixth year.
On the tenth day of the third month in the twelfth year, he passed away at Fuyang while lying on his right side with his arm as a pillow, having met his end without illness.

His final memorial, consisting of two scrolls of the *Niansong yi* (Ritual for Recitation) intended for presentation to the Emperor, was submitted. He was sixty-one years of age and twenty-nine years since his ordination (*laba*). His remains were cremated, and [relics] were recovered from the ashes.
There were over a hundred grains of relics. Later, a stupa was erected to the east of the capital city.
Tang Shengong was a native of Xianglu in Muzhou; however, it is unknown from where his family lineage originated. From childhood, he possessed a powerful memory;

his aspirations were great and his speech lofty, such that the senior monks all marveled at his capacity. He followed a teacher to enroll for his studies at Shengde Temple, relying upon his paternal aunt.
The master Sūkaigen (Sukāiyuán) and Dōkō (Dàohéng) studied the Vinaya. [Sukāiyuán] especially cherished his diligence and prudence.

Later, he lectured and taught in Weyang and authored the *Shùnzhènglù* (Record of Accordance with Correctness) in ten fascicles. The world called him the Master of the Huainan Records; he styled himself the Śramaṇa of Mount Qinglíng. Thus it is said.
Tang Shenqing, style name Lingyu, was surnamed Zhang and was a native of Changming in Mianzhou. All three of his brothers had left the household life;

Shenqing was the middle one and was renowned for his virtue. While still in her womb, his mother had loathed pungent and fatty foods. In childhood, whenever he encountered a Buddhist image, he would immediately pay it homage.
At the age of thirteen, he relied upon Dharma Master Bianzhi of Kaiyuan Temple. He recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa Sūtra*, and others.
When the authorities sent someone to test his mastery of these studies, the local Governor Qiao Lin was struck by his excellence and shaved his head for him;

this was during the Dali era. At the age of seventeen, the assembly requested that he lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*. Those who listened were so deeply impressed and convinced that they submitted to his teaching. Upon completing his term of study, he followed Huiyi.

Sengru received full ordination as a *vinaya* master and soon traveled to the capital. There, due to his superior literary talent and extensive learning, he entered the imperial court to serve as an attendant.
Later, after losing a close relative, he returned to Huiyi Temple to propagate and guide others. During the Yuanhe era, he passed away at the summit of the mountain behind the temple.
His remains were enshrined in the Bailmen Aranya, located outside the northern outer gate of Qi City; this is what is known as Beishan.

He composed ten fascicles of the *Fahua xuanyan jian* (Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra), thirty fascicles of the *Shishi nianzhi* (Chronicle of the Buddhist Community), and ten fascicles of the *Xinlü shuyao tan* (Essential Discourse on the New Vinaya Commentary), also known as the *Qingchao*.
He also authored one fascicle of the *Erzong chuxue yi* (Ritual for Beginners of the Two Schools) and seventy-five [fascicles] of the Youzong.
*Fashu* (Commentary on the Dharma), one fascicle; also titled *Fayuan ji* (Record of the Source of the Dharma).

It is so named because it provides a detailed and comprehensive exposition of the essential nature, functions, and activities of the phenomena categorized within the five positions of the Hīnayāna—namely, matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitta*), non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).

*Shixin lun* (Treatise on the Consciousness-Mind); *Chengguan lun* (Treatise of Chengguan); *Jushelun yishao* (Explanatory Notes on the Meaning of the Abhidharmakośa); *Beishan canxuan yulu* (Recorded Sayings on Investigating the Profundities from Beishan); and the works of his disciple, Yiji.
Jiangsi was exceptionally skilled in the two treatises, the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Awakening of Faith*.
Tang Cheng’en, whose origins are unknown, pursued his studies seeking out masters and vied with others in the academies. He took particular delight in teaching and nurturing students;
his excellence in lecturing and discussion drew disciples from all quarters. Toward the end of the Tiānbǎo era, when the Guāngzhōng region fell into chaos, he consequently sought refuge elsewhere.

In Guzang, the multitude followed him with one accord. He then reflected that because the borders of the barbarians were fragmented and customs were prone to change, this was actually a blessing for the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, he recompiled the *Śataśāstra-ṭīkā* along with its abridgment (*piṇḍārtha*) and put them into circulation. After he had passed into *parinirvāṇa*, [the works remained].

The śramaṇa Faxin submitted a memorial to Zhang Chaoyi, the Regional Commander (Jiedushi) of the original province, requesting that the Great Virtuous Ones (Dade) of the two monasteries and three schools be commissioned to conduct a detailed determination [of the matter].
An imperial edict granted this permission, and furthermore, the monk was bestowed with purple robes (zijī) to serve as the Great Virtuous One of the province;
this occurred in the third month of the fourth year of the Xiantong era.
Tang Danfu had long practiced the discipline of the *śīla* regarding what is permitted and what is prohibited under Master Hengwen.

Toward the end of the Xiantong era, his disciple Zhizhang transmitted this lineage down to the present day.

Hui Pu of the Tang dynasty was the son of the Song family from Qishui in Qi. Having been scrupulous in his observance of the *śīla* since his ordination, he made it his primary vocation to recite and uphold the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
In the twelfth year of the Yuanhe era, he built a dwelling on Mount Guangji to facilitate his practice.
Regarding this great sūtra, he was able to memorize all forty-two fascicles. When others, harboring doubts, tested him, he indeed [recited them perfectly].
His breath flowed freely without any obstruction. In the third year of the Dazhong era, he gathered his assembly, sat in the full lotus posture, and passed away as if entering meditative absorption.
His disciples enshrined his entire body in a stupa on a mountain peak, and the incense and lamps have remained unextinguished until the present day.

Tang Xuanchang, whose courtesy name was Shenzhi, was the son of the Chen family of Xuancheng. At the age of nine, he relied upon the Venerable Qingyi of Xishui Temple in Jing County to study the sutras and the Dharma.
At nineteen, he received the tonsure; one year later, he received full ordination at the Doushuai Precept Platform in Fuzhou.
He was particularly diligent in his mastery and study of the Vinaya-piṭaka. His travels through Yuezhong had brought him complete satisfaction.
Upon hearing this extraordinary account, he hurried to the Ximing Monastery in the capital to follow Master Huizheng.
There, he extensively investigated the eminent traces of the Venerable Vinaya Master Xuan’s practice of the Way, and subsequently received the office of Great Virtue for the Three Studies.

When the teachings were suppressed during the Huichang era, the assembly deliberated that it would be appropriate to submit a memorial as a remonstrance, hoping that the Emperor might heed it and rescind the previous edict. Thereupon, Lingyan, the Monastic Registrar of the two streets, and Bian...

Zhang and others collectively recommended Huichang as their leader. They recorded the deeds of the emperors of successive dynasties and submitted them for imperial review, but [the Emperor] would not grant his ear.
At the beginning of the Dazhong era, he was granted a purple *kāṣāya* robe and a decree appointing him as a Great Virtuous One (*mahāsattva*) of the inner and outer altars.

During the Xiantong era, he was summoned by imperial decree to serve as the head of the Zui Fu Yuan (Retribution Monastery) and concurrently as the *karmadāna* of Zongchi Temple; he was appointed as an *upādhyāya*. He cultivated the methods of repentance and added ten thousand Buddha names to his recitations.
Wuqian concurrently requested that one copy of the *Bodhicittabhūmi-parivarta-sūtra* (Xindi guan jing) in eight fascicles be included in the Tripitaka; the Emperor granted this by imperial decree.

At the beginning of the Qianfu era, he was bestowed the title Fabao. On the twenty-first day of the third month in the second year, he passed away at the age of seventy-nine and with fifty-nine years of ordination seniority.
On the twenty-fifth day of the fourth month of that same year, he was interred at Gaoyang in Chang’an County.
Xiaoliang Village. In the fourth year [of the reign], Cui Hang, Minister and Vice-Minister of the Ministry of Rites, composed the inscription for its stele, followed by a panegyric of his virtues.
Tang Xuanyue was born into the Zhang family of Zhengping. In his youth, he entered Longxing Temple in his native village, where he studied and recited a thousand words daily.
Having undergone tonsure, he received the full set of precepts (*pūrṇa-saṃvara*) and delved into the *Piñjū* (the Vinaya). He spent many years investigating these profound mysteries.

Guàn was revered and looked up to by all. He arrived at Shèngshòu Monastery in Chāng'ān, where he presided over the ordination platform to lecture on the Vinaya and concurrently taught the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* more than forty times.

He also composed the twenty-fascicle *Jinhua Chao* to clarify the essential tenets of the treatise. His reputation was weighty throughout the regions of Fén and Qìn, and he had more than a hundred disciples who studied under him.
He passed away at the age of seventy-six, in the fifth month of the fifty-sixth year [of the Kaihuang era]. The funeral rites were performed.
Having obtained the śarīra relics, he constructed a brick stūpa to the west of the prefectural city.

Liang Yanhui, surnamed Sun, was a native of Wuyang County in present-day Dongjing. While still in his swaddling clothes, he would laugh with joy whenever he heard his father recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, as if he had grasped its meaning.
Furthermore, when his family once held a vegetarian feast for the monks, as soon as the *kangling* and the *fan* bells were struck together, he would immediately join in.
