He chanted "Namo. At the age of fifteen, he followed his teacher to Taiyuan, Jingzhao, and Luoyang to study. He received full ordination at Shaoshi Temple on Mount Song.
He thoroughly mastered the depths and boundaries of the *Prātimokṣa* and the *Vinaya*, and subsequently explored the sūtras and śāstras, reaching the very source of their profound depths.
It is said: "The ways of practicing goodness differ, yet they all lead to the same governance. This governance consists of *śīla* (precepts), *samādhi* (concentration), and *prajñā* (wisdom).

These are the ultimate means for entering the state of sainthood (*ārya*). For this reason, the people of Southern Yan called him the "Son of the Buddha. Initially, while presiding over the Mingfu Monastery, he lectured on the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*;

the elite scholars from across the four seas flocked to him like clouds and waves, with his audiences always numbering in the hundreds. He subsequently lectured on the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* and the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*.

He produced approximately one hundred fascicles in total, which were included in the *Shuaitai Chao* (Commentary on the Huatai Monastery) and circulated in the world. He passed away on the third day of the eighth month in the autumn of the first year of the Qianhua era.
He was seventy-two years of age and had been a monk for fifty-two years.
In his youth, Liang Congshen shaved his head at Chanzhi Temple in Jiangdu. In the fifth year of the Xiantong era, he proceeded to Fufu Temple on Mount Yan to receive full ordination.

Thereafter, he traveled extensively through various scenic and significant sites. Later, he returned to lead the monastic community, earning the respect and submission of those below him through his mastery of the Vinaya and the Dharma.
Nevertheless, he was devoted solely to the recitation of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, never for a moment showing the slightest negligence. In the second year of the Zhenming era, three...
On the eighteenth day of the month, he suddenly contracted a slight illness and passed away the following day. During the cremation, śarīras were obtained;
they were enshrined in a stone cairn at Jūnyuen, where the śramaṇa Linghu composed an inscription for them.
During the Later Tang dynasty, he received the *upāsaka* precepts from Master Jia Yong of Yue’er. Having taken the vows, he immediately carried his book-satchel (*fengji*) to the capital to study;

he mastered the scriptures and was proficient in the treatises (*śāstra*), never ceasing his efforts to propagate the teachings. During the Xian Tong era, he repeatedly responded to imperial summons to offer hymns of praise for the Emperor’s birthday.

He subsequently served as the Director of Rituals (*jianyi*) for the Left Ward (*zuo jie*). His contemporaries bowed in submission before him. During the Guang Ming era, when Huang Chao breached the capital, he fled to Yue to escape the turmoil, whereupon he opened [a school].

Regarding the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, I have provisionally relied upon the commentaries of the various masters of Qiányǎ Temple. As for the *Chóngfú* commentary, it is overly verbose and lacks conciseness.

During the Tóngguāng era, I consequently composed the *Yìpíng Chāo* (Commentary on the Evaluation of Meaning) in fourteen fascicles. Furthermore, I compiled a sub-commentary (*chāojiě*) on the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*.

The prefaces were written by Jia Zeng, a Palace Attendant, and the śramaṇa Yuánhuí. Other works include [commentaries on] the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Śata-dharma-prakāśamukha-śāstra*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.

In the chapter "The Meaning of the Distinct Practices of Consciousness," [Huiyuan] was solely frugal and impetuous, rarely harmonizing with the world. He maintained disciples, yet in the end none could satisfy his mind.
He once personally handled the hearth to prepare food; when the firewood was damp, the flames would flicker on and off. In anger, he poured water upon it.

He did not eat again for the rest of the day. In his later years, his vision grew dim and he suffered from dizziness; whenever he gave a lecture, he would always carry a bamboo staff, as it was not scorched by the sunlight.
Some might have criticized him for showing such disrespect to the assembly, yet he accepted these remarks with composure and took them to heart.

When the Regional Commander, the Military Protector (Wuxu) Qian Wang, was touring the provinces and arrived at Yue, he went out to pay his respects. The King, who had long admired his reputation, treated him with exceptional courtesy. (The year was) Qiànhuā.
In the middle [period], he was summoned to serve as the *jiantan* (Supervisor of the Ordination Platform) for the bestowal of the precepts. This office originated with him in the Wu-Yue region.

During the Tongguang era, King [Qian Liu] recommended him to the imperial court, requesting that he be granted purple robes. When the imperial decree arrived, just as he was about to ascend the platform to lecture on the preface to his commentary on the *Sūtra of Maitreya’s Rebirth Above*, he said:

"It is like a vast furnace that receives all things in its emptiness. Suddenly setting down his fly-whisk (*chushi*), he looked at the assembly and said: "I have attained fame, yet it lacks canonical authority."

"Is it truly so? "What is meant by 'receiving [the mandate] in vain'? The assembly explained the circumstances in detail. The King sighed and said, "This monk shall not attain glory or longevity; his words were indeed a prior prophecy.
In the year of Yiyou (1345), he received the imperial decree of succession and descended to the Yuan Shuai-fu.
At that time, the empire was fragmented like the slices of a melon. The arrival of the envoys necessarily required them to cross the sea from Qingzhou to the south.
In the perils of wind and waves, it takes more than a single month to reach the shore.
It was only upon reaching this point that he learned that the day he boarded the ship was precisely the day foretold by the prophecy. How could Wu Fuk have possessed such prescience!
Later, Jingxiao of the Xü clan of Danqiu was born. Initially, he relied upon Master Biao to study under the guidance of Acharya Shouyan, who expounded the teachings in his native village;
Jingxiao then admired him and followed him there. By nature, he was upright and principled, yet he was impetuous and lacked tolerance.

Consequently, few people associated with him. Although his appearance was quite plain and inferior, his temperament was rather fierce. After receiving the precepts, he immediately began instructing beginners at East Baishan in Jinhua.
At that time, the Vinaya Master Huiyou from Jiangxi, who prided himself on his scholarly achievements, arrived at the temple leading his disciples;
it happened that he was there when [the Master] encountered him. This man had authored a work known as the *Guijian lu* (Tortoise Mirror Record), which was currently circulating in the world.

During the night, he attended a lecture on the *Ji-chi-pian* (Chapter on Observance and Transgression), listening silently to the exposition and admiring it for a long time; his reputation consequently grew even more eminent.
He composed the twenty-fascicle *Jian-ji* (Record of Rectification) to refute heterodox and deluded views. King Qian of Wusuku summoned him to preside over Lin’an Zhulin Temple.
In the second year of the Tiānchéng era, he officiated at the ordination platform at Beita Monastery, and later passed away at Nan Zhen.
His remains were enshrined in the Shēnbǎo Pagoda Temple at Dàcí Mountain, and he was posthumously granted the pagoda name Qīngliáng.
Later, during the Zhēnhuì era of the Later Táng, there was a man surnamed Bāo, a native of Chángshū in Wú. At the age of thirteen, he received the tonsure at Lóngxīng Temple in his home prefecture.
By nature, he was grave, serene, and diligent; barely a year after beginning his studies, he could recite the *Lotus Sūtra* from memory, and he practiced daily recitation twice a day.

He made this his constant practice. At the age of nineteen, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*). He traveled extensively through the regions of Yi, Luo, He, and Fen to investigate and exhaustively master the sutras and śāstras.
In the first year of the Tiānyòu era of the Táng dynasty, he arrived at Xiāngguó Temple in Bì to expound and guide others;

he recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* about ten times daily, yet people initially did not know of it. By the time the Liáng dynasty established its capital, followers gathered from all directions like clouds. In the second year of the Zhēnmíng era—
In the first year of the era, Marshal Duke Kong Shafeng provided the funds to establish a hall within the West Pagoda Courtyard.

He invited Master Hui to lecture extensively on the scriptures, while Hui’s attendants read the texts of the Great Tripitaka. Twice daily they performed the ritual practices, and they continued to recite the Lotus Sūtra with diligent perseverance without interruption.
Furthermore, he once earnestly told his disciples: "The doctrines of heterodox schools muddle and disorder the true mind; one must be careful not to hear them. I wish for you to be liberated."
He turned his shoulder toward the inner courtyard of Maitreya; he had no further aspirations for other realms.

On the eleventh day of the second month in the second year of the Qingtai era, he suddenly joined his palms toward the sky and said, "The assembly of sages welcomes me; I am now departing. The multitude also all heard the sound of celestial music.

Shortly thereafter, he passed away. His age was seventy-three; his years since ordination were fifty-four. On the eighteenth day, his remains were moved to the grounds of the East Suburb Temple Estate for burial.
Later, Guiyu of the Later Tang dynasty was surnamed Mei and was a native of Shouchun. His father, Yuanxu, was a man of great virtue and skilled in physiognomy; because of this—

"It is fitting that you leave the household life. He granted permission. He served under Master Daozong of Kaiyuan Temple. Before long, he had memorized and mastered the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, and other scriptures.
Upon reaching the age of twenty, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*). Furthermore, he studied under various masters whose lectures were highly esteemed by the community.

Later, hearing of the flourishing study of the sūtras and śāstras in Luoyang and Jingzhao, he traveled there to seek teachers and friends. For nearly ten years, he mastered both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, encompassing both the *Xing* (Nature) and *Xiang* (Characteristics) schools of thought.

As for the treatises such as the *Nyāyapraveśa*, the *Abhidharmakośa*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, as well as the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Sūtra on the Ascent to the Tuṣita Heaven*, they all delve into profound depths and exhaust the most abstruse mysteries;
yet no one had previously scrutinized them. Furthermore, he sought out Master Huī of Southern Yan to verify and rectify them.

However, as the new commentaries were not yet refined, he further edited and corrected them at the Xiangguo Temple in Dongjing. His disciples attained realization, and his reputation reached the imperial hearing. Thus, he once [associated] with the later...

The Emperor, having shared his studies with him since childhood, issued an imperial decree to seek him out upon ascending the throne. Knowing he could not escape, [Zhaozuo] entered the palace for an audience.

As it happened to be the Qiaqing Festival, when an edict had been issued to prohibit all monks and Daoists throughout the realm, an imperial favor was bestowed upon him alone at the island retreat, granting him a purple *kāṣāya* and the title "Great Master of Dharma Propagation" (*Fanyan Dashi*).
The ceremonial guards of the two monastic districts escorted him to the temple, and by imperial decree, the Imperial Portrait Hall of the East Pagoda was renamed [the Zhaozuo Cloister].
He was appointed as the head lecturer of Changjiang Monastery. The provincial governor of Min presented him with three hundred rolls of silk as a gift for his long life.
This brought great luster to the Buddhist teachings. On the tenth day of the third month in the third year of the Qingtai era, he said to his disciple Hongyan, "My time has come to an end.
You must advance in your practice without slackening. He burned incense, joined his palms, and passed away at the beginning of the night.

He was seventy-five years of age and fifty-five years of *śrāmaṇera* seniority. On the eighteenth day of the intercalary month, he was enshrined in a stupa on the eastern ridge of the temple estate at Dongjiao.
Later Tang: Lingyin, a native of the Yang family from Wenxiang in Shanfu. Having left the household life, he traveled extensively to study under eminent masters of the Amitābha tradition.
Among the various treatises on the *Śata-dharma* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, his interpretations were particularly profound and refined.

From that time forth, his reputation spread far and wide, and lay devotees came to take refuge in him. He traveled to Changshui in Luonan, where he established a monastery and propagated the teachings within it.

In the intervals between instructing his disciples, he would separately recite the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha-sūtra* as his regular practice. In this manner, for nearly thirty years, he never allowed himself even the slightest slackening. During the Qingtai era...

In the second year [of the reign], he passed away at the monastery where he resided. He was seventy-one years of age and fifty-one years since his ordination. His body was cremated, and his *śarīra* relics were enshrined in a stupa at the foot of the mountain.
The Chinese monk Zhao, a native of the Zhang clan from Yan’ang, was fourteen years old when, with an appearance of remarkable stature and a mind of brilliant intelligence, he...

The śrāmaṇera spent another year at Minzhong Temple, where he was already able to recite from memory such sutras as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Within just a dozen years, he had already mastered their profound texts and abstruse meanings. During the Tiānyòu era...
Carrying his staff and alms bowl, he traveled south. At Zhongshan, the Regional Commander Wang Chuzhi invited him to reside at Fahua Temple.
Upon reaching Yiding, the Grand Tutor Li Gong of Longxi submitted a memorial of recommendation. By imperial decree, he was granted a purple cassock and the title "Great Master Zhen.

Marquis Ma of Fufeng requested that he serve as the Sangha Rectifier (Sengzheng), but this was not his aspiration. He proceeded to Luoyang, where he was sometimes commissioned to expound the *Lotus Sūtra* at Falin Temple.
The assembly at the sutra seat was vast and magnificent, with people gathering like the spokes of a wheel; many were those who took his teachings to heart and carried them away fully laden.

On the twenty-sixth day of the third month in the first year of the Qianguo era, he manifested his passing at the age of seventy and with fifty-four years of *śrāmaṇera* and *bhikṣu* ordination (*varṣa*).
At that time, Li Gongfang, the Grand Tutor, was serving as Chancellor in Luoyang; he personally oversaw the funeral rites. On the third day of the fourth month, the cremation was performed.
To the south of the city, he obtained relics that were luminous and moist. General Ding Gong of Jiyang erected a stupa and interred them on the southern ridge of Guanghua Temple.
Han Ju Min, surnamed Ren, was a native of Xihe. His father, Ben, delighted in the seclusion of the gardens and groves, finding joy in the cultivation of the arts. His mother was Lady Wang.

He was devoted to the study of Buddhism and received the eight precepts of the *aṣṭāṅga-śīla*, remaining pure and free from other thoughts. When Minsheng was only seven years old, his will and spirit were already resolute and destined for accomplishment.
Once, his parents took him into the Jingxin Monastery in the commandery; there, the Master Lunshi Xuanyuan was staying in his quarters.

Upon seeing him, the Master felt as if they shared a karmic bond from a previous life and wept, begging to take him as his disciple. His parents could not dissuade him. At ten years of age, he established a daily routine of recitation.

Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, upon reaching full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), he immediately studied the Vinaya and delved deeply into the principles of the Mahāyāna.
As for the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Tarkajvālā-śāstra*, and the *Vyākhyāyukti-śāstra*, he expounded them all more than ten times each. He also extensively researched secular classics.
An imperial edict ordered him to reside at Tiantangyuan (Tennō-in). A multitude of fellow monks gathered there, and the government provided all necessary provisions so that nothing was lacking.

In the first year of the Ganguo era, an edict dispatched court officials to bestow upon him purple robes and the title of Great Master Yuánzhì. Shortly thereafter, an edict transferred him to the Lecture Hall of Chongfusì (Shūfuku-ji), where he concurrently served as the *Sengzheng* (Sōjō) for the管内 (*guǎn nèi*, jurisdictional district).
He disciplined the fourfold assembly with such authority that they were like grass bowed down by the wind. In the eleventh month of the second year...
On the fifth day of the month, he passed away without illness at the age of seventy-three, having lived for fifty-four years of the Xia calendar. Upon cremation, śarīras were obtained;
this was reported in detail to the throne. By imperial decree, he was buried at Tiantong Temple on the Western Hills, posthumously titled Dashik (達識).

Fahui was from the Liu family of Sanxiang in Luoyang, descending from the Han dynasty. From his youth, he was quick-witted and intelligent; however, his resolve was firm and he sought to leave the secular world.
His parents consented, and he took up the tonsure at Zhuge Monastery in the district.

Having received full ordination at Songyang, he subsequently went to Changshui to study under Master Yin, receiving instruction in the *Amitābha-sūtra*, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, and the *Śata-dharma-prakāśamukha-śāstra*. At that time, Master Yin was advanced in years and appointed Fahui to act on his behalf.

He traveled to respond to the invitation of Bu Jin. During the Qingtai era of the Later Tang, because he had received repeated summons from [Master] Yin, he ascended the Dharma seat three times daily for the sake of the assembly, manifesting his diligent intent.
His summer retreats were especially long-lasting; he perused the scriptures of the Tripiṭaka and cultivated himself with such refined austerity that no one could surpass him.
On the first month of the second year of the Ganyou era, he passed away due to illness at the age of fifty-three and with thirty-two years of ordination. He was cremated.
His remains were collected and enshrined in a stupa.

In a dream, a son of the Yang family from Changshui County in Luoyang saw him; he had left the household life to be affiliated with Xuanquan Monastery, where he recited the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and lectured on the *Śata-dharma-vidya-śāstra*.
During the Qingtai era of the Later Tang dynasty, he was invited by Guanghua Monastery in Longmen to expound the Dharma for the assembly.
Yan. When the Emperor visited his temple, he was summoned for an audience; his responses were in accord with the Imperial will, whereupon an edict was issued granting him a purple *kāṣāya*.

He declined and would not accept it. He was diligent in instructing others. In his later years, he ate but one meal per day, practicing the Way and prostrating before the Buddha. For over twenty years, he met the Buddha’s compassion and forbearance as if it were but a single day.
In the third year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty, he passed away due to illness at Tiangong Temple, his place of residence.
The monastics and laypeople, mourning him with deep longing, erected a stupa for him.

Han Xijue, whose courtesy name was Shunzhi, was surnamed Shang. His family had resided in Jinling for generations, later moving to Yin yang, where Xijue was born. He had originally pursued a career as a Confucian scholar.

During the chaos at the end of the Tang dynasty, he fell into dire straits and had nowhere to turn; he once supported himself by hiring out his services as a copyist. Through this work, he gained access to the imperial library.
At that time, Master Luo was living in seclusion at his home. The Master happened to speak with him and took pity on him, saying, "My son, why have you come to this?
He then gave him much money and encouraged him to study. In the first year of the Wende era, at the age of twenty-five, he traveled to Wenzhou and entered the monastic order under Kaiyuan Temple.
During the Longji era, he received full ordination and subsequently studied the Vinaya-piṭaka at Ximing Monastery.
As for Master Huize, he was the foremost disciple of the Great Master Fabao. During the Guangming era, he fled from the Guanzhong region to the banks of the Zhe River.
It was there that Jingjue first met him at Tiantai. When Huize passed away, Jingjue continued his lectures and instructions in Wenzhou.
Shortly thereafter, Qian Hua—the younger brother of the Prince of Wusu—came to serve as governor. He treated him with increased courtesy and respect.
When someone falsely accused him of a minor transgression, he released him without inquiry. He moved his residence to Dacian Temple in Qiantang.

King Wenmu appointed him to preside over the new monastery of the Thousand Buddhas and granted him the purple robe; privately, he was honored with the title of Great Master Wenguang. Not long after, due to old age and illness...
He requested to be relieved of his office and lived in seclusion in a mountain hermitage, finding joy in the Way. At the time of his passing, he was eighty-five years old.

His literary works include the *Zenghui ji* (Collection of Augmented Radiance) in twenty fascicles, the *Ningjiangdong chanyu* (Imitating the Jiangdong Letters of Censure) in five fascicles, and miscellaneous poems and prose in fifteen fascicles.
Zhou Zhizhuan was surnamed Zhang and was a native of Yongji in Ye. At the age of nine, he entered the service of a master at Wangshecheng Temple in Linqing.

Upon receiving full ordination, he applied himself diligently to Buddhist affairs. In his leisure time from reciting the sutras, he performed prostrations and circumambulations, never failing to do so three times during the day and three times at night.
Subsequently, his preceptor sent him to follow Master Hui of Mingfu Temple in Huatai to study.

Within less than a month of his training, he suddenly grasped the profound essentials. Among the dozens of disciples who had previously been hailed as preeminent at Master Huī’s gate, all now fell beneath him.
Thereupon, responding to the request from Xuyang, the Dharma-blessing poured forth like rain.

After a long time, a faithful layman in the capital of Bian donated his residence to establish the Wansui Baiyuan Monastery, where he took up residence. He subsequently traveled to various patrons' dwellings.

He received offerings from the populace and provided meals for three hundred thousand monks over the course of his career. The three clans of Zhang, Guo, and Dai of Tianxiong Army invited him to the Guanyin Monastery;
was this not to support him during a time of decline, old age, and exhaustion? Quan was exceptionally well-versed in the *Śata-dharma-prakāśamukha-śāstra* (The Hundred Dharmas).

When ascending the seat to preach, he was eloquent and fluent, never relying on written texts. Whenever he perused the Tripitaka, he did so to augment his insight and understanding; his recitation was performed with sincere devotion. When...
In the deep of night, when all was silent, there were those heard outside the room snapping their fingers in praise. The Wei Province Commander, Chen Junsirang, was deeply devoted to the faith;
he submitted a memorial recommending [the Master] for the purple robe and the title of Guizheng Dashi.
In the fifth year of Xiande, at the age of eighty-three, he suddenly commanded his disciples Fengyan and others to construct a wooden bier, saying: "It must be according to the Western rites."
I cremated him. On the eleventh day of the eleventh month of that year, he suddenly passed away; his remains were enshrined in a stupa.

Zhou Cheng was of the Zong clan from the state of Chu, though his specific hometown remains unknown. His family had maintained a life of Confucian simplicity for generations, and his mother, Zhao, was likewise pure and austere.
On the evening of Bǔ’s birth, a brilliant light illuminated the entire room, leaving the neighbors in amazement. At the age of seven, he happened to enter a temple.

Whenever he saw a Buddha image, he would immediately prostrate himself in worship. Returning home, he asked his father, "As for those with the golden-colored marks sitting upon lotus flowers—is it only the Buddha who is thus, or can others also do so?
His father replied, "If even all sentient beings, down to the most minute insects, can attain Buddhahood, how much more so can human beings?
Fàn was delighted and wished to leave the household life; at the age of ten, he entered the monastery of Xiangguo Temple under Master Ming...
The disciple Zhi was distinguished in both character and appearance, setting him apart from his peers. Those who recognized his potential knew him to be a preeminent vessel for the Dharma-gate.

Once he had received full ordination, he devoted himself to the study of the new scriptures; regarding the profound depths of the Vinaya, he alone was able to penetrate them deeply, such that none among his contemporaries could rival him.

Consequently, he was titled "The Tiger of the Vinaya. Princes, dukes, and high officials visited his door daily to seek his instruction. During the Tianfu era, an imperial edict summoned him to enter the inner monasteries.
He was granted a purple *kāṣāya* robe and the title of Great Master Zhenfa, and appointed as the Patriarch of the New Chapter.

Whenever consorts or members of the royal family entered the path, he would invariably confer the precepts upon them. On the eleventh day of the tenth month in the sixth year of the Xiande era, he faced north with his head toward the west and passed away without illness.
He was seventy-one years old and had fifty years of *varṣa*.

Song Chuan was surnamed Peng and was a native of Dongming in Kaifeng. His father, Yin, worked as a farmer and was particularly well-versed in the principles and interpretations of Buddhist scriptures.
His mother, Xing, dreamed of visiting a monastery; she grasped a ritual object and subsequently conceived. She immediately told her father about the dream, and he said joyfully:
He was destined to father a son, whom he would cause to leave the household life. At the age of eleven, he was sent to serve Bi Gong of the district as a disciple;
Bi Gong taught him the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Ratnaketuparivarta*, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras, which he was able to recite from memory after a single reading.

Once he had shaved his head, he followed his teacher to Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, whereupon he received full ordination. At that time, Qinglang of Xun-jiao and Daoya of Suiyang were both renowned for their refinement and elegance.
While he took the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as his basis, his teacher relied upon the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. Both were cases of internal substance with external names.
Thus, Zhang Huo traveled extensively to seek out the secret transmissions to support his exposition. As the dharma assemblies were spread and the seats opened, his disciples gathered in circles;

for nearly twenty years, he never ceased for even a moment. During the Guangshun era of the Zhou dynasty, the Grand Master Guangzhi, Director of Monks for the Left Street, presented his recommendation to the throne.

In the morning, he was granted a purple square-cut robe. In the second year of the Qiandé era, upon the recommendation of Dàoshēn, the Director of the Left Street Monastic Registry, he was conferred the title of Great Master Yìmíng.
Shortly thereafter, he manifested illness and passed away at the age of fifty-five and thirty-six years of religious seniority.
On the sixteenth day of the eleventh month of that year, his body was cremated on the Southern Plains of the capital. His tongue remained unburnt. At first...
When his father passed away and was cremated, his tongue likewise remained unimpaired. One can thus know that the efficacy of reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is such as this.
In the fifth year of the Kaibao era, his disciples erected a stupa and buried him there together. The inscription was composed by Grand Master Qinghui of Xiangguosi Temple, Yi Bing.
Song Jilun, whose secular surname was Cao, was a native of Jinyang. He entered the monastic path at a tender age.

His teacher initially had him practice the recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, whereupon he was able to memorize three more pages each day than his peers. At that time, the assembly marveled at his quick-witted intelligence.

By the time he received full ordination, he was twenty-one years old. Beyond his mastery of expounding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he further studied the two treatises on *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and *Hetuvidyā*.

He expounded the teachings with sudden brilliance. His assembly was grand, numbering a constant one hundred and fifty. Lun’s appearance and nature were compassionate and patient; his precepts and conduct were firm and pure.

His demeanor moved others like the wind, and all who beheld him submitted their hearts in reverence. Even when the Liu family held power over Bing and Fen, they still accorded him respectful greetings and conferred upon him the honorary title of "Dharma-Treasure Grand Master" (Fǎbǎo Dàshī).
He was appointed to record the affairs of the Right Street Monastery, and the fourfold assembly relied upon him for their spiritual cultivation and progress. Thus it was.

In the winter, he manifested illness and composed a verse, expressing his vow to be reborn in the Heaven of Contentment (Tuṣita) within Maitreya’s inner court. After he passed away, the crown of his head remained warm for more than half a day;
this was the third year of the Kaibō era. He attained a lifespan of fifty-two years. It is said that after his cremation, his relics were divided and offered as objects of veneration.
Songyi’s secular surname was Pei. He was a native of Anyang in Xiangzhou. His two younger uncles both left the household life and attained renown and high standing through their religious practice.
The elder, named Xiujin, once performed a prostration for every single character of the *Lotus Sūtra*; furthermore, he daily recited the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*.
He is now a great virtuous master presiding over ordination platforms in Lixia. The younger, named Shenglun, [is also a monk of great virtue].
He had previously recited the *Mahākaruṇā* and *Śūraṅgama* mantras each one hundred million times. He now presides over Qingqiu Xiangyan Monastery.

When Chu was seven years old, he came to visit his two fathers at the command of his parents; Jin subsequently ordained him as a monk. Having received full ordination, he studied diligently without slackening.

Regarding the *Abhidharmakośa* school, he penetrated its subtleties to the ultimate degree, and thus transmitted the *Yuanhui* commentary, lecturing on it ten— (Note: The text provided ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the available portion.)
I have permitted this comprehensive collection. However, those in the world who are ignorant have employed various texts from the teachings and frequently resulted in errors and contradictions.

Therefore, I have thoroughly refined and categorized them all, so that the meanings, principles, and realities of the entire Tripitaka may be clearly manifest and their efficacy evident, leaving no room for doubt for scholars who take up the pen or wield the tongue.
Thus, for the sake of truth throughout the world, I have begun this work during the Kaiyun era of the Jin dynasty.
Two years later, in the first year of the Xiande era of the Zhou dynasty, the work was completed.

It comprised fifty sections in total, arranged into four hundred and forty chapters, and was titled *The Six Compendia of the Śākya School* (*Shishi liutie*). This was modeled after the works of Bai Juyi of the Tang dynasty.

Upon its presentation to the throne, an imperial edict granted him the purple *kāṣāya*, the title of Great Master Mingjiao, and the work was submitted to the Historiography Bureau. He passed away at the Longxing Monastery during the Kaibao era.
His age was seventy-four, and his years since ordination were fifty-four. In his later years, Master Chu considered himself blind;
he repented his transgressions, saying, "How could my writings escape being cut down and pruned? Do they not violate the Buddha’s intent and shatter the chapters of the Dharma?
Subsequently, his sight was restored. Commentators attribute this to the response of his utmost sincerity. Regarding his book, Prime Minister Wang Gong (Wang Pu) composed a preface for it.
It is said that Song Yizhuang, surnamed Zhang, was a native of Huaitai. As a youth, he followed his local community to Kaiyuan Temple, where he studied the scriptural teachings.

Upon receiving full ordination, he immediately took up his book-bag and traveled to Luoyang to listen to the exegesis of the *Lotus Sūtra*. His conduct was austere and he held a profound distaste for worldly things; his insight surpassed that of his contemporaries.

The public requested that he reside at Jiuyao Temple. At the beginning of the Jianlong era, Shen Gong, the Left Attendant-in-Ordinary, submitted a memorial on his behalf, and he was granted purple robes.
In the eighth month of the third year of the Taiping Xingguo era, he passed away at the age of seventy-eight, having been a monk for fifty-nine years.
In the second month of the following year, his funeral carriage was moved to the west of Longmen Bodhi Temple, where he was interred in a stupa.
Song Pusheng, surnamed Zhang, was a native of Luzhai in Shenzhou. In his youth, he entered the monastic order under Master Chao-hua of Huayan Monastery on Mount Wutai.

By nature, he possessed an exceptional memory; upon reading any commentary or treatise only once, he mastered it entirely. Within a few years, he earned the reputation of a "blue" (disciple) among the "green" (senior monks).
Furthermore, he revised and supplemented various works to produce the *Zhenbian chao* (The Authentic Discernment Commentary) in four fascicles for circulation. He opened [the path].
In the intervening years, he was granted a purple robe by imperial decree and conferred the title Xuanchao (Proclaiming the Teaching).

On the fourth day of the seventh month in the fourth year of the Taiping Xingguo era, he manifested illness and passed away at Jingtu Yuan (Pure Land Cloister). He was sixty-three years of age and forty-three years since his ordination.
A stupa was erected to inter his śarīra on a western mound of Longmen Mountain at Baoying Temple.
The eulogy says:
The Mahāyāna Dharma is like a flowing spring; Its vapor gathers and its pulse issues forth.
As it courses through the earth without partiality, It may encounter pits where its function is not manifested. Yet with it one cooks and steams, And with it one irrigates and waters.
Day by day, one should provide only morning and evening meals; throughout the year, let there be no drought or parching heat. In the pursuit of learning, one must follow this path:
remain in profound stillness and solitude, enjoying leisure and unhurried progress. Accumulate knowledge without indolence, and nurture it without negligence.
Once what has been heard is vast and expansive, apply it with vigor, so that its beneficial influence reaches far and wide.
*The Newly Compiled Classified Biographies of Monks of the Six Studies*,
Volume Twenty-three and Volume Twenty-four,
composed by the Śramaṇa Tán’è of Eastern Zhejiang.
Jingxun Xuegantongke (精進學感通科) was a person from Jin’an whose origins were unknown. He was well-read and skilled in discourse. During the Yongjia era, throughout the realm...
During a great epidemic, Huize prayed to Heaven at night, requesting that divine medicine be bestowed early so as to save the common people.
One day, he went out from the monastery and saw two stones as large as jars; upon inspection, they were filled with water. He gave this to the sick, and there was none who did not recover.
Later, while residing at Dashi Temple in Luoyang, he wrote a copy of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* on yellow silk, making it into one scroll with characters the size of soybeans.
The calligraphy was exquisitely refined, comprising some ten scrolls in total. One set was given to the wife of Zhou Zhongzhi; her mother, Lady Hu, carried it with her when crossing the river.
One night a fire broke out, and in the frantic confusion, she had no time to retrieve them. She lamented that they were irretrievably lost.
When the fire was extinguished, they were found amidst the ashes; the scrolls remained undamaged, as if newly made. They are now preserved by the nun Jianjing.
In the temple, there was also one named Kang Huichi, whose miraculous traces were exceedingly renowned.
Zhu Fayi of the Jin dynasty—his clan name being lost in historical records—was skilled at lecturing on the Lotus Sutra and was close friends with Wang Dao and Kong Fu.
During the Xingning era, he returned to Jiangzuo and settled at Baoshan in Shining. He had more than a hundred disciples who constantly attended to his worship of an image of Avalokiteśvara.
In the second year of the Xi'an era, he suddenly suffered from heart ailments. One night, he dreamed of a person who cut open his abdomen and washed his intestines.

Upon his awakening, he was immediately healed. He passed away in the fifth year of the Taiyuan era. By imperial decree, a stupa was erected for him. His disciple Tanshuang lived in a hut beside it and subsequently founded a monastery named Xinting Jingshe.
Bai Faqiao of Zhongshan was a monk of the Jin dynasty. He delighted in chanting, yet his vocal resonance never reached its full potential.
Thereupon, he abstained from grain and prostrated himself before Avalokiteśvara to offer prayers. On the seventh night, he felt that his throat and lips were suddenly unobstructed;

he immediately sought water to swallow and rinse his mouth two or three times, saying, "It is sufficient. From then on, he was able to memorize and retain [the scriptures] without forgetting, reciting fluently some hundreds of thousands of words.
He chanted with such pathos and elegance that it moved and inspired those who heard him. He passed away in Hebei during the Yonghe era at the age of over ninety.
Tanyi of the Jin dynasty was born into the Yao clan and was a Qiang person. At the age of sixteen, he took Master Dao’an as his teacher; he was renowned for his mastery of the Vinaya.

His name was [Hui]yi. He had thoroughly mastered the essentials of all three Piṭakas, and his contemporaries of the time held him in the highest esteem. While traveling through Shu, the Regional Inspector Mao Qu provided him with a midday meal.
As Yi was receiving the rice from the serving tray, he first ate some of it himself. Mao Qu, believing that Yi was innocent despite the circumstances, treated him with great respect.
Later, Mao Qu sent Yi a gift of a thousand *shi* of rice, which Yi distributed among various monasteries. At that time, Master Dao’an was at Tanxi, and Changsha...
The Prefect, Teng Hanfang, was then at Jiangling, where he donated his residence to establish a monastery. He requested Hui’an to appoint a monk to take charge of its administration.
Hui’an said, "No one but [Hui]yi can do it. This is the present Changsha Monastery. Later, having fled to Shangming to avoid the turmoil, he established another monastery there.
Upon returning to Jiangling, he again repaired the Changsha Monastery. Thereupon, he experienced a miraculous manifestation of vajra-relics during a vegetarian feast. He then felled timber...

On Mount Jun in Dongting, a deity appeared in a dream expressing his joy. On the eighth day of the second month in the nineteenth year of the Taiyuan era, a light suddenly flashed forth from north of the city.
Monks from Baima Temple rushed there and saw the image, but were unable to lift it. Daoyi was then able to carry it back;
it was indeed that which he had long earnestly prayed for. Upon examining its side, he found it inscribed with Sanskrit script.
It is said that on a certain month and day in a certain year, King Anru (Aṅga) passed away peacefully before the image at the age of eighty.
At the same time, there was a monk named Wei, whose scholarly achievements were highly renowned and whom Yin Zhongkan held in great esteem.
Tanjie of the Jin dynasty, also known as Huijing, was a native of Nanyang from the Zhuo clan. He was devoted to learning;

having first heard Tanfa Dao lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (The Light-Emitting Prajñā), he went with his relatives and friends to listen. He subsequently attained a profound realization of the subtle principles and abandoned his household life to study extensively under Master Dao’an, thoroughly investigating the Tripiṭaka.
He would recite more than five hundred thousand words daily and perform five hundred prostrations each day. Later, when his illness became severe, he maintained the *Maitreya* [contemplation].

He never ceased reciting the name [of Amitābha] from his mouth. At the time of his death, his disciple Zhisheng attended him and asked, "Do you not wish to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang)?
He replied, "I and eight other monks made a vow together to see Maitreya. Now that the Master has attained the Way, he shall lead me there first.
Having finished speaking, light illuminated his body; his countenance became radiant and serene, and he passed away. He was buried to the right of the An-ta pagoda at the age of... (years).

Seventy. Sengji of the Jin dynasty was a man of unknown origin. Toward the end of the Taiyuan era of the Jin, he went to Mount Lu and studied the various Mahayana and Hinayana sutras under Master Huiyuan.
His lectures were highly esteemed by his contemporaries. Shortly thereafter, he fell ill; Huiyuan then handed a torch to Sengji.

He said, "If one can direct the mind toward the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī) and compete with the passing moments of the various outflows (āsrava), one may rely on a small table to pass the lamp to a neighboring monk.

Suddenly, he dreamed of an extraordinary omen; rising from his seat, he called for his sandals, stood facing the void, and said, "I am now departing. He then passed away while lying on his right side at the age of forty-five.
Zhu Tanyou (also known as Fayou) of the Jin dynasty was a native of Dunhuang. From his youth, he maintained rigorous discipline and excelled in meditative contemplation.

He traveled to Shan County and resided in a stone grotto on Mount Shicheng. Once, while begging for alms at the home of a person afflicted by a *gū* (a type of malevolent spirit), he invoked a blessing to expel its poison and then consumed the food himself.
Later, he moved to Mount Chicheng in Shifeng. A pack of tigers arrived and crouched submissively, listening as Huiyou recited the sutras without ceasing.
One tiger fell asleep; Huiyou struck its head with his *ruyi* (monk’s staff) and said, "Why are you so drowsy? The tigers immediately all departed.
Furthermore, there was a large snake that raised its head and opened its mouth toward Huìyòu, appearing as if it wished to swallow him. Huìyòu remained unmoved, and the snake departed.
A mountain deity then appeared and said, "The Dharma Master’s majestic virtue is most profound and weighty. You have come to this mountain; I, your disciple, wish to offer this land for a vihāra.
I beg you to depart from here. Huìyòu asked, "Would it be possible to dwell together? The deity replied, "I fear indeed—"

"It would be improper for you, being of low station and burdened by worldly ties, to encroach upon and defile this pure sanctuary. Sengyou asked, "If I were to leave, where would I go? The spirit replied, "I am a son of the Xia Emperor.
My family has resided on this mountain for nearly two thousand years; if you depart, you may rely upon my maternal uncle at Mount Hanshi."
Thereupon, they offered three caskets of incense, whereupon [the deities] sounded drums and blew horns, ascending into the air and departing.

Zhiyou then led more than ten practitioners up the rocky cliffs by means of a ladder to sit in meditative retreat. They constructed bamboo conduits to transport water for their ritual ablutions and offerings.

Wang Xizhi once visited him and stayed for two nights before returning. The cliffs extend in succession toward Mount Tiantai and Mount Siming; it is traditionally said that there was once a monastery there.
Above it, those who have attained the Way reside. Water cascades down into the ravines, and stone bridges span the void; yet all are so perilous and steep that they cannot be traversed.
When Huiyou first intended to visit the monastery, he heard a voice from the air saying, "You have not yet attained deliverance."
"It will be possible only after another ten years. Huiyou was filled with regret. That night he stayed overnight in a rock cave and heard the sound of *brahman* chanting.
At dawn, he saw an elderly man who said, "Would you not mind defiling this sacred temple with your body, which is subject to birth and death?
Huiyou asked, "Elder, how have you come to be here? The old man replied, "I am a mountain deity. Suddenly, he vanished from sight, and the clouds and mist closed in, filling all the hollows.
There was a voice. Daoyou closed his eyes and remained as he was. After a short while, a man wearing pleated robes arrived and said, "This is my dwelling.
I had just gone out on other business and did not have the opportunity to welcome you. Now that my entire household has moved elsewhere, I hope you will remain.

Thereupon, the cliffs and valleys opened wide, and a strange monk emerged from a vihāra to meet him. He burned incense and prepared a meal. When the meal was finished, Daoyou expressed his wish to take refuge [in the monk].
He stopped. The monks said, "He shall come here after ten years. Thereupon, [Hui]you took his hand and led him out. During the Taiyuan era, a comet appeared;
[Hui]you was summoned to pray for seven days, and the comet withdrew. A small boy dressed in green came to repent his transgression. At the end of the Taiyuan era, he passed away;
his corpse remained silver-green in color, showing no signs of decay even to this day.
Zhu Huida of the Jin dynasty was born into the Liu clan; he was also called Sahe. A native of Xihe in Bingzhou, he made his living as a hunter.
After he died, he traveled through the various hells and was struck with great terror. There, a practitioner of the Way comforted him and preached the Dharma to him, saying:
"I was your teacher in a previous life. You should go quickly to Danyang, Kuaiji, and Wujun to seek out the stupa and image of King Aśoka.
There, repent and wash away your past transgressions; you shall then be reborn. He subsequently left the household life to become a śramaṇa. During the Ningkang era, he arrived at the capital.

At night, he saw that the tip of the spire at Changgan Temple was of an unusual color. He immediately went there, prostrated himself, and circumambulated it. Suddenly, light flashed down from beneath the spire.
Upon digging with a pickaxe, he discovered three stone tablets covering an iron casket. Opening the iron casket, he found a silver casket; opening that, he found a gold casket.
Inside were enshrined three śarīra relics, a fingernail, and a single coil of deep blue hair that, when drawn out, measured several zhang in length.
The sides of the casket bear an inscription stating that it was one of the eighty-four thousand [stupas] constructed by King Aśoka during the reign of King Xuan of Zhou.
Emperor Jianwen previously erected a three-story stupa to enshrine it. This was in the sixteenth year of the Taiyuan era.

Emperor Xiaowu further added three tiers above it. During the Xianhe era, Gao Kui, the Governor of Danyang, excavated the Kāṅhū Bridge (Zhanghóu Qiáo) marsh and discovered a golden image without a pedestal.
Upon close inspection, there was a script written in *pārśvākṣara* (side-writing) which stated: "Created by the fourth daughter of King Aśoka.
Kui loaded it onto his cart and returned home; when he reached Changgan Lane, the cart would not move, so he followed where the ox led.

He immediately entered the monastery and was subsequently retained there for another year. At that time, a man from Linhai named Zhang Xi, who had been fishing at the mouth of the estuary for generations, discovered a copper lotus pedestal.
Fearing he might not be permitted to keep it, he presented it to the county office. An imperial edict was issued to use it to secure the feet of a golden image.
It was as if a key had been found to fit its lock. At that time, five Brahman monks arrived at Hui-ku’s residence and said to him: "In the past, we obtained a statue in India.
Upon reaching Ye, we encountered the chaos of war and buried it by the riverbank. We subsequently searched for it but lost its location.

Recently, we dreamed that the statue appeared in Jiangdong and was recovered by you; therefore, we have come to pay our respects. Hui-ku accompanied them to Changgan Temple, whereupon the statue immediately emitted light. The five monks said: "Its..."
Behind the crown of the head, there was still a mark of the circular halo (prabhāmaṇḍala), which he would later obtain.

In the first year of the Xiangan era, Dong Zongzhi, a Duan fisherman from Hepu in Jiaozhou, while gathering pearls in the sea, unexpectedly obtained it. Regarding it as a rare and auspicious omen, he presented it to the throne.

By imperial decree, it was installed upon the back of the statue, fitting like a lid to its box. Over the course of more than forty years, it had been scattered and lost in various directions, only to be reunited once again.
Is this place not extraordinary? Da served there for a long time before eventually traveling east. Upon reaching Wu Commandery, he paid homage to the stone image. Regarding this stone image:
in the first year of the Jianxing era, there was a fisherman on the Songjiang River who saw a light every night.

Suspecting it was the sea deity, he spread the news among both the clergy and the laity. The lay practitioner Zhu Ying, accompanied by the nun Bo of Dongling Temple, went to the mouth of the Hudu River and beheld it.
Two giants emerged from the water and approached. Upon inspection, they were found to be of stone; on their backs were inscriptions: one was named Vipaśyin and the other Kāśyapa.
He welcomed them and enshrined them at Tongxuan Temple. Da remained at Tongxuan for three years, performing repentance rituals with unwavering diligence.
He then traveled to Kuaiji, where he paid homage and visited the stupa on Mount Mao. This stupa was also constructed by King Aśoka, and a miraculous light frequently emanated from it.

Ding Da poured out his sincere heart in repentance and cleansing, fully fulfilling the admonitions of the man from the Hell Path. After Da’s passing, nothing further was known of his end. During the Jin dynasty, there was a monk named Fa’an, also known as Ciqin.

His origins were unknown. He served Master Huiyuan as his teacher. He was skilled in lecturing and study, possessed strict observance of the precepts, and also practiced the discipline of meditation (*dhyāna*).
During the Yixi era, he passed through Xinyang County. The local inhabitants lived in close proximity to one another, like the interlocking teeth of a dog. One hundred...
The other families found this extremely strange and closed their doors. When they questioned him, they learned that there were many tigers; there was a local shrine situated beneath a large tree.
Dao’an consequently sat down in meditation there. After a short while, a tiger carried a carcass and placed it before Dao’an, leaping about with joy as it displayed its claws and tail.
Hui’an consoled him. Thereupon, the tiger crouched on the ground with eyes closed; Hui’an preached the Dharma for him and departed.

When the pursuers arrived the following morning, they saw Hui’an and were greatly astonished, regarding him as a deity. The calamity caused by the tigers subsided from that point on. Consequently, the shrine was converted into a monastery, and Hui’an remained there to dwell.
His fields and gardens were all designated as permanent property of the Sangha. Later, his final whereabouts remained unknown.
Bai Sengguang—also known as Tanguang—was a man of unknown origins from the Jin dynasty.

At the beginning of the Yonghe era, he arrived at the foot of Mount Shicheng in Jiangdong and asked the local elders for the way into the mountains. The elders all said, "The mountain is infested with fierce beasts;

you must not go there. Yet Sengguang was determined to proceed. After traveling several li, a storm of wind and thunder broke out with rain, and a tiger roared, shaking the valleys and peaks. Sengguang sat down upon a rock.
In the middle of the month, on the following day, he entered the village to beg for food. Upon his return, he sat in meditation for three days, during which time his dreams were particularly strange.
After another three days, the mountain deity manifested its form and spoke of his aspirations, saying: "I wish to move Mount Han-shi at Zhang’an to provide a dwelling for you.
Thereupon, Guang built a hut among the trees; after a long time, it became a temple named Yin’gao. Whenever Guang entered meditative absorption, he would remain there for seven days before emerging.
He rose and remained [in this state] for fifty-three years, reaching the age of one hundred ten. He passed away while covering his head with his monastic robe.

When he first entered this state, his disciples regarded it as ordinary and did not examine it closely; only after seven days had passed did they strike the chime to rouse him from his meditative absorption, by which time it was too late.
In the second year of the Jianwu era of the Song dynasty, Guo Hong was serving as an official in Shan County; he entered the mountains to pay his respects to him. As it was...

He pried open the bird’s breast; the feathers were destroyed and the flesh wasted away, leaving only the white bones remaining. Daohong fashioned a niche for its image and had it sculpted, which remains there even now.
Zhu Fakuang of the Jin dynasty was born in Gaoshi; his ancestors were from Xiapi, but he lived as a guest in Wuxing. Orphaned at a young age, he served his late father’s successor.

His mother was renowned for her filial piety; he personally tilled the land to support her. He observed the funeral rites with full propriety. Upon the completion of his mourning period, he took the śramaṇa Tanyin as his teacher. Tanyin was a man of lofty conduct.

Once, when Tanyin was critically ill, Huikuang offered prayers and repentance with such sincere devotion that for seven days he did not cease. One night, five-colored light suddenly illuminated Tanyin’s chamber.
Tanyin felt someone’s hand rubbing and massaging him, and his illness was immediately cured. Later, he took leave of his teacher to travel, and eventually returned.
He dwelt in a stone grotto at Qian, taking the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Amitāyus-sūtra* as his essential practice. When there was a congregation, he would lecture;
when dwelling alone, he would recite. Xie An visited him from Wuxing; first, he dismissed his attendants and approached the seat on foot.

They took their leave after conversing joyfully all day. While Sima Jianwen was serving as Chancellor of State, he dispatched Qu An, the Governor of Tangyi, to inquire after his well-being and to perform rites for averting the calamity of the comet.
[Huiyuan] replied: "In the past, when Lord Jing of Song cultivated virtue, the comet withdrew its quarters.

You should diligently cultivate virtuous governance to block the Heavenly reprimand; thus the world would be most fortunate. Shortly thereafter, the comet vanished. This occurred during the Xingning era.

He traveled east to the Cave of Yu, letting his spirit roam among the mountains and waters. Upon reaching Yuya, he took a liking to a secluded pool and desired to build a hut there to cultivate his will.
Xi Chao and Xie Qingxu frequented him most often. At that time, an epidemic was ravaging the eastern lands;

since Zhu Dao’s nature was compassionate and he was skilled in divine incantations, he went out from the city to stay at Changyuan Temple to provide salvation. The villages relied upon him for relief. [The biography of] the śramaṇa Zhu Dao...
Línzào built a stupa and image of Amitāyus. Xuánguǎng led those with spiritual affinities to erect a great hall.
Emperor Xiaowu admired his character and issued an edict for him to leave the capital and reside at Chánggān Temple. He passed away in the Yuánxīng era at the age of seventy-six.
Tansui of the Jin dynasty was a man of unknown origins. He resided at the Baima Monastery in Heyin and recited the Lotus Sūtra.
One night, someone knocked on his door and said, "I request that you, Venerable Sir, come to view the sūtra. Tansui did not grant permission; however, when the visitor insisted, he finally consented.
Accompanied by a single disciple, they went together. Upon waking, he found himself inside the shrine of the White Horse Mound deity. From then on, every day [the deity appeared] in the dark.
He went there, but no one recognized him. A group of monks passed by the shrine and saw Master Sui’s disciples sitting facing each other on high seats, delivering a lecture.

Only then did both the clergy and the laity come to respect and marvel at them. At the conclusion of the summer retreat, Shen Shi presented him with a white horse, five white sheep, and ninety bolts of silk.
Zhi Tanlan of Jin was a native of Qingzhou. He could recite thirty thousand words of the scriptures. During the Taiyuan era, he traveled to Shan County and settled at Mount Chicheng in Shifeng.
Suddenly, a man several *zhang* tall appeared and rebuked Tanlan, ordering him to leave. This was followed by strange-looking snakes and beasts that coiled around him and lunged about.
Tanlan sat in meditation, remaining unperturbed. The man then bowed and said, "I am Zhu Qi, the maternal uncle of the Wang family."
"It is on Mount Weiqing; you may rely upon it for residence. Now, this mountain is offered to you, Venerable Sir. Thereupon, he vanished.

Three years later, there was one who approached the King with a pearl as a deceptive gift. He saw [the monk] there, wearing a ceremonial cap and robes with pleated folds, his appearance refined and elegant.
Twenty-two people, including his wife and children, surrounded him in a dense throng of carriages and horses. They prostrated twice and requested to receive the precepts. At that—

Lan herself took up the incense burner and straightened the ritual table. She personally conferred the five precepts upon each person. Finally, she departed after receiving ten thousand coins and two jars of honey as offerings.
At that time, more than ten of her disciples were present, attending and witnessing the exchange of questions and answers; these were no different from those of the worldly realm.
She passed away during the Yuanxi period at the age of eighty-three.
Huiyisheng of the Song dynasty was surnamed Liang. His origins were unknown. He possessed a refined and elegant bearing and was thoroughly versed in the sutras and treatises.
During the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, he departed from the capital, saying that he had once encountered a Daoist named Facheng in Jizhou who, at the time of his death, told his disciple Puyan:
"The deity of Mount Songgao said that General Liu of Jiangdong shall receive the Mandate of Heaven. I..."
There were thirty-two jade discs and one ingot of gold as tokens of sincerity. At that time, the High Ancestor was residing in the residence of the Prince of Song;

upon hearing of this, he said to Dao Yi, "Would it be possible for you to seek this out on my behalf? In the seventh month of the thirteenth year, Dao Yi traveled to Mount Song and prayed there for a response.
He immediately had a dream in which a long-bearded man with a staff pointed and said, "It is beneath this rock."
The following day, Fayi traveled through the mountains and recognized the place of his dream; he obtained the jade disc and gold, exactly as specified in number, and offered them [to the temple].
In the first year of the Yongchu era, Fan Tai, the General of Chariots and Cavalry, established Zhihuan Temple, for which Fayi served as the director of rituals.
He passed away at Wuyi Temple in the twenty-first year of the Yuanjia era at the age of seventy-three.
Sengquan of the Song dynasty was a native of Haiyang in Liaoxi. From his youth, he was renowned for his extensive learning and traveled between Yan and Qi.
He discarded his robes and cap to become a śramaṇa, becoming thoroughly versed in the sūtras and śāstras. Later, he crossed the Yangtze River to lecture, his fame shaking the capital.
Zhang Gong of Wu Commandery invited him to reside at Xianju Temple; later, he stayed at Huqiu Temple. Prior to this, Sengquan had constructed [an image] at Huanglong Temple.

He fashioned a sixteen-foot golden image, and further created a "human-gold" (human-sized) image at Mount Huqiu. He maintained himself with purity and integrity, possessing no personal stores or accumulations.
Meng Yi of Pingchang established Fangxian Temple in Yuhang to invite Sengquan; however, Sengquan, being fond of extensive reading, contracted the disease of double blindness.
When his condition became severe, he constantly saw the two images he had made on the western wall. His disciple Fa... [text ends]
In a clear dream, several people appeared carrying a golden platform to him. When he questioned them, they replied, "We have come to welcome Dharma Master Quan.
The next morning, he indeed passed away at the home of Official Dong in Lin’an. The County Magistrate Ruan Shangzhi ordered his burial to the right of the tomb of Guo Wenju on Mount Tushan.
Tandi of the Song dynasty was born into the Kang clan. His ancestors were originally from Kangju; during the reign of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty, they came to settle in Guanzhong.
At the end of the Han, amidst the great chaos, the family moved to Wuxing. His father, Yong, had previously served as the Regional Aide (Biejia) of Jizhou.
Tandi’s mother, Lady Huang, dreamed that a monk called to her and entrusted her with a fly-whisk and an iron-inlaid book-seal. Upon waking, both objects were there. She was greatly astonished.
When Sengdi was five years old, his mother presented him with two objects. He laughed heartily and said, "These are merely gifts sent to me by the King of Qin.
His mother asked, "Do you remember where these were placed? Sengdi looked blank and replied, "I do not recall."
At the age of ten, he left the household life. All that he realized and understood did not derive from the instruction of teachers.

Once, while traveling with Rong through Fandeng and passing through Guanzhong, he habitually called [Qi] by name. The presiding monk Shi scolded him, saying, "A mere child calls me by my name; who has incited you to do so?"
He said, "Just now I suddenly thought of my novice monk who was gathering vegetables for the assembly of monks when a wild boar happened to graze near his feet.
That novice seemed to be you, Master; I happened to recognize his name and unconsciously let out a cry.

Xie was greatly astonished and questioned Rong, who recounted the beginning and end of the matter. He then produced the *zhuchi* (whisk) and the iron-inlaid book-seal, which Xie examined. Weeping, Xie said:
When the late Master Hongjue was lecturing on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for Yao Chang in the past, I served as the assistant lecturer (*dujiang*).
The two items [the staff and the bowl] were provided by Yao Chang; furthermore, the incident of him plucking vegetables and injuring his foot can both be verified.

Consequently, when I later calculated the date of Master Hongjue’s passing, it coincided exactly with the day those items were entrusted to him. I read through the account carefully until I could recite it from memory. Later, I entered the Tiger Hill Monastery.

He lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, each for fifteen assemblies. He sported with ease in the *Book of Changes*, the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, and the *Zuozhuan*.

Skilled in literary composition, he had a collected works in six volumes. By nature, he delighted in mountains and waters; he settled permanently at Mount Zhangkun and lived on water from mountain streams for over twenty years.
He passed away at the end of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty. He was sixty years of age. His teacher, upon whom he relied, is lost to history.
Song Jingdu was a native of Wuxing; the histories do not record his clan name. In his youth, he joined a hunting party to shoot game.

He once dropped a pregnant doe’s fetus, yet even as it died, the animal licked it before passing away. Struck by this, he broke his bow and arrows, left his home to become a śramaṇa, and recited more than three hundred thousand words of scripture.
He frequently dwelt alone among the mountains and marshes, disciplining himself through meditative contemplation. He heard that in the local district...
Senghui immediately went there and offered his own body as a lamp, burning it until dawn in worship. He maintained this practice as a constant for many years.
Suddenly, he called to his disciples, and after they had prepared the incense and bathed him, he recited several thousand verses and passed away in profound stillness.
From the void above, the sound of drums and music was heard, leading the way as fragrant incense drifted down; everyone witnessed this. At the same time, there was another monk named Sengcong.

He practiced the contemplations of the five gates with diligence and abstained from grains, subsisting only on dates and chestnuts. He resided at Pùbù Mountain in Shǐfēng and lived for over a hundred years before passing away in the mountains.
Sòng Dàojiǒng was born to the Mǎ family; a native of Fúfēng, he became a śramaṇa and served as a disciple to the Dharma Master Dàoyì. When Dàoyì fell ill, [Dàojiǒng attended him].
He sent four of his disciples, including Sengjiong, to Mount Huo to carry torches into a deep cavern to gather stalactites.

After traveling about one *li*, they encountered a massive ravine; three of them perished while attempting to cross the water. Sengjiong alone recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and maintained mindfulness of Avalokiteśvara.
He saw a light like a firefly, which he pursued until he emerged from the cavern, thereby escaping with his life. He then traveled south to the capital and took up residence there.

At Nanjian Temple, Changye practiced the *pratyutpanna-samādhi*. During the night while in meditative concentration, he saw someone arrive in a carriage. He assisted Jiong in ascending the carriage, and they soon reached Shenqiao Bridge behind the commandery.
There they saw a man in magnificent attire seated upon a *huchuang* (Hindu-style chair), with several hundred attendants surrounding him.
They all rose in alarm, but Jiong said, "I am merely a practitioner of *zichan* (seated meditation). The man on the *huchuang* looked at his attendants and said, "Just now I intended to..."
"It is enough to let him know the location of the Dharma Master; why must you trouble yourself to come here? Thereupon, he prostrated at his feet and escorted him back.

When Sengjiong arrived at the temple, the gate was still closed; he knocked for a long time before it finally opened. In the twentieth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he passed away in Guangling.
Tanyi of the Song dynasty was a native of Yuhang. He possessed extraordinary conduct. Initially a śramaṇa, he relied upon Huiyuan of Mount Lu; later, he traveled to Guanzhong to rely upon Kumārajīva.
Subsequently, he returned to the east and built a hermitage on the northwest peak of Qinwang Mountain. There, he drank from mountain streams and recited the Lotus Sūtra.
Moved by his devotion, Samantabhadra appeared in the form of a woman, carrying a bamboo basket containing a white pig and two garlic bulbs. She arrived at [the hermitage].
The girl said, "I entered the mountains on business and am about to return when evening falls. Wolves and jackals are blocking the path;
what shall I do? I pray you let me stay for one night. Yi Jian refused her. The girl’s pleas were even more earnest, so he finally allowed her to stay outside the eaves.

At midnight, she cried out, saying her belly ached and asking Yi Jian to massage it. Yi Jian would not agree. When she pleaded incessantly, he then wrapped his staff head in cloth and massaged her from a distance.
He rubbed it. By dawn, auspicious clouds suddenly gathered from all sides; the pig became an elephant, and the garlic became lotus flowers.
Soaring into the air, [the deity] said to Fayi: "I have observed your mind; it is like the moon in water—pure and unstained. Before long, you shall return to my assembly.
At that time, Meng Yi, the Grand Governor of Kuaiji, was sitting on the hall at dawn attending to his duties when he suddenly saw light radiating forth.

At the edge of the courtyard, there was a faint sound like that of metal, stone, strings, and bamboo instruments. Upon inquiry, he discovered its source; he then reported to the court that Daoxing had manifested such spiritual power through his wings.
By imperial decree, the Fahua Jing-she (Lotus Precinct) was renamed Fahua Temple. Initially, Daoxing had heard the śramaṇa Fazhi reciting the Lotus Sūtra while disguised as a pheasant.
After seven years, Daoxing passed away, and Fazhi buried him. One night, Fazhi dreamed of a youth who bowed to him and said: "Now..."

By the power of this scripture, he was born into the Wang family at Mount [Name]. One day, when the Wang family was preparing a vegetarian feast and summoned him, as Zhi was about to enter the gate, the child said, "My monk is coming.
Zhi had him undress and examined his armpits; indeed, there were three feathers of a pheasant there.
He subsequently followed Zhi to leave the household life and was named Tanyi. He passed away in the twenty-seventh year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty. [Prayer:]

Seventy. Among those who studied with Tan under the guidance of Yi, there was one named An, whose hermitage was called Leli Jing-she (Joyful Forest Monastery), situated not far from Yi’s own hermitage.
There was also Daojing, a descendant of Wang Xizhi; he possessed profound learning in the Way and was strict in observing the Vinaya, his conduct being exceptionally pure and rigorous.
Wang Pān of the Song dynasty was a native of Chánglè. In her youth, she followed her younger paternal uncle as he traveled to Jiànyè.

At the age of thirteen, she visited Master Yuǎn of Lúshān and vowed to become a śramaṇī. While traveling through Liāngzhōu, she was plundered by bandits; she prayed secretly to Guānshìyīn and was thereby spared.
She then proceeded to Héjiān, where she studied the methods of dhyāna under Dharma Master Xuángāo. On the way, she encountered the Tǔyù...
When the Hu forces arrived, he traveled through the capital city. There, he was invited by the retired scholar Fei Wenyuan to establish the Qihuan Monastery, where he resided.

He propagated his teachings throughout Xichuan. When the Regional Inspector Zhang Yue entered the imperial court, he praised [Huiwang] in the capital. Emperor Xiaowu of the Song dynasty, having heard of his reputation, invited him to reside at Zhongxing Monastery;
however, Huiwang submitted a memorial earnestly declining. Later, when Liu Kaokao governed the prefecture, he requested that Wang [Huiwang] deliver lectures.
He spoke thus and then accepted the invitation. During the Daming era, Wang Jingmao provided him with lodging at Fu Yan Temple.
He passed away in the first year of the Taishi era. Sengkao had a stupa erected for him at the temple gate.
Famin of the Song dynasty was a man of unknown origins. He was a scholar-monk who resided at Wuceng Temple in Jiangxia.
When the śramaṇa Sengchang was constructing a stūpa, Xie Hui, the Regional Inspector of Jiangling, intended to demolish it. Famin went to remonstrate with Hui, but Hui would not listen.

Consequently, Famin withdrew to Mount Yuelu in Changsha, where he remained for the rest of his life and never emerged again. Xie Hui brought wine and meat to the temple and raised the drums to intimidate him.
He hacked and mutilated the images. Suddenly, clouds and mist darkened the sky, and wind-blown dust rose from all sides. Huì was struck with terror and fled. Later, he was executed for rebellion.
Mǐn composed the *Xiànyàn lùn* (Treatise on Manifested Verification) to clarify the law of cause and effect, and also wrote a commentary on the *Dàdào dì jīng* (Sūtra of the Stages of the Great Way).
He passed away in the mountains at the age of eighty.
Qi Fadu was a native of Huanglong; the histories have lost his clan name. He became a śramaṇa in his youth and was learned in the sūtras and śāstras.
He disciplined himself with rigorous austerity and traveled to the capital. There was Ming Sengshao of Qijun, who lived in seclusion on Mount Nie in Langya; [Fadu] took him as his teacher.
Fadu abandoned his residence to establish the Xixia Vihāra and took up his dwelling there. After more than a year, suddenly a standard and banners arrived at his gate.

A messenger announced his arrival, saying: "Jin Shang’s appearance is most majestic. Upon bowing and rising, he declared himself a disciple and said, "Your Majesty has possessed this mountain for seven hundred years;
it is the abode of divine beings, and by principle, it must not be disturbed. However, as the Master’s virtue and wisdom are lofty and great, I wish to offer [it to you]."

He resided there to propagate the Dharma, thereby bestowing blessings upon this region. It was said that those who lived on that land invariably died; only after [Hui]du arrived did they cease to suffer such calamities. The deity requested to receive the five precepts.
Du said, "As a patron (*dānapati*), you maintain ancestral sacrifices involving blood offerings. This is something the Buddha’s precepts prioritize forbidding; how can you do so?
The deity replied, "If I am fortunate enough to be accepted, I shall first eliminate these practices. At dawn, he delivered ten thousand coins.

Incense, candles, and a knife were presented; there was a record stating that they were offered by the disciple Jin Shang. On the fifteenth day, he was ordained, and a ritual assembly was held for him.

Shang even participated with the assembly in the practice of the Way and departed after receiving the precepts. Subsequently, the temple priest had a dream in which the deity told him: "I have received the precepts from Master Du;
henceforth, my sacrifices shall cease, and I shall subsist on vegetarian food. Later, while Du was lying ill, he saw [the deity].

Huishang came and prostrated himself at [Seng]du’s feet. Huishang used a lapis lazuli bowl to scoop some water, which he had [Seng]du sip; it tasted intensely sweet and cool, and his ailment was immediately relieved.
At that time, there was a śramaṇa named Fashao, whose debates were of equal caliber to [Seng]du’s, and they were known as the "Two Sages of Beishan.
Fashao was a native of Baxi. Zhou Yong of Runan went from Chengdu to welcome them to the mountain, where they resided together with [Seng]du in the Zici Vihāra.
He was honored as a teacher by Prince Ziliang of Jingling and Prince Yaoguang of Shigan. He passed away in the second year of the Yongyuan era at the age of sixty-four.

His disciple Senglang was proficient in the *Avataṃsaka* and the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*). Hui Kai of Pengcheng and Fakai of Yuhang were both accomplished lecturers and scholars, whose reputations were equal to those of Daozhao.
Hóngmíngshēng of the Zhì family was a native of Shānyīn, Huìjī. In his youth he became a śramaṇa and possessed great virtue in observing the precepts.
He resided at Yúnmén Temple, where he recited the Lotus Sūtra; the water in his pitcher would fill itself spontaneously, and a young boy descended from heaven to serve as his attendant.
A tiger never entered the room to lie down, yet Ming rose and sat as usual. Once, a young boy came to listen to the sutras; Ming preached the Dharma for him, but suddenly he was gone.
On another occasion, a mountain spirit arrived; Ming pointed at it and laughed. The spirit seized Ming and bound him with its belt;
after a long time, it could not loosen it. Ming cried out, "Release me! Release me! The spirit said, "I dare not come again," and so Ming released it. Later, he resided at Yongxing.
He [Dharmakṣema] resided at Shaohuan Temple and later at Bolin Temple, where he passed away at the age of eighty-four.
Tanchao of the Qi dynasty was born into the Zhang family of Qinghe. His stature was tall and slender, reaching eight chi in height; his appearance and voice were exceptionally refined.

By nature, he was focused and serene, delighting in exploring the mysteries of the Way. He practiced the single-meal discipline and remained constantly seated. While traveling through Shixing, he stayed overnight beneath a tree, where a tiger came to rely upon him.

He followed [the invitation] and arrived in Jinling during the Daming era. When Emperor Taizu of the Qi dynasty ascended the throne, he issued an edict for him to go to Liaodong to propagate and promote the methods of Chan.
After residing there for two years, he retired to Mount Lingyuan in Qiantang. During a year of severe drought, one night he saw an old man bowing before him and say, "I am a dragon, your disciple.
I dwell on Mount Chitingshan in Fuyang. All the dragons of that mountain are my kinsmen."
"Brother, however, the nature of dragons is prone to poisonous wrath. Only I, a disciple who studies the Buddha's teachings, am somewhat benevolent.

Now, the people of Fuyang have, for no reason, excavated the foot of the mountain and severed the geomantic veins of the earth. Consequently, the dragons are enraged and have not sent down rain for over two hundred days.
Although I have earnestly remonstrated with them, they will not listen. Only the Master, whose virtue and Way are most exalted, can [bring them to compliance]."
