"Go and preach the Dharma to instruct them; by praying for blessings on behalf of all living beings, you will bring great benefit to the multitude of dragons—this would be most fortunate.
Hui-chao declined, saying, "The road is steep and far away; it is not a place where one can reach with staff and sandals. The old man said, "This is easy.
If the Dharma Master is willing, I shall serve as your bed and seat; what need is there for concern? Suddenly, a donkey appeared carrying Hui-chao, and they traveled until they reached the mountain.
Immediately, a heavy rain fell. The district magistrate learned of this and hurriedly had the people prepare boats to welcome Hui-lin and Hui-fan back.
Later, the old man came to Hui-chao to express his gratitude. Hui-chao told him that the area lacked good drinking water and it would be difficult to settle the community there.
The old man clapped his hands and a spring gushed forth; its taste was sweet and crisp. This is the present-day Lingyuan Fuzhang Spring (Clapping-Hands Spring).
Sengjing of Qi was a native of Nanhai. He became a śramaṇa in his youth and was extensively learned in the sūtras and śāstras.
After traveling through Jingzhou and Chu for a long time, he returned to serve as the presiding abbot of Haishan, Xiuyunfeng, and Yong’an monasteries; both clergy and laity took refuge in him.

Once, a novice monk was struck by a ghost with great force. Sengjing reviled and cursed it, whereupon the leader of the ghosts manifested its form and apologized, saying, "This was the transgression of my subordinate."
"I have offended you, Master Dharma. I look up to your great compassion; I pray that you will accept my repentance. Having said this, he prostrated himself again and departed.
At the time of his death, a wondrous fragrance filled the room, which did not dissipate for an entire day.

Fapeng of the Liang dynasty was surnamed Feng and was a native of Haiyan. His ancestors had resided in Guanjun, Nanyang. From his youth, he bore the aspiration to transcend the mundane world; however, his parents would not permit it.

He pleaded with them persistently, to which they replied, "Once you have married, you may do as you please. At the age of eighteen, he took a wife, but after only half a year, he abandoned her and left home.
He joined the monastic order at Guangxing Temple and shaved his head. He traveled to the capital and resided at Xinghuang Temple, where he followed [Master Huiyuan].
Daomeng and Tanqi studied the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* with such diligent devotion day and night that Zhang Rong of Wu Commandery sent a letter to Zhou Yong, saying:
"The ancients still left behind their children and women to carry on the family lineage; yet Master Fapeng has transcended the mundane world as if casting away snot and spittle."
Such aspirations are great and far-reaching. Later, he followed the monk Zhou of Changle Temple to study the *Samyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma*.
Tanyin of Zhuangyan Temple had traversed the virtues of various schools, extracting the profound and analyzing the abstruse; his character and spirit were preeminent.
Prince Ziliang of Jingling of the Qi dynasty once held a gathering for the discussion of doctrine at Xidi, entrusting the affairs to Zhixiu of Yecheng. Zhixiu said to Chong: "When..."

This was the response. "How do you compare to me? he asked. He replied, "First you were pleased, then you rejected me; in this, I am not your equal. You have established the names and defined the realities;
in this, you are not my equal. Xiu turned pale with shame. At the age of thirty-eight, at Zhengsheng Temple, Fayuan was skilled in the arts of divination.
He told Wang Chong that he would die at forty. Chong also looked into a mirror himself and saw a black vapor over his face. At this—
He exhausted all his wealth on robes and alms bowls, using those resources to purchase incense and lamps. He returned to the Guangxing Hall, shut his door, and engaged in ritual repentance.
For forty years, he forgot to eat or rest during the day and did not sleep at night. On a winter evening toward the end of that period, his two ears suddenly became swollen and painful;
he redoubled his vigilance and continued his repentance until the fourth watch. Then he heard a voice from outside saying, "Your karma of death has already been exhausted."
He hurriedly opened the door and saw nothing at all. When he looked there the next day, the black vapors had vanished, and the *shougǔ* (occipital eminence) behind his ear had become prominent.
In the seventh year of the Tiānjiàn era, an imperial edict appointed him as the *Sēngzhèng* (Patriarch/Chief Administrator of Monks). He moved his residence to Xuānwǔ Temple;

the temple was originally named Tiānbão, but the Emperor renamed it Xuānwǔ to cultivate merit for King Xuānwǔ and issued an edict to renovate and adorn it in preparation for his reception of imperial favor. In the fourth year of the Pǔtōng era, he experienced a spiritual resonance.

He suffered from wind-disorder (rheumatism), yet he did not cease reading scriptures or performing prostrations. He passed away on the sixteenth day of the third month in the fifth year [of the Kaihuang era].
He was seventy-four years of age. He was buried at Dinglin Temple. At that time, Zhiguo, surnamed Guan, was a native of Wu; he also resided at Guangxing Temple in Haiyan.
Sengshu resided at Gongche Monastery in Shan County; he was well-versed in various sections of the sutras, though the histories do not provide detailed accounts of him.
Huichao of the Liang dynasty was surnamed Lian; his ancestors were from Yangping in Zhaojun, but they fled to Chaoge in Zhongli to escape the turmoil.

He subsequently registered his residence there. At the age of eight, he entered the monastic life under Huitong of Jian’an Temple in Linzhi County. Huitong was a man of simple character who possessed no specialized skills;

however, Sengchao followed him with utmost obedience and never grew weary. He applied himself particularly diligently to listening to and studying the teachings, never declining to do so even amidst wind, rain, mud, or mire.

Once, a foreign monk saw him and marveled at his extraordinary qualities, saying, "He will either become a teacher of the five assemblies or a governor of the eight provinces. Later, he traveled south...

He resided at Nanjian Temple, where he received the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and other scriptures from the monk Zongshou. From that time on, he became a man of long-standing virtue and a renowned master who had experienced much;
he was particularly devoted to the school of the *Amitāyus Sūtra*. Xie Yue of the Ministry of Personnel praised him, saying, "What a gentleman this man is!

At the beginning of the Liang dynasty, an imperial edict appointed him as the Sangzheng (Director of Monks). The Emperor provided him with an official messenger, a sheep-cart, and a group of swift-footed attendants.

He was honored with ceremonial insignia and other marks of favor. Furthermore, as he held that the meaning of *prajñā* was the primary tenet of the True Dharma (*paramārtha*), he was uniquely charged with the task of conversion and guidance;
consequently, inquiries and challenges arose in abundance, yet his eloquence flowed like a cascading river.

Previously, while he had gathered disciples at the capital to lecture on the meaning of the *bodhicitta*, he saw a powerful benevolent deity of exceptionally magnificent appearance one night, who told him that on another day he would lead together those with a common affinity.
"Come and listen. When he arrived, the hall was suddenly filled with people of extraordinary appearance; they dispersed as soon as the session ended, and no one recognized them.

Such was his spiritual resonance. Furthermore, he was by nature fond of mountains and rivers; wherever he went, people were aware of him, and those who followed him as attendants extended for several li.

Upon seeing him, he transcended [worldly concerns], carrying only a staff and sandals. Hunters would consequently stop their pursuit to rest beside him. During the Tianjian era, an imperial edict was issued for him to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
He was further invited to lecture on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra in the Huilun Hall, which the Emperor personally attended.

On the sixteenth day of the fifth month in the seventh year of the Putong era, he passed away in his quarters at the monastery. His age and years of ordination are not recorded in the historical records.
Sengrong of the Liang dynasty resided at Donglin Temple in Jiujiang. He took the propagation of the Dharma through travel as his primary mission.

Previously, a family in Jiangling had been devoted to a local deity; later, Sengrong exhorted them to receive the precepts and serve the Buddha. Consequently, they demolished the shrine and sent the materials to the temple to cultivate merit.
On the seventh day, the mother of that family saw a ghost holding a red rope, intending to bind her. The mother was filled with great terror and thereupon requested [Sengrong’s intervention].

The monk had completed his recitation of the sutras and his practice of the Way. In his later years, he returned to Mount Lu; coincidentally encountering snow and rain, he stayed alone overnight at an inn.
At night, he saw a great multitude of ghostly soldiers. One ghost in particular was exceptionally robust and imposing, wearing armor and clutching a blade, while carrying a folding chair.
Facing Rong as he sat, the ghost scolded him angrily, saying, "Why is it that you always claim there are no ghosts or spirits in this world?
You may be dragged from your seat and beaten to serve as a warning for the future. Just as the ghosts were about to step forward, Rong suddenly and silently recited the name of Avalokiteśvara.
Before his thought had even ceased, he saw behind the wooden chair where the ghosts were sitting a celestial general approximately one zhang tall, wearing yellow leather trousers and a tunic.
He raised a vajra and brandished it; the ghosts were all startled and dispersed, and their armor and weapons were reduced to dust and powder.

Furthermore, in Jiangling, there was a husband and wife who had been falsely accused by bandits. The husband had already fled, but the wife was arrested. She encountered Daorong in Luoyang and pleaded for a method to save herself.
Daorong instructed her to recite the name of Avalokiteśvara. Although she was imprisoned, she continued to recite it without ceasing.
He paused for a short while. At night, he dreamed that a śramaṇa kicked him to wake him up; upon waking, all three wooden stocks were completely removed.

However, the door was bolted and locked, and the gatekeeper stood guard, so there was no way to leave. He fell back asleep, and again a voice said in his dream: "The door shall open of its own accord; you should depart quickly."

Upon exiting, the gate was indeed open, and there was no one there to question her. At that time, the sky was dark and gloomy; after traveling several li, she became suspicious that pursuers might be following her and sought refuge among the grass.

However, someone was already hidden in the grass. When she questioned him, it turned out to be her husband. Overcome with both grief and joy, they embraced and led each other away, feeling certain they would escape punishment.
Wei Chaoda’s clan and native place are unknown. When the Tuoba clan first entered China, they strictly prohibited books such as the *Chen* (prophecies) and *Wei* (astronomical portents).

Inspections were conducted with particular severity wherever these texts were found. Someone falsely accused Chaoda of possessing a great many such works, and he was immediately ordered by the authorities to be taken to the prison in Yongyang for interrogation.
Although subjected to all manner of torture, Chaoda answered truthfully and remained steadfast, refusing to confess. At that time, [the official] Bo...

Lord Lingwei received the imperial decree and subjected him to a frame-up, ordering that his neck be bound to the rim of a chariot wheel and guarded according to protocol, not permitted even the slightest moment of release during the night.
Da believed he was certain to die; nevertheless, he focused his mind single-mindedly on reciting the names of the Ten Great Bodhisattvas without ceasing.
At the fourth watch, the chariot wheel suddenly slipped away, and his neck followed by being lifted off. Looking back, he saw that all the guards were...
He fell into a deep sleep, intending to flee far away to escape. However, having been bound for a long time, his feet were cramped and he could not walk.
Limping along until dawn, the pursuers’ cavalry suddenly caught up with him. He then hid among the grass, where the raiders let their horses trample over him;
the grass was completely crushed, yet they ultimately did not discover his whereabouts. Da looked up at the raiders, seeing that each of them had something like a cowhide covering their eyes.

Thus, even though they were face-to-face, he did not see him. Alas, how extraordinary! Furthermore, there was the monk Ming, who was the head of the Shikusi (Stone Cave Temple) on the Northern Terrace.
At that time, the Emperor suspected that the śramaṇas were thieves; he ordered them all to be arrested and executed. Several hundred were captured, and Ming was actually their leader.
Consequently, he was bound in fetters and awaited his execution. Ming said, "The *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* can save one from suffering."
How could this be a falsehood? As he recited the scriptures aloud and focused his mind in prayer without ceasing, at midnight he felt his bonds grow slightly looser.

By dawn, they had all snapped and fallen away entirely, and he finally escaped. When the officials reported the matter to the Emperor, the Emperor sent men to track him down, finding no other cause for his release.
Thus, the official above also awakened to his error and repented; consequently, they both escaped harm.
Wei Daotai was a man of unknown origin who left the household life to reside at the Hengtang Vihara in Changshan.

He once dreamed that someone said to him, "When you reach forty-two years of age, it will be time for your end. At that time, Daotai was already advanced in years, and he thought to himself privately: [...that he would not live to see that age.]

Failing to regain his life, his mind was filled with profound aversion toward it. When the appointed time arrived, he fell gravely ill; believing himself unable to escape death, his anxiety and fear intensified.

Thereupon, he exhausted his resources to perform Buddhist rites, seeking to see what would come of them. A friend of his who was knowledgeable in the *Śāsanavāhana* (the vehicle of the teachings) said to him:
"I have heard that the merit of making offerings to sixty-two billion bodhisattvas is equal to that of reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara once."

"The name of Avalokiteśvara is the same as yours; why do you not take refuge in him with a sincere heart? If you do so, how could your wishes not be fulfilled? Tai was moved to realization by these words.
Thereupon, for four days and four nights, he recited the name with single-minded devotion and without slackening. Suddenly, a light shone from beneath the curtain where he sat.
Upon looking, he saw a golden figure entering through the door; between its ankles, there was a brilliant, radiant illumination.
He said to Tai, "Do you recollect Avalokiteśvara? Tai rose immediately, drew back the curtain, and intended to pay his respects, but [the apparition] vanished at once.
Consequently, he wept with a mixture of grief and joy; his body and mind felt instantly refreshed, and the ailment he suffered also healed from that point on.
It was only after a long time that he began to speak of this to others. Even in his old age, he remained remarkably robust and healthy.
During the late Wei dynasty, there was a śramaṇa named Fali, whose origins are unknown. He was resolute and practiced asceticism with great diligence.
He resolved to establish a monastery in the land of Lu, but as the necessary resources were not easily gathered, he set out for Shanggu with the novice Mingchen to beg for alms.
They obtained a cartload of hemp and returned; however, upon reaching an open marsh, a wild fire spread from all four directions, and they found themselves downwind while Fali was already exhausted.
He lay down and did not wake; Zhen cried out in distress. After a long while, smoke and flames blazed up fiercely. He rose with all his might and raised his voice, chanting the name of Guanyin.
However, before he had even reached the two characters for "World-Sound" (Shiyin), the wind shifted and the flames subsided, and he ultimately attained safety and peace.
Furthermore, when Fazhi was still a layman, he was traveling alone through a vast marsh when wild fires closed in from all sides. Judging that the situation was beyond escape...
He was spared. He then prostrated himself upon the ground and invoked the name of Avalokiteśvara while awaiting death. After a long time, he felt nothing;

looking up, he saw that the fire had already been extinguished. Rising slowly to examine the site, he saw that all the grass and trees there were reduced to ashes, yet the spot where his body lay was only large enough for him to fit—nothing else remained. From this, he knew it was the protection bestowed by the Bodhisattva.
This was the beginning of Zhì’s renunciation. Furthermore, there was Dàojí, who once traveled to the western mountains of Shòuyáng.
There he encountered two bandits who bound him to a tree and seized all his possessions. They were about to kill him, but Dàojí silently recited the name of Avalokiteśvara without ceasing.

The bandits repeatedly drew their knives to strike him, yet they could inflict no injury or damage. Believing him to be possessed by a deity, they fled in terror. Dàojí relied upon this [practice] for his safety.

Duo. Furthermore, there was the monk Chan. Once, while traveling with a companion through the mountains, they encountered bandits. Chan and his companion focused their minds solely on the recitation of Avalokiteśvara’s name;

the bandits were unable to advance. Whenever they shot at them, their bows and arrows would suddenly fall away. Terrified, the bandits cast their weapons upon the ground and surrendered themselves in sincere devotion.
This account is recorded in detail in the *Guanyin Ganying Zhuan* (Biographies of Avalokiteśvara’s Responsive Manifestations).
Senglang of the Wei dynasty was a native of Liangzhou. In the seventh year of the Shiguang era, the imperial army of the Wei attacked Xia and laid siege to Liang.
The defending general, finding his forces too few, mobilized all the monks residing within the city walls to take up positions on the ramparts. When the city fell, three thousand men were captured;
Emperor Taowu ordered them to stand before his tent and said to them, "Monks should practice seated meditation and cultivate the Way; why then have you acted as bandits?"
"Yes. Tomorrow they must all be executed. At the time of the morning meal the following day, the diviner reported that a red omen had pierced the sun;

it was not appropriate to kill the practitioners of the Way. Furthermore, the Heavenly Master Kou Qianzhi submitted a memorial to the Emperor, stating that during the campaign at Chengpi, these were truly not matters that could be settled by practitioners of the Way.
He argued that to kill them would bring misfortune. By imperial decree, their death sentences were commuted.

They continued to treat them as slaves and distributed them among the various chieftains; however, Lang and several other monks, including Sengyi and Zhan, were separately assigned to the troops under the command of Zhang Xia and sent back.
Lang and his companions plotted to escape, but as the army was just then forming ranks and marching through the mountains, there was no way to break free.
Only at one corner to the east and west was there a sheer cliff where no guards had been stationed; yet it was so steep and precipitous that it was difficult to find a foothold.

He was able to do so. Looking around, he saw a great tree nearby that grew with spreading branches and hung low; he therefore fastened the rope from his flagpole to the tree. At nightfall, he descended by means of the rope.
Once it was pitch black, the intertwining vines and sharp thorns made it difficult to move;

he could faintly hear the sounds of his comrades calling out as they searched for him, and he was seized with such terror that he could not control his ascent or descent. He said to himself, "Now I am dead. I must simply exert myself and maintain mindfulness."
The World-Honored One’s Ear. Thereupon, each struck the rock with his head, reciting silently without ceasing. After a short while, they perceived a great radiance;

even those places previously hidden from view became visible, allowing them to find their way across the level terrain. Yet it grew dark again as before. Exhausted, they lay down to sleep, using one another as pillows.
At dawn, they beheld overlapping mountain ridges and did not know where they were emerging from; they simply followed the path of the sun. Suddenly, a great...
A tiger was before them. Someone said, "We have fortunately escaped the calamity of the barbarians, yet now we enter the tiger's mouth;
what shall we do? Lang replied, "Have you gentlemen also awakened from your former darkness to this light? Is this not due to the power of your mindfulness?

Furthermore, how can you know that the arrival of this tiger is not itself a manifestation intended to guide your way? The manifestations of Bodhisattvas accord with whatever one encounters; how could it be anything other than peace?"
It cannot be fathomed by ordinary consciousness. Thereupon, he followed the tiger as it went; the tiger proceeded straight ahead, matching Lang’s pace exactly.

By noon, they reached a great highway, and the tiger was lost from sight. After seven days, they arrived at Quchi. He then traveled south through Lianghan and eventually stayed in Jingzhou for the remainder of his life.
The Wei dynasty monk Sengzhao resided at Danling Temple on Mount Tai. During the Putai era, he happened to go to Mount Rong and saw a cave beneath a cascading waterfall that could be entered.

He entered the cave and traveled for five or six *li* before emerging. Following a narrow path like a bird’s track, he traveled northeast for several more *li* until he reached a stone channel two or three paces wide, where water flowed westward, crystal clear and covered with medicinal herbs.
To the north of the canal was a three-bay tiled house. In the courtyard, ears of rice were piled high, being lightly pecked at by birds and sparrows.
On a wooden rack in the eastern room were several scrolls of yellow paper; inside were two iron mortars, along with cauldrons and other vessels, all covered in layers of dust.
There was no trace of cooking or fire anywhere. In a western dwelling sat a śramaṇa in meditative posture; green moss covered the four walls, while outside stood a dense forest.
A mountain stream hung down, cutting off all paths. After a short while, a monk about sixty years of age arrived, his eyebrows being over ten feet long.
A wooden bowl hung from his ear. Seeing him, [Zhao] was delighted. He asked where Zhao had come from and comforted him for a long time. Furthermore, he said of himself:
"Three of my fellow students have lived here to avoid the world. One has gone out on a journey and has not yet returned; another died long ago."
He appeared as if entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and was placed in a western room; yet he had never been seen there before.
He was asked again, "What is the name of the world-ruler's clan, and what is the name of his kingdom? He replied, "The kingdom is named Wei. [The other] said, "In that case, his clan is not Cao.
He replied, "My clan is Yuan; it is not Cao. Having taken pears and jujubes hidden beneath leaves from within the grove and eaten them, he later pounded the rice ears.
He prepared a meal for him and instructed him to eat his fill, saying, "Do not suspect me because I do not eat.

He asked which sutra he was studying, and [the other] replied, "The Lotus Sutra. Nanyue nodded and said, "Excellent. Since I can recite every word of the sutra hanging on the beam in the eastern house, would you like to hear it?
Zhaohui joined his palms and said, "I wish to hear it. Nanyue then recited it through the entire night until dawn. Zhaohui—

He immediately fell into a deep sleep. [The monk] said, "Just sleep; this is indeed my habitual practice. The next day, he again prepared food. [Zhaohui] apologized, saying, "I have had the good fortune to pay my respects.
I beg to take my leave for a short while; we shall make another appointment later. That monk showed no sign of lingering interest, saying only, "I am going on a journey.
My fellow student will return soon; you should wait to see him, for he will bring you great awakening. Since [Zhaohui] was now determined...
Cihao departed. After Zhao returned, he sought companions and traveled toward the mountain, but eventually lost his way and desisted.
When Master Cheng of the Wei dynasty was still alive, he had recited the *Lotus Sūtra* with diligent and tireless devotion. Upon his death, he was reborn as the fifth son of the Xue family in Hedong.
He was able to recount his past lives and expressed a particular desire to leave secular life. His father held an official post in Beisi.
The Provincial Governor followed him to Qidi Temple. There, he found the disciple from his previous life and said to him, "Do you perhaps remember when I took you across the water to Mount Lang?
I was the Meditation Master. He pointed to the spirit-tablet in the room and said, "This is my very body;
it can be removed and sent away. From then on, the family treated it with even greater reverence, fearing it might escape, and subsequently provided it with a wife.

Consequently, his supernormal power of knowing past lives was lost. Furthermore, at the beginning of the Tahe era, a eunuch in the capital suffered from the affliction of being castrated and requested permission from the Emperor to leave the household life.
An imperial edict granted his request. At the start of that summer, he returned to the mountains to shave his head and receive ordination;

he recited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and performed prostrations and repentance with great diligence. By the end of the summer, a beard and mustache had grown upon his chin and jaw. When this matter was reported to the authorities...
The Founder of the Wei dynasty marveled at this extraordinary event. From that time on, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* became highly esteemed in the capital.
During the Northern Wei, Huìníng traveled to Luoyang; he once fell ill and passed away, only to revive after seven days. He said:

"I initially followed a common laborer and was led before King Yama. I stood beneath the hall while the King sat upon it. The King ordered an official to inspect the registers. The clerk claimed there had been an error."
He was merely being pursued; his life span was not yet exhausted, so he was released and returned home. At that time, there were five other śramaṇas present:
Zhi Sheng of Baoming Temple, Ruo Dao-pin of Ban Temple, Tanmu-zui of Rongjue Temple, Daoheng of Chanlin Temple, and Baoming of Lingjue Temple.
The King sat at his desk and interrogated them all regarding their deeds throughout their lives. Zhi Sheng...
He said, "I have devoted myself solely to *dhyāna*. Daopin said, "I have recited forty-one fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Tanmozui said, "I lecture on the two sutras, the *Nirvāṇa* and the *Avataṃsaka*, and lead several thousand disciples.
Daoheng said, "I have exhorted the fourfold assembly of donors to produce all the scriptures and to carve and cast ten statues of the Buddha, [all] radiant with jewels."
He said, "Before I left the household life, I served as the Governor of Longxi and constructed Lingjue Temple. Since my ordination, I have never failed to pay my respects there.
When the King had granted his request, he further exhorted him, saying, "The Way of the śramaṇa requires that one must restrain the mind through meditation and recitation.
One should not boast of village virtues, nor engage in seeking favors, nor strive for fame and reputation. As for those who preach the sutras..."

They distinguish between self and others; relying on their own abilities, they treat all things with arrogance. Those who recruit people to create scriptures and images do so scheming for wealth and giving rise to greed, thereby becoming fully possessed of the three poisons.

Those who establish monasteries while holding office rely on their power to oppress the people. As for those who feign goodness to evade punishment, exclude them from the wisdom and sacred path of the Buddhas.

It is appropriate that such individuals be sent as common servants to deliver others to heaven. Furthermore, those such as Tanmozui, Daoheng, and Baoming should all be dispatched [to serve as attendants].

The guards in black robes escorted him away to be delivered to hell. When the matter was reported to the court, Empress Dowager Hu issued a secret edict to Xu He, the Attendant-in-Ordinary for the Yellow Gate, ordering him to search throughout the capital to inquire whether the temple name and the names of the monks mentioned by [Zhang] Ning were true or false.
Shortly thereafter, a report arrived stating that the temple’s plaque and the monks’ names were indeed in perfect agreement with what Neng had described, without any error.

Thereupon, the Empress Dowager marveled at this marvel. She issued an edict requesting one hundred monks who practiced seated meditation and recited the sutras to be constantly supported within the inner palace. Furthermore, she decreed:
"From now on, bhikṣus shall not be permitted to carry scriptures or images while wandering through the streets to beg for alms. If they have private wealth for the purpose of construction..."
[The Emperor] granted his request. Zhi Ning retired to Mount Bailu. From this time on, the Central Plains generally esteemed meditation and recitation.
Qi Zhenyu was of the Dong family of Yidu in Qingzhou; he was born blind in both eyes and was also orphaned, having no means to support himself.
Her mother took pity on her. Zhì vowed not to marry; when she was only seven years old, her mother had a skilled artisan teach her the lute (pipa) so that she might provide for their livelihood.

However, because of her brilliant nature and quick intelligence, within less than ten days she mastered the subtleties of all musical variations. It happened that there was a vegetarian assembly and lecture in her home village;
her mother took her along to listen. Yù said with joy, "If I could always obtain [instruction] such as this, how would I, a child, ever worry about [not being able to provide for our needs]?"
He was a master of ritual methods. His mother consequently abandoned all family affairs and devoted herself exclusively to guiding him; she disregarded wind, rain, frost, and snow.
Yu Bao briefly declined his advances, yet he resisted and subdued the various elites with a power that could not have been produced by mere academic learning alone.

Upon his mother’s death, he lived in a hut at her grave for five years, through both winter and summer. The scholar-officials esteemed and honored him. During the Tianbao era, Emperor Wenxuan extensively propagated [his teachings].
At the Dharma assembly, Yubiao was the preeminent leader; when he ascended the seat, his discourse exhausted the ultimate truths and fathomed the profound mysteries, being truly inconceivable.
Moreover, upon merely hearing a voice, he would immediately recall it; though separated by many years, he could still identify their names and surnames.

Among his hundreds and thousands of disciples, all had thoroughly investigated the nature of their own minds. Whenever anyone had a desire to act, he would invariably bestow upon them exhortations and admonitions. He once ordered an attendant to read a sutra.
He said: "The world-system of the Pure Lotus Flower Buddha’s land in the east is no different from the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha in the west.
He then sighed, saying: "How could the pure lands of the Buddhas be restricted to a particular direction? Yet everyone rushes toward the west."
Having no longing for the east, he used this resolute mind to find it difficult to complete his dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*).
He then made a vow to be reborn in the land of the Buddha Padmottara. Morning and night he applied himself with diligence, vowing not to remain long [in this world].

Suddenly, he brought out various garments, utensils, and implements, bestowing them as gifts upon his disciples according to their respective ranks; the assembly initially did not understand this. After the *poṣadha* ceremony, he fell ill while staying in Ye City.
The patron from the north, a member of the Wang clan, appeared in spirit, voice, and speech just as he had in life. Those who came to inquire after him flocked from the entire capital;

yet suddenly, smoke and clouds drifted in from the east, and a wondrous fragrance filled the courtyard and halls. From within it issued sounds like those of chanted hymns, clear, resonant, and lovely.
His feet gradually grew cold, yet he continued to murmur prayers and recite mantras without ceasing. Ten days after his passing, the fragrance...
His breath then ceased. The brothers of the Wang family prepared mourning garments for him, as if he were their own close relative.
The Qi monk Da was surnamed Li; he was a native of Shanggu. His physical appearance was extraordinary: he had a tiger’s head and long ears, and his two front teeth exceeded one inch in length.
Those who saw him were struck with wonder. At the age of *zhìxué* (the time for beginning formal studies), he first shaved his head and donned the robes of a monk.

He immediately set out on travels to observe the grandeur of the lecture halls at Mount Dai in the north. Having completed two years of the *jūjū* (formal monastic training), he proceeded to study the *Vinaya*. At that time, the Wei dynasty was still in power;

Emperor Xiaowen invited him to propagate and expound the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* within the imperial temple. His discourses and debates were timely and adaptive, and everyone praised his excellence. Shortly thereafter, he again took up his monk’s staff and departed.

In Luoyang, he received the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* from the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati. After residing there for a long time, Ratnamati passed away; the assembly honored his posthumous lectures, and their fame shook the regions of Yi and Gu.
Shortly thereafter, hearing that Master Daoguang had made significant revelations regarding the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, he subsequently received the Bodhisattva precepts from him.
Having long heard that Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty was propagating the Dharma, he immediately crossed the Yangtze River to the south to have an audience.

By imperial decree, the Prince’s son-in-law Yin Jun was ordered to escort him into the Chongyun Hall, where they sat together for seven nights. He expounded upon the secret and subtle mysteries, requesting to receive the precepts and become a disciple.

The Emperor then ordered him to appear before the throne every ten days. An edict was issued for him to reside at Tongtai Monastery so that he might provide instruction. Once, he encountered Master Zhi, who said: "Great..."
He was a man of great merit. Thus, the Emperor often remarked that both Dharma Master Luan and Dharma Master Da were *saṃbhogakāya* bodhisattvas in human form.

He remained for one *yuga* (twelve years) before returning to Yanzhou. At that time, Hou Jing was governing the Administration Bureau (*xingtai*) and had constructed the Changliu Temple on Mount Tianguan to welcome him.
However, Da reflected that his own body was merely a vessel of suffering, insufficient to sustain the Dharma, and suddenly—

He consumed only medicinal fungi and abstained from grains, vowing to remain in this state until the end of his retribution. Shortly thereafter, Emperor Fei of the Wei dynasty issued an edict for Daoren to travel to the capital of Ye with Gao Longzhi;

there, they jointly conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon Prince Zhongshan. When the Qi dynasty succeeded the Wei and Emperor Wenxuan ascended the throne, he treated him with exceptional courtesy and respect.
He returned to pay his respects and receive honors on ten occasions in total, including an imperial decree to reside at the foot of Huanghua Ridge on Mount Linlü.
He established Honggu Temple. He also converted the old shrine of Shenwu into Dingkou Temple, allowing people to come and go and dwell there.
When he first arrived and was about to undertake the construction of Honggu, a tiger blocked his path so that he could not enter. He prayed, saying: "I wish to build this temple here."
"By means of this merit, may the spirit be comforted. If you permit it, I shall depart. The tiger immediately left.

One day, while they were deliberating on returning to Ye but had not yet set out, they saw at night someone in yellow robes prostrating and kneeling. He identified himself as Dai Shan Hu and said, "The King has prepared offerings for you in the Three Valleys;
I pray that you do not return. Da replied, "If we remain in the mountains, those who benefit will be few; if we stay in the capital, those who..."
"The benefit will be great. I, a poor monk, act according to the capacities of beings; do not discourage me.

That night, an old woman entered the room and offered him rice cakes, saying, "I am but a servant of the mountain deity. Now that you, a monk, are performing the ritual of prostrating before the Buddha, you have omitted my name alone—is this not partiality?
It would be well if you could include me in the invocation as well. Da refused the cakes but granted her request.
He continued his practice there. After he had been reciting scriptures for the mountain deity for over a month, he lost the dog he kept.

Da heard of this and said, "This must have been because the minor Daoist was not careful, and you, donor, warned him, thereby bringing calamity upon the dog. He questioned him in detail, and the Daoist replied:
I was originally reading the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, but by mistake I had substituted it with the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. Thereupon, I made this vow:
"Although I read other scriptures yesterday, may their merit also belong to the donor. Not long after, a dog emerged from a hole;
looking at its crown, I saw marks of a tiger’s bite, thereby knowing that [the previous danger] was due to a tiger. This occurred on the seventh day of the sixth month in the seventh year of Tenpō.

He finally passed away at Kutsugū-ji at the age of eighty-two. The Imperial carriage rushed to the site, and the courtiers wailed in mourning; the six armies cried out in such grief that their voices shook the mountains and forests.
He was buried in the valley, and a stele was erected beneath a cliff.
Sengquan was by nature gentle and quick-witted. While traveling and practicing at the Ye capital, he studied the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* at Dazhuangyan Monastery.
In the summer of the fourth year of the Wuping era, a visiting monk fell ill and sought refuge in the monastery; the community loathed him and no one was willing to accept him.

Quan, however, observed that his discernment and capacity were vast and profound, and his conduct was upright and refined, so he invited him into his own quarters and lived with him. Even when the visitor became filthy and unclean, Quan did not turn away from him.

They felt compassion for him. As their feelings of intimacy grew day by day, they occasionally inquired about what he was studying. When he replied that it was the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, they all rejoiced all the more because he shared their same field of study.
Furthermore, they would periodically extract difficult passages from the sutra to question him, and he would unravel and explain them all without the slightest hesitation.
Tong was increasingly delighted. He personally prepared medicinal decoctions for him and attended to him morning and evening without showing the slightest sign of weariness.

Once, at night, he took a cup of wine and offered it to him, saying, "This will dispel dampness and relax the qi; taking it according to the regulations does no harm. The guest then frowned, took a single sip, and stopped.
When the summer retreat ended and the guest prepared to depart, Tong said, "The time for the distribution of winter robes is fast approaching. This is the custom of our official monastery..."

"I have received some robes as a gift; you may wait for three or five days, and I shall have something to bestow upon you. The guest firmly declined, but Sengtong also insisted on keeping him and presented him with the robes.
As they were about to part, he took Sengtong’s hand and cautioned him, saying: "In cultivating the Way, one must not deceive even in a dark room.
Yesterday, you honored me with wine; this was improper. At that time, I did not dare refuse you abruptly only for fear of offending your kind intentions."
"From now on, you should sever this and no longer attend to such matters. Later, he added, "As for Drumshan Shikusi (Drum Mountain Cave Temple), will you ever be able to reach it?
The temple where this humble monk resides is exactly five *li* north of the cave. To the east of the winding stream station, there is a small valley;
exiting toward the east, one finds the small temple known as Zhulin (Bamboo Grove). If there is a karmic affinity, I hope you will not begrudge the journey."
Once, Tong said, "I deeply appreciate these admonitions. I intend to express my gratitude through action.

The following summer, an imperial decree was issued stating that as there were few monks at Shikusi Temple, it was appropriate to assign over one hundred monks from the official temples of Zhuangyan, Dingguo, Xingsheng, and Zongchi to serve as a single rotation at Shikusi for the summer retreat.
Tong happened to be included among their number; however, he reflected alone that this was like [being a bamboo shoot].

"The appointment regarding the forest can be sought from you. Whenever I inquired about that temple during various assemblies, the crowd would invariably laugh and say, 'This is merely a vulgar and false tradition;
do not believe it. Tongxi was always telling the assembly that the account of the traveling monk was not a false tradition."
The multitude marveled at this. Together they carried incense and flowers and followed the path as it led on.
Upon ascending a ridge, they saw an old man with a cloth tied around his forehead, wearing a loincloth and coarse garments, holding a hoe and driving a horse as he cleared the wasteland on the slope.

Seeing the monks from afar, he let go of the horse and stepped forward, saying, "What kind of practitioners are you, who do not take the road but come directly here? They replied, "We are monks from the stone cave; we wish to go [there]."
"Zhulin, have you not lost your sense of direction? The old man suddenly spoke with angry reproach: "The monks of that official temple are truly beyond reproach.
Last year they let their livestock graze there, devouring my field crops. My son tried to protect them and was nearly beaten to death."
"Now, with what face shall you see me? he cried, and finally dragging his hoe, he pursued the assembly of monks. Thereupon, the monks fled in all directions toward the eastern valley to return home;
however, he alone did not pursue Tong. He said to Tong, "I release you to enter the mountains to be devoured by tigers.
Tong then went out another several li to the east. The mountain stream he passed through was clear and shallow, while the forest trees were lush and dense. Following the stream to the east, he heard—
On the southern ridge, there was the sound of chanting. Tongge called out through the forest to ask where the bamboo grove was located.
In response, it was said: "Where have you come from? Are you not Master Yuantong? Tong replied, "I am. The monk immediately cleared a path through the woods and emerged.
Overwhelmed by a mixture of grief and joy, they briefly recounted their long separation. Then [the monk] said, "This place is insufficient for a detailed conversation; we must go to my small temple."
After proceeding several li further, there was a gate flanked by twin towers and long corridors with double walkways. Pines and bamboos cast a dense shade over the area.

Outside the gate, horse troughs were filled to the brim with millet and beans; they were all lacquered black with golden fittings, their spouts adorned with rings, and each was over a hundred feet long, arranged in ten rows.

The hoofprints of many animals were visible nearby; the place was swept and tidied with extreme care and purity. A monk-attendant stood to the left of the gate and said, "I shall announce you to the Great Master.
After a short while, he was led into the lecture hall and made to stand beneath the western eaves. The Master sat upon a large couch;
he appeared to be about seventy years of age and was surrounded by five or six young clerks as they consulted legal documents. An attendant offered his salutations.
Tong went to pay his respects to the Upādhyāya, who said, "The official temple provides such generous offerings that it is difficult to leave;
why have you deigned to visit? Tong fully explained the circumstances. Once he had been settled, the monk took Tong on a tour of the quarters to inquire after them.

Upon reaching two rooms, they were adorned with magnificent curtains and necklaces of pearls. The host sat there with an air of indifference, waving his hand and saying, "Why must this man be sent away?"
The monk felt ashamed. He looked at Sengtong and said, "Our inclinations differ; you are obstructing my purpose. For now, go and rest in your small room.

Thereupon they lingered together in conversation, and he provided them with a midday meal. The food tasted like ordinary worldly fare. After eating, they toured the images, gardens, ponds, pavilions, and galleries.
Sengtong thought of staying there and informed the monk of his intention. The monk replied, "It is indeed a humble monk's [dwelling]."
This is my heart’s intention. However, you must inform the Great Abbot [Dàhéshàng]. We shall sleep together tonight; at dawn, we will go together to inform the Abbot.

The Abbot said, "I fully understand your purpose and do not begrudge a single room. Nevertheless, since you have already accepted an invitation from an official and yet wish to stay here as well, this would be to register your name in two places.
A monk following the Vinaya may not register his name in two places. For now, you should return; wait until after the mourning period."
He said, "I have come from Guan Temple; let us be reconciled. Please do not harbor resentment. He then dismissed the monk, sending him out.
Tong was filled with regret and could not bear to part. From this point on, he set out toward the west, looking back again and again with lingering affection.

At first, the temple gate still appeared to be a hundred paces away, but after traveling another two li, it suddenly vanished from sight. All the places where the old man had cleared the wasteland the day before were now overgrown with weeds.
There are only *mianjing* shrubs and *zhen* bushes, where foxes appear and disappear. The *Ruren ruzhong lun* (Treatise on Entering the Mahāyāna) states:
"The Venerable Piṇḍola, Rāhula, and the other sixteen great arhats are scattered among various mountains and islands. Another sutra further states:
"Nine hundred and ninety million great śrāvakas all took voting sticks before the Buddha and remained in the world for their entire lifespans, all dwelling together in the three [realms]."
Somewhere within the mountains and seas, there is one who protects the True Dharma; is this not the very person encountered by Tong?
It is indeed so. Daofeng of Qi had three disciples who lived together at Gushan in Xiang; they did not practice begging for alms.
He maintained a furnace for fire and used yellow and white medicinal herbs to provide for himself. Once, Emperor Gaozu passed by and questioned him;

his responses were not premeditated, yet they were appropriate to each matter. The Emperor consequently granted him wine and a steamed piglet, which he immediately drank and ate until he was drunk and full, without declining anything.
After the Emperor had departed, Fēng summoned his disciples and said, "Clear away the objects beneath my bed. When they lifted the bed, [they found...]
Upon returning, he found that the steamed pig, wine, and other items were still there exactly as before; people considered this a marvel.

At that time, there was a monk at Shikusi Temple who believed he had attained realization through his own practice of *zazen*. Every evening, he would gaze toward the mountain peak to the east and see a golden image eighteen feet tall.
The monk rejoiced in private, claiming that the sacred image appeared solely for him and that others could not perceive it. He read...
More than two months later, while lying in bed at night, he heard a voice from between his pillows saying, "There is no other Buddha in the world;
now you have already attained the Way—you are a Buddha yourself. You must cherish yourself; do not treat the Buddha-body with such negligence.
Thereupon, the monk became arrogant and self-important, regarding his peers as mere weeds. Whenever he spoke, he would point to his chest and look at the assembly, saying: [He was a Buddha.]

"Do you also recognize the true Buddha? Since clay stupas, niches, and painted images are incapable of preaching the Dharma or saving sentient beings, yet you all take them to be the Buddha and falsely pay them homage and respect—how then can you be said to know the true one?

This is an act that leads to rebirth in the Avīci Hell. Furthermore, [those who do so] have eyes that are entirely bloodshot and cry out incessantly for impermanence; thus, an entire monastery regards [such objects as the Buddha]."
He was insane. They carried him to the residence of [Wang] Feng and had him treated. Feng hurriedly asked, "Did you see the golden Buddha on the eastern mountain?

He replied, "Yes. Feng asked again, "Did you hear voices from between your pillows? He replied, "Yes. Feng said, "This is merely a loss of mind due to wind; if not treated early, it will be difficult to control.
He then applied needles to three points, and [the patient] recovered well. When Feng was about to pass away, he pointed this out to his [son].
The disciple said by the side of the hearth, "I have long labored for you fetching water from the valley; now I repay you with this.
He then took a square stone from that spot, and a dark spring appeared, clear and reflecting.
Despite passing through droughts and floods, it neither overflowed nor ran dry, and it remains to this day.
Sengbao of the Qi dynasty possessed a strong memory; he was able to recite more than two hundred fascicles of sutras by heart.
In the third year of the Wuping era, while traveling from Bingzhou toward Ye, he lost his way at Ailing and mistakenly entered a range of chaotic mountains.

At dusk, seeking a place to lodge for the night, he saw from afar a single chamber beneath a cliff that appeared to be inhabited. Upon approaching it, however, it was silent. Exhausted, Sengbao sat down before the chamber.
Upon the rock, he looked up and saw pine branches from which a stone chime (qing) hung more than ten feet above the ground; his mind was already struck by its extraordinary nature.
At the second watch of the night, a monk clad in grass garments arrived from outside. He remarked, "How can such worldly air be present here? Bao hurried forward to pay his respects.

He related the circumstances of his arrival in detail. After a short while, he asked Baohui, "In which country do you currently reside, and what is your surname? Baohui replied, "I am from the state of Qi, and my surname is Gao.
Baohui then asked, "How long has your venerable master resided here? He replied, "I have been here since the time of the Later Han dynasty. Baohui further asked, "Which sutra is your field of study?"
Baofang, relying on his own extensive learning, was somewhat arrogant in his responses. The monk said, "A practitioner of the Way should not be like this.
Which sutra do you also enjoy hearing? I shall recite it for you. Baofang replied, "I enjoy hearing the *Avataṃsaka*. The monk recited it;
the tone and rhythm were harmonious, fluent, and perfectly resonant—truly beyond anything to be found in the mundane world. In a mere moment, the entire volume was completed. The rest...
He recited them all in this manner. Bao was struck with awe and marveled that he could not equal him. The monk said, "You possess a mind of conditioned action (*saṃskṛta-citta*);
I possess a mind of non-action (*asaṃskṛta-citta*). For one who has forgotten their attachment to things, things truly cannot create any obstruction.

Bao awakened to his spiritual sanctity and requested to remain under his guidance. The monk said, "Since you have come here for the sake of material offerings (*lābha-satkāra*), how can you possibly find peace [in my company]?"
"How desolate! Moreover, since your emotional attachments have not yet been cast off, it would be of no benefit for you to remain here.
At dawn, he took his leave and departed. Sengyun of the Qi dynasty was skilled in rhetoric and eloquence; he had long been well-versed in the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras.
He resided at Baoming Temple in Ye, where it was his constant custom to recite the precepts every half-month during the summer retreat. One year, Yun suddenly addressed the assembly, saying:
Now, as for the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, those who have left the household life are able to recite it from memory; why then should it be recited so many times as to weary the great assembly?
From this day forward, one monk should be appointed to expound its meaning, so that future generations may gain enlightenment through hearing and seeing.

The assembly followed this proposal, and none dared to oppose it. When the time for the *Pravāraṇā* ceremony arrived and he was about to ascend the seat, Daoyun’s whereabouts were lost; thereupon, [the crowd] surged and scattered in all directions.
He went out in pursuit and found him inside an ancient tomb about three *li* from the side of the monastery. His entire body was covered in blood, as if he had been struck by sharp blades.

When asked the reason for this, he replied: "A man appeared, brandishing a great sword three feet long, with a fierce expression and shouting at the clouds, 'How dare you recklessly change the *poṣadha* ceremony into a formal lecture? He intended to mince and stab my body, and thus I have been mangled."
He collapsed; his suffering was unbearable, and the multitude carried him home. He repented with all his heart, and for ten years he did not fail in his regular duties.
On the day of his death, his countenance remained undisturbed, and a rare fragrance welcomed him. This was indeed the proof of his self-reproach and diligent cultivation.

Seng’an of the Qi dynasty was a man of unknown origins. He was rigorous and meticulous in observing the Vinaya, and his expositions on Chan and the sutras were elegant and fluent; thus, contemporary acclaim was bestowed upon him.
During the reign of Emperor Wenxuan, Seng’an gathered some two thousand disciples at Mount Wangwu to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

As soon as he began the introductory discourse, a female pheasant came and settled beside his seat as if listening. At mealtime, it would go out to drink and peck for food, and by the time of the evening lecture, it would return to settle and listen as before.
At the beginning, [the hen] had not returned after reaching the third fascicle. The assembly marveled at this. Dao’an said, “The hen has now been born into the human realm.
In the fourth year of the Wuping era, while Dao’an was practicing the dhūta austerities in Yuezhou, he went directly to a certain house and called out for a female hen.
A girl came out to meet him, prostrated herself, and rejoiced. The girl’s parents considered this strange and invited him in to provide food. Dao’an asked why...
"Why is this girl named 'Cock Hen'? He replied, "It is because when she was first born, her hair resembled the feathers of a pheasant.
Dao'an laughed heartily and recounted the original circumstances of the name. Upon hearing this, the girl wept bitterly and earnestly requested to leave the household life.

Her parents joyfully granted her permission. At that time, the girl was fourteen years old; when the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was preached for her, she understood it immediately upon hearing it. This continued until the third fascicle, where—

He was unable to communicate anything further. From that time on, he ascended the seat to preach, and people from far and near flocked to attend. He spoke of his past causes, and the assembly urged him even more.
Zhou Daomiao, whose religious name was Sengmiao, was originally a native of Jizhou and later moved to Pufan in Hedong. He was intelligent and wise.

He attained maturity at an early age. He maintained the Vinaya with rigorous discipline and read extensively across all categories of literature. He was particularly adept at lecturing and exposition; yet, by nature, he was humble, modest, and retiring.
Whether in joy or anger, he never allowed his emotions to be seen upon his countenance. Every time he descended from his seat, he would invariably join his palms in repentance, saying:
"How could the Buddha’s intent be fathomed by an ordinary person? What I have now preached was transmitted to me by my former teachers; it was by no means my own invention. I hope..."
The great assembly examined his conduct to discern right from wrong; they were filled with joy at his acts of giving, and consequently, followers gathered like clouds.
He soon returned to Changnian Temple in his native village—which was Renshou Temple—where Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty showed him exceptional respect.

During the Datong era, when Buddhist relics were presented from the Western Regions, an imperial edict ordered them to be sent to Miaosi for veneration. [Sengxiu] received them upon his head and circumambulated them day and night, gazing up at them as if they were the Buddha himself.

This was one year later. Suddenly, at midnight, light radiated from within, filling the entire room. It wound its way out through a crack in the window, spreading in all directions until it illuminated the world beyond heaven and earth.
Everyone thought a fire had broken out and rushed to rescue [the house]. Upon arriving, they saw a golden vase shimmering brilliantly.
Everyone offered praise without exception. Miaoshan then burned incense and knelt to petition, saying, "The sentient beings have already beheld the holy traces;

I pray that you may now conceal this numinous image, returning to stillness and merging with the void. Thereupon, the light gradually spiraled and entered the vase. That night, the sound of joyful shouts was heard for dozens of li.
Yet there was one monk in the temple who, lying within his room, alone did not perceive it; even when others shook him and called out to him, he remained unaware.
He remained as he was. Before long, he suffered from a pestilential illness; it is said this was brought about by his karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*).

As for what is currently called "Buddha-bone," since the passing of Miaozhi, its radiance has no longer appeared. Nevertheless, the *Nityaparinirvāṇa-sūtra* contains certain passages and phrases [that address this].

Adapting to circumstances and making decisive judgments, his lectures varied with each occasion; thus, the most eminent scholars among his disciples were won over by his excellence and followed his teachings.
In the regions where his influence flourished, the consumption of alcohol and meat was entirely eliminated, and even onions and garlic were suddenly forbidden and suppressed.
The customs beyond the river changed abruptly—could this not have been brought about by his instructions? Written by the disciple Tanyan. (See separate entry).

Biography. Zhou Huitian was a native of Shangdang. He resided at the Kaifu Temple established by the Yuan clan within the commandery. He lived alone in a single room, dedicating himself to the practice of dhyāna and repentance.
In the sixth year of the Jiande era, an imperial edict abolished the Buddhist teachings; Huitian took the scriptures and images and fled into the deep mountains. A band of robbers...

They plotted to kidnap him, yet Li Tan was unaware of it at first. Suddenly, he saw a man over ten feet tall with handsome whiskers and a fine countenance, wearing a gauze cap and a green robe, with a golden belt adorned with nine rings and boots made of *jibao* leather.

Mounted on a white horse with crimson mane, the man came straight from the mountain peak to Tan’s presence. Dismounting, he saluted him and said, "Thieves will arrive tonight; you should flee at once. Tan looked toward his residence.
The cliffs were so precipitous that they were not a place for human passage; yet, having happened to encounter him there, he felt that this must surely be due to the mountain’s numinous spirit.
He then said, "In this region, the Buddha-Dharma has been nearly extinguished, let alone for a poor monk such as myself.

If I am not protected by the grace of your patronage, my life will end in death. Even if I wished to avoid these bandits, where could I possibly go? The man replied, "Since you have spoken with such sincerity, Master..."
The disciple dared not disobey. "I would be fortunate indeed to remain here; there is no other purpose," [the deity said], and then it vanished.

That night, a heavy snow fell, reaching nearly a zhang in depth. On another day, the bandits' schemes were still not at an end. The deities of the various villages below the mountain dreamed that their god was proclaiming everywhere:

"The bandits are plundering Master Tian; you must surely rescue him! Thereupon, they admonished one another and each prepared weapons before entering the mountains, where they encountered the bandits.
On the way, the multitude fought with great vigor, and the rebels then scattered and fled. From that time on, Yuan Tian constantly relied upon this [place] to advance in his studies.
Later, Dao Mu of Songzi during the Liang dynasty, who by nature loved springs and rocks, entered Shenshan in Jingzhou to live in seclusion.

Suddenly, there arose a thunderous storm with fierce winds; rocks were dislodged and trees uprooted, while snakes and tigers roamed about him on all sides. Yet Dao Mu remained exceptionally calm and undisturbed.

Terrified and cowed, the one in meditative concentration gazed far and high for seven days and beheld that land: to the east it leaned against a deep ravine, and to the west it overlooked a profound stream.

He was moved by a sense of resolve to spend his final years there. Thereupon, a mountain deity manifested its form and identified itself as Tian Boyu to apologize for its transgressions, requesting to receive the precepts.
From that time on, the local community ceased all sacrifices involving pungent herbs and meat, and [the region was spared from] drought.
Lao responded to prayers for rain and drought. He resided there for thirty years, and among his visiting friends and guests, there were none from whom he did not welcome them, regardless of distance.
Among the śramaṇas were Sengzhan and Sengan; among the eminent scholars were Liu Qiu and Che Zui.
Prince Xiangdong Yi, admiring his pure virtue, erected a pavilion and a stele to commemorate their bond of friendship. Emperor Jianwen composed a eulogy to narrate his [virtue].
His character was refined and dignified. He erected his monument at the summit; it was only after ascending to the highest peak in his later years that he passed away.
Thus, his resolve remained unchanged from beginning to end. He lived to the age of seventy.
Tánxún of the Sui dynasty was born into the Yang clan of Huáyīn in Hóngnóng; later, his family moved to Héduō.

At the age of twenty-two, he traveled to Línluò Quán Temple on the northern slopes of Báilù Mountain. Delighted by its tranquility and seclusion, he took refuge under the Zen Master Tánzhǔn and received the tonsure.
Having received full ordination, he practiced the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*. At that time, Zen Master Sēngchóu was leading his disciples at Cānggǔ. On the way—

The terrain was extremely remote and obstructed. Whenever he contemplated performing his devotions, he would press through thorns and brambles, trample over sand and gravel, and scale heights by pulling himself up along ledges, bypassing established paths and heading directly toward the site as his guide for practice.
As he traveled back and forth seeking instruction, his resolve remained fixed upon right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).

Though he encountered hardship and difficulty, he never faltered in his progress; he would often say: "Rather than losing the Way and yet happening to reach my destination, it would be better to remain here."
He lived there until his life came to an end in accordance with the Way. Shortly thereafter, he moved again to Lùtǔ Valley. Where the springs had run dry, they overflowed once more;
deer and elk became tame and docile, leading the students to rejoice together. Once, someone who had stolen vegetables from the garden was stung by a swarm of bees;

his entire body swelled with pain as he neared death. When Xun was consulted on how to treat him, he recovered. On another occasion, while walking alone, he encountered two tigers fighting; Xun parted them using his ritual staff (*xi-zhang*).
Yi said, "We have lived together in these woods; in my estimation, there has been no great disagreement between us. It would be fortunate if we were each to depart.
One day, a person came forward to pay his respects and said, "I am a man of Zhao. Recently, I died from illness, and King Yama declared that I deserved to be sent to prison for my offenses.
However, thanks to the plea of Dhyāna Master Tanxun for my life, I have been released and returned here. Furthermore, I have long been a stranger to the Master."
Having been born, I have received such profound grace; how could I dare not offer my prostrations of thanks? I once inquired whether he remained fixed for seven days;

even though a tiger’s den was at his door, he felt no concern. Consequently, the courtyard grew overgrown with weeds and the paths became filthy, as birds and beasts shared his dwelling. Yet, wherever his fame and radiance reached, [all were transformed].
Those to the north of the River submitted with joy; carrying staffs and wrapping themselves in provisions, they flocked there until the doorsteps were filled with visitors.

During the Kaihuang era, the Emperor issued an edict to Yuan Shou, a General of the Third Grade, to convey his sincere devotion by sending incense and offerings. He passed away in the nineteenth year at Bajian Mountain Temple.
He was eighty-five years old and had fifty-five summer retreats. When he first manifested signs of illness, there were extraordinary occurrences of divine light and fragrant incense.
A bird with a white neck and a red body flew about, crying out mournfully as it circled the monastery grounds; it gradually approached the hall steps and came even to his sitting mat.

It grew so familiar with people that it showed no fear. When he closed his eyes, the bird cried out in extreme distress; its blood boiled from within its eyes, and it whirled through the empty air before alighting [upon him].
He passed away upon the earth. Clouds darkened and mists grew gloomy; forests and mountain streams were choked and obstructed. The signs of decay within the mountains are beyond full description.
On the twelfth month of the fifth year of the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, his disciples Jinglin and others performed the cremation.
They constructed a stupa for his remains and erected a stele, with the śramaṇa Mingze composing the inscription.
Hongyang of the Sui dynasty was a native of Ye. By nature he observed the monastic precepts and resided at Daci Temple in Xiangzhou.

Having lost his sight in both eyes due to the exhaustion of his lifelong study and recitation, he required assistance for every movement; consequently, people grew weary of him, and he lived constantly in a single room.

He performed his daily liturgical recitations without ceasing morning and evening. In the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era, a voice suddenly resounded from the air, identifying itself as a *prajñā* donor who had come to receive the precepts from him.
From that time on, he conversed with it several times, as was the common custom of the world.
Master Senggang, who had previously shared a cell with Xian, once went up to the hall for midday meals; at that moment, *Prajñā* offered him a robe.

Houxian presented it, saying, "I have labored to perform these religious services; the benefit [thereby] provided is no small matter. He insisted that it must be accepted. Shortly thereafter, Hui-gang returned and was surprised to find his robe and satchel missing.

He searched throughout the temple until he finally found them inside Houxian’s box. Houxian felt deeply ashamed and begged for forgiveness, claiming the items were actually offerings for the *Prajñāpāramitā* service.
However, Hui-gang ultimately did not believe him. Soon after, the interior of Hui-gang’s room became a scene of disorder, with its chests and caskets overturned.
[The spirit] was perverse. He overturned the mats and bedding, broke the poles and fans, and threw them away. From mid-air, he reviled Gong, saying:
"In your entire life, you have never made offerings to the Triple Gem. Now I am merely giving you a small warning; later, great calamity shall befall you.

Although Gong was blind, his conversation with the Prajñā [spirit] was as clear as if he were seeing before him. He once said to Gong: "My companions are extremely numerous; they are all in the Purple [Palace]."
"On the banks of the Mo River, there are only thirty people accompanying me. You may now provide a meal for the temple community.

Once the meal is finished, you may then praise its excellence from the air as a token of gratitude. Furthermore, since the net has not provided a vegetarian feast, he intends to bring disaster upon the net."
Having no other choice, Daoweng then prepared the offerings according to the Dharma. A voice from the air announced, "Since you are able to do this, I shall rejoice with you.
He further presented two rolls of silk as an offering, instructing that one be given to the assembly and the other used to compensate Daoweng.
It is said that Daoweng relied on these offerings to further advance in his practice. Later, he eventually passed away at the monastery.

Faqing of the Sui dynasty resided at Ningguan Temple northwest of the capital. In the third year of the Kaihuang era, he was constructing a sixteen-foot standing Śākyamuni image made of layered cloth and lacquer at the temple;
however, before the lacquer and cloth were applied, Faqing passed away. On that same day, the monk Dazhi of Baochang Temple also passed away.
Three days later, he revived and said: "At first, I drifted as if riding upon the wind, traveling for what seemed like a hundred [li]."

After about a *li*, he saw the palace gradually coming into view, magnificent and ornate like the residence of a sovereign. A man sat there wearing the *guǎnmian* robes and crown, with his attendants and ceremonial guards standing solemnly on either side.
After a short while, Sengqing suddenly arrived, looking deeply distressed. Yet another moment later, the image appeared and said to the seated man, "Sengqing has not yet finished constructing me;
why have you died so abruptly? The seated man hurried down from the hall to prostrate himself, calling out to his attendants and questioning them.
He asked, "Is Qinghe about to die? He replied, "Her life-force is not yet exhausted; it is simply that her food has run out.
Those sitting there said, "If this is so, let us provide lotus leaves for her to sustain her life until its end. Subsequently, they lost sight of both the image and Qinghe's whereabouts.
Thereupon, Baochang immediately dispatched someone to go and observe Ningguan, and everything he had said was proven true. From then on, Qinghe ceased her fasts and consumed six lotus leaves daily.
Eight pieces for the midday meal. The method is to first soak them in hot water to soften and moisten them before consuming them.
Furthermore, one should exert all effort and exhaust all resolve to complete the image, performing prostrations and repentance throughout one's entire life.
Huiyun of the Sui dynasty was a native of Fanyang. At the age of twelve, he left home to study under a teacher, traveling about without ever flagging in his diligence.
When he reached eighteen, he returned to visit his family; at that time, he was riding a donkey that was swift, spirited, and lovely. His paternal uncle, Gui, desired to possess it.
Consequently, when Huiyun stopped at his father’s house, his father intended to kill him in order to take the donkey; just as he was grasping a blade, he saw a man in yellow robes to the east.
Beneath the wall, he raised his fist and shouted, "This is surely a Great Being who circulates the Dharma; you must not harm him.
His father was terrified and returned home to tell his wife. The wife said, "Your eyes are playing tricks on you; how could such a thing exist?
The father went back again and saw the man in yellow robes from before beneath the western wall, repeatedly shouting, "Do not kill! Do not kill! If you kill, calamity will descend upon you!"
Huiyun was about to visit his elder sister’s house. His father feigned reluctance, saying, "The road is perilous and impassable;

I wish for you to have an escort. Thereupon, he took up a knife and followed Huiyun. Later, he lay in wait to strike Huiyun, but suddenly his sister’s servant stood by the side. The father was immediately filled with shame and apologized.
During the Kaihuang era, the Buddhist teachings flourished, and Huiyun was particularly renowned throughout the land for his extensive mastery of the sūtras and śāstras.

Leading five hundred disciples, he traveled to his hometown to visit his paternal uncle. The uncle and his wife were filled with remorse; they offered ten bolts of silk and requested that Yun perform a rite of repentance for their sins.
It was through this that Yun first learned of the matter, yet even then, he never harbored resentment or regret. He would always recount this incident as an example.
Jiemen said: "How could the beauty of things merely burden oneself? It also burdens the thoughts of others. Later, his final whereabouts were unknown.
Huigong of the Sui dynasty was the son of the Zhou family in Chengdu, Yizhou; he entered the monastic order and was particularly close with Huiliang of the same monastery.

Qicheng: After Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty abolished the Buddhist teachings, Huiyuan traveled far to the Guanzhong region, while Fayong respectfully visited the Jing and Yang regions to pursue his studies and gather teachings.
In this way, they were separated for more than thirty years. When Huiyuan returned to lecture in his native village, Fayong also arrived from Jiangnan.
Having been parted for so long, their joy at this brief reunion was beyond words. Thereupon, from dusk until dawn, Fayong recounted all that he had acquired. Fayong—
Hui-gong remained silent and said nothing at all. Hui-yuan pressed him persistently, so Hui-gong thanked him with humility, saying, "My nature and understanding are dull and obscure;
truly, I do not know how to be enlightened. Hui-yuan asked, "Can you not at least recite a single scripture? Hui-gong, having no other choice, suddenly replied:
He could only recite a single scroll of the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*. Yuan was incensed and rebuked him, saying, "The *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* is something recited by mere children.
Why do you, sir, bring such disgrace upon yourself? Furthermore, you have practiced the Way since your youth, vowing to ascend to the stage of fruition;
yet you now recite a scripture that is barely the size of a finger. Your indolence is such that you offer no benefit to my three virtues. I request that we sever our friendship. Gong—
He said, "Although this scripture is small, it was proclaimed from the Buddha’s own mouth. Those who honor it shall gain merit; those who treat it with contempt shall incur transgression.
I pray that you, Dharma Master, will appease your anger and deign to listen to it once. Only after that shall we part ways—is this not appropriate?

Yuan laughed and said, "As for me, I have mastered the *Abhidharmakāya*, the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Dharmaskandha*, the *Tattvasiddhi*, the *Vibhāṣā*, and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*."

"The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* and other treatises have all been studied by me both superficially and deeply, such as the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*—which is indeed the 'Universal Gateway' chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
I have lectured upon it a hundred times already. Is what you are now reciting any different? Truly, I have no desire to hear it.

Wishing to shake his head and depart, he was respectfully entreated by Zeng (Gong) two or three times until he finally consented to stay. Zeng then established an altar in the courtyard and set up a seat.
Upon the altar, he circumambulated it several times, prostrated himself, and ascended the seat. At a distance, he took his place upon a low stool, leaning slightly to one side.

When the Master began to chant the title with reverence, he immediately perceived a pervasive, swirling fragrance. As the text was entered, celestial music played above and four kinds of flowers fell in profusion.
When the sutra concluded and he descended from the seat, having personally performed the ritual for concluding the session (*jie zuo fan*), both the flowers and the music ceased together.
Huiyuan started with a start, rose in alarm, and prostrated himself on the ground. Weeping, he apologized for his transgression, saying, "I, Huiyuan, am but a foul and filthy corpse;
how dare I venture beneath the light of heaven and sun? I beg you to stay but a moment and grant me your instruction. Huigong replied, "This is not within my power; it is the power of the Buddhas.
Thereupon, he offered a long farewell bow and departed.
Daoyou of the Sui dynasty was a monk who resided at Qisheshi Temple in Dazhou. He was well-versed in both the sutras and the śāstras.
During the Renshou era, he lectured on the *Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* along with its commentary at his own temple; those who came to listen numbered over a hundred.
Once, at noon, while sitting upon a rope bed with his eyes closed, he saw a man of extraordinary and magnificent appearance, who declared, "I am Śakra Devendra."
