"I have come here for no other reason than to entreat you to preach the sutras for the sake of the various devas. When they heard this from the underworld, their hearts were filled with singular regret and they took no pleasure in death.
Consequently, they sent word saying: 'We are currently constructing a Buddha hall; there are matters that prevent us from attending easily.
Upon waking, he related this to the Dharma Master Ruru, who was serving as his attendant. Ruru said, 'This is indeed a rare occurrence in the world. As for the person who passed away—'"
"I am to die once and for all. If I wish to be reborn in the heavenly realms, how could that possibly be achieved? Now, by good fortune, I have been summoned by the Heavenly Emperor;
furthermore, I have obtained the opening of the benefits of the Dharma to bring me salvation and increase. Such merit is immense. How insignificant, then, would a Buddhist hall be in comparison?"
Youxin thought this was so. After some time, he again dreamed as before, and Youxin finally granted his request.
Tian then placed a small amount of incense in Youxin’s palm and set a time to come and welcome him. Upon waking, the fragrance from his palm perfumed the entire monastery.
Thereafter, he lectured repeatedly without weariness. One day he said, "The appointed time has arrived. He then took up the incense burner, stood upright, and passed away. At that time—
Monastics and laypeople saw from outside that vapors were emerging from within the temple, ascending straight into the sky like a white silk ribbon until they vanished.
Huihuan of the Sui dynasty was born into the Guan family of Yunyang in Jingzhao. Having admired the Way since his youth, he was constrained by worldly burdens;
only after renouncing official service and marriage did he manage to don the black robes at the age of thirty-seven. He then began his studies at Qingchan Temple.

Master Chong consulted him regarding the definitive Dharma and the regulation of the duration of his breaths; he attained a state of serene clarity. Furthermore, having severed all worldly distractions, he remained with only his physical form and shadow as companions.
As the years passed through cycles of stars and frost, his adherence to these practices became increasingly rigorous. Once, while walking in meditation, he happened to fall onto a rocky ledge;
though the precipice was more than ten feet high, he sat upright and silent in the lotus posture, as if nothing had occurred.
As for the Master Zhijue: at the beginning of the Daye era, the Great Chan Ding Temple was established in the capital to honor the posthumous merit of Emperor Wen.

By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside there. He passed away in the second month of the sixth year in his quarters at the temple, at the age of sixty-nine. His final instruction was that his body be given to wild animals to devour;
however, his disciples and lay patrons could not bear this and buried him in Bianzizhu Valley on Mount Zhongnan, where they erected a stupa and inscribed a commemorative stele.
He thus composed this work to commemorate him.

Huǐhǎi of the Sui dynasty was surnamed Zhāng and was a native of Wŭchéng in Qīnghé. In his youth, he relied upon Dharma Master Jiǒng of Kuàngguó Temple in the capital Yè to study the *Nirvāṇa* and *Laṅkāvatāra* sūtras.
After five years had passed, his recitations were thorough and fluent, earning the admiration and submission of his fellow students. He further received...
The *Mahāyāna-abhidharma* [treatises] were [translated] by the Dharma Master Daoyou at Daye Temple in Qingzhou. Daoyou possessed unimpeded wisdom and eloquence, yet he served as a maritime official;

this was indeed appropriate for him. In the second year of the Daxiang era of the Northern Zhou dynasty, he came to Taopu and founded Anle Temple, where he constructed a multi-storied pavilion with the aspiration to be reborn in the Pure Land.
Suddenly, there appeared a monk named Daoquan, who carried a painted image of Amitābha Buddha.

It is like a single scroll. It records that from Qizhou, it was said: "This is the Five-Supernatural-Powers Bodhisattva of the Kītamukha Monastery in the Western Heaven, traveling through the air to the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Regarding what was depicted therein, the ocean meets with the profound; he applied himself with even greater diligence.
Having beheld the divine light, his joy and gratitude became all the deeper. In the fifth month of the fifth year of the Daye era, he raised his five fingers and addressed his disciples:
He said, "I shall pass away at this very place. On the night of the fifth day, he rose from his seat, faced west, and performed prostrations;
at dawn, he passed away. He was sixty-nine years of age. He had lectured on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* thirty times and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* fifty times.
On the ninth day of that very month, he was buried at the monastery. Wang Shen of Langye, a Secretariat Scholar, composed the inscription for his stele.

Zhitong of Sui was from Yi-zhi in Hedong; his surname was Cheng. He entered the monastic order at the age of ten and recited the scriptures and prostrated before the Buddha without the slightest negligence.
When he reached the age of fifty, even though it was a time when the Dharma gate was in decline, he followed Master Yan Zhun.
The Dharma Master traveled about to propagate his teachings. When the Sui dynasty first arose, he returned to Puzha to establish a monastery.

There, he provided for the destitute, the orphaned, the solitary, the infirm, the aged, and those with no one to turn to, numbering in the thousands every day. At the beginning of the Renshou era, he once again cast off his shoes to dwell among the crags, following the ancient model.
In the seventh year of the Daye era, he fell ill; he immediately commanded his attendants to recite the name of Amitābha and prayed for [his own rebirth].
He was reborn in that land. Shortly thereafter, the *karmadāna* struck the bell to assemble the community, but the pestle broke.

Those who understood the signs knew that he would not rise again. At that time, his disciple Dinggai was attending by his side. Tong said to him, "Today, food should be prepared in the kitchen. Dinggai questioned him, "For whom will this food be required?
He replied, "There will be high-ranking officials and various nobles arriving. Dinggai said, "This refers to those born into the human realm."
Regarding the signs he perceived: the Master’s cultivation had reached such a state that at nightfall, he gazed straight ahead without blinking.

After a long while, he suddenly snapped his fingers and exclaimed "Inconceivable! two or three times. When someone asked him from the side what the reason was, he replied, "I see jeweled banners, flowered canopies, and the magnificent adornments of stupas and temples.
Later that night, he again asked where the bright pearl was and said, "It is burning brightly."

He asked, "Is this a lamp? Because the light was dim and obscured by a screen, he cried out in reproach. Thinking that the radiance must have grown even more intense, he said, "How could you deceive me?
This room is as dark and obscure as ever, yet what the Master perceives must surely be a superior sign.
He immediately joined his palms and said, "I shall be reborn in the Pure Land," whereupon his breath ceased. This was on the twenty-fourth day of the tenth month at Sanji.
The building shook; doors and windows cracked and split open; pheasants in the forest flew up and cried out.

For several days, the temple monk Daohui had a dream in which the western ridge was entirely covered with multi-storied pavilions, and people were traveling westward through the air. Furthermore, his mother, Lady Yu, was particularly devoted to the faith;
at the time of her death, she saw red and blue lotuses, as large as five-hu jars, covering the grounds of the residence. The Buddha and...
The Bodhisattva and [the Master] arrived together to welcome her; at that moment, her mother passed away. This was in the second month of the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era.
She was of the Li clan of Dikao in Jincheng, [formerly of] Suilinggan. Her grandfather, Xiangfeng, held the fief of Shangdang, and they subsequently moved their residence there.

At the age of fourteen, he entered the Da Zhuangyan Temple in the capital city of Ye to take ordination under Master Yan. Whenever he entered the lecture hall, he cultivated the perception of it as a celestial palace.

At eighteen, he gave a recitation-exegesis (*fujiang*) on the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which was immediately praised by the assembly. He received full ordination at the age of twenty.
He was single-mindedly devoted to the Vinaya. During the upheaval caused by Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty, he lived as a layperson yet observed the precepts according to the Dharma.

With the rise of the Sui dynasty, an imperial edict included him among the ranks of the Bodhisattva-saṃgha, and the state provided all his necessities; he was subsequently stationed at Shaolin Monastery.

In the third year of the Kaihuang era, he underwent re-ordination at Jingtu Monastery in Luozhou together with Dharma Master Haiyu, where they lectured on and expounded the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. In the seventh year, an edict summoned him to reside at Xing[shan Monastery].

Shansi was a śramaṇa who served as a proofreader for the translation of scriptures. In the seventeenth year [of the Kaihuang era], he fell into a state of unconsciousness and had not yet been encoffined.
Upon regaining consciousness, he said: "At first, I saw two officials holding documents standing outside the door of my room, saying, 'The authorities require to see you, Master.

A short while later, I felt as though I were walking through empty space. I arrived at a grove of trees made of the seven precious gems, as magnificent and upright as a painting. Thereupon, the two officials took their leave."
Looking toward the east and west, there was nothing within the range of vision that was not precious treasure; it was so brilliantly radiant that one could not gaze upon it directly.
Beneath every tree there was a flower-seat, though some were occupied while others were empty. Whenever one heard someone calling their name, they would go to look.
Huiyuan then realized that this was indeed the Dharma-body. He bowed and inquired of him, asking, "What land is this? He replied, "This is Tuṣita. Master Sengxiu is seated on the southern throne;
I shall be reborn there together with him. Furthermore, he saw that neither Sengxiu nor Huiyuan appeared in their original forms;
both were wearing crowns and robes of brilliant colors, their radiance surpassing that of the world. However, they could still recognize each other’s voices. Huiyuan spoke to him again, saying:
"My disciples have all been born here. In the third year of the Renshou era, an imperial edict was issued to send śarīra relics to Hanwang Temple in Luzhou;

the details of these auspicious responses are recorded in a separate biography. At that time, Prince Han Liang, who was stationed at Jinyang, heard that Dao-gan had erected a stūpa at that temple and dispatched an envoy from afar to bestow offerings.
When Empress Xian passed away, Dao-gan once recited a liturgy for the Emperor on her behalf, which met with the Sovereign's approval, and he was subsequently granted silk.
Two hundred bolts [of silk]. In the third year of the Daye era, the Great Chan-ding Monastery was established, and by imperial decree he was appointed as the Abbot (Upādhyāya).
On the twenty-ninth day of the first month of the eighth year, he passed away at the age of seventy-eight. He was subsequently cremated on the northern slope of Zhongnan Mountain.
Previously, Hui-gan had constantly practiced the visualization of the Lotus World-Ocean and the Tuṣita Heaven Palace of Maitreya; when his illness reached its terminal stage, his eyes rolled upward.
Looking upward, he did not face anyone. After a long time, it remained as before. The śramaṇa Tongzhen asked, "What do you see?
He replied, "Just now two youths dressed in blue came to summon me. We reached the outskirts of Tuṣita City but had not yet entered.
Therefore, I stood on tiptoe to gaze at the jeweled trees and flowered canopies within the city; had I stood upright, there would have been nothing to see. Tongzhen said, "It is so."
"Did you not achieve your wish? Gan replied, "Celestial bliss is not lasting; one will ultimately fall back into the cycle of saṃsāra. The Flower Treasury World (Huazang) is my true aspiration.
Shortly thereafter, his breath ceased again, but he revived. Zhen asked him once more. Gan said, "I saw vast waters everywhere, with lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels.
I sat upon one of them. Thereafter, he passed away. Lingbian was Gan’s younger cousin, whom he had raised from childhood.
He was well-versed in the great classics and currently resided at Shenguang Temple.

Xingjian of the Sui dynasty was a man of unknown origins who made the practice of meditative concentration his constant vocation. During the Daye era, he traveled east to Mount Tai and stayed overnight beneath the eaves of a temple.
Suddenly, a person arrived, dressed in magnificent robes and caps, with a solemn and dignified bearing, accompanied by attendants shouting out his arrival. Xingjian—
He thought to himself that this was a spirit, and as he rose from his seat, he silently recited various sutras. The spirit immediately spoke to him without the slightest fear.
He then asked, "The world says that the official here governs ghosts; is this so? The spirit replied, "It is. [Seng] Jian asked, "Do you wish to see those who have passed away? Jian said:
Recently there were two of my fellow students; where are they now? The spirit, having learned their names, replied:
"One of them has already attained rebirth, while the other, owing to the gravity of his offenses, remains bound in prison and must endure great toil.
Suddenly they arrived at a place where the walls were all made of iron and ablaze with fire; from within, cries of lamentation reached out to the exterior. Peering through a window...
If there were anyone among them, their skin and flesh would all have rotted away so that no one could recognize who they were.
He then returned and questioned the deity for a method to save and spare them. The deity said, "Transcribe the Avataṃsaka Sūtra; this will likely suffice. At dawn the next day, he took his leave.
He immediately sought out skilled artisans to repair the scripture as if by divine means. On another day, he built a temple again.
The deity suddenly informed him that his fellow student had attained a superior reward through the power of his efforts regarding the scripture. Later, Huijian’s end remained unknown.
Fatai of the Sui dynasty was a native of Longshan County in Meizhou. His surname was Lü.

He had initially left secular life to become a Daoist for over ten years when he suddenly attained self-awakening and shaved his head to receive full ordination. He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* until he mastered it thoroughly;
furthermore, he produced a copy with sincere devotion, which frequently manifested miraculous signs. On one occasion, he commissioned a skilled artisan in Chengdu to bind and mount the volume.
He had a man carry two baskets as he traveled. In one basket he placed the scriptures, binding two thousand coins upon them;
in the other basket he placed his clothing and belongings. Upon reaching Zuo Bridge, the bridge broke, and both the baskets and the carrier fell into the water together.
Tài remained alone behind, unharmed. Once the carriers had emerged, the basket drifted away and sank; its whereabouts were unknown.
Tài beat his breast and wailed loudly, saying, "The money and robes are matters of little consequence, but what shall become of the sūtra? He then hired divers to search for it underwater.
They recovered the money and robes, but not the sūtra. Tài’s grief grew even deeper; he followed along the bank, weeping uncontrollably. After a short while—
From afar, he saw a bundle upon some grass on a separate island. He hurriedly took it and looked; it was a scripture, yet it was not the slightest bit dampened.

Even though it had been submerged in water, he firmly declined to accept payment for it. Having had it bound and decorated, he brought it back to his residence at Bisen-ji Temple, where he enshrined it with solemn purity.
Every night, a fragrant aroma wafted forth, and Hui-tai invariably recited and upheld it until the end.
At dawn, [Seng]xiao led the group through one recitation. At that time, Dharma Master [Zhi]biao was giving a lecture at that monastery and was troubled by the clamor of their voices.
The next day, he went in person to request that they lower their voices. Suddenly, he saw Sengtai standing before him, as if there were a great assembly kneeling with palms joined.
[Biao] finally withdrew, not daring to speak further. Sengtai passed away at the age of eighty.
Continued Biographies of Monks Classified into the Six Studies, Volume Twenty-four and Volume Twenty-five.
Compiled by the Sramana Tan’uo of Eastern Zhejiang.
Jingxunxue Gantongke was a native of the Shu family of Jimo in Lai Prefecture during the Tang dynasty. In his youth, he followed Daozang of Daozang Temple in Qingzhou.
The Dharma Master received the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the *Bhūmi-vastu*, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, and other treatises.
Later, he resided at Youde Temple, which was founded by Zong himself. Once, while he was lecturing on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, heavenly flowers swirled around the hall and chambers;

after a long time, they flew away without once falling to the ground. The assembly marveled at this rarity, yet Zong never regarded it as extraordinary. He subsequently moved to reside at Huiri Temple.
In the temple, Ying and Yan gathered together and constantly expounded the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*. He entered the Pass and resided at Shengguang Temple;

subsequently, he was invited to the Palace of Hongyi for a Dharma assembly, where the various princes and high officials all attended in rows to listen. From then on, his turnings of the wheel of Dharma continued without fail.

In the sixth year of the Wude era, he passed away at his residence at the age of sixty-one. While the Emperor Taizong was still in the Qin Prince’s residence, he issued an edict providing two types of funeral offerings.
One hundred sections. He was buried at the southern cliff of Zhixiang on Mount Zhongnan.
Dao Lin of the Tang dynasty was born into the Li clan of Taiyang in the region. At the age of thirty-five, he left the household life and entered a remote and secluded place in Mount Taibai.

There, he subsisted on wild fruits and drank from mountain streams, refining his fundamental nature. At the beginning of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, an imperial edict selected him for his talent.
There were seven virtuous men who were registered in the public records and ordained as monks, manifesting the Emperor’s intent to transform the administration and show reverence for the Dharma.

When the relevant officials received the imperial decree, they sought out Lin Yingzhi. The Emperor himself personally exhorted him; however, Lin firmly declined, saying it was not possible, and fled back to his residence to resume his former work.

When this matter was reported, an imperial edict was issued to arrest and bring him before the court. He underwent interrogation without being disgraced. Thereupon, the Emperor felt even greater regret.
He was held in high esteem. [The Emperor] bestowed upon him incense burners and other articles, and invited him to reside at Daxingguo Monastery in Fengyi.

Shortly thereafter, he again fled to the southern slopes of Liangshan, where he excavated a cave and sat in meditation within it. After some time, he felt slightly unwell. His disciples and lay devotees gathered daily around him to attend to his well-being.
Suddenly, they heard the sound of an empty space like the blowing of a *vaṃśa* flute, and a strange fragrance rained down, its droplets as large as peaches and jujubes.

He gathered [the remains] and cremated them; the fragrance was exceedingly intense. The multitude regarded this as an auspicious omen. After three days, his spirit became clear and lucid, and he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.
This was in the seventh month of the seventh year of the Wude era. His shrine remained open for seven days, and his countenance appeared as if alive.

He was buried on the Western Mountain, with some ten thousand people attending the funeral procession. While Lin Le delighted in seclusion and simplicity, Daomiao followed him in advancement; such was his regard for women.

People had never before encountered him face-to-face, much less heard him preach the Dharma or receive his alms. At the time of death, there were sometimes those who came suffering from the same illness;
Hui-lin would invariably perceive this beforehand and immediately send someone to decline them, refusing to let them enter. Nevertheless, he was compassionate and sympathetic toward all beings.
Regarding insects such as fleas and lice, he allowed them to wander and bite him at will, never daring to shake his robes to frighten them away.

Táng Fǎtōng, surnamed Guān, was a native of Hù in Jīngzhào. He entered the monastic order at a young age; he was so frail and weak that he could not even bear the weight of his own clothes, and would fall prostrate at the slightest touch.
Consequently, his fellow monks mocked him. Every time, he would weep as he prayed before an image of Avalokiteśvara, saying:
Tongwen heard that the Bodhisattva’s compassion was such that his wishes would surely be granted; he beseeched him to grant him guidance so that he might avoid such negligence.

He then recited the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* morning and night without ceasing. More than a year later, while visiting his mother at her lay residence, he fell into a light sleep beneath a tree in the courtyard after finishing his meal.
Shortly thereafter, saliva and froth flowed from his mouth in an amount of about three liters. His mother became alarmed and hurriedly woke him, asking what was the cause.
Tong said, "I recently dreamed that someone gave me three chopsticks to carry on a donkey and told me to eat them all. I had barely eaten one when I woke up;
I regretted losing the other two. Since then, my skin and flesh have become firm and tight, and my appearance has grown majestic and powerful.
Yet, those who come and go do not initially realize that I possess such strength. The monk Kanfen, in particular, is exceptionally robust and courageous."
Tong secretly took his *kāṣāya* and placed it beneath a pillar. When Kan saw this, he thought Tong was speaking with spirits and deities.

Tong laughed and lifted the pillar to retrieve the *kāṣāya*, doing so with extreme ease. Kan was greatly startled and filled with admiration. Thereupon, all those from the four quarters who were renowned for their physical strength came to visit Tong to request instruction.
Tong pulled the oxen of a cart until they walked backward; he merely took a handful of beans and wheat, and they were instantly ground to powder.
[The stone] was shattered. On South Mountain there was a stone mortar, large and weighing five hundred *jin*. Tong carried it back to the monastery and used it until the present day;
it remains exposed to the open air, filled with water to provide for the birds. During the reign of Emperor Gaozu of the Sui dynasty, a powerful man from the Western Regions was presented at court.

An imperial decree ordered Tong to wrestle against him. The strong man stepped forward and grappled with Tong, yet Tong remained unmoved. After a while, Tong gradually seized the strong man by both hands, whereupon blood splattered [from the man’s body].
He fell prostrate on the ground begging for his life. Tong hurriedly released him, saying, "I refrain from killing, and that is why I did so; otherwise, I would have shattered your bones.

During the final years of Emperor Yang, he went into hiding in the Southern Mountains to escape the chaos. Before long, he encountered the mourning period for his mother; after performing the funeral rites, he returned home.

However, his natural disposition was one of sincerity and frugality, and he never once offended anyone even slightly. His contemporaries held him in high esteem. He passed away at the beginning of the Wude era.
The temple where he resided was Fahai Temple. He was fifty-six years of age.
Huìyīn of the Táng dynasty was born with the secular surname Yú; he was a native of Hǎiyán in Wújùn. He was a descendant of Yú Bǎo, the Grand Music Master of the Jìn dynasty.

His grandfather, Yú Pǔ, served as the Court Gentleman for the Interior during the Liáng dynasty, and his father, Yú Yuǎnxiǎn, served as the Secretariat Drafter during the Liáng dynasty; both were men of profound learning and outstanding talent who maintained their family’s legacy through successive generations.
His excellence was such that at the age of twelve, he entered the monastic life under Dharma Master Huixi of Kaishan Temple.
At fifteen, he studied the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* under Dharma Master Jing of Jianchu Temple. Even before his full ordination, his reputation had already spread far and wide.
Yet, his heart yearned for the joy of dhyāna; he therefore went to Mount Zhong to request the methods of contemplation from Huixiao and Zhiquan. He also visited Changgan Temple.

The Dharma Master Bian studied the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*). After a long time, Bian withdrew from the world and departed for distant places, entrusting more than three hundred of his disciples to [the Master] to guide them.
For nearly thirty years, at the beginning of the summer retreat in the eighth year of the Taian era of the Chen dynasty, he suddenly appeared to pass away while seated;
however, his limbs remained supple and warm as before. After seven days had passed, he revived. His disciples then questioned him.

For this reason, Xu said, "Try looking inside the chest to see what is there. The attendant looked as instructed and found two bundles of silk, saying, "These are the inner linings for the funeral garments.
Thereupon, the initial messenger led the retinue, with string and wind instruments playing in welcome, saying, "The King invites the Dharma Master.
Subsequently, one wearing ceremonial robes and a crown was seen entering solemnly; it was said to be King Yama. This took place within the hall.

While observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*) and lecturing on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, he frequently beheld the various manifestations of the hells and the successive torments of the five sufferings.

He thought to himself: "It has already been three months; why do these visions still appear so frequently? Alas! Is this not due to deluded thoughts and inverted views? The Vice President Xu Ling and the Minister Mao Xi both paid him the highest respect.
In the third year of the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty, an imperial edict appointed him as an administrator (*karmadāna*) at Chanding Monastery.

Zuo frequently expounded the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) and composed commentaries on them. Upon entering the imperial court, he was appointed to one of the sixteen virtuous positions responsible for monastic affairs.
As the temples of the capital had long venerated the Bodhisattva Precepts, those who subsequently received full ordination followed his ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*) without exception.
Xiao Yu, the Left Vice-Director of the Chancellery, and Shen Shuan’an, the Minister of Justice, both held him in profound esteem and reverence.
Having received [the precepts] at this time for twenty years, he passed away on the thirteenth day of the second month in the first year of the Zhenguan era at Dazhuangyan Temple.
He was eighty-nine years of age. Previously, his disciple in the precepts, Faren, had exhorted him to dwell in accordance with the Dharma so that not a single day of his life would pass in vain.
When the final watch of the night arrived, he adjusted his appearance and sat upright; the assembly heard a wondrous fragrance fill the chamber. Upon his passing...
The secular authorities escorted him to the south of the city, where they again heard the sound of celestial music; consequently, they erected a stupa and inscribed a stele there.
The text was composed by Xiao Jun of Lanling. Ren was also diligent in his studies and possessed a reputation for excellence.
Tang Yisu was a person of unknown origin. He was pure and had few desires, devoting his days solely to the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

His count reached no fewer than several thousand repetitions. During the chaos at the end of the Sui dynasty, one Tang Liu of Meiquan Township in Liquan County, Yongzhou, invited him to his home to provide for his needs.
At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, as he was about to pass away from illness, he spoke to his friend Hui...
Kuo said, "Recently, I intended to use the miraculous efficacy of my recitation of the sutras to awaken the common people and spread the goodness of their faith.
Now that I am about to die, it will ultimately be of no benefit to the world. You may bury my corpse for ten years and then exhume it; perhaps the root of my tongue will not have decayed.
It would be fitting to erect a stupa so that this may endure for a long time. After he died, they indeed buried him. When the period arrived—
In the eleventh year, his tomb was opened and his tongue was found; consequently, a brick stupa was erected on the southern cliff of Gan-gu.
Furthermore, there was a man named Shi He-yan from Feng-gu County, who served as a provincial secretary. He was humble and modest toward others, never riding on horseback throughout his life.

He took the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Anrakugyō* (Peaceful Practices) as his standard, being diligent in recitation; even while walking in meditation, he would silently perform his daily recitations. When he went...
Whenever he came or went, he invariably took the narrow path; because it was secluded and quiet, his thoughts were focused and single-minded.
Although ten years had passed since his death and burial, when his tomb was opened, only his tongue remained. Those who heard of this could not help but marvel at it.
Tang Xiu was a monk of Suihua Temple in Huangzhou. Throughout his life, he made the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra* his primary vocation.
He frequently experienced miraculous signs, yet some remained unconvinced. During a period of intense summer heat, Xiu had never before felt any internal coolness.
A person fond of such wonders went at night to invite him; outside Xiu’s room, they beheld a magnificent display of carriages, horses, and ceremonial guards. Thereupon, that person...
He was startled and retreated. He then called his followers to look around the four walls; it was the same everywhere. Looking up into the air, they saw it was filled to the horizon.
They all rushed together to ask Xiuzhi about the reason for this, but Xiuzhi declined, saying he did not know. At the end of the Sui dynasty, he passed away at the temple where he resided.
Dharmaprabha (Wǎnguāng) of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Park (Pǔ) and was a native of Silla in Chinhan. His family had been engaged in Confucian studies for generations.
At the age of twenty-five, he crossed the Bohai Sea northward to Jinling to pursue his learning. During the Chen dynasty, literary arts were said to have reached their zenith;
thus, he was able to associate with the ranks of scholar-officials and gentlemen to collate and verify the Classics and Histories. There, he met the Venerable Min of Zhuangyan.

When his disciple Jiang delivered a lecture, [Dao’an] listened once and it permeated his spirit; he then looked upon Confucianism as mere chaff. Consequently, he submitted a petition requesting permission to enter the Way, which was granted by imperial decree.
After shaving his head and receiving full ordination, he traveled extensively, diligently studying the *Abhidharmakośa* (Cheng shi) and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

In the evening, he cultivated the practice of meditative concentration at Mount Huqiu in Wu. Disciples seeking dhyāna arrived like clouds, and he consequently formed the intention to remain there for the rest of his life.

Sometimes he resided at the foot of the mountain; when requested to come forth and propagate the teachings, he initially declined but was eventually persuaded. He provided guidance to the fourfold assembly, and from that time on, their hearts were satisfied.

His reputation grew even more prominent throughout the coastal regions. Upon receiving the imperial summons, he took up his pack and followed it, as the Sui dynasty had suddenly come to possess all under heaven.

When the soldiers entered the capital of Yangzhou, Huiguang was captured by the enemy generals and was about to be executed. The commanding general saw from afar that light was reaching the pagoda and temple;
upon going to inspect it, he found that Huiguang was bound beneath the pagoda, yet there was no fire at all. Finding this strange, the general released his bonds.

In the ninth year of the Kaihuang era, he came to the capital, whereupon he began to lecture on the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (She lun), and the assembly filled the seats. Shortly thereafter, the King of his own country, Jin... [text ends].

The Master repeatedly submitted petitions requesting to return to his native country. An imperial edict granted him leave with words of consolation and sent him on his way. Upon his arrival, both the old and the young rejoiced as if the Buddha had descended to earth.
His clothing, medicine, and food were provided by the imperial palace until he reached the camp; no one was permitted to assist him, so that he might enjoy this merit exclusively.
Once he entered the inner quarters, he was allowed to use a palanquin and was attended by his disciples. In the fourth year of the Zhenguan era, he fell ill for seven days.
He sat upright in meditation and passed away at his residence, Huanglong Temple, at the age of ninety-nine.

His funeral was provided with ceremonial insignia according to royal rites, and he was buried in the suburbs. His disciple Yuan’an succeeded him in his noble legacy; after traveling extensively, he returned once more to the capital temples.
Xiao Yu, the Special Advancer, petitioned for him to reside there, and he subsequently established Jinliang Temple in Lantian. This is its account.
Master Guang remarked that he was particularly well-versed in this matter.

Mingjing of the Tang dynasty was a native of Gaodi. He left home to become a monk in his youth and devoted himself to the study of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). He practiced seated meditation on Mount Meng by the seashore.

Several decades later, he traveled south to the various mountains of Kuaiji and Tiantai. Once, while begging for alms in a village, he encountered a pack of tigers on his return path who opened their mouths toward him.
Jing, seeing that they were hungry, suddenly scooped up some rice and placed it into each of their mouths.
He then ate the remaining rice himself with composure. He then said to the tigers, "I regret that the food is too little to truly sustain you."
The following day he did the same, and his companions marveled at this extraordinary feat. After some time, he returned to live at the foot of Mount Meng.
During a severe drought, when shamans and diviners performed sacrifices without success, Jing requested permission to sweep and clean a single room, where he stayed alone.
He vowed that it would rain within seven days, and the rain fell in abundant measure. In the third year of the Zhenguan era, from winter until summer, the capital experienced six successive...

It did not rain for months. The people were distressed and anxious. Various methods and arts of the Daoists and Buddhists were tried, and offerings were sent to the shrines of the mountains and rivers;

yet none of these efforts proved effective. At that time, there was an attendant surnamed Pan who had previously served as Governor of Mi. He informed the Emperor of the former services rendered by Sengjing. An imperial edict summoned Jing to inquire what he desired.
Jing replied, "I desire nothing, other than being granted the official registration for privately ordained monks and nuns. The Emperor then bestowed [the requested favor].
The new temple name for the entire realm was thus established; the Emperor granted this by imperial decree and further bestowed fragrant oil.
He entered nirvana at Zhuangyan Temple. On the morning of the seventh day, the officials guarding the site looked toward the northwest and said, "There shall be a white rainbow.
Upon looking, they saw it and believed them. They said, "The rain is coming. Shortly thereafter, torrential rain fell for an entire day. Thereafter, the multitude...

The Emperor praised the aforementioned virtues and purified the offerings previously requested; however, before they could be implemented, agricultural work had suddenly begun and the seedlings were already in the ground.
When the rain failed to follow, the seedlings withered and dried up. Left Vice-Director Fang Xuanling prepared a purification ritual and went to visit [the Emperor], saying:

"The realms of the unseen and the seen share one and the same principle. You granted permission but did not respond; how does this accord with principle? Upon hearing this, the Emperor issued an edict.
He suspended all official duties for another seven days of fasting, and it indeed rained. That year there was a bountiful harvest.

By imperial decree, three thousand additional monks were ordained beyond those previously promised, in order to console his pure intentions. Not long after, he returned to his hometown and resided at Yisheng Temple.
There was a monk named Huirong who had long practiced Chan and was able to cure illnesses by consecrating water; by imperial decree, [Huirong] was summoned to reside at Puguang Temple in the capital.
The two monasteries honored him with successive missions of dispatch.
Tang Faxi was a native of the Li clan from Xiangyang. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and relied upon Chan Master Hao, residing at Chanding Monastery.

Having served him for a long time, he maintained himself with profound reverence and discipline; yet while Hao specialized in the practice of meditative concentration, [Faxi]—prior to Hao’s passing—one...
In the evening, the wall of the room where he resided collapsed without any apparent cause. Daohao said, "My circumstantial retribution has already become disordered;
it is time for me to depart. He then sat upright and passed away. At that time, Sengxi was still a śrāmaṇera, serving the monastic community at Qingxi Temple in Jingzhou.
By night, he would burn firewood and recite the sutras. Although he studied various sections of the canon, the Lotus Sūtra was his primary devotion; every time he ate...

Recently, he would invariably recite one fascicle of a scripture until it was completely mastered; for the remainder of the time, he remained constantly in samādhi. Whenever he slightly succumbed to drowsiness or distraction, he would return to his practice of rehearsing the texts.
During the Renshou era, an imperial edict appointed him to the Chan Ding Monastery to oversee the protection of the Buddha’s tooth relic.
After some time, he vowed to recite the Lotus Sūtra one thousand times to honor the spirit of his late teacher, Master Hao. Morning and night, he focused his mind on this goal for eight full years.
His illness worsened and became increasingly severe. Among the monks of the temple, there was one who saw a white ox pulling a precious carriage enter the Xifang (Joyful Chamber);
he followed its tracks, but nothing remained there. Furthermore, he was diligent in providing for the sick and suffering, remaining indifferent even when his body was immersed in excrement and urine.
In the fourth year of the Wude era, Xiao Yu, the Right Vice-Director of the Chancellery, built Jinliang Temple in Lantian and invited him to reside there.
Donors arrived in great numbers. In his later years, he established a residence on a mound south of Mount Li and lived there until his end.

In the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, he contracted a slight illness. On the twelfth day of the tenth month, he told his disciples: "Impermanence has already arrived; be careful not to cause any commotion.

From time to time, he would chant: "The three realms are empty and illusory; they are but the single mind. Suddenly, to the north of the grove, there was the sound of music and carriages and horses. He heard it with joy.
He then exclaimed, "I have long since cast off karmic retribution; how could I be reborn again in a place of pleasure?

Thereupon he entered meditative absorption for a brief moment, at which the sound ceased and a fragrant aroma filled the room. It was the fifth watch of the night when he passed away while sitting upright, at the age of sixty-one.

Initially, during the first year of the Zhenguan era, wherever he stayed, there were always auspicious signs of blazing flames. Furthermore, he once traveled to the mountains to make a prediction in advance.
Regarding the burial site: they were about to excavate a niche to enshrine him when he was due to depart the following day.

However, that night there was a heavy snowfall, accumulating nearly a foot in depth over a distance of only two *li*. When they reached the midpoint of their journey, his spirit possessed a disciple and said, "I wish to bestow my body upon sentient beings;
how can you bury me and thus contravene my original vow? Therefore, they merely left the niche exposed above ground.

After his burial was completed, his countenance remained unchanged for a long time without decaying. When Lord Yu of Song saw this, he sighed in wonder at the marvel. Later, he happened to lift the monk’s shroud;
looking at it, he found it to be entirely a skeleton, with only the crown of the head remaining intact. Was this not indeed the fulfillment of his original vow?
Tang Zhixing was the son of the Song family in Luozhou. He maintained himself with humility and restraint, while further sharpening his moral conduct.

Throughout the day and night, he recited essential verses from various sutras, his mind and mouth acting as teachers for one another without ceasing. He resided at Chanding Monastery—what the world calls Dazhuangyan Monastery—where he followed the Vinaya Master Shou in his lectures.
When meeting with his companions to engage in dialectical inquiry and debate, the sharpness of his rhetoric was startling and preeminent. In the fifth year of the Daye era.
In winter, he served as the *karmadāna* (rector) of Ren Temple. He was most diligent and devoted in observing the method for striking the bell.

There was a monk named Sanguo whose elder brother had accompanied the imperial procession on its southern journey to Jiangdu; the brother died along the way without anyone receiving news of his passing.

Thereupon, his wife dreamed of him, who said: "I traveled as far as Pengcheng when I unfortunately fell ill and died. I have been born in hell, where the suffering is beyond description. Fortunately, this month's first day..."
The monk Zhixing of Chanding Monastery struck the bell, causing its resonance to shake the hells;
those suffering there together were all simultaneously liberated and reborn in a place of bliss. To repay his kindness, one should present him with ten rolls of silk to express my intent.
When his wife awoke, she told this to others, but no one believed her. Shortly thereafter, the dream recurred, and when a shaman entered a trance, the words he uttered were exactly as such.

Accordingly, he offered the silk as received, yet because it was not his own merit, he transferred it all to the great assembly. When someone asked him about the reason why his striking of the bell had brought about such a spiritual response, he replied:

"I saw in the *Dharmatrāta-avadāna* (Fu fa zang zhuan) the account of King Kanishka and how the wheel of fire from his sword was halted, as well as the merits of the bell-sound in the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
Following these accounts, I practiced this with diligence and did not dare to be negligent. As for its striking:
At the beginning, the ritual master says: "May all the sages and worthies enter this dharma-assembly together.

He strikes the bell three times; this is to manifest reverence. When it comes to the long striking, he says: "May those in the evil realms hear the sound of my bell and all be freed from their suffering.
This must be completed in three rounds; this is to give full expression to compassion. On nights of severe cold or at mornings of extreme frost, [the skin...]
His flesh was torn and his skin cracked; yet he still held his mallet with his bare hands, the blood coagulating within his palms, showing no sign of reluctance or fear—this was all there was to it.
What other skill could he have possessed? In the third month of the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, he fell ill and foretold the day of his death.

He distributed his personal belongings and food, summoned the assembly, and made his final farewells. He was forty-five years of age when he passed away. He was buried at Ducheng. His disciple Shanyin lectured on the *Four*... [text ends].
He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* from the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā* to dedicate merit for the deceased.

Dao’ang of the Tang dynasty was a native of Wei Commandery; his clan lineage is unknown. He left the household life under Dharma Master Lingyu and studied the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* at Hangling Mountain Temple, where he propagated the teachings at that time.
Yet, his aspiration was set upon rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). One day, he suddenly ascended...

At Baoying Monastery, while sitting upon the high seat and holding an incense burner to bestow the Bodhisattva precepts upon the fourfold assembly, Huiang looked up and saw gods and humans gathered in great numbers with the sounds of pipes and strings resounding.
A voice cried out, "The Tuṣita Heaven comes down to welcome you! Huiang said, "The heavenly realms are subject to the cycle of saṃsāra;
they do not bring an end to birth and death. My original aspiration was for the Pure Land—why has this sincerity not been fulfilled? Having spoken, he passed away.
When his words were finished, the celestial beings immediately vanished. Then, fragrant flowers and musical instruments were seen coming from the west, circling back above his head.
He called out to the great assembly, saying, "Cultivate yourselves well; be careful not to let one another down. Suddenly, the incense burner slipped from his hand and fell.
Finally, he sat upright and passed away upon his high seat at the age of sixty-nine. This was in the eighth month of the seventh year of the Zhenguan era.

It was the month of the moon. His spirit-shrine was returned for burial on Mount Hanling. Initially, Seng’ang kept a dog that was deaf yet clever; whenever Seng’ang reduced his own food, he would give it to the dog.
When Seng’ang passed away, the dog also vanished from its place. Furthermore, he once lectured at night when the hall was dark and dim.

When Aṅga raised his palms, light radiated forth, and he could see even the finest hairs. When questioned as to where this light had come from, he replied, "This is something humans constantly possess;
why is it considered strange that it has reached such a state? Upon viewing the patterns on his feet before his cremation, they formed the characters for "Hall of Universal Radiance" (Puguangtang).
Alas, how extraordinary! Furthermore, there was the śramaṇa Lingzhi of Xiangzhou, who was also a disciple of Master Yu. Regarding Aṅga and Shishi, they were brothers...
In his youth, he frequently served as the *dūjiàng* (debate moderator) under Master Yu, gaining renown throughout the region of Changye.

In his later years, he suddenly ceased all correspondence and petitions, devoting himself exclusively to the practice of meditative concentration. In the eighth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away at the age of seventy-five.

Tang Hongman, surnamed Liang, was a native of Anding. When he was fifteen years old, before he had yet left the household life, he suddenly suffered from a contraction and lameness of both feet that no number of medicines could cure.

He thought only of the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* to pray for a miraculous efficacy. After three years had passed, a monk happened to appear before him carrying a water jar and stood there without speaking.
Hongman asked, "Where has the Master come from? The monk replied, "I have come because of you, the donor."

The Emperor saw him and summoned him; thus he had come. Faman then bowed his head and asked, "What karma did I commit in my previous lives that I now receive this retribution of being both hunchbacked and lame?
The monk said, "Because you once bound and imprisoned others, this is your retribution. Simply close your eyes, and I shall treat you.
Faman followed these words, and he felt only that his two knees were light and refreshing, as if they had been pulled out. Six.
A seven-inch long nail [pierced his body] as if it were burning; he immediately opened his eyes, performed a prostration to express his gratitude, and then lost sight of where the monk had gone.
Thereupon, Mǎn’s gait returned to normal, and he awoke. That monk was indeed Avalokiteśvara. From that time on, Mǎn redoubled his self-exhortation, vowing never to marry for the rest of his life.
He was able to sit in dhyāna, entering into meditative absorption for three or seven days at a time. At the beginning of the Kaihuang era...

He received the tonsure and resided at Jiudu Temple during the Daye period. He later moved to reside at Fahai Temple, where he passed away in the thirteenth year of the Zhenguan era at the age of eighty-three.
Huicong of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Wang; he resided at Fuhua Temple in Yizhou and was devoted to lecturing and reciting the scriptures, never letting them leave his hands.

He said to himself, "In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is told that the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging did not exclusively recite the scriptures, but merely practiced prostrating to the fourfold assembly and yet attained the purification of the six sense faculties. Why then should I fail to pay homage to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones?

Thereupon, in a separate hall, he closed the door and, relying on the sūtra, chanted the names of fifteen thousand Buddhas while performing prostrations. The monks of the monastery once [observed him] at the wall...
Peering through a crack, he saw that Sengcong was prostrating before the Western Dragon and the Eight Divinities, who all stood in a circle surrounding him, following his every movement;

this occurred not just once, but repeatedly. Whenever anyone entered his courtyard, they would invariably leave with their hearts trembling. A strange fragrance was constantly perceived, wafting forth luxuriantly.
He passed away during the Zhenguan era. From that time on, the traces of human traffic to and from the courtyard ceased, yet every night there were those who performed prostrations.
While walking in meditation, he made the sound of snapping his fingers.

During the Tang dynasty, there was a monk named Tanzang, surnamed Yang, a native of Huayin in Hongnong. When he was fifteen years old, some predicted that he possessed the physical marks of an early death.
His parents immediately sought to arrange a marriage for him in hopes of securing his lineage, but this was not his intent;

he therefore departed in secret, wishing to become a monk, yet had not yet found such a person. While silently reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara, he encountered on the road a man from Qian leading two oxen.

He asked the man for a place where he might stay overnight, and the man replied, "If you travel westward, there is a temple; you will soon hear the sound of the bells. He followed the direction and indeed saw the temple.

The monastic community there was particularly numerous; moreover, they were shaven-headed and showed no signs of distress. Upon completing his task, he immediately left the gate, but after walking only a hundred paces, he looked back and saw nothing.
From this, he knew it had been a realm of transformation. At dawn, he hurried westward to the ridges and then returned to the capital.

He resided at Jingshan Temple, where he ascended the platform to receive precepts and studied the sutras and śāstras. Whenever he encountered doubts regarding their meaning, he would go [to seek clarification].
Shandong examined him against the standards of the venerable masters of old; his mastery of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* was without obstruction.

Later, he returned to be registered at Guangming Temple. After Empress Xian passed away, he was summoned to reside at Chanding Temple. During the reign of the present dynasty, when Huichang Temple was constructed, an imperial decree appointed him as its head (upādhyāya).

During the translation projects of the Zhenguan era, he was summoned to certify the meaning of the texts. He was further decreed to preside over Xingshan Temple. When the Tripitaka Master firmly declined the appointment, he recommended Run of Huaganshi Temple in Lantian.
The Dharma Master, by his own merit, truly fulfilled the imperial will. When the Crown Prince fell ill, [Fazang] entered the palace to bestow the precepts, and the prince recovered.

The Emperor bestowed upon him silk and robes, issued an edict to ordain three thousand monks, and commissioned the construction of Puguang Temple, placing it under his jurisdiction. The Emperor further inquired whether it was permissible to receive the precepts from afar.
Fazang, citing the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, stated that if no precept master is present, one may generate a great vow and thereby obtain the Bodhisattva precepts. Consequently—

He advanced his treatises for imperial review. Furthermore, the Emperor ordered him to recite the Imperially Composed Text on Repentance before the imperial library. When the Empress fell ill, he was summoned by imperial decree to the inner palace to confer the precepts upon her;
she bestowed upon him abundant gifts. On the eighteenth day of the third month in the ninth year, he passed away at Huichang Temple.

He was sixty-nine years old. Both palaces were stricken with profound grief. He was buried to the west of the capital, where a stupa was erected and his likeness depicted to ensure his legacy endures imperishably.
Yu Zhining, Duke of Liyang and Director of the Household of the Crown Prince, composed the inscription for his stele.
The one who showed the steps to the Tang Emperor was the Mohe of Liaoxi Loucheng. When he was young, he happened to find a bronze image about two inches high somewhere;
regarding it as a divine spirit, he kept it in a leather pouch and carried it with him whether sleeping or rising.
Every time he ate or drank, he would invariably offer a portion as a sacrifice; he made no distinction even regarding leftover wine or scraps of meat.

At the age of eighteen, he entered Goryeo, where they mistook him for a spy, captured him, and were about to execute him by beheading. Even after three strokes of the blade, he was not wounded. Suspecting that he possessed some occult arts, they questioned him.
He replied, "I have none. They asked, "If so, how is it that you have come to this? He said, "Throughout my life, I have had [certain things]..."

Perhaps it was due to his spiritual power? He brought it out to show me; upon its back, there appeared what seemed like slight damage, but when examined closely, it was clearly the mark of three sword wounds.
He then released the animal and sent it back to China, saying, "The Great Tang is currently flourishing in the Buddha-dharma;
perhaps there you may fulfill your aspirations. Thereupon, [the monk] enrolled at a monastery in Youzhou and left the household life.

Tang Daoxun, surnamed Zhang, was a native of Yuxiang in Hedong. From his youth, he had mastered the various scriptural collections, specializing in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* as his ultimate doctrinal principles.

His younger brother, Daoxian, was also a disciple of Dharma Master Tan Yan. Later, they resided at Renshou Temple in Puzhou, where they gathered disciples to propagate their teachings and established their religious foundations at major thoroughfares.
Their reputation spread from the royal courts and the offices of the central government down to all levels of officialdom.

He would often turn his carriage aside to visit and seek instruction from [his teacher], yet sometimes he was too hurried and failed to meet him; in such cases, he felt ashamed and anxious, as if he were carrying a heavy burden.
He maintained himself through virtue and regarded the noble and the humble as equals; even when people came and went, he never engaged in the formalities of welcoming or seeing them off.
During the chaos of the Daye era, he traveled to the capital via the Dao Pass and stayed overnight at an inn. His family consisted of five sons who were all bandits.

The horse ridden by Xu was exceptionally powerful and fine, so the thief plotted to steal it. Seeing ten men beside the horse, of heroic and imposing stature, clad in armor and grasping weapons, standing there in a rage, the thief retreated and fled.
He looked back slowly, but they were no longer there. He advanced again, and what he saw was just as before;
this happened four or five times until it finally ceased. Terrified, the thief went the next day to Xu, confessed his intentions, and sought repentance.
When our dynasty rose in righteous rebellion, Pú had not yet been captured. Among the temple monks was one named Sùrú, who had previously behaved with insolence toward Xuǎn;

he even intended to defect to the enemy with the city. Subsequently, the city fell and he was captured. As he was about to be executed as a public warning, Xuǎn wept and pleaded with his captors, saying:
"This monk’s transgression is truly due to my own failure in instruction. I pray that you spare him and instead execute me. His captors [granted his request].
The authorities took pity on his sincerity and released him. During the Zhenguan era, someone requested that he lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

He firmly declined, but was repeatedly urged. Daosun said, "It is not that I dare decline; I fear I shall not finish this seat. Furthermore, I am troubled by this, so let us go to Wangcheng Valley and I shall lecture there for you.
The next day, Daosun arrived at the valley and ascended the seat. Monastics and laypeople gathered together. Suddenly, he said, "The world..."

It was the natural law of the realm that he would soon pass away. He ventured to address the great assembly, saying, "What [is the meaning of] this verse? Afterward, he requested to be reborn in a future life;

thus, he set aside his commentary up to the title and proceeded to the verse. Thereupon, his illness flared up, and after three days, he passed away amidst the mountain valleys at the age of seventy-five.
On the evening following the burial of the corpse, extraordinary flowers sprang up surrounding the site.

Their stalks were about one or two chi in length, and their brilliant colors were like those of the *kuan-tung* (Helleborus), yet their form and appearance were by no means similar to it. If some were plucked and placed in a vase, they remained as fresh as ever even after a year had passed.
A scholar from Jin Prefecture, who was fond of hunting, had previously known Sui; upon hearing that Sui’s death had been accompanied by such auspicious omens, he was deeply moved.
He then went to that spot and wept in repentance for his transgressions. After a short while, he obtained a flower just like the previous one, measuring about one chi in length.

Daoxuan had studied under those who possessed the realization of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) and was renowned throughout the empire; however, he soon realized that the Renshou Road where he resided was situated at a major thoroughfare.

Tired of the constant demands of social interaction, he departed to travel among the mountains and rivers; finding the excellence of Wangcheng Valley particularly appealing, he settled there to dwell.
In the first year of the Zhenguan era, Xun passed away, at the age of sixty-seven. His son Weikui could not overcome his grief at the loss.
His disciple Daoji performed the cremation and collected the remains, erecting a stupa and a stele. The monk Xingyou composed the inscription to commemorate his virtues.

The monk Ming was a man of unknown origins. He resided at the ancient Sāṃba Monastery on Mount Wutai, where he constructed more than twenty rooms and gathered various scriptural volumes to support his practice of meditation and recitation. He said to others:
"When I was seventeen years old, I followed my teacher eastward to Huilin Mountain. There, I paid homage to Mañjuśrī and entered a stone valley that was exceedingly deep and perfectly circular."

There was a stone mortar and a wooden pestle. Two majestic figures stood in the midst of the sun without casting shadows; they had long eyebrows and disheveled hair, and their eyelids covered their eyes.

Master [Dao]shi suddenly prostrated himself, praying for their pure acceptance. One of them said, "Your grain smells foul; you should move a short distance away. He asked, "Where have you come from? [Dao]shi replied, "From Shaoguo Temple.
I have lived here in seclusion within this Sahā world, practicing meditation and cultivating the Way for several decades. However, I eat only..."
"Grain! I pray that the Bodhisattva will compassionately protect us. He said, "We must consult with the assembly. Shortly thereafter, another person arrived;

he was quite tall and robust, wearing a garment of tree bark. He said, "You may follow me to the temple. They walked together along the side of a great rock, when suddenly the mountain valley transformed beyond measure.
Courtyards and corridors surrounded them, appearing like a celestial palace. There sat some fourteen or fifteen venerable elders.

They conversed with laughter and also asked where he had come from. After they had discussed matters for a long time, he was sent out; he was suddenly bewildered and lost his way, unable to find it again.
Ming died in the sixteenth year of the Zhenguan era at the age of eighty-one.

Tánróng of the Táng dynasty was born into the Zhāng family of Jiǔmén in Dìngzhōu. At the age of nineteen, he became a scholar and applied himself with earnest intent to the profound principles of the Way.

It happened that while the Dharma Master Língyù was lecturing on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, Tánróng stayed to listen; upon hearing it, he attained a realization. He subsequently served Língyù and received the tonsure.
Having received full ordination, he traveled extensively through the monasteries of the Vinaya and the various schools of doctrine. Furthermore, he did not survive the calamities of the Zhōu period.

In place of his regular duties, at the beginning of the Sui dynasty, he withdrew to live among the mountains of Shangdang, Lu, and Li. Upon reaching the age of forty, his meditative virtue became widely renowned, and students flocked to him in great numbers.

Moved by his supreme grace, even during the chaos at the end of the Sui dynasty when war and famine repeatedly struck, Rong practiced the Vaipulya and Pratyutpanna samādhis during the spring and summer, while in autumn and winter he devoted himself exclusively to seated meditation. Those who engaged in recitation were assigned to separate courtyards.
He enshrined them there; thus, there were four locations for them. Furthermore, he established the *chánhuì* (repentance) ritual at Yansheng Temple in Hanju.

The Regional Inspector Feng Tongren presented three *śarīra* relics. Tongrong led three thousand monastics and laypeople to welcome them, each placing a water bowl and incense burner before them, saying:
"The virtue of the *śarīra* manifests in infinite ways. If one’s karmic burdens..."
By making offerings and requests, [the relics] could be obtained. From night until dawn, more than four hundred pieces were recovered.

At that time, local officials wished to prohibit this practice, but when a calamitous omen appeared, they were struck with fear and desisted. In the ninth year of the Wude era, while performing a ritual at Jiaozhang Village in Lucheng, the hall suddenly collapsed;
yet the niche, the image, and the śarīra emerged unharmed. In the seventh year of the Zhenguan era, the lay devotee Chang...
Yi Bao requested that Rong perform the Fangdeng (Vaipulya) Repentance Ritual at Fazhu Temple in the provincial seat.
On the fourteenth day of the seventh month, within the ritual hall, the śramaṇa Sengding of the main temple beheld five-colored light penetrating from above to below.
Within it appeared the marks and signs of the Seven Buddhas, most extraordinary. The Buddha spoke to Ding, saying: "I am Vipaśyin Tathāgata, the Arhat."

"The Truly Realized Ones, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, have come to bear witness because your offenses have been extinguished. However, as they were not your original teachers, they did not bestow upon you a prophecy.
Thus it was with all six Buddhas, who spoke these same words. The last Buddha said, "I am your original teacher, Śākyamuni.
Because your offenses have been extinguished, I have come to bestow a prophecy upon you. Within this Bhadrakalpa, Tanrong—
He was named Fubing Buddha. You, too, shall in turn become a Buddha named Puming.
While he was lying ill in bed and weeping, his disciple Yuanzong asked, "Does the Master have anything that is not to your liking? He replied, "I am now about to die.
My only regret is that I shall no longer have the opportunity to wash away the karmic burdens of the seven assemblies. On the twelfth day of the tenth month in the thirteenth year, he passed away.
She lived to the age of eighty-five.
Huíyú of the Táng dynasty was surnamed Cén and was a native of Xiāngyáng. Having lost both her parents at the age of three, she was raised by her maternal relatives.

At five years old, she accompanied her maternal grandfather to hear a lecture at Chángshā Temple; upon seeing a Buddha statue, she wept with longing and devotion, vowing to remain there, and thus took up residence in the temple.

This Dharma Master Jiukū (Jiuku) had a shorn head. Within fifty days, he was able to recite the entire text of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* from memory. Later, he investigated the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises).
During the chaos at the end of the Sui dynasty, he sought refuge in the mountains at Yùquán, where he sat in meditation within a thatched hut.

For twenty-three years, his practice remained as constant as a single day. Beside the mountain temple there was a spring, though its name was unknown; could this perhaps be what is called "Jade" (*yù*)?
Is this perhaps the spring? A black snake about twenty feet long dwells there, appearing and disappearing unpredictably as if acting as its guardian.

The bandits were warned not to approach it. Among them was one named Zhang Heqia, the ringleader, who was exceptionally fierce and brave; taking up two blades, he led a dozen or so of his wicked followers with the intent to kill the snake.
The snake opened its eyes and emitted light for more than two hundred paces. The thieves were struck with terror and fell prostrate once again.
On that day, when Yu heard of this, he hurried there and recited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* for him. He prayed for the snake, which followed Yu as he traveled;
seven of the bandits died, while three were restored to life at that moment. Thereupon, offerings from all directions accumulated in great abundance.

In the tenth year of the Zhenguan era, the monastics and laypeople of Jingzhou requested that he expound upon the Three Treatises and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* at Shengjue Temple. In the fourteenth year... [seventh month].

On the twenty-second day of the seventh month, the temple attendants all saw a multitude of stars fall into the well. On the seventeenth day of the eighth month, while lecturing on the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he reached the passage on rebirth;
before it was finished, he took up his *cāmara* whisk and passed away in his seat. He was seventy-nine years old.
Huileng of Tang was the son of the Shentu family from Xilong. He was born after his father had already passed away, and for three years he was raised solely by his mother.

At the age of three, he already understood the existence of the Buddha-dharma and wished to hear its teachings. His mother, out of pity for him, took him to travel to Xiangyang. At that time, Dharma Master Run was expounding the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises).
Upon first approaching the edge of the lecture seat, Huileng attained a profound realization. At the age of eight, he lost his mother and subsequently relied upon [the Master].
At the age of sixteen, Tanxi Temple’s Master Dan was able to grasp the general meaning and extraordinary principles of the sutras.

He went to inquire with Dharma Master Ming of Maoshan in Jingzhou; there, he received specialized instructions in a private chamber regarding the non-existence of existence, continuing for three years.

He profoundly grasped the essential meaning [of the teachings]. Later, he followed Master Gao of Anzhou to enter Shu; during the period when he was reciting and expounding [the texts], he especially captured Gao’s intent.
Consequently, people called him "De-yi Leng" (Leng who has Grasped the Essence). When Gao was unjustly imprisoned in the Chengdu County jail, Leng was also held in custody.

The assembly requested that he lecture on the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises); he had barely delivered five sections when the imperial decree arrived for his release, and no further questioning took place. It happened that [Master] An...
The province suffered from famine. Sengyao valued [Seng]ling as if he were a pearl; [Seng]ling begged for food daily to sustain himself. [Seng]gao and [Seng]hongyan never grew weary of him.

When [Seng]gao fell ill, [Seng]ling took his place without showing any sign of reluctance. At that time, there were over thirty eminent and talented scholars at the lecture hall, all of whom held that their own interpretations of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* entirely contradicted [Seng]gao’s principles.
When [Seng]gao recovered from his illness, he requested that the matter be settled. Thereupon, [Seng]gao summoned [Seng]ling before him.
In his prefaces, [Hui]xu always said: "This is because you have not yet submitted. Before his death, Seng’ao grasped Huileng’s hand and said:

"Do not covet gain and offerings; do not shrink from toil. Be cautious and apprehensive, as if treading upon blades and swords; only then can you transmit the lamp and continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom.
Prior to this, Huileng had dreamed that he lost his eyes, and furthermore, someone brought him a radiant jeweled mirror and pressed it against his body.
This was a sign of his realization. Not long after, in the fifth year [of the Zhenguan era], he returned to Zijin Monastery in Xiangzhou to propagate the Mahāyāna teachings.
In the eighth year, he expounded the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, and other scriptures at Xumi Monastery.

In the third month of the twelfth year, he dreamed that the birds at his monastery were flying away and dispersing; consequently, he disbanded his assembly. In the first month of the fourteenth year, Dharma Master Chang of Gantong Monastery had a dream.
King Yama said to him, "I have now invited Master Ling to lecture on the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises) and Master Ba to lecture on the *Fahua* (Lotus Sutra).
Upon hearing this, Ling rejoiced and said, "I made a vow to dwell perpetually in hell to transform sentient beings; if this vow is fulfilled, what cause for regret could there be?

In the ninth month, the regional governor, Prince Jiang, seeing that he was physically frail, sent powdered stalactite from Shaoshan to him to take as medicine. That night, he dreamed of wearing official robes and cap.
The precepts state: "Do not consume. King Yama has adorned his *bodhimaṇḍa* and possesses an abundance of medicinal milk.

On the fifteenth day of the tenth month, he suddenly informed his disciples that his five viscera had already collapsed, yet he felt no pain. At the fourth watch, he rose and sat up, addressing the temple master, Baodu, saying:
"I observe the events of my youth as clearly as if they were before my eyes. Suddenly, he heard a great sound outside.
The voice said, "The Dharma Master rose early and burned incense; the messenger has arrived. Huidu asked who the messenger was, and the reply was, "He is a messenger from King Yama.
At the time of the morning meal, Tanleng assumed a solemn expression and passed away on the sixteenth day of the tenth month in the fourteenth year.
He lived to the age of sixty-five.

Huìtiáo of the Táng dynasty was surnamed Zhuāng; he was a native of Xiāngzhōu. Having left home to become a monk in his youth, he traveled to study among the various prefectures of Qí, Xú, Qīng, and Hǎi.
At the end of the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty, he returned to reside at Bàośàn Temple in his hometown. At that time, there was also Xiàngwáng Zhé.
Master Gong was then expounding the Three Treatises at Xialongquan Temple. When Tiao heard of this, he ridiculed him, saying, "The Three Treatises clarify emptiness;
that man must surely be attached to emptiness. Before he had finished speaking, Tong’s tongue protruded for about three feet, and blood flowed from his eyes, nose, and ears.
He remained unconscious for seven days. The Vinaya Master Fu passed by and said to him, "The sin of disparaging the sutras is more severe than..."
Regarding the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), you should burn incense and repent for your past transgressions. Following this advice, his illness was swiftly and completely cured.

He subsequently carried [the image] to the residence of Master Zhe, where he made a vow to take refuge. After Master Zhe passed away, he moved to Xiangshan Shenzu Temple. There, he regularly gathered the assembly during the four seasons to expound the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and atone for his former misdeeds.
On the third day of the fourth month in the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era, while he was once at the pine tree behind the temple...

While Tanliao was sitting in meditation in the forest, three men suddenly appeared, their appearance and attire both magnificent. They prostrated themselves and requested that he confer upon them the Bodhisattva precepts.

After a moment, they spoke again, saying, "Master, you possess sharp faculties and are suddenly able to have deep faith in the Mahāyāna. Had it not been so, even if a thousand Buddhas were to appear in the world, you would still remain in hell.
Tanliao immediately wept uncontrollably. He then converted both clergy and laity, and together they produced the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* Sūtras.
He bestowed one hundred copies each of the *Avataṃsaka*, *Vimalakīrti*, *Akṣayamati*, and *Buddhapiṭaka* treatises.
On the ninth day of the third month in the thirteenth year, he passed away before the Buddha. During his diligent practice, his age was over eighty years.
Tang Famín was surnamed Sūn and was a native of Danyāṅ. At the age of eight, he entered the monastic order under Master Yīng.

He went to Māoshān to study the *Sanlùn* (Three Treatises) under Master Míng, and later relied upon [Master] Dōng'ān to investigate its essential meaning. At twenty-three, he followed Master Shí of Gāolǐ;
after Shí passed away, he traveled with Master Yìn to Shǔ. There, however, the dharma seat had declined and fallen into ruin, as the Chen dynasty had lost its governance.
He returned to his original robes. After three years, he was finally able to withdraw from worldly affairs.
He sought refuge at Liang’an Temple in Qianyao, where he led a group of ten śrāmaṇeras and continuously expounded the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Three Treatises* without interruption.

In the first year of the Zhenguan era, he returned to his hometown to propagate the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, guiding the fourfold assembly. In the second year, Lord Tian, the Commander-in-Chief of Kuaiji, welcomed him back with due ceremony.
He resided at Yizhong Temple. Over seventy states sent more than two thousand śramaṇas learned in the doctrines to attend this great assembly, along with three hundred nuns;
the number of laymen and laywomen was beyond reckoning. In the nineteenth year, he moved to reside at Jinglin Temple to expand the lecture series on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
In the sixth month of summer, he finally ascended the seat. As he entered into the text, a golden-colored snake appeared, emitting light of five colors and measuring seven [chi] in length.

It was about one chi in height; it hung from the roof beam and remained directly above Hui-min’s head until the lecture ended, after which it vanished. Not long afterward, he again relaxed the retreat at Yiyin.
At night, he saw two men dressed in red robes who paid him homage, saying: "The merit of the Dharma Master is immeasurable.
Why not go to other regions to teach and transform? We have now come from the east to welcome you. On the full moon of the eighth month, there were three consecutive days of profound darkness.
He could no longer distinguish between night and day. The day of his passing was the twenty-third. Furthermore, the great brightness lasted as long as day throughout the night.
He was seventy-six years of age. As he was about to be interred, the stupa’s spire emitted a brilliant light, the earth shook, and a wondrous fragrance spread in all directions.
Tang Shiyu was the son of the Chen family of Taizhou. Orphaned at a young age, he supported himself as a hired laborer before eventually leaving that life behind.
He then traveled far to follow Master Lun of Zhenxiang Temple in Mianzhou to enter the monastic order; this was the twelfth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty.
He practiced the single-meal discipline and remained seated constantly, maintaining the dhūta ascetic practices. Not long after, he moved his residence to Jizhu Temple in Lizhou. Later...
He resided at Mount Yingxiang in Mianzhu County, Yizhou, for an exceptionally long time. The mountain was so deep and remote that it was utterly devoid of human habitation;
he relied solely on four monkeys who would occasionally provide him with fruits and gourds. Once, a lay devotee named Moqiu Sheng brought grain to offer to him.

On his way back, halfway up the mountain, he encountered two guests whose complexions were a deep blue. Each held a lotus flower, a sugarcane, and a taro root, saying, "We come to present these as offerings to the Dhyāna Master."
