The Master said, "I do not know from where they have come. For six periods of the day and night, I practice the Way with birds and beasts as my companions.

During three years, the food I consumed amounted to no more than one *shí* and seven *shēng* of rice. When I first drew water from a spring, suddenly a second spring emerged beneath it; its clarity and sweetness were delightful.
At the beginning of the *Zhèngguān* era, I happened to dream that four dragons entered the center of my eyes; since then, I have attained silent realization."
Regarding the fundamental tenets of the Three Treatises (Sanlun), he subsequently relied upon Dharma Master Lingrui at Dashi Temple in Mian to rectify their meaning.

He then restated them in subsequent expositions, all of which accorded with the commentaries and sub-commentaries. Suddenly, while at Chongle Temple, he said to his friend, "I shall now travel abroad.
His friend admonished him, saying, "The Way is omnipresent; why must you travel abroad? Thereupon, he returned to Dashi Temple. Then—
At first, no one knew that he had passed away while seated in his room. Suddenly, a fragrant aroma was perceived emanating from the room.
Following the scent, someone entered the room and saw him there; three gold coins were found together at the place where he sat. Yet he still held the incense burner in his hands.
This occurred on the eighth day of the fourth month in the nineteenth year [of the reign]. He was sixty-three years of age. Prefect Liu Dewei composed [the memorial inscription].
The entire body was enshrined within a niche; after three years had passed, its appearance remained as if alive.

Hui-xuan of the Tang dynasty, whose secular surname was Dong, left home to become a monk at a young age in Xiangyang. When the Northern Zhou abolished the Great Teaching, he fled south to the Chen dynasty, where he followed Master Ming of Maoshan in Danyang to study the *Sanlun* (Three Treatises).
He further investigated the *Sijun* (Four Treatises), the *Dapin* (Large Perfection of Wisdom Sutra), the *Niepan* (Nirvana Sutra), and others.
The Dharma Master Xianbu of Qixia later resided at Dalin Temple in Anzhou, where he received the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*) from Dharma Master Yuan.
Subsequently, he returned to his hometown and stayed at Guangfu Temple. During a period of turmoil, he took refuge within the city.

The Governor, Lord Lu, invited him to the government granary to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, gathering more than one thousand five hundred eminent disciples. Because of this, the rebels subsequently lifted their siege and departed. The State...
Having received his family’s command, he resided at Longquan Temple. He continued to propagate and expound the great *Tri-svabhāva-śāstra* (Sanlun) without the slightest negligence.

In the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era, the assembly requested that he open a lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. On the night of the eighth day of the fourth month, someone informed him, saying, "Dharma Master, before long you shall be reborn in the Western Land.
On the fourteenth day of the seventh month, he presided over a session for the *Ullambana Sūtra*; as soon as his exposition was concluded, [he passed away].

Suddenly, he folded his hands and said, "The offerings I have received in faith throughout my life—from now on, even down to a single hair's breadth, shall all be used to provide for the monks of the ten directions.
As for myself, though impoverished, I am but a beggar. He then proceeded to his seat and passed away at the age of seventy-nine. Huixuan was by nature serene and tranquil;

in his conduct toward himself and others, he was loyal and empathetic, ever delighted to encourage and promote the worthy. He nurtured those junior to him with benevolence and tempered them with righteousness.
He was truly a model for his generation. He was skilled in discourse on the *Zhuangzi*, *Laozi*, and the histories, and was particularly well-versed in the records of the Geng and Jiang families.
Each time he was invited to their military encampments, they would seek his counsel. Once, he grew weary of Guangfu’s distance from water and intended to relocate elsewhere.
Shortly thereafter, a divine being in a purple robe, approximately one zhang in height, detained him, saying that [staying there] would bring great benefit through the Mahayana.
"The world cannot overcome this. Since you require water, it is easy enough; I shall go myself to the Great Spring on Mount Cimuzi in Jiannan to summon the Dragon King.
Shortly thereafter, a great wind arose from the southwest, and thunder and rain poured down suddenly.
When the storm subsided slightly, a spring emerged to the north of the monastery, its water sweet and fragrant. Later, when he moved to Longquan, that spring also dried up.
Tang Zhicong was a man of unknown origins. He was well-versed in the Three Treatises (Sanlun). Initially, he resided at Baima Monastery in Yangzhou; later, he stayed at Zhi guan Monastery.

After the Chen dynasty was overthrown by the Northern [Wei], he crossed the Yangtze River and settled at Anle Monastery. During the chaos of the Daye era, he returned southward, but his path was blocked and obstructed.
He hid himself among the reeds and recited the Lotus Sūtra for seven days without food. Four tigers then circled around him.
Beside him, a voice suddenly spoke in human speech, saying: "It has been ten days since I last ate. Everyone says that the tiger will surely devour me;
otherwise, my life will not last much longer, and I shall simply die of hunger. The tiger declined, saying that such a thing was utterly impossible.
At that moment, an eighty-year-old old man appeared, carrying a boat under his armpit, and wished to be ferried across, saying: "Xiqia."
"This secluded and magnificent place is fit for dwelling. Please board the boat at once so that we may cross. The four tigers all shed tears, as if unable to part from him.
Thereupon, Sengcong requested to accompany the four tigers; once they had crossed over, he ultimately lost sight of the old man.
From then on, Sengcong resided west of the Śāri-kūṭa Stūpa at Xiqia. Together with eighty others, they sat in meditation and did not lie down to sleep.
Four tigers relied upon him; whenever there was an ominous event, they would invariably provide advance notice, whereby the community was led to maintain a sense of vigilance and awe.

Furthermore, grain was particularly scarce in the mountains. Moreover, there were three hundred households among the local faithful who sent a messenger saying, "We shall provide one *shí* of grain to sustain you for a year.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era, after the light meal, he paid homage to the image of Zhiyi.
After paying his respects at the graves of Fuli and Xinghuang at Zhi guan Temple, he returned and passed away while seated in his room at Qixia.

Throughout the entire city of Danyang, everyone perceived a wondrous fragrance. Three thousand disciples, both monastics and laypeople who had received precepts from him, rushed to the site, wailing in grief.
At that time, he was ninety-nine years old.

The monk Ché was born into the Jìn clan of Wànquán in Hé-dōng. Having long felt weary of the mundane world, he entered the monastic life immediately upon the passing of his two parents and practiced the *āraṇyaka* (forest-dwelling) discipline.
In the district there was Jiè Village, which was the former site of [Jiǎng] Zītūī; on its southern slope...

Mount Jie consists of precipitous and inaccessible crags and ledges. Sengche then took refuge there to cultivate the Way. After some time, people collectively built structures until they were sufficient to provide shelter.
Yet, he still suffered from a lack of water. One day, he noticed that the slope and the masonry were damp;

as soon as he dug there, clear spring water gushed forth. It never ran dry when drawn. Fang Renyu, the Prefectural Governor of Taizhou, submitted a memorial requesting that a temple be established there.
A monastery was established to commemorate his virtue; this is likely the present-day Jianquan Temple.

When a prince of the Xu residence descended to govern the region, he invited [the Master] back to reside at the local temple for the sake of paying him reverence. Shortly thereafter, he returned to the mountains to cultivate the practice of tranquility, never ceasing his innate compassion.
Wild birds would regularly come to take food from his palm, and wild beasts would sleep beneath the eaves of his hall. At the age of seventy-seven, he said to his disciples:
Tudu said, "I am leaving. He dismissed all his attendants and left only one person to serve him, instructing him to wait for his mother’s touch.

After a long time had passed since his breath ceased, as if he had entered meditative absorption, the servant shook him and found he was already deceased. For three days, the trees on the mountain turned white.
When the body was moved for burial, the weather became clear and bright, and six-petaled white flowers drifted and danced through the air, resembling ice crystals.
The snow was bright, pure, and lovely; men and women vied with one another to catch it on the hems of their robes, yet it melted away as soon as it was grasped, leaving nothing behind.
Tang Lin, the Minister of Revenue, composed an inscription for a stele to commemorate this, ensuring its legacy would endure imperishably.
Tang Huixiang’s surname was Zhou; historical records have lost track of his native place. From the age he first resolved to pursue learning, he left secular life to enter the Way.
He practiced the dhūta austerities with particular vigor, such that no one could fathom the depth of his realization. Soon thereafter, he received the Three Treatises (Sanlun).

He constantly admired the spirit of Āryadeva exposing his own belly and Dharmapāla defending the Dharma. As he traveled through the markets of the Dharma, whenever he saw those whose dignified deportment was not self-disciplined, he would look back [in disapproval].
He said to the people: "Wait until after I have received full ordination; if I am to serve as the abbot of this temple, I shall certainly ensure that [the monks] study the Vinaya.
At the age of nineteen, he lay ill for three months, and medicine could not cure him. Rising from his bed in the middle of the night, he sighed and said:

"A great man’s original intention was to take his body upon himself to shoulder the Great Dharma. Now I am beset by the demons of illness—what is to be done? Then, at dawn, he saw a person over ten feet tall who said to him:

It was sufficient merely to recite the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* for him to recover. After reciting it for three days, he was cured. While residing at Guoning Temple, he expounded the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, and his assembly remained disciplined and solemn.
Toward the end of the Daye era, during the summer retreat, while having his midday meal, he suddenly obtained a *śarīra* (relic) in his mouth.
He spat it out onto the ground, but it immediately returned to his mouth; this occurred several times in succession. He then tested it by placing it on a mortar.

The mallet did not change in appearance, yet it struck the bell to assemble the assembly of both monastics and laypeople for prayers. After a short while, it emitted light of five colors, and a wondrous fragrance pervaded the city and its suburbs;
those who witnessed this were inspired to renounce their ways, such that hunters changed their occupations and there were no meat stalls in the market.

Subsequently, the fourfold assembly erected a nine-story stupa over one hundred feet high for him. His auspicious physical form was full and fair, measuring eight chi in height; he appeared majestic from afar.
He was exceptionally magnificent. When the Regional Inspector Li Shengming arrived at the temple, he jokingly said to his colleagues, "This practitioner must eat one sheep a day.

Immediately, [Li] felt his hands and feet go numb and paralyzed, unable to lift them; he fell from his bridle and could no longer ride. He hurriedly apologized and repented, whereupon the symptoms ceased.
The Grand Commissioner Quan Mao prepared a detailed report on coarse food and tested him; after seven days, [the monk] recovered and became even more robust and flourishing.

Mao bowed in shame and submission. In the eighth month of autumn, he suddenly gave instructions to his disciples, saying: "You all should each advance in your practice; perhaps then my school will not come to total extinction.
Thereupon, holding a scripture in his hands and kneeling with his right knee on the ground, he passed away. Those near and far marveled at this. He was seventy years of age.
Furthermore, a wondrous fragrance filled the city and its suburbs, as if it were the time when śarīras were being manifested.
Tang Lingrui was originally from Yingchuan and was a descendant of the Chen clan. Having migrated to Yichang in Shu, his family had served the Daoist tradition for generations.

His mother once visited a Daoist temple and prayed for a son; upon returning home, she dreamed at night that while sitting beneath a pine grove, a bowl made of the seven treasures flew from the treetop into her mouth.
Upon waking, she became pregnant. Consequently, she took no pleasure in the smell of meat or pungent flavors. When he was born...
Sometimes, when he advanced [in his practice], both mother and son suffered from headaches that could not be cured; consequently, they eventually set him aside entirely.

At the age of eight, he accompanied his parents to a Daoist temple, where a Daoist priest ordered him to practice reciting the *Buxu ci* (Verses on Walking in Emptiness). Suddenly, blood began to flow from his face.
One day, he encountered Dharma Master Zhisheng in a field; the Master seized his robe and said, "To serve the Buddha is my vow. He then followed him from afar.
While serving as a śrāmaṇera at Shengye Monastery in Yizhou, he was able to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* from memory by the end of the summer retreat.
At the beginning of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Master Yin of Goguryeo opened the Three Treatises (*Sanlun*) and entered the capital, where everyone relied upon him to receive instruction.

Not long after, Rui returned to reside at Faju Monastery. In the second year of the Wude era, Master Gao of Anzhou resided at Dajianchang Monastery, and Rui followed him there. He remained for three years.

There was a follower of heterodox teachings at the temple—his name has been forgotten—who repeatedly attempted to harm him but ultimately failed. He subsequently moved to Longji Temple in his home village to seek refuge.
In the first year of the Zhenguan era, the donor Qian Chanshi of Tongzhou provided for all his needs throughout his life.

With more than three hundred listeners, he requested that [the Master] constantly propagate and expound [the Dharma]. On the night of the twenty-fourth day of the eighth month in the twentieth year, three...

A great wind arose, and a voice rang out clearly and resonantly, saying: "The Dharma Master Lingrui shall, in the tenth month of next year, attain rebirth on the western slope of Mount Guangming in the Great Country of the Southern Sea, in the presence of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. When the appointed time arrived...
On the third day, the multitude saw banners and flowers filling the temple. In the evening, after the lecture concluded, he entered his room and continued reading as usual.
At times, he would speak of auspicious signs; then, slowly grasping his scroll, he stepped out the door and stood still until his passing. His staff remained firmly planted and did not lean or fall.
When they carried him to his bed, he rose again at midnight and sat in the full lotus posture as if alive. He was eighty-three years of age.
Tang Mingdu resided at Shibi Temple in Bingzhou. Throughout his life, he devoted himself exclusively to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as his primary practice.
Toward the end of the Zhenyuan era, a dove nested among the eaves; when spring arrived, it produced two fledglings within the temple.
Every morning, Sengdu would sell his hair and use the proceeds to feed him, always reciting a prayer: "By the power of my recitation of the sutras, may you surely achieve success.

Shortly thereafter, Xuefei fell from flight to the ground and died. More than ten days later, Sengdu saw two small boys in a dream who said, "We were originally born from eggs, but now we have received the merit of the Venerable One’s dedication of virtue;
we have been reborn as humans. Ten *li* to the east, there is such-and-such a family."
This was indeed so. Dujue (Du-jue) immediately recorded it on the wall to keep it in mind.
Furthermore, he used his dream to verify it with those who came and went, and all regarded it as credible. When ten months had passed, he went to her home; indeed, she had given birth to two sons.
He then had his mother take them out and called out, "Pigeon-children" (He'er). They immediately nodded their heads and smiled.

Master Ci’en’s secular surname was Lü. He was a native of Ji in Weizhou. Both his ancestors had served as Regional Inspectors (*zhōu cìshǐ*) of that prefecture, and his father, Xun, was the Governor of Muling under the Sui dynasty.
When he was two years old, his parents frequently saw a Buddhist monk with white hair and elegant eyebrows, who appeared before them flanked by two attendants holding banners.
The monk said, "I wish to be your son. His parents immediately prostrated themselves before him, but he suddenly vanished from sight. Thereupon, she conceived. The following year...
On the night of the eighth day of the fourth month, she was born at the fourth watch. A rare fragrance filled the room, appearing like two banners on either side.
After reaching the age of five, she constantly beheld white light that remained unchanged until her death.

In the ninth year of the Wuping era of the Qi dynasty, when she was only nine years old, her father took her to the Chan Master Min, the Head Monk (Sengxuantong) at Yunmen Temple, where she received the Dharma from these two masters.

When it was known that she had given birth to auspicious signs, he immediately ordained her as a novice. After the Qi dynasty fell, at the age of sixteen, he studied the Four Foundations of Mindfulness and recited the Lotus Sūtra.
He attended upon Master Xuantong while they traveled east and west to evade the perils of war, never flagging in his devotion.

At the beginning of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, when the Emperor held the Buddha-dharma in high esteem, Daolun was twenty-three years old; he once received instruction for nearly half a year from Vinaya Master Li of Wuyang.
In the summer, the assembly saw five-colored light, like a chariot wheel, illuminating the space between Hui-lun’s chest and heart.
After he finished prostrating before the fifty-three Buddhas, the light remained; he then prostrated before twenty-five more Buddhas, after which it vanished.

Shortly thereafter, he accompanied the two masters Fang and Yuan into the various mountains of Taihang for over twenty years. Toward the end of the Daye era, when the world was in turmoil, he led his disciples to Weizhou.

He continued to serve as the abbot of Longshan Temple during the Later Xia dynasty. In the fifth year of the Wude era, he entered Baodushan on Mount Taihang to instruct those who came to study with him using his own practice.
In the fourth year of the Zhenguan era, the regional governor Pei Wansheng, along with his peers, requested to receive the Bodhisattva precepts from him.
On the thirteenth day of the first month in the twenty-third year, at the fourth watch of the night, he rose and said to the people:
"I have attained liberation through all dharmas," he said, yet the Lord of Devas suddenly came to welcome him, and he passed away.
At the time of his enshrinement, the sky was exceptionally clear and cloudless, yet a fine rain fell in gentle drizzles; everyone considered this a marvel. He was eighty-five years old at the time.
*The Newly Compiled Classified Biographies of Monks of the Six Studies*, Scroll Twenty-Five and Scroll Twenty-Six.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Tán’è of Zhèdōng.
Jingxue Gantong (感通) of the Tang dynasty,
surnamed Sun, was a native of Qi. He was skilled in the *zhangcao* (cursive) script and regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
This was her lifelong practice. On the twelfth day of the second month in the first year of the Yonghui era, she died suddenly at night.
When they felt her chest, there was a slight warmth remaining. After some time, she revived and said: "Initially, two youths dressed in blue robes led me to the presence of King Yama.
The King asked what kind of practice I had cultivated throughout my life. I replied, 'I have done nothing but recite the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra. The King said, 'Excellent.'"
How extraordinary! How can it be fully described? If the Master recites [the name] ten thousand times or more, he will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
Although the disciple wishes to see the Master again, it shall not be possible. From that time on, Xu Jun redoubled his diligent asceticism, surely fulfilling the required number.
He passed away in the second month of the following year; the monks of the monastery all heard celestial music and a wondrous fragrance, they say.
Huiwu of the Tang dynasty left secular life at a young age and lived in seclusion among the Taibai Mountains. He was exceptionally diligent and devoted in his recitation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Suddenly, a lay devotee arrived from afar and invited Huiwu to a vegetarian feast. Huiwu, considering the distance, did not grant the invitation immediately.
The layman smiled and said, "There is no need for you to go; there shall be a way to bring you here. Thereupon, the layman placed Huiwu within the fold of his robe and ascended into the void.
After the discourse on emptiness was concluded, he went to a certain place of practice where he saw five hundred holy monks all gathered together upon that ground.

Awakening was struck with awe and trepidation, so he hurriedly approached to take a lower seat. The layman said, "Master, you who take the *Avataṃsaka* as your primary teaching have truly realized the realm of the Buddha;
how can those of the Lesser Vehicle be worth mentioning? Yet you remain so humble. He then led Awakening to sit above him. After the meal was finished, [he gave] what he had obtained...

The alms-offerings he bestowed upon others were even more abundant and generous. The layman remarked, "This vegetarian feast was specifically prepared for the sake of awakening," yet five hundred holy monks arrived unexpectedly during the proceedings.
Judging by the era, this must have been during the Yonghui period; it is recorded in detail in the *Huayan Yingyan Lu*.
Tang Tuō was the son of the Xing family from Jiachuan in Taiyuan. He entered the monastic order in his youth and devoted himself to the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Initially, he resided at Zhaogu Temple; later, he withdrew to Foguang Temple on the southern side of Mount Wutai.

The region abounded in flowering trees, and whenever summer arrived, a Clear and Cool Pond (*Qīngliáng Chí*) would emerge at its side—a place where Mañjuśrī constantly dwelt and rested. Tuō once three times...
Upon seeing this, Yun said to Yude: "If you simply repent and take responsibility for your transgressions from beginningless time, you will be able to enter the Way.

Thereupon, he practiced these instructions with a sense of awe and did not dare to disobey, until his mind became peaceful and still. Furthermore, he was moved that the Buddha had manifested his body for him and spoken these verses.
The verse said: "The profound Dharma of the Buddhas' quiescent extinction was attained only now after cultivation through vast eons.
If one can illuminate this light of the Dharma, all Buddhas will rejoice. Having spoken, he suddenly vanished. [The seeker] then asked, "What is this Dharma of quiescent extinction?
A voice from the sky replied: "Skillful means and wisdom serve as the lamp; they illuminate and reveal the realm of the mind. If you wish to investigate the truth..."
Shishi was a man of true realization who saw nothing at all. He dwelt within the Buddha’s light for forty years, and his followers numbered only seven or eight hundred.
He passed away during the Yonghui era. Today, his miraculous body remains within the cave, and more than ten of the temple’s original halls still stand without having collapsed.
At one hundred and six years of age, Master Yao was still able to recount the events of that time.
He said: "The Master Jie-tuo saw Mañjuśrī at Dafu Lingjiu Temple, thirty *li* southeast of Zhongtai.
At that time, I was only fifteen years old. Furthermore, Chan Master Puming of Sopo Temple also sought to see Mañjuśrī and requested the Dharma.
Suddenly, a voice from the air said: 'You have not yet attained meditative concentration; you should take medicine to hope for longevity. Ming—"
He did not know where the medicine was located and harbored doubts. A voice from the air replied, "It is the tall pine tree in front of the hermitage.

Its nature is non-toxic and its flavor is pungently fragrant; by taking it, one can attain immortality. Ming took it for a long time, and one day he announced to his friends that he was departing for the heavens.
Master Sengguan, a Chan master who formerly belonged to Jianguo Temple in Xiurong, Xing, was eighty years old when he moved to reside on Mount Wangren.
The laity revered and followed him, gathering like a market to seek blessings; yet none could fathom the depth of his spiritual attainment.
During the Yonghui era, there was a blind man of unknown origin who was able to transpose the entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* onto the lute.
Playing it with his hands while reciting it orally, his tone was clear and elegant. He, too, would frequently head toward Mount Wangren.
Tang Jingzhi’s surname was Zhao; he was a native of Gaoling in Yongzhou. Initially, his parents sought to obtain an heir by reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara.
Once she became pregnant, the mother strictly refrained from eating pungent vegetables, which was unlike her former habits.

When Jingzhi was only seven or eight years old, he followed the texts to practice the contemplation of Amitābha and the contemplation of white bones, achieving success in both. He constantly aspired to leave the household life, but his parents, having only this one son, would not permit it.
He was not permitted [to do so]. Before long, his father was posted to office in Shu. Shortly thereafter, his father passed away. He intended to immolate himself as an act of filial retribution;

however, someone cited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to him, suggesting that sacrificing one's body was not as meritorious as upholding the sutra. Consequently, he shaved his head and became a monk, specializing in the practice of meditative concentration under Master Jiang.
At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, he lived in seclusion at Guanghua Temple on Mount Peng by the Dao River. He remained seated in meditation for over ten years.
He did not reside in a separate room. Those who received his instruction numbered more than two hundred at all times, practicing with diligence day and night without weariness.
He subsequently moved to the deep mountains of Lingyan, where tigers lived alongside him without causing any offense; he was naturally well-disposed toward them.

Later, at the invitation of Chan Master Daoli of Lizhou, he went to dwell on Mount Qiongfu north of Jiegao Pass, accompanied by some ten fellow practitioners. They stored four *shí* of rice for the summer retreat.
When three months had passed, he had still not finished eating one *shí* of food. Suddenly, his nose became congested with a fleshy growth that could not be cured by any means.
A monk instructed him to recite the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* ten thousand times; when he reached five thousand recitations, the flesh fell away and he was healed.
Once, while in Qinzhou, he was bitten by a venomous snake; the pain was extreme, but through the power of *samādhi*, it was immediately eliminated.
Later, when he suffered from illness, it was likewise. Consequently, he compiled a single scroll titled *Zhujia guanmen* (The Contemplation Gates of Various Schools), which circulated in the world.

In the third year of the Xianqing era, an imperial edict summoned him to reside at Ximing Monastery. On the twenty-seventh day of the second month in the fifth year, he passed away lying on his right side;
he was fifty-seven years of age. Before his death, the cassias, walnuts, and hazelnuts in the temple where he resided in Lizhou suddenly withered.
Fragment. *Nao-ba*. The temple halls collapsed and were buried, yet the statue remained almost entirely undamaged. Surely there must have been some profound connection [between them].
During the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty, Zhiqin—a member of the prominent Zhu clan of Deng—received śarīra relics from the imperial palace.
By imperial decree, Great Xingshan Temples were established in every famous prefecture throughout the realm to enshrine them, and monks were ordained to oversee the offerings. Zhiqin...

Being young, he received the tonsure through his [mother's] grace and was enrolled in this temple. He was indeed sincere and intelligent in his conduct, and whatever his will was directed toward, it invariably brought about auspicious responses.
Initially, when he prayed to Avalokiteśvara on account of his mother’s illness, a Buddha image suddenly grew upon the branches and leaves of a tree in his family garden;
his mother subsequently recovered and remained free from ailment. During the chaos of the Daye era at the end of the Sui dynasty, all temples were devastated and ruined.
Nothing was left behind, except that the scriptures and images in his temple remained intact; this was likely because Sengqin had been able to resist and defend them even unto death.

One day, when a great force of rebels arrived, Sengqin changed into lay clothes and hid himself. When the rebels saw him, they intended to kill him, but they heard a voice from the air saying, "You may remove your lay clothes.

He immediately removed them. The rebels were surprised and delighted, and they promptly prostrated themselves before him, seeking his blessings. They then escorted him back to their camp and [treated him with respect].
He lived there for a long time before entering Shu to listen to Dharma Master Gao lecture. At that time, the assembly numbered three thousand;

yet the Master entrusted him entirely to diligent care and protection, so that throughout the entire course of the lectures, no discord or deviation occurred. Later, he expounded the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* and the *Three Treatises* (Sanlun) more than twenty times in each of his local villages.
He subsequently moved to seclusion in the Northern Mountains, where he practiced the Way day and night; when exhausted, he would merely lean against something to stand, never once sleeping.
Once, while traveling among the rocky peaks, he beheld a building, serene and deep, resembling a great monastery. He entered it at once to pay his respects.

He went back and forth like this two or three times, after which it suddenly vanished. Furthermore, as he suffered from a lack of food, he noticed that the spot where he practiced walking meditation (caṅkrama) began to swell up.
Though he tilled the ground in the evening, it returned to its former state; however, large red grains of grain gradually emerged, and upon digging deeper, he obtained more grain.
He [could carry] twenty-odd *shi* [of weight]. He resided in the mountains for over ten years, and the manifestations he invoked were of this nature.

Subsequently, as the Buddha-dharma was declining in the prefecture, both monastics and laypeople joined in pressing him to leave the mountains and reside at Daxingguo Monastery. Furthermore, they commissioned him to inspect and certify the monks and nuns of the local jurisdiction;
various princes and regional inspectors came to receive the precepts from him. At the beginning of the Yonghui era, he shut his door to read the Tripitaka, frequently encountering divine beings.
People stood by his side as if listening. Throughout the beginning, middle, and end of the night, they heard the sounds of finger-snapping and clearing one's throat.

In the fourth year of the Xianqing era, an imperial decree arrived for the construction of Ci’en Temple; he was diligent and did not yield. In the fifth month of that year, he commanded his disciples to repair all the dilapidated parts of the temple.
On the fifteenth day, the trees suddenly withered and their leaves fell. On the sixteenth day, at dawn, [he performed] as he had done in the past.
While listening to the sutra, a divine being bowed before him. Qin Zhi said, "Do not bow. The attendant heard these words but had no idea that anyone was there.
Thereupon, [the deity] shaved his head, donned robes, and holding an incense burner, sat cross-legged upon the rope bed.

He instructed his disciples to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* until they reached the "Chapter on Rebirth in the Pure Land," whereupon he chanted "Nirvāṇa" (extinction). After several days had passed, his complexion showed no change whatsoever.
A fragrant aroma pervaded the entire monastery. He was seventy-four years old.

Zhi Xian of the Tang dynasty entered the monastic life at a young age and resided at Huming Temple in Liaozhou. His observance of the precepts was upright and rigorous, and his practice of Chan meditation was courageous and sharp;
no one knew the depths of his spiritual attainments. Toward the end of the Sui dynasty, bandits rose up everywhere. Whenever he encountered them, they would clash with him in a battle of blades.

They engaged in a contest to determine who was superior, and the proceedings lasted for several weeks. Daoyuan constantly mediated between them during their interactions, and over time the multitude came to admire and rely upon him.
Later, while traveling with both monastics and laypeople, they encountered the Tujue (Turks), who proceeded to plunder them. Daoyuan suddenly made himself invisible so that he could not be found;
after some time, they found him again, and he said, "It is because I recite the name of Avalokiteśvara that I am able to do so. There was [a monk named] Xian.
His fellow student had long remained in seclusion on Mount Ji. One day, hunters seized all of his provisions. Xian perceived this from afar and sent him rice as a gift.
His heart in rescuing those in suffering was beyond measure; his embodiment of compassion was boundless, manifesting universally according to the various types of beings.
Although his conduct and spiritual station were exceptional, he may still be considered nearly worthy of emulation. Later, nothing was known of his final end.
Tang Fachong, surnamed Chen, first entered the monastic order and resided at Changle Temple in Suzhou. Later, he received the tonsure at Qixia Temple on Mount She.

He was able to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* before long and soon mastered it. Furthermore, he visited the seats of the two Dharma Masters Yiyin and Huimin in Kuaiji to listen to their lectures;
his mental burdens were completely cleared away, and he attained freedom from all hindrances. During the Zhenguan era...
In the fifteenth year, he traveled to propagate the teachings in Suzhou, Hangzhou, and other prefectures; those who received his instruction numbered three hundred.
From that time on, he circulated and expounded the *Avataṃsaka* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras more than twenty times.

In the nineteenth year, the spirit of Lord Gao of Jiaxing County descended into his shrine and said to the recorder: "Request Dharma Master Cōng to receive the Bodhisattva precepts for me. Having been requested, he received them.
[The deity] issued a command, saying: "From this day forward, you must completely abstain from alcohol, meat, and the five pungent herbs.
Whenever there is one who seeks blessings, you must invite a monk to the shrine to perform a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*) and conduct the ritual services.

In the twenty-first year, at a vegetarian assembly in Hǎiyán County, the Lord of Póyáng descended upon his medium and said: "On my behalf, invite Dharma Master Cōng to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. [He then] lectured.
On several more sheets of paper, he further issued a decree: "The karmic obstacles of those in the divine realms are many;

this body suffers various afflictions, being constantly bitten by small insects within its scales and shells. Having now received the benefit of the Dharma Master’s exposition and instruction, I have attained a light ascension.
You may request him once again to lecture on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. In the winter of the first year of the Xianqing era, he said to his disciples: "I..."
After relinquishing his karmic retribution, he immediately gave [his remains] to various birds; yet he continued to lecture without ceasing.
One day, he suddenly saw his fly-whisk fall from its seat to the ground. Upon looking at it, he was found sitting upright, having passed away at the age of seventy-one.
Tang Minghui sought the Mahāyāna with resolute intent; throughout the nights of his lectures and recitations, he never once slept.

In the first year of the Linde era, when the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang passed away at the Yuhua Palace in Beifang, Jingzhao, Minghui was then at the Great Ci’en Monastery, circumambulating the Buddha hall at night during the third watch.
He beheld four white rainbows piercing the sky from south to north and east to west.

Below the well, it reflects upon the monastery courtyard. Huinian considered that according to what is recorded in the biographies, when the World-Honored One entered nirvana in the past, twelve white rainbows pierced the Taiwei constellation.
Although their number today has decreased by two-thirds of the World-Honored One’s original count, none but a sage is worthy of such a phenomenon.
Could it be that the Dharma Master of Yuhua has suddenly become like this? He questioned her on this matter.

He reported the matter to the assembly, but they did not believe him. Nine days later, the news arrived, and everyone was greatly moved to admiration. Yuanxiang of the Tang dynasty was a native of Shu.
He entered the monastic order at the age of seven and resided at Faju Monastery, where he mastered both Buddhist and secular learning.

He was skilled in literary composition and was known at the time as a "prodigious child. In the first year of the Longshuo era, he passed away due to illness. At the moment his breath ceased, a long rainbow suddenly appeared.
When he practiced ascetic refinement, the roof of his room would pierce through to the stupa above, and the bells on the cords would all ring loudly.

The murals on the walls of the three gates peeled away, and for over a hundred days, the sounds of drums and horns were heard every night. Consequently, birds and sparrows no longer nested in his house.

In the fourth year of the Xianheng era, sweet dew descended upon the branches and leaves of the *tāla* trees in front of the lecture hall. His collected works, consisting of thirty fascicles, were circulated in the world.
Tang Qingxu was a monk of Huiyi Monastery in Zizhou, Shu. Throughout his life, he had always been devoted to the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
If he devoted himself to the study of the sutras, he would constantly dwell in the mountains, where seven deer grew tame and familiar with him.
Furthermore, when a neighboring house caught fire and the entire complex of interconnected roofs and beams was consumed by the flames, the building where he resided alone remained unharmed.

In the second year of the Chang’an era, while wandering by chance to Wuzhen Temple in Lantian, he stayed in the northern courtyard of the upper section, where there had previously been no well or spring. At that time, the Great Master of the Avataṃsaka, Fazang, heard of this.
Regarding the virtue of Xu, he requested that a spring be prayed for. Xu immediately entered the Maitreya Pavilion to recite sutras, continuing from night until dawn three times.
It appeared as though he saw three jade maidens using knives to carve away the earth on the northwest slope of the mountain. The next day, they dug there and found a spring at that very spot.
In the fourth year, he spent the summer retreat at Shaolin Temple. Some people claimed that there was a demonic presence in the Buddha Hall atop the mountain.

A malevolent spirit had been killing people; through the performance of exorcistic rites, the calamity was brought to an end. In the twentieth year of the Qinglong era, an imperial edict summoned him to the palace to pray for rain.

After praying for seventeen days, snow finally fell. The Emperor, considering this insufficient to meet the expectations of the people, ordered him to perform devout prayers within the Buddha hall of the temple.
Thereupon, Xu held up one finger and a heavy rain poured down. When his finger was charred, it reappeared as it had been before. The temple stood by a river;

whenever the waters rose to the level of the buildings, they would invariably submerge them, yet Xu’s courtyard alone remained entirely unaffected. Other miraculous manifestations were generally of this kind.

Chan Master Tang’an was a native of Bingzhou. Throughout his life, he cultivated the practice of the Pure Land. During his meditative states, he frequently beheld the two Bodhisattvas, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
at times, their complete forms would appear in the void, and people vied with one another to witness this marvel.
Master Tang’an thought he should have them depicted so that they might be transmitted for posterity, yet there were no skilled artisans in the world. One day, two men appeared from—
A man from the Western Capital came and said, "I am about to travel to Mount Wutai to visit Master An; let us join our efforts in this work of painting.

Afterward, he presented his paintings alongside what he had seen within the empty space [of the mountains]. They were remarkably lifelike, and Master An was so delighted that he immediately offered him a generous reward, but the man would not accept it.
He took only two pairs of straw sandals and departed. After a long time, Master An gathered his disciples and said, "I must now certainly..."

He was reborn in the Pure Land. Was there perhaps someone who made a vow to accompany him? At that time, a young boy attending by his side stepped forward and said, "I am fortunate to have served you with staff and sandals.
He then sent the boy back to inform his parents of his decision. His parents thought he was deceiving them and treated him with amusement;
however, they bathed him and dressed him in clean robes according to the ritual. Once he had entered the place of practice, he indeed invoked the Buddha and passed away in an instant.
An said with a sigh, "In the end, I have been surpassed by this son. He immediately took up his brush and composed a hymn in praise of the two Bodhisattvas:

"Avalokiteśvara assists from afar to receive; Mahāsthāmaprāpta aids in welcoming at the encounter. The precious vase is manifest upon the crown; The transformation Buddha is clear before the ushnisha.

Together they roam through the lands of the ten directions, Holding flowers and awaiting the nine births. I pray that with your hands of compassion, You will uplift and encourage me as we travel west together. He then sat cross-legged.
He passed away on the seventh day of the first month in the first year of the Chuigong era.

At that time, he was barely eighty years of age. His secular surname was Song, and he was a native of Kuaiji. Having left home at a young age, he relied upon a monk of Changshou Monastery to practice dhyāna and contemplation;
the abbot of Changshou highly commended him. Later, he produced a commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in eighty fascicles. At that time, there was Zheng Qingshu... [the Minister].
While serving as the Prefectural Administrator of Fangling, he submitted a memorial requesting that the teachings be expounded; however, [the Master] refused and would not go.

In the second year of the Jinglong era, the Censor-in-Chief Feng Si suddenly died and then revived, saying: "At first, I saw from afar a massive tree with lush branches and foliage, capable of shading several mu of land.
Two youths arrived there holding registers and warrants, and after verifying my transgressions, they said: 'This is the Hall of the Judge.'"
He was there. His former acquaintance, Zhang Siyi, was sitting beside the Judicial Assistant. [The monk] beckoned and called out, "I am your uncle.
I served as a granary official in Luoyang, and the high-ranking official falsely accused me of a crime and had me executed.

Now, because I borrowed money from Taiping Temple and used it for oil and flour, I have not yet been released. Your current predicament is due to nothing else but the fact that you once [visited] the Empress Dowager’s Palace..."
The internal turmoil was merely incidental. If one can indeed produce the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and cast a bell, that would suffice.
Zhang then led Feng to inspect the various offices to determine which were of minor or major importance. As they were about to depart, he instructed him, saying:
"The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* must be the version transmitted by Master Lízōng to Tiantái. This scripture is surely protected by benevolent deities, and its merit is vast."
His [merit] was beyond compare. He further remarked, "Alas, how pitiable it is that those born in Jambudvīpa do not cultivate merit.
He also said, "In my home, within Dao Guang Ward of Luo City, at the third intersection of the crossroads, there is a residence with the scenic beauty of ponds, pavilions, bamboo, and trees;
I pray you will kindly inquire after the well-being of my wife and children. Subsequently, Feng sought out a good manuscript, but he was unable to find one.
He obtained it suddenly. He entered the underworld again, established a time limit, and only ceased once the task was completed. From then on, he remained in the world for forty-eight years;
as for Zongzhi, he remained in the world for ninety-seven years.
The Huayan Master resided north of the city of Youzhou. He made the study of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* his daily practice.
His chanting could be heard from near and far, as if he were right beside one’s ear. Consequently, people called him the "Huayan Master.
During the Wansui Tongtian era, the Regional Commander Zhang Renyuan rose at dawn and said to his wife, "Last night, the sound of the scriptures..."
"Did you hear it? he asked. "I did," he replied. "In what place do you think the sound originated? "It must have come from before the yamen," he said.
"No," [the master] replied. "It originated north of the city. Even now, people are still reciting it and have not yet finished.
His wife said, "North of the city is far from here; how could it have been heard? Thereupon, he sent a young servant on horseback to investigate, and the report was confirmed.
His wife was greatly alarmed. One day she said to Renyuan, "Since you have made this vow in your heart, why not fulfill it promptly? Renyuan replied, "I agree;
I am currently manufacturing five hundred monastic robes to bestow upon the Arhats. She asked, "Do you wish to know the dwelling place of these Arhats?
It is none other than Zhulin Temple on Mount Mian Shan right here. On another day, as she had said...
It is said that when they sought for one, they found a temple; yet, among those who had received the kashaya, there was one person missing.
When this person was sent back to Master Huayan, it became known that Huayan, too, was an arhat.
Wenzhao of the Tang dynasty was a youth who received the precepts from Dharma Master Tanyan at Baiti Temple in the region of Hedong.

There he shaved his head and devoted himself exclusively to reciting various sutras, yet he remained ignorant of their exegesis and elucidation. He often reflected upon the impurity of his own faculties and felt a profound sense of frustration and yearning for enlightenment.
At one time, while he was dozing, he suddenly dreamed of the Dharma Master, whose body was over ten feet tall and whose eyes radiated light in all directions.
He said to Zhao, "As for what you wish to obtain, how could I possibly procure it for you?
I have here only a single scroll of the *Cōngmíng jīng* (Scripture on Wisdom). Recite it diligently; do not neglect it. He then drew it from his sleeve and handed it to him.
Upon taking it up and examining it, he found it was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He recited it seven times and attained awakening.
From that time forth, his understanding of the meaning and his eloquence gathered within him; truly, this was not something achievable through worldly scholarly effort.
Tang Daojian was born into the Feng family of Wu Commandery. He resided at Lingyan Mountain Monastery in Lixia and was renowned in his time for his spiritual practice.

He died at the age of seventy-eight. During the Yuanhe era, a man from Wu Commandery named Feng, who was awaiting selection for office after passing the examination on the Classics, was staying in Chang’an.
One day he encountered an elderly monk, who said to him, “I share the same surname as you and am from your native region; do you not have [any kin]?”

"I wish to travel together with you. Thus, they went back and forth without interval. After more than a year had passed, Sengzhao was about to depart for his post as Commandant of Dongyue and was preparing his luggage.
Sengqie also took up his staff to bid him farewell. Sengzhao asked, "Where are you going? He replied, "I dwell beneath the western corridor of Lingyan Temple in Qi.
I have been traveling in the capital for nearly ten years now. I am now returning home; if you do not disdain me," he continued, "..."
"I hope you will kindly visit me another day. The Master (Sheng) gave his promise. Shortly thereafter, he went to visit him, but [the monk] was nowhere to be found.

The Master thought to himself alone, "Master Jian is pure and upright; how could he speak falsely? Thereupon, he wandered aimlessly through the temple until he reached the western corridor, where he saw a mural that bore a striking resemblance to Jian.
Furthermore, beside it was a stone inscription which read: "The son of the Feng family, a native of Wu Commandery."
At the age of eighteen he became a Buddhist monk; he passed away at seventy-eight. His words were not at all different from those spoken by the old monk in the past.
Upon hearing this, Sheng was struck with wonder and departed. Furthermore, as for Lingyan Temple in Gusu, it was the Guvagu Palace of King Helu of Wu, located twenty li west of the city.
In the fifteenth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, the lay practitioner Cao arrived there as a guest.
Ink and wash painting. In the northwest corridor at the corner of the hall, he painted images of Indian monks, each one foot five inches tall.
Against the plastered walls, their divine countenances were extraordinary and ancient; their spiritual traces and miraculous deeds had long benefited the world.

In the second year of the Xiāntiān era, Lord Lù Xiàngxiān fell ill and sought medical treatment, but it was ineffective. The Lord feared the illness would worsen and was deeply distressed. Just then, a monk—
While begging for alms, he passed by the gate. Entering to look inside, he sought water with which to sprinkle the patient, and the illness was immediately cured.

The official was delighted and offered a generous gift of silk in thanks, but he would not accept it. When asked where [the monk] resided, he replied, "He is at West Lingyan Temple in Wuxian County, Suzhou.
If you, young master, travel through that region on your journey, you might perhaps deign to visit him. Later, Lu Zi was indeed appointed to the Ministry of Personnel (Shangshu).
The Director of the Sacrificial Bureau was transferred to the position of Intendant of the Gui Circuit;

intending to take a circuitous route through that monastery to pay his respects and reflect upon the past, he searched everywhere with great effort, yet in the end could not find it. Suddenly, he beheld a painted image and, fixing his gaze upon it, said:
"Is this not the deceased who appeared before me yesterday? Thereupon, the monks of the monastery spoke at length of the events concerning its spiritual resonance and miraculous responses.

Lu Ziyi provided tens of thousands of strings of cash for incense and offerings, expressing his profound devotion. At the beginning of the Huichang era, [the Bodhisattva] appeared in a dream to Lu Xuan, a neighbor of the mountain, saying:
"I am now about to return west to India. Xuan immediately commissioned artisans to copy the painting.
Five years later, by imperial decree, more than forty monasteries throughout the empire were destroyed, and Lingyan was among them. Once the Dazhong era had begun...
He further instructed that the temple should remain as it was. In the seventh year of the Xiántóng era, a severe locust plague arrived;
they covered the heavens and stretched across the wilds, leaving no edible vegetation behind. When they reached the city walls, they even gnawed at the clothing, skin, and hair of the people.
The common folk suffered greatly from this. At that time, several hundred people, including Qíwén and Wú Yuànràng, burned incense and wept before the painted image, praying for the locusts.
In the fifth year of the Qiánfú era, the monks of the temple went to the imperial court to request the bell for use as a ritual implement.
Having submitted their petition to the Right Shèncè Army, the officials were surprised and said, "Yesterday, there was already a monk who requested a bell;

the temple name registered with the local prefecture and county matches exactly with this one. Is it perhaps a duplicate, or has another been produced? They then carefully investigated its markings, and it was indeed an image [of the Buddha]. Later...
Regarding the account of Bodhisattva Zhijī, it is said that this was the first instance of a Brahman monk coming to pay his respects, which is indeed so.
Táng Fǎjiāng was a native of Jiāngdōng. He traveled to Shǔ and resided at Fǎjù Monastery. This monastery was originally built by the Sui Prince of Shǔ, Xiù;
during the Rénshòu era, he once enshrined śarīra relics there, and thus it possessed many extraordinary features. One day, Fǎjiāng suddenly said to his [disciples]:
A fellow practitioner said, "Outside there are more than ten thousand donors who are all currently suffering under arrest;
they have no one to whom they can appeal. We must rescue them urgently. His companion immediately went out to look, but saw nothing.
He only saw fishermen carrying baskets of snails on their backs. He hurried back to report this to Jiang, who paid money to redeem them and cast them into the water. Furthermore—
Daxingshan Monastery in Chang’an was originally the Shaivati Monastery of the Sui dynasty. During the Tianxian era, it was reduced to ruins by fire, leaving but a few survivors.
A Daoist priest from the Dongming Guan named Li Rong, a native of Baxi who was frivolous and fond of jesting, composed a verse for the occasion:

“What is good about the Way? It has never been good. What is meant by ‘flourishing’? Yet it does not flourish. The Tathāgata has been burned to ashes; There remains only a flock of monks. The assembly [was moved].
Upon hearing this, he was both incensed and stirred; however, the undertaking required such great expense and effort that it could not be brought to completion.

Suddenly, a man dressed in a single robe, with a humble and unattractive appearance, dropped a tattered sack on the ground and said, "May you fortunately restore this to the Buddha Hall," before departing at a rapid pace, his whereabouts unknown.
Upon closer inspection, no one recognized him. He then overturned the sack and found a thousand taels of gold within. Consequently, he made the offering.
These were the four assemblies. Thus, the temple was completed with great speed.
The Tang governor was a man from Min who resided at Tong'ai Temple; he was skilled at exhorting and guiding the officials and commoners of Min, inspiring them with joy.

He relieved their urgency and resolved their difficulties as if they were his own hunger and thirst. Wherever there were monasteries or hermitages, they all achieved completion. In the tenth year of the Kaiyuan era...
They deliberated at that temple to construct a bathhouse for the convenience of the assembly. However, the terrain was higher than elsewhere, and a spring flowed beneath it;
moreover, it was distant and difficult to access, such that even a well-drawing wheel, jars, and ropes were of no use.
Subsequently, the source, which had been low and remote, suddenly dried up one night. Suddenly, a clear spring gushed forth, located some twenty paces from the bathhouse, yet close at hand.
Those who understood him considered this to have been moved by his sincere virtue.

During the Tang dynasty, Fashou left home life to reside in a Buddhist temple in the capital. He frequently traveled among the mountains and waters of Zhongnan, constantly exhorting the assembly to accomplish virtuous tasks.
Even until old age, he never grew weary of this. Toward the end of the Kaiyuan era, he dreamed that someone instructed him with a hand-towel.
He donated five hundred items of *kāṣāya* robes each to a temple for dedication. Upon waking, he prepared those objects exactly as numbered;
yet, when he subsequently inquired everywhere for the location of the dedication, no one knew. Suddenly, a monk said to Xiu, "I know where the dedication was made."
"You bring with you these offerings and a catty of famous incense; if you follow me, you shall attain the merit of dedication. Thereupon, Xiu consented.
After traveling for two days, he first became aware that the terrain was extremely deep, remote, and isolated. Proceeding further, he saw a set of millstones lying across the side of the road.
Xiu thought to himself, "This place is not one that can be reached by the tracks of wheels. And so...

Seeing that there were tools such as grinding and milling stones, he realized that human habitation was not far away. He then took out the incense he was carrying and burned it upon the grinding stone, prostrating and praying with deep sorrow several times.
From noon until dusk, the valley was shrouded in dense fog on all sides; one could not see anything even at a distance of a few feet.
After a short while, the sky cleared and brightened, and from afar he saw gold and azure hues shimmering halfway up the cliff. He faintly discerned a signboard which read:
The temple for which this was dedicated, the monks who accompanied me, and the efforts of those who assisted by my side, have all reached their end;

the bells and chimes have been cast, and now the shadows fade and the sounds subside. The following morning, the attendant led me to pay my respects to the Abbot in the hall and explained the purpose of my visit.
The Abbot ordered that the offerings be distributed among the various quarters, and the items thus distributed numbered four hundred and ninety-nine.
He went through the other rooms in the same manner; the occupants were all there, with no one else present.
When he reached the next room, it was covered in dust and its windows were dark. Suddenly, an old monk said to Xiu, "This is indeed the room of your master, the Emperor of Tang."

"While we lived together, you made some progress in cultivation, yet by nature you were fond of musical sounds. In the end, you violated the precepts and fell back into the realm of the ordinary—how regrettable!
I have thus picked up the jade flute on the wall. I said to Xiù, 'This too was what your master used in his daily life.
However, if you now present it along with the hand-towel and the *kāṣāya* robe that you offered, it will still be sufficient to honor the mountain.'"
In the interim, he did not forget his intention, doing so merely to hasten his return. Later, Xiu indeed met the Emperor;
the Emperor immediately took up a jade flute eight *chi* long and blew it, and the sound was exactly as it had been through his past practice.

Huifu of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Qi and was a native of Zhujia in Yue. In his youth, he possessed great physical strength; he was a man of chivalrous spirit who did not engage in worldly occupations.
Consequently, he entered the monastic life at Xiangyan Temple under a master. After receiving full ordination, he was able to rectify his conduct and soften his heart.
Suddenly changing his initial practice, he maintained the Vinaya and dwelt in dhyāna. He studied and investigated the sūtras and śāstras;
after some time, he entered Tianzhu Peak on Mount Huo in Qin County and built a hermitage there to reside. After a long while, a giant serpent opened its mouth toward Daofu as if to devour him.
Daofu spoke to it slowly, saying: "I have a karmic debt from the past; I request that you repay it now. If you are bound by your own karma..."

If you wish to escape quickly, you should change your form and come; once I have conferred the precepts upon you, [you may go]. Subsequently, there was indeed a youth who wished to rely on the talisman to transcend the world.
He then shaved his head, donned the monastic robes, and departed. Some reported his private ordination to the authorities. The talisman (Fu) responded with a full account of the facts.
The officials observed that this was extraordinary and released him. Throughout his life, he was skilled at reciting mantras. Upon returning to his hometown...

Li suffered from a carbuncle and requested that he perform a ritual recitation; it was healed instantly. He passed away in the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era. When his remains were cremated, his bones and joints were found to be linked together in a chain, refusing to disperse.
Tang Chujì was the son of the Zhou family from Zizhou in Shu. Having left the household life and received full ordination, he served Master Bǎoxiū as his teacher and attained the Dharma of the mind.
He lived in seclusion at a hermitage to the north of the mountains, practicing the dhūta austerities; his name became known throughout the realm.

During the reign of Empress Wu, she summoned him for an audience and bestowed upon him a monastic robe (*saṃghāṭī*). He declined the honor with earnestness and was permitted to return to the mountains, where he sat cross-legged on a wooden chair at all times.
He sat constantly day and night, never falling into slumber. A tiger would crouch beneath him as if to guard him.
For forty-six years, he never once left the mountain, yet his spiritual wonders became widely renowned. At that time, Master Muxiang of Silla came from his own country to pay him a visit.
Before his passing, Jing instructed his attendants to sweep and clean the premises, saying, "A distant guest has arrived.

At the beginning of the Kaiyuan era, when Wang Ye was appointed as the Prefectural Governor, he issued an edict to the monks, commanding that they must attend the prefectural office to present their congratulations; otherwise, the clerks were to investigate and penalize them for their offense.

Thereupon, Jing did not go. His disciples spoke against this, but Jing said, "Karmic conditions have their own course; as long as I am not yet dead, even if it be Wang Ye himself, what can he do to me?"

What happened? Later, Huaiyue, out of arrogance regarding his meditative visions, became enraged and summoned all the monks. He had them sit in the main hall and questioned them about the state of Daoji. Suddenly, Huaiyue collapsed to the ground;
his attendants hurriedly supported him and carried him into a screened area, where he died. It appears that Huaiyue was formerly a Taoist priest (*huángguān*).

During the Jingyun era, he rose to a position of minor official rank and was subsequently appointed to govern a district with its people and lands. Nevertheless, he never showed the slightest concern for our Teaching.
Ji died in the first month of the twenty-second year [of the Kaiyuan era]. He was eighty-seven years old.
Tang Deyou was the son of the Sun family of Fuyang. From his youth, he transcended the mundane world; at an early age, he perfected his precepts and discipline.
His heart of compassion and salvation for all things sought primarily to uproot suffering and bestow happiness upon all sentient beings, so that they might all be joyful and free from distress.
When one is weary and distressed, one’s aspirations may finally be considered fulfilled. Nevertheless, the realm of the unseen world suffers most from the affliction of hunger and emptiness;
therefore, whenever food or drink is offered, one must invariably wait until the night is deep and still, performing visualization, chanting, and prayers according to the prescribed ritual.
From beginning to end, he was free from transgression and remained true to his original vows. The people along the banks of the Zhe River truly revered and looked toward him.
Later, when he manifested his passing at Mount Ding, his traces were marked by extraordinary and supernatural wonders; this occurred in the first year of the Tianbao era.

When his remains were moved to be enshrined within a stupa, seven *śarīra* relics suddenly rained down from the sky. His disciples placed them in a jar and buried them within the stupa. After a long time, someone inadvertently opened it.
As for that stupa, its exquisite appearance was as if it were alive. Shells [śarīra] adhered to its teeth like grains of millet;

consequently, it was repaired and expanded into a great pagoda. Furthermore, a white snake appeared, entering and exiting as if to provide protection; for this reason, neither woodcutters nor herdsmen dared to approach it.

Tang-seng (the monk from Tang) was born into the Zhao clan of Yanmen. In his youth, he entered a local school; although he applied himself with the utmost diligence, he never attained anything of substance.
When he encountered monks and nuns, he could do no more than join his palms in reverence and stand in awe of them.

At the age of twelve, his parents sent him to rely upon Master Jingjue of Huayan Monastery on Mount Wutai to undergo tonsure. Having received full ordination, his nature became increasingly dull and obscured.
He was dull-witted, yet he carried firewood and drew water; at that time, the community marveled at him.
When he reached the age of thirty-six, he made a vow to behold Mañjuśrī in person and beg for wisdom, hoping thereby to advance his studies and complete his vocation.
During the height of midwinter snow, he suddenly ascended barefoot to the summit of Mount Dōngtái. There he saw an old man sitting by a fire. Yun asked where he had come from, and the man replied:
Descending from the mountain, he said, "I have come down from the mountain; there are no other tracks. Could you possibly be deceiving me?
Yun replied, "The snow preceded me. The old man then asked Yun, "Why do you walk barefoot through such deep snow?
Yun told him the reason. The old man said, "Excellent! However," he continued, "since I was unable to see the Bodhisattva here, why do you, Master, wish to..."
"Where should I seek him? Yun said. "He must have gone to the Northern Terrace. The old man nodded and said, "My thought is the same. You should go first; do not linger.
Yun then traveled extensively across the secluded and magnificent peaks of the terrace.
Upon bidding farewell to the old man, he reached the Northern Terrace as dusk fell. There, at the very summit, he again saw the old man sitting by a fire just as before. Amazed, he...
When asked about the reason for his prior arrival, he replied, "I simply know the direct path. Yun thought to himself, "If it were not for a Bodhisattva, how could one be capable of such a thing?
He immediately prostrated himself at the old man’s feet. The old man firmly declined, saying, "I am but a layman. Yun continued his prostrations without ceasing.
The old man said, "Let me simply enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*) for your sake and observe. Thereupon, he closed his eyes; after a short while, he opened them again.
He said to Yun, "The Master was a water-dam ox in your previous life. Because you once exerted great strength pulling a boat carrying the Tripitaka, you have obtained this monastic reward.
However, that dull and obtuse nature still persists because there is a mass of congealed flesh from kalpas past remaining within your heart."
"Now I shall depart. You may go to the Dragon King Hall and fetch a hoe. Yun then respectfully closed his eyes and said, "I will not hear your voice;
do not open them. Shortly thereafter, he felt a hoe being applied to his chest, yet there was no pain, only an extraordinary sense of refreshment.
The old man said, "The necrotic flesh has been removed. Now open your eyes. As soon as he opened his eyes, it was Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
He stood before Sa and said to Yun: "From this day forward, you have both skillfully memorized and maintained the scriptural teachings without any loss.
Furthermore, you have a particularly deep affinity with the eastern cloister of the Huayan Gorge. You should apply yourself with diligence and receive my entrustment."

Yun prostrated himself in sorrowful gratitude. Before he had even raised his head, the vision suddenly vanished. Later, while Yun was observing the summer retreat within the monastery, he circumambulated the Śākyamuni Stūpa (King Aśoka’s Stūpa), walking back and forth while reciting the scriptures.
Toward the first watch of the night, he saw a single beam of light shining directly from the summit of the northern terrace onto the site of the stūpa;
it remained there for a long time without dispersing. Within it appeared a jeweled pavilion, upon which a golden plaque was inscribed with the characters "Śubhavyūha" (Well-Abiding). Yun said:

In the past, the Bodhisattva had already bestowed a prophecy upon him; how could he dare to forget it? Thereupon, he resided in Dongjianyuan, having constructed a pavilion according to the manifestation [of his vision].
He was highly esteemed by the world and was called Niuyun (Ox-Cloud), which was said to be a manifestation of the Bodhisattva.
In the twenty-third year of the Kaiyuan era, he passed away without illness at the age of sixty-three and with four years of *śrāmaṇera* ordination.
14. Huixiu of the Tang dynasty was born into the Li clan of Chenliu. In his youth, he took refuge at Tiangong Monastery in Luoyang and received full ordination.

During the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, she frequently invited him into the palace to inquire about the Dharma. Whenever he spoke of future events, his predictions of fortune and calamity invariably proved accurate; consequently, people of the world generally revered and served him. This occurred repeatedly.
At Ziseng Temple in the capital, he was inaugurating the monastery. One day, he instructed his disciples not to light lamps at night;
even the perpetual lamps before the Buddha were to be extinguished. The disciples would not obey. Xiu then said, "The danger of a spreading fire must be prepared against.
Furthermore, because a certain temple failed to prepare, the disaster reached its main hall; another temple’s bell tower was likewise destroyed."
The temple and its scriptural repository were likewise destroyed; all that remains until today is mere regret. Is it possible to repent for what has passed?

At that time, everyone took these words to be mere generalities and did not understand their significance. That evening, at the third watch, the temple was consumed by fire, and only these three items remained as unburnt relics.
Only then did they realize that the objects he had pointed out were none other than these. When the Emperor Xuanzong was still the Prince of Lu, he [the Master] accompanied the various princes...
Fashi left behind a single flute as a parting gift for Daoshou. Daoshou immediately took it and instructed his disciples, saying, "Conserve this with care;

you must certainly use it to present as an offering in the future. During the Kaiyuan era, the disciple Damo took it to present to the Emperor, explaining that this was the specific instruction Daoshou had previously given.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor was struck with wonder and granted him lavish rewards. Daoshou subsequently fell ill and passed away at the age of... [years].

At the age of one hundred, Huaidao of the Tang dynasty entered the monastic order and was registered at Aitong Temple in Fuzhou. From his early years, he devoted himself to seeking instruction from masters and was particularly diligent in ritual worship and recitation.
One day, while prostrating, he obtained a pearl that was perfectly round and lustrous; he suspected it could not have been produced from the womb of an oyster. Later, at that temple...
He fashioned a statue of Mañjuśrī, for which the forehead jewel (ūrṇā-kośa) was particularly renowned. Furthermore, he once obtained śarīra relics that were likewise extraordinary;
he subsequently enshrined them within the Nanjian Pagoda. His disciple, the monk Sengchang, presided over the affairs of the pagoda and was able to recite the *Lotus Sūtra* from memory.
Daodu ordered him to recite it, and he did not dare cease day or night. In the second year of the Zhide era, a single white *kāṣāya* robe suddenly descended into the pagoda.
Among such cases as these, none can be fully understood. Some say they were brought about by the power of sincere resolve; is this not so?
Daobada was a monk of Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou during the Tang dynasty. He had long been renowned for attaining worldly efficacy through the recitation of secret mantras.

Therefore, the courtyard where he resided contained ritual implements such as sand-stamping beds and mirrors for reflecting the Buddha. The tides of the Zhejiang River are more perilous and magnificent than those anywhere else in the world;
when the autumn is high and the air is crisp, the waves surge with violent force, destroying embankments and overrunning city walls, causing great distress to the common people.
Thereupon, he performed prayers for averting calamity. Suddenly, one night, he beheld a majestic figure wearing a dark cap and crimson robes.
Yi, leading his followers, went before him and said to Da: "I, Daizi, am the Wu-yuan of Gai Wu.
In the past, with the intent to avenge my grievances and wipe away my shame, I harbored my indignation between heaven and earth, causing harm to all living beings;
thus, I incurred much reproach from those of virtuous character. Now, I rely upon you, Master, through your compassionate and sorrowful sincerity, to bring an end to my affliction."
"Once you are freed from the fetters and hindrances, you will surely be able to ascend and cross over. Having finished speaking, he vanished. Later, sand indeed rose on the western bank;
people said this was brought about by the spiritual response of Da.
Tang Yuanjiao was a native of Lingwu. He had long made his livelihood through the practice of recitation and clear invocations.

At the end of the Tianbao era, Emperor Xuanzong fled to Shu, and Crown Prince Suzong, gathering troops to plan the recovery of the two capitals, subsequently ascended the throne in accordance with public sentiment.
In the second year of Zhìdé, the imperial carriage headed for Fúfēng, and an edict was issued for Huìjiǎo to depart ahead. Previously, Huìjiǎo had enjoyed a fine reputation throughout Guānshǎn;
when the Emperor returned from the east, he particularly wished to have him accompany him as a monk of pure conduct. Thereupon, the official attendants nominated Huìjiǎo for the post.

The imperial decree reached Fengxiang. Thirty-seven monks were selected to establish a Bhaisajyaguru-samādhi ritual site at Kaiyuan Temple, where they lit lamps, recited sutras, and performed the path-practice (xingdao) during the six periods of the day.
Suddenly, within the ritual site, forty-nine branches of wild plum trees sprouted from the ground. When this matter was reported, the Emperor was greatly pleased.
On the eighteenth day of the fourth month, Jingjiao and others submitted a memorial of congratulations. The imperial reply stated: "The auspicious plums have flourished in abundance."
This is an omen for the flourishing of the nation; how much more so within a Buddhist monastery! It is sufficient to add glory to the Bodhi tree.
Moved by these extraordinary auspicious signs, I share in the celebration with you, Master. [Signed: Jiaoshu, Inner Attendant.
During the Jinglong era of the Tang dynasty, Huaiyi of Lengqia Monastery in Fuzhou exerted great effort to construct a vihāra to the east of Aitong Monastery.
Once the construction was completed, however, the site lacked a water source, causing distress among the community. Suddenly, two birds appeared, wheeling and dancing above the ground.

Someone immediately ordered the earth to be excavated; after digging only a foot or so deep, gushing springs welled up to provide for their daily needs and seasonal festivals, remaining constant even during floods.

It overflows during times of flood yet does not diminish during droughts; were it to overflow or diminish, the fortune or misfortune of the temple would depend upon it. Some call it the "Numinous Spring.
In the second year of the Yongtai era, it manifested its extinction.
Tang Zilin was of the Fan clan. His family had resided for generations in Dafan Village in Qianfeng County, Yanzhou. His father, Fan Junchao, took no pleasure in the Three Jewels;
whenever he saw them, he would spit upon and revile them, or even strike them with his hand. Zilin’s childhood name was Lin’er. When he was only a few years old, he showed reverence toward monks.
At the beginning of the Kaiyuan era, Vinaya Master Qingxiu of Guang’ai Temple in the Eastern Capital traveled to Mount Tai; on his way, he passed through [Yanzhou].
A man of the Fan clan saw him from a distance, prostrated himself, and requested to leave the household life. He asked, "Have your parents given their permission? He replied, "I have not told them;
had they known, I would have been subjected to flogging. The Master went on ahead while he followed behind. Before five li had passed, the Vinaya Master had already traveled some distance.
Yet his neighbor suddenly caught up with him. Sengzun followed him, adopting his robes and shaving his head as if they had been bound by a long-standing karmic bond.
In the eleventh year, Sengzun suddenly took leave to return home for a visit; at that time, his father had been blind for three years and his mother had passed away.

Nevertheless, Senglin wished to know where his mother was located, so he went to the Temple of Mount Tai at night, prepared his ritual implements, and recited the Lotus Sūtra, seeking an audience with the King of Tianqi. The King indeed summoned him.
