A neighbor asked for the reason. The neighbor said, "Since your mother, Lady Wang, passed away, the period of mourning has already ended; may I ask where she is now?
King [Wang] looked at his clerks and replied, "Lady Wang is currently imprisoned in jail and suffering. The neighbor asked, "For what crime? King [Wang] said:
When Master Zuo was alive, he ate chicken eggs. Furthermore, he took the head sores of Bai Fu (Bai Juyi).

His neighbor wailed in grief and exhaustion, entreating the King for clemency, saying, "Karma cannot be avoided by the power of others. As for a plan for your teacher, you should go at once to Mount Mao to pay homage to the Aśoka Stūpa.
The next morning, the neighbor followed the path to the temple; before the Śarīra Stūpa, he cast a tally and prostrated himself.

He performed prostrations until he reached forty thousand. Suddenly, he heard the voice of someone calling for his neighbor; looking up, he saw his mother amidst the clouds, who said, "I thank you for your efforts.

I have been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and have come specifically to repay your kindness. He returned to the Guanzhong region, where he gained renown through his lectures and exegesis. During the reign of Emperor Suzong, he was selected to enter the inner palace;
his skill in divination and narrative was such that none of his contemporaries could equal him. By imperial decree, he was granted a purple square-cut robe and appointed as a ritual attendant.
Respectfully submitted. During the Yongtai era of Emperor Daizong, Amoghavajra retranslated various scriptures; [the author], Lin, was selected for an official post in the Imperial Library.
Tang Xuanzong was a native of Yongjia. In his youth, he followed Master Changjing at Baoshou Temple on Mount Yongding in his hometown and left the household life.
After receiving full ordination, he traveled to study in all quarters and received the Dharma-seal from Ci at Jiangling.
Later, Master Lang moved his staff to Mount Zijin, where he built a dwelling to practice *jñāna-vipaśyanā* (wisdom-insight) and to cultivate the multitude.
Previously, this mountain had been plagued by many violent tigers; however, from the time Zong arrived, such violence ceased entirely.

One day, while he was preaching the Dharma surrounded by his disciples, an old man suddenly hurried forward and prostrated himself in accordance with the rites. Zong asked, "Who are you? Have you come by mistake?"
"How is it that we have never before been acquainted, yet you show me such respect? There must surely be a reason for this.

The old man said, "In my previous life, due to my sinful karma, I fell into the body of a tiger. Had it not been for the Chan Master’s instruction, I would have continued to devour living beings and would now be suffering the retribution of hell.
Now, fortunately, I have attained this heavenly state; how could I not know its origin and forget it? Suddenly—
He offered his thanks and, having finished speaking, vanished. In the second year of the Dali era, Zong passed away at the age of eighty-six.
He was a monk from Qixian Temple in Hanzhou, Sichuan, during the Tang dynasty. The temple’s former name was Lingyi; previously, there had been one named Shen Cang.

Because he was not careful in upholding the Vinaya, a divine being hurled him down from the mountain for a distance of about seven *li*; yet he was injured by only a single toe on his foot, which served as a warning.
Ultimately, he reformed himself and became a virtuous man. At the beginning of the Dali era, the northern mountain suddenly turned the color of gold.
The patterns on the rock formations all resemble multi-storied pavilions, with the traces of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas walking upon them.

Within these, one can practice the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa). Among the people of Mianzhu, there are none who do not revere and serve them. One day, a person died while serving as a lay donor (dānapati) for the elephants.
The donor prepared the funeral rites with great completeness. Just as the spirit-carriage was about to be lifted, two deer suddenly came forward and led it back to their monastery.
Yet, no one knew from where these deer had come. When the carriage reached the threshold of the gate, the temple plaque fell to the ground without apparent cause.
People near and far were struck with wonder and sighed in admiration; thus, they established a shrine within the monastery to enshrine his image.
Tang Huai-gan’s surname and native place are unknown. He was a man of great learning and diligent practice, whom people from all quarters looked up to as a model.

He alone harbored doubts regarding the various sutras and treatises concerning the efficacy of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha's name), specifically how one could be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss without requiring the passage of many lifetimes.

He subsequently went to visit Shan-dao to inquire about this. Shan-dao replied: "You transmit the teachings and deliver sentient beings; if you were to expound these lectures, it would be for the sake of your own self-conviction."

Only after that did he lecture. Furthermore, was it not because he lacked self-confidence that he lectured tentatively, merely to indulge in deception and heresy? He replied, "If one does not believe the sincere words of the Buddhas, one should not lecture on them.

Huida said, "If what you have observed is indeed true, then how could the teachings on mindfulness of the Buddha and rebirth in the Pure Land found in the various sutras and treatises be the words of Māra?
Thereupon, he entered the ritual arena for twenty-one days; considering his own karmic obstructions to be deep and heavy, he practiced with great earnestness.
He felt it was a regret not to have beheld a spiritual omen and intended to fast until death. Zhi Dao did not permit this, instead urging him to redouble his diligence.

Three years later, he indeed beheld a golden hue and a jade-white ūrṇā-kośa, thereby attesting to the *nienfo samādhi*. He composed the *Jueyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) in seven fascicles and passed away facing west with palms joined.

Dharma Master Fa-shen of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Sun. His mother conceived him after dreaming that she had swallowed a bright pearl. Upon his birth, he possessed extraordinary features and an unusual appearance, unlike other children.
He followed a teacher to shave his head and received full ordination according to his age; thereafter, he cultivated his nature beyond mere physical form, living in seclusion in self-attainment.
Thereupon, the Great Master Dienenzheng entrusted him with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the *Bodhisattva Precepts*, and the *Awakening of Faith*.
One night he dreamed that he was crossing the sea by boat when a mountain appeared before him; yet the boat he was riding upon surged over the peak and reached the other side unimpeded.
Upon waking, he broke into a cold sweat and was overcome with joy beyond measure. From this experience, he composed verses to string together the flowers [of the teachings].
His realization of the Dharma was profound and free from any stagnation. In the sixth year of the Tiānbǎo era, he painted an image of Vairocana at Chánglè Monastery in Sūzhōu.
In the second year of the Dàlì era, at the request of the assembly, he went to Longxīng Monastery in Chángzhōu to expound the teachings.

Just as he was about to ascend the Dharma seat, a divine light suddenly appeared, like a trailing red thread that gradually grew larger and brighter, swirling in the air. Those who had practiced cultivation for a long time were the first to behold it.
On the seventh day of the eleventh month of the thirteenth year, the śramaṇa Huìjué dreamed that a massive three-tiered stupa sank into the earth.
Subsequently, Dàoxuēn passed away due to illness; he was sixty years of age and had been ordained for forty-three years. His disciples Tàichū, Zhèngjué, and Shénxiù succeeded him.
As for his tomb, Master Zhòu of Wǔxīng composed a stele inscription, and Master Sù of Hángchéng composed a eulogy.
Tang Qihan, whose courtesy name was Dengzhi, was the son of Shen of Wuxing. His grandfather and great-grandfather had served the Chen and Sui dynasties before entering the present dynasty;

for three generations, they had maintained their virtue in seclusion. Qihan himself lacked the worldly flair suited to common society. On the fifth day of the eighth month of the eighth year of the Tianbao era, by imperial decree, he received the tonsure and was registered at Yongding Temple.
In the tenth month of the ninth year, he ascended the Five-Part Platform and received the *ubhayato-bhāga-vimukta* precepts.
He was transferred to Kaiyuan Temple. During the Dali era, he was further transferred to Huqiu Temple at the request of the monastics and laypeople of those two prefectures.

Zhihan specialized in the commentaries on the *Sifenlü* (Four-Part Vinaya), and he was particularly proficient in the *Lotus Sūtra*. He transformed the regions of Wuzhou, Suzhou, and Huzhou; whenever there were matters of great merit, he would undertake them.
He never failed to welcome [the image] as his master. In the tenth year, he entered the Water-Flowing Buddha-Mindfulness Dharma Hall.

Within the state of right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), the various signs of the Western Paradise suddenly appeared; this was surely brought about by his pure sincerity. Consequently, in that same year, he passed away at Huqiu.
His age was sixty-eight; his years since ordination were twenty-six.

Fǎzhào of the Táng dynasty was a man of unknown origin. In the second year of the Dàlì era, he took up residence at Yúnfēng Temple on Mount Héng, where he practiced his cultivation without slackening.
Once, during the morning congee in the Sanghārāma, he beheld five-colored cloud-gas suddenly rising within his alms bowl, and the mountain...
The reflection of the temple appeared within it. Fifty *li* to the northeast of the temple was a mountain; at the foot of the mountain was a ravine. To the north of the ravine stood a stone gate.
Upon entering the stone gate and traveling for about five *li*, there was a temple with a golden plaque inscribed:
"The Great Sage Bamboo Grove Temple. At that moment, my eyes perceived it clearly while my mind remained skeptical, as it was a place I had never visited in my life.
On another day, the various temples of Mount Tai appeared once more within the clouds of his midday alms bowl;

their towers, pavilions, ponds, and grottoes were all adorned with myriad jewels, devoid of any mountains, forests, or impure things. Furthermore, the pure and lovely Buddha-lands of the ten directions manifested together before him.
After he finished eating, they vanished. Thereupon, Zhào questioned the two masters Jiāyán and Tánhuī regarding their former travels to the Five [Mountains].

Master Tai’s words accorded even more closely with what was witnessed. In the fourth year, he subsequently established the Five-Assembly Nianfo (Buddha-recitation) Dharma-hall at Hengzhou Hudong Temple.
On the second day of the sixth month, auspicious clouds completely covered the entire temple;

within the clouds, the reflections of pavilions and towers appeared, along with several monks in the form of Brahmās, each about one zhang in height, holding *khakkhara* staffs and walking along the path. Amitābha Buddha... [text fragment]
Surpassing Samantabhadra, ten thousand bodhisattvas—tall and majestic—were all present. From the hour of zi until you reached you (the hour of wu), they gradually vanished.
Those among the local people who saw them were for the most part moved to tears and paid their respects.

When it was evening, Huizhao was outside the site of practice when he encountered an old man who said to him, "Master, you previously made a vow to go to the Golden World to pay homage to the Great Sage; you may go now. Zhao [departed].
He replied, "The times are perilous and the roads are treacherous; it is not yet possible. The old man said, "Simply go quickly and do not fear. Suddenly, he vanished.
On the thirteenth day of the eighth month, he gathered his companions and set out from Mount Heng.

On the fifth day of the fourth month of the fifth year, they reached Mount Wutai, where they already saw several streaks of white light to the south of Foguang Temple. The next day, they went to the temple and gazed [upon it].

The scene was exactly no different from what had previously appeared in his alms bowl. At the fourth watch of the night, another light came from the northern mountain and shone directly upon his body.
As soon as it illuminated him, he entered the hall and questioned the assembly. The assembly replied, "This is the inconceivable light of a Great Sage;
it constantly serves to awaken those with whom he has a karmic connection. Thereupon, Zhaoying assumed a dignified posture and followed the light toward the east of the monastery.
Traveling fifteen *li* to the north, one indeed finds a stone gate at a mountain stream and other features.
There, two young attendants named Sudhana and Nanda, aged eight or nine, stand outside the stone gate; if they have been waiting for you, they will lead you through the gate.

Traveling five *li* further north, one passes the Golden Gate Tower. Upon entering the gate, there is the Great Sage’s Bamboo Grove Monastery (*Zhulin Si*). The ground is composed entirely of pure gold, from which [streams] flow...
The grove of flowers was only twenty *li* in extent, with corridors surrounding it on both sides and one hundred and twenty courtyards;
compared to what he had seen within the bowl, this appeared somewhat more distinct. In the center of the lecture hall, upon the lion throne, Mañjuśrī sat to the west.
Samantabhadra was situated to the east, surrounded on all sides by a multitude of great bodhisattvas. The sound of his preaching the Dharma could be heard clearly and distinctly.
[The assembly] looked toward him and paid homage, asking: "Ordinary beings of the final age possess shallow wisdom and deep obscurations.

The ocean of the Dharma is profound and vast; though we wish to practice it, we find no way to grasp its essentials. We only pray that the Great Sage will point the way and reveal its location. Mañjuśrī replied:
Among all gates of practice, none surpasses mindfulness of the Buddha. Regarding the two adornments of merit and wisdom, there is nothing left unattained.

Because I practiced mindfulness of the Buddha throughout past kalpas, I have now attained the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā). For this reason, among all the pāramitās, [mindfulness of the Buddha is supreme].
"Even unto all Buddhas, they arise from mindfulness of the Buddha. You should practice mindfulness diligently and not allow it to cease.
Zhao then asked, 'What is this mindfulness? [The Master] replied, 'To the west of this world is Amitābha Buddha. The power of that Buddha’s vows is inconceivable.
You should fix your mindfulness upon him so that it remains uninterrupted; then, after the end of your life, you will certainly attain rebirth there. Having spoken these words,"
Then the two bodhisattvas extended their golden hands, touched his head in blessing, and conferred upon him this prediction:
"By the power of your merit from recollecting the Buddha, you shall before long realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
If there are sons or daughters of good family who truly desire to swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood, they need only recollect the Buddha. Thereupon, the two bodhisattvas each spoke [as follows].
Gāthās were used to illuminate this for him. Upon seeing the light, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; the net of his doubts was instantly removed.

He prostrated himself in thanks and stood by the side with palms joined. Mañjuśrī led him to tour the various courtyards of the bodhisattvas, where he everywhere requested their instructions and admonitions.
They also visited a garden of seven-jeweled fruit trees; as soon as the fruit ripened, it was as large as a bowl. He took one and ate it, and his body and mind became tranquil and at ease.

Xuan Ci took his leave of the Bodhisattva and departed. Following the green-clad attendant to the gate, he suddenly lost sight of him. He then paced back and forth and gazed out from afar, his grief and emotion redoubled.
On the thirteenth day, he again accompanied more than fifty monks to the Vajra Cave to follow the traces left by Asaṅga and pay homage to the names of the twenty-five Buddhas;
at that time, Zhao alone saw the ground shining like lapis lazuli and palaces [appearing there].
The assembly was solemn and pure; Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and ten thousand bodhisattvas, including Buddhāpālita and others, were seated or standing with dignified composure.
As for the other monks, they saw nothing. At the third watch that night, he again saw five lamps atop the western tower of Huayan Monastery, where he was staying.
He silently prayed, "I wish for these to multiply into a hundred lamps," and immediately they became so. He then said, "I wish for them to become a thousand lamps."
It was likewise so. Furthermore, the orderliness of its arrangement was beyond anything the world could emulate.
He then proceeded alone to the Vajra Cave to see the Great Sage. Buddhāpālita led him into the sacred temple; the details are recorded in the *Jùjuéjiù zhuan* (Biography of Jùjuéjiù).

On the twelfth day of the month, at the temple’s Nian (Recollection) Hall—the site of the Buddha’s place of enlightenment—he vowed to abstain from grain and resolve to be reborn in the Pure Land. During the night of the seventh day—
Just as the chanting for the Buddha was about to begin, a Brahman monk arrived at the ritual site and said to Zhao, "Why do you not also circulate the realms you have perceived?

Zhao did not respond. At the hour of Shen the following day, an elderly Brahman monk appeared and said, "Mystical and extraordinary matters should be shown universally to sentient beings so that they may give rise to the bodhicitta. Zhao replied, "I did not dare to conceal them."

[This is] indeed so. However, I fear only that the sentiments of the common folk will give rise to slander. The monk said, "When the Great Sage resided on this mountain, slanderous discourse was rampant and could not be stopped;

how much more so regarding the realm you have seen? Furthermore, both inherent goodness and inherent evil are equally Bodhi, and thus the drum of the 'poisoned paint' (tú-dú) must naturally be unfailing in its conditions.
In the first month of the sixth year, the monk Chonghui of Huayan Monastery...
Over thirty people, including Mingqian, erected a stone inscription on the grounds of the Prajñā Hall within the Vajra Cave.

At that moment, they suddenly heard the sound of a bell, elegant and resonant, with its rhythmic intervals clearly defined. The assembly was struck with even greater wonder and marvel, concluding that what Huizhao had revealed could not possibly be false.
Later, Huizhao further constructed the Zhulin Monastery as a means of manifesting his own realization. 12.

On the thirteenth day of the ninth month of that year, Zhao led his disciples Chunyi and Weixiu, along with Zhizhuan, the novice Weiying, and the lay follower Zhang Xiling—eight people in total—to ascend the Eastern Terrace. There, they first beheld white light appearing four times.
Strange clouds gathered and billowed; when the clouds parted, they were crimson in hue. Mañjuśrī rode upon a blue-maned lion within a five-colored light that permeated his entire body.
As fine snow drifted and fell, the halo of light completely illuminated the mountains and valleys. This is recorded in detail in the account by Wang Shizhan, a military official of Jiangzhou.

Tang Daoyi was a native of Siqu in Zhedong. At the beginning of the Kaiyuan era, he arrived at Mount Tai and hung up his staff at Qingliang Temple, where he resided in the Buyu Hall and served as the *diànzuò* (the monk in charge of the refectory).
He would carry firewood and timber daily, yet finding the labor too arduous, he would weave bamboo sandals and trade them for those who were stronger to take over his tasks.
Once, wearing a patched robe, he went out for a stroll; traveling northeast for about five li, he encountered...
An old monk lived at the foot of Mount Laṅkā; his appearance was simple and ancient, yet his spirit was serene and refined.
A youth followed behind him, though he was actually unacquainted with Daoyi. Suddenly, the monk called out the youth’s name, Jueyi, and sent him to invite Daoyi to the temple to drink tea.
Together they entered the temple and toured all the courtyards, where they beheld a great three-storied pavilion, both above and below.
The nine bays were all golden in color, their brilliance dazzling to the eye. Shortly thereafter, the old monk said to Huaiyi, "This mountain is cold and difficult to dwell in;
you should return early. Huaiyi assented and took his leave. After only about a hundred paces, he looked back at the site and found it to be nothing but a vast wilderness of mountains and forests.
At the beginning of the Dali era, Huaiyi submitted a memorial describing the circumstances. By imperial decree, Jinguesi Temple was established on that very spot.

Ten administrative districts provided assistance for the expenses. The Śramaṇa Cunda from the Western Regions served as the chief supervisor. Once the construction of the temple was completed, an imperial edict was issued to bestow [the temple] upon the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra.
The Tang dynasty smith Tang Cao was the son of the Cao family of Luling; his courtesy name was Bolian. He possessed a stern and resolute countenance, yet his heart was gentle and virtuous.
He constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, always carrying its scrolls in a bamboo tube which he wore upon his person. He vowed to remain celibate for the rest of his life.
At that time, the world was unsettled due to the An Shi Rebellion, and peace was nowhere to be found, the situation being particularly dire in Jiangnan. Great...
In the seventh year of the [Dali] era, in the eleventh month, Lü Dàfū rebelled in Guangzhou.

The Prefectural Governor, Liu Níng, received a dispatch from the Regional Headquarters in Hóngzhōu, led by Lù Sīgōng, ordering him to recruit three thousand men to recapture Pányú. Bólíán was among those selected;

after he had presented himself for inspection, he was further appointed as a minor general of the expeditionary force. Bólíán grew weary of this and consequently fled as a fugitive. The headquarters immediately...
An order was issued to pursue him through all strategic points. He was subsequently captured at Yangkou in the prefecture and sent in shackles for the local authorities to dispose of.

The prefect ordered his execution at Zhumiao Bridge; however, when he was beheaded three times, the blade failed to penetrate the flesh each time. The prefect marveled at this and asked for the reason. He replied: "I am naturally timid and cowardly.
When I was conscripted into the army, I feared that my lack of martial prowess would bring disgrace upon the military prestige; therefore, I fled. Nevertheless, [the third time...]"
That those who were struck down did not even realize it—what can this truly be said to be?
Is it not perhaps the power of the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra*? When asked where the sūtra was now, he replied: "When I was captured, it fell several hundred paces away;
how could I have expected to find it so quickly? Indeed, there were three sword-marks upon the bamboo tube. How extraordinary it was to hear such an account!
The monk was popularly known as the "Three-Sword Master. His name was registered at Longxing Temple in the prefecture.
Zhi Deng of the Tang dynasty, whose origins are unknown, received the tonsure and enrolled as a student at Tianchong Temple in Jingzhou.

He had long studied the *Vinaya* and especially devoted himself daily to the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. During the Zhengyuan era, he fell ill and died; seven days later, he returned to life.
Sengdu said: "At first, I saw a man whose robes and cap were like those of a king. He was surrounded by officials and soldiers as he sat upon the hall.
When I arrived, he descended the steps and greeted me with a bow of great respect. He invited me onto the hall, and we exchanged the roles of host and guest. Once seated, he said:

'Because you, Venerable Monk, possess the merit of reciting the sutras, I have specifically granted you ten years of extended life. You should resume your cultivation to sever the cycle of rebirth. Sengdu asked:"
Within the Sangha, *yiyiren* (coix seed) was used as a medicinal food after meals. [The King asked,] "Is this permissible? The King replied, "This is not found in the Vinaya.

Daoping said, "The Vinaya contains provisions for what is strictly forbidden and what is permitted under certain conditions; how can you say that? The King replied, "These were added by later generations;
they do not reflect the Buddha’s intent. Daoping ultimately did not know his final destination.

Tang Puming was a man of unknown origins. He had long practiced meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and was particularly adept at proclaiming the vehicle of the *dharmaparyāya* to awaken the multitudes.
At the beginning of the Dali era, he accepted an invitation to reside at the Hermitage on the River in Zu County. Students flocked to him in numbers like ants.
The lay patrons who provided him with material gifts arrived at his door every day.

Jia Dan, the Right Vice President of the Imperial Secretariat and Military Governor of Huazhou (Yicheng Commandery), had long been deluded by the arts of lead and mercury and did not show respect toward śramaṇas;

yet upon seeing Ming, he descended from the steps, left his seat, and prostrated twice, welcoming him according to the rites. He subsequently invited him to Longxing Temple in the prefecture, where Ming’s Way—

The flourishing of the Dharma reached its zenith during his time. On the tenth day of the intercalary twelfth month in the *Ren-shen* year of the Zhenyuan era, he suddenly passed away while seated in meditation.

His remains were cremated, and the resulting *śarīra* relics were collected; a stupa was erected at that monastery. Ten years later, the Song dynasty succeeded the Zhou through abdication and launched a western campaign against Liu Min.
At that time, a man from Huai, named Chai Qing, renowned for his prowess, was dispatched as a scout. He remained hidden by day and traveled by night to avoid detection.
While on patrol, Chang Ruo-ming constantly led the way before them, and they eventually reached the border of the state without mishap;
was this not perhaps a miraculous manifestation of his spirit? Indeed, it was only natural that Qing would always pay homage to his image whenever he was in his hometown.
Tang Zizhao was a native of Wangdu in Boling. In his youth, he followed the śramaṇa Zhiquin at Kaiyuan Temple to leave the household life.

In the second year of the Zhide era, he received ordination after passing the scriptural examinations and immediately took full precepts. He further studied the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma at Chanfa Temple in Lingshou County;
for nine years, he investigated and contemplated them until he had mastered their most profound and secret depths. In the ninth month of the first year of the Dali era—
He moved his residence to Chonglin Mountain Temple in Pingshan County. With its clear streams and white stones, it was truly a sublime place for reclusion.
He wandered about with bare shoulders and bare feet, gathering wild vegetables and acorns for food; he took no heed even when tigers and wolves crossed his path.

In the fifth month of the second year, the Regional Commander, Lord Zhang, came to the mountain due to a severe drought to visit Jue and pray for rain; as soon as the prayer was made, [the rain fell].

[The work] was completed with abundant sufficiency. From then on, Master Zhang served [the deity] with diligent devotion, casting a forty-nine-foot statue of the Great Compassionate Thousand-Handed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara.
This was intended to manifest the forty-nine vows he had made throughout his life.
He first constructed a small hermitage beside it to house the craftsmen and laborers; later, he expanded it until it became a great temple—this is what is known today as...
As for Dabeizi (Great Compassionate One): while he was chanting the Buddha’s name during the night, at the third watch, he suddenly saw three paths of golden light illuminating the ground.
Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta stood in the air; the Buddha alone extended his arm and stroked Jue’s crown.
Furthermore, he called out the name of Jue, saying: "You must benefit sentient beings and maintain your resolve without wavering.
On the full moon of the second month in the eleventh year of the Zhenyuan era, he again heard a divine being report: "The Master will surely enter parinirvāṇa this year.
On the thirteenth day of the sixth month of that year, he indeed passed away at Beici Temple. On the eighteenth day of the fourth month in the thirteenth year, his spirit-shrine was moved.

It was buried to the south of the temple. At the beginning of the Xiande era during the Five Dynasties period, an imperial edict ordered the Ministry of Finance to melt down its image to provide for state expenditures.

While they were working with blazing charcoal, the artisan suddenly collapsed. To this day, the statue still has perforations through its chest and crown. When the Song dynasty received the abdication of the throne, an edict ordered it to be restored to its original completeness.

There was a monk from India during the Tang dynasty whose name has been lost to history. When Wei Gao (style name Wuzi) was three days old, his family held a vegetarian feast for the monks in their hall.
As the nursemaid carried Gao about to seek blessings, a certain Indian monk spoke alone to the father, saying: "Take good care of him;
in the future, he will surely establish merit on the western frontier and advance to a high position at the northern palace. The prestige of the Wei clan shall depend upon him."
He arose from his seat. His father then asked for the reason, and he replied: "This child was Zhuge Wuhou in a previous life.

When Wuhou assisted Shao- lie in upholding the Han lineage, the people of Shu were so deeply grateful and moved by him that they have now recognized the birth of Cheng as being destined for your family;
thus, the fortune of your house shall surely be equal to that of this child. Furthermore, since Wuhou already possessed [great virtue]..."
In Shu, those who come now shall enjoy their retribution; this is precisely what our Buddha calls "karmic conditions.
His father thought this was so. Later, Gao was recommended by Zhang Yi to take charge of Longzhou.
When Li Chulin killed Yi, Gao immediately led the forces of Fengxiang to execute him. Zhu Ci bestowed upon him the posthumous name Fengyi to honor his service, and further promoted Gao.
He served as Minister of Rites. At the beginning of the Xingyuan era, he was summoned to serve as General of the Left Golden Myriad Guards.

During the Zhenyuan era, while serving as the Governor of Chengdu, the Southern Barbarians and the Tibetans launched incursions; he repeatedly achieved military victories and was enfeoffed as Prince of Nankang Commandery, subsequently promoted to the rank of Grand Marshal.
He eventually attained high status and prominence in Shu; thus, what the monk said was indeed true and not false.

Tang Wuzhu was a native of Yongjia. From his youth, he possessed firm resolve and integrity. Having left the household life and received full ordination, he immediately studied the Mahāyāna without the slightest negligence.
Traveling through various regions, he arrived at Yunhua Temple in the capital, where he relied upon Master Chengguan to investigate the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
He was a guide who penetrated the Dharma-realm; there were no sutras or treatises that he did not extensively expound.

In the second year of the Dali era, he traveled to Mount Wutai and took up residence at Huayan Monastery. It was the fifth month, and while he was sitting in the summer retreat hall, during a break for tea, he saw an old monk of very haggard appearance sitting naked upon the northern couch.
He asked him, "You have come from the south; may I borrow the rosary you are holding?"
Upon seeing him, Daozhu hurriedly handed it over. In the blink of an eye, the old monk had vanished from sight. Daozhu considered this a marvel and thought to himself:
"In the past, there were those who saw a stone mortar and wooden pestle here and ultimately attained entry into a sacred temple; perhaps I am one such as they.
He then ascended the Prajñā Sūtra Pavilion to look out, when a *śrī-vatsa* bird suddenly appeared, soaring and dancing in the midst of the void, its wings—

Mao Qianxuan spread her wings and flew toward the northeast. The next day, two streaks of white light pierced through the door and entered, illuminating the interior of the temple with brilliance before fading after a long while.
Her fellow resident, Fǎděng, made a vow, saying: "If you are indeed a Bodhisattva who has turned your attention toward me, the light should appear again.
Indeed, it appeared as before. Thereupon, she went alone to the Vajra Cave to pay her respects; becoming weary, she dozed off for a moment upon the stone.
Third, while hearing the sound of a cow being scolded as it drank water, he awoke and beheld an old man whose appearance and attire were exceptionally simple and ancient.

The master rose, took the man’s hand, and asked where he had come from. The man replied, "I have come from outside the mountains seeking provisions. The master asked, "Where do you reside? He replied, "Mount Tai. The master asked further, "Master, why are you here?
He replied, "I have long heard of the Vajra Cave, so I have come here out of a sense of sympathetic joy. The master said, "What does the Master wish..."

"Are you sleeping? Please come to my quarters and drink some tea. Thereupon, they proceeded together toward the northeast. At a distance from the monastery, the elder knocked on the door and called out "Juntei!
three times. A boy answered the call and came out; he was about fourteen or fifteen years old, with hair reaching his eyebrows.

His short, coarse garment barely reached his calves. The old man handed him the lead-rope and had him lead the ox in first. Then, he ascended directly to the hall and sat down, bowing as the other took his seat beside him.

After the youth had served tea, he further presented *sukara* (butter-milk) and curd; its flavor was exquisite and lingering, and upon swallowing it, the inner sanctuary of the spirit felt clear and refreshing.
Furthermore, the buildings, beds, seats, and utensils were all made of gold, jade, ivory, and tortoise shell, their splendor beyond compare.
It was magnificent and extraordinary; it was certainly not of this human world. The old man asked what he was cultivating and practicing.
He replied, "I have merely dipped my fingers into both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The old man said, "If that is so, then when you first left the household life, what did you intend to seek?

He replied, "I strove to seek the Mahāyāna. The old man said, "Then you have already obtained what you sought from your initial resolve. Furthermore, tell me your age. He replied, "Thirty-one. The old man said, "Master is pure..."
Shu was thus. From now until the thirty-eighth day, the roots of merit and the sprouts of virtue shall flourish and grow deeply in this place.
Suddenly rising, Shu thanked him and said, "I am old and weary; I wish to rest. You, Master, may depart. Zhuo requested that he stay for one night.
[Shu] said, "You have two companions waiting for you to return; can you truly stay? Furthermore, it is because your attachment to worldly emotions is not yet exhausted that you wish to remain. Zhuo—

The Master replied, "As for clinging to worldly emotions, this is something those who study the Buddha-dharma ought to exhaust completely; how could you, my companion, dare to harbor such attachments? He asked, "Do you carry the three robes?
[The monk] replied, "I have carried them since receiving the precepts. The Master said, "Yet it is also said that one must exhaust all clinging to emotions.
Having said this, he suddenly rose, waved his hand in farewell, and hurried out. The old man said, "Listen to one verse from me," and immediately sang: "One thought of pure mind"
This is Bodhi. It surpasses the construction of stupas made of the seven treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
though those stupas may ultimately be crushed into dust, a single thought of pure mind achieves perfect enlightenment. [He] called out "Jumti" and placed [him] down. Again, he patted him on the back.
Together with the boy, they went before the Vajra Cave. He asked the boy, "What is the name of this temple? The boy replied, "What do you, Master, think of this cave?"

[The Master] asked, "What is its name? [The boy] replied, "It is called 'Vajra' (Diamond). Beneath 'Vajra,' there are two characters; can you recall them, Master? [The Master] said, "I cannot. Could they be the characters for Prajñā?
The youth smiled and said, "This is precisely Prajñā Temple. He then chanted again: "When there is no anger on the face, it is an offering;
when there is no anger in the mouth, it emits wondrous fragrance; when there is no anger in the heart, that is the true treasure."
That which is unstained and unsullied is the true eternal. Suddenly, all vanished together.
Looking back toward where the old man had been encountered, white clouds drifted away, and from the earth about ten feet upward, a five-colored rainbow emerged.

Upon it sat a Bodhisattva riding a lion, while other Bodhisattvas surrounded him, dispersing in all directions. After a short while, white clouds rose from the east and gradually covered and disappeared. Nothing remained.
Upon their subsequent visit, six monks—including Xiu Zheng, the abbot of Bodhi Monastery in Fenzhou—also went to the cave to pay their respects.

They happened to encounter Daozhu there. When Zhu asked them about what they had attained, they replied that they had heard nothing but the mountain rocks vibrating and roaring like the sound of thunderclaps.
Zhu then recounted the previous events to them; the six monks were filled with regret and sorrow, realizing all the more how they were burdened by their own karmic obstructions.

It is said that he remained in seclusion within the mountains for the rest of his life. During the Yuanhe era, his disciple Wen Yi recorded these events in a memorial, which has circulated in the world.
During the Changqing era, the Tang monk Fazhao frequently saw him amidst the commoners of Shanfu, speaking with a stammering voice as if possessed by something.
He was reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. One day, while taking shelter from the rain at an inn, it had already passed midday.

Realizing that he could not go out for alms, he sent his young attendant to buy a shoulder of pork in the market. He cooked it thoroughly, sliced it thinly, spread it over a flatbread (*hu-bing*), and rolled it up to eat.
In a short while, they were all gone; he acted as if no one else existed around him. Those who saw this were incensed and reviled him, considering his conduct improper.
The youth was so intent on beating him that he waited until nightfall, when he entered the room and closed the door. Sengzhao continued his recitation as usual.

After a short while, a brilliant light permeated the walls of the house and a fragrant aroma filled the courtyard. Some people followed one another to prostrate themselves before him in repentance for their offense, yet Sengzhao remained seated cross-legged, unmoved.
Tang Shousu was by nature high-minded and upright; his character remained unchanged whether he was in poverty or prosperity during his travels with others.
He resided at Daxingshan Temple in Jingzhao for many years, never once stepping outside his door. He recited the Lotus Sūtra thirty-seven thousand times.

He was moved by the devotion of a marmot, which would come to him at night to listen to the sutra in a docile manner, and by crows and magpies, which would come to his palm at noon to take food. In the courtyard of the temple stood four green paulownia trees.
A grove of paulownia trees. These were originally planted by Su himself; in the summer months, their cool shade is lush and spreading, making them especially lovely.
During the Yuanhe era, many scholar-officials sought coolness and avoided the world at this temple.

Suddenly, the paulownias began to exude a sweat that dripped like ink, splashing onto the clothes of visitors so that they could not be washed clean. The travelers were distressed by this, whereupon Su prayed to them, saying: "I have nurtured..."
"I embrace you, yet you remain thus; I shall now strike you down. Thereupon, the sweat did not emerge. Was the resolve of Su then truly so easy to fathom?
Tang Huizong was surnamed Cai and was a native of Jingzhou. In his youth, he joined the monastic order at Gong'an Temple and received the tonsure. During the Changqing era...

At first, he was suddenly stricken with a wasting disease. Although skilled physicians applied medicines and treatments, none were sufficient to cure him. With his internal organs obstructed and his body emaciated, he could not even manage his own food and clothing.
Consequently, he made a vow to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for the rest of his life in order to pray for rebirth in a favorable realm.

When he had reached the fiftieth recitation, he dreamed one night that someone ordered him to open his mouth. Once he had opened his mouth, [the person] extracted over a thousand hairs from his throat.
He also dreamed that he vomited earthworms about an inch long; after barely a month had passed, he was cured.
Jiankong of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Qi and was a native of Wu Commandery. His original name was Junfang. His family had been scholars for generations.

He read books to grasp their general meaning rather than striving to memorize them, yet he frequently suffered from ailments while engaged in his writings. Being poor, he sought patronage among various officials in the regions of Wu and Chu.
Whenever he encountered no patronage and obtained only enough money to fill a single string of cash, his illness would flare up; he would spend it all on medicine and only then recover.
At the beginning of the Yuanhe era, he traveled to Qiantang. As the year was plagued by a great famine, he thought of begging for his midday meal at Tiantzhi Temple.

Upon reaching the west of Gushan Temple, however, he was so famished and exhausted that he could not proceed; sitting upon the embankment by the lake, he shed tears and sighed deeply. Suddenly, there appeared a monk...
A monk standing nearby laughed and said, "The Dharma Master is a scholar; have you not traveled far enough?
At this, Kō heard his call and, finding it strange, became suspicious. He replied tentatively, "I have traveled far enough. Moreover, when you address me as 'Dharma Master,' who are you speaking of?
The Indian monk said, "Do you not recall reciting the Lotus Sūtra at Tōdai-ji Temple in the capital of Luoyang?"
Kong said, "I am already forty-five years of age, yet my footprints have never once been set upon the soil of the capital of Luojing.
How, then, could I know of Tongde Temple? [The other] replied, "You are currently being consumed by the fire of hunger; it is only natural that you cannot know.
He then reached into his bag and produced a jujube fruit about the size of a fist, saying, "This is a product of our country, eaten only by those of superior wisdom."

He was able to comprehend the three periods of time. With inferior wisdom, he had only understood his previous life. He scooped up water with his empty hands and drank it; then, he leaned against a rock and fell asleep.
Upon waking, he clearly remembered the events of the Dharma lecture given by his fellow practitioner as if they were from yesterday. He immediately asked, "Where is Master Zhen?
[The spirit] replied, "Because his attachments were not yet severed, he was reborn in Shu as a monk. Now they have been severed. [Zhi] said, "Spirit..."
"Where is the Venerable Master? [The messenger] replied, "By the power of his former vows, he has gone to propagate the teachings in lands where the Buddha-dharma does not exist.
[The messenger] asked, "Where is the Dharma Master Wuzhuo? [The messenger] replied, "He once made a vow before a stone Buddha statue at Mount Xiangshan, saying:
'If I do not realize unsurpassed bodhi, I shall become a warrior to alleviate the national crisis. Now I have heard that he has already entered government service as a Great General."
The Indian monk then spoke again to Kong, saying: "At that time, including myself and you, there were five of us companions.
Among them, I alone have attained liberation. Although those three others have not yet transcended birth and death, they still continue their cultivation."

He did not fall into inferiority. As the only son, he extensively expounded heterodox views from the lion’s throne, causing scholars to waver between doubt and awakening regarding the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

This led them to give rise to false conceptualizations and become negligent in self-restraint, perhaps even lacking the "jewel of precepts. Such karmic retribution is only natural; there is no cause for regret.
Kongju bowed hurriedly and said, "O Monk, through your compassion, I pray you will deign to grant me mercy and salvation. The Indian monk probed...

From his robe, he produced a mirror whose front and back were both translucent and bright, saying, "The distinctions between the noble and the lowly in this world, the length of one's lifespan, and the flourishing or decline, the rise or fall of the Buddha-dharma—all of these can be known by gazing into this. Kong looked at it once and expressed his gratitude, saying:

I respectfully wear these instructions upon my person. The Indian monk then placed the mirror back into its case and departed. After walking some ten paces, he suddenly vanished from where he had gone.

That evening, Daoxing went to Lingyin Monastery to have his hair shaved under the guidance of his master; he received full ordination and traveled to various regions to study, his conduct becoming increasingly solitary and austere.
In the first year of the Taika era, he visited Tiantzhusi Temple at Longmen in Luoyang and recounted these matters to Liu Li of Hedong.

Kong’ou said, “My lifespan will reach seventy-seven years, and my *saṃghāṭī* age will be thirty-two. With nine years remaining for me to beg for alms with my bowl, will the Buddha-dharma decline after my death?
When Liu Li questioned him further, he remained silent and gave no answer; instead, he sought out a brush and inscribed [the following]:
The Inscription on the Northern Wall of the Sūtra Repository states: "To raise one grain of sand and [count] the sands of the Ganges; to set snares for hares and nets for dogs;
when oxen and tigers encounter one another, their horns and fangs clash—yet the flower of the precious sandalwood tree shall never perish. Later, it was unknown where he ended his life.
Tang Dingguang entered the monastic order at Fugan Temple in Chengdu, which is what is commonly known as Dashisi (Great Stone Temple).
An Aśoka stūpa containing śarīra relics was located there. Originally, the stūpa stood to the southwest of the temple.

Toward the end of the Tiānbão era, Zhangqiu Jianqiong came to serve as the Regional Inspector (Chángshǐ). Upon reaching Jiànmén Pass, he saw a man over ten feet tall holding a halberd who blocked his horse, saying:
"I am the guardian deity of the pagoda at Woguk Temple. Hearing that you, sir, have received your official decree to oversee the affairs of the district, I have come here to welcome you.
However, there is a minor matter I wish to represent to you; I pray that you will deign to listen. At present, the location of the pagoda is not perfectly auspicious.
If it were moved forty-two paces to the northeast, it would be acceptable. Furthermore, there is a large rock beneath it; I beseech you not to [disturb it]."
"Dig it up. Qiu consented. Having been in the commandery for only a few days, he reported what he had seen to the governor and proposed the relocation of the stupa.
He ordered the ground to be excavated first; indeed, they found a large stone that could not be moved. Although they chiseled and hacked at it, it would immediately become level and full as before.
Thereupon, he dispatched officials and soldiers to keep watch by its side at night. They saw several dozen white pigs using their snouts to push aside the broken stones.
Wherever he plugged the holes made by the chisels, he would lick them with his tongue, and they would become as hard and solid as iron; it was truly beyond human capability.

In the end, he moved the stupa just as the deity had instructed, and the temple was named after the stone. After Emperor Wuzong suppressed the Buddhist teachings, Guang returned to wearing Confucian robes.

During the reign of Emperor Jianxuan, the establishment and propagation of the Dharma-gate flourished even more. Guang was able to return to the temple and diligently restored what had fallen into decline.

He subsequently solicited over ten thousand jin of red gold to cast a great bell. While the hammering and striking were underway, suddenly there appeared smoke and flames of five colors, like a rainbow or a celestial halo.
The [light] divided into two streams, emerging from atop the *cakra* of the stupa and meandering through the entirety of space;

those who witnessed it were filled with wonder. Tang Faxiang, surnamed Yu, was a native of Changshui in Wu. At the age of seven, his teacher had him practice the recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
in barely three weeks, he had mastered the entire work. His proficiency far surpassed that of other children. During the Dali era, he received the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
At An Guo Temple in the capital, he subsequently comprehensively studied the Vinaya texts for eleven years, until he had achieved a profound mastery.
Upon his return, students flocked to him like a marketplace. The Prefect submitted a memorial requesting that a *śīla-maṇḍala* (ordination platform) be established at Kaiyuan Temple;

he was appointed as the presiding master (*xiang*) and charged with the administrative leadership of the monastery. Having ascended the platform, he served as the primary refuge for the assembly, constantly bestowing [precepts].

Clad in white robes, he observed the precepts and carried a water-strainer, using it wherever he went. Throughout his life, he never kept any possessions beyond what was necessary. On the ground where he sat, crows would always perch;

though they were driven away, they would not leave. On the tenth day of the second month in the first year of the Huichang era, he said to his disciples Qingjun, Qinggao, and others, "I am about to depart.
Thereupon, he sat with his feet stacked one upon the other and lay down on his right side. The assembly—
He heard celestial music sounding during the day and beheld auspicious light in the evening. He lived to the age of eighty-nine and had been a monk for sixty-nine years.
In the fourth month of that year, his reliquary was moved to the plains of La-su.

In the second year of the Jingfu era of the Later Tang dynasty, his disciples, along with Cao Xin, the Regional Inspector of Yizhou, and Wu Fang, the Judicial Assistant of Dali, reopened the stupa to re-consecrate it; therein they discovered the remains.
His remains were the color of copper; his tongue was like a lotus flower; his teeth were complete, numbering forty-two.
After being bathed with fragrant water, he was interred on the twenty-fifth day of the fifth month of that year.
Fazheng of the Tang dynasty resided at Kaiyuan Temple in Jiangzhou. He specialized in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, reciting it thirty-seven times daily without ever failing.
At the beginning of the Changqing era, he died suddenly from illness but then revived, saying: "At first, someone led me to a place that resembled a government office.
A king, dressed in the ceremonial robe and crown, was seated upon the throne. He questioned Fazheng, saying: 'During your life...'"
"What is it that you practice? [The Master] replied, "Precisely this sutra. The King hurriedly gestured for him to ascend the hall and ordered a high seat to be prepared.
He was made to mount it and recite the scripture. As soon as he began the title, the King rose up in awe, and all the attendants joined their palms at the foot of the stairs.

The clamor of interrogation, flogging, beating, and litigation suddenly ceased. When the recitation reached the seventh repetition and concluded, those who had been covered by [the King's] punishment were [granted] merit.
Thus, those of virtue were reborn in the good realms. As they cheered and danced, they embraced one another. Thereupon, the King said to Zheng:

"From this day forth, you shall live in the world for thirty more years. It is my hope that you will continue to practice and uphold [the teachings] even more diligently so as to reach the stage of fruition.
He then dispatched an envoy to escort him back. Upon returning, Zheng encountered a pit in his path, which caused him to stoop down.
He peered inside. Suddenly, [the monk] pushed him into it. He eventually regained consciousness. Subsequently, he indeed lived until over eighty years of age before passing away.
A famous monk of the Tang dynasty once stayed as a guest in a Buddhist temple in Dongjing. He provided money to have a lay attendant (jìng rén) purchase wine.
The temple community became angry and plotted to humiliate him. Someone said, "There is no need; you should simply not give him any to drink. After a short while, the lay attendant...
He returned home carrying wine in a jar. The assembly snatched the jar and smashed it against the cypress trees in the courtyard; the wine adhered to the trees, solidifying and not flowing away.
The monk hastily caught it with another vessel, and as the wine entered the container, there was not even the slightest mess.
The monk then drank from it quite naturally. Someone asked him what technique he used to achieve this; at first he declined to say he did not know, but when pressed further, he said: "I..."
I have always maintained the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. However, it is essential that one first drinks [water] so that the voice and breath may flow harmoniously;

if one recites without having drunk, the opposite occurs. Now, desiring to perform this recitation, I ventured to trouble the lay attendants (*upāsaka*), for which you gentlemen were provoked to anger.
"I believe it is certain that he would not have been able to drink [the poison], yet it happened thus. Was this perhaps brought about by his extraordinary physical strength?
Even I cannot know for certain. The crowd dispersed in astonishment.
Tang Jianyuan’s origins are unknown. He possessed supreme conduct and was able to maintain the monastic precepts as a model for his contemporaries, not merely engaging in empty discourse.
Furthermore, he was profoundly versed in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; whenever he lectured, the hall would be filled with scholar-officials, earning him the reputation for hosting "excellent assemblies.
Moreover, although the granaries contained barely several hundred *hu* of grain, yet along—

From summer into autumn, the offerings for morning sales and midday meals provided for a thousand people daily were never lacking. Could this be possible without the influence of a profound spiritual resonance?
The temple where he resided was filled with many miraculous signs. Meditation Master Huiguan was a venerable elder of that monastery.
It was said that at night, more than three hundred monks could invariably be seen holding lotus-shaped lanterns, ascending clearly into the air.

During the Kaiyuan era, Lord Cui Ning of Ji doubted this as being false; he personally stayed overnight in the mountains to observe, while simultaneously prohibiting anyone within thirty li of the mountain from lighting fires.
At first, he saw nothing, but on the third night, he saw over a hundred.
A lantern appeared in the air, and further, a light of crimson hue manifested for over a thousand chi.
Thereupon, Lord Ji prostrated himself with urgency, exclaiming that such a thing had never occurred before. Suddenly, from amidst the pines, a golden hand emerged, approximately seven chi in length;

two bodhisattvas of yellowish-white complexion also appeared, so dazzling that one could not look directly at them. On the following day at noon, a single lantern appeared atop the cypress trees in the courtyard. Together with...
The sun’s brilliance vied with it. Extending for about three *li* across the Glass Mountain, there was a single precious gem, one *zhang* in diameter, shimmering and lovely to behold.
Above the mountain gate on the western ridge, a great rainbow bridge arose;

upon the bridge, a Brahmin monk, an elderly man, and a youth emerged holding two torches, moving back and forth through the air as if in a ritual of welcoming and seeing off. Below them, pairs were matched.

Four bodhisattvas were manifested, their entire bodies emitting light of various colors, standing sixty or seventy feet tall. Suddenly, they displayed the temple’s name plaque amidst a great pine forest;

later, they inscribed the characters for the "Three Studies" in seal script. Furthermore, two ornate silk ribbons hung down from a brilliantly glowing lamp that descended through the night between the eastern groves of Mount Jinshan.
When the moon was at its zenith, there appeared two lamps—one of gold and one of silver—standing in a row and illuminating the site.

The site beside the tomb of Dharma Master Xuan is truly a most extraordinary place. Every year in the third month, Wei Gao, Prince of Nan’gang, would come to the monastery to host a vegetarian feast for three hundred bodhisattvas.
After the Chief Minister Bai Minzhong had renovated the various halls and buildings, he further documented all its sacred traces and submitted them to the throne.
In the eighth year of the Dazhong era, an imperial edict changed the name to Kaizhao; thus it became known as the East Stream Vinaya Monastery.
He was the master who ultimately traced back the source [of the lineage].
Tang Weizhong left home to become a monk in his youth and was registered at Fating Temple in Pei County, Chengdu. His aspirations and conduct were firm and prudent.
He was naturally revered and admired by his fellow villagers. The temple had long possessed a stupa that was exceptionally lofty and imposing.
One day, a thunderclap struck with such force that a thick mist enveloped everything; suddenly, a wooden beam from the center of the stupa emerged on its own and came to rest on the ground nearby.
Zheng himself did not know how this could have happened. Previously, the Maitreya statue of the temple had manifested extraordinary spiritual responses. Consequently, Zhong...
I pray that you consider this: the stupa is the repository for the śarīra of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and it is that which devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts ought to protect.
If it is suddenly shaken in such a manner, it will give rise to the idle speculations of the world and result in the sin of slandering the Dharma.
Therefore, a Bodhisattva would rather sacrifice their own body and life than allow sentient beings to suffer the consequences of such slander.

"This is a transgression against the Dharma. We pray that the Great Being will bestow his protection upon us. After a long time, the wooden pillar returned to its place within the stupa exactly as it was before;
the transformations of thunder, lightning, and dark mist were no different than they had been yesterday.

Some even saw four divine beings, their bodies equal in height to the stupa, supporting and guiding the pillar. Was this not indeed the response to his loyalty? Eventually, Zhong passed away at the temple.
Lingyou of the Tang dynasty was a man of unknown origins who resided at Dàwēnguó Temple in the Capital.

He once died suddenly and then revived, after which he went to Zhōnglí Temple in Háo Prefecture to seek out stone inscriptions of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Thereupon, he carefully examined them and discovered that all the versions circulating in the world were deficient by one section:
the passage following "There is no dharma that can be preached; this is called preaching the Dharma. He subsequently memorialized the imperial court regarding this matter.

Add this [to the record] and distribute it throughout the world. When he first entered the underworld, he saw the one known as King Yama, who asked him what his primary occupation had been throughout his life.
He replied that he had recited the sutras. The King then ordered him to recite them until the end of a single scroll. The King said:
"It is good, indeed; yet it is not yet perfectly good. He then spoke to him regarding the missing passages and said, "I shall extend your life by ten years;
you may now proceed to compose the work as previously instructed. The deceased respectfully accepted the command and did not dare to disobey.

Tang Weigong resided at Faxing Monastery in Jingzhou. His character was unruly and he lacked proper conduct; nevertheless, he was particularly diligent in the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
There was another in the same monastery named Lingkui whose behavior was similar; people referred to the two of them as "The Two Harms."
One day, while Sui was out for a stroll about a li from the monastery, he encountered six or seven youths whose countenances were quite handsome and whose robes were elegant and clean.
They held musical instruments in their hands, such as those used in the Kucha style.

When they asked Sui where Sengcong was, Sui suspected they must have come to the monastery to offer incense and wished to know Cong’s whereabouts. He told them the truth without hesitation. The following day...
Upon returning to the monastery, he reached the gate and heard the sound of a bell. He said, "Gong passed away last night at the second watch.
Inferring from this, the youth he had seen must have been a celestial musician coming to welcome him.

Had Gong devoted himself single-mindedly to goodness throughout his life, would the power of his recitation of the sutras have resulted in nothing more than rebirth in heaven? Thereupon, Kui was moved to realization.
The heights he attained cannot even be mentioned in the same breath as those of [Master] Gong.
Tang Sui-duan, surnamed Zhang, was affiliated with Derun Temple in Mingzhou. Throughout his life, he made it his constant practice to specialize in the recitation of the Lotus Sūtra.
In the second year of the Xiantong era, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture; shortly thereafter, a blue lotus flower appeared.
Seven stalks emerged from his mouth; those near and far vied to behold them, considering it a rare wonder. He was buried on East Mountain, where light and radiance frequently manifested.
After more than twenty years, the multitude again opened his tomb to look upon him; his countenance was as if alive.
Thereupon, they welcomed him back to the monastery and, having reinforced him with lacquer and cloth, enshrined him in the Hall of the True Body. This monastery was that of Prince Wu.
This is the Hall for Reading Books of Kan Ze, the Grand Tutor and Marquis of Duqing; its plaque reads "De-run" (Virtuous Moisture), which is Ze’s courtesy name.

Zhi Bian of the Tang was diligent in his studies and possessed a remarkable memory; his comprehension reached a divine level, such that what he understood could not be produced by ordinary intellectual consciousness.
When he lectured, his voice was clear and resonant, and his analysis was incisive and profound. Nevertheless, among the disciples who relied upon him...
No one came at all. He sighed alone, saying, "Have I truly severed the seeds of the Buddha? How is it that my affinity with others is so lacking?

A man of long-standing virtue passed by and instructed him, saying, "You should prepare plenty of cakes and snacks, go to a place in the forest where birds and beasts congregate, and scatter them there morning and evening.
Furthermore, you should pray, saying: 'I vow that in a future life, may they become my followers in the Dharma and attain [enlightenment].'"
"Bodhi. Thereupon, Bian followed these words exactly; for twenty years, he did not neglect them for even a single day.

Later, he propagated the teachings at Kaiyuan Temple in Ye, attracting a multitude numbering in the thousands. When their ages were compared, they were all barely twenty years old; thus, [Bian] was a teacher of long-standing virtue.
The evidence of this result is not false.
Master Ning of Tang was a native of Qiyang; his surname was Ning, and people of the time habitually called him by his surname alone, as his given name has been lost.

At the beginning of Emperor Zhaozong’s reign, Ning suddenly passed away at the temple where he resided. After three days, he revived. When the assembly gathered in astonishment to question him, he said:
"I have entered the underworld. There, I first saw an official sitting at his desk, just like those in a worldly government office.
He immediately said to me, "The Master has a long life but no merit; what a pity! He then inspected the registers and said, "There are only three piculs of dried lotus leaves.
He ordered an attendant to lead me through the various sections. Thus we arrived at a place where a signboard over the gate read: "Li Kuei-yung. Ning peered inside and saw—
First was a one-eyed black dragon, shackled upon an iron pillar. Next was one who said he was Zhu Quanzhong;
he saw a green-haired, white-browed tiger that had just been bound and chained, with blood and flesh scattered before it as if it had just devoured something. Next was one who said he was Wang Jian.
He saw a white rabbit lying upon a golden bed; next, he saw Li Maozhen, with several female attendants and a king wearing a ceremonial crown sitting there.
When it came to Yang Xingmi, however, everything was shrouded in shadow and nothing could be seen.
He questioned his guide, who replied, "This is your future lord. The other places were all dark and deep, and he knew not where they had gone. Thereupon, [he proceeded].

He returned, and the official then allowed him to go home, admonishing him, saying: "Simply recite the *Gongde jing* (Sutra of Merit) as much as possible. Ning asked which sutra was the *Gongde jing*;

the official replied, "It is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. This matter was reported to the regional commander of Qiqihar, who, loathing how it deluded the public, prohibited it with great severity.
Later, the results were proven to be no different from before. At that time, the world called Ning "The Monk Who Entered the Netherworld," and he lived out his life accordingly.

He ate lotus leaves and passed away at his place of residence. During the Tang dynasty, Fazang resided at Baotai Temple in Fu Prefecture. His character was simple and honest, yet he possessed great capability. He once solicited offerings along the Weishui River to construct a monastery; its halls and pavilions were extremely magnificent, such that the people of his hometown all marveled at it, saying: [...omitted...
