He was unable to reach it. Suddenly, he died of a sudden illness but revived. He immediately transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with even greater diligence than before, reciting it morning and night without ceasing.
When questioned about this, he said: "When I was dying, it was exactly like being in a dream. I saw a monk from India who said to me:
'It is truly good that you have risen to perform this work; its merit is immeasurable. However, you have intermingled the property of the Three Jewels.'"
"What can be done? I shall at least confess my transgressions to reveal them before others. Furthermore, I urge you to copy and recite this sutra;
it will not only eliminate your sins but will also suffice to prolong your life. This is why I dare not forget it. He passed away one hundred and ten years later.
Tang Shen-zhi, surnamed Li, was a native of Yiwu in Wuzhou. In his youth, he studied under the śramaṇa Weixiao of Yunmen Temple and received the tonsure.
At the age of twelve, he practiced eating only once a day and devoted himself to the recitation of the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī with exceptional diligence and intensity.
During the Huichang suppression of the Dharma, although he changed his appearance and attire, his resolve did not undergo the slightest alteration.

At the beginning of the Dazhong era, when the Buddhist teachings were being restored, he traveled to Zhuji in Yue province, where he built a dwelling to practice meditation and tranquility; he also used consecrated water to treat illnesses.
Those who sought him from near and far mostly obtained results. Consequently, seekers came daily, and the community was provided for.
Before long, he entered the capital, where he met the Chancellor Pei Xiu. The Chancellor had once dreamed of a monk and had long been able to recall his appearance;

upon seeing Zhi, it was exactly as in the dream. He held him in great reverence and affection. Furthermore, his daughter had been possessed by a spirit, suffering from madness and delirium that could not be cured. Zhi—
After seven days of prayers, he was suddenly cured. Lord Pei thereupon reported his noble conduct and great achievements to the Emperor.

The Emperor bestowed upon the temple the name "Dazhong Shengshou" (Great Zhong Holy Longevity) and further granted it one bell cast by the Shen-ce Army, fifty scrolls of the Buddhist canon embroidered by Empress Wu, and the temple’s hall plaque, which was written by the Lord’s own hand. The second year of the Guangqi era, the tenth month...
At the end of the second month, he passed away at the age of sixty-eight and with forty-eight years of ordination seniority. His stupa was erected on the Southern Mountain of the county.
Liang Hongchu, whose courtesy name was Fangwai, was surnamed Tang and was a native of Yongjia. In his youth, he followed his cousin to leave the household life at Longgong Temple in Yue.
After receiving full ordination, he returned to his hometown. At that time, the regional governor Zhu Biao was well-acquainted with his reputation and held him in high esteem.
He was held in high esteem. During the Dàshùn era of the Táng dynasty, he requested that the abandoned Dàyún Monastery south of the city be entrusted to him for restoration as his residence;
the Emperor granted this by imperial decree. Thereupon, Zhǔ collected offerings and mobilized craftsmen to restore the monastery to its former splendor.

At the beginning of the Qiánhuà era, the Qián family of Wúyuè summoned Zhǔ to Lóngxīng Monastery in Qiántáng to preside over the ordination platform and bestow the precepts. Furthermore, they submitted a memorial requesting that he be granted the purple robe and the title of Master.

He was titled [as such]. Because Xiao Chu considered his virtue to be cool and insufficient to match his robes, he declined the honor with great sincerity. The poet Zheng Shuo praised his integrity and presented him with a collection of verses.
Xiao Chu was particularly well-versed in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; he presided over more than fifty assemblies for its public exposition.
He also once pricked his own blood to transcribe the scripture as an act of offering. In the third year of the Changxing era, a lotus flower suddenly grew from [the ground].
Within the lecture hall, the flowers had double calyxes and double petals, and their fragrance was rich and pervasive.

On the night of the fifth day of the sixth month, while he was still practicing the Way and reciting the sutras, his attendants suddenly perceived that his voice had grown faint and the lamps had dimmed. Upon going to look at him, they found him sitting cross-legged, having passed away.
He was seventy-five years of age and fifty-two years since his ordination (*varṣa*).
During the Tianfu era of the Shi Jin dynasty, there was a monk who spent the summer retreat at a Chan monastery in Xiangyang; Zhiben was also present there.
Once the retreat had concluded, that monk said to Ben: "I left the household life at Zhulin Monastery on the western mountains of Yedu."

"Before the temple, there is a stone pillar as a landmark. If you have leisure at another time, do not hesitate to visit; when you strike that stone pillar once, I shall certainly come to welcome you.
After a long while, the Master indeed followed the agreement and went to the capital city of Ye (Yecheng). He searched everywhere for what was called Zhulin Monastery, but it was nowhere to be found.
Someone pointed to a certain place with a casual gesture, saying, "According to the traditions of the elders, this is where it is located."
"This is where the worthy sages dwell; yet it is but an empty name, devoid of any substantial trace. Why, then, must one subject oneself to such hardship?
Originally, seeing a stone pillar rising steeply and alone, he thought to himself: "In the past, that monk surely had something to teach me.

He struck it once, and at once wind and clouds gathered from all sides, so that not a foot's breadth could be seen. After a short while, the sky cleared and brightened, and the towers and pavilions stood out abruptly.
I was already at the mountain gate. After a short while, a monk emerged from within, and we exchanged greetings as old friends;
our joy was great. We then took each other’s hands and ascended the steps to the secret hall. There, the venerable elder sat upon a large couch and questioned me repeatedly.
I recounted in full detail the origins of our friendship. The elder said, "You may stay for a meal and then depart. After the meal, I requested to remain, but the monk— [text ends] —[refused].
Because his past lives were so venerable, it was not possible to part from him hastily; we knew not where he had gone.
In praise, it is said:
Vertically, he is the three periods of time; Horizontally, he is the ten directions. In the center there is a single thing That cannot be measured.
From the very beginning, the radiance has been penetrating and pervasive; between the Buddha and sentient beings, there is not the slightest gap.
Here one feels, and there one responds; this side and that side interpenetrate like the great void.
The void is serene and still—who can distinguish "this" from "that"? Even regarding this resonance and penetration, the principle is likewise so.
One should contemplate entering nirvana; one should contemplate birth. Do not allow the active manifestation of good or evil to arise anew.
*The Newly Compiled Classified Biographies of the Six Studies of Monks*, Scroll Twenty-six;
*The Newly Compiled Classified Biographies of the Six Studies of Monks*, Scroll Twenty-seven.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Tanne from Eastern Zhejiang:

"Cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*) leads to realization for one's own practice; spiritual transformation for the benefit of others—all these arise from meditative concentration. Why is this so?"
To speak of this is to clarify one's nature, yet it is obscured by darkness. However, if one seeks the means to restore it, one must observe;
through observation, it becomes clear and reaches the state of illumination. Quiescence is one's nature, yet it is disturbed by movement.
However, if one seeks the means to restore it, one must cease; through cessation, it returns to its original state.

Furthermore, when one ceases [mental activity], there is stillness that leads to quiescence (*śānti*). Now, does one first stabilize the illumination of contemplation and then achieve this quiescence?
Therefore, if awakening is triggered from quiescence, the realization attained will be profound; if transformative activity arises from illumination, the spiritual manifestations will be vast.
Thus, these two categories—realization and spiritual transformation—should appropriately be appended under the study of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Also: The biography of Sengxian of the Jin dynasty, who attained realization. His secular surname was He, and he was a native of Huoshuo. He sat in meditation within mountain forests for several days without showing any signs of hunger. The Grand...
Toward the end of the Han dynasty, when Liu Yao invaded Luoyang, Daoxian traveled south to visit famous mountains, having no fixed dwelling.
Once, while lying ill, he focused his mind on the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). He then beheld Amitābha Buddha, whose light illuminated his body and healed him.

That evening, he changed his clothes and bathed, telling his attendants that what he had seen were all extraordinary matters. At dawn, he sat upright and passed away in tranquility, leaving a fragrance that filled the room.
The room [remained closed] for over ten days before it finally ceased.
Zhu Fahui of the Jin dynasty was a native of Guanzhong. He was upright and resolute by nature, and he protected himself according to the Vinaya. He served as a disciple to Fotudeng of Mount Songgao.
In the first year of the Jianyuan era, he arrived in Xiangyang and stayed at Yang Shuzi Temple. Whenever he went out to beg for alms, he would not...
He accepted a special invitation and carried his own rope bed with him every day. Upon arriving at a secluded and open space, he would immediately set it up as a seat.
When it rained, he would cover it with an oil-silk cloak; when the rain ceased, upon looking at it, he saw only the rope bed and had lost sight of Hui. Only then did he feel startled and amazed.
Yet Huì remained composed upon his bed, and no one could discern how he was feeling. He said to his disciple Fǎzhào, "In a past life, you broke the leg of a rooster;
the retribution for that has now arrived. Shortly thereafter, Fǎzhào was mistakenly injured in the leg by someone.
It is further said that there was a man capable of being saved living in Xinye. Hui went to see an old man who was then plowing; he asked him for his ox, but the old man would not give it to him.

Hui stepped forward and seized the ox by its nose, whereupon the old man became afraid and gave it to him. Hui walked seven paces and made a vow to return the ox. Not long after, the old man passed away.
Yu Zhigong, the General Who Conquers the West, was stationed at Xiangyang and grew envious of Hui’s ability to delude the masses.
Huì also said, "My karmic retribution from past lives has arrived; I shall indeed be killed by Zhìgōng. He was fifty-eight years old when he faced execution.
At the time of his death, he said, "Three days after my death there will be a torrential rain. Subsequently, the rain fell to a depth of over one zhang, and many residents died.
Huiyuan of Jin was a native of Hebei. The histories do not record his clan name. He was a man of pure and ultimate integrity; those around him never saw him display expressions of joy or anger.
He would sit upright for the entirety of the day. He resided at Pingshan Temple in Wuling, where more than twenty disciples applied themselves to the Way with diligent austerity.
He passed away in the fourteenth year of the Taiyuan era. Later, his followers entered Mount Wudang and saw [him there].
His countenance and expression remained composed as he sent word to the monks of the temple, telling them to practice with diligent effort and not to be indolent.
From then on, this man constantly heard the sound of a stone chime in the air; following it, he gathered the assembly, never failing to arrive at the appointed time.
The Jin dynasty monk Shi Huikai was a man of unknown origins. Initially, he traveled to Chang’an and stayed at the Great Monastery (Dasi).
After a long time, he departed to practice meditation in the mountains and valleys. One night, a headless ghost suddenly stood before him. Huikai was not afraid;

he spoke calmly, saying, "Since you have no head, you are spared the burden of headaches—how fortunate for you! The ghost immediately vanished. A short while later, another ghost appeared, this one without a belly.
The woman arrived. Sengwei said, "Since you have no belly, you are merely spared from the affliction of hunger and thirst; what joy could there be in that?

In this manner, she manifested a hundred strange forms, and Sengwei sent each one away as it transformed. One night, during a great snowfall when human tracks had vanished in all directions, a beautiful woman suddenly appeared, knocking at the door and seeking lodging.
She said, "I am a celestial maiden. Because the Venerable One possesses the virtue of precepts, I have come."
She came to offer her condolences. Sengwei said, "Your coming was merely because you wished to see me; now that you have seen me, you should depart.

Furthermore, you are an obstacle to the Path for the Dharma; how could you stay overnight? Thereupon, the woman ascended into the air and departed, saying, "The rivers may run dry, and Mount Sumeru may be overturned, but that Superior Man holds fast to his will with unwavering integrity. During the reign of Emperor An, she [was with] the Dharma...
He manifested his journey to the West; later, his ultimate end was unknown.
Xuanhu of the Jin dynasty was born into the Sun clan and was a native of Liangzhou. He traveled to Guanghan and resided at Yanxing Temple. He had long practiced meditative contemplation.
At the time of his death, light issued from his mouth, illuminating everything in five colors. His final instruction was that he must be cremated according to the Indian dharma and not buried.
Later, a single finger was found among the ashes in the furnace; a stupa was erected for it called the "Finger Stupa" to manifest this occurrence.
Faxu of the Jin dynasty was born into the Hun clan. A native of Gaochang, he possessed noble conduct and recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Vimalakīrti*, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* sutras.
He entered Shu and dwelt among the tombs of Master Liu, where he practiced meditative contemplation; tigers served as his companions and attendants.

When he passed away during the height of summer, he offered his body to insects and birds, yet it did not decay for seven days. At night, a brilliant light illuminated the surrounding villages, and its fragrance persisted for many days.
After ten days, he finally ceased [his practice]. An elder enshrined him upon his tomb mound.
The Song dynasty monks Saṃghadatta and Saṃgharakṣa were both profoundly versed in the methods of dhyāna. While Saṃghadatta was sitting in meditation, he thought that the time for a meal had arrived;
a bird then brought fruit as an offering. Saṃghadatta thought to himself: "When the monkey offered honey, the Buddha accepted it."
"What could I not do for him? In the eighteenth year of the Yuanjia era, Prince Kang of Linchuan invited him to stay at Guangling;
later, he moved to Jianye and passed away there. At the end of the Jingping era, Luochu arrived in Jianye, begging for food among the people and sitting in meditation beneath the trees.
He came and went with effortless ease, neither seeking intimacy nor distance from the world. He eventually settled on the southern slope of Mount Zhong, where he remained until his life’s end.
Song Xuangao was born into the Wei family of Wannian in Fengyi. His mother, Kou, originally held heterodox views, whereas his elder sister was particularly devoted to the faith.
She prayed to her mother that she might give birth to a son free from false views, one who would serve the Great Dharma and establish the family lineage.

Suddenly, Kou dreamed of a foreign monk scattering flowers from the air as she conceived. When Xuangao was born, fragrant light filled the air for days and nights; consequently, he was named Lingyu (Numinous Nourishment). The local community...
Revered sir, his other name was Shigao. At the age of twelve, he sought to leave the household life, but his parents objected on account of his youth.
One day, a scholar who intended to retire to live in Mount Zhongchang stayed overnight at Gao’s home. His parents entrusted him to this man.
That evening, they saw many elderly people coming to bid him farewell; the next morning, they all returned to his house once more.
He then realized that those who had come previously were likely spirits sent to welcome him. He stayed with the lay student Gao Liu for two days;

having found his teacher, he changed his name to Xuangao and received the tonsure. At the age of fifteen, he sought the essentials of the Way from the meditation master Buddhabhadra at Shiyang Temple.
Before long, he suddenly attained profound realization, such that Buddhabhadra did not dare [to claim superiority].
He visited him with the etiquette due to a teacher and subsequently resided at Maiji Shan. There he befriended the eminent and high-practicing śramaṇa Tánhóng.

At that time, Dharmapriya arrived from the northwest in Liáng; he was masterful in dhyāna and contemplation. Tánhóng also associated closely with him for ten days, during which Dharmapriya repeatedly questioned him on points of doctrine that had remained unresolved.
When Dharmapriya was about to return westward, a sorcerous bhikṣu, jealous of Tánhóng, slandered him to the Governor of Hénán.
The Crown Prince Man said, "Now this man has gathered a following and will bring harm to the state; I believe he should be killed.

His father, the King of Henan, did not permit it, but instead banished Gao to the north of the Yellow River. Once Gao arrived, he dwelt on Mount Linyang Tang, which was indeed the abode of terrestrial immortals.
At night, he heard the sound of bells and stone chimes. Among his more than one hundred disciples at the gate, there was one named Xuan Shao.
He once pointed at the ground and water gushed forth for the assembly. There were eleven others like Shao; Tanhong was especially honored by King Hong of Henan.
On one occasion, he said to the king, "Gao is a rare omen of this age. Why do you exclude him? I truly regret this for Your Majesty. The king welcomed Gao;
when Gao was about to leave the mountains in response to the summons, the vegetation along the way withered and broke.

A fallen rock blocked the road, making it impassable. Daogao said, "My resolve lies in propagating the Way; yet if I remain stagnant in this mountain cave, it will be of no benefit even to you spirits.
Thereupon, the road became passable. The King came out to meet him at the outskirts of the capital and appointed him as State Preceptor.
He traveled through the territory of Liang, where Juqu Mengxun treated him with exceptional reverence. Among his disciples, Sengyin claimed to have already attained the stage of Arhat.

During the Northern Wei dynasty, when the Emperor Tuoba Tao occupied Pingcheng, he frequently invaded the territory of Liang. The Emperor’s maternal uncle, the Prince of Yangping, Shou, invited Daogao to join him.

Daogao lent him his supernatural powers so that, while in a state of meditative concentration, he could hear the various teachings expounded by the Buddhas throughout the infinite worlds of the ten directions. He committed these to memory over the course of a single summer retreat;

yet, upon reviewing what he had perceived, he found it inexhaustible. Filled with shame and trepidation, he performed repentance. At that time, Tuoba Tao was ruling from Pingcheng and repeatedly incursions into the borders of Liang. The Prince of Yangping, Shou, requested that Daogao accompany him.
He returned to the capital of Wei. Crown Prince Tuoba Huang took him as his teacher. Once, Huang was slandered, and Tuoba Tao became suspicious of him.

Huang spoke of this to Gao, who performed the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* repentance ritual for him. Thereupon, Tao dreamed that his ancestors admonished him, saying he should not harbor suspicions toward the Crown Prince because of slander.
Upon waking, Tao recounted the dream to his ministers, all of whom declared that the Crown Prince was without fault.
He treated him as he had before. A decree was issued intending to abdicate the throne and to have the Crown Prince govern the state.

The court officials and common people addressed him as their sovereign and submitted petitions in the manner of a formal memorial, distinguishing them only by using plain white paper. Cui Hao and Kou Qianzhi were both favored ministers of Tuoba Tao;
fearing that Huang’s succession would not be beneficial to themselves, they said to him: "The Crown Prince actually harbored a plot previously, but..."

Jie Xuan said, "I employed my arts of the Way to bring about the passing of the former Emperor; I fear this will happen to Your Majesty as well. If you do not execute Xuan, he will surely cause great harm.
Daohui was greatly incensed and issued an edict to arrest and kill Xuan. He was only forty-three years old at the time, which was the twenty-first year of the Yuanjia era.
At that moment, the śramaṇa Huichong of Liangtu was also killed with him. His disciple Xuanchang was then in Yunzhong when he suddenly—
Seeing a man approaching, he said, "Your master is in great distress; lend him your horse. It could travel six hundred li in a single day.

Upon reaching the capital of Wei before the sun had set, the man wept and said, "The Dharma Master possesses supernatural power; you must rise for my sake. Thereupon, Baogao opened his eyes wide and gazed at him.

He said to his disciples: "The manifestation of the Great Dharma follows conditions in its flourishing and decline. While its flourishing and decline pertain to its outward traces, the underlying principle remains eternally serene.
I only regret that your practice does not match my own; may only Xuanchang’s journey south be free from misfortune.

After you have passed away, the Dharma shall surely flourish again. Cultivate your minds well and do not allow yourselves to feel regret later. Having finished speaking, he immediately manifested his transformation. [Thus ends the account of] the śramaṇa Dharmakṣema.
Fada cried out, "The Sage has departed from this world; what use is my life? As he spoke, he saw [Hui]gao in the clouds above.
Fada prostrated himself and begged for deliverance. Gao said, "I do not forget all beings; how could I forget you alone? Fada asked, "Where have both the Master and Master Chong been reborn?
He replied, "My wish was to be born in the evil realms to rescue and protect sentient beings. Master Chong has already been born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī)."
Yi Da asked, "To what stage has the Master already ascended? Gao replied, "Among my disciples, there are those who know.
Yi Da went to visit his disciples, and they all said, "He is a Bodhisattva who has attained patience (kṣānti-labdha)."
The Song dynasty monk Zhou was of unknown origin. He possessed noble conduct and deeply concealed his identity. He resided in a stone grotto on Mount Song.
When the Wei Emperor Daowu suppressed the Buddha-dharma, Zhou had foreseen this in advance; he and several śramaṇas went into hiding at Hanshan near Chang’an.
Later, Daowu repented due to illness and immediately executed the families of Cui Hao, Kou Qianzhi, and others, whereupon the Buddha-dharma was restored.
Upon hearing of Zhou’s reputation, Emperor Xing dispatched an envoy to invite him. Zhou firmly declined on the grounds of old age and illness, and his disciple Sengliang went in his stead.
After Sengliang had departed, that very night Zhou entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (fire-light samādhi) and passed away; his remains were enshrined in a stupa within the mountains.

When Sengliang arrived at the capital, Prince Yongchang went out to the suburbs to welcome him. He preached the Dharma for him in Guanzhong and renovated the monasteries, extensively ordaining śramaṇas—all at the recommendation of Sengliang.

Huitong of the Song dynasty was a native of Guanzhong; his family name has been lost to history. Having received the tonsure in his youth, he resided at Taishou Temple in Chang’an, where he recited the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
He also studied the methods of dhyāna and contemplation under the Chan Master Huishao of Liangzhou, dedicating himself single-mindedly to praying for rebirth in the Pure Land.
Once, while suffering from a slight illness, he beheld the radiance of Amitābha Buddha illuminating his body, accompanied by a wondrous fragrance. For a long time...
He eventually passed away after a long time, at the age of fifty-nine.

Sengfaqi was born into the Xiang family; he was a native of [郫] in Shu Commandery. Orphaned at a young age, he served his elder brother with such filial piety that he was renowned throughout the local villages.

At the age of fourteen, he left home to receive full ordination. He received the Dharma from the meditation master Zhimeng and practiced meditative contemplation together with the śramaṇa Falin of Lingqi Temple;
both attained realization. Later, he followed Xuanchang and traveled to Jiangling.
Of the ten stages of the *Vihāra-dhyāna*, he had already mastered nine, with only the *Siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* remaining incomplete. Xuanchang sighed and said, "I have gone to the West..."
He traversed the shifting sands and reached the remote deserts to the north; at times he explored the Cave of Yu and ascended Mount Heng and Mount Huo.

Among the many eminent companions he encountered, you alone possessed the branches of Chan practice, yet you ultimately passed away at Changsha Temple. Your divine radiance and extraordinary fragrances perfumed and illuminated both near and far.
He lived for sixty-two years. At that time, there was also the śramaṇa Daoguo of Longhua in Shu, who was likewise renowned for his meditative contemplation; his fame was equal to that of [Hui]qi.
Hui'an of the Song dynasty was a man of unknown origin. In his youth, he was taken as a captive by others and sold to a wealthy family in Jingzhou, where he performed manual labor.
He was extremely diligent. His master loved him. At the age of eighteen, he was permitted to leave the household life as a śrāmaṇera and resided at Pipa Temple in Jiangling.

His appearance and demeanor were plain and unassuming, so the community largely looked down upon him. Nevertheless, whenever it was time for the monks' midday meal, he would invariably rise to serve the water, proceeding from the highest seat to the lowest;
yet the water was never exhausted. The assembly marveled at this marvel. When he received full ordination, his spiritual traces became even more manifest. Once, while with...
The śramaṇa Huìjì was presiding over the *poṣadha* ceremony when he ascended the hall. Before the doors had even opened, [Huí]’ān grasped Huìjì’s finger and it passed through a crack in the wall;
the withdrawal was likewise. Huìjì was greatly terrified and did not dare to speak. Huì’ān said to Huìjì, "I am about to travel far away; I now bid you farewell.
Looking up, he saw beautiful flowers filling the air, the sounds of string and wind instruments, and a rich fragrance of celestial incense. Huìjì—
Yu was so terrified that he could not speak. Dao’an said, “What you have seen during your travels with me—be careful not to speak of it recklessly;
to do so would bring you misfortune. Only in the southwest is there a lay bodhisattva who has newly resolved his mind; you may speak with him.

Thereupon, Yu took his leave and boarded the vessel of a great merchant, traveling into the region of Xiang. On the way, he suffered from dysentery and was on the verge of death. He said to the merchant, “When I die, I must certainly...”
He exposed his corpse on the riverbank; there was no need to provide a coffin. When asked the reason for this, he said, "I wish to give it as alms to insects and birds.
The merchants followed his instructions and cast the corpse onto the bank. At night, flames would constantly emerge from his body, which terrified the merchants greatly.

They rowed their boat toward the middle of the Xiang River, where An had already arrived beforehand. Although they wished to speak with him, they were unable to do so. Only after they had crossed did they reach him.

At Zhiqui Temple, he visited the recluse Liu Qiu and conversed with him through the night. When [Hui]ji arrived, Liu Qiu immediately paid him homage from afar, saying, "This is one who has attained the *tejodhātu-samādhi*.
At that time, there were also the monks Senglan and Fawei in Shu, both of whom possessed divine anomalies; the world suspected they had attained the Way.
Sengdaofa of the Cao clan was a native of Dunhuang. In his youth, he became a śramaṇa; he was diligent and austere, possessing lofty conduct.
His prayers and incantations were divinely efficacious. He traveled to Chengdu at the invitation of Wang Xiuzhi and Fei Kengzhi, where he resided at the two monasteries of Xingle and Xiangji.

When it was time, he went out to beg for alms and did not accept private invitations. Once, while entering meditative absorption, he ascended to the inner courtyard and beheld Maitreya from the navel [downward].

A wheel emitted light, illuminating the sufferings of the three miserable realms. Thereupon, she redoubled her resolve to remain constantly seated without reclining. In the second year of the Yuánhuí era, she passed away;
her countenance remained as if alive.
Pǔhéng of the Gù clan was a native of Chéngdū during the Sòng dynasty. In her childhood, she saw a strange bhikṣu preaching the Dharma in the air.
He recounted this to his relatives and expressed his wish to leave the household life. Upon reaching adulthood, he became a śramaṇa and resided at Anle Temple in Luoyang.
He delighted in secluded and quiet places, withdrawing and gathering his mind. He was a close friend with the Śramaṇa Tao of Shu. He claimed that he had once entered the fire-light samādhi;
from between his eyebrows, it extended down to the limits of the vajra-water. Within the light, he beheld various forms and images. First...
Regarding matters such as the retribution for his physical karma, he passed away while ascending into clarity at the age of seventy-eight. He bent three fingers of his hand;

though people tried to force him to believe otherwise, it was impossible. Throughout his life, his appearance had been dark and emaciated, yet thereafter he became remarkably plump and fair-complexioned, whereupon they knew he had attained the Way.
When his body was cremated, smoke formed five colors for a long time, and a wondrous fragrance wafted forth intensely.
Qi Anamo—translated here as Bao-yi (Jewel-Mind)—was surnamed Kang and was a native of Kangju. In the early years of the Jianzhong era, he arrived at Jianye and resided at Waguan Temple.
He frequently sat in meditation beneath trees, was well-versed in the sutras and vinaya, and was skilled in the recitation of divine incantations.

By rolling several hundred cowrie shells, he could immediately discern good or bad fortune. By applying incense to his palms, he could perceive the past lives of others. Emperor Shizu [used] a bronze spittoon...
He gave the bowl to Shi. One night it was lost; he then offered a prayer over an empty scroll on his mat. Three nights later, the bowl was found within the mat.
He passed away at the end of the Yongming era.
Liang Zhi was surnamed Hao and was a native of Fuzhou in Zizhong. He initially served as an official in the commandery of Baxi.
Once, by the order of the Governor Zheng Zhen, he traveled to the capital to present offerings. At the beginning of the Putong era, the Emperor was greatly promoting the Buddhist vehicle;

stupas and temples were magnificently adorned, surpassing the finest residences, and the status of monks and nuns was equal to that of princes and dukes. Liang Zhi admired this and subsequently left the household life. Upon his return to Shu, his wife and children...

They all shaved their heads and donned the monastic robes. During the Dàtóng era, they encouraged one another to cultivate their practice with even greater diligence, observing the practice of eating once a day and remaining seated at all times, never wavering until the end of their lives.
At that time, there was a monk named Fǎ'ài in Nán Wǔdū who was venerated by the world for his incantatory arts; Tánxiāng went to visit him.
That evening, he saw a figure approaching dressed in magnificent robes and cap. The Master remained unmoved.

The figure then lifted the rope bed upon which the Master sat—about four or five feet high—and immediately vanished. After a short while, it returned and lifted the bed again, moving only one corner before departing.
After another brief interval, it came forward and stood before him as it had been at first. The Master remained entirely motionless. A moment later, he suddenly beheld its face.
The ridgepoles and rafters on the roof made a sound of great crashing and splitting, yet Xiang remained almost motionless. The man hurriedly prostrated himself, seeking repentance.
The next day, he said to Ai, "If you wish to abandon heterodox teachings, it would be well for you to depart. Xiang had grown up in a remote and uncivilized border region.
However, his speech and delivery were common and unrefined. Later, when he went to the lecture halls of the Yi Prefecture to study, the crowd treated him with contempt and ridicule;

yet Faxiang did not take this to heart. Once, while traveling on official business, he stayed overnight at a Daoist monastery. The Daoist master had long heard of Faxiang’s reputation and, fearing he might seduce his disciples, refused to pay him due respect.
When the night was well advanced, a pack of tigers howled near the place where Faxiang was lying. All [the others]...
The Daoist could not find peace all night long. At dawn, he followed [the monk] to request the precepts.
He also saw someone fishing by the waterside of Hongnong; the monk exhorted him not to kill, but the man was exceptionally arrogant and spat into the water.
Suddenly, a large snake appeared with its head raised, looking about and charging toward the fisherman. The fisherman repented and subsequently served him as a disciple. Not long after...
He gathered several disciples at Mount Qingcheng. Xiao Hui, the Prince of Liang, held him in particularly high esteem.

One day, he said to his disciples: "I have no meritorious deeds by which to be reborn in a Pure Land. However, the sufferings of the three miserable realms and the pleasures of heaven are not places where I shall be born.
Since there is no other alternative, I shall continue to be born in this world to teach and transform you all. You must therefore exert yourselves."

He practiced the Way and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture at the age of thirty-four. Thereupon, the local Liao people gathered to witness him and marveled at his extraordinary nature;
they were inspired to emulate his example, and thus the customs of the barbarians were transformed.

Previously, he had constructed Bailin Temple to the west of Mian City and personally planted a single *wutong* tree beneath the hall, which grew exceedingly lush and flourishing. However, at this time, it withered and fell without any apparent cause.
At dawn, the *vina* struck the bell and missed the sound. The senior monk (*upādhyāya*) rose and said to the others, "This must portend a great calamity.
They immediately fled in haste. Shortly thereafter, news arrived that the temple was more than four hundred li from Qingcheng, yet the spiritual resonance was such as this.
How could this be fathomed by ordinary sentiments? Toward the end of the Liang dynasty, Daoxiang and Senglang were both possessed of divine anomalies; they are not recorded here in detail.
Huisheng of the Liang was a native of Jiaozhi who resided at Xianzhou Mountain Temple. He made it his constant practice to recite one fascicle of the *Lotus Sūtra* every day.
Later, he studied various contemplative practices under the foreign meditation master Dharmadeva. He would remain in meditative concentration for entire days and nights.
Liu Hui of Pengcheng, who had been appointed as the governor of Nanhai, heard of his reputation and respectfully invited him; taking him with him, he returned home and settled him at Youqi Temple.
Throughout the day, [Hui] remained silent as if an idiot. The longer one associated with him, the more venerable he became. He went on alms rounds...
In his leisure time, he would shut his door and attend to no other affairs. In the fifth year of the Yongming era, he moved to reside at the Yanxian Vihāra on Mount Zhong;
its location was remote and secluded, making it particularly renowned for its spiritual excellence. He passed away during the Tianjian era at the age of seventy.

Tanzhi was a native of Shanren in Qizhou during the Wei dynasty. He left the household life at Juntuoshan Caosi. This monastery was originally a *bodhimanda* established by Guṇavarman of the Song dynasty;
even in Tanzhi’s time, its grand scale had not yet declined. Tanzhi devoted himself exclusively to the recitation and upholding of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
On the day he was about to pass away, the Liang dynasty śramaṇa Baozhi foresaw this in advance and said to Emperor Wu...
The Emperor said, "Today, at the Grass Temple on Mount Ren in Renshan County in the north, a noble monk who has attained the fruit of Srotāpanna entered parinirvāṇa.
When the monastics and laypeople of the capital heard this, there were none who did not turn toward the north to pay their respects.

Thus, when Hui-zhan reached his end, he passed away in silence without illness or distress; he did nothing more than slightly curl a single finger on each of his two hands. This was his final consciousness.

Some believe that in Western India, the realized stages of fruition were verified in this manner: specifically, it is said that one finger signified the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), while two fingers signified the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
Thus we know that the first fruit was so profound and substantial that when the stupa was built on Mount Makuṭabandhana, neither birds nor beasts could defile its lime mortar or clay.
Buddhatara of the Wei dynasty was a man from the Western Regions. Having already practiced meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he further resolved to observe the world and benefit sentient beings.
He had six companions, five of whom had already realized the fruits of the path (*phala*). Only Buddhatara had not yet realized them;

his frustration and yearning were so intense that he could hardly contain himself. Thereupon, his friends who had realized the fruits said to him, "The Way is attained through a mind free of grasping."
"It cannot be achieved by mere force. Furthermore, you shall have special karmic conditions in Zhendan (China) where you will save two disciples and bring benefit to the world;

the merit you shall thereby obtain will be great indeed. Why not go? Consequently, he traveled on again until he reached Beitaishan (North Terrace Mountain) in Heng’an of the Wei dynasty, where he stayed.
At that time, Emperor Xiaowen was greatly promoting our teaching and treated him with profound courtesy and hospitality.

They carved stone to house him in a grotto and provided grain to satisfy his companions; thus, signs of spiritual response appeared repeatedly, causing those who understood these matters to marvel at him.
Within the city, the Kang family possessed abundant wealth and built a monastery for him so he might continue his regular practice.
One day, a young boy peered through a crack in the door and saw nothing else, but only a great, blazing fire. He ran home to inform his family.
He had them peer inside, but nothing was seen. From this, he knew that his attainment of realization was not false.
When the capital was moved to the Yi and Luo regions, an imperial edict was issued to construct a monastery at Shaoshi Mountain to house him; this is the present-day Shaolin Temple.

He would often say to the assembly, "This vihāra shall never lack for anything in the future; I have indeed separately summoned the numinous spirits to guard and protect it. Thus, it has reached down to this day.
For two hundred years, although calamities and famines occurred repeatedly during that interval, the temple’s endowments remained full and abundant;

was this not perhaps due to the power of Tanyao’s vow? He was particularly skilled in the science of phonology (*śabdavidyā*). Later, while in Luoyang, he ordained two disciples, Huiguang and Sengchou.

At first, he would strike their heads with a staff; recognizing them as vessels of the Dharma (*dharmabhājana*), he subsequently ordained them. In time, they both became famous throughout the world. Thus it is recorded.

Each has its own biography. Because Tuo was elderly, he did not participate in the communal assembly; he was moved by a benevolent deity who accompanied him in eating, drinking, and daily activities, listening solely to the deity's guidance.
He would also occasionally prepare offerings for the deity’s ritual feasts. Later, he painted the deity’s image on the wall of his room.
Not long after, he passed away.
Wei Huida, also known as Suhe, was surnamed Liu. He was a member of the Jihu (Qiang) people from Dingyang in Sancheng, northeast of Xianyang.

He was brave and possessed great physical strength; he took pleasure in hunting and archery and lived a life of unrestrained independence. Consequently, he did not enjoy much praise from his fellow villagers.

Nevertheless, he managed his household with such abundance that his parents and brothers were all filial and fraternal toward one another. He served as a "sudden-attack general" (tūjiāng) at Liangcheng and later defended Xiangyang. Once...
Having contracted an illness from drinking wine, he died and underwent the various sufferings of the hells. Consequently, he left the household life and resided at Anmin Temple in Cizhou.
Later, he traveled again to Yue to pay homage to the śarīra relics; his rigorous and diligent cultivation is detailed in his separate biography.

In the first year of the Taiyan era, he traveled west to Fanhe in Liangzhou and, gazing toward the northeast at Yugu, prostrated himself and said: "In the future, there shall be a sacred image upon this cliff."
It appeared, sometimes complete and sometimes incomplete; the order or chaos of the world depended upon it.

At the beginning of the Zhengguang era, there was a sudden great wind and rain with a swift thunder that split a mountain, whereupon a stone image eighteen *zhang* tall was seen standing erect. It was solemn and dignified, yet lacked a head.

People vied with one another to carve heads and place them upon it, but as soon as they were placed, they fell off. Seeing that its form could not support them, they desisted. Thus, during the decline of the Wei dynasty—

From this point it began. Reaching the time of Zhou Xing, light emanated from a stream seven *li* east of the city. He dug there and recovered the head; when he lifted it and joined it to the statue, they fit together as if they had never been parted.
At the beginning of the Baoding era, an imperial edict was issued to build a temple on that site, which was named Ruixiang (Auspicious Image).

At the beginning of the Jiande era, the head of the statue fell off again, and the omens for the extinction of the Dharma appeared. During the Kaihuang period of the Sui dynasty, the statue was restored to a state of exceptional perfection. Great...
The work was completed in five years. The Emperor personally paid him homage and issued an edict changing the name of the temple to Gantong (Responsive Manifestation) to commemorate this marvel.
Now, according to the prophecy of Xiang, eighty-seven years passed before the image actually appeared; another forty-odd years passed before it joined with its head;
and another ten-odd years passed before the head fell off. With each union and each falling, the events were verified exactly as recorded in the prophecy. This is...
How divine he was! Da died and was buried at Jiuquan by Su. Upon cremation, fragments of bone were recovered resembling sunflower seeds.
The common people beyond the passes have, to this day, venerated him with temple images, calling him "Master Buddha Liu."

Sengchou of the Qi dynasty was surnamed Sun; his ancestors were from Changli, and he now resided in Xingtao, Julu. By nature he was filial and trustworthy, and he had mastered the classics and histories;
thus, contemporary opinion held him in high regard. He was summoned to serve as a Doctor at the Imperial Academy, yet he grew weary of worldly turmoil and defilement.

Upon first perusing the Buddhist scriptures, his spiritual understanding was suddenly awakened. At the age of twenty-eight, he entered the service of Dharma Master Shi of Jingming Temple in his hometown as his preceptor for tonsure.
Furthermore, he made five vows to revere the Triple Gem and to bring merit to the four debts of gratitude.
Initially, he studied the practice of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* under Chan Master Fang, a disciple of Guṇabhadra. He then traveled north to Jiayu Mountain in Dingzhou, where he withdrew [into seclusion].

As he focused his mind in contemplation, he realized there was absolutely nothing to be attained. He then intended to leave the mountains to propagate the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for the sake of saving the world.
At that time, a monk arrived from Mount Tai; Hui-chou informed him of his intention. The monk earnestly exhorted him with the path of dhyāna, seeking to dissuade him from any other resolve.
He said, "All sentient beings possess the dhyāna of the 'taste of the first stage' (*āsvāda-dhyāna*). If one simply focuses the mind on this, there is no one who will not attain it.

He followed this instruction, and within ten days he indeed attained concentration. He constantly relied upon the noble practice of *nirvāṇa* and the method of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).

Whether sleeping, dreaming, or awake, he was entirely free from thoughts of desire. After five summer retreats, he went to see Chan Master Daoming of Mount Zhanghong in Zhaozhou, where he received the ten [precepts].

He practiced the six dharmas of special excellence with such diligent devotion that for ninety days his food consisted of only four *dou*. He would sit alone upon a stone, the coarse fibers of his clothing digging into his skin.

Sometimes, while his meal was not yet cooked, he would sit in silent oblivion for the duration of a watch; by the time the hungry vultures and famished monkeys had finished consuming everything he possessed, he remained unmoved.
Furthermore, he constantly cultivated the contemplation of death; whenever bandits came, they were struck with fear, yet he showed no sign of alarm. Because of this—

He preached to them concerning all karmic actions. [The spirits] all broke their bows and snapped their arrows, received the precepts, and withdrew. Once, at Mount Que, he moved a deity through his graceful postures and seductive gestures;
the spirit embraced his shoulders and pressed against his waist, pouting its lips and blowing air, increasing its disturbances.

Yet, because his mind was fixed on death as his essential goal, nine days passed before he emerged from his meditative absorption. His thoughts were clear and serene, realizing that ultimately there is nothing worth pursuing in the world.
Lè went to the Venerable Tripitaka Master Bhadra at Shaolin Temple to present his realization.

The Tripitaka Master said, "Regarding the study of Chan east of Mount Song, you are the foremost. He remained at the Shaoshi Monastery on Mount Song. The monastery had a spring that was always sufficient to provide for the community.
Occasionally, a woman in tattered clothes was seen sitting on the steps with a broom, listening to the sutras. A monk scolded her.
The woman became extremely resentful; she trampled the spring with her foot, and the spring immediately dried up. The woman also sank and disappeared.

From then on, the assembly suffered from the lack of water at the spring and informed Sthiramati of it. Sthiramati hurried to the site of the spring and called out three times for the *upāsikā*. The woman emerged.

Huida said, "The assembly of monks is practicing the Way; it is fitting that you provide them with protection. At the spot where the woman had kicked the spring with her foot, the water immediately gushed forth as before.
Later, while traveling to Mount Wangwu in Huai Prefecture, two tigers were in the midst of a furious fight; Huida resolved their conflict with his *xi-zhang* (monk’s staff), and they each dispersed.
Suddenly, two scrolls of a *xian-jing* (immortal scripture) appeared upon the bed where he resided. Huida said, "I seek the path of the Buddha."
This was all. Longevity is not something to be cultivated [by such means]. Shortly thereafter, he lost the whereabouts of his books.

He moved to Mount Qingluo, where those suffering from various chronic ailments, leprosy, sores, and fevers all brought him offerings. He accepted them; though they were pus, blood, and foul-smelling odors, he felt no aversion.

As he sat for a long time and grew weary, his legs gradually became stiff. Suddenly, a deity emerged from the ground to support him, causing him to return to the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). Once settled, he remained fixed therein.

He set a period of seven days; such was his practice in his later years. He moved to Mount Mátou in Huai Prefecture, where he did not respond to the three imperial edicts of Emperor Xiaoming of the Wei dynasty.
In the first year of the Yongxi era, Emperor Xiaowu established a meditation chamber for him at Shangshu Valley.

His followers gathered in great numbers, and the provisions provided were abundant and lavish. By imperial decree, Lou Rui, the Regional Inspector of Dingzhou, and Gao You, the Prince of Pengcheng, were ordered to welcome him.

Reaching as far as the Great Dark Mountains of Wenmo, he first established the precepts for the regions of Gui, Jie, Yan, and Zhao. Those who were moved by his sincerity were so numerous that none dared to offer sacrifices involving animal blood.
Whenever there were those stubbornly attached to fame and profit, he would explain gāthās for them to dispel their delusions;

those among the recluses who sought to still the mind were encouraged to advance toward what they had not yet attained. Both the monastic and the laity relied upon him. This continued until the time of Emperor Wenxuan of the Qi dynasty, who especially held him in high esteem and respect.
In the second year of the Tenpō era, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "I have long heard of your virtue and character, and I desire to propagate your teachings.
I hope you will accept this gift and travel briefly to the Imperial Court to transform sentient beings; it is not right that one should seek excellence for oneself alone.

When the time comes for you to return to the mountains, you shall be free to go east or west without being detained. Having thus decreed that Dingzhou should provide transport to Ye, Tanchou departed from the mountains on that very day.
Suddenly, both mountain peaks shook, and the sound was piteous and cutting. Birds and beasts fled for three days. The Imperial Carriage went out to meet him at the suburban altar;

he was escorted into the palace, where he knelt to hear the essentials of the Dharma. His hair stood on end and sweat poured from him. Having received the methods of the Śāsana, he was fit to attain profound realization.

He was conferred the Bodhisattva Precepts, and an edict was issued for the Director of the Imperial Kitchen to cease serving wine and meat, for the tiger cages to release hawks and dogs, and for all hunting throughout the empire to be strictly prohibited.

On the sixth day of every month and the third day of each season, the people observed fasts and abstinence. On another occasion, he said to Sengchou, "The Way is propagated by men; sincerity does not fail to elicit a response. You, Master, need only set your mind at ease.
How would it be if I, your disciple, were to serve as an external patron (*dānapati*) to protect you? Sengchou replied, "A Bodhisattva takes the protection of the Dharma as his heart's purpose.
Your Majesty accords with Heaven and complies with the people, acting as a pillar and beam for the Triple Gem. This is most fortunate for the Gate of the Teaching."

He was consequently detained within the imperial palace for over forty days. In the third year, an edict was issued to construct Yunmen Monastery on the southern slope of Longshan Mountain, eighty *li* to the southwest of the capital, to provide him with a residence; he was also appointed to preside over Shikusi.

Furthermore, an edict was issued to establish numerous Chan monasteries throughout the various prefectures and commanderies within the realm, as the Emperor intended to abolish the recitation and lecturing services at all other monasteries. The Emperor remarked, "The Buddha-dharma..."
"The Great Tradition takes a tranquil mind as its foundation. These various Dharma masters are merely causing unnecessary clamor;

how could they possibly propagate and explain [the teachings]? Is it appropriate now to abolish them all? Sengchou remonstrated, saying: "The Dharma masters circulate the Tripiṭaka and follow the four reliances by imperial decree.

These are the primary foundations for mental cultivation and the precursors to the Buddha Vehicle. They are the gradual means by which faith is inspired and the ignorant among the people are enlightened. The Emperor was greatly pleased.
From then on, it was deliberated that the national treasury should be divided into three parts; excluding public expenditures and private use, all surplus was to be dedicated to Sengchou.
An edict was issued to establish a storehouse within the monastery to accumulate money and silk. Those who arrived to deliver these goods followed one another in endless succession along the roads.

Sengchou urgently submitted a memorial refusing them, which the Emperor praised. Sengchou usually stayed in a small room for his daily life; even when the Emperor visited him in person to inquire after his well-being, he never [left his quarters].
His disciples said this to him. Sengchou replied, "In the past, when Piṇḍola invited a king for seven paces, it caused the king to lose his kingdom for seven years.
My true virtue does not equal his; I do not dare to deceive others regarding my physical appearance. The reason I did not rise was also in the hope that the Sovereign might obtain merit.
Later, someone indeed slandered Chou to the Emperor on account of his arrogance. The Emperor became enraged and was about to—
He went in person to inflict harm upon him. Daochou knew of this in his heart. He instructed the kitchen staff in advance to prepare a grand offering.

He then mounted a bullock cart and traveled twenty li through the night. Arriving at the mouth of the valley, he stood alone by the roadside. After a short while, the carriage arrived; the Emperor asked in surprise for the reason.
Daochou replied, "I feared that my own blood might be impure and defile the monastery; therefore, I have come ahead to wait here. The Emperor was greatly astonished.
He dismounted from his horse and prostrated himself, filled with remorse that knew no end. Turning to the Chancellor Yang Daoyan, he said, "How could one possibly defame such a True Man?
He then requested to carry Daochou back to the monastery to apologize for his transgression. Daochou firmly declined.

When the Emperor inquired between times what kind of being he had been in his previous life, Daochou replied, "A Rākṣasa king; this is the result of your habitual tendency toward killing. He then performed a rite over a basin of water and showed it to him.

He saw him alone, and his appearance was like that of a rākṣasa as depicted in the world’s paintings. Ji Jiang, the Gentleman Attendant for the Eunuchs, together with several great virtuous ones, requested the extraction of the essentials of dhyāna;
[Huiyuan] then composed two fascicles on the *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation), which circulated in the world.

He passed away on the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the first year of the Qianming era. His age was eighty-one; he had been a monk for fifty summers. Prince Xuan of Xiangle issued an imperial decree to offer condolences.

It is said: Therefore, the Great Dhyāna Master’s resolve and diligence were refined and arduous; his attainment of the fruit was inevitable. He settled his mind in silent stillness, departing empty-handed but returning with reality.

His wondrous deeds and profound influence were esteemed by both the monastic and lay communities. Now that his life has passed and his spirit has departed, we are truly filled with lamentation and bewilderment.
To further honor his legacy and express our sorrowful respect, we shall bestow five hundred rolls of silk and provide offerings for a thousand monks at Yunmen Monastery. —The Huangjian Era.

In the fifth month of the second year, his disciples, including Tanxun and others, submitted a petition requesting that a stupa be erected for him. The imperial edict stated: "The late Great Chan Master’s virtue and achievements were lofty and far-reaching;
he was a pillar of the Triple Gem. His causal conditions having ended and his transformation complete, his spirit now roams beyond the mundane world.

You may follow the Western Regions custom by cremating him and erecting a stupa. We grant one thousand rolls of silk and shall establish a vegetarian feast for one thousand monks, thereby commemorating his fragrant legacy and providing an example for future generations."
The Right Vice-Director Wei Shou composed the inscription for the stele.

The monk Sengyae was surnamed Mou; his ancestors were from Fuling. In the ninth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, when Zhu Lingshi campaigned against Shu, three hundred households of the Min people from Fuling followed the army and settled in the Jinyuan Valley of Guanghan.

In time, his descendants settled there to make their home. When Ya was young, he was precocious; he spoke little and laughed rarely, and he utterly refrained from play. Whenever he drank water, he would invariably offer a prostration.
He would often sit for an entire day, gazing intently without blinking. When asked the reason for this, he said, "I contemplate how loathsome this body is;
it shall one day be burned. Later, as he grew up, he became exceptionally upright and resolute. One day, while fishing with others, he divided the catch.
He threw what he had caught into the water and said, "Killing is not a wholesome practice; I now vow to sever it completely.

He then burned his hunting gear and ceased hunting altogether. Furthermore, he saw a strange snake, red from head to tail, initially about a foot long and two inches thick, which in an instant suddenly grew over ten feet long and approximately five or six feet in circumference. It emerged from a pond dug by the *mlecchas*.
In the pond, [the dragon] suddenly ascended into the clouds and vanished. The multitude was struck with terror, but Huaiya said, "Fear not; it is enough simply to sever the karma of killing.

Furthermore, he exhorted them to completely abolish the embankments and reservoirs used for keeping fish. Although the multitude still did not consent, before long the dykes broke and collapsed, exactly as he had warned.
He then entered the monastic life under Master Xisi, serving him with exceptional diligence and care. During the month of deep winter, while practicing meditation...
The Master ordered fire to warm his feet. Huai set up a large brazier before him. The Chan Master rebuked him for having so much fire, to which he replied, "I need the fire to ward off the cold;
yet when I obtain the fire, I complain that it is too much. If one's disposition is like this, how can one be said to have attained the Way? The Chan Master then had him place his hand into the fire;
immediately, upon hearing the command, he burned off a finger without any sign of distress. The Chan Master inwardly marveled at him. On another day, the other disciples...
The boy pushed himself into the midst of the smoke and flames; although his body became covered in sores, he remained joyful and smiling as usual.
The Chan Master said to him, "If you act like this, will you not delude and disturb the common people? He replied, "The Buddhas attained the Way through the suffering of their bodies;

how much more so for someone like me? If I could obtain tonsure for even a single day, that would be enough. The Chan Master then performed the tonsure for him himself, yet he felt it was as easy as calling out the name "Good."
The Master came forward; the Chan Master immediately set aside his knife, adjusted his robes, and prostrated, saying, "Dharma Master Ya has come to be my teacher;
I request to be your disciple. Ya merely declined with humble apologies. From that time on, his spiritual transformations gradually became manifest, and those he rescued and benefited were numerous.
He was over seventy years old, yet his mental and physical faculties remained robust.

In the sixth month of the first year of the Wucheng era, in the middle of a great thoroughfare west of the city of Yizhou, he wrapped his five fingers on each hand in cloth and set them ablaze. As the flames grew fierce, someone asked him whether it was painful.
He replied, "Pain arises from the mind. Since the mind has no pain, how could the fingers possibly feel pain? Some people suspected that he had suffered a stroke or a mental affliction.

[The interlocutor] said, "Why do you not mend them? He replied, "The body is entirely empty; what use is there for mending it? [The interlocutor] asked again, "The four great elements and the five sense organs possess resistance;
how can they be called empty? He replied, "As for the four great elements and the five sense organs, where else could they abide?

When Master Dui of Xiaoci Temple saw that his understanding was so thorough and unimpeded, and having heard of him thus from Yuankai, he led his disciples to pay him homage and bestowed upon him clothing and other requisites. Upon withdrawing, he said to the assembly: "Yuankai..."
Regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, he had attained true realization rather than merely engaging in verbal discourse. Consequently, people vied with one another to address him as a Bodhisattva;

monks and laypeople gathered from all four quarters, redoubling their reverence and faith. As days passed in this manner, the fingers of his left hand were completely consumed until the fire reached his palm and the marrow within his bones began to boil;
yet even as the flames were about to die out, he suddenly used the remaining fingers of his right hand to stir up the blaze once more.
Someone asked, "Why do you subject yourself to such hardship? He replied, "It is because sentient beings do not practice patience; I wish merely to exhort and inspire them.
At the height of the smoke and flames, as his two arms were burning fiercely, he remained motionless on the cliff, his countenance unchanged, preaching the Dharma with encouragement.

Practicing loving-kindness, he abstained from killing. He would further recite the sutras for the fourfold assembly; when he reached the most critical phrases and essential meanings, he would nod his head and smile.

At that time, there were those who grew weary or indolent. Huikaya looked back at them and said: "In this age of the final dharma, people are disrespectful. They look upon images as if they were wooden stumps, and hear the sutras as if the wind passing by a horse's ears.
When I was in the mountains, I did not know a single character; yet now, hearing the teachings of the sutras, every sentence accords with my own mind."

[The Master] replied, "It should be so; therefore, I shall burn my own hands to inspire faith and reverence. Otherwise, how could these hands ever become firewood? Thereupon, tens of thousands of men and women gathered around him.
While Fatai sat calmly in the center of the cliffs, a light drizzle suddenly began to fall. He immediately withdrew his thoughts and entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
The clouds dispersed and the moon shone as before. Once the five bones of his palms were consumed by the flames, they suddenly rose up together in full form.
They emerged, each three inches long, pure white and lovely. The assembly all said, "After the Bodhisattva’s parinirvāṇa, we vow to enshrine these śarīras, erect a stūpa, and make offerings to them.
The cliff then bit out the bone that had grown from it with its mouth and spat it before the assembly, saying, "This may serve as a stūpa.
On the fourteenth day of the seventh month, there was a sound like the earth collapsing and the heavens splitting; everyone was struck with awe and alarm. Furthermore—

He saw dogs, sheep, dragons, snakes, military weapons, and elephants in the sky; after a short while, they vanished. Someone asked him the reason for this, and he replied, "It was merely a dream within my *samādhi*.
I wish to cast off my body, and therefore I have manifested these signs. He then dispatched messengers to prepare the necessary offerings.
Subsequently, to the southeast of Chengdu County, he piled firewood to form a tower several *zhang* high, upon which he placed a small amount of dried hemp.
He moistened the chamber with oil. Chan Master Dao of Xiaocai Temple offered a six-runged *khakkhara* staff and a purple robe.
Sengyuan of Jianwei offered a variegated *kaṣāya*. At that time, people from near and far flocked together, and their offerings piled up like a mountain.
Initially, no one knew that these were the items donated by the two virtuous masters. On the morning of the fifteenth day, Huiyi said to his attendant, Fata: "You take the staff..."
Carrying his staff and wearing purple robes over his patched saffron dharma-cloak, he arrived and immediately took the palanquin to the cremation site.

At that time, several hundred thousand monastics and laypeople crowded around the palanquin, weeping. Huiyuan said, "Simply maintain the bodhicitta; do not weep. He then ascended the high seat and preached the Dharma.
After looking up toward the lecture hall and smiling alone, he lay down on his right side. His breath ceased entirely, and his appearance was like a wooden puppet. Suddenly—
Dongqi said, "The time has come. He then descended from his seat and addressed the assembly, saying, "The Buddha-dharma is difficult to encounter; you should all protect and uphold it together.
Having finished, he walked slowly to the foot of the tower, circumambulated it three times, and paid obeisance at all four gates.

Once he had ascended, he looked down and addressed the fourfold assembly, saying, "I pray that you will single-mindedly recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* to assist me in raising this tower. The donor was Wang Zhuan, who intended for it to be so.
"I have built this tower to burn the Bodhisattva; how could I not incur sin? Yà remained silent, but he knew [the truth].

He called Zhuàn up to the tower, took Zhuàn by the head with his arm, and said, "Do not worry that building this tower will bring you sin; rather, it is the means by which you shall obtain merit. He immediately ordered the fire to be extinguished.
The assembly all stood with hands folded in reverence, none daring to step forward. Yà placed the torch on the ground and personally used his own arm [to put it out].
He held a torch and set fire to the northwest corner of the room; next, it reached the southwest. The hemp was dry and the oil thick; the flames blazed together in a brilliant conflagration.
Amidst the raging fire, he cast away the torch and performed his prostrations. By the time he had completed two bows, his face and body were scorched and split open.

When he wished to prostrate again, his body collapsed onto the glowing coals. In a moment, the fuel was exhausted and the fire extinguished; his flesh and bones were all consumed, leaving behind only his heart, liver, and intestines.
[The body was reduced to] kidneys alone. The heart remained uniquely red, moist, and supple; its inherent nature could not be destroyed by external forces.
Consequently, forty cartloads of firewood were added to refine it further. Yet, while the intestines and kidneys were seen to shrink and curl up, the heart remained largely unchanged.
He then ordered it to be collected and preserved for burial. This was because, in the past, whenever a Bodhisattva was asked a question, he would say: "My body may perish, but my mind..."
[He] was ever-present. Those who heard of this took it to mean that this was merely the spirit. But how could the spirit ever have a time of decay or dissolution?
Furthermore, after Ya’s death, miraculous traces were even more numerous; for the most part, they were all manifestations of compassionate transformation that uprooted suffering and bestowed joy.
I shall not record them in detail here, but will briefly cite one or two to illustrate the moment of his transition between life and death. Monk Fǎ of Xià'ài Temple...
Xing followed worldly customs in his eating and drinking. Later, moved by the events at Yajue, he made a vow to abstain from alcohol and meat.

When he returned to the monastery in the evening, he saw a golden-colored person who said to him, "It is excellent that you can abstain from meat. However, if you were to eat the flesh of even a single sentient being..."
One thus eats the flesh of all sentient beings; all sentient beings are, in fact, the flesh of one’s own parents and kinsmen.
If one must eat it, one should regard it as the worms within a corpse—the worms being the very flesh itself. Furthermore, one hears a voice in the air saying:
"Be diligent in observing the fast, and vow that all sentient beings may attain a body that is not eaten, and that the bodies of hungry ghosts may always be fully satiated. As he was about to...
At that time, the śramaṇa Ratnasāgara asked: "Since it is one and the same fire, why is it that when the Bodhisattva undergoes this burning, there is no appearance of pain?
He replied: "Sentient beings experience pain because they possess marks [of selfhood]. The Bodhisattvas, however, always say: 'I shall take upon myself the suffering of sentient beings.'"

"Is this actually attained or not? He replied, "Since one has already resolved to take [the suffering] upon oneself in their stead, why would it not be attained? "Question: The karmic offenses of sentient beings have ripened, and each must undergo their own suffering.
How can a Bodhisattva burn themselves and thereby substitute for them? "Answer: A single thought of wholesome roots is capable of extinguishing evil."
"Is this not a matter of substitution? Master Fapha said, "The two schools have debated the great meaning together, yet in the end it has not been resolved.
One maintains that Buddha-wisdom takes the markless principle as its object; the principle is the object-condition (*ālambana*), and wisdom is the subjective condition (*ālambaka*).

The other maintains that the elimination of delusion and the cessation of inversion is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Of these two doctrines, which is correct? Yuanya said, "Buddha is precisely the markless."

"Because their characteristics are distinct. Master Hai said, "The Buddha is formless; the characteristic of the formless has no distinct characteristics from the beginning. If this is so, then is the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni or Avalokiteśvara? Yaya replied, "I am an ordinary person who vows to enter hell to undergo suffering on behalf of sentient beings, wishing for them to attain Buddhahood. Master Hai asked, "For what reason did the previous Buddhas attain Buddhahood so early? He answered: [He attained it] because he had already fulfilled his vows. Master Hai said, "If you have already fulfilled your vows, why do you not become a Buddha now? Yaya replied, "I am a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage. Because I vowed to undergo suffering in hell on behalf of sentient beings, I have not yet attained Buddhahood. Master Hai said, "If that is so, then all Buddhas must have been Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage before attaining Buddhahood. Yaya replied, "That is so. Master Hai said, "If that is so, then I shall now become a Buddha. Yaya replied, "If you become a Buddha, I shall also become a Buddha. Master Hai said, "If I were to become a Buddha, I would immediately ascend to the Tuṣita Heaven and dwell there. You would then be unable to see me. Yaya replied, "Even though you ascend to the Tuṣita Heaven, I shall still be able to see you. Master Hai said, "If you can see me while I am in the Tuṣita Heaven, then I shall indeed become a Buddha. "In the past, when the former Buddhas had already completed the deliverance of all sentient beings, they asked the holy ones such as Bhaiṣajyarāja, 'For what reason have you also attained Buddhahood, while now you alone, O Bodhisattva, have not yet attained Buddhahood? This seems to be a different path from that of the former Buddhas. They replied:

'In former times, sentient beings had already attained the intention of Bhaiṣajyarāja; now, sentient beings have not yet attained my intention. Because I am beginning my transformation, it is like gathering fallen flowers.'"
His responses were all of this nature. Among those present was one who doubted that Huiya was a sage;
Huiya then called out that person’s name by it and said, "The Buddhas appear in the world without a fixed form; they may manifest as the sick, the ugly, or as animals of various species.
I pray that you, donor, do not give rise to thoughts of frivolous contempt. During the sequence of lighting the funeral pyre, everyone beheld auspicious signs.
In some places, a circular canopy covered a cliff, where three practitioners of the Way sat cross-legged upon it.

In other places, five-colored lights appeared in human forms within a chamber of hemp at its four gates. On a wooden tower, light shone like the sun’s disc, and in both instances, flowers rained down in various sizes.
Furthermore, the sound of celestial drums was heard, deep and resonant from afar. After a long time, a person from Bei County [encountered this] by the banks of the Bei River.
He saw a cliff in the sky where a person was riding in an oil-silk palanquin, followed by five or six hundred monks, gradually fading away toward the west.
When the heart-relic reached the Bao-guo Temple, there was again a light in the shape of a cluster of flowers that brightly illuminated the courtyard and buildings.
Monk Hui-sheng of A-ka-ni-ta Temple was suffering from illness; feeling particularly despondent because he believed he would not witness such a superior auspicious event, he suddenly dreamed—
Huiya took a śrāmaṇera and wrapped about three *hu* of incense in a cloth. He then divided sandalwood powder into four heaps and circumambulated the image while burning them.
The image appeared terrified and said, "I am but an ordinary person; I cannot yet burn my own body. Huiya replied, "Do not fear;

I am using this to fumigate your illness. Immediately, the image felt refreshed and robust. Thereupon, he requested a manifestation of a spiritual sign. The image answered, "My name is Samantaprabhāsa-ratnagarbha Bodhisattva."
