Zen Master Zhouyou, surnamed Yang, resided at Duobao Monastery in Yizhou for over forty years. Day and night, he devoted himself exclusively to recitation.

Later, he depicted the nine meditations on impurity (*navasaṃjñā-vikṛti*) upon the walls of his room. He placed a rope bed out in the open, covering it with a *tāla* palm mat to protect it from rain and dew.
During the day, he joined the monks in their labors; at night, he practiced meditative concentration within that space. As soon as the sun had barely risen...
He ate it as his regular diet, gradually increasing the duration until he did so for seven days or even a month. Sengshu took pleasure in this and did not find it strange.
In this manner, twenty years passed without anyone taking notice or showing concern. Suddenly one night, there was a violent wind and rain;
the painted walls of the building collapsed, and the neighboring monk Yiyou was buried beneath them. When [Sengshu] went there at dawn, only the rope bed remained; nothing else was left.
[This is] a record. Later Liang’s Monk Jing was a man of unknown origins. He resided at Mount Yang on the northern bank of the Li River. He had attained realization regarding the Way.
Mount Yang borders the Peach Blossom Spring; it is a place where immortals, spirits, and ghosts dwell in seclusion. Jing lived there in tranquil obscurity.

The echoes resounded, and snakes and tigers served as its messengers. Should anyone approach with an evil thought, they would immediately be struck with terror and confusion, not knowing where to turn.
However, if one came simply to inquire about the Way, there was no harm. Chan Master Huicui, a spiritual disciple of Master Huisi of Mount Nanyue, heard of this and went to visit him.
[The deity] remained silent all day long, refusing to be questioned. Huicui, therefore, persisted in his earnest efforts time and again.
He followed this with weeping. Thus it continued for ten days and nights until they were finally able to converse.
Cui withdrew and sighed, saying, "I have encountered eighteen noble spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and in each case I was able to enter their gate and ascend to their hall;
yet none were as lofty as the walls of this man, nor as steep the steps leading up. Later, nothing was known of his final destination.
Huiyi of the Sui dynasty was surnamed Li and was a native of Linyuan. He was single-mindedly devoted to the study of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and also studied Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras.
When the Yuwen clan suppressed the Dharma, he traveled south to the Liang court, where he became a fellow disciple of the śramaṇa Huiling of Xiancheng Mountain.

Shortly thereafter, he moved to the former hall of Master Cong in the capital, where he remained in a constant sitting posture day and night. His radiance was so brilliant that those who saw him were startled, taking him for a lamp.
There was a man named Liu Jing in his home village who had previously served as the Governor of Deguang Commandery.

He had long been a non-believer, so he separately invited [the Master] to his own home to receive offerings for a hundred days. Furthermore, he sent his four sons, Yi, Bing, and the others, to go there at night to spy on him.
They indeed saw that his room was brilliantly illuminated. From this, Jing finally turned toward the faith. He passed away at the beginning of the Kaihuang era; on that day, it was said—
The disciple Huixing said, "When guests arrive, we should prepare an abundance of vegetarian offerings. By midday, however, those coming to offer condolences had filled the gates.
Master Yong was a native of Nangxiang; during the Liang dynasty, Emperor Ming once provided him with offerings. At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, [he arrived].

He passed away while seated. Those who heard the music and smelled the fragrance did so for seven days and nights. Only then was his corpse exposed upon the mountain under a canopy, and he was not yet buried.
Dharma Master Quan of the same monastery suddenly approached the corpse and said, "I pray you remain for seven days to wait [for me]. When the seventh day arrived, Quan died;
the corpse was then carried out and laid on its side, and only then did Yong’s corpse begin to decompose.
Daoshun of the Sui dynasty was a man of unknown origins. He built a thatched hut on Mount Yangtou in Zezhou, a place traditionally said to be where the Lord of Shenong tasted medicinal herbs.
It was a tranquil, secluded, and remote location, truly a dwelling place for immortals and sages. Daoshun ate but once a day and remained in constant meditation;
throughout the year, he never slept. Snakes and rats bred beneath his rope bed, and tigers would often crouch and stare at him.
He would stand to one side and appear to listen as he preached the Dharma. If someone came and told him to leave, he would invariably depart exactly as instructed.

Or if someone said, "Please do not come tomorrow," it would invariably turn out to be so. Thus, those among his followers who were with him never encountered any opposition, and his efficacy in transforming sentient beings was generally like this.
His robes were tattered and he walked barefoot; those who met him could not recognize him. At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, he carried a water jar and a staff while begging for food.
In a village where many villagers had gathered to seek the dharma of receiving the precepts, he encountered a young woman who immediately said, "You shall be reborn among the cattle;
the signs are already manifest. Even if you receive the precepts, it will be of no benefit. She then stepped on his heels to make him leave, but he was unable to do so.
He said, "A cow relies on its tail for strength. If its tail is stepped upon, can it suddenly wish to depart? This is surely but the shadow of one's karma.

Moreover, having looked back at this, do you not feel regret? Thereupon, the woman emptied her entire household wealth to cultivate merit and perform repentance. Her heart was filled with even greater compassion;
she frequently visited the homes of those afflicted by pestilence to offer incantations and treatment, never shrinking from the task. In her later years, she went to the forest.
He concluded with the peaks of Luyong, Honggu, Pan, and Ting.
Daoxian (also known as Sengxian) of the Sui dynasty was a native of Kangju in the Western Regions.

In his youth, he engaged in trade, traveling back and forth between the rivers and seas of Wu and Shu on two ships, amassing wealth worth tens of thousands of strings of cash. At that time, Master Sengda resided in Zizhou.
At Mount Niutou in Xincheng Prefecture, an immortal couple visited him. Da preached the Dharma to them, saying:
"In the cycle of birth and death, there must be separation from all that is loved. Even this body is like this; how much more so external things? He also once went to knock on Da’s door.

Fotuo did not respond; he merely peered through the door and saw that the room was filled with water alone. Those who understood the matter believed this was because Fotuo had entered the water for contemplation.
Thereupon, the Immortal Da was greatly enlightened; he immediately sank both ships, took leave of his wife and children, and shaved his head at Zhulin Temple on Mount Guankou.
Facing the assembly, he made a vow, saying: "If I do not attain the Way, I shall never leave this mountain."

Huiyi withdrew to a remote and secluded place, where he built a hut to practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Whenever he entered samādhi, he would remain there for four or five days before emerging;

consequently, he was able to speak of future events, all of which were verified without the slightest discrepancy. When guests arrived the following day, he would first announce their number during the night. His divine anomalies gradually became widely renowned.
When Xiao Dan, the Prince of Shixing of the Liang dynasty, was stationed in Shu, he treated Huiyi with the etiquette due to a teacher and escorted him to Shan. This was during the Tianjian era.

In the sixteenth year, he traveled to Qingxi Mountain, intending to establish his residence there. Prior to this, the Daoist Li Xuezhu and others had occupied the site for their own construction projects;

whenever the Immortal arrived, they would clear and cultivate the land. Although the Daoists repeatedly rebuked and tried to stop him, he paid them no heed, clearing only enough space for a single meditation seat.
Before long, a fire broke out, and when the Daoists saw it from afar, they looked at one another and thought: [it was his doing].
Furthermore, when the Immortal was reduced to ashes, [the official] hurried to inspect him; the Immortal sat upright amidst the blazing flames, remaining as composed as ever.

From this, it was known that he had attained the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (fire-element samādhi), such that even Daoist practitioners followed suit in honoring him. Later, when the meditation hall was completed...

His power was truly great. Through a profound and mysterious resonance, he manifested the Four Heavenly Kings at Liang Tai Temple. On six consecutive *zhai* days, he established a great assembly for offerings;
the Immortal (the Master) went there to attend, and from the crowns of the Four Kings’ heads, five-colored light radiated, its brilliance shining near and far.
The incense burners they held did not require fire to ignite, yet smoke rose from them spontaneously. The Regional Inspector, Prince of Poyang—
Hui personally received his instructions and precepts. When Taiwei Lu Fahe was still of humble status, he admired Hui and attended at his side, providing him with water and firewood for twenty years.
Once, when a guest treated him somewhat disrespectfully, Hui repented and said, "This is a noble official of the Three Dukes; how could one revile or insult him?"
Once, while lying ill, he saw a youth dressed in pale blue garments holding medicine; emerging from the waters of the Qingxi Stream, the youth knelt and presented it to him.
His illness was promptly cured. He soon returned to Shu, having remained in Shan for twenty-eight years. Upon his arrival, the people of Shu regarded him as they would their own parents.
During a great drought, they requested him to pray for rain. The immortal slowly tapped the dragon pool with his staff and asked, "What do you crave?"
He slept in this manner. Before long, a torrential rain poured down. The people followed him in song and dance, praising his virtue and repeatedly requesting [him to remain].
As they touched his elbows and armpits, they obtained śarīra relics at the mere thought of it. When the Sui dynasty unified the realm, Prince Xiu of Shu summoned him; he did not go.
Enraged, the Prince arrived with his troops, his power being truly formidable. Upon hearing of this, the Immortal donned his saṃghāṭī robe and waited while recollecting the Buddha. Then, Heaven—
The atmosphere suddenly changed; clouds and mist became dark and gloomy, hail and snow fell in torrents, and mountain streams surged with rapids, blocking the roads.

The soldiers were discouraged and unable to advance. The King, filled with fear, repented his transgressions, whereupon the weather cleared. Upon meeting the immortal, he paid him homage and listened to the Dharma.

He then welcomed him to Zhongjing Monastery in Chengdu. During the Kaihuang era, the immortal returned to his mountain temple. As he was about to depart, the mountain spirits swept the path ahead of him.
Except for the road, once he had returned, there was a visiting monk staying in his room; he rose suddenly and dragged him out. Shortly thereafter, the house collapsed and buried them.
Alas, how can the depth of his compassion be measured? He passed away at over one hundred years of age and was buried in the mountains.
To this day, the common people call him "Master Immortal" (Xian Shali).
During the Sui dynasty, Huìyán resided at Chóngxuán Monastery in Sū. He constantly sat in his quarters practicing meditation and never once went out for recreation.

Whenever he did go out, he would eat and drink freely and laugh and talk without restraint, failing to maintain the discipline of the precepts. People regarded him as mad and treated him with contempt and regret. Yet he was always alone and joyful;
facing the assembly, he would point and direct them, saying, "This place is the main hall," "This place is the lecture hall," and even extending it to the corridors, the kitchens, and the stables.
The entire monastery was in a state of disorder. After more than a month had passed, he told those who knew him: "A bell has fallen from the stupa; this is the time of my departure.
He then locked his door from the inside and did not open it for a long time. Shortly thereafter, a bell from the stupa indeed fell down.

The multitude broke through the barriers and entered, only to find him sitting upright upon the cliff, having passed away. When the city heard of this, they rushed there in such numbers that the streets were choked with people;
they vied with one another to offer gold and silk for the support of the monastery’s permanent endowment.

They provided ample funds for its reconstruction, yet the structural layout and positioning remained exactly as he had described before they ceased. It flourished and became a renowned monastery, and his physical remains still remain there today.

By nature compassionate and loving, even birds of prey and wild beasts would become docile upon hearing him preach the Dharma until they could be employed for service. Once, a tiger used its head...
He lay with his head resting on his knees; Yue also entered meditative absorption and was unaware of it. His reputation spread throughout the three regions of Chu.
Toward the end of the Kaihuang era, when Emperor Yang resided at the Jin Prince’s residence, he dispatched the Palace Attendant Wang Yanshou to summon him to the Huiri Monastery.
Following him to the capital, people everywhere were converted. Later, he returned to Yangzhou, where he passed away midway. His body was placed upon a boat, which remained as if he were still alive.
People saw a light emanating from his feet at night and entering through the crown of his head; it continued to circulate in this manner without ceasing until dawn.
Marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence, the King issued a special decree ordering that he be returned for burial on the mountain, thereby honoring his extraordinary nature.
Suihui Kan was the son of the Tang family of Qu’acha in Jinling. In his youth, he studied under Master He, who was particularly endowed with spiritual wonders that no one of the world could fathom.
Nevertheless, he treated sacred images as if they were living beings; seeing a standing image, he did not dare to sit, and he exhorted others to necessarily commission seated images.
Whenever he encountered those in distress or hardship, he would rescue them without withholding his efforts. Once, he saw a herd of pigs that had been bound.
Huihe chanted, "The *Śūraṅgama* is liberation; bondage shall spontaneously dissolve. The pig bolted away, and the owner followed after it to let it go.
Whenever he gathered with the multitude, he would preach the Dharma to awaken them. In his later years, he flourished in his propagation at Ye.
Those who turned toward him praised his virtue even unto this day. He eventually passed away in Ye. As he was about to die, someone asked him what realization he had attained.
He said, "I have merely attained the ripening of my roots of goodness. Initially, Hui-kan had received a formal transmission from Huiguo;

later, he went to Lingnan to rely on Paramārtha, where he devoted himself exclusively to meditative stillness. Toward the end of the year, he resided at Xiqia Temple and subsequently went to the capital city of Yangdu to visit Dharma Master Zai.

Zai, who had long been aware of his spiritual practice, received him with due reverence. As they were about to part, Zai requested that he manifest supernatural powers. Hui-kan replied, "I grant you this."
Furthermore, what was his difficulty? He immediately extended his arm through the window; it was several tens of *zhang* long and reached as high as the lintel of the Buddha hall at Qi-xi Temple.
He held it back into his room and said to Sui, "I simply feared that the people of the world would be startled by this marvel, and for that reason, I did not deign to perform it.
At the beginning of the Daye era, he passed away at Da-guishan Temple in Jiangzhou at the age of eighty-two. On the day he was about to die, he suddenly cast [his arm]—
He placed his three robes in a cloth bag upon the hall floor and said, "I return these three robes to you, the community of monks; I am now dead. He then hurriedly closed the room and entered it.

The assembly was struck with astonishment and rose to follow and look inside; there was only a set of white bones sitting cross-legged upon the bed. When they shook them, they made a jingling sound and did not disperse.

He was deeply devoted to and close with the Venerable Yi of Jiangling and the Venerable Ming of Xiancheng; for many years he requested instruction from them. His practice surpassed that of the entire assembly, and his virtue stood preeminent among all the worthy ones.

He was victorious. After the Sui dynasty had assumed the mandate, he entered the Songgao Mountains to the north, where he ingested medicinal herbs and practiced seated meditation.

Upon Yong’s deposition, he moved his residence to Dingshui. There he met Master Lan, who invited him to Wuzhen Temple in Langu Valley; they lived in seclusion together for eight years.

later, he declined on account of illness, and the Emperor granted him leave to return home. When the Imperial House first commenced its mandate, his reputation remained as weighty as it had been in former times. Thus, eminent monks such as Huiyin and Baogong [honored him].
They all came to dwell with him. Before long, he lay ill. His disciples knelt and asked about his state of mind regarding his own life’s mission.
He replied, "To feel no joy at birth and no sorrow at death is my natural disposition. Thereupon, he sat facing west and said, "The emptiness of the primary truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā).
He then passed away, appearing as if entering meditative absorption. This was the sixth day of the twelfth month in the fifth year of the Wude era. He was seventy years of age.

Tang Huichao was born into the Shentu clan; he was a native of Lu in Shangdang. Since his renunciation of the world, he resided in the Daxingguo Monastery in Jinyang, where he practiced the discipline of dhyāna.

Within his meditation hall, he displayed a profusion of ritual images, banners, and flowers to adorn it, and he gathered various kinds of exotic incense, burning them so that the smoke would swirl and billow. Huichao himself, however, wore pure, clean robes.

Sitting upright in meditative absorption, he would invariably obtain śarīra relics that filled his flask; as soon as he took them out, more appeared, and when compared with their original count, they had never diminished.
Yet, no one could fathom where they came from. During the Renshou era, by imperial decree, he resided at Chanding Monastery, where his practice of the Way elicited auspicious signs just as before.
In the first year of the Wude era, he returned once more to Xingguo Monastery. In the winter of the seventh year, he suddenly summoned the assembly of the monastery.
He said to him, "We have lived together for many years; it is only natural that ordinary sentiments may create distance, and there may have been some disagreements.
I hope you will forgive these matters. Human birth is difficult to attain, and virtuous conditions are rarely met. You should seek your own liberation and do not bring error upon your future lives.

Thereupon, he folded his hands and remained silent, his countenance showing no change whatsoever. Had it not been for the fact that his breath had ceased, those observing him would never have known he was dead. At that time...
He was over seventy years old. In the twelfth month, his corpse was conveyed on a rope bed and interred at the side of Kaehwa Temple on Lungfu Mountain.
Although many years have passed, his remains have become increasingly firm and intact; those who pay homage and make offerings continue without ceasing to this day.
Tánlún of the Táng dynasty was the son of the Sūn family from Jùnyí in Bì. At the age of thirteen, he entered the monastic life under Master Duàn of Xiūfú Monastery.
Master Duàn practiced the gradual meditation (ānupūrvika-vipaśyanā) and once instructed him, saying: "Bind your mind to the tip of your nose; you shall thereby attain concentration."
Lun said, "If there were a distracted mind, one would fix it upon the tip of the nose. But since the mind is fundamentally not distracted, why then should one fix it?

From that time on, he entered samādhi every time he sat. Later, while being sent by his teacher to carry an alms bowl to the hall, before he had even reached the hall, he suddenly sat upright in the lotus position and entered meditative absorption, yet continued to hold the bowl with perfect composure.
His teacher greatly praised him for this. On another occasion, the teacher said to him, "Remove the veil of delusion."

It was like peeling onions: they had to be peeled away layer by layer until they were completely gone before one could attain purity. Lun replied that since there had been no onions from the very beginning, why even bother to peel them?
The Master alone recognized that his spiritual capacity was extraordinary and treated him with secret respect; he did not dare employ him for labor.
Even when performing prostrations to the Buddha or reading the sutras, the Master did not press him to do so; he merely swept a single room and remained shut inside his door all day long.

In his four modes of conduct, he was free from all discursive thought. By chance, he was appointed as the *zhisui* (the official in charge of the year’s provisions) to guard the property of the Sangha.
He repeatedly admonished his subordinates, "Do not feed the Sangha’s rice gruel to the dogs. His subordinates ignored him entirely; the dogs then vomited the gruel.
The subordinates again considered this a mere coincidence and continued to feed the dogs gruel as usual. Thereupon, a pack of dogs vomited the gruel right before the monks. If there were...
When those who employed him first became greatly afraid, they regarded Senglun as a deity. Senglun was by nature serene and composed; in his daily life, he did not display outward ostentation.

When questioned on matters of principle and doctrine, he answered each query immediately without any impediment. In the second year of the Renshou era, he constructed a meditation chamber to offer posthumous merit for the Empress Dowager.
By imperial decree, he was appointed to this task. Upon arriving, he swept the room and closed the door as usual. Those of the time [marveled at this].

Regarding the *Wolun* (臥倫) [treatise], the Dharma Master Shanjian (善粲) of Xingguo Temple was a man of vast learning and great eloquence, who styled himself the "Champion of the Three Kingdoms Debates.
He eventually composed a discourse on the *Wolun* teachings; for three days and nights, no one could fathom it.

When he expounded the meaning of *prajñā*, he stated that it is like flowers in the sky or bubbles on water—ungraspable—and that the fundamental nature is pure, like the great void. Shanjian bowed repeatedly, regarding him as a sage beyond compare.

He was able to reach [the capital]. Residing in the capital, only the Vinaya Master Xuǎnwǎn, the Dharma Master Jìnglín, and his disciples Sēngjiāng, Jìng, and others came and went to receive the Dharma.
As for those who sought audience with him, they were as numerous as fish eggs. However, toward the end of the Wǔdé era, he lay ill at Zhuāngyán Temple.
When someone asked where he would be reborn, he replied, "The world of inexhaustibility. Again, when asked what would happen after he relinquished his life, he said:
"How is it? he asked. [The monk] replied, "It is merely that he has been wrapped in coarse mats and cast away. He added, "The four elements are fighting;

they have already reached the knees. The master of the house simply watches. Sengqie suddenly felt the sensation of coldness and, withdrawing, said to the man, "The sensation of cold has indeed reached the knees.
When the four elements separate, one should be reborn in the realms of suffering. Lun knew this from afar and said, "The realms of suffering..."
Kong. After a short while, he asked, "Has the fifth-watch bell been struck yet? They replied, "Not yet. When the bell was struck, he looked at him and found he had already passed away.

He was over eighty years old. His disciples, following his final instructions, carried his body out to expose it in the wilds of South Mountain. Among those who transmitted his story was the Layman Bao, known as Maitreya.

Tang Daohui resided at Fuyuan Temple in Xinfeng, Yongzhou. Later, he built a thatched hut in a secluded valley on Mount Li to the south of the temple, where he practiced the dhūta austerities and devoted himself especially to meditative stillness. Whenever he entered samādhi, he would invariably emerge after seven days;

yet he continued to carry his staff and hold his alms bowl to beg for food without the slightest lapse. Consequently, the lay devotees of the surrounding villages prepared elaborate meals on those scheduled dates to offer him.

He went out to meet them at the head of the road; when they rested, he joyfully inquired after their well-being and instructed them in kindness and compassion. Once they had finished eating, he then conferred the *śaraṇa-gamana* (refuge) precepts upon them.
The multitude escorted him into the mountains before departing. In this manner, forty years passed as if they were a single day. In the summer of the third year of the Zhenguan era,

When the appointed time arrived and he did not emerge, they went to the hermitage to observe him; he sat with hands folded in the *añjali* mudrā and legs crossed in the *paryaṅka* posture, motionless.

The assembly thought he had entered into meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and hastily agreed to stay overnight to guard his side. After a long time, they perceived that his breath had ceased; they then locked the door together, fearing some calamity might occur.
Although the cold and heat alternated in succession, his countenance remained as it was. In the winter of the following year, those among his fellow villagers who were seekers of the Way added...
He plastered and lacquered the temple buildings to ensure their solemn veneration, a tradition that continues to this day.
Daoying of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Chen and was born in Yishi of Puzhou. His family had long been engaged in trade.

When he reached the age of eighteen, his younger paternal uncle, Vinaya Master Xiu, exhorted him to leave the household life; however, his parents opposed this, so they immediately arranged for him to marry a wife in order to distract him.

Zhi’s wife was exceptionally harmonious and compliant; even though they shared a bed, their bodies never touched. This continued for five years. Her parents were at peace of mind, believing that Ying had no other intentions.
However, every night Ying would have his wife hold a candle while he composed literary drafts and left instructions for those with whom he shared property.
He then secretly departed to shave his head and become a monk, having no lingering attachments or regrets. He relied upon Master Ju of Bingzhou to receive the teachings of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
In various sutras, it is said that at that time the woman had not yet married; she returned to her hometown to see her parents and spoke of the benefits of studying the Buddha-dharma.

Her parents regretted having heard of it so late. In the tenth year of the Kaihuang era, an imperial edict was issued to ordain monks and nuns throughout the land, and she was finally able to register her name in the official records.

As she walked alone, she thought to herself: "The characteristics of dharmas are easy to understand, but the delusions of the mind are difficult to cure. What is to be done? Thereupon, she entered [the mountains].

At Baitisi on Mount Taihang in Hexian, he practiced *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. He realized the emptiness of persons at the southern slope and realized the emptiness of phenomena on the northern ridge.

Thereafter, while managing monastic duties and examining his mind through these activities, he soon traveled to Shengguang Temple in the capital to hear Master Tanqian’s lectures on the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*.
Tanqian said to those under his care: "You all merely seek the literal text while neglecting its underlying meaning."

Having already attained diligence and reached the ultimate, only Daoying has mastered its subtlety. Furthermore, relying upon the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he made vows to provide offerings to the Sangha as a means of self-discipline.
He would often say: "When I sit with my eyes closed, it seems as though I have attained something regarding the nature of reality;
yet as soon as I open my eyes, I lose it, and it returns to merging with consciousness. Therefore, during the course of daily activities, I must ensure that there is constant cultivation."
"May it be so! Thereupon, he sat constantly with his eyes open; for more than two nights, they did not even blink. Only then did his spiritual realization begin to differ from the ordinary.
In the ninth year of the Daye era, while serving as the temple’s *zhisui* (steward), a layperson encroached upon temple land.
After a long dispute failed to resolve the matter, he suddenly said to the layperson, "I am about to die. He then abruptly collapsed, his breath ceasing. The layperson, believing him...
They vied with one another in seizing needles and piercing his fingernails, yet he did not move in the least. Within a short while, his complexion turned bluish and his flesh swelled.
The common people were terrified and urgently took refuge in him, requesting that they donate their land to the monastery so that there would be no further disputes. Daoying rose and sat as usual;
he happened to stand upon the Longtai Marsh and saw a school of fish leaping about with great joy. He slowly removed his robe and had his disciples hold it to keep watch over him.
He eventually entered the water and said, "How could I not reach the fish? He remained submerged for six nights before emerging.
Upon coming out, he told his attendant disciple, "I am not covered by soil; how could I leave it and ascend to the bank?

It was the height of winter, and though the heavy snow had just cleared, beyond the four suburbs the ground was as level as a spread mat or a polished mirror. Ying then remarked, "It is this evenness..."
In the Pure Land, he struggled to remain awake; he eventually removed his robes and lay on his back for three days and nights before rising.

He laughed heartily, saying, "I nearly died of the heat. In the evening, he returned to Puzi Temple in his native village, where he established three estates to provide for his followers and manage the community.
Those who arrived there forgot their own labors and yearned for his Dharma-medicine. Once, he rose from a night lecture.
Entering the "Gate of the Truth of the Treatise on Faith," he suddenly entered meditative absorption and remained so for several days.
Daoxun of Hedong was his former fellow student; their residences were separated by one hundred and fifty *li*. On the evening of Daoxun’s death, Sengying already knew of it.

At dawn, he led several friends to go and offer condolences, only to encounter the news of the funeral along the way. Those who understood him marveled at his spiritual resonance. In the ninth month of the tenth year of the Zhenguan era, the assembly...
Birds cried out in lamentation and flew about, gathering upon the buildings. Xuanying said to his disciples, "We must prepare ourselves early;

fetch water for a cleansing ritual, for our departure is very urgent. He donned his great robe and sat for a long time. His disciple Zhibao was attending at his side when he saw two youths dressed in blue entering with flowers;

a purple light issued from Xuanying’s body, its flames soaring up to the ridgepole of the hall. When the assembled crowd questioned him later, [he explained that these were the Bodhisattvas Guanyin and Mahāsthāmaprāpta].
Shishi said, "The Buddha has clear teachings; if one can practice according to them, there will be no further entanglements. Why do you speak thus?
He then expounded the essentials of the Dharma and recited the verse of the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. When the light of dawn appeared, he passed away at the age of eighty.
At that time, a mist darkened the area for twenty li, and it did not clear until three days later. The oxen he had kept would not eat grass or drink water, and their urine flowed [as tears].
He wailed and roared with such intensity that his voice reached several *li* away. When the seventh day arrived and the enshrouding was about to take place, people from near and far rushed to attend.

He was buried to the south of the manor on East Mountain in Xia County. At the moment the grave pit was first opened, the earth shook violently, and two white rainbows appeared, spanning continuously across the burial site.
Second, the anomaly of the white swans and the *ēng* bird’s cry.

Huixian of the Tang dynasty was a native of Baekje. In his youth, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and lectured on the *Three Treatises*, attaining a profound mastery in both that rivaled the teachings of his masters.

He resided at Xiude Temple in the northern part of that country, where he would lecture and recite the scriptures. When the time for his own impermanence drew near, people from the four directions heard of his reputation and flocked there.
Xian grew weary of the clamor and disturbances, and moved to Mount Danna in the south—a place of profound precipices and remote seclusion.
Throughout the year, no one came; thus, Xian was able to devote himself exclusively to his practice within it.
When he passed away at the age of fifty-eight, his fellow students carried his corpse and placed it inside a stone cave, awaiting wild jackals or tigers to devour it.

Eventually, the flesh and bones were entirely consumed, leaving nothing but the skull and the tongue. After three cycles of winter and summer had passed, the color of the tongue became even more vibrant.
It was red, soft, and pliable, and did not decay. Later, it suddenly turned purple and as hard as stone. The multitude built a stupa together and enshrined it within.
This was at the beginning of the present Zhenguan era.
Huifang of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Zhao. A man from Laiqiang in Xindu, Jizhou, he entered the monastic life at nine years of age at Linluoquan Temple on Mount Sumen.

He remained seated in meditative concentration throughout the day, such that no one could fathom the depths of his realization. Whether instructed in the nine successive stages or the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*), he attained realization upon hearing them.
As many years passed through the cycles of heat and cold, he did not undergo even the slightest change. During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty...
Yu then established a temple in the capital to dedicate merit for the posthumous benefit of the Empress Dowager.

He was subsequently summoned by imperial decree to reside there, where the ritual offerings were lavish and abundant. Nevertheless, his longing for the mountain forests never once departed from his heart.

In the sixth year of the Daye era, he returned to his former retreat, where his fellow practitioners gathered like clouds. Toward the end of Emperor Yang’s reign, as the world fell into turmoil, he moved again to Jiji.
During the Tang Dynasty, Longshan Temple was restored and he returned to Sumen, where he renovated the buildings and further advanced his studies.
Once, while conversing with friends about the profound mysteries of the profound teachings beneath the corridors, a novice monk overheard them from the side.
Suddenly, a voice rang out from the air as if scolding or reviling him; the novice fled in terror and died on the spot. It was only after a night had passed that he revived. Just then—
He then entered parinirvāṇa during the first month of winter in the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era. He was ninety-three years of age.
He was buried ten li north of the prefecture, on the southern slope of Yuangang Hill, on the seventeenth day of that same month.

Tang Tongda was a native of Yongzhou. He first entered the monastic life at the age of thirty. He had no fixed dwelling place, making the pursuit of teachers and the quest for the Way his sole urgent priority.
After a long time, he encountered no one who could guide him; he then entered Mount Taibai, where he subsisted on wild grass and sheltered beneath trees, sitting in meditation for five years.
One day, he struck a clod of earth with a piece of wood, and the clod shattered into fragments without remainder. Thereupon—
Dawu later resided at Lüzàng Temple in the capital. He wore only a single skirt and a single robe, remaining unchanged through both cold and heat.
Once, while discussing profound mysteries during a lecture, those who were unworthy contradicted him at every turn; yet when it came to eating and drinking, he was no different from ordinary people.
Dà remarked, "Is the study of the Mahāyāna truly like this? If one points to such [worldly] inclinations as the noble intention of a sage, then such a person is merely an ordinary commoner. Left.
When the Vice Director Fang Xuanling heard of this, he deemed it correct. He welcomed him to his residence and treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher.
Da Xing was unrestrained in nature and his speech was always unrestrained; yet Fang Xuanling placed him beyond worldly affairs, and none of their interactions were discordant.

From the beginning of the Zhenguan era, he gradually manifested supernatural anomalies. Whenever he visited a person's home, joy and laughter portended good fortune, while sorrow and gloom portended misfortune. At times, he would request certain things.

"It would be appropriate to grant him [the request]. Otherwise, it will also be a loss. For this reason, the noble and the humble throughout the capital all waited upon him to divine their fortune or misfortune.
When the Great General Xue Wanjun brought him to provide for his needs, [the Master] suddenly broke his precepts by eating at night and further desired to enter the inner quarters to sleep.
The General’s younger brother, enraged, beat him nearly to death. He then hurriedly ordered hot water to be prepared, saying, "My body has been defiled..."
"It is as filthy as this. Can you not bathe once? The boiling water was surging and bubbling; [Huiyuan] immediately undressed and leaped into the cauldron.

He moved about and rubbed himself with ease, and then told the cook to add more fire. Xue’s family was filled with shame and alarm. From then on, he was permitted to sleep and stay wherever he wished.
He once intended to hold a great vegetarian assembly and first ordered the monastery to draft an invitation for the guests. At that time, the rice was just—
Prices soared and provisions became scarce. When several thousand people arrived the following day, the monastery did not know how to provide for them.
The assembly blamed Da, but Da said, "He promised to send offerings; it cannot be a lie. By midday, those who had come were about to disperse.
Suddenly, he saw a carriage full of exquisite food filling the roads, which was used for the ritual offering until there was more than enough to satisfy all;
yet, when he sought out those who had brought the offerings, no one could be identified. Only then did he realize that his virtue reached both the hidden and the manifest realms.
During the late Sui dynasty, Fa-kong of the Tang served as an Eagle-Attack Colonel (Yingji Langjiang) in the administration of Yanmen Commandery at the age of forty.
Admiring the Buddha-dharma, he said to his wife and children: "I have long been burdened by you all. Wandering east and west, what have I ultimately achieved?
From now on, each of you may make your own plans; I shall likewise resolve to depart from here. He then packed his provisions and took up his bundle.

He entered Mount Wutai. In hunger, he ate pine and cedar; in cold, he sheltered in bitter caves. He focused exclusively on contemplating the essential meanings within the sutras, without seeking out questions from others.
At that time, the region was in turmoil, and the authorities suspected him of being a thief, arresting and interrogating him.

Yet he remained in the lotus posture, unmoving, for five days without food, drink, or even the relief of nature’s calls. Consequently, they released him without further questioning, and he went into seclusion.

For more than thirty years, he lived in close intimacy with birds and beasts. When his wife went searching for him, wishing to provide him with provisions, Hui-kong said, "Since I have grown weary of the mundane world and come to this place, you should especially set aside your efforts to transport these supplies; do not concern yourself with such trivial matters.
From now on, there is no need for us to see one another. After he had lived there for a long time, he perceived at night the sound of someone calling out, "Hui-kong, Zen Master!"
The Chan practitioner of the Void awakened alone and took this as the realm of the mind; he dispelled it through the Dharma, whereupon he subsequently attained tranquility.
He first studied the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and finally studied the Mahayana Middle Way that realizes the signless definitive meaning.
Those who followed him were likewise instructed by him in this manner. His ultimate end remains unknown.

Tang Xuanshuang was the son of Liu of Nanyang. Having married by the age of twenty, he grew weary of worldly life and left home to become a monk. His studies spanned both the schools of Emptiness and Existence;
he also once attended the lectures of Dharma Master Xuan of Longquan, gaining renown in his time. Meanwhile, Chan Master Xin was flourishing in his propagation of the teachings.
Thereupon, he hurried to Qizhou to request instructions on the Path. Later, he returned to his native village, where he practiced mindfulness without lying down to sleep.
The śramaṇas Āi, Ming, Leng, Fa, and others—all renowned masters of the Chan school—became his close friends.

On the ninth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Yonghui era, he passed away in the mountain valley where he resided. The śramaṇa Huipu had long relied upon the Faxian Monastery in Xiangyang.

He devoted himself to the study of the Vinaya-piṭaka for over twenty years. As the surrounding cities bowed in submission to him, he later specialized in the gate of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

When Prince Ji established his seat of governance, he intended to restore the abandoned temples of the former sages and appointed [Huiji] to oversee these affairs. He was able to replace licentious sacrifices with benevolent shrines, thereby transforming the local customs of Chu.
Furthermore, he renovated and constructed thirty sites, including the Mingyin Monastery, achieving the highest excellence in architectural splendor. His fame was manifest.
In the third year of the Qianqing era, he passed away at his residence at the age of eighty; all of these were paragons of Hanyin.
Huixian of the Tang dynasty was born into the Zhao clan of Pufan in Hedong. In his youth, he remained entangled in worldly ties, but in his later years, he renounced them entirely.

Upon reaching the age of forty, he finally received the tonsure and ordination. He constantly regarded the two sections of the *Avataṃsaka* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras as the ultimate beginning and end of the Tathāgata’s teaching.

He chanted even more fervently, savoring the flavor of the teachings, and carried the scrolls with him at all times as if they were a pair of wings. He said to others, "These two Dharma-treasures are now like wish-fulfilling jewels;
do not neglect or abandon them for even a moment. Wherever he stayed, whether at a strategic crossroads or amidst illness and hardship, there was no one who did not look up to him in devotion.

Through the power of the Venerable Xianci’s roots of goodness, it was sufficient simply to have him recite the Buddha’s name; there was nowhere he went that he did not provide salvation. At the temple—

The buildings were in ruins, and even the ten-foot-tall great elephants were covered in dust and disarray. He gathered offerings and constructed new structures, which were so radiant with pearls, gems, gold, and lapis lazuli that their brilliance dazzled the eyes.
After some time, he dreamed of a monk who told him, "In the winter of next year, you shall arrive at impermanence."
If one wishes to prolong [one's life], one should exert effort early; however, since this present life has already been fixed, even if it were prolonged, it would merely increase one's karma.
In the ninth month of the following year, he manifested a slight illness and sent his attendant to summon the various virtuous ones to confer the Bodhisattva precepts upon him.
As the virtuous monks did not attend, he took up the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* himself and recited it. He stopped, his voice choked with emotion; he was both sorrowful and joyful.
That night, celestial seers stood in rows before and behind him, appearing and disappearing as if visible, their discourse audible to the ears. Some even beheld Buddha-images entering his chamber.
At noon the following day, he suddenly rose from his seat, joined his palms, offered a final instruction, and passed away at the age of seventy-five. Forever...
On the seventeenth day of the eleventh month in the sixth year of the Huigong era, the Chan Master Hu of the same monastery— who was renowned in the capitals of Jing and Luo—
often maintained that immortals must be born in Tuṣita Heaven to behold Maitreya; he likely examined his own conduct and practices to obtain such a sign of verification.
Tang Sengxuan was a native of Bingzhou. Having left the household life, he had long been renowned for his learning and conduct.
At the age of ninety-six, he first encountered Chan Master Daocuo lecturing on the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra* and saw the *Anle ji* (Collection on Peaceful Bliss);

only then did he realize that the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha truly must not be neglected. Thereupon, day and night, he set himself a daily task of performing one thousand prostrations to Amitābha Buddha and reciting [the Buddha’s name].
He recited the Buddha’s name eight million times over the course of five years without the slightest laxity. As his end approached, he said to his disciples:
"Amida Buddha has personally bestowed this robe upon me; its fragrance is worthy of mindfulness. Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta stand arrayed before me, and transformation Buddhas fill the sky.
From here to the west, all is the Pure Land. Having spoken these words, he passed away. At that time, there was one named Kihō-en.
The two Dharma Masters Guo resided at Wuzhen Temple in Lantian. Together before an image of Avalokiteśvara, they made a vow to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
They then took a branch of willow and inserted it into the hand of the image, saying:

"If we are certain to attain rebirth in the Pure Land as we have vowed within this summer, then this willow branch shall remain unfaded for seven days. Indeed, it did not wither until the seventh day.
One day, she practiced mindfulness of the Buddha and recited the sūtras according to the Dharma. Subsequently, in a fragrant dream, she found herself within a great pond;
suddenly, she flew into a magnificent jeweled canopy to the east. There, a monk told her that by focusing exclusively on mindfulness of the Buddha, she would surely be reborn there.

She further dreamed of Avalokiteśvara sitting with his feet hanging down; she then took hold of his feet and placed them upon the crown of her head. Beside him was a lotus pond, and [there stood] Amitābha...
Just as Amitābha Buddha had arrived from the west, Fang asked the Buddha, "Can the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa rely on the sutras to attain birth here by mindfulness of the Buddha?
The Buddha replied, "Do not doubt; they will certainly be born in my land. Furthermore, he saw that the Sahā world consisted entirely of mountains and rivers.
The Land of Ultimate Bliss is level and pure; with music and jeweled canopies, one proceeds from the west without any interruption.
Suddenly, there appeared a monk named Dharmākara, who met the fragrance riding upon a great carriage.
Seeing his body seated upon a lotus flower made of a hundred jewels, he had attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment. Śākyamuni Buddha and Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva praised him.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is further seen that to the immediate west there are three paths of precious stairs. On the first path, all are white-robed laypeople;

on the second path, they are half black-clad monastics and half white-robed laypeople; and on the third, they are entirely black-clad monastics. It is said that these are all those who have attained rebirth [in the Pure Land].
Tang Shanfu, also known as Dengzhao, was surnamed Jiang and was a native of Yixing in Changzhou. He was born with white hair.

At the age of five, he followed his elder brother, Dharma Master Cai, to receive the precepts at Anguo Temple. In the third year of the Zhenguan era, the Regional Inspector, Lord Dou, having heard of his talent and learning, summoned him to serve as a teacher in the local school.
Despite this, Shanfu continued to read Buddhist scriptures without ceasing. When the State Doctor reprimanded him for this, he replied: [text continues]
He sought to broaden his observations; in questioning others, he encountered no obstructions. Consequently, among the students in the academy, there was none who did not respect and submit to him.
Shortly thereafter, he studied the Four Scriptures and Three Treatises under Dharma Master Bi at Liushui Temple in Su. He then relied upon Dharma Master Min of Yue.
Finally, he met Chan Master Chao of Tiantai and attained the essential meaning of the visualization of the Western Pure Land. Thereupon—

He traveled south through Jiaozhi, Guangzhou, and Xunzhou; northward to Jingzhou and Xiangyang. In Qi, he met Master Xìn; at Mount Lu, he paid homage at Master Yuǎn’s Hall for Contemplating the Pure Land.
Upon returning to his home village, he received the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*) from Master Yán in Rùn.

Later, together with Masters Huī and Cái, he practiced the contemplation of compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*) and was conferred the precepts for spirits and ghosts. There were sorcerers who used slaughter as sacrifice; [he] confronted them with violence...
When he finally revived, he said, "I received the precepts from Master Fu; I vowed never to eat meat. How could you kill it for me? Out of pity for your ignorance, I shall spare your life for now.
Should you violate this again in the future, I will certainly not show leniency. From that time on, all offerings of raw or cooked meat were discontinued at sacrifices.
Once, there were two men from Wuzhou who were traveling together selling hemp and flax; one of them made an offering of vegetarian food to the River God.

First was the sacrifice involving the slaughter of living beings. Upon reaching the shore, those who had performed sacrifices through slaughter were entirely drenched with moisture, while those who had offered vegetarian sacrifices remained dry.

Although they were on the same boat, there was such a difference between the dry and the wet that this was a manifestation of the efficacy of the precepts. Even so extreme was it that fish and meat could not be easily obtained in the market for the sacrificial rites;

consequently, the local authorities reduced their tax quotas. As for the Magistrate of Yixing, he might have been unable to believe this, fearing it would delude the masses, and thus intended to take action against them.

Regarding this matter, his kinsmen and brothers paid bribes and he was thus spared. Before long, however, his household was plagued by strange occurrences: snakes and dogs would climb onto the bed and bite people. A divination stated:

"The offense stems from profaning the worthy and the sagely; the calamity cannot be absolved. Ultimately, he incurred reprimand and was stripped of his official title, returned to the status of a commoner.
In the second year of the Yonghui era, Sengfu was again summoned by the authorities and compelled to return to his lay attire; nevertheless, he maintained his integrity and principles.

He redoubled his efforts. The assembly gathered once more to seek the essentials of the Dharma. His teachings and practices were, for the most part, based on the *Fifteen Contemplations* and the *Treatise on the Four Clarities*.
It is said that after he had resided for a long time at Mount Funiu, in the fifth year of the Xianqing era, he sought seclusion on Mount Heng to avoid slander.

As his disciples gathered again and he was about to expound upon the subtle and profound [teachings], he suddenly remarked: "All things are impermanent; the span of one's breath is difficult to preserve."

At nightfall, everyone dispersed, for their karmic conditions had ended and they were about to depart; at that time, no one could fathom what was happening. Huìjiān then firmly barred the door and remained silent.
That evening, all of Hèng’s bells, chimes, flutes, pipes, and every instrument capable of making sound, began to ring and resonate of their own accord, continuing without ceasing until dawn.
Upon breaking through his delusions and views, he sat upright in meditation and passed away. This was immediately reported to the throne.

Yuanxiao of the Tang dynasty was the son of the Xie family from Xiangzhou in the kingdom of Silla. He entered the monastic path at the age of seven and traveled with his teacher to study, having no fixed abode.

At that time, the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang was converting the Central Kingdom; Yuanxiao accompanied a friend intending to visit him. The details of this matter are recorded [in the *Da Tang Xiyu Ji*].
The Biography of Dharma Master Xiang. Since his circumstances had become adversarial, his tracks diverged; he wandered at ease according to his own nature, without any fixed abode.
It happened that King [Wenxuan] established a hundred lecture seats and summoned men of renowned virtue from various provinces to preach the *Renwang Jing*.

Because of Xiang’s long-standing reputation for erudition, some might have invited him, yet others slandered him as being of impure conduct and did not accept him. Not long after, the King’s consort contracted a brain abscess; neither medical treatment nor prayers were effective. A divination was performed...
He said, "It is fitting that a divine elixir be brought to the land of the Central Kingdom. Thereupon, he dispatched an envoy to cross the western sea.

Amidst the surging depths of the ocean, he suddenly saw a man who invited him to the abode of the Dragon King. The palace was solemn and magnificent, and the attendants were grand and imposing; it was truly beyond the reach of the ears and eyes of this world.
The Lord called himself Qianhai (Seal of the Sea) and said to the envoy, "Your lady is the third daughter of the Green Emperor. Her...

I possess a particularly strong power of aspiration toward the Buddha-dharma. The *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* is that which perfectly reveals the two types of awakening and demonstrates the practice of a bodhisattva.
I have previously obtained it, yet it has not been easily circulated. Now, because of the illness of my lady, the catalyst for its transmission has been activated;
thus, it will benefit not only her alone. Consequently, I took a knife and slit my calf muscle, opening it to insert [the scripture].
It consists of approximately thirty sheets of paper, wrapped both inside and out in waxed paper and coated with other medicinal substances.

He said, "I have done this because I fear that demonic obstacles may arise during my travels. He further stated, "If the Great Master An (Dae-an) were to arrange and compile it, and the Dharma Master Wonhyo were to compose a commentary and lecture upon its explanation, then even the *agada* medicine of the Snowy Mountains [would be surpassed]."
However, Da’an was unusual; his appearance and attire were always eccentric. He would frequently go through the marketplace striking a bronze bowl and chanting, “Great Peace!
Great Peace! When the King finally summoned An with urgency, An said, “Simply bring the sutra. He then analyzed it according to its principles and divided it into eight sections before departing.
Yet he ultimately refused to see the King. Once he had mastered the sutra, he transcribed it upon an ox cart.
It was completed in five fascicles. He then set out a table with brushes and inkstones between the two horns of an ox and declared:

"The two types of awakening—the Original and the Arising—are the purport of this sutra; I have merely used these to represent them. Soon after, he fixed a date to expound and propagate it at Huanglong Temple.

Those who were frivolous and shallow were jealous of his ability; they stole the work and fled. The King issued a decree setting a three-day deadline, and [the thief] further produced three fascicles of an abridged commentary in haste.

In his medical treatments, he was skilled at inducing emesis with a composed and dignified manner. His eloquence was sharp and incisive; as he praised and rebuked others, the sound of his finger-snap resounded through the air.
He said, "In the past, when the hundred rafters were being gathered, I was not included in the assembly; yet today, when placing the single ridgepole, I alone am capable.
Thus, he mocked their former slanders. The crowd turned red with shame. Later, nothing further was known of his end.
Tangsheng was a native of Zangxi River. Having renounced worldly life at a tender age, he devoted himself to the practice of a dhūta ascetic.
He was particularly renowned for his dedication to the Pure Land practices; he recited the name of Amitābha Buddha countless times. One day, he suddenly fell ill and lay down.
Addressing his disciples, he said, "A moment ago, as my eyes closed, I attained travel to the Land of Ultimate Bliss and beheld many noble and virtuous beings scattered about."
Huā paid his respects and said, "Now the devas and humans will come in succession to welcome you. Thereupon, he joined his palms and passed away with serene composure.
Zhengshou of the Tang dynasty had long frequented the monastic communities of Chan; having attained insight upon meeting Master Kǎo at the Southern Pagoda, he followed Kǎo to reside in Handong.
At Shanguang Temple, Prince Chongfu of Qiao—the second son of Emperor Zhongzong—was particularly devoted to Daoxiao and had prepared a stupa for him in advance, seventy feet in height.
When Daoxiao’s illness became critical, the Prince sent someone to ask who could succeed him. Daoxiao replied that Daoshou was fit.
Thereupon, Daoshou was summoned; he immediately informed Daoxiao of his request to test the stupa, whereupon he entered the stupa and sat in the full lotus position.

He passed away while seated; consequently, the world came to call him Master Shouta (Tomb of Longevity). Upon hearing of this, the King sighed in admiration and subsequently commissioned a separate stupa to enshrine Dao’s remains.

During the Tang dynasty, Shending was expansive and unconstrained, never grooming himself. He would regularly carry a peck-measure and beg in the Chang’an market; whenever he obtained [alms], he would...
He would eat whatever was available at that spot before departing. Sometimes he was given scraps of cloth or silk, which he would patch and sew onto his *kaṣāya*.
His hair hung down in locks, covering the area between his eyebrows; he spoke little and seldom smiled, finding serene joy in tranquility.

One day, while Dharma Master Lìzhēn was lecturing in the temple, Fǎdǐng happened to arrive and listened intently from the front of the assembly. He asked, "Are all things fixed? Zhēn replied, "They are fixed. Dǐng said, "Why, O *śramaṇa*..."
If Li says it is fixed, then high banks become valleys and deep valleys become hills; the dead are born and the living die;
one wanders through the six realms, cycling in saṃsāra without end—how can there be anything fixed? Zhen said, "It is not fixed. Li asked, "If it is not fixed..."
"Why not point to heaven as earth, or point to earth as heaven? Why not summon the stars as the moon, or summon the moon as the stars?
How could it not be indeterminate? Zhen was unable to respond, and the assembly marveled at his eloquence.

When Zhang Wencheng saw this, he said to him, "Master, since your talent and eloquence are such as these, are you not perhaps a person who has attained the fruit-stage of a Bodhisattva? Ding replied, "A Bodhisattva experiences joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure."
Nothing was sufficient to disturb his inner being; fame, profit, honor, and disgrace were insufficient to move him outwardly.
When the internal and external are one and the same, then his birth comes as something spontaneous, and his death departs with a sense of ease.

This is what is called "attaining life and death while remaining detached from life and death. How could people like us ever reach such a state? Having said this, the assembly joined their palms and dispersed.
Huilang of Tang was a native of Su’an. At the age of twenty-two, he resolved to seek ordination, yet had not yet found a teacher.
Someone told him that on North Mountain in Quzhou there was one who excelled in the Southern School; he went there, but the man said, "I am not your teacher.
You must certainly go to Tiantai. Upon arriving at Shicheng Temple in Shan, he saw an old man whose appearance...
He was extraordinary and ancient, his spirit refined and refreshing. He asked Hui-lang, "Where are you going? Lang replied, "I am going to Tiantai to seek the Great Dharma of the Buddha.
The old man then traveled with him for several dozen li before resting among the trees. The old man told him, "The Dharma is eternally quiescent;
why must you still travel so far? You have a karmic affinity with your own village; you should return there to propagate and transform others. Do not delay. Having finished speaking, he vanished.

He then went into seclusion. Hui-lang also attained sudden enlightenment of mind. He subsequently lived for several years on a mountain peak, pecking at grain and drinking from mountain streams, before later residing at Huian Temple in the city.
There, while still a layman (*avadāta-vasana*), he practiced the dhūta ascetic precepts. Not long after, Mount Qinwang shook unexpectedly.
A great tortoise emerged from it; all who saw it considered it a marvel. Shortly thereafter, Sengbian arrived from Yunmen.
He was eight chi and four cun tall, with a prominent nose and large eyes, his radiance striking those around him.

He was thoroughly versed in the *Siyi*, *Dapin*, and *Weimo* sutras, as well as having mastered and synthesized various śāstras. The assembly revered him as a deity, and Hui-lang wished to serve him as his teacher. Bian examined...

Regarding the meaning of the *Vimalakīrti*, Lang’s responses were exceptionally transcendent. During the Jinglong era, several dozen households—including Yu Shaoxing, the County尉 of Ruchuan, and Yu Ren, the County Magistrate of Xinchang—acted as patrons (*dānapati*) and took turns inviting him to visit.
One night, they suddenly beheld a divine light emanating from his crown, illuminating the surrounding mountains and rivers for over eighty li. Because of this, Master Bian returned [to his home].
He treated Lang with the etiquette due to a teacher, yet Lang ascended the seat and preached the Dharma, displaying transformations beyond measure.
Monastics and laypeople rejoiced and marveled, saying, "In the past, mountains shook and tortoises emerged; this auspicious sign was surely not for the sake of Master Bian.

From then on, scholars from the four quarters gathered like clouds. In the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era, the regional governor Li Sichuan selected a site on the southern slope of Longshan and constructed [a monastery].
The monastery welcomed him and established a great ordination platform, widely inviting masters of the Vinaya. Both Master An of Guangzhou and Master Chao of Kuaiji were present;

they conferred the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon Falang, whose reputation for the Way grew even more honored. In the seventh year, the Regional Inspector Wei Liji embraced the teachings and turned toward the transformation [of the Dharma].
In the eighth year, Xu Sigong, the Prefectural Administrator of Shixi, invited him to his seat of government. Every time Falang...
He ascended the seat. A bear followed the assembly, gathering in reverence and prostrating before him as if listening to his teachings.

In the thirteenth year [of the Dali era], on the twenty-first day of the ninth month, he gathered his disciples to announce his passing, saying: "I was to be born in this place for three lifetimes; now I have completed but one.

Having finished speaking, he entered a state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). He was sixty-four years old. His disciples, following his final instructions, prepared the funeral pyre and erected a stupa. (The *Dali* era...)
In the twelfth year [of the Kaiyuan era], his dharma heirs—Daochin, Huiyou, and Daocan of Kaiyuan Temple; Bianhai of Longxing Temple;
Jin Yu of Ningguo Temple; Youpai, Yuanzheng, and others of Baolin Temple in Yuezhou; and Yixing and others of Zhulin Temple in Hangzhou—erected a stele.
Xiao Ding, the Governor of Xinding, composed the inscription, and Liu Changqing, the Regional Secretary, calligraphed it.
The Prefectural Governor Li Kui inscribed the title.
Tang Zhen was a man from the kingdom of Baekje; for generations his family had practiced hunting. Zhen was particularly agile and skilled at archery.

During the Kaiyuan era, while pursuing game in the wild, he grew weary and rested among the mounds and fields. Seeing that the frogs were exceedingly numerous, he thought to himself alone: "This cannot be..."

"Shall we have some soup? he asked. He then took willow branches and skewered about thirty [frogs], placing them in deep water. He then pursued game by another path and returned, forgetting to retrieve what he had skewered.
The following spring, while hunting at that same spot as before, he heard the croaking of frogs; upon approaching to look, those he had skewered were all gasping and moving about as usual.
He was filled with great shame and reproached himself, saying: "I have allowed my mouth and belly to become a burden to living beings."
Thinking thus, "How can this sin be avoided? he immediately drew the sword he wore at his waist, shaved off his hair, and fled into the mountains to repent.

He vowed that he would personally receive the precepts of a bhikṣu from Maitreya Bodhisattva. Day and night he circumambulated [the mountain], striking his head until it bled, his mind never ceasing for a moment.
After seven days and seven nights had passed in this manner, he beheld the hand of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.

Carrying his golden mendicant’s staff, he was first inspired by the preparatory rites for receiving the precepts; he attained sudden awakening, and joy pervaded his entire body, causing him to redouble his diligent practice.
On the fourteenth day, a great ghost suddenly appeared with a terrifying form, pushing him so that he fell to the bottom of a deep precipice.
Yet his body remained unhurt. Beside him stood a stone altar; he crawled forward and ascended it. Though the demons caused a tumultuous disturbance, he paid them no heed.
After twenty-one days, as dawn began to break, he heard the voices of birds crying, "The Bodhisattva has come!

White clouds gathered at the four horizons like a spread of fine powder, filling the mountains and rivers so that there was no longer any distinction between high and low; they became a world of silver. The Lord of Tuṣita...
Īśvarī was surrounded by her attendants at the stone altar. At that time, Maitreya slowly approached the site of the altar and, stroking the crown of [the disciple’s] head with his hand, said:
"Excellent, great man! To seek the precepts in such a manner—even Mount Sumeru could be cast aside.
Your mind is firm and cannot fall back. Having praised and caressed him two or three times, he then conferred [the precepts].
The Dharma brings harmony and joy to both body and mind; it cannot be compared to any worldly pleasure. Soon thereafter, he attained the divine eye, seeing all things clearly and without obstruction.
Maitreya personally bestowed upon him three robes and an earthen alms bowl, and conferred upon him his true name.
Suddenly, from beneath his knees, two divination sticks emerged; one was marked with the number nine, and the other with eight. Examining the sticks, they were neither ivory nor jade.

However, as he ultimately did not know what had caused this, he sent a letter stating: "In the future, if someone comes to you seeking the precepts, you should first cause that person to repent for their transgressions.
For merit and fault arise from upholding or violating [the precepts]; such is the method for repenting transgressions."
Whether for ninety days, forty days, or twenty-one days, one shall set a period.

When the period is complete and one wishes to know whether the transgressions have been extinguished or not, one should add one hundred and eight slips. On these slips, one shall write the names of the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*).
Using the two aforementioned slips, one shall join them and cast them toward the void. If the one hundred and eight slips fly...

The [divination sticks] are scattered across the four sides. As for the two sticks, eight and nine, which stand upright alone at the center of the altar: this is the sign of having attained the highest grade of precepts (*śīla*).

If, among the one hundred and eight sticks, only one or two sticks intersect with the two sticks [numbered] eight and nine, one should simply examine which affliction (*kleśa*) the intersecting stick represents;
thus one will know that these afflictions have not yet been exhausted, and that such a person should be instructed accordingly.
It is appropriate to further repent for one's transgressions. Thereafter, take the previously mentioned "intersecting" divination stick and combine it with either the eighth or ninth stick;
cast them into the air. If the sticks do not intersect but fly far apart, this is called the sign of the medium grade of precepts.
If, among the one hundred and eight bamboo slips, the final eight or nine slips are obstructed and concealed, the transgression is not extinguished and one does not obtain the precepts.

Even if one can sincerely repent for the offense and, after ninety days have passed, performs the aforementioned ritual again without obstruction or concealment, one obtains the lower grade of precepts.
Furthermore, it is said that "eight" refers to new conditioning and "nine" refers to innate habit; subsequently, these fade away like withered flowers.
The incense and cannons [faded], and the mountains and rivers lay desolate. Thereupon, he donned his robes and took up his alms bowl to become a great bhikṣu.

Intent on descending the mountain to benefit sentient beings, he found that the grasses and trees bowed low and the valleys and gullies became level. Auspicious birds and rare beasts flew, danced, and submitted themselves before and behind him.
Furthermore, voices resounded from the air, saying: "The Bodhisattva has come out of the mountains; why do you not go out to welcome him? For this reason—
The people of the village looked at one another, some spreading their hair on the ground and others stripping off their clothes;

they spread out felt, woolen blankets, mats, and rugs along the path, all trampling them underfoot to fulfill his wish. A woman spread out half a piece of white felt and waited, but he suddenly startled and avoided her, departing for elsewhere.
The woman, finding this inconsistent with his intent, questioned him, and he replied: "It is not that I have no intention; it was just that I recently beheld..."
"Between the layers of felt are all piglets. I fear they might be harmed, so I am merely avoiding them. It can be known from this that the woman was originally from a butcher's family;
this is the reason for the presence of the felt. Usually, two tigers attend to her left and right.
She said to them, "I shall not enter the city walls now. If there is another place where I may practice my cultivation, you two lead the way. Thereupon she traveled thirty li and sat down.
He stopped on a hillside; for his outer appearance, he hung his staff upon a tree branch and sat upon spread grass.
Lay devotees arrived from the four directions, and in an instant, a monastery was established, named Jinshan Temple. Today, the portrait hall and ritual implements still remain.
Tang Huaiyu, surnamed Gao, was a native of Danqiu. Having shaved his head and donned the robes at an early age, he was affiliated with Yongquan Temple.

He specialized in the Vinaya and frequently practiced the methods of repentance. Each day, he recited the name of Amitābha fifty thousand times; moreover, he never failed to chant the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
It is said that the total number of scrolls he recited throughout his life amounted to three hundred thousand. The first month of the sixth year of the Tiānbǎo era...
On the ninth day of the month, he suddenly saw transformed Tathāgatas filling the realm of space. One [Tathāgata] entered through the window carrying a silver platform.
Sengyu said, "I will not go unless I have a golden platform. Thereupon, the silver platform vanished of its own accord. Sengyu redoubled his diligent practice beyond what was usual.
Later, a voice from the air announced: "A halo has now appeared above your head; you may now form the mudrā with your hands."
He sat cross-legged in the *paryaṅka* posture, awaiting the arrival of the Buddha. After a short while, a brilliant light filled the chamber.

Emperor Yu immediately signaled for the onlookers to withdraw, saying, "This is the light of the Buddha; be careful not to touch it. At the hour of the Ox (2–4 a.m. on the thirteenth day, a white *ūrṇā-kośa* radiance suddenly appeared.
Emperor Yu said, "If you smell a strange fragrance, my life will be coming to an end. His disciple Huiming asked, "Where will he go?"
Kṣa replied with a verse, saying: "Pure and radiant, free from dust and defilement; born by transformation from a lotus flower as my parents.
Having practiced the Way for ten kalpas, I have appeared in the human realm to undergo manifold sufferings. Through one lifetime of asceticism, I have surpassed ten kalpas;
forever leaving Saṃsāra, I shall return to the Pure Land. Once he had spoken the verse, light and fragrance filled the entire realm of space. Ā...
Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with a great assembly whose bodies were the color of purple gold, arrived riding upon a vajra platform to welcome her.
Yuyin smiled and passed away while seated. Later, the Regional Inspector Duan Huairan composed a poem in praise of her, saying:

"My Master, in a single thought, ascended to the First Ground; The music of the Buddha-land has come twice to greet her. Only the ancient huai tree before my door Remains as a witness to this wondrous event."
The branches bend low only to hang from the silver terrace.

Tang Ziyu, whose courtesy name was Zhenying, was surnamed Shen and was a native of Deqing in Wuxing. Before he had even reached the age of ten, he took leave of his parents to enter the monastic life at Dayun Temple in his home prefecture.
During the Ruyi era, a general amnesty was proclaimed, and an imperial edict was issued for the entire realm to ordain individuals in order to pray for [the welfare of the state].

The state reorganized its religious affairs, and he subsequently obtained tonsure and received full ordination at Dafuxian Temple in the capital of Luoyang. Among those who attained spiritual clarity and sanctity, he returned to hold the staff of the Vinaya, establishing the regulations for the pure assembly.
In his daily life, he personally performed the worship of fifteen thousand Buddhas and concurrently practiced the Compassionate Repentance (Cibei chanfa), being diligent and devoted day and night.
Suddenly, there were nine individuals who snapped their fingers and walked the path, who then vanished without a trace; when questioned about them, no one knew where they had gone.
Only after this did those who knew him recognize him as a holy monk. Sometimes, while sitting at night without lamps or candles, his body would emit a brilliant light.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era, Dharma Master Zú of Lín'ān died; after three nights, he revived and said, "I saw Yu in the underworld.

He said to the King: 'Zú is capable of lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; please grant him clemency. The King replied: 'I have heard that Yánlún was able to lecture on it, but [I have not yet heard of you].'"

[The Emperor] heard of this and was pleased, yet he did not grant [the request]. Fayu strove to argue for it. It is said that throughout his life, Fayu transcribed the scriptures totaling three collections, amounting to sixteen thousand scrolls.
In the eleventh year, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. The following year, when his body was cremated and the coffin opened for inspection, [his remains were found intact].
His complexion remained entirely unchanged, and those who saw him felt a sense of reverence.
Da Xing of Qi State during the Tang dynasty lived constantly on grass clothing and wooden-fruited food, practicing the Lotus Samādhi within the rocky ravines of Mount Tai.
He subsequently experienced a manifestation of Samantabhadra appearing before him. Later, he sighed to himself, saying that this life was coming to an end, but what would become of future lives?

He understood this. Regarding the stage where he would receive retribution, he searched the Tripitaka and obtained various sutras from the Western Regions. Thereupon, he practiced and cultivated according to the Dharma.

After twenty-one days, suddenly one night, his mind and eyes became luminously clear; he beheld the lapis lazuli ground and the Buddhas of the ten directions, appearing like reflections in a bright mirror.
Not long after, he was summoned into the inner court, granted the title of Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent (Chang Jingjin), and enfeoffed as the Duke of Kaiguo.
After a long time, he manifested a slight illness and passed away lying on his right side. He was buried at Mount Tai.
