An Jing of the Tang dynasty was a man from the Western Regions; in the fifteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, he traveled east to China and arrived at Dingtao.
There, he inquired as to the location of the layman Ding’s grave, eventually locating it and opening it up, whereupon five-colored clouds and vapors billowed forth from the earth.
Inside, his bones were all golden in color, linked together in an unbroken chain. When pulled, they extended for about five *zhang*.
When struck, their sound was sharp and clear. He carried them on his back using a staff as a pole, seeking another location where he could build a stupa to inter them.
After a long time, when the task was completed, Jing also passed away. Originally, while the layman was practicing the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*), he attained the Dharma of the mind at Mount Song.
When Chan Master Pujì was about to pass away, he sat in the lotus position with his palms joined; the bells and chimes of all the monasteries within the city resounded in response.
This was already extraordinary at the time, yet people’s reverence and admiration for him increased further upon this event.

Furthermore, there was the master Xu Guo of Chengdu Prefecture, whose appearance was like that of one who is demented, yet whose words frequently hit the mark; he was thus a disciple of the same lineage as Master Zhì.
Indeed. When Tang Mingzan first visited Chan Master Pujì of Mount Song, he received the Dharma.

He subsequently traveled to Mount Heng, where he served at Nanyue Temple for twenty years without ever speaking of weariness or hardship. He then retired to live in seclusion on Shilin Peak. To the utmost...
As for Daoqu: Li Mi was then young and devoted himself to study; he delighted in solitude and seclusion. He had once built a dwelling not far from that place.
One night, hearing the sound of Buddhist chanting, he went to see what it was. It happened to be exactly when Huizang was lighting a fire with cow dung to take out taro roots to eat.
Bi then bowed before him. Zàn slowly pointed to the ground beside the incense burner and said, "You may sit here upon this.
He then broke off half of a taro root and fed it to Bi, saying nothing more. The Regional Inspector used to perform the annual sacrificial rites at the shrine of Mount Yue;
however, a massive fallen rock was obstructing the path. He dispatched village headmen to pull it away, employing several hundred laborers. Zàn took pity on their agitation and [removed it] entirely.
He took his leave. After a short while, he raised his foot and kicked it; the stone rolled down the mountain with a sound like a thunderclap.

Tigers had been causing great havoc, but Zàn sat alone and summoned a large tiger to prostrate before him. He produced a one-foot-long whip and made the tiger take it in its mouth, saying, "You should use this to severely lash all those who have harmed people.
The large tiger departed, and from that time on, the tigers' violence ceased entirely. The world generally regarded him as a man of divine and extraordinary power.
He was posthumously bestowed the title of Chan Master Daming. His composed lyrics are recorded in the *Chuandeng lu*.
Huai Kong of Tang left Shu for Langzhou, where he was born into the Liang family. In his youth, he received ordination at Guangfu Temple on Mount Qishu in his hometown.
Having received full precepts, he traveled to various regions and met Daji at Zhongling, from whom he received a prediction of enlightenment. Later, he hung [his robe]...
Xi resided in seclusion at Mount Anfeng in Pengcheng, never seeking audiences with officials. Yet donors came to him of their own accord.
He passed away after several years, leaving behind a great monastery. Occasionally, there were monks who traveled through the air to his dwelling;
they would circumambulate the walls day and night without ceasing, and lotus flowers would sprout wherever they stepped. Those who witnessed this marveled at it, and it continued for several days.
Xuankong suddenly took his leave, saying, "In three or five years, I shall return to rely upon you once more. Thereupon, he ascended into the air and departed.
In the first year of the Xingyuan era, Xuankong manifested his passing; he was eighty-eight years old. On the second month of the first year of the Changqing era, he was finally interred in a stupa.

Wulou of the Tang dynasty, surnamed Jin, was a prince of the kingdom of Silla. From his youth, he admired the integrity of Lord Yanling and ultimately renounced the position of crown prince to devote himself to the Dharma of Śākyamuni.
Having boarded a ship to travel west to China, he subsequently crossed the shifting sands of the Taklamakan Desert.
He ascended the Pamir Mountains, intending to pay his respects at the sacred sites of India.
There he met a strange bhikṣu who said to him, "Your name does not appear in the ancient records; how can you venture there so recklessly?
You must first subdue the venomous dragon to advance your fortitude, and pray to Avalokiteśvara to strengthen your wisdom and vows. Thereupon, he manifested as a dragon.
He was granted the precepts of the Three Refuges. Alternatively, while dwelling in meditative concentration before an image for forty-nine days, the Bhikṣu still regarded him as his spiritual son;
this connection was particularly well-known in the land of Tang. Consequently, he built a hermitage at the White Reed Valley on Mount Helan.
During the An Shi Rebellion, when Suzong was marshaling his troops at Lingwu, [the Master] repeatedly appeared in dreams before him as a golden-colored person.

He chanted the name of the Tathāgata Ratnaśrī and consulted his ministers; they all replied that he was suffering from a mental affliction (*srotas*). The Emperor immediately summoned him for an audience, but he did not rise.
Later, when the Vice Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Frontier, Guo Ziyi, the Director of the Secretariat, personally went to deliver the imperial decree, he finally complied with the command.
Upon ascending the steps to have an audience, the Emperor stared at him and said, "This is truly the one I saw in my dream. He then retained him within the Inner Sanctuary (*nai-daochang*).

After making offerings, the rebellion was quelled. The hundred officials escorted the imperial carriage back to the capital. [The Master] submitted a memorial requesting to return to the mountains, but the Emperor granted him an honorable reply, refusing his request.
In the third year of the Shangyuan era, he suddenly passed away. His twin feet appeared upon the right leaf of the inner sanctuary gate, hovering about several chi above the ground.
When the officials reported this, the Emperor rode in his palanquin past the spot and recovered the remains.
He set forth the intent of what he had reviewed: his words pointed toward nothing more than seeking to return for burial at his native mountain.

The Emperor granted the request and dispatched an imperial envoy to supervise the ceremonial procession and escort him home, while establishing an official residence in Huaiyuan County—presumably because it was the place through which he had traveled throughout his life.
When the funeral carriage arrived there, it could not be moved despite all efforts; consequently, a separate hall was constructed to enshrine it.
Its physical form has remained unchanged to this day. The doors and panels within the hall are the very same as those of the inner sanctuary (antarmandala).
Furthermore, it is said that the traces of the two feet manifested at that time still remain.

The Great Master of Guangling during the Tang dynasty was physically unimposing and humble in appearance. By nature, he was straightforward and did not concern himself with formal decorum or monastic discipline.
He resided as a guest at Xiaogan Temple, where he would daily frequent the marketplaces to drink and eat with groups of youths.

They would go so far as to gather to slaughter dogs and pigs, plunder money and goods, gamble, and engage in brawls—there was nothing they would not do. Yet when he returned home at night, his room would be silent and still; he almost never made a sound. Occasionally...
An elderly man rebuked him, saying, "Though you do not value yourself, do you have no concern for the Buddha-dharma?
Guangling laughed and said, "How can a swallow or a sparrow know the ambition of a wild goose? Subsequently, the door to his room remained closed long past midday.
Someone peered through a crack and saw him sitting on his couch as if having entered meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), with a divine radiance emanating from between his eyebrows.
The light shone brightly throughout the space between the rafters and illuminated the four walls. He was greatly startled and hurried to report it to the monastics and laypeople near and far.
They crowded the corridors and together pushed against the door to inspect the room, but he had already passed away. Furthermore, during his lifetime, he had been entirely without fame;
yet the one later known as the "Great Master of Guangling" was so designated merely because of what was subsequently observed, thereby affixing a title of respect to him.
It is so. Shenhui of the Tang dynasty was originally a man from the Western Regions. Later, his grandfather entered China and adopted the surname Shi, settling in Fengxiang.
Shenhui possessed innate, intuitive understanding that no one in the world recognized. At the age of thirty, he went to Shu to visit Master Wuxiang.

Master Śāriputra possessed sharp faculties and attained sudden enlightenment, his mind in secret resonance with the Seal of the Mind. Without manifest form, he sighed and said, "My Way rests in you. For the most part, his realization was transcendent;
free from discursive thought, his tranquil illumination was utterly still. When he remained in profound stillness, devoid of outward signs, his substance was like that of earth or wood.

Yet when it came to his wondrous function, his silent salvation was like the movement of clouds and the falling of rain. The common masses were molded by his transformative teaching; they beheld his countenance and [were transformed].

By means of this, he encouraged the transformation toward goodness; hearing his words, people reformed their errors. He reached the point where narrow boundaries and dogmatic attachments were swept away and the dust of mental obscurations was thoroughly cleansed.

All those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities were led to enter [the path] according to their respective portions. How could such a state be fathomed by those of shallow views and meager understanding?
On the twelfth day of the eleventh month in the tenth year of the Zhenyuan era, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed away at Jingzhong Temple in Chengdu, at the age of seventy.
Fifteen. Thirty-six. Twelve years later, on the twenty-second day of the second month, the monastic and lay communities moved his seat to the northern corner of the monastery.
The fourfold assembly grieved with such longing that the colors of their faces changed as they turned toward the mountain forests.
Prince of Nankang, Wei Gao, erected a stele for him, composed the inscription, and personally wrote it; he paid his respects in person. His disciple was Nathi (Nadi).
Tang Daoqi was the son of the Zhao family of Qiantang. From his youth, he was intelligent and quick-witted; while reading in the local school, senior scholars regarded him as exceptionally talented.
One day, standing by the roadside, he saw a monk begging for alms who was reciting the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.

Hearing this, he rejoiced and said, "How could such words be spoken by those of the secular world? He immediately invited the monk back to his home, prepared a meal for him, and questioned him about [the teaching].
He resided at Ding-shui Monastery. His parents subsequently requested and granted him permission to leave the household life. At the age of seventeen, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

He studied the Vinaya and further investigated the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Lingyin Monastery, where he practiced meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and the ascetic practices (*dhūta*).
While traveling, he once sat in meditation in a stone grotto at an Indian temple. Suddenly, a massive python emerged from its side, appearing as if it intended to swallow him;
yet he remained silent and composed as usual. He lived among tigers, leopards, deer, and wild boars, becoming especially tame and docile toward them. At the mountain peak, water was scarce.

When he struck the ground with his staff, a spring gurgled forth. In the twenty-first year of the Zhenyuan era, when the assembly requested him to lecture on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, the season was at its frozen height;
yet they found extraordinary flowers amidst the ice and snow, shaped like lotuses, shimmering and radiating brilliant light.
Those who witnessed him marveled at his excellence. After a long time, he passed away in a mountain temple.

During the Tang dynasty, there was a man from the Chen clan who suffered from illness; he lost his father when he was seven years old and his grief and emaciation exceeded the bounds of propriety. Upon completing his period of mourning, he addressed his mother.

He sought to leave the household life, but his mother found this difficult to accept. He immediately cut off one of his fingers to demonstrate his resolve, whereupon he proceeded to Guoqing Temple to shave his head and receive full ordination.
Because he constantly desired to substitute himself for the suffering of all sentient beings, he was given that name. After some time, he traveled abroad and arrived at Lingjiao.
At that time, Heyang was suffering from a severe drought; as the illness befell him, he applied the methods of the scriptures and painted eight dragons.

The King established a *maṇḍala* to offer prayers. Indeed, a great rain poured down, providing sufficient moisture for a thousand *li*. Previously, in that region, violent winds and hail had broken out during the summer;
the crops were laid low and uprooted, and the battlement walls all crumbled. Those with discernment attributed this to the machinations of a venomous dragon.
He performed a rite using esoteric mantras to ward off the illness, and from then on, he was free from affliction. The people erected a shrine and worshipped him with an image of his likeness.
In the first year of the Dali era, he ascended Mount Taihang and entered Mount Huo, where he built a thatched hut in a secluded place to live in seclusion.

When some thieves came to steal his belongings and were about to depart abruptly, two tigers blocked the path at the entrance. It happened that a sick man returned from elsewhere; the thieves bowed their heads and explained [their situation] to him.
Feeling remorse, the patient consoled him and drove away the tiger, sending it on its way. The thief looked back and begged to remain in service by his side for the rest of his life.
The shrine at Zhongshan was particularly numinous and extraordinary. In the past, when Shendiao first raised his army of righteousness, he was once thwarted by dark rain and lost his way there;

yet the deity secretly assisted him, leaving behind traces of its merit. Upon ascending the throne, Shendiao issued an edict to carve stone images and enroll the shrine in the official liturgical canon. When the patient arrived...

He thought that these [images] were being used for slaughter and food in the regions between Jin and Jiang. Thereupon, he went before the images in the courtyard and spoke, commanding them to receive the Buddha’s precepts from him.
The image suddenly nodded its head as if granting permission, but when it looked toward the image of the divine consort, she remained almost entirely motionless.
He then destroyed it, saying: "What kind of stubborn, base metal is this, capable of harming sentient beings in such a way? The common people reported this to the Regional Governor (Taishou).

The Prefect was enraged and had him imprisoned. The gates and doors of Jiaquan Temple were fastened with very strict locks. After ten days, when they opened them to look at him, he was sitting in meditation, unmoved and as composed as ever.
When the crowd heard of this, they flocked there; some struck the sounding-stone to rouse him from his samādhi, but the Prefect sent messengers to invite him, and he would not listen.
When the messengers went a second time, he made a pact with them, saying: "If you insist on not coming, then cut off my head and bring it here."
The sick man feigned cutting off his own finger and gave it to the messenger. The Governor was moved by this and eventually went in person to offer his apologies.
He then moved the sick man to Dafansi (Great Brahma Temple) and constructed a stupa to bury the finger-joints. From then on, offerings from the faithful poured in like mountains.
A jealous person bribed a poor woman and offered her poisoned wine, saying, "My husband is skilled at brewing; today he has prepared..."
The wine was brewed with such sincerity that it was exceptionally fine. "I would be honored if the Venerable Master would partake of a small measure to plant the field of merit," [the woman] said.

The Sūtra states that the Buddha does not go against the wishes of sentient beings. The Venerable Master, out of compassion for her illness, asked, "Are you not a Buddha? The poor woman joyfully told him everything about her situation.

The Venerable Master laughed and finished his drink, saying, "The ground upon which I sit shall split open. He looked down slowly, and indeed it did split. The severity of its poisonous vapor was such that...

He appeared as if he were meditating. It was from this time that the common people began the practice of making offerings of wine. Whenever there was a famine, he would invariably solicit grain to establish assemblies for the purpose of satisfying the hungry;

he held such assemblies eight times, and the regions of Yan and Zhao relied upon his aid. On the eighth day of the seventh month in the fourteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, he sat cross-legged before the assembly as if entering a state of dhyāna.
His disciples, fearing he might not pass away, arranged incense and flowers to make offerings as they usually did.
After one year had passed, the flesh of his skin was felt to have become firm and shriveled; subsequently, lacquered cloth was applied to ensure its permanence.

During the reign of Emperor Wuzong, it was carried away and hidden within an abandoned kiln, where wind and rain offered no protection. Soon thereafter, extraordinary grasses grew and entwined themselves over the top of the head.
Emperor Xuanzong again provided instructions, having a pavilion built and the relic moved there. The joints of the *jiaquan* (the "auspicious spring") remained undecayed throughout a century.
His muscles and nails became increasingly lustrous, like the color of yellow gold.
A Tang dynasty śramaṇa whose name has been lost lived in seclusion on Mount Zhongliang in Baocheng, Xingyuan.
His conduct was straightforward and forthright, and he was not constrained by worldly conventions; he drank wine and ate meat as usual, which his peers all condemned.
Thus it was. However, because he was senior in both age and monastic standing (*kalpa*), he attained the administrative office of the temple;
his deliberations and implementations were all appropriate, and people consequently submitted out of awe, honoring him collectively as the *sthavira* (Elder).

Among the youths and juniors, some occasionally emulated his conduct. Upon hearing this, the Elder was startled and said: "Without having attained the Ground of Pure Mind (*śuddhabhūmi*), how dare you act thus? My younger brother should [behave]..."
He subdued them. One day, he instructed the cook to prepare an abundance of cakes and snacks and invited the assembly to tour among the graves.

He sat alone on the ground, picking up withered bones and rotting flesh; he spread out the cakes and snacks, wrapping the meat in them and eating it as if it were a fresh, delicious, and savory delicacy.
The assembly looked around in a circle, retching and vomiting uncontrollably. The Elder looked at the group and said, "Can you eat this? Can you eat it?"
This suggests that he was perhaps fit to eat meat. When Lord Liu Zhongying was stationed at Xingyuan, he personally went to pay his respects;
[the Master] passed away at the age of eighty or ninety.
Tang Wenshuang had been a monk at Chongfu Temple in Taiyuan since his youth. His spirit was exceptionally clear and lucid; he never once slept.

Later, he dwelt among hills and mounds, practicing the dhūta austerities with the utmost diligence. At one time, after heavy rain had lasted for ten days, snakes, seeking refuge from the flooding waters, gathered together and coiled upon Wenshuang’s palm.
When someone invited him to a vegetarian feast and saw this, they were struck with terror and fled. The snake—
It also slithered away. The man then came forward and made his request, but Xiang Shuang declined on the grounds that it was past noon and would not consent to go.
Consequently, the man remained to wait for the next day; meanwhile, a wolf opened its mouth toward Shuang, appearing as if it wished to bite him.
Shuang said to it, "Are you hungry? I offer this foul sack of mine to you, so that you may achieve a firm and solid body. You shall receive it."
"I shall give [myself] so that we may together realize Bodhi. Thereupon, he lay prostrate upon the ground; the wolf immediately lowered its ears and departed.

On the day of his death, the sound of bells and stone chimes resonated throughout the air, the shadows of banners and streamers obscured the sun, and a wondrous fragrance filled the cold air, yet none knew from whence these things came.
Whenever Tangben Jing saw him in Min, he would attend upon various Chan masters until he attained realization. Later, he lived in seclusion at Mount Huotong in Changxi County;

apart from his almsrounds, he devoted himself solely to quietude and silence. The mountain was particularly numinous and extraordinary, being the very site where the Bodhisattva Tianguan preached the Dharma as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Furthermore, the dragon of this "poisonous den" displayed constant and unpredictable spiritual transformations. At his hermitage—
He stayed by his side. Whenever he called out, [the tiger] would respond and arrive at his summons; its ferocity ceased and the tracks of woodcutters vanished.
Once, Jing happened upon the tiger and stroked its head, admonishing it. From that time on, all became peaceful. Once, nine eminent men sought lodging; beneath the lamp, they conversed at length.
When dawn broke, they suddenly took their leave, refusing to stay even when urged. As he escorted them slightly to the gate, they suddenly transformed into cranes and flew away.
He flew up into the air and departed; his final resting place thereafter was unknown.

During the Tang dynasty, there was Qingguan, whose courtesy name was Mingzhong. He was the son of the Qu family of Linhai. At birth, his hands and feet were marked with webbed membranes (*jālāhastapāda*).

By the time he reached the age of childhood, he was remarkably intelligent and outstanding. His resolve to leave the household life was firm, and neither his parents nor others could dissuade him. He subsequently served Master Yuan of Guoqing Temple.
Master Dharma-Teacher Zhang devoted himself to the study of the sutras and the vinaya. At the age of eighteen, he received full ordination.

He attained mastery in the principles of the Three Contemplations of Tiantai, as well as in the various texts of the Confucian scholars and the hundred schools of thought, and excelled in poetry, composition, calligraphy, and painting.

Whenever high-ranking officials or imperial envoys heard of his reputation, they would visit him to pay their respects; yet he would immediately return their offerings to the monastic community (the *changzhu*). His disciples requested that he keep them for use in times of emergency.
He said, "I regret that I have not yet been able to give away my head, eyes, marrow, brain, and ears.

During the beginning of the Dazhong era, when the Buddhist teachings were revived, he went to the capital to visit the Court Scholar (Xue-shi) Liu Gongquan and had him write the temple's plaque. He then obtained a great bell and a collection of the Tripitaka scriptures to bring back with him.
In the seventh year, there was a succession of famines in Jiangnan. Corpses lay scattered everywhere, and the monastic community all went elsewhere to seek food.
Guanding alone sat in meditation within his quiet chamber. He said to his disciples, "If you do not die, wait until the autumn harvest is ripe;

then you shall strike the chime to rouse me. His disciples did not dare disobey him. When they struck the chime in autumn, he indeed arose as expected. Once, while attending a vegetarian feast in the countryside, it rained at night.
The Zhangxi River has waves and rapids that surge with great speed; it is difficult to cross and extends for about twenty li.

The hostman thought that the Master would certainly not go there, yet in an instant he was seated [on the other side], appearing entirely free from any trace of wetness or mud. Were it not for the attainment of supernatural powers (*ṛddhipāda*), how could such a thing be possible?
His reputation spread in all directions, and those who came to pay their respects increased day by day. He then sought seclusion from the clamor in a monastery on Mount Cuiping.

After a long time, the assembly requested that he serve as the State Preceptor (Zhōngsēngzhèng), but he again feigned madness to escape. Du Xióng, the Prefectural Governor, reported his conduct to the court.
By imperial decree, he was granted a purple *kāṣāya*. Guǎnwǎng Zī was unhappy with this and later passed away without illness.
Tang Yong’an was a native of Hongya in Meizhou, Shu. He was short in stature and of unattractive appearance, yet his temperament was vast and expansive;
those who met him could not easily fathom his character. His contemporaries called him "Master Wulou" (The Stainless One), which was appropriate given his realization.
Some claimed it was because he had never set foot in a latrine. In the eighth year of the Dazhong era, Bai Minzhong served as the military governor of Chengdu.
An went to pay his respects and was lodged at Seongan-sa Temple. Minjung dispatched five or six monks to guard him day and night. He remained there for ten days;
although his food and drink were the same as those of others, he was utterly devoid of any dualistic conduct. Consequently, both those near and far were struck with wonder.
Even when he was over eighty years old, Lu Qiu, the District Magistrate, would still speak of him with admiration whenever they met. This was when he was still a youth.
His character was so harmonious and refined that it was easy to perceive.
Yuan Biao of the Tang dynasty was a native of Goryeo. During the Tianbao era, he traveled west to China with the intention of journeying to India to visit sacred sites.
There, he encountered the Bodhisattva Mind-King (Cittarāja), who told him that Mount Zhiti was the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva Heavenly Crown (Dharmamukuṭa).
Thereupon, carrying the eighty fascicles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* upon his head, he traveled south to Minyue and settled on this mountain.
On another day, fierce beasts, venomous insects, and malevolent spirits abounded on the mountain; it was a place where no human could dwell.

Once, a monk stayed overnight and found that his body had been cast ten or more li away from the foot of the mountain, having been thrown there by a divine spirit. It happened that a great assembly was being held.
Emperor Chang abolished the teachings. [The monks] used *huālǚ* wood to case the scriptures and concealed them within a stone chamber.
At the beginning of the Dazhong era, Chan Master Huiping of Baofu learned of this; he then led various lay devotees to welcome them out from the Gānlù Dūwèi Monastery.
It is said that the paper and ink appear as if newly made.
This head monk (dūta) was originally from a lowly family; he spent his days grinding stones for hire. Nevertheless, the dūta’s natural disposition was pure and virtuous.

He was devoted to the study of Buddhism. His conduct was characterized by a compassionate and benevolent disposition. While he was still living at home, his father sent him to herd donkeys. One night, while turning the millstone, he became exhausted from hunger and thirst;

Puṇyadatta would then release the animals to provide them with water and fodder, taking their place himself to turn the stone. His father was greatly moved to realization and established a separate business for him.
From that time on, Puṇyadatta also shaved his head and donned the robes of a monk. Once he had received full ordination, his practice became even more earnest and steadfast.
He wore robes made of discarded rags weighing several jin, and he used the same bedding for thirty years without ever changing it.
While residing at Longxing Temple in Zhenzhou, all the people—whether old or young, noble or humble—knew to revere him.
The Chan practitioner of Zhurong Peak during the Tang dynasty was unconventional in his conduct and did not observe formal etiquette.

Yet, when it came to proclaiming the essence of the school, he was concise, direct, and rigorous; those who heard him knew where to turn for refuge. Once, while drinking water, he encountered poison and immediately vomited;
his robes were all tattered and torn, yet his body felt no discomfort whatsoever. Whenever he walked or sat, snakes and tigers would invariably attend him as guards. This continued until his death.
After the cremation, a single bone was found that resembled the hollow of a lute; it was then placed in even more intense flames and re-forged.

While being forged, its color was no different from the fire itself, but once the fire was extinguished, it was whiter than snow. Is this not what the sutras refer to as the "solidly established śarīra" that remains when the entire body is cremated?
Later Tang Quan-zai was the son of the Shen family of Qiantang. In his youth, he relied upon the Great Master Fa-jie of Mount Jing to receive the tonsure.

Having received full ordination, he immediately practiced the dhūta austerities, seeking realization through meditative contemplation. While traveling to various regions, he finally received instruction from Shi.

He visited the residences of various eminent masters. Later, he entered Mount Tiantai and dwelt at Andian Rock for twenty years. His conduct became increasingly rigorous, and his reputation grew ever more prominent.

Even the spirits of the wood and the goblins of the stone served him as attendants. In the fifth year of the Tiānchéng era, he returned to Mount Jìngshān to spend his final years, where he passed away.
A mad monk from the Han dynasty first appeared in Gaocheng County of Luoyang. He traveled through the villages begging for stone and mineral ash, which he carried on his back with great effort.
He entered the two mountains, Da-liu and Xiao-liu, where he worked day and night without ceasing, saying, "I shall use this to construct a palace.
People regarded him as a lunatic and paid him no heed. When he had gathered approximately several thousand *shí*, he sealed them tightly with his own hands; suddenly, he vanished.

Its departure left no trace. At the beginning of the Qianguo era, the Emperor ascended the throne; not long after, he passed away. His last will designated Daliu Mountain as Rui Ling (the Imperial Tomb).
The relevant authorities calculated that several million bricks and tiles were required, along with an incalculable amount of mineral ash.
While the bricks and tiles could be obtained by firing them in kilns, they knew not where the mineral ash originated. Those in charge were just then considering it—
The village headman reported this, whereupon [the authorities] released him and provided for him with just enough.
At that time, there was an anonymous monk in Tanzhou of the Han who recited the *Lotus Sūtra* from memory and never spoke of anything else.

Emperor Wen Zhao of the Ma family treated him with exceptional courtesy and distinction, summoning him to the Tiance Fu and providing for him at the Xiangxi Yuan. Nevertheless, his speech and conduct were remarkable.
His conduct was always eccentric and startling to the world; thus, those who lived with him would secretly laugh at him.

During the Qianyou era, he summoned the temple attendants to urgently carry the Buddha statues and place them in the two side halls. His movements were exceedingly frantic, leading those who heard of it to believe he had gone mad.
Shortly thereafter, he suddenly vanished. When they searched for him slowly, they found him sitting upright upon the throne in the main hall, having passed away. This, too, was remarkable.
Did you perhaps scrutinize his attainments with a calculating mind?
As for the Arhat Wangluo of the Song dynasty, he was a monk of Qianfu Temple in Mingzhou. By nature he was simple and straightforward, and he made no distinctions in what he ate or drank.

He was particularly fond of pork. His speech was like that of one who is dull-witted, yet his foreknowledge was as if divine. When people came to beg for anything he possessed, he never begrudged them even slightly.
Once, while he was drying his robes, a thief pulled them away; the Arhat feigned sleep and allowed him to take them. In the first year of the Kaibao era (968 CE).

His sitting practice concluded in the sixth month. By the third day, his complexion became even more radiant and lustrous, so they lacquered and clothed him. Shortly thereafter, a sound like sighing was heard coming from between his two cheeks.
The assembly suspected that because he had become putrid and rotten, such a sound was occurring. Or perhaps it was said in a dream one night: "The lacquering and clothing are very good;
however, I am extremely dazed and distressed—what can be done? The next day, several people reported this, all saying the same thing. Thereupon...
He summoned artisans and had them completely remove the lacquered cloth; the flesh color was red and white, most lovely to behold.

Countless round and lustrous śarīra fell to the ground, which the temple collected for veneration to this day. The King of Hantan, the Qian clan, privately conferred upon him the title "Venerable Honored One of Secret Cultivation and Divine Transformation."
Songzong was a native of Minyue. He was upright and possessed few desires; those who understood him held him in deep respect and faith.

In his youth, he was affiliated with Yanshou Monastery in Tanzhou while Jia Pian, a Grand Master for Remonstrance, was serving as the prefectural governor. Songzong once went to visit him, and Jia, recognizing his spiritual attainment, recommended him for office.

He presided over Wenshu Monastery. One day, he ascended the hall, took leave of the assembly, and prepared his travel gear. Crossing the Pengli Lake, he arrived at Huangzhou Post Station, where he passed away standing.
People from near and far gathered to observe the proceedings. An imperial messenger arrived with funds to manage the funeral rites, and a stupa was subsequently erected at that site.
It is now known as the Shinshin-in (True Body Hall), having been established in the second year of the Kaibō era.
Song Dao lived at Dà'ān Temple in Míngchí. As a person, he was profound and detached, prone to change, and unfathomable. He would often say to himself:
"I shall maintain myself through the virtue of frugality and respond to the world through guileful means. Frugality simplifies affairs; guile eliminates right and wrong.
He kept a black dog with whom he slept and rose; every day he cooked millet in an iron bowl and ate it together with the dog.
Once [the master] died, the dog also died. The temple preserved both bodies by lacquering and wrapping them in cloth;
to this day, they are especially venerated in Luoyang, with incense and flowers daily crowding their reliquary niches.
Song Shi-yun was a native of Jin-hua. In his youth, he traveled with National Teacher Shao. By nature, he was jocular and fond of sarcasm;

being frivolous, many treated him with familiarity and contempt, and he was not particularly esteemed by virtuous scholars or gentlemen. Only the National Teacher regarded him with constant intimacy and affection.
He would often say to others: "Although I have lived with Yun for the longest time, I have never been able to fathom the limits of his character."
This is truly extraordinary. In the seventh month of the sixth year of the Kaibao era, he passed away without illness, as if entering a state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
For twenty-one days, his body did not wither or decay. During the cremation, *śarīra* relics were obtained; his tongue was exceptionally bright and moist, standing out from the rest.

The assembly marveled at this and added more wood and charcoal to intensify the fire, yet it remained even firmer and more beautiful—evidently due to the power of the secret practices he had cultivated throughout his life. Yuan.
He once commissioned a monk to compose a text for repentance, in which he stated that he had recited scriptures and performed invocations numbering up to several hundred *zang*.
At first, [the author] did not believe him; yet looking back now, it was indeed not false.
When Yun resided at Bore Monastery on Mount Tiantai, he previously vowed to cast himself down beneath the stone bridge at Yanzuo Peak; thus, the firmness and resolve of his will can be seen.
Later, a small stupa was constructed and his tongue was enshrined within it, so that those who cultivate goodness might know how to be encouraged.
Some say that Huiyun never spoke of his surname, age, or seniority in the monastic order to others; yet at this time, judging by his appearance, he must have been over eighty years old.
Master Song Kuang was from Haitan County in Fuzhou. The son of a frontier soldier, he left home life to reside at Lenggaya Monastery.
From the age of eight, he took a liking to wild vegetables; whenever he saw them being tilled or weeded, he considered it the taking of life.

Whenever he saw fish or shellfish being prepared for cooking, he would throw sand and ash into them so that they could not be eaten. When he received the tonsure, his head emitted a fragrance as if incense were being burned.
Shen Tan said to the people, "The pagoda at Kaiyuan Temple was built by me during the Sui dynasty. His accounts of past events were remarkably corroborated and thus credible;
he was then popularly known as the "Holy Monk. At that time, the Censor-in-Chief Huangfu Zheng served as the Acting Governor of the prefecture.
He was invited to the provincial residence for an offering. A single vegetarian meatball was presented alongside a hundred non-vegetarian meatballs.
Chong took only the vegetarian one and cast all the others away. Chong was struck with amazement. He died at the age of thirteen; this is indeed what he himself recorded.
The Praise says:
The Bodhisattva advances in cultivation, Passing through birth and death; Traversing three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, He must awaken before he ceases.
How is this awakening? It is difficult for things to be conceptualized or compared; At the final moment of the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), Wisdom first arises.
Like awakening from a dream, like a lotus flower blooming, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, emitted light and manifested auspicious omens.
They praised him, saying, "Excellent! You turn the Great Wheel of Dharma! To meet the capacities of beings and sustain the lineage, the heavens rained down the four flowers;
the earth shook in six ways; Śakra and Brahmā followed with joy; and the Māras and heretics were struck with alarm.
*The Newly Compiled Biographies of Monks Classified into Six Categories of Study*,
Scroll Twenty-Eight and Scroll Twenty-Nine.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Tán’è of Zhèdōng.

Section on the Miraculous Transformations of the Vinaya Master Zhú Sēnglǎng of Jīn: A native of Jīngzhào, he traveled extensively in his youth, coming and going through Guāngzhōng. He took it upon himself to lecture and expound the teachings. Once...
He went with his peers to attend an invitation. On the way, he suddenly said, "Your belongings have been left at the temple and are now being stolen.
If you return quickly to pursue them, you may avoid losing them. The group followed his words and indeed escaped the loss. While residing on Mount Tai, he associated with the recluse Zhang Zhong.
When Zhong passed away, he moved to Mount Kunlun in Jinyu Valley to the northwest of Mount Tai. Students came to him there.

Fu Jian frequently bestowed offerings upon him. Later, during the purge of the monastic community, Lang alone was renowned for his spiritual conduct and thus was not included in the list of those to be eliminated.
Previously, the mountain had suffered much from tiger attacks, but from that time on, they reportedly ceased entirely.

Whichever guests arrived—whether many or few, noble or humble—he would always know of them in advance and would invariably instruct his disciples to prepare the necessary provisions beforehand. He passed away at the age of eighty-five. At that time, there was also [the monk] Zhi...
Seng Dun was well-versed in the sutras and śāstras and proficient in the Mahāyāna; he authored the *Treatise on the Origin of Sentient Beings*, which circulated throughout the world.
Ghandhara of the Jin dynasty was a man from the Western Regions who had long resided in Luoyang, yet people did not recognize his extraordinary nature. To the southeast of the city was Mount Panqi;
Ghandhara pointed to a site at the foot of the mountain and said to the people, "This is the foundation of an ancient monastery. He then began to excavate it.
As a result of this, he obtained bricks, tiles, and other utensils, whereupon they built a monastery together and appointed him as its head.

The monastery was about one hundred li from Luoyang. Whenever Shi Le entered the city to attend meals at various donors' homes, he would beg for a bowl of oil in the evening and return to the monastery to offer it to the Buddha;
he made this his regular practice. His pace was so swift that even a galloping horse could not catch up with him. He once had someone hold his robe and sash, yet...
He perceived the sound of wind passing by his ears. In a short while, he arrived at the monastery; thereafter, nothing more was known of his end.

Hālaka of the Jin dynasty was a native of Fanyang. He possessed a refined bearing and a lofty, pure disposition. Having left the household life, he was able to recite two million words of scripture from memory.
He practiced *dhūta* austerities amidst the mountain forests; during the freezing winter, he sat upon stone steps and did not lie down at night.
In the first year of Taikang, he arrived at Luoyang. At that time, those afflicted by pestilence were lying piled upon one another;

yet when he exhausted his prayers for them, the sick rose and the dead returned to life, beyond counting. In the first year of Yuankang, he went west to Mount Luzhi. Inside a stone chamber, the room was far from water.
People wished to excavate a pond and channel a mountain stream to facilitate drawing water. Jie said, "Why go to such trouble? Immediately—
He pressed his left foot against the western stone wall of the chamber until it sank in; as he withdrew his foot, water gushed out, fragrant, clear, and delicious.
He drank of it, which quenched his hunger and thirst and cured his ailments. He passed away eight years later. When his body was cremated, his entire form remained seated in the lotus posture.
He was then moved to a stone chamber for veneration. At the beginning of the Xianhe era, a man named Zhu Ding’an from the Western Regions heard of this and marveled at it.
He went in person to the stone chamber and beheld the remains; they were as solemn and intact as if [the master] were still alive, though he had been dead for thirty years.
Buddhayaśas (Fotu Cheng) of the Jin dynasty was a native of India. In the fourth year of the Yongjia era, he came to Luoyang, claiming to be over one hundred years old.

He constantly practiced the cultivation of vital energy (*qi*) for self-nourishment and was able to abstain from food for many days. He was skilled in reciting divine incantations and could command spirits and deities.
There was an opening on the side of his abdomen which he plugged with cotton wool. When reading by night, he would pull out the wool so that its light would illuminate the room.
When fasting, he would go to the water and draw out his intestines and stomach through the opening to wash them, after which he would return them.

Whenever he listened to the bells of a pagoda, they would foretell good or bad fortune; all were remarkably accurate. During the rebellions in Luoyang, he hid in the wilds to observe the changing situation. Shi Le stationed his troops at Ge...
Shi Bei practiced slaughter exclusively, and many śramaṇas met with harm. Fo Tucheng went to visit Shi Le’s general Guo Heilüe, who hosted him in his residence.

Later, when Heilüe followed Shi Le on military expeditions, he would invariably predict victory or defeat in advance. Shi Le questioned him, saying, "I am not aware that you possess such extraordinary strategy;
how is it that you always know the auspiciousness or misfortune of military operations? Heilüe replied, "The General is divinely gifted..."
Shenwu was aided by mysterious spirits. Recently, he obtained a śramaṇa who possessed extraordinary abilities and could interpret speech.
"General, once you have briefly brought order to the realm, he shall become your teacher. Everything that had been reported previously was his word. Shi Le summoned Fotudeng to test his arts.
Fotudeng took an alms bowl, filled it with water, burned incense, and offered prayers; suddenly, a lotus flower grew within the bowl, its radiance and color brilliant.
Shi Le, through this, came to revere and believe [in him]. When Shi Le returned from Gepei to the north of the River and passed by Fangtou, his enemies raided the camp at night.
Fo Tucheng had previously said to Hei Lue, "The enemy will arrive in a moment; you should inform the Duke. Subsequently, because they were prepared, they escaped harm.

Shi Le once donned his helmet and armor, grasped a sword, and sat through the night. He sent a messenger to ask where Fotudeng was. Fotudeng said to the messenger, "The General has been out at night; where has he been?
Fotudeng then asked the messenger, "When there are no bandits during the day, why do you maintain such strict military precautions at night?

One day, Shi Le became enraged over a certain matter and intended to kill all the Daoist practitioners, intending to subject Fotudeng to the same suffering. Fotudeng hid himself in the house of Heilüe and said to his disciples: "If..."
The General sent someone to see him; when questioned, [Tong] deceived him by saying he did not know. That night, the General indeed sent people there, but they could not find him.
Returning to report this to Shi Le, Le said in alarm, "I have erred! I have erred! As soon as an evil thought arose, Tong abandoned me and departed like this.
He could not sleep all night, longing to see him. Then Tong went to pay his respects to Le and asked, "What was it like last night?"
Shi Le said, "I was angry, so I merely avoided him; now that I have changed my mind, I dare to come here. Shi Le laughed and said, "Is it not a mistake for you, a man of the Way, to act thus?
The source of the water for Xiangguo City was located five li northwest of the city moat, and it had suddenly run dry.
Shi Le asked Da Cheng what would cause the water to return. Da Cheng replied, "I shall command the dragon. Thereupon, he went with his disciple Fasheng and others to the source of the water.
Shangzheng sat upon a rope bed, burned frankincense, and offered prayers. Suddenly, a small dragon about five or six inches long emerged, playing in the water with a slight, shimmering flow.
In an instant, the water rose greatly until the moats and ditches were all filled. The Xianbei leader Duan Mo-bo was attacking Shi Le’s forces with a vast army.
Fearing for his life, Shi Le questioned Zhongtong, who replied: "The temple bell sounds; it says that at mealtime tomorrow, [the enemy] shall be captured."

Duan Mopuo was atop the city walls of Leding, observing from afar. He could see no trace of Mopuo’s army behind him and, turning pale with alarm, said, "If Mopuo is like this, can he possibly be captured so quickly?
He sent Kui An again to inquire of Fotudeng, who replied, "Mopuo has already been captured."
At that time, ambush troops emerged from north of the city and captured Mopa. Fo Tucheng consequently urged Shi Le to pardon his crime and allow him to return to his own country;
Le followed this advice and ultimately made use of his services. Liu Yao dispatched his younger brother Yue to attack Le, who sent his own brother Shijilong to resist him.
Yue was defeated and retreated to take refuge at Shiliangwu, where Shijilong erected strong stockades to guard it. At that time, Tucheng was with his disciples.
From the official temple to the Central Temple, he suddenly sighed and said, "Liu Yue is pitiable.
His disciple Fazuo asked for the reason, and Fo Tucheng replied, "Yesterday at the hour of Hai, Yue was defeated and captured. It soon turned out to be exactly so.
When Liu Yao personally attacked Luoyang and Shi Le intended to resist him, his attendants advised that it would not be advisable. Le consulted Fo Tucheng, who replied, "The stūpa’s *cāmarī*..."
The sound of the bell was: *Xiūzhī tìlìgāng píngǔ qútùdāng*. This is the Qie-yun (Kharosthi) script.
*Xiūzhī* means "army"; *tìlìgāng* means "to set out"; *píngǔ* refers to Liu Yao’s Huns; *qútùdāng* means "to seize. Thus, it signifies:
"The army sets out and seizes Yao. Thereupon, Xu Guang alone urged Shi Le to march. Shi Le left his son Shi Hong to garrison Xiangyang.
The commander of the state led infantry and cavalry toward Luoyang, where Shi Kan’s soldiers captured Yao alive in the water.

At that time, Fotudeng took sesame oil mixed with *yanzhi* (vermilion) and smeared it upon his palms; he then had a youth observe them after the youth had purified himself through fasting. The youth looked in astonishment and said:
He saw a vast multitude of troops and horses. Among them was a man who was tall, large, and fair-skinned, with his elbows bound by crimson cords. Fo-t'ung said, "This is Yao.
He immediately informed Shi Hong, who addressed him as the Heavenly King of Zhao and acted as the Emperor. His reverence for Fo-t'ung became even more profound.

At that time, Shi Chong was about to rebel. Fo Tucheng cautioned Shi Le, saying, "This year there are insects within the onions; eating them will surely harm people. You should order the common people not to eat onions.
Shortly thereafter, Shi Chong indeed fled. From then on, Shi Le consulted Tucheng before undertaking every matter and addressed him as "Great Monk" (Dàhéshàng).
Shi Le’s son, Bin, died suddenly; Shi Le sighed and said, "Gaozi, the Prince of Guo, [was saved by] Bian Que..."
"Can he be brought back to life? Great Master, surely you have no intention [to help]? Zhicheng then took willow branches and moistened them with water, sprinkling it over him while reciting prayers.
He then took Hui-bin’s hand and said, "Arise, arise! Bin then came back to life. From that time on, Shi Le issued an imperial decree for his sons to raise him in the monastery.

On every fourth day of the fourth month, he would personally visit the temple to perform the ritual ablution of the Buddha and make vows. This was in the fourth year of the Jianping era, in the fourth month.
The sky was calm and windless, yet a single bell atop the stupa rang out alone. Fotudeng said, "The sound of the bell says: 'The state will suffer a great national calamity;

it will not pass beyond this year. In the seventh month, Shi Le indeed passed away. His son, Shi Hong, succeeded him on the throne, but shortly thereafter, Shi Le deposed him and established himself as ruler.
He moved the capital to Ye and devoted his heart and service to Fotudeng, clothing him in silk gauze and brocade and having him ride in an ornately carved carriage during court assemblies.

He was led up to the palace hall; the attendants and those below them all assisted in lifting the palanquin. The Crown Prince and the various dukes supported him as he ascended, while the presiding official proclaimed, "The Great Monk!
Upon this, everyone seated rose. Li Nong, the Minister of Works, personally inquired after his health morning and evening, and the Crown Prince and the dukes visited him once every five days.
The people all venerated the Buddha, competing with one another to build stupas and monasteries; among those who had left the household life, both the genuine and the false appeared side by side.
There was considerable transgression and usurpation. Shi Le issued an edict to investigate and rectify the matter. Wang Du, the Director of the Bureau of Historiography, submitted a memorial stating:

"The Buddha is a deity of foreign lands; he is not one whom the people of China should worship. When the Han dynasty transmitted his Way, they permitted only the eight monasteries in the Western Regions to worship their own deity.
Han people have never before left the household life. Wei inherited the institutions of Han and likewise followed its precedents. Now..."

Those who seek liberation should not pay respects at various temples, but must exclusively follow the ancestral rites. This prohibition shall apply to all officials, from the high ministers down to the common serfs.
Any who violate this shall be punished with the same penalty as those who practice illicit worship. As for the śramaṇas, they were ordered to disrobe.
Many court officials submitted petitions for their ordination; because of Fotudeng, Shi Le issued an edict stating: "I am of humble origin from the frontier barbarians."
Having the honor of dwelling among the various states of the Central Xia, as for sacrifices and offerings, one should follow one's own ancestral customs;

however, since the Buddha is a deity of the Rong tribes, he should be venerated concurrently. As for the common people of the Yi and Zhao regions who take pleasure in serving the Buddha, let them be permitted to do so.
Formerly, Fo Tucheng dispatched his disciple Fachang northward to Xiangguo. Fachang’s younger brother, Fazuo, came from Xiangguo and met him at the foot of Liangtai City. They faced one another...
While traveling by carriage at night, when Sengcheng was about to return home, Cheng smiled and said, "So you were discussing your teacher with Fachang while riding in the same carriage?
As the ancients said: 'Is it not called reverence when one does not change even in the presence of what is hidden? Is it not called caution when one is not negligent even when alone?'"
"Solitude is the foundation of reverence and caution; do you not understand this? Zuo was struck with awe and apologized in shame.

Thereupon, the people of the state warned one another not to give rise to evil thoughts, saying, "The Great Monk knows you. Whereever Fo Tucheng was, no one dared to spit, sneeze, or relieve themselves toward him.
Crown Prince Sui of Emperor Jilong had two sons in Xiangguo; Tucheng said to Sui, "The younger..."
"Ami! He will likely fall ill soon. Dao Sui immediately dispatched a messenger to visit him; indeed, he had already fallen sick.
The great physician Yin Sheng and a foreign Daoist both claimed they could cure him, but Fotudeng said to his disciple Fachai, "Even if a sage were to appear once more, he could not cure him.
Shortly thereafter, he died as predicted. Dao Sui, intending to oppose him, said to the palace attendants, "The Master..."

"If the Way of the Gods should manifest its schemes against me, I must eliminate them first. When Fotudeng was about to enter the capital for an audience, he said to his disciple Senghui, "There is someone I must pass by;
you may stop me there. As Fotudeng passed, Yao Sui invited him up onto the Southern Terrace. Senghui pulled at his robes and urged him to decline the invitation, returning to the monastery.
He sighed, saying, "The omen of disaster has already appeared. Consequently, he gently admonished Shi Jilong, but in the end, Jilong could not be dissuaded.

When the event occurred, [Shi] Fang finally realized that his words had been prophetic. When Guo Heilüe was leading a campaign north of Chang’an and fell into a Qiang ambush, Fotudeng changed his expression and said, "Master Guo is now in peril.
He then called out for the assembly of monks to offer prayers, and Fotudeng himself also offered prayers.

After a short while, he said, "He has escaped. Later, Guo Heilüe recounted the events himself: just as he was breaking through the encirclement and attempting to flee, his horse’s strength failed him; suddenly, someone pushed him [out].
He lent his horse to [the man], who was thus able to escape. That day was precisely the time when Fotudeng had offered his prayers. During a severe drought, Jilong prayed for rain without success;
he requested that Fotudeng go there himself, whereupon two white dragons descended into the shrine at the mouth of the Zhang River, and rain fell over several thousand *li*.
Fotudeng sent a disciple to the Western Regions to purchase incense. Once the disciple had departed, Fotudeng said, "I see in my palm that he will encounter bandits."
As he was about to die, he offered a prayer. His disciples returned and reported that bandits were about to kill them; suddenly, for no apparent reason, they fled in terror.

It was said that the *yuán* fish would not appear in the Yellow River, yet suddenly someone caught one and presented it as an offering. When Shi Le (Ji Long) examined it, he sighed and said, "Will it not be long before Huan Wen enters the River?
Huan Wen’s courtesy name was Yuanzi. Shortly thereafter, this proved true. [This was followed by the account of] the Grand Marshal of the puppet state, Yan Gong Bin.
He served as the Governor of Youzhou. Fo Tucheng said to Shi Jilong, "Withdraw your horses immediately; by autumn, Qi will suffer from festering sores.
Jilong did not understand this and immediately issued orders to all locations to collect the horses. That autumn, someone slandered Shi Bin; Jilong summoned him and whipped him three hundred times.
He also killed his mother, Qi, and Li Long, and subsequently slaughtered five hundred people before finally ceasing. Fo Tucheng [continued to predict the consequences].
He said, "The mind must not be indulged; death cannot be brought back to life; and ritual propriety must not be treated with intimacy. To kill would be to wound the spirit of benevolence.

How could there be a Son of Heaven who personally carries out punishments? When the Jin army emerged from the Huai and Si rivers and all the cities north of Long were besieged and pressed by attack, the three frontiers sent urgent pleas for help.
Shi Le (Ji Long) said in anger, "I have honored the Buddha and provided for the monks, yet in return I am met with invaders. The Buddha has no divine power! At this, Fo Tucheng...
Rang said, "Your Majesty was a merchant in a previous life and once held a great assembly at a temple in Kaśmīra.
Among the sixty arhats present at that assembly, I was one of them. A holy sage declared: 'When this donor's life ends, he will be reborn as a rooster.'"
"In the future, I shall return once more to rule the land of Jin. Is it not now, Your Majesty, that this is the retribution for your service to the Buddha and your support of the Sangha?

That border regions are subject to incursions is the constant reality of possessing a state; why then do you harbor resentment and slander against the Triple Gem, even giving rise to such poisonous thoughts?
Shi Le knelt and apologized, then said to Fotudeng, "The Buddhist Dharma prohibits killing. Yet I hold the power of life and death over the empire; how can I reconcile this?"
Tancheng said: "When emperors serve the Buddha, they do so by embodying reverence and following the Way with a compliant mind, manifesting support for the Dharma and refraining from violence.

They must not harm the innocent. If there are among the people those who commit evil and do not repent, how can they not be executed? However, executions must not involve indiscriminate punishment; one must be cautious.
At that time, the Shangshu (Minister) Zhang Li and Zhang Liang were wealthy and devoted to Buddhism. When [the temple] was being constructed...
The stupas and temples were exceptionally magnificent. Fotudeng said to him, "To serve the Buddha lies in purity and freedom from desire.

Although you and your kind revere the Buddha, your greed and meanness are unceasing, and your hunting is unrestrained. What benefit is there in building thousands of stupas? Later, Shi Le dreamed that a flock of sheep carrying fish came from the north.
Upon waking, he questioned Fotudeng about it. Fotudeng replied, "This is not auspicious. The Xianbei will possess the Central Plains."

Later, all these things were proven true. Once, as [Dao]cheng ascended to the central hall, he suddenly cried out in alarm, "Change! Change! He called for wine and spat it toward the source. Laughing, he said, "Stop.
At that moment, someone arriving from Youzhou reported that there had been a fire on that very day. A sudden rainstorm came from the southwest and extinguished it; the rain smelled of wine.
When Shi Xuan was about to kill Shi Tao, he passed by Cheng’s residence. One bell on the stupa rang; Cheng—
He said, "Do you understand the sound of the bell? The bell replied, "The Master from the West has been delivered. Xuanshe changed color and asked, "What words are these?
Fotucheng then feigned surprise and said, "This old barbarian practices the Way, yet he cannot dwell in the mountains; instead, he enjoys wealth and honor with heavy carpets and fine food."
"Is this not a sign of your passing? Later, when Sengtao arrived, Fo Tucheng gazed at him intently for a long time. Terrified, Taò asked why. He replied, "I merely find your blood smell foul.
Shi Le had a dream in which a dragon flew from the southwest and fell from the sky; he questioned Tucheng about it, and he replied:
"Calamity is about to arise; father and son must be compassionate and harmonious, and exercise great caution.

When Shi Jilong and his wife, Lady Du, went to inquire after him, Fotudeng said, "There is a thief beneath your ribs; within ten days, from the west of the temple stupa to the east of the hall, blood shall flow everywhere.
Be careful not to travel to the east. His wife asked, "Are you senile, Master? Where could there be a thief? Fotudeng then feigned...
He said, "That which is received by the six senses is all a thief. Laozi was certainly in his old age; it would have been best simply to ensure that the younger ones did not become deluded.
Two days later, Xuancheng indeed killed Tao within the monastery. He intended to take advantage of Shi Le's presence at the funeral to kill him as well.

Because Sengcheng had previously maintained his precepts, he was spared. When Sengxuan was subsequently arrested, [Sengcheng] remonstrated with him, saying: "They are all Your Majesty's sons; why inflict such heavy calamity upon them?
If you can cast aside your anger as if it were compassion, there are still more than sixty years remaining [for the dynasty]. Otherwise, Sengxuan shall become a comet."
The lower palace of Ye was swept clean. Shi Le ultimately placed Xuan in shackles, dragged him onto a pyre of firewood, and burned him to death.
Afterwards, a horse with a shaggy mane and tail both bearing marks of burning entered the Zhongyang Gate and exited through the eastern side of the Xianyang Gate;
it could not enter the Eastern Palace and fled toward the northeast, disappearing from sight in an instant. Fotudeng sighed and said, "The calamity has reached its peak. Shi Le—
When Shi Le hosted a great banquet for his ministers in the Great Wu Anterior Hall, Fotudeng chanted: "The hall! The hall! Thorns have formed a forest; they will tear the clothes of men.
Shi Le ordered that the area beneath the stones of the hall be excavated, and indeed thorns were found growing there. Later, during the rebellion of Ran Min, the Shi clan was nearly exterminated.
Ran Min’s childhood nickname was "Thorn Slave" (Jinu). When the Great Wu Hall was first constructed, [the walls] were painted with images of ancient loyal ministers and filial sons.

The sons, the loyal warriors, and the chaste women all transformed into the appearance of barbarians; their heads were entirely retracted into their shoulders, with only their crowns and hair protruding.
Shi Jilong loathed this and remained silent, while Fotudeng wept before him. He then personally opened a tomb at Zimo in the western suburbs of Ye, sitting there and speaking to himself:
"Will I have three years? He answered himself, "No. Then he said again, "Will I have two years? One—
"Is a hundred days a month? He replied, "I cannot say. Thereupon, he ceased speaking. After a long time, he said to Fazuo, "In the year Wushen, calamity and chaos will gradually sprout;
in Jiyou, the Shi clan shall perish. I have already undergone transformation before these events occur.
He then wrote a letter to Jilong to bid him farewell. When the Emperor arrived, he consoled him, saying, "How can you, O Monk, so suddenly abandon me?"

Huh? Cheng said, "To emerge from life and enter into death is the constant way of the Dao. Longevity and brevity are determined by one's lot; there is no means by which they can be increased or diminished.

However, the Dao prizes the completion of practice, and virtue prizes the absence of indolence. If one's conduct and virtue are without blemish, then even in death it is as if one were alive. Is this not so? All agreed that it was so.

"What benefit would even a thousand years bring? Yet there is something lamentable: although the state has set its heart upon the principles of the Buddha, establishing monasteries and ordaining monks, it ought to have received blessings and fortune.
However, its administration was harsh and empty, punishments and rewards were both excessive and indiscriminate, and it specifically contravened the sacred scriptures without ever reforming itself;
this is why the mandate of the state did not endure. After Shi Le (Ji Long) had wailed with grief and sobbed, Fo Tucheng (Fo Cheng) sat peacefully and passed away.
This was the fourth year of the Yonghe era of Emperor Mu of the Jin dynasty. A śramaṇa came from Yong and claimed to have seen Fotudeng entering Guanzhong in the west.
Shi Le opened the tomb to inspect it, but saw nothing but a single stone. Displeased, Shi Le said, "The stone is I myself; it has buried me and departed. I shall surely die soon.
Consequently, he fell ill, and the following year there was great chaos. Fotudeng had once said to Shi Le...
The dragon said, "Two hundred li to the east of the capital, on such-and-such a day in such-and-such a month, you shall send a most extraordinary man; do not kill him.
As appointed, there was a beggar in the marketplace of Wei County wearing a hempen jacket and cloth trousers; he was commonly known as "Hemp-Jacket" (Maju).

His speech was unconventional, like that of a madman. Whenever he obtained rice or grain by begging, he would not eat it but would instead scatter it upon the main road, saying, "This is to feed the celestial horse."
Zhao Xing, the Governor of Taishou, borrowed [the monk] and escorted him there. Shi Jilong spoke with him, but he made no unusual remarks.

His younger brother said, "Your Majesty shall ultimately become the 'Single Pillar under the Hall' (Yizhu Dianxia). Jilong did not understand this. He was sent to see Fotudeng, who said upon meeting him: "In the past, we met during the Guanghe era; suddenly it is now.
The Western Rong have received the mysterious mandate and their calendar has been severed. The time for the military camp has arrived; the metal element has departed and dissolved."
It is ruined. The borderlands cannot follow it; they drive away its sacred traces. Though the descendants and branches flourish, how can one accumulate a period of auspiciousness for eternity?
As for joy, Tancheng said: "The heavens turn and the cycle reaches its limit; misfortune will not be sustained. The Nine Woods cannot be remedied by artifice.
Although the profound revelation remains, the world is unable to uphold it. The foundation must surely collapse. Having wandered long in Jambudvīpa, it is a place of turmoil."
She frequently exhibited such eccentric behavior. Once, she ascended into the clouds and met with those who roam in the void;
her words were incomprehensible to others. Shi Jilong sent her back to her home county by courier. Once they had left the city, she insisted on walking, saying, "I must pass through a certain place;
I cannot depart yet. She said, "Stop at Hekou Bridge and wait for me there. When the courier arrived at the bridge, Ma Ru was already there ahead of him.
When Murong Jun threw Ji Long into the Zhang River, he leaned against a bridge pillar and did not float; this was the fulfillment of the "Single Pillar" prophecy.
When Emperor Yuan succeeded to the throne in the region south of the Yangtze, it was the fulfillment of the "Celestial Horse" prophecy.
Shandao Kai of the Jin dynasty was a native of Dunhuang. He recited forty thousand words of the scriptures. He abstained from grain, subsisting on cypress seeds;
when these were not always available, he did not even supplement with pine resin. Instead, he ate small pebbles, swallowing several at a time, taking this dose once every few days.
Whether much or little, he would occasionally eat a piece of ginger and pepper. In this manner, for seven years, he feared neither cold nor heat;
he sat day and night without lying down. The mountain deities and tree spirits beheld his extraordinary form, yet he remained unafraid.

During the time of Shi Jilong, he once traveled from Xiping, covering seven hundred li in a single day. A certain śrāmaṇera, fourteen years of age, was able to keep pace with him on the journey. Upon arriving—
The Governor of Qinzhou sent [Buddhabhadra] to Ye, where Shi Fotu Cheng was made to converse with him; they were on good terms.

He resided in the shrine of Fa-chin west of the city. Later, he moved to the Zhaode Monastery in Linzhang, where he constructed a multi-storied pavilion about eighty or ninety feet high within his quarters.
On top, he wove reeds to create a meditation chamber, where he constantly sat. Shi Jilong provided him with very generous support, and Dao-kai likewise [did so].
He gave [the food] to others. When people came to consult him regarding the Way of the Immortals (*xiandao*), he remained silent and did not answer.

Instead, he spoke a verse, saying: "I pity all who suffer; I have left the home-life to benefit the world. To benefit the world, one must study the luminous [truths]; by studying the luminous truths, one can sever evil.

This mountain is remote and grain is difficult to obtain; thus I have made this plan of fasting. This is not for the sake of seeking companions among the immortals; I pray you do not spread this word abroad. Each day he consumed only *zhentian* (sedative herbs).
He kept several medicinal pills, each as large as a *wuzi* (nutmeg) seed, which possessed the aroma of pine, honey, ginger, cinnamon, and *fuling* fungus.
He would occasionally drink only one or two liters of tea and *su* soup. He claimed he could cure eye ailments, and those who sought his treatment all found it effective.
Observing his conduct, people regarded him as if he possessed divine powers. Fotucheng said, "This Daoist is observing the rise and fall of the state; if he departs, there will be great chaos."
Toward the end of the reign of Shi Le (Ji Long), Daokai crossed the Yangtze to Xuchang. During the great chaos in Ye, in the third year of the Shengping era, he arrived at the capital.
Later, he traveled to Nanhai and entered Mount Luofu, where he lived alone in a thatched hut, living in serene detachment from the mundane world.
At over a hundred years of age, he passed away in his mountain dwelling. He instructed his disciples to place him in a stone cave; they then moved his remains into the rock.
Kong. During the Chen dynasty, Yuan Hong served as the Governor of Nanhai. Together with his younger brother Yingshu and the śramaṇa Zhifafang, he ascended Mount Luofu.
Upon reaching a stone chamber, they encountered Daokai; his physical remains were as if alive, and the incense burners and earthenware vessels remained intact.
Yuan Hong said, "The Dharma Master’s spiritual practice was extraordinary; this is surely his shedding of the cocoon."
Zhu Fotiao of the Jin dynasty was a native of India. He served Fo Tucheng as his teacher. By nature, he was unadorned by worldly refinements.

Having resided in a mountain monastery for many years, there was a man whose surname has been lost who received the Way from Fotiao. When his wife fell gravely ill, they moved their residence outside the monastery to treat her.
His younger brother, who lived at home, became quite anxious about this. Furthermore, seeing Fotiao coming from outside, the brother...
He sent a message inquiring after his elder brother and sister-in-law. Tiao replied, "Regarding your brother's illness, which has been as it was before, he has already begun to feel gradually better;

however, your younger brother has followed him to pay his respects at the monastery, where the Master has condescended to visit. His brother was startled and said, "How could the Master have ever come out to speak such falsehoods?

The brothers disputed this incessantly, so the brother questioned Tiao. Tiao laughed but did not answer. Tiao then wrapped some parched grain and rice cakes and traveled alone deep into the mountains.
He traveled for years until his return; his provisions of parched grain and rice were always in surplus, and he would sometimes carry them with him.

When evening came and it snowed heavily, he would invariably stay overnight in a tiger’s den. Some people were terrified by this, but after a long time, he set a date and announced his passing. The people gathered to watch, and Sengzhao said:
"Mountains, rivers, heaven, and earth all undergo change and extinction; how much more so for humans? Yet one can attain longevity, provided one is able to focus the mind in purity."
He cast off the three poisons. Although their physical forms were distinct, their essential meeting was one and the same.
Having finished speaking, he immediately covered his head with his robe, sat upright, and passed away. Later, eight disciples of the Master entered the Western Mountains.

Suddenly they saw Tiao standing atop a cliff, his robes bright and clean, his bearing majestic and expansive. The eight men prostrated themselves and said, "Is the Master truly free from ailment? Tiao laughed.
He nodded his head in agreement, and immediately he vanished from sight. Upon returning home, they opened his tomb to look for him; only his sandals remained.

Qi Yu, a man from India, arrived in Xiangyang during the reign of Emperor Huai. When he wished to cross the Han River, the boatman, regarding him as a foreign śramaṇa, cast him out and would not take him aboard.
By the time the boat reached the northern bank, Qi Yu was already there ahead of them. The boatmen [were amazed].
Everyone was dazzled and marveled at this. On the road there were two tigers; Daoyu pressed one tiger’s head down with his hand and stamped his foot to drive away the other.
Thereupon, both tigers retreated. Wherever he went, children clamored and pursued him.
When tens of thousands of monks from Luoyang came to pay their respects, Daoyu sat upright and received them without saying a word. He pointed only to Zhi Fayuan and said: [The text ends here.]
"This bodhisattva has come from among sheep. He then pointed to Zhu Faxing and said, "This bodhisattva has come from among the devas.
He further remarked, "The robes of these bhikṣus are all adorned with flowers; this violates the Buddha’s dharma regulations and is improper.

Looking toward the palace buildings, he said, "In general, they resemble the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. However, those were produced by the power of the Path, whereas these are merely produced by the power of karma. He continued:
The śramaṇa Jīvamitra said, "The one who constructed this palace came from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; having completed it, he returned immediately to heaven.
Beneath the tiles on the roof ridge, there should be the tools used for its construction. Upon searching, fifteen hundred implements were indeed found.
Teng Yongwen, the Grand Administrator of Hengyang, was residing at Manshui Temple when he suffered from a wind-paralysis ailment. Daoyi sprayed him with water, and [he was cured].
A man with a withered leg was immediately able to rise and walk. In the monastery, there were several *cintāmaṇi* trees (trees of contemplation) that had been withered for a long time;

Faxu consecrated them with water, and suddenly their flowers and leaves became lush and vibrant. In the Imperial Workshops (*shangfang shu*), there was a man suffering from a malignant tumor who was about to die;
Faxu placed his alms bowl upon the patient’s abdomen, covered it with a cloth, and recited incantations for thousands of words. Suddenly, a foul odor emerged, whereupon he lifted the cloth.
He spread [the cloth] over it, and within the alms bowl there was mud. The sick man then revived. During the chaos in Luoyang, Fayi took his leave to return home.

The Indian śramaṇa Zhu Faxing requested of him, saying, "I pray you grant me a single word that I may practice throughout my life. Fayi then assembled the monastics and the laity, ascended the high seat, and said:
"Guard your mouth, restrain your body, and control your mind; be careful not to commit any evils. Cultivate all forms of goodness. As it is said: [The verse follows].
"This constitutes attaining transcendence. Having finished speaking, he remained silent. Xing said, "I pray that you will accept this Dharma which I have not yet heard.
If a child of eight years can recite such a verse, it is not what one expects from a man of the Way.

Huiri laughed and said, "If an eight-year-old can recite it, yet a hundred-year-old does not practice it, what benefit is there in reciting it without practicing? Everyone knows to revere those who have attained the Way, but..."

"To know and practice for oneself is the way to attain the Dao. How tragic! At this, [the monk] pulled his arm and departed directly. Several hundred people blocked his path and bowed, requesting that he stay for the midday meal before proceeding.
Daoyu granted their request. The following morning, more than five hundred households all claimed that Daoyu was there; it was as if he had manifested multiple bodies.
