Once he had departed for the region south of the Yellow River, he traveled so slowly that his pursuers could not catch up.
He then drew lines on the ground with his staff and said, "I part from you here. On that very day, some saw him leaving Chang’an, while others saw him still within the monastery.
Furthermore, the merchant Hu Shiden returned from the Western Regions and reported: "On this day, I saw him in the shifting sands; by my reckoning, he has already [passed through]."
It was nine thousand *li*.
Jin Shengong was a man from the Western Regions who became a śramaṇa in his youth. During the time of Fu Jian, he entered Chang’an;

he practiced tranquility and the regulation of breath (*qi*), abstaining from the five grains. He could travel five hundred *li* in a single day and spoke of future events with a precision as if pointing with his finger.
Fazang was able to summon divine dragons through secret incantations. Whenever there was a drought, Yao Xian would always have him offer prayers to the dragon to request rain.

Shortly thereafter, a dragon would descend into his alms bowl, and it would invariably rain heavily. Yao Xian and his ministers would personally approach the bowl to observe this. Fazang passed away in Chang’an.
Later, after a great drought had persisted for some time, Fu Jian said to his Secretary of the Palace Secretariat, Zhu Tong: "If Master She were still here, how could we worry about this?
Buddhayaśas (translated into Chinese as Jueming) was of Brahmin descent from the kingdom of Kaśmīra. His family had followed non-Buddhist paths for generations.
There was a bhikṣu who went to that house to beg for alms. Yaśas’s father, enraged, drove him away, whereupon the bhikṣu’s hands and feet became convulsed and he became lame.
A divination stated: "This is due to offending a great man. Yaśas immediately sought out the aforementioned bhikṣu and repented; consequently, the bhikṣu was healed.

His father was greatly astonished and had Yaśas take him as his teacher. At that time, Yaśas was thirteen years old. Once, while following his teacher in the wilderness, they encountered a tiger. The teacher, feeling distressed, wished to flee and hide, but Yaśas—

Shè said, "Do not fear; the tiger has already departed. When the Master asked him the reason, he replied, "The tiger was already full; when I went forward, I saw its remains. The Master marveled at this.
At the age of fifteen, he could recite thirty thousand words daily. A strange monk, pitying his exceptional wisdom and acuity, [took him under his care].
He shared his portion of alms with others so that they would not neglect their recitation and study. At the age of nineteen, he had memorized several million words of Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras.
By nature, he was lofty and simple; with his vast knowledge and insight, he regarded himself as superior to the world, such that no one could serve as his teacher.

Because of this, people disparaged him. Yet, upon seeing his refined demeanor, when he spoke and laughed, they were suddenly struck with a sense of clarity and lost all grounds for their previous judgment.

He felt regret. Because of this, he returned to his youth and became a śrāmaṇera once more. He followed his maternal uncle even further to study the various treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
At the age of twenty-seven, he finally received the full precepts. He regularly provided meals for the assembly of monks at the house of the King of Śākala.

The crown prince Dharmamitra spoke with him and took a liking to him, so he invited him to remain and provide offerings. Later, Kumārajīva arrived; they again engaged in mutual study with great joy. It happened that...
When Kumārajīva returned to Kucha with his mother, the Prince of Śākala succeeded to the throne. At that time, Lü Guang was attacking Kucha;
the King of Kucha sent an appeal for assistance to Śākala, but before the troops arrived, Kucha had fallen. Kumārajīva was captured by them, while Guṇabhadra remained alone to convert Kucha.
Ten years later, while Kumārajīva was in Guzang, he sent a letter inviting Guṇabhadra, but the people of the country detained him, and another year passed.

At night, he set out secretly with his disciples. A disciple asked, "What shall we do if we are pursued by daylight? Thereupon, Kumārajīva consecrated medicine and threw it into the water in his bowl;

they washed their feet and traveled. By dawn, they had covered several hundred li. He asked the disciples what they perceived; they replied, "We heard only the sound of a violent wind and our tears fell.
He again consecrated medicine and threw it into the water; they washed their feet and stopped. Upon reaching Guzang, Kumārajīva was there.
When Chang’an heard that Yao Xing was pressuring him with a woman, he sighed and said, “How could one take fine cotton and cast it into a thorny forest?
When Kumārajīva urged Xing to welcome him, the messenger arrived. Guṇavarman laughed and said, “Your gracious decree has descended from afar;

I shall immediately travel by post to honorably respond to the donor’s diligent hospitality toward scholars. However, if I am treated with the same courtesy as Kumārajīva, then I shall indeed be poor.”

Dao said, "I have not yet dared to receive your command. He sent a messenger back to report this. Emperor Xing sighed, remarking on his prudence and circumspection. He dispatched envoys to urge him with gentle persuasion, whereupon he finally consented to come.

Emperor Xing went out to the suburbs to welcome him and constructed a separate vihāra within the Xiaoyao Garden. Although lavish offerings were prepared, [Sengrui] accepted nothing; when the time came for almsround, he would take but a single meal.
At that time, Kumārajīva was translating the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, and [Sengrui] had doubts and had not yet taken up the brush. When he reached—
This was a definitive assessment. Yan She was a man with red whiskers who was well-versed in the *Vibhāṣā*; he was thus known at the time as "Red-Whiskered Vibhāṣā.

Furthermore, because Kumārajīva took him as his teacher due to his Way, he was called "Great Vibhāṣā. Yao Shuang, the Commandant of the Capital Guard, requested that the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* be translated.
Daoxing doubted there were omissions or errors in it, so he tested him by having him recite fifty thousand words from the *Bhaiṣajyavastu*.
Furthermore, he translated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* in forty-four fascicles. He offered ten thousand bolts of silk for the production of the *Dīrgha-āgama* and other scriptures;

the total amount he donated accumulated to fill an entire house, yet he never once inquired as to their whereabouts. It is said that he eventually sold them to fund the construction of a temple south of the city.
Upon returning to the Western Regions, he reached Kapiśa, where he obtained one fascicle of the *Ākāśagarbha-sūtra*, which he entrusted to a merchant to carry back.
Regarding the old friend from Liangzhou, the Jin-era monk Tanhuo: it is unknown where he was from. He delighted in dwelling among tombs and beneath trees.

At that time, Tufan Lulugu, a Xianbei chieftain from Hexi, had usurped authority in Xiping and established the era name Jianhe. During this period, Huo carried a single *khakkhara* staff and [traveled] from the Yellow River...
He traveled southward. He would cause people to kneel before him and say, "This is the Eye of Prajñā; those who receive it may attain the Way.
When people offered him clothing, he would accept it and cast it upon the ground or into water. Later, the garment would return of its own accord to the donor's house, unstained by anything.

His gait was as swift as the wind; even if one tried to pursue him with all one’s might, one could not catch up. It was said that his pronouncements regarding fortune and misfortune were always verified. Once, someone playfully hid him away...
As for that alms-staff, Huo narrowed his eyes for a long while, immediately knowing its place of concealment; he rose, took it away, and asked no questions.
Huo’s younger brother, the General-in-Chief Rutan, wielded great influence throughout the entire state. Huo repeatedly exhorted him to serve the Buddha, to which Rutan replied:
"In my previous life, I served Heaven and Earth; now I serve the Buddha. I fear that this may violate the instructions of my ancestors.
If you can go without food for seven days, I shall follow you. He then had people keep watch over him. Murong Tan secretly sent him cakes and snacks.
Huo said to the śramaṇa Zhi-xing, "Whom am I deceiving? Am I deceiving the King? In the end, he did not eat as promised. Thereupon, Murong...
Tantun believed him and was convinced. Tantun’s daughter fell ill, and he requested that she be saved. Huo said, "The boundaries between life and death are fixed;

even a sage cannot alter them. One can only roughly know the time of their occurrence. Despite his firm request, the gates of the inner palace remained closed for a long time. Huo hurried to have them opened and said:
When the gates opened, he was born; before they had opened, he died. Guo Gongmen passed away before the palace gates could even open.
He often said to Fu Rutan, "If you can remain settled and act without striving, then the world may be pacified and the state's fortune will flourish.
If, however, you exhaust your troops and delight in slaughter, calamity will surely follow. Fu Rutan was unable to follow this advice. Later, amidst military chaos, Guo Bu-zhu met his end.
Sengzong of Jin was a man of unknown origins. He wore a hempen robe with a coarse cloth cloak over it and was known as the "Hemp-Cloth Daoist.
His moods were unpredictable, and his body was afflicted with ringworm and scabs. Every day he would sit at the Baitu Dam in Guangling, singing and strumming a lute to his own satisfaction;
one could not tell where he stayed overnight. When Tan Qi, the Magistrate of Jiangdu, summoned him, his speech was without bounds or limits.
On the bank, he asked for paper and composed a poem, saying: "To have desire is to suffer from insufficiency; To be without desire is to be without sorrow.
Yet none compare to those who are pure and empty, Wearing rope belts and donning dark robes. Floating through this world, Like a drifting boat with no mooring.

One must surely cast off worldly entanglements And settle one’s will upon the ancient mountain mounds. Tandhi found this extraordinary and bestowed several pieces of cloth upon him. Zong immediately gave these away to others. At that time...
There was a man carrying a basket on a staff who, at dusk, sought lodging with the Magistrate of Haiyan.

He saw a young boy tending geese and ducks and asked the Magistrate to lend him [the boy], saying, "I shall return him in a few days. The Magistrate granted his request. The man then led one of the boys up a mountain.
On the mountain was a house of several rafters. There were three or four practitioners of the Way who greeted one another with words of greeting;
what they said, the boy did not understand at all. He ate only a small bowl of food, like dried mugwort. He asked a man, "Do you know Shi Zong? When will his banishment finally end?
The man replied, "He is at Bai-tu-dai in Guangling, north of the river in Xuzhou. Judging by his words, [the boy] knew that his journey would soon come to an end.
The questioner wrote a letter and handed it to a man, saying, "Deliver this for me. He then tied it to the boy’s sash and returned to Haiyan.
When he asked Xi what was inside the chest, Xi replied, "It is merely a letter. However, Xi would not eventually show it to him;
when Xi wished to steal a look at it, the man would always move it elsewhere at night and then take his leave, saying, "I..."

"I originally intended to stay for a short while, but since you constantly harbor thieving intentions, how could I possibly remain? The Magistrate then called the boy and questioned him about the previous incident.
The boy said, 'Previously, when I was seized by the staff, I drifted away; I heard only the sound of waves beneath my feet.'"

He arrived at a mountain where a man living there sent him a letter, saying: "A-shang of Shang-dai. He immediately pulled back his robe-belt to open and read it, yet he could not understand its meaning.
A young boy went to Shi Zong, who was greatly astonished and said, "Have you come from Mount Penglai?
Later, as they passed by Yu-liang, they saw fishermen catching fish; Shi Zong then bathed in the upper reaches of the stream, and the fish all [disappeared].
He may be captured. Furthermore, he conversed at night with the śramaṇa Daokai and heard much concerning the affairs of Penglai.

Tanshi of the Jin dynasty was a native of Guanzhong; his family name has been lost to history. Toward the end of the reign of Emperor Dazhuan, he traveled to Liaodong and transmitted the teachings of the Triple Gem.
This marked the beginning of the circulation of Buddhism in Goguryeo. At the beginning of the Yixi era, he returned to Chang’an. Furthermore—
He greatly propagated the Buddhist teachings, and his fame resounded throughout the Three Commanderies. At first, when he walked through the mud with bare feet, they remained unstained;
thus he was called the "White-Footed Monk" (Bai-zu Heshang). There was a man named Wang Hu whose uncle had been dead for several years.

Suddenly, the uncle returned home and took Hu by the hand, leading him on a tour of the hells, where he exhorted him, saying, "You must serve the Arhat White-Footed. Upon returning, Hu searched everywhere to find him.
He served [the deity] in this manner, whereupon divine wonders became manifest. At the end of the Jin dynasty, the Xiongnu came from Shuofang and ravaged Guanzhong, killing many.
When they first encountered [Shi] Shi, their blades could not harm him. Helian Bobo marveled at this marvel and issued an amnesty, sparing the remaining śramaṇas from execution.
Shi had previously been dwelling in seclusion among the mountains and forests, practicing dhyāna and recitation; shortly thereafter, Tuoba Tao ruled Chang’an, while Ren Cui...
Inspired by the words of Kou Qianzhi, Tuoba Tao decided to execute all śramaṇas in order to sever their Dharma, so that they would no longer cause harm to the people.
Tao believed him; in the seventh year of Taiping, he dispatched troops to burn Buddhist monasteries, release the monks and nuns from the path, and arrest and execute those who fled.
The entire region was left empty. After some time, he finally realized they were capable of being transformed; thus, during Tao’s Great Assembly (Yuánhuì),...

He said, "Carrying my staff, I have arrived at the palace gate. The *wubo* (gatekeeper) reported, "A man of the Way has arrived. Daowen said, "Bring the executioner's blade quickly; let it fall so that it does not wound him.

When this was reported to Daowen, he became greatly enraged and drew his girdled sword, striking with all his might to cut him down, yet he could not cause even a wound; the sword left only a slight mark.

He was like a thread; when placed inside a tiger's cage, the tigers all crouched in fear, not daring even to blink. Daowen then invited him up to the hall, where he prostrated twice in repentance and apology.
Only then did [Seng]hao begin to preach the Dharma for him. Daowen felt such shame and remorse that he fell ill, while both [Seng]hao and [Seng]qian also suffered from malignant diseases.

Upon his death, Daōfēn, in a fit of rage, executed both families for their crimes. He then issued an edict to restore Buddhism. After Daōfēn died, his grandson Jūn succeeded him, and the Buddha-dharma flourished once more.
The beginning of this period is known, but its end remains unknown.
As for the Jin dynasty practitioner Beidu, his surname and given name were unknown, nor was it understood where he was from. When first seen in Jizhou, he appeared like one who is deranged;
he carried a wooden cup and would invariably ride upon it when crossing water, hence he was popularly known as Beidu (Cup-Crosser). He once sought lodging at the home of a wealthy man.
There was a golden image in a shrine, which he stole and departed with. Although horses pursued him as he walked slowly, they could not catch up with him.
He boarded a raft and crossed the Mengjin Ford, arriving at the capital. At that time he was about forty years old; his appearance was haggard and distressed, and his moods were inconsistent.

His speech was devoid of artifice or ornament. Even in the height of winter, he would pierce the ice to bathe; sometimes he would climb mountains wearing wooden clogs, or walk barefoot through the marketplace.
Carrying a single reed basket, he went to the śramaṇa Fayi at Yanxian Temple, where Fayi provided him with lodging.

He was particularly diligent. Suddenly he abandoned his practice and went to Guabù, intending to board a boat. Before the boatman could respond, he immediately boarded a bowl and reached the northern shore.
In a village at Kuānglíng, there was a man of the Lǐ family who was just then feeding monks; he crossed directly and entered, placing [the bowl] in the courtyard of the reed hut.
While he sat among the assembly, the crowd gazed at him with wide eyes. Fadu remained composed as before. Among those seated was one who grew angry.
Seeing that a reed basket was obstructing the path for people to pass, the Li family wished to move it; though they exerted great strength, they could not budge it.

When the meal was finished, Fadu lifted it up, departed with a smile, and called out, "Four Heavenly Kings! Four Heavenly Kings! Bless the house of the Lis! At that time, a young boy secretly looked inside the basket and saw four...
The children were all several inches tall, with eyebrows and eyes as if painted. Li was struck by this marvel and pursued them, but they vanished from sight.
After three more days, he saw them sitting beneath a dense tree on the western boundary; he prostrated himself and requested that they return home, where he served and attended to them.

They ate and drank without discrimination between various foods. Liu Boxing of Pei State, serving as the Governor of Yanzhou, dispatched a messenger to summon them; they carried a reed basket upon their backs.

He arrived at Boxing’s residence and was treated with great respect. Peering inside, he saw nothing but tattered rags and a wooden bowl. When they spoke, [Boxing] did not understand him, so he returned to the Li family estate.
One day, he suddenly asked for his *kāṣāya* robe; [Boxing] hurriedly prepared it for him, and he took it away. That night, a wondrous fragrance was perceived throughout the entire region.
At dawn, he went to search for him on the northern bank and found him lying stiff upon his mat, the *kāṣāya* still draped over him, while blue lotus flowers grew all around him. He shook him...
He passed away. A few days later, a person came from Pengcheng and said that he had seen the ferryman at the home of the white-robed Huang Xin.
Xin was faithful and devout, yet poor, eating only wheat porridge daily. The ferryman found it delicious and stayed for half a year.
Suddenly, he ordered Xin to prepare thirty-six reed baskets (*lu-chui*). Xin said, "I have only ten. The ferryman made him arrange them in the middle courtyard exactly according to that number.
Suddenly, gold and silk filled [the boat], totaling more than one million in value. He gave these to Xi and then departed.

He stayed at the home of Zhu Wenshu in the capital, where Wenshu bowed his head and begged for deliverance. Fudu did not answer. Wenshu said joyfully, "The silence of the Buddha-dharma is surely a sign of consent.
He also traveled through the Wu region, begging for fish from fishermen; when he obtained some that were emaciated, he threw them into the water, and they swam about alive.
He departed. On another day, he again begged for some fish, but the fisherman scolded him in anger and refused to give any. Huidu took two pebbles and threw them into the net;
suddenly, two oxen began fighting in the water, tearing the net apart, and the oxen vanished without a trace. He then traveled east to Mount Tiantai and later returned to the capital.
He visited the Śramaṇa Saṃghadatta at Changgan Temple. A Śramaṇa named Sengwu shared the same quarters as Datta;
once, while peering through a crack in the door, he saw Datta taking up a *kṣatriya* staff and playing with it. From this, Sengwu’s reverence for him increased.
Furthermore, there was one Zhang Nu who encountered Datta. Datta said, "I went east to see Cai Dun, south to inquire after Ma Sheng, and north to see Wang Nian."
"I was now intending to go to Bei-du, little expecting to recognize you here. Zhang Nu had composed a poem on a locust tree;
its diction was exceptionally brilliant and grand, and Za’s response was also worthy of admiration. When Bei-du saw Nu, he treated him as he had in his lifetime.
Furthermore, [Bei-du] stayed with the Chen family of Nanzhou. Some say there was another Bei-du in the capital. The five sons of the Chen family went to visit him.
What he saw was no different [from before], yet he remained in doubt. Thereupon, [Dao'an] set out honey, a knife, incense of *guggulu*, and hand-towels, leaving them before him.
His two younger brothers immediately returned home and saw what had been provided; it was exactly as it had been. They said to Chen, "The knife is dull; it should be sharpened.
Subsequently, those in the capital moved to Lingjiu Temple. Chen suddenly requested yellow paper.

Two scrolls. He composed a letter; though the characters were not fully formed, he joined the backs of the sheets together. When Chen asked the venerable man what kind of document this was, Du did not answer.
Zhu Lingqi of Wu Commandery was returning from Goryeo when his ship encountered a gale and was driven to an island. On the island there was a mountain, which was exceedingly high and large.
Following his intuition, he traveled some ten li and heard the sound of midday chanting. He entered a temple; the temple was made of the seven treasures.
The figures were all stone statues of monks. When someone called out to them as they were about to turn back, Lingqi bowed twice.
He received food that was fragrant and delicious, unlike anything found in the world. One person said, "From here it is more than two hundred thousand *li* to the capital.
Do you know the monk Beidu? Lingqi replied, "I know him. The man pointed to a bag on the northern wall and said, "His..."
He had a bowl with an ear-handle. He took it and gave it to him, placing a letter inside the box and saying, "When you see someone crossing [the river], you should hand this to him.
He also sent a single bamboo staff, instructing him to place it at the prow of the boat, saying, "You may reach Shitou in three days.
Upon arrival, he lost the bamboo staff. A short while later, the ferryman came to take the letter and received the bowl. He laughed loudly and said, "I have not seen this bowl for some time."
Four thousand years have passed. [He] threw [the staff] into the clouds and caught it again; furthermore, he wrote the six characters "Fúdé mén líng rén xiáng" (The Gate of Merit and Virtue:
A Spirit Descends) upon the door-panel of the Chen family and then crossed over, leaving no trace. In the capital, however, the practice still persists.

In a mountain village, there was a man named Yu Chang whose maidservant stole property and fled. Chang followed her tracks and questioned a ferryman. The ferryman pointed and said, "She died in Jinling."

By the riverbank, there was an empty tomb; he frequently hurried there to inspect it, and indeed, it was as he had suspected. Kong Sheng, a Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gate, fell ill and requested that Du perform a ritual for his crossing over [to the afterlife].
Du said, "He has already been harmed by a ghost; it cannot be done. Kong Sheng died shortly thereafter. Furthermore, there was Hu Shi, the wife of Qi Xie.

He was ill and requested Du Zhu to perform a rite for him. After the rite was performed, he recovered. He left ten thousand coins, entrusting them to Xie He to provide a meal for the monks before departing.
He passed away upon reaching Chishan Lake; this was the ninth month of the third year of the Yuanjia era. Xie He buried him on Fuzhou Mountain in Jianye.
On the eighth day of the third month of the fifth year, Du returned to Xie’s household accompanied by three gentlemen: Lü Daohui, Du Tianqi, and Shuiqiu Xi.

He was there. Upon seeing him, he was greatly startled and immediately prostrated himself twice. Sengdu said, "This year will be very inauspicious; you must cultivate meritorious deeds without hesitation.
The monk Fayi is a man of high virtue whom you may approach to avert calamity. Suddenly, a monk appeared above the lintel of the gate and called out to Du.
Du looked up at him and immediately took his leave.
Falarong of the Song dynasty was a native of Gaochang. His clan name has been lost to history. In his youth, he became a śramaṇa;
he was diligent and austere in his practice. His teacher, Fajin, also possessed lofty conduct. Once, while sitting in meditation with his door closed, Jìn suddenly saw Lang standing before him.

Jìn asked, "By what means have you come here? Lang replied, "I entered through the keyhole. He was then joined by several other monks. As midday approached, [Lang] requested that [Jìn] provide them with food.
Sengjin went forward to prepare a meal for him, but he heard only the sound of the spoon and bowl; at first, no person was visible. Sengjin was greatly surprised by this.
He used the *kāṣāya* robe presented to him by Huiyuan of Mount Lu as an undergarment. Daolang said, "The assembly of monks has set down their spoons and chopsticks and departed;
they shall come to take it back another day. Soon after, the cook was seen taking the *kāṣāya*. Sengjin joyfully handed it over to him. The next day...

When questioned, the cook had nothing to offer; he was, in fact, a manifested body (*nirmāṇakāya*). During the time when the Wei barbarians were destroying and diminishing the Buddha-dharma, Lang traveled west to Kucha.
The King of Kucha once prayed to the venerable ones of his kingdom, saying: "May one who has attained the Way arrive."
"Please report this to me; I wish to serve him. Lang reported this to the Honored One, who spoke to the King, saying, "The King’s Master honors him as a Buddha.

Shortly thereafter, he passed away while sitting in meditation. On the day of his cremation, springs gushed from between his two eyebrows and splashed into the air. The King collected the remains and erected a stone stupa for him in Kucha.
At that time, there was also a śramaṇa named Zhizheng in Liangzhou, who likewise possessed extraordinary conduct.

Sengcheng of the Shi clan, whose courtesy name was Huilan, was a native of Liquan during the Song dynasty. In his youth, he and Xuangao were both renowned for their practice of silent contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
While traveling through the Western Regions, he carried a Buddhist alms bowl upon his head. Upon reaching Kaśmīra, he sought instruction on the essentials of dhyāna from the bhikṣu Dharmada.
Dharmada once entered meditative absorption and ascended to Tuṣita Heaven to receive the precepts from Maitreya Bodhisattva; he subsequently transmitted these rules of discipline to Huilan. Huilan...

He returned to Khotan and conferred the precepts upon the bhikṣus there. Subsequently, he departed via Henan for Tuhu-yun, where Muye, the heir apparent of the Tu-yü-hun, and others paid him reverent homage.
He dispatched an envoy to establish Zuojun Temple in Shu to extend his influence. He also moved to Tiangong Temple on Mount Luofu.
Emperor Wen issued an imperial decree inviting him to the capital, where he transmitted the sublime meanings of the Dharma. After a long time, he passed away during the Shou era of the Daming period.
60. Shao Shi of the Song dynasty was a native of Kangju. He had a wide mouth and large eyes, and his appearance was like that of a madman. Wherever he went, children would treat him with contempt.
Occasionally, when he joined a group of drinkers entering the market to drink heavily, the drinkers would mostly push and shove him away.

When he went away, [the others] would simply give him drink without any dispute. However, whenever he saw a Buddha image, he would prostrate himself a hundred times, sighing with grief until tears flowed.
He fathered three sons and two daughters; the eldest son was named Huisheng and became a śramaṇa. Later, Shuo also became a śramaṇa and was styled Gong.
Whether it was night or day, he would go out for walking meditation whenever he felt the inclination to do so. He traveled through various counties in the Yizhou region.
He spoke of all matters with humorous wit, eliciting laughter from others while exhorting them toward goodness. Consequently, every household delighted in him.

If he were to wish for something and then lie down on the ground, that family would suffer the calamity of a death; if he begged for a fine mat and lay upon it, there would be the joy of a son being born.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, when the images were welcomed into Chengdu, Shi once crawled among the crowd and played with the lion puppet.
He manifested this as a personal response. On that same day, he was also seen in Pei County; it is said that he had divided his body.
Both the Provincial Governor Xiao Huikai and Liu Mengming served him with reverence. Once, Mengming sent two concubines dressed in men’s clothing to attend upon the Master.
The Master immediately composed verses in rhyme to dismiss them, saying: "I would rather beg for fine wine to pass the end of the year than..."
He was able to grow old as a husband. When the Senior Scribe Mengming’s friend, Shen Zhongyu, revised the regulations on the use of the whip and staff, he remarked:
"The world cries out in distress from this very practice. If these regulations were abolished, one might obtain the post of Regional Inspector.

Upon hearing this, Zhongyu removed them. When Mengming passed away, Zhongyu took charge of the affairs of the province. On the first day of the ninth month of the first year of the Yuanhui era, he spoke thus to Tong of Mount Min.
The śramaṇa Yún said, "When I die, my remains may be exposed beneath the pines; however, both feet must be provided with sandals.
Yún followed this advice and subsequently passed away. His corpse was carried out and exposed, but when they went to look at it the following day, it had vanished.
Shortly thereafter, someone arriving from Pí County said, "Yesterday I saw you walking through the marketplace; one foot was wearing a sandal. [Yún] said, "Tell Yún this for me."
The Duke said, "These young children have deceived me; they gave me only a single sandal. He went forward in surprise and questioned the śrāmaṇera.
The śrāmaṇera replied, "When we were carrying the corpse, one sandal fell off; we traveled so hurriedly that there was no time to re-tie it."
Qi Fekui was born into the Wan clan. A native of Yuqian in Wuxing, he served as a disciple to the Śramaṇa Zhiguan Fakai during his youth.
Fakai served as a teacher to Wang Xuan and Wang Su of Langya due to his mastery of the Way and its learning. As for Fekui’s character, he was reverent, sincere, and simple;

he spoke little, maintained his integrity, and did not associate with worldly people. He recited the *Lotus Sūtra*. There was a Dharma Master named Sheng at the monastery who was elderly and infirm; Fekui [tended to him].
He relied upon the protection of the guardian spirits. Having attained victory, he was buried according to the Dharma. A funeral monument was erected, and a sandalwood image was fashioned.

Once the image was completed, a great assembly was held to celebrate it. His family resided in the great marketplace of the capital city. On the day before his passing, he went to visit Dinglin Monastery, Zhizhi Garden, and all those in his household for a meal.
Upon returning, he closed his room, lay down, and passed away. His corpse was fragrant and soft; when two fingers were bent, [it returned to its original state].
Knowing that he had attained the fruit [of arhatship], Emperor Wu heard of it and went in person to offer condolences; Emperors Wenxuan and Wenhui accompanied him.
A stupa was erected at Zhiguan Monastery in the seventh year of the Yongming era.

Seng Huisheng of the Qi dynasty was of the Liu clan; his place of origin is unknown. He lived as a guest in Jingzhou for several decades, serving at Zheshan Temple, which had been established by Liu Lie of Nanyang.
He appeared to be about fifty or sixty years old. By nature he lacked dignified deportment. When he visited the homes of the sick, people would take his reaction as a prognostication:
if he became angry, the patient would surely die; if he showed joy, they would surely recover. Even when encountering people he had never met before, he behaved in this manner.

He would immediately know their kinship and manifest the details of their survival or demise. Once, he sought to cross a river from a ferry official, but the official declined on account of the boat being too small;

shortly thereafter, Hui was seen having already crossed and walking along the bank. At that time, Zhen Tian of Zhongshan and Che Tan of Nanping both invited Hui on the same day, and he went to attend them both.
Crown Prince Wenhui invited him to the capital, and upon passing by Baozhi, Baozhi patted his back.
He said, "The Red Dragon Son has nothing further to say. Upon returning to Jingzhou, he encountered Liu Jingrui, the Regional Inspector’s Chief Secretary, and suddenly began to wail in grief.
Shortly thereafter, Jingrui was indeed killed by the Provincial Governor. His final whereabouts remained unknown.
At that time, there was also a śramaṇa named Huiyuan in Changsha who possessed miraculous traces; it was said he could manifest multiple bodies to attend various invitations.
Qí Huītōng was a man of unknown origins. During the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty, he was seen in Shòuchūn wearing tattered clothes and sleeping in the open fields;
he called himself Zhèng Sànjì. His predictions of future events were all proven accurate. There was a man named Biān Sēngguī in Jānglíng who...
While traveling from Shangyu to Shouchun, he was about to return home when Tōng came to entrust him with some goods. The monk, fearing that his carrying pole would become too heavy, refused;

however, Tōng insisted on adding more, yet the monk’s pole did not feel heavier at all. After walking several li, Tōng took her leave and said, "I have an elder sister named Huìxù who lives at Sān céng Temple;
please convey my regards to her. Suddenly she vanished. When the monk looked back at the items entrusted to him, they were also gone. The monk returned home.
He was greatly astonished. Upon arriving, he sought out Huixu to question him. Huixu said, "I have no younger brother. He then went to seek out Sengtong but did not see him.
When Sengtong arrived in Jiangling, Huixu had also died. [Sengtong] entered his room to offer condolences and inquire in detail; consequently, he remained in Jiangling.
Whenever he saw the tombs of people's families, there were none that did not mention their clan names and the dates of their deaths. The people of Jiangling...
Everyone looked at one another in astonishment and wonder. At times, he would point from afar and describe the crimes of thieves and robbers;

consequently, when the bandits saw him, they would conceal their tracks and flee. Suddenly, he went to the home of Ren Yang and urgently demanded wine, saying, "I am traveling far away and shall not see you again.
To bid farewell to my spiritual friends, you should each strive with diligence to cultivate goodness. Having first drunk himself into intoxication, he lay down beneath a wall.
He thus underwent transformation. After several days, someone saw him again walking through the marketplace; they pursued him and conversed with him for a long time before he vanished.

Baozhi of the Liang dynasty was a man whose origins were unfathomable. During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, a woman of the Zhu family in Jinling heard the crying of a child within an eagle’s nest on the day of Shangsi.
She climbed the tree and retrieved it, raising it as her own son. His face was square and his complexion luminous.
He was as transparent as a mirror. His hands and feet were all webbed with bird-like claws. At the age of seven, he departed and became a novice under the great śramaṇa Sengjian at Mount Zhong.
Upon reaching adulthood, he shaved his head and devoted himself to the practice of dhyāna and contemplation; he would often sit for ten days at a time.

After a long period, he suddenly ceased to have a fixed residence, frequently traveling between Mount Wan and the Jianling range. He went about with hair unshorn and barefoot, wearing a brocade robe, and his eating and drinking were like those of ordinary men.
In his time, the common folk would constantly carry scissors, mirrors, silk, and other such items, leaning on staffs as they hurried through villages.

Children would clamor and chase after him; sometimes he would beg for a little wine, or at other times he would not eat for several days. Once, he asked a man who was eating minced fish for some of the same.
When the eater gave it to him, he felt a sense of revulsion and immediately spat it into the water, where it all turned into live fish that swam away. This happened from time to time.
He composed poems that were initially unintelligible, yet later all came to be verified. During the Jianyuan era, his miraculous traces became widely renowned.
Prime Minister Gao Song spoke of him to Emperor Wu, who received him with ceremonial rites from Mount Wan and welcomed him to the capital.

He was lodged in the residence of General of Chariots and Cavalry Chen, where the image of Avalokiteśvara spontaneously manifested itself, its face adorned with twelve heads. Its expression was both compassionate and majestic, so wondrous and beautiful that the entire city was captivated.
Huan Guan praised him. Later, the Emperor became incensed that he was deluding the masses and had him arrested and sent to the prison in Jiankang.
Yet, as he walked through the market streets, he did not change his demeanor in the slightest; those who were with him in the prison remained composed as usual.

One night, the official was sent to fetch food from outside the gate, and it so happened that Crown Prince Wenhui and Prince Jingling provided offerings by filling two carriages with rice served in golden bowls and sending them to Jiankang.
The Magistrate of Kang, Lü Wenxian, reported the matter to the Emperor. An imperial decree was issued to welcome him into the inner palace.
Shortly thereafter, another decree was issued to clear the inner quarters for a family banquet. The official was also dismissed from his post according to precedent.

Yet, the Emperor later saw the Master on Mount Jingyang leading seven bhikṣus in the performance of a ritual. Enraged, the Emperor ordered an investigation, but they could not find his whereabouts. The official replied, "The Master has departed."
"It has been a long time. He is currently in the Secretariat. When the official went to see him, the man’s body was like one smeared with ink. Upon hearing this, the Emperor was greatly shocked.
Chen Xian-da was stationed at Jiangzhou, and Yin Qizhi was accompanying the Grand Marshal; they went to take their leave of the Duke.
He drew a crow on a strip of paper and gave it to him, saying, "This may be used in times of urgency. When Xian-da rebelled, Qi-zhi fled.

Xian-da sent cavalry in pursuit; they were about to overtake him. Qi-zhi was in great distress. At that time, the evening light was fading into darkness, and the trees and forest were shrouded in deep shadow.
Seeing no one about, flocks of crows cawed upon him; he then thought of the painting bestowed upon him by the Duke the day before and intended to hide it in that place to avoid [the summons].
Later, when the Prince of Zhonglie of Poyang was dining with his younger brother, he placed a branch of *jīng* (hedge-hyssop) on the gate as he departed.

Shortly thereafter, the Emperor issued an edict appointing the Prince to govern Jingzhou. Hu Xie, the Commandant of the Imperial Guard, fell ill and sent a letter inviting him, the language of which was particularly earnest. The Master...
He inscribed the end of the book, saying: "The next day, the corpse indeed emerged.

The monk Fǎzhèng wished to offer his robes as a gift and sought them at both Longguāng and Jìbīn Monasteries, but they were nowhere to be found. [Fǎzhèng] said, "Last night he stayed here; at dawn he departed.
Lì Hòubó, with whom the Master was on intimate terms, also searched his home. Hòubó said, "Yesterday you came to my house..."
He was weary from walking the path and was lying down, having not yet risen. When those seeking him looked for him, he laughed and got up.
While at the Huālínyuán (Flower Grove Garden), he suddenly donned three layers of cloth caps, though it was unknown how he had obtained them.

Shortly thereafter, Emperor Wu passed away, followed by the deaths of Crown Prince Wénhuì and Prince Wénxiàn of Yùzhāng; from this point on, the Qi dynasty began its decline. [This occurred at] Língwèi Monastery.
The śramaṇa Bǎoliàng wished to offer the Master a monastic robe (*nàpì*), but before he could speak, the Master suddenly came forward, took the robe himself, and departed.

Zhòngxióng once asked the Master about the highest rank he had attained in his official career; the Master simply untied the left cord from the end of his staff, threw it to him, and said, "After Zhòngxióng."
He eventually rose to the rank of Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs. During the Yongming era, he resided in the Rear Hall of the Eastern Palace.

Every morning and evening when he entered or exited through the various gates, nothing unusual occurred. Toward the end of his life, he suddenly began to pull up his robes and run away, claiming that there was blood on the person at the gate.

Later, when the Western Capital (Xichang) executed Emperor Yulin and issued the initial order, they transported the corpse to the home of the former eunuch Xu Longju; this was where his ox-drawn carriage had been.

Blood from his neck flowed over, completely covering the threshold of the door. During the Jianwu era, Emperor Ming persecuted various students and men of high integrity; Jiang Bi was deeply distressed by this.

Prince Zilin of Nan’gang visited the Master to inquire about the fortune or misfortune of the public. The Master took a censer and overturned it, covering its ashes, and said: [The disaster shall not fall upon you].
"Everything will come to an end, everything will come to an end. Afterwards, it all happened exactly as he had said. When Xu Ling was a child, his father took him to see the Duke.

The Duke patted him and said, "He is a stone qilin from the heavens. When San Yan, a cavalry officer, plotted treason, the Duke saw him and brandished his hand like a halberd, shouting, "Do you intend to hack off my head and bore through my chest?
Yan broke into a cold sweat and did not dare look up. When the Liang dynasty received the abdication of the throne, Emperor Wu...

Previously, the imperial court had been overly restrictive; at this time, an edict was issued to release him. [The Emperor] once asked, "My disciple’s afflictions and delusions have not yet been eliminated;
how should they be treated? He replied, "In the twelve. He asked again, "What is the meaning of the twelve? He replied, "It lies within the time and measure of the strokes when writing characters.
He asked again, "When can one attain a pure mind for cultivation? He replied, "In the 'Peaceful Joy' (Anle) section of the *Jin* (Prohibitions). He asked again about the year.
Zu Yuanjin said, "Yuanjia, Yuanjia. The Emperor was delighted and considered that his reign would last twice as long as that of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty.
In the winter of the fifth year of Tianjian, there was a drought; although the ritual sacrifices for rain (*yujì*) were performed exhaustively, the rain did not fall.

Daoshi said to his attendants, "My illness has not improved, and I have come to the officials to beg for my life. If I do not submit this petition, the officials will surely suffer calamity. He then immediately submitted a memorial, wishing that—
At Huaguang Hall, he was invited to preach the Śrīmālā-sūtra to pray for rain. The Emperor immediately commanded the śramaṇa Fayun to lecture upon it; by the end of the night, snow fell.
Zhi also placed a knife across the surface of a water basin, and after a long while, rain fell. At first, the Emperor had been severe in his punishments.

The Master, employing supernatural powers, caused him to see the High Ancestor undergoing extreme suffering beneath the earth. From then on, the Emperor reduced his use of capital punishment. He then issued an edict for the court painter Zhang... [to paint the scene].

Zhang Sengyao was commissioned to paint the Duke’s portrait, but as soon as he set brush to canvas, he could not find his composure. He bowed his head in earnest supplication, and the Duke laughed, saying:

"Vipaśyin Buddha applied his mind long ago, yet until this very day you have still not attained the sublime. Once, when the Emperor happened to accompany the Duke to the riverbank, they gazed out across the water.
A creature was seen swimming upstream; the Duke raised his staff and beckoned it, and it followed the staff until it reached them—it was, in fact, [a dragon].
It was purple sandalwood. The Emperor issued an edict for the attendant Yu Shao to carve an image of the Master; it was completed in an instant, its expression appearing as if alive.

The Emperor was greatly pleased and placed it within the inner court for the perpetual blessing of his descendants through the generations. At that time, Master Yunguang of Fayun Temple was lecturing on the sutras, and the heavens rained down flowers.
The Emperor, considering this a sign of spiritual realization, burned incense and offered a petition at night in the Hanguang Hall, requesting an audience with him.

Zhi recorded that Yunguang invited the Four Elders of the Great Master (Fotuo Dashi) for a vegetarian feast. On the following day, Yunguang did not arrive. The Master had once listened to Fayun lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*;

when they reached the passage, "Suppose there were black winds," he asked, "Does the wind actually exist? Fayun replied, "According to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it exists; according to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it does not.
The Master said, "If its essence is merely provisionally existent, then even this [existence] cannot be understood, can it? Fayun remained silent.
However, when the Master himself presided as both host and guest, his arguments and refutations emerged like sharpened blades; not a single person in the assembly could follow them.

Once, when the Emperor was conversing at ease, he asked whether the dynasty’s mandate would face calamities. The Master pointed to his own throat and looked at him. During the rebellion of Hou Jing, people later reflected upon those words with great regret.
There was a monk named Yirou (Stonehead) who came to visit the Emperor while floating a cup; the Emperor was just then playing chess with a guest.
He composed a verse, saying: "I shall kill him. When the game of chess was finished, he asked where the monk was. The attendants reported, "Just now we received Your Majesty's command;
he has already been killed. The Emperor sighed in lamentation and questioned the Master. The Master said, "Your Majesty’s previous incarnation was an earthworm.
This monk was once a grass-cutter who mistakenly killed an earthworm; this is merely the repayment of that debt. In the thirteenth year of the Tianjian era, the Master moved to Huālín Garden.
The image was placed in his quarters. When the Emperor heard of this, he said, "Is the Great Master about to depart from me?
In the twelfth month of that year, he suddenly issued an order for string and wind instruments to be played day and night. On the sixth day, he passed away at Xinghuang Temple;

as he drew his last breath, he lit a single candle and entrusted it to Wu Qing, an attendant of the rear palace, to inform the Emperor. The Emperor sighed and said, "The Great Master will not remain with us any longer. [He then took] the candle...
"Is he entrusting me with his final affairs? The Emperor once visited Master Gong at Dinglin Temple on Mount Zhong and pointed to the Dulong Ridge ahead, saying, "This shall be my burial site;
it will ensure the longevity of my lineage. The Emperor asked, "Who shall obtain it? Zhi replied, "He who dies first shall have it.
Consequently, [the Emperor] exchanged one hundred and twenty thousand *jin* of gold for that land to bury him there. The Imperial Princess...
Princess Yongkang passed away. She bestowed all her bridal ornaments and jewelry as alms, and erected a five-story stupa upon her tomb, which was further crowned with a priceless precious pearl.
Furthermore, she established the Kaishan Vihara, and by imperial decree, Lu Chui composed an inscription to be placed within the tomb.
Wang Jun inscribed a stele at the temple gate, and his portrait was circulated everywhere. When the construction was completed, the Emperor visited the temple;

the Master suddenly appeared amidst the clouds, and the ten thousand people cheered with a roar that shook the mountains and valleys. By imperial decree, he was posthumously titled Great Master Guangji.
The beginning of the Master’s public manifestation was approximately fifty or sixty years ago, and even at his passing he did not appear aged. There was one Xu Qidao, who was ninety-three years old;
he claimed to be the younger brother of the Master’s maternal uncle and was four years younger than the Master. Calculating from the time of his own death, Xu Qidao must have been ninety-seven.

Liang Mingda, surnamed Kang, was a native of Kangju in the Western Regions. He entered the monastic order in his childhood, and upon receiving full ordination, his conduct became increasingly austere.

His side never touched the mat, and he took no more than one meal per day. At the beginning of the Tianjian era, when he arrived in the Yi region, the Man and Yi tribes of Ba and Xia were plundering and looting with impunity.
The regional and local authorities were about to mobilize troops to suppress them, but Mingda took pity on those being caught in the conflict.

He killed [the man] and then galloped to the rebels' camp to offer a plea for their surrender. Before the rebels had even understood his intent, a storm of wind, rain, thunder, and lightning suddenly broke out.
The rebels were terrified and begged him for mercy and rescue. Da ordered a thousand lamps to be arranged as an offering; immediately, it became bright and clear as before.

The rebels also withdrew and returned to their farming, while those traveling back and forth on official business no longer suffered from the calamities—all this was due to Da’s power. Once, while traveling, he encountered...

When he was binding a pig, the pig prostrated itself on the ground and spoke in human speech, saying, "I pray that the Supreme Sage will release my bonds. Da immediately stripped off his clothes to redeem it.
Furthermore, one night as they were returning from the fields, a disciple washed his feet with hot water, but the mud would not come off.
Da said, "This is fish grease; how can it be washed away with hot water? He then changed the water to plain water, and the mud came off immediately. They eventually arrived at Zizhou.

Suddenly, he made a vow to construct a vihāra, intending to relocate the stūpa to Mount Niutou. However, from the outset, he had never purchased timber and yet immediately sought out skilled craftsmen;
no one who heard of this failed to laugh at his audacity. At that time, it was the third month, and the Fei River was extremely low.
Soon after, he sent men to dig in the water and extract massive timbers to serve as pillars. In the fourth month, the waters rose in a great flood, and the timber was carried down by the river;
when it was retrieved, it was piled up like a mountain. Before long, the temple and the pagoda were completed together, their towering and magnificent splendor ranking foremost in the region.
A śramaṇa named Sengjiu had long suffered from a lameness and paralysis; he requested treatment from Fotudao, who gave him a staff and ordered him to walk.

He walked with quick steps; though he returned with nothing, he felt no distress. A thief peeked at his *poṣadha* robes and attempted to carry them over the wall, but was ultimately bewildered and did not know where to go.
Finally, [the monk] retrieved them from within the monastery, comforted the thief, and sent him on his way. Thereafter, he occupied a rope bed and entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Smoke and flames blazed forth; when the crowd rushed to extinguish them, there was in fact no fire at all. This was in the fifteenth year of the Tianjian era.
He passed away at Jiangling at the end of the twelfth month, at the age of fifty-five.
The Master Tan-te of the Northern Wei, also known as Hui-feng, was one who practiced "stamping and kicking" (a form of ascetic discipline) yet did not follow the restraints of the precepts;

his eating and drinking were identical to those of common worldly people. However, his speech and silence were unpredictable, and whenever he spoke of future events, they invariably came true. While residing in Wuwei, he was particularly wild and unrestrained.

He acted with unrestrained license. The Provincial Governor, Yuwen Zhonghe, welcomed him to his residence and toured the treasuries and stables, saying, "Why do you, sir, keep the property of another official?
Zhonghe angrily dismissed him and forbade him from re-entering the city. Not long after, Zhonghe defied imperial orders and refused to comply.
The Emperor dispatched Du Gu Xin with his own troops to capture him, and all of his possessions were confiscated.

As for his background: at that time, Emperor Wen of the Northern Zhou was serving as Chancellor and governing the state. Having heard of Tan Te’s extraordinary nature, he dispatched a letter summoning him.
Upon arriving at Qifu, he encountered Gao Huan’s invasion of Yubie. Tan Te remarked, "How could a dog ever pass through the Dragon Gate? Indeed, Gao Huan did not reach the Dragon Gate and retreated.
Later, when Hou Jing was about to rebel against Eastern Wei, Tan Te suddenly carved the head of a macaque on the tip of his staff.

He had the form of a monkey. He was constantly ordered to face west day and night to seize [the sun] as he traveled. He also requested a horned bow and pulled it along. After a short while, the solar halo descended.

Soon after, he rebelled and returned to the Liang dynasty. In the spring of the seventeenth year of the Datong era, he suddenly began wearing a cloth cap and entered and exited the Prime Minister’s residence.
His attendants asked him in astonishment about this, and Tan-te replied, "You all wear them; the King wears them too. This continued for three months.
When Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty passed away, he again wore a white silk cap. When his attendants questioned him about this, his response was as before.
Later, when his wife passed away, he again wore one; subsequently, when his second son, the Duke of Wuyi, passed away, the events were similarly presaged. Shortly thereafter, he fell ill and died.
During the Xiaochang era of the Northern Wei, the so-called "River Shaveling" (He Tushi) wandered through the marketplaces of Jinyang in the guise of a śramaṇa.

He was sometimes foolish and sometimes wise, such that he could not be fathomed or identified. People vied with one another to call him "River Shaveling," yet in the end, no one knew his surname, given name, or place of origin.
At that time, Emperor Shenwu of the Qi resided at his former palace, where Empress Dowager Wuming gave birth to Emperor Wenxuan.

During the Yangshi era, Empress Dowager’s family was extremely impoverished. One day, while speaking with her relatives, she remarked, "In this state, I fear nothing more than dying of cold and hunger.
Wenxuan had been in his swaddling clothes for only a few months; hearing these words, he immediately replied.
Because he spoke when he should not have spoken, they considered him a portentous child and were all greatly alarmed. It happened that they heard of the Shramana Tulu.

He insisted on inviting [the monk] to his presence and had him produce all the records from the time of Wenxiang of the Wei Yongxi era. He then questioned him extensively regarding future fortunes and ranks, yet [the monk] offered no predictions whatsoever.
Only when it came to Wenxuan did he raise his hand toward the heavens and do so repeatedly; clearly, his intention lay therein.
Venerable Lènnànméntí was a man from the Western Regions who resided at Yongning Monastery in Luoyang during that time. His learning was unfathomable.
Qímǔ Huáiwén was a man of ingenious intellect; whenever the state undertook the construction of palaces or the manufacture of implements, he was always consulted on their designs.

He had previously served as the Regional Inspector (Cishi) of Xìnzhōu, and upon his return, an imperial edict ordered the restoration of the monastery where Lènnànméntí resided. Consequently, [he] was able to...

He maintained a frequent correspondence with Tí. However, in his heart he knew that Tí possessed extraordinary arts; thus, he constantly presented him with gifts and offerings, hoping to receive some instruction.

Yet Tí treated him as if he were an ordinary person. Huáiwén harbored a private resentment toward him. During the height of the Rouran's power, whenever an envoy arrived, they would invariably lodge him at the Xuanwu Post Station.
There was one envoy who was particularly fond of Tí, and Tí was likewise exceedingly generous toward this envoy. Once, while riding on horseback...
They wore skins and visited him daily. They conversed using the language of the Yi people, yet he showed no sign of weariness. Huaiwen listened from the side, unable to understand anything.
He said to Zhiyi, "I have long been fond of the Buddha-dharma and am skilled in Confucian studies; furthermore, I am somewhat practiced in worldly arts and crafts.
Lately, I have shown my utmost respect in hopes that you, Master, would deign to lower yourself for me, yet you have never granted me the benefit of even a single word."
"These are merely the northern barbarians, what the ancients called the Xianyun. They have human faces but the hearts of beasts; they slaughter living beings and feast on blood.
Truly, what is there to speak of them? Yet you treat them with such intimacy. Tí said, "How can one be contemptuous of those who are evil?

Although the people of the Central Kingdom may read ten thousand scrolls of books, when compared for their actual abilities and knowledge, they will certainly not surpass them. Huáiwén said, "If that is so, I wish to calculate it."
Shu proposed a wager with him, betting on the horse he rode. It was then the seventh month, and the fruit was flourishing in abundance.
Ti immediately pointed to a jujube tree in the courtyard and said, "Regarding the fruit produced upon this tree, can you know its exact number?"
Huaiwen laughed and said, "How could this be mere arithmetic? I cannot know it. Tí said, "The Rouran know it.

Huaiwen still did not believe him, so he made a wager with the Rouran on a horse-racing contract, challenging him by saying, "You must know exactly how much of it is ripe, how much is unripe, how much has seeds, and how much is seedless. However—
The stake was subsequently determined according to the tally. The Rouran nodded in agreement;
he then drew from a leather pouch at his waist a device shaped like a scale-beam, strung with threads of five colors, which were in turn threaded with white pearls.

He used these to measure the tree’s height, its four sides, and its circumference. He stood for a long time, lingering as if engaged in calculation, until everything matched exactly what Huaiwen had required.
He first recorded the number [of trees] and sent someone to fell them all to verify [the count]. Indeed, it was not false; they were almost entirely gone, with nothing remaining.
In the end, he drove away the horses that had been wagered. One day, Ti sighed and said:

"I wish I could take the two mountains of Songgao and Shaoshi, use them as a pillow, and let the waters of the Luo River perhaps escape the toil of being harnessed for transport and felled for timber, so that every household might be provided for."
When there was sufficient firewood for the hearth, he would then release them to return home. This was indeed very easy within my own practice;
yet I fear that those in the world who are deluded, thinking they have personally realized sainthood, do not dare to do so.

One day, as he retired to his room for rest, a disciple happened to see him through a crack in the door, suspended in mid-air while holding his bedding. Thereupon, they informed one another and gathered to peer through the opening, where they heard him clearing his throat.
After a short while, he rose from his meditation seat and lay down as before. He called out, saying, "Why have you not come in?
I was merely finding my bed too hot and moving to another place to lie down; do not mistakenly take this for something strange. Not long after, he passed away.
As for the ācārya Zhōuxiāng, his origins were entirely unfathomable. At the beginning of the Liáng dynasty, he was seen at Fēifù Temple on Mount Qīngchéng in Yìzhōu.
According to custom, on the third day of the third month of the year, men and women would go there to enjoy themselves;

they invariably carried wine and meat into the mountains, becoming intoxicated and satiated as a source of pleasure. Although he repeatedly issued warnings and admonitions, they never listened. Later—
The Master had someone dig a pit one *fangzhang* (ten feet) square at another location while incense was being prepared.

When those who came for the excursion and appreciation had gathered as before, he said to them, "Donors, do you not think of the silence and stillness of the incense? Thereupon, the assembly collectively offered wine and meat, which were presented to him.
Whenever Xiang was served food, he would finish it all until the end of his meal; he never once set down a cup or chopsticks.

He received with his mouth and stored in his belly until he was so full that it was as if a great chasm were being filled. Onlookers marveled at this. At dusk, he looked to his disciples and said, "Support me, support me!
I am drunk and satiated, and I wish to vomit. He went to a pit to vomit so as not to soil the ground; as soon as he reached the pit, he vomited profusely, as if pouring out a vessel.
The chickens that had been slaughtered for meat flew away when they emerged; the sheep that had been slaughtered for meat ran off when they emerged.

When the wine and food were brought out, the water overflowed the pits, and fish, shrimp, geese, and ducks swam about in confusion. The multitude was consequently struck with terror and their spirits were moved with grief; they vowed to renounce the consumption of pungent roots and the taking of life.

The news spread throughout the four quarters as a means of both warning and encouragement. Before long, the Regional Inspector Luo Yan went to the capital for an audience with the Emperor. When Master Zhi asked Yan about the price of incense in Yizhou, Yan replied, "It is very cheap.

At first, he did not realize that the Master was referring to him. Zhi said: [...]* *Note: The source text provided here is incomplete, ending abruptly after the Master's response. The ellipsis indicates the missing portion of the narrative.*
"Since you have been despised by others, how can you remain here for long? Yan did not understand this at all.

Later, when he spoke of it to those of discernment, they said, "Could this not refer to the Venerable Master Xiang of Qingcheng? Yan then went into the mountains and related his experience to Master Xiang.
Xiang said, "You, a lay devotee, have come from afar; could your words be false? That very night, the disciples [of the deceased] finally passed away.
When they were preparing the tomb for the enshrouding, they found that his coffin was remarkably light. Surprised, they opened it to look inside and found nothing but his staff and sandals.
Whenever the monk Sengduo was seen in Yizhou, he appeared to be mad or deluded; yet his speech and gestures often contained prophecies.

The discerning among them gradually cautioned one another not to become familiar or disrespectful. While the Prince of Zhao was stationed in his fief, there was a man from [郫] County with whom he had previously been on intimate terms.
Later, due to a minor rift, he intended to raise troops in rebellion. Someone reported this situation to the king, but the king did not believe it.
Subsequently, that man led his troops to attack the king at the west of the city; the king likewise occupied a tower at the west of the city, protecting himself with three thousand cavalrymen.
Before the battle had even begun, the man was sitting cross-legged on a couch in the middle of the main street west of the city, directing his followers.
At that moment, Sengdu placed one boot upon his head, urinated from the western side of the city, and fled, discarding the boot beneath the Panṭa Stūpa.
The crowd marveled at this; even the man himself could not fathom it. He looked around for paper and brush to inquire about the omen, but Sengdu was already holding them.

He wrote the characters "zhòuduó" (周度) with brush and paper. The man rejoiced, saying, "Since that state has 'duó' (度) and I have received it, this is like choosing a day for a journey and finding it is a 'wǎngmíng' (往亡)—my going there will cause their death; its auspiciousness is evident. Shortly thereafter, King Zhao signaled his troops to advance.
In a single battle, [the enemy] was captured and killed, with over a thousand men slain. A *jingguan* (京觀) mound was constructed at Pandita.
Beneath the stupa, he then realized that the matter was indeed a manifestation [of his own karma]. "Pí" refers to leather; "pí" refers to leather footwear.
Footwear cannot be placed upon the head. That he now wears it is because this man has lost all reason and, conversely, has elevated what should be beneath him.
If he were to urinate while fleeing and discard his boots, these would both be signs of defilement, defeat, and the portents of death. As for...

The character for "Zhoudu" (the second character read with the *tu* and *ge* initials) is formed by reversing the order of its phonetic components; when sought through its phonetic analysis, it becomes the character for "beheading.
This precisely indicates that the person in question ought to be treated in such a manner. It may be said that this was verified without the slightest discrepancy.
After some time, someone reported this matter to the King, who dispatched messengers four times to summon him, but in the end he could not be found, and so the matter ceased.
Sengcheng of Zhou was the son of the Cheng family from Lingwu in Xianyang. Even as a child, his ambition was revealed when he would playfully heap sand into stupas;
yet, he remained entangled by worldly attachments. It was not until late in life that he took the tonsure, at which time he was already twenty-six years old.

Having found refuge under the guidance of Dharma Master Daoyuan, he subsequently had audiences with Emperor Xiaowen and repeatedly received the Emperor’s personal honors. Indeed, Master Yuan was truly a renowned master of the Wei dynasty. (Tahe)

Before he had yet reached Luoyang, he encountered the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati and received the teachings on dhyāna. Regarding the profound and esoteric mysteries, he possessed innate knowledge from his past lives.
Ratnamati marveled at him and would often say, "The study of the mind has flowed eastward; is this man not one who can reach its ultimate depths? During the Datong era, [he...]
When Emperor Zhou Zu was presiding over the hundred officials, he issued an edict stating: "The Master’s eyes are beautiful with double pupils, resembling those of Yu Shun;
his back is hunched and stooped, much like that of the Duke of Zhou. His moral character is pure and sublime, and the measure of his conduct is difficult to emulate.

His words are treasures for the age, and he is steadfast in his commitment to upholding the Dharma. Regarding matters of Buddhist practice that ought to be promoted and secular affairs that ought to be abolished, these shall be presented through formal memorials."

His administration was effective. At the beginning of the Baoding era, the Director of the Three Treasuries (Zhaoxuan) was summoned by imperial decree to be elevated to the rank of State Tripitaka Master.
Upon reaching the capital, he joined with more than fifty great virtuous monks from Jingzhou, Liangzhou, and Yizhou; they examined the subtle and profound essentials of the True Dharma together.

His responses were elegant and lucid, penetrating both the Northern and Southern traditions. He resolved hidden difficulties and revealed insights beyond the reach of ordinary sentiment; all were humbled by his vast erudition.
One day, he suddenly said to his disciples, "The main hall of a certain temple in Jiangnan is about to collapse and crush [the people inside].

You must quickly attend to the incense and lamps and recite the name of Avalokiteśvara to save it. At that time, several hundred monastics and laypeople from the capital of Yangdu were gathered in a lecture hall for a dharma assembly when they smelled a fragrance coming from the northeast and heard the sound of music; thereupon, they rushed toward the empty hall.

As he was about to emerge to listen, the hall collapsed along with him; fortunately, the assembly suffered no injury. On the eighteenth day of the seventh month in the third year, he passed away at Daizhuyuan Temple at the age of eighty-eight.
When the news of his death reached the Emperor, he was struck with profound grief and, on that very same day, [issued a decree].
He was interred outside the eastern city gate. An imperial decree was issued for the authorities to establish the Dafutiian Monastery and to depict his likeness upon its walls.
His disciples, including Tancheng and others, erected a stele at the tomb, with the text composed by Yi-cheng Gong Yu Xin.
Zhou Tanxiang was born into the Liang family of Liangtian in Yongzhou. He resided at Dafu Tian Monastery and was particularly close with the monk Sengshi.
He was intelligent and quick-witted; he could read seven lines of text at a single glance. Possessing great compassion, he was devoted to guiding and encouraging others.
Whenever he saw creatures in distress due to arrows, snares, or nets, he would request to take their place, ensuring they were set free before he would stop.
Shishi said to others: "I am far inferior to Tanxiang in many respects. Shishi once visited Xiang’s quarters at night;
they sat facing each other for some time without a single word of question or answer. Those who understood him knew that the Way was preserved in their silent gaze.

Whenever there were epidemics, droughts, floods, or military incursions, he would briefly mention them when questioned, yet his words could not be fully comprehended. By the time [the events] reached...
When examined at that time, it was indeed true. As for Li Shunxing and Qianglian, people considered Shunxing to be a "dragon in the womb" (a latent sage), while Qianglian was a secular immortal.
Shunxing’s nature was characterized by many desires, and Qianglian’s nature delighted in wandering; both were means by which they assisted the Buddha in propagating his transformation of the world.

When the Great Tang suppressed the Dharma, they retreated deeply into mountain valleys. At the beginning of the Kaihuang era, they were the first among the monastic community to shave their heads and emerge from among the common people.
In the second year [of the reign], on the eighth day of the fourth month, he passed away at Wei-yin. His portrait remains today in a Chan monastery in the capital.
At the time of his death, he left a final testament stating that he was now reborn in the West;
one named Hui-kuan, also known as Hui-duan, was the disciple who inherited his lineage. These matters are recorded in his separate biography.
Fahang was a *śiṣya* (disciple) of the Dharma Master [Seng]lun; the biography of Lun is found in a separate tradition.
Fahang had no fixed dwelling place, appearing sometimes in mountain valleys and sometimes in market towns. However, Qingxi was a place he frequented regularly.
One day, while traveling by way of Fuchuan, he ascended to its summit. Admiring the flowing springs and lush trees, he looked back at his disciples and said, "In ten years..."
Thereafter, a person of great merit and wisdom shall establish this site as a monastery; furthermore, when a wise man accomplishes [this task], his prior announcement will accord with that prophecy.
Moreover, he once stood at Dangyang holding a bamboo bow and shooting at the city wall. Subsequently, mountain bandits attacked and besieged the city.
However, he frequently predicted in advance the fortunes and misfortunes of the state. Emperor Xuan detested him and sent an envoy to summon him to the capital. [He] went...
He refused to comply with the command, saying, "I shall simply repay my life debt at this very spot; I have nowhere else to go.
Subsequently, an imperial envoy arrived and ordered that he be executed on the spot. As he faced his death, he recited a verse expressing the meaning that karmic retribution cannot be evaded;
the words and principles were all profoundly poignant. Most of them cannot be fully recorded here. After the execution, there was no blood, and soon thereafter, [the body] vanished.
Shi said: "The late Minister Yu of Tang stated that because his ancestors had continued the lineage, they had caused the killing of a sage; thus, their sin was grave.
He frequently visited the Sishang Mountain monastery to perform repentance on behalf of Emperor Xuan."
Fǎcōng of the Liáng dynasty was surnamed Méi. A native of Xīnyě in Nányáng, he entered the monastic order at the age of eight.

As he grew up and attained maturity, he practiced pure giving in succession, dedicating all his possessions toward the construction of a scripture repository containing over three thousand fascicles. Furthermore, regarding all discourses that could be propagated and extolled, he [promoted them].
There were none who did not gather [his disciples] to serve him. At the age of twenty-five, he traveled east to Mount Song and west to Mount Wudang, propagating the teachings wherever he went;
yet his sole pursuit was quietude and silence. He built a dwelling on Sangai Mountain in Xiangyang to provide a place for his lodging.

When Prince Jin’an, hearing of his reputation, came to visit him, his horses and riders attempted to advance but were forced to retreat. The Prince became enraged and ultimately turned back; that night, he experienced a sinister dream. Furthermore—
He went again at evening, but the men and horses were struck with terror as before. The King then purified himself and paid his utmost respects, arriving at the temple;
he saw only the mouth of the valley filled with a fierce, blazing fire. After a short while, waves surged up, and when the water subsided, the temple buildings finally became visible.
He then verified the facts of what had occurred: it was because Sengcong had just entered the meditative concentration of water and fire. Sengcong sat upon a rope bed, with [a monk] by his side.
Two tigers stood as if in attendance. When the King retreated and fled, Sengcong caused the tigers to bow their heads and close their eyes, then led the King forward.
He informed the King that his territory was plagued by many tigers. Sengcong entered a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and, in an instant, summoned seventeen large tigers.

He administered the precepts of taking refuge to them and bound them by oath not to harm or harass the common people. He further ordered his disciples to tie old pieces of cloth around the tigers' necks, setting a time for [their release].
He returned after seven days. On the very day appointed, when the King had prepared a vegetarian feast and the assembly had just gathered, a tiger also arrived in a pack.
[Tanchong] suddenly removed the cloth from its mouth and gave it food; from this point on, there was no further trouble from tigers.

While traveling with the King to the White Horse Spring (Baimaquan), a white tortoise emerged from the spring and took food from Tanchong’s hand. He said, "This is a male dragon. They also traveled to the Spirit Spring (Lingquan).
There were five-colored carp, which were said to be female dragons. On that day, the King bestowed great gifts upon him and departed.
To his left and right, there were several dozen men who were cruel and greedy; they plotted to plunder the bestowed goods at night, but a tiger roared and blocked their path.
He saw a giant leaning against a pine tree; the tree reached only to his knees. Holding a vajra, he appeared wrathful in countenance. The plotter was so terrified that he did not dare step forward;
he remained agitated until dawn, and it was only after noon that he was able to return. When the King questioned him about the reason, he told him the truth.
Thereupon, he memorialized the throne, and an imperial decree was issued to build Chanju Monastery to entice [the master]. Daecung, however, sent someone else in his stead.
He did not go there himself. Furthermore, by imperial decree, Xu Chi was ordered to go to that site to establish Lingquan Monastery. White deer and white sparrows came to dwell there.
Once, while walking through the fields, he encountered a butcher driving several hundred pigs toward the market.

Sengcong recited the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* three times, and the pigs all scattered and fled without exception. The butcher, enraged, was about to drive them back, but his hands and feet—as if—[became paralyzed].
As for the "Bondage," it cannot be moved. There was once a fisherman on the Han River who saw it; he recited [the mantra] three times as before, yet whenever he raised his net, he caught nothing.
During a prolonged drought in Jingzhou, a monk from Changsha Temple went to Sengcong to beg for rain; indeed, the rain fell in abundance.
An imperial edict summoned the Prince of Luling to the capital; however, he firmly declined and subsequently traveled to Mount Lu.

After the Prince of Weiwang, the General of the Flying Cavalry, had received the precepts, he wished to escort him back to the palace. [Hui]qian fled secretly to Xiangdong, where the Prince personally served him as his teacher.
He dispatched his trusted attendant, Chen Min, to convey his intent, saying to Min: "If he does not grant permission, you shall be punished. Having no other choice, [Min] returned with the message.
