Once, while visiting the capital region, he happened upon Qingxi. Jiang Lu, the Magistrate of Jiangling, came to him in the mountains and erected a lofty pavilion for him.
In the third year of the Taicheng era, the High Ancestor passed away and Prince Xiangdong took over the administration.

He converted the palace formerly occupied by the Emperor into a monastery, naming it Tiangong (Heavenly Palace), and invited Fayin to reside there. Furthermore, the Prince provided cypress wood sent from the governor of Baxia to construct the imperial bedchamber.

The Hall emitted light that pervaded the ten directions for many days. The King immediately ordered that the name of the monastery be changed to Baoguang (Jewel Light). He constructed a stupa, monastic quarters, and a lecture hall;
he donated his personal treasures to create a dew-receptacle (*lupan*) atop it. On days of leisure, the King would expound upon the meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā* there.
On the nights he expounded the meaning of the teachings, light would invariably radiate for several li. By the time of Emperor Xuan, his reverence was even greater;
in his final years, when he entered the dharma hall, he could not restrain himself from weeping profusely. In the ninth month of the fifth year of the Dading era, he passed away without illness.
He sat upright as if alive; his body remained supple and the crown of his head was warm. His fingers were curled into two. A rare fragrance lingered for an entire month. He was ninety-two years old.

The Great Being Chen Shanhui was born on the eighth day of the fifth month of the fourth year of the Jianwu era (497 CE) of the Xiao Qi dynasty, under the *dingchou* stem-branch combination, at the home of Fu Xuanci in Shuanglin Township, Yiwu County, Wuzhou. A divine light filled the room, and his features were extraordinary.
As he grew older, he was named Xi and styled Xuānfēng. At the age of sixteen, he took Liu Miaoguang as his wife, who gave birth to Pú.
He built [the temple] together with his two sons, Pu and Cheng; this was during the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty. At the age of twenty-four, he went fishing with his father at Jiting Bay.
Whenever his father caught something, he would immediately throw it back into the water. Although his father was angry, he took no heed of it.
The world regarded him as a fool. It happened that a monk arrived from India who said, "I am Sthūlakoṭīviśa;
let us visit him. He asked, "I and you made a vow together before the Buddha Vipaśyin. The robes and alms bowl in the Tuṣita Heaven remain even now.
On what day shall we return? Thereupon, they went together to the water’s edge to look into it, and they saw the reflection of the Great Being, his halo and jeweled canopy blazing with light.
However, he was fully endowed [with these qualities]. The Master smiled and said, "As long as sentient beings have not yet been delivered, why should I take pleasure in this?
Thereupon, he retired to the summit of Mount Song, where he sustained himself by farming with his own hands. He once spoke a verse: "Empty-handed, I grasp the hoe;
Walking, I ride a water buffalo. People pass over the bridge; The bridge flows, but the water does not. Or, when someone stole the plants he had cultivated, [he would say]: "Great..."
Whenever a man encountered him, he would immediately hide in the grass and cast him into a bamboo basket to be carried away. Once they were all gone, he would join others in manual labor;
at night, he traveled the roads. Śākyamuni, Suvarṇapuṣpa, and Dīpaṃkara—the three Tathāgatas—accompanied him on his rounds.

One day, while he was in meditative absorption, light appeared before him forming the characters of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*. In the second year of the Datong era, he sold his wife and children and obtained [the funds].
Fifty thousand coins were used to establish an unobstructed great assembly (*anavaraṇa-mahāpariṣad*). At that time, the Dharma Master Huìjí heard the teaching and attained realization;
he regarded the Great Being as an emanation of Maitreya. Fearing that this would delude the masses, the Great Being suddenly rebuked and stopped him.
On the twenty-eighth day of the first month of the sixth year, he dispatched his disciple Fù Yǎng to deliver a letter to Emperor Gāozǔ of the Liáng dynasty, which began: "The two *shāla* trees..."

"Regarding the lower [vehicle], there shall be liberation in the future. The Great Being of Good Wisdom addressed the World-Ruling Savior Bodhisattva: 'Now, I wish to set forth the superior, middling, and inferior excellences.

Those who are able to receive and uphold the superior excellence do so by taking a humble mind as the foundation, non-attachment as the principle, the absence of signs as the cause, and *nirvāṇa* as the fruit.
As for the middling excellence, it briefly takes the cultivation of the self as its foundation. [The text continues with "cultivating..."]
The state is the foundation. In both the heavens and the human realm, the retribution is peace and happiness.

Among those who are good, there are those who briefly provide for and protect sentient beings by excelling in non-violence and abandoning killing, so that all the common people may universally observe the six days of fasting.

Now, having heard that the Emperor honors the Dharma and desires to extend his discourse on its principles, yet has not yet fulfilled his aspirations, he has therefore dispatched his disciple Fu Yang to report this. Yang is currently the Director of the Grand Music Bureau.
He Chang submitted [the letter] for presentation. He Chang said, "Master Huìyuē, the National Teacher, still deigns to send a formal petition.
Since Xi is merely a subject and not a senior elder, he is by no means humble; how could I dare present it? Huìyuē burned his hand on the royal road to demonstrate his sincerity.
He Chang then hurried to Tongtai Monastery to consult Dharma Master Hào, who urged him to submit it immediately. On the twenty-first day of the second month.

He presented the book. When the Emperor read it, he immediately dispatched an imperial edict to welcome him. Upon his arrival, the Emperor asked, "Whom have you served as your teacher since you first came?
He replied, "I have come from nowhere; I have come from no place. My service to a teacher is likewise so. Prince Zhaoming asked, "Why does the Great Being not engage in the discussion of doctrine?
He replied, "That which the Bodhisattva speaks is neither long nor short, neither broad nor narrow, neither possessing limits nor—"
"Boundless. According to suchness and correct principle, what further words could there be? The Emperor asked again, "What is the ultimate truth? He replied, "Cessation, yet not extinction.
The Emperor said, "If it is cessation yet not extinction, then this must possess form. Because it possesses form, it is dull. If it is thus, the householder cannot escape the common world.
He replied, "When facing wealth, one does not seek gain through dishonest means; when facing peril, one does not seek escape through dishonest means. The Emperor said:
The Layman Da Shi bowed in greeting and said, "All dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent. The Emperor replied, "I respectfully receive the Layman’s teaching.
The Layman continued, "In the great trichiliocosm, all forms and phenomena do not fail to return to emptiness.

Just as the myriad rivers flow together but do not exceed the sea, so too the immeasurable wondrous dharmas do not transcend True Suchness (Tathatā). For what reason, O Tathāgata, [did you teach] within the three realms for ninety..."
Amidst the six realms of existence, he alone transcends them all; he regards all sentient beings as if they were his own infants, or even as himself.
In this world, nothing that is not the Way brings him peace, and nothing that is not in accordance with principle brings him joy. The Emperor remained silent. The Great Being took his leave.

On another day, the Emperor invited the Great Being to the Shouguang Hall to lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Great Being ascended the seat, took up the clapper, and chanted the scripture.
It consists of forty-nine verses. In the fifth year of the Datong era, he petitioned to donate his residence at the foot of Mount Song;
because of two twin *tao* trees, he founded a monastery named Shuanglin (Twin Forest). These trees were joined at the trunk and surrounded by auspicious mists, and a pair of cranes nested therein.
In the second year of the Taicheng era, the Great Being vowed not to eat, intending to offer his own body by cremation on the Buddha’s birthday.

On that day, more than sixty monastics and laypeople abstained from food in his stead, while three hundred people burned their bodies. They pierced their hearts and drained their blood, mixing it with incense, and entreated the Great Being to remain in the world.
Moved by compassion, the Great Being complied with their request. In the third year of the Chengsheng era, he again surrendered his family wealth for the sake of the assembly.
He was born. Making offerings to the Triple Gem, he spoke a verse, saying: "I relinquish all for the sake of the multitudes, to serve and honor the God among Gods.

I look up and pray for the rain of ambrosia to flow down and nourish all boundlessly. In the second year of the Tianjia era, the Great Being practiced the Way atop Mount Song, circumambulating a twin-trunked tree.
The Seven Buddhas followed him; Śākyamuni led the way from the front, and Vimalakīrti followed behind. Only Śākya...
The Venerable One frequently looked back at him and spoke with him, saying, "I am to be your successor. Suddenly, yellow clouds rose from the mountain, swirling like a canopy;
for this reason, it was named Mount Yellow Clouds (*Yunhuang Shan*). At that time, Dharma Master Huìhé passed away without illness, and Sengtou entered *nirvāṇa* at Lingyan Temple on Mount Ke.
The Great Being knew this in advance and said, "Master Seng is waiting for me in Tuṣita Heaven; he must certainly not [die yet]."
He remained for a long time. At that moment, the flowering trees on all four sides, which were just beginning to blossom and bear fruit, suddenly withered and became desolate.

On the twenty-fourth day of the fourth month of the first year of the Taian era (the Jichou year), he addressed the assembly, saying: "This body is utterly loathsome; it is a collection of manifold sufferings.

One must be cautious regarding the three karmas and diligently apply oneself to the six perfections. If one falls into hell, it will be extremely difficult to escape. One must constantly practice repentance."

He expressed regret. He further said, "After I have departed, you must not move my sleeping couch. Seven days from now, a venerable monk named Fa Meng will arrive carrying an image and a bell to establish them here.
When his disciples asked what should be done with his physical remains after his passing, he replied, "Burn them on the mountain peak."
He asked again, "If it does not succeed, what should be done? He replied, "Be careful not to enshroud him in a coffin. Instead, pile up bricks to construct an altar and place the corpse upon it.
Surround it with screens and cover it with crimson silk. Erect a stupa above, and place an image of Maitreya beneath it.
He asked again, "When all Buddhas enter nirvana, they always speak of their merits; may I hear of the master's own departure? He replied, "I..."
He has come from the fourth heaven (*Tuṣita*) for the sake of delivering you all and shall succeed Śākyamuni. If Pu-min (Pumen) is mentioned, it is Mañjuśrī;
Hui-ji (Huìjí) is Avalokiteśvara; and He-chang (Hécháng) is Ānanda. All of these have come together to assist me.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "There is a bodhisattva who comes from Tuṣita, whose faculties are sharp and keen, and who swiftly [attains] parinirvāṇa."
"If it is appropriate, then I am that very person. Having spoken these words, he sat in the lotus posture and passed away at the age of seventy-three.
Shortly thereafter, Master Xunmeng arrived with the fruit. He wove an image of Maitreya and left behind a nine-milk bell to serve as a guardian; both vanished in an instant.

The bodhisattva’s ritual implements, numbering more than ten, remain visible to this day. On the tenth day of the sixth month in the ninth year of the Tianfu era of the Jin dynasty, the year of Jiachen (904 CE)...

After seven days, King Qian dispatched an envoy to open the stupa and extract sixteen fragments of sacred bone, along with purple-gold relics and ritual implements, which were brought to Longshan south of the prefectural city to establish Longhua Temple, where they were enshrined. Furthermore, he fashioned an image using these sacred bones as the core.
*The Newly Compiled Classified Biographies of Monks of the Six Studies*, Scroll Twenty-Nine and Scroll Thirty.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Tanyu of Eastern Zhejiang.
Section on the Spiritual Transformations of Dingxue (2):
Tong Jin of the Sui Dynasty, surnamed Li, was a native of Mianzhou in Shu. He left the household life during the Zhou period and traveled about as a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*).
He traveled in all directions. However, he was dissolute and lacked propriety; he was addicted to drinking alcohol and would say to people, "This can be used to irrigate the Dharma-body.
During the campaign against Qi, an imperial edict required the procurement of toxic drugs, which were to be collected and prepared at places such as Jianzhou and Luzhou.

The method involved using dozens of ingredients, including the head of a viper (*fù*), *tiěxīng* (iron-ape), the root of *qín*, large bees, wild yam (*yěgě*), and the feathers of a poison-fowl (*zhèn*). These were fermented together in an iron vat.
Once it was completed, those who wished to approach were covered in skins and had their eyes shielded with glass;
otherwise, wherever the vapors reached, they would cause sores and even lead to death. If even a drop of the residue were to touch them, their flesh and sinews would instantly rot.
When Jin heard of this, he went directly to the prison. The wardens mocked him, saying, "If you can drink, you shall have a drink."
"Is this so? Jin laughed and said, "The ancients used five *dǒu* to dispel their drowsiness; asking for one *shēng* is not much.
The supervisor said, "Drink as much or as little as you wish; why discuss one *shēng*? Jin immediately took an iron ladle from within the jar, filled it once, and drank it.
His expression remained unchanged, and his joking conversation did not diminish from his usual state. The Daoist practitioners living nearby all...
The crowd gathered to observe and verify its transformation. Jin slowly raised a ladle to offer it cheerfully, but [the beast] recoiled in terror and ran away to hide.
Someone said to the supervisor, "You let him drink, and for that reason you have killed him. To kill a person is a crime; I am truly afraid for you.
Jin then looked back and said to the supervisor, "What crime have I committed? I merely wished to drink myself. Furthermore, it was not—"
"Who is it that you employ? What crime have you committed? Afterward, he remarked with wonder, "It is only today that I have finally attained a full intoxication.
He lay down upon a square stone, and shortly thereafter, he discharged urine; the stones upon which the urine fell all shattered. After a long while he awoke, his spirit and vigor as usual.

From then on, his food and drink increased twofold. At the beginning of the Sui dynasty, he was tonsured and ordained. He spent his final years traveling among monasteries at the age of ninety-something.
At the end, his clothing, bedding, and mats were permeated with the scent of incense and lacked the odor of wine.
Fǎjìn of the Sui dynasty was a native of Xīnfán in Shū. While living as a layman, he had long practiced the Way and maintained the precepts;

even while engaged in agricultural labor, he would strike his plowshare and mattock so that their sound resembled bells and chimes to regulate his recitations. He waited for the sun’s shadow to reach noon before eating, continuing his cultivation of the fields.
He was especially protective and sparing of insects and ants. Suddenly, a voice from the air said, "The time has come for Master Jin to leave the household life.
This occurred four or five times. People raised their voices and heard it. Thereupon, he went to a mountain pass and shaved his head to become a monk.

He practiced the dhūta austerities exclusively and did not register his name with any monastery. Prince Xiu of Shu dispatched the military aide Yu Jiulü Changxiang to lead ten officials and attendants to him.
Upon arriving at the mountain, they made their request. As they were about to depart, the King said, "If he does not come, you must apply the laws of the state.
The King further said, "There is no need for intimidation; simply extend an invitation with propriety. He will surely meet you tomorrow; do not delay.
When Changqing emerged from the city gate of Chengdu, he looked back at his ten companions and said, "Now that we have ascended to Tuṣita Heaven through our efforts, Maitreya may be reached."
How much more so for a solitary practitioner in the mountains! At dusk, they arrived at the foot of Mount Jiyang, where a tiger crouched by the roadside.
He shot at it, but his horse retreated in great fear. He immediately wished to stay overnight in a village house, but he hesitated because this would violate his agreement with the King.
Suddenly, a monk appeared carrying a bundle, intending to ascend the mountain. Changqing therefore left all his attendants behind and went alone with the monk to the temple. They proceeded...
When Jin summoned Changqing to enter and face the tiger he had previously seen, the tiger happened to be beneath the couch.

Changqing trembled with fear and did not dare to step forward. Jin perceived this and shouted at the tiger to leave; only then did Changqing advance. He reported his intentions to the King, yet his speech and countenance still lacked composure.
Jin laughed and said, "When you, Dānapati, first left the city gates, your heroic and magnificent bearing was certainly not like it is now."
This was extraordinary. Changqing prostrated himself but remained silent, not knowing how to respond. At dawn, he again sent Changqing back first to report on his progress;

by the time they reached Wangxiang Terrace, [the Master] had already arrived. They then went together to pay their respects to the King, for whom he conferred the precepts. Immediately thereafter, he took his leave and departed.

He offered a set of undergarments as a gift, but [the King] would not accept them. He immediately went to the Dharma Assembly Temple (Hozu-ji) and spoke to his attendants, saying, "When I saw Master Jin, I could not help but feel my spirit tremble with awe;
whenever I see him from afar, I invariably pay him homage. Master Jin often rebuked the King, saying, "The poor monk and Your Majesty each have our own ground of peace and happiness;
why do you trouble yourself to press and harass me? The other monks remonstrated with him, considering it improper.
[The Emperor] may frequently oppose the King. [Hui]jin said: "The Great Virtue fears death and seeks only to comply with and flatter the King's will.
How can this be considered propagating the Teaching? I shall certainly reprimand him for his transgressions; though I face death, I have nothing to fear.

He entered the palace precincts repeatedly, yet he declined all fine banquets and delicacies, contenting himself only with the comfort of a simple rope bed and the satisfaction of steamed cakes. Upon reaching—
When he bestowed the precepts upon the queens and concubines, he caused them to be free from negligence and to contemplate impermanence with great intensity.
At that time, there was not a single person among the commoners of the marketplace who did not go to him; such were the traces of his compassionate salvation through his emanations.

Initially, Jñānagarbha served as a teacher at the royal court and concurrently held monastic office, yet the administration of the state was exceptionally severe. Nevertheless, because of the King, the various monks...
Tongren (Huijing) went so far as to petition Daojin to request that Zangqiao be removed from his position. Daojin would not permit it, saying, "His nature is such; can he truly accept my words?

Although the assembly continued their pleas without ceasing, Daojin ultimately allowed Zang to remain in his office. When Zang came out to welcome him, Daojin suddenly said, "The Dharma-gate rests upon you, yet you have been too extreme.
Zang’s stern demeanor subsided. After returning to the mountains, some time passed before he went to a lay patron’s home for a meal. At the seat...
The Master suddenly burst into laughter. A fellow monk asked him the reason, and he replied, "I saw a temple attendant at a mountain monastery piercing a wall to steal honey;
that is why I laughed. He passed away during the Kaihuang era at the age of ninety-six.
Zhi Kuang of the Sui dynasty was surnamed Wang. His ancestors were originally from Taiyuan, but later his father moved from Xu to Jingzhou, where they subsequently registered their residence.
When his mother was pregnant with Kuang, she dreamed that a young boy riding a precious boat entered her embrace while she was bathing in water;
upon waking, he was born. From birth, he was quick-witted and wise, upright and principled, possessing a firm character. At the beginning of the Taiching era, successive disasters and chaos ensued.
Once, when he raised an army for an eastern expedition, he was renowned for his vast vigor and courage; yet when he responded to the call to join the ranks, he was captured and never recovered.

From this, he grew weary of the world’s falsehoods and completely renounced marriage. Initially intending to escape the secular life, he was enticed by those in head-cloth and coarse garments who spoke of immortals, saying:
"One must first receive talismans and registers, and subsequently present petitions and perform sacrificial rites. Kuang said: "If that were so, it might be possible."
"Is this the Way? He replied, "The registers (*lù*) are for protecting the body; the talismans (*zhāng*) are for summoning wealth. To have attained the Way is not yet the case.
Kuang asked, "I venture to ask how one attains the Way. Thereupon [the master] showed him the method of abstaining from grains (*pígù*).

He said, "If you can do this for even seven days, though you might ascend to the Jade Purity (*Yùqīng*) is possible. Thereupon, he did not eat for seven days, but there was no sign of efficacy. [The master] said, "You are still drinking water."
[He] heard [this]. He fasted for seven days by water, but there was no sign. [Kuang] said, "You were sleeping at night. He sat upright for seven days, yet again there was no sign.

Eventually he abandoned his practice and followed a śramaṇa to receive the five precepts, becoming a disciple of the Buddha; however, he practiced in secret and attained realization through hidden means, gradually manifesting miraculous powers.
Zhang Quan of Jiangling had been blind since birth; Kuang said to him, "Inside your family tomb, there is an ancient well..."
"The coffin has merely filled the opening. If you can now relocate it to its tomb so that the well may once again be used by people, you will have avoided disaster.
Following his words, it was indeed so. Furthermore, he said there was an ancient bell in the ravine that could be excavated; they dug it up and obtained the bell, proving him not mistaken.
The Regional Inspector of Renzhou considered this to be deluding the masses; he whipped his back a hundred times and imprisoned him. Yet, his skin did not appear bloodied and his flesh was not torn.
The jailer tried to fit him with eight-foot shackles and beat his knees, and those watching thought for certain that his bones would be shattered and his tendons severed;
yet when they felt him, there were no marks at all. The officials playfully cut off his food and provisions, and though it lasted a long time...
He never showed the appearance of hunger; yet he was frequently encountered in the marketplace, while remaining as if nothing were amiss even when imprisoned.

In the third year of the Dading era, he requested straw sandals from within the prison, saying, "Tonight I must travel with great haste. The officials and guards suspected him of attempting to escape.
At midnight, a fire broke out in the city; the common people fled in haste toward the city gates, but those who could not reach them in time perished.
There were seven thousand people. Kuang led two hundred prisoners along a mountain path; no one knew of it at all. Once they had been tonsured and ordained, Kuang was already forty years old.
He immediately began practicing *dhūta* austerities on Mount Sisheng to the north of the prefecture, saying, "This is a land of merit and should be a place established by the Son of Heaven.
Before long, offerings poured in like clouds, and suddenly a magnificent structure was completed—this is what exists today.
This is the Kai-ōji Temple. In the second year of the Shōmei era, both the Kyōhei and Sōrin Imperial Mausoleums were situated near the temple;

thus, its reputation as a site of merit and virtue was all the more firmly established. On one occasion, when the summer floods threatened, an empty boat on the opposite bank came to them of its own accord upon being called out, and they were thereby delivered.
The multitude marveled at this even further. Kō, however, cautioned them not to spread the story again. Later, when he renovated the Butsuseki-ji Temple in Seiyō, [the same thing occurred].
The temple had a draft ox that was about to give birth, but the calf could not come out. The mother cow was on the verge of death.

When the monastery administrator reported this to Daokuang, Daokuang said, "In a previous life, this calf was a lay devotee of this temple. It has come to repay its debt for stealing the property of the Sangha.
However, the reason its head extends and retracts without emerging is due to its sense of shame. Toward its mother, it harbors no intent to cause harm. Because of this...
Holding the incense burner, she stood at the railing; suddenly, a sense of reproach arose.

On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month of the twentieth year of the Kaihuang era, she passed away without illness at the age of seventy-five. At the time of her death, celestial fragrance filled her chamber and music resounded throughout the sky.
It was as if he were departing toward the southwest. Within two years of his passing, he frequently spoke of stomach pain and again predicted matters concerning his afterlife.
Suddenly, he asked the Vinaya Master, "Do those who have attained the stage of Anāgāmin suffer from illness? The Vinaya Master did not know how to answer;

[the Master] answered himself, saying, "It is the natural law of the retribution-body (*vipākakāya*). After he passed away, he bent three fingers of his hand. This was in the first year of the Renshou era.
The monk Fagui of Yongji Temple died and then revived, saying: "I saw King Yama when a palace of the *khang-seng* (vast vehicle) descended from the sky.
The sinners rejoiced, saying, 'A sage of the third fruit has come to save us! Thus, it is certain that Kuang had attained the third fruit."

The Chan Master Wuxiang of the Sui dynasty was a man of unknown origins. He suddenly appeared at Xiangsi Temple in Fuzhou, where he lived among the common monks, appearing no different from any ordinary monk.
The temple was situated on the southern bank of the Fu River; to its north, a cliff rose up like a screen.
Upon it was an inscription, carved upon a patch of ground measuring about five chi square, with characters roughly the size of a palm. Over time, the stone had peeled away.
The inscription was eroded and blurred, such that it could not be recognized; moreover, no one knew the number of characters. Below this were two marks of the Buddha’s footprints, nine chi apart.
Each footprint was approximately three chi in length. Those who take pleasure in such things would invariably seek out Ji’an to view them when they visited the temple.
One day, although Wuxiang had already crossed over with the crowd, the multitude suddenly turned back first, leaving Wuxiang behind. Thus, Wuxiang—
I wandered alone, gazing back until my interest was exhausted, wishing to catch the boat that had turned back, but it was already too late.
Without any apparent reason, he placed his alms bowl in the water and said to me playfully, "Why do you trouble yourself? I have been carrying you for a long time."
"You may now cross the water yourself as well. He then took a leaf from a plantain tree and floated it upon the water;

he stood upon it to cross, followed by his bowl. If there were anything that could have caused him to sink, in an instant he reached the southern bank and departed, with no one knowing where he had gone.
Fǎ'ān of the Sui dynasty was surnamed Péng. A native of Chūgū in Āndìng, he entered the monastic life in his youth and resided at the Jiǔlǒng Vihāra on Mount Tàibái.
Wearing coarse garments and eating simple food, he devoted himself to the practice of dhyāna, intending to do so for the remainder of his life.

During the Kāihuáng era, he traveled to Jiāngdū to pay his respects to Emperor Yáng, who was then stationed there as the Prince of Jìn. However, the gatekeeper, because of his short stature and humble appearance, did not [allow him entry].

Tong’an arrived at the gate. Although the King used metaphors to dismiss him, he was unwilling to leave. When the King heard of this, he summoned him for an audience; they regarded each other as old acquaintances.
The King immediately appointed him to reside at Huiri Temple and always accompanied him wherever he traveled. Once, while traveling to Mount Tai, they encountered thirst and exhaustion.
Looking in all directions, there was only a rocky cliff from which it seemed impossible to obtain water. Tong’an drew his knife and pierced the rock; water gushed forth in torrents. The King—
He marveled greatly and asked, "By whose power has An arrived here? An replied, "It is by the power of Your Highness’s merit.
They then entered the desert and reached the muddy sea; all the calamities they encountered were averted so that they suffered no harm, thanks entirely to An.

Just as they were about to pass through Shentong Temple and enter the valley, they first saw a monk riding a white donkey approaching. The King asked, "Who is this man? An replied, "This is Master Lang."
"Because Your Highness intends to construct [a temple], we have come to welcome you. Shortly thereafter, a monk arrived carrying a sealed letter and requested that Dao’an deliver it to the donor.
Upon reaching the temple, he saw a divine being sitting upon the *chīwén* (ornamental ridge-end) of the lecture hall, looking down at the crowds of people passing by.
The King asked who he was, and Dao’an replied, "This is the deity of Mount Taibai; he is one who follows Your Highness."
Other matters are not recorded here in full. At the beginning of the Daye era, the Emperor was particularly devoted to luxury and extravagance, and he held Seng’an in even higher esteem.
Consequently, he ordered An to summon all the hidden recluses—such as Guo Zhibian, Shi Zhigong, Sengcheng, and Beidu—to Huiri Monastery.
Furthermore, he established the Baoyang Daochang in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang) and assembled over two thousand practitioners of the Way and the arts within it.
He practiced the Way for eleven years. In the spring of the eleventh year, when difficulties arose in all directions, Dao’an finally passed away without illness at the age of ninety-eight.
Before his death, he had secretly informed the Emperor in advance of future calamities and failures; therefore, when the Emperor faced these crises, he was able to remain without fear.
During the final years of the Chen dynasty, there was one Fa-ji who was then gaining renown in the southern regions until he received imperial favor under the Sui.

He was peerless in his encounter with the world; yet he was diligent and possessed few desires, such that none among his peers could rival him. He frequently stayed overnight within the imperial palace, yet never once was seen to exhibit a dejected countenance or seductive demeanor.
Emperor Wen established Xiangtai Temple in Chang’an, and Emperor Yang established Longtian Daochang in the Eastern Capital (Luoyang).
One [temple] was for the purpose of providing relief and provisions, while Jie [the other] resided within the palace. Jie once rode a white horse that had been bestowed upon him by the Emperor.

Sometimes he would announce that someone was ill; when they were given consecrated water to drink, they were immediately cured. He could also exorcise malevolent spirits and speak of events before they had occurred.

In the fourth year of the Daye era, he suddenly came to the Emperor to take his leave, saying, "The Mandate of Heaven is not constant; I must return to a future life. I only wish that you will extensively protect and sustain all living beings.
Thereupon, he sat upright and passed away. When his hair was being shaved off for the funeral shroud, in an instant, hair grew back, reaching a length of about half a foot.
It was about one cun [in height]. The Emperor said, "The Chan Master has entered the samādhi of cessation; how can he be buried? We shall strike the great bell for over a month to bring him out.
Thereafter, the court sessions were suspended, and he was buried in Jiangzhou in plain dress. At every location reached along the way, vegetarian feasts were held.

The expenses were borne by the government offices. For the dukes and nobles below the rank of Prince of the Eastern Capital, forty thousand large banners were produced, and one hundred monks were provided with daily vegetarian feasts;
each monk was given twenty-five bolts of silk as an offering. Calculating this across the full seven weeks, the total expenditure reached over one million coins. Oh, how magnificent!
The Dharma Master Cen of the Sui dynasty resided at Chanju Temple in Xiangzhou. The temple was situated amidst mountain thickets and marshes where grain provisions were insufficient.
Every day, he would go into the city with a ceramic jar to beg for wine; he would drink from it on the spot until the jar, which could hold about three *dǒu*, was empty.

He would then beg for another jar and return home, drinking as he walked. By the time he reached the temple, the jar would already be exhausted. Rising in the morning to break his fast, he would thus take the jar with him.

The kitchen prepared gruel, which he carried on a staff as he proceeded to the hall. There, he set down the vessel, cast off his staff, and struck the heads of the monks, starting from the highest-ranking and moving downward.
Each monk received one blow; the assembly believed that by being struck in this manner, calamities could be dispersed. Thus, they accepted it without protest.
In his room, Cen kept a brindled dog, along with several thousand rats within the monastery. Whenever gruel was served, Cen never [failed to partake].
This was a song. [Hui]cen used all [the food] to feed his dogs and rats. Consequently, the dogs and rats increased in number until they crowded the courtyard.

Once, by chance, he lost a rat. Cen felt deep sorrow and lamented, rebuking the dog. The dog suddenly gnawed a dead rat and brought it to him. Cen looked at it with great resentment and beat the dog with a staff.
He buried the rat and wailed so bitterly that he could not control himself. Sometimes a rat would gnaw at the monk’s robes or his chest, and the monk would report it to him.
Cen then summoned all the rats and made them vouch for one another. Those who had no one to vouch for him, Cen would immediately beat, saying, "Why have you been disturbing things?

The rats finally submitted and did not dare move. Because the monastery’s permanent provisions were exhausted, Cen subsequently planned to relocate the kitchen, storehouse, and granary to the marsh below the White Horse Spring; however, at that time the water was overflowing, and the crowd laughed in secret.

When he summoned craftsmen to fell timber for construction, that site suddenly became level ground, and the buildings were completed in an instant. Subsequently, the temple indeed flourished and prospered.
It is further said: "Sixty years hence, a foolish man shall erect a multi-storied pavilion in the southern corner of the temple, thereby causing the temple to incur litigation.
This prediction was fulfilled during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty with the record of the pavilion's construction.
Fǎxǐ of the Sui dynasty was a native of Nánhǎi. His physical appearance was plain and unattractive, and he was about forty years of age.
The elders all claimed to have seen him as a child; his complexion had not changed at all from what it was then, leading some to believe he was already three hundred years old.

He also frequently said of himself that he had known Dharma Master Huiyuan at Mount Lu in the past; moreover, when discussing matters of the Jin and Song dynasties, his descriptions were as vivid as if they had occurred only two nights prior.
He remained silent in ordinary circumstances, yet whenever he encountered someone, he would invariably mock and deride them.

However, his words and intentions often struck directly at future fortunes and calamities; consequently, those who were self-composed and dignified did not like to see him. At that time, Chen Youguo was one day riding a horse...
Jing was the Prefect of Guangzhou. Whenever he traveled through the provinces on official circuit, he invariably led tens of thousands of armored troops to display his majesty along the frontiers.
Upon first assuming office, he joyfully proceeded directly to the administrative hall, where he drew the head of a horse on the ground to show his son before departing.

Not long after, Jing died and was falsely accused by others of plotting treason against the Emperor. The Emperor dispatched the Marquis of Linru to observe the situation, who reported: "He has indeed rebelled."
He was executed immediately; had it not been so, he would simply have replaced him. Lord Chen of Linru took advantage of his lack of vigilance to execute him and seize the throne.
Emperor Yang’s temple heard of this anomaly and issued an edict for him to come to the imperial residence.

At that time, a new palace had recently been completed at Jiangdu, and upon joyfully ascending the steps, he looked around and suddenly retreated, crying out, "I nearly crushed to death! That very night, a torrential rain fell, the roof collapsed, and several people were killed.
Later, he again traveled throughout the palace, searching for the heads of sheep. The Emperor detested this and issued an edict to lock him up in a single room.

After several days, the officers and soldiers of the Three Guards saw him in the marketplace; he was as relaxed and composed as usual. Someone reported this at the time, and the Emperor ordered an inspection and questioned the guards, but they all claimed there was nothing amiss.
When the door was opened and the interior of the room was searched, a *kāṣāya* robe was found covering a white skeleton.

His neck bones remained bound by shackles as before. The Emperor’s suspicion and astonishment increased further; he again summoned the Regional Administrator Wang Heng to investigate, and the report proved true.
Thereupon, the Emperor began to feel reverence and trepidation, exclaiming, "The sage’s spiritual transformations are boundless; how could he possibly be encountered through worldly means?
It happened that the guards reported that Xī was approaching the Emperor's presence. The Emperor immediately issued an edict to break the shackles, remove the door bolts, and release him.

Shortly thereafter, he fell ill and took his own life by removing his mats and bedding, lying askew upon a wooden plank bed while placing burning charcoal beneath it until half his body was scorched and rotted away;
he died after several days. He was buried beside Xiangshan Temple. Four years later, Huixi was released from captivity and returned to the South Seas, whereupon he submitted a memorial of thanks.
An imperial decree ordered his coffin to be opened, but it was empty.
Fú Pǔ'ān, surnamed Guō, was a native of Jìngzhào Jīngyáng. In his youth, he followed Master Yuán to renounce the householder’s life;
later, he joined Master Āi, through whom he mastered the *Sanlùn* (Three Treatises). Nevertheless, he always took the *Huáyán* as his primary practice.

When Emperor Wǔ suppressed the Dharma, he withdrew to live on the western slope of Gěngzǐ Valley in Zhōngnán Mountain. At that time, there was Master Jìngyuān, with whom he resided together and from whom he received support.

He penetrated and elucidated the profound mysteries of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Furthermore, he practiced asceticism with such selfless devotion for the sake of others that, on a small scale, he would expose his body to feed mosquitoes and gadflies, and on a large scale, he would surrender his life to nourish jackals and tigers.
All these acts of injury to himself were brought about by the permeation of his compassion and the resonance of his pity, undertaken to fulfill his original vow.
Whenever he went among herds of wild beasts, he was nearly devoured by them; yet he also gathered those who had sought refuge from danger.

The monks, fearing no public execution despite violating the state’s strict edicts, personally practiced begging for alms; thus, their food and clothing became abundant, and their diligence was twice that of usual times.
Some plotted to seize An and hand him over to the authorities in hopes of receiving rewards, but An went to them and said:
"You are so poor; I shall certainly provide for your welfare. Consequently, they entered the capital together and submitted a petition. By imperial decree, he was released.
[The Emperor] considered that a practitioner of the Way ought to find refuge in the mountains, yet he had instead been detained here;
this was as if forcing him to have no place to escape death. Liu Baizhe and Sengkuai were particularly cruel; when the order arrived for An to be arrested, Baizhe declined to comply.
I ventured to visit him. Upon my release and return, I passed by Master Jing’ai at the residence of Du Yingshi in Yigu Valley.
It happened that Yingshi had excavated a cave to hide Jing’ai, so I was able to pay my private respects to him there. Jing’ai sighed and said, "Master An’s spirit and resolve are beyond compare;

his refusal to avoid those who are powerful or oppressive is truly difficult to emulate. An then invited Jing’ai to return with him. When the Sui dynasty rose like a dragon, [the Master]... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. This translation reflects the available portion.)
The Emperor issued another decree, summoning more than thirty monks from the Bianzi Valley to reside together in the state temple. Only Dao’an remained steadfast and did not move.
Later, someone carved a niche and constructed a hermitage by the confluence of the streams in the Ziwu and Hulín Valleys to welcome him.
Just as he was about to enter, a large rock above collapsed; its momentum was directly upon the niche. Dao’an silently recited: "If..."
When he moved slightly to another location, it was as if his wishes were fulfilled. The rock then responded by shifting its position elsewhere.

An said, "This is the power of the *Avataṃsaka*. A villager named Sotuo lived to the left of the stream; out of jealousy toward An’s virtue and harboring resentment, he went with two companions and drew their bows to shoot at him.

However, they were unable to release their arrows. Their eyes bulged and their tongues became stiff; their voices shook and their complexions turned pale. They stood paralyzed through the night, unable to leave the village.
Li bowed his head and requested, saying, "The power that brings about this salvation and peace is that of the *Avataṃsaka*. How could I have known it myself?
In Weicun, Zhang Hui used a five-sheng jar to steal the oil for the Buddha statue at night; when he reached the gate, he fell into a stupor as if someone had bound and fettered him.
Dao'an also said it was due to the power of the *Avataṃsaka*. As for Minister Zhang, who had stolen money, his affliction of muteness vanished after he performed repentance.
When Cheng Huohe was already dead, he was called by name and revived. An old woman of the Bai village suffered from a loss of speech for a hundred days;
when Dao’an arrived, she rose to welcome him and conversed as usual. At that time, Tian Yisheng encountered Dao’an while providing alms for a poor girl.
She gathered two feet of coarse cloth and more than ten grains of rice and millet; by offering these as alms, she attained deliverance and became a nun.
Once, when three pigs were bound for slaughter, Dao’an paid ten times their original price for them, and furthermore, she cut flesh from her own thigh to ransom them.
Consequently, for fifty *li* outside the southern and western suburbs of Chang’an, chickens and pigs were kept in pens, yet families observed the precepts of fasting;
was this not all due to the power of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*? In the eighth year of the Kaihuang era, an imperial edict appointed him as the tutor to the Crown Prince.

The Princess of Chang’an established Jingfa Chan Temple and again by imperial decree he resided there. On the eleventh month of the fifth year of the Daye era, he passed away at Jingfa Temple at the age of... [years].

80. At the end of the Southern Pagoda, by the side of Xiangsi Temple, there was the Master Qin of the Sui dynasty, whose origins were unknown. At the beginning of the Daye era, he was seen in Guangping; his physical appearance and spirit were unlike anything recognized in the world.
He would sometimes remain silent and sometimes speak, having no fixed time for these acts. Upon reaching Luozhou, Lingtong Temple was then constructing a five-story pagoda.
The tiers were all constructed of glazed tiles. They were polished, carved, and inlaid, striving for the utmost grandeur and splendor.
The labor was immense and the expenses extravagant. Qínwàng looked on with a smile and said to the temple monks, "Why bother building this beacon tower?"
How could it be that such things are necessarily so by virtue of merit and Buddhist affairs? If that were the case, what room would there be for the path of pure quiescence?
At that time, his contemporaries all took offense at his words, saying, "That madman is not worth taking seriously.
Within nine years, bandits rose up on all sides and the government troops maintained strict vigilance; before the stupa was even finished, watchtowers were already being constructed upon it.
Fire! Alas, the principles governing order and chaos are suspended from Heaven; those of supreme virtue know them.
Once, while the youth Ma Shida was playing with a group of common children in the marketplace, he happened to see Qin suddenly transform his body and enter a pigsty.
The piglets immediately mingled with him as if he were one of their own kind. Thereupon, Shida and the others remained there to observe him.
He stood by for a long while, wishing to see whether he would regain his human form. Suddenly, Qin let out a great cry from behind the group of children, saying, "What do you all intend to look at?
The children were instantly startled and prostrated themselves. The world fell into great chaos, and Qin’s voice and traces likewise vanished.
Senglang, also known as Falang, was the son of the Xu family of Nanyang. When he was over twenty years old, he earnestly sought ordination.

He had no fixed place of residence and frequently appeared and disappeared in Ezhou. His appearance was extraordinary and ancient; his eating and drinking were no different from those of ordinary people.

He was always accompanied by two large monkeys, one yellow and one red, as well as a dog. When it was time for his midday meal, he would receive food in an alms bowl and eat from it, giving the leftovers to the monkeys and the dog.
Once the monkeys and the dog had finished eating together, the monkey would place the bowl on its head and ride upon the dog, leading them forward with a bright and cheerful gait.
