He paid his respects. The elder said, "Have you not brought with you the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*?

The sentient beings of this land have committed much sinful defilement, and even those among them who have left the household life are no different. This is a secret method for sincerely invoking blessings to extinguish obstacles;
if you do not bring it, what benefit is there in your coming? Even if you were to see Mañjuśrī himself, you would not recognize him. If you can go back and retrieve it, then..."
This is to universally honor all the sages, extensively benefit all classes of beings, and repay the kindness of all Buddhas.
When the scripture arrived, the disciple showed the Master the place where Mañjuśrī was located; Li, hearing this, was so overcome with joy that he could not contain himself.

Just as he was about to wipe away his tears and prostrate in thanks, in the brief blink of an eye, the old man suddenly vanished. Li’s devotion increased manifold, and for a long time he remained profoundly reverent as he honored it.
When the scripture arrived, an imperial edict was issued for Du Xingyi, the Director of Guests at the Honglu Temple, and the Tripiṭaka Master Rizi to translate it at the Inner Court of the Daochang.
Thirty rolls of fine silk were provided as offerings, and the Emperor personally retained the scripture within the palace.

Lìlì wept and said, "The reason I did not shrink from the journey back and forth was solely because I wished to benefit all beings. Moved by his sincere devotion, the Emperor returned the Sanskrit manuscript to him.
Lì sought out the śramaṇa Shùnzhēn and retranslated [the text] at Xìmíng Sī; it differs slightly from the version translated by Du Lìng.

Li’s ultimate end was unknown; some say he took the Sanskrit manuscript and hid it within the Vajra Cave in the mountains, where a stūpa still exists today on Longshǒu Gāng in Yǒngxīng. During the Dàlì era, the śramaṇa of Yúnfēng Sī on Mount Nán...
The monk Fazhao entered the palace to pay homage at the Vajra Cave. When night fell, he began to reproach himself, intending to throw himself against a rock to die in his quest for his vow.
Suddenly, he saw a monk about seven chi tall, whose Brahma-voice was resonant and flowing; this was none other than Buddhatārali.
He asked Fazhao, "Is it not exhausting for you, Master, to act in such a manner? Furthermore, what do you hope for? Fazhao replied, "I hope to see..."
Mañjuśrī, while he was removing his sandals upon a stone slab, in the blink of an eye he had already entered a monastery.

Its name was written as "Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Monastery"; the calligraphy was forceful and vigorous, its radiance dazzling the eyes. The courtyard was adorned with various extraordinary treasures beyond description;
the towers and pavilions were layered and the halls and buildings stood side by side, numbering some two hundred. Within them were stored and sealed all the secret sūtras.
His physical presence was magnificent and imposing, such as rarely seen before. As the Great Sage occupied his exalted position, his attendants gathered from all directions in great numbers.

He spoke words of comfort and encouragement to them. After distributing tea and assigning food, he commanded Zhilong (Zhao) to lead the way out. Fotiao (Zhaodao) requested to remain behind, saying he wished to observe the suffering [of the world].

Zhilong urged him to advance in his cultivation, saying, "You may stay for your next rebirth. When Fotiao returned, he found only the sandals left upon the wooden board; he suddenly lost sight of where Zhilong had gone.
The monk Tangeng originally did not know where he had come from. At the beginning of the Longshuo era, he was registered at Longxing Temple on Mount Mingyang.
Upon reaching Linhuai, he acquired land donated by the Heba clan of Xinyi Ward and subsequently established a monastery named Puzhao Wang.

When he first dug the earth, he discovered an inscription on a stele that read: "The Fragrant Accumulation Monastery of the Qi Dynasty. He also found a golden image, upon whose robes and foliage an inscription was carved reading:
"The Buddha King Universal Radiance" (Puzhao Wangfo). Heba Shi was deeply moved and marveled at these wonders; however, he still had no intention of donating his residence.
One night, while he was sleeping in his home, someone peered in and saw that his head and feet were each about three chi longer than the bed. Not long after, he again...

He was seen manifesting the form and features of Avalokiteśvara, possessing distinct eyes, ears, mouth, and nose, totaling eleven faces. Thereupon, the entire clan took refuge in him, and the temple was thus established.
Originally, it had been known by the ancient name Xiangji (Fragrant Accumulation). In the second year of the Jinglong era, an imperial decree summoned him to the Inner Court of the Way.

When the Emperor presided over the Dharma assembly, he inquired in detail about auspicious and inauspicious omens; his divinations and responses were consistently accurate. Consequently, the Emperor bestowed a new title upon the temple in recognition of his merit.
His name was Puguangwang (Universal Radiance King). Because it avoided the taboo name of the Empress Dowager, the character "Zhào" (Radiant) had been changed [to "Guāng"].

In the fourth year, the gengxu year, he manifested illness. An imperial edict ordered him to be moved to Jianfu Monastery for his care. On the second day of the third month, he passed away; his countenance remained as if alive.

The Emperor was deeply grieved and bestowed three hundred bolts of silk. He was buried on the banks of the Huai River. Later, the Emperor occasionally asked Master Wanhui, "What kind of person was that Śākyamuni?"
He was regarded as an incarnation of Avalokiteśvara. During the Taiping Xingguo era of the Song dynasty, an imperial edict restored the temple’s name to Puzhao.
The miraculous responses he manifested both during his lifetime and after his passing are fully recorded in the official annals; they shall not be recounted here in their entirety.
Heba’s name was Xuānjì, who was said to have attained realization in the Way. His disciples were Huìyǎn, Huì'àn, and Mùchā.
During the Tang dynasty, Fēnggān resided at Guōqīng Monastery on Mount Tiāntái. He stood over seven feet tall, with hair cropped even with his eyebrows.

He wore a coarse cloth robe, which he never changed regardless of the heat or cold. Daily, he performed the labor of pounding grain to provide for the assembly. When anyone consulted him regarding the Buddha-dharma, he would respond with the two characters "Sui-shí" (according to the occasion).
At times, he would ride a tiger back and forth along the pine-lined paths. Every night, he would sing songs within the monastery grounds.
He reached dawn. Monastics and laypeople alike came to revere him. After a long time, he manifested his passing at the temple.
During the Xiāntiān era, Lǚ Lìyìn of Jīngzhào was about to take up an official post in Tiantái when he suddenly suffered from a headache. Common physicians were unable to provide relief.

Before long, Fēnggānchēng arrived from Tiantái to visit him and requested that he treat his ailment. [Fēnggānchēng] immediately drew water to fill a pure vessel and sprayed it [upon him]; the illness was promptly [cured].
When he had finished speaking, Dao Yin was greatly delighted. He invited him to sit and conversed deeply with him, inquiring extensively about any notable figures at Tiantai whom he might meet.
[The monk] said, "In the future, you, Excellency, must not forget Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. Dao Yin questioned who they were, to which he replied, "They are none other than Hanshan and Shide.
These two had long been affiliated with Guoqing Temple; upon arrival, one should simply seek them out at Guoqing.

This was all there was to it; yet, even more so, it could not be grasped by outward appearance alone. Once Zhenyin had taken up his official duties, he proceeded to build a temple according to their agreement.
At that time, the temple monk Daoqiao was in charge of receiving guests. Zhenyin first inquired of him as to where Master Fenggan resided.
He found the tiger tracks filling the old quarters behind the storehouse, and there he saw Han Shan and Shide together tending the fire, looking at one another beneath the hearth.

He burst into loud laughter. Dao Yin hurriedly bowed to him, but he scolded him, saying, "You do not even know Amitābha; why do you prostrate before me? He added, "Seal, Seal! You chatterbox, you chatterbox!
Then, taking Dao Yin by the hand, he walked straight out. As for Hanshanzi, it was initially unknown where he came from. His appearance was emaciated and haggard;
he wore a birch-bark cap and wooden clogs, with a coarse cloth tunic and trousers. He lived in seclusion in Shifeng County.

He lived in a cold rock cave; thus, the world came to call him Hanshan (Cold Mountain). His speech was full of profound meaning, and his phrasing was so elegant and grand that it was beyond the reach of ordinary scholars.
Once, Lü Qiū personally sent him medicinal decoctions and clothing, but Hanshan suddenly shouted at a rock, causing it to split open, and entered within.
As he went in, he repeatedly cried out, "Thief! Thief! and further said, "I announce this to all of you people."
Each must strive for themselves. Once they had entered, the stone doors closed together without a trace or crack. Lüqiu ordered Daoqiao to record their poems;
those found upon tree leaves, cliffs, rocks, and the walls of the hermitage numbered over three hundred in total. This collection was compiled and has been transmitted to the present day.
As for Shide, he was named because he "picked up" [the child]. Formerly, when Feng Gan was traveling to Chicheng, he heard a child crying.

By the side of the road, he picked him up and brought him home. Lingyi took charge of his care and nurtured him. When he grew slightly older, he was assigned to serve as the "Holy Monk" (shèngsēng) for offerings at the hall.
However, he would sit upon the table every day and eat the offerings himself; furthermore, he would revile the Holy Monk, calling him a minor fruit.

Someone reported this to Lingyi, who sent him to serve as the offering for the Temple Guardian (gālánshén), intending to humiliate him. Yet, crows and vultures began pecking at the offerings in the temple.
Shide then struck the deity with his staff, saying, "If you lack the power to protect what you eat, how can you protect this monastery?
That evening, the deity appeared in a dream to the monks of the temple and said, "Shide has beaten me; what am I to do?

The next day, the assembly of monks recounted their dreams, and as everyone’s account was identical, they could not help but marvel at the strangeness. Thereupon, they went to the district magistrate's office to submit a petition describing the situation, which the district office then reported upward.
The provincial authorities issued an edict to the temple, stating that it was fitting to honor a man of virtue; thus, Shide became renowned throughout the world.

Nevertheless, he never once left Guoqing Temple. He was especially close friends with Hanshanzi. Whenever the midday meal was over and he had finished washing the dishes, he would strain the vegetable scraps into a bamboo tube to await the arrival of Hanshan, who would then carry them away.
At other times, they would mingle with woodcutters and herdsmen, wandering freely in the open.
Zi-le (Self-Enjoyment) was once attending the *poṣadha* ceremony when he suddenly rode a bull through the gate.
The *śrāmaṇera* head seat scolded him, whereupon Zi-le stood on the steps below amidst a herd of cattle. He called out the names of the deceased monks of the monastery one by one;
whenever he called a name, a specific cow would respond with a lowing sound and stand at his side until all had been called. The assembly was filled with shame and fear. Later, because...
Lüqiu fled in haste, but in the end, he did not know where [the other] was.
During the Tang dynasty, Wanhui was the son of the Zhang family of Wenxiang in Guozhou. In his youth, his appearance was dull and turbid; saliva, foam, mucus, and tears covered his face.
He ran about wildly, stumbling along, sometimes laughing and sometimes weeping, with no fixed time for these outbursts. The children of the neighborhood all took him to be...
His parents, lacking wisdom, insulted him; they harbored resentment, yet when he returned, they accepted him peacefully and never once showed him compassion.
When he was ten years old, his elder brother had been stationed in Liao-yang for a long time and all communication between them had ceased.

The family held a vegetarian feast to pray for blessings, and Hui suddenly said to his mother, "The condition of my brother’s daily life is extremely easy to know; why must you worry? After the meal, he wrapped up some steamed buns.
The provisions went out the gate, yet no one knew where they had gone. Returning in the evening, he took his brother’s letter from the sleeve of his robe;
when asked where he had obtained it, he did not answer. When the military service at Liao-yang ended, his brother said that Hui would arrive on that very day.

They took the cakes and provisions and ate them together, while urgently searching for the letter to announce his return; in the end, they could not discern from where it had come. Now, Liao and Guo were [separated by]...
He traveled ten thousand *li*; his journeys back and forth were more than merely passing through eastern and western lodgings. Was this not indeed the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*)?
From this, the name "Wanhui" (Ten Thousand Returns) first became renowned. When the court and the commonalty heard of it, they all revered and marveled at him.

Toward the end of Emperor Gaozong’s reign, Empress Wu repeatedly summoned him into the inner palace, where she bestowed upon him a brocade robe and a jade belt, with two palace maidens attending him on either side. This continued until she succeeded to the Zhou calendar.

An imperial edict conferred upon him the title of Dharma-Cloud Master (Fayun Gong). At that time, the gates for reporting secrets were wide open, and cruel officials engaged in the practice of "roasting" (fabricating charges against others).
Among the high-ranking ministers, there was not one who escaped. When it came to the mother of Cui Xuanyi of Boling—Lady Lu—she commanded Xuanyi to invite Wei Hui to inquire about her fate.
The mother wept and prostrated herself, offering gold spoons and chopsticks as a gift. Hui hurriedly descended the steps and threw the spoons away.
He tossed his chopsticks onto the roof of the house and strode away with his arms flung out. The family considered this an ill omen. Later, they sent someone up a ladder to retrieve the chopsticks;
beneath them, they found a book of prophetic lore (*chanwei*). They hurriedly burned it.

Shortly thereafter, the authorities indeed dispatched clerks and soldiers to enter the house and search extensively for such books of prophecy. They lifted every tile until nothing was found, and only then did they desist. This was truly a cruel magistrate.
Having cast him into this situation, they sought to frame him with a crime. In the second year of the Shenglong era, an imperial edict was issued for his tonsure;

a special altar was established for him to receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*). At that time, Empress Wei was involved in the administration of state affairs, and every time she encountered [Hui]hui, she would insult him, saying:

"How can you be so rebellious? I shall soon cut off your head! When Princess Jincheng went to marry into the Tibetan court, the imperial carriage escorted her as far as Shiping. Cui Ri... (text fragmentary).
Wu Pingyi, Song Zhiwen, Shen Quanqi, Cen Yi, and Xue Ji all followed Huiri to welcome the imperial carriage and stood to the left of the road.
The gentlemen requested a word from him; Huiri patted Quanqi and said, "You are truly a man of talent.
To Pingyi, he said, "You should be named 'Buddhist Child Without Sorrow' (Futong Wuyou). He looked at Xi and Ji with an expression of displeasure. The Emperor asked in between:
When asked who Huí was, [the master] replied, "He is an emanation of Guanyin. When Emperor Ruizong was still in his private residence, he would occasionally go out on excursions.
Whenever he arrived at a location, Huí would be the first to announce, "The Son of Heaven is coming!

Once, when Prince of Linzi (later Emperor Xuanzong) was accompanied by Zhang Wei and others to visit Huí, Huí hurriedly called for a staff and drove Zhang Wei and the others outside. He then personally pulled the Prince inside and bolted the door from within.
He then patted the king’s back and said, "The Son of Heaven shall rule for fifty years; after that, nothing more is known.

Fu Wei and the others overheard this secretly from outside the gate, whereupon their devotion and reverence increased all the more. On the road, they encountered the carriages and retinues of the two princesses, Daiping and Anle.
He would immediately move away to avoid it. He repeatedly exclaimed, "Bloody! Bloody! Taiping requested to build him a residence in Huaiyuan Ward, where he lived alone as usual.
In the second year of the Jinglong era, he manifested illness; suddenly, he called out loudly for the water from his native village.

His attendant thought, "The distance is great and it will not be easy to obtain," and was distressed, having no solution at hand. Turning back, he pointed to the ground before the hall and said, "This..."
It was indeed so. Thereupon, [the tomb] was excavated and water was drawn forth; he drank one full vessel and passed away.

When the report reached the Emperor, he was struck with grief and issued an edict posthumously conferring upon him the title of Minister (Situ) and the Duke of Guo, and his portrait was enshrined in the Jixian Academy.
Previously, during the Zhenguan era, the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang had traveled to India and visited Shizang Temple. While casually inspecting a room, he saw a folding chair and a monk’s staff.
Having finished, he questioned the man, "Where does the one who lives here reside now? The man replied, "In Wenxiang, in Zhendan.

When the Dharma Master returned and inquired for confirmation, just as he was about to visit, the man’s family hosted him overnight and urged him to prepare a vegetarian meal, saying, "A distinguished guest will arrive tomorrow.
Upon the Dharma Master's arrival, they conversed with him regarding the mountains and rivers of India.

The details of this matter are as follows. Although there were places that even Master Huaiji had not personally visited among those he mentioned, the full account of these events is contained in the *Bi-zhuan* (Separate Biography).
At the end of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, Daoyi once presided over Zhongshan in Fuzhou. Suddenly, a monk appeared at his seat;

his body was covered in scabies and leprosy, his robes were tattered and filthy, and pus, blood, lice, and nits lay scattered about. Those who saw him avoided him, and other monks would not associate with him.

The residents all cautioned one another not to approach him with familiarity; only Yi treated him with special care, frequently washing and wiping him down, and even seeking out fine medicines to administer for his treatment.
At the end of the summer, he took his leave. When Yi asked where he was going, he replied, "To the hermitage east of Daeheung-sa Temple.
Yi said, "I am well-acquainted with this area, yet there is no such place as a hermitage here. He replied:
"If you do not believe me, you should come one more time another day. Later, when he went once more, the monk had already come out to greet him with a smile outside the gate.
The pavilions and halls were magnificent; he stayed for two nights. When the monk escorted him out of the mountain and they had already waved their hands in farewell, [the traveler] departed.
Looking back slightly, there are merely red cliffs and verdant walls, ancient trees and strange rocks.
Wuxiang of the Tang was the son of the King of Silla. In the sixteenth year of the Kaiyuan era, he traveled by sea to the capital.
Having presented himself at court, an imperial decree ordered him to be attached to Chanding Monastery. Later, he went to Zizhong in Shu to pay his respects to Chan Master Zhishen.

The Master had attained awakening. Previously, he had met the extraordinary monk Chuji, who recognized his potential and treated him with great hospitality, bestowing upon him a nine-panel *mona* robe granted by Empress Wu Zetian and instructing him, saying, "I hope you will not forget me. Thereupon, the Master withdrew to live among the mountain streams and valleys;
whenever he sat in meditation, he would remain in *samādhi* for five days before emerging. Once, during one night, two black calves appeared, locking horns and kneeling before him.
Beneath his bed, he moved slightly closer. Suddenly, he felt a hairy hand, extremely cold, slip its sleeve into his own and reach down to his abdomen.
Furthermore, once a great snowfall had finally cleared, two starving tigers came from outside; he stroked them and lay naked before them, waiting to be eaten.
The tigers merely sniffed his head and feet and departed. After a long time, his hair grew long and his clothes became worn out. He was a hunter.

Others suspected he was not human; they drew their bows to shoot him, but then desisted. At the end of the Tianbao era, because of old acquaintances, he was received by the Retired Emperor at his temporary residence.

Yang Yi, the Magistrate of Chengdu County, considered him a demon and ordered his officials to arrest him. When the officials arrived, they were all seized with trembling and none dared to step forward.
Suddenly a great wind arose, driving sand and stones through the curtains and tossing them about the audience hall. Yang Yi was terrified.
He prostrated himself with his head to the ground in repentance for his transgressions, and then ceased. The four surrounding monasteries were the Jingsong, Daci, Puti, and Ningguo monasteries;
however, he resided exclusively in the rear courtyard of the Jingsong Monastery. He subsequently excavated two small ponds in front of the monastery, naming them "Left Soup" and "Right Rice.
Whenever resources were lacking, he dredged and deepened them, accepting offerings and donations from those who came.

This was repeatedly verified. A pagoda stood outside the gate of the monastery, exceptionally lofty and prominent. Beneath it, he planted young cypress trees and said, "When the Cypress Pagoda Monastery is destroyed, [the truth of my words] shall be known.
During the upheaval of the Huichang era, this began to be believed. There were those who offered to serve as laborers within the monastery using firewood for cooking, yet would not accept wages;
however, no one knew from where they came. This was likely because Xiang had left the household life...
When he entered China, his elder brothers also passed away one after another. The people of the state then established his younger brother on the throne.
That younger brother constantly feared that his brother would return to depose him; he sent a guest to Chengdu to assassinate the brother by ambush.

One night, a woodcutter found him and killed him, whereupon the assassin fled. Upon hearing this, the brother sighed and said: "The retribution for my enmity has arrived; what burden does it place upon me?"
On the nineteenth day of the fifth month in the first year of the Zhide era, he passed away without illness at the age of seventy-seven.
His stupa was named the Great Master of the Eastern Sea. During the Qianyuan period, the Prefect Han Hu composed a stele inscription for him.

Tang Huichong was a man of unknown origins. At the beginning of the Yongtai era, when the First Patriarch Guoyi first entered Mount Jing, Huichong sat in meditation one day beneath a stone screen on the Northern Peak.
He saw a person dressed in white who claimed to be a man from Jingshan at Mount Tianmu.
Prostrating himself before him, the figure said, "The deity of that mountain has informed me that the Buddha-dharma in Chang’an will soon face calamity."
"Send me to save him; if it were not for my monastic appearance, it would not suffice to lend weight to the Dharma-gate. I pray that you allow me to shave my head under your guidance.
Mount said, "What ability do you possess that could save the Dharma? Daichong replied, "I am able to recite the *Avalokiteśvara* mantra and the *Koṭi* dhāraṇī, among others.
Mount then tested him by ordering him to strike a stone screen behind his seat. Upon his striking it, the stone split into three pieces. Thereupon, Mount [granted him ordination].
He had his hair shaved. Daichong then took his leave and traveled to the capital, where he stayed at Zhangjing Temple.

On the twelfth day of the ninth month in the third year of the Dali era, Shi Hua, a Daoist priest of the Taiqing Palace, submitted a memorial stating: "Your Majesty loves both the teachings of the Buddha and the Way."
There was no difference in their relative skill. The subject wished to compete with those among the monks renowned for their talent and technique;

he hoped that by doing so, Your Majesty would realize that the ancestral teachings cannot be viewed as equal [to secular arts], and that the whole world might change its perspective—this would be most fortunate. The imperial decree granted his request.
The next day, Hua performed at Dongming Guan, where he constructed a "sword-ladder" (a series of steps). He climbed it as if it were level ground, without the slightest pain or distress.
Those assembled among the monks all recoiled in fear and did not dare look up at him. At that time, Yu Chaoen was the Governor of the Capital;

Daochong immediately submitted a petition, vowing to compete with him. The following day, a ladder was erected in the courtyard of the temple where he resided, made twice as high as the previous one, with blades so sharp and its height so formidable that it was impossible to touch.
Yet Daochong climbed it up and down barefoot, with no one able to grasp or hold onto him. Those standing by—

They trembled with fear; some even plunged their hands into boiling oil, ate hot iron, or sat in meditation amidst masses of fire. Upon seeing this, the elite looked at one another in terror and scattered.
When the Emperor heard of this, he was pleased and dispatched an eunuch to proclaim an imperial summons to question him. He asked, "Whom do you take as your teacher? Daoyi replied:

The eminent monk Fachin of Mount Jing was my teacher. The Emperor comforted and praised him repeatedly, bestowing upon him purple robes and appointing him as Court Gentleman for State Ceremonies (Honglu Qing), with the title "Tripitaka Master Guardian of the Nation. By imperial decree, he was to reside at An Guo Temple.

When Chongyi declined on the grounds that he had not yet received full ordination and did not dare accept the honors, the Emperor specially ordered the establishment of an ordination platform and summoned ten masters to confer the precepts upon him. Only then...

During the *karmavācanā* ceremony, light suddenly emanated from atop the altar; it manifested as the form of a white lunar disc and then vanished. The Emperor was struck with wonder and awe, and posthumously conferred upon him the title "Great Master Xingkong" (Master of the Nature of Emptiness).
Dao Wu of the Tang dynasty had long lived in seclusion on Mount Tao in Wenzhou, cultivating his practice without ceasing, yet no one knew of him. Having now revealed himself...
When he passed away, his remains remained firm, intact, and uncorrupted. His disciples then applied lacquer to preserve them as if he were still alive.

Five years later, he suddenly raised his right hand in the gesture of preaching the Dharma and transmitting the incense. The local commandery reported this matter to the throne, who issued an edict bestowing upon him a purple *kāṣāya* robe and the posthumous title "True Aspect" (*Shixiang*).
To this day, the commandery prays to him for rain and fine weather; his spiritual efficacy is particularly manifest.

Tang Puman was an individual of unknown origin from the region between Fen and Jin. He manifested many extraordinary traces, leading the world to regard him as a peer to Qianglian, Wan Hui, and others.
At the beginning of the Jianzhong era, he inscribed a poem on a Buddhist temple in Luzhou, which read: "This water connects with the Jing River;
the twin vermilion flows fill the valley. The blue ox leads the red tiger; this shall be called the Year of Great Peace. He subsequently vanished.
Its location remains unknown; yet, as for the meaning of this poem, no one has been able to fathom it.

It was during the rebellion of Zhu Ci, the Regional Commander of Jingyuan, that the imperial carriage took refuge in Fengtian. Troops from all quarters mobilized to assist the king, fighting incessantly.
His younger brother, Zhu Tao, assisted him. It was not until the first year of Xingyuan (Yichou) and the second year of Zhenyuan (Bingyin) that the rebellion was finally suppressed.
Thus we know that this water is *cǐ*; the pair of vermilion characters are *cǐ* and *tāo*.
The blue ox is *yǐchǒu*, and the red tiger is *bǐngyín*. What they indicate is perfectly clear; how truly marvelous!
The Master Azu of the Tang dynasty is not well known as to his origins; he resided mostly in Wenxiang in Guo.
In character, he appeared as if lacking wisdom, yet whenever he spoke, his words invariably hit upon matters of fortune and misfortune.

Because people regarded him as possessing the style of Master Fayun, those who came to pay their respects followed one after another in endless succession. Although offerings from donors accumulated like mountains, he never once turned his attention toward them even slightly. Zhang...
In a wealthy family in Shenxi, there was but one son. His appearance was coarse and ugly, and his nature was dull and ignorant; moreover, he was gluttonous and insatiable.
His parents doted on him and allowed him to act as he pleased; even when he squandered their assets and ruined their livelihoods, none dared to restrain him.
One day, he passed by Ajatu and told him the reason for his visit, requesting that Ajatu provide compassionate salvation.
Ajatu closed his eyes for a long time and said, "Your grievances shall not cease for several more years. However, as I now pity your extreme diligence, I shall eliminate them for you.

He then had a day chosen to arrange a great vegetarian feast (*mahāpariṣad*), assembling both monastics and laypeople. Along the riverbank, they prepared and arranged abundant food and drink to be consumed.
After a short while, he ordered several strong men to seize his son and throw him into the river.
His son sank and rose again four or five times before finally drowning. Zhen watched from the side in utter astonishment; then, suddenly, his son leapt out of the water.
Brandishing his halberd, he cursed him, saying, "To me, you were neither father nor mother; you were merely an enemy.

I intended to take revenge upon you, but fortunately encountered a holy man who explained the matter for me. From this point forward, there shall be no further trouble. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
From this, the fame of Azu became even more renowned.
During the Kaicheng era of the Tang dynasty, there was a monk who lay ill on Mount Wutai. A certain attendant looked after him with exceptional diligence.
Once the monk’s illness had healed, he took leave of his caregiver and said to him: "I reside in Jiulong County, outside the Sword Gate (Jianwai)."

"I went to Mount Chalong. On another occasion while traveling abroad, I hoped you would visit me there. Later, when I entered Shu, I inquired everywhere about what is called 'Chalong,' yet no one recognized it.
On the road, I met a young boy who said, 'I am indeed a servant of that mountain; I would be honored to lead you there.
Upon arriving, the temple halls and towers rose high into the air, and the monastic quarters filled the valley. The master welcomed me with a smile at the gate."
Outside, he met a monk who had previously been ill on Mount Wutai. They embraced and conversed regarding their long separation.
When it was time for the evening rites, the monk rose and took his leave, saying, "I have obtained this single meeting through our past affinities; however, I cannot remain here.

I pray you, apply yourself diligently to cultivation so as to realize the state beyond outflows (*anāsrava*). Then I shall come to welcome you; the day is not yet late. He then ordered a youth to escort him out, and they departed.

One who encompasses heaven and earth and participates in the transformation of creation cannot be sought within the mundane world.
The Master Dadian of the Song dynasty was a descendant of the Meng clan. During the Guangzheng era, he resided at Lingjiu Temple in Dayi County, south of Gongyang.

Although he had undergone tonsure and entered the monastic life, his character was expansive and unrestrained; whenever he engaged in discussion with others, he would invariably provide repeated guidance and instruction.
To verify this matter, he was thus named according to local custom. Whenever invited to vegetarian feasts or banquets with meat, he would accept without inquiry;

the villagers likewise took this as a matter of course and did not mock or criticize him. Every evening when he returned from outside, he would purchase yellow and white paper, brushes, and ink, tucking them into his sleeves to compose his writings.
He would then shut his door and remain in silence, such that his neighbors hardly ever noticed him.
He heard the sound of coughing and clearing his throat. The chamber had no four walls; those who wished to approach it invariably lost their way.

Once, a novice monk tried to observe what was being done by tiptoeing into a hidden spot. He saw [the Master] holding a candle, squatting with legs spread apart, and arranging paper, brush, and ink before him.
After rebuking [his disciples] for a long time, he then wrote rapidly, making large characters as if issuing a formal decree of judgment. [The novice] gradually became aware [of his presence].
There were several officials and jailers standing in rows beside him, all with strange forms and unusual attire, none of whom could be identified.
The śrāmaṇera was struck with awe and retreated; he attempted to question them, but they did not answer. Later, nothing was known of his final whereabouts.
The praise says:
The Bodhisattva’s transformation body pervades lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; his marks and signs and radiant light are primordially complete, yet he alone conceals them.
He manifests in accordance with ordinary beings, appearing in forms according to their kind, and acts as their kinsman.
Wherever the mind arises, there is no distance near or far; mountains, rivers, walls, and barriers cannot obstruct it.

Like spring traversing the earth where clusters of flowers bloom, or like the moon descending upon water where its reflection spreads across the waves—this inconceivable power dispels hardships and eradicates demons. This is truly the Prajñāpāramitā.
